c-group-culture: The archaeologist George A. Reisner named the culture with a letter, as it has no central site and no written record of what its people called themselves. It arose after his A-Group and B-Group cultures, around the end of the Old Kingdom in Egypt. Its origins are still debated: some scholars see it as growing out of the A/B-Group, while others think it was brought by migrants or invaders, perhaps from the drying Sahara, who mingled with the local people. Linguists have proposed that its people spoke a Berber language, on thin evidence, and more recent work suggests a Cushitic language whose closest relative is Beja.

Most of what is known comes from Lower Nubia and the Dongola Reach. The culture's northern limit lay near el-Kubanieh by Aswan, while C-Group sites have been found as far south as Eritrea. In the Egyptian Sixth Dynasty, Lower Nubia was described as a set of small states, among them Setju, Wawat and Irjet, while the Kingdom of Kerma was emerging upstream; early Kerma shows clear likenesses to the C-Group. The Middle Kingdom conquered much of C-Group Lower Nubia, and Kerma took control after the Egyptians left. From the conquest of Nubia by Tuthmosis I in the late 16th century BCE, the C-Group merged with the Egyptians.

The C-Group were farmers and semi-nomadic herders who kept large herds of cattle in land now too dry for them. Cattle gave milk, blood and hides and stood at the centre of their art, burials and religion. Their pottery, with fine incised designs often showing cattle and herding, held liquids in small jars rather than grain, and vessels were deliberately broken as a funerary rite. Once thought peaceful, they in fact buried daggers, short swords and battle-axes with their dead.

Early tombs were simple stone circles; later the body lay in a stone-lined chamber, with an offering chapel to the east whose standing slabs bore cattle images. They supplied Egyptian garrisons with milk and meat and traded between Egypt and lands to the south. In the New Kingdom, at the Fadrus cemetery, the dead were laid out on their backs in the Egyptian manner and cattle decoration disappeared.
c-p-ramaswami-iyer: Chetput Pattabhiraman Ramaswami Iyer, popularly known as Sir C. P., came from a Tamil Brahmin Iyer family whose ancestral place was Chetput in North Arcot. His father, C. R. Pattabhirama Iyer, was a judge. He studied at Wesley College High School and Presidency College, Madras, where he won prizes in English, Sanskrit and Mathematics, and then at the Madras Law College. He had wanted to become a professor of English, but followed his father's wish into the law. In 1895, at the age of 16, he was married to the nine-year-old Seethamma.

From 1903 he built one of the leading practices at the Madras bar. In 1912 he won the custody case of Jiddu Narayaniah against Annie Besant, but later joined Besant in the Home Rule League, edited her paper New India while she was interned, and in 1917 became Secretary of the Indian National Congress. He drew away from the national movement over his disagreements with Mahatma Gandhi on Non-Cooperation. He was Advocate-General of Madras from 1920, and on the Governor's executive council from 1923 he laid the foundation of the Pykara Dam, began the Mettur Dam and improved the ports of Cochin, Visakhapatnam and Tuticorin. He later sat on the Viceroy's council and attended the Third Round Table Conference in 1932.

As Diwan he brought the Indian Aluminium Company to Aluva and founded Fertilizers and Chemicals of Travancore, India's first fertiliser plant; capital punishment was abolished and a midday meal scheme introduced through the Vanchi Poor Fund. In October 1946 his police and army crushed the Punnapra-Vayalar revolt; the historian A. Shreedhara Menon put the dead at about 1,000. On 25 July 1947 he survived multiple stab wounds at a concert. Ramachandra Guha has written that British ministers encouraged his independence plan for access to Travancore's monazite, while family sources say he sought only greater autonomy.

He later served as Vice Chancellor of Banaras Hindu University and Annamalai University at the same time and chaired the Hindu Religious Endowments Commission from 1960 to 1962. On 26 September 1966 he died suddenly at the National Liberal Club in London while researching a book. Edwin Samuel Montagu called him one of the cleverest men in India, while Jawaharlal Nehru called him an admirer of dictatorship and an ornament of autocracy in an Indian state.
c-r-swart: Charles Robberts Swart, nicknamed Blackie, was born on 5 December 1894 on the farm Morgenzon in the Winburg district of the Orange Free State. He was the third of six children of Hermanus Bernardus Swart and Aletta Catharina Robberts. The Second Boer War began when he was five. His mother and the children were interned at the Winburg concentration camp, where one of the three boys died, and his father was wounded and captured at the Battle of Paardeberg and held as a prisoner of war.

Swart attended the government school in Winburg and later a Christian National Education school set up by Afrikaners in answer to Lord Milner's anglicisation policy. He became a barrister in 1914, spent a brief period acting in silent films in Hollywood, took a degree in journalism at Columbia University in 1921–22, and practised law in Bloemfontein from 1919 to 1948.

Swart was elected to the House of Assembly for Ladybrand in 1923 and held the seat until 1938. He was a member of the Ossewabrandwag, and in 1941 he became leader of the National Party in the Orange Free State and member for Winburg. When the National Party came to power in 1948 he was appointed Minister of Justice and was responsible for legislation strengthening the powers of the South African Police to suppress anti-apartheid activity. He held the education portfolio in 1949 and 1950 and was Deputy Prime Minister from 1954 to 1959.

Swart was appointed Governor-General, though like his predecessor Ernest George Jansen he was a staunch republican. In a referendum a small majority of white voters endorsed a republic. In 1961, after signing the new republican constitution into law, he asked the Queen to release him from office, and Parliament elected him state president, the ceremonial head of state replacing the monarch and the Governor-General. Nelson Mandela and other underground leaders planned a three-day general strike of non-white workers against the change, but the government averted most of it through extensive use of police force. Elected for seven years, Swart served six and retired in 1967.

Swart died on 16 July 1982, aged 87. He was known as Blackie, since swart means black in Afrikaans, or as Oom Blackie, oom being a respectful word for an older man. The tallest building in Bloemfontein was named the President CR Swart Building, and in 2015 it was renamed the Fidel Castro Building. Protesting students destroyed his statue at the University of the Free State in late February 2016. His portrait was on the South African coins from 1 to 50 cents dated 1968, struck to commemorate him as the first state president.
c-rajagopalachari: Chakravarti Rajagopalachari was born on 10 December 1878 in the village of Thorapalli, near Hosur, in the Madras Presidency. His father was the munsiff of the village, and the family was Hindu and Brahmin. He was a weak and sickly child whose parents feared he might not live long. He passed his matriculation examinations in 1891, graduated in arts from Central College, Bangalore, in 1894 and in law from Presidency College, Madras, in 1897.

One of Gandhi's earliest political lieutenants, Rajagopalachari joined the non-cooperation movement, the Vaikom Satyagraha and the Civil Disobedience movement, and in 1930 he led the Vedaranyam Salt Satyagraha in answer to the Dandi March. After the Congress won the Madras elections of 1937 he became the first Congress premier of the Presidency. His government passed an Agricultural Debt Relief Act in 1938 and the Temple Entry Authorization and Indemnity Act of 1939, which removed restrictions on Dalits and Shanars entering Hindu temples.

He resigned in protest at the declaration of war by the Viceroy and was jailed in December 1940. He later urged co-operation in the war effort, opposed the Quit India Movement and favoured talks with Muhammad Ali Jinnah and the Muslim League, which led to a proposal known as the C. R. formula. His stand angered many colleagues in Congress. After independence he was the first Governor of West Bengal, then served as Governor-General from June 1948 to 26 January 1950, the last holder of the office and the only Indian to hold it. He later sat in Nehru's cabinet as Home Minister and was Chief Minister of Madras State from 1952 to 1954.
In 1959 he left Congress and founded the Swatantra Party. It won 45 Lok Sabha seats in 1967, and he helped assemble the alliance that ended Congress rule in Madras that year.

Rajagopalachari wrote in Tamil and English. His Tamil retelling of the Ramayana, serialised in the magazine Kalki from 1954 to 1955 and published as Chakravarti Thirumagan, won the Sahitya Akademi Award in 1958. He received the Bharat Ratna in 1954 and was a strict vegetarian and a campaigner for prohibition. Critics fault his compulsory Hindi teaching and the Modified Scheme of Elementary Education of 1953, which they called a hereditary education policy. He died on 25 December 1972, aged 94, and was given a state funeral.
c-v-raman: Raman was born on 7 November 1888, the second of eight children of R. Chandrasekhar Iyer and Parvathi Ammal. His father was a school teacher on a modest salary, who in 1892 took a post in physics at a college in Visakhapatnam. There Raman attended St Aloysius' Anglo-Indian High School, passed matriculation at eleven and the First Examination in Arts at thirteen, and took first place in both. He published a first paper on the diffraction of light in 1906, and in February 1907 took first place in the entrance examination for the Indian Finance Service.

Posted to Calcutta, Raman was impressed by the Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science, founded in 1876 as India's first research institute. With Ashutosh Mukherjee's support he won permission to do research there in his own time. His article on Newton's rings in polarised light, published in Nature in 1907, was the institute's first research paper. Between 1916 and 1921 he published on bowed string instruments and the wolf tone in violins and cellos.

During a voyage in September 1921, with a pocket spectroscope and a Nicol prism, he saw that the Mediterranean looked bluer than the sky's reflection would explain, contradicting Lord Rayleigh's account. He and K. S. Krishnan then sought a scattering with a changed wavelength, and found it on 28 February 1928, a day now marked in India as National Science Day. Raman moved to Bengaluru in 1933 as the first Indian director of the Indian Institute of Science and founded the Raman Research Institute in 1948.

Grigory Landsberg and Leonid Mandelstam in Moscow independently reported the effect in 1928 and were nominated with Raman in 1930. The Nobel Committee held that they had seen it only in crystals, while Raman and Krishnan had shown it in solids, liquids and gases. Raman also disagreed for decades with Max Born, who worked at the Institute in 1933 and 1934, on lattice dynamics, and most physicists favoured Born's view. He resigned from the Royal Society, to which he was elected in 1924, in 1968.

He had a cardiac arrest in his laboratory at the end of October 1970 and died on 21 November 1970, aged 82. Two days earlier he urged a former student not to let the Academy's journals die. His honours included the Hughes Medal in 1930, the Bharat Ratna in 1954 and the Lenin Peace Prize in 1957.
cabanagem: Until 1822 Grão-Pará had been a viceroyalty separate from Brazil, reporting directly to Portugal; after independence it joined Brazil. Leaders of the struggle there, among them the canon and journalist João Batista Gonçalves Campos, the Vinagre brothers and the farmer Félix Clemente Antônio Malcher, were pushed aside once a provincial government named by the emperor took office. The causes of the revolt included extreme poverty, imperial oppression and the province's political irrelevance, and even its elite agriculturists resented a central government dominated by the Southeast and Northeast.

The name refers to the huts of the poorest people along the waterways, chiefly caboclos, freed slaves and indigenous people. In 1833 the province had 119,877 inhabitants: 32,751 Amerindians, 29,977 black slaves, 42,000 people of mixed race and a white minority of 15,000. The provincial president Bernardo Lobo de Souza answered the separatists with repression, and in 1834 Batista Campos took refuge on Malcher's fazenda, where rebels gathered; on 3 November troops killed Manuel Vinagre and seized Malcher.

On the night of 6 January 1835 the rebels took Belém, killed President Lobo and the army commander, and made Malcher president. He sought to keep the province within the empire, while Francisco Vinagre and Eduardo Angelim wanted to separate; Malcher was killed and his body dragged through the streets. A squadron under the English admiral Taylor drove the rebels into the interior, but they attacked Belém again on 14 August and retook it after nine days of fighting, in which Antônio Vinagre died. Angelim became president.

In 1836 Brigadier Francisco José de Sousa Soares de Andrea was named president and attacked the capital, and naval forces under John Pascoe Grenfell blockaded and bombarded Belém; on 10 May Angelim fled and was captured. The rebels fought on from the interior for three more years. An amnesty was declared in 1839, and the last group, under Gonçalo Jorge de Magalhães, yielded in 1840.

Over the five years of fighting the population of Pará is estimated to have fallen from about 100,000 to 60,000. The Memorial da Cabanagem, designed by Oscar Niemeyer, stands at the entrance to Belém. It was inaugurated on 7 January 1985 for the revolt's 150th anniversary and has held the remains of Eduardo Angelim and Canon Batista Campos, with symbolic ashes for three more leaders, among them Malcher.
cabimas: Cabimas lies on the Costa Oriental del Lago de Maracaibo in Zulia State, with Lake Maracaibo to the west, the municipalities of Santa Rita and Miranda to the north, Lara State to the east and Simón Bolívar and Lagunillas to the south. The terrain is mainly flat, sandy and low, with depressions that were once lagoons. The weather is hot and humid. The name comes from cabima, a word of Carib origin for the copaiba tree, whose trunk yields an oil with medicinal and craft uses.

Cistercian monks founded the place in 1758 as the Mission of Saint Ambrosio of Punta de Piedra, and Archbishop Mariano Marti described the town after a visit in 1771. It grew as a fishing village on the lake shore until the Venezuelan Oil Concessions found oil with the Santa Barbara well in 1917. The well Los Barrosos 2, which blew out in December 1922 at 100,000 barrels a day, made newspaper headlines around the world and marked the beginning of Venezuela's modern history as a major oil producer. The La Rosa field was granted in concession by President Juan Vicente Gómez.

Oil companies and workers came from other parts of Venezuela and abroad, mostly American and Dutch personnel, and the city grew round oil camps, so its development was not planned. Its main avenues were named after a coordinate system the company Shell used to locate its wells. Settlers came from the east, the Andes and Falcón, and also Syrians, Lebanese, Chinese, Italians, Spanish, Portuguese and Greeks, which shaped the local markets. In 1936 Jorge Hernández founded the Oil Workers and Employees Union, the first workers' union in Venezuela.

Cabimas remains an important centre of production from the fields in and beneath Lake Maracaibo, including La Rosa on land and La Salina in the lake. The port of La Salina is one of the main oil tanker docks on the lake. The union's building on El Rosario street still serves it, and a mechanical pump is a monument at the site of the Barroso well. Our Lady of the Rosary Cathedral is the seat of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Cabimas.
cabyle: Cabyle, also written Kabile and known as Calybe or Kalibe, stood in the interior of ancient Thrace, west of Develtus, on the river Tonsus. Its acropolis occupied the easternmost part of Zaichi peak. The southern entrance was a gate cut into the rock, and on one of these rocks is carved a relief of Cybele, the Great Mother of the Gods. Because that is the Phrygian name of the goddess, Prof. Velizar Velkov suggested that the town's name was pronounced Cabyle in the Thracian language. In later times the town was called Diospolis and Goloë.

The settlement was founded around 2000 BCE on the Zaychi Vrah Heights and became one of the most important centres of south-eastern Thrace. After its conquest by Philip II of Macedon it became part of the empire of Alexander of Macedon, and Philip settled rebellious Macedonians there. Thracians governed it again in the 3rd century BCE, when it was a major trading and military centre, and ancient writers including Demosthenes, Polybius, Strabo, Pliny the Elder and Stephanus of Byzantium mention it.

Troops of the Roman Republic under Marcus Lucullus took the city in 71 BCE. After 45 BCE it was part of the Sapaean Thracian kingdom, a Roman client state, and after 46 CE of the province of Thracia. It remained one of the chief cities of Thrace after the reforms of Emperor Diocletian. The Goths seized it in the late 4th century, and it was finally destroyed by the Avars and never settled again, though a small medieval settlement stood on part of its territory.

The site lies near the village of Kabile, less than 10 kilometres from Yambol. The city and its surroundings were declared a territory of national importance in 1965 and made an archaeological reserve of about 65 km2, with a museum on site. Under the name Diospolis in Thracia it remains a titular see of the Roman Catholic Church.
cacamatzin: Cacamatzin, also called Cacama, was a son of King Nezahualpilli of Texcoco by one of his mistresses. Texcoco was the second most important city of the Aztec Empire, and its kings were traditionally elected by the nobility from the ablest members of the royal family. His election was said to have been made under heavy pressure from Moctezuma II, lord of Tenochtitlan, who wished to lessen Texcoco's power in favour of greater centralisation in his own city.

After the Spaniards, lodged in the palace of Axayácatl, found the treasure of Moctezuma's grandfather, Hernán Cortés demanded that Moctezuma's vassals pay all the gold they had. In Texcoco the task fell to two of Cacamatzin's brothers, Tetlahuehuezquititzin and Netzahualquentzin. Suspected of treason after a misunderstanding, Netzahualquentzin was sentenced by Cortés to hang; Moctezuma interceded and the sentence was suspended, but he was flogged.

Angered by these events, Cacamatzin called on his vassals and neighbouring rulers to rise against the Spanish: his cousin the lord of Coyoacán, Totoquihuatzin of Tlacopan, Cuitláhuac of Iztapalapa and the lord of Matlatzinco. Moctezuma, who did not want war in Tenochtitlan, warned Cortés, who tried to make peace. Cacamatzin refused, saying he would not be persuaded as Moctezuma had been. He gave an ultimatum of four days, urged his uncle to be a lord and not a slave, and declared that his war was for his vassals and the defence of their land and religion.

On the orders of Cortés, Moctezuma had Cacamatzin arrested in his own palace while he was discussing preparations for war; the lords of Coyoacán, Iztapalapa and Tacuba were also seized. Cacamatzin is credited with a poem, the Song of Cacamatzin, which invokes his father and grandfather and seems to protest against the attack of Pedro de Alvarado during the festival of Tóxcatl.
cachar: Cachar district occupies 3,786 square kilometres in the Barak valley of Assam. It is bounded on the south by Mizoram, on the east by Manipur and on the north by the Barail and Jayantia hill ranges. The Barak River is its main river, with tributaries including the Jiri and Jatinga from the north and the Sonai and Daleswari from the south. The district is mostly plains with several hill ranges, and the wetlands sometimes flood and form lakes. It is mostly tropical evergreen forest, with large tracts of rainforest in the north and south, and its annual rainfall exceeds 3,000 millimetres.

In the late medieval period a conflict between two Dimasa Kachari princes led the younger, Dakhin, to build a new capital in the Barak valley, and his followers became known as the Twipra Kingdom. In 1562 King Chilarai of the Koch dynasty captured the valley and gave his brother Kamal Narayan authority over it. His descendants ruled until the 18th century as the Khaspur kingdom. When the last Koch ruler, Bhima Singha, died without sons, the Dimasas of Maibang moved to Khaspur, through his daughter Kanchani's marriage to the Dimasa prince Laxmichandra, and the two kingdoms merged as the Kachari kingdom.

The British moved into Assam in 1824 during the First Anglo-Burmese War. They sent the army officer T. Fisher to oversee the region and annexed the plains of Cachar on 14 August 1832, justifying the step by the doctrine of lapse. Northern Cachar remained a separate principality until the British occupied it in 1854, citing the misconduct of its rulers. Cachar became part of the Chief Commissionership of Assam on 6 February 1874. After the partition of India in 1947 the Karimganj sub-division of Sylhet joined the district, and later Dima Hasao, Karimganj and Hailakandi were separated from it.

Silchar is the district headquarters. At the 2011 census Cachar had 1,736,617 inhabitants; Bengali is spoken by about three quarters of them, and Hinduism is the main religion. Rice and tea are the main crops. At Khaspur, 20 kilometres from Silchar, the Sun Gate, the Lion Gate, the king's palace and a temple survive from the 17th century Kachari kingdom. Barail Wildlife Sanctuary, the only one in the district, was established in 2004.
cacheu: Cacheu lies on the Cacheu River in north-western Guinea-Bissau and is the capital of the region of the same name. It stands in the territory of the Papel people, and its name is of Bainuk origin, from Caticheu, meaning the place where we rest. Its strategic position on the river made it one of the earliest European colonial settlements in sub-Saharan Africa.

From the late sixteenth century a European and Afro-European population grew up through informal settlement by Portuguese traders, adventurers and outcasts known as lançados. Portugal also sent degredados, people condemned to exile. In 1567 the English slaver John Hawkins raided the settlement. After this and a period of conflict with the Papel, the traders asked the king of Cacheu in 1589 for permission to build a fort and in 1591 moved into the new stockade. The Papel stormed it without success before an agreement allowed both to live together. A priest was appointed in 1598, and in 1605 the crown offered a municipal charter, when about 1,500 people lived there, 500 of them white.

Cacheu was an important slave-trading point for the Portuguese in Upper Guinea and a centre of boat-building, with mostly African artisans. The lançados, Papel and other traders regularly broke the crown's supposed monopoly. In 1676 the Portuguese launched the Company of Cacheu and Rivers and Commerce of Guinea, the first of several companies that failed to control the trade. In 1684 the slave trader Bibiana Vaz captured the captain-major, and the so-called Republic of Cacheu refused to let the company's representatives land. In 1878 a Portuguese force attacked Cacanda, the first of the campaigns that ended in the conquest of the region in 1914. As Portuguese Guinea grew, Bolama, Bissau and Canchungo overtook Cacheu as administrative centres.

A stone fort built in the 1640s still stands. The Cacheu Memorial of Slavery and Black Traffic, a museum, gives historical context to the area, and the Cacheu River Mangroves Natural Park lies nearby. A regular market serves the surrounding districts, which export coconuts, palm oil and rice. Cacheu is twinned with Lisbon.
cacique: The word cacique, sometimes spelled cazique, with the feminine form cacica, comes from the Kalinago word kassiquan, which means to keep house. It first entered English in 1555, defined as prince. Among the Taíno the kasike rank was hereditary and sometimes established by democratic means. A kasike's importance depended on the size of his clan rather than on skill in war. Kasikes lived in a larger rectangular hut at the centre of the village and had reserved places from which to watch the ceremonial dances and ball game. The kasike's word was law.

The Spanish took over the term and used it for the local leader of almost any Indigenous group in Spanish America. Caribbean caciques who did not at first resist became middlemen between their communities and the Spanish, but their cooperation was often provisional. Most of the early caciques revolted and died in battle or by execution. Two of the best known are Hatuey, from what is now Cuba, and Enriquillo, on Hispaniola.

The Spanish had more success with the leaders of the more hierarchical societies of Central Mexico, who became loyal intermediaries in the colonial system. Cooperative elite men often replaced rivals with better hereditary claims. The Spanish treated Indigenous nobles as a European-style nobility: caciques and their families were allowed the honorifics don and doña, and gained rights to carry swords or firearms and to ride horses or mules. Some held entailed estates called cacicazgos, and many engaged in sheep and cattle ranching and silk raising. By the late colonial period the title had lost any dynastic meaning, and the last special privileges were abolished with Mexican independence in 1821.

In the Andean region the local term kuraka was preferred, and the Spanish let kurakas keep their titles if they swore fealty to the Spanish monarch. The 1781 rebellion of Túpac Amaru II was led by a kuraka claiming descent from the Inca royal line.

In Hispanic and Lusophone countries the word also came to mean a political boss, like a caudillo, exercising power in a system of caciquism. In Mexico after independence it kept its meaning of Indigenous leader but also came to mean any local or regional leader. Caciquismo appeared in Spain in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, and Benedict Anderson coined the term cacique democracy for the Philippines. Scholars do not agree on the origins of caciquismo.
cadair-idris: Cadair Idris lies in the Meirionnydd area of Gwynedd, near the town of Dolgellau. It is built of a fractured and folded pile of sedimentary and igneous rocks of Ordovician age, folded and faulted during the Caledonian Orogeny: mudstones and siltstones of the Ceiswyn Formation in the south, basalts and tuffs of the Pen y Gadair Volcanic Formation above Llyn Cau, and on the north side great cliffs of microgranite.

The chair of the name is a bowl-shaped hollow carved by a cirque glacier during several ice ages. Its crater-like shape gave rise to the mistaken claim that the mountain is an extinct volcano, a claim Charles Kingsley rejected as early as 1872 in his book Town Geology. Teardrop-shaped knolls above Llyn Cau are roches moutonnées shaped by the moving ice.

The name means Idris's Chair. Idris is usually taken to be a giant, said to be skilled in poetry, astronomy and philosophy, or else Idris ap Gwyddno, a 7th-century prince of Meirionnydd who won a battle against the Irish on the mountain and who is called Idris Gawr, Idris the Giant, in some medieval genealogies. The poet Lewys Glyn Cothi wrote the form Cadair Idris in the second half of the 15th century; the spoken form Cader had developed by the end of the Middle Ages.

Legend holds that some of its lakes are bottomless and that anyone who sleeps alone on its slopes will wake either a madman or a poet. In Welsh mythology it is a hunting ground of Gwyn ap Nudd and his hounds, the Cŵn Annwn. In 1800 Mary Jones, a girl from Llanfihangel-y-Pennant at the foot of the mountain, walked 25 miles to Bala to buy a Bible, a journey that was a major factor in the founding of the British and Foreign Bible Society in 1804.

Much of the area was made a National Nature Reserve in 1957 and is home to Arctic-alpine plants such as purple saxifrage and dwarf willow. Three main trails, the Pony Path, the Fox's Path and the Minffordd Path, lead to the scree-covered summit, which has a trig point and a stone shelter. In June 2016 Snowdonia National Park chose the spelling Cader Idris for its signs.
caddo: The Caddo are thought to descend from the Woodland period Fourche Maline and Mossy Grove cultures, who lived in the area between 200 BCE and 800 CE; the Wichita and Pawnee, who also spoke Caddoan languages, are related. By 800 CE some villages had become ritual centres where leaders directed the building of platform mounds around swept plazas, and by 1200 extensive maize farming supported denser settlement. The Spiro Mounds in present-day Oklahoma were built by ancestors of the Caddo and Wichita. Archaeological evidence shows unbroken continuity from these people to the present Caddo Nation.

In the Caddo creation story the people emerged from a cave called Chahkanina, the place of crying, led by Moon, until the wolf looked back and the way closed. Caddo religion centres on Kadhi háyuh, the Leader Above, and in early times a head priest, the xinesi, could commune with spirits near the temples.

The Caddo first met Europeans in 1541, when the expedition of Hernando de Soto clashed with the Tula near present-day Caddo Gap, Arkansas. Spanish Franciscan missions and French traders followed in the 18th century, and smallpox, measles, influenza and malaria caused epidemics with high death tolls. The name Texas comes, through the Spanish Tejas, from the Hasinai word táysha, meaning friend. In 1835 the Kadohadacho signed a treaty to move to Mexican Texas; after 1845 the Hasinai and Kadohadacho were forced onto the Brazos Reservation, and after a vigilante attack on a Caddo camp on 26 December 1858 many were moved to Indian Territory in 1859.

In the late 19th century many Caddo took up the Ghost Dance, and the Caddo and Delaware medicine man John Wilson introduced the Big Moon peyote ceremony. The Caddo opposed the allotment of their land under the Dawes Act and lost much of it in the decades that followed.

Under the Indian Reorganization Act and the Oklahoma Indian Welfare Act the Caddo restored their tribal government, ratifying a constitution on 17 January 1938 and a new one in 1976. The Caddo Nation of Oklahoma, headquartered in Binger, is a federally recognised tribe of some 6,000 enrolled citizens, governed by an elected council of eight with a chairperson. The Hasinai Society and the Caddo Culture Club teach and perform Caddo songs and dances.
cadmus: In the usual telling Cadmus was the son of Agenor, ruler of a Phoenician kingdom, and his wife Telephassa, although some sources give other parents. When Zeus carried off his sister Europa, Cadmus was sent by his father to find her and told not to return without her. Unsuccessful, or unwilling to go against Zeus, he came to Samothrace, the island sacred to the Great Gods, where he took Harmonia as his bride; according to Diodorus Siculus the wedding was the first on earth to which the gods brought gifts.

Cadmus went to Delphi, where the oracle told him to follow a cow marked with a half moon and to build a town where she lay down exhausted. The cow led him to Boeotia, where he founded Thebes. He killed the dragon that guarded the Ismenian spring and, on Athena's instruction, sowed its teeth. Armed men called the Spartoi sprang up and fought one another until five survived, who helped him build the Cadmeia, the citadel of Thebes, and became the ancestors of its noblest families.

The dragon had been sacred to Ares, and the family met with misfortunes. Cadmus abdicated in favour of his grandson Pentheus and went with Harmonia to Illyria to fight beside the Enchelii, and he founded the cities of Lychnidos and Bouthoe. Troubled by his ill fortune, he said that if the gods so loved the life of a serpent he might wish it for himself, and he began to change; Harmonia asked to share his fate.

Herodotus credited Cadmus with bringing the Phoenician alphabet to the Greeks. Modern scholarship almost unanimously agrees that the Greek alphabet came from the Phoenician, but the earliest Greek inscriptions match Phoenician letter forms of the late 9th or 8th centuries BCE, far later than Herodotus supposed. Frederick Ahl suggested that the legend might preserve memories of Linear B, which has been found in abundance at Thebes.

Albert Schachter suggested that Cadmus was an invented hero named after the Theban acropolis and made Phoenician through the influence of eastern immigrants. Others have proposed that he was a Mycenaean, a Cretan or an Argive.
cadwallon-ap-cadfan: Cadwallon ruled from around 625, succeeding his father Cadfan ap Iago; the genealogies of the kings of Gwynedd trace his line to Maelgwn Gwynedd and Cunedda. The historian Alex Woolf has argued instead that the genealogists inserted Bede's Cadwallon into an unrelated pedigree, and that he was Catguallaun liu, a ruler of the Hen Ogledd, the Brittonic north. Little is known for certain of his early life, and the main source, Bede's Ecclesiastical History of the English People, is strongly hostile to him.

Edwin of Northumbria, the most powerful king in Britain, conquered the Brittonic kingdom of Elmet and extended his rule to the Isle of Man and Anglesey. The Annales Cambriae record Cadwallon besieged on Glannauc, now Puffin Island, in 629, and Welsh poetry and the Welsh Triads tell of a battle at Digoll and a stay in Ireland before his return. Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia Regum Britanniae, a much later account that has him living until after the Battle of the Winwaed, has him defeating the Mercians at Exeter and forcing Penda into alliance.

At Hatfield Chase on 12 October 633 Edwin and his son Osfrith fell, and Northumbria divided into Deira and Bernicia. Besieged by Osric of Deira in a strong town, Cadwallon broke out and destroyed him and his army; Eanfrith of Bernicia was killed when he came to negotiate peace. Bede says Cadwallon ruled the Northumbrians for a year like a rapacious and bloody tyrant, sparing neither women nor children. The historian John T. Koch warns against taking this at face value, since Cadwallon was allied with the Anglo-Saxon Penda.

Cadwallon was defeated by Eanfrith's brother Oswald at Heavenfield, though, in Bede's words, he had most numerous forces, and was killed at a place called Denis's-brook. The Britons remembered him as a national hero and the Northumbrians as a tyrant, while the name of Cædwalla of Wessex, derived from his, suggests a better reputation among the West Saxons. Uniquely among Welsh kings of his century, three poems are associated with him, and englynion in Peniarth MS 21 are said to be his own.
cadwgan-ap-bleddyn: Cadwgan was the second son of Bleddyn ap Cynfyn, king of both Powys and Gwynedd. After Bleddyn was killed in 1075 by Rhys ab Owain of Deheubarth and the nobles of Ystrad Tywi, Powys was divided among three of his sons, Cadwgan, Iorwerth and Maredudd. Cadwgan is first heard of in 1088, when he and Trahaearn ap Caradog attacked Deheubarth to avenge his father and forced its king, Rhys ap Tewdwr, to flee to Ireland; Rhys returned the same year with a fleet from Ireland and defeated the men of Powys.

When Rhys was killed in 1093 Cadwgan attacked Deheubarth again, though it was the Normans who gained from Rhys's death, and about then he married a daughter of the Norman lord Picot de Sai. In the Welsh revolt of 1094 he defeated a Norman force at the Battle of Coed Yspwys, and with his brothers he took Montgomery Castle and came close to taking Pembroke. In 1098 he stood with Gruffudd ap Cynan of Gwynedd against Earl Hugh of Chester and Earl Hugh of Shrewsbury, until a Danish fleet hired by Gruffudd took a higher Norman offer and the two fled to Ireland in a skiff.

Returning the next year, he recovered part of Powys and Ceredigion by doing homage to Earl Robert of Shrewsbury. When the earl fell out with the king in 1102, Iorwerth helped defeat him and handed their brother Maredudd to the king, but broke with the crown when his promised lands went to Normans, and his imprisonment in 1103 left Cadwgan sole ruler of the parts of Powys not in Norman hands. In 1109 Cadwgan's son Owain abducted Nest, wife of Gerald of Pembroke, from the castle of Cenarth Bychan, and Cadwgan could not persuade him to return her.

Richard de Beaumais, the justiciar of Shropshire, promised lands to other members of the house of Powys who would attack Cadwgan and Owain. Owain fled to Ireland and Cadwgan was left with one border vill, until Henry I returned Ceredigion for a fine of £100 and a promise to have nothing to do with Owain. After Madog ap Rhiryd killed Iorwerth in 1111, Cadwgan briefly ruled all Powys, but Madog killed him at Welshpool later that year. Another son, Madog ap Cadwgan, began the line of the lords of Nannau, which ran to the 13th lord in the 16th century.
caedmon: The only source of original information about Cædmon's life is Bede's Historia ecclesiastica. According to Bede, he was a lay brother who cared for the animals at the monastery of Streonæshalch, now Whitby Abbey, during the abbacy of Hilda. One evening, while the monks feasted and passed round a harp, he left early to sleep with the animals because he knew no songs. In a dream a man asked him to sing the beginning of created things. After first refusing, he produced a short poem praising God as Creator of heaven and earth.

In the morning he remembered the verses and added more. His foreman took him to the abbess, who with her counsellors judged the gift to be from God and set him a test, a poem on a passage of sacred history or doctrine. When he returned the next day with it, he was invited to take monastic vows, and the abbess had scholars teach him sacred history, which he turned into verse.

Bede credits him with a large body of vernacular religious poetry: accounts of creation, versions of the Old and New Testaments, and songs of future judgment, the horrors of hell and the joys of heaven. He says Cædmon never composed anything foolish or trivial, only what concerned devotion. Only his first poem survives. The poems of the Junius manuscript match Bede's description in part, but they differ in style from the Hymn, and scholars no longer attribute them to him.

Cædmon's Hymn has nine lines and is known from 21 manuscript copies, in two dialects and five recensions. It survives in manuscripts of Bede's History, as a gloss to his Latin or as a replacement for it in the Old English translation. The oldest version is Northumbrian, dated to at least the mid-8th century. Some scholars accept the texts as accurate transmissions, while others argue they are back-translations from Bede's Latin.

Bede reports that Cædmon had a premonition of death, asked to be moved to the abbey's hospice, and died after receiving the Eucharist, with his friends around him. Bede gives no dates. His activity is placed between the abbacy of Hilda and the events of the 680s, and most scholars see no reason to doubt that a poet named Cædmon existed. He is venerated as a saint in several churches, with a feast day on 11 February, and in 1898 Cædmon's Cross was erected in his honour at St Mary's Church in Whitby.
caedwalla: Cædwalla was born about 659, according to Bede's statement that he was about thirty at his death. His name is a Saxon form of the Welsh Cadwallon, and a number of early West Saxon kings had Celtic names. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle makes him the son of Coenberht and a descendant of Cerdic, but later scribes tried to link every king to Cerdic, so the genealogy must be treated with caution. He is first mentioned in the Life of St Wilfrid as an exiled nobleman in the forests of Chiltern and Andred. In 685 he began to contend for the kingdom, defeated and killed Æthelwealh, king of Sussex, and was soon expelled by Æthelwealh's ealdormen Berthun and Andhun.

In 685 or 686 Cædwalla became king of the West Saxons after Centwine retired to a monastery. Bede says that before his reign Wessex was ruled by underkings, though this has been questioned. He attacked Sussex again and killed Berthun. He conquered the Isle of Wight, then an independent pagan kingdom. Bede says he set out to kill every native and resettle the island with his own people, though the natives remained a majority. Arwald, king of the island, left two young brothers, who were found at Stoneham and killed on his orders after a priest persuaded him to let them be baptised. Cædwalla was wounded in this conquest.

He controlled Surrey, as a charter of 688 granting land at Farnham for a minster shows, and invaded Kent in 686, installing his brother Mul as king. Mul was burned in a Kentish revolt, according to the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, and Cædwalla returned and laid waste to the land, possibly ruling Kent directly after that. He gave land to churches and, according to the Life of Wilfrid, sought out Wilfrid as a spiritual father.

In 688 Cædwalla abdicated and set out on pilgrimage to Rome, perhaps because his wounds were killing him. Bede says he wished to receive baptism at the shrine of the Apostles. He stopped in Francia at Samer and at the court of Cunincpert, king of the Lombards. In Rome Pope Sergius I baptised him on the Saturday before Easter, giving him the name Peter, and he died on 20 April 689, still in his white garments. He was buried in St Peter's Basilica, and his epitaph called him King of the Saxons. Ine succeeded him, and his departure appears to have led to instability in the south of England.
caelian-hill: The Caelian Hill is a promontory about 2 kilometres long and 400 to 500 metres wide, rising to about 50 metres in the park near the Temple of Claudius. According to a tradition recounted by Varro, it took its name from the Etruscan folk hero Caelius Vibenna, who either settled there or was honoured after his death by his friend Servius Tullius. Other authors linked the name to the Latin caelum, "heaven", and the earlier name was probably Querquetulanus mons, for its oaks.

Under Tullus Hostilius the whole population of Alba Longa was forcibly resettled on the hill. It is said to have been included in the city under Ancus Marcius, and under Augustus it became Regio II Caelimontium. Most of it lay outside the pomerium, so temples to foreign divinities, such as the Temple of Minerva Capta, could be built there. It was a fashionable district of wealthy houses. Pliny the Elder records that Mamurra, a soldier who served under Julius Caesar in Gaul, first encrusted the walls of a Roman house with marble there, and Horace and Catullus mocked him.

The Temple of Claudius was raised on a huge platform, begun by his widow Agrippina after his death and deification in 54 CE and finished under Vespasian, and Nero added a nymphaeum supplied by a branch of the Aqua Claudia. Septimius Severus built a barrack for the mounted imperial guard there between 193 and 197, and the decisive battle of the mint workers' revolt of 271, led by Felicissimus, was fought on the hill. Jerome says that Marcus Aurelius was born there in 121. Alaric's sack of 410 badly damaged the buildings, and the hill was increasingly abandoned.

In the 6th century the hill fell within the ecclesiastical region of the Lateran basilica. Churches followed, including the Basilica of Saints John and Paul, the Basilica of the Four Crowned Martyrs and the Basilica of Saint Stephen in the Round, with monasteries and noble towers, mainly in the 10th and 11th centuries. It suffered again in the sack of 1084.

The hill forms the Rione of the same name and keeps its tradition of care in the Policlinico Militare del Celio. Its monuments include the Temple of Claudius, the Arch of Dolabella and the Villa Celimontana. The philosopher George Santayana lived at the Convent of the English Blue Sisters on the hill from 1912 until his death.
caen: In Roman times the site was known as Catumagos, from Gaulish words for combat and field, and it remained a minor settlement. In 912 Caen became the western capital of the Duchy of Normandy, and the patronage of the dukes brought a major development of commerce in the 10th century. Around 1060 William the Conqueror began the Château de Caen, one of the largest medieval fortresses of Western Europe, which became the centre of the ducal court.

His wife, Duchess Matilda of Flanders, founded the Benedictine Abbey of Sainte-Trinité at about the same time and was buried in it. Caen succeeded Bayeux as capital of Lower Normandy, beside Rouen as the second ducal capital, and William was buried in the city. Philip II of France took it on 21 May 1204, and it passed with the rest of Normandy into the Kingdom of France.

During the Hundred Years' War Edward III of England stormed and sacked the city on 26 July 1346, in less than a day, killing 3,000 citizens and burning much of the merchants' quarter on the Île St-Jean; only the castle held out. Henry V captured it after a siege in 1417 and treated it harshly as the first town to resist his invasion. French forces recaptured it in 1450. The University of Caen was founded in 1432 by John of Lancaster, Duke of Bedford, and Henry VI of England.

German forces occupied Caen after the Battle of France in 1940. After the Allied landings of Operation Overlord, the British Second Army fought the Battle of Caen from 6 June to 6 August 1944 to dislodge German forces. Allied bombing raids heavily damaged the city and caused many French civilian casualties, and little of prewar Caen remained. Reconstruction of whole districts and the university campus took fourteen years, from 1948 to 1962. A Canadian Army Film and Photo Unit recorded the recovery in the film You Can't Kill a City. The city has since built the Mémorial de Caen, a museum dedicated to peace.

Caen is the prefecture of the department of Calvados, on the River Orne about 15 km from the coast and 200 km northwest of Paris. The city proper has 105,512 inhabitants. A canal built under Napoleon III links it to the English Channel at Ouistreham. It remains known for the buildings of William the Conqueror's reign, including the castle and the abbeys.
caerleon: Caerleon, in Welsh Caerllion, lies in the Vale of Usk, about 5 miles (8 km) north-east of Newport city centre, and is now a community within Newport. The area has important Neolithic sites. By the Iron Age it was home to the Silures and seems to have been the centre of a wealthy trading network. From the 5th century BCE a hillfort at Lodge Wood Camp, defended by three lines of ramparts and ditches and the largest fortified enclosure in South Wales, crowned the hill above the river. An excavation in 2000 found it occupied continuously until the Roman fortress was built. There is no evidence that it was taken militarily, and its abandonment may have been part of the terms of peace.

Caerleon was the headquarters of the Second Legion Augusta from about 75 to 300 CE. The Romans called the place Isca after the River Usk, and the name Caerleon may derive from the Welsh for fortress of the legion. The military amphitheatre, baths and barracks have been excavated, and a Roman harbour was found in 2011.

In the Middle Ages Caerleon was an administrative and religious centre of the Kingdom of Gwent and an early see associated with Saint Dubricius. After a Norman castle was built, the Welsh lords and the Normans contested the town. In 1171 Iorwerth ab Owain destroyed it and burned the castle, which William Marshal seized and rebuilt in stone in 1217. Rhys Gethin took it in 1402 during the Glyndŵr Rising.

In his Historia Regum Britanniae, about 1136, Geoffrey of Monmouth made Caerleon a major centre of British history, naming Belinus as its founder and describing it as the place of Arthur's coronation feast. Early Welsh poetry and Geoffrey named it as Arthur's capital, and the amphitheatre has been linked with the Round Table, although it shows no sign of sixth-century occupation. Gerald of Wales wrote in 1191 that the Roman ambassadors had been received at Arthur's court there. Until the docks at Newport were built, Caerleon was the major port on the Usk.

The remains of Isca Augusta, the National Roman Legion Museum and the Roman Baths Museum draw visitors and school parties, and a heritage trail marks the town. Caerleon has 86 listed buildings, among them Saint Cadoc's Church and the Round Tower. An arts festival has been held each July since 2003, together with a Roman military display in the amphitheatre.
caernarfon: Caernarfon lies on the eastern shore of the Menai Strait in Gwynedd, opposite the island of Anglesey, with Snowdonia to the east and south-east. The mouth of the River Seiont forms a natural harbour. The name combines caer, meaning fortress, either the Roman fort of Segontium or the Norman castle near the mouth of the Seiont, with Arfon, meaning opposite Môn, Anglesey, and so means the fortress in the land opposite Anglesey. The town is the historic county town of Caernarfonshire.

The resources of the Menai Strait supported prehistoric habitation. During the Roman conquest the fort of Segontium was established around 80 CE to subjugate the Ordovices, a Celtic tribe. Roman rule ended in 382, after which Caernarfon became part of the Kingdom of Gwynedd. In the late 11th century William the Conqueror ordered a motte-and-bailey castle to be built there as part of the Norman invasion of Wales, but the invasion failed and Wales remained independent until about 1283.

Llywelyn ap Gruffudd, ruler of Gwynedd, refused to pay homage to Edward I of England, and the English conquest of Gwynedd followed. The present castle was built between 1283 and 1330 on Edward's order, and its banded stonework and polygonal towers are thought to imitate the Walls of Constantinople. The town walls, with eight towers and two gateways, were built between 1283 and 1285. In 1284 the Statute of Rhuddlan created the county of Caernarfonshire, and Edward granted the town a charter making it a borough and the seat of English government in north Wales. St Mary's Church was begun in 1307 as a chapel for the castle and garrison.

When the Welsh House of Tudor came to the English throne hostilities eased and the castle fell into disrepair. In the 19th century Caernarfon was an important port, exporting slate from the Dyffryn Nantlle quarries, helped from 1828 by the Nantlle Railway.

Caernarfon is a royal town, a status granted by Queen Elizabeth II as a royal borough in 1963 and amended in 1974. The castle and town walls form part of the World Heritage Site of the Castles and Town Walls of King Edward in Gwynedd, which UNESCO listed in 1986. Gwynedd Council has its headquarters there. The town has the highest percentage of Welsh speakers of any community in Wales, and its residents are known colloquially as Cofis. It has hosted the National Eisteddfod several times, from 1862 to 1979. Tourism, the harbour and the marina are central to its economy.
caerphilly-castle: Caerphilly Castle lies in the Rhymney Valley, alongside the Rhymney River, at the centre of a network of paths and roads and beside a former Roman fort. It covers around 30 acres and is the largest castle in Wales, built from Pennant sandstone on a natural gravel bank. It introduced concentric castle defences to Britain, and its defences include large gatehouses and what the historian Allen Brown called the most elaborate water defences in all Britain. The core, with luxurious accommodation, stands on a central island among artificial lakes, a design Gilbert de Clare probably took from Kenilworth, where he fought in the siege of 1266.

The earls of Gloucester had been charged with subduing Glamorgan since 1093, and the de Clare family acquired the earldom in 1217. Gilbert de Clare, called Red Gilbert, inherited in 1263 and faced the Welsh prince Llywelyn ap Gruffudd. After the baronial revolt was crushed in 1266–1267, he began the castle in 1268, and most of the work was done within three years. Llywelyn burned the site in 1270, Henry III sent two bishops to take it over in 1271, and the following February de Clare's men seized it back. Work stopped about 1290.

The castle withstood attacks in 1294, in the rising led in Glamorgan by Morgan ap Maredudd, and in 1316, when Llywelyn Bren attacked it. In 1317 it passed to Eleanor de Clare and her husband Hugh le Despenser, who enlarged the Great Hall in 1325 to 1326. Edward II and Despenser sheltered there in late 1326 before fleeing, and William la Zouche besieged the garrison until March 1327. The castle declined after 1486, the lakes drained and the walls were robbed of stone, as for Thomas Lewis after 1583.

The Marquesses of Bute acquired the castle in 1776, and the third and fourth marquesses restored it, the fourth from 1928 to 1939. The fifth marquess gave it to the state in 1950, and the water defences were re-flooded in the 1950s and 1960s. The Welsh heritage agency Cadw manages it. It is a scheduled monument and a grade I listed building.
caerwent: Caerwent lies about 5 mi (8.0 km) west of Chepstow and 11 mi (18 km) east of Newport. Its name joins Venta, an ancient British word for a market, to the later Welsh Caer, a fortified settlement. Roman writers called the town Venta Silurum to tell it apart from other tribal markets such as Venta Belgarum, modern Winchester, and Venta Icenorum, modern Caistor St Edmund.

The Romans founded the town in 75 CE as a market for the defeated Silures, as the Civitas Silurum stone, now in the parish church, confirms. Its walls still rise to 5 metres in places; the historian John Newman called them the most impressive town defence to survive from Roman Britain. A 4th-century temple with its temenos and a mosaic of fish found in 1881 survive, but most houses were plain, few with mosaics or heated floors, and the town never matched the sophistication of other Romano-British tribal capitals.

Caerwent remained important after Roman rule, where the road from Gloucester to Caerleon met the road from Shrewsbury through Monmouth and Trellech to the sea at Portskewett. Brooches and pins of the 5th–7th centuries and many Christian burials of the 4th to 9th centuries have been found, and it has been suggested that it was the birthplace of Saint Patrick. A monastery was founded there some time before the 10th century.

During World War II a Royal Navy Propellant Factory was built north of the A48 road. Between 1967 and 1993 it was a storage station for the Royal Air Force and the United States Army, and it later became an army training facility.

The modern village is built around the Roman ruins, with houses over half the site of the old market place, and had about 1,200 people in 2021. The Church of St Stephen and St Tathan has parts dating to the 13th century.
caesar-rodney: Rodney was born on 7 October 1728 on Byfield, his family's plantation on St. Jones Neck in Kent County, Delaware. His grandfather William Rodney had come to the colonies with William Penn in 1681–1682 and was speaker of the Colonial Assembly of the Delaware Counties in 1704; his mother was a daughter of the Rev. Thomas Crawford, Anglican rector of Christ Church at Dover. Byfield, a farm of 849 acres worked by enslaved labour, sold wheat and barley to Philadelphia and the West Indies.

He attended the Latin School of the academy and College of Philadelphia until his father died in 1746, when the Orphan's Court placed him under the guardianship of Nicholas Ridgely. In 1755 he was elected sheriff of Kent County, then held posts as Register of Wills, Recorder of Deeds, justice of the peace and judge; from 1769 to 1777 he was an associate justice of the Supreme Court of the Lower Counties.

Though he belonged to the Anglican gentry of Kent, Rodney sided with his brother Thomas with the minority Country Party, which favoured independence, working with Thomas McKean against George Read. He was a delegate to the Stamp Act Congress in 1765 and sat in the Delaware Assembly from 1761/1762 to 1775/1776, presiding on 15 June 1776, when it voted to sever ties with Parliament and the king. He signed the Declaration on 2 August, and a backlash in Delaware cost him election to the state's constitutional convention.

As president of Delaware from 31 March 1778 and major-general of its militia, he relied on his standing with the General Assembly, where real authority lay, and on the militia's loyalty. He gathered money, supplies and soldiers for the war and held down Loyalist activity, above all in Sussex County, scene of the Black Camp Rebellion of 1780. Failing health led him to resign on 6 November 1781.

Rodney suffered from asthma all his life and for years from a facial cancer, wearing a green scarf to hide his face. He died on 26 June 1784, before the end of the Legislative Council session that had chosen him as its speaker. At his death he held 18 enslaved people; his will freed three of advanced age and set a schedule for freeing the rest. He lies in an unmarked grave on his family's former farm, and the stone at Christ Episcopal Church is a monument only. A statue of him on horseback stood in Rodney Square in Wilmington from 1923 until its removal in 2020.
caesarea-mauretaniae: The town stood on the northern coast of Africa, about 100 km west of present-day Algiers. Phoenicians from Carthage founded it around 400 BCE as a trading station and named it Iol or Jol. It later became part of the kingdom of Numidia under Jugurtha, who died in 104 BCE, and grew important to the Berber monarchy and the generals of Numidia; the Berber King Bocchus II lived there. Because of its strategic position, new defences were built during the 1st century BCE.

Juba II had been brought up in Rome under the tutelage of Julius Caesar and had learned Greek and Latin. Once Augustus entrusted the kingdom of Mauretania to him, he and his wife Cleopatra Selene II, daughter of Cleopatra VII and Mark Antony, rebuilt the town on a lavish scale as a Graeco-Roman city, with street grids, a theatre, an art collection and a lighthouse like the one at Alexandria. Its buildings mixed Egyptian, Greek and Roman styles, and most of its people were of Greek and Phoenician origin, with a minority of Berbers.

The client kingdom lasted until 40 CE, when its last king, Ptolemy of Mauretania, was murdered on a visit to Rome. A bloody revolt and war with Rome followed, after which Emperor Claudius divided Mauretania into two provinces. The city was settled with Roman soldiers and given the rank of a colonia as Colonia Claudia Caesarea. It came to have a hippodrome, an amphitheatre, a basilica, temples, a school of philosophy, an academy and a library, and soon passed 30,000 inhabitants; the historian Gsell put its later population at nearly 100,000. The future emperor Macrinus was born there in about 165 CE.

Berber tribes sacked the city during a revolt in 371/372, but it recovered. Christianity spread quickly in the 4th and 5th centuries: a bishop named Fortunatus attended the Council of Arles in 314, the town became a Donatist centre, and Augustine of Hippo publicly confronted the Donatist bishop Emeritus there in the autumn of 418. The Vandals, who reached Africa in 429, burnt the town and turned many of its buildings into citadels, though they also restored much of the damage. The Byzantine Emperor Justinian I took the city in 533, and it declined thereafter.

The site is the modern town of Cherchell in Algeria. The Royal Mausoleum of Mauretania, where Juba II and Cleopatra Selene II were buried, can still be seen. Caesarea is also used as a titular see for Catholic and Eastern Orthodox bishops.
caesarion: Caesarion, whose name means Little Caesar, was born in Egypt in 47 BCE; an Egyptian demotic stele from the Serapeum at Memphis records his birth on 23 June 47 BCE. He was conceived during Julius Caesar's stay in Egypt, when Caesar supported Cleopatra's claim to the throne against her brother Ptolemy XIII. Mark Antony later testified before the Roman Senate that Caesar had privately acknowledged the boy as his son, but Caesar never recognised him legally as his heir, and when his will was read after his assassination on 15 March 44 BCE, Caesarion was omitted and Octavian was named as heir.

Cleopatra returned to Alexandria with her two-year-old son in mid-April 44 BCE, and on 2 September 44 BCE Caesarion was proclaimed King of Egypt at the age of three, although Cleopatra kept absolute authority. She presented herself as the goddess Isis and him as Horus. In 34 BCE, in the Donations of Alexandria, Antony granted lands and titles to Caesarion, proclaimed him a god and King of Kings, and declared him Caesar's true son and heir. That threatened Octavian, whose position rested on his adoption by Caesar, and he used Roman resentment of the Donations to win support for war against Antony and Cleopatra.

When Octavian invaded Egypt in 30 BCE, Caesarion was seventeen. Plutarch says he was sent with much treasure towards India, and that his tutor Rhodon persuaded him to return by saying that Octavian invited him to take the kingdom. Octavian took Alexandria on 1 August 30 BCE.

Octavian is supposed to have had Caesarion killed in Alexandria in late August 30 BCE. According to Plutarch he followed the advice of Arius Didymus, who said that too many Caesars was not good. Little is recorded of the death. Caesarion was the last of the Ptolemaic line and the last pharaoh.
caesars-civil-war: The main issue was how Julius Caesar, who had been in Gaul for almost ten years, was to be reintegrated into Roman politics after accumulating immense power and wealth there. He had allied himself with Crassus and Pompey in the First Triumvirate during his consulship in 59 BCE, but the alliance frayed in the mid 50s BCE. By late 50 BCE both Caesar and the anti-Caesarians, among them Pompey and Cato, seemed to believe the other would back down, and trust had eroded.

On 7 January 49 BCE the Senate was persuaded to demand that Caesar give up his post or be judged an enemy of the state. Caesar crossed the Rubicon on the 10th or 11th of January, which marked the formal start of hostilities.

Caesar marched west and in June 49 BCE defeated a Pompeian army under Lucius Afranius and Marcus Petreius at Ilerda, which put all of Spain under his control. His lieutenant Curio was defeated and killed at the Battle of the Bagradas River in August. In 48 BCE Caesar crossed the Adriatic, but Pompey forced him to withdraw at the Battle of Dyrrachium. The larger Battle of Pharsalus in Greece was won by Caesar, and Pompey's army disintegrated. Pompey fled to Egypt, where he was murdered on arrival.

Caesar became involved in the dynastic dispute between Ptolemy XIII and Cleopatra, and then defeated Pharnaces II at Zela in a few weeks. He crossed to Africa on 25 December 47 BCE and defeated Metellus Scipio at the Battle of Thapsus in 46 BCE. Cato and Metellus Scipio died by suicide soon after. In 45 BCE Caesar defeated the last Pompeians at the Battle of Munda in Spain, led by his former lieutenant Titus Labienus. The Spanish campaign was marked by atrocities, with Caesar treating his enemies as rebels.

Caesar held four triumphs, over Gaul, Egypt, Asia and Africa, and the Senate made him dictator perpetuo in 44 BCE. A group of senators, including Marcus Junius Brutus, assassinated him on the Ides of March of that year. Some scholars, such as Erich Gruen, see the war, triggered by miscalculation rather than design, as the event that set off the collapse of the Republic. Others see it as a symptom of that collapse. Caesar's death left a power vacuum, and his heir Octavian eventually took complete control and formed the Roman Empire as Augustus.
caete: The Caeté were one of the Tupi peoples of the Brazilian coast, alongside the Tupiniquim, Tupinambá, Potiguara, Tabajara, Temiminó and Tamoio, related by language but not united and often at war with one another. In the 16th century their lands ran from the mouth of the São Francisco River to the island of Itamaracá, with the Potiguara to the north and the Tupinambá, their traditional enemies, to the south. They grew corn, peanuts, tobacco, squash and cotton, and like other Tupi peoples they practised a ritual cannibalism of captured enemies, believing that it passed on a brave warrior's strength.

The Portuguese allied with the Tupinambá, and the Caeté suffered from smallpox and other European diseases and from mass enslavement, which reached its peak in the 1550s. On 16 June 1556, in Alagoas, they captured and ate Bishop Pero Fernandes Sardinha and the 90 sailors shipwrecked with him. A holy war followed from 1556 to 1558: under Jerónimo de Albuquerque the Portuguese carried out a brutal extermination of the Caeté between the São Francisco River and the Cabo de Santo Agostinho, and a decree of Catherine of Austria allowed the perpetual enslavement of every captive. The persecution eased only with Brazil's first law on slavery in 1570, which the Jesuit Manuel da Nóbrega had worked for.

In 1587 Cristóvão de Barros campaigned against them to avenge his father, Antonio Cardoso de Barros, whom they had eaten. In the 1580s Caeté groups moved north to the lands between the Caeté and Turiaçu rivers, where the Capitania de Caeté, the Caeté Captainship, was created in 1622 and Jesuit missions grew into towns. A quarrel over the village leadership led to the Caeté Upheaval, and in 1753 Vila de Souza was moved and became Bragança.

The Caeté entered Brazilian literature as enemies. In the epic Caramuru by Santa Rita Durão, written in 1781, they oppose Caramuru and Paraguaçu. Nísia Floresta, by contrast, made a Caeté the hero of her poem A Lágrima de um Caeté, against the Indianist habit of choosing heroes from peoples friendly to the Portuguese.
caffaro-di-rustico-da-caschifellone: Caffaro was born in the village of Caschifellone, now part of Serra Riccò, in either 1080 or 1081. While still a teenager he travelled to the Holy Land with a Genoese contingent on the First Crusade, from August 1100 until January 1101, and he went back to the Holy Land in the 1130s.

On the strength of his fame as a crusader, Caffaro became a captain in the Genoese navy and fought in several battles against the Republic of Pisa and other Mediterranean powers. Between 1122 and 1149 he served eight terms as one of the consuls of Genoa. Towards the end of his life he turned to diplomacy, carrying out missions for Genoa to the courts of Pope Callixtus II, the Emperor Frederick I and King Alfonso VII of León and Castile, and also to Pisa.

Caffaro began the Annales ianuenses, the Genoese annals, which became the official history of the republic and were continued by his successors down to 1294. His imperfect Latin kept the work from greatness as literature, but it was the first chronicle of its kind in Genoa and remains an important record, not least for the careers of the early Embriaco family.

He also wrote the Ystoria captionis Almarie et Turtuose, an account of the siege of Almería, from 1 August to 17 October 1147, and of the siege of Tortosa, from 1 July to 30 December 1148. Perhaps in 1155-56, while Genoa was in dispute with the Kingdom of Jerusalem, he wrote De liberatione civitatum orientis, On the Liberation of the Cities of the East, a work on the First Crusade, on relations between the West and the Byzantine Empire, and on the distances between the cities of the East.
cagliari: Cagliari stands on the southern coast of Sardinia, at the head of a bay, on a position between the sea and a fertile plain. It is surrounded by two marshes, which gave defence against attacks from inland, and high mountains nearby offered a refuge if the settlement had to be abandoned. Its natural resources have always been its sheltered harbour, the strongly fortified hill of Castel di Castro, the salt of its lagoons, wheat from the Campidano plain and silver and other ores from the Iglesiente mines. Its mild climate allows many subtropical plants to grow.

The area has been inhabited since the Neolithic, and under the modern city lies a continuous stratification of settlement over some five thousand years. The legend told by the Latin writer Gaius Julius Solinus says that Caralis was founded by Aristaeus, son of Apollo and the nymph Cyrene, who introduced hunting and agriculture to Sardinia. Remains of the ancient city of Karalis include the Tuvixeddu necropolis, the largest Punic necropolis still in existence, the Roman amphitheatre, traditionally called Is centu scalas, and an aqueduct.

Cagliari was ruled by the Byzantine Empire, apart from a short occupation by the Ostrogoths in 551 and 552 during the Gothic War, and became the capital of a gradually independent Judicate, which was born around 1020 and overthrown by the Republic of Pisa in 1258. Pisa and Genoa both valued Sardinia as a base for controlling the trade routes between Italy and North Africa. The Pisan Lamberto Visconti forced the judikessa Benedetta of Cagliari to give him the mount east of Santa Igia, and Pisan merchants founded there the fortified city of Castel di Castro, ancestor of modern Cagliari.

The Crown of Aragon conquered Sardinia from the Pisans in the 14th century. During the siege of Castel di Castro, from 1324 to 1326, the Aragonese under Alfonso IV built a stronghold on the hill of Bonaria. Cagliari was the capital of the Kingdom of Sardinia from 1324 to 1848. In 1718, after a brief Habsburg rule, Cagliari and Sardinia came under the House of Savoy. In 1848 the Perfect Fusion merged the Savoyard possessions into one state with its parliament in Turin, which then became the formal capital.

Cagliari is the capital and largest city of Sardinia, an autonomous region of Italy, with about 145,981 inhabitants. It is the seat of the University of Cagliari, founded in 1606, and of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Cagliari, since the 5th century. The Feast of Sant'Efisio on 1 May is its most important religious event, with a procession to Nora, where according to tradition the saint was beheaded. Its native language, official alongside Italian, is Sardinian, in the Campidanese dialect.
cahokia-woodhenge: The circles were found during salvage archaeology by Warren Wittry in the early 1960s, ahead of a planned highway interchange about 850 metres west of Monks Mound. Among the house remains were unusual post holes, 2 metres long, with sloping ramps for raising posts an estimated 6 metres tall. Plotted, they formed arcs of evenly spaced holes, and Wittry, suspecting a calendar, named the circles woodhenges after the monuments of England. Robert L. Hall found more holes and central posts in 1963, and Wittry's excavations of the late 1970s confirmed five circles, now numbered Woodhenge I to V.

Four of the circles overlap, so they are thought to have been built in sequence, each generally larger and with twelve more posts than the last: 24 posts in Woodhenge I, 36 in II, 48 in III and 60 in IV, while V may have been planned with 72, though only 13 were found, in an arc facing sunrise. Archaeologists suspect that large trees were becoming scarce by then.

The posts were of red cedar, the area's only native evergreen and a tree held sacred by many Native American groups, and traces of red ochre suggest they were painted. Woodhenge III, thought to date from about 1000 CE, was completed by William R. Iseminger's excavations of 1985 and reconstructed in its original holes, half in red cedar and half in black locust.

Archaeologists think the circles served as a solar calendar for the farming year and religious observances. At the equinoxes the sun, seen from the centre, appears to rise out of the front of Monks Mound, and the moving and enlarging of the circles may have followed the mound's growth. In Woodhenge III the central post was set 1.7 metres east of the true centre so that perimeter posts marked the solstice sunrises; at the winter solstice the sun would have risen over Fox Mound and its temple across the grand plaza.

A ceremonial beaker bearing a cross in a circle, found in an offertory pit near the winter solstice post, suggests ritual meaning too. The Illinois Historic Preservation Division holds sunrise observations at the equinoxes and solstices, without ceremonies, out of respect for Native American beliefs.
cahors: Cahors lies in a meander of the Lot, surrounded by steep, dry limestone hills, 115 km north of Toulouse. It covers 64.72 km2, and its altitude ranges from 105 to 332 metres. It is the historical centre of the Quercy and the main town of the Lot department.

The town's original name was Divona, or Divona Cadurcorum, Divona of the Cadurci. Divona was a fountain, now called the fontaine des Chartreux, worshipped by the Cadurci, a Celtic people of Gaul. They were among the last Celtic tribes to resist the Roman conquest in the 50s BCE. Romanisation was rapid and thorough, and Cahors became a large Roman city whose remains include the Arc de Diane, a relic of Roman baths.

In the Middle Ages the town was notorious for financiers known as Cahorsins, Christians who charged interest on loans. The church held that this was the sin of usury, so Cahors became a byword for it, and Dante's Inferno names it alongside Sodom. Pope John XXII, born Jacques Duèze, came from Cahors, the son of a shoemaker. On 7 June 1331 he granted a charter to the University of Cahors, which was annexed to the University of Toulouse in 1751.

The Valentré Bridge, the symbol of the town, was begun in 1308 and finished in 1378. A Devil's Bridge legend is attached to it, and when the bridge was restored in 1879 the architect Paul Gout placed a small sculpture of the devil on one of its towers.

Cahors is the prefecture of the Lot department and the seat of a diocese. Its monuments include the Saint-Étienne cathedral, a national monument, and the Valentré bridge, a World Heritage Site as part of the pilgrimage path to Santiago de Compostela. The wine of the Cahors appellation is a robust, tannic red that must contain at least 70% Malbec.
cai-lun: Cai Lun was born in Guiyang Commandery, in what is now Leiyang in Hunan, to a poor family. His year of birth is unknown, and estimates run from about 50 to about 62. Almost nothing is known of his early life, and it is not known how he came into imperial service in Luoyang. He is known to have been a eunuch official by 75 CE, and eunuchs were the only people eligible for certain tasks of the Han imperial household. Around 80 CE he was promoted to Xiao Huangmen, a messenger between the palace and the outer court.

In 82 CE Lady Dou, who wished to place her adopted son Prince Zhao in line for the throne, falsely accused Consort Song of witchcraft and ordered Cai to interrogate her and her sister; both killed themselves. When Prince Zhao became Emperor He in 88 CE, at the age of ten, Dou ruled as empress dowager and promoted Cai to Zhongchang shi, the highest post open to eunuchs, and made him Prefect of the Palace Workshop, responsible for instruments and weapons. Emperor He overthrew the Dou family in 92 CE but left Cai undisturbed.

In 105 CE Cai announced a new composition for paper and a new process. It used bamboo and also hemp waste, old rags, fishnets and, above all, tree bark, probably mulberry, boiled to a pulp, beaten, mixed with water, sieved and dried. Before then writing was usually on heavy bamboo and wooden slips or on costly silk. The Hou Hanshu records that he submitted the process to the emperor and that the paper came to be called the paper of Lord Cai. In 110 CE he oversaw a new edition of the Five Classics, and in 114 CE he was made a marquis.

After Empress Dowager Deng's death in 121 CE, Emperor An, remembering Cai's part in the death of his grandmother Consort Song, ordered him to answer to the Ministry of Justice. Cai bathed, dressed formally and drank poison.

Paper existed in China as early as the 3rd century BCE, so scholars regard his work as an improvement, not an invention, though paper did not see widespread use until his changes. Papermaking spread across China and by the 600s appeared in Turkestan, Korea and India. Chinese prisoners from the Battle of Talas passed the knowledge to the Arabs of the Abbasid Caliphate, and it reached Europe, where paper was widely made by the 12th century. In China Cai was deified in the early Tang dynasty as god of papermaking, and Leiyang is still a centre of paper production.
cai-yong: Cai Yong, courtesy name Bojie, was born in a substantial family in Yu County, Chenliu Commandery, near present-day Qi County, Kaifeng, Henan. His family had a reputation for not dividing its territory for three generations. After his father Cai Leng died he lived with his uncle Cai Zhi and cared for his mother for her last three years. He then studied composition, mathematics, astronomy, pitch-pipes and music under Hu Guang, one of the highest-ranking officials at the Han court. He was an astronomer, calligrapher, historian, mathematician, musician and writer.

In the early 160s the senior eunuchs recommended him to Emperor Huan for his skill with the drums and the guqin, but he feigned illness on the way to the capital and returned home. In the early 170s he served as a clerk under Qiao Xuan, then as a county magistrate and a Consultant in the capital, editing and collating texts in the library. In 175, fearing that parties would alter the Confucian classics, he and other scholars petitioned to have the Five Classics engraved in stone. Emperor Ling approved, and the Xiping Stone Classics were completed in 183.

He urged the restoration of ceremonial practice and often criticised the eunuchs. In 178 his reply on ill omens attacked eunuch pretensions, and the eunuchs accused him and Cai Zhi of extortion. The death sentence was remitted to exile on the northern frontier, and after he returned to the capital he fled south to Wu and Kuaiji commanderies for twelve years. When Dong Zhuo took power in 189 he summoned Cai Yong to Luoyang, threatening to eliminate whole clans, and made him Left General of the Household in charge of revising rituals.

When Wang Yun killed Dong Zhuo in May 192, Cai Yong was imprisoned and sentenced to death for allegedly expressing grief at Dong's death. He asked to finish his history of the Han, but Wang Yun refused, comparing him to Sima Qian, and Cai Yong died in prison. Many of his works were lost in the turmoil of the following decade, but he had entrusted most of his library to his protégé Wang Can, through whom works survive in compilations like the Book of Later Han. His works include Duduan on ceremonial, Qin Cao on the guqin and Zhuan shi on seal script. His daughter Cai Yan, also called Cai Wenji, was a poet and musician.
cai-yuanpei: Cai Yuanpei was born in Shanyin County, Shaoxing, Zhejiang, and was appointed to the Hanlin Academy at the age of 26. From 1898 he administered schools, serving as superintendent of the Shaoxing Chinese-Western School, head of the Shanshan College and director-teacher of a special class at Nanyang Public School, the predecessor of Shanghai Jiao Tong University.
