The chronicle then follows the royal line down to Adittaraja and his war with the Mon kingdom of Lavo to the south, ending in his victory and the finding of the relic still enshrined in Wat Phra That Hariphunchai.

The text survives as a palm-leaf manuscript in the Tai Tham script, kept at a monastery in northern Thailand. The only complete edition of the Pali appeared in 1920 with a Thai translation; five years later George Cœdès published a French translation of chapters 12, 13 and part of 14, and Donald Swearer's full English translation followed in 1998.

Early Western scholars searched the text for historical facts, and Cœdès criticised it for lacking them. Modern scholars read it instead as a religious foundation myth linking Mon Haripunjaya with Lamphun, confirming the visit of the Buddha to the region that tradition records and legitimising the relic and its temple. Popular veneration of the queen has revived in northern Thailand, centred on a memorial statue in Lamphun.
cambodia: Cambodia covers about 181,035 km2 and lies entirely within the tropics, with a 443 km coastline along the Gulf of Thailand. Its landscape is a low-lying central plain surrounded by uplands and low mountains, including the Tonle Sap, the Great Lake, and the upper Mekong delta. The Tonle Sap's most distinctive feature is its flooding, from about 2,590 km2 in the dry season to about 24,605 km2 in the rainy season, and the plain around it, devoted to wet rice cultivation, is the heartland of the country.
The highest peak is Phnom Aural, at 1,813 metres. The Khmer name derives from the Sanskrit Kambujadeśa, the land of the sons of Kambu, after a sage from whom the Khmer kings claimed descent.

Cambodia has been inhabited for over 5000 years. The cave of Laang Spean, with radiocarbon dates around 6000 BCE, is considered the most ancient archaeological site in the country, and the first rice farmers came from the north from the third millennium BCE. Iron was worked by about 500 BCE. In the 3rd, 4th and 5th centuries the Indianised kingdoms of Funan and its successor Chenla coalesced in what became Cambodia and southwestern Vietnam, and for more than 2,000 years the region absorbed influences from India and passed them to other Southeast Asian civilisations.

In 802 Jayavarman II declared himself king, uniting the warring Khmer princes of Chenla under the name Kambuja, and the Khmer Empire became the centre of power. Over 600 years it facilitated the spread of first Hinduism and then Buddhism across Southeast Asia. In the 15th century Cambodia declined and lost territory to its neighbours, and during the Post-Angkor period Vietnam and Thailand each attempted to vassalise it. It became a French protectorate in 1863 and secured independence in 1953.

The Khmer Rouge regime carried out the Cambodian genocide from 1975 to 1979 and was deposed by a Vietnamese intervention and occupation, though insurgencies continued until 1999. By 1993 a United Nations peacekeeping mission had restored the monarchy and established a democratic constitution with elections. Cambodia is a constitutional monarchy. About 17 million people live there, 95.8% of them ethnic Khmer.
cambodian-peoples-party: Nationalists in Cambodia, Vietnam and Laos believed they had to work together to free themselves from France, and formed the supranational Indochinese Communist Party in 1930. The Japanese triumph in the early part of the Second World War crippled French rule and fed nationalism, and in Cambodia national pride joined with historical mistrust of the neighbouring countries. On 28 June 1951 Cambodian nationalists split from the Indochinese party to form the Kampuchean People's Revolutionary Party. In 1955 it set up a subsidiary, the Pracheachon, to contest that year's national election. The name became Workers' Party of Kampuchea on 28 September 1960 and Communist Party of Kampuchea in 1966, whose members Prince Norodom Sihanouk termed the Khmer Rouge.

On 5 January 1979 the Cambodian communists who overthrew the Khmer Rouge regime, ending the genocide, held a congress and re-established the Kampuchean People's Revolutionary Party. They declared themselves the true successors of the party of 1951, labelled the gathering its Third Party Congress, and did not recognise the 1963, 1975 and 1978 congresses of the Communist Party of Kampuchea. The party allied itself with Vietnam and the Soviet Union, in contrast to the pro-Chinese Pol Pot, and ruled the People's Republic of Kampuchea from 1979 to 1989, then the State of Cambodia until 1991. It took on a more reformist outlook in the mid-1980s under Heng Samrin. Hun Sen was prime minister from 1985 to 1993.

In 1991, during a United Nations-sponsored peace process, it took its present name, Cambodian People's Party, with Chea Sim as president and Hun Sen as vice-president, abandoning the one-party system and Marxism–Leninism. It took a large part in the negotiations behind the Paris Peace Accords of 23 October 1991. In 1997 it ousted Norodom Ranariddh in a coup in which thirty-two people died.

The party won 64 of 123 National Assembly seats in 1998, 73 in 2003 and 90 in 2008, with 58 percent of the vote that year. It lost 22 seats in 2013. In 2018, after the main opposition, the Cambodia National Rescue Party, was banned, it won all 125 seats and 58 of 62 Senate seats. After the 2023 elections it held 120 of 125 seats. Hun Sen became its president in 2015, though he had held de facto control earlier.

Its leaders describe a centrist middle path between capitalism and communism, while the academic John Ciorciari observed that it kept communist-era party structures and that many top members came from the old party. Political scientists have classed it as left-wing. It belongs to the Centrist Democrat International and hosted a Socialist International meeting in 2004.
cambodian-vietnamese-war: The Cambodian and Vietnamese communists had fought side by side against France and later against the anti-communist regimes in Saigon and Phnom Penh. Yet the Khmer Rouge under Pol Pot feared that the Vietnamese wanted an Indochinese federation which Vietnam would dominate. They also held irredentist feelings about the Mekong Delta, and had grievances reaching back to Vietnamese intervention in Cambodia from the 17th century and the annexation under Minh Mang after 1834.

After the communist victories of April 1975 the Khmer Rouge expelled North Vietnamese forces from Cambodia and attacked the Vietnamese island of Phú Quốc on 1 May 1975. A major attack on Vietnam followed on 30 April 1977. Vietnam retaliated at the end of 1977 and withdrew in January 1978 without bringing the Khmer Rouge to the table. In April 1978 the Khmer Rouge carried out the Ba Chúc massacre of over 3,000 Vietnamese civilians.

On 21 December 1978 two Vietnamese divisions moved on the town of Kratié. Of the 19 divisions of the Kampuchea Revolutionary Army, 10 fired along the border with Vietnam on 23 December. On 25 December Vietnam launched a full-scale invasion with 13 divisions, estimated at 150,000 soldiers, supporting Cambodian dissidents in exile. The country was occupied in two weeks and the Khmer Rouge government was removed, ending the Cambodian genocide, which had killed between 1.2 and 2.8 million people.

On 8 January 1979 the pro-Vietnamese People's Republic of Kampuchea was established in Phnom Penh. The Khmer Rouge withdrew to the jungle near the Thai border, where they fought on with the Khmer People's National Liberation Front under Son Sann and FUNCINPEC under Norodom Sihanouk. These groups formed the Coalition Government of Democratic Kampuchea in 1982, which the United Nations continued to recognise.

Vietnam could not defeat the Khmer Rouge remnants, and the war isolated it from everyone but the Eastern Bloc. Most United Nations members, including China and North Korea, denounced the use of force. Vietnamese advisers sat at every level of Heng Samrin's government, and many Cambodians came to see the occupation as no liberation. Hun Sen, prime minister from 1985, opened talks with the coalition's factions.

Under diplomatic and economic pressure Vietnam adopted reforms and withdrew completely in September 1989. The Paris Peace Agreements of 1991 began a process of reconciliation, leading to a United Nations transition and the restoration of multi-party rule and a constitutional monarchy in September 1993.
cambridge: Cambridge is the county town of Cambridgeshire, on the River Cam about 55 miles north of London. It stands on level, low-lying ground just south of the Fens, between 6 and 24 metres above sea level, and the town was historically surrounded by wetlands that were drained as it expanded. Its river link to the farmland around it and its road connections to London made it an important regional trading post.

The earliest clear evidence of settlement is a 3,500-year-old farmstead found at the site of Fitzwilliam College, and an Iron Age settlement stood on Castle Hill from the 1st century BCE. A small Roman fort, Duroliponte, was built on Castle Hill around 70 CE and converted to civilian use some fifty years later. After the Roman withdrawal around 410 the Anglo-Saxons were settling the area by the end of the century, and their settlement was called Grantebrycge, Granta bridge. By the 7th century Bede described it as a little ruined city holding the burial place of Æthelthryth. It sat on the border between the East and Middle Anglian kingdoms.

Henry I issued the earliest known municipal charter in the early 12th century and granted the town a monopoly on river trade. A charter of King John in 1207 permitted the appointment of a mayor, and the first recorded mayor, Harvey FitzEustace, served in 1213. Fairs such as Stourbridge Fair and Midsummer Fair drew merchants from across the country. Hobson's Conduit, built in the early 1600s after repeated outbreaks of pestilence, brought fresh water from Nine Wells into the centre. The railway reached Cambridge in 1845, and with changing patterns of retail distribution it reduced the town's importance as a market town.

The town expanded rapidly in the 19th century, and inclosure acts of 1801 and 1807 allowed it to spread over the surrounding open fields. Members of the university drew up the first rules of association football in 1848, the Cambridge Rules, first played on Parker's Piece, and they influenced the Football Association rules of 1863.

Cambridge received city status in 1951. Its university, founded in 1209, has buildings that include King's College Chapel, the Cavendish Laboratory and the University Library, one of the largest legal deposit libraries in the world. The city lies at the centre of a high-technology district known as Silicon Fen and is completely enclosed by green belt.
cambridgeshire: Cambridgeshire is a ceremonial county in the East of England and East Anglia, bordered by Lincolnshire, Norfolk, Suffolk, Essex, Hertfordshire, Northamptonshire and Bedfordshire. The north and east are dominated by the Fens, an extremely flat, drained marsh maintained by drainage ditches and dykes, where Holme Fen is the lowest physical point in the United Kingdom, 2.75 metres below sea level. The south and west are gently undulating. The principal rivers are the Nene, the Great Ouse and its tributary the Cam, which flows through Cambridge.

Must Farm quarry at Whittlesey has been described as Britain's Pompeii for the best-preserved Bronze Age dwellings ever found in the United Kingdom, and many archaeological finds from the Stone Age, the Bronze Age and the Iron Age have come from East Cambridgeshire. Anglo-Saxons settled the area from the fifth century. Genetic testing of seven skeletons from Anglo-Saxon graves at Hinxton and Oakington found that five were migrants or descended from migrants from the continent, one was a native Briton and one had both continental and native ancestry, suggesting intermarriage.

The Domesday Book records the county as Grantbridgeshire, a name related to the river Granta. In 1888 separate county councils were set up for the area around Cambridge and for the liberty of the Isle of Ely. In 1965 these were merged as Cambridgeshire and the Isle of Ely, and under the Local Government Act 1972 this merged with Huntingdon and Peterborough, formed in 1965 from Huntingdonshire and the Soke of Peterborough. The resulting county was called simply Cambridgeshire. Since 1998 Peterborough has been a separate unitary authority.

Because of the flat terrain and the nearness of the continent, many airfields were built in the county in the Second World War for RAF Bomber Command, RAF Fighter Command and the American air forces. The Cambridge American Cemetery and Memorial lies at Madingley.

Peterborough is the largest settlement, and the county also contains the cities of Cambridge and Ely and the towns of Wisbech, Huntingdon and St Neots. Most of it is agricultural. The University of Cambridge, the second-oldest university in the English-speaking world, stands in Cambridge.
cambyses-ii: Cambyses was the eldest son of Cyrus the Great and Cassandane, and his younger brother was Bardiya. In April 538 BCE Cyrus appointed him governor of northern Babylonia, and he received the royal sceptre in the temple of Marduk at the New Year festival. Cyrus dismissed him after nine months, for unknown reasons. Babylonian records give both men the title King of Babylon, King of the Lands, which suggests that Cyrus made him co-ruler some years before his campaign against the Massagetae. Cambyses was sent back to Persia before Cyrus fell in that campaign, and he had his father's body carried to Pasargadae for burial.

The conquest of Egypt had been planned by Cyrus, who wished to unite Babylonia with the Trans-Euphrates lands. Cambyses seized Cyprus, founded the Achaemenid navy with men and equipment from Phoenicia and Asia Minor, and made a treaty with the Arabs of the desert between Gaza and Egypt for water. In the spring of 525 BCE he defeated Psamtik III at Pelusium, then besieged and captured Memphis. By summer all Egypt was under Persian suzerainty. The Greeks of Cyrene and Barca acknowledged his authority, and he set a garrison at Elephantine against Kush. At Sais he was crowned in the temple of Neith and took the titles of the pharaohs.

Greek writers such as Herodotus accuse him of brutality, of looting temples, of killing the sacred Apis bull, and of madness. Pierre Briant holds that this bias casts doubt on Herodotus's account. An epitaph and sarcophagus show that Cambyses took part in the burial of an Apis, and the Demotic Chronicle says that he reduced the income of most Egyptian temples, which may explain hostile stories spread by priests. Herodotus also reports a disastrous expedition against Kush, but archaeology shows a Persian stronghold at Dorginarti.

In the spring of 522 BCE Cambyses left Egypt in haste to put down a revolt in Persia. On the way through Syria he received a wound in the thigh that became gangrenous, and he died about three weeks later, probably at Hama. Herodotus tells of an accident with his sword, Ctesias of a self-inflicted wound, and some modern historians suspect assassination. He died childless and was succeeded by his brother Bardiya, whom Darius the Great soon overthrew. Cambyses was buried at Neyriz in southeastern Persis. At his death the empire stretched from Cyrenaica to the Hindu Kush.
camden-south-carolina: Camden lies in the Midlands of South Carolina, in the south-central part of Kershaw County, on the north-east side of the Wateree River, a south-flowing tributary of the Santee River. It is the county seat and the largest city in the county. It stands near the centre of the Cofitachequi chiefdom that existed in the 1500s. Its roads link it to Columbia, about 32 miles to the south-west, and to Charlotte, North Carolina, 76 miles to the north.

In 1730 King George II ordered eleven inland townships to be established along South Carolina's rivers. Camden's was laid out in 1732 as Fredericksburg in the Wateree River swamp, south of the present town, but few settlers took lots there and chose the higher ground to the north. In 1758 Joseph Kershaw from Yorkshire came into the township, set up a store and renamed the town Pine Tree Hill. It became the main inland trade centre of the colony, and Kershaw proposed the name Camden in honour of Lord Camden, a champion of colonial rights in the British Parliament. In the 1770s John Bartlam established an early American porcelain factory there.

After Charleston fell in May 1780, Lord Charles Cornwallis and 2,500 Loyalist and British troops marched to Camden and made it the main British supply post for the Southern campaign. The Battle of Camden, the worst American defeat of the Revolution, was fought near the town on 16 August 1780. On 25 April 1781 General Nathanael Greene, with about 1,400 men, fought 950 Loyalists and British under Lord Francis Rawdon at the Battle of Hobkirk's Hill. It was a costly win for the British and forced them to leave Camden and retreat to the coast.

After the Revolution Camden grew rich as an interior trading town, sending goods to Charleston on flat-bottomed riverboats until the railroad came in 1842. It supplied six Confederate generals in the Civil War, and parts of Sherman's army burned a full block of downtown buildings at the war's end. From the mid-1880s wealthy northern families wintered there, and the town became associated with horses; the Carolina Cup steeplechase has been run since 22 March 1930, and the National Steeplechase Museum stands near its course. The population was 7,788 at the 2020 census.
camel: The camel is an even-toed ungulate of the genus Camelus, marked by fatty deposits known as humps. Three species survive. The one-humped dromedary makes up 94% of the world's camel population and the two-humped Bactrian camel 6%. The wild Bactrian is a distinct species, not the ancestor of the domestic Bactrian. Camels provide milk, meat, fibre and felt, and are a vital means of transport for passengers and cargo.

The hump is a reservoir of fatty tissue, a reserve of calories and not of water, as is commonly believed. A dromedary can drink as seldom as once every 10 days even in great heat, and can lose up to 30% of its body mass through dehydration.

Camelids originated in North America during the Eocene. Paracamelus, the ancestor of modern camels, crossed the Bering land bridge into Asia during the late Miocene, around 6 million years ago. The camels that stayed in North America were wiped out 10 to 12,000 years ago, when the first indigenous peoples spread there from Asia, although fossils have never been associated with definitive evidence of hunting.

When humans first domesticated camels is disputed. Dromedaries may have been domesticated in Somalia or South Arabia in the 3rd millennium BCE, and the Bactrian in central Asia around 2,500 BCE, as at Shahr-e Sukhteh in Iran. A study of 2016 using mitochondrial DNA suggested that the dromedary was first domesticated in the southeast Arabian Peninsula.

Excavations in the Timna Valley in 2009 to 2013, led by Lidar Sapir-Hen and Erez Ben-Yosef, found what may be the earliest domestic camel bones in Israel or outside the Arabian Peninsula, dating to around 930 BCE. The find drew attention because camels appear in the biblical stories of Abraham, Jacob, Esau and Joseph, and it is taken as strong evidence that those stories were written after that time. The archaeologist William F. Albright had earlier seen the camels of the Bible as an anachronism.

Camels introduced to Australia as transport animals in the 19th and early 20th centuries became a large feral population. The United States Camel Corps experiment of the 19th century also brought camels to the Southwestern United States.
camera-degli-sposi: The room is also known as the Camera picta, the painted chamber. In the fifteenth century the Gonzaga kept Mantua independent of its stronger neighbours Milan and Venice by hiring out their support as a mercenary state, and Ludovico III Gonzaga commissioned the paintings to give his rule more cultural standing at a time when courts such as Ferrara were ordering painted chambers of their own. The room, on the first floor of a north-eastern tower overlooking the Lago di Mezzo, served as Ludovico's bedchamber, a gathering place for family and close courtiers, and a reception room for important guests.

Before work began the room was made nearly square, about eight metres each way and seven metres high. Mantegna painted it as a classical pavilion. On the north wall, above the fireplace, the Court Scene shows Ludovico seated with his secretary Marsilio Andreasi, his wife Barbara of Brandenburg, several of their children and his dog Rubino, with courtiers waiting on the steps. Ludovico reportedly sat in front of this portrait when receiving distinguished visitors, so that its unflattering likeness would vouch for the rest.

The west wall shows the Meeting Scene, in which Ludovico greets his son Francesco Gonzaga, newly made a cardinal, in the company of Emperor Frederick III and King Christian I of Denmark. The meeting never took place, and it leaves out Duke Galeazzo Maria Sforza, the main employer of Mantua's soldiers. On the ceiling, painted reliefs show scenes from the lives of Arion, Orpheus and Hercules, and putti hold medallions of the first eight Roman emperors.

The room became known as a masterpiece of trompe-l'œil and of di sotto in sù, painting seen from below, soon after it was finished. In the oculus, courtiers lean over the balustrade and look straight at the viewer, and a heavy planter rests on a loose beam above. This idea of a painting that answers the viewer's presence was new in Renaissance Italy, and the ceiling set a standard for the ceiling paintings of Correggio and later Baroque painters.
camera-obscura: The effect is a natural phenomenon. Perforated gnomons that projected a pinhole image of the sun are described in the Chinese Zhoubi Suanjing, and the Mozi explains that the image is inverted because light crosses at the pinhole: rays from a person's foot strike below it and form the top of the image. The Greek philosopher Aristotle, or a follower, asked in the Problems why sunlight passing through square gaps in wickerwork forms round images.

Al-Kindi, who lived from about 801 to about 873, used pinhole images to show that light travels in straight lines. Ibn al-Haytham, known in the West as Alhazen (965 to 1040), gave the first experimental and mathematical analysis of the phenomenon in the early 11th century.

A camera obscura is a box, tent or room with a small hole in one side or the top. Light from the scene outside passes through the hole and forms on the opposite surface an image that is inverted and reversed left to right, with colour and perspective kept. A smaller hole gives a sharper but dimmer image, until diffraction spoils it, so practical instruments use a lens, which allows a larger aperture. Mirrors can set the image upright.

Leonardo da Vinci wrote the oldest known clear description in 1502 and drew about 270 diagrams of it, though his writings were deciphered and published only in 1797. The oldest published drawing is in Gemma Frisius's book of 1545, where he used it to watch the solar eclipse of 24 January 1544. The name first appears in Johannes Kepler's book of 1604. From 1611 David and Johannes Fabricius and Christoph Scheiner projected the sun to study sunspots, since looking at it directly could damage the eyes.

As a drawing aid it allowed an image to be traced and was valued as an easy way to achieve correct perspective. Lenses were fitted from the second half of the 16th century. In the first half of the 19th century camera obscura boxes were used to expose light-sensitive materials, and the technology developed into the photographic camera.
camerino: Camerino stands in the Apennines on the border with Umbria, between the valleys of the rivers Potenza and Chienti, about 64 kilometres from Ancona. It occupies the site of ancient Camerinum, whose inhabitants became allies of Rome in 310 or 309 BCE, bound to it by an equal treaty, the foedus aequum. Under the empire the town was a municipium. No ancient building is visible today, since the Roman remains lie as much as a metre below ground level.

Camerino was part of the Exarchate of Ravenna until 592, when the Lombards captured it. Under them it was the seat of a marquisate and then of a duchy, which the Franks later conquered. Around 1050 Boniface III of Tuscany occupied the duchy and ceded it to his daughter Matilda, who donated it to the Papal States. After the year 1000, however, it had become an independent commune. The troops of Manfred of Sicily destroyed it in 1256 and killed much of its population. Gentile Da Varano, one of the refugees who returned in 1262, founded a fiefdom for his family that lasted three centuries.

In 1382 Giovanni da Varano built a wall 12 kilometres long to defend the city, and Giulio Cesare Da Varano built a Ducal Palace, now one of the most important Renaissance buildings in central Italy. Giulio Cesare's daughter Camilla Battista da Varano was canonised in 2010. Cesare Borgia nearly extinguished the family in 1502. The university was founded in 1336, was recognised by the Kingdom of Italy in 1861 and became the public University of Camerino in 1958.

Camerino is a town in the province of Macerata in Marche. Its Ducal Palace is the seat of the university's Faculty of Jurisprudence. Its cathedral was rebuilt in the early 19th century, and the Porta Malatestiana dates from 1511.
cameroon: Cameroon covers 475,442 square kilometres in Central and West Africa, on the Bight of Bonny, part of the Gulf of Guinea. It is often called Africa in miniature because it has the coast, desert, mountains, rainforest and savanna of the continent. The country divides into five major geographic zones, among them a hot and humid coastal plain and the South Cameroon Plateau, covered by equatorial rainforest.

A chain of mountains, hills and plateaus, the Cameroon range, runs from Mount Cameroon on the coast, the highest point at 4,095 metres, almost to Lake Chad in the north. Volcanism there has created crater lakes. On 21 August 1986 one of them, Lake Nyos, released carbon dioxide and killed between 1,700 and 2,000 people.

Excavations at Shum Laka in the Northwest Region show human occupation dating back 30,000 years. The Baka are counted among the longest continuous inhabitants, and Bantu migrations into eastern, southern and central Africa are believed to have begun from this area about 2,000 years ago. The Sao culture arose around Lake Chad about 500 CE and gave way to Kanem and its successor, the Bornu Empire, while kingdoms, fondoms and chiefdoms arose in the west. Portuguese sailors reached the coast in 1472 and named the Wouri River Rio dos Camarões, the Shrimp River, after the ghost shrimp they found there. In 1896 Sultan Ibrahim Njoya created the Bamum script for the Bamum language.

Germany built a warehouse on the Wouri estuary in 1868, and in 1884 the German Empire claimed the territory as the colony of Kamerun after Gustav Nachtigal made a treaty with a local king. The people resisted in the Bafut Wars and Adamawa Wars. Commercial companies ran local administration and used forced labour on banana, rubber, palm oil and cocoa plantations, a policy criticised by other colonial powers. After World War I the territory was divided between France and the United Kingdom as League of Nations mandates. The French-administered part became independent as the Republic of Cameroun in 1960 under Ahmadou Ahidjo, and the southern part of British Cameroons federated with it in 1961.

Yaoundé is the capital and Douala, the economic capital and main seaport, is among the largest cities. Cameroon is a unitary presidential republic. Its official languages are French and English, and its people speak some 250 native languages. Christianity is the majority religion, with significant minorities practising Islam and traditional faiths. Cameroon is a member of the African Union, the United Nations, the Commonwealth of Nations and the Organisation Internationale de la Francophonie.
cameroon-grassfields: The Western High Plateau, also called the Western Highlands or Bamenda Grassfields, lies along the Cameroon line, a series of volcanic swells running from the Atlantic Ocean in the southwest of the plateau to the Adamawa Plateau in the northeast. It consists of massifs, mountain ranges and volcanoes. The region borders the South Cameroon Plateau to the southeast, the Adamawa Plateau to the northeast and the Cameroon coastal plain to the south. Its dormant volcanoes include the Bamboutos Mountains, Mount Oku and Mount Kupe. The plateau rises in steps from the west and ends in the east in mountains between 1,000 and 2,500 metres high.

The core of the plateau is volcanic rock ringed by plutonic rock, above a crystalline and metamorphic base of gneiss and granite dating to the Precambrian period. A layer of basalt covers this, and volcanism has produced fertile black and brown soils. Crater lakes dot the plateau where dead volcanoes have filled with water.

The climate is equatorial of the Cameroon type, with a long wet season of nine months and a short dry season of three. Rainfall averages 1,000 to 2,000 millimetres a year, and the high elevation makes the region cooler than the rest of Cameroon; the average temperature at Dschang in the West Region is 20°C. The relief and rain make it a major watershed: the Manyu, which rises in the Bamboutos Mountains and becomes the Cross River downstream, and the Nkam, known as the Wouri on its lower course, both rise here, as do important tributaries of the Sanaga River. Ekon Falls near Nkongsamba is 80 metres high.

The plateau was once heavily forested, but repeated cutting and burning has driven the forest back to the waterways and let grassland spread. Sudan savanna is the dominant vegetation, consisting of grassfields, which give the name Bamenda grassfields around the city of Bamenda, and short shrubs and trees that shed their leaves in the dry season. Raffia palms grow in the valleys.
camille-pissarro: Jacob Abraham Camille Pissarro was born on 10 July 1830 at Charlotte Amalie to Frederick Abraham Gabriel Pissarro, a merchant of Portuguese Jewish descent who held French nationality, and Rachel Manzano-Pomié. His father's marriage to his late uncle's widow caused a stir in the small Jewish community, and the four children were sent to an all-black primary school. In 1855, at 25, Camille moved to Paris and worked as an assistant to the painter Anton Melbye. He found the teaching at the École des Beaux-Arts and the Académie Suisse stifling and asked Corot for instruction instead.

His first painting was accepted by the Paris Salon in 1859. Corot inspired him to paint outdoors, and at the Académie Suisse he met Claude Monet, Armand Guillaumin and Paul Cézanne, who shared his dissatisfaction with the Salon. During the Franco-Prussian War he moved his family to Norwood near London, since he had only Danish nationality. Of the 1,500 paintings he left in France, only 40 remained, since soldiers had used many as floor mats. In 1871 he married Julie Vellay, with whom he had seven children, six of them painters. The family settled at Éragny-sur-Epte in April 1884.

The first Impressionist exhibition, in 1874, shocked critics, who found the subjects vulgar and the brushwork sketchy. Pissarro showed five landscapes, and Émile Zola praised them. In 1885 he met Georges Seurat and Paul Signac and for about three years used their method of small dabs of pure colour, showing such works in 1886 at the eighth exhibition. By the end of the 1880s he found the method too restrictive, but kept a stronger attention to colour. He was also drawn to anarchist circles, and in 1889 made an album of thirty drawings, Turpitudes sociales.

In 1892 Monet helped Pissarro and Julie buy the Éragny house, and in 1893 Pissarro converted the barn into a studio. In old age a recurring eye infection kept him from working outdoors except in warm weather, so he painted from hotel windows in Rouen, Paris, Le Havre, Dieppe and London. He died in Paris on 13 November 1903, aged 73, of sepsis, and was buried in Père Lachaise Cemetery. The art historian Diane Kelder wrote that no member of the Impressionist group did more to mediate the disputes that threatened to break it apart. Cézanne said that Pissarro had been a father for him.
camille-saint-saens: Saint-Saëns was born in Paris, the only child of Jacques-Joseph-Victor Saint-Saëns, an official in the French Ministry of the Interior, and Françoise-Clémence, née Collin. Less than two months after the christening his father died of consumption. The boy was taken to the country for his health and lived for two years with a nurse at Corbeil, 29 kilometres south of Paris. He always considered himself a true Parisian.

On leaving the Conservatoire in 1853, Saint-Saëns became organist at Saint-Merri, where weddings and funerals gave him a comfortable income and spare time to compose. In 1861 he took his only teaching post, at the École Niedermeyer, in charge of piano studies. He scandalised some austere colleagues by introducing his students to Schumann, Liszt and Wagner, and Gabriel Fauré remembered the lessons with lasting gratitude.

In 1870, with Romain Bussine, he discussed a society to promote new French music. He served in the National Guard in the Franco-Prussian War. The Société Nationale de Musique, with the motto Ars Gallica, was founded in February 1871, with Bussine as president and Saint-Saëns as vice-president. He was elected to the Institut de France in 1881, and in 1906 and 1909 he made successful tours of the United States as pianist and conductor.

Saint-Saëns was the first major French composer to write piano concertos. The Second, in G minor (1868), became one of his most popular works, and the pianist Zygmunt Stojowski said it begins like Bach and ends like Offenbach. The Fifth, the Egyptian concerto of 1896, was written while he was wintering in Luxor. His Third Symphony has prominent parts for piano and organ and is dedicated to the memory of Liszt.

He wrote twelve operas. Henry VIII became a repertory piece in his lifetime, but since his death only Samson et Dalila has been regularly staged. He composed more than 140 mélodies and set Victor Hugo most often. Committed to the structures of earlier French composers, he came into conflict in later years with the impressionist and expressionist schools.
camillo-benso-count-of-cavour: Camillo Benso was born in Turin on 10 August 1810, during Napoleonic rule, into a family that had acquired estates during the French occupation. His godparents were Napoleon's sister Pauline and her husband, Prince Camillo Borghese. He joined the Engineer Corps of the Royal Sardinian Army in 1827. Reading Jeremy Bentham and Benjamin Constant made him a liberal and a suspect to the police, and he resigned his commission in November 1831. He managed the family estate at Grinzane and served as its mayor until 1848, held that economic progress had to come before political change, and backed railways and canals.

The Revolutions of 1848 let him enter politics, and he founded the newspaper Il Risorgimento. After the Piedmontese defeat at Novara and the abdication of Charles Albert in favour of Victor Emmanuel II, he became minister of agriculture, commerce and the navy in 1850 and of finance in 1851. His railway programme gave Piedmont 800 kilometres of track by 1860. With Urbano Rattazzi he formed a coalition that brought down Massimo d'Azeglio's cabinet in November 1852, and he became prime minister. His methods included heavy use of emergency powers and rigging elections, and the national debt rose sixfold. Piedmont joined the Crimean War on 10 January 1855, which earned it a place at the Congress of Paris.

At Plombières in July 1858 Cavour agreed with Napoleon III that France would help Piedmont fight Austria in return for Savoy and Nice. After Magenta and Solferino Napoleon signed the Armistice of Villafranca on 11 July 1859, and Cavour resigned in fury. Recalled on 20 January 1860, he ceded Savoy and Nice to France to annex Tuscany and Emilia. Garibaldi's thousand volunteers landed at Marsala on 11 May 1860 and conquered Sicily and then Naples. Cavour invaded Umbria and Marche to stop them marching on Rome, and Garibaldi handed the south to the king.

In 1861 Victor Emmanuel II declared the Kingdom of Italy and Cavour became its first prime minister. He held that Rome should be the seat of a free church in a free state. Exhausted, he fell ill, presumably with malaria, and was bled several times. He died on 6 June 1861 and was buried at Santena. Venice joined Italy in 1866 and Rome in 1870. Cavour had at first aimed to expand Piedmont rather than to unite Italy, but by his death the state was five times its earlier size and ranked among Europe's great powers.
camilo-henriquez: Henríquez was born on 29 July 1769 in Valdivia, in a house belonging to his grandmother Margarita de Castro; his father, Félix Henríquez y Santillán, had been a Spanish infantry captain. At nine he was sent to Santiago to study at the Convictorio Carolino, and in 1784, at fifteen, to Lima under his maternal uncle Juan Nepomuceno González, a member of the order known as the Buena Muerte. Taught there by Friar Isidoro de Celis, a strong proponent of science and rationality, he joined the order as a novice in 1787 and was ordained a priest on 28 January 1790.

Influenced by the French Enlightenment, he read books banned by the Spanish government, among them Jean-Jacques Rousseau's Social Contract. In 1809 the Spanish Inquisition arrested and interrogated him; he never explained why, and the reading of forbidden books is only the most commonly cited reason. After his release his order sent him to Quito to found a convent, where he witnessed royalist violence that he later drew on in his play Camila o la Patriota de Sud América.

Back in Chile in 1811, he wrote the Proclama de Quirino Lemachez under a pseudonym formed from an anagram of his name, urging support for pro-independence candidates for the First National Congress. Drawing on the social contract theorists, it argued that since the patriots had never consented to a pact with Spain, they should establish their own government; it was reprinted in Europe. He sat in the Congress as interim deputy for Puchacay and became president of the senate in 1813. The first issue of La Aurora de Chile appeared on 13 February 1812, and its successor, the Monitor Araucano, on 17 April 1813.

After the Disaster of Rancagua, where his brother José Manuel was killed defending one of the trenches of the town's plaza, Henríquez fled to Mendoza and later escaped to Buenos Aires. There he contributed to La Gaceta de Buenos Aires and El Censor, and he reportedly studied mathematics and medicine while in exile.

He came back to Chile at the request of Bernardo O'Higgins, became librarian of the National Library of Chile and edited the Gazeta Ministerial de Chile. He was a deputy for Chiloé in 1823 and for Copiapó in 1824, and sat on the nine-member conservative senate that advised the Supreme Director, Ramón Freire. He died in Santiago on 16 March 1825, and the government declared a national period of mourning. In all he edited at least ten newspapers in Santiago and Buenos Aires.
camilo-torres-tenorio: José Camilo Clemente de Torres Tenorio was born on 22 November 1766, the son of Francisco Jerónimo Torres and María Teresa Tenorio. At the Seminary of Popayán he met future leaders of the independence movement such as Francisco Antonio Zea and his cousin Francisco José de Caldas. He studied jurisprudence at the Colegio del Rosario in Santafé, taking a degree in canon law in 1790 and a doctorate in 1791, and opened a law office there. In 1802 he married María Francisca Prieto y Ricaurte; they had six children.

His generation had seen the Insurrection of the Comuneros of 1781, and students of the Colegio del Rosario, Torres among them, were persecuted after Antonio Nariño translated the Declaration of the Rights of Man in 1794. When Ferdinand VII abdicated, Torres backed a junta loyal to the king. His Memorial de agravios complained of the slight representation the American colonies were given in the Supreme Central Junta, yet it praised Spanish authority and hoped the colonies would not secede. After the junta of Santafé was formed on 20 July 1810, he was among the signers of its Act of Independence.

From 1811 he led the federalists, who stood for provincial autonomy, against Nariño's centralists. He was president of the congress of the United Provinces from 1812 to 1814 and became a friend of Bolívar, whose federalist troops forced centralist Cundinamarca to surrender in 1814. The years of strife are often called la Patria Boba. He was president of the United Provinces from 1815 to 1816.

Ferdinand VII, restored to the throne, sent an army under General Pablo Morillo, which took Santafé on 6 May 1816. Torres fled to El Pital near Neiva and tried to sail for Argentina from Buenaventura, but the ship left without him, and in July 1816 he was captured by the troops of Juan Sámano. He was shot for treason in Santafé on 5 October 1816. His property was confiscated, and when Bolívar became president he gave part of his own monthly stipend to Torres's family. His face has appeared on Colombian peso banknotes.
camino-de-santiago: The Camino de Santiago is a network of pilgrim routes leading to the shrine of the apostle James in the cathedral of Santiago de Compostela in Galicia, where tradition holds that his remains are buried. The main route follows an earlier Roman trade road that continues to Cape Finisterre on the Atlantic coast, which the Romans called Finisterrae, the end of the world. Pilgrims can take one of dozens of routes, and traditionally the way begins at one's own home. The Camino Francés, the French Way, is the most popular, and the Via Regia forms its last portion.

The Way was established in the early 9th century after the discovery of the relics of Saint James the Great, and the earliest records of visits to the shrine come from the time of the Kingdom of Asturias and Galicia. The earliest recorded pilgrims from beyond the Pyrenees came in the mid-11th century, and by the early 12th century the pilgrimage was highly organised.

Pope Callixtus II promoted it and began the Compostelan Holy Years. The Codex Calixtinus, published around 1140, served as the guide: four routes from France met at Puente la Reina, and from there a defined road crossed northern Spain through Burgos, León and Astorga.

Hospitals along the route met the pilgrims' needs, and contributed to the modern idea of the hospital. Romanesque churches with massive arches were built for the crowds, and pilgrims took home a Galician scallop shell as proof of completion, which became the badge of the pilgrim. The Church also imposed the pilgrimage as penance for grave sins. The Black Death, the Reformation and political unrest in the 16th century brought a decline, though in 1779 John Adams followed part of the route in reverse on his way to Paris. Few modern pilgrimages predate the 1957 publication of Walter Starkie's The Road to Santiago.

Whenever St James's Day, 25 July, falls on a Sunday, the cathedral declares a Holy Year. In 1987 the Camino was named the first Cultural Route of the Council of Europe, and the French Way and the Northern routes in Spain were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List, followed by the routes in France in 1998. Pilgrims come mostly on foot, some by bicycle or horse, and many walk the final 100 kilometres to earn the Compostela certificate.
camino-frances: The French Way follows the long-distance footpath GR 65 and is the most popular of the routes of the Way of St. James. It begins at Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port on the French side of the Pyrenees, crosses to Roncesvalles and runs another 780 kilometres to Santiago de Compostela through Pamplona, Logroño, Burgos and León. Walking the whole route usually takes at least four weeks, with one or two rest days on the way.

Paths from Tours, Vézelay and Le Puy-en-Velay meet at Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port. A fourth French route, from Arles in Provence, crosses the frontier between Somport and Canfranc, follows the Aragonese Way and joins the French Way at Puente la Reina, south of Pamplona, about 700 kilometres from Santiago de Compostela.

In 1993 the French Way and the Spanish routes of the Camino de Santiago were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List, for their importance in Christianity as a major pilgrimage route and as a testimony to the exchange of ideas and cultures along them.

The Pilgrim's Office in Santiago counts the pilgrims who receive its certificate. In 2024 over 235,000 of them, about 47 per cent, took the French Way. Most began in Sarria, and 14 per cent at Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port, where nine in ten came from neither France nor Spain. Of the 2024 pilgrims on the route, 94 per cent travelled on foot and 2 per cent by bicycle; about 300 rode horses and 170 travelled in wheelchairs, and most finished between May and September.
camino-real-de-tierra-adentro: Long before Europeans arrived, peoples of the north-central steppe of Mexico had established the route as a thoroughfare for hunting and trade. It linked the peoples of the Valley of Mexico with those of the north through the exchange of turquoise, obsidian, salt and feathers, and by 1000 CE a trade network reached from Mesoamerica to the Rocky Mountains. After Tenochtitlan was subdued in 1521, Spanish conquistadores and colonists followed these native trails in expeditions meant to extend their domains.

In April 1598 military scouts led by Juan de Oñate, newly appointed governor of the province of Santa Fe de Nuevo México, lost their way in the desert south of Paso del Norte. A captured local man named Mompil drew in the sand a map of the only safe passage to the Río del Norte. The party reached the river in late April, crossed it, and then mapped and extended the route to what is now Española, where Oñate established the province's capital. The road became the northernmost of the four main royal roads linking Mexico City to Acapulco, Veracruz, Guatemala and Santa Fe.

After the Pueblo Revolt of 1680 forced the Spanish out of Nuevo México, the Crown organised the conducta, a system of wagon caravans that left Mexico City every three years to supply the missions, presidios and ranchos of the north. The journey took six months. Floods and droughts caused delays, and the most feared stretch was the Jornada del Muerto beyond El Paso del Norte, nearly 100 km of desert without water. Bandits threatened the caravans, and from southern Zacatecas northward the Chichimecas attacked, chiefly for horses. Presidios along the way provided relays of troops.

In the 18th century the road carried silver from the northern mines and a growing trade. San Felipe el Real, today Chihuahua, founded in 1709, became its leading commercial centre, and Albuquerque, founded in 1706, traded cattle, wool, textiles and salt. Fairs at San Juan de los Lagos, Saltillo, Chihuahua and Taos were authorised along it. After 1821 American merchants arrived by the Santa Fe Trail, and in 1846-1847 American forces marched along the road during the Mexican-American War.

In 2010 UNESCO listed 55 sites and five existing World Heritage Sites along the Mexican section, between Mexico City and Valle de Allende in Chihuahua. In the United States the 650-kilometre section was proclaimed a National Historic Trail on 13 October 2000, and the El Camino Real de Tierra Adentro Trail Association works with the National Park Service to preserve it.
camp-de-tarragona: The Camp de Tarragona takes in the counties of Tarragonès, Alt Camp, Baix Camp, Conca de Barberà and Priorat. It borders Penedès and Central Catalonia to the east, Ponent to the north and the Terres de l'Ebre to the west. At its heart is a central plain, enclosed on the west and north by the Pre-Coastal Range, open on the east to the sandy Mediterranean beaches of the Costa Daurada and closed to the south by the Coll de Balaguer. Its main rivers are the Francolí, the Gaià and the Foix.

The modern region roughly follows the old vegueria of Tarragona, which was abolished in 1716 after the Nueva Planta decrees and replaced by the Castilian corregimientos. The Parliament of Catalonia defined it as a statistical region in the Territorial Planning Laws of 1987, and it became one of the nine vegueries of Catalonia in January 2010. Before that, several organisations and citizens of Reus had asked that it be called simply Camp and that Reus share the role of capital with Tarragona, so as to spread administration and economic activity more widely.

The capital is Tarragona, and the largest towns are Tarragona, Reus, Valls and Cambrils; the region had 564,162 inhabitants in 2025. It hosts a large chemical complex and one of the main ports, and produces hazelnuts, olives, wine and fish. Its past survives in the Roman remains of Tarragona, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and in the Catalan Modernisme buildings of Reus, the hometown of Gaudí. The University of Rovira i Virgili, founded in 1991, has facilities in Tarragona, Reus and Vila-seca, and the Costa Daurada, with Salou and the PortAventura theme park, draws many visitors.
campania: Campania lies in the south-west of the Italian Peninsula, with a coastline of about 500 km on the Tyrrhenian Sea. It also includes the Phlegraean Islands of Ischia, Procida, Vivara and Nisida, and the island of Capri. The mountainous interior is broken into several massifs, while close to the coast stand the volcanic massifs of Vesuvius and the Campi Flegrei. The Romans knew the region as Campania felix, the fertile or happy countryside.

From the beginning of the 1st millennium BCE the interior was inhabited by Oscan-speaking Italic tribes, among them the Osci, Samnites, Sidicini, Hirpini and the Campanians, after whom the region is named, and by Etruscans. Between the 8th and 7th centuries BCE its coastal areas were colonised by the Greeks of Magna Graecia. Capua was then the leading city, while Naples was predominantly Greek-speaking.

By the end of the 4th century BCE Campania was a full part of the Roman Republic, valued for its pastures and rich countryside. Naples made it a centre of Hellenistic culture for the Romans. In 275 BCE the Romans under the consul Curius Dentatus won the Battle of Beneventum in the Samnite city of Maleventum, which they renamed Beneventum. During the Second Punic War, in 216 BCE, Capua allied with Carthage and was cut off from the rest of Campania, which stayed loyal to Rome; Naples resisted Hannibal behind its walls.

In the Middle Ages the area held many duchies and principalities, in the hands of the Byzantine Empire and the Lombards. The Normans brought the smaller states together within the Kingdom of Sicily. The kingdom then passed to the Hohenstaufen, and Frederick II founded the University of Naples, making the city the intellectual centre of the kingdom. In 1266 Pope Innocent IV crowned the Angevin duke Charles I as king, and Charles moved the capital from Palermo to Naples. In September 1943 Salerno was the scene of Operation Avalanche, and from February to July 1944 it was the temporary capital of the Kingdom of Italy.

Campania is an administrative region of Italy with Naples as its capital and more than five million people. It has ten of Italy's UNESCO sites, including Pompeii, Herculaneum, the Royal Palace of Caserta, the Amalfi Coast, the Longobardian Church of Santa Sofia in Benevento and the historic centre of Naples. Other ancient sites include Oplontis, Paestum, Stabiae and Velia. Its agriculture is known for tomatoes, nuts and the buffalo milk used for mozzarella di bufala.
campeche: Campeche lies in southeast Mexico, bordered by Tabasco, Yucatán and Quintana Roo, by the Petén department of Guatemala to the south and the Orange Walk District of Belize, with 523 kilometres of shoreline on the Gulf of Mexico. The name derives from Can Pech, the Maya name of a chiefdom of the southwestern Yucatán Peninsula at the time the Spanish arrived; its capital, Ah-Kin-Pech, stood where the city of Campeche is now. The native name means place of snakes and ticks.

The Maya were the first people to dominate the area, and their main cities were Edzná, Xtampak and later Calakmul and Becán. The civilisation reached its height between 600 and 900 CE, and from about 1000 the cities were abandoned for unknown reasons. In 1517 Francisco Hernández de Córdoba and Antón de Alaminos landed at Can-Pech and renamed it San Lázaro. At Champotón Hernández de Córdoba was attacked and died of his wounds, so the Spanish called the bay the Bay of the Bad Fight. The conquest of the peninsula began in earnest in 1540 under Francisco de Montejo, father and son, and the capital was founded that year.

The city was a rich port during the colonial period and suffered more than 21 major pirate attacks. After the sack of 1685 by English and French buccaneers, who plundered the surroundings for two months, fortifications were begun that took 24 years to complete: a wall with four main gates, three to the land and one to the sea, and forts including San Carlos, Santa Rosa, San Juan and San Francisco. Only one pirate, Barbillas, found a way in, in 1708. After Mexican independence the city declined, and Campeche split from the province of Yucatán in the mid-19th century, mostly because of political friction with Mérida.

Campeche is one of the 31 states that, with Mexico City, make up the 32 federal entities of Mexico, and has thirteen municipalities. Much of its territory is filled with archaeological sites, almost all Maya, among them Calakmul, Edzná, Becán, Chicanná and Río Bec. The Calakmul Biosphere Reserve was created in 1989. The historic buildings of the capital, formally San Francisco de Campeche, are protected by decree.
campi-flegrei: The Phlegraean Fields are a large volcanic caldera west of Naples, part of the Campanian volcanic arc, which also includes Mount Vesuvius. The caldera area consists of 24 craters and volcanic edifices, most of them under the Gulf of Naples. Part of the city of Naples is built over it, and the area also takes in Pozzuoli, Bacoli, Ischia and Procida. The Solfatara crater has steaming fumaroles and many pools of boiling mud, and was believed in ancient Rome to be the home of Vulcan, the god of fire. Lake Avernus fills one of the tuff craters.

Geologists distinguish three phases. In the first, about 39,280 years ago, the Campanian Ignimbrite eruption, rated VEI 7, spread ash across a large part of eastern Europe; one theory holds that it contributed to the extinction of the Neanderthals. The second period, 35,000 to 10,500 years ago, produced the Neapolitan yellow tuff, with Pozzuoli at its centre; the last major eruption came about 12,000 years ago. The third, from 8,000 to 500 years ago, formed Lake Avernus and Monte Nuovo, which an eight-day eruption built as a new hill in 1538.

The ground rises and falls slowly, a process called bradyseism, most evident at the Macellum of Pozzuoli, where bands of holes bored by marine molluscs in marble columns show that the level of the site against the sea has varied. Between 1982 and 1986 an uplift raised the ground by 1.8 metres.

The ancient Greeks had a colony at Cumae, seat of the Cumaean Sibyl. Lake Avernus was believed to be an entrance to the underworld and is portrayed so in Virgil's Aeneid. Baiae was a fashionable coastal resort with summer villas of Julius Caesar, Nero and Hadrian, who died there.

Pozzuoli has the Flavian Amphitheatre, the third largest in Italy, and Baiae, now partly submerged, had the largest ancient dome before the Pantheon. Quarries of piperno stone supplied much of the building stone of Naples from Roman times to the early 20th century. The tombs of Agrippina the Elder and Scipio Africanus lie in the area. In 2022 the International Union of Geological Sciences listed the site among 100 geological heritage sites, for its part in the development of volcanology in the 18th and 19th centuries.
campine: The Campine takes in a large northern and eastern part of Antwerp Province and neighbouring parts of Limburg and the far north of Flemish Brabant in Belgium, and in the Netherlands parts of North Brabant south-west of Eindhoven and Dutch Limburg around Weert. The river Demer forms its southern edge, the Meuse valley its eastern one, and to the east it runs on into the related Groote Peel. Beneath it lies the Campine Basin, Devonian and Carboniferous rocks on the northern flank of the Brabant Massif. The Medieval Latin name Campania, first recorded in the mid-11th century by Stepelinus, a monk of Saint-Trond, comes from a root meaning field and denotes uncultivated land.

Its poor sandy soil left few old or large towns, and most of them, such as Hasselt, Diest, Lier, Breda, Tilburg and Eindhoven, stand at its rim; Turnhout, with its printing trade, and Herentals, a textile centre whose cloth hall survives, are exceptions. The quiet of the thinly peopled heath drew monks to the abbeys of Achel, Postel, Westmalle and Tongerlo. The first pines were sown in the Gierlebos at Vosselaar in 1667 for Amalia van Solms, and pine later covered large areas to supply pit props for the coal mines.

Industry arrived from the later 19th century: silica sand was quarried at Mol from 1872, Philips was founded in Eindhoven in 1891, and metalworks grew at Balen, Overpelt and Lommel. The Campine coal basin was worked above all after World War II, bringing new industry to Geel, Beringen and Genk, while Belgium's first nuclear installation opened at Mol in 1962 and military bases were placed on the open land. Writers such as Hendrik Conscience and Georges Eekhoud set many books there, and painters such as Jakob Smits painted its landscapes.

Parts of the old heath, marsh and forest survive in reserves such as the Kalmthoutse Heide and the Hoge Kempen National Park near Genk, opened in March 2006 and placed on UNESCO's Tentative List in May 2011. The open-air museum of Bokrijk keeps much of the region's rural heritage, including its long-facade farms.
camulodunum: Camulodunon, the stronghold of Camulos, a British god of war, is named on coins minted by the chieftain Tasciovanus between 20 and 10 BCE. Its earthworks, begun in the 1st century BCE but mostly of the 1st century CE, are considered the most extensive of their kind in Britain. The River Colne guarded the site to the north and east and the Roman River valley to the south, and the dykes closed the western gap, enclosing 1,000 ha. Under Cunobelinus it replaced Verlamion as the most important settlement of pre-Roman Britain.

After Cunobelinus died around 40 CE, his son Caratacus ruled from Camulodunon. In 43 Aulus Plautius led four legions to Britain with the town as their main target, and the Emperor Claudius arrived with reinforcements, including artillery and elephants, to lead the attack. Caratacus fled to the Ordovices and Silures in Wales. The first permanent legionary fortress in Britain was built within the oppidum for the Twentieth Legion, and the colony that followed held the province's only classical-style temple, the centre of the Imperial Cult.

Rebuilt after the revolt, the town, officially Colonia Claudia Victricensis, grew to 45 ha and flourished in the 2nd and 3rd centuries, though the procurator's office moved to Londinium. Its walls, completed by 80, were the first town walls in Britain, and their Balkerne Gate is still Britain's largest Roman gateway. The town had two theatres, Britain's only known chariot circus and more than 50 mosaics, was for a time the province's only producer of samian ware, and may have reached a population of 30,000.

In the crises of the late 3rd century the Balkerne Gate and Duncan's Gate were blocked. A church at Butt Road, dated from 320 to about 425, may be one of the earliest in Britain. Life continued at a much reduced level after Roman administration collapsed in 409–411. Colchester re-entered the written record in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 917, when King Edward the Elder retook it from the Danes.

The Roman walls survive to a height of over 6 m, part of the precinct wall of the Temple of Claudius can be seen near the castle, which alone used over 25,000 cubic metres of reused Roman tile and brick, and the Norman chapel of St Helena stands in a corner of the Roman theatre.
camulogenus: Camulogenus, also written Camulogene, came from one of the Aulerci tribes, Celtic-speaking peoples of northern Gaul in the 1st century BCE. His name goes back to the Gaulish *Camulogenos, probably formed from *camulo(s), champion or servant, and *genos, birth or descendant. Since the name Camulos is attested in the period, it may mean descendant of Camulos, and some scholars have seen in it a reference to the Gaulish god Camulus. Little is known of his life before the Gallic Wars. In his Commentarii de Bello Gallico, Julius Caesar describes him as an Aulercan elder with an exceptional knowledge of warfare.

After six years of Roman invasion and conquest, the Gauls rose under Vercingetorix in 52 BCE. Caesar sent his lieutenant Titus Labienus with four legions to campaign along the Seine, and the Gauls living along the river chose Camulogenus to organise their defence because of his skill and experience. When the Romans had taken the Senonian town of Metiosedum (Melun) and moved against Lutetia in the lands of the Parisii, he turned to scorched earth, ordering the town burned and its bridges cut.

On hearing of Caesar's defeat at Gergovia and that the Bellovaci were mobilising to help the Gauls, Labienus tried to cross the Seine and rejoin Caesar at Agedincum. Camulogenus blocked his path, and the armies met on the plain of Grenelle in the Battle of Lutetia. Camulogenus was killed and his forces scattered, leaving Labienus free to march to Agedincum.

Lutetia was rebuilt after the battle and grew into a Roman city and, in time, into Paris. For his part in its history Camulogenus has come to be counted in the story of Paris, and the Rue Camulogène in the 15th arrondissement is named after him.
can-vuong: The Nguyễn dynasty, restored at Huế in 1802 with help from French missionaries and merchants, revived Confucian institutions to reassure the scholar-gentry but did little for the peasants, and its reign was marked by unrest. The French took southern Vietnam between 1859 and 1867, and in 1882 Henri Rivière captured Hanoi while the court kept negotiating and sidelined mandarins who wanted to fight. After the emperor died without an heir in 1883, factions at Huế quarrelled. In July 1885 General de Courcy arrived at Huế, demanded that the emperor come down from his throne to greet him, rejected the court's gifts and threatened to arrest the regent Tôn Thất Thuyết.

With few French troops in Annam to attack, the insurgents turned on Vietnamese Christians, long seen as allies of the French. The numbers are disputed, but between late July and late September 1885 Cần Vương fighters probably killed around 40,000 Christians, nearly a third of the country's Christian population, some 24,000 of them in Quảng Ngãi and Bình Định. In September de Courcy enthroned Hàm Nghi's brother Đồng Khánh, and the queen mother Từ Dũ returned to Huế.

At Ba Đình in Thanh Hóa province, Đinh Công Tráng built a fortified camp and held it through a two-month siege until the survivors broke out on 20 January 1887; the French lost 19 dead, the Vietnamese thousands. In the south a column from Cochinchina under the Vietnamese commander Trần Bá Lộc took Bình Thuận in 1886, and by June 1887 the provinces south of Huế were under French control, followed by brutal reprisals.

After Hàm Nghi was captured and deported to Algeria, Confucian scholars carried on the Văn Thân resistance until about 1892. Phan Đình Phùng held Hà Tĩnh province with his troops until his death from dysentery, and Đề Thám fought on in the Yên Thế mountains until a settlement in 1897. The Sino-Japanese War of 1894 closed the Chinese border to supplies. The movement brought royalty, scholar-gentry and peasants together, but its roughly 50 groups never acted in concert, and its defeat marked the end of the last independent Vietnamese dynasty.
canaan: Canaan was an ancient Semitic-speaking civilisation and region of the southern Levant in the late 2nd millennium BCE. Egyptian texts of that millennium use the name for an Egyptian-ruled colony whose boundaries broadly match those of the Hebrew Bible: the Mediterranean Sea to the west, the vicinity of Hamath in Syria to the north, the Jordan Valley to the east and a line from the Dead Sea to around Gaza to the south. The Egyptians also called the Levantine coast Retjenu, and the region between Ascalon and the Lebanon, inland to the Sea of Galilee, Djahy.

The name appears as Kinâḫna in the Amarna letters of the 14th century BCE. Its origin is uncertain; one early explanation derives it from a Semitic root meaning to be low or subjugated. The Akkadian word kinahhu referred to purple-dyed wool, a key export, and the Greeks may have taken the name Phoenikes for the Canaanites from their word for crimson or purple.

Scholars use several periodisations. Metalworking Ghassulian settlers entered Canaan around 4500 BCE, at the start of the Chalcolithic. In the Early Bronze Age Ebla was incorporated by about 2300 BCE into the Akkadian Empire of Sargon the Great and Naram-Sin. In the Middle Bronze Age, from 2000 to 1550 BCE, urbanism returned and the region was divided among small city-states, of which Hazor seems to have been the most important, within a wide international trading network.

In the early Late Bronze Age, Canaanite confederacies centred on Megiddo and Kadesh were fully brought into the Egyptian and Hittite empires. By the Early Iron Age the southern Levant was dominated by the kingdoms of Israel and Judah, the Philistine city-states, and Moab, Ammon, Aram-Damascus and Edom. The Neo-Assyrian Empire conquered the whole region in the 10th and 9th centuries BCE and held it for three hundred years.

The name Canaanites is attested many centuries later as the endonym of the people the Greeks called Phoenicians from about 500 BCE, and the Punics of North Africa used a form of it of themselves. In the Hebrew Bible Canaan and the Canaanites appear some 160 times, and Canaan is the land of the Promised Land. The biblical scholar Mark Smith, citing archaeology, holds that Israelite culture largely overlapped with and derived from Canaanite culture.
canada: Canada is the second-largest country by total area, encompassing 9,984,670 square kilometres, and has the world's longest coastline, of 243,042 kilometres. It shares the world's largest land border with the United States, spanning 8,891 kilometres. The country has seven physiographic regions, among them the Canadian Shield, the Interior Plains and the Western Cordillera. It has over 2,000,000 lakes, and boreal forests prevail throughout. Canadian Forces Station Alert, on the northern tip of Ellesmere Island, is the world's northernmost settlement.

Indigenous peoples have continuously inhabited what is now Canada for thousands of years, and they include the First Nations, Inuit and Métis. Their population at the time of the first European settlements is estimated at between 200,000 and 2 million, and it declined by 40 to 80 percent as a consequence of colonisation, through European diseases, conflicts over the fur trade, conflicts with colonial authorities and settlers, and the loss of land.

British and French expeditions explored and later settled along the Atlantic coast from the 16th century, and France ceded nearly all of its colonies in North America in 1763. Early interactions were relatively peaceful, but friendship and peace treaties gave way to the dispossession of Indigenous lands.

Canada was formed in 1867 through Confederation as a federal dominion of four provinces. Settler colonialism peaked in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, when the government funded Indian residential schools administered by Christian churches. These are considered part of a genocide of Indigenous peoples because of their forced assimilation and the large-scale removal of children from their families. A reconciliation commission was formed in 2008. Autonomy from the United Kingdom grew through the Statute of Westminster, 1931, and the Canada Act 1982 severed the remaining legal dependence.

Canada has ten provinces and three territories, with Ottawa as the capital and Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver as the three largest metropolitan areas. It is a parliamentary democracy and a constitutional monarchy, and it is officially bilingual in English and French in the federal jurisdiction. The 2021 census enumerated 36,991,981 people, and the population is estimated to have passed 40,000,000 in 2023. About 80 percent live within 150 kilometres of the border with the contiguous United States. Multiculturalism is official state policy.
canada-east: Canada East covered the southern part of present-day Quebec. In 1851 it had an estimated 890,000 people, only 15 per cent of whom lived in towns. The rest were farmers, habitants as they called themselves, who built their own stone houses and wooden furniture, made their own clothes and grew their own food; the main farm products were potatoes, rye, buckwheat, maple sugar and livestock.

Lumber was the most important natural resource. Hundreds of workers felled trees and floated the logs down the St. Lawrence River on the spring floods to sawmills that cut planks and boards for markets in the United States, and factories made windows, shingles, washboards and door frames. At Confederation, Montreal, with 107,225 people, was the largest city of the British North American colonies.

Lord Durham's report on the causes of the rebellions in Upper and Lower Canada recommended uniting the two colonies, and the Act of Union 1840, passed by the Parliament of the United Kingdom, created the Province of Canada with effect from 1841. Its parliament was elected in a mixture of multi-member and single-member districts. The names Canada East and Canada West came into use while the old names had no constitutional status, but an interpretation act of 25 April 1849 gave Lower Canada and Upper Canada legal meaning again.

As English-speaking Canada West outgrew it in population, the even division of seats made no provision for representation by population, and most in Canada East resisted taking over the Hudson's Bay Company's lands west of Lake Superior, which would have changed the balance of the legislature. Because the St. Lawrence was full of ice for half the year, many supported a railway through Canada East to Halifax as an all-British route for trade and defence. In 1866 Fenian raids south and east of Montreal were repulsed by local militia and British regulars, and as Confederation approached the Francophones feared that their heritage would be overwhelmed.
canadian-american-reciprocity-treaty: When Britain repealed the Corn Laws in 1846, ending imperial preference for colonial produce, the business community of Montreal looked south, and merchants threatened to press for annexation to the United States unless London secured a free trade agreement. The treaty took its other name from its negotiators, James Bruce, 8th Earl of Elgin, and William L. Marcy. In the United States it was backed by manufacturers seeking cheaper raw materials and larger markets, and by free traders and their Democratic Party allies, while protected interests, represented by the Republican Party, opposed it.

The treaty applied to British North America: the Province of Canada, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland. It admitted most Canadian raw materials and farm produce, timber and wheat above all, to the American market free of duty, ending a 21% tariff on natural resources. In return Americans gained fishing rights off the east coast, and each side received some rights of navigation on the other's lakes and rivers. It was in force from 1854 to 1866.

Canadian exports to the United States grew by 33% and American exports by 7%, and trade between the two countries doubled within ten years; Nova Scotia's coal mining gained in particular. In 1968 the economic historians Lawrence H. Officer and Lawrence B. Smith argued that railways, the American Civil War and the poor harvests and Crimean War of 1855 explained most of the growth, and that open trade had replaced smuggling.

The United States ended the treaty in 1866, its critics objecting to the Cayley–Galt Tariff on manufactures and angry at British and colonial help to the Confederacy. Canada's later National Policy of tariffs began in 1879. In 1911 Wilfrid Laurier's Liberals negotiated a new treaty of the same name with President William Howard Taft, but the Conservatives warned of annexation and won that year's election, and Robert Borden's government rejected it. Free trade returned only with the Canada–United States Free Trade Agreement of 1988.
canadian-red-ensign: A Red Ensign bearing a Canadian emblem was used on land and at sea from as early as 1868, soon after Confederation, on an informal basis. Prime Minister Sir John A. Macdonald constantly made use of it, and an 1891 memo of the Governor General, Lord Stanley, noted that the Dominion Government encouraged its use on public buildings. In 1892 an Admiralty warrant authorised it for ships registered in Canada, which the Canada Shipping Act of 1934 confirmed. The original shield bore the arms of the four founding provinces, and flag makers often added wreaths and crowns or enlarged the badge as provinces joined.

The ensign flew over the Parliament Buildings until 1904, when the Union Flag replaced it, and it featured in recruiting and patriotic displays in the First World War. The flag carried by the 5th Canadian Infantry Battalion at the Battle of Vimy Ridge in 1917 survives and is possibly the oldest Canadian flag in existence. It was given to the Imperial War Museum, which lent it to the new Canadian War Museum in Ottawa in 2005 and took it back in 2008.

On 26 April 1922 an order-in-council placed the new shield of the arms of Canada, designed by the College of Arms, on the ensign; its maple leaves were green until 1957. In 1924 the flag was approved for government buildings outside Canada, and on 5 September 1945 Order-in-Council P.C. 5888 named it a distinctive Canadian flag for federal buildings within or outside Canada, so that it once again flew over Parliament.

After the Great Flag Debate the Maple Leaf flag was adopted in 1965, but the ensign kept broad sympathy, and the provincial flags adopted by Ontario in 1965 and Manitoba in 1966 are red ensigns. In 2007 the Public Register of Arms, Flags and Badges of Canada recognised it as a national symbol of Canada. It flies beside the Maple Leaf at war memorials such as the Canadian National Vimy Memorial and is part of the Royal Canadian Legion's colour party. In the 2010s some far-right and white nationalist groups adopted it, which drew protests from the Legion and others.
canal-du-midi: A canal between the Atlantic and the Mediterranean was an old idea. Leaders including Augustus, Nero, Charlemagne, François I, Charles IX and Henry IV are said to have dreamed of it. In 1516 François I brought Leonardo da Vinci to France and commissioned a survey of a route from the Garonne at Toulouse to the Aude at Carcassonne. Such a waterway would spare ships and goods a voyage around the Iberian Peninsula that could take a month and carried the danger of piracy.

Royal authority for the work came in October 1666, when Jean-Baptiste Colbert authorised it by edict after a committee of experts had studied the route for several months. Colbert believed that trade favoured the Dutch rather than the kingdom, and grain prices and wine production had fallen. The edict gave the work to its designer, Pierre-Paul Riquet, and his descendants, with rights of expropriation, a tax-exempt fief and the right to levy tolls.

The canal is about 240 km long. It was first called the Canal Royal en Languedoc and was renamed the Canal du Midi in 1789. It climbs from Toulouse over 52 km to the Seuil de Naurouze, its summit level at 189.43 m, and then descends 188 km to Les Onglous on the Étang de Thau. The central difficulty was bringing water from the Montagne Noire to the summit. Riquet sent François Andreossy and Pierre Roux there to work on the supply, which uses the reservoirs of Lampy, Cammazes and Saint-Ferréol and channels called rigoles.

The first locks, rectangular and built on wooden stilts, collapsed, and Riquet redesigned them with thicker, rounded walls, a form later called Baroque. Construction lasted from 1666 to 1681. Riquet died in October 1680, shortly before completion, and the first inspection began on 2 May 1681. In 1686 Vauban found the canal in poor repair and ordered new work, including the Cammazes tunnel and a strengthening of the Saint-Ferréol reservoir.

At first the canal was used mainly by small sailing barges with lowered masts, hauled by gangs of men. By the middle of the 18th century horses had largely taken over, and steam tugs appeared in 1834. By 1838 273 vessels worked the canal regularly, and mail boats carried passengers. The record year for trade was 1856, with nearly 100,000 passengers.

Railways then took the traffic. In 1858 Napoleon III entrusted the canal for 40 years to the railway company Chemins de fer du Midi, which favoured its own line, and boat traffic declined. Commercial shipping ended around the late 1980s, and the canal is now used mainly by boaters and tourists. It was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1996.
canaletto: Canaletto was born in Venice, the son of the painter Bernardo Canal and Artemisia Barbieri, and takes his name, "little Canal", from his father. He was apprenticed to his father and to his brother, a theatrical scene painter. In 1718 he travelled to Rome, having already worked on sets for operas by Antonio Vivaldi and others, and took inspiration from the Roman view painter Giovanni Paolo Pannini. After returning he began painting topographical views, and studied under Luca Carlevarijs, quickly becoming his equal. In 1725 an agent urged a buyer to prefer him, saying that his work was like Carlevaris's "but you can see the sun shining in it".

Much of his early work was painted from nature, unlike the usual practice of finishing in the studio. He owned a camera obscura, though several experts now think it gave inspiration rather than being used for tracing. Owen Swiny urged him in the late 1720s to paint small views for tourists, and before 1728 he began his association with Joseph Smith, an English merchant living in Venice, later British Consul, who became his principal agent and patron.

The War of the Austrian Succession reduced the number of British visitors, and in 1746 Canaletto moved to London to be nearer his market. He lived in Beak Street in Soho and painted views of London, the new Westminster Bridge, Northumberland House and Warwick Castle. His English work grew repetitive, and the critic George Vertue suggested the painter was an impostor; his reputation never fully recovered in his lifetime. Back in Venice he was elected to the Venetian Academy in 1763.
