He kept painting until his death in 1768, often from old sketches, and was buried at San Lio, the church where he had been baptised. His pupils included his nephew Bernardo Bellotto and Francesco Guardi. Smith's collection went to George III and forms the bulk of the Royal Collection's works by him. His later pictures, with their atmospheric effects and strong local colours, are said to anticipate Impressionism. In July 2025 his Venice, the Return of the Bucintoro on Ascension Day sold at Christie's in London for £27.5 million.
canary-islands: The Canary Islands are an archipelago in the Atlantic Ocean, about 100 kilometres off the northwest coast of Africa. The seven main islands, from largest to smallest by area, are Tenerife, Fuerteventura, Gran Canaria, Lanzarote, La Palma, La Gomera and El Hierro. All are volcanic in origin, and with the Azores, Cape Verde, Madeira and the Savage Isles they form the Macaronesia ecoregion. Historically the chain was called the Fortunate Isles.

The western islands, El Hierro, La Palma and La Gomera, are influenced by the moist Canary Current and carry extensive subtropical laurisilva forest, while Fuerteventura and Lanzarote, nearest to Africa, are effectively desert or semi-desert. Mount Teide on Tenerife is the highest peak in Spain.

Linguistic, genetic and archaeological analyses indicate that indigenous peoples were living on the islands at least 2,000 years ago, possibly 3,000, and shared a common origin with the Amazighs of the nearby North African coast. They may have reached the islands in several small boats, landing first on Lanzarote and Fuerteventura. They came to be known collectively as the Guanches, although that name had belonged only to the indigenous inhabitants of Tenerife.

According to a 2024 study by the University of Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, archaeological evidence shows that the Romans were the first to establish contact, between the 1st century BCE and the 1st century CE. During the Age of Sail the islands were the main stopover for Spanish galleons on the way to the Americas, which sailed that far south to catch the prevailing northeasterly trade winds.

The archipelago is the southernmost autonomous community of Spain, established in 1982. It has two provinces, Santa Cruz de Tenerife and Las Palmas, created by splitting the Province of Canary Islands in 1927, and the cities of Santa Cruz de Tenerife and Las Palmas de Gran Canaria are joint capitals.

The name Islas Canarias probably derives from the Latin Canariae Insulae, meaning Islands of the Dogs, from Pliny the Elder's account of vast multitudes of very large dogs on Canaria. The canary bird takes its name from the islands. San Cristóbal de La Laguna on Tenerife is a World Heritage Site, as is Mount Teide.
canassatego: Little is known of Canassatego's early life, since he appears in British records only in the last eight years of his life. Most modern scholars think he was not one of the fourteen Onondaga hereditary royaner who sat on the Haudenosaunee Grand Council, although one historian holds that he bore the League title of Tadadaho. In the 1730s a faction of Haudenosaunee leaders, working with Pennsylvania's interpreter Conrad Weiser, agreed that the colony would recognise the Haudenosaunee as owners of all Indian lands in Pennsylvania and that they would sell land only to it.

Canassatego probably attended the treaty of 1736 at which Haudenosaunee chiefs sold land along the Susquehanna River traditionally occupied by the Lenape. At the conference of 1742, where the final payment was made, he persuaded Governor Thomas Penn to pay more than the original price, and at Penn's urging he ordered the Lenape off the lands of the Walking Purchase of 1737, berating them as women who had no right to sell land.

At Lancaster in 1744, with King George's War under way, Maryland and Virginia agreed after a speech by him to pay for land in their colonies, although Virginia's deed gave it much more than the Shenandoah Valley the Haudenosaunee believed they had sold. Witham Marshe, a Marylander present, described him as tall and strong, about 60 years old, with a lively manner of speech. He repeated his call for colonial unity at another conference in 1745.

His last treaty conference was at Philadelphia in August 1749, where he complained of settlers on the Susquehanna and agreed to sell the land, again under a document ceding more than had been negotiated. He was reportedly poisoned in September 1750. Contemporary accounts said he was killed for taking bribes to sell communal lands, or by agents of New France; the historian William Starna argued that pro-French Haudenosaunee probably killed him.

His words on union became central to the Iroquois Influence Thesis, the disputed proposal that the Haudenosaunee Confederacy was a model for the United States Constitution. John Shebbeare portrayed him as wise and honest in the novel Lydia: or Filial Piety (1755), and the US Navy named a harbour tug, USS Canasatego, after him.
canberra: Canberra lies near the Brindabella Ranges, part of the Australian Alps, about 150 km inland from Australia's east coast. Its urban area has an elevation of about 580 m, and the highest point near it is Mount Majura at 888 m. The Molonglo River was dammed to form Lake Burley Griffin, and it then flows into the Murrumbidgee. The area was a flood plain before the lake was filled.

The name derives from the Ngunnawal language of a local clan that the first British colonists called the Canberry, Kanberri or Nganbra tribe. Joshua John Moore, the first European landowner in the region, named his grant Canberry in 1823. The form Canberra began to appear around 1857. Suggested meanings include meeting place.

The first peoples of the area include the Ngunnawal and Ngambri. Archaeological evidence suggests human activity there 21,000 years ago. The Canberry or Nganbra clan lived mostly around Sullivan's Creek and had ceremonial grounds at the base of Galambary (Black Mountain), while the Pialligo clan had land around what is now Canberra Airport. The people managed the land with fire, farmed yams and hunted. Galambary was a meeting and business site, mainly for men, and an initiation site.

European settlement began in the first half of the 19th century. The federation of the Australian colonies was achieved on 1 January 1901, and the new capital was founded and formally named Canberra in 1913, as a compromise between Sydney and Melbourne. It is an entirely planned city, based on a design by the American architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, influenced by the garden city movement and aligned with landmarks such as Black Mountain, Mount Ainslie and Capital Hill.

Canberra is the capital of Australia and the largest population centre in the Australian Capital Territory, with an estimated 484,630 people. It is the country's largest inland city. It is the seat of the federal government, with Parliament House, Government House and the High Court, and it hosts all foreign embassies in Australia.

Among its national institutions are the Australian War Memorial, the Australian National University, established in 1946, the National Gallery, the National Museum and the National Library. The Royal Military College Duntroon is also there, and Floriade is the largest flower festival in the Southern Hemisphere.
canche: The Canche, Kwinte in Dutch, is one of the rivers that flow from the plateau of the southern Boulonnais and Picardy into the English Channel, of which the Somme is the largest. Its basin covers 1,274 square kilometres in the south of the Pas-de-Calais. It rises at Gouy-en-Ternois and passes Frévent, Hesdin and Montreuil-sur-Mer before leaving the chalk to reach the coast between Étaples and Le Touquet-Paris-Plage. A gentle gradient gives it a meandering course through an alluvial valley 1 to 2 kilometres wide of marshes, meadows and small woods. Its main tributaries, the Ternoise, Planquette, Créquoise, Course and others, all join from the north.

The fertile valley has been settled since ancient times, and its villages have lived by farming, fishing and the harvesting of reeds. Peat was cut in the marshes of the lower river by the 16th century, both for heating and as a fertiliser, and alders planted on the wet ground bound the soil, gave timber and helped to drain it. In the 18th century fields were enclosed with hedges and ditches, and the authorities encouraged the draining and planting of the peat marshes to feed a growing population.

In the 19th century steam engines replaced windmills in the drainage works, and the valley dried out downstream as far as Hesdin. Late in the 20th century the authorities began to protect the marshes they had earlier helped to destroy. In 1976 the estuary became the first site on the coast of northern France to be saved by a conservation campaign, when local people, associations and scientists stopped a plan from the 1960s for a harbour and marina, offered as compensation for taking water from the Canche at Hesdin to supply Lille.

The river and its valley have formed part of a national nature reserve since 1987. The estuary, with its sandbars and spits, is typical of the region, and its dunes, marshes and valley hold 485 kinds of plants and seventy-five kinds of nesting birds, among them the nightjar, woodlark, common snipe, oystercatcher, merlin and common buzzard.
cancho-roano: Cancho Roano, sometimes written Cancho Ruano, lies three miles from Zalamea de la Serena on the road towards Quintana de la Serena, in a small valley beside the stream Cagancha. It is the best preserved Tartessian site. The main body of the building is square and faces east, and it was surrounded by a deep moat that was kept permanently filled with water.

The site goes back to at least the 6th century BCE, and the dating of the objects found there puts its beginning at about 550 BCE. The building was later expanded and modified. At its end it appears to have been ritually burned and sealed in rammed earth, in a manner similar to Etruscan practice. Its exact purpose is unknown. The altars make its religious character certain, while its defences suggest it may also have been a palace.

Excavations directed by John Maluquer de Motes began in 1978 and continued until 2001, uncovering the building with its moat, its many rooms and its altars. The site was declared a National Monument in 1986 and is open to the public, with an interpretation centre.

Interpretations of the building differ. Its sacred character and many small rooms have suggested to some a temple of sacred prostitution, perhaps dedicated to the Phoenician goddess Astarte, an idea supported by looms found in two of the rooms, which recall the weavers of the goddess Asherah in the Temple of Jerusalem. Similar rites have been seen in the imagery of other Phoenician sites in Hispania, such as Gadir, Castulo and La Quéjola. Another view sees a palace housing a harem whose members took part in the temple's rites.

Richard Freund proposed that Cancho Roano was a memorial city standing for the lost city of Tartessos, which he identified with Atlantis, reading concentric circles on a stele from the site as Plato's Atlantis. Scholars have widely dismissed the theory, and the sign is regarded as a typical warrior's shield of the kind engraved on the Southwestern Stelae of the Iberian Peninsula.
cancor: Cancor was the son of a noble lady, Williswinda. Since her only known husband before she was widowed was named Robert, or Rodbert, it has been proposed that Cancor's father was Robert, Count or Duke in the Hesbaye, who lived in the 8th century; Robert II of Hesbaye may have been his brother or his nephew. Cancor married a noblewoman named Angila, of unknown parentage, probably before 766.

Together with his widowed mother, Cancor founded Lorsch Abbey in 764 as a proprietary church and monastery on their estate of Laurissa. They entrusted its government to Cancor's cousin Chrodegang, Bishop of Metz, who dedicated the church and monastery to Saint Peter and became its first abbot, and the founders later enriched the new abbey with further donations. In 766, shortly before his death, Chrodegang resigned as abbot because of his duties at Metz and sent his brother Gundeland, also a kinsman of Cancor, to Lorsch as his successor.

Cancor died in 771. He and Angila had four children: Heimrich, Count in the Upper Rheingau, who died on 5 May 795 in the Battle of Lüne, a campaign of Charlemagne's Saxon Wars; Embert, Bishop of Worms from 770 to 803; and Rachilt and Euphemia, both nuns at Lorsch.

Through Heimrich, Cancor was the great-grandfather of Poppo I of Grabfeld, progenitor of the Popponids, the early or Franconian House of Babenberg. Several later dynasties descended from them, including the Austrian House of Babenberg, the Wittelsbach, the Henneberg, the Schweinfurt and the Babonids. The recurring name Poppo, also found as Bubo, Pabo and Babo, is likely a variation of Robert, the name of Cancor's father.
candarl-halil-pasha-the-younger: Çandarlı Halil Pasha was the fourth and penultimate member of the Çandarlı family to be grand vizier of the Ottoman Empire. His father, Çandarlı Ibrahim Pasha the Elder, his uncle Çandarlı Ali Pasha and his grandfather Çandarlı Halil Pasha the Elder had held the post, and his own son, Çandarlı Ibrahim Pasha the Younger, would hold it later. The family had grown extremely wealthy from more than a century of influence, possibly more so than the ruling Ottoman house. Halil was appointed in 1439 after the deposition of Nizamüddin Pasha.

Under Murad II, a man more interested in religion and the arts than politics, Halil Pasha enjoyed unlimited trust. Twice Murad retired to Manisa, and Halil Pasha had a castle built in a nearby town for his protection, renaming it Çandarlı after his family; meanwhile Halil held effective control in Edirne with the child Mehmed II as nominal sultan. When Murad abdicated in 1444, Halil urged him to return; Murad marched against the Crusaders and won the Battle of Varna on 14 November. After Murad again left the throne to Mehmed in 1445, Halil organised his return during the Buçuktepe rebellion of 1446. Murad remained sultan until his death in 1451. Halil ensured the immediate transfer of power to Mehmed.

Mehmed, deposed twice because of Halil, resented him. Halil opposed the siege of Constantinople and was suspected of taking bribes from the Byzantines. When Constantine XI sent a message asking for an increase of the annuity of Mehmed's cousin Orhan, a possible pretender, or his release, Halil is recorded as answering that the schemes of the Byzantines would be fruitless.

Constantinople was taken on 29 May 1453. Mehmed imprisoned Halil Pasha on 1 June, and he was executed on 10 July 1453 and buried in İznik in an open tomb without a roof, unlike his ancestors. He was the first Ottoman grand vizier executed by a sultan. The Turkish historian Y. Oztuna held that his execution ended the struggle between the Turkish aristocratic party and the devshirme party, which the latter won. The Çandarlı family became provincial notables based in İznik, although his son later served briefly as grand vizier.
candaules: Candaules, also known as Myrsilos, was a king of the ancient Kingdom of Lydia in the early years of the 7th century BCE. According to Herodotus, he succeeded his father Meles as the 22nd and last king of the Heraclid dynasty. His name was traditionally assumed, from an ambiguous line of the poet Hipponax, to mean hound-choker in Lydian, and J. B. Bury and Russell Meiggs describe it as a Maeonian name with that meaning. More recently it has been suggested that the name or title Kandaules is cognate with the Luwian hantawatt(i), meaning king, and probably has Carian origin. It gave its name to candaulism, a sexual practice which legend attributed to him.

Several accounts tell how the Heraclid dynasty ended and the Mermnad dynasty of Gyges began, mostly in a mythical vein. The earliest is Herodotus's, of the fifth century BCE. He says Candaules thought his wife the most beautiful woman on Earth. He does not name her, though later artists and writers have called her Nyssia. Candaules urged his favourite bodyguard, Gyges, to see her naked, and Gyges, who first refused out of respect for the queen, hid in the bedroom and watched her undress. She saw him leave. Herodotus remarks that among the Lydians, as among most non-Greek peoples, it was thought highly indecent even for a man to be seen naked.

The queen swore revenge. Next day she gave Gyges two choices: kill Candaules and take the throne with her as his wife, or be executed at once by her trusted servants. Gyges hid in the bedroom again and stabbed the sleeping king. Many Lydians at first did not accept him, so to prevent civil war Gyges offered to let the Delphic Oracle confirm or refuse his position, agreeing to restore the throne to the Heraclids if it declared against him. The Oracle supported him, adding that the Heraclids would have their revenge in the fifth generation of the Mermnadae. In Plato's Republic a different story has Gyges use a magical ring of invisibility to usurp the throne.

Bury and Meiggs reject Herodotus's tale and hold that the family of Candaules, though descended from Heracles himself, had become degenerate, so that Gyges assassinated him and began a new era under his own Mermnad clan. Herodotus's version appears in Michael Ondaatje's 1992 novel The English Patient, and Alexander von Zemlinsky's opera Der König Kandaules is based on André Gide's play Le roi Candaule.
candide: Voltaire was already a well-established author when he wrote Candide, which became a model for the contes philosophiques of the 18th and early 19th centuries, a genre that included his earlier Zadig and Micromegas. Several events lie behind it: the publication of Leibniz's Monadology, the Seven Years' War and the Lisbon earthquake of 1755, which posed a problem for the optimism founded on the theodicy of Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, which insisted on God's benevolence in spite of such disasters.

It is not known exactly when Voltaire wrote it. Scholars estimate that it was mainly composed in late 1758 and begun as early as 1757, in part at Les Délices near Geneva. A popular legend that he wrote it in three days probably rests on a misreading of an 1885 book. He did not openly admit his authorship until 1768, and signed it until then as Doctor Ralph.

The story has thirty short chapters. Candide, the illegitimate nephew of a baron in Westphalia, lives in the baron's castle, where the tutor Pangloss teaches that all is for the best in the best of all possible worlds. Expelled for his love of the baron's daughter Cunégonde, he is swept through war, earthquake and cruelty, first in Europe, then in the Americas, where he reaches El Dorado, and finally back to Europe and the Ottoman Empire. Many of the events are based on real happenings.

Its method is to set great tragedy against comedy, told in a matter-of-fact tone. At Portsmouth Candide sees an admiral, thought to stand for John Byng, shot for failing to engage a French fleet, merely pour encourager les autres, a phrase Voltaire is credited with originating. The book ends with Candide dismissing optimism but offering no system in its place, only the practical precept that we must cultivate our garden, and critics still dispute what that means.

Immediately after publication the work and its author were denounced by secular and religious authorities because it openly derides government and church, and it was widely banned on grounds of blasphemy and sedition. A sequel by other hands appeared in 1760. Candide is the most widely read of Voltaire's works and is listed in Harold Bloom's The Western Canon. Its parody and picaresque methods influenced later black humorists such as Joseph Heller, Thomas Pynchon and Kurt Vonnegut.
candlemas: The feast rests on Luke 2:22–40. Under the rules of Leviticus 12 a woman was to be purified 33 days after a boy's circumcision by presenting a lamb as a burnt offering and a young pigeon or dove as a sin offering. Egeria recorded the feast in Jerusalem in the 380s: a procession to the Anastasis, sermons on the passage in which Simeon and Anna saw the child, and the sacrament, with great joy, as at Easter. In the West, Christmas was kept on 25 December from at least 354, and forty days from 25 December inclusive is 2 February. In the East the emperor Justinian established the Hypapante.

Pope Gelasius I helped spread the feast but did not invent it, and it appears to have become important around the Plague of Justinian in 541. The Jerusalem feast fell on 14 February because Jerusalem placed Christmas on 6 January; it became the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary on 2 February as it spread to Rome and elsewhere from the mid-7th century.

Candlemas is the last feast of the Christmas cycle, and in some countries Christians take down their Christmas decorations only after it. In France, Belgium and Swiss Romandy it is also the day of crêpes, a custom tradition ascribes to Gelasius I, who had pancakes given to pilgrims in Rome. In Germany the day marked payment deadlines and the start of the farmer's year, and ended the servant's year, when servants were paid the rest of their wages and might change employer.

In Luxembourg children walk the streets with lanterns, singing at each house for sweets or small change. In Hungary they dress as bears, light candles and eat honey, in keeping with the folklore that bears go back to sleep if they see their shadows. In Mexico whoever finds the figure of the Christ child in the Epiphany cake dresses the niño dios on Candlemas and prepares tamales for a family meal.

The Virgin of Candelaria, patron of the Canary Islands, takes her name from the feast. According to tradition, around 1392 or 1400 two Guanche shepherds on Tenerife found an image of the Virgin on the shore, and in 1497 the conqueror Alonso Fernández de Lugo held the first Candlemas festival dedicated especially to her. The German belief that a hedgehog would cast a shadow if the sun appeared on Candlemas was the origin of Groundhog Day, since many early Pennsylvania settlers were German.
candomble: Enslaved Africans first reached Brazil in the 1530s. Those of the 16th century came largely from the Guinea coast, those of the 17th mostly from Angola and Congo, and between 1775 and 1850 most were Yoruba and Dahomean from the Gulf of Benin. Around four million Africans were taken to Brazil, more than to any other part of the Americas, and they were concentrated in Bahia. Candomblé arose among these communities in the 19th century, blending the religions of the Yoruba, Fon and Bantu with the Roman Catholicism of the Portuguese colonists.

The earliest terreiros, or houses of worship, appeared in Bahia in the early 19th century. According to what the scholar Stefania Capone calls the founding myth, the first was the Ilê Axé Iyá Nassô Oká, or Casa Branca, founded in Salvador in 1830, from which the Nagô tradition descends.

Candomblé has no central authority, and each terreiro is independent, run by a priestess, mãe de santo, or a priest, pai de santo. Its believers hold that a distant creator, Olorun or Olodumare, stands above spirits called orixás, inkice or vodun, depending on the tradition, which are linked with Catholic saints. Each person has a tutelary orixá residing in the head. The main traditions, called nations, are the Ketu or Nagô, the Jeje and the Angola, which draw on Yoruba, Ewe and Bantu languages respectively.

Practice centres on drumming, singing and dancing so that an orixá possesses a member, on offerings including food and sacrificed animals, and on divination with cowrie shells. A force called axé, the vital energy of the universe, is held to be concentrated in objects such as leaves, roots and blood. Initiation is called making the head.

Brazil's constitution of 1891 enshrined freedom of religion, but the Roman Catholic establishment kept Candomblé on the margins, often linking it to crime. In the 1930s it became more public under President Getúlio Vargas, whose Law Decree 1202 recognised the legitimacy of terreiros and whose Penal Code of 1940 protected them. In the 1920s it also influenced the formation of Umbanda.

One census report found about 1.3 per cent of Brazilians identifying as followers, and a 1997 count recorded 1,144 terreiros in Salvador. On 2 February, Iemanjá's Day, hundreds of thousands gather on the beach and cast offerings to her into the sea. Followers have faced intolerance and attacks, and some evangelical and Pentecostal groups target them in what they call spiritual war.
cangas-de-onis: Cangas de Onís is a municipality in the eastern part of the province and autonomous community of Asturias, in the north-west of Spain. Its Asturian name, Cangues d'Onís, is explained as the valleys of Onís. More than seventy square kilometres of the municipality form part of the Parque nacional de los Picos de Europa. Because of its range of heights it has many kinds of plants, among them mountain shrubs, heather, oak and ash, surrounded by grassland. The municipality is divided into eleven parishes, and the capital is the parish of Cangas de Onís, with 4,326 inhabitants according to the figures of 2005.

Within the national park lies the village of Covadonga, where the battle of Covadonga, about 722, was the first major victory of a Christian military force in Iberia after the Islamic conquest and is taken to mark the starting point of the Reconquista. Cangas de Onís is known as the first capital of the Kingdom of Asturias and is the site of the first church built in Iberia after the conquest, Santa Cruz de Cangas de Onís of 737, which was built on an ancient dolmen.

A parish named Cangas de Onís is attested for the 14th century, and the stone bridge over the Sella River was built in the 14th or 15th century. The town was represented in the Junta General of the principality of Asturias in 1504. Covadonga began to develop as a pilgrimage site in the 16th century, which attracted commerce, and the settlement of Cangas de Onís grew rapidly in the middle of the 19th century. It was bombarded several times in the Spanish Civil War, and it was the seat of the Regional Council in the pre-autonomous regime of 1978 to 1981, before the Statute of Autonomy of the Principality of Asturias came into force on 31 January 1982.

The main economic activities of the region are agriculture, cattle rearing and rural tourism, and the nearby Covadonga Sanctuary and its surrounding lakes are among the main tourist destinations in Asturias, within the national park.
cangrande-i-della-scala: Christened Can Francesco, he was born in Verona on 9 March 1291, the third son of Alberto I della Scala, ruler of Verona, and Verde da Salizzole. His early strength and wit earned him the name Cangrande, big dog, later echoed in the dog's head crest of the Scaliger lords. He first fought in the campaigns of his brother Alboino I della Scala against Azzo VIII of Este, and in 1308 began to share rule with him and married Giovanna, daughter of Conrad of Antioch; they had no heirs.

Emperor Henry VII made the brothers Imperial Vicars of Verona, and in 1311 Cangrande commanded the Italian levies at the siege of Brescia. He became sole ruler on Alboino's death on 29 November 1311 and took Vicenza in February 1312, opening a long war with Padua. On 17 September 1314 he rode from Verona to Vicenza in three hours and routed a Paduan army in its suburbs, and the peace of October 1314 recognised his hold on the city.

In December 1317 he took Monselice and stormed Este, and in February 1318 Padua ceded both, with Castelbaldo and Montagnana. A Ghibelline convention at Soncino named him Captain and Rector of the Imperial Party of Lombardy, and he ignored the excommunication of Pope John XXII. On 25 August 1320 Henry III of Gorizia routed his army at Bassanello. Cangrande then won Feltre, Serravalle and Belluno by political means, and on 10 September 1328 he entered Padua as its ruler.

Cangrande made his state entry into Treviso on 18 July 1329 but was already ill, according to contemporary accounts after drinking from a polluted spring, and died on 22 July. Tests on his mummified body in 2004 found lethal amounts of digitalis, which points towards poisoning; his successor Mastino II hanged one of his physicians. His tomb over the entrance of Santa Maria Antiqua in Verona was topped by an equestrian statue, now in the Museum of Castelvecchio.

Of his conquests only Vicenza outlasted Mastino II's reign, but his revision of Verona's statutes lasted to the end of the Scaliger period. Dante Alighieri was his guest at Verona, generally dated between 1312 and 1318, and praised him in Canto XVII of the Paradiso, and Giovanni Boccaccio portrayed him as a wise ruler in the Decameron.
canh-thinh: Nguyễn Quang Toản was the eldest son of Nguyễn Huệ, Emperor Quang Trung; according to the Đại Nam chính biên liệt truyện his mother was the Empress Consort Phạm Thị Liên. He was named Crown Prince after his father's coronation, and in 1790 China granted him the title An Nam quốc vương thế tử, Crown Prince of Annam, recognising his right to succeed. On his deathbed in 1792 Quang Trung called him a clever boy but too young.

Crowned at nine, he made his stepmother Bùi Thị Nhạn empress dowager, and the Grand Preceptor Bùi Đắc Tuyên became the real ruler, angering many ministers and generals. In 1793 he helped his uncle Nguyễn Nhạc against the Nguyễn lord and then annexed his territory. In a coup the generals Vũ Văn Dũng, Phạm Công Hưng and Nguyễn Văn Huấn surrounded Tuyên's house while the emperor was inside and forced him to give Tuyên up; Tuyên was executed with Bùi Đắc Trụ and Ngô Văn Sở. Ruling directly, the young emperor could not end the quarrels among his commanders, and further purges in 1798 left them fearing for their lives.

Nguyễn Ánh took Quy Nhơn in 1799 and, while Võ Tánh held the main Tây Sơn army there, marched on the capital. Revolts broke out in Thanh Hóa and Tonkin, and Vientiane and Muang Phuan attacked Nghệ An. The emperor ignored Nguyễn Thiếp's advice to move the capital to Phượng Hoàng trung đô. In 1801 his navy and its hired Chinese pirates were almost destroyed at the Nộn estuary, and he fled to Thăng Long, taking the era name Bảo Hưng. The Jiaqing Emperor of Qing China refused him aid after captured pirates confessed to Tây Sơn support.

In 1802 he led around 30,000 men against Nguyễn Ánh at the Linh River and was beaten. After Thăng Long fell he fled across the Nhị River and was captured by villagers at Phượng Nhãn; his brother Nguyễn Quang Thùy and Bùi Thị Nhạn took their own lives. He was taken to Phú Xuân, and according to the Đại Nam thực lục he and three brothers were executed by slow slicing and their bodies torn apart by five elephants.
canice: Much of what is known of Cainnech comes from tradition and legend, though he is mentioned by Adomnán, abbot of Iona, in his Life of Columba. Cainnech moccu Dalánn was born at Glengiven, near Dungiven in Ulster. His father, Lughadh Leithdhearg, was a bard of the Corco Dalann who became tutor to the son of the chief of Cianachta, and his mother, Maul or Mella, was honoured for her holiness by a church beside Kilkenny.

In 543 he became a pupil of Finnian at Clonard, one of the twelve students later known as the Twelve Apostles of Ireland, and there became a friend of Columba. He then studied under Mobhí Clárainech at Glasnevin, and when plague scattered that community he went to Cadoc's monastery of Llancarfan in Wales, where he was ordained priest in 545. After a journey to Rome he returned to Glengiven in 550 and converted his foster brother, Geal Breagach, who helped him found Drumachose near Limavady.

In 565 Cainnech joined Columba in Scotland, where he is known as Kenneth. Adomnán tells that Columba foresaw his coming and that God gave him a calm crossing to Iona on a stormy day. He is said to have built a church at the place now called Saint Andrews, cells on the islands of Ibdon and Eninis, an oratory on Loch Laggan and a monastery in Fife on the Eden.

Back in Ireland he won the favour of Colmann son of Feradach, king of Osraige, who granted him land including Aghaboe, the field of the ox, which became his chief monastery. Tradition holds that in 597 he led a Christian force against the last stronghold of druidic rule at Kilkenny and founded a monastery near the present St. Canice's Cathedral.

In old age he retired to an island in Loch Cree and wrote a commentary on the four Gospels, known as the Glas-Chainnigh or Chain of Cainnech, which was long kept in his church. He was buried at Aghaboe. The see of Ossory stood there until the twelfth century, when it moved to Kilkenny, and in 1346 Diarmaid Mac Giollaphádraig burned Aghaboe and destroyed his shrine and relics. His feast is kept on 11 October, and he is also a patron saint of the shipwrecked.
canillo: Canillo is the name of one of the seven parishes of Andorra and of its main town. It borders France to the north and east and is the largest parish of Andorra, at 121 square kilometres. Its localities include Soldeu, El Tarter, Incles, Prats and Meritxell, and the Estany de Juclà in the Incles valley is the largest lake in Andorra. Much of the parish is still characterised by active farms.

The name of the parish is pre-Roman in origin. It is first documented in the 9th century, in the deed of consecration of the cathedral of La Seu d'Urgell, as Kanillave, and appears as Canilau in 1176. At Prats stands the sanctuary of Roc de les Bruixes, a set of rock engravings dating from the Bronze Age to the early Middle Ages. Remains of the late 7th and 8th centuries show early Christianity in Andorra. The church of Sant Joan de Caselles, Romanesque and from the end of the 11th century, holds a 12th-century Romanesque Majesty on a mural painting.

Canillo is also the site of the sanctuary of Our Lady of Meritxell. According to legend a shepherd found an image of the Virgin under flowering roses, and when he took it home it returned three times to the same place, so a chapel was built there. In 1873 she was declared patron saint of the country, and 8 September 1921 was declared the national holiday. The Romanesque sanctuary burned down in 1972, and the architect Ricardo Bofill Levi designed the new one, inaugurated in 1976.

The parish had 4,826 inhabitants in 2011 and is a tourist destination, notably for the ski resort of Soldeu-El Tarter, though farming continues. The sanctuary of Meritxell was declared a minor basilica in 2014.
cankili-ii: Cankili II, in Tamil Caṅkili Kumāraṉ, was a nephew of King Ethirimana Cinkam of Jaffna. When the king died in 1617 there were three claimants to the throne: Cankili, the king's brother Arasakesari and a powerful chieftain, Periye Pillai Arachchi. The late king's young son was proclaimed king with Arasakesari as regent, but Cankili killed the regent, the other claimants and further princes of royal blood in a palace massacre and took the throne himself.

The Portuguese in Colombo refused to recognise his regency, and Cankili refused to pay them tribute. The massacre stirred unrest in the kingdom. In August and September 1618 Migapulle Arachchi, son of Periye Pillai Arachchi, drove Cankili to Kayts with Portuguese help. Cankili turned to Raghunatha Nayak, ruler of the Thanjavur Nayak kingdom, who sent 5,000 men under Khem Nayak, also called Varunakulattan, to put down the rising.

By June 1619 the Portuguese had sent two expeditions. Khem Nayak's troops drove back the naval force, but a land army of 5,000 under Filipe de Oliveira defeated Cankili. The Portuguese beheaded his remaining soldiers without trial.

Cankili was taken to Goa, tried by a High Court for treason and sentenced to be beheaded. In prison he was visited by friars of the convent of St. Francis and asked to become a Christian; he was baptised as Dom Filipe and his queen as Dona Margarida of Austria, with Archbishop Dom Frey Cristvao de Lisboa as godfather. Father Fernao de Queyroz described his execution on a platform hung in mourning in the courtyard of the Custom house, after which he was buried in the friars' chapter-hall in the habit of St. Francis.

The surviving royal family were taken to Goa and asked to enter holy orders, and most did, so that no further claimants to Jaffna appeared. With him ended the Aryacakravarti line, which had ruled the kingdom for over 300 years.
cankiri: Çankırı lies about 140 kilometres north-east of Ankara, some 800 metres above sea level. Its ancient name Gangra seems to mean a goat in Paphlagonian. The earlier town stood on the hill behind the modern city, where the ruins of a late fortress remain, while the Roman city occupied the site of the present one.

Gangra seems once to have been the capital of Paphlagonia, since Strabo says that Deiotarus Philadelphus, the last king of Paphlagonia, lived there, though he also calls it only a small town and a garrison. It was absorbed into the Roman province of Galatia on the king's death in 6 or 5 BCE. It was later named Germanicopolis, after Germanicus or possibly the emperor Claudius. In Christian times it was the metropolitan see of Paphlagonia, and its bishop Hypatios, venerated as a saint in the Orthodox tradition, was killed by Arians on his return from the Council of Nicaea in 325.

In the 4th century Gangra was the scene of an important synod, whose date is disputed. Twenty-one bishops met to act against Eustathius of Sebaste and his followers, who disowned marriage and denounced riches. The synod issued twenty canons, declared ecumenical by the Council of Chalcedon in 451, and said it condemned not virginity but the dishonouring of marriage, and not poverty but disparagement of honest wealth. In 1400 and 1401 the patriarch Matthew I appointed George Kontophe metropolitan of Gangra, at the request of its people, who were threatened by the Turkomans.

Çankırı is the seat of Çankırı Province and of Çankırı District, with about 90 thousand inhabitants. Wheat, maize, beans and apples are grown in the surrounding fields, and Çankırı Karatekin University was founded there in 2007.
cannes: Cannes is a resort city on the French Riviera, in the Alpes-Maritimes department of Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur. Le Suquet, the old town on its hill, overlooks the Promenade de la Croisette, the waterfront avenue with palm trees, beaches and luxury hotels. Off the coast lie the Lérins Islands, and the history of Cannes is closely tied to theirs. Cistercian monks are the only inhabitants of the smaller Île Saint-Honorat, where monks have lived since 410 CE. On the Île Sainte-Marguerite the Man in the Iron Mask was held; his identity has never been proven.

By the 2nd century BCE the Ligurian Oxybii had established a settlement known as Aegitna. In 154 BCE it was the scene of a short conflict between the Oxybii and the troops of Quintus Opimius. By the 10th century the town was known as Canua, a name that may derive from the word for a reed. An attack in 891 by the Saracens, who stayed until the end of the 10th century, devastated the country, and the insecurity of the islands forced the monks to settle on the mainland at the Suquet. A castle was built in 1035, and around 1530 Cannes became independent of the monks who had controlled it for hundreds of years.

Henry Brougham, 1st Baron Brougham and Vaux, bought land at the Croix des Gardes around 1838, when the place was little more than a fishing village, and built the Villa Eleonore-Louise. His improvements attracted English aristocrats, who built winter residences. In the late 1860s casinos, villas, hotels, roads and a railway followed, cutting the journey from Paris to 23 hours. After the First World War winter tourism gave way to summer tourism, and the city council proposed an international film festival shortly after the Second World War.

The Cannes Film Festival, founded in 1946, is held annually, usually in May, at the Palais des Festivals et des Congrès. The city also hosts the Cannes Lions festival of creativity, Midem and the trade markets MIPIM and MIPCOM. In 2021 it was designated a City of Film by the UNESCO Creative Cities Network. Its economy rests on tourism, trade fairs and aviation, and the technopolis of Sophia Antipolis lies in the hills beyond it.
canning: The Dutch are noted as the first to tin food: their navy is reported to have carried cleaned and brine-cooked salmon in tin-plated iron boxes as early as 1772. Shortly before the Napoleonic Wars the French government offered a cash award of 12,000 francs for a cheap and effective way of preserving military rations for the Grande Armée.

In 1809 Nicolas Appert, a confectioner and brewer, observed that food cooked inside a jar did not spoil unless the seals leaked, and developed a method of sealing food in glass jars. Count Montelivert, the minister of the interior, awarded him the prize in 1810. The reason the food kept was unknown, since it would be about 50 years before Louis Pasteur demonstrated the role of microbes in spoilage. The Grande Armée tried issuing canned food, but the process was too slow for the wars to benefit.

The tin can process was allegedly developed by the Frenchman Philippe de Girard, who used the London merchant Peter Durand as his agent to patent the idea in 1810. Durand sold the patent in 1811 to Bryan Donkin and John Hall, and Donkin developed the packaging of food in sealed airtight cans of tinned wrought iron. Each large can was made by hand and could take up to six hours to cook, so the food was too dear for ordinary people. By 1817 Donkin had sold £3000 of canned meat in six months, chiefly to the British Army and Royal Navy.

Arctic expeditions carried canned food, among them William Edward Parry's in 1824. Robert Ayars set up the first American canning factory in New York City in 1812. The Crimean War, the American Civil War and the Franco-Prussian War introduced working-class men to canned food, and companies such as Underwood, Nestlé and Heinz later sold it to urban households. By the 1860s smaller machine-made steel cans were possible and cooking times had fallen from about six hours to thirty minutes.

In the mid-19th century canned food was a status symbol among middle-class European households. Early cans were sealed with poisonous lead solder. Max Ams invented the double seam in 1888, which made an airtight seal without solder and sped up manufacture. Can openers did not appear for another thirty years, and soldiers at first opened cans with bayonets or rocks.

In the First World War armies needed vast quantities of cheap food, and British soldiers lived largely on canned pork and beans, bully beef and Maconochie's stew. After complaints about quality, the French Army issued canned dishes such as coq au vin from 1917. Peter Durand's cans largely replaced fragile glass jars in commercial canneries, though glass remains common in home canning.
cannon: The word cannon derives from the Old Italian cannone, meaning large tube, from the Latin canna and the Greek kanna, reed. It has referred to a gun since 1326 in Italy and 1418 in England. The earliest known depiction of cannons may appear in Song dynasty China as early as the 12th century, but solid evidence does not appear until the 13th century. The cannon was probably a parallel development or evolution of the fire lance, a short-range weapon combining a gunpowder-filled tube and a polearm, whose paper and bamboo barrels were eventually replaced by metal.

Elsewhere the dates are less settled. There is no clear consensus on when the cannon first appeared in the Islamic world, with dates ranging from 1260 to the mid-14th century. Documentary evidence of cannons in Russia does not appear until 1382, and Ivan III established the first Russian cannon foundry in Moscow in 1475. Cannons reached the Javanese Majapahit Empire when a Mongol-Chinese army under Ike Mese invaded Java in 1293.

A cannon has the form of a truncated cone with an internal cylindrical bore that holds the charge and the projectile. The thickest and strongest part lies near the charge, which is ignited through a thin tube called the vent. The main body is divided into the chase, the reinforce and the cascabel, and a cannon's calibre is determined by the diameter of its bore. By the 16th century cannons were made in great variety, and the general rule was that the longer the barrel, the longer the range.

Cannons were used primarily as anti-infantry weapons until around 1374, when large cannons were recorded breaching walls for the first time in Europe. In 1464 the Ottoman Empire cast the Great Turkish Bombard, which weighed 16,000 kilograms. Larger guns forced engineers to build stronger castle walls, and in India the fort of Raicher had gun ports built into its walls for defensive cannons. Field artillery became more important after the introduction of the limber, which greatly improved mobility.

In the 1770s a cannon was manned by two gunners, six soldiers and four officers of artillery. The bore was cleaned with a wet sponge, powder was added, then wadding and the ball, which was rammed down; at 45 degrees the ball had its utmost range. Decoys also had a use: the Quaker gun, a painted log, was used by Colonel William Washington's Continental Army in 1780, when about 100 Loyalists surrendered rather than face bombardment.
canossa-castle: The castle stands on the summit of a rocky hill at Canossa, in the province of Reggio Emilia in northern Italy. It was built around 940 by Adalbert Atto, son of Sigifredo of Lucca, a Lombard nobleman. Besides his residence it held a convent of 12 Benedictine monks and the church of Sant'Apollonio, all protected by a triple line of walls, with the barracks and the servants' houses between the outer two.

In the Middle Ages it was one of the strongest castles in Italy. In 950 Adelaide of Italy, the widow of King Lothair II, took refuge there, and Berengar II of Ivrea besieged it for three years without success. Its owner at the time of the meeting of 1077, Matilda of Tuscany, was on friendly terms with Gregory VII and arranged for her lands to pass to the Church after her death in 1115, though her heirs refused to accept it.

Troops of Reggio destroyed the castle and its church in 1255. It returned to the Canossa family, was again held by Reggio from 1321 until 1402, when Simone, Guido and Alberto Canossa regained it, and in 1409 they ceded it to the House of Este, which kept it, apart from a short spell under Ottavio Farnese, Duke of Parma, in 1557, until 1796.

In 1502 Ercole I d'Este named the poet Ludovico Ariosto castellan, and he lived there for six months. It was granted as a fief to the Counts Rondinelli in 1593 and entrusted to the Valentini in 1642, who were driven out in 1796 by local people joining the Republic of Reggio.

After being returned to the Valentini, the castle was bought by the Italian state in 1878 and declared a national monument. It remains best known as the scene of the Road to Canossa, the meeting of Emperor Henry IV and Pope Gregory VII during the Investiture Controversy in 1077.
cantabria: Cantabria is bordered on the east by the Basque Country, on the south by Castile and León, on the west by Asturias and on the north by the Cantabrian Sea, part of the Bay of Biscay. It belongs to Green Spain, the strip of land between the Bay of Biscay and the Cantabrian Mountains, named for its lush vegetation, which results from a wet, temperate oceanic climate. The region has a coastal strip of low, wide valleys, meeting the ocean in a line of cliffs, and mountains to the south. Its rivers are short and rapid and flow at right angles to the coast, except for the Ebro.

Cantabria has archaeological sites from the Upper Paleolithic, and the first signs of human occupation date from the Lower Paleolithic. The cave of Altamira, with paintings from about 37,000 BCE, was declared a World Heritage Site by UNESCO along with nine other Cantabrian caves. The region corresponds to the territory of the Cantabri in the second half of the 1st millennium BCE. The first written reference to the name appears around 195 BCE, when Cato the Elder wrote in his Origines that the Ebro rises in the land of the Cantabri. The origin of the name is uncertain.

After the Roman Empire collapsed, Cantabria regained its independence from the Visigoths. In 574 King Liuvigild captured the south of the country, including the city of Amaya, and established there a Visigothic province, the Duchy of Cantabria, as a frontier zone against the Cantabri and the Vascones. In 714 a mixed Arab and Berber army invaded the upper valleys of the Ebro and captured Amaya, forcing the Cantabrians back to their traditional frontiers, where they joined forces with the Kingdom of Asturias.

The modern province was constituted on 28 July 1778 at Puente San Miguel, Reocín. During the War of Independence of 1808 to 1814 Bishop Rafael Tomás Menéndez de Luarca promoted himself as Regent of Cantabria and set up the Cantabrian Armaments in Santander to detain French troops at the mountain passes. In 1936 the Republican Federal Party drafted an autonomy statute for a Cantabrian-Castilian Federal State, which the Civil War prevented from passing.

Cantabria is an autonomous community and province of northern Spain with Santander as its capital. Its Statute of Autonomy, approved on 30 December 1981, gave it its own institutions of self-government, and it is called a historic community in the statute. Spanish is the official language, and remnants of the Cantabrian language, a dialect of the Astur-Leonese continuum, survive in the west and in the Pas and Soba valleys. The traditional sport is bolos, or skittles.
cantabrian-wars: The wars closed a Roman conquest of Hispania that had lasted two centuries, in what are now Cantabria, Asturias and León. The Cantabri, Astures and Gallaeci, the last independent Celtic peoples of the peninsula, were known to Rome long before: Cantabrians had served as mercenaries in Hannibal's army, helped break the Roman siege of Numantia and, by Julius Caesar's account, fought at Ilerda in 49 BCE, while Astures served Hasdrubal Barca at the Metaurus in 207 BCE. Roman historians justified the campaigns as revenge for raids on the Meseta, though Asturian gold and Cantabrian iron were probably also an aim.

Statilius Taurus campaigned against the Cantabri, Astures and Vaccaei in 29 BCE, and Calvisius Sabinus and Sextus Apuleius won triumphs in the next two years, but the northern peoples stayed free. Augustus came to Segisama in 26 BCE to direct the war himself, one of only two campaigns he led against barbarians, and withdrew to Tarragona a year later, presumably through illness. Eight legions and auxiliaries, about 50,000 soldiers, were committed, and a fleet from Gallia Aquitania closed the coast, while the Cantabri answered with ambushes and quick retreats in the mountains.

In spring 25 BCE the Astures gathered by the Astura River to attack three Roman winter camps, but the Brigaecini warned Augustus, and the general Publius Carisius drove the Astur forces into the hillfort of Lancia. They then held out on Mons Medullius, which the legions ringed with a fifteen-mile ditch; according to Orosius the defenders killed themselves with their weapons and yew poison rather than surrender.

The major fighting ended in 19 BCE, with smaller rebellions until 16 BCE, and the Romans unusually took no prisoners; Strabo wrote that the captives sang hymns of victory on the cross. Two legions, X Gemina and IV Macedonica, stayed in the region for seventy more years. The Roman army took from the Cantabri the cavalry tactics called the circulus cantabricus and the cantabricus impetus, and a standard, the Cantabrian lábaro, that it still carried three centuries later.
cantar-de-mio-cid: The poem is anonymous and survives in a 14th-century codex in the Spanish National Library in Madrid, which lacks its first page and two others in the middle. A colophon names Per Abbad, in English Abbot Peter, and puts the date 1207 after his name. Current thinking is that this claim was simply copied with the text of an earlier manuscript now lost. Ramón Menéndez Pidal counted the work among the poems passed down and varied by minstrels, while others believe a single learned author wrote it. Date and authorship remain open to debate.

The original title is unknown, and the present one was proposed by Menéndez Pidal. Cid comes from the Arabic sidi or sayyid, a title like Sir. The poem has been translated into English many times since 1879, among others by John Ormsby, W. S. Merwin and Burton Raffel.

Since 1913 the poem, of more than 3,700 verses, has been divided into three parts. In the first, enemies accuse Rodrigo Díaz of keeping tribute owed to King Alfonso VI, who exiles him from Castile and León. He leaves his wife, Doña Ximena, and his daughters, Doña Elvira and Doña Sol, at the monastery of Cardeña and grows rich from raids on Moorish territory. In the second he takes Valencia and defeats the Almoravid king Chufa ibn Tashfin, and the king pardons him and allows his daughters to marry the infantes of Carrión.

In the third part the infantes show cowardice, fleeing a lion in the court and a campaign against the Moors. In revenge they beat their wives and leave them tied to trees at Corpes. The Cid asks the court of Toledo for justice, his men defeat the infantes in a duel, and his daughters marry the heirs of Navarre and Aragon. The tone is realist, with no magic: the archangel Gabriel appears only in a dream.

The poem is the oldest preserved Castilian epic and is considered a national epic of Spain. It departs from history: it does not mention the Cid's son, and his daughters were not called Elvira and Sol. It echoes the plot devices of the Song of Roland.
cantarell-field: Cantarell lies 80 kilometres (50 mi) offshore in the Bay of Campeche. The complex comprises four major fields, Akal (by far the largest), Nohoch, Chac and Kutz, with a fifth block, Sihil, beneath Akal, where light oil was discovered in 1998 in Jurassic strata. The main reservoirs are carbonate breccia of Late Cretaceous age, rubble from the asteroid impact that created the Chicxulub crater. After the impact the carbonate platform collapsed, leaving coarse breccias overlain by finer ones from the tsunamis that followed, sealed by a shaly layer rich in ejecta. Folding from the early Miocene to the Pliocene formed the trap into which the oil migrated.

The fisherman Rudesindo Cantarell Jimenez noticed oil stains in 1972, and the field was discovered in 1976. By 1981 it was producing 1.16 million barrels per day, falling to 1 million in 1995. In 2000 a nitrogen injection project began, with the largest nitrogen plant in the world installed onshore at Atasta, Campeche, and output rose to 1.6 million barrels a day, then 1.9 million in 2002 and finally 2.1 million. The nitrogen, however, migrated into the gas and lowered its heating value. In cumulative production Cantarell became the largest oil field in Mexico.

The decline was fast. On 12 August 2004 Luis Ramírez Corzo, head of exploration and production at PEMEX, announced that output was forecast to fall by 14% a year from 2006; it fell 13.1% in 2006 and by January 2009 stood at 772,000 barrels a day, pulling Mexico's total oil production down 9.2%. By September 2009 it had reached 500,000 barrels a day, one of the most dramatic declines seen in the oil industry, and that year the Ku-Maloob-Zaap complex replaced it as Mexico's most productive field. The shortfall hurt the government's budget and the country's sovereign credit rating.

Production kept falling, to 408,000 barrels a day in April 2012 and 340,000 in June 2014. PEMEX planned to spend 6 billion US dollars until 2017 to hold output at around 325,000 barrels a day, but it had fallen to 159,300 barrels a day by 2019 and to 158,300 in 2022.
cantares-mexicanos: The manuscript is kept in the National Library of Mexico in Mexico City. Its songs are made up of short stanzas of about thirty words on average, written as hanging paragraphs, of which there are about 1,700 in all. Many songs have eight stanzas and most have more; the longest has 114. The collection is described in the census of prose manuscripts in the native tradition in the Handbook of Middle American Indians.

The songs themselves and the ethnography of Sahagún and other observers of the time show that they were performed to drums: the upright skin drum, huehuetl, and the horizontal log drum, teponaztli, each able to sound two tones an interval such as a fifth or a major third apart. Gongs, horns and other instruments could join them, and a full performance might include costumed dancing, often with mimicry.

The Mexican scholar Ángel María Garibay Kintana published a Spanish edition and translation of much of the manuscript in the second and third volumes of his Poesía náhuatl in 1965 and 1968. The whole collection was first rendered in Spanish in the two-volume translation edited by Miguel León-Portilla and published by the National Autonomous University of Mexico.

In 1985 John Bierhorst published a complete paleographic transcription with an English translation, Cantares Mexicanos: Songs of the Aztecs, together with a dictionary and concordance. Scholars valued his transcription for its accuracy, but criticised his translations as misleading and shaped by his view that the Cantares are ghost songs, part of a colonial revitalisation movement like the ghost dances of the Plains Indians. Garibay and León-Portilla, by contrast, saw the songs as part of a long aesthetic and philosophical tradition older than the Spanish conquest.
canterbury: Canterbury lies on the River Stour, not far from its mouth on the Strait of Dover, in east Kent. The site has been occupied since prehistoric times. The Roman name Durovernum Cantiacorum means Durovernum of the Cantiaci, and replaced an earlier British name reconstructed as Durouernon, meaning stronghold by the alder grove. In Sub-Roman Britain it was Cair Ceint, the stronghold of Kent, and the Jutes who occupied it called it Cantwareburh in Old English.

Canterbury was first recorded as the main settlement of the Cantiaci. In the 1st century CE the Romans captured it and rebuilt it with a grid of streets, a theatre, a temple, a forum and public baths. They kept no major garrison, but its position on Watling Street, in relation to the ports of Richborough, Dover and Lymne, gave it strategic importance. In the late 3rd century they built an earth bank and a wall with seven gates round it. It later served as capital of the Jute kingdom of Kent.

A large Viking army besieged Canterbury in 1011, and the city was pillaged. Remembering the destruction caused by the Danes, its inhabitants did not resist William the Conqueror in 1066, and William ordered a wooden castle built beside the Roman wall, rebuilt in stone in the early 12th century. In the mid-16th century Canterbury hosted the first congregation of Huguenot refugees in England, founded around 1548 and scattered in 1553–4 under Mary I. In 1647, during the English Civil War, the Plum Pudding Riots broke out, and the trial of the rioters led to a Kentish revolt.

Canterbury is a World Heritage Site and its cathedral is the seat of the Archbishop of Canterbury. Its surviving past includes a city wall founded in Roman times and rebuilt in the 14th century, the Westgate Towers, the ruins of St Augustine's Abbey and the Norman castle. The Canterbury and Whitstable Railway, which ran from 1830 to 1953, was the first regular passenger steam railway in the world. The city's economy rests on tourism, higher education and retail.
cantigas-de-santa-maria: The Cantigas de Santa Maria, meaning Canticles of Holy Mary, are 420 poems with musical notation, written in medieval Galician-Portuguese during the reign of Alfonso X of Castile, called El Sabio (1221–1284). Traditionally all were attributed to Alfonso, but scholars have established that the musicians and poets of his court wrote most of them. The authors are unknown, though studies suggest the Galician poet Airas Nunes may have written many. Alfonso, named Affonso in the songs, is believed to have written some, since he refers to himself in the first person. The language was fashionable for lyric in Castile, and Alfonso had spent part of his early years in Galicia. His other major works, histories and prose, were in Castilian.

Every song mentions the Virgin Mary, and every tenth is a hymn. Of the 420 poems, 356 are narratives of Marian miracles; the rest, apart from an introduction and two prologues, are songs of praise or concern Marian festivals. The Virgin is depicted in a very humanised way, often playing a part in earthly episodes. The metres vary widely: 280 different formats for the 420 songs, the commonest being the virelai and the rondeau, with lines of between two and 24 syllables. In many songs the narrative voice describes an erotic relationship with the Divine in the troubadour fashion. The notation resembles that used for chant but also gives some information about note lengths.

The songs survive in four manuscripts: two at El Escorial, one at the National Library in Madrid and one in Florence. The Toledo codex, To, is the earliest, with 129 songs and no illustrations. The E codex, the codex of the musicians, holds the most, 406 cantigas plus the introduction and prologue, with 41 detailed miniatures of musicians playing a wide variety of instruments. The Códice Rico, T, has 195 surviving cantigas, each illustrated with six or twelve miniatures, and its sister F in Florence has 111, seven of them with miniatures only.

F was never finished, so its empty staves never received music. The codices are generally thought to date from Alfonso's lifetime, To perhaps from the 1270s and T, F and E from the early 1280s until his death in 1284.

The musical forms are still being studied, and rhythm in particular is much debated, for little beyond pitch is reliable. Early music groups have recorded the songs, among them Eduardo Paniagua and Música Antigua, Federico Bardazzi and Ensemble San Felice, Esther Lamandier and Jordi Savall, and because the notation is ambiguous the recordings differ greatly.
canton-system: The Kangxi Emperor twice banned all maritime trade while Ming loyalists such as Koxinga and the Three Feudatories resisted the new Qing dynasty. After Taiwan was taken in 1683, he opened the seas by an edict of 1684, and customs stations were set up along the coast from Guangdong to Jiangsu. In 1686 a Foreign Goods Hong was created at Canton, the basis of the later Thirteen Factories, and in 1704 the Baoshang system licensed Chinese merchants to trade with Westerners if they collected the duties. Most Westerners already chose Canton, closer to Southeast Asia.

In 1757 the Qianlong Emperor closed every customs office but Canton's to non-Russian ships after a petition about armed Western merchant ships along the coast. The historian Angela Schottenhammer links the decision to the Flint affair: James Flint, an East India Company supercargo who spoke Chinese, sailed north to Zhejiang in 1755 and in 1759 went to Ningbo to complain of corruption at Canton. He was imprisoned at Macau from December 1759 to November 1762, and new regulations barred winter trade, confined foreigners to the factories and forbade Chinese to borrow from or work for them.

The restriction mainly affected British traders and those without other treaties, Dutch, French, American, German and Nordic traders; Russians traded overland through Kyakhta, and the Portuguese and Spanish could also use Xiamen. Western demand for tea and Chinese demand for silver led the East India Company to sell Indian opium for shipment to China, where it was illegal, and Chinese efforts to stop the trade led to the First Opium War. Article V of the Treaty of Nanking of 1842 abolished the system.

In 1760 the Hong merchant Puankhequa and nine other firms in the Western trade joined to form the Cohong, which bought goods for foreigners, deducted duties and gained imperial authority to tax them. They worked under the Guangdong Customs Supervisor, known as the Hoppo, and the governor-general. Each foreign ship had to anchor at Whampoa Roads for inspection and was guaranteed by a local merchant responsible for its crew and taxes. By 1866, after trade had moved to Hong Kong and the northern ports, only 18 foreign firms kept offices in Canton.
cantonal-rebellion: The Glorious Revolution of 1868 overthrew Isabella II. Amadeo of Savoy, elected king in 1870, faced the assassination of Joan Prim and the Third Carlist War from 1872, and abdicated on 11 February 1873, when the First Spanish Republic was formed. The Federal Democratic Republican Party, which won the 1873 election, was split between benevolents, who sought a federal republic by legal means, and intransigents, who wanted it built from below by revolution. Prime Minister Francesc Pi i Margall, the founder of the federalist movement, sought conciliation, but the intransigents rose to found cantons on the Swiss model.

In July 1873 intransigents in Cartagena seized the city council and proclaimed the Canton of Cartagena under Juan Contreras y Román and Roque Barcia, taking the warships in its port, most of the Spanish Navy. Pi resigned on 18 July and was replaced by Nicolás Salmerón, and over the following days cantonalists took Algeciras, Cádiz, Granada, Seville, Salamanca, València and other towns, chiefly in the south and east, from which troops had been withdrawn to pacify the Carlist rebellion. Members of the Spanish Regional Federation of the International Workingmen's Association joined, hoping to turn the rising into a social revolution.

Manuel Pavía led 3,000 soldiers to Seville, which he took after two days of fighting, and Arsenio Martínez Campos subdued the Canton of Valencia after two weeks. By mid-September 1873 only Cartagena, protected by its walls and naval base, still held out; one of its leaders appealed to the United States for protection before military officers in the city surrendered.

The rising strengthened the army's hold on politics. Salmerón gave way to Emilio Castelar, and on 3 January 1874 Pavía deposed Castelar in a coup and installed Francisco Serrano; within a year Martínez Campos led another coup that restored the Bourbon monarchy under Alfonso XII. The anarchist newspaper El Orden reported that prison authorities had drowned 66 participants of the Canton of Cádiz, whose mayor Fermín Salvochea was sentenced to life imprisonment. Federalism declined, and many federalists turned to anarchism, which grew in influence in the late 19th century.
canu-heledd: The poems are rare among medieval Welsh verse in being set in the mouth of a woman. As the scholar Dorothy Ann Bray summarised them, they are a statement of mourning from which a background story has been deduced: Cynddylan, prince of Powys, his brothers and his warband are killed defending their country against the English in the mid-seventh century, and his sister Heledd, one of the few survivors, sees the battle and the destruction of his hall at Pengwern. She has lost her brothers, her sisters and her home, and the poems suggest she blames herself for the ruin because of some ill-spoken words.

As with the other saga englynion, among them Canu Llywarch Hen and Canu Urien, it is uncertain how the poems were performed. They are usually thought to have accompanied a prose narrative, to which they gave emotional depth, but this is not certain. In the stanzas called Ffreuer, Heledd wakes and weeps at daybreak for her brothers and her land.

The poems survive chiefly in the Red Book of Hergest, written between about 1382 and 1410. They were also in the White Book of Rhydderch, where they are now lost through damage, but later copies descended from it survive, made by Thomas Wiliems in 1596 and John Jones of Gellillyfdy in 1607, and John Davies of Mallwyd made two copies before 1631. All appear to descend from one lost original. Though written in largely Middle Welsh spelling, the poems are thought to have been composed in Old Welsh, given their archaic style; Jenny Rowland, their editor, dates the cycle to around 800 to 900.

Neither Cynddylan nor Heledd appears in historical sources such as the Harleian genealogies, but Cynddylan is the subject of a lament, Marwnad Cynddylan, thought to date from his own time, and scholars have not doubted that both were historical figures of seventh-century Powys. Other evidence suggests that relations between Mercia and Powys were then more cordial, while English invasions marked the ninth century, so the poems are now generally read as a ninth-century imagining of the seventh. Heledd's later reception has been surveyed by Marged Haycock, and she appears in Kate Roberts's novella Tywyll Heno.
canu-llywarch-hen: The poems are the best known of the early Welsh cycles of englynion about heroes of post-Roman North Britain. They contemplate martial, masculine culture, fate and old age from a critical standpoint. In the poem Gwên and Llywarch, set during a watch at Rhodwydd Forlas, the speakers tell of a thin shield on the left side, of the horn with its band of gold that Urien gave Gwên, and of the boast that no old man was a weakling in youth.

As with the other saga englynion, above all Canu Urien and Canu Heledd, it is uncertain how the poems were first performed. They are usually assumed to have accompanied a prose narrative to which they gave emotional depth, but this is not certain. In most manuscripts they are preceded by the poem Claf Abercuawg, which the White Book of Rhydderch calls the englynion of Mabclaf son of Llywarch; modern scholars do not see it as originally linked to the cycle.

Llywarch Hen may have been a historical figure: early Welsh royal genealogies place him in sixth-century north Britain as a cousin of Urien Rheged, the subject of the stylistically similar Canu Urien. The poems instead tie him to Powys, and it is generally accepted that later tradition moved his story there. The cycle may have been built up from little more than the genealogies, with his epithet inspiring his portrait as an old man. Their archaic style and occasional archaic spelling suggest that most were composed in Old Welsh and transmitted orally or in writing, and Jenny Rowland places the two poems on Gwên among the earliest saga englynion, older than some of those on his other sons.

The chief witness is the late fourteenth-century Red Book of Hergest. The poems were also in the White Book of Rhydderch but were lost there through damage, and survive in two copies descended from it: Peniarth 111, made by John Jones of Gellillyfdy in 1607, and British Library Add. MS 31055, made by Thomas Wiliems in 1596. Dr John Davies of Mallwyd copied the cycle twice from lost manuscripts before 1631. All these descend from one lost original, which makes a critical edition fairly straightforward; Ifor Williams edited the poems in 1935 and Rowland in 1990.
canusium: Canusium, the modern Canosa, lies on the right bank of the Ofanto river, the ancient Aufidus, nearly 20 kilometres from the Adriatic Sea. The town stands on the edge of the Murgia plateau at between 105 and 140 metres above sea level. Its soil is sand or clay over a layer of soft limestone tuff, which is easily excavated. This allowed the digging of underground grottoes and a hypogeum, and the stone taken out of them went into buildings above ground.

The ancient Greeks and Romans ascribed the foundation of the town to the Homeric hero Diomedes. Archaeologists place human presence in the area as far back as the 7th millennium BCE. The surrounding fields were one of the main centres of the Dauni, a northern branch of the Iapyges, and buildings and tombs at Toppicelli point to a wealthy aristocracy. The town became an important commercial centre for craftsmen, above all of ceramics and pottery, and is thought to have become a Greek polis in the age of Magna Grecia.

After Hannibal defeated the consuls Paullus and Varro at Cannae in 216 BCE, Canusium sheltered the fleeing remnants of the Roman army within its walls. In the second year of the Social War it joined the rebels and resisted a Roman siege. It suffered heavily in that conflict or in the civil wars that followed, but became a self-governing municipium in 88 BCE. Some of its bishops are known from the 4th century, and it came to be called the city of bishops. Bishop Stercorius attended the Council of Sardica in 343, and the diocese reached its height under Saint Sabinus (514 to 566), later the town's patron saint.

Earthquakes damaged the town repeatedly, notably in 1361, 1456, 1627, 1659, 1694 and 1851. It was sacked by the Tarantini in 1451 and by Napoleon in 1803. As a fief it passed through several families, and Tiberio Capece was named prince of Canosa in 1712.

Canosa di Puglia is a town and comune in the province of Barletta-Andria-Trani in Apulia, between Bari and Foggia, and is counted among the oldest continually inhabited cities in Italy. Its Cathedral of San Sabino was founded in the 8th century by Duke Arechis II of Benevento and was named after Sabinus in 1101. Bohemond I of Antioch, a commander of the First Crusade, is buried in its mausoleum. The so-called castle is the acropolis of the ancient town, and the remains of a Roman amphitheatre lie at its southern foot. The archaeological museum, founded in 1934, holds about 2,000 finds from the tombs and the town.
canute-lavard: Canute Lavard, born on 12 March 1096, was the only legitimate son of King Eric I of Denmark, who died in 1103, and Boedil Thurgotsdatter. As a minor he was bypassed in the election of 1104. He grew up in close contact with the noble family of Hvide, who later became among his most eager supporters. His byname Lavard is cognate with the English Lord.

In 1115 his uncle, King Niels of Denmark, placed him in charge of the Duchy of Schleswig in order to end the attacks of the Slavic Obotrites. Over the next fifteen years he established peace in the border area so well that he was titled Duke of Holstein and became a vassal of the Holy Roman Empire. He was the first Duke of Schleswig and the first border prince who was both a Danish and a German vassal, a position leading toward the later double position of Southern Jutland.

He seems to have been the first member of the Danish royal family attracted by the knightly ideals of medieval Germany, and he changed his title to Duke of Schleswig. His appearance made him popular and a possible successor to Niels, but he acquired mighty enemies among Danish princes and magnates, who apparently questioned his loyalty and feared his bond with Emperor Lothair III, who had recognised him as sovereign over the western Wends.
He married Ingeborg of Kiev, daughter of Mstislav I of Kiev and Christina Ingesdotter of Sweden. They had four children: Margaret, Christina, Catherine and Valdemar I of Denmark, born in 1131.

Niels and his son Magnus the Strong seem to have been alarmed by the emperor's recognition. On 7 January 1131 Canute was trapped in the Haraldsted Forest near Ringsted on Zealand and murdered by Magnus. Some sources consider the death a murder by Magnus, others attribute it to Niels himself. Ringsted Abbey became his first resting place, and in 1157 his remains were moved to a new chapel at St. Bendt's Church in Ringsted.

After his death the Obotrite lands were partitioned between the chiefs Pribislav and Niklot, and a civil war continued intermittently until 1157, ending with the triumph of his posthumous son Valdemar I. At Valdemar's request Canute was canonised in 1170. His feast day, Knutsdagen, was originally 7 January and later moved to 13 January. A Canute Guild in Tallinn was named in his memory, and a 4-metre crucifix was raised near the site of his death in 1902.
canute-vi-of-denmark: Canute VI was the eldest son of King Valdemar I and Sophia of Polotsk. On 25 June 1170, at the age of seven, he was proclaimed and crowned co-king of Denmark with his father, in the first coronation in Danish history, performed by Archbishop Eskil of Lund at Ringsted. In 1177 he married Gertrude, daughter of Duke Henry the Lion of Saxony; the marriage produced no children. Contemporary sources describe him as an earnest, strongly religious man.

After his father's death in 1182 Canute became sole ruler. He at once faced a peasant uprising in Skåne, where the peasants refused to pay Absalon's tithe. The nobles of Halland and Skåne defeated them at Dösjebro, and Canute then punished the region with fire and sword so relentlessly that Absalon begged him to stop.

Emperor Frederick Barbarossa had compelled Canute's father to acknowledge him as overlord. In 1184 he demanded the same of Canute. Canute did not reply. Absalon answered for him that Canute was as free a king as the emperor. The emperor ordered his vassal Bogislaw I of Pomerania to invade, and Bogislaw gathered 500 ships. Absalon assembled the Danish fleet and, according to the account, attacked the Pomeranians in fog, capturing 35 ships. Canute ordered two invasions of Pomerania and in 1185 forced Bogislaw to acknowledge him as overlord. From then until 1972 the kings of Denmark used the title King of the Wends. In 1197 Canute personally led a crusade against the pagan Estonians.

His brother Valdemar, Duke of Southern Jutland, was twelve when their father died, and Bishop Valdemar of Schleswig was appointed his regent. The bishop plotted with Count Adolf III of Holstein against the king. In 1192 the young duke had the bishop arrested, and he was held in Søborg Tower for thirteen years. Valdemar defeated Adolf at the Battle of Stellau in 1201 and captured him.

Absalon, Canute's friend and chief adviser, died on 21 March 1201, and Canute died suddenly on 12 November 1202 at the age of 39. As he had no children, he was succeeded by his brother Valdemar II, who ruled from 1202 to 1241.
cao-cao: Cao Cao, courtesy name Mengde, came from Qiao County in Pei State, in present-day Bozhou, Anhui. His father, Cao Song, bought his way into the office of Grand Commandant under Emperor Ling and served less than half a year; Cao Song was the foster son of the eunuch Cao Teng. Nominated as a xiaolian around the age of 19, Cao Cao became Commandant of the North District of Luoyang and later Chancellor of Jinan State, where he proposed dismissing about 80 percent of its officials for corruption.

In 189 Cao Cao spent his family fortune on an army to oppose Dong Zhuo, and between 191 and 192 Yuan Shao made him Administrator of Dong Commandery, which marks the start of his career as a warlord. His attacks on Tao Qian in Xu Province followed the murder of his father there, and he massacred thousands of civilians. In 196, on the advice of Xun Yu and Cheng Yu, he received Emperor Xian, who had escaped his captors, and set up the capital at Xuchang. The emperor and government came under his control, though he kept up nominal allegiance.

After defeating Yuan Shao at the Battle of Guandu in 200, he spent seven years defeating Yuan Shao's sons and allies and brought much of northern China under his rule. In 208 he marched south but was defeated at the Battle of Red Cliffs by Sun Quan and Liu Bei, when disease had also broken out in his army. Emperor Xian made him Duke of Wei in 213 and King of Wei in June 216, with privileges once reserved for emperors.

Cao Cao died in Luoyang on 15 March 220.
