In November 220 his son Cao Pi accepted the abdication of Emperor Xian and founded the state of Cao Wei, an event commonly seen as a usurpation, and gave his father the title Emperor Wu. Opinion of Cao Cao has been divided since the Jin dynasty: some praise his poetry and career, others condemn his cruelty and alleged treachery. Traditional Chinese culture stereotypically shows him as a sly tyrant opposed to Liu Bei, a portrait shaped by the 14th-century novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms.
cao-huan: Cao Huan was born with the name Cao Huang. His father, Cao Yu, the Prince of Yan, was a son of Cao Cao, the father of Wei's first emperor, Cao Pi. In 258, at the age of 12, Cao Huan was instated as the Duke of Changdao District.

In June 260 the emperor Cao Mao was killed in an attempt to seize back state power from the regent Sima Zhao. Cao Huang was selected to succeed him. His name was then changed to Cao Huan, because the old name was a homonym of many common words, including those for yellow and for emperor, and so hard to avoid.

During his reign the Sima clan controlled the state, and Cao Huan was a figurehead and head of state in name only. In the first years of the reign the rival state of Shu Han, under the general Jiang Wei, attacked repeatedly, though these attacks were largely repelled.

Sima Zhao then ordered a counterattack on Shu with 180,000 men under Zhong Hui and Deng Ai. In late 263 the Shu emperor Liu Shan surrendered to Deng Ai, ending the state of Shu. In early 264 Zhong Hui plotted with Jiang Wei to restore Shu, and the Wei generals killed both men. Shu's former lands were annexed by Wei.

In December 263 Sima Zhao again pressed Cao Huan to grant him the nine bestowments, and this time accepted them, which signalled that a usurpation was near. In May 264 he became King of Jin. After he died in September 265, his son Sima Yan inherited his position and on 4 February 266 forced Cao Huan to abdicate. Cao Huan was sent to the city of Ye, where he lived for the rest of his life, and Sima Yan founded the Jin dynasty on 8 February.

Little is known of Cao Huan's life as a prince. Sima Yan allowed him to keep imperial banners and wagons and to worship his ancestors with imperial ceremonies. He died in the reign of Emperor Hui, was buried with the honours due an emperor and was given the posthumous name Yuan. The title of Prince of Chenliu stayed within the Cao clan until it was abolished in 479.
cao-kun: Cao Kun, courtesy name Zhongshan, was born on 12 December 1862 to a poor family in Tianjin. During the First Sino-Japanese War in 1894 he went with the army to fight in Joseon. After the war he joined Yuan Shikai in training the New Army, known as the Beiyang Army. Admired by Yuan, he rose quickly, and by the time of the Xinhai Revolution of 1911 he commanded the Beiyang 3rd Division. He was a staunch supporter of Confucianism and an opponent of liberalism and communism.

Made a general in the Beiyang Army, he led the Zhili clique after the death of Feng Guozhang. In the 1918 election Duan Qirui promised him the vice-presidency, but the office remained vacant after most of the National Assembly left and it lost its quorum. Cao felt betrayed by Duan and defeated him in battle in 1920. In March 1922 he tried to launch an airline, Beijing-Han Airlines, with a Handley Page aircraft; its three-day trial tour ended when the plane crashed on approach to Beijing, killing all 14 on board. He also had a family connection to the Chinese Muslim commander Ma Fuxing, who lived in Xinjiang.

After forcing the resignations of Xu Shichang and Li Yuanhong, and engaging in bribery, Cao became president of China in Beijing on 10 October 1923 and served until 2 November 1924. He acquired the office by threats, extortion and bribing assembly members with 5,000 silver dollars each. The episode brought disrepute to the Beiyang government and to the National Assembly, which lacked a quorum even to hold elections, and it turned rival factions against him. His relations with his chief protégé Wu Peifu soured, though the two stayed together against the Fengtian clique. He promulgated the draft 1923 Constitution in an effort to legitimise his claim. Hastily drafted, it was deemed the most democratic and progressive charter yet, but like earlier charters it was ignored.

During the Second Zhili–Fengtian War against Zhang Zuolin in October 1924, Feng Yuxiang betrayed and imprisoned him in the Beijing coup and forced him to resign. His brother Cao Rui killed himself during Cao's house arrest. Feng released him in 1926 as a goodwill gesture to Wu Peifu. Cao died at his home in Tianjin on 15 May 1938.
cao-pi: Cao Pi was the second son of the warlord Cao Cao, but the eldest of the sons of Cao Cao's concubine, later wife, Lady Bian; the eldest of all, Cao Ang, died early. In 211 he became General of the Household for All Purposes and Vice Imperial Chancellor, second only to his father.

For years it was unclear whom Cao Cao intended as heir. He favoured his third son Cao Zhi, known for his literary talent, and in 216 Cao Zhi's party falsely accused two officials who supported Cao Pi, Cui Yan and Mao Jie; Cui Yan was executed. In November or December 217 Cao Cao, by then King of Wei, named Cao Pi heir apparent.

When Cao Cao died in spring 220, Cao Pi declared himself King of Wei before Emperor Xian had confirmed it, and sent his brothers, Cao Zhang and Cao Zhi among them, back to their fiefs. In the winter of 220 he pressed Emperor Xian to yield the throne. He declined three times, a pattern later usurpers in Chinese history followed, and then accepted, founding the state of Cao Wei. This ended the Han dynasty and began the Three Kingdoms period.

Sun Quan briefly submitted to Wei, and Cao Pi rejected the strategist Liu Ye's advice to attack him, granting him the title King of Wu instead; most historians believe this choice confined Wei to northern and central China. After the Battle of Xiaoting in 222 Sun Quan broke with Wei and founded Eastern Wu, and Cao Pi's attacks over the next years made no significant advances. In 225 he remarked that Heaven created the Yangtze River to divide the north and the south.

Historians view him as a competent but unspectacular administrator. He formally established Chen Qun's nine-rank system as the basis of civil service nomination, but he reduced the princes' power and restricted their use of military force. He named Cao Rui crown prince only in summer 226, when seriously ill, and entrusted him to Cao Zhen, Chen Qun and Sima Yi.

Cao Pi was a poet and scholar like his father and his brother Cao Zhi. His Yan Ge Xing is the first Chinese poem with seven syllables to the line. He also wrote over a hundred articles, and the collection of strange tales Lieyi Zhuan is attributed to him. After his death Cao Rui gave him the posthumous name Emperor Wen and the temple name Gaozu.
cao-wei: Late in the Eastern Han dynasty northern China came under Cao Cao, chancellor to the last Han ruler, Emperor Xian. In 213 the emperor made him Duke of Wei, and in 216 King of Wei. Cao Cao died on 15 March 220, and his son Cao Pi inherited the title. On 11 December that year Cao Pi forced Emperor Xian to abdicate and established the state of Wei. Liu Bei contested the claim and declared himself Emperor of Han a year later. Sun Quan, nominally a vassal king under Wei, declared independence in 222 and proclaimed himself Emperor of Wu in 229. The capital was first Xuchang and later Luoyang.

Cao Pi ruled until his death on 29 June 226 and was succeeded by his son Cao Rui, who ruled until 22 January 239. Between 228 and 234 the Shu chancellor Zhuge Liang led five campaigns against Wei's western borders, aiming at Chang'an, but Wei armies repelled them. Fighting with Wu through the 220s and 230s mostly ended in stalemate. In 238 Sima Yi invaded Liaodong and, after a three-month siege, captured the Gongsun capital of Xiangping. In the Goguryeo–Wei Wars from 242, Wei defeated Goguryeo and destroyed its capital Hwando in 244.

Imperial authority collapsed in 249 when the regent Sima Yi seized power from his co-regent Cao Shuang, reducing the emperor Cao Fang to a puppet. His son Sima Shi deposed Cao Fang in 254. In 263 Wei armies conquered Shu. On 4 February 266 Sima Yan forced Cao Huan to abdicate and replaced Wei with the Jin dynasty.

Wei's government inherited much from the Eastern Han. Cao Pi set up bodies to reduce the authority of the Imperial Secretariat, and cut provincial governors to inspectors, with military affairs handled by regional officers. The minister Chen Qun developed the nine-rank system for civil service nomination, adopted by later dynasties until the Sui. It also set rigid lines in law between commoner and noble households and enabled hereditary officeholding by aristocratic families, whose bonded clients and retainers paid no state taxes or labour service. The kaishu style of calligraphy and the Jian'an poetry style developed in this period, as did the Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove.
caodaism: Caodaism began in 1925 in Saigon as a Spiritualist club called AĂÂ, founded by Cao Quỳnh Cư, Cao Hoài Sang, Lê Văn Trung and Phạm Công Tắc, clerks in the colonial government who practised mediumship and ouija sessions. After a séance in 1926 the group believed it had received a revelation predicting a universal religion, and Ngô Văn Chiêu signed the Declaration of the Founding of the Cao Đài Religion on 7 October 1926.
Ngô Văn Chiêu declined the office of Pope and founded the separate Chiếu Minh branch; Lê Văn Trung became acting Pope, and after his death in 1934 Phạm Công Tắc took the role.

The full name is Đại Đạo Tam Kỳ Phổ Độ, the Great Faith for the Third Universal Redemption. This monotheistic faith combines ethical precepts from Confucianism, practices from Taoism, karma and rebirth from Buddhism and a hierarchical organisation from Catholicism. Its God, Cao Đài, is accompanied by the Holy Mother, Diêu Trì Kim Mẫu, and they stand for yang and yin. Followers hold that history has three periods of revelation: in the first two, figures such as Gautama Buddha, Laozi, Confucius and Jesus founded religions that later became corrupted, and the third comes through Cao Đài. Victor Hugo, Sun Yat-sen and Trạng Trình are named as its main prophets.

Adherents practise prayer, ancestor veneration, nonviolence and vegetarianism, aiming at union with God and release from saṃsāra. The church is headed by a Pope over an Executive Body, with a Legislative Body under the Hộ Pháp. Lê Văn Trung was the only Pope ordained at Tây Ninh, and the office has stayed vacant.

By 1940 Caodaism had over a million members, between a fifth and a quarter of the population of Cochinchina. From 1941 to 1946 Phạm Công Tắc and other leaders were jailed in French penal colonies in Madagascar. During the First and Second Indochina Wars, Caodaists took part in political and military struggles against the French and against Ngô Đình Diệm.

After the fall of Saigon in April 1975 the communist government banned the practice; legal recognition came in 1997. Between 1934 and 1975 the religion split into as many as thirty sects, of which eleven have been recognised by the authorities. Estimates of followers in Vietnam differ widely, up to about six million, and the Holy See at Tây Ninh is a major pilgrimage site.
caonabo: Caonabo was not native to Hispaniola: he was born among the Lucayan people of the Lucayan Archipelago of the Bahamas and later migrated to the island. The historian Bartolomé de las Casas, one of the first Spanish settlers in the Americas, wrote that because he stood out as a man of war and of peace he came to be king of that province and was highly esteemed by all. He ruled Maguana, one of the island's five cacicazgos, most likely from what is now San Juan de la Maguana in the Dominican Republic.

In 1492 Christopher Columbus's ship the Santa María was wrecked on the north coast on Christmas Day, and it was salvaged to build the fort of La Navidad, where Columbus left some of his crew. Caonabo's attack on the fort in 1493 left 39 Spaniards dead. His wife Anacaona, the sister of the cacique Bohechío, later explained that, angered at the Spaniards' treatment of the natives, she had moved him to it.

When Columbus returned and found La Navidad destroyed, Caonabo came to be considered one of the strongest leaders on the island; the cacique Guacanagaríx of Marién told the Spaniards he was responsible. Bartholomew Columbus then received word that Caonabo planned to attack the Spanish fort of Santo Tomás, and Columbus sent Alonso de Ojeda into the interior with four hundred men to subjugate the natives.

Accounts of his capture differ, and the historian Samuel M. Wilson considers the story likely embellished and romanticised by the Spanish. In Las Casas's version Ojeda offered him polished handcuffs and chains as a gift, said to be worn by kings in Spain, and locked them once Caonabo tried them on.

The capture led to the first Native American uprising against the Spanish. Caonabo's brother Manicatex gathered around 7,000 natives to rescue him but was defeated, largely through the Spaniards' use of cavalry, and taken prisoner. To prevent further risings the Spanish sent both brothers to Spain, and Caonabo died during the voyage and was buried at sea.
cap-haitien: Spanish explorers took the Taíno name Guárico for the area. Puerto Real, one of the first Spanish towns of Hispaniola, was founded near Cap-Haïtien in 1503 and abandoned in 1578. Cap-Français was founded in 1670 by a dozen colonist-adventurers under Bertrand d'Ogeron, and its formal foundation dates from 1711. The French built large sugar plantations on the northern plains and imported tens of thousands of African slaves. Cap-Français became the colony's main commercial centre and its capital until 1770, when the capital moved to Port-au-Prince, and its wealth earned it the nickname Paris of the Antilles. Two thirds of its 15,000 inhabitants in 1790 were enslaved.

The Haitian Revolution began nearby. At Bois Caïman, on 14 August 1791, the maroon leader Dutty Boukman and a mambo named Cécile Fatiman led a Vodou ceremony at which those present swore to die rather than endure slavery, and the insurrection began on 22–23 August. At Vertières, on 18 November 1803, Jean-Jacques Dessalines's army defeated a French army under the Comte de Rochambeau, and Haiti declared independence in 1804. Henri Christophe renamed the city, and it was the first capital of his Kingdom of Haiti until 1820.

Cap-Haïtien is the capital of the department of Nord, with about 300,000 people. Near Milot stand the Citadelle Laferrière, a mountaintop fortress built by Henri Christophe, and the ruins of his Sans-Souci Palace, damaged in the earthquake of 7 May 1842, which destroyed most of the city. UNESCO listed both as a World Heritage Site in 1982. After the United States occupation of Haiti from 1915 to 1934, the streets of the central city were renamed with letters running north to south and numbers running east to west. Its well-preserved 19th-century architecture, with gingerbread houses, resembles that of New Orleans.
capacocha: The name joins the Quechua qhapaq, meaning noble, solemn, principal, mighty or royal, and hucha, meaning crime, sin or guilt. In Inca culture the dead were a link between the people and the gods, and the rite was meant to appease gods who might otherwise punish the people's sins with floods, earthquakes and famines. The children became servants of the gods, or of the emperor when the rite followed his death, and guardians of the places where they died.

No region was exempt. Boys were no older than ten; girls could be up to sixteen but had to be virgins, and all had to be free of any blemish. Families often counted selection an honour, and noble families sometimes offered children to win the emperor's favour. Girls were often first placed with the mama-kuna in the House of Chosen Women, where they learnt to weave and to prepare chicha; at about fourteen some became priestesses, the prettiest were sent for sacrifice, and others became servants, concubines or secondary wives.

From Cuzco the children, priests and companions went home not by the royal road but in straight lines across valleys and mountains, possibly along the ceque lines, a journey that could take months. At the shrine the children were given an intoxicating drink, and death came by strangulation, a blow to the head, suffocation or burial alive while unconscious. Spanish reports of hearts being removed have no archaeological support. Graves were dug with sharpened sticks, never metal, and the dead were buried in a fetal position with paired figurines of gold, silver and spondylus shell, cloth and pottery.

The fullest description is Cristóbal de Molina's, which ties the rite to a monarch's accession. Archaeology has not confirmed sacrifice on the scale the chroniclers describe: Bauer found surface evidence of human burial at only three of Cuzco's shrines. Molina's stress on high peaks and the offerings he lists do match the finds at the more than 100 Inca ceremonial sites on or near the high summits of the Andes Mountains.

At Llullaillaco, at about 6,739 metres, hair samples of the three children show a marked change of diet in the year before death and a procession begun months before. On Quehuar, looters' dynamite damaged the remains of a girl of about twelve. At Ampato, DNA showed that Juanita was related to people of northern Peru and Argentina, and a CT scan that a blow to the head killed her; three more children found there had been damaged by lightning.
cape-coast: Cape Coast lies on the Gulf of Guinea, about 130 km from Accra. Its traditional name is Oguaa, from the Guan Awutu word gua, meaning market. Early Portuguese navigators called it Cabo Corso, short cape, which the British later corrupted to Cape Coast. It became the principal town of the Fetu Kingdom, an old Guan kingdom whose paramount seat lay about 16 km to the north. A market called Ogua grew into an active commercial centre, and the King of Fetu appointed a chief to represent it.

The English navigator William Towerson, the first documented English visitor to reach the Guinea coast, landed in 1555. Around 1650 Hendrik Carloff bought a plot from the King of Fetu for Dutch privateers working against the Dutch West India Company. The fort built on the site of Carolusborg changed hands several times before 1664, when a joint English and Dutch force captured it from the Dutch. The Danes built Fort Frederiksborg on a hill plot, which the English later bought.

The Asante invaded the coast in 1806. Cape Coast escaped the attack, but the townspeople's confidence in British protection fell. The town had been largely burnt down in 1817. It was the most important anchorage on the coast until Sekondi Harbour was built in the 1890s. Cape Coast was capital of the Gold Coast from 1821 until 1877, when the seat moved to Accra, which badly damaged its economy.

Cape Coast is the capital of the Central Region of Ghana. Its 2010 census population was 108,374, mostly Fante. Cape Coast Castle is a World Heritage Site. The University of Cape Coast, established in 1962, helped make it an educational centre. The main festival is Fetu Afahye, held on the first Saturday of September.
cape-coast-castle: The first fort was built for the Swedish Africa Company by Hendrik Caerloff, a former official of the Dutch West India Company, who in 1650 won the king of Fetu's permission to build at Cabo Corso, Portuguese for short cape, later corrupted to Cape Coast. The timber lodge was named after King Charles X Gustav of Sweden and traded in timber and gold. In 1657 Caerloff, now serving Denmark, drove the Swedes out, and after disputes in which the king of Fetu sold it back to the Swedes, the Dutch occupied it in 1663, a year before the English took it in 1664, during the prelude to the Second Anglo-Dutch War.

The English strengthened it so far that the Dutch admiral Michiel de Ruyter judged it impossible to take, and Cape Coast became the capital of the English possessions on the Gold Coast. The Royal African Company, given a monopoly of English trade on the west coast of Africa in 1672, expanded it, and from 1750 the Company of Merchants Trading to Africa took it over.

The castle was a market where gold, ivory, mahogany and enslaved captives were bartered for cloth, spices, sugar, silk and other goods, and enslaved people became the main trade. Vaulted dungeons cut into the rock beneath the parade ground, probably built by 1682, could hold about a thousand people awaiting shipment, while the Europeans lived in relative luxury above. At times the castle could not feed its prisoners, and in June 1683 a factor warned that they would starve. The company also kept castle slaves who worked at the fort: in 1777 they numbered 288 men, women and children.

Pirates were hanged there, among them Duncan Mackintosh in 1689 and 52 men of Bartholomew Roberts's crew in 1722. After a French squadron nearly captured it in 1757, during the Seven Years' War, the castle was largely rebuilt, with new bastions and dungeons below Grassle's Bastions.

George Maclean, President of the Committee of Merchants from 1830 to 1844, and the poet Letitia Landon, who died there within two months of their marriage, are buried in the courtyard. The British Public Works Department first restored the castle in the 1920s; at independence in 1957 it passed to the Ghana Museums and Monuments Board, and it was restored again in the early 1990s. It now holds a museum and is visited on guided tours, and it appears in Yaa Gyasi's novel Homegoing and the film Sankofa.
cape-cod: Cape Cod extends into the Atlantic Ocean from the south-eastern corner of Massachusetts and is coextensive with Barnstable County, running from Provincetown in the north-east to Woods Hole in the south-west. It is divided into fifteen towns. Most of the land consists of glacial landforms, terminal moraine and outwash plains, which mark the southernmost extent of glacial coverage in south-eastern New England. Geologically it is young, laid down some 16,000 to 20,000 years ago. Since 1914 the Cape Cod Canal has separated most of the peninsula from the mainland.

The Wampanoag have lived on Cape Cod for centuries. They lived from the sea, farmed, and lit controlled fires to keep the underbrush in check. They helped the Pilgrims, who arrived in the fall of 1620, to survive at Plymouth Colony, and later gradually lost their lands through cessions and violent conflict with settlers. The Wampanoag tribe was federally recognised in May 2007.

Bartholomew Gosnold coined the name Cape Cod in 1602, and it is the ninth-oldest English place-name in the United States. It applied at first only to the tip of the peninsula. The Cape was among the first places settled by Puritan colonists, with Sandwich founded in 1637 and Barnstable and Yarmouth in 1639. The canal was developed from 1870 to 1914. Lighthouses were built from 1797, and from the end of the 19th century improved rail transport made the Cape a summer haven for city dwellers from Boston.

Cape Cod has a year-round population of about 220,000 and a tourist season in the warmer months. Henry David Thoreau wrote about his 1849 travels there in Cape Cod, published in 1865, and Henry Beston's The Outermost House of 1928 describes a year spent in a cottage in Eastham.
cape-cod-bay: The bay measures 604 square miles (1,560 km2) below a line drawn from Brant Rock in Marshfield to Race Point in Provincetown. It is enclosed by Cape Cod to the south and east and by Plymouth County to the west, with Massachusetts Bay and the Atlantic Ocean to the north. It is the southernmost extremity of the Gulf of Maine and one of the bays that give Massachusetts the name Bay State, with Narragansett Bay, Buzzards Bay and Massachusetts Bay.

Most of Cape Cod is made of glacially derived rocks, sands and gravels, and at the end of the last glaciation, which ended about 12,000 years ago, the bay was probably a large freshwater lake. The Provincetown Spit, the land north of High Head in North Truro, formed from marine deposits over the last 5,000 to 8,000 years and created the bowl of Provincetown Harbor. Currents generally move counter-clockwise, south from Boston to Plymouth, then east and north to Provincetown.

The Italian navigator Giovanni da Verrazzano was the first European to reach the bay, in 1524, as a map of 1529 that clearly outlines Cape Cod shows. In 1620 the Pilgrims first sheltered in Provincetown Harbor, where they signed the Mayflower Compact, and while at anchor there they shot unsuccessfully at a whale. Since 1914 the Cape Cod Canal, which divides the towns of Bourne and Sandwich, has connected the bay to Buzzards Bay.

The bay supports bluefin tuna, striped bass, bluefish, flounder and Atlantic mackerel as well as seals, dolphins and whales; the severely endangered North Atlantic right whale feeds there, and humpback whales come from April to December. Roseate terns and piping plovers use its shores, and the Brewster Flats near Brewster are the widest expanse of tidal flats in North America. Nitrogen from backyard sewage systems and polluted runoff threaten its waters, where blooms of Phaeocystis and of Alexandrium, the cause of red tides, occur.
cape-colony: An expedition of the Dutch East India Company (VOC) led by Jan van Riebeeck established a trading post and naval victualling station at the Cape of Good Hope in 1652. Its aim was a harbour of refuge for company ships on the long voyages between Europe and Asia. Within about three decades the Cape held a large community of vrijburgers, or free citizens, former company employees who undertook to farm the land for at least twenty years in exchange for tax exemption and loans of tools and seeds. In 1688 the company also sponsored the immigration of nearly two hundred French Huguenot refugees.

Colonists on the frontier, known as Boers, moved far beyond the colony's first borders, and some, the trekboers, became permanently nomadic. The period of company rule saw bitter, genocidal conflicts between the colonists and the Khoe-speaking peoples, and later the Xhosa, who were seen as competitors for farmland. The company also imported thousands of slaves from the Dutch East Indies and other parts of Africa. By the end of the eighteenth century the population included about 26,000 people of European descent and 30,000 slaves.

In 1795 Britain occupied the Cape after France occupied the Dutch Republic, defeating the company's militia at the Battle of Muizenberg. The Treaty of Amiens returned it to the Batavian Republic in 1803, but Britain took it again after the Battle of Blaauwberg and set up a colony on 8 January 1806. The Dutch formally ceded sovereignty in 1814. British settlers arrived at Port Elizabeth in 1820, and slavery was abolished in 1834. Resentment among the Boers of this change and of English language and culture led many to trek inland in the Great Trek and form the Boer Republics.

The colony became a Crown colony with representative government in 1853 and elected its first parliament in 1854, with a franchise based on a property qualification regardless of race. It achieved responsible government in 1872 under its first Prime Minister, John Molteno.

The colony stretched from the Atlantic coast inland and eastward along the southern coast, about half of modern South Africa, with its eastern boundary at the Fish River after several wars against the Xhosa. In 1910 it joined three other colonies to form the Union of South Africa and became the Province of the Cape of Good Hope. In 1994 the Cape Province was divided into the Eastern Cape, Northern Cape and Western Cape, with smaller parts in North West province.
cape-guardafui: Cape Guardafui, in Somali Raas Caseyr, is a headland in the federal state of Puntland that forms the geographical apex of the Horn of Africa. Its shore, at 51°27'52"E, is the second easternmost point on mainland Africa after Ras Hafun. It is named after the offshore Guardafui Channel, which connects the Gulf of Aden with the Somali Sea, and the archipelago of Socotra lies off the cape. A sighting of the cape marked a milestone for passing vessels, because of a sharp westerly change of direction and the contrast between hazardous currents to the east and comparatively calm seas to the north.

The ancient Greeks called it the Aromata promontorium, and the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea described it in the 1st century CE together with other flourishing commercial settlements on the northern Somali coast. The name Guardafui arose in the late Middle Ages among sailors using the Mediterranean Lingua Franca, in which guarda fui means look and escape, a reference to the danger of the cape.

In the early 19th century Somali seamen kept foreign ships out of their ports and traded with Aden and Mokha in their own vessels. Because of the many shipwrecks, the British made an agreement with Sultan Osman Mahamuud of the Majeerteen Sultanate, which controlled much of the northeastern coast, to pay annual subsidies to protect shipwrecked British crews and guard wrecks against plunder. It remained unratified, as the British feared that it would give other powers a precedent for agreements with the Somalis. Sultan Yusuf Ali Kenadid of the Sultanate of Hobyo later gave concessions to a French hotel proprietor and a former French Army officer to build a lighthouse, but the project failed.

Britain ceded the disputed region to Italy in 1894. Italy wanted the cost shared by the maritime powers that would benefit, but Britain, suspecting a coaling station to rival Aden, refused to contribute, and the lighthouse came only in the 1920s. The Francesco Crispi Lighthouse, a metal-framed tower, opened in April 1924, and troops guarding it repelled two attacks by rebels against Italian rule, in November 1925 and January 1926. A stronger stone lighthouse opened in 1930 in the shape of a Fascio littorio, with a stone axe blade. It is no longer in use.

Many of the nomads who cross the cape are also fishermen, because of the abundance of fish offshore. In 2013 the Puntland government created a region named Gardafuu, coextensive with the cape and carved out of the Bari region, with its capital at Alula.
cape-horn: Cape Horn lies on Hornos Island in the Hermite Islands group, at the southern end of the Tierra del Fuego archipelago in southern Chile, at about 56 degrees south. It is not the most southerly point of South America, which is Águila Islet, but it marks the northern boundary of the Drake Passage, the strait between South America and Antarctica, and the place where the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans meet. The cape lies in Chilean territorial waters, within Cabo de Hornos National Park, and the Chilean Navy maintains a station on the island with a residence, chapel and lighthouse.

The Dutchmen Willem Schouten and Jacob Le Maire first rounded the cape in 1616 and named it Kaap Hoorn after the city of Hoorn in the Netherlands. The Strait of Magellan, between the mainland and Tierra del Fuego, had been used for trade well before the Horn was discovered, but is narrow, and for decades Cape Horn was a major milestone on the clipper route by which sailing ships carried trade around the world. The need to round it was greatly reduced by the opening of the Panama Canal in August 1914.

The passage is regarded as perhaps the most dangerous ship route in the world, and many ships have been wrecked and many sailors have died attempting it. Winds in these latitudes blow from west to east almost uninterrupted by land, and the Andes and the Antarctic Peninsula funnel them into the narrow Drake Passage. The waves become shorter and steeper over the shallow water south of the Horn, and rogue waves of up to 30 metres are reported west of it. Icebergs are a further hazard. Passage from east to west, against the winds and currents, was a particular problem for traditional sailing ships.

There are no regular commercial routes around the Horn, although cruise ships and vessels bound for the Antarctic Peninsula pass it. Rounding the Horn remains one of the major challenges in yachting. A memorial near the station, a sculpture by José Balcells of the silhouette of an albatross, was erected in 1992 in remembrance of the sailors who died attempting to round the Horn. The cape belongs to the commune of Cabo de Hornos, whose capital is Puerto Williams.
cape-juby: Cape Juby, in Arabic Ra's Juby and in Spanish Cabo Juby, is a cape on the coast of southern Morocco near the border with Western Sahara, directly east of the Canary Islands. The surrounding area, including the towns of Tarfaya and Tan-Tan, is called the Cape Juby Strip, the Tarfaya Strip or the Tekna Zone, after the Tekna, the native Saharawi tribe. It lies in the far south of internationally recognised Morocco and forms a semi-desert buffer between Morocco proper at the Draa River and Western Sahara.

On 28 May 1767 the Sultan of Morocco, Mohammed ben Abdallah, signed a treaty with Charles III of Spain in which Morocco admitted it could not guarantee the safety of Spanish fishermen south of the Noun River, since it did not control the Tekna tribes. On 1 March 1799 Sultan Slimane recognised that the Saguia el-Hamra and Cape Juby regions were not part of his dominions. In 1879 the British North West Africa Company set up a trading post near the cape called Port Victoria. Moroccan soldiers attacked it on 26 March 1888, killing its director, and in 1895 the company sold it to the Sultan of Morocco.

In 1912 Spain negotiated with France, then in charge of Moroccan affairs, for concessions on Morocco's southern coast. Francisco Bens occupied the region for Spain on 29 July 1916. It was administered as one entity with Spanish Sahara and the Ifni enclave, as Spanish West Africa. The Spanish area covered 33,000 square kilometres with a population of 9,836. Its main town, founded as Villa Bens and now Tarfaya, was a staging post for airmail flights. After Morocco regained full independence in 1956 it asked for the areas held by Spain, and after the fighting of 1957 in the Ifni War, Spain ceded the Cape Juby Strip in 1958.

In 1877 the Scottish engineer Donald Mackenzie proposed a Sahara Sea. He wanted a channel cut from a lagoon north of Cape Juby to a plain that Arab traders called El Djouf, which he believed lay up to 61 metres below sea level. Flooding it would give an inland sea of 155,400 square kilometres suited to navigation and farming, with a canal giving access to the Niger River. He had never travelled in the area. The lowest depression near the cape, Sebkha Tah at 55 metres below sea level, covers under 250 square kilometres and lies 500 kilometres north of El Djouf, whose average elevation is 320 metres.
cape-mesurado: Portuguese sailors named the headland Cape Mesurado in the 1560s; it is also called Cape Montserrado. It is the promontory on which African-American settlers established the city now called Monrovia on 25 April 1822. A lighthouse was built on the north-western part of the cape, in what is now the Mamba Point neighbourhood of Monrovia, in 1855.

Before the settlers came the cape was a base of the illegal slave trade. In 1815 Governor William Maxwell of Sierra Leone sent an armed force there, which seized ships and goods and freed enslaved Africans working at the trading posts; their owners, Robert Bostock and John McQueen, were sentenced to fourteen years' transportation to New South Wales. The following year HMS Queen Charlotte of the West Africa Squadron seized the Le Louis, suspected of slaving.

The American Colonization Society's first settlers had suffered a high death rate on swampy Sherbro Island, so in 1821 the society sent Dr. Eli Ayers to buy healthier land further down the coast. With the help of the naval officer Robert F. Stockton, who led the talks with leaders of the Dei and Bassa peoples, he obtained a coastal strip 36 miles long and 3 miles wide for trade goods, supplies, weapons and rum worth about $300. The local ruler, Zolu Duma, known as King Peter, was reluctant and was forcefully persuaded, at gunpoint according to some accounts.

The new colony faced scarce supplies and unhealthy conditions, and local peoples who resented the settlers' efforts to end the slave trade attacked it. Led by Lott Carey and Elijah Johnson, the colonists organised their own defence and refused British help that would have meant raising the Union Jack on the cape. At the Battle of Fort Hill on 1 December 1822, a colonist named Matilda Newport is supposed to have repelled an attack by firing a cannon with an ember from her pipe; Matilda Newport Day, a holiday created in 1916, was abolished in 1980.
cape-of-good-hope: The Cape of Good Hope is a rocky headland on the Atlantic coast of the Cape Peninsula in South Africa, about 2.3 kilometres west and a little north of Cape Point. It is a common misconception that it is the southern tip of Africa; the southernmost point is Cape Agulhas, about 150 kilometres to the east-southeast. Following the western African coastline from the equator, however, the Cape of Good Hope marks the point where a ship begins to travel more eastward than southward. Cape Town lies about 50 kilometres to the north, in Table Bay.

Herodotus records that around 600 BCE Necho II reputedly commissioned Phoenicians to sail from the Red Sea around Africa to the mouth of the Nile, which would be the first completion of the Cape Route. The account came to him by oral tradition. Eudoxus of Cyzicus, a Greek navigator for Ptolemy VIII, found in about 116 BCE the wreck of a ship that appeared to have come from Gades, and concluded that it had sailed round Africa; his own later attempt failed and his fate is unknown. The Fra Mauro map of 1450 depicts the Indian Ocean as connected to the Atlantic and records a voyage by an Indian junk around 1420.

The first European to reach the cape was the Portuguese explorer Bartolomeu Dias, who named it the Cape of Storms, Cabo das Tormentas. John II of Portugal renamed it the Cape of Good Hope because of the optimism the opening of a sea route to India and the East engendered. The Khoikhoi lived in the area when the Dutch first settled in 1652. On 6 April of that year Jan van Riebeeck established a resupply camp for the Dutch East India Company in Table Bay, which developed into Cape Town and became known as the Tavern of the Seas. On 31 December 1687 a community of Huguenots arrived from the Netherlands, since the Company needed skilled farmers.

British troops occupied the Cape Colony in 1795, after the Dutch Republic was occupied by France, and again on 19 January 1806 following the Battle of Blaauwberg. The colony existed from 1795 to 1802 and again from 1806 to 1910. Today the cape is a section of Table Mountain National Park, with fynbos vegetation that belongs to the Cape Floristic Kingdom, and at least 250 bird species, including a mainland colony of African penguins. In legend it is the home of the Flying Dutchman, and the poet Luís de Camões invented the giant Adamastor in Os Lusíadas, first printed in 1572, as a symbol of the dangers of rounding the Cape of Storms.
cape-palmas: The cape is a small, rocky peninsula joined to the mainland by a sandy isthmus. The estuary of the Hoffman River lies just to the west, and about 21 kilometres to the east the Cavalla River reaches the sea on the border with Côte d'Ivoire. The International Hydrographic Organization takes the cape as the western limit of the Gulf of Guinea. Offshore lies Russwurm Island, joined to the peninsula by a breakwater, and a lighthouse warns ships of the many shoals nearby.

In 1458 Prince Henry the Navigator of Portugal sent his captain Diogo Gomes down the coast of West Africa as far as this point, where the shore stops running south and turns east. Gomes named it Cabo das Palmas, the Cape of the Palms, and the river Rio das Palmas, later the Hoffman. The name appears on the Cantino planisphere of 1502, the earliest map known to carry it, at a time when Europeans called this stretch of coast the Malaguetta Coast.

In December 1831 the Maryland legislature appropriated US$10,000 for 26 years to carry free black people and former slaves from the United States to Africa, and the Maryland State Colonization Society, once a branch of the American Colonization Society, was formed for the purpose. It named its settlement Maryland in Africa on 12 February 1834. The colony became a state on 2 February 1841, and after independence in 1854 it was annexed to Liberia by treaty on 18 March 1857. Its first black governor, John Brown Russwurm, gave his name to the island off the cape. The Episcopal missionary Elizabeth Mars Johnson Thomson taught there from 1835 to 1862.

The city of Harper, founded by the society in 1835, runs inland along the Hoffman estuary and has a small harbour; a white masonic lodge hall with a large golden orb on its roof is a landmark seen from the sea. The name Cape Palmas is often used for the whole of Maryland County and for Harper, its county seat.
cape-province: The Province of the Cape of Good Hope, known in Afrikaans as Kaapprovinsie, was commonly called the Cape Province, and colloquially the Cape. When the Union of South Africa was formed in 1910, the original Cape Colony was renamed the Cape Province. It was by far the largest of the four provinces, the others being Transvaal, Natal and the Orange Free State. It had annexed regions such as British Bechuanaland, not to be confused with the Bechuanaland Protectorate, now Botswana, and Griqualand East, around Kokstad, and Griqualand West, around Kimberley. It encompassed two thirds of South Africa's territory, about 717,000 square kilometres, and included Walvis Bay.

Before the union the Cape Colony had a non-racial franchise, in which qualifications for suffrage applied equally to all males regardless of race. In the union negotiations the Cape prime minister, John X. Merriman, fought unsuccessfully to extend it to the rest of South Africa, since the former Boer republics strongly opposed it, being determined to entrench white rule. After union the Cape Province was permitted to keep a restricted version, and it became the only province where Coloured and Black African men could vote.

Successive acts eroded this roll. In 1931 the restricting qualifications were removed for white voters but kept for Black and Coloured voters, and in 1956 the apartheid government removed all remaining suffrage rights for non-whites, appointing many extra senators to force the change through.

During the apartheid era the policy of homelands carved territory out of existing provinces. In the Cape Province the Transkei was declared independent in 1976 and the Ciskei in 1981, and Griqualand East was transferred to Natal after Transkei's independence cut it off. Walvis Bay was ceded to Namibia two months before the first fully democratic elections of April 1994. After the Interim Constitution the homelands were reincorporated, and the Cape Province was divided into the Western Cape, Eastern Cape and Northern Cape, with parts absorbed into the North West.
cape-town: Cape Town stands on the shore of Table Bay, at a latitude of about 33.55 degrees south. Table Mountain, with near vertical cliffs and a flat summit more than 1,000 metres high, forms a mountainous backdrop with Devil's Peak and Lion's Head on either side and creates the City Bowl, which holds the central business district. To the south the Cape Peninsula runs 40 kilometres into the Atlantic Ocean and ends at Cape Point, and many suburbs lie on the Cape Flats, a plain that joins the peninsula to the mainland. Robben Island in Table Bay is part of the city, and Table Mountain National Park lies within its boundaries.

The earliest known remains of human occupation in the region were found at Peers Cave in Fish Hoek in the late 1920s; earlier estimates of an upper Pleistocene origin have since been revised to the mid-Holocene. Bartolomeu Dias, the first European to reach the area, arrived in 1488 and named it the Cape of Storms. John II of Portugal renamed it the Cape of Good Hope, because the opening of a sea route to India raised such optimism, and Vasco da Gama recorded sighting it in 1497. In 1510, at the Battle of Salt River, the Portuguese admiral Francisco de Almeida and sixty-four of his men were killed by the Khoikhoi Goringhaiqua, who used cattle trained to respond to whistles and shouts.

Ships of several nations, mainly Portuguese, regularly stopped in Table Bay in the late sixteenth century on the way to the Indies. They traded tobacco, copper and iron with the Khoikhoi clans of the region for fresh meat and other provisions. In 1652 Jan van Riebeeck and other employees of the United East India Company were sent to establish a way-station for ships travelling to the Dutch East Indies, and they built the Fort de Goede Hoop, later replaced by the Castle of Good Hope.

The settlement grew slowly because adequate labour was hard to find. The shortage led the local authorities to import enslaved people from Indonesia and Madagascar, many of whom are ancestors of the present Cape Coloured and Cape Malay communities.

Cape Town is the legislative capital of South Africa, the seat of its Parliament, and the capital of the Western Cape. It is the country's oldest city. It has the highest density of Cape Dutch buildings in the world, a style that combines the architectural traditions of the Netherlands, Germany, France and Indonesia. Mostert's Mill in Mowbray, built in 1796, is the only complete windmill in South Africa. The Cape Floristic Region, including Kirstenbosch National Botanical Garden, was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2004.
cape-verde: Cape Verde is a horseshoe-shaped cluster of ten volcanic islands, nine of them inhabited, and eight islets, with a land area of about 4,033 square kilometres. They lie between 600 and 850 km west of Cap-Vert on the Senegalese coast, from which the country takes its name. Cap-Vert comes from the Portuguese Cabo Verde, meaning green cape, a name Portuguese explorers gave to the headland in 1444. The islands are divided into the Barlavento or windward group in the north and the Sotavento or leeward group in the south. Santiago is the largest and holds the capital, Praia.

The islands were uninhabited before the arrival of Europeans. Genoese and Portuguese navigators found them around 1456. Portuguese records credit the first discoveries to António de Noli, born in Genoa, who was later appointed governor by King Afonso V. In 1462 Portuguese settlers founded Ribeira Grande on Santiago, today called Cidade Velha, the first permanent European settlement in the tropics.

In the 16th century the islands prospered from the Atlantic slave trade. The English privateer Francis Drake sacked Ribeira Grande twice in 1585, when it was part of the Iberian Union, and after a French attack in 1712 the town declined relative to Praia, which became the capital in 1770. The decline of the slave trade in the 19th century brought economic crisis, but the islands' position on mid-Atlantic shipping lanes made them a good place to resupply ships, and the harbour of Mindelo grew into a commercial centre. In 1951 Portugal changed the status of Cape Verde from a colony to an overseas province in an attempt to blunt nationalism. The country became independent in 1975.

Cape Verde is a unitary semi-presidential republic whose constitution was adopted in 1980 and revised in 1992, 1995 and 1999. Praia is the capital and largest city. Portuguese is the official language, and Cape Verdean Creole, called Kriolu, is the mother tongue of virtually all Cape Verdeans. The people descend from Africans, free or enslaved, and Europeans of various origins, and the diaspora outnumbers the people on the islands.
cape-verdean-creole: The early history of Cape Verdean Creole is hard to trace because of a lack of written documents and because the language was shunned under Portuguese administration. Scholars hold three theories of its formation. One holds that the Portuguese simplified their own language to make it accessible to enslaved African people, a view associated with Prudent, Waldman, Chaudenson and Lopes da Silva. A second, put by Adam and Quint, holds that enslaved African people built it on the grammar of West African languages and replaced the African vocabulary with Portuguese words.

A third, from linguists such as Chomsky and Bickerton, holds that it arose spontaneously among the population born on the islands, through universal grammar. Its phonology comes mainly from Portuguese of the 15th to 17th centuries, and it keeps some consonants that today's Portuguese has lost.

Between 90 and 95 per cent of its words come from Portuguese, and the rest from West African languages such as Mandingo, Wolof, Fulani, Temne, Balanta and Mandjak. Its grammar, however, is very different from Portuguese, and resembles that of other creoles. The basic order is subject, verb, object. Verbs have only two forms, the same for every person, and tense, mood and aspect are shown by small particles.

There are no definite articles, only demonstratives, and only nouns for people and animals have gender. Double and even triple negation is possible. Each of the nine inhabited islands has its own variant, grouped into the southern Sotavento creoles, which include Santiago and Fogo, and the northern Barlavento creoles, which include São Vicente and Santo Antão.

Almost all Cape Verdeans learn Creole as their first language, but Portuguese remains the official language and is used in schools, administration and foreign relations. The two live in a state of diglossia, and speakers switch between them in informal talk. The only writing system recognised by the authorities is the Unified Alphabet for the Writing of the Cape Verdean Language, ALUPEC, approved on an experimental basis by Decree-Law No.

67/98 in 1998 and institutionalised by Decree-Law No. 8/2009 in 2009. It is neither required nor always used, and the law allows other systematic models. Writers have long used Creole for literature and song: Eugénio Tavares wrote poems in the Brava variant, and the lyrics of Nôs Ráça by Manuel d'Novas are in São Vicente Creole.
capernaum: The original name, Kfar Naḥum, means "village of comfort" in Hebrew, and there is apparently no connection with the prophet Nahum. Josephus wrote it in Greek as Kepharnōkón, and in Arabic the site is called Talḥūm, taken to mean the ruin (tall) of Ḥūm.

The village had no defensive wall and stretched along the northwestern shore of the lake. Fishing was a major source of income, and the remains of an ancient harbour lie west of the modern one built by the Franciscans. Tabgha, 2.5 kilometres away, seems to have been farmland, judging by the many oil and grain mills found there.

The houses were built of coarse basalt blocks reinforced with stone and mud, without mortar. Each stood around a courtyard that held a circular furnace, grain mills and stairs to the roof, and several extended families shared courtyards and doorless passages. Most finds are of clay, together with fish hooks, net weights, weaving bobbins and basalt mills for grain and olives. From the 4th century the houses were built with good mortar and fine ceramics, yet differences in social class are not noticeable.

The synagogue visible today was built of white limestone brought from distant quarries, standing out among the black basalt of the other buildings. It seems to date from the 4th or 5th century. Its prayer hall measured 24.4 by 18.65 metres, and it carries inscriptions in Greek and Aramaic naming benefactors, with carvings of palm trees and of five- and six-pointed stars. Loffreda suggests that a basalt foundation beneath it belonged to a 1st-century synagogue, though others read the paved surface there as an open market area. The village was re-established northeast of the earlier site in about 700, in the Early Islamic period.

Edward Robinson found ruins in 1838 without linking them to Capernaum, and in 1866 Charles William Wilson identified the site, then known as Tell Hum. The Franciscans bought much of the land in 1894, and Kohl and Watzinger began their study of Galilean synagogues in 1905. A Greek Orthodox monastery and church were built on the eastern part of the site in 1931.

Excavators concluded that a compound called the sacra insula held a house venerated as Peter's from the 1st century, with an octagonal church built over it in the middle of the 5th century. A modern memorial church, dedicated in 1990, stands on eight concrete stilts over the remains, with a glass floor that lets visitors look down on them.
capetian-dynasty: The Capetian dynasty, also called the House of France, is of Frankish origin. Agnatically it is a branch of the Robertians, and it descends from the Carolingians through female lines. It takes its name from its founder, Hugh Capet, whose nickname Capet has an unknown meaning; one suggestion links it to the Latin caput, head. Nineteenth-century historians applied the name to the ruling house of France and to all the male-line descendants of Hugh; it was not a contemporary practice. In 987 Hugh Capet was elected to succeed Louis V, the last of the Carolingian dynasty that had ruled France for over three centuries.

The Capetian monarchy began as one of the weakest in Europe, its direct rule confined to the Île-de-France. The early Capetians associated their elder sons with them in the kingship, which established hereditary succession and turned a theoretically elective kingship into a sacral one. By the reign of Philip II Augustus, who became king in 1180, the hold was so strong that the practice was dropped. The kings extended their power slowly while the great peers of the realm lost theirs in succession crises. The senior line ruled until the death of Charles IV in 1328.

Charles IV died without male heirs, and the French lords, who rejected the claim of Edward III of England through his mother Isabella, made Philip of Valois king. From then on the succession excluded females and claims through the female line, a rule known as Salic law. The crown passed to the House of Valois and then to the House of Bourbon. The Revolution abolished the monarchy in 1792 and Louis XVI was executed in 1793. The Bourbons returned in 1814 and left the throne in 1830 for Louis Philippe I of the House of Orléans, the last Capetian king of France, who reigned until 1848.

By tradition, younger sons and brothers of the king received appanages to maintain their rank and discourage them from claiming the crown. Capetian cadets therefore aimed at foreign thrones, and the family has reigned in Portugal, Sicily and Naples, Navarre, Hungary, Poland, Spain and Sardinia, in the grand duchies of Lithuania and Luxembourg, and in the Latin and Brazilian empires. Cadet branches of the House of Bourbon still reign in Spain and Luxembourg.
capetian-house-of-anjou: The Capetian House of Anjou, also called the House of Anjou-Sicily, was a cadet branch of the Capetian dynasty and one of three royal houses called Angevin. Its founder, Charles of Anjou, was a younger son of Louis VIII of France. His brother Louis IX, who came to the throne in 1226, named him Count of Anjou and Maine, and he was invested in August 1246. Charles married Beatrice of Provence, an heiress of the County of Provence, and so became Count of Provence. After fighting in the Seventh Crusade he was offered the Kingdom of Sicily by Pope Clement IV, because of the conflict between the papacy and the Holy Roman Empire, which the ruling House of Hohenstaufen represented.

Charles was invested by the pope as King of Sicily in June 1265 and crowned on 5 January 1266. At the Battle of Benevento on 26 February 1266 he defeated King Manfred. In 1271 he acquired Albanian territory from the Despotate of Epirus and in February 1272 took the title King of Albania. The War of the Sicilian Vespers in the 1280s split the kingdom: the island of Sicily passed to the Crown of Aragon, while the kingdom of Naples stayed under Angevin control. The Angevins held Durrës until 1368.

The house divided into branches. Anjou-Hungary ruled Hungary and, from 1370 to 1399, Poland; Anjou-Taranto ruled the remnants of the Latin Empire; and Anjou-Durazzo ruled Naples from 1382 to 1435. Charles II married Mary of Hungary in 1270, and their eldest son, Charles Martel of Anjou, claimed the Hungarian crown without gaining enough support from the magnates. His son Charles Robert won a civil war and ruled from 1308 to 1342. Louis I of Hungary became king of Poland in 1370 under the Privilege of Buda of 1355, but the union ended after his death in 1382, when his daughter Hedwig was crowned in Poland.

In Naples, Robert the Wise left his kingdom in 1343 to his granddaughter Joanna, making no mention of Andrew, who was thus denied the right to reign beside her. Andrew was later strangled by noble conspirators at Aversa; the involvement of Joanna is unproved. The senior Durazzo line died out in the male line with King Ladislaus of Naples in 1414 and completely with his sister Joanna II in 1435. Over the Middle Ages the house had ruled the counties of Anjou, Maine, Touraine, Provence and Forcalquier, the principalities of Achaea and Taranto, and the kingdoms of Sicily, Naples, Hungary, Croatia, Albania and Poland.
capetian-house-of-burgundy: The House of Burgundy was a cadet branch of the Capetian dynasty, descending from Robert I, Duke of Burgundy, a younger son of King Robert II of France. He lived from 1011 to 1076, and his brother was Henry I of France. The house ruled the Duchy of Burgundy from 1032 to 1361. Besides Robert I, the notable members of the main line include Hugh III, Odo IV and Philip I, Duke of Burgundy, together with Margaret of Burgundy, the first wife and queen of Louis X of France, and Joan the Lame, the first wife and queen of Philip VI of France.

The main line passed from father to son through Hugh I, Odo I, Hugh II, Odo II and Hugh III, then Odo III, Hugh IV, Robert II, Hugh V and Odo IV, who died in 1349. His grandson Philip of Rouvres, who succeeded in 1349 and is numbered Philip I in the genealogy, was the last member of the house. He died childless in 1361, and the duchy reverted to his liege, who two years later created his own son the new duke of Burgundy, beginning the Younger House of Burgundy.

The house also had cadet lines. The Montagu branch descended from Alexandre, Lord of Montagu, who died in 1205, and held a number of lordships in Burgundy over later centuries, including Sombernon and Couches. Other younger sons included Louis, King of Thessalonica, who lived from 1297 to 1316, and Robert, Count of Tonnerre.

The Portuguese House of Burgundy was founded by Henry, Count of Portugal, in 1093, and he was the father of the first Portuguese king, Afonso Henriques. The senior legitimate line went extinct with the death of King Ferdinand I of Portugal in 1383, but two illegitimate lines, the Houses of Aviz and Braganza, continued to rule in Portugal, with interruptions, until 1910, and later in Brazil until 1889. Through this branch the house achieved the recognised title of King of Portugal.
capital-cities-and-tombs-of-the-ancient-: The sites lie in Ji'an, in Jilin Province, and Huanren, in Liaoning Province, in north-east China. They belong to Goguryeo, also written Koguryo or, in Chinese, Gaogouli, a Korean kingdom that lasted from 37 BCE to 668 CE and lay in the northern and central parts of the Korean Peninsula and the southern and central parts of Manchuria. The site was designated a cultural World Heritage Site in 2004 under the first five of the six criteria for cultural heritage. Its designation includes the remains of three fortress-cities, Wunü Mountain City, Gungnae and Hwando, and forty identified tombs of Goguryeo imperial and noble families.

Wunü Mountain City, known in Korean as Onyeosanseong, was the first capital of Goguryeo and has been only partly excavated. Gungnae and Hwando were also capitals. Gungnae lies within the modern city of Ji'an and served as a supporting capital after the main capital moved to Pyongyang. Hwando holds many remains, among them a large palace and many tombs. The capitals are an early example of mountain cities that neighbouring cultures later imitated, and the system represented by Gungnae and the mountain city influenced the later capitals built by the Goguryeo state. They are also described as a blending of human construction with rocks, forests and rivers.

The forty tombs were built by Goguryeo rulers and nobles. Some have elaborate ceilings designed to roof wide spaces without columns, able to carry the weight of a stone or earth mound placed above them. The wall paintings show artistic skill and a specific style, and also strong influence from various cultures.

North Korea began trying to register the sites for World Heritage from around 2000. Registration was scheduled for 2003, but China opposed North Korea's sole registration and applied for the Goguryeo ruins scattered in Jilin Province. The remains of both countries were therefore registered together in 2004. A dispute exists between North Korea and China over the history of Goguryeo. In 2010 the Chinese government established the Ji'an Gaogouli National Archaeological Park, which includes all the Goguryeo World Heritage sites in Ji'an and Jilin, but not those in Liaoning, such as Wunü Mountain City.
capitalism: Capitalism in its modern form is traced to agrarian capitalism and mercantilism in the early Renaissance, in city-states such as Florence. Capital had existed on a small scale for centuries in merchant, renting and lending activities. During the Islamic Golden Age, Arabs promulgated policies such as free trade and banking, and their use of Indo-Arabic numerals facilitated bookkeeping; these innovations reached Europe through Venice and Pisa.

In 16th-century England the manorial system broke down, land became concentrated in fewer landlords and workers were increasingly employed in a money-based economy instead of as serfs. From the 16th to the 18th centuries mercantilism prevailed, a system of trade for profit, though goods were still largely produced by non-capitalist methods. Most scholars see it as the origin of the modern system, but Karl Polanyi held that capitalism required generalised markets for land, labour and money, and so could not be said to exist before 1834, when a competitive labour market was established in England.

Capitalism is an economic system based on private ownership of the means of production and its use to obtain profit. Its elements include private property, the profit motive, capital accumulation, competitive markets and wage labour. Its forms, among them laissez-faire, state and welfare capitalism, differ in their degree of free markets, public ownership and regulation. There is no universally agreed definition.

The term capitalist, meaning an owner of capital, dates to the mid-17th century. Louis Blanc in 1850 and Pierre-Joseph Proudhon in 1861 are credited with the first modern use of capitalism, and Karl Marx wrote of the capitalist mode of production in Das Kapital (1867). Because socialist critics coined the word, Robert Hessen called it a term of disparagement.

The Industrial Revolution of the 18th century made capitalism the dominant mode of production, characterised by factory work and a complex division of labour. It spread across the world in the 19th and 20th centuries. In the 19th century it was largely unregulated; after World War II it became more regulated through Keynesianism, followed from the 1980s by a return of less regulated capitalism termed neoliberalism.
capitoline-hill: The Capitoline Hill lies between the Forum and the Campus Martius. It was earlier known as Mons Saturnius, after the god Saturn. The word Capitolium first meant the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus and then came to cover the whole hill. Ancient sources connected the name with caput, Latin for head, through a tale that a man's head was found when the temple's foundations were laid. The Romans regarded the Capitolium as indestructible and adopted it as a symbol of eternity. On its eastern lower slopes stood the Vulcanal, a sacred precinct of the 8th century BCE.

The temple of the Capitoline Triad was started by Rome's fifth king, Tarquinius Priscus, and completed by the last, Tarquinius Superbus. It was nearly as large as the Parthenon. Temples of Juno Moneta and of Virtus also stood on the hill. When the Senones Gauls raided Rome in 390 BCE, the Capitoline was the one part of the city they did not take, because its defenders had fortified it. According to legend, the sacred geese of Juno warned Marcus Manlius Capitolinus of the attack. In the Year of Four Emperors, 69 CE, Vespasian's brother and nephew were besieged in the temple, and it burned down.

In the Middle Ages the hill's religious role was overshadowed by its use as the seat of Rome's civic government, revived as a commune in the 12th century. After a revolt against the pope and the nobles in 1144, a senator took up residence there. His palace turned its back on the ancient Forum, a change of orientation that Michelangelo later accentuated. Pope Paul III commissioned Michelangelo Buonarroti in 1536 to redesign the piazza, partly to impress Emperor Charles V, who was expected in 1538. The work ran from 1536 to 1546, and the Campidoglio was completed in the 17th century. Michelangelo faced the new piazza towards St. Peter's Basilica, and the paving design was finished only in 1940, on the order of Benito Mussolini.

The Palazzo dei Conservatori, the Palazzo Nuovo and the Palazzo Senatorio enclose the trapezoidal Piazza del Campidoglio, which is approached by the wide ramped stair called the cordonata. The first two palazzi, with the Palazzo Senatorio, now house the Capitoline Museums, and the Palazzo Senatorio is also the Roman city hall. The equestrian statue of Marcus Aurelius in the piazza is a modern copy; the original is in the Palazzo dei Conservatori. The church of Santa Maria in Aracoeli stands beside the square, and the English word capitol derives from Capitolium.
capitulare-de-villis: The capitulary is one of several issued by Carolingian rulers on the running of their estates, and it may belong to the later years of the reign of Charlemagne. Its origin is disputed: the manuscript has been claimed for Fulda or the Rhineland, and its date and the circumstances of its making are debated. It was probably written as the court settled at a fixed palace, to solve the problem of supplying food and equipment to an administration far from its estates.

A study of 1912 argued that Louis the Pious wrote it for his estate reform in Aquitaine in 794, citing plants that grew only in southern France. Others have linked it to the famine of 792–3, to curbing abuses on the royal estates, or to supplying the army. No answer has won general support.

Its seventy chapters follow no logical order. Most of the text sets out the duties of the iudex, the official in charge of royal properties: to avoid corruption, guard the estates against theft, prosecute criminals fairly, present certain items to the king each year, and above all keep an accurate inventory and send the estate's food, money and goods to the court. The stewards also dispensed justice in the king's absence.

Fish ponds, byres, pigsties, sheepfolds, goat-pens, mills and barns are prescribed, with how much land to keep as forest and how much to clear, and villae kept ready to receive the king. Wine receives special attention, as do horses and puppies, while crops are mostly given as quotas. Craftsmen from blacksmiths to weavers were to work on each estate.

A comparison with the Brevium Exempla, which records real audits of several estates, shows that the capitulary was largely aspirational and did not always, if ever, match reality. It is no longer used to explain the whole economic and social order of the Carolingian world, but remains important for its material culture and administration. Its carts and produce for the army and its care for horse breeding point to preparations for war. It also shows the queen with authority over the stewards: her orders sent through the butler or seneschal were to be obeyed, and she could set a penalty when the iudex's orders went unheeded.
capitulary: Capitularies came from the Frankish court of both the Merovingian and the Carolingian dynasties, above all that of Charlemagne. The name comes from capitulum, a diminutive of caput, head or heading. Once a capitulary was composed it was sent to the archbishops, bishops, missi dominici and counts, and a copy was kept by the chancellor in the palace archives. After the reign of Louis the Pious they grew long and diffuse, and the last emperor to issue them was Lambert of Italy, in 898. The Lombards also had capitularies, which continued their own laws.

The editor Alfred Boretius divided them into classes. Capitula legibus addenda added to the laws of the peoples, such as the Salic, Ripuarian or Bavarian law, and were promulgated in local assemblies where the people's consent was asked. Capitula ecclesiastica gave force to the canons of councils of bishops, capitula per se scribenda were political decrees binding on all subjects, and capitula missorum were instructions to the missi on their circuits. Other documents were joined to them, among them the Capitulare de villis on the royal estates and the partitions of the kingdom in the Divisio regnorum of 806 and the Ordinatio imperii of 817.

No capitulary survives in its original form; they are known from copies in manuscripts going back to the 9th and 10th centuries. In 827 Ansegisus, abbot of St. Wandrille, gathered them in four books, which Louis the Pious was citing after 829. By 858 a writer calling himself Benedictus Levita had added three more books mixing in Roman law, church canons and spurious provisions, and modern historians avoid citing them. Étienne Baluze published a new classification in 1677, and the Monumenta Germaniae Historica edition was begun by Boretius in 1883 and continued by Victor Krause.
capitulation-of-wittenberg: Since the Treaty of Leipzig of 1485 the lands of the House of Wettin had been divided between the senior Ernestine branch, which held the electoral dignity, and the junior Albertine branch, which ruled as dukes. In the early Reformation the two lines took opposite sides: the Ernestine Elector Frederick III supported Luther, while his Albertine cousin George, Duke of Saxony, tried to halt the new movements. The Reformation took hold in the Albertine lands under George's brother Henry IV.

Henry's son Maurice was also a Lutheran, but in 1546 he sided with Emperor Charles V against the Protestant princes of the Schmalkaldic League, which was led by his Ernestine cousin John Frederick I. In the Schmalkaldic War of 1547 John Frederick was taken prisoner at the Battle of Mühlberg, and the emperor, aided by the Duke of Alba, went on to take Wittenberg.

Alba presided over a court-martial that condemned John Frederick to death. To save his life the elector conceded defeat, and his sentence was commuted to imprisonment for life. He resigned the offices of Prince-Elector and Arch-Marshal of the Holy Roman Empire, and the electoral title passed to Maurice with large parts of the Ernestine lands, including the core Duchy of Saxe-Wittenberg. Maurice became the first Saxon elector of the Albertine line.

The treaty brought a radical territorial reshaping of the Electorate of Saxony. John Frederick was released with imperial consent on 1 September 1552 and returned to the remaining Ernestine domains in a triumphal march, moving the seat of his government to Weimar. Several questions still open between the Ernestine and Albertine branches were settled later by the Treaty of Naumburg of 1554.
capitulations-of-santa-fe: The agreement followed a form used in Catalonia since the 14th century, in which the king agreed specific conditions with those who built ships and went to sea, set out in chapters, or capítulos. The first documented capitulation dates from 1363. When Columbus's proposal was first rejected, Queen Isabella called another assembly of sailors, philosophers, astrologers and others, who judged his estimate of the distance to the Indies absurd. A group of influential courtiers, among them Hernando de Talavera, the notary Luis de Santángel and the chamberlain Juan Cabrero, persuaded the monarchs that they would lose little if the project failed and gain much if it succeeded.

Juan II Coloma, secretary to Ferdinand II, was ordered to draw up the text, which took three months to prepare because the monarchs were busy with other matters. Besides the titles and the share of riches, it granted Columbus the honorific don. It was sealed at the Santa Fe encampment, which had been built outside Granada as a base during the siege of the city. Columbus asked for agreements that applied only in the Catalan-Aragonese kingdom, since the Catholic Monarchs ruled their realms under their separate legal systems.

The original document has not survived. The earliest copy is in the confirmations the Crown issued in Barcelona in 1493, as the Capitulations were binding in Catalan law. The text does not mention Asia, which has led some historians to suggest that Columbus never meant to go there, only to discover new lands. In 2009 UNESCO inscribed the Capitulations on the Memory of the World International Register.
capitulations-of-the-ottoman-empire: The capitulations, known in Ottoman Turkish as ahidnâmes, were grants made by successive sultans to Christian states, following a policy the Byzantine Empire had already pursued towards the European powers. They were first granted to each state separately, beginning with the Genoese in 1453. Later documents summed up earlier concessions and added whatever had been granted to any other state, a clause that became a most favoured nation article.

France is generally seen as having initiated them. The first well-documented agreement was concluded in 1569 between Charles IX of France and Selim II. Historians have questioned references to earlier agreements between Louis XII and Bayezid II in 1500 and between Francis I and Suleiman the Magnificent in the mid-1530s, the latter being generally viewed as only a draft.

Under the capitulations, foreign traders were exempt from local prosecution, local taxation and local conscription, and their homes could not be searched. Foreigners resident in the empire were subject to the laws of their own countries, so that the French consul, for example, judged disputes involving French merchants instead of the Islamic sharia courts. An ahidnâme did not in itself signify a reciprocal engagement, unlike a treaty (mouahede), but later confirmations gave the grants a lasting force.

The 1673 renewal between Louis XIV and Mehmed IV made the French monarchy protector of all Christians in the empire, a role the Pope never acknowledged. The Ottoman-French Treaty of 1740 marked the height of French influence in the eighteenth century, and grants to Britain and the Netherlands (1737), Naples (1740), Denmark (1756) and Prussia (1761) were meant to balance it. After the Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca of 1774, rivalry between France and Russia over the protection of Christians did much to ignite the Crimean War.

On 8 September 1914 the ruling Committee of Union and Progress abrogated the capitulations unilaterally, amid diplomatic manoeuvring with Germany and the United Kingdom over whether the empire would enter the First World War. The German, Austro-Hungarian, British, French and Russian ambassadors protested jointly, and the decision took effect in early October.

For Turkey the capitulations were abolished by Article 28 of the Treaty of Lausanne in 1923. In Egypt they ended in 1949, as laid down by the Montreux Convention Regarding the Abolition of the Capitulations in Egypt of 1937. Over their history, capitulatory treaties were signed with states from Venice and England to the United States (1830), Brazil (1858) and Bavaria (1870).
capo-colonna: In Roman times the promontory was called Promunturium Lacinium. A sanctuary of Hera stood there from the 7th century BCE, closely linked to the Greek colony of Kroton nearby, and became one of the most important sanctuaries of Magna Graecia. The temple was said to be still fairly complete in the 16th century, when it was pulled down to build the episcopal palace at Crotone; the surviving Doric column with its capital is about 8.2 metres high.

In 194 BCE, after the Second Punic War, Rome founded a maritime colony at the cape, entrusted to the triumvirs Cn. Octavius, L. Aemilius Paulus and C. Laetorius. At least 91 farms occupied its hinterland, and the colony may have counted around 1,500 citizens with their families. In 190 BCE the prefect of the Roman fleet inspected ships here before they sailed against Antiochus III. The town covered the northern end of the promontory on a rectangular street plan that left the sanctuary on its own alignment.

Wealthy houses rose from the late 2nd century BCE, and in 80–70 BCE the duumvirs Lucilius Macer and Annaeus Trasus turned an older public building into baths with mosaic floors. The walls were rebuilt after pirate raids and the siege by Sextus Pompeius in 36 BCE. Decline probably began after the Augustan era, and the settlement shrank around the sanctuary, appearing as Licenium on the Peutinger Map; an altar of 98–105 CE dedicated for Ulpia Marciana, the sister of Trajan, shows that Hera Lacinia was still honoured.

In 982 the Battle of Cape Colonna was fought here, in which the forces of the Fatimid Caliphate defeated the army of the Holy Roman Empire under Otto II. Many German nobles and churchmen were killed, as was the Emir of Sicily, Abu'l-Qasim.

The whole peninsula lies within the Capo Colonna Archaeological Park, and a museum nearby holds important finds. Excavations from 2014 have greatly increased knowledge of the site, and the cape keeps its modern name from the one remaining column of the Temple of Hera Lacinia.
captaincies-of-brazil: The Portuguese crown had used captaincies, land grants with extensive governing privileges, to settle Madeira, the Azores and other Atlantic islands. After the expedition of Martim Afonso de Sousa in 1530, with brazilwood to exploit and rumours of silver and gold in the interior, the crown decided on permanent colonies but lacked the people and money to found them itself. King John III began the grants in Brazil with Pernambuco, by the royal Golden Letter of 24 September 1534.

The first captaincies were drawn as strips parallel to the equator, from the coast west to the Tordesillas Line, each nominally fifty leagues wide, though pairs of rivers set the real boundaries. Initially fifteen, they went to twelve donees: five to Martim Afonso de Sousa and his brother Pero Lopes, cousins of the finance minister António de Ataíde, one to Pero de Gois, and the rest to military men and court bureaucrats. Four donees never took possession of their lands and four more quickly succumbed to the Indians.

Only São Vicente, Pernambuco, Ilhéus and Porto Seguro survived past 1549. When Bahia reverted to the crown after the massacre of its donee Francisco Pereira Coutinho and his settlers by indigenous people, John III placed a royal governor there and rescinded some of the donees' privileges.
