Pernambuco, which thrived on sugarcane, saw no royal governor until the 17th century, and São Vicente prospered through the bandeiras into the hinterland. The captaincies continued as governments subordinate to the governors-general and viceroys, and the last private one reverted to the crown in 1754.

Their boundaries in the later 18th century became the basis of the provinces of Brazil, and in 1815 all existing provinces and crown captaincies became provinces of the United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves. Thirteen modern states bear the names of their predecessor captaincies, which also preserved many Tupi-guarani names of rivers and mountains, and the huge fazendas of the 18th and 19th centuries were allotted from the captaincies' land holdings.
cara-al-sol: To give the Falange a song of its own, its leader José Antonio Primo de Rivera called a committee that met on 2 December 1935 in the home of Marichu de la Mora Maura. Those present included José María Alfaro, Rafael Sánchez Mazas, Agustín de Foxá, Pedro Mourlane Michelena, Dionisio Ridruejo, Agustín Aznar and Luis Aguilar. After further review by a sub-committee at the Cueva del Orkompon, a Basque bar in Madrid, the result was provisionally called the Himno de Falange Española.

The music, credited to Juan Tellería and Juan R. Buendia, was based on Tellería's 1935 piece Amanecer en Cegama (Dawn at Zegama). The words are usually credited to Primo de Rivera, under whose editorship they were written together: Foxá, Ridruejo, Alfaro and Mourlane are each named for particular lines, and the last four lines were existing Falange slogans.

The song opens with the new shirt, the plain blue working-class shirt of the Falangist uniform, embroidered over the heart with the party's red yoke and five arrows. Later lines allude to the arrows of that Yoke and Arrows symbol and to the Falangist youth movement, and pay homage to fallen comrades. It closes with a version of the rally chant España Una, Grande y Libre and the Falangist cry Arriba España in place of the more usual Viva España.

The song's popularity grew after Primo de Rivera was executed on 20 November 1936 and glorified by the Spanish Nationalists. It was the Falange's anthem throughout the Spanish Civil War, when Falangist units fought beside the insurgent army. In Francoist Spain, where the Falange was merged into the single legal party, it became a national song alongside the Carlist Oriamendi and the anthem of the Spanish Legion, often played with the official Marcha Granadera; a decree of 1942 ordered the national songs to be saluted with a Roman salute at official events.

After the war the anthem's words gave the name new shirts to those who had joined the party during or after the war, as against the old shirts who had joined before it. A slow version, Amanecer, close to a love ballad and sometimes sung by a woman, appeared after the war. Since the Spanish transition to democracy the song has often been played at far-right rallies.
caracalla: Caracalla was born Lucius Septimius Bassianus at Lugdunum in Gaul, the elder son of Septimius Severus and Julia Domna. At seven he was renamed Marcus Aurelius Antoninus as part of his father's attempt at union with the families of Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius.

His father, acclaimed Augustus in 193, had himself adopted posthumously by Marcus Aurelius, and Caracalla was made Caesar in 195 or 196. On 28 January 198, aged nine, he became joint Augustus, on the day of his father's triumph over the Parthian Empire, and in 202 he was consul with his father.

Severus died at Eboracum on 4 February 211 while on campaign in Caledonia, leaving Caracalla and his brother Geta as joint rulers. On 26 December 211, at a reconciliation meeting arranged by their mother, Geta was killed by Praetorian Guards loyal to Caracalla, and it is widely accepted that Caracalla ordered it. He persecuted Geta's supporters, and the Senate pronounced a damnatio memoriae on Geta, whose name it became a capital offence to speak or write; an estimated 20,000 people were massacred. Julia Domna took on more of the government, since Caracalla found administration mundane.

In 212 he issued the Constitutio Antoniniana, granting full Roman citizenship to all free inhabitants of the empire except the dediticii. In 213 he left Rome, never to return, and campaigned against the Alamanni on the German frontier, defeating some tribes and settling others by diplomacy. In December 215 he slaughtered a deputation of leading citizens at Alexandria after the city mocked his claim to have killed Geta in self-defence, and set his troops loose on the city for several days of looting.
He raised the annual pay of a legionary from 2,000 sesterces to 2,700 to 3,000, and the cost led him to debase the coinage. In 215 he introduced the antoninianus, intended as a double denarius.

In 216 Caracalla began a campaign against the Parthians after King Artabanus IV refused a marriage proposal. On 8 April 217, travelling from Edessa to Carrhae to visit a temple of the moon god Sin, he was stabbed by a Roman soldier, Justin Martialis, and the two Praetorian tribunes completed the killing. Macrinus succeeded him three days later, and had him deified.

Cassius Dio, Herodian and the Historia Augusta portray him as a cruel tyrant and a soldier first and an emperor second, a view that has largely persisted. The Constitutio Antoniniana goes almost unnoticed in the classical records. In the late 18th century French painters revived his image, as the tyranny ascribed to him seemed to parallel that ascribed to Louis XVI.
caracas: Caracas lies along the Guaire River in the Caracas Valley of the Venezuelan Central Range, a small and irregular valley close to the Caribbean Sea. A steep range, Cerro El Ávila, rises 2,200 metres between the valley and the shore, and about 15 kilometres of El Ávila National Park separate the city from the coast. The valley floor lies between 870 and 1,043 metres above sea level, and the historic centre stands at about 900 metres. The highest point of the Capital District, Pico El Ávila, reaches 2,159 metres.

The Guaire crosses the city and empties into the Tuy River. The city is occasionally struck by earthquakes, notably in 1641, 1812 and 1967. The region was formed in the Late Cretaceous, and the city sits mostly on metamorphic rock.

Before the city was founded in 1567, the valley was populated by indigenous peoples. Francisco Fajardo, the son of a Spanish captain and a Waikeri cacique, began establishing settlements around La Guaira and the Caracas valley between 1555 and 1560. His plantation of 1562 did not last, as natives of the region led by Terepaima and Guaicaipuro destroyed it, as they had destroyed the Villa de San Francisco founded by Juan Rodríguez de Suárez in 1561.

The settlers who eventually founded Caracas came from Coro, the capital of the German colony of Klein-Venedig, which Spaniards had controlled in practice from the 1540s. Moving eastward, they founded inland towns including Barquisimeto and Valencia before reaching the valley. In 1591 Simón de Bolívar, an ancestor of the liberator Simón Bolívar, petitioned King Philip II for a coat of arms. The king granted it by Royal Cedula on 4 September 1591 and declared Caracas The Most Noble and Very Loyal City of Santiago de León de Caracas.

Caracas is the capital and largest city of Venezuela and the centre of a metropolitan region estimated at over 5 million people. Its historic centre is the Caracas Cathedral on Bolívar Square. The Central University of Venezuela, founded in 1721, is the oldest university in the country, and its campus, designed by the architect Carlos Raúl Villanueva, was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000.

In the 1940s and 1950s, after the Second World War, a wave of European immigrants, mainly Spanish, Italian and Portuguese, settled in the country, and the city has been shaped by many ethnic and cultural groups. The Caracas Metro has operated since 27 March 1983.
caracazo: During Carlos Andrés Pérez's first presidency, from 1973 to 1979, high oil prices encouraged heavy borrowing, and a fall in oil prices in the mid-1980s brought an economic crisis. Pérez won the 1988 election with 53% of the vote after campaigning against the International Monetary Fund. When he took office on 2 February 1989, international reserves stood at US$300 million, the national debt at US$34 billion and the poverty rate at 70%. On 16 February he announced a package of shock measures recommended by the IMF, El Gran Viraje (The Great Turn), which its critics called El Paquetazo.

The package was rejected by all political parties, including his own, but Pérez ignored them. Gasoline prices rose 100 per cent over the weekend of 25–26 February. Public transport fares were officially to rise 30 per cent from 1 March, but bus drivers applied the increase on 27 February, a day before payday.

Rioting began on the morning of 27 February in Guarenas, about 30 kilometres (19 mi) east of Caracas, and spread to Caracas and other towns. Pérez dismissed warnings and ordered Plan Ávila, a military contingency plan in place since the 1960s. On 28 February the government imposed a state of emergency and martial law and suspended constitutional rights, among them individual liberty, the inviolability of the home, freedom of expression and the right to peaceful protest.

Troops fired on crowds and into poor neighbourhoods. In Petare twenty people were reported killed by troops, and in 23 de Enero young, inexperienced soldiers fired automatic weapons at apartment blocks, killing unarmed residents. Gunfights between radical groups and the army began on 1 March, and the last documented death came on 5 March.

Initial official figures gave 276 dead; after hundreds of unmarked graves were found, many estimates put the toll above 2,000 and up to 5,000. The Comité de Familiares de Víctimas del Caracazo estimates that 97% of the dead were killed in their homes. In 1999 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights found that the government had committed violations of human rights, including extrajudicial killings, and the Venezuelan government accepted full responsibility.

According to Velasco, the Caracazo is widely held to be a turning point that exposed a deep fissure in the social pact between political elites and voters set up after the 1958 revolution. Hugo Chávez described it as the beginning of his Bolivarian Revolution; his MBR-200 accelerated its preparations for a coup, and two attempts followed in February and November 1992.
caradog-ap-gruffydd: Caradog belonged to a dynasty whose strongholds were the kingdoms of Glywysing and Gwent. His grandfather Rhydderch ab Iestyn, King of Glywysing, had held the throne of Deheubarth from 1023 until his death in 1033. His father, Gruffudd ap Rhydderch, received the lordship of Caerleon in 1031, inherited Glywysing and became King of Deheubarth in 1045. The family descended from Owain, son of Morgan Hen, the last ruler of a unified Kingdom of Morgannwg.

Gruffudd ap Rhydderch was said to have resisted raids by the Danes and attacks by Gruffudd ap Llywelyn, but in 1055 Gruffudd ap Llywelyn killed him in battle and took Deheubarth. After a further victory near Glasbury in 1056, Gruffudd ap Llywelyn was recognised as King of Wales by 1057, and Caradog received Caerleon. From the family's base in Gwent he appears to have added his inheritance in Morgannwg.

When Harold Godwinson defeated Gruffudd ap Llywelyn in 1063, the old lineages of the south were restored. Caradog became ruler of Glywysing at about the time Maredudd ab Owain ab Edwin, the male-line heir of Hywel Dda, took Deheubarth. In 1065 Caradog destroyed the hunting lodge Harold was building at Portskewett and ravaged the district. After the Norman Conquest the Normans sacked south-east Wales and parts of Gwent, and Maredudd, who chose not to resist them, was rewarded with lands in England in 1070.

Caradog then set out to add Deheubarth to his realm, as his father and grandfather had done. In 1072 he defeated and killed Maredudd in a battle by the Rhymney River, and in 1074 he took control of what was left of war-ravaged Gwent from his kinsman Cadwgan ap Meurig. In 1078 he killed Rhys ab Owain, Maredudd's successor, and by 1081 he had forced the next prince, Rhys ap Tewdwr, to flee to St David's Cathedral.

Rhys ap Tewdwr found an ally in Gruffudd ap Cynan, who had come from Ireland to seize Gwynedd from Trahaearn ap Caradog; the two met at St David's and made their alliance with the blessing of the Bishop of St Davids. Caradog answered by allying with Trahaearn. The armies met at Mynydd Carn, about a day's march north of St Davids, and Caradog and Trahaearn were both killed. His son Owain ap Caradog kept Gwynllwg and founded the line of the Lords of Caerleon, while Iestyn ap Gwrgant became King of Morgannwg.
caral: Caral lies in the Supe District of Peru, near the present town of Caral, 182 kilometres (113 mi) north of Lima, 23 kilometres (14 mi) from the coast and 350 metres above sea level. It is the best studied and one of the largest sites of the Norte Chico civilisation, with a population of around 3,000. Nineteen other temple complexes were scattered across the 90 square kilometres (35 sq mi) of the Supe Valley, and the area may have held 20,000 people sharing the same culture.

Closely related was an early fishing city, Áspero, on the coast near the mouth of the Supe River. The date of 2627 BCE for Caral rests on radiocarbon dating of reeds and woven carrying bags used to haul stone for the temples. Excavators describe it as the oldest urban centre in the Americas, a claim challenged by the discovery of other ancient sites nearby, such as Bandurria.

Max Uhle found Caral in 1905 during a survey of ancient Peruvian cities but did not recognise the hills as pyramids. Paul Kosok studied it more fully in 1948, and others doubted the age he claimed. In 1975 the architect Carlos Williams recorded most sites of the Supe valley. Ruth Shady then explored the city, which was inhabited from about 2600 BCE to 2000 BCE.

The city had two halves divided by the Supe River valley. The Upper Half held six monumental complexes, each with a pyramid, open plaza and houses, where food remains such as sea lion bones point to elites. The Lower Half had smaller houses, with diets of mostly crops and some fish, and one complex, the Temple of the Amphitheater. The present explanation is that the city was planned this way, so that the layout expressed political power and social inequality. The main temple is 150 metres long, 110 metres wide and 28 metres high.

Shady found no sign of warfare at Caral, such as battlements, weapons or mutilated bodies. One temple held 32 flutes made of condor and pelican bones, and a collection of 37 cornetts of deer and llama bone and 33 flutes was also found. Excavators labelled a knotted textile a quipu, which they take as evidence that this record-keeping system was older than thought. A geoglyph of a human face lies west of the site.

UNESCO declared the city a World Heritage Site in 2009. Scholars believe that research at Caral may answer questions about the origins of Andean civilisations, since its urban design seems to have been a model for later ones.
caranus-of-macedon: In the Greek myth, Caranus was a son of Temenus, king of Argos, a descendant of Heracles. Temenus, Cresphontes and Aristodemus were the three Doric leaders who invaded the Peloponnese and divided the conquered lands, Temenus receiving Argos. After Temenus died, his sons quarrelled over the kingship, and one of them, Pheidon, defeated his brothers in battle and took it. Caranus then resolved to find a kingdom of his own. Plutarch agrees on his Heraclid descent and argues that Alexander the Great descended from Heracles through him.

Caranus first consulted the Oracle of Delphi, where the Pythia told him to raise the chief city of a state where he saw white-horned goats. He and his followers travelled north and found a green valley rich in game and goats. There he built a city, which he named Aigai, the present-day Vergina, a site of much archaeological work.

Other writers give different versions. Justin, citing Marsyas of Pella, says Caranus came to Emathia with a large band of Greeks, followed a herd of goats fleeing a downpour and seized the city of Edessa while its people were taken unawares in rain and fog. He renamed it Aegae and thereafter kept goats before his standards. The Chronicon of Eusebius says he gathered forces from the Argives and the rest of the Peloponnese and went to the aid of the king of the Orestae against the Eordaei, receiving half of that king's territory as promised, and ruled there for 30 years.

According to Eusebius, Caranus died in old age and was succeeded by his son Coenus, who was king for 28 years. Livy counts twenty monarchs from Caranus, the first king, down to Perseus. Caranus is first reported by Theopompus and is regarded as the mythical founder of the Argead dynasty. Herodotus names Perdiccas I as the first king instead.
caratacus: Dio Cassius names Caratacus as a son of the Catuvellaunian king Cunobelinus. From the distribution of coins he appears to have been the protégé of his uncle Epaticcus, who expanded Catuvellaunian power westwards into the territory of the Atrebates. After Epaticcus died in about 35 CE the Atrebates under Verica regained some land, but Caratacus seems to have conquered them completely, since Dio says that Verica was ousted and fled to Rome to appeal to the emperor Claudius. This gave Claudius the excuse for his invasion of Britain in the summer of 43. Coins minted in his rule bear the beginning of his name, CARA, which scholars connect with the Welsh Caradog.

The invasion targeted Camulodunon, modern Colchester, the former seat of Cunobelinus. Caratacus and his brother Togodumnus led the first defence against the four legions of Aulus Plautius, thought to have numbered about 40,000 men, mainly by guerrilla tactics. After defeats at the Medway and the Thames they lost much of the south-east, and Camulodunon became the first Roman colonia in Britain. Dio reports that Togodumnus was killed, though Miles Russell and John Hind argue that he survived.

Tacitus next shows Caratacus leading the Silures and Ordovices of Wales against Plautius's successor as governor, Publius Ostorius Scapula. In 50 CE Scapula defeated him in a set-piece battle in Ordovician territory and captured his wife and daughter, and his brothers surrendered. Caratacus fled north to the Brigantes, whose queen Cartimandua handed him over to the Romans in chains. The site of the battle is unknown: Tacitus's description fits neither of the places of legend, Caer Caradoc and British Camp, and Blodwel Rocks at Llanymynech has been proposed instead.

Caratacus was sent to Rome as a war prize, presumably to be killed after a triumphal parade, but he was allowed to address the Senate. Tacitus records a version of his speech in which he says that his stubborn resistance made Rome's glory the greater, and that if he were spared he would be an eternal example of Roman clemency. He made such an impression that he was pardoned and allowed to live in peace in Rome.

A genealogy in the Welsh manuscript Harley MS 3859, written about 1100, lists Caratauc, son of Cinbelin, son of Teuhant, which corresponds to Caratacus, son of Cunobelinus, son of Tasciovanus. He does not appear in Geoffrey of Monmouth's History of the Kings of Britain, though he seems to match Arviragus, who keeps up resistance to the Romans. Two hills in Shropshire are called Caer Caradoc, and his speech to Claudius has been a popular subject in visual art.
carausius: Carausius was of humble origin, a Menapian from Belgic Gaul who had once worked as a pilot. He distinguished himself in Maximian's campaign against the Bagaudae rebels in northern Gaul, and was appointed to command the Classis Britannica, a fleet based in the English Channel, with the task of eliminating Frankish and Saxon pirates raiding the coasts of Armorica and Belgica. He was suspected of letting pirates raid and collect loot before attacking them, and of keeping the captured treasure for himself. Maximian ordered his execution, and when Carausius learned of the sentence he declared himself emperor in Britain and northern Gaul.

His forces comprised his fleet, augmented by new ships, the three legions stationed in Britain and a legion he had seized in Gaul, together with foreign auxiliary units, a levy of Gaulish merchant ships and barbarian mercenaries drawn by the prospect of booty. Maximian prepared an invasion of Britain in 288 or 289, which failed. A panegyric to Constantius Chlorus blames bad weather, while Eutropius says hostilities were in vain because of Carausius's military skill, and a peace was agreed. It has been suggested that he built the fortifications of the Saxon Shore.

Coinage is the main source for his rule. It came from mints at Londinium, Rotomagus (Rouen) and a third site, possibly Colchester, and he issued the first proper silver coins in the Roman Empire for generations. Some coins show three portraits and the legend PAX AVGGG, implying recognition by Diocletian and Maximian, and others read CARAVSIVS ET FRATRES SVI, Carausius and his brothers. Legends such as Restitutor Britanniae appealed to British dissatisfaction with Rome, and Expectate veni alludes to a line of Virgil's Aeneid. A milestone from Carlisle names him Invictus Augustus.

In 293 Constantius Chlorus marched into Gaul and reclaimed it. He besieged the port of Gesoriacum (Boulogne-sur-Mer) and invaded Batavia to secure his rear against Carausius's Frankish allies, but could not yet attack Britain without a fleet. Carausius's grip was fatally weakened, and his finance minister Allectus assassinated him and took power. Allectus's rule lasted three years before he was defeated and killed by Constantius's subordinate Julius Asclepiodotus. A hoard of over 52,500 Roman coins found near Frome in 2010 held 766 coins of Carausius's reign.

In Geoffrey of Monmouth's History of the Kings of Britain, completed in 1136, he is a Briton of humble birth who becomes king after defeating Bassianus. The Welsh town of Tregaron is very likely named after him.
caravaggio: Caravaggio was born in Milan on 29 September 1571, where his father, Fermo, served the marquess of Caravaggio as household administrator and architect-decorator. The family moved to the town of Caravaggio in 1576 to escape a plague, and his father and grandfather both died there in 1577. He began his apprenticeship in Milan in 1584 under Simone Peterzano. In 1592 he left for Rome in flight after certain quarrels and the wounding of a police officer, and worked in the workshop of Giuseppe Cesari, painting flowers and fruit.

Caravaggio's innovation was a radical naturalism combining close observation of the model with a dramatic use of chiaroscuro known as tenebrism. He worked rapidly from live models, preferring to forgo drawings. In 1599 he was contracted to decorate the Contarelli Chapel in San Luigi dei Francesi, and The Martyrdom of Saint Matthew and The Calling of Saint Matthew, delivered in 1600, were an immediate sensation. Opinion among artists was polarised, but the young gathered around him.

He was also notorious for brawling and was often arrested. After he killed Ranuccio Tomassoni in a brawl in 1606 he was sentenced to death and fled to Naples, where he painted the Madonna of the Rosary and The Seven Works of Mercy. In 1607 he travelled to Malta and on to Sicily, pursuing a papal pardon, and in 1609 he returned to Naples.

He died on 18 July 1610 while travelling from Naples to Rome, and was buried at Porto Ercole. Rumour held that the Tomassoni family or the Knights of Malta had him killed, and historians have suggested syphilis, malaria and lead poisoning; research published in 2018 concluded that he died of sepsis from a wound received in a brawl in Naples. His influence appears in the work of Rubens, Ribera, Bernini, Velázquez and Rembrandt. His style fell out of favour, and interest revived in the twentieth century.
caravanserai: The word caravanserai is Persian, combining karvan, a group of traders, pilgrims and travellers, with sarai, a building with enclosed courts. Depending on region and period such buildings were also called khan, funduq and wikala. Rural staging posts are ancient: an early forerunner appears at an Urartian site of the 8th or 9th century BCE in western Iran, and Herodotus reports royal stations and excellent caravanserais along the Royal Road of the Achaemenid Empire. In the Islamic period their use grew, linked to a shift from wheeled vehicles to camels and caravans for long-distance travel. The oldest identified Islamic example is a courtyard structure at Qasr al-Hayr al-Sharqi, an Umayyad complex of the early 8th century in the Syrian desert.

A caravanserai was typically a square or rectangular building with a single entrance wide enough for laden camels. Its central courtyard, open to the sky, was surrounded by identical stalls and chambers for merchants, their animals and merchandise. A fountain or well supplied water, and many had a small mosque, shops, fodder and sometimes a hammam. Rural examples stood about a day's journey apart, which in Iran meant 30 to 40 km in open country and about 10 km or less in mountains. Seljuk examples in Iran and Central Asia were of brick with decorated façades, while those of Anatolia were of stone with tall carved portals.

Rural caravanserais let merchants and travellers rest safely along the way. Urban ones, concentrated near the main bazaars of cities such as Damascus, Aleppo, Cairo and Istanbul, lodged merchants, especially foreign ones, stored their goods and served as places to do business. The oldest surviving urban example is the Khan al-Mirjan in Baghdad, from 1359. Many earned revenue for charitable or religious buildings through a waqf, an endowment guaranteed under Islamic law. Under the Safavids their number grew to encourage trade with India, especially under Shah Abbas I, who ruled from 1587 to 1629, and in the Indian subcontinent they stood along the Grand Trunk Road.
caravel: The caravel developed from small, single-masted fishing vessels used in the thirteenth century along the coasts of Galicia, Portugal and Atlantic Andalusia. Mediterranean trade carried lateen rigging westward through the Strait of Gibraltar, and shipwrights there adapted it to small, shallow-draft open boats built for the swells and river mouths of the Atlantic coast. These boats first weighed less than 20 tons and had a crew of five, but grew larger through the fourteenth century, and records of 1307 note caravels of up to 30 tons in Biscay. By the early fifteenth century decked versions were widely used across the Iberian Peninsula.

In the mid to late fifteenth century Prince Henry the Navigator of Portugal wanted better ships to explore the Atlantic and the African coast. At Sagres he brought together experts in mapmaking, navigation, astronomy and ship design. The caravel could sail in difficult winds and open ocean, and was easier to steer than the square-rigged barca. It became the main vessel of Portuguese explorers such as Diogo Cão and Bartolomeu Dias, and of Christopher Columbus's expedition of 1492, in which the Pinta and Niña were caravels and the Santa María a small carrack.

Fifteenth-century caravels averaged 12 to 18 m in length and carried 50 to 60 tons, which made them fast and manoeuvrable but limited their cargo. Columbus re-rigged the Niña with square sails for the Atlantic crossing. Towards the end of the 15th century the Portuguese developed a larger round caravel with a square-rigged foremast, used as an escort on the routes to Brazil and round the Cape.

Caravels found new trade routes, but their small size made them poor cargo ships, and on commercial routes the much larger carrack replaced them. After the colonisation of the Americas the galleon replaced them as well, being stronger and able to carry more. The caravel remains a poorly understood type, since few wrecks have been investigated that are likely to be caravels.
carcassonne: Carcassonne lies in the plain of the Aude, about 80 kilometres east of Toulouse, between the historic trade routes linking the Atlantic to the Mediterranean Sea and the Massif Central to the Pyrénées. Settlement there dates to about 3500 BCE. The hill site of Carsac, a Celtic place-name, became an important trading place in the 6th century BCE, when the Volcae Tectosages fortified it as an oppidum. The popular story of a lady named Carcas and the ringing of bells is a modern reconstruction of a 16th-century depiction.

The Romans fortified the hilltop around 100 BCE and made it a colonia; the lower courses of the northern ramparts date from Gallo-Roman times. In 462 the Romans officially ceded Septimania to the Visigothic king Theodoric II, who had held Carcassonne since 453. The first count known by name is Bello, of the time of Charlemagne, who founded the Bellonid dynasty. In 1067 the county passed to Raimond-Bernard Trencavel through his marriage with Ermengard, sister of the last count.

In August 1209 the crusading army of the Papal Legate, the abbot Arnaud Amalric, besieged the city, a stronghold of Occitan Cathars. Viscount Raymond-Roger de Trencavel was imprisoned while negotiating its surrender and died in mysterious circumstances three months later. The people were allowed to leave with nothing but the shirts on their backs, and Simon de Montfort became the new viscount and added to the fortifications. The city submitted to France in 1247 and became a border fortress against the Crown of Aragon under the 1258 Treaty of Corbeil. Edward the Black Prince failed to take it in 1355, though his troops destroyed the lower town.

The Treaty of the Pyrenees of 1659 moved the border away and reduced Carcassonne's military importance. A decree of 1849 ordered the decayed fortress demolished, but a campaign led by the mayor Jean-Pierre Cros-Mayrevieille and the writer Prosper Mérimée saved it, and Eugène Viollet-le-Duc restored it from 1853 until his death in 1879. His slate roofs and pointed tips, more typical of northern France, were criticised in his lifetime. The citadel was added to the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1997, and Carcassonne is the prefecture of the Aude.
cardiff: Cardiff is the county town of the historic county of Glamorgan. The centre of the city is relatively flat and bounded by hills to the east, north and west, and the River Taff flows past Cardiff Castle. The highest point in the local authority area is Garth Hill, at 307 m. The position, with easy access to the coalfields of the South Wales Valleys, influenced the city's development as the world's largest coal port. The Welsh name, Caerdydd, derives from Middle Welsh Caerdyf, meaning the fort of the Taff, the fort probably being the one the Romans established.

People had settled in the area by about 6000 BCE, in the early Neolithic, and burial chambers such as Tinkinswood and St Lythans lie a few miles to the west. Four Iron Age hill forts and enclosures have been identified within the county boundary, among them Caerau Hillfort, which encloses 5.1 hectares. Cardiff Castle has stood in the centre of the city since the Norman period, within the walls of the old Roman fort. Welsh was the majority language from the 13th century until the Victorian growth of the city; as late as 1850, five of the twelve Anglican churches within the present boundaries held services only in Welsh.

In 1536 the Laws in Wales Acts made Glamorganshire and Cardiff its county town, and in 1538 Henry VIII closed the Dominican and Franciscan friaries. John Crichton-Stuart, 2nd Marquess of Bute, born in 1793, spent his life building the Cardiff docks and was later called the creator of modern Cardiff. A boat service to Bristol opened in 1815. Dic Penderyn was tried and hanged in 1831, after unrest that followed the Napoleonic Wars. Cardiff became a county borough on 1 April 1889, with more than 123,000 people.

Edward VII granted Cardiff city status on 28 October 1905, and in 1955 it was proclaimed capital of Wales. National institutions followed, including the National Museum of Wales and the Welsh National War Memorial, though the National Library of Wales went elsewhere, partly because its founder, Sir John Williams, thought Cardiff had a non-Welsh population. Since 1922 the city has included Llandaff, with its cathedral. The Senedd, the Welsh Parliament, has sat in Cardiff Bay since 1999, when it was founded as the National Assembly for Wales, and its building opened on 1 March 2006. The 2021 census counted 362,400 people in the city.
cardigan-bay: Cardigan Bay, in Welsh Bae Ceredigion, is a large inlet of the Irish Sea that indents the west coast of Wales between Bardsey Island in Gwynedd in the north and Strumble Head in Pembrokeshire in the south. It is the largest bay in Wales. Much of the coast around it is fertile farmland, dotted with towns and seaside resorts including Fishguard, New Quay, Aberaeron, Aberystwyth, Aberdyfi, Tywyn, Barmouth, Porthmadog, Criccieth and Pwllheli. Many rivers flow into the bay, among them the Glaslyn, Mawddach, Dysynni, Dyfi, Rheidol, Ystwyth, Aeron and Teifi.

Until the early 20th century Cardigan Bay supported a strong maritime industry. Cardigan lies at the mouth of the River Teifi, hence its Welsh name Aberteifi, meaning mouth of the Teifi. At the turn of the 19th century, the heyday of its port, more than 300 ships were registered there, seven times as many as at Cardiff and three times as many as at Swansea.

The central and northern parts of the bay are the site of the Cantre'r Gwaelod of Welsh legend, the drowned Lowland Hundred or Hundred under the Sea. A forest near Borth, which 4,500 years ago stretched over boggy land as far as Ynyslas, was buried under layers of peat, sand and saltwater as sea levels rose. In the winter storms of 2014 parts of it reappeared on the shoreline as preserved tree stumps.

The Cardigan Bay Special Area of Conservation protects the wildlife of the sea and the foreshore. The bay's main marine mammals are harbour porpoises, grey seals and bottlenose dolphins, of which it has the largest population in the UK, and minke whales, Risso's dolphins, common dolphins, puffins and basking sharks may also be seen. A military testing range was first set up in the bay during the Second World War. Controlled from a base near Aberporth, it has played a part in developing and testing weapons, and its danger area covers some 6,500 square kilometres of the bay.
cardinal-richelieu: Armand du Plessis was born in Paris on 9 September 1585, the fourth of five children, and was delicate from childhood. His family belonged to the lesser nobility of Poitou; his father, François du Plessis, seigneur de Richelieu, was a soldier and courtier who died of fever in the French Wars of Religion when Armand was five. In 1606 Henry IV nominated him to the Bishopric of Luçon, which the family held. Since he was below the canonical minimum age, he travelled to Rome for a dispensation from Pope Paul V and was consecrated bishop in April 1607. On his return he was heralded as a reformer and became the first bishop in France to implement the reforms of the Council of Trent.

In 1614 Richelieu represented the clergy of Poitou at the Estates-General. He rose by serving the queen mother Marie de' Medici's favourite, Concino Concini, and in 1616 was made Secretary of State with responsibility for foreign affairs. He became a cardinal in 1622 and Louis XIII's principal minister in 1624. His policy had two aims: to centralise power in France and to oppose the Habsburg dynasty, which ruled in Austria and Spain. In 1626 he abolished the position of Constable of France and ordered all fortified castles razed, except those needed against invaders, which made him hated by most of the nobility. In 1627 he personally commanded the troops besieging the Huguenot stronghold of La Rochelle.

Abroad he subsidised the Dutch Republic against Spain, and in 1629, alarmed by Emperor Ferdinand II's growing influence, he gave money to incite Sweden to intervene in Germany. He encouraged Louis XIII to colonise the Americas through the Company of New France, and the Ordonnance of 1627 deemed Indians who converted to Catholicism natural Frenchmen. He also renovated the Sorbonne and patronised the arts.

Near the end of his life Richelieu faced a plot by the marquis de Cinq-Mars, whom he had introduced at court. He suffered from recurrent fevers, intestinal tuberculosis and migraine, and he died on 4 December 1642, naming Jules Mazarin as his successor. He left his library, with some 900 manuscripts, to be open to scholars. Historians credit him with replacing a largely feudal political structure with centralised power, work that Louis XIV continued. He is also noted for authoritarian measures: he censored the press, kept a network of spies and had those who conspired against him prosecuted and executed.
cardwell-reforms: Five royal commissions dealt with army reform before 1870. The most controversial, in 1857, heard Sir Charles Trevelyan campaign against the purchase of commissions, when a captaincy cost £2,400 and promotion to lieutenant colonel £7,000; selection by merit and education was found only in the artillery and engineers. An army of only 25,000 in the Crimea had stripped Britain of almost every trained soldier, and the Indian Mutiny again required almost the whole usable army. Reform was resisted by senior officers led by the commander-in-chief, Prince George, Duke of Cambridge, and the German victory over the Second French Empire in the Franco-Prussian War gave it new urgency.

In 1868 Cardwell abolished flogging in peacetime, though it remained on active service until 1881, and in 1869 he began withdrawing troops from the self-governing colonies, which were encouraged to raise their own forces; by 1871 some 26,000 had returned to Britain. The Army Enlistment Act 1870 introduced short service: men enlisted for twelve years, served six with the colours in the infantry, eight in the line cavalry and artillery, and passed the rest in the reserve, paid fourpence a day. The War Office Act 1870 reformed the administration of the War Office.

The Regulation of the Forces Act 1871 divided the country into 66 brigade districts based on county boundaries and population. Each line infantry regiment was to have two battalions sharing a depot and recruiting area, one serving overseas while the other trained at home, with the local militia usually as a third; the linking of regiments was completed only under the Childers Reforms of 1881. When a bill reimbursing officers for their commissions was defeated, the government announced that all purchase was abolished, and the House of Lords then passed the remedial legislation. Second lieutenant replaced the ranks of cornet and ensign.

A change of government removed Cardwell in 1874, but his reforms survived attempts to undo them. Garnet Wolseley, his principal military adviser from 1871, went on defending short service, and by 1900 the reserve numbered about 80,000 trained men; in 1899 it allowed Britain to assemble for the Second Boer War the largest army it had ever deployed abroad. Historians of the army have generally praised the reforms as essential to modernisation, while a minority, among them Theodore Hoppen, call them partial at best, since no planning department or chief of staff was created.
carhaix-plouguer: Carhaix-Plouguer, commonly called Carhaix, lies in the Poher, an important territory of Brittany between the Arrée Mountains to the north and the Black Mountains to the south. The town grew mainly on a plateau about 140 metres above sea level, bounded on the north by the valley of the Hyères, which in Roman times required the building of an aqueduct to cross it. Carhaix and Plouguer became separate communes at the French Revolution and merged in 1957.

In the Roman Empire the city was called Vorgium and was the chief town of the Osismii. Modern archaeological digs have uncovered evidence of the Roman city, including its aqueduct system. Its function as a crossroads persisted, together with a decline in the late empire, and this may explain why the Osismii, although Carhaix was their capital, did not leave their name to it, as happened more often in Gaul.

The oldest form of the name, Carahes, appears in a charter of Hoel, Count of Cornouaille, written before his death in 1084; the Breton prefix kaer means a fortified place. In the 19th century it was believed that the name came from Ahès, the daughter of Gradlon in Breton tradition who brought about the loss of the city of Ys. In the continental romances Carhaix is thought to be the Carohaise of King Leodegrance, where King Arthur meets Guinevere.

Carhaix is in the department of Finistère, in the region of Brittany. It has the only lycée of the Diwan schools, which teach in Breton, moved there from Brest in 1999. The town holds the Vieilles Charrues music festival every July and the Book Festival in Brittany every October.
carians: When the Carians enter history is unclear. They may be the Karkiya or Karkisa of Hittite records, who aided the Assuwa League against the Hittite king Tudhaliya I, gave asylum in 1323 BCE, at the request of King Arnuwandas II, to the deposed Manapa-Tarhunta of the land of the Seha River, and fought on the Hittite side at the Battle of Kadesh in 1274 BCE. The link is uncertain, since the location of Karkisa is unknown, but it suits the language: the Phoenicians called the Carians KRK, and Old Persian krka.

Archaeology has given mixed answers. Surveys by J.M. Cook and G.E. Bean in the 1950s found Caria almost devoid of prehistoric remains, while excavations in the 1970s revealed Mycenaean buildings at Iasus and Protogeometric and Geometric cemeteries and pottery. As Neolithic Caria was nearly empty, the Carians may have been of Aegean origin, settling in south-western Anatolia during the second millennium BCE.

Homer has the Carians, of incomprehensible speech, holding Miletus and Mount Mycale and joining the Trojans under Nastes, son of Nomion, whose golden armour or ornaments may recall a reputation for Carian wealth. Herodotus reported that the Carians thought themselves natives of Caria, while ancient writers agreed they had been a seafaring people gradually pushed inland. Thucydides held that they settled the Cyclades before Minos of Knossos expelled them, and in the Athenian purification of Delos more than half the graves opened were Carian.

Strabo wrote that the Carians, more than other non-Greeks, roamed Greece serving on expeditions for pay. Inscriptions in Egypt and Nubia name Carian mercenaries under Psammetichus I and II. Plutarch says the Persians called them cocks for the crests on their helmets, and that Artaxerxes II honoured the Carian soldier who killed Cyrus the Younger by letting him lead the army with a golden cock on his spear.

Carian belongs to the Luwic group of Anatolian languages, with Lycian and Milyan; its ancestor was very close to Luwian, though probably not a direct descendant. At Mylasa, their first capital, the Carians worshipped a warrior god whom Herodotus called the Carian Zeus, admitting only Lydians and Mysians besides themselves, a sign of the kinship told in the myth of Car, brother of Lydus and Mysus. On Mount Latmos they worshipped Endymion, and the goddess Hecate may have originated among them.
caribbean: The Caribbean is a region of thousands of islands, islets, reefs and cays centred on the Caribbean Sea and lying largely on the Caribbean plate. Island arcs mark its northern and eastern edges: the Greater Antilles, including Cuba, Hispaniola, Jamaica and Puerto Rico, in the north, and the Lesser Antilles in the east and south. The Bahamas, the Turks and Caicos Islands and Barbados are counted as part of the region though they do not border the sea. The term West Indies is often used interchangeably with the Caribbean. The region takes its name from the Caribs, after whom Spanish colonists named it.

The oldest evidence of human presence is at Banwari Trace in southern Trinidad, where remains about 7,000 years old have been found. Consistent dates of 3100 BCE appear in Cuba and of 2000 BCE in Antigua. At the time of European contact the dominant groups were the Taíno of the Greater Antilles and the Island Caribs of the southern Lesser Antilles, and the population is estimated to have been about 750,000.

Christopher Columbus arrived on Hispaniola in 1492. The Spanish assigned enslaved people to conquistadors under the encomienda system, and the Laws of Burgos of 1512 were meant to protect the rights of the native peoples. Smallpox and measles, to which they had no immunity, and social disruption sharply reduced the Amerindian population, and from 1503 enslaved people from Africa, among them Kongo, Igbo, Akan, Fon and Yoruba, were brought in. England, the Netherlands and France sought colonies of their own, and colonial rivalries made the region a battleground of European wars for centuries. Spain ceded Jamaica to England, while Martinique and the western third of Hispaniola passed to France.

The principal official languages are Spanish, French, English and Dutch, with Haitian Creole and Papiamento, and almost every country has a creole language or dialect as its everyday speech. Christianity is the main religion, alongside Hinduism, Islam and Rastafari. The islands hold about 8 per cent of the world's coral reefs. In 1973 English-speaking states created the Caribbean Community, CARICOM, in Guyana.
caribbean-community: The Caribbean Community was first called the Caribbean Community and Common Market. It was established by the Treaty of Chaguaramas, signed by the leaders of Barbados, Guyana, Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago and in effect from 1 August 1973. It superseded the Caribbean Free Trade Association of 1965-1972, which had kept up an economic link between the English-speaking countries of the Caribbean after the West Indies Federation dissolved. That federation had lasted from 3 January 1958 to 31 May 1962.

CARICOM began as an organisation of the English-speaking Caribbean, and English was its sole working language into the 1990s. It became multilingual as Suriname joined in 1995 and Haiti in 2002, and Spanish was added as a fourth official language in 2003. On 5 July 2001 the heads of government signed a revised Treaty of Chaguaramas at Nassau, which cleared the way for the CARICOM Single Market and Economy and established the Caribbean Court of Justice. Haiti's participation was suspended from 29 February 2004 until June 2006.

CARICOM took part in founding wider bodies. The Association of Caribbean States was formed on 24 July 1994, from a recommendation of the West Indian Commission that CARICOM's heads of government set up in 1989. CARICOM was also involved in creating the Community of Latin American and Caribbean States in 2010.

The Conference of Heads of Government and the Community Council, made up of ministers responsible for community affairs, are the two principal organs. The chairmanship rotates among the heads of government. The Secretariat in Georgetown is the chief administrative organ; its Secretary-General is the chief executive, with a five-year term that may be renewed. Its main activities are coordinating economic policy and development planning, running a regional single market, handling trade disputes and devising projects for the less developed members. Its flag, first flown on 4 July 1984, shows two interlocking Cs as broken chain links, which stand for unity and a break with the colonial past.
cariboo: The Cariboo is an intermontane region of British Columbia, centred on a plateau that stretches from the Fraser Canyon to the Cariboo Mountains. Its name refers to the caribou that were once abundant there, and Governor Douglas used it for the area in dispatches to Britain as early as 1861. The grasslands of the Cariboo are home to the regionally endangered American badger.

The Cariboo was the first part of the interior north of the lower Fraser River and its canyon to be settled by non-indigenous people, and it played an important part in the early history of the colony and province. Its boundaries in the historical sense are debatable. At first the name meant the region north of the forks of the Quesnel River, between that river's mouth on the Fraser at Quesnel and the northern end of the Cariboo Mountains, mostly in the Quesnel Highland, where several gold-bearing creeks rise near the head of the Willow River.

The richest of those creeks, Williams Creek, is the site of Barkerville, which was the capital of the gold rush and the seat of government officials for decades afterwards. As settlement spread south along the route of the Cariboo Road, over the rolling plateaus and benchlands of the Cariboo Plateau and the lands along the Fraser and Thompson rivers, the name came to cover a much wider area than the goldfields alone.

The goldfields, once the most settled and most significant part of interior British Columbia, are thinly populated, and Barkerville is a museum town. The region's towns include Quesnel, Wells and Likely in the north, Williams Lake, Horsefly and 150 Mile House in the centre, and 100 Mile House, Lone Butte and Clinton in the south.
cariboo-wagon-road: The road was begun in 1860 on the orders of James Douglas, governor of the Colony of British Columbia, in response to the Cariboo Gold Rush. It replaced a dangerous mule trail, a rough cliffside path wide enough for a single animal, and was meant to lower the cost of supplies to the mining settlements. The colonial government employed local men as well as the Columbia Detachment of the Royal Engineers, who built toll bridges among other works, including the original Alexandra Suspension Bridge of 1863. It was also known as the Great North Road or the Queen's Highway.

Between the 1860s and the 1880s the road existed in three versions. The first, surveyed in 1861 and built in 1862, followed the Hudson's Bay Company's Harrison Trail from Lillooet through Clinton and the mile houses to Soda Creek and Alexandria. The mile houses of the Cariboo take their names from Mile 0 of the Lillooet route, sometimes called the Old Cariboo Road, where Bactrian camels were tried for freight in 1862. The second, the Yale Cariboo Road of the stagecoach and freight companies based at Yale, ran from 1865 to 1885 through the Fraser Canyon over Hell's Gate and Jackass Mountain to Clinton.

After the Canadian Pacific Railway was completed in 1885, the station at Ashcroft became the southern end of the road. Railway building, washouts and the Great Flood of 1894 destroyed much of the canyon section, which was not rebuilt until plans for the Fraser Canyon Highway in the 1920s.

The road cost nearly one and a quarter million dollars and left a standing debt of £112,780, one of the costs of serving the gold colony that pushed it into union with Vancouver Island in 1866 and then into Canada in 1871. More than six and a half million dollars' worth of gold travelled along it. Douglas had hoped to carry the road across the continental divide into Rupert's Land, but the plan was dropped when he retired in 1864. British Columbia Highway 97 largely follows its route.
carignan-salieres-regiment: The regiment was formed in 1659 by merging the Carignan Regiment, raised in Piedmont in 1644 by Thomas Francis of Savoy, Prince of Carignano, with the Salières Regiment, raised in Germany early in the Thirty Years War by Johann von Balthazard. The Carignan had fought in Lombardy, Tuscany and Piedmont and for the royalists at the Battle of the Faubourg St Antoine in 1652. Henri de Chastelard de Salières commanded the merged unit.

New France, with 3,035 people in 1660, could not hold off the Haudenosaunee raids of the Beaver Wars. After Louis XIV made it a royal province in 1663, he and his finance minister Jean-Baptiste Colbert sent the regiment to end the threat and secure the fur trade.

The first ship left La Rochelle on 19 April 1665, and the companies reached Quebec between June and September, the last two transports with 35 dead on the voyage. The soldiers built Fort St. Louis, now Fort Chambly, Fort Saint-Jean and Fort Sainte Thérèse, restored Fort Richelieu and built Fort Sainte Anne on Isle La Motte. The Huguenots in the ranks were coerced into recanting.

Governor Daniel de Rémy de Courcelle's winter march of January 1666 went astray without its Algonquin guides, attacked cabins near Schenectady and turned back; the Jesuit Relations counted over 60 dead from hunger. A second strike under Pierre de Saurel turned back when the Mohawk returned their prisoners. In the autumn Alexandre de Prouville de Tracy led 600 soldiers, 600 Canadien volunteers and 100 Algonquin and Wendat warriors to the four Mohawk villages, found them abandoned, claimed them for Louis XIV on 17 October 1666 and burned them.

Soldiers who stayed were offered money or rations, officers seigneuries along the Richelieu, placed as a buffer against the Haudenosaunee and the English. Many married Filles du Roi, and their soldiers' nicknames became family surnames and place names. Back in France the regiment fought in the Franco-Dutch War, became the Soissons Regiment in 1676 and the Perche Regiment in 1690, and its line ran on to the 24th and 50th Infantry of the Line.
carinthia: Carinthia is the southernmost and least densely populated Austrian state, in the Eastern Alps, noted for its mountains and lakes. Most of the larger towns and lakes lie in the Klagenfurt Basin in the southeast, which covers about one fifth of the area, while mountainous Upper Carinthia reaches in the northwest up to the Alpine crest. The name has not been conclusively explained: the Ravenna Cosmography, about 700, referred to a Slavic tribe called Carantani as the eastern neighbours of the Bavarians.

About 300 BCE Illyrian and Celtic tribes joined in the Kingdom of Noricum, known for its salt and iron. The Roman Empire incorporated Noricum in 15 BCE, and under Diocletian it split into two provinces. From 591 the Frankish king Theudebert I tried to break into the region and Bavarian settlers entered from the Puster Valley, but Slavic tribes, themselves pressed by Avar horsemen, repulsed them. About 600 the Slavic principality of Carantania arose along the valleys of the Drava, Mur and Sava, and the Prince's Stone in the Zollfeld valley bears witness to the investiture of its rulers, performed exclusively in Slovene.

Emperor Otto II separated the Duchy of Carinthia from the Bavarian duchy in 976, the first newly created duchy of the Holy Roman Empire, comprising for a short time lands from the Adriatic almost to the Danube. The March of Carniola was separated in 1040, and about 1180 Styria became a duchy of its own. After the death of Duke Henry VI of Gorizia-Tyrol in 1335 Carinthia passed to the Habsburg dynasty, represented by Albrecht II and Otto IV, which ruled it until 1918. In 1867 it became a crown land of Austria-Hungary. After the First World War Slovene volunteers and the Yugoslav army occupied the south, and fierce fighting around Völkermarkt alarmed the Allies at the Paris Peace Conference.

Carinthia is an Austrian federal state with its capital at Klagenfurt; Villach is its other statutory city. German is the official language, and a Slovene-speaking minority, the Carinthian Slovenes, lives mainly in the south and southeast. Its sights include the Romanesque Gurk Cathedral, Maria Saal, the abbeys of St. Paul's, Ossiach, Millstatt and Viktring, and the castle of Hochosterwitz.
carita-parahyangan: The text survives in a single manuscript, registered as Kropak 406, which came from the collection of the Bataviaasch Genootschap voor Kunsten en Wetenschappen (Batavian Society of Arts and Sciences) and is now kept in the Perpustakaan Nasional, the National Library of Indonesia in Jakarta. It consists of 47 leaves of lontar palm leaf, each about 21 by 3 cm, with four lines of Old Sundanese script on every leaf. Its name comes from the Parahyangan highlands of West Java, from Sundanese words meaning the abode of the hyangs, or gods.

The chronicle follows the Sunda Kingdom from the Galuh period, in the time of Wretikandayun and King Sanjaya, down to the fall of Pakuan Pajajaran, the Sundanese capital, when it was invaded by the Banten Sultanate with help from the Cirebon and Demak Sultanates.

The manuscript holds two texts. The larger is the Carita Parahyangan proper, an account of Sundanese kings and kingdoms of the pre-Islamic period. The second, which its modern editor called the Fragmen Carita Parahyangan, fills 13 leaves, or 25 pages, and differs in its hand: it has an irregular number of lines, from three to six a page, and small differences of script. It contains three main stories of rulers of the Sunda kingdom at Pakuan Pajajaran, and its second, larger part is of interest for social and economic history. Scholars hold that the two texts were brought together in one manuscript at an early stage.

The scholar Holle identified the text under this name in 1882, and it was published by Holle that year and by Pleyte in 1914; Poerbatjaraka later gave a complete transliteration. In 1962 the scholar Noorduyn restored the order of the leaves, which had fallen into disarray, and published an annotated transliteration and translation of the first part, adding corrections in 1966 after rereading the original.

Working from Noorduyn's order of the leaves, Atja and Danasasmita published a new transliteration with an Indonesian translation and notes in 1981. In 1995 Darsa and Ekadjati produced a further edition and translation, which printed the Fragment for the first time, and in 1999 Darsa examined how the two texts of Kropak 406 relate to each other.
carl-benz: Carl Benz was born Karl Friedrich Michael Vaillant on 25 November 1844 in Mühlburg, in the Grand Duchy of Baden, to Josephine Vaillant and Johann Georg Benz, a locomotive driver, whom she married a few months later; the child then took the name Benz. His father died of pneumonia when he was two. His mother, living in near poverty, gave him a good education, and he passed the entrance examination for mechanical engineering at the Karlsruhe polytechnical school on 30 September 1860, aged 15. He graduated on 9 July 1864.

In 1871 Benz joined August Ritter in founding an iron foundry and mechanical workshop in Mannheim, and when it went badly his fiancée Bertha Ringer bought out Ritter's share with her dowry. They married on 20 July 1872. He finished a petrol two-stroke engine on 31 December 1879 and patented it on 28 June 1880. While perfecting it he patented the speed regulation system, battery spark ignition, the spark plug, the carburettor, the clutch, the gear shift and the water radiator. In 1883 he founded Benz & Cie. with Max Rose and Friedrich Wilhelm Eßlinger.

Benz applied for a patent on his motorcar on 29 January 1886 and drove it publicly on the Ringstrasse in Mannheim on 3 July 1886. Patent number 37345 followed in November, and the vehicle became known as the Benz Patent-Motorwagen. He began selling it in the late summer of 1888. On 5 August 1888 Bertha Benz took one with her sons Eugen and Richard on a trip of 104 km from Mannheim to Pforzheim, repairing faults on the way and having leather nailed to the brake blocks.

Benz & Cie. grew from 50 employees in 1889 to 430 in 1899, and in 1899 it produced 572 vehicles, making it the largest automobile company in the world. Benz announced his retirement from design management on 24 January 1903 but stayed on the board. On 28 June 1926 the firm merged with Daimler Motoren Gesellschaft as Daimler-Benz, and he died at Ladenburg on 4 April 1929, aged 84.
carl-blegen: Carl William Blegen was born on 27 January 1887 in Minneapolis, Minnesota, the eldest of six children of Anna Regine and John H. Blegen, who had emigrated from Lillehammer in Norway. His father taught at Augsburg College in Minneapolis for more than 30 years and was prominent in the Norwegian Lutheran Church of America, and his younger brother Theodore C. Blegen became a historian. He took his bachelor's degree at the University of Minnesota and began graduate studies at Yale University in 1907.

As a fellow of the American School of Classical Studies at Athens from 1911 to 1913 he worked on excavations in Locris, at Corinth and at Korakou. During the First World War he did relief work in Bulgaria and Macedonia, and Greece awarded him the Order of the Redeemer in 1919. He completed his doctorate at Yale in 1920 and was assistant director of the American School until 1926, excavating at Zygouries, Phlius, Prosymna and Hymettos.

In 1927 he joined the University of Cincinnati, where he was professor of classical archaeology until he retired in 1957. Work at the Palace of Nestor resumed in 1952 and continued until 1966; many of its finds are in the Archaeological Museum of Chora. Honorary degrees came from Oslo, Thessaloniki, Oxford, Cambridge and Athens, among others, and in 1965 he became the first recipient of the Archaeological Institute of America's Gold Medal for archaeological achievement.

In 1924 Blegen married Elizabeth Denny Pierce, whom he had met at the American School. She had at first broken off their engagement because she did not wish to end her long relationship with Ida Thallon, and the two couples, Blegen and Pierce with Thallon and Bert Hodge Hill, married at the same time and lived together in Athens, calling themselves the Family or the Pro Par.

Widowed in 1966, Blegen died in Athens on 24 August 1971, aged 84. He is buried with his wife in the Protestant corner of the First Cemetery of Athens, near the graves of Thallon and Hill. He left a large collection of his papers to the American School, whose Blegen Library bears his name, as does the Carl Blegen Library of the University of Cincinnati.
carl-friedrich-gauss: Gauss was born on 30 April 1777 in Brunswick, in the Duchy of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, into a family of relatively low social status. His father, Gebhard Dietrich Gauss, worked variously as a butcher, bricklayer, gardener and treasurer of a death-benefit fund. His mother, Dorothea, was nearly illiterate.

He graduated as a Doctor of Philosophy in 1799, from the University of Helmstedt rather than Göttingen as is sometimes stated. The Duke then granted him the cost of living as a private scholar in Brunswick. The Duke's promise of an observatory ended when he was killed at the battle of Jena in 1806, and the duchy was abolished the next year, which stopped Gauss's financial support.

In November 1807 the University of Göttingen hired him as full professor and director of the observatory, and he kept the chair until his death. In his doctoral thesis he proved the fundamental theorem of algebra. On 1 January 1801 Giuseppe Piazzi discovered Ceres but could follow it only briefly. Gauss predicted a position for its reappearance in December 1801, and it was found within half a degree of it by Franz Xaver von Zach and independently by Heinrich Olbers.

Legendre published the method of least squares in 1805, but Gauss claimed in Theoria motus in 1809 that he had used it since 1794 or 1795, which began a priority dispute. His geodetic survey of Hanover led him in 1828 to a work that marks the birth of modern differential geometry of surfaces. In 1828 he became head of the Kingdom of Hanover's board for weights and measures.

Gauss married Johanna Osthoff on 9 October 1805; she died on 11 October 1809. He married twice and had six children. He died on 23 February 1855, and his brain was removed and studied. In 2013 a neurobiologist in Göttingen found that it had been mixed up with that of the physician Conrad Heinrich Fuchs, so that most later studies concerned Fuchs's brain.

Gauss is frequently regarded as one of the three most important mathematicians of all time, with Isaac Newton and Archimedes, and has been called the Prince of Mathematics. More than 100 mathematical and scientific concepts are named after him. Among his students, Richard Dedekind and Bernhard Riemann became influential mathematicians.
carl-gustaf-emil-mannerheim: Mannerheim was born on 4 June 1867 at Louhisaari Manor in Askainen parish, into a Swedish-speaking aristocratic family. The Mannerheims, originally from Germany as Marhein, became Swedish noblemen in 1693. His great-grandfather, Count Carl Erik Mannerheim, became the first head of the executive of the newly autonomous Grand Duchy of Finland after Sweden lost Finland to the Russian Empire in 1809. His father, heavily in debt, left the family in 1880, and his mother died the following year.

In 1882 he entered the Hamina Cadet School, and in 1889 he was hired as a cornet in a dragoon regiment at Kalisz in Poland. He married Anastasia Arapova in 1892; they had two daughters. He served in the Russo-Japanese War, travelled through Turkestan to Beijing as a secret intelligence officer, and fought on the Austro-Hungarian and Romanian fronts in the First World War, rising to lieutenant general in April 1917.

After Finland declared independence in December 1917, the Senate of Finland faced the socialist Reds in a civil war. On 13 January 1918 Mannerheim was given command of the army of the Whites, about 24,000 mostly untrained men, against some 30,000 Red Guards. At Vaasa he surrounded a Russian garrison of 1,500 to 2,000 men with recruits, only the front rank of them armed, and the garrison surrendered its weapons. The Whites held a victory parade in Helsinki in May.

He was regent from December 1918 to July 1919, won recognition of independence from several Entente powers and ratified the republican constitution although he was a monarchist. He lost the first presidential election to K. J. Ståhlberg in 1919 and held no public office in the interwar years. As chairman of the Defence Council from 1931 he prepared for a possible war with the Soviet Union, and after the Soviet attack of 30 November 1939 he became commander-in-chief at 72, a post he held for five years.

In 1944 the Parliament of Finland unanimously appointed Mannerheim president, and he oversaw peace negotiations with the Soviet Union and the United Kingdom. Finland had made him a field marshal in 1933 and gave him the title Marshal of Finland in 1942, which no one else has held. In poor health, he resigned in March 1946, wrote his memoirs at a sanatorium in Montreux, Switzerland, and died there on 27 January 1951.

Mannerheim is often called the father of modern Finland. According to the historian Tuomas Tepora, a cult of personality grew around him after the civil war, and the Mannerheim Museum in Helsinki memorialises his life.
carl-gustav-jung: Carl Gustav Jung was born on 26 July 1875 in Kesswil, in the Swiss canton of Thurgau, the first surviving son of Paul Achilles Jung, a rural pastor in the Swiss Reformed Church, and Emilie Jung, née Preiswerk. His grandfather and namesake was a noted physician and professor of medicine at Basel. In 1903 Jung married Emma Rauschenbach, daughter of the owner of IWC Schaffhausen, whose shares in the watchmaking firm ensured the family's financial security. Emma became his assistant at Burghölzli and a noted psychoanalyst.

Jung worked as a research scientist at the Burghölzli psychiatric hospital in Zurich under Eugen Bleuler. He sent Freud his Studies in Word Association in 1906. Freud saw the younger man as his heir, and secured his appointment as president of the International Psychoanalytical Association. But Jung's research and personal vision made it hard to follow the older man's doctrine, and they parted ways in 1913. The division was painful, and Jung went through a period of isolation, describing a confrontation with the unconscious. This led to his Red Book, published partially and posthumously in 2009.

During the First World War he served as an army doctor and became commandant of an internment camp for British soldiers. He emerged with Psychological Types (1921), one of his most influential books, and in 1922 bought land at Bollingen, where he built a tower. Statements he made in the 1930s have been cited as evidence of both contempt and sympathy for Nazism.

Jung founded analytical psychology. Its central concept is individuation, the lifelong process by which the self is differentiated from conscious and unconscious elements, which he considered the main task of human development. He distinguished the personal unconscious from the collective unconscious, shared by all people, and described archetypes as universal and recurring mental images or themes. His typology of extraversion and introversion grew from early word-association experiments. He died on 6 June 1961.
carl-linnaeus: Carl Linnaeus was born on 23 May 1707 in the village of Råshult in Småland, Sweden, the first child of Nicolaus (Nils) Linnaeus and Christina Brodersonia. His father, a Lutheran minister and amateur botanist, taught him Latin as a small child, and the family moved to the rectory of Stenbrohult when his father became rector there. Linnaeus liked plants from his earliest years, and his father gave him his own patch of land to grow them.

In 1727, at the age of 21, he enrolled at Lund University. Most of his higher education was at Uppsala University, where he began giving lectures in botany in 1730. In May 1732 he set out on an expedition to Lapland, funded by a grant from the Royal Society of Sciences in Uppsala, curious about the Sami people.

In April 1735 Linnaeus travelled to the Dutch Republic to study medicine at the University of Harderwijk, and he published the first edition of his Systema Naturae in the Netherlands. After returning to Sweden on 28 June 1738 he worked as a physician at the Admiralty in Stockholm and helped found the Royal Swedish Academy of Science, becoming its first Praeses by drawing of lots. He later became professor of medicine and botany at Uppsala, and in the 1740s he was sent on several journeys through Sweden to find and classify plants and animals.

He taught many students, 17 of whom he called his apostles, and they made botanical expeditions around the world, so that his system spread without his travelling outside Sweden again. He was ennobled in 1761. Illness troubled his last years, and he died on 10 January 1778 in Hammarby.

The first edition of Systema Naturae, printed in 1735, ran to twelve pages. By its 10th edition in 1758 it classified 4,400 species of animals and 7,700 species of plants. Linnaeus's main contribution to taxonomy was the establishment of universally accepted conventions for naming organisms, and his work marks the starting point of the consistent use of binomial nomenclature.

The Linnaean system placed nature in a nested hierarchy of three kingdoms divided into classes, orders, genera and species. His taxonomy of human races has been criticised in the 21st century: some regard him as a forebear of scientific racism, while others hold that his classification was stereotyped but did not imply that any race was superior.
carl-menger: Carl Menger von Wolfensgrün was born on 28 February 1840 in Neu-Sandez, in the Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria in the Austrian Empire, now Nowy Sącz in Poland. His father, Anton Menger, was a lawyer. He studied law at the universities of Prague and Vienna and received a doctorate from the Jagiellonian University in Kraków. In the 1860s he reported and analysed market news for the Lemberger Zeitung and then the Wiener Zeitung, and noticed a gap between what classical economics said about prices and what people in markets believed.

In 1867 Menger began a study of political economy that led in 1871 to his Principles of Economics. In 1873, aged 33, he received the chair of economic theory at the University of Vienna. From 1876 he tutored Archduke Rudolf von Habsburg, the crown prince, accompanying him on journeys through Europe and the British Isles; their association lasted until the prince's death in 1889.

His Investigations into the Method of the Social Sciences (1883) set off a dispute with the historical school. Gustav von Schmoller reviewed it unfavourably and used the term Austrian school as a gibe, and in 1884 Menger answered with The Errors of Historicism in German Economics, opening the Methodenstreit, or methodological debate. His disciples included Eugen von Böhm-Bawerk and Friedrich von Wieser. He headed a commission to reform the Austrian monetary system, and in 1903 he resigned his chair to concentrate on study.

Menger rejected the cost-of-production theory of value held by Adam Smith, David Ricardo and Karl Marx. His subjective theory of value held that price is determined at the margin and that both sides gain from exchange. Unlike William Jevons, he did not believe that goods provide units of utility; goods are valuable because they serve various uses whose importance differs. He explained money as a development of exchange, in which gold and silver, being especially saleable, came to be a general medium of exchange. Friedrich Hayek wrote that the fundamental ideas of the Austrian school belong fully and wholly to Menger.
carl-peters: Peters was born on 27 September 1856 at Neuhaus an der Elbe in the Kingdom of Hanover, the son of a Lutheran clergyman. He studied history and philosophy at Göttingen, Tübingen and Berlin, where he was a student of Heinrich von Treitschke, and wrote a prize-winning dissertation on the Treaty of Venice of 1177. Rather than teach, he went to London to stay with his uncle, the composer Carl Engel, refused an offer to become a British subject, and on his return to Berlin founded the Society for German Colonization.

The treaties he made in Usagara in 1884 were written in German and had little legal value; Karl Jühlke, a member of the expedition, conceded that the chiefs were probably not clear what they signed. Otto von Bismarck at first refused support, but Peters threatened to sell his gains to King Leopold II of Belgium, and the charter was granted on 27 February 1885. Peters had no business experience, and when the company was refinanced in 1887 he lost control of it.

In 1888 he led an expedition, avowedly to relieve Emin Pasha but in fact to extend German influence into Uganda, seizing food from the local people; the Danish explorer Peder Scavenius later found burnt villages and skeletons along its route. His treaty with Kabaka Mwanga II of Buganda was voided by the Heligoland–Zanzibar Treaty of 1 July 1890. As Reichskommissar at Kilimanjaro from 1891 he had his servant Mabruk hanged and, in January 1892, Jagodjo, one of the African women the Germans kept as sex slaves, whom he suspected of spying. August Bebel made the killings public in the Reichstag on 13 March 1896.

Deprived of his commission and pension, Peters moved to London and explored the Zambezi region for a gold mining company, identifying the medieval mines of the Kingdom of Mutapa with the ancient land of Ophir. In 1914 Emperor Wilhelm II restored his title and gave him a pension. He published an autobiography in February 1918 and died on 10 September that year.

A proponent of Social Darwinism and Völkisch thought, he was called Hänge-Peters (Hangman-Peters) by critics in the German press and mkono wa damu, the man with blood on his hands, by Africans. Colonial circles hailed him as a national hero, Adolf Hitler rehabilitated him by decree in 1936, and a 1941 propaganda film starred Hans Albers as Peters. Many German streets named after him were later renamed, among them Berlin's Petersallee on 23 August 2024.
carl-philipp-emanuel-bach: Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach was born on 8 March 1714 in Weimar to Johann Sebastian Bach and his first wife, Maria Barbara. The composer Georg Philipp Telemann was his godfather. At ten he entered the St. Thomas School in Leipzig, which his father directed as Thomaskantor, and he was trained in music almost entirely by his father. Like his brothers, he also studied law, at Leipzig University in 1731 and at Frankfurt an der Oder in 1735. He took his degree in 1738 at the age of 24 but never practised law, and turned at once to music.

A few months after graduating, Bach was appointed at Berlin to the service of Crown Prince Frederick of Prussia, and when Frederick came to the throne in 1740 he joined the royal orchestra. His reputation was made by two sets of sonatas, dedicated in 1742 to Frederick the Great and in 1744 to Charles Eugene, Duke of Württemberg. In 1746 he became chamber musician, serving alongside Carl Heinrich Graun, Johann Joachim Quantz and Franz Benda. In Berlin he wrote nearly two hundred sonatas and other keyboard pieces, symphonies, songs and a Magnificat of 1749, and was known as the Berlin Bach, to tell him from his brother Johann Christian, the London Bach.

In 1768, after long negotiations, he was released from court service to succeed Telemann as Kapellmeister in Hamburg, and was named court composer to Frederick's sister, Princess Anna Amalia. The post required steady music for Protestant services, and he turned more to church and choral music: twenty-one settings of the Passion, some seventy cantatas, litanies and motets, and the oratorios Die Israeliten in der Wüste and Die Auferstehung und Himmelfahrt Jesu. In 1773 he wrote an autobiography, one of the first by a composer.

Bach was the chief representative of the empfindsamer Stil, the sensitive style, working between his father's Baroque and the Classical style that followed. His keyboard works, especially the fantasias, are full of dramatic silences and harmonic surprises. His treatise Versuch über die wahre Art das Clavier zu spielen, written in Berlin, became a definitive work on keyboard technique, studied by Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven. He died in Hamburg on 14 December 1788 and was buried in the Michaeliskirche. His reputation stood above his father's in the later 18th century, fell into neglect in the 19th, and revived chiefly from the 1960s.
carl-rover: Carl Georg Röver was born on 12 February 1889 in Lemwerder. In the First World War he served first with the regular army and then in the propaganda department of the Oberste Heeresleitung, the army's supreme command. He joined the Nazi Party in 1923 and joined again in 1925, after the period in which it had been banned. He also joined the Sturmabteilung (SA), rising to the rank of Obergruppenführer on 9 November 1938, and gained the same rank in the National Socialist Motor Corps on 30 January 1939.

Röver entered Oldenburg's municipal council in 1924, became a local party leader in April 1925 and district leader for Oldenburg and East Friesland in July 1927. On 20 May 1928 he entered the Oldenburg Landtag, and Adolf Hitler made him Gauleiter when Gau Weser-Ems was founded on 1 October 1928. He was elected to the Reichstag in September 1930 and kept the seat until his death. As minister-president from 16 June 1932 he held the highest party and state offices in his region at once.

In September 1932 he attacked the African pastor Robert Kwami in racist tirades, together with the Norddeutsche Mission and the Lutheran church council that had allowed Kwami to preach in St. Lambert's Church, Oldenburg; the sermon went ahead on 20 September 1932, and the episode became known as the Kwami Affair. Made Reichsstatthalter of Oldenburg and Bremen on 5 May 1933, he took part in the Holocaust, personally signing the order for every Jew deported from Bremen in his lifetime.
