He resisted Hermann Göring's wish to fold Bremen into Prussia and persuaded Hitler to refuse it. A favourite of Martin Bormann, he saw Weser-Ems supply most of the party's staff in the occupied Netherlands.

Röver is said to have suffered a stroke in May 1942 and died in Berlin on 15 May. Some sources give pneumonia as the cause and others heart failure. Hitler attended his lavish state funeral at the Reich Chancellery, where Alfred Rosenberg spoke the eulogy, and Paul Wegener succeeded him as Gauleiter. Bormann's biographer Jochen Von Lang concluded that Röver was killed by agents sent by Bormann, and attributed Röver's increasingly erratic behaviour to dementia brought on by late-stage syphilis, which Bormann ordered kept secret.
carl-schurz: Carl Schurz was born on 2 March 1829 at Liblar, now part of Erftstadt, in Rhenish Prussia, the son of a schoolteacher, Christian Schurz, and Marianne Jussen. He studied at the University of Bonn, where he befriended his professor Gottfried Kinkel. With Kinkel he founded the Bonner Zeitung, which advocated democratic reforms, and in 1849 he joined the revolutionary army in the campaign in the Palatinate and Baden as adjutant to the artillery commander Fritz Anneke.

When the army was defeated at the fortress of Rastatt, Schurz, knowing that the Prussians intended to kill their prisoners, escaped to Zürich. In 1850 he returned secretly to Prussia and rescued Kinkel from prison at Spandau. Forced out of France in 1851, he lived in London, teaching German, until he emigrated to the United States in 1852, shortly after marrying Margarethe Meyer.

In Wisconsin Schurz joined the anti-slavery movement and the Republican Party, and in 1858 he was admitted to the bar. Lincoln sent him as minister to Spain in 1861, and in April 1862 he became a brigadier general of Union volunteers. As a major general he led a division of the XI Corps at Chancellorsville and Gettysburg. The corps broke at both and was heavily criticised in the press. In 1865 he reported to the Senate on conditions in the South, finding that Reconstruction had not protected the rights of the freed people.

He was elected to the Senate from Missouri in 1868, the first German-born American in it. He broke with President Ulysses S. Grant, helped found the Liberal Republican Party and presided over its convention of 1872, which nominated Horace Greeley. Grant won by a landslide, and Schurz lost his seat in 1874 to Francis Cockrell.

President Rutherford B. Hayes made him Secretary of the Interior in 1877. Schurz held that merit should be the main consideration in appointments, though his efforts against patronage had limited success. He prosecuted land thieves, drew attention to forest preservation and opposed the transfer of the Indian Office to the War Department, which he thought corrupt. His policy towards Native Americans, which continued forced removal and later became assimilationist, was repressive, and promises made to chiefs were often broken.

Later he led the Mugwump movement against James G. Blaine in 1884, was president of the National Civil Service Reform League from 1892 to 1901, and as an anti-imperialist supported William Jennings Bryan in 1900. He died in New York on 14 May 1906.
carl-ulrich: Carl Theodor Johann Ulrich was born in Braunschweig on 28 January 1853, the son of a shoemaker. He left school in 1867, trained as a mechanical engineer and in 1872 travelled through Saxony, Hesse, Bavaria, Baden, Bohemia and Switzerland. In 1874 he settled in Offenbach in the Grand Duchy of Hesse, worked in a machine tool factory and joined the metalworkers' union. Jailed for 30 days that December for labour organising, he was one of the youngest delegates at the founding congress of the Socialist Workers' Party of Germany in 1875, and the same year became editor of the Neue Offenbacher Tages-Zeitung.

In 1885 Ulrich was elected to both chambers of the Hessian parliament, becoming with Franz Jöst the first social democratic deputies in Hesse. He sat in the lower house and its successors without a break until 1931, 46 years, the longest service of any legislator in German history. In 1886 he, August Bebel, Ignaz Auer and others were sentenced to nine months under the Anti-Socialist Laws. By the end of the 1880s he led the party in Hesse, and he sat in the Reichstag from 1890, apart from 1903 to 1907. A pragmatist who kept out of the party's quarrels over theory, he said in 1898: "We don't float in the clouds, we live on the earth."

When the Hessian monarchy was abolished on 11 November 1918, Ulrich became head of the new republican state, leading a cabinet of the SPD, the German Democratic Party and the Zentrum. After the SPD won the elections of January 1919 he formed a second such cabinet, and he continued as State-President under the constitution of 20 March 1920, his government being returned in 1921, 1924 and 1927. From 1922 he also ran the education ministry and worked for universal primary schooling.

Known as the red grand duke, he received a letter of congratulation from the former Grand Duke Ernest Louis on his 75th birthday in 1928, and retired that year in favour of Bernhard Adelung. He died in Offenbach on 12 April 1933, and the Carl-Ulrich-Brücke over the Main bears his name.
carl-von-clausewitz: Carl von Clausewitz was born on 1 July 1780 in Burg bei Magdeburg, in the Prussian Duchy of Magdeburg, the fourth and youngest son of a family that claimed noble status, which he accepted. The family said it descended from the Barons of Clausewitz in Upper Silesia, though scholars question the connection. His grandfather, the son of a Lutheran pastor, had been a professor of theology, and his father, once a lieutenant in the army of Frederick the Great, held a minor post in the Prussian internal-revenue service.

Clausewitz took part in the Rhine campaigns of 1793 and 1794, including the siege of Mainz, and fought in the Napoleonic Wars from 1806 to 1815. In 1801 he entered the Kriegsakademie in Berlin, where he won the regard of General Gerhard von Scharnhorst. With Hermann von Boyen and Karl von Grolman he was among Scharnhorst's chief allies in reforming the Prussian army between 1807 and 1814. At the Battle of Jena-Auerstedt on 14 October 1806 he was one of 25,000 prisoners taken as the Prussian army disintegrated.

On 10 December 1810 he married Countess Marie von Brühl, whom he had met in 1803. She was well educated and politically connected, played an important part in his career and thinking, and edited and published his collected works. He eventually reached the rank of major general.

Clausewitz drew on the campaigns of Frederick the Great and Napoleon for his principal book, Vom Kriege (On War). It was unfinished at his death and contains material from different stages of his thinking, so some passages seem to contradict each other; many of these apparent contradictions come from his dialectical method. It treats chance, the fog of war, friction, centres of gravity and the culminating point of the offensive, and holds that war belongs to the social realm rather than to art or science.

His line that war is the continuation of policy with other means is one side of an argument, and the synthesis is his trinity of violent emotion, chance and rational calculation. B. H. Liddell Hart argued that his followers, Moltke the Elder among them, carried his teaching to an extreme he had not intended.
carlisle: Carlisle lies on a slight rise at the confluence of the rivers Eden, Caldew and Petteril, about eight miles (13 km) south of the present Anglo-Scottish border, which earned it the nickname of the Great Border City. Its name comes from the Cumbric Caer Luel. Luguvalium took its name from a native name reconstructed as Brittonic Luguwaljon, the city of Luguwalos, a Celtic given name meaning strength of Lugus.

The earliest recorded inhabitants were the Carvetii. Luguvalium was founded to serve the forts along Hadrian's Wall, though it may have earlier origins. After Roman rule the region was the British kingdom of Rheged, whose capital, associated with Urien and his son Owain, has been identified with the Cair Ligualid listed by Nennius. Rheged came under Northumbrian control before 730, and for the rest of the first millennium Carlisle was contested between the kingdom of Strathclyde and Anglian Northumbria. In 685 St Cuthbert was shown its walls and a Roman fountain.

A priory built in the early 12th century became Carlisle Cathedral in 1133, when the Diocese of Carlisle was created, and as a diocesan seat the town gained city status. It was county town of Cumberland, and its earliest recorded charter was issued by Henry II.

Mary, Queen of Scots was held in the castle in 1568. In 1539 Henry VIII employed the engineer Stefan von Haschenperg to modernise the defences. Carlisle has been besieged at least ten times, and the reiving of the border families was suppressed more firmly after James VI of Scotland became James I of England in 1603. In the 19th century textile mills and engineering works opened in the Caldew Valley and Carlisle became a railway town, with seven companies sharing its station.

Carlisle is the only city in Cumbria and its largest settlement, with a population of 77,730 in 2021. The castle houses the Border Regiment Museum, and Tullie House Museum, opened in 1893, shows the Roman occupation, Hadrian's Wall and the Border Reivers. The cathedral remains the seat of the Diocese of Carlisle.
carlism: Carlism aimed to place on the Spanish throne a branch of the Bourbon dynasty descended from Don Carlos, Count of Molina, who lived from 1788 to 1855. It grew out of an early 19th-century dispute over the succession and out of dissatisfaction with the Alfonsine line of the House of Bourbon. Spanish kingdoms had traditionally allowed daughters to inherit in the absence of sons, but when the French Bourbon Philip V acceded on 1 November 1700, the Salic law of the French royal house led to a semi-Salic system excluding women unless all male descendants of Philip had died out.
Carlists defended that rule. The term carlistas for followers of Carlos María Isidro emerged in the mid-1820s, and the supporters themselves cautiously began to accept the name in the 1840s.

The First Carlist War, from 1833 to 1840, was fought between supporters of the regent Maria Christina, acting for Isabella II, and those of the late king's brother Carlos de Borbón, whose goal was a return to absolute monarchy. Portugal, France and the United Kingdom supported the regency and sent volunteers and even regular forces. A minor Catalan uprising from 1847 to 1849 made up the Second Carlist War, and a third war began in 1872.

After the fall of Isabella II in 1868 and the strong support of Pope Pius IX, many conservative Catholics joined the movement, and it had about 90 members of parliament in 1871. After its defeat in 1876 it returned to peaceful politics, building under the Marquis de Cerralbo a mass party around local assemblies called Círculos.

In July 1936 the Carlists joined the Nationalist rising uneasily. Their militia, the Requetés, took over Pamplona on 19 July, and in a few days almost all of Navarre was occupied. Under Franco the movement was gradually marginalised. In the first democratic elections of 1977 only one Carlist senator was elected, and Carlists have since remained outside parliament.

The motto Dios, Patria, Fueros, Rey, meaning God, Fatherland, Local Rule and King, summed up its principles: Catholic faith as the basis of Spain, patriotism seen as a nesting of communities, regional self-rule under fueros, and a king limited by the Church's doctrine and the laws and usages of the kingdom. Its flag was the red cross of Burgundy on white, and the red beret was its emblem.

Cultural and political regionalism in Spain is described as largely Carlist in origin, and Sabino Arana, a founder of Basque nationalism, came from a Carlist background. Writers including Ramón María del Valle-Inclán, a Carlist himself, wrote novels about it.
carlist-wars: When King Ferdinand VII died in 1833, his widow, Queen Maria Cristina, became regent for their two-year-old daughter, Queen Isabella II. The country split into the Cristinos, or Isabelinos, who backed the regent and were the party of the Liberals, and the Carlists, who backed Infante Carlos of Spain, Count of Molina, the late king's brother. Carlos denied the validity of the Pragmatic Sanction of 1830, which abolished the semi-Salic law; he had been born before it.

The Carlists wanted a return to autocratic monarchy and rallied to the cry of God, Country and King, defending Spanish tradition, meaning Legitimism and Catholicism, against liberalism. The wars also had a strong regional side, because the new order called into question regional laws and customs kept for centuries.

The First Carlist War lasted more than seven years and at one time or another spread over most of the country, though the main fighting was in the Basque Country and in Aragon, Catalonia and Valencia. The Carlists were rural and traditionalist and at first did better through guerrilla tactics, but they were defeated by liberal forces led by General Baldomero Espartero. More than 120,000 people, about 5% of the pre-war population, died, which makes it one of the bloodiest wars in Spanish history.

A minor Catalan uprising in 1846 to 1849 tried to install Carlos, Count of Montemolín. The French detained Don Carlos so that he could not join, which doomed the effort. The last war began after Queen Isabella II was overthrown in 1868 and the Cortes replaced her with Amadeo, Duke of Aosta. After the elections of 1872 brought government violence against Carlist candidates, the pretender Carlos VII decided that only force could win him the throne, and the war lasted four years.

The war ended in 1876 with Carlos VII defeated and Alfonso XII installed as King of Spain. The wars brought serious instability to nineteenth-century Spain, slowing economic development and reducing its international standing. Carlist violence could not reverse the liberal reforms but slowed them, so that even in the early twentieth century Spain was not fully centralised. Historians count three wars, while other authors and popular usage speak of two main ones and treat the events of 1846 to 1849 as a minor episode. The tensions behind the wars were never fully resolved.
carlo-cattaneo: Cattaneo was born in Milan on 15 June 1801, the son of Melchiorre Cattaneo, a goldsmith, and Maria Antonia Sangiorgi. He studied law at the University of Pavia and graduated in 1824. A republican by conviction, he took part in his youth in the Carbonari movement in Lombardy. He met the philosopher Giandomenico Romagnosi, whose stress on practical solutions and interdisciplinary work drew him, and hoped to turn the Italian people away from romanticism and rhetoric towards the positive sciences.
In 1839 he founded the review Il Politecnico in Milan to set out these ideas. In 1835 he married his longtime fiancée Anne Pyne Woodcock, and from 1840 to 1848 he lived at the Palazzo Gavazzi.

During the Five Days of Milan (18-22 March 1848), Cattaneo formed a council of war with the young democrats Enrico Cernuschi, Giulio Terzaghi and Giorgio Clerici, with its headquarters at Palazzo Taverna in via Bigli. When Field Marshal Radetzky sounded out the rebels about terms, some leaders were ready for an armistice that would let Piedmontese troops arrive, but Cattaneo demanded the complete evacuation of Lombardy. On 21 March he again refused an armistice, saying it was better to die of hunger than on the gallows.

When the Austrians returned in August 1848 he fled to the canton of Ticino. From 1852 to 1865 he taught philosophy at the new lyceum of Lugano and shaped its teaching. He wrote a history of the 1848 revolution and the Archivio triennale delle cose d'Italia (1850-1855), revived Il Politecnico in 1860, and in 1858 received an honorary Swiss bourgeoisie from the Grand Council of Ticino.

Cattaneo opposed Camillo Benso di Cavour for his unitarian views and for ceding Nice and Savoy to France in the Treaty of Turin. In 1860 Giuseppe Garibaldi called him to Naples to help govern the Neapolitan provinces, but he would not accept union with Piedmont without local autonomy. Elected office required an oath to the monarchy, which he would not take; in 1868 he agreed to stand for the Chamber of Deputies but withdrew at the last moment. He died on 6 February 1869 at Castagnola in Switzerland.

Some have judged him too bitter a partisan, and his ideas of local autonomy were thought inopportune at a time when unity seemed essential. Gaetano Salvemini counted him among the men of genius of 19th-century Italy, with Giacomo Leopardi, Cavour and Francesco de Sanctis.
carlo-i-tocco: Carlo was the son of Leonardo I Tocco, count of Cephalonia and duke of Leukas, and Maddalena de' Buondelmonti, sister of Esau de' Buondelmonti, the ruler of Ioannina. His grandmother Margherita Orsini was a sister of Nicholas Orsini and John II Orsini, rulers of Epirus, so he inherited a claim to Epirus from both families. He succeeded his father in 1376 and shared power with his brother Leonardo II, who received Zante as an appanage in 1399. His marriage to Francesca, daughter of Nerio I Acciaioli, Duke of Athens, gave him a claim to Corinth and Megara, which he seized in 1395.

His islands could not raise a large army, so he hired mercenaries, mostly Albanians, rewarding their leaders with gifts and fiefs. From 1405 he held fortresses on the mainland, including Angelokastro, and in February 1411 the people of Ioannina invited him to succeed his uncle Esau. The Albanian clans under Yaqub Spata of Arta defeated him in 1412 but failed to take the city; after Yaqub was killed in 1416, Arta surrendered, and the Tocchi held every major town in Epirus. In 1415 Manuel II Palaiologos granted him the title despotes, and he signed his letters and decrees in Greek.

In 1421 he bought Glarentza in the Morea from Oliverio Franco. A raid on the animals of Albanian herders in late 1426 brought war with the Byzantines, and in 1427 John VIII Palaiologos's fleet defeated his at the Battle of the Echinades. In the settlement his niece Creusa married Constantine Palaiologos, later Constantine XI, who received Glarentza as her dowry.

Carlo died on 4 July 1429. He had no children with Francesca but five illegitimate sons and two daughters, one of whom married the Ottoman prince Musa Çelebi in 1412. He was succeeded by his nephew Carlo II Tocco, son of Leonardo II. The Chronicle of the Tocco, written by a contemporary and covering 1375 to 1425, is a main source for his rule.
carlo-maderno: Maderno was born in Capolago, in today's Ticino, which was then a bailiwick of the Swiss Confederacy. He began his career in the marble quarries of the far north and moved to Rome in 1588 with four of his brothers to assist his uncle Domenico Fontana. He worked at first as a marble cutter, a background that helped shape the sculptural quality of his architecture. He is often called the brother of the sculptor Stefano Maderno, but this is not universally agreed.

His first solo project, in 1596, was the facade of the ancient church of Santa Susanna, built between 1597 and 1603. A dynamic rhythm of columns and pilasters with a protruding central bay, it was among the first Baroque facades to break with the Mannerist conventions seen in the Gesù. It brought him to the attention of Pope Paul V, who appointed him chief architect of St Peter's Basilica.

At St Peter's Maderno had to modify Michelangelo's plans and design an extended nave with a palatial facade, completed in 1612 and built to allow papal blessings from the balcony above the central door. The extension turned the Greek cross into a Latin cross and has been criticised for blocking the view of the dome from the piazza, though the approach avenue is modern. His last work there was the Confessio, a crypt-like space under the dome lit by 95 bronze lamps.

Most of his work was the remodelling of existing buildings. Santa Maria della Vittoria, built 1608-20, is the main building he designed apart from a facade. At Sant'Andrea della Valle he designed the facade and built the dome, the third largest in Rome. He also worked on the Quirinal Palace, Castel Gandolfo and the Palazzo Barberini, and his Palazzo Mattei dates from 1598 to 1618.

Maderno died in Rome on 31 January 1629, aged 73, and was buried in San Giovanni dei Fiorentini, where he had directed the building of the dome and main body. At his death the facade of Sant'Andrea della Valle was half built, and Carlo Fontana completed it to his design. Francesco Borromini and Bernini both worked on Maderno's buildings, and their works were influenced by his.
carloforte: Carloforte is a fishing and resort town and comune in the province of Sulcis Iglesiente, in the autonomous island region of Sardinia. It stands on the Isola di San Pietro, or Saint Peter's Island, about 7 kilometres off the south-western coast of the Sardinian mainland. Its Tabarchino name, U Pàize, means the village or the town. Ferries link its port with the mainland at Portovesme and with Calasetta on the island of Sant'Antioco, another fishing port that has a community of Tabarchini.

According to a legend, a church on the island, the Chiesa dei Novelli Innocenti, was founded in the early 14th century in honour of hundreds of participants in the Children's Crusade of 1212 who died in a shipwreck just off the island in a gale. It was the only visible building the settlers found when they came.

The town was founded in the 18th century by around 30 families of coral fishers. They descended from people of the Ligurian town of Pegli, near Genoa, who had left it in 1541 and settled on the island of Tabarka, off the coast of Tunisia, to fish for coral. After centuries the coral there was exhausted. On their way back towards Italy the families found plenty of coral in the sea off western Sardinia, and they asked Charles Emmanuel III, King of Piedmont-Sardinia, for permission to settle on the then uninhabited island of San Pietro. When he agreed, the island was colonised and the town was named Carloforte in his honour, meaning Charles the Strong or Carlo's Fort.

Carloforte has 5,851 inhabitants and keeps strong cultural ties with Pegli and Genoa. Most of its people speak tabarchino, a variety of Ligurian separate from both Italian and Sardinian, which most children also use and which is taught in the island's schools. The town has a long tradition of wooden boatbuilding, and traditional lateen-sail fishing boats can be seen in its harbour. North of the town stand the buildings of a former communal tuna-processing plant, which served the island's tonnare tuna fishing. The Capo Sandalo Lighthouse, on the far side of the island, dates from the 1880s. Fishing and tourism are its main sources of income, with money sent home by merchant mariners from Carloforte.
carloman-i: Carloman was born on 28 June 751, the second surviving son of Pepin the Short and Bertrada of Laon. At the age of three he was anointed King of the Franks, with his father and his brother Charlemagne, and given the title Patrician of the Romans by Pope Stephen II, who had left Rome to ask the Frankish king for help against the Lombards.

On Pepin's death the kingdom was divided between the brothers. Carloman's share lay in the centre of the realm, with its capital at Soissons, and took in the Parisian basin, Provence, Burgundy and Alemannia among other regions. It was easier to defend than Charlemagne's lands but poorer. The brothers disliked each other, though the reasons are unclear. When Aquitaine rebelled, Carloman marched to help Charlemagne but quarrelled with him at Moncontour and withdrew, which damaged his standing. Rosamond McKitterick argues that there is no evidence of lasting animosity.

In 770 their mother Bertrada began diplomacy that left Carloman isolated. Charlemagne married Desiderata, daughter of the Lombard king Desiderius, and Bertrada won him the friendship of Tassilo III of Bavaria. Carloman sought the support of Pope Stephen III, but after Desiderius had the papal official Christopher the Primicerius murdered the pope favoured the Lombards and Charlemagne. Charlemagne then repudiated his Lombard wife, and Desiderius appears to have allied with Carloman.

Carloman died on 4 December 771 at the villa of Samoussy. The death was set down to natural causes, and a severe nosebleed is sometimes named. He was buried at Reims and reburied in the Basilique Saint-Denis in the 13th century. His widow Gerberga fled with her two sons to Desiderius, after his supporters invited Charlemagne to annex his lands, and Desiderius asked Pope Hadrian I to anoint the boys as kings. Charlemagne responded by invading Italy and ending the Lombard kingdom. What became of Gerberga and her sons is unknown.
carloman-mayor-of-the-palace: Carloman was the eldest son of Charles Martel, mayor of the palace and duke of the Franks, and his wife Chrotrud of Treves. When Charles died in 741, Carloman and his brother Pepin the Short succeeded to their father's positions, Carloman in Austrasia and Pepin in Neustria. Charles had left nothing to his half-brother Grifo, the son of his second wife Swanachild. When Grifo demanded a share, the brothers besieged him at Laon in 741, took him captive and forced him into a monastery.

On Carloman's initiative the two mayors installed the Merovingian Childeric III as king in 743, though the throne had been vacant since the death of Theuderic IV in 737. For seven years the brothers worked together and campaigned jointly against Hunald I of Aquitaine, against the Saxons in 742 and 743, and against Odilo, Duke of Bavaria, their brother-in-law.

In his realm Carloman supported the Anglo-Saxon missionary Winfrid, later Saint Boniface, whom he charged with restructuring the church in Austrasia. In 742 he helped convene the Concilium Germanicum, the first major synod in the eastern Frankish lands, which he chaired jointly with Boniface. It ruled that priests might not bear arms or keep women in their houses and that they must root out pagan belief. Carloman also gave the land for the monastery of Fulda, one of Boniface's most important foundations.

He could also be ruthless. After repeated revolts, in 746 he summoned the Alemanni magnates to an assembly at Cannstatt and had most of them, said to number in the thousands, arrested and executed for high treason in the Blood Court at Cannstatt. This destroyed almost the whole tribal leadership and ended the independence of the duchy of Alemannia, thereafter governed by counts appointed by the Franks.

On 15 August 747 Carloman renounced his position and was tonsured in Rome by Pope Zachary. The sources agree that his withdrawal was voluntary, though some have speculated that Pepin asked the pope to keep him in Italy. He founded a monastery on Monte Soratte and then went to Monte Cassino. In 754 he left it at the request of the Lombard king Aistulf to ask Pepin, now king, not to march on Italy. Pepin refused, and Carloman died soon afterwards at Vienne on 17 August and was buried at Monte Cassino. Norman Cantor called him the first of a new type of saintly king.
carloman-of-bavaria: Carloman was the eldest son of Louis the German, king of East Francia, and Hemma, daughter of a Bavarian count. His birth date is unknown, probably around 828 or 830. He first appears as the leader of reinforcements from Bavaria and Alemannia whom he brought to his father at Worms in 842 during the civil war with his uncle Lothair. Notker of Saint Gall called him bellicosissimus, 'most warlike'.

In 856 his father appointed him governor of Carantania, and in 864 commander of the southeastern marches. In 861 he expelled several frontier commanders without his father's consent and sided with Rastislav of Moravia; in 863 Louis invaded, forced him to submit and took him into custody. He escaped in 864 and was reconciled with his father. In 865 the Division of Frankfurt assigned him Bavaria and the southeastern marches after Louis's death.

In 870 Carloman established Frankish domination over Great Moravia, when Svatopluk handed over his uncle Rastislav. He captured Svatopluk in 871 but reinstalled him to pacify the country, and Svatopluk then turned on the Franks and inflicted severe losses. Louis the German died on 28 August 876, and Carloman became king of Bavaria. He refounded the palace and monastery at Ötting and made the scholar Baldo his chancellor.

After Louis II of Italy died on 12 August 875, Carloman led an army into Italy, declaring himself the chosen successor, but Charles the Bald, whom Pope John VIII favoured, paid him a large sum to leave. When Charles died on 6 October 877, Carloman was elected king of Italy by the nobles assembled at Pavia. He confirmed bishops as royal representatives, granted Bishop Wibod of Parma authority outside the city walls, and had pennies minted at Milan and Pavia.

In 879 Carloman was incapacitated, perhaps by a stroke, and lost his voice though he could still write. His illegitimate son Arnulf took control in his name, but in November Carloman's brother Louis the Younger came to Bavaria and forced a settlement. Carloman abdicated Bavaria to Louis, and Italy passed to Charles the Fat. He died in 880 and was buried in the chapel of his palace at Ötting.

Regino of Prüm called him learned in letters, just and very warlike. Most sources place his death in March, but one gives 21 September. Arnulf continued as margrave of Carinthia, became king of East Francia in 887 and emperor in 896.
carlos-andres-perez: Pérez was born on 27 October 1922 at the hacienda La Argentina near Rubio in Táchira state, the eleventh of twelve children. His father, a Colombian-born coffee planter and pharmacist, was ruined by falling coffee prices and harassment by henchmen allied to the dictator Juan Vicente Gómez, and died of a heart attack in 1936. The widow moved the family to Caracas in 1939. Pérez became active in politics at 15 and was a founder of the Democratic Action party. In 1945 he became private secretary to Rómulo Betancourt, and after the military coup of 1948 he spent a decade in exile. He served as Minister of Interior and Justice from 1959 to 1964, when he was known for his tough response to guerrillas.

Elected in December 1973 with 48.7 per cent of the vote, Pérez took office just as petroleum prices rose sharply. He nationalised the iron and petroleum industries, tripled public spending and promoted state industrial projects. His administration was nicknamed Saudi Venezuela for its ambitions, and the party lost the 1978 election to the Social Christian Party. Abroad he restored relations with Cuba, opposed the Somoza and Pinochet dictatorships, helped settle the transfer of the Panama Canal, and co-founded SELA in 1975.

Elected again in 1988, he turned to economic liberalisation with an International Monetary Fund loan, in a programme called El Gran Viraje. A rise in transport fares set off the Caracazo riots from 27 February 1989, and deaths ranged from an official 277 to unofficial estimates of up to 5,000. Lieutenant-Colonel Hugo Chávez led a coup attempt on 4 February 1992, and a second, bloodier one followed on 27 November. On 21 May 1993 the Supreme Court accepted charges of embezzling 250 million bolívars of a discretionary fund, and Congress removed him from office on 31 August.

He was sentenced in May 1996 to 28 months in prison, and was later prosecuted again on other charges. He lived in exile from 1998, mostly in Miami, and died there on 25 December 2010. His remains were returned to Venezuela and buried in October 2011. He is remembered as a founder of Acción Democrática and as the first Venezuelan president impeached by the Supreme Court.
carlos-antonio-lopez: Carlos Antonio López Ynsfrán was born at Manorá, near Asunción, on 4 November 1792, one of eight children. He graduated from the Real Colegio y Seminario de San Carlos and began a law practice, which let him form influential connections. He attracted the hostility of the dictator José Gaspar Rodríguez de Francia, his reputed uncle, and went into hiding for several years.

López was briefly secretary of the military junta led by Colonel Mariano Roque Alonso, which ruled from 1840 to 1841 after the death of Francia. On 12 March 1841 Congress chose López and Roque Alonso as joint consuls for three years. In 1844 he exiled Roque Alonso and assumed dictatorial powers. A new constitution soon changed the title of head of state to president and elected López for ten years. It gave him powers almost as sweeping as Francia's and contained no guarantees of civil rights; the word liberty was not in the text. He was re-elected in 1854 for three years and in 1857 for ten more, with the power to nominate his own successor.

His government developed Paraguay's primary resources, strengthened its armed forces and built the Fortress of Humaitá, hiring numerous foreign technicians, most of them British. It signed commercial treaties with Brazil in 1850, with Great Britain, France and the United States in 1853, and with Argentina in 1856. It set up a railway line and steamship routes on the rivers, expanded primary schools, reopened the seminary, and established textile factories and shipyards. The Ybycuí Iron Foundry produced iron tools and cannons. He released political prisoners soon after taking power and took measures to abolish slavery.

Disputes with Brazil, the United States and the British Empire several times nearly led to war. In 1858 the United States sent a nineteen-ship squadron after President James Buchanan threatened reprisals for Paraguay's refusal to ratify the treaty of 1853, among other grievances. López resolved to make Paraguay so strong that further intervention would be impossible. He died on 10 September 1862 and was succeeded as president by his eldest son, Francisco Solano López. A barrio of Asunción is named after him.
carlos-camacho: Carlos Garcia Camacho was born on 16 November 1924 in the village of Hagåtña, Guam, to Felix Martinez Camacho and Antonia Cruz Garcia. He attended Aquinas College in Grand Rapids, Michigan, from 1946 to 1949, and in 1952 earned a D.D.S. degree from Marquette University in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. A Republican, he sat in the Guam Legislature from 1965 to 1967.

At the age of 44 he was appointed governor by President Richard Nixon, succeeding Manuel F.L. Guerrero, with Kurt Moylan as lieutenant governor. In December 1969 he travelled to Vietnam to spend Christmas with the Chamoru troops serving there. His appointed term lasted only eighteen months, because the Guam Elective Governor Act of 1968 let Guamanians choose their own governor from 1970. In that first election Camacho and Moylan defeated the Democratic ticket of Ricardo Bordallo, and they were inaugurated on 4 January 1971 at the Plaza de España in Agana.

Camacho offered incentives through the Guam Economics Development and other help to private business, and his years saw a wave of hotel building, including the Hilton, Okura and Reef hotels. He began road projects that his successors continued, among them the widening of Marine Drive, now Marine Corps Drive. He is credited with drawing educated Chamorros such as Tony Palomo and Joseph F. Ada back to Guam, and he kept able administrators of the other party. In the 1974 election he won a plurality against Bordallo, but after a challenge that went to the U.S. Supreme Court, Bordallo won the runoff.

Camacho returned to dentistry and kept a private practice until his death on 6 December 1979, at the age of 55. He is buried at the Pigo Cemetery in Anigua. He and his wife, Lourdes Perez Camacho, had seven children: their son Felix Perez Camacho served as Governor of Guam from 2003 to 2011, and their daughter Mary Camacho Torres became a senator in the Guam Legislature.
carlos-castillo-armas: Carlos Castillo Armas was born on 4 November 1914 in Santa Lucía Cotzumalguapa, in Escuintla, the son of a landowner but born out of wedlock, so that he could not inherit the property. He graduated from the military academy in 1936. In 1944 he joined the rebels who overthrew Federico Ponce Vaides, as a protégé of Colonel Francisco Javier Arana. After Arana's failed coup of 1949 he went into exile in Honduras. When Jacobo Árbenz launched the land reform known as Decree 900, the United Fruit Company lobbied the US government, and in 1953 President Dwight Eisenhower authorised Operation PBSuccess to overthrow him, with Castillo Armas as its leader.

On 18 June 1954 Castillo Armas led about 480 CIA-trained men over the border from Honduras. They made little headway, but the Guatemalan army grew unwilling to fight, believing the US would intervene. Árbenz resigned on 27 June, and Castillo Armas became president on 7 July. In October 1954 he won an election in which he was the only candidate, with 99 percent of the vote.

His government arrested many thousands of opponents as communists; historians estimate more than 3,000 arrests, and about 1,000 agricultural workers were killed by his troops on Finca Jocatán alone. A National Committee of Defense Against Communism investigated nearly 70,000 people. Parties, labour unions and peasant organisations were outlawed. Of 529,939 manzanas expropriated under Decree 900, 368,481 were returned to landowners. The government depended on US aid, and in histories of the period Castillo Armas has been called a dictator.

On 26 July 1957 Castillo Armas was shot dead in the presidential palace by a guard, Romeo Vásquez Sánchez, who was reported to have killed himself afterwards. There is no conclusive information on whether he acted alone. His reversal of the reforms of his predecessors sparked leftist insurgencies, which led to the Guatemalan Civil War of 1960 to 1996.
carlos-davila: Carlos Gregorio Dávila Espinoza was born on 15 September 1887 in Los Ángeles, Chile, to Luis Dávila and Emilia Espinoza. He graduated from the School of Arts and Crafts, now the University of Santiago, in 1907, and entered law school at the University of Chile in 1911 but left three years later to work for El Mercurio. In 1917 he founded La Nación in Santiago, which he directed until 1927. From 1927 to 1931 he was Chilean ambassador to the United States, and in 1929 he received honorary doctorates from Columbia University and the University of Southern California.

Dávila was a member of the Government Junta that ruled Chile from 4 June to 8 July 1932, and its president from 16 June. On 8 July he dissolved the junta, took power as Provisional President of Chile and called new congressional elections. He held the office until 13 September, one of six people who led the country as president or head of a junta that year. He also founded the magazine Hoy in 1932.

In 1933 he was visiting professor of international law at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill under the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. He then worked for many years in the United States with the Editors Press Service and as correspondent for South American newspapers, received the Maria Moors Cabot Award from Columbia University in 1941, and wrote We of the Americas (1949). His Dávila plan of 1940 created the Inter-American Development Commission, which became part of the Organization of American States in 1948. He sat on the council of the United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration from 1943 to 1946.

Having contributed to the founding of the organisation, he was chosen secretary general of the OAS in August 1954. He married the artist Herminia Arrate in 1918 and, after her death, Frances Adams Moore in 1950. He died on 19 October 1955, 14 months into his term.
carlos-de-siguenza-y-gongora: Sigüenza was born in Mexico City on 14 August 1645, the eldest son among nine children of a father from Madrid, who had tutored the Spanish royal family, and a mother born in Seville, through whom he was related to the poet Luis de Góngora. He entered the Society of Jesus as a novice in 1660 but was dismissed in 1668 for repeatedly breaking its discipline by going out at night, and his plea to return was refused. Ordained a secular priest in 1673, he had no parish and spent his life seeking posts to support his extended family.

He won the chair of mathematics and astrology at the university on 20 July 1672, though he held no doctorate, and taught mainly astronomy. In his Philosophical Manifest Against the Comets of 1681 he tried to separate astronomy from astrology, and when the Tyrolean Jesuit Eusebio Kino criticised his views he answered with the Libra Astronómica y Filosófica of 1690, arguing that authority had no place in these sciences, only proof. In the 1680s he made the first map of all of New Spain, and in 1692 King Charles II named him royal geographer; that year he took part in the expedition of Andrés de Pez to Pensacola Bay, which he mapped along with the mouth of the Mississippi.

During the riot of 8 June 1692, when a crowd set fire to the viceregal palace, he saved most of the archive's documents at the risk of his life, and his letter to Admiral Pez is a main Spanish account of the riot. He was chaplain of the Hospital del Amor de Dios from 1682 until his death.

A criollo patriot, he designed the triumphal arch for Viceroy Cerda y Aragón in 1680 with the twelve Aztec rulers as models of political virtue, and he held that the Mexican Indians descended from Naphtuhim, son of Misraim, the founder of Egypt, and that St Thomas the Apostle was Quetzalcoatl. He learned Nahuatl and received the manuscripts of the historian Fernando de Alva Ixtlilxochitl from the historian's son, and his attribution of the Nican mopohua to Antonio Valeriano persists today. Los infortunios de Alonso Ramírez (1690), once read as a novel, is now shown by archival research to rest on a true story he edited. He died on 22 August 1700, after asking for his body to be autopsied.
carlos-duke-of-madrid: Carlos de Borbón y Austria-Este was born on 30 March 1848 in Ljubljana, then the capital of Carniola, the elder son of Prince Juan, Count of Montizón, and Maria Beatrix of Austria-Este. As an infant he lived briefly in London with his family, where his younger brother Alfonso was born. His father, considered too liberal for Carlist tastes, left their mother, and the boys grew up with her in Modena. Her brother Francis V, Duke of Modena, was largely responsible for their education and was the chief influence in their early lives. Carlos was known for Traditionalist views that differed greatly from his father's.

Carlos became the Carlist claimant to the Spanish throne as Carlos VII in 1868, when his father renounced his claim. After his father's death in 1887 he also held the Legitimist claim to the French throne, under the name Charles XI. He organised and led the Third Carlist War, fought between 1872 and 1876.

On 4 February 1867 he married Princess Margherita of Parma, daughter of Charles III, Duke of Parma, at Schloss Frohsdorf in Austria. They had five children, Blanca, Jaime, Elvira, Beatrice and Alice. Margherita died in January 1893, and on 28 April 1894 Carlos married Princess Marie-Berthe de Rohan in Prague, in the private chapel of her distant cousin Cardinal Schönborn. Marie-Berthe had a dominant personality, and the marriage was very unpopular among Carlists. According to one assessment, all writers agree that it was disastrous for Carlos, his family and the Carlist party.
Carlos died in Varese in 1909 and is buried in the Cathedral of San Giusto in Trieste. His son Jaime, Duke of Anjou and Madrid, followed him in claiming both the French and Spanish thrones.
carlos-finlay: Finlay was born Juan Carlos Finlay y de Barrés in Puerto Príncipe, now Camagüey, to a Scottish father, the physician Edward Finlay, and a French mother, Elisa de Barrés. Cuba was then part of the Kingdom of Spain. Because the University of Havana would not recognise his European credits, he enrolled at Jefferson Medical College in Philadelphia, where John Kearsley Mitchell, a proponent of the germ theory of disease, and his son Silas Weir Mitchell supervised his studies. He graduated in 1855, opened an ophthalmology practice in Havana in 1857 and studied in Paris in 1860–61.

Finlay did his work in the 1870s, but it came to prominence only in 1900. In 1881 he was the first to theorise that a mosquito carried the organism causing yellow fever, so that a mosquito that bit a victim could infect a healthy person. He presented this at the 1881 International Sanitary Conference, where it was ridiculed. A year later he identified a mosquito of the genus Aedes as the carrier, and he recommended controlling the mosquito population to control the disease.

The Walter Reed Commission of 1900 confirmed his hypothesis nearly twenty years later. Reed credited Finlay with the discovery of the vector, cited his papers and said so in his correspondence. General Leonard Wood, the American military governor of Cuba, compared the confirmation with Jenner's introduction of vaccination. William C. Gorgas used the discovery to reduce mosquito-borne disease among the workers on the Panama Canal from 1903, when about 10 per cent of the workforce had died each year from malaria and yellow fever. Finlay was chief health officer of Cuba from 1902 to 1909.

Finlay wrote about 40 articles on yellow fever, and others on leprosy, cholera, gravity and plant diseases. He often treated patients who could not pay. He was nominated seven times for the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, but never won it, and he received the French Legion of Honour in 1908. He died of a stroke at his house in Havana on 20 August 1915.

In 1928 Cuba established the National Order of Merit Carlos J. Finlay, and in 1942 the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene awarded him the Walter Reed Medal posthumously. Havana has a medical history museum named for him, founded in 1962, and a monument in the shape of a syringe at Marianao. A statue stands on the bayfront at Panama City, and UNESCO's Carlos J. Finlay Prize for Microbiology is named after him.
carlos-frederico-lecor: Lecor was born on 6 October 1764 in the parish of Santos-o-Velho in Lisbon, the son of Louis Pierre Lecor, a French émigré, and Quitéria Maria Krusse, through whom he had German, Dutch and Spanish ancestry. The eldest of five sons of a merchant family, he was meant for a commercial career, but after moving to Faro in the 1770s he enlisted in the Portuguese Army in 1793 as a gunner, at the age of 29.

He rose to sergeant at the Fortress of Santo António da Barra in Tavira and became first lieutenant in the Artillery Regiment of Algarve in 1794. In 1795 and 1796 he served with the artillery of the Nau Príncipe da Beira, flagship of a fleet escorting merchant ships to Salvador in Brazil. Back in Lisbon he joined the Light Troops Legion and became aide-de-camp to the Marquis of Alorna, rising to major in 1802 and lieutenant-colonel in 1805.

When Junot invaded Portugal in November 1807, Lecor is credited with spotting the French army north of Abrantes and informing the Prince-Regent, the future King John VI. Unwilling to serve in the Légion Portugaise raised for Napoleon, he fled to Plymouth, where he helped create the Loyal Lusitanian Legion after the Portuguese uprisings of June 1808. Returning to Portugal with Colonel Robert Wilson, he became colonel of the 23rd Infantry Regiment at Almeida in December 1808.

From 1809 to 1813 he commanded brigades and the Beira Baixa region from Castelo Branco, served in the Bussaco campaign and on the Lines of Torres Vedras under Rowland Hill, and became brigadier general on 8 May 1811. Promoted major general on 4 June 1813, he fought at Sorauren, commanded the 7th Division at the Nivelle and led the Portuguese Division to the end of the war. He was the first Portuguese officer to command a division of British troops in Wellington's army.

After a short time as military governor of the Alentejo, he was made lieutenant general in June 1815 and given the Prince's Royal Voluntary Division, mostly Peninsular veterans, for service in Brazil. With it he conquered the Banda Oriental from the Federal League of José Gervasio Artigas and ruled the Cisplatina Province himself until the war of 1825–1828, in which he held Montevideo against an Argentine-Uruguayan siege. When Uruguay became independent under the peace treaty, he returned to Brazil.
carlos-fuentes: Carlos Fuentes Macías was born in Panama City on 11 November 1928, the son of Berta Macías and Rafael Fuentes, a Mexican diplomat. As the family moved with his father's career, he spent his childhood in several Latin American capitals, an experience he later said gave him the ability to see Latin America as a critical outsider. From 1934 to 1940 his father was posted to the Mexican Embassy in Washington, where he attended an English-language school and began to write. In 1940 the family moved to Santiago, Chile, where his interest in the poetry of Pablo Neruda led him to socialism.

He lived in Mexico for the first time at 16, when he went to study law at the National Autonomous University of Mexico with a diplomatic career in mind, and he later attended the Graduate Institute of International Studies in Geneva.

In 1957 Fuentes became head of cultural relations at the Mexican Secretariat of Foreign Affairs. His first novel, Where the Air Is Clear, appeared in 1958 and made him a national celebrity, allowing him to write full-time. In 1959 he moved to Havana after the Cuban Revolution. He served as Mexico's ambassador to France from 1975 to 1977 and resigned in protest at the appointment of the former president Gustavo Díaz Ordaz as ambassador to Spain. He taught at Cambridge, Princeton, Harvard, Columbia and other universities.

He was long a critic of the Institutional Revolutionary Party government that ruled Mexico from 1929 until 2000. In the 1980s he broke with the poet Octavio Paz over the Sandinistas, and a feud began that lasted until Paz's death in 1998. He received the Miguel de Cervantes Prize and, in 1999, Mexico's highest award, the Belisario Domínguez Medal of Honor. He died on 15 May 2012.

Fuentes named Cervantes, William Faulkner and Balzac as the writers most important to him, and his main theme was Mexican history and identity. Where the Air Is Clear is built around Federico Robles, a former revolutionary turned powerful financier, and presents Mexico City in vignettes. The Death of Artemio Cruz (1962) begins like Citizen Kane with its protagonist on his deathbed and tells his life in flashbacks: a soldier of the Mexican Revolution who becomes wealthy through violence, blackmail and bribery. Fuentes was a leading figure of the Latin American boom of the 1960s and 1970s, with Gabriel García Márquez, Mario Vargas Llosa and Julio Cortázar.

Terra Nostra (1975) tells the story of Hispanic civilisation, moving between the sixteenth and twentieth centuries. The Old Gringo (1985), loosely based on the disappearance of Ambrose Bierce during the Mexican Revolution, became the first United States bestseller by a Mexican author. His work has been translated into 24 languages.
carlos-humberto-romero: Carlos Humberto Romero Mena was born on 29 February 1924 in Chalatenango, after the death of his father, José María Romero. He studied at the Captain General Gerardo Barrios Military School and the Command and General Staff School, and from January to March 1962 he took a course in counter-insurgency at the School of the Americas in the Panama Canal Zone. In the 1960s he served as an intelligence officer, and he later commanded the Cavalry Group and the First Infantry Regiment and became chief of staff of the Armed Forces General Command.

A member of the National Conciliation Party, Romero was captured with President Fidel Sánchez Hernández, whose chief of staff he was, during the failed coup of 25 March 1972. The new president, Colonel Arturo Armando Molina, made him Minister of Defense and Public Security, in charge of all police and paramilitary activity, and the landowning oligarchy came to see him as its protector against communists and against Molina's agrarian reforms. In February 1973 he announced a terrorist plot by the Communist Party, which led to the arrest of about 100 members of the Christian Democratic Party with no link to it. He is also accused of having ordered the student massacre of 30 July 1975.

Chosen as candidate for his opposition to reform, Romero was declared the winner of the election of 20 February 1977 over Colonel Ernesto Antonio Claramount Roseville; the historian Michael Krennerich speaks of massive fraud. On 28 February the National Police attacked an opposition protest in the Plaza Libertad in San Salvador, killing up to 200 people by some counts, though official records gave 8. In November 1977 he enacted a law that legalised repression of opposition groups, and death squads such as the White Warriors Union, some commanded by his officers, operated during his term, while left-wing groups attacked officials and the security forces.

After the fall of Anastasio Somoza Debayle in Nicaragua in July 1979, United States officials privately urged Romero to resign. He sent his family abroad on 14 October 1979, and after the bloodless coup of the following day he went into exile in Guatemala, replaced by the Revolutionary Government Junta. He later returned and died in Colonia Escalón, San Salvador, on 27 February 2017.
carlos-ibanez-del-campo: Carlos Ibáñez del Campo was born on 3 November 1877 to Francisco Ibáñez and María Nieves del Campo. His father's family descended from an Irish captain, John Augustine Evans of Galway, who reached Chile in 1730 after the shipwreck of HMS Wager, and his mother's from a Frenchman, Giles Du Champ, who settled in Concepción in 1700. He grew up on his father's San Francisco estate at Vega de Ancoa and attended the Linares Boys' Lyceum, whose director, Rogelio Cuéllar, recommended him for the Military School, which he entered on 12 March 1896.

In 1924 the armed forces, led by General Luis Altamirano, banged their sabres on the floor of Congress in protest at the government of President Arturo Alessandri, who left the country as Altamirano set up a junta. Colonel Marmaduke Grove and Lieutenant Colonel Ibáñez led a second coup that deposed Altamirano, and the two men invited Alessandri to return.

Alessandri came back in 1925, and Ibáñez became Minister of War and later of Home Affairs. When Emiliano Figueroa Larraín, who had won 71 percent of the vote, resigned in 1927, Ibáñez became vice president as home affairs minister and won the presidential election of 22 May with 98 percent, his only opponent being the communist Elías Lafertte.

In his first term Ibáñez ruled largely by decree, named the members of the Senate and Chamber of Deputies himself, and had opponents, among them Grove, arrested and exiled. The historian Frederick Nunn judged that he was not a true dictator but a rigid authoritarian. His government also issued social legislation, including a labour code that was the first in Latin America.

After the crash of 1929 loans were called in and the value of copper and nitrate exports fell by 89 percent between 1927-1929 and 1932. Protests, a student strike and rioting in July 1931 left about 20 dead, and Ibáñez went into exile on 26 July 1931.

In 1952 he was elected again with 47 percent, promising to sweep away corruption with his broom and nicknamed the General of Hope. Inflation rose to 71 percent in 1954 and 83 percent in 1955, and fell to 33 percent by the end of his term with the help of the Klein-Sacks mission. He repealed the law banning the Communist Party. He was succeeded in 1958 by Jorge Alessandri Rodríguez, and he died in Santiago on 28 April 1960. The region of Aysén bears his name for his efforts to integrate Aysén and Magallanes into Chile.
carlos-manuel-de-cespedes: Carlos Manuel de Céspedes del Castillo was born on 18 April 1819 in Bayamo, into a sugar-producing family. He studied at the University of Havana, graduating in 1840, and then went to Spain for law studies, where he took part in revolutionary activities, was arrested and was forced into exile in France. In 1844, back in Cuba, he bought La Demajagua, an estate with a sugar plantation near Bayamo. Convinced that only armed opposition could bring independence, he made contact with other opponents of Spanish rule, among them Salvador Cisneros Betancourt, Bartolomé Masó and Pedro Figueredo, most of them from sugar families in the poorer east of the island.

On 10 October 1868 Céspedes made the Cry of Yara, declaring Cuban independence and beginning the Ten Years' War. That morning he sounded the bell of La Demajagua, which told his slaves it was time to work, and announced that they were free and invited them to join the war. In April 1869 he was chosen President of the Republic of Cuba in Arms. The war pitted tobacco planters and farmers of the east, joined by mulattos and some slaves, against the sugar-growing west and the Spanish governor-general; Hugh Thomas summarised it as a conflict between criollos and peninsulares.

The Spanish authorities captured Céspedes's son Oscar and offered to exchange his life for the president's resignation. Céspedes answered that Oscar was not his only son, since every Cuban who died for the revolution was also his son, and Oscar was shot.

Céspedes was deposed in 1873 in a leadership coup. The new government would not let him go into exile or give him an escort, and Spanish troops killed him in a mountain refuge on 27 February 1874. The war ended in 1878 with the Pact of Zanjón, which freed the slaves and Chinese who had fought with the rebels but gave neither general emancipation nor independence. Cubans call him the Father of the Homeland, and three of his children died during his fight. His portrait was on the 10 peso note until 1960, and an order of merit named for him was created in 1926.
carlos-menem: Carlos Saúl Menem was born on 2 July 1930 in Anillaco, a small town in northern La Rioja Province, to parents of Syrian Arab ancestry from Yabroud. He was raised a Muslim and later converted to Roman Catholicism to pursue a political career. On a visit to Buenos Aires in 1951 he met Juan Perón and Eva Perón, which led him to become a Peronist. He studied law at the National University of Córdoba. Elected governor of La Rioja in 1973, he was deposed and detained after the coup of 1976 and not released until 1978. He was re-elected governor in 1983 and again in 1987 with 63% of the vote.

In 1989 Menem defeated Antonio Cafiero in the Peronist primaries by building a broad coalition, and took office after hyperinflation and riots forced Raúl Alfonsín to leave early. He abandoned party orthodoxy for a market-oriented policy in line with the Washington Consensus and in 1991 introduced the Convertibility plan, complemented by privatisations and at first a success. Argentina aligned itself with the United States, joined the Gulf War and re-established relations with the United Kingdom. His government suffered two terrorist attacks, on the Israeli embassy on 17 March 1992 and on the AMIA centre in 1994.

Menem pardoned the leaders of the military juntas convicted in the 1985 Trial of the Juntas, despite popular opposition, and put down a mutiny led by Colonel Mohamed Alí Seineldín, the last military mutiny in Argentina. The Pact of Olivos with Alfonsín allowed the constitutional amendment of 1994 and his re-election in 1995. A new economic crisis began in his second term, and an opposition coalition won the 1999 presidential election.

Menem ran again in 2003 and led the first round with 24%, but withdrew before the run-off against Néstor Kirchner, who was likely to win by a wide margin. He was arrested in 2001 over a weapons export scandal and later received a sentence of seven years for arms trafficking and four and a half years for embezzlement, but his position as senator, to which he was elected in 2005, protected him from imprisonment. He died on 14 February 2021 at the age of 90.

He is regarded in Argentina as a polarising figure, chiefly because of corruption and economic mismanagement. Supporters credit his first presidency with ending a period of economic uncertainty and bringing stability. Contrary to Peronist tradition he addressed the public through television rather than rallies at the Plaza de Mayo.
carlos-montufar: Montúfar was born in Quito on 2 November 1780, the third son of the Creole nobles Juan Pío de Montúfar y Larrea, II Marquis of Selva Alegre, and Teresa de Larrea y Villavicencio. He graduated in 1800 from St. Thomas Aquinas University, where he studied philosophy and the humanities.

In 1802 he joined the German scientist Alexander von Humboldt and the French botanist Aimé Bonpland, who had reached Quito that January. The choice caused jealousy: the Colombian inventor Francisco José de Caldas, who had been turned down, complained of it. Montúfar climbed volcanoes of the Andes with them, including Chimborazo in June 1802, and travelled on through Peru, Mexico and Cuba to the United States, where he met political figures in Washington, D.C. in 1804 after Thomas Jefferson invited Humboldt there.

He went with Humboldt to Paris in 1804, living with him among a group of young South Americans that included Simón Bolívar. In 1805 he began military training at the Royal Academy of Nobles in Madrid. In the Peninsular War he served as aide-de-camp to General Francisco Javier Castaños at the Battle of Bailén in 1808, and he was then named royal commissioner for the Court of Quito, with broad autonomy from the viceroys of Peru and New Granada.

Learning that his father had taken part in the Quito Revolution, he returned in 1810 and helped form the short-lived State of Quito, which adopted its own constitution under Bishop José de Cuero y Caicedo. He led its defence against Toribio Montes, Melchor Aymerich and Juan de Sámano. After the defeat at Ibarra on 1 December 1812 he hid on haciendas in Cayambe and the Los Chillos Valley, was arrested, tried for treason and sent towards Spain, but escaped at Panama and joined the Liberation Army in New Granada, where he rose to colonel.

After the Pasto Campaign under General Manuel Roergas Serviez ended in defeat, Montúfar fought at the Battle of Cuchilla del Tambo on 29 June 1816. Captured and sentenced to death by Juan de Sámano, he was shot in the back as a traitor at Buga on 31 July 1816. Humboldt later wrote of him with sorrow. For the centenary of the Battle of Pichincha in 1922 his remains were taken to Quito Metropolitan Cathedral, and the moth Hellinsia montufari bears his name.
carlos-prio-socarras: Carlos Manuel Prío Socarrás was born on 14 July 1903, and was the first president of Cuba born in an independent Cuba. In 1940 he was elected senator for Pinar del Río Province. When his fellow Auténtico Ramón Grau became president in 1944, Prío served in turn as Minister of Public Works, Minister of Labor and Prime Minister. He won the presidency on 1 July 1948, and he was the last Cuban president to gain office through universal, contested elections.

Known as el presidente cordial, the cordial president, Prío sought a rule marked by civility and respect for freedom of expression; public works and the founding of a National Bank and a Tribunal of Accounts are counted among his successes. The historian Charles Ameringer called the eight years under Grau and Prío a time of constitutional order and political freedom, though not golden years. Violence between political factions and reports of theft and self-enrichment in government marred his term, and the public came to see his administration as ineffectual against them.

With elections due in mid-1952, rumours spread of a coup planned by Fulgencio Batista, a long-shot candidate. Prío saw no constitutional basis to act. On 10 March 1952 Batista and his collaborators seized military and police commands and occupied the main radio and television stations, and Prío, mounting no resistance, flew into exile. According to Arthur M. Schlesinger Jr., Prío later said: "They say that I was a terrible president of Cuba. That may be true. But I was the best president Cuba ever had."

Prío lived in exile in the United States for 25 years. In 1953 he appeared in court on charges of conspiring to export arms without a licence under the Neutrality Act, and pleaded not guilty. Weeks before his death he travelled to Washington with other Miami Cubans to oppose any détente with Cuba before Secretary of State Cyrus Vance. He shot himself and died on 5 April 1977 in Miami Beach, aged 73, a week before he was to be interviewed by Gaeton Fonzi of the House Select Committee on Assassinations.
carlos-saavedra-lamas: Carlos Saavedra Lamas was born in Buenos Aires on 1 November 1878 into a family descended from an early Argentine patriot, and he later married a daughter of President Roque Sáenz Peña. He studied at Lacordaire College and then at the Faculty of Law of the University of Buenos Aires, where he earned a doctorate in law summa cum laude in 1903. After further study in Paris he became a professor of law and constitutional history at the University of La Plata, beginning a teaching career of more than four decades.

Saavedra Lamas entered public life in 1906 as director of public credit and became secretary-general of the municipality of Buenos Aires the next year. Elected to Parliament in 1908 for two consecutive terms, he sponsored laws on coastal water rights, irrigation, sugar, finance, colonisation and immigration, and he helped preserve Argentina's arbitration treaty with Italy during a crisis of 1907 and 1908. Many saw him as a conservative patrician who favoured British intervention, particularly in railway building. As minister of Justice and Public Instruction from 1915 he reorganised public education and developed vocational and technical training.

President Agustín P. Justo appointed him foreign minister in 1932. He brought Argentina back into the League of Nations after a thirteen-year absence. In 1932 he initiated the Declaration of August 3 in Washington, by which American states agreed not to recognise territorial changes made by force. He drafted the Treaty of Nonaggression and Conciliation, signed by six South American countries in October 1933 and two months later by all American states at the Seventh Pan-American Conference in Montevideo.

A scholar of labour legislation and international law, he supported the founding of the International Labour Organization in 1919 and in 1928 presided over its Geneva conference while leading the Argentine delegation. His publications include the three-volume Código nacional del trabajo (1933) and La Crise de la codification et de la doctrine argentine de droit international (1931). In 1935 he arranged mediation by six neutral American countries that ended the Chaco War between Paraguay and Bolivia. He was elected president of the Assembly of the League of Nations in 1936.

After leaving the ministry in 1938 he was rector of the University of Buenos Aires from 1941 to 1943 and taught there until 1946. He died in Buenos Aires in 1959 and was buried at La Recoleta Cemetery.
carlota-of-mexico: Charlotte was born on 7 June 1840 at the Palace of Laeken, the fourth child and only daughter of Leopold I of Belgium and Louise of Orléans. Her first name honoured Princess Charlotte of Wales, her father's first wife. Leopold, at first disappointed by a daughter, came to treat her as his favourite child. Through her mother she was a granddaughter of Louis Philippe I, and through her father a first cousin of Queen Victoria, and she spent long holidays in the French royal residences and at Windsor Castle.

In 1856 two suitors sought her hand, Prince George of Saxony and King Pedro V of Portugal, the favourite of Queen Victoria and Leopold. She declined Pedro, writing that crowns were heavy burdens. She married Maximilian of Austria, whom his brother Emperor Franz Joseph I appointed Viceroy of Lombardy-Venetia in September 1857. In Milan Maximilian soon neglected her, and she complained of loneliness and boredom.

Napoleon III selected Maximilian as figurehead of a proposed French empire in Mexico, and Charlotte overcame her husband's doubts. A Mexican delegation, persuaded by conservatives who wrongly promised broad support, offered the crown, and the couple were informally proclaimed at Miramare Castle on 10 April 1864. After a blessing from Pope Pius IX in Rome on 19 April, they reached Mexico City. Maximilian let her rule as regent during his absences, so she is considered the first woman to rule in the Americas.

When Napoleon III ordered the withdrawal of French military aid, the imperial couple's position became untenable. On her own initiative Charlotte sailed for Europe, landing at Saint-Nazaire on 8 August 1866. At Saint-Cloud she met the ailing Napoleon III on 11 August, and later the Pope, and both refused her. In Rome her mental health seemed to fail, and a doctor advised confining her at Miramare Castle.

Maximilian was deposed and executed under Benito Juárez in June 1867, and Charlotte, not knowing she was a widow, was taken to Belgium. She learned of his death in January 1868. She lived at Tervuren, Laeken and, from 1879, Bouchout Castle in Meise, for 48 years in a poor mental state. She saw only family, embroidered, played cards and listened to a gramophone. The cause of her illness is uncertain; some authors suspect poisoning in Mexico.

Charlotte died at Bouchout on 19 January 1927, aged 86, of pneumonia after influenza. Six former Belgian legionaries who had served in Mexico carried her coffin on 22 January, and she was buried in the Royal Crypt of the Church of Our Lady of Laeken. Much of her fortune was managed by Leopold II and was used to finance the Congo colonial enterprise.
carlsbad-decrees: The Carlsbad Decrees were a set of restrictions introduced in the states of the German Confederation by resolution of its parliamentary body, the Bundesversammlung, on 20 September 1819, after a conference at the spa town of Carlsbad in the Austrian Empire. The Austrian minister Prince Klemens Wenzel von Metternich called the meeting after the liberal Burschenschaft student Karl Ludwig Sand murdered the conservative writer August von Kotzebue on 23 March 1819, and after the apothecary Karl Löning attempted to kill the Nassau president Karl von Ibell on 1 July 1819. Metternich feared that liberal and national tendencies at German universities might lead to revolutionary activity threatening the monarchical order, and the two outrages served as a pretext for action.

The decrees were organised in three sections. The first provided for a special representative of each state's ruler at every university, to enforce regulations and watch the spirit of the lectures. It also provided for the removal of teachers judged to propagate harmful doctrines, who could not then be appointed in another state, and for the dissolution of the Allgemeine Burschenschaft, a union across universities. Students expelled from one university could not be received at another.

The press law required that daily publications and serials of up to twenty sheets receive official approval before printing. The Diet could suppress writings on its own authority, with no appeal, and an editor of a suppressed periodical could not edit a similar one for five years. The third section set up an extraordinary commission of investigation of seven members at the federal fortress of Mainz, the Mainz Central Investigation Commission, to inquire into revolutionary plots and demagogical associations.

The decrees effectively dissolved the student associations and sports organisations, forced reformers out of many local governments, and by 1820 all significant liberal and nationalist reform movements had ended. The Confederation treated liberal and nationalist ideas as sedition and persecuted those who spread them as demagogues, a persecution especially vigorous in Prussia. The Carlsbad Decrees also affected the independent academic jurisdiction that had partly existed for centuries. After the Hambach Festival in 1832 the persecution was renewed for the last time. The German Bundestag abrogated the decrees on 2 April 1848, after the March Revolution.
carmagnole: The song takes its title from the carmagnole, the short jacket worn by working-class militant sans-culottes, adopted from a Piedmontese peasant costume named after the town of Carmagnola. Its verses sarcastically celebrate triumphs over Queen Marie Antoinette as Madame Veto, King Louis XVI as Monsieur Veto and the French monarchists in general. Like Ah! ça ira, it had simple words that illiterate people could easily learn, understand and sing, which helped make it popular.

It served mainly as a rallying cry and entertainment for revolutionaries and as a way to insult opponents: a popular punishment was to make anti-revolutionaries, from marquises and princes to bishops and cardinals, sing and dance the Carmagnole. After the storming of the Tuileries Palace on the night of 9–10 August 1792 and the massacre of the king's Swiss Guard, the Paris crowd was described as dancing and singing it to celebrate the victory.

It was also a battle song. At the Battle of Jemappes on 6 November 1792 the sans-culottes in the army were said to have rushed the enemy singing La Marseillaise and La Carmagnole. It accompanied festivals and the planting of liberty trees, some 60,000 of which were planted during the Revolution, giving many occasions for public singing.

Carl Schurz recalled French exiles in England dancing the Carmagnole and singing Ça Ira at the news of Napoleon III's coup of 2 December 1851, and Victor Hugo, in Les Misérables, set it against the Marseillaise. It appears in Charles Dickens's A Tale of Two Cities, Baroness Orczy's The Scarlet Pimpernel, Gertrud von Le Fort's The Song at the Scaffold and Umberto Giordano's opera Andrea Chénier. On Samos, under Ottoman rule, it named the Karmanioloi faction, which opposed the landholding notables and led the island into the Greek War of Independence in 1821. Later versions include the anarchist La Ravachole.
carmarthen: Carmarthen lies on the River Towy, 8 miles (13 km) north of its estuary in Carmarthen Bay. Its Welsh name, Caerfyrddin, is widely held to mean Merlin's fort, though another reading is sea-town fort, and one explanation is that the name Merlin comes from the town's name rather than the reverse. It has a claim to be the oldest town in Wales and stands on the site of a Roman town. In the 16th to 18th centuries it was the most populous borough in Wales, described by William Camden as the chief city of the country, until the growth of settlements in the South Wales Coalfield overtook it by the mid-19th century.

As the civitas capital of the Demetae under Roman Britain it was known as Moridunum, sea fort, and is recorded by Ptolemy and in the Antonine Itinerary. The Roman fort is believed to date from about 75 CE. Nearby is one of seven surviving Roman amphitheatres in Britain, excavated in 1968, with an arena of about 46 by 27 metres. The Norman William fitz Baldwin probably built a castle about 1094. Llywelyn the Great destroyed it in 1215, it was rebuilt in 1223 with a town wall, and Owain Glyndŵr captured the town and sacked the castle in 1405. In the Middle Ages there were twin settlements, Old Carmarthen around the priory and New Carmarthen around the castle, merged into one borough in 1546.

Geoffrey of Monmouth, writing in 1188, began the legend that Merlin was born in a cave outside Carmarthen. The Black Book of Carmarthen, of about 1250, is associated with the town's Priory of St John the Evangelist and St Teulyddog and includes poems referring to Myrddin. The Black Death of 1347 to 1349 arrived with the river trade. Edmund Tudor, 1st Earl of Richmond, died of plague in Carmarthen in 1456, three months before the birth of his son, the future Henry VII, and was buried in the Grey Friars church. Bishop Robert Ferrar of St Davids was burned at the stake in the market square in March 1555, during the Marian persecutions.

Carmarthen is the county town of Carmarthenshire, and the county council has its headquarters on the site of the castle. At the 2021 census the community had a population of 14,636. Little of the medieval castle remains, but its gatehouse still dominates Nott Square. St Peter's church, a Grade I listed building, has the longest nave of any parish church in the Diocese of St David's. The revival of the Eisteddfod as an institution took place in Carmarthen in 1819, and the town hosted the National Eisteddfod in 1867, 1911 and 1974.
carmarthenshire: Carmarthenshire is bounded by Ceredigion to the north, Powys, Neath Port Talbot and Swansea to the east, the Bristol Channel to the south and Pembrokeshire to the west. Much of it is upland, with the Black Mountain range in the east and the foothills of the Cambrian Mountains north of the Towy valley. The county top is Fan Foel at 781 metres. The River Towy, the longest river flowing entirely within Wales, drains it, and the best farmland lies in the broad Tywi Valley, which gives the county its name the Garden of Wales.

Stone tools from Coygan Cave near Laugharne show hominins, probably Neanderthals, in the area at least 40,000 years ago. Before the Romans the land was part of the kingdom of the Demetae, one of whose chief settlements, Moridunum, is now Carmarthen. The Roman fort at Carmarthen dates from around 75 CE, and with a Roman amphitheatre nearby this probably makes it the oldest continually occupied town in Wales. In the High Middle Ages the area was part of the Kingdom of Deheubarth, with its court at Dinefwr, and then disputed between the Normans and Welsh lords, with many castles changing hands several times.

After Edward I's conquest, the Statute of Rhuddlan reorganised the region in 1284 into Carmarthenshire, with Carmarthen as its capital and the seat of his courts of chancery and exchequer. The Normans made Carmarthen an international trading port, the only staple port in Wales. Owain Glyndŵr captured Carmarthen Castle in 1405. The Parliamentarians recaptured it in 1648 in the English Civil War, and Oliver Cromwell ordered it slighted.

The first industrial canal in Wales was built in 1768 to carry coal from the Gwendraeth Valley to the coast, and by the end of the nineteenth century Llanelli was the world centre of tin-plating. Around 1840 Carmarthenshire was at the centre of the Rebecca Riots, when farmers and agricultural workers dressed as women rebelled against higher taxes and tolls.

Carmarthen is the county town, though Llanelli is by far the largest town. The county has the largest area of the historic counties of Wales and its population was 183,777 at the 2011 census. Carn Goch, near Llandeilo, is one of the most impressive Iron Age forts, and the county has castles at Carreg Cennen, Dinefwr, Kidwelly, Laugharne and elsewhere. The Dolaucothi Gold Mines were worked by the Romans, and Laugharne is associated with the poet Dylan Thomas.
carmelites: Historical records of the order's origin are uncertain. Berthold of Calabria and Albert of Vercelli are traditionally associated with its founding, but few clear records survive. Tradition gives 1185, but that rests on a pilgrim's story whose interpretation is questionable; the oldest reliable written accounts of Latin hermits on Mount Carmel date from 1220 and 1263.
