The Carmelites look back not to a founder but to the prophet Elijah and his disciple Elisha, whom they regard as their spiritual fathers. A written rule of life for the hermits, centred on prayer, is dated 1209 and was requested, tradition says, from the Latin Patriarch of Jerusalem, Albert of Vercelli.

In Europe the hermits met difficulties. Their solitary life did not suit their new settlements, and they competed with other mendicant orders. In 1274 the Second Council of Lyon disestablished all mendicant orders founded after 1215; only the Franciscans, the Order of Preachers, the Carmelites and the Augustinians remained. The Carmelites, barely spared, had to change from hermits to friars. They settled across Europe, among other places at Aylesford in Kent in 1242 and in Paris in 1259.

After the Black Death had reduced the number of members, a majority of Carmelites asked Pope Eugene IV in 1432 to mitigate the rule because of its severity. John Soreth, Prior General from 1451 to 1471, worked to restore a stricter life. The Teresian reform of the 1560s created the Discalced Carmelites, who faced opposition from unreformed houses: Carmelites at Toledo imprisoned John of the Cross. The French Revolution suppressed the order, and the Compiègne Carmelites were guillotined.

The Carmelites are a mendicant order for men and women. The order of Carmelite nuns was formalised in 1452, and John Soreth had a leading part in founding the Third Order for lay members. Their distinctive garment is a scapular of two strips of dark cloth worn on the breast and back. Tradition holds that the Virgin Mary gave it to Simon Stock and promised that those who die wearing it with faith and piety would be saved.
carnatic-sultanate: The Carnatic was the old province of southern India that stretched from the Krishna River to the Kaveri, bounded on the west by the Mysore kingdom and Dindigul, with Madras on its coast; its northern part was called the Mughal Carnatic and its southern part, with the Maratha fortresses of Gingee and Ranjankudi, the Maratha Carnatic. After the decline of the Vijayanagara Empire the Nayakas of Madurai, Tanjore and Kanchi made themselves independent, but soon paid tribute to the kings of Golconda and Bijapur. In 1692 the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb appointed Zulfiqar Khan the first subahdar of the Carnatic, seated at Arcot, as a reward for his victory over the Marathas under Rajaram I.

As Mughal power declined the province became an independent state, ruled by nawabs under the legal purview of the Nizam of Hyderabad. Nawab Saadatullah Khan I moved his court from Gingee to Arcot, and his successor Dost Ali Khan annexed Madurai in 1736. In 1740 a Maratha army attacked Dost Ali in the pass of Damalcherry, where he, his son Hasan Ali and other leading men were killed; Arcot then surrendered, and Chanda Sahib and his son were sent captive to Nagpur.

Muhammad Ali Khan Wallajah took power in 1749, was crowned only in 1752 and was recognised as an independent ruler by the emperor in Delhi in 1765. He backed the English against the French and against Hyder Ali, which left him deeply in debt and forced him to give up much of his territory to the East India Company. The English businessman Paul Benfield lent him large sums after he had conquered the Maratha state of Tanjore with English help.

When the thirteenth nawab, Ghulam Muhammad Ghouse Khan, died, the British annexed the state under the doctrine of lapse. His uncle Azim Jah was made the first Prince of Arcot by Queen Victoria in 1867 and given a tax-free pension in perpetuity. The nawabs' rule spans the period in which Mughal authority on the Carnatic and Coromandel Coast gave way first to rising Maratha influence and then to British India.
carnatic-wars: After the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb died in March 1707, central control over the empire declined. Nizam-ul-Mulk established Hyderabad as an independent kingdom, and after his death his son Nasir Jung and his grandson Muzaffar Jung disputed the succession, France aiding Muzaffar Jung and Britain Nasir Jung. The Carnatic, ruled by Nawab Dost Ali Khan, was under the Nizam's legal purview, and at Dost Ali's death his son-in-law Chanda Sahib, backed by the French, and Muhammad Ali, backed by the British, struggled for power. Joseph François Dupleix, who became governor of the French East India Company in 1742, sought to extend French influence beyond a few outposts, chiefly Pondicherry, and was met by the young British officer Robert Clive.

The First Carnatic War (1746–1748) was an extension of the War of the Austrian Succession. The French captured Madras on 21 September 1746, and a 10,000-man army sent by the Nawab was repulsed by a small French force at the Battle of Adyar. By the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle Madras went back to the British in exchange for the fortress of Louisbourg. Clive, taken prisoner at Madras, escaped and gained his first military experience.

The Second Carnatic War (1749–1754) was a proxy war. In 1751 Clive led British troops to capture Arcot and then defended it. The Treaty of Pondicherry in 1754 recognised Muhammad Ali Khan Walajah as Nawab of the Carnatic, and Charles Godeheu replaced Dupleix. The Third Carnatic War (1757–1763) followed the outbreak of the Seven Years' War. The British took Chandernagore in 1757, and in the south Sir Eyre Coote defeated the Comte de Lally at Wandiwash in 1760. Pondicherry fell in 1761.

The Treaty of Paris in 1763 returned Chandernagore and Pondicherry to France and let the French keep trading posts without administering them. France agreed to support British client governments, which ended its ambitions of an Indian empire and made Britain the dominant foreign power there. The dominance of the British company eventually led to its control over most of India and to the British Raj.
carnation-revolution: The Estado Novo grew out of the coup of 28 May 1926 and was renamed in 1933; António de Oliveira Salazar was prime minister until 1968. Elections were mostly shams, and the political police, the PIDE, persecuted opponents, who were often tortured, imprisoned or killed. After Salazar's stroke in 1968 Marcelo Caetano promised reform, but censorship stayed until 25 April 1974. Independence movements had begun in Mozambique, Angola and Portuguese Guinea, and the colonial war of 1961 to 1974 took up to 40 per cent of the budget. The war became unpopular, and many young men avoided conscription by emigrating.

By December 1973 officers including Vasco Lourenço, Vítor Alves and Otelo Saraiva de Carvalho were preparing a coup, and the Armed Forces Movement, the MFA, took shape. The coup, code-named Operation Historic Turn, had two signals: the song E Depois do Adeus, broadcast at 22:55 on 24 April, and Grândola, Vila Morena, by the banned singer Zeca Afonso, broadcast at 00:20 on 25 April.

Within six hours the government gave way. Though the MFA urged civilians to stay home, thousands filled the streets. Celeste Caeiro, a restaurant worker, offered carnations to soldiers, and others put them in gun barrels, which gave the revolution its name. Caetano took refuge in the barracks at Largo do Carmo and ceded power to General António de Spínola. The siege of the security police's headquarters lasted until the next morning, and four civilians were killed by its warning shots.

Power passed to the National Salvation Junta and then the Revolutionary Council, in a turbulent period that culminated in the Hot Summer of 1975. Portugal's first free election was held on 25 April 1975 to write a new constitution, and the first constitutional government, led by the socialist Mário Soares, took office after a further election in 1976.

Portuguese troops were withdrawn from Guinea in 1974, and in 1975 Cape Verde, Mozambique, São Tomé and Príncipe and Angola became independent, and East Timor declared independence. More than one million Portuguese, the retornados, left the African territories. 25 April, Freedom Day, is a national holiday.
carnegie-institution-for-science: The institution was founded on 29 January 1902 with an endowment of $10 million from Andrew Carnegie, who proposed an institution in Washington that would encourage investigation, research and discovery and show the application of knowledge to the improvement of mankind. At first it supported both individual investigators and institutional research, but over time it stopped funding outside researchers and worked through its own laboratories and departments. Within its first decade it had ten major research departments, among them the Desert Laboratory, the Department of Terrestrial Magnetism, the Geophysical Laboratory and Mount Wilson Observatory.

The Desert Laboratory, opened in Tucson, Arizona, in 1903, studied desert plants in their natural habitats and became a centre of early ecology, with Forrest Shreve and Frederic Clements on its staff. The Department of Terrestrial Magnetism, founded in 1904, measured the Earth's magnetic field at sea, its ship Carnegie, built in 1909, completing seven cruises before it was destroyed by an explosion and fire. At Mount Wilson the institution funded the Hooker 100-inch telescope envisioned by George Ellery Hale, on which Edwin Hubble showed in 1923 that the universe extends far beyond the Milky Way and in 1929 that it is expanding.

When the United States joined World War II, the institution's president was Vannevar Bush, who had persuaded President Franklin Roosevelt to create the National Defense Research Committee in 1940. Bush housed the agency in the institution's headquarters at 16th and P Streets in Washington and supervised projects from there, including the Manhattan Project; Carnegie scientists helped develop the proximity fuze and the mass production of penicillin. Nobel laureates on its staff included Thomas Hunt Morgan, Alfred Hershey and Barbara McClintock.

The institution also took part in eugenics. In 1918 the Eugenics Record Office at Cold Spring Harbor, New York, founded by Charles Davenport in 1910 and a centre of pseudoscientific research, was donated to it, and it funded the office until closing the department in 1939. In 2020 it issued a statement acknowledging and apologising for this past involvement. The Las Campanas Observatory in Chile, established in 1969, became the site of its Magellan Telescopes. The name Carnegie Institution for Science came into informal use in 2007 and Carnegie Science in 2024, while the legal name remains Carnegie Institution of Washington.
carniola: Carniola, in Slovene Kranjska and in German Krain, was divided into Upper Carniola, Lower Carniola (with White Carniola) and Inner Carniola. The region is crossed by the Julian Alps and the Karawanks, and its highest peak is Triglav at about 2,800 metres. Its main rivers include the Sava, Ljubljanica and Krka, and its lakes include Bled and Bohinj. In 1914 it had a population of slightly under 530,000, of whom 95 per cent were Slovenes.

In 1991, 47 per cent of the population of Slovenia lived within the borders of the former duchy. Slovenes there still tend to identify with its traditional parts. From about 900 until the 20th century Carniola's ruling classes and towns spoke German, while the peasantry spoke Slovene.

Before the Romans came, about 200 BCE, the Taurisci, Pannonians and the Celtic Iapodes or Carni lived in the region. After the fall of the Western Roman Empire in 476 it passed to Odoacer's Kingdom of Italy and then, in 493, to the Ostrogothic Kingdom. Towards the end of the sixth century Slavs settled in the area Latin writers called Carniola, 'little Carnia'. About 623 they joined the tribal union of Samo, and after his death in 658 they fell again under Avar rule.

The Franks governed the region about 788 and Christian missionaries came from Aquileia. It became an independent margraviate with its own Slavic margrave at Kranj, subject first to the governor of Bavaria and after 976 to the Dukes of Carinthia. Frederick II of Austria obtained the title of duke in 1245, and in 1268 Ulrich III willed his lands to Ottokar II of Bohemia. When Duke Henry of Carinthia died in 1335, Albrecht, Duke of Austria, received Carniola, and Rudolf IV proclaimed it a duchy in 1364. It then stayed Habsburg almost continuously until 1918, though Ottoman raids from the 15th century and local rebellions troubled it.

The capital moved from Kranj to Kamnik and finally to Ljubljana. French troops occupied the region in 1797 and in 1805-1806, and by the Treaty of Vienna it joined the French Illyrian Provinces in 1809-1814, with Ljubljana as capital. It was returned to Austria and from 1816 to 1849 belonged to the Kingdom of Illyria. In 1849 it became a crown land in its own right and in 1867 part of Cisleithania. It then covered 9,904 square kilometres.

In 1918 the duchy ceased to exist, and its territory joined the State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs and then the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes. Its western part, including Postojna and Idrija, was annexed to Italy in 1920 and included in Yugoslavia in 1947. Since 1991 the region has been part of independent Slovenia.
carnival-of-oruro: The area of Oruro, called Jururu (Uru Uru) in ancient times, was a pilgrimage centre of the Andean world, where pilgrims came to the Sacred Mountain of the Urus to call on protective deities, among them the hill toad Jamp'atu Qullu, the hill lizard Argentillo Arankani, the viper Quwak and the condor. The Spanish banned the native Itu ceremonies in the 17th century, but the Uru kept the festival as a Catholic rite at Candlemas, with Christian icons concealing Andean gods and saints standing in for lesser divinities.

According to legend, in 1756 a mural of the Virgin Mary appeared in a mineshaft of the richest silver mine in Oruro, and the festival has since honoured the Virgen de la Candelaria, or Virgen del Socavón. Catholic ideas of the Virgin and the Devil merged with the native Pachamama and Tio Supay.

The carnival opens with a ceremony to the Virgen del Socavón, and on Sunday marching bands compete in the grotto of Pie de Gallo as a greeting to the Virgin. Its high point is a parade of three days and three nights in which 48 groups of folk dancers process to the sanctuary of the mineshaft. Before it people visit the symbolic condor, and a week after it the snake south of the city, the toad to the north and the ants to the east. The pilgrimage ends with two mystery plays, one on the Spanish conquest and one in which the Archangel Michael defeats the Devil and the Seven Deadly Sins, introduced by Catholic clergy in 1818.

Over 28,000 dancers and about 10,000 musicians in 150 bands take part, before some 400,000 visitors. The diablada, or devil dance, leads the dances, which come from the Altiplano and the Yungas, the valleys of Cochabamba, Tarija and Chuquisaca, and the eastern plains; morenada, caporales, tinku and kullawada are among them.

An international jury chaired by the writer Juan Goitisilo, with members including Alpha Oumar Konare, Carlos Fuentes and the Bolivian singer Zulma Yugar, proclaimed the carnival a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity on 18 May 2001.
carnuntum: Carnuntum stood on the Danube in what is now Lower Austria, halfway between Vienna and Bratislava, near the villages of Petronell-Carnuntum and Bad Deutsch-Altenburg. It was a Roman legionary fortress and the headquarters of the Pannonian fleet from about 50 CE, and it grew into a city of roughly 50,000 inhabitants. It was a major trading centre for amber, because the main arm of the Amber Road crossed the Danube there.

Carnuntum first appears in history in 6 CE, when Tiberius made it his base in the campaigns against Maroboduus. It became the garrison of the Legio XV Apollinaris before 14 CE, and in about 50 CE the emperor Claudius ordered a legion to be stationed on the Danube to protect the defeated party in a dispute between the Quadi and the Marcomanni. Legio XIV Gemina made it its permanent quarters in 117–118 and stayed for three centuries. Hadrian made it a municipium, and it became the capital of Pannonia Superior.

Marcus Aurelius lived there for three years, 172 to 175, during the war against the Marcomanni, and wrote part of his Meditations there. Septimius Severus, then governor of Pannonia, was proclaimed emperor by his soldiers there in 193; under the Severan dynasty the city boomed, and Caracalla raised it to colony status. In 308 Diocletian chaired the Conference of Carnuntum with Maximian and Galerius to settle tensions within the Tetrarchy. An earthquake damaged it around 350, and in 374 Germanic invaders, the Quadi and Iazyges, destroyed it. Valentinian I partly restored it, but it never regained its importance. Vindobona became the chief military centre.

The site was eventually abandoned, used as a cemetery and a source of building stone, and its remains became buried and forgotten. The Carnuntum Archaeological Park now covers 10 square kilometres. It includes a rebuilt Roman house, palace ruins, an amphitheatre for about 15,000 spectators, and the Heidentor, the ruin of a triumphal arch put up between 354 and 361, probably under Constantius II. A gladiator school was found in 2011 by aerial photography and ground-penetrating radar.
carnutes: The name Carnutes is Gaulish and literally means the horned ones, probably a reference to their combat helmets, from the stem carno-, horn; it is related to the Brittonic name behind the Welsh Kernyw, Cornwall. Caesar and Livy call them Carnutes, Strabo writes Karnoútōn, Ptolemy Karnoũtai, and the Notitia Dignitatum has Carnunta. Little is recorded of them before the middle of the 1st century BCE, although a tradition of legend counted them among the peoples who joined the migration of Bellovesus into Italy.

Their large territory stretched across the modern departments of Eure-et-Loir, Loiret and Loir-et-Cher, between the basins of the Loire and the Seine, with the Loire as its boundary with the Bituriges. From the early 2nd century BCE people gathered in open lowland settlements, some later followed by fortified oppida on nearby heights. Cenabum was a bridge town whose bridge is dated by tree rings to 159 BCE. The archaeologist Sandrine Riquier has argued that the people comprised a northern and a southern group, set apart by their coins and burial rites.

They struck potin and bronze coins, some bearing the name of the king Tasgetios. Caesar does not say that the druids' meeting place was a wood, and the scholar Sophie Krausz holds that the image of a forest of the Carnutes may be a modern construction. Its site is unknown; the vast Roman sanctuary of Saint-Martin-au-Val at Chartres, one of the largest known in Roman Gaul, has been proposed as a candidate.

At the time of the Gallic Wars the Carnutes were clients of the Remi. Roman legions wintered in their territory in 57 BCE, and Caesar made Tasgetius, a man of royal descent and a loyal ally, their king. Some of his own people killed him in 54 BCE, in the third year of his reign, and the Carnutes submitted the following year.

They were among the chief instigators of the revolt of 52 BCE, and the killing of the Roman traders at Cenabum was led by Cotuatos and Conconnetodumnos. A further campaign was fought in their country at the start of 51 BCE, and Caesar later had the gutuater, whom he called the chief author of the war, put to death. Under Roman rule the civitas kept two centres, Cenabum in the south and Autricum in the north, an arrangement described as without parallel in Gaul.
carol-i-of-romania: Carol was born Karl Eitel Friedrich Zephyrinus Ludwig on 20 April 1839 at Sigmaringen in southern Germany, the second son of Prince Karl Anton of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen and Princess Josephine of Baden. His family belonged to the Catholic Swabian branch of the House of Hohenzollern, was related to the Prussian royal family and, through both grandmothers, to the Bonaparte family. He trained at the cadet school in Münster and the artillery school in Berlin and served as a Prussian officer until 1866, taking part in the Second Schleswig War.

In 1866 a coup removed Alexandru Ioan Cuza, the prince of the united Moldavia and Wallachia, and the country risked disintegration. Philip of Flanders refused the throne. Napoleon III then suggested Karl, and the politician Ion Constantin Brătianu went to negotiate with his family. Karl travelled incognito through Switzerland under a Swiss passport, was elected Domnitor on 20 April 1866 and entered Bucharest in May, swearing his oath in French because he did not yet speak Romanian.

On 29 June 1866 parliament adopted a constitution modelled closely on that of Belgium, which guaranteed freedom of speech and the press and separated powers. It also barred non-Christians from citizenship, which heavily affected the Jewish population. In 1869 Carol married Princess Elisabeth of Wied. Their only child, Maria, born in 1870, died in 1874, and the throne later passed to his nephew Ferdinand.

In the Russo-Turkish War Romania declared independence on 10 May 1877. After the Russian advance stalled at Pleven, Carol took command of the combined Russian and Romanian forces there, and Osman Nuri Pasha surrendered the town on 28 November 1877. The Treaty of Berlin recognised Romanian independence on 13 July 1878 and gave Romania Northern Dobruja. The constitution was amended in March 1881 and Carol was crowned king on 10 May, wearing a crown made from steel of a captured Ottoman cannon.

He built Peleș Castle in the Carpathian mountains and ordered the engineer Anghel Saligny to build a bridge over the Danube between Fetești and Cernavodă. In 1883 he arranged a secret alliance with the Central Powers, unknown to parliament and the public until the First World War. A peasant revolt in 1907 was bloodily suppressed. Romania gained Southern Dobruja in 1913. Carol died on 10 October 1914 (27 September, Old Style), and Romania, neutral at first, joined the Allies in 1916.
carol-ii-of-romania: Carol was born in Peleș Castle as the son of Crown Prince Ferdinand and Crown Princess Marie, the first male member of the royal family to be born in Romania. He spent much of his childhood under his domineering great-uncle, King Carol I, who kept his parents out of his upbringing. His marriage to Zizi Lambrino, who was not of royal lineage, was dissolved, and in March 1921 he married Princess Helen of Greece and Denmark, with whom he had a son, Michael.

His affair with Elena Lupescu ended the marriage. The National Liberal Party used it to argue that he was unfit to be king. In 1925 he renounced his rights to the throne in favour of Michael and went into exile in France with Lupescu. Michael inherited the throne at the age of five on the death of Ferdinand in 1927, and Helen divorced Carol in 1928.

Carol returned to Romania on 7 June 1930 in a coup engineered by the National Peasant prime minister Iuliu Maniu, deposed Michael, who was still under a regency, and was recognised as king by Parliament the next day. After the December 1937 elections no coalition could be formed. On 10 February 1938 he suspended the constitution, proclaimed martial law and set up a royal dictatorship, abolishing all parties and forming the National Renaissance Front.

When the Second World War began he proclaimed neutrality. After the fall of France in 1940 Carol moved towards Nazi Germany in the hope of avoiding invasion. In June the Soviet Union demanded Bessarabia and northern Bukovina by ultimatum, and Carol gave way without fighting. The Treaty of Craiova ceded Southern Dobruja to Bulgaria, and the Second Vienna Award of 30 August 1940 gave northern Transylvania to Hungary. Demonstrations demanded his abdication, and General Ion Antonescu forced him to abdicate on 6 September 1940 in favour of Michael.

Carol left Romania by train with thirty truckloads of his fortune; the Iron Guard shot at the train at Timișoara in a failed attempt to kill him. He went to Portugal and then to Cuernavaca in Mexico, where from 1941 he tried to organise a Free Romania movement, which gained no recognition. He married Lupescu in Rio de Janeiro on 3 June 1947 and died at Estoril in 1953. The historian Stanley G. Payne called him the most cynical, corrupt and power-hungry monarch of twentieth-century Europe. His remains were returned to the Curtea de Argeș monastery in 2003.
caroline-islands: The Caroline Islands form a widely scattered archipelago of about 500 small islands in the western Pacific Ocean, north of New Guinea and east of the Philippines. They stretch for approximately 3,540 kilometres, from Tobi in Palau in the west to Kosrae in the east. Most are low, flat coral atolls, though some rise high above sea level. Yap lies 1,900 kilometres from Manila, and the group was once called Nuevas Filipinas, or New Philippines, because it formed part of the Spanish East Indies and was governed from Manila.

Different islands tell different stories of their origins. On Pohnpei, the people divide their pre-colonial history into three eras: building or peopling before 1100, the reigns of the Saudeleur from 1100 to around 1628, and the era of the tribal chiefs, the nahnmwarki, from around 1628 to 1885. According to Pohnpeian legend, the Saudeleur came from beyond the islands and imposed an increasingly oppressive centralised rule. A foreigner named Isokelekel invaded, overthrew them and set up the more decentralised nahnmwarki system.

The Portuguese navigators Diogo da Rocha and Gomes de Sequeira, carried east by a storm in 1525, were the first Europeans to reach the islands. In 1528 Álvaro de Saavedra Cerón claimed the Ulithi Islands for the king of Spain. Francisco de Lezcano, arriving at Yap in 1686, named the group Las Carolinas in honour of Charles II of Spain. A missionary, Juan Antonio Cantova, was killed in 1731, and Spain broke off relations until 1787. Whaling ships from Britain, the United States and Australia called there through the 19th century, the first known being the London whaler Britannia at Ngatik in December 1793.

In 1885 a Spanish representative signed an agreement with the chiefs of Koror and Artingal establishing Spanish sovereignty. When Germany and the United Kingdom disputed Spain's right to collect customs duties, Pope Leo XIII arbitrated and decided in Spain's favour west of the 164th meridian east. After the Spanish-American War, Spain sold the Carolines and the Northern Marianas to Germany in 1899 for 25 million pesetas. Japan occupied the islands in 1914, received a League of Nations mandate over them in 1920, and kept a large base at Truk Lagoon in World War II. The islands then became a United States trust territory.

The group is divided between the Federated States of Micronesia in its central and eastern parts, which became independent in 1986, and Palau at its western end, independent from 1994. Pohnpeian, Chuukese, Carolinian, Kosraean, Palauan and Yapese are among the languages spoken. Yap is known for its huge stone discs quarried in Palau, which serve as tokens of wealth.
caroline-of-zweibrucken: Caroline Henriette Christiane Philippine Louise was born on 9 March 1721, the daughter of Christian III, Duke of Zweibrücken, and his wife Caroline of Nassau-Saarbrücken. On 12 August 1741, in Zweibrücken, she married Louis IX, Landgrave of Hesse-Darmstadt. The marriage was arranged for the two families and proved unhappy. Caroline's interests lay in music and literature, while her husband cared chiefly for military matters, and for much of their married life the couple lived apart from each other.

She was counted among the most learned women of her time. The name by which she became known, the Great Landgräfin, was given to her by Johann Wolfgang von Goethe. She befriended several of the writers and philosophers of the day, among them Goethe, Johann Gottfried Herder and Christoph Martin Wieland, and Wieland wrote that he wished he had the power to make her Queen of Europa. In 1772 she advanced the career of the politician Friedrich Karl von Moser.

Caroline also corresponded with Frederick II of Prussia, the Alte Fritz, and was one of the few women whom he respected. He called her the Glory and Wonder of our century. She died on 30 March 1774. After her death Frederick sent an urn to Darmstadt bearing the Latin words femina sexu, ingenio vir, a woman by sex, a man by spirit.

Caroline is remembered both for the literary circle she gathered and for her place in the genealogy of Europe's royal houses. When Charles III became King of the United Kingdom in 2022, Caroline and her husband Louis IX became the most recent common ancestors of all the current sovereigns of the hereditary monarchies of Europe, every one of whom descends from the couple.
carolingian-civil-war: From 830 the reign of Louis the Pious was shaken by revolts of his sons. In the first, Lothar, ruling Italy, and King Pippin I of Aquitaine sided with rebellious nobles, and Louis's second wife Judith, mother of Charles the Bald, was imprisoned. In 833 Louis the German joined his brothers, and at the Field of Lies the emperor was captured with Judith and Charles; Lothar ruled for ten months until Louis the German restored their father in February 834. Shortly before his death in June 840, Louis sent the imperial sceptre and crown to Lothar, who then claimed the whole empire, disregarding the partition planned in 839.

Lothar forced Louis the German from the Rhineland in August 840, then crossed into Neustria and made a truce with Charles at Orléans in November. Their nephew Pippin II pressed his claim to Aquitaine. On 13 May 841 Louis routed Lothar's army in Alemannia at the Battle of the Ries, where its commander Adalbert was killed, and joined Charles. Reinforcements from Aquitaine reached both sides, and at Fontenoy on 25 June Lothar and Pippin were routed, though the battle did not settle the war.

On 14 February 842 Louis and Charles swore the Oaths of Strasbourg, Louis in Romance and Charles in German so that each other's armies understood, and their armies swore matching oaths. They met Lothar's army on the Moselle in March, and he withdrew towards Burgundy, giving up Aachen. Bishops assembled there declared Lothar unfit to rule, and the two kings divided the empire north of the Alps between themselves.

Faced with this, Lothar sought terms, and by June 842 a three-way division had been agreed in principle. In October 120 commissioners, 40 from each brother, met at Koblenz, and because a poor harvest made all three kings anxious to keep the peace, they agreed that envoys should first describe and inventory the empire's bishoprics, monasteries, palaces and estates; the description was due by 14 July 843 and no copy survives. The brothers signed the Treaty of Verdun in August 843.

The chief narrative is that of Nithard, a partisan of Charles whose lands Lothar confiscated, though charters show Lothar had the widest support in the first two years. Angelbert's poem on Fontenoy and Florus of Lyon's Lament on the Division of the Empire mourned the war.
carolingian-dynasty: The Carolingian line began with two rival Frankish families, the Pippinids and the Arnulfings, whose fortunes became intermingled in the early 7th century. Pippin I of Landen and Arnulf of Metz, from whom historians take the family names, appear in the Continuations of Fredegar as advisers to Chlotar II of Neustria, who incited a revolt in 613 against King Theuderic II and Brunhild of Austrasia.

As a reward Chlotar gave Arnulf the bishopric of Metz in 614, with the management of the Austrasian capital and the education of Chlotar's son, the future Dagobert I. Pippin became mayor of the palace of Austrasia in 624. The mayor of the palace mediated between the king and the magnates and has been described as the most important non-royal person in the kingdom.

Beginning with Pippin II, the Carolingians set out to put the kingdom of the Franks back together after it fragmented following the death of the Merovingian king Dagobert I. The historian Bernard Bachrach argues that their rise is best understood as a grand strategy, resting on a political alliance with the aristocracy and on the late Roman military organisation, in which civilians owed military service according to their wealth.

The dynasty made the offices of mayor of the palace and dux et princeps Francorum hereditary. In 751 the Merovingian dynasty was overthrown with the consent of the Papacy and the aristocracy, and Pepin the Short, son of Charles Martel, was crowned king of the Franks. The dynasty reached its peak in 800 with the crowning of Charlemagne as the first emperor of the Romans in the West in over three centuries.

After Charlemagne's death in 814 the dynasty began slowly to crumble. His kingdom was split into three parts, each ruled by one of his grandsons, and only the eastern and western parts survived, becoming the predecessors of modern Germany and France. The Carolingians were displaced in most of the realms of the empire by 888, ruled in East Francia until 911 and held the throne of West Francia intermittently until 987.

Cadet branches continued in Vermandois and Lower Lorraine but never sought the royal or imperial thrones. One chronicler of Sens dates the end of Carolingian rule to the coronation of Robert II of France as junior co-ruler with his father, Hugh Capet, which began the Capetian dynasty.
carolingian-empire: The Carolingian dynasty had ruled as kings of the Franks since 751 and as kings of the Lombards in Italy from 774. Its rise rested on Charles Martel, who took neither the title of king nor of emperor but was the absolute ruler of virtually all of continental Western Europe north of the Pyrenees. He earned his surname, Martel, meaning the Hammer, through his defence of Christian Europe against a Muslim army at the Battle of Tours in 732. In 800 Pope Leo III crowned his grandson Charlemagne as Roman emperor in return for political protection, disregarding the universalist claims of the weakened Byzantine Empire.

Under Charlemagne the empire covered most of Western Europe, as the Roman Empire once had. His son Louis the Pious, originally crowned king of Aquitaine at the age of three, became emperor unexpectedly after the deaths of his older siblings. His reign was overshadowed by a dynastic struggle that ended in a civil war from 840 to 843. In 843 his three sons settled the partition in the Treaty of Verdun. Lothar received the imperial title, the kingship of Italy and the lands between the Rhine and the Rhone. Louis took the lands east of the Rhine, and Charles those west of the Rhone.

After the death of Charles the Bald in 877 the empire was attacked by the Vikings in the north and west and faced internal struggles from Italy to the Baltic. In 884 Charles the Fat reunited all the Carolingian kingdoms for the last time, but the Frankish nobility deposed him in 887, and the empire dissolved when he died in 888. The legitimate line was restored in the western kingdom in 898 and ruled until 987, with an interruption from 922 to 936.

The empire had no permanent capital, since the court moved from place to place, as in other Western European kingdoms. Charlemagne began building the Palace of Aachen in the 780s, and its chapel, completed in 796, later became Aachen Cathedral. Aachen was meant as a meeting place for aristocrats and churchmen, where patronage was distributed, assemblies were held and laws written. The language of official acts was Latin. Carolingian Empire is a modern term, not used by contemporaries.

Frankish forces campaigned almost every year. Charlemagne gathered an assembly around Easter and launched a campaign through the summer,. The population is estimated at between 10 and 20 million, and the empire held Franks, Alemanni, Bavarians, Frisians, Lombards, Romans, Celts, Basques and Slavs, whose ethnic identities helped decide which law codes applied to them.
carolingian-minuscule: Carolingian minuscule grew out of an effort to create a clear, uniform way of copying books. It derives from scripts that all descend from late Roman cursive and uncial. Individual scriptoria, partly in response to Charlemagne's reforms, improved their scripts, starting from a Merovingian script and adding Insular and half-uncial features; later the scripts conformed to one style. Charlemagne, never fully literate, understood the value of a uniform script in running his empire, and sent for the English scholar Alcuin of York to run his palace school and scriptorium at Aachen, where Alcuin was master from 782 to 796. The script spread first from Aachen and then from Marmoutier Abbey at Tours, where Alcuin restructured the scriptorium.

The script is uniform and rounded, with clearly distinguishable letters. It gave word spacing, more punctuation and conventions such as capitals for titles and lower case for the body of a text. It has few ligatures, though et, æ, rt, st and ct are common. Under Charlemagne letter forms still varied between regions; in the ninth century regional hands grew into an international standard, and modern forms such as s and v began to appear. From the twelfth century the letters became more angular and closer together. Charters continued to be written in a Merovingian chancery hand, and documents in local languages used traditional local scripts.

The script spread most widely where Carolingian influence was strongest. The Roman Curia resisted it, England and Ireland took it up only after church reforms in the middle of the tenth century, and in Spain the Visigothic hand survived. More than 7,000 manuscripts in the script survive from the eighth and ninth centuries alone, and scholars of the Carolingian Renaissance used it to copy Roman texts that had been forgotten. Blackletter replaced it, but humanists of the early Renaissance took old Carolingian manuscripts for Roman originals and modelled the humanist minuscule on them. Through it, and printers such as Aldus Manutius, it is a direct ancestor of most modern lower-case Latin typefaces.
carolingian-renaissance: The expression does not imply that Western Europe was barbaric before the Carolingians. Pierre Riché points out that the ancient schools did not vanish abruptly after the fall of the Western Roman Empire, and that Martianus Capella, Cassiodorus and Boethius kept the liberal arts alive. Irish monastic scriptoria spread over Europe, and Charlemagne's union of most of Western Europe brought peace and an economic revival.

Charlemagne found that many parish priests could not read the Vulgate Bible, which alarmed him because the clergy were to instruct his subjects. His Admonitio generalis of 789 and his letter De litteris colendis served as manifestos, and a capitulary of 787 ordered schools to be created. He drew leading scholars to court, among them Peter of Pisa, Paul the Deacon, the Spanish Goth Theodulf of Orléans and Alcuin of York, a Northumbrian monk who headed the Palace School from 782 to 796.

Alcuin wrote textbooks and word lists and established the trivium and quadrivium as the basis of education. Theodulf produced a scholarly edition of the Vulgate from manuscripts of Spain, Italy and Gaul, and the original Hebrew. At Corbie and Tours scribes developed Carolingian minuscule, a book-hand with lower-case letters, consistent letter heights, punctuation and spaces between words. Renaissance humanists later took it for Roman script. Carolingian workshops produced an estimated 100,000 manuscripts in the 9th century, of which some 6,000 to 7,000 survive, and the earliest surviving copies of Cicero, Horace, Lucretius and Julius Caesar are Carolingian.

Conrad Leyser notes that fewer than 2,000 Latin manuscripts survive from before 800, against over 7,000 from the century after. The Carolingians preserved texts through their own values, and Christian works were favoured, though secular texts were also kept. Some historians contest the word renaissance, since the project was a top-down initiative driven by royal patronage, unlike the later Italian movement, and recent writing tends to see it as a religious reform. Its effects were mostly limited to a small group of court scholars. John Contreni describes its effect on education and culture as spectacular, on art as debatable and on the moral regeneration of society as unmeasurable.
carpathian-mountains: The Carpathians form an arc across Central and Southeast Europe, about 1,500 kilometres long and covering 190,000 square kilometres. After the Alps they are the most extensive mountain system in Europe. They do not form an uninterrupted chain but consist of several geologically distinct groups, which run from the Western Carpathians through the Eastern Carpathians to the Southern Carpathians. Their width varies from 12 to 500 kilometres. The highest peak, Gerlachovský štít in the Tatra Mountains of Slovakia, rises 2,655 metres. About half the range lies in Romania, 21 per cent in Slovakia and 10 per cent each in Poland and Ukraine.

The mountains are separated from the Alps by the Danube and are surrounded on all sides by plains, among them the Pannonian plain to the south-west. They form the watershed between the northern seas and the Black Sea. They arose in the Alpine orogeny, in the Mesozoic and Cenozoic eras, and iron, gold and silver were found in great quantities in the Western Carpathians.

The name Carpates is first recorded in the Geographia of Ptolemy in the second century CE, though in most languages the modern form of the name is a neologism. It is strongly associated with the Dacian tribes called Carpes or Carpi, who lived east of the mountains. Late Roman documents called the Eastern Carpathians the Montes Sarmatici, the Sarmatian Mountains. Hungarian documents of the thirteenth to fifteenth centuries called them Thorchal or Tarczal, or less often Montes Nivium, the Snowy Mountains, and the Rus' chronicles called them the Hungarian Mountains.

The origin of the name is not firmly established. Some connect it with a root meaning rock or rugged, others with one meaning to turn, referring to the bend of the range. After the Roman emperor Trajan conquered Dacia, he brought back to Rome over 165 tons of gold and 330 tons of silver.

The mountains stretch through Austria, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Hungary, Poland, Ukraine, Romania and Serbia. They are habitat for the largest European populations of brown bears, wolves, chamois and lynxes, and they hold over a third of all European plant species. Romania has one third of Europe's thermal and mineral waters, many of them in the Carpathians. The area is the most seismically active in Central Europe, and the last volcanic activity occurred at Ciomadul about 30,000 years ago.
carpathian-ruthenia: The region rests on the southern slopes of the eastern Carpathian Mountains, bordered to the east and south by the Tisza River and to the west by the Hornád and Poprad rivers. It borders Poland, Slovakia, Hungary and Romania. The landscape is mostly mountainous and the region is predominantly rural and infrastructurally underdeveloped. Its two major cities, Uzhhorod and Mukachevo, each have about 100,000 people. Most inhabitants regard themselves as Ukrainians or Rusyns, and there are also Hungarians, Romanians, Slovaks and Poles. Jews made up over 13 per cent of the population in 1930.

In the 8th and 9th centuries the Slavic tribe of White Croats densely settled the valleys on both slopes, and Kievan Rus' conquered those who stayed in the late 10th century. The Hungarians crossed the Carpathians in 896. In 1526 the region was divided between the Habsburg Kingdom of Hungary and the Eastern Hungarian Kingdom, which became the Principality of Transylvania from 1570. The Union of Brest of 1595 and the Union of Uzhhorod of 1646 brought the region's Orthodox churches under the jurisdiction of Rome as Eastern Catholic churches. After 1867 it lay in the Hungarian part of Austria-Hungary.

After the First World War the region was briefly claimed by the West Ukrainian Republic, but for most of 1918 and 1919 it was held by the Hungarian Democratic Republic. The Treaty of St. Germain of 10 September 1919 granted the Carpathian Ruthenians autonomy, which Prague upheld only in part. In 1928 Czechoslovakia was divided into four provinces, one of them Subcarpathian Rus, with Užhorod as its capital until 1938. Under the First Vienna Award of November 1938 Czechoslovakia ceded the south of the region to Hungary, and in December the rest was renamed Carpathian Ukraine.

In March 1939 Carpathian Ukraine declared independence under Avhustyn Voloshyn, and Hungary occupied and annexed it, setting up the Governorate of Subcarpathia. The Red Army secured most of the region by 28 October 1944, and on 29 June 1945 Czechoslovakia signed a treaty with the Soviet Union ceding it. It became part of the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic and remained part of Ukraine when the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991.
carpathian-sich: The Sich, formally the National Defense Organization Carpathian Sich, was formed on 9 November 1938 from units of the Ukrainian National Defense, organised in Uzhhorod by Ukrainian nationalists under Stepan Rosokha. It was based in Khust, the temporary capital after Uzhhorod, Mukacheve and Berehove passed to Hungary under the First Vienna Award, and was led by Dmytro Klympush. Its leaders were local Transcarpathian Ukrainian nationalists, but most of its men were Ukrainian activists who crossed the mountains from Galicia.

By February 1939 the Sich had up to 15,000 members, of whom only 2,000 were organised to fight; its five garrisons housed some 2,000 men, only 300 to 400 of them armed, with Czech weapons. Ten district commands ran military and political training, and members served in the police and with the border guards. Its uniforms and ranks, from Ataman to Sichovyk, were modelled on Ukrainian formations of 1917–20. It published the weekly Nastup, edited by Rosokha. Inspired by Nazi German stormtroopers, it terrorised Jews and the pro-Russian parts of the population.

On 13 March 1939, as Czechoslovakia fell apart, the Sich, according to the historians Paul R. Magocsi and Ivan Pop with the encouragement of the SS, prepared a coup against the Carpatho-Ukrainian government of Avgustyn Voloshyn and attacked Czechoslovak troops, at the cost of several Czechoslovak soldiers and many Sich members. When Carpatho-Ukraine declared independence, the Sich became its national army under its commander, Serhii O. Yefremov. Hungary invaded on 15 March, Voloshyn fled to Romania, and by 18 March the Hungarian army held all of Carpatho-Ukraine.

Hundreds of Sich members died in the fighting, many after retreating into conflict with Polish border guards. Survivors fled to Romania and Slovakia or hid in the mountains; the Romanians handed many over to Hungary, which gave Galicians to the Poles and executed the prisoners it kept. In September 1939, 600 veterans of the Sich formed a battalion, authorised by the Abwehr, that took part in the German invasion of Poland and was soon disbanded. In March 2019 Ukraine granted former members official veteran status.
carpentras: Carpentras is a commune in the Vaucluse department of Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur in south-eastern France. It stands on the banks of the river Auzon, a tributary of the Sorgue, 23 kilometres south-west of Mont Ventoux and 23 kilometres north-east of Avignon. Its climate is borderline between humid subtropical and hot-summer Mediterranean, with cool winters and hot summers. Its Provençal Occitan name is Carpentràs, and its Latin name was Carpentoracte.

Greek merchants used the site as a commercial centre in ancient times. The Romans knew it at first as Carpentoracte Meminorum, a name mentioned by Pliny, and then renamed it Forum Neronis, the Forum of Nero. A Roman triumphal arch survives, enclosed by the bishops' palace, which was rebuilt in 1640 and is now a law court, along with a machicolated city gate, the Porte d'Orange.

At the beginning of the Avignon Papacy, Pope Clement V took up residence in Carpentras with the Roman Curia in 1313. His successor, Pope John XXII, settled definitively at Avignon. As capital of the Comtat Venaissin, the town was frequently the residence of the Avignon popes, and the Papal States kept the Venaissin until the French Revolution. Until 1791 Carpentras belonged to the Papal States, not to the Kingdom of France. After the coup of 18 Fructidor on 4 September 1797, counter-revolutionaries attacked its Hôtel de Ville on 22 October.

In the 18th century the Hôtel-Dieu was built between 1750 and 1760 at the commission of Joseph-Dominique d'Inguimbert. It now houses the Bibliothèque Inguimbertine. Carpentras has long been an important centre of French Judaism, and its synagogue, opened in 1367, is the oldest in France. In May 1990 the Jewish cemetery was desecrated, which caused a public uproar and a demonstration in Paris attended by 200,000 people, including President François Mitterrand.

Carpentras is a commercial centre for the Comtat Venaissin and is known for its black truffle market, held every Friday morning in the winter months. Its traditional confectionery is the berlingot, a small hard candy with thin white stripes, originally made from the syrup left over from preserving fruit. The Renaissance composer known as Carpentras, Elzéar Genet (c. 1470 to 1548), and the politician Édouard Daladier, prime minister of France at the start of the Second World War, were born there.
carrack: The carrack evolved from the single-masted cog and was first used for European trade between the Mediterranean and the Baltic. As the Portuguese and Spaniards pushed their trade south along Africa's Atlantic coast in the 15th century, they needed larger, more durable ships. They developed their own oceanic carracks by combining features of the ships they knew, with a more advanced rig that sailed well in the heavy winds and waves of the Atlantic and a hull that carried larger cargoes.

In its most developed form the carrack was carvel-built, stable in heavy seas and large enough to carry a big cargo and the provisions for very long voyages. Later carracks were square-rigged on the foremast and mainmast and lateen-rigged on the mizzenmast, with a high rounded stern, aftcastle, forecastle and bowsprit. The São Gabriel, a typical three-masted carrack, had six sails.

From 1498 Portugal began direct and regular exchanges with India through the Cape Route, a voyage of about six months that required substantial vessels. On average four carracks connected Lisbon to Goa, carrying gold to buy spices, mainly pepper, and from Goa one went on to Ming China to buy silk. From 1541 the Portuguese traded with Japan, exchanging Chinese silk for Japanese silver, and from 1550 the Crown leased the annual captaincy to Japan, giving exclusive rights to a single carrack each year. In 1557 they acquired Macau for this trade, which lasted until 1638, when Japan's rulers banned it for smuggling in Catholic priests. The Japanese called the ships Black Ships, kurofune, after their hulls.

Among the carracks named in the sources are the Grace Dieu, commissioned by Henry V of England and one of the largest ships in the world when launched in 1418, the Santa María of Columbus's voyage of 1492, the São Gabriel, flagship of Vasco da Gama in 1497, and the Flor de la Mar, built in 1502, which sank in 1512 with Afonso de Albuquerque and a large booty. The first galleons were developed from the carrack in the middle of the 16th century and came to replace it, although carracks were still in use in the middle of the 17th century because of their larger cargo capacity.
carrara: Carrara is a town in Tuscany on the Carrione River, some 100 kilometres west-northwest of Florence, notable for the white or blue-grey marble quarried there. Its name likely comes from a pre-Roman element, kar, meaning stone, through the Latin carrariae, quarries. Its motto, Fortitudo mea in rota, or My strength is in the wheel, refers to the wheel of the cart that carried marble blocks from the quarry. The Pantheon and Trajan's Column in Rome are built of Carrara marble, and many sculptures of the Renaissance were carved from it.

The Apuan Ligures lived in the region as early as the ninth century BCE. The present town grew from a borough built for workers in the marble quarries that the Romans opened after conquering Liguria in the early second century BCE. In the early Middle Ages it was a Byzantine and then a Lombard possession, and then it fell to the bishops of Luni, to whom Emperor Otto I gave it. It became a city-state in the early 13th century. The bishops regained it in 1230, and their rule ended in 1313, after which it passed to the republics of Pisa, Lucca and Florence, and later to Gian Galeazzo Visconti of Milan.

After the death of Filippo Maria Visconti in 1447 the Malaspina family fought for Carrara, and moved the seat of their lordship there in the second half of the 15th century. Carrara and Massa formed the Duchy of Massa and Carrara, which passed to the Duchy of Modena through the last Malaspina, Maria Teresa, who married Ercole III d'Este. At the end of the 19th century Carrara became the birthplace of Italian anarchism, above all among the quarry workers and stone carvers, who led the Lunigiana revolt of January 1894. The Congress of Carrara in 1968 founded the International of Anarchist Federations.

The town lies in the province of Massa and Carrara. Its sights include the 12th-century cathedral and the Ducal Palace, also called the Palazzo Cybo Malaspina, which now houses the Fine Arts Academy and combines a 13th-century castle with a Renaissance palace begun in the late 16th century.
carraresi: The family came from Carrara Santo Stefano near Padua and traced itself to a certain Gamberto or Gumberto, probably of Lombard origin to judge from his name and that of his son Luitolfo, who founded the abbey of Carrara in 1027. Gumberto was lord of the castle of Carrara San Giorgio. Loyal to the emperors over many generations, the family became lords of Pernumia before rising in Padua. Its device was a four-wheeled cart, a carro, and its colours were red and white in a checkerboard.

As lords of Padua the Carraresi held wide estates in the surrounding countryside and much property in the city, and their power was comparable to that of the Scaligeri of Verona and the Visconti of Milan. In 1338 they drove the della Scala of Verona out of Padua. Under their rule Padua conquered Verona, Vicenza, Treviso, Feltre, Belluno, Bassano, Aquileia and Udine, controlling much of the Veneto and part of Friuli.

In 1388 a coalition of Milan and Venice forced Francesco il Vecchio to abdicate in favour of his son, Francesco Novello; the elder Francesco died a prisoner of Giangaleazzo Visconti at Monza in 1393. The Venetian annexation of Padua in 1405 ended the prospect of a large regional state with Padua as its capital. One of Francesco Novello's sons, Bishop Stefano, escaped to Rome, where he lived until 1448, and all but two of Padua's bishops until the end of the Venetian Republic in 1797 were Venetian nobles.

The family is known above all for its patronage. Francesco il Vecchio was a patron of Petrarch, who spent his last years at Arquà, a Carrara fief, and left Francesco his picture of the Virgin by Giotto; Francesco also commissioned frescoes, now destroyed, illustrating Petrarch's De viris illustribus, employing Guariento among others. The Baptistery of Padua served as the family's mortuary chapel, though its Carrarese tombs were later removed. Part of their palace survives, including the Loggia and the Sala dei Giganti, and the church of the abbey of Santo Stefano holds the tomb of Marsilio da Carrara.
carrick-on-suir: The town's Irish name, Carraig na Siúire, means rock of the Suir. It lies on both banks of the river at its tidal limit, in the south-eastern corner of County Tipperary, 21 km east of Clonmel and 27 km northwest of Waterford. Most of it stands north of the river in the townland of Carrig Mór, the rest on the south bank in Carrig Beag, which is in County Waterford. The town grew on an island upstream of Waterford and remained one until the 18th century, when small rivers were diverted to form dry land north and west of it.

The earliest records date from 1247, when Matthew Fitzgriffin, a Cambro-Norman lord of the manor, was granted three fairs a year, and the place was first called Carrig Mac Griffin. By the early 14th century it was home to the Butlers: Edmond Butler was created Earl of Carrick in 1315 and built two castle keeps on the north bank. A four-towered castle followed in the 15th century, and Edmund MacRichard Butler built the first bridge over the estuary in 1447. Archbishop Dermot O'Hurley, one of the 24 Irish Catholic Martyrs, was arrested in the manor house in 1583.

In 1649, during the Cromwellian conquest of Ireland, English Parliamentarians took Carrick by stealth through an undefended gate, and Ulster troops under a Major Geoghegan who tried to retake it were beaten off with the loss of over 500 killed. James Butler, 1st Duke of Ormond, founded a woollen industry in 1670, and by 1799 the population had reached around 11,000. Taxes on the woollen trade, unemployment, emigration and the Great Famine later reduced it. In the Civil War the town was held by the Anti-Treaty IRA until it fell to the Free State army in 1922, and tanning brought steady work from the 1930s until the Pollack & Plunder tannery closed in 1985.

The Tholsel, a four-storey townhouse of about 1500 at the West Gate, survives from the old town, and the manor house, refurbished by the Irish State in the 1990s, is open to the public. The town is linked to Limerick and Waterford by the N24 road and by rail.
carrickfergus: Carrickfergus sits on the north shore of Belfast Lough, 11 miles (18 km) from Belfast. Its name comes from the Irish Carraig Fhearghais, the rock of Fergus. The town is said to take it from Fergus Mór, a king of Dál Riata of the old stories, whose ship, according to one tale, ran aground on a rock by the shore. Belfast Lough itself was known as Carrickfergus Bay well into the 17th century, and for a long time the town was both larger and more prominent than Belfast.

Carrickfergus became an inhabited town shortly after 1170, when John de Courcy invaded Ulster. De Courcy was expelled between 1203 and 1205 by Hugh de Lacy, who finished the castle's gatehouse, drum towers and outer ward. After the Earldom of Ulster collapsed, the castle remained the only English outpost in Ulster for four centuries. Edward de Bruce captured the town in 1315 and the castle in 1316, and the Scots largely destroyed the town in 1402. In November 1597 the Battle of Carrickfergus, part of the Nine Years War, ended in defeat for the forces of Elizabeth I at the hands of the MacDonnell clan.

Sir Arthur Chichester, appointed to govern the castle and town in 1599, brought in English and Scottish settlers and built the town wall. In 1642 chaplains with the Covenanter army set up the first presbytery in Ireland there. The castle withstood several days of siege by the forces of William of Orange before surrendering on 28 August 1689, and William landed at the town on 14 June 1690.

In February 1760 French troops under François Thurot held the town to ransom, and in 1711 it saw the last witchcraft trial in Ireland. In April 1778 John Paul Jones fought and defeated HMS Drake off the town. William Orr was hanged there on 14 October 1797, and in 1798 Henry Joy McCracken was captured on its outskirts.

Carrickfergus had a population of 28,141 at the 2021 census. It forms part of the Belfast Metropolitan Area and, since 2015, of the Mid and East Antrim Borough Council. Segments of the town wall are still visible, and Carrickfergus Castle is one of the best-preserved Norman castles in Ireland. The town gave its name to a folk song, a 19th-century translation of an Irish song from Munster.
carrie-chapman-catt: Carrie Clinton Lane was born on 9 January 1859 in Ripon, Wisconsin, and moved with her family to Charles City, Iowa, when she was seven. After graduating from high school in 1877 she enrolled at Iowa Agricultural College, now Iowa State University, paying her way by washing dishes, working in the library and teaching in rural schools. At the Crescent Literary Society she demanded the right to speak extemporaneously, which led to women gaining the right to speak in its meetings.
In 1885 she married the newspaper editor Leo Chapman, who died of typhoid fever in August 1886. In 1890 she married George Catt, a wealthy engineer, who encouraged her suffrage work.

From 1890 to 1892 Catt was state organiser of the Iowa Woman Suffrage Association and began working for the National American Woman Suffrage Association (NAWSA). In 1893 she coordinated the campaign in Colorado, where she visited 29 of the state's 63 counties; Colorado passed women's suffrage that November, the second state to do so and the first by popular vote. She served as NAWSA president from 1900 to 1904 and from 1915 to 1920.

She also led the international movement. At the first meeting of the International Woman Suffrage Alliance in Berlin, with 33 delegates, she was elected president, and she held the post from 1904 until 1923. The alliance grew to include associations in 32 nations.

In January 1915 Catt and Jane Addams called a meeting of more than 3,000 women that formed the Women's Peace Party. In 1917, with Catt as president, NAWSA offered the women's services to the government, while stating that its work for suffrage would continue. In March 1919 she proposed a League of Women Voters, and she founded it on 14 February 1920, six months before ratification of the Nineteenth Amendment.

Catt's views on race and immigration changed over her life. In the 1880s and 1890s she gave speeches that echoed anti-immigrant sentiment and referred to the ignorant foreign vote, though she proposed education and reform rather than disenfranchisement. In September 1917 the NAWSA board under her leadership resolved to stand for a democracy that knows no bias of race, color, creed or sex.

Catt died of a heart attack at her home in New Rochelle, New York, on 9 March 1947 and was buried at Woodlawn Cemetery in The Bronx beside her companion of more than twenty years, Mary Garrett Hay. Mary Church Terrell, an African American suffragist, wrote of the loss of a great woman who had pleaded with the world to deal justly with all human beings.
carrigafoyle-castle: Built by Conor Liath O'Connor-Kerry in the 1490s and counted among the strongest of Irish fortresses, Carrigafoyle was a large tower house of a type common across the north of Munster. It stood on a rock in a small bay off the southern bank of the Shannon estuary, and its name anglicises the Irish Carraig an Phoill, rock of the hole. It was called the guardian of the Shannon because it commanded the shipping lanes that supplied Limerick, some 32 km upriver.

A wooded island shielded the bay from the estuary on the north. A double wall defended the castle-rock on the west and south: the inner wall enclosed a bawn, and around it lay a moat covered on three sides by the outer wall, where a smaller tower stood. The keep was 86 feet high, the steep sides of the rock were faced with brick and mortar, and at high tide the walled landing inside the moat could take a ship of 100 tons.

During the Second Desmond Rebellion the castle was held for Gerald FitzGerald, 14th Earl of Desmond, by 50 Irish and 16 Spanish soldiers who had landed at Smerwick in the Papal invasion of 1579, with women and children. An Italian engineer, Captain Julian, had been strengthening its defences under the direction of Desmond's countess, Eleanor. At Easter 1580 Sir William Pelham, with Sir George Carew and a fleet under Sir William Winter, brought three demi-cannon and a culverin ashore and bombarded the castle for six hours on each of two days.

An assault on the first day was beaten back from the sea-wall. On the second, reinforced from the ships, troops under Captains Humfrey Mackworth and John Zouche attacked; the great west wall collapsed, crushing many inside, and most who fled were shot or put to the sword, the rest hanged, Captain Julian three days later. Askeaton and other Desmond strongholds were then abandoned, though the rebels fought on until the earl was killed at Glanageenty in 1583. The castle was never repaired, and its ruins, with the outer defences and moat, still show the bombardment.
carrion-de-los-condes: Carrión de los Condes is a municipality in the province of Palencia, in the autonomous community of Castile and León. It stands on the River Carrión, 40 kilometres upstream from the provincial capital, on the French Way of the Way of Saint James.

One tradition has the town taken from the Moors by Alonso Carreño at some point between 791 and 842, when it took the name Carrión. In the poem Cantar de Mio Cid it was the home of Diego and Fernán González, the fictitious sons-in-law of El Cid. In 1072, after losing the nearby Battle of Golpejera, Alfonso VI of León took refuge in the Church of Santa María de las Victorias, also called Santa María del Camino, and ultimately chose exile, going to Toledo, then in Moorish hands. In 1209 Gonzalo Rodríguez Girón, a Palencia magnate who became steward of the king, founded the Hospital de la Herrada to help pilgrims on the Way of Saint James and other travellers.

The town was inhabited by Jews at an early date, and they outnumbered the Christians in numbers and in property. In 1126 they submitted to the victorious Alfonso VII, who was favourably disposed to them, and in 1160 many settled in neighbouring Palencia. In 1290 the community paid 92,000 maravedís in taxes, not much less than that of Burgos.

The Romanesque church of Santa María de las Victorias dates from the 12th century, as does the church of Santiago, which houses a Pantocrator considered a masterpiece of Romanesque sculpture. The monastery of Santa Clara dates from the 13th century, and the monastery of San Zoilo, built between the 11th and 16th centuries, has a Plateresque cloister. The town also has Romanesque tombs of the counts who lived there, and the churches of Belén, San Andrés and San Julián.
carrowmore: Carrowmore, in Irish An Cheathrú Mhór, the great quarter, stands on a small plateau between 36.5 and 59 metres above sea level, at the centre of a ritual landscape dominated to the west by Knocknarea and the great cairn of Miosgán Médhbh on its summit. Thirty tombs survive and another 25 have been destroyed since 1800, many by quarrying and field clearance. With Carrowkeel, Loughcrew and Brú na Bóinne it is one of the big four clusters of megalithic tombs in Ireland.

Most tombs are satellites of the largest monument, the restored cairn of Listoghil, or Tomb 51, erected c. 3500 BCE and 34 metres across. Each satellite was a small dolmen of five upright stones under a capstone, ringed by 30 to 40 boulders, usually of gneiss, and most face the central area. The burials were mostly cremations of several people, with antler and bone pins, beads, pendants and quartz fragments, and the chambers were reused in the Bronze and Iron Ages.

Gabriel Beranger drew the monuments in 1779, George Petrie surveyed and numbered them for the Ordnance Survey of 1837, and William Gregory Wood-Martin made the first recorded excavations in the 1880s, after the landlord Rodger Walker had dug there for antiquities. The Swedish archaeologist Göran Burenhult, who excavated in 1977–1982 and 1994–1998, read his radiocarbon dates as showing that hunter-gatherers built the tombs, but a later review with 25 new dates placed them between about 3750 and 3000 BCE. Ancient DNA showed a man buried in Listoghil to be related to people buried at Newgrange, Millin Bay and Carrowkeel.

Carrowmore is a protected National Monument. A plan of 1983 by Sligo County Council for a landfill dump near the complex was rejected by the Supreme Court in 1989, the first explicit legal recognition of an architectural landscape. Most of the site is now in public ownership, with a visitor centre in a farmhouse near the R292 road.
cartagena-colombia: Cartagena faces the Caribbean Sea in the north of Colombia, on a bay with two entrances, Bocachica in the south and Bocagrande in the north. Its position between the Magdalena and Sinú rivers gave easy access to the interior of New Granada and made it a main port for trade between Spain and its overseas empire, with its importance established by the early 1540s. Settlement by indigenous peoples around the bay dates from about 4000 BCE, and the Puerto Hormiga culture of the nearby coast produced the oldest ceramic objects found in the Americas.

Rodrigo de Bastidas travelled to the Pearl Coast and the Gulf of Urabá in 1500-01. On 14 January 1533 Pedro de Heredia entered the Bay of Cartagena under contract to Queen Joanna of Castile with three ships, 150 men and 22 horses. He found the village of Calamari abandoned, fought an all-day battle at Turbaco, and returned to Calamari in April with gold, including a solid gold porcupine weighing 132 pounds. In later expeditions he raided the gold tombs and temples of the Sinú. The city was founded on 1 June 1533 and named after Cartagena in Spain, and by extension after Carthage; Heredia governed it for 22 years and died on his return to Spain in 1544.

Cartagena was a centre of political, church and economic life in the Spanish Empire, a key port for exporting silver to Spain and for importing enslaved Africans under the asiento system, and it could be defended against pirate attacks. In the 18th century, after the Bourbon dynasty ended the Carrera de Indias convoys, it became the gateway to the Indies of Peru under the Viceroyalty of New Granada. It had 13,700 inhabitants by 1777. The Battle of Cartagena de Indias was fought here in 1741 during the War of Jenkins' Ear between Spain and Britain.

Cartagena was under Spanish rule for more than 275 years. On 4 June 1810, after the Peninsular War began, the Royal Commissioner Antonio Villavicencio and the city council banished the Spanish governor Francisco de Montes. A Supreme Junta was formed, and on 11 November a declaration of independence proclaimed a free and sovereign state, helped by the artisan leader Pedro Romero. The city is now the capital of the Bolívar Department, with 876,885 people at the 2018 census. Its colonial walled city and fortress were designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1984.
cartagena-manifesto: The document's original title was Memoria dirigida a los ciudadanos de la Nueva Granada por un caraqueño, Memorial Addressed to the Citizens of New Granada by a Man from Caracas. Simón Bolívar had been an officer in the Venezuelan army. The First Republic fell to movements that confronted and exploited one another: royalists fighting for the old order, supporters of independence fighting for creole supremacy, and pardos, blacks and slaves fighting for their liberation. The conflict was worsened by shortages of provisions and the 1812 Caracas earthquake.
Bolívar left La Guaira on a Spanish ship, stayed briefly in Curaçao and reached Cartagena, where he accepted a commission in the army of the United Provinces of New Granada.

Bolívar set out a framework meant to keep New Granada from suffering Venezuela's fate, since its territory followed the same colonial pattern of loyal juntas turning into independent governments. Beyond the federal system, which he judged weak for wartime, he named the bad management of public income by the republican government, the earthquake, the impossibility of raising a permanent army against the resistance of the population, and the Roman Catholic Church, which he accused of secretly spreading anti-republican views.

Against the infighting of city, state and national authorities, he called for a strong central government with a powerful executive. Government, he wrote, must adjust itself to the times, men and circumstances in which it acts: gentle and protective when they are prosperous and serene, but severe and armed with a strength equal to the dangers when they are calamitous and turbulent.

The manifesto is the first of Bolívar's public documents, and his later fame as the Liberator of five nations made it well known. It argued that continued royalist control of Venezuela threatened New Granada's own independence and urged its authorities to take the offensive and recapture Caracas. It set out the conceptual framework of the agenda he then carried out in the field, and New Granada later gave him permission to lead a force into Venezuela.
cartago-costa-rica: Cartago was founded in 1563 by Juan Vásquez de Coronado and was the first successful establishment in Costa Rica. King Philip II of Spain granted it a coat of arms in 1565, and the Cortes gave it the title Muy Noble y Muy Leal in 1814. It served as the first capital of Costa Rica.

In 1823 the republican leader Gregorio José Ramírez moved the capital to the larger city of San José. Cartago had wanted to unite the newly independent province of Costa Rica with Iturbide's Mexican Empire, while San José and Alajuela supported a republican system. Major earthquakes severely damaged the city in 1822, 1841 and 1910. The eruption of the Irazú Volcano in 1963 badly damaged farmland around Cartago, but not the city itself.

Cartago stands at 1,435 metres above sea level at the base of the Irazú Volcano, and is the head city of Cartago canton in Cartago Province. Its Basílica de Nuestra Señora de los Ángeles is the country's principal church, to which many pilgrims come on the feast day of the Virgin of the Angels, 2 August. It holds a statue of a Black Madonna known as La Negrita, believed to have healing powers.

According to folklore, an indigenous girl found the statue in 1635, though the only inhabitants of the area were then enslaved black and mulatto people living in a village named La Puebla. The rock where it was found is kept as a relic in the basilica. In the Plaza Mayor stand the Santiago Apóstol Parish Ruins, which are not true ruins but an unfinished building damaged by the 1910 earthquake. The Costa Rica Institute of Technology and the city museum are also in Cartago.
cartersville-georgia: Cartersville lies in south-central Bartow County, 42 miles north-west of downtown Atlanta and 76 miles south-east of Chattanooga, Tennessee. The Etowah River flows through a broad valley south of the downtown and on to Rome, where it forms the Coosa River. The city limits extend upriver as far as Allatoona Dam, which forms Lake Allatoona. Its highest point is the summit of Pine Mountain at 1,562 feet. The Etowah Indian Mounds, an archaeological Native American site, lie south of the city.

The town was founded by English-Americans in 1832 and was first called Birmingham. It was incorporated as Cartersville in 1854, taking the name of Col. Farish Carter of Milledgeville, the owner of a large plantation. It became the seat of Bartow County in 1867, after Sherman's March to the Sea during the American Civil War destroyed Cassville, and it was incorporated as a city in 1872. Amos Akerman, who lived there for a long time, was United States attorney general under President Ulysses S. Grant and led the federal prosecution of members of the Ku Klux Klan, which made him one of the most important public servants of the Reconstruction era.

On 26 February 1916 a mob of fifty men and boys took Jesse McCorkle, a Black man arrested the night before on an accusation of assaulting a woman, from the jail and lynched him in front of city hall. The evangelist Samuel Porter Jones also lived in Cartersville, and his house, Rose Lawn, is now a museum.

Cartersville is a city in north-western Georgia and the seat of Bartow County, at the north-west edge of the Atlanta metropolitan area, with 23,187 inhabitants in the 2020 census. Manufacturing, tourism and services are part of its economy. Its museums include the Booth Western Art Museum, the Tellus Science Museum and the Bartow History Museum in the old courthouse of about 1870. A Coca-Cola sign painted in 1894 on a downtown pharmacy wall is described as the world's first outdoor Coca-Cola sign.
carthage: Carthage was founded on the eastern side of the Lake of Tunis. Tradition credits Queen Elissa, or Dido, originally from Tyre, though her historicity has been questioned. In the myth she asked a local tribe for land and was told she could have as much as an oxhide could cover, so she cut the hide into strips and laid out the perimeter of the city. The name derives from the Punic qrt-ḥdšt, new city, implying a new Tyre. The Carthaginians were Phoenician settlers who spoke Canaanite, a Semitic language, and followed a local variety of Canaanite religion. Unlike other colonisers who required only respect from their colonies, Carthage is said to have sent its own magistrates to govern overseas settlements.

The city stood on a promontory between Sicily and the Tunisian coast, so that every ship crossing the sea passed it. It had two artificial harbours, one for a navy of 220 warships and one for trade, and walls described as 37 kilometres long, with the 4.0 to 4.8 kilometres across the isthmus truly massive and never penetrated. The Byrsa citadel stood roughly in the middle. The surrounding farmland, the Chora, was worked by Punic owners, and a retired general named Mago wrote a 28-volume work on agriculture in Punic, later translated into Latin and Greek and now lost except for passages in other Latin works.

Carthage contested the western Mediterranean with Greek cities in the Sicilian Wars and the Pyrrhic War, and with Rome in the Punic Wars. The Roman Republic destroyed the city in 146 BCE after a siege of nearly three years, the Byrsa being the last place to fall.

Gaius Gracchus founded a short-lived colony there by 122 BCE, and Julius Caesar built a new city between 49 and 44 BCE. By the first century it was the second-largest city in the western half of the Roman Empire, with a peak population of 500,000, and the centre of the province of Africa. In 698 Hasan ibn al-Nu'man defeated Emperor Tiberios III in the Battle of Carthage, and the Umayyad forces destroyed Roman Carthage, tearing down its walls and cutting its aqueducts to prevent a Byzantine return. In the 13th century the Crusaders took it from the Hafsids, massacring its inhabitants in the Eighth Crusade, and the Hafsids then destroyed its defences.

Christian Tuxen Falbe surveyed the site in 1830, and Charles Ernest Beulé, Alfred Louis Delattre and French archaeologists after 1921 excavated it. Scholars disagree on whether child sacrifice was practised in ancient Carthage. Carthage became a municipality in 1919 as a suburb of Tunis, and the ruins are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
carthaginian-iberia: The Phoenicians, traders mainly from Tyre, Sidon and Byblos, founded many trading colonies around the Mediterranean, including some in Spain, and in 814 BCE founded Carthage on the coast of what is now Tunisia. After Phoenicia fell to the Babylonians and then the Persians, Carthage became the most powerful Phoenician city and annexed other colonies of the western Mediterranean, such as Hadrumetum and Thapsus, along with territory in Sicily, Africa and Sardinia. Its province in Iberia covered the Mediterranean part of the peninsula.

After Carthage's defeat in the First Punic War, the general Hamilcar Barca crushed a mercenary revolt in Africa and trained a new army of Numidians, mercenaries and other infantry. He led it to Iberia hoping to win a new empire to make up for the territories lost to Rome and to serve as a base for revenge.
