His success began at Gadir, and by force and diplomacy he secured around half of the peninsula and founded the city of Akra Leuke, before dying in battle in 228 BCE. His son-in-law Hasdrubal the Fair carried the conquest to the Tagus River by his death in 221 BCE and founded Qart Hadasht, New Town, around 227 BCE.

The province fell in the Second Punic War. In 209 BCE the Romans under Scipio Africanus captured New Carthage, the centre of Punic power in Iberia. At the Battle of Baecula they could not stop Hasdrubal Barca marching to reinforce his brother Hannibal in Italy. The defeat of the Carthaginian forces at Ilipa in 206 BCE sealed the province's fate, and Gades, which had already rebelled against Carthage, fell to Rome. In 205 BCE Mago tried to retake New Carthage while the Romans faced a mutiny and an Iberian rising, but was repulsed and sailed for Italy from the Balearic Islands.

Iberian soldiers made up a large part of the army that Hannibal led into Italy. Gadir drew closer to Rome soon after the war, and Qart Hadasht became the present-day city of Cartagena. Carthage itself was destroyed in 146 BCE at the end of the Third Punic War, about 50 years after it lost Iberia.
carthago-delenda-est: Rome won the first two Punic Wars but suffered humiliations and damaging reverses, above all at the Battle of Cannae in 216 BCE, and won the Second Punic War through Scipio Africanus in 201 BCE. Carthage was then reduced to a small territory equal to what is now north-eastern Tunisia and no longer threatened Rome. In 152 BCE Cato the Censor, a veteran of that war, visited the city as a member of a senatorial embassy sent to arbitrate a conflict between Carthage and Massinissa, king of Numidia and an ally of Rome. He was shocked by Carthage's wealth, which he considered dangerous for Rome.

Cato then called relentlessly for the city's destruction and is said to have ended all his speeches with the phrase, even when the debate concerned another matter. The Senate did not follow him at first. Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica Corculum, son-in-law of Scipio Africanus and the most influential senator, opposed war, arguing that fear of a common enemy was needed to maintain Roman unity. He is said to have ended his own speeches with Carthago servanda est, 'Carthage must be saved'.

Cato prevailed after Carthage attacked Massinissa, which gave Rome a pretext, since the treaty of 201 BCE forbade Carthage to declare war without Rome's assent. In 146 BCE Scipio Aemilianus, grandson of Africanus, razed the city and its remaining population was sold into slavery. Africa became a Roman province. The notion that Roman forces sowed the city with salt is a 19th-century invention.

No ancient source gives the phrase exactly as it is quoted today. Pliny the Elder in his Natural History, Aurelius Victor and Florus all quote it in indirect speech, as a demand that Carthage be destroyed. Plutarch's Life of Cato the Elder gives only a Greek paraphrase: 'It seems best to me that Carthage no longer exist'. The modern short form was made by English and French scholars at the turn of the 18th and 19th centuries, while German scholars have used the longer Ceterum censeo Carthaginem delendam esse.

The phrase has been quoted or paraphrased as a learned reference to total war. In 1673 the English minister Anthony Ashley Cooper, 1st Earl of Shaftesbury, revived it as Delenda est Carthago in a speech before Parliament during the Third Anglo-Dutch War, comparing England to Rome and the Dutch Republic to Carthage. In 1899 Leo Tolstoy kept the form Carthago delenda est as the title of a pacifist essay condemning war and militarism. In 1930 José Ortega y Gasset coined Delenda est Monarchia. The opening words, ceterum censeo, now refer on their own to a statement a speaker repeats again and again.
carthago-nova: The city may have been built on an earlier Iberian or Tartessian settlement, and Cartagena has traditionally been identified with Mastia, named in the Ora maritima of Avienus and in the second treaty between Rome and Carthage of 348 BCE. The coast of Cartagena and Mazarrón was coveted for its lead, silver and zinc, worked since Phoenician times, and its waters gave fish for salting. Strongly walled, the city was the main market for goods arriving by sea and for inland produce sent overseas.

Hamilcar Barca, seeking a dominion for his family in Iberia after the First Punic War, made the region the centre of his operations, and under the Barcid family the city, Qart Hadasht, became the chief Carthaginian city of Hispania. From there Hannibal set out for Italy at the start of the Second Punic War in 218 BCE. After Scipio Africanus took it, it was a tributary community, received Latin rights under Julius Caesar and became the colony Colonia Vrbs Iulia Nova Carthago in 44 BCE. Around 40,000 enslaved people are said to have worked in its silver and lead mines.

Under Augustus the city gained a large theatre and forum. From the 2nd century it declined, perhaps as the mines were exhausted, and its eastern quarter was abandoned until Diocletian made it a provincial capital in 298, when buildings rose again from Augustan materials and trade turned to the fish sauce garum. The Vandals plundered it in the 5th century, and in 461 Emperor Majorian's fleet of 45 ships gathered there was destroyed at the Battle of Cartagena. After a time under Visigothic control, Emperor Justinian I made it the capital of the Byzantine province of Spania, renamed Carthago Spartaria.

Remains of the Roman city stand within modern Cartagena: the Republican amphitheatre beneath the bullring, the Augusteum and forum, the Casa de la Fortuna with its wall paintings and mosaics, and the Roman theatre, discovered in October 1988 and one of the largest in Roman Hispania. Finds are shown in the Municipal Archaeological Museum, the National Museum of Underwater Archaeology and the Roman Theatre Museum, opened in 2008.
cartimandua: Cartimandua, also written Cartismandua, was a first-century queen of the Brigantes, a Celtic people of what is now northern England, and she is known through the writings of the Roman historian Tacitus. Her reign is dated from about 43 to about 69. Although Tacitus first mentions her in 51, her rule may already have been established when the emperor Claudius began the conquest of Britain in 43.

She may have been one of the eleven kings who surrendered without a fight according to Claudius's triumphal arch, or she may have come to power after the defeat of a revolt of part of the Brigantes by Publius Ostorius Scapula in 48. Tacitus calls her of distinguished birth, so she probably inherited her power. Her name may be a compound of Celtic roots meaning chase and pony.

In 51 the British resistance leader Caratacus, defeated by Ostorius Scapula in Wales, sought sanctuary with her, and she handed him to the Romans in chains. Tacitus says this brought her wealth and the wanton spirit that success breeds. She later divorced her consort Venutius, who had been loyal to Rome, and took his armour-bearer Vellocatus as consort, an act Tacitus calls scandalous.

Venutius made war on her, though she had seized his brother and other relatives as hostages, and then on her Roman protectors, and he built alliances outside the Brigantes. During the governorship of Aulus Didius Gallus, in the years 52 to 57, he invaded. The Romans sent cohorts, and the fighting stayed inconclusive until Caesius Nasica arrived with the legion IX Hispana and defeated the rebels.

In 69, during the Roman year of four emperors, Venutius revolted again with help from others. She asked for troops, but the Romans could send only auxiliaries, and she was evacuated, leaving Venutius in control of a kingdom at war with Rome.

After the evacuation in 69 Cartimandua disappears from the sources. Tacitus portrays her notoriously, as a ruler who betrayed Caratacus under the pretence of sanctuary and who put a common military man beside her. His account is the only substantial one, and he wrote of her as a client queen defended by Roman arms. He records that the throne was left to Venutius and the war to Rome.
cartography: What counts as the earliest known map is debated, partly because the term map is not well defined and some artifacts that might be maps may be something else. A wall painting that might depict the ancient Anatolian city of Çatalhöyük has been dated to the late 7th millennium BCE, and prehistoric alpine rock carvings at Mount Bego in France and Valcamonica in Italy, dated to the 4th millennium BCE, are widely interpreted as showing cultivated plots.

Other maps of the ancient world include the Minoan House of the Admiral wall painting of about 1600 BCE, showing a seaside community in oblique perspective, and an engraved map of the Babylonian city of Nippur from the Kassite period. The oldest surviving world maps are from Babylonia of the 9th century BCE; one shows Babylon on the Euphrates, surrounded by Assyria, Urartu and several cities, all encircled by a bitter river.

Cartography is the study and practice of making and using maps, combining science, aesthetics and technique. Its traditional objectives are to select the traits to be mapped, to represent terrain on flat media through map projections, to remove irrelevant characteristics through generalisation, and to arrange the elements of the map to convey its message.

Maps are divided into general maps, made for a general audience, and thematic maps, which concern specific geographic themes, such as a map of corn production. A topographic map describes a place, with contour lines showing elevation, while a topological map disregards scale and detail to communicate route information; Beck's London Underground map is the usual example.

About 1,100 medieval European mappae mundi survive, of which some 900 illustrate manuscripts. In 1154 the Arab geographer Muhammad al-Idrisi produced his atlas Tabula Rogeriana, and his world map, mostly Ptolemaic in conception, remained the most accurate for the next three centuries. In 1492 Martin Behaim, advisor to King John II of Portugal, made the oldest extant globe, and Hartmann Schedel was among the first to use the printing press for maps.

The Selden map, made by a Chinese cartographer around 1620, though historians debate the date, shows trading routes, a compass rose and a scale bar. Enlightenment maps used copper plate intaglio rather than woodcut, and mapmakers often plagiarised: Herman Moll's Beaver Map of 1715 closely reproduces Nicolas de Fer's work of 1698. Some scholars argue that maps are inherently biased, and that cartography served imperial power in the conquest of Africa.
casa-da-india: Its forerunners arose with the Portuguese exploration of the African coast. A Casa de Ceuta was founded in Lisbon as early as 1434, and around 1443 the Casa de Arguim and Casa da Guiné were set up at Lagos, in the Algarve, to manage Prince Henry the Navigator's monopoly on African trade; King Afonso V moved them to Lisbon after Henry's death in 1460. In 1482 King John II reorganised them as the Casa da Mina e Tratos de Guiné, with a separate naval arsenal, and in 1486 he added the Casa de Escravos, a slave-trading department.

After Vasco da Gama opened the sea route to India in 1497–99, the house was reorganised as the Casa da Índia e da Guiné, first named in a royal letter of 1501; from 1511 its offices stood on the ground floor of the Ribeira Palace on Terreiro do Paço. It organised the annual India Armadas, and by 1510 the crown drew a million cruzados a year from spices alone, so that Francis I of France called Manuel I the grocer king. Between 1506 and 1570 it enforced the royal monopoly on spices, silk and shellac and on exports of gold, silver, copper and coral.

Costs in Morocco and reliance on foreigners for many services consumed much of the income, and by about 1560 it no longer covered expenses. After 1642 the house lost its trade monopolies and became solely a regulator and customs agency. The Great Lisbon Earthquake of 1755 destroyed its headquarters, many of its tasks passed to ministries from 1822, and King Miguel I dissolved it in 1833, its functions going to the Alfândega de Lisboa.

A director and three treasurers oversaw the house, with five secretaries and a chief factor who corresponded with the trading posts; the chronicler João de Barros was appointed factor in 1532. Its departments dealt with the spice trade, finance, ship scheduling and legal matters, and it also kept archives, appointed royal officials overseas and ran one of the first postal services. The separate Armazém built and supplied the ships, and in 1547 the post of chief cosmographer was created for the mathematician Pedro Nunes. The house kept a secret master map, the Padrão Real.
casa-de-contratacion: Queen Isabella I of Castile created the House of Trade of the Indies eleven years after Christopher Columbus's landfall in the Americas in 1492; its official name was La Casa y Audiencia de Indias. It was the Spanish counterpart of the Portuguese Casa da India of Lisbon. Its first officers were Sancho de Matienzo as treasurer, Jimeno de Bribiesca as contador and Francisco Pinelo as factor, and they soon controlled the economic development of Hispaniola. Until the Council of the Indies was founded in 1524, the Casa had broad powers over overseas affairs.

Unlike the later chartered East India Companies of the Dutch and English, the Casa was an arm of the crown. It approved every voyage of exploration and trade, licensed captains and emigrants, administered commercial law, kept secret information on routes and discoveries, and settled the estates of Spaniards who died overseas. In theory no Spaniard could sail without its approval, though smuggling was common. It levied the quinto real, a 20 per cent tax on all precious metals entering Spain, and other duties of between 10 and 40 per cent, while each ship had to carry a clerk to log its goods.

The Casa kept the Padrón Real, the official and secret map from which every Spanish ship's charts were copied, first made in 1508. Amerigo Vespucci was its first piloto mayor from 1508 until his death in 1512, training pilots in its navigation school; later cosmographers included Sebastian Cabot, Alonso de Santa Cruz and Pedro de Medina. Trade itself passed through the merchants' guild of Seville, the Consulado de mercaderes, and the convoys of the Flota de Indias and the Manila galleons.

By the late 17th century the Casa had fallen into bureaucratic gridlock as Spain struggled to pay for both its wars in Europe and a global empire, and the riches carried from Manila and Acapulco were often signed over to the crown's creditors before the galleons reached port. The Bourbon kings reduced its power and that of Seville, moving it to Cádiz in 1717. Charles III limited its powers further, and his son Charles IV abolished it in 1790, a reorganisation that also ended the treasure fleets.
casa-de-la-vall: The house stands in the historic centre of Andorra la Vella on a rocky spur, the roc de la Vall, overlooking the valley. Before the Council bought it, it was known as Casa Busquets; the keystone of its entrance arch bears the family's tree emblem, the date 1580 and an abbreviated form of the name Antoni Busquets. It follows the type of a large Pyrenean manor house, an almost square block with thick walls, and has machicolations, corner turrets with loopholes and a defensive tower over the old royal road into the town.

Above the door is the quartered coat of arms of Andorra, with the motto Virtus unita fortior, and beside it an older relief signed Escoter me fecit, regarded as the oldest surviving representation of the Andorran arms. Inside, a hall carries 16th-century paintings of the Passion, and the council chamber holds a chapel of Saint Ermengol and the Cupboard of the Seven Keys, the Council's old archive, which opens only when the keys of every parish are present.

The Council of the Land had met in church porches and cemeteries before it agreed on 19 December 1701 to buy the house for 1,650 lliures. The house also held the criminal court, the Tribunal de Corts, and from the 18th century a prison. Because sittings could last several days, councillors ate in the kitchen and slept in the attic, later divided into one room for each parish. On 5 April 1933 young Andorrans besieged the Council there, an episode remembered as winning universal male suffrage, and in 1991 and 1992 the attic hosted the commission that drafted the Constitution of 1993.

In the early 1960s the Catalan architect Joaquim Ros de Ramis remodelled the house, stripping the render to bare stone and adding a second corner turret. The architect Enric Dilmé and the historian Quim Valera later called the exposed stone a historical fake, which nonetheless became a model for Andorran building. Dilmé restored the interior in 2025, and the house reopened on 22 December 2025 with the Saint Thomas session. It is protected as a bé d'interès cultural and appears on the Andorran 1 euro coin.
casablanca: Casablanca stands on the Atlantic coast of the Chaouia plain in the central-western part of Morocco. It has about 3.22 million inhabitants in the urban area, making it the most populous city in the Maghreb, and its port is one of the largest artificial ports in Africa. Before the 15th century the settlement was called Anfa. The sociologist André Adam favoured a Tamazight origin for the name, such as anfa meaning hill or promontory on the sea, though he found the information insufficient to say which.

Berbers settled the area by the seventh century BCE, and the Phoenicians and then the Romans used it as a port. Under the Merinids in the 14th century Anfa rose in importance as a port, and after the last Merinids were ousted in 1465 it became independent again, a safe harbour for pirates and privateers. The Portuguese bombarded it into ruins in 1468, and the town that grew up around it was called Casa Branca, white house.

Sultan Mohammed ben Abdallah built the port and rebuilt the town between 1756 and 1790, after the earthquake of 1755. It was named ad-Dār al-Bayḍāʼ, the Arabic translation of Casa Branca. In the 19th century it grew as a supplier of wool to the British textile industry. The Treaty of Algeciras of 1906 formalised French preeminence in Morocco, and the Treaty of Fez of March 1912 established the French protectorate. The population rose from about 12,000 to 110,000 by 1921, largely through shanty towns.

Casablanca hosted the Anfa, or Casablanca, Conference in January 1943, where Winston Churchill and Franklin D. Roosevelt discussed the progress of the war, with Charles de Gaulle and Henri Giraud attending in minor roles. In the 1940s and 1950s it was a major centre of anti-French rioting.
casale-monferrato: Casale Monferrato lies in the province of Alessandria in Piedmont, about 60 kilometres east of Turin, on the right bank of the Po, where the river runs at the foot of the Montferrat hills. An ancient Roman municipium, it has been the most important trade and manufacturing centre of the area for centuries. Its origins are fairly obscure. A Gaulish settlement called Vardacate stood on the Po here, and by the beginning of the 8th century a small town under Lombard rule, probably called Sedula or Sedulia, occupied the site.

The cult of Saint Evasius, said by late and unreliable accounts to have been beheaded here with 146 followers, flourished, and by 988 the town was known as Casale di Sant'Evasio. In the time of Charlemagne it came under the bishops of Vercelli, and Frederick Barbarossa freed it from their power. Troops from Vercelli, Alessandria and Milan sacked it in 1215, and it was rebuilt and fortified in 1220. It fell under the Marquess of Montferrat in 1292 and later became the capital of the marquessate. The Visconti of Milan held it from 1370 to 1404. The condottiere Facino Cane was born there.

In the 15th and early 16th centuries Casale was the capital of the House of Palaiologos, and in 1471 William VIII, Marquess of Montferrat, made it the permanent seat of his court. In 1536 it passed to the Gonzagas of Mantua, who fortified it strongly. It was besieged during the War of the Mantuan Succession. In 1745, after the Piedmontese defeat at the Battle of Bassignano, French and Spanish troops occupied it and damaged many buildings; the Baroque rebuilding that followed shaped the town's appearance. During the Wars of Italian Independence it resisted the Austrians in 1849 and was strengthened in 1852. Its Jewish ghetto lasted until the emancipation of the Jews in Piedmont after Charles Albert granted a constitution in 1848.

Limestone deposits in the nearby hills led to the opening of several cement factories in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, and Casale became known as the cement capital of Italy. An Eternit asbestos-cement factory operated there from 1907 to 1986, and some 1,800 deaths from mesothelioma and other asbestos-related diseases in the area have been linked to it.

The historic centre is built around Piazza Mazzini, the site of the Roman forum. Nearby are the Lombard Romanesque cathedral of Sant'Evasio, founded in 742 and consecrated in 1107, and the 11th-century Torre Civica. The castle of the Paleologi is a 15th-century hexagonal fortress with four round towers and a moat. The synagogue, built in 1595, is recognised as one of the most beautiful in Europe and its women's galleries hold a Jewish museum. Casale is also known for krumiri biscuits.
casamance: Casamance is the area of Senegal south of the Gambia, including the Casamance River. It consists of the Lower Casamance, which corresponds to Ziguinchor Region, and the Upper Casamance, made up of the Kolda and Sédhiou Regions. The region is low-lying and hot, with some hills to the southeast, and has a tropical savanna climate with more rain than the rest of Senegal. Most areas receive over 1,270 millimetres between June and October.

According to local legends, the Jola and Bainuk have inhabited the Casamance for over a thousand years. Jola leaders ruled portions of the region, frequently under the nominal rule of Wolof and Serer kingdoms to the north. From the 15th to the 18th century the Bainuk kingdom of Kasa, in the Lower Casamance, was the dominant state in the south. In the 15th century Portuguese slave traders and navigators set up a trading station and formed relations with local Jola chiefs and the king of Kasa. The name is most widely explained as coming from the Manding Kasa mansa, king of Kasa, which the Portuguese rendered Casamansa. A less common view derives it partly from Portuguese casa, house.

The region was subject to both French and Portuguese colonial efforts, until a border was negotiated in 1888 between the French colony of Senegal and Portuguese Guinea. Portugal lost the Casamance, then the commercial hub of its colony. The region has kept Casamance Creole, a variant of Upper Guinea Creole, and its Creole community carries Portuguese surnames such as Da Silva, Carvalho and Fonseca. Because the Jola, the dominant group in the Casamance, are only 4 per cent of Senegal's population, a sense of economic disenfranchisement contributed to the founding of the Movement of Democratic Forces of Casamance in 1982, which sought independence or autonomy. Its armed wing was established in 1985 and a low-level insurgency began in 1990.

The Casamance is mainly inhabited by the Fulani, Jola and Bainuk, with significant Balanta and Mande minorities. Its people practise Islam, Christianity and traditional African religions. The largest city is Ziguinchor, and the economy relies largely on rice farming and on tourism, which benefits from the beaches of the coast, particularly at Cap Skirring.
casbah-of-algiers: The Casbah lies at the centre of Algiers and forms its historic core, on a slope with a height difference of 118 metres facing the Mediterranean. It has a triangular shape with its base on the Bay of Algiers, so that from the sea it appears as a pyramid or triangular amphitheatre. Its narrow, winding streets, some ending in dead ends or vaulted passages called sabat, are closed to cars, and donkeys have been used for rubbish collection since the Regency. The name comes from the citadel above, the Arabic al-qaṣabah, and originally meant the highest point of the old city before it came to mean the whole medina.

A Phoenician port called Ikosim was probably founded at Algiers after the late 6th century BCE, and it later became a Roman city, Icosium. The medina itself was built in the 10th century by Bologhin Ibn Ziri of the Zirid dynasty on the ruins of the Roman city, in the territory of the Berber Beni Mezghenna. The name Al-Djaza'ir, the Islets, probably refers to the islands that once faced the port.

In 1529 the Barbarossa brothers expelled the Spanish from the Peñón islet, and Aruj Barbarossa joined it to the mainland to make a port, turning Algiers into the main base for corsairs in the western Mediterranean and capital of its regency. Charles V's expedition failed in 1541, and the city was then enclosed with a wall and gates such as Bab Azoun and Bab El Oued. The citadel was begun in 1597 and became the seat of the dey's power in 1817.

The French entered Algiers on 5 July 1830. They demolished much of the lower Casbah, built what is now Place des Martyrs and pulled down the walls. In 1956 leaders of the FLN, among them Abane Ramdane, Larbi Ben M'hidi and Krim Belkacem, settled in the Casbah, which offered hideouts, couriers and clandestinity for urban guerrilla warfare. After independence many native families moved to European-style apartments elsewhere.

The Casbah has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1992. Its houses, typically 30 to 60 square metres and presenting a single façade, are grouped close together, a pattern thought to date from the Zirid era. Its palaces include Dar Aziza and Dar Hassan Pacha, and its mosques include Jamaa Ketchaoua, Jamaa el Kebir and Jamaa el Jdid. The Thaâlibiyya Madrasa of 1904 is in the neo-Moorish style. Many films were shot there, among them Pépé le Moko (1937) and Gillo Pontecorvo's The Battle of Algiers (1969).
casilinum: Casilinum stood some 3 miles north-west of ancient Capua, where the Via Appia and the Via Latina met and crossed the river Volturnus by a three-arched bridge that still exists. The town lay where the modern city of Capua now stands, while ancient Capua occupied the site of present-day Santa Maria Capua Vetere. Its place at this junction of roads gave it considerable strategic importance during the Roman Republic.

The original pre-Roman town, doubtless dependent on neighbouring Capua, stood entirely on the left, or south, bank of the river, which surrounded it on three sides. The Roman town spread to the right bank as well. Its remains have been found some 25 feet below the present ground level, as the bed of the river has since risen considerably.

During the Second Punic War, Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus first occupied Casilinum in 217 BCE. Troops from Praeneste and Perusia then defended it against Hannibal, who took it in the winter of 216-215 BCE after a stubborn resistance. Roman forces recaptured it the following year, and the town afterwards served the Romans as a base of operations against Capua, which had rebelled.

Casilinum later lost its independence and became a praefectura. Julius Caesar founded a colony there in 59 BCE, which Mark Antony renewed in 44 BCE, and the veterans settled in the town took the side of Octavian after Caesar's death. The town appears to have been united with Capua some time before the reign of Vespasian: Pliny does not list it among the independent communities and describes it as falling into decay. Only its position at the meeting of major roads seems to have saved it from insignificance. When it finally declined or was destroyed is uncertain, but by the 9th century no town stood on the spot.
casimir-i-of-kuyavia: Casimir was the second son of Konrad I of Masovia and his wife Agafia of Rus, and was probably named after his grandfather, Casimir II the Just. His father gave him Kujawy, without Dobrzyń, in 1233. In 1239 he gained the castellany of Ląd as the dowry of his second wife, Constance, a daughter of Henry II the Pious, and in 1242, in support of his father's turbulent politics, he conquered the district of Wyszogród from the rulers of Gdańsk.

When Konrad I died on 31 August 1247, most of Masovia passed by his will to Bolesław I and Sieradz-Łęczyca to the youngest son, Siemowit I. Dissatisfied, Casimir attacked his brothers' lands while they were at their father's funeral in Płock and took Siemowit's inheritance; when Bolesław died unexpectedly and without issue early in 1248, Casimir used the confusion to capture Dobrzyń. In the 1250s he worked for the conversion of the Yotvingian tribes and for peace with them, but the Teutonic Order, which had the Pope on its side, opposed him, and relations with the Order were normalised only in 1263.

Ląd brought a long conflict with Greater Poland. In 1258 Bolesław the Pious, allied with Wartislaw III, Duke of Pomerania, attacked Kujawy to recover it. In 1259 a stronger coalition with Bolesław V the Chaste, Siemowit I and Daniel of Galicia forced Casimir to surrender on 29 November and promise to cede the castellany. He refused, and after a further attack in 1261 and the demands of his eldest son, Leszek II the Black, he gave up Ląd and granted Sieradz to Leszek as a separate district.

Casimir died on 14 December 1267 and was buried in the Cathedral of Włocławek. His first marriage, to Hedwig, probably a daughter of Władysław Odonic, was childless. Constance bore him Leszek II the Black and Ziemomysł. His third wife, Euphrosyne, daughter of Casimir I of Opole, whom he married in 1257, bore Władysław I the Elbow-high, King of Poland from 1320 to 1333, Casimir II, killed in battle against the Lithuanians in 1294, Siemowit, and Euphemia, who married Yuri I of Galicia.
casimir-i-of-opole: Casimir was the eldest child and only son of Duke Mieszko Tanglefoot of Racibórz and his wife Ludmilla, probably a Bohemian princess of the Přemyslid dynasty. His birth was the occasion of an agreement with Casimir II the Just, High Duke of Poland, who wished to break Mieszko's alliance with Mieszko III the Old: he gave Mieszko the Lesser Polish districts of Bytom, Oświęcim and Pszczyna and stood godfather to the boy, who was named after him. After the death of his brother Bolesław I the Tall in 1201, Mieszko conquered the Duchy of Opole.

Casimir succeeded his father in 1211. He first joined the coalition of the junior dukes Leszek the White, Konrad I of Masovia and Władysław Odonic against Władysław III Spindleshanks and Henry the Bearded, working closely with the church and with Bishop Wawrzyniec of Wrocław. At the Congress of Wolbórz in 1215 he granted the church great privileges and immunity, the origin of the semi-independent district of Ujazd. As Henry grew stronger in the 1220s, Casimir allied with his cousin; his troops joined Henry's failed expedition against Kraków in 1225, and in 1227 he annexed the frontier fortress of Czeladź.

Following Henry's example, he encouraged German settlers. Towns were founded under German town law at Leśnica in 1217, in the bishops' lands of Ujazd in 1222, at Biała and Gościęcin in 1225 and at Olesno in 1226. Settlement helped the duchy's economy, though less than in Lower Silesia. Emigrants from Lesser Poland also served him, among them Klement of Brzeźnica of the Gryfici family, who paid part of the cost of the city walls of Opole.

Casimir died suddenly on 13 May 1230 and was buried at Czarnowąsy, a monastery he had generously patronised. He married late, probably between 1212 and 1220; the origins of his wife Viola are unknown, though the chronicler Jan Długosz said she came from Bulgaria. Their children were Mieszko II the Fat and Władysław, both dukes of Opole-Racibórz, Wenzeslawa, a nun at Czarnowąsy, and Euphrosyne, who married Casimir I of Kuyavia and later Mestwin II of Pomerania. Henry the Bearded became regent for the young sons.
casimir-ii-of-leczyca: Casimir was the fourth son of Casimir I of Kuyavia, the second from his third marriage, to Euphrosyne, daughter of Casimir I of Opole; he was probably named after both his father and his maternal grandfather. On his father's death in 1267 he and his full brothers inherited their share of the lands under the regency of their mother until 1275, when they began to rule jointly. He was Duke of Brześć Kujawski from 1267 and of Dobrzyń from 1275.

In 1288 the death of his childless half-brother Leszek II the Black brought him the Duchy of Łęczyca in the centre of Poland. The next year he and his brother Władysław I the Elbow-high backed Bolesław II of Płock's bid for the throne of Kraków, and on 26 February 1289 their forces defeated Silesian troops under Henry III of Głogów, Bolko I of Opole and Przemko of Ścinawa at the Battle of Siewierz. When Bolesław dropped his claim, Władysław tried to win Lesser Poland for himself, with Casimir's close help, in a war against King Wenceslaus II of Bohemia.

The policy failed in the autumn of 1292, when a Bohemian expedition captured both brothers, and under the peace of 9 October that year they had to pay homage to Wenceslaus. They did not give up. On 6 January 1293 they met Przemysł II of Greater Poland and Jakub Świnka, Archbishop of Gniezno, at Kalisz and made a secret agreement for the recovery of Kraków, pledging 300 pieces of fine silver a year from the salt mines once the city was taken.

On 4 June 1294 a Lithuanian force under Vytenis attacked Łęczyca. According to the chronicler Jan Długosz it numbered 1,800 Lithuanians, Prussians and Samogitians, plundered the collegiate church and carried off many people. Casimir pursued the raiders with his knights and was killed in the fighting on the bank of the Bzura river on 10 June; Długosz writes that the Polish knights then fled in all directions and many drowned in the river. He died unmarried and childless, and Władysław I inherited his duchy. His burial place is unknown, but he was probably buried in the collegiate church of St. Mary and St. Alexius at Tum near Łęczyca.
casimir-ii-the-just: Casimir was the sixth, but fourth surviving, son of Bolesław III Wrymouth and his second wife Salomea, daughter of Count Henry of Berg. He was born on 28 October 1138, after his father's death but on the same day, so the will did not mention him and he was left without land. He lived with his mother at Łęczyca and, after her death in 1144, was cared for by his brother Bolesław IV the Curly. When he came of age in 1151 he still received nothing.

In 1157, after the campaign of Emperor Frederick Barbarossa, Casimir was sent to Germany as a hostage for his brother's loyalty. His fate at the imperial court is unknown, and he was back in Poland by 21 May 1161.

When his brother Henry was killed on a Prussian crusade without issue, his will named Casimir heir to the Duchy of Sandomierz. Bolesław IV divided the duchy and gave Casimir only the district of Wiślica. Casimir rebelled with the support of Mieszko III, Archbishop Jan of Gniezno, Bishop Gedko of Kraków and most of Lesser Poland, but the rising was quickly stopped. When Bolesław died in 1173, Mieszko III became High Duke and gave the whole of Sandomierz to Casimir.

Mieszko's dictatorial rule caused deep disaffection, and in 1177 the nobles, Bishop Gedko, Mieszko's son Odon and Casimir rose against him. Mieszko was defeated and forced to flee. After helping Bolesław the Tall in Silesia, Casimir took Kraków and became High Duke. To secure hereditary succession for his line, he called an assembly of nobles at Łęczyca in 1180 and granted privileges to the nobility and the Church, lifting a tax on the clergy's profits and giving up his rights over the lands of dead bishops.

In 1186 the sickly Duke Leszek of Masovia left Casimir all his lands, though Mieszko occupied Kuyavia. In 1191, while Casimir was involved in the affairs of Rus', Mieszko seized Wawel Castle at Kraków, but Casimir regained the capital without a fight on his return.

Early in 1194 Casimir led an expedition against the Baltic Yotvingians, which ended in success. He died unexpectedly on 5 May 1194, after a banquet to celebrate his return, and some historians believed he had been poisoned. He was probably buried at Wawel Cathedral and was succeeded by his son Leszek I the White. He was generous to Cistercian monasteries such as Wąchock and Jędrzejów. The title the Just was not contemporary and first appeared in the 16th century.
casimir-iii-the-great: Casimir was born on 30 April 1310 in Kowal in Kuyavia, the third son of Władysław I Łokietek and Jadwiga of Kalisz. His father was crowned king in Kraków on 20 January 1320, and in 1325 Casimir married Aldona of Lithuania, daughter of Grand Duke Gediminas, an alliance sought against the Teutonic Order. The war against Bohemia, Brandenburg and the Teutonic Order went badly for Poland, and when his father died on 2 March 1333 Casimir inherited a small, weakened realm of two ravaged provinces, Lesser Poland and Greater Poland.

Casimir was crowned at Wawel Cathedral on 25 April 1333. John of Bohemia was still widely regarded as the rightful king of Poland, and Casimir's main strength was his alliance with Hungary. An arbitration at Visegrád in November 1335 returned Dobrzyń Land and Kuyavia to Poland, while Casimir renounced Pomerania and the Chełmno Land to the Teutonic Order. He accepted the loss of Silesia to Bohemia and turned east, conquering Galicia-Volhynia, known as Red Ruthenia, which roughly doubled the kingdom and opened access to Black Sea trade.

At the Sejm in Wiślica on 11 March 1347 he sanctioned civil and criminal codes for Greater and Lesser Poland, which earned him the title the Polish Justinian. About thirty towns received walls and some fifty castles were built, and towns grew under Magdeburg rights. In 1364, with the permission of Pope Urban V, he founded the University of Kraków. On 9 October 1334 he confirmed the privileges granted to Jews in 1264 and allowed them to settle in large numbers.

Casimir left no legitimate son. In 1355, at Buda, he named his nephew Louis I of Hungary as heir should he have no male child. After Casimir died in 1370, Louis travelled quickly to Kraków, had a will that adopted another heir set aside by bribing the nobles with future privileges, and was proclaimed king. Casimir was the last Piast king of Poland.
casimir-iv-jagiellon: Casimir was the third and youngest son of King Władysław II Jagiełło and his fourth wife, Sophia of Halshany, who was 40 to 50 years younger than her husband. This prompted rumours of adultery, and after Casimir's birth Sophia swore an oath of innocence and the charges were dismissed. Many of the children closely resembled their elderly father. Casimir was baptised on 21 December 1427.

In 1440, after the assassination of Sigismund Kęstutaitis, Lithuanian magnates led by Jonas Goštautas invited the thirteen-year-old Casimir to Vilnius, and the Council of Lords proclaimed him Grand Duke of Lithuania on 29 June 1440, contrary to the wishes of Polish nobles. In his reign the rights of the Lithuanian nobility were put on an equal footing with those of the Polish szlachta.

Władysław III died at Varna in 1444, and after a three-year interregnum Casimir was elected King of Poland and crowned on 25 June 1447. In 1454 the Prussian Confederation asked his help against the Teutonic Order, and the Thirteen Years' War began. The Polish army crushed the Teutonic force at Świecino in September 1462, and the Order's fleet was sunk at the Vistula Lagoon a year later. In the Second Peace of Thorn in 1466 the Order recognised Polish sovereignty over Royal Prussia and overlordship over the rest of its state.

In 1454 Casimir married Elizabeth of Austria, which tied the house of Jagiellon to Hungary and Bohemia. His son Vladislaus II was crowned King of Hungary in 1490, having been King of Bohemia. Casimir's Code of 1468, the Grand Duchy's first unified code of criminal and procedural law, was written in Ruthenian.

Casimir died on 7 June 1492 and was buried in the Holy Cross Chapel of Wawel Cathedral, in a red marble tomb by Veit Stoss. John I Albert succeeded him as King of Poland and Alexander became Grand Duke of Lithuania. His children included Vladislaus II, three kings of Poland and Saint Casimir, who chose religious life. Under Casimir the Jagiellonian dynasty became one of the leading royal houses of Europe.
caslav-klonimirovic: Časlav belonged to an exiled branch of the Serbian dynasty of the Vlastimirović and was brought up in Bulgaria as a political hostage. His grandfather Strojimir and Strojimir's brother Gojnik had been expelled to Bulgaria by their brother Mutimir. His father Klonimir, born about 850, married a Bulgarian noblewoman, a match initiated by the Bulgar khan Boris. Časlav was born before 889, probably at the Bulgarian capital Pliska, and his father tried to take the Serbian throne from Petar Gojniković but was killed in 897. The Byzantine emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus recorded the history of the Serbian principalities in De Administrando Imperio, composed between 948 and 952.

In 925 or 926 the Bulgarian ruler Simeon sent a large army against the Serbian ruler Zaharija, who fled to Croatia. Časlav was with it, and the Bulgars called the Serbian župani, or counts, to accept him as ruler, then captured them and Časlav and imprisoned them in Bulgaria. Serbia was devastated and came under nominal Bulgarian rule.

Simeon died on 27 May 927, and Časlav escaped with four followers and took the Serbian throne without the Bulgarian ruler's consent. The Byzantine emperor Romanos Lekapenos helped him and moved Serbian refugees to Serbia. Časlav swore loyalty to Romanos and was recognised as archon of Serbia, taking precedence among the Serbian principalities. According to the De Administrando Imperio, he organised and settled the country. His accession is most recently dated to 927 or 928.

The Magyars raided Byzantine territory in 933 and 943, and Časlav may have defended the lands south of the Sava and Danube as a Byzantine ally. His death is dated to 943 or 944, or to an unknown time, as the Byzantine sources that mention him were recorded before Romanos was ousted in December 944.

A later account based on folklore, the Chronicle of the Priest of Duklja, says that the Magyar chieftain Kys raided Bosnia and was killed by Časlav's men, and that Časlav was then captured in Syrmia and thrown bound into the Sava river. The chronicle is considered unreliable for the early Middle Ages, though its personal names tend to be true. After the De Administrando Imperio, Serbia as a political entity disappears from Byzantine sources until the mid-eleventh century, and it seems to have broken up through infighting among the nobility.
caspar-david-friedrich: Friedrich was the sixth of ten children, raised in the strict Lutheran creed of his father Adolf Gottlieb Friedrich, a candle-maker and soap boiler. Records of the family's finances are contradictory; some sources say the children were privately tutored, others that they lived in relative poverty. He knew death early: his mother Sophie died in 1781, a sister a year later, and another sister in 1791. In 1787 he witnessed his younger brother Johann Christoffer, aged thirteen, fall through the ice of a frozen lake and drown.

He studied in Copenhagen from 1794 to 1798, then settled permanently in Dresden. There he made etchings and designs for woodcuts, but he worked mainly in ink, watercolour and sepia, and did not work extensively in oils until his reputation was more established.

His landscapes, mostly of northern Germany, were inspired by trips from 1801 to the Baltic coast, Bohemia, the Krkonoše and the Harz Mountains. He made pencil studies of places such as the cliffs on Rügen and the Elbe, but rendered the atmospheric effects of mist, sun and moon from memory. His key innovation was to treat landscape not as a backdrop subordinated to human drama but as a self-contained emotive subject. He often used the Rückenfigur, a person seen from behind, to draw the viewer into sharing the contemplation of nature.

Resentment of the French occupation of Pomerania in 1813 led him to put motifs from German folklore in his work. In Old Heroes' Graves (1812) and Fir Forest with the French Dragoon and the Raven (c. 1813) he conveyed political symbols by means of the landscape alone, a first in the history of art. He suffered depressive episodes, and after 1826 vultures, owls, graveyards and ruins became permanent motifs, while his colours grew darker.

Friedrich married Caroline Bommer on 21 January 1818, and found patrons in Russia: Grand Duke Nikolai Pavlovich visited his studio in 1820, and the poet Vasily Zhukovsky helped him for decades. His reputation nevertheless fell over his last fifteen years, and he lived as a recluse in relative poverty. A first stroke in June 1835 greatly reduced his ability to paint. He died in Dresden on 7 May 1840, little noticed by the artistic community.

A Berlin exhibition of thirty-two of his works in 1906 began a renewed appreciation. He influenced Expressionist artists and the Surrealists, among them Max Ernst. The Nazis used his work to promote their ideology in the 1930s, and the association damaged his reputation for decades. Scholars later placed him in a purely art-historical context, and since the 1970s he has been regarded as one of the most important artists of German Romanticism.
caspe: Caspe lies 104 kilometres south-east of Zaragoza on the banks of the Guadalope river, a few kilometres from the Ebro, in one of the most arid areas of Aragon. A popular belief derives the name from ancient inhabitants from the Caspian Sea, but this lacks philological support. The name appears in Andalusi sources as Qsp, Qasp or Qasb, and may be related to an Arabic word or to an Indo-European root meaning oak.

The area was among the last of Lower Aragon to be settled, although a biface of 150,000 to 100,000 years ago shows the passage of Neanderthal hunter-gatherers. Towns and tumular necropolises of the Celtic Hallstatt culture appeared around the 8th century BCE. From 713 to the Christian reconquest in the first half of the 12th century the lands of the Ebro formed the northernmost mark of Al-Andalus. King Alfonso II of Aragon took Caspe between June and September 1169, in a campaign led by Arnau Mir de Tost, Count of Pallars. Until 1610 Christian and Muslim communities lived in the town, each with its own municipal area.

Because of its position Caspe suffered in many of Spain's conflicts from the 17th century. In the War of the Spanish Succession it supported the Bourbon cause while its neighbours chose the Austrian claimant. French troops occupied it from June 1809 to 1813, and the local lawyer Agustín de Quinto, who collaborated with them, was named commissar of the left bank of the Ebro, which made Caspe capital of the lower half of Aragon. In June 1813 Colonel Ramón Gayán retook it after a siege of fifteen days, using tunnels to blow up part of the castle where the French were barricaded.

The Statute of Autonomy of Aragon of 1936, also called the Statute of Caspe, was drafted in the town. During the Spanish Civil War it was the seat of the anarchist Regional Defense Council of Aragon, which a military intervention dissolved in August 1937, when the 11th Division under Enrique Líster arrested its president, Joaquín Ascaso.

Caspe is the seat of the comarca of Bajo Aragón-Caspe, and its municipality of 503 square kilometres is the fourth largest in Aragon. Its heritage includes the Plano del Pulido cave paintings, declared a World Heritage Site in 1998, the Roman Miralpeix Mausoleum and the remains of the Castle of the Commitment, built by the knights of the Hospital Order.
caspian-flotilla: Russia's presence on the Caspian Sea goes back to the reign of Alexei Mikhailovich (1645-1676), who sought to expand trade with Persia and protect the trade routes along the Volga. The flotilla itself was formally created in November 1722 in Astrakhan by order of Peter the Great, under Admiral Fyodor Apraksin, and took part in Peter's Persian campaign of 1722-1723, though most of the gains of that conflict were later lost. It is the oldest flotilla in the Russian Navy not operating in a body of water connected to the open ocean.

In the reign of Catherine the Great a Russian naval presence was re-established, and it helped the army to take Derbent and Baku in the Persian Expedition of 1796. By the Treaty of Gulistan of 1813, which ended the Russo-Persian War of 1804-1813, the flotilla remained the only naval flotilla on the Caspian. Baku, an ice-free port, became its main base in 1867. By the early 20th century it had only two gunboats and a few armed steamers.

In 1918 the Soviets formed a flotilla at Astrakhan to help the Red Army, but its ships were captured in August by the Centrocaspian Dictatorship and regained after the overthrow of the Musavat government.

The British Royal Navy supported the White forces on the Caspian, and by May 1919, after a victory at the Battle of Alexandrovsky Fort, it had driven the Bolsheviks from the sea and up the Volga. Once the Civil War ended the Red forces regained full control.

The Soviets established the Caspian Fleet on 1 May 1920 and renamed it the Caspian Flotilla on 27 June 1931. The Stalin purges of the 1930s hit its officers, among them a former commander, Grigory Kireyev. In the Great Patriotic War of 1941-1945 it secured shipping for army units and equipment, especially during the Battle of Stalingrad and the battle for the Caucasus, and in 1945 it received the Order of the Red Banner.

After the dissolution of the Soviet Union the flotilla shrank. Russia, Azerbaijan, Turkmenistan and Kazakhstan agreed at Baku on 16 April 1992 to divide its 50 small and medium-size vessels, bases and a navy school. Azerbaijan first claimed 75 percent of them but settled for less, and the Kazakh contingent became the basis of Kazakhstan's naval service. The Russian Federation inherited most of the ships, and the headquarters, in Baku from 1867 until 1991, are now at Astrakhan. On 7 October 2015 Russia's defence minister announced that four warships of the flotilla had fired 26 cruise missiles at positions in Syria.
caspian-sea: The Caspian Sea is an endorheic basin lying east of the Caucasus, west of the steppe of Central Asia, south of the plains of Southern Russia and north of the Iranian Plateau. It covers 371,000 square kilometres, stretches 1,200 kilometres from north to south with an average width of 320 kilometres, and lies about 27 metres below sea level. Its salinity is about a third of that of average seawater. The Volga, Europe's longest river, is its main freshwater inflow, entering at the shallow north end.

Like the Black Sea, it is a remnant of the ancient Paratethys Sea, and it became landlocked in the Late Miocene, about 5.5 million years ago, through tectonic uplift and a fall in sea level. The Caspian seal is the only aquatic mammal endemic to it, and the sea is known for its caviar and oil industries.

The earliest hominid remains found around the Caspian are from Dmanisi, about 1.8 million years old, and finds in the Hotu and Kamarband caves in Iran suggest human habitation south of the sea as early as 11,000 years ago. The sea's name derives from the ancient Caspi people, who lived to its southwest. Strabo wrote that the territory called Caspiane was named after the Caspian tribe, as was the sea, but that the tribe had disappeared. Greeks and Persians in antiquity called it the Hyrcanian Sea.

Other names reflect later powers. Arabic writers called it the sea of the Khazars, and Turkish, Azerbaijani and Turkmen still call it the Khazar sea after the Khazar Khaganate, a large empire based north of the sea between the 7th and 10th centuries. Since the medieval period traders reached it by portages linking the Volga with the Don and with rivers flowing into the Baltic, and canals followed from the early 18th century. Its shores were bordered in turn by Safavid, Afsharid, Zand, Qajar and Pahlavi Iran, and by the Tsardom of Russia, the Russian Empire and the Soviet Union.

Five states border the sea along about 4,800 kilometres of coastline: Kazakhstan, Russia, Azerbaijan, Iran and Turkmenistan. A treaty of 1931 between Iran and the Soviet Union stated that the sea belonged to both. The five long debated the question of its legal status as a sea or a lake, because the answer decides access to oil and natural gas, fishing and international waters.
cassander: Cassander was a son of Antipater and a contemporary of Alexander the Great. He was taught by the philosopher Aristotle at the Lyceum in Macedonia and educated beside Alexander with Hephaestion, Ptolemy and Lysimachus. His family were distant collateral relatives of the Argead dynasty. At 25 he still sat upright at dinner, evidently not having killed a boar unaided, which has been taken to suggest ill health or disability.

He is first recorded at Alexander's court in Babylon in 323 BCE, sent by Antipater, most likely to uphold his father's regency, though a later hostile writer claimed he went to poison the king. He returned to Macedonia and helped his father govern, and from 321 to 320 BCE served as chiliarch to Antigonus, probably to watch him.

When Antipater neared death in 319 BCE he gave the regency to Polyperchon, not Cassander. Cassander rejected this, sought the support of Antigonus, Ptolemy and Lysimachus, destroyed Polyperchon's fleet, put Athens under Demetrius of Phaleron and declared himself regent in 317 BCE. He besieged Olympias in Pydna, and when the city fell in spring 316 BCE she was killed; Alexander IV and Roxana were confined at Amphipolis. Cassander married Alexander's half-sister Thessalonike and founded Thessalonica and Cassandreia, and rebuilt Thebes.

Alexander IV and Roxana were secretly poisoned in 310 or 309 BCE, and Cassander bribed Polyperchon to kill Heracles. He proclaimed himself king in 305 BCE. From 307 to 304 BCE he fought Athens, and Demetrius Poliorcetes drove him from central Greece. He then rebuilt the coalition with Lysimachus, Ptolemy and Seleucus against Antigonus, who was killed at the Battle of Ipsus in 301 BCE.

After Ipsus Cassander held Macedon undisputed, but he died of dropsy in 297 BCE. His dynasty did not last: his son Philip died of natural causes, and his sons Alexander and Antipater fought each other. Demetrius I ended it by killing Alexander V and founding the Antigonid dynasty.

Cassander stood out among the Diadochi in his hostility to Alexander's memory; Arrian reported that he could not pass a statue of Alexander without feeling faint. He is seen as ambitious and unscrupulous and was responsible for the deaths of more Argeads than other Diadochi, but John D. Grainger argues this owes much to stories spread by his rivals. His refounding of Therma as Thessalonica, named for his wife, was of lasting significance.
cassava: Cassava, Manihot esculenta, is a woody shrub of the spurge family, native to South America and grown for its starchy tuberous root. Its wild ancestor, a subspecies called flabellifolia, is centred in west-central Brazil, where cassava was likely first domesticated no more than 10,000 years ago. Cassava pollen appears in the Gulf of Mexico lowlands by 4600 BCE. The oldest direct evidence of cultivation comes from the 1,400-year-old Maya site of Joya de Cerén in El Salvador. By the time of European contact in 1492 it was a staple of peoples of northern South America, southern Mesoamerica and the Taino of the Caribbean, who grew it by a high-yielding form of shifting agriculture.

Cassava is grown in sweet and bitter varieties. Both contain cyanogenic glycosides, but the bitter ones hold far more, up to about 1,000 milligrams of cyanide per kilogram of fresh root against as little as 20 in sweet ones. Improper preparation can therefore cause poisoning. The Indigenous peoples of the Caribbean removed the poison by peeling, grinding and mashing the root, pressing the mash through a basket tube called a sebucan or tipiti, and drying and sieving it into flour. Cassava starch is called tapioca, and the Brazilian farofa and West African garri are coarse flours made by grating, pressing and roasting the root.

Cassava is the third-largest source of carbohydrates in the tropics, after rice and maize, and more than 500 million people depend on it. It tolerates drought and poor soil, and it yields more food energy per hectare each day than rice, wheat or maize. It has several uses besides food, including cassava beers such as the Brazilian cauim, animal feed and laundry starch. Haitian bambouri and Jamaican bammy combine Indigenous Caribbean cassava cooking with African practice, and the Tupí myth of Maní tells that manioc sprang from the grave of an Indigenous girl of that name. Viruses remain a serious threat, such as the African cassava mosaic virus, which caused a major famine in Africa in the 1920s.
cassiodorus: Magnus Aurelius Cassiodorus Senator was born at Scylletium, near present-day Catanzaro in Calabria, into a family of Syrian origin. Senator was part of his surname, not his rank. His family had served the state for generations: his great-grandfather held a command defending the coasts of southern Italy against Vandal sea-raiders, his grandfather appears in a Roman embassy to Attila the Hun, and his father of the same name served Odovacer and then Theoderic the Great, finally as Praetorian Prefect. Cassiodorus began his career about his twentieth year as his father's consiliarius, a legal adviser in complex cases.

He was quaestor sacri palatii from about 507 to 511, consul in 514 and later magister officiorum under Theoderic and under the regency for Theoderic's young successor Athalaric. At Ravenna his rhetorical skill led to his drafting important public documents. He rose to praetorian prefect for Italy, effectively the head of the Ostrogothic civil government. James O'Donnell considers it almost indisputable that in 523 he accepted advancement as the immediate successor of Boethius, who was imprisoned and later executed, and notes that Cassiodorus's letters never mention it.

Athalaric died in early 534, and the rest of Cassiodorus's public career was dominated by the Byzantine reconquest and Ostrogothic dynastic intrigue. His last letters were drafted in the name of Vitiges. Around 537–38 he left Italy for Constantinople, where he stayed for almost two decades, concentrating on religious questions. He had earlier worked with Pope Agapetus I on a plan for a library of Greek and Latin texts to support a Christian school in Rome. In retirement he founded the monastery of Vivarium on his family estates on the shore of the Ionian Sea.

His writings include the Chronica, ending at 519, a Gothic History of 526 to 533 known only through the abridgment by Jordanes, the Variae epistolae, Theoderic's state papers, and an Exposition of the Psalms. The Institutiones divinarum et saecularium litterarum, written between 543 and 555, guided the monks' studies in place of the school he had planned in Rome. Its first book treats Christian texts and its second the liberal arts, which he valued mainly as aids to the study of divinity. His last known work, De orthographia of about 580, was completed when he was 93.

Vivarium had a communal monastery and a retreat for hermits, apparently without a strict rule. Cassiodorus had a complete Bible in a single volume, the Codex Grandior, made for his monks. Ceolfrith bought it in 679–80 and took it to Wearmouth Jarrow, where it served as the model for the Codex Amiatinus. The library was later dispersed, but his promotion of regular manuscript copying in monasteries helped preserve classical and Christian literature.
cassius-dio: Lucius Cassius Dio was the son of Cassius Apronianus, a Roman senator of the Cassia gens who was born and raised at Nicaea in Bithynia. Byzantine tradition holds that his mother was the daughter or sister of the Greek orator and philosopher Dio Chrysostom, though this has been disputed. Although Dio was a Roman citizen he wrote in Greek. He kept a love for Nicaea, which he called my home, while he described his villa at Capua as the place where he spent his time whenever he was in Italy.

For most of his life Dio served the state. He was a senator under Commodus and became a suffect consul in about 205. After the death of Septimius Severus he was governor of Smyrna, and he was also proconsul in Africa and in Pannonia. Severus Alexander held him in the highest esteem and made him consul a second time in 229. In his later years Dio went back to Bithynia, where he died. He was either the grandfather or the great-grandfather of another Cassius Dio, consul in 291.

Dio's Roman History, written in Greek in 80 books, began with the arrival of Aeneas in Italy and the founding of Rome by his descendant Romulus, and ran through the Republic and Empire to 229 CE. By his own account he spent ten years collecting the achievements of the Romans down to the death of Severus in 211, and twelve more composing the work. Until the first century BCE he gives only a summary of events; after that his accounts become more detailed. It is one of only three written Roman sources for the revolt of Boudica in 60 to 61 CE.

The work survives unevenly. The first 21 books are partly reconstructed from fragments and from the 12th-century epitome of Joannes Zonaras, and books 22 to 35 were already lost by his time. Books 36 to 54, covering 65 to 12 BCE, are nearly complete, as are books 56 to 60, from 9 to 54 CE. For the last twenty books only fragments and the abridgement by the 11th-century monk John Xiphilinus remain. Dio has often been dismissed as unreliable, but some recent scholars have stressed the sophistication of his political and historical interpretation.
cassivellaunus: Cassivellaunus is known from Julius Caesar's Commentarii de Bello Gallico, where he is given command of the combined British forces opposing Caesar's second invasion of Britain. His name, Cassiuellaunos in Common Brittonic, comes from a word uellaunos meaning chief or commander. The meaning of the prefix cassi- is debated, but it possibly signifies tin or bronze.

Caesar does not name Cassivellaunus's tribe, but his territory north of the Thames corresponds to that inhabited by the Catuvellauni at the time of the later invasion under Claudius. According to Caesar, he had been in near-constant conflict with his neighbours and had recently brought down the king of the Trinovantes, the most powerful tribe in Britain. The king's son, Mandubracius, fled to Caesar in Gaul.

Cassivellaunus harried the Romans to prevent them from foraging, but Caesar advanced to the Thames. The only fordable point was defended and fortified with sharp stakes, yet the Romans crossed it. Cassivellaunus dismissed most of his army and relied on his knowledge of the land and the speed of his chariots. Five British tribes, the Cenimagni, Segontiaci, Ancalites, Bibroci and Cassi, surrendered to Caesar and revealed the location of his stronghold, which Caesar besieged.

Cassivellaunus sent word to the four kings of Kent to attack the Roman camp on the coast, but the Romans defended it successfully. On hearing of the defeat and the devastation of his territory he surrendered, on terms mediated by Caesar's Gallic ally Commius. Hostages were given, a tribute was agreed, and Mandubracius was restored as king of the Trinovantes. Caesar returned to Gaul, and the Roman legions did not return to Britain for another 97 years.

Cassivellaunus appears in Geoffrey of Monmouth's 12th-century Historia Regum Britanniae as Cassibelanus, a king of Britain who twice repels Caesar before his nephew's death in a quarrel leads to a rift with Androgeus, who allies with Caesar. In Welsh literature he is Caswallawn, son of Beli Mawr. In the Second Branch of the Mabinogi he is a usurper who seizes the throne while Bran the Blessed is at war in Ireland, using a cloak that makes him invisible.

Many Welsh Triads mention Caswallawn, some drawing on a tradition not found in Roman or surviving medieval sources. The scholar Rachel Bromwich suggests that these fragments relate to a narrative of him that has been lost.
casta: Casta is an Iberian word, found in Spanish, Portuguese and other Iberian languages since the Middle Ages; it is first recorded in Spanish in 1417, and the Portuguese casta gave English the word caste in the early modern period. Its colonial use grew out of limpieza de sangre, purity of blood, an idea that developed in Spain after the reconquest of Al-Andalus and spread through the Spanish Inquisition, holding that new converts to Christianity were prone to heresy and prompting genealogical inquiries to exclude families that had not been Christian.

The Inquisition checked the Old Christian standing of its officials in the Americas, and by the end of the 1500s some records listed categories such as black and mulatto, and sometimes mestizo and indio. From the late 16th century some inquiries into ancestry treated any link with black Africans, and sometimes with Indians, as a stain.

The categories described a person's calidad, or quality, which combined legal status as a tributary liable to a head tax with culture and race. Placement was flexible: people could pass as another group to hold offices reserved for whites, or change labels to match a spouse's. In 1617 Christóbal de Toro was described as a mulato although white, showing that the term could mark calidad rather than appearance.

The crown divided the population into the República de Indios and the República de Españoles, the latter taking in Spaniards, black people and the mixed castas. From the late 16th century royal decrees sought to keep black and Indian people apart; black people were forbidden to live with Indians in Peru in 1580, in Chile in 1586 and in Lima in 1587, though repeated orders suggest the decrees often failed. Laws from 1577 eased the collection of taxes from the castas and barred black and mulatto people from carrying weapons.

During the Mexican War of Independence José María Morelos called for ending the formal distinctions between racial groups, calling them one and all Americans, and casta designations were abolished at independence in 1821. The idea of a colonial caste system was developed in the 1940s by Ángel Rosenblat and Gonzalo Aguirre Beltrán; later studies by Pilar Gonzalbo, Joanne Rappaport, Berta Ares and Ben Vinson have challenged it.
caste: A caste is a fixed social group into which an individual is born within a system of social stratification. Members are expected to marry only within the same caste, to follow lifestyles often linked to a particular occupation, and to hold a ritual status within a hierarchy. Interaction between castes follows cultural notions of exclusion, with some castes considered more pure and others more polluted. The standard ethnographic example is the division of India's Hindu society into rigid groups, whose roots lie in South Asia's ancient history. Scholars have used it as a model for studying caste-like divisions elsewhere.

The English word comes from the Spanish and Portuguese casta, which a Spanish dictionary of 1569 defined as race, lineage, tribe or breed, and which derives from a Gothic word for a group of animals. The Portuguese, the first Europeans to reach India by sea in 1498, were the first to use casta in its modern sense, applying it to the thousands of endogamous, hereditary Indian groups they met. The spelling caste with this meaning is first attested in English in 1613.

In India the system rests on an old four-fold theoretical classification called varna, Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya and Shudra, laid over the social groups called jāti. One 2016 genetic study concluded that endogamous jatis originated during the Gupta Empire. From 1901 British census authorities sorted all jatis into the four varna categories. Today there are around 3,000 castes and 25,000 sub-castes in India.

Writers have reported caste systems in many regions. In Nigeria the osu caste among the Igbo is determined by birth and brings ostracism. In Rwanda and Burundi the Maquet study of 1961 described the Tutsi, Hutu and Twa as ranked by birth. The Songhai economy was based on a caste system, with metalworkers, fishermen and carpenters among the most common groups. In Bali, ethnographers described three or four castes modelled on the Indian pattern. For centuries the Cagots of the Pyrenees and the Basque provinces were treated as an inferior caste and obliged to use separate church doors.

In colonial Spanish America, mixed-race groups were called castas, but the social order was otherwise fluid, and scholars dispute how far the Latin American and South Asian systems can be compared. The term is also used in biology for groups of ants and bees, which early observers named after the Indian system. Some scholars, such as Heidi Fjeld for pre-1950s Tibet, argue that other societies were functionally caste systems, while others reject the label.
caste-war-of-yucatan: After independence in 1821, Yucatán's congress passed laws that eased the spread of henequen and sugar plantations onto Maya communal lands, and by the 1840s many Maya peasants had become indebted labourers on haciendas. Rebel leaders also named oppressive taxation: Jacinto Pat wrote in 1848 that they wanted liberty and not oppression. In 1839 Santiago Imán armed Maya against the central government, promising land free of tribute, and in the struggles between Mexico, Miguel Barbachano's faction at Mérida and Santiago Méndez's at Campeche, many Maya served as soldiers and kept their arms.

In June 1847 Méndez executed the Maya leader Manuel Antonio Ay at Valladolid and burned Tepich. Cecilio Chi and Jacinto Pat attacked Tepich on 30 July 1847, and Chi ordered all non-Maya killed in reprisal for the massacres of Maya. The siege of Mérida broke, according to some historians because the Maya went home to plant their crops, according to others because their supplies ran out. Yucatán rejoined Mexico on 17 August 1848, and with Mexican guns, money and troops pushed the Maya back from more than half the state.

From 1850 the Talking Cross, believed to be God's voice, urged the war on, and Chan Santa Cruz became the centre of resistance; the United Kingdom recognised it as de facto independent because of its trade with British Honduras. The Yucatán government sold Maya prisoners into slavery in Cuba. Other Maya groups, the Ixcanha and the Icaiche under Marcus Canul, followed their own paths; Canul routed British troops at San Pedro Yalbac on 21 December 1866. A treaty of 1893 between the United Kingdom and Mexico closed British Honduras to the rebels' trade in guns and gunpowder.

In 1901 General Ignacio Bravo occupied Chan Santa Cruz and on 5 May telegraphed that the war was over, the date most often given for its end. Smaller fighting continued, and measles and smallpox carried by his troops cut the Cruzob's numbers. Governor Salvador Alvarado, sent in 1915, introduced reforms that eased the grievances behind the war, and a last skirmish at the village of Dzula in April 1933 killed five Maya and two soldiers. An estimated 40,000–50,000 people died in the hostilities. In 2021 the governments of Mexico and Guatemala apologised to the Maya people.
castel-nuovo: Castel Nuovo, often called the Maschio Angioino, stands in front of Piazza Municipio and the city hall in central Naples. Charles I of Anjou, moved the capital from Palermo to Naples and wanted a new castle near the sea, because the Norman Castel Capuano was judged inadequate as a royal residence. The French architect Pierre de Chaulnes designed it, and building began in 1279 and took only three years. The king never lived there. After the War of the Sicilian Vespers cost the House of Anjou the crown of Sicily, the new palace stood unused until the death of Charles I in 1285.

Charles II moved in with his court and enlarged it. On 13 December 1294 Pope Celestine V abdicated in its main hall, and the cardinals elected Boniface VIII there on 24 December. Under Robert, King of Naples, from 1309, it became a centre of culture, hosting Petrarch and Boccaccio, and Giotto painted the Palatine Chapel in 1332. Joanna I fled in 1347 as Louis I of Hungary advanced to avenge the death of her husband Andrew, and his army looted the castle. A legend says that Joanna II had her lovers thrown through a trapdoor to sea monsters, and another tells of a crocodile in the dungeons.

Alfonso V of Aragon set up his court in the castle in 1443 and had it rebuilt in Catalan Gothic style by Guillem Sagrera, with five round towers suited to the guns of the time. Its main gate became a marble triumphal arch commemorating his entry into Naples in 1443, which modern authors attribute to Francesco Laurana, and the work was finished in 1479. In the Hall of the Barons, Ferdinand I had barons who had conspired against him arrested at a wedding feast, and some were put to death. Charles VIII of France looted the castle in 1494, and under Spain it was a garrison and the viceroy's residence until the early 17th century.

The Italian state took the castle for civil purposes, and restoration lasted until 1939. The castle holds a civic museum, opened in 1990, which includes the Palatine Chapel, the only surviving element of the 14th-century castle of the House of Anjou, and the Neapolitan Society of Homeland History has its headquarters and library there. The Hall of the Barons, 26 by 28 metres, has an octagonal star vault, and until 2006 it hosted the city council of Naples. The triumphal arch is 35 metres tall, with a statue of Saint Michael at its top.
castel-santangelo: The tomb of the Roman emperor Hadrian was erected on the right bank of the Tiber between 134 and 139. Originally it was a decorated cylinder with a garden on top and a golden quadriga. Hadrian's ashes were placed there a year after his death at Baiae in 138, together with those of his wife Sabina and of his first adopted son, Lucius Aelius, who died in 138. The remains of later emperors were also deposited there, the last recorded being Caracalla in 217. Hadrian also built the Pons Aelius, which faces the mausoleum and still gives an approach from the centre of Rome.

The building became a military fortress in 401 and was included in the Aurelian Walls under Flavius Honorius Augustus. Visigoth looters scattered the urns and ashes during Alaric's sack of Rome in 410. When the Goths besieged Rome in 537, the defenders threw the original bronze and stone statuary down upon them, as Procopius recounts. Stone from the tomb was later reused: Giorgio Vasari writes that columns were taken from it for Saint Peter's. The capstone of a funerary urn, probably Hadrian's, ended up in Saint Peter's Basilica, covered the tomb of Otto II and was later built into a Renaissance baptistery.

The popes turned the structure into a castle, beginning in the 14th century, and linked it to Saint Peter's Basilica by a covered fortified corridor, the Passetto di Borgo. Pope Clement VII took refuge there from the Landsknechte of Charles V during the Sack of Rome in 1527. Leo X built a chapel, and Paul III added a rich apartment so that a pope would have a fitting place to stay in any later siege. The Papal State also used it as a prison, and Giordano Bruno, held there for six years, and Benvenuto Cellini were among its prisoners.

According to legend, the Archangel Michael appeared on top of the mausoleum and sheathed his sword to mark the end of the plague of 590, which gave the castle its present name. In 1536 Raffaello da Montelupo made a marble statue of Saint Michael to stand on the roof. Peter Anton von Verschaffelt's bronze statue of the same subject replaced it in 1753, and Montelupo's can be seen in a courtyard inside. The castle is the setting for the third act of Giacomo Puccini's opera Tosca of 1900. It was decommissioned in 1901 and is now the Museo Nazionale di Castel Sant'Angelo.
castell-dinas-bran: The name is usually taken as the crow's fortress, since dinas meant a defended enclosure in Middle Welsh and brân is a crow; others derived it from a person named Brân or, as Thomas Pennant and Edward Lhuyd held, from a dark stream at the foot of the hill. In English it has been called Crow Castle since at least the 18th century. Around 600 BCE the Ordovices built a large hillfort on the summit, with an earthen rampart and a deep ditch on the gentler southern slopes. A wooden castle of the princes of Powys Fadog, perhaps of Madog ap Gruffydd Maelor, founder of Valle Crucis Abbey, preceded the stone one and was destroyed by fire.

Gruffydd II ap Madog, an ally of Llywelyn ap Gruffudd, built the stone castle as one of several raised after the Treaty of Montgomery; Dolforwyn Castle may be the work of the same master mason. When Edward I invaded North Wales in 1277, Henry de Lacy, Earl of Lincoln, came from Oswestry to take it, but its defenders, probably the younger sons Owain and Gruffudd, had already set it alight. After the war of 1282 the castle passed to John de Warenne, Earl of Surrey, who built a new castle at Holt instead.

Rectangular stone walls run east to west above a steep northern slope, with a rock-cut ditch 6.1 metres deep and a counterscarp bank on the gentler southern and eastern sides; the ditch also served as a quarry. The two-storey keep stood at the south-eastern corner beside a gatehouse with two towers, once reached by a wooden bridge. On the south side stand the Great Hall, with its enlarged windows, and the D-shaped Welsh Tower, which held the kitchens below and living quarters above. A postern gate in the south-western corner allowed the garrison to sally out.

The castle first appears in literature in the 13th-century romance Fouke le Fitz Waryn, where the Norman knight Payn Peveril spends a night in the ruined Chastiel Bran and kills the giant Gogmagog. The 14th-century love story of Myfanwy Fychan of the castle and the poet Hywel ab Einion probably inspired the words of Joseph Parry's song Myfanwy of 1875. J. M. W. Turner and Richard Wilson painted it. A scheduled ancient monument kept by Denbighshire County Council with Cadw, it saw its first archaeological investigation in 2017, followed by an excavation around the gatehouse in 2021.
castell-y-bere: The Welsh princes had traditionally built no castles, living instead in undefended courts called llysoedd, while the Normans, advancing into Wales from the late 11th century, had set up the Welsh Marches in the south. In 1221 Llywelyn the Great took Meirionnydd from his son Gruffydd, with whom he had fallen out, and began the castle to control the local population and guard his new south-western border, which included the mountain trade routes between Gwynedd, Powys Wenwynwyn and Deheubarth. It was the first of several stone castles he built.

His grandson Llywelyn ap Gruffudd, who took power in 1255, added a tower to the south, probably for more accommodation. After his death near Builth in December 1282, forces under Roger Lestrange and William de Valence besieged the castle and took it on 25 April 1283. Edward I of England visited three times in 1284 and founded a small town beside it, whose charter of that year barred Jews from living in the borough. Walter of Huntercombe, made constable, spent £47 on a new chamber, and a further £262 was spent between 1286 and 1290.
