In 1294 the revolt of Madog ap Llywelyn reached the castle, which was under siege by late October, and its constable Robert FitzWalter was sent to lead a relief expedition. It was probably taken by the Welsh late that year and burnt. Edward did not repair it: unlike his new coastal castles, it could not be supplied by sea. In the 16th century the poet Gruffydd Hiraethog described it as destroyed and cast to the ground.

The ruins stand on a rocky outcrop, with ditches cut into the stone on the south and east sides. The entrance on the west leads through a barbican with two gate towers, probably built by Edward I, into a courtyard with a large well. The north and south towers are apsidal, or D-shaped, a design characteristic of Welsh castles of the early 13th century. The castle also had decorative sculpture, including statues of soldiers, and decorated floor tiles, features found among Welsh castles only here and at Criccieth.

The site was cleared of undergrowth in the 1850s, when its owner William Wynne made the first archaeological investigations. In 1949 Charles Corbett, the last private owner, placed the ruins in the guardianship of the state, and Cadw now cares for them as a scheduled monument.
castelvecchio-verona: Castelvecchio, the Old Castle, is the most important military building of the Scaliger dynasty that ruled Verona in the Middle Ages. It is a square, compact compound of red brick with very little decoration, one of the prominent examples of Gothic architecture of its age, with M-shaped merlons along the walls of the castle and its bridge. It has seven towers and a raised keep, the maschio, with four main buildings inside, and it is ringed by a ditch, now dry, once filled from the Adige. It stands on the probable site of a Roman fortress outside the Roman city.

Cangrande II della Scala had the castle and its bridge built as a deterrent to powerful neighbours such as Venice and the Gonzaga. Construction ran from 1354 to 1376, though Cangrande died in 1359. The fortified bridge was meant to let the lords escape northwards to the Tyrol in case of rebellion, since the Scaligeri were allies of the Holy Roman Empire, and when the family lost Verona its surviving members left Italy and founded a German branch.

Under Venetian rule the bridge was further fortified with cannons. French troops damaged the castle in 1796–7 in reprisal for the Pasque Veronesi, a violent revolt of the city's people, and Napoleon stayed there on his visits to Verona. The Austrians turned it into barracks. It was restored in 1923 and again in 1963–1965, and the bridge, destroyed by the retreating German army in 1945, was rebuilt in 1949. The castle now houses the Castelvecchio Museum and the local officers' club.
castillo-de-san-marcos: St. Augustine was founded in 1565 by Pedro Menéndez de Avilés on the site of a Native American village called Seloy. After Sir Francis Drake attacked it in 1586, nine wooden forts were built over the next 80 years. When the English privateer Robert Searles burned the town in 1668, Mariana, Queen Regent of Spain, approved a masonry fort, and Governor Francisco de la Guerra y de la Vega ordered it. The design was by the engineer Ignacio Daza, and work began on 2 October 1672 under Governor Manuel de Cendoya. Native Americans from the nearby missions did most of the labour, with skilled workers from Havana and African slaves owned by the Spanish.

The Castillo is a star fort of coquina quarried at the King's Quarry on Anastasia Island and ferried across Matanzas Bay. It has four bastions, San Pedro, San Agustín, San Carlos and San Pablo, with a ravelin guarding the sally port, a glacis on the two landward sides and a moat that could be flooded with seawater. The coquina absorbed cannonballs, which sank into the walls instead of shattering them. From 1738 the engineer Pedro Ruiz de Olano rebuilt the interior with vaulted ceilings, raising the outer wall from 26 to 33 feet.

The fort was a refuge for slaves escaping from Carolina, whom the Spanish freed if they converted to Catholicism, which led to Fort Mose, the first free Black settlement in the future United States. Possession changed five times, always peacefully. As Fort St. Mark under the British it held Christopher Gadsden; as Fort Marion under the United States it became a military prison. Osceola was held there in 1837, and that November Coacoochee and nineteen other Seminoles escaped. From 1875 western prisoners were held there under Richard Henry Pratt, whose experience led to the Carlisle Indian Industrial School, and from 1886 to 1887 about 491 Apaches, at least 24 of whom died.

The fort became a national monument in 1924, passed to the National Park Service in 1933 and took back its Spanish name in 1942. In 1964 its Freedom Tree was a gathering place for civil rights demonstrators.
castillo-san-felipe-del-morro: El Morro, the promontory, stands at the north-western point of the islet of Old San Juan and is named in honour of King Philip II of Spain. Its construction began in 1539 on the orders of King Charles V, under the conquistador Diego Ramos de Orozco, with a tower and a water battery below it; by 1555 it had eight bronze cannons as a defence against French privateers.

In 1587 Field Marshal Juan de Tejeda and the Italian engineer Bautista Antonelli drew the final design, part of a plan that also fortified Havana, Cartagena, St. Augustine and other ports. Work began in March 1589 with stonecutters, masons and smiths and the labour of 150 slaves, adding a hornwork across the headland with two half-bastions, Tejeda and Austria, joined by a curtain wall behind a moat. A plan of 1765 by Alejandro O'Reilly and Tomás O'Daly, approved by King Charles III, added three cisterns and walls 5.5 to 12.2 metres thick, and by 1790 San Juan was one of the strongest places in the Americas.

Sir Francis Drake attacked San Juan from the sea without success in 1595. In 1598 George Clifford, 3rd Earl of Cumberland, came over land and took the fortress, the only time El Morro fell in battle, but dysentery forced the English to leave. In 1625 the Dutch under Boudewijn Hendricksz sacked and burned the city while El Morro held out, and in 1797 Captain General Ramón de Castro repelled a British force under Ralph Abercromby and Henry Harvey.

On 12 May 1898 United States warships shelled the fort in a day-long bombardment, and after the Treaty of Paris it became part of the United States Army post of Fort Brooke. In March 1915 Lt. Teófilo Marxuach ordered shots fired from it at the German merchant ship Odenwald, and during World War II the army added a concrete bunker to watch for German submarines.

The army left in 1961 and the fort passed to the National Park Service. In 1992 its esplanade was cleared of palm trees, roads and parking lots and restored to its open colonial appearance, and today more than two million visitors a year come to the fort.
castizo: The origin of the word is uncertain; a chart accompanying a study of casta paintings calls its origin uncertain. It is recorded from 1543 with the meaning class, condition or social position. In colonial usage it named the child of a Spaniard and a mestiza, herself the child of a Spaniard and an indigenous woman, and it stood beside other labels of the period such as mestizo and cuarterón de indio.

Marriage licences required each partner to declare a racial status. Although castizos were widely distributed throughout New Spain, they did not appear in great numbers in parish documentation. In the censuses of white and mestizo households, the three categories of mestizo, castizo and español gave census takers a broader framework for recording differences of appearance. Some people were classified as castizos rather than españoles, but that status let them keep a raised standing within the wider mestizo population. Different labels were sometimes used side by side in the same documents.

In the census of 1778, carried out under King Carlos III by Viceroy Juan José de Vértiz y Salcedo in the territory of present-day Argentina, castizos and criollos together made up the 69,804 people counted as white, 37.54% of the population.

An 18th-century visitor to colonial Mexico held that the stigma of descent from a Spaniard and an Indian vanished at the third step: a Spaniard and an Indian produced a mestizo, a mestizo and a Spaniard a castizo, and a castizo and a Spaniard a Spaniard. Indian descent was no blemish, he added, since Philip II had granted mestizos the privilege of becoming priests. In the early 21st century the word has also come to mean light-skinned people of mixed descent, as against groups with darker skin such as mulattos, pardos, cholos, moriscos and coyotes.
castle: The emergence of castles in Europe has been much debated. Discussions have typically attributed it to a reaction to attacks by Magyars, Muslims and Vikings and to a need for private defence, together with the breakdown of the Carolingian Empire, which privatised government. The link between insecurity and building is not always straightforward, however: some high concentrations of castles occur in secure places, while some border regions had relatively few.

From 1000 onwards references to castles in charters increased greatly, and archaeological dating of ceramics supports a sudden increase in their number. In Italy the increase began in the 950s. In 950 Provence had 12 castles, by 1000 it had 30, and by 1030 over 100.

Scholars define a castle as a private fortified residence, built and owned by a local feudal lord for himself or for his monarch, which distinguishes it from communal defences such as the Anglo-Saxon burhs or walled cities like Constantinople. Many early castles were a motte, an earthen mound with a flat top, with a bailey, a fortified enclosure for the lord's household, garrison and workshops. The keep, a great tower serving as the main living quarters, was called a donjon in the medieval period.

Curtain walls enclosed the bailey; a typical wall could be 3 metres thick and 12 metres tall, studded with towers. Arrowslits did not become common in Europe until the 13th century, for fear they would weaken the wall. The gatehouse, usually the weakest point, gained portcullises and projecting towers, and moats, wet or dry, kept siege towers from the walls.

A castle was a centre of administration from which a lord controlled his lands. An average motte has been estimated to have taken 50 people about 40 working days to build. Garrisons were expensive and often small: in 1403 a force of 37 archers defended Caernarfon Castle against two assaults by allies of Owain Glyndŵr.

Artillery powered by gunpowder reached Europe in the 1320s, and around 1500 the angled bastion developed in Italy, leading to star forts. Between 75,000 and 100,000 castles are estimated to have been built in western Europe, about 1,700 of them in England and Wales. In the English Civil War many were refortified and then slighted so that they could not be used again.
castle-bravo: Castle Bravo was the first in a series of high-yield thermonuclear weapon tests, Operation Castle, conducted by the United States at Bikini Atoll in the Marshall Islands. The device, called SHRIMP, used the Teller–Ulam design with the same basic radiation-implosion configuration as the earlier Ivy Mike device. But where Ivy Mike used cryogenic liquid deuterium, which needed elaborate cooling equipment, SHRIMP used lithium deuteride, a solid at room temperature. The test made the cryogenic design obsolete, since it showed a practical, deliverable fusion bomb, although the device tested was not itself weaponised.

The device was mounted in a shot cab on an artificial island built on a reef off Namu Island. It was detonated at 06:45 local time on 1 March 1954. Within one second it formed a fireball almost 4.5 miles across.

The yield was 15 megatons, well above what its designers had predicted. The cause was an error at Los Alamos National Laboratory: the designers had counted only the lithium-6 isotope in the lithium deuteride as reactive, and assumed that lithium-7, about 60 percent of the lithium, reacted too slowly to add to the yield. The fission of the natural-uranium tamper made a great deal of fallout, and with the larger yield and a wind shift it fell on inhabited places and on the test personnel, some of whom sheltered in bunkers for several hours.

Fallout fell on the inhabited atolls of Rongelap and Utirik, whose people were evacuated and suffered radiation sickness. Ultimately 15 islands and atolls were contaminated. In 1957 the Atomic Energy Commission allowed 82 people to return to Rongelap, but their staple foods had disappeared or made them ill and they were removed again. By 1963 thyroid tumours were appearing, including in 20 of the 29 Rongelap children who had been present at the test. The Japanese fishing boat Daigo Fukuryū Maru was also caught in the fallout; its 23 crew were contaminated and the chief radioman, Kuboyama Aikichi, died six months later. The official American position at first denied that the crew had been harmed by fallout.

Traces of radioactive material reached Australia, India, Japan, the United States and Europe, and the test became an international incident that prompted calls for a ban on atmospheric testing. In 1958 Eisenhower set an unwritten rule that no American test should exceed the yield of Castle Bravo, and in 1963 the Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty ended non-underground tests.
castle-rushen: The castle stands in Castletown, the island's historic capital, above the Market Square and the harbour, on a site fortified to guard the entrance to the Silver Burn. It began as a square stone keep, reinforced with towers to the west and south by 1313, and in the 14th century gained an east tower, gatehouses and a curtain wall. The keep's limestone walls are 12 feet thick at the base, its north tower rises to 80 feet, and an outer wall 25 feet high carries five towers. The entrance has a drawbridge, two portcullises and murder holes, and a clock presented by Queen Elizabeth I in 1597 still works.

Magnús Óláfsson, the last King of Mann and the Isles, died at the castle in 1265, and the island passed to Scotland under the Treaty of Perth. On 18 May 1313 Robert the Bruce landed at Ramsey; Castle Rushen, defended by Dungal MacDouall, was the only resistance and fell on 12 June after a three-week siege. After further changes of hands the English prevailed, and from 1405 to 1738 the Stanley family held the island.

In the English Civil War James Stanley, 7th Earl of Derby, kept a Royalist court there. After his capture at Worcester and execution at Bolton in October 1651, a rising led by Illiam Dhône and a mutiny of her garrison forced his wife Charlotte to surrender the castle to Parliamentarian forces under Colonel Robert Duckenfield. Later it housed a mint, a law court and the Manx law books, and the House of Keys met there at times.

It also served as a prison. Bishop Thomas Wilson was held there in 1722 after a dispute with the Lord of Mann, and by the 1880s conditions had become so miserable that a new prison was built, opening in 1891. The last execution in its grounds, of John Kewish, took place in 1872.

The castle passed from the Crown to the Isle of Man Government in 1929 and to Manx National Heritage in 1988, and opened as a museum in July 1991. It tells the history of the Kings and Lords of Mann, is still in use as a court house, and appears on the Manx £5 note.
castor-and-pollux: Castor and Pollux, or Polydeuces, are twin half-brothers whose mother was Leda. The sources disagree about their parentage. In the Homeric Odyssey they are sons of Tyndareus alone, the king of Sparta, and in the Hesiodic Catalogue of Women sons of Zeus. Pindar's Nemean Odes gives the conventional account, in which only Pollux was fathered by Zeus, which explains why Pollux was granted immortality and Castor was mortal. In the Iliad, Helen says that her brothers are dead and buried at home in Lacedaemon, which suggests that in some early traditions both were mortal. Scholars connect them with the Indo-European horse twins, such as the Vedic Ashvins.

Both brothers were excellent horsemen and hunters. They took part in the hunt of the Calydonian Boar and joined the crew of the Argo, on which Pollux defeated King Amycus of the Bebryces in a boxing contest. When Theseus abducted their sister Helen, they invaded Attica to rescue her and took Theseus's mother Aethra to Sparta as her slave.

They then carried off the Leucippides, Phoebe and Hilaeira, who were betrothed to their cousins Idas and Lynceus. A cattle raid ended in a quarrel, and Idas fatally wounded Castor with a spear. Pollux killed Lynceus, and Zeus struck Idas dead with a thunderbolt. Zeus then offered Pollux a choice between all of Olympus and sharing his immortality with his dying brother. Pollux chose to share it, so the twins alternate between Olympus and Hades; they became the two brightest stars of the constellation Gemini and were said to appear to sailors as St. Elmo's fire. They were regarded as patrons of travellers, sailors, horsemen and athletes, intervening at moments of crisis.

The twins were important at Sparta. A symbol of them was two upright posts joined by crossbars, called dokana, and it was carried before the army in the field. Their grave-shrine was at Therapne, across the Eurotas from Sparta. The Etruscans venerated them as Kastur and Pultuce.

The Romans revered them from the 5th century BCE, probably through the Greek colonies of Magna Graecia. According to legend the twins fought at the head of the Roman army at the Battle of Lake Regillus and brought the news of victory to Rome, and the temple of Castor and Pollux was built in the Roman Forum to fulfil a vow made after that battle. On 15 July, their feast day, 1,800 equestrians paraded through Rome. After the rise of Christianity, Pope Gelasius I in the 5th century still attested a cult of the Castores that people did not want to abandon, and the church adopted Saints Peter and Paul in place of the twins as patrons of travellers.
castries: Castries stands on a flood plain and is built on reclaimed land, laid out in a grid. Its sheltered, deep-water harbour gave the settlement its first name, Carénage, a French word meaning safe anchorage. The harbour receives cargo vessels, ferries and cruise ships. Morne Fortune, a hill of 258 metres, rises above the city and carries Fort Charlotte.

In 1650 a group of 40 Frenchmen led by de Rousselan founded a fort near the Petit Cul-de-Sac and the Carénage river, when the island of Saint Lucia had been purchased from the French West India Company by du Parquet and Houel. Governor Baron de Micoud moved the capital to the south side of the harbour in 1769. The village of Carénage was renamed Castries after Charles Eugène Gabriel de La Croix, marquis de Castries, the French Minister of the Navy and Colonies; his title comes from a commune in southern France.

Castries has been rebuilt many times after major fires, on 15 October 1805, on 6 April 1813 and, most severely, on 19 June 1948. Under British rule a wharf was built to serve the coal trade, and the first steamship, the RMS Solway, arrived in 1841. On 9 March 1942 the German submarine U-161 entered the harbour at night and sank two Allied ships, among them the Canadian ocean liner RMS Lady Nelson, which was refloated and taken to Canada to be converted into a hospital ship.

Castries is the capital and largest city of Saint Lucia and the seat of government, with an urban population of about 20,000 and a district of just under 70,000. Landmarks include the Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception, the Government House and Derek Walcott Square, renamed from Columbus Square for the island's Nobel Prize-winning poet, who was born in the city, as was the economist Arthur Lewis. The city also hosts the secretariat of the Organisation of Eastern Caribbean States and the headquarters of the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court.
castro-of-santa-trega: The hillfort lies on the slopes of Mount Santa Trega, 341 metres above sea level, overlooking the mouth of the river Miño. It belongs to the Castro culture. According to classical authors such as Pliny the Elder, Pomponius Mela, Appian and Ptolemy, this corner of Galicia was home to the Grovii, whose chief town was Castellum Tyde, now Tui. A wall of stones bound with clay, up to 160 centimetres thick and without a foundation, marked the edge of the settlement rather than defending it.

The settlement arose when the Romanisation of the north-west of the peninsula had already begun, yet its building kept to the Castro tradition with little Roman influence. Most houses are small, free-standing and circular or oval, set on the bedrock, their walls about 40 centimetres thick and plastered with lime and sand mortar, sometimes tinted. Many have a foyer, which experts see as a Mediterranean influence. Door jambs and lintels carry intertwined geometric patterns, and small blocks in the walls show spirals, triskelions and Celtic roses. Hearths found where a central post was expected suggest roofs resting on the walls.

Houses and rougher storehouses were grouped around small, often paved courtyards in household units, with rainwater channels cut into the rock. The finds suggest a peaceful farming community with some buying power: local and Roman pottery, Roman glass, glass beads and game tokens, bronze situlas, knives and two gold-plated torc ends. Petroglyphs such as the Laja del Mapa, or Sacred Rock, with its spirals and concentric circles, are some 2,000 years older, from the final stage of the Galician Neolithic.

Stonemasons found a bronze figure of Hercules in 1862, and the ruins were described by Ramón López García in 1864 and by Manuel Murguía in his History of Galicia of 1888. Ignacio Calvo directed excavations from 1914 to 1923 and first linked the site with Mount Medulio, where classical writers placed the last Gallaecian resistance against the Roman Empire. Cayetano de Mergelina y Luna of the University of Valladolid uncovered many houses on the western slope between 1928 and 1933. The site, declared a National Historical and Artistic Monument in 1931, then lay abandoned until 1983, when Antonio de la Peña Santos of the Museum of Pontevedra began systematic excavation of its northern part.
castro-urdiales: Castro Urdiales was originally called Portus Amanum and was the chief city of the Autrigones. In 74 a Roman colony was established there under the name Flaviobriga, in the reign of Vespasian, most likely to mine the abundant iron of the area. A Roman milestone opposite the Church of Santa María dates to 61, and the water channel of El Chorrillo is a Roman work of hydraulic engineering.

The town received its municipal charter in 1163. It lay at the western tip of the coastline of Navarre until 1200, when Alfonso VIII of Castile invaded the kingdom. It profited from its place at a crossroads of trade between northern Europe and Castile. It remained in Biscay until at least 1476, and until the 18th century it tried to rejoin Biscay, attempts that Bilbao refused because they could tip the balance against its own trade. The French destroyed the town in 1813, but it was rebuilt and fortified. Its growth dates from iron mining and railways after 1879.

Castro Urdiales is a port on the Bay of Biscay in Cantabria. Its chief industries are tourism, fishing and the oil-packing of fish, especially sardines and anchovies. The old quarter, the Puebla Vieja, was declared a Conjunto histórico in 1978. The Gothic church of Santa María de la Asunción was built in the 13th century under Alfonso VIII, finished in the 15th and declared a National Monument in 1931. The Castle of Santa Ana stands near the port. The Cave of El Cuco holds Paleolithic rock carvings and paintings of deer, goats and horses.
castruccio-castracani: Castruccio Castracani degli Antelminelli was born in Lucca into the noble Antelminelli family, which belonged to the Ghibelline party. In 1300 the Black Guelphs, then dominant in the city, exiled him with his parents and others of their faction. Orphaned at nineteen, he served as a condottiero under Philip IV of France in Flanders and then with the Visconti in Lombardy, before joining the Ghibelline leader Uguccione della Faggiuola, lord of Pisa, in 1313.

Castruccio helped Uguccione capture Lucca in 1314 and was the main author of the victory over the Guelph League led by the Florentines at the Battle of Montecatini in 1315. His growing popularity led Uguccione to imprison him and condemn him to death, but a rising of the people of Lucca drove Uguccione and his party out, and Castruccio regained his freedom and his position. On 12 June 1316 he was elected lord of Lucca as lifelong consul.

He fought the Florentines almost without pause, while at home he renovated the Ponte della Maddalena over the River Serchio. He first supported Frederick of Austria, who in 1320 made him imperial vicar of Lucca, Lunigiana and Val di Nievole. After the Battle of Mühldorf he went over to Emperor Louis the Bavarian and served him for many years, receiving the title of duke of Lucca, Pistoia, Volterra and Luni. He also captured Pisa and was made its imperial vicar. His relations with Louis later cooled, and in 1327 the papal legate excommunicated him in the interest of the Guelphs.

Castruccio died on 3 September 1328, and the fortunes of his young children were ruined in the Guelph triumph that followed. Niccolò Machiavelli later wrote a Life of Castruccio Castracani, a work understood to be fictional in many places and built on classical aphorisms; Leo Strauss considered it significant for understanding Machiavelli's political philosophy. Mary Shelley based her novel Valperga; or, The Life and Adventures of Castruccio, Prince of Lucca, published in 1823, on his life, with the dates slightly changed.
castrum: Castrum appears in Oscan and Umbrian as well as Latin, which suggests an origin at least as old as Proto-Italic. Julius Pokorny traces it to a root meaning to cut, with the sense of a tract of land cut off and prepared. A military camp would then be a piece of land cut off from the common land and modified for military use. Castra in the plural meant a camp, and castrum in the singular a fort. Latin phrases distinguished permanent camps (castra stativa), summer camps and winter camps.

From the most ancient times Roman camps were built to an ideal pattern, described in the De Munitionibus Castrorum and the works of Polybius. Latin also used castrum and castra as place names, from which come the Welsh prefix caer, as in Caerleon and Caerwent, and the English endings caster and chester, as in Winchester and Lancaster.

A castrum was the fortified base of a legion, a detachment of one, or of auxiliary units, giving a secure place for training, administration and defence. They ranged from temporary marching camps to large permanent fortresses housing a whole legion. The site was chosen for defensibility, access to water and timber, and flat ground, and surveyors laid out a rectangular perimeter with the aid of a groma. Soldiers dug a ditch, the fossa, threw the earth inward to make a rampart, the agger, and set a palisade of stakes on it, which they carried on the march. In time a palisade might be replaced by brick or stone.

The plan had four gates, the main one, the porta praetoria, facing the enemy. The via praetoria led to the central section, where stood the principia, or headquarters, and the praetorium, the commander's residence, along with a hospital, a bathhouse and storehouses. It crossed the via principalis at right angles, and a road, the via sagularis, ran round the inside of the wall. The ideal plan was altered to suit the terrain, and not every camp had the standard streets and buildings.

Villages grew around the camps: canabae near legionary fortresses and vici near auxiliary forts, home to merchants, craftsmen and soldiers' families and centres of trade with the army. Permanent castra often became the foundations of towns and cities across the Roman Empire, many of which still bear traces of their origins in their layouts and names. Castro is a common Spanish family name and a place name in Spain, Italy and the Balkans, and the emperor Caligula was called Castrorum Filius, son of the camps.
castulo: Castulo, Kastilo in Iberian, lay north of the Guadalquivir River near modern Linares, in the Andalusian province of Jaén. Finds show people living there from the Neolithic period. It became the seat of the Oretani, an Iberian people who settled the area from the sixth century BCE, and it is probably the ancient Castax.

In 211 BCE Castulo was the scene of a crushing victory by Hasdrubal Barca over a Roman army, won with roughly 40,000 Carthaginian troops and Iberian mercenaries. The Romans afterwards made a pact with the townspeople, who betrayed the Carthaginians and became foederati, allies of Rome. According to Livy, they had been intimidated by Scipio Africanus's order to massacre the inhabitants of neighbouring Illiturgis.

Bishops of Castulo appear in the fourth century, at the Councils of Elvira and Sardica. Under Visigoth rule a bishop of Castulo, by then a suffragan of the Metropolitan of Toledo, attended the Third Council of Toledo in 589, and bishops of the see appear at later councils down to the Tenth Council of Toledo in 656. The Diocese of Baeza later took its place.

Known in the Middle Ages as Cazlona, the town lost more of its importance under Islamic rule, while nearby Linares grew around its castle, first an Arab fortress and later rebuilt by the Christians after the Reconquista. The walls of Castulo were destroyed in 1227, and the town was depopulated soon afterwards.

The Catholic Church lists Castulo as a Latin titular see, nominally restored in 1969. Among its remains is a late-antique building once taken for a church, which researchers have proposed may have been a synagogue: its square plan could have held a central bimah, a lamp fragment may bear a menorah, and no clearly Christian objects were found nearby.
catalan-atlas: The Catalan Atlas is a medieval world map, probably made in the late 1370s or early 1380s and often conventionally dated 1375. It was produced by Cresques Abraham, a Jewish cartographer and the leader of the Majorcan cartographic school, whom a contemporary described as a master of world maps, compasses and illuminated manuscripts. It was in the royal library of France by 1380, in the reign of Charles V. It originally consisted of six vellum leaves, each about 64.5 by 50 centimetres, painted in various colours including gold and silver. They were later mounted on five wooden panels in a leather binding made by Simon Vostre about 1515, restored most recently in 1991.

The first two leaves carry Catalan texts and illustrations on cosmography, astronomy and astrology, stressing the Earth's spherical shape and giving sailors information on tides and on telling the time at night. The other four leaves form the map itself, with Jerusalem near the centre. Two show the Orient, and two show Europe with North and West Africa. Cities are drawn with a cross if Christian and a dome if not, and a flag marks each one's allegiance. The western part resembles contemporary portolan charts but has the first compass rose known on such a chart. The eastern part combines older world maps with travel literature, especially Marco Polo's Book of Marvels and Mandeville's Travels, and many Indian and Chinese cities can be identified.

Its captions name rulers across the known world. The Mali Empire appears under Mansa Musa, called Musse Melly, who is described as the richest and noblest lord of that region because of the gold taken from his lands. The Sultan of Delhi, the Il-Khanate ruler at Tabriz, Jani Beg of the Golden Horde and Kublai Khan are also shown. In the central Sahara a King of Organa is placed; no medieval African kingdom bore that name, and historians have suggested it stands for Kanem–Bornu, Ife or Ghana.

The atlas has been described as the most important map of the Middle Ages in the Catalan language and as the zenith of medieval map-work. Its caption on Mansa Musa is often misquoted in modern media as a claim about the richest man in the world, and Hadrien Collet has examined it as one of the earliest European stages in the long making of the Mansa Musa wealth myth. The manuscript is still preserved in the Bibliothèque nationale de France.
catalan-civil-war: The quarrel began within the royal family. John II, King of Navarre through his first wife Blanche I of Navarre, kept her lands after her death in 1441 and dispossessed their son Charles, Prince of Viana; father and son fought openly in Navarre in the early 1450s. On succeeding his brother Alfonso V in 1458, John refused to recognise Charles as his first-born, probably to keep that title for Ferdinand, his son by Juana Enríquez. When he had Charles arrested at Lleida on 2 December 1460, Catalonia rose in protest.

The Catalan Courts ruled that the king had broken the Usatges de Barcelona and the Constitucions de Catalunya, and an army under the Count of Modica forced him to give way. By the Capitulation of Vilafranca of 21 June 1461 Charles was recognised as heir, and the king could no longer enter the principality without the permission of the Generalitat. Charles died of tuberculosis in Barcelona on 23 September 1461, and the rivalry of the Busca and the Biga factions revived.

Fighting opened in February 1462 with the rising of the remença peasants under Francesc de Verntallat. By the treaties of Sauveterre and Bayonne in May 1462, Louis XI of France lent John 700 lances in return for 200,000 écus, with Roussillon and Cerdagne as surety. The Consell del Principat deposed the king, and the Catalans offered the crown in turn to Henry IV of Castile, who renounced it on 13 June 1463; to the constable of Portugal, acclaimed as Peter V, who was defeated at the Battle of Calaf on 28 February 1465 and died in 1466; and to René the Good, Count of Anjou and Provence.

Supplies from Aragon, Valencia, Sardinia and Sicily sustained the king. René's son John II, Duke of Lorraine, defeated Prince Ferdinand at the Battle of Viladamat on 21 November 1467, but the duke's death at Barcelona on 16 December 1470 and the withdrawal of French troops in 1471 turned the war. Barcelona, besieged by land and sea from 1 January 1472, surrendered on 16 October by the Capitulation of Pedralbes.

The settlement granted a general pardon, though not to Hug Roger III, Count of Pallars Sobirà, and approved the acts of the Catalan government since the death of Charles of Viana, while the Capitulation of Vilafranca was rejected. Roussillon and Cerdagne proved harder to recover: the French conquered Roussillon in 1474, and in October 1478 John ceded both counties to France until he could redeem them. The Catalan historians Santiago Sobrequés and Jaume Sobrequés saw in the rebels' cause a new idea of a community bound by common laws, and the French historian Joseph Calmette called the rising the first of modern revolutions.
catalan-company: The almogavars were elite light infantry formed on the Iberian peninsula in the 13th century by the demands of the Reconquista, and the Crown of Aragon used them in its Mediterranean ventures, above all the War of the Sicilian Vespers. They fought in companies of 20 to 50 men under a chief of proven skill. The Peace of Caltabellotta of 1302 left them without employment, and James II of Aragon and Frederick III of Sicily feared the threat they posed to order. Many were therefore gathered into a company of companies under Roger de Flor, to be paid in Byzantine service.

The Company left Messina with 36 ships carrying about 8,000 men, by the count of Ramon Muntaner, although the Byzantine historian Nicephorus Gregoras gives only 1,000. Emperor Andronikos II Palaiologos married Roger de Flor to his niece Maria Asanina and named him Megas Doux. The newcomers angered the Genoese, and some 3,000 of them were killed in the Genoese massacre of September 1303.

In Anatolia the Company defeated the Karasid Turks at the Battle of the Cyzicus in October 1303, relieved Philadelphia after the Battle of Aulax in 1304 and won the Battle of Kibistra on 15 August 1304. Greek historians recorded heavy looting and abuse of the Byzantine population by the almogavars. On 30 April 1305 the emperor's son Michael IX Palaiologos had Alan mercenaries murder Roger de Flor at Adrianople, and the Catalans answered by killing the Byzantines of Gallipoli and defeating Michael at the Battle of Apros in July 1305.

After quarrels among its leaders, in which Bernat de Rocafort was arrested and starved to death in Naples in 1309, the Company moved west. It pillaged Chalcidice and Mount Athos, failed to take Thessalonica and reached Thessaly by 1309. Its leader Roger Deslaur then took service with Walter V of Brienne, Duke of Athens, whose refusal to pay led to the Battle of Halmyros on 15 March 1311.

The Company held the Duchy of Athens and made Thessaly into the Duchy of Neopatras, ruling as feudal lords. In 1312 it accepted the overlordship of the Aragonese crown of Sicily and took a seal with the head of St George, and in 1318 the Pope excommunicated its members for refusing to give the duchies back to their heirs. It held them until it was defeated by the Navarrese Company and the troops of Nerio I Acciaioli of Corinth. Muntaner later wrote a chronicle of its history, and the monks of Mount Athos barred Catalans from the mountain until 2000.
catalan-courts: The Courts grew out of the comital court of the counts of Barcelona, of about 1000, modelled on the Frankish curia regis, and out of the assemblies of the Peace and Truce, which met from 1021 to end wars and feudal violence. Townspeople first took part in such an assembly in 1192. The Royal Court of 1214, called at Lleida by the papal legate Cardinal Peter of Benevento after King Peter fell at the Battle of Muret, received the oath of the six-year-old James I, and the Court of 1218 is counted as the first General Court.

Each estate formed an arm. The ecclesiastical arm, under the Archbishop of Tarragona, included the bishops, abbots and cathedral chapters; the military arm, under the Duke of Cardona, the titled nobles, knights and lords with vassals; and the royal arm, under the Chief Councilor of Barcelona, the síndics of the towns under royal jurisdiction. Barcelona sent five, Perpignan three and most towns one, each bound by an imperative mandate from its municipality. Laws proposed by the king were called Constitucions, those of the estates Capítols de Cort. Majorca sent its representatives to these Courts, which often met at Monzón or Fraga.

In 1289 at Monzón the Courts appointed a standing delegation to collect the tax they granted the king, and in 1358-1359, under King Peter IV, they named twelve deputies with powers over taxation. This body, the Deputation of the General or Generalitat, was headed by Berenguer de Cruïlles, bishop of Girona. The Courts of 1480, the first of Ferdinand II, approved the Constitution of the Observance, which bound the king to respect the constitutions and let the Generalitat revoke unconstitutional orders.

Under the Habsburgs the Courts were summoned less and less. The Courts of 1626, at which Philip IV sought the Union of Arms of his minister Gaspar de Guzmán, Count-Duke of Olivares, were never concluded, and the tensions led to the Reapers' War of 1640-1652. The last Court, under the Habsburg claimant Charles III in 1705-1706, extended individual rights such as the secrecy of correspondence. Between 1214 and 1705 the Courts were convened 104 times, and the Parliament of Catalonia, founded in 1932, is considered their successor.
catamarca-province: Catamarca lies in the northwest of Argentina and covers 102,602 square kilometres. It borders Salta, Tucumán, Santiago del Estero, Córdoba and La Rioja, and to the west the country of Chile. Eighty percent of the territory is covered by mountains, which fall into four systems: the Pampean sierras in the east and centre, the Narváez-Cerro Negro-Famatina system in the west, a cordilleran transition area at the western extreme, and the Puna, an elevated portion in the northwest.

The province is semi-arid, and the scarce water determines where people live: agriculture is concentrated in pockets and valleys between the mountains, and in the east the population gathers around watercourses from which canals and ditches carry the water. The Puna in the extreme west has a desert climate with very low precipitation, and snow cover is permanent at the highest peaks of the Sierra del Aconquija.

Before the Spanish conquest most of what is now Catamarca was inhabited by the Diaguita people, among them the fierce Calchaquí. In 1558 Juan Pérez de Zurita founded Londres de la Nueva Inglaterra, but it was constantly attacked by indigenous people, its population stayed small, and it was re-founded several times at new sites with new names. The sixth foundation, by Fernando de Mendoza Mate de Luna on 5 July 1683, bore the name San Fernando del Valle de Catamarca. The name of the province is believed to come either from Quechua cata, slope, and marca, fortress, or from Aymara catán, small, and marca, town.

When the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata was created in 1776, Catamarca became a subintendencia under the Salta intendency. In 1821 the province claimed its autonomy and elected Nicolás Avellaneda y Tula as its first governor. The mountains kept it isolated from the rest of Argentina until 1888, when the railways first reached it. Its valleys and dry climate attracted immigrants from Lebanon and Iran, who found it reminiscent of the orchard-lined mountain valleys they had left.

Catamarca is a province of Argentina with its capital at San Fernando del Valle de Catamarca, usually shortened to Catamarca. Its population was 429,556 at the 2022 census, and other important cities are Andalgalá, Tinogasta and Belén. The province is divided into sixteen departments.

Mining is important in its economy, notably the Bajo de la Alumbrera copper and gold mine. Among its sights are Antofagasta de la Sierra, the San Francisco Pass, the archaeological park Las Huellas del Inca and prehistoric petroglyphs.
catania: Catania faces the Ionian Sea at the base of the active volcano Mount Etna. The Sicels, the ancient indigenous people of Sicily, named their villages after features of their location, and the Siculian word katane means grater or skinning place, or a crude tool apt to pare. The geographer Strabo observed that the site was both a curse and a blessing: eruptions have destroyed large parts of the city, while volcanic ash makes fertile soil, especially suited to vines. The city has been buried by lava seventeen times, and the Roman city and the earlier Greek settlement lie beneath the present one.

Around 729 BCE Chalcidian Greek settlers from nearby Naxos occupied the village of Katane under a leader named Euarchos, and the native population was rapidly Hellenised. In 263 BCE, during the First Punic War, the city was one of the first in Sicily to submit to Rome. The Vandals under Gaiseric sacked it in 440 and 441. The Byzantine Empire reconquered it in 535, and an Islamic emirate ruled it for two centuries until the Normans of Roger I of Sicily took it. In 1232 it rebelled against Frederick II, who later built the Castello Ursino and made Catania a royal city, ending the dominance of the bishops. Sicily's first university was founded there in 1434.

Etna's eruption of 1669 devastated the surroundings, though the city's walls diverted most of the lava into the port. In 1693 an earthquake nearly destroyed Catania, and it was rebuilt in the Baroque style that now characterises it. Garibaldi's expedition of the Thousand conquered Sicily in 1860, and from the following year Catania was part of unified Italy.

Catania is the second-largest city of Sicily, after Palermo, with 296,984 people in the city proper. It is the industrial, logistical and commercial centre of the island and has its main airport. The central old town, with late-Baroque architecture built after the 1693 earthquake, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, part of the Late Baroque Towns of the Val di Noto. The elephant fountain, u Liotru, assembled in 1736 by Giovanni Battista Vaccarini, is the symbol of the city. The composer Vincenzo Bellini and the writer Giovanni Verga were natives.
cataphract: The word comes from the Greek kataphraktos, composed of kata and phraktos, meaning covered or protected, and is read as fully armoured. Heavy cavalry of this kind originated in Central Asia and developed in several places at once, among the peoples of the Silk Road and in Greater Iran. Reliefs at Nimrud are the earliest known depictions of riders in plated-mail shirts of metal scales, and under Tiglath-Pileser III (745-727 BCE) the Neo-Assyrian kingdom is believed to have formed crude regiments of cataphract-like cavalry.

By the 6th century BCE, peoples near the Aral Sea such as the Massagetae, Dahae and Saka armoured the horse as well as the rider. Selective breeding was a prerequisite, since the horses had to carry a heavy load of armour and a rider through the strain of battle.

A cataphract was clad in scale armour, made of overlapping plates of bronze or iron sewn to a leather or hide undergarment, or less often in lamellar armour, with chain mail for the rider. The horse's armour was usually sectional, tied around the animal's waist, flank, shoulders, neck and head to give it freedom of movement. A full set of about 1,300 scales could weigh about 40 kilograms. The usual weapon was the kontos, a long lance, and some riders carried bows. Only wealthy men of noble birth could afford the panoply and the cost of several war horses.

Cataphracts served as shock troops, supported by infantry and archers, and were used to break enemy formations. At the Battle of Carrhae in 53 BCE the Parthians combined horse archers and cataphracts. The archers encircled the Roman infantry, forcing the legionaries into the testudo formation, which made them immobile and vulnerable to the lances of a cataphract charge.

The Greeks first met cataphracts in the Greco-Persian Wars, and the Seleucid Empire adopted them widely after Alexander the Great's death. The Parthians, who took Persia from the last Seleucid kingdom in the East in 147 BCE, relied on them. The Romans met cataphracts in the Hellenistic East, with varying success: they did well at Carrhae and less well against Lucullus near Tigranocerta in 69 BCE. In 38 BCE Publius Ventidius Bassus defeated Parthian armoured cavalry by making extensive use of slingers.

Rome adopted cataphract-like units in the late 3rd and 4th centuries, and the emperor Gallienus and his general Aureolus are thought to have contributed much to this. In East Asia the Xianbei used cataphracts widely from the early 4th century, and Chinese armies of the Jin dynasty and the Northern and Southern Dynasties readopted them in large numbers. The Eastern Roman Empire's contact with them may have influenced later European knights.
catapult: The word catapult comes from the Latin catapulta, from the Greek katapeltēs, formed from kata, downwards, and pallō, to toss or hurl. A catapult launches a projectile at a great distance without gunpowder, by the sudden release of stored energy: tension or torsion built up slowly in springs, bows, twisted rope or elastic. King Uzziah of Judah is recorded as equipping the walls of Jerusalem with machines that shot great stones, and Jaina texts record that Ajatashatru of Magadha used catapults against the Licchavis in the 5th century BCE. In China the mangonel appeared in the same century.

Greek catapults were invented in the early 4th century BCE. Diodorus Siculus describes a mechanical arrow-firing catapult devised by a Greek task force in 399 BCE and used at the siege of Motya in 397 BCE. It developed from the gastraphetes, or belly-bow, a foot-held crossbow that stored more energy than ordinary bows.

An Athenian arsenal inscription dated between 338 and 326 BCE is the first clear evidence for torsion catapults, which were more powerful than crossbow types and came to dominate Greek and Roman artillery. The change was probably spurred by the engineers of Philip II of Macedonia, who used arrow-firing machines at the siege of Perinth in 340 BCE. Alexander the Great used catapults at the Battle of Jaxartes and in sieges. The Romans began to use them in their wars against Syracuse, Macedon, Sparta and Aetolia, and later fitted ballistae to warships.

Medieval armies used ballistae, springalds, mangonels and trebuchets against castles and walled cities, throwing stones, incendiary missiles, and sometimes carcasses or garbage over the walls. The trebuchet was probably the most powerful, in a traction form worked by people and a counterpoise form worked by a counterweight. At the siege of Stirling Castle in 1304 the army of Edward I built a giant trebuchet called Warwolf, which levelled a section of wall.

Defences improved until catapults were largely ineffective, and the Viking siege of Paris in 885–6 used nearly every siege instrument known to the classical world to little effect. Leonardo da Vinci designed a catapult powered by a leaf spring and winding drum, which enthusiasts have since built. The last large-scale army use was in the trench warfare of the First World War, when catapults threw hand grenades into enemy trenches until small mortars replaced them. Catapults also launched aircraft from ships, from British experiments in 1917 to common fittings on major warships by the 1930s.
cataract-surgery: Cataract surgery has a long history in Europe, Asia and Africa. The earliest account comes from the Stoic Greek philosopher Chrysippus of Soli. Couching, in which the clouded lens is pushed out of the line of sight rather than removed, was the original form of the operation and was used from antiquity; it is still occasionally found in traditional medicine in parts of Africa and Asia, though mainstream medicine no longer uses it.

The Indian contribution has been questioned. A paper in the journal Annals of Translational Medicine found that much of the ophthalmological literature crediting the operation to Sushruta copies earlier papers without checking the original sources, and the ophthalmic historian Julius Hirschberg judged that whether Indians invented the operation could so far be neither confirmed nor denied.

A cataract is an opaque or cloudy area that forms in the eye's natural lens through metabolic changes in its fibres, though some infants are born with one and environmental factors can cause them. Early signs include glare from lights at night, faded colours, blurred or double vision and halos around lights, and blindness can be the end result. Cataract remained the leading cause of blindness in the world in 2020, and it accounts for about half of the blind people of Africa.

In the modern operation the clouded lens is removed and usually replaced by an artificial intraocular lens, which restores the eye's ability to focus. It is normally done by an ophthalmologist under local anaesthesia, with the patient going home the same day, and well over 90 per cent of operations restore useful vision.

Two main techniques are now in common use. In phacoemulsification an ultrasonic probe, commonly vibrating at 40 kHz, breaks up the lens, which is removed by suction through an incision small enough to need no stitches. Extracapsular extraction takes the lens out in one piece through a cut of 10 to 12 mm, leaving most of the lens capsule in place to hold the implant. Manual small incision surgery, an evolution of that method through a self-sealing tunnel in the sclera, needs far less equipment and is popular in the developing world. The older intracapsular method has been largely superseded wherever surgery under a microscope is possible.
catawba-people: The Catawba call themselves Ye Iswąˀ, people of the river, after the river now named for them; the Haudenosaunee called them Totiri or Toderichroone. People have lived in the region since about 10,000 BCE. In the 19th century Henry Rowe Schoolcraft claimed that the Catawba had come from Canada and reached the Catawba River by 1660, but the anthropologist James Mooney dismissed this as absurd, noting that the Spanish expedition of Juan Pardo had recorded them there by 1567. Spanish explorers of the mid-16th century estimated their number at 15,000 to 25,000.

In the 1720s and 1730s the Catawba fought Lenape and Seneca raiders as far north as the Potomac. Smallpox struck in 1738 and in 1759, when it killed nearly half of them, and in 1763 Shawnee killed their chief, King Hagler. That year South Carolina confirmed a reservation of 225 square miles on both sides of the river. The Catawba supported the colonists in the Revolutionary War, and nineteen men fought for the Confederacy in the Civil War. By the Treaty of Nation Ford of 1840 South Carolina took all but one square mile of the reservation, a treaty invalid from the start because only the federal government could make it.

Federally recognised in 1941, the tribe was terminated in 1959. After decades of land claims, Congress passed a settlement act on 27 October 1993 that restored recognition and, with South Carolina, settled the claims for $50 million. The Nation opened the Catawba Two Kings Casino at Kings Mountain, North Carolina, on 1 July 2021.

The Catawba were sedentary farmers who also fished and hunted, and their women are known for pottery and baskets; their pottery tradition is believed to be the oldest surviving east of the Mississippi. Many Catawba became members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints after missionaries came around 1883. The reservation lies in two sections in York County, east of Rock Hill. Citizens must descend from someone on the tribal rolls of 1943, 1961 or 2000, and the Catawba language is being revived.
catechetical-school-of-alexandria: The Catechetical School of Alexandria, also known as the Didascalium, was a school of Christian theologians, bishops and deacons in Alexandria. It was one of the two major centres of biblical exegesis and theology in late antiquity, the other being the School of Antioch. According to Jerome it was founded by Mark the Apostle, and its first head was Justus, later the sixth bishop of Alexandria. Another opinion holds that it was founded in the middle of the second century, about 190. The first great Christian figures in Egypt were scholars rather than bishops, and the school's purpose was to supply defenders of the Christian faith.

It did not gain wide fame until Pantaenus became its teacher, around 180. He was a native of Sicily and a Stoic philosopher before his conversion, and he united theology with philosophy. His supporters held that philosophy was a gift of God for the Gentiles, preparing them for the Gospel as the Law had done before, and that it trained the mind and could serve the faith. Tertullian and Cyprian opposed this union. Clement of Alexandria succeeded him in about 190, was attended by large numbers of pagans and wrote works for those who could not hear him. In 202 he fled to Palestine because of the persecution of Septimius Severus, and returned after four years.

Origen then gave the school its high character for biblical studies. He is generally regarded as the father of biblical criticism, and he was the first to distinguish the literal, moral and mystical or allegorical senses of scripture. Other notable people connected with the school include Gregory Thaumaturgus, Heraclas, Dionysius the Great and Didymus the Blind, while Jerome and Basil visited to meet its scholars.

The school taught more than theology. Philosophy, science, mathematics, Greek and Roman literature, logic and the arts were also taught. Its question-and-answer method of commentary is said to have begun there. The school was destroyed by riots after the Council of Constantinople of 381, according to one account. It was reopened in a different location in 1893 as the Coptic Theological Seminary, which claims continuity with the ancient school.
caterina-sforza: Caterina Sforza was born in Milan in 1463, one of four illegitimate children of Galeazzo Maria Sforza and his mistress Lucrezia Landriani. In 1473 she became betrothed to Girolamo Riario, a nephew of Pope Sixtus IV, who gave him the lordship of Imola. She was ten, and the marriage is said to have been consummated when she was fourteen. In Rome she became an intermediary between the Roman court and other Italian courts, especially Milan. Her first child, Ottaviano, was born on 1 September 1479.

In 1480 the Pope also gave Girolamo the lordship of Forlì. Pope Innocent VIII confirmed him in both lordships, but his appointment as captain-general was only nominal. Girolamo had abolished taxes to win favour, but when the city ran out of money at the end of 1485 he was forced to levy them, which made him unpopular. After more than a half dozen failed attempts, a conspiracy led by the Orsi family, a noble family of Forlì, killed him on 14 April 1488. Caterina and her six children were made prisoners, and she then ruled the lordship as regent for her son Ottaviano.

In 1499 Louis XII came to Italy and allied himself with Pope Alexander VI, who in return was to support his son Cesare Borgia as ruler in Romagna. A papal bull of 9 March 1499 invalidated the investiture of the feudal lords, including Caterina. Left without Florentine help, she recruited and trained soldiers, stored weapons and food and reinforced the fortress of Ravaldino, where she resided. Cesare obtained custody of her from the French general Yves d'Allègre, promising to treat her as a guest, and took her to Rome, where she was imprisoned in Castel Sant'Angelo.

The Pope accused her of trying to kill him with poisoned letters in November 1499, and historians remain unsure whether the charge was well founded. She was released on 30 June 1501 by Yves d'Allègre. She then lived in Florence, where she fought a legal battle over the custody of her son Giovanni, who was returned to her in 1504. After Alexander VI's death on 18 August 1503 she pleaded her case to Pope Julius II, but the people of Imola and Forlì opposed her return, and the domain passed to Antonio Maria Ordelaffi on 22 October 1503. She died on 28 May 1509.

Caterina kept a manuscript of 454 recipes in cosmetics, chemistry and medicine, later published as Experimenti by the historian Pier Desiderio Pasolini. Her only child to inherit her militant personality was Giovanni delle Bande Nere, and she was nicknamed La Tigre. Machiavelli tells that when conspirators threatened her children she mocked them, saying that she could make more.
caterino-zeno: Zeno was born in Venice on 12 July 1418 into the noble Zeno family, the son of Dragone Pietro Zeno and Anna Morosini. He took part in expeditions to Alexandria and Tanais in 1445 and 1446, and from 1448 held public offices, serving as State Advocate for the minor curiae and several times on the Council of Forty. In 1453 he married Violante Crispo, daughter of Nicolò Crispo; their son Pietro later became ambassador to Constantinople. He financed a trade route to Syria and Beirut in 1455, commanded a ship in 1463 and was a port officer in Venice in 1467.

On 7 March 1471, after two other candidates had declined, he was chosen as ambassador to Uzun Hassan, with the aim of building an alliance against the Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II. He reached the ruler's court in April 1472 and stayed about a year and a half, becoming a personal friend of Uzun Hassan and on friendly terms with Theodora Despina Komnene and her daughters, whom he met again in Damascus in 1473. The alliance he prepared outlasted his return, and Giosafat Barbaro and Ambrogio Contarini took his place.

On his way back he risked capture by the Ottomans and ran so short of money that he had to give one of his servants as a slave to continue the journey. He sought further alliances with Emperor Frederick III, the King of Poland and King Matthias Corvinus of Hungary, without great results, though Matthias knighted him on 20 April 1474.

In Venice he took part in missions to Rome and Naples in 1474, became a governor of the revenue in January 1475 and was appointed to the Council of Ten on 29 September 1476, serving several times as its head or inquisitor. In May 1477 he was elected patron of the Arsenal. He died before June 1478, probably of the plague, and was buried in the church of the Crociferi. His great-grandson Nicolò reworked and expanded his writings and published them in 1558 as the Commentari, and his fame as a traveller inspired fiction such as Vincenzo Formaleoni's Storia Curiosa of 1783.
cathal-mac-finguine: Cathal belonged to the Eóganacht Glendamnach, a sept of the Eóganachta whose lands lay south-west of Cashel in the middle valley of the Blackwater. The Eóganachta kingship had its seat at Cashel and its chief church at Emly, and dominated the southern half of Ireland while the Uí Néill and Connachta held the north. His father Finguine mac Cathail, his uncle Ailill mac Cathail, his grandfather Cathal Cú-cen-máthair and his great-grandfather Cathal mac Áedo had all been kings of Cashel. His mother Gormgel and his wife Caillech both came from the Uí Liatháin, southern neighbours of his sept.

In 721 Cathal and Murchad mac Brain, king of Leinster, wasted Mag Breg, the lands of the southern Uí Néill, and the high king Fergal mac Máele Dúin struck back at Leinster. The partisan Annals of Inisfallen claim that Fergal then submitted to Cathal. After Fergal was killed by the Leinstermen at the Battle of Allen on 11 December 722, the Uí Néill kings were weak for some years, and Cathal sought to extend his power over Leinster, but Áed mac Colggen of the Uí Cheinnselaig defeated him in 731 and again in 735, when well nigh countless Munstermen died and Cathal escaped.

In 733 Domnall Midi of Clann Cholmáin drove him off from Tailtiu, though he defeated Fallomon mac Con Congalt at the Hill of Ward and the Leinstermen at Bealach Ele in 734. In 737 he met the high king Áed Allán at Terryglass; the historian Byrne doubts that Cathal accepted his authority, and the law of Patrick was then proclaimed in force across Ireland.

Cathal is widely regarded as the most powerful Irish king of the first half of the 8th century and the strongest historical king from Munster before Brian Bóruma. His son Artrí mac Cathail was also king of Cashel, and the O'Keeffes of County Cork descend from his line. Later Middle Irish tales made him a character, not always sympathetic: in the satire Aislinge Meic Con Glinne a demon of gluttony, planted by spells on apples, possesses him and brings famine to Munster until the scholar Mac Conglinne cures him.
catharism: Few Cathar texts survive, and much of what is known of Cathar thought comes from Catholic denunciations of the movement. Most historians of the 20th century agreed that its beliefs came from the East, from the weakening Byzantine Empire, along the trade routes, and spread from the First Bulgarian Empire towards the Netherlands. The movement appears to have been strongly influenced by the Bogomils of the First Bulgarian Empire, and may have begun among followers of the Paulician movement in Armenia and eastern Anatolia who were resettled in Thrace. The name Cathar, from the Greek for the pure ones, was coined by Catholic theologians; in their own texts the believers called themselves Good Men, Good Women or Good Christians.

According to Catholic sources, Cathars held that there were two Gods, a good God of the spiritual realm and an evil god who made the physical world and whom they identified with Satan. Some communities held a mitigated dualism, in which Satan had once been the true God's servant before he rebelled; others, probably a majority over time, held an absolute dualism of two equal principles. Human souls were thought to be sexless spirits trapped in matter, reincarnated until they were freed through the consolamentum, a rite that removed sin and made the believer a Perfect. The Cathars honoured Jesus but denied his physical incarnation and resurrection.

The Perfecti lived in austerity, avoided animal food and anything produced by sexual reproduction, and travelled in pairs to minister to the people. Ordinary believers were called credentes. Women could be Perfect and administer the consolamentum. By about 1140 a liturgy and doctrine had been set, and bishoprics were created, first at Albi around 1165, then at Toulouse, Carcassonne and Agen after the council of 1167 at Saint-Félix-Lauragais.

Papal missions from 1147 onwards had little lasting effect. In January 1208 the papal legate Pierre de Castelnau was murdered after excommunicating Raymond VI, Count of Toulouse. The crusade that followed besieged Béziers on 22 July 1209, and the Treaty of Paris of 1229 ended the official war, leaving the princes of Languedoc dispossessed of much of their lands. Persecution by the Inquisition continued: Peire Autier, leader of a revival in the Pyrenean foothills, was executed at Toulouse in April 1310, and the last known Perfect in Languedoc, Guillaume Bélibaste, in 1321.

Since the 1990s some historians, notably R. I. Moore, have questioned whether Catharism existed as an organised religion at all, arguing that churchmen largely constructed it from a broader spiritual revival. The region of Cathar castles such as Montségur and Carcassonne is now called Pays cathare. The Cathars have also been tied, without sound basis, to the Holy Grail and the Knights Templar.
cathay: The name comes from the Khitans, a nomadic people who ruled the Liao dynasty in northern China from 916 to 1125 and later formed the Qara Khitai. They called themselves Qidan, but in the language of the ancient Uyghurs a final -n became -y, and this form may be the source of Khitai for later Muslim writers. It reached medieval Europe through Muslim and Russian sources. In 1026 envoys of the Liao ruler visited the Ghaznavid court, where he was called Qatā Khan. Nizam al-Mulk appears to treat Khita and China as two countries. When the Mongols destroyed the Jin in 1234, Persian historians called the conquered land Khitāy.

European and Arab travellers reaching the Mongol Empire described northern China, under the Mongols, as Cathay. The name appears in Giovanni da Pian del Carpine and William of Rubruck and in Marco Polo's account of Kublai Khan's China, while Polo, Rashid al-Din and Ibn Battuta called the south, ruled by the Song, Mangi, Manzi, Chin or Sin. Mangi came from a Chinese word meaning barbarians of the south, which the Mongols adopted. Medieval maps used it into the 16th century.

About 1340 the merchant Francesco Balducci Pegolotti compiled a guide to trade in China, which he called Cathay, noting the size of Khanbaliq and how merchants could exchange silver for paper money. The division of China ended in the late 13th century, when the Yuan conquered the south.

After the Portuguese reached the Pearl River in 1513, it was not clear to Europeans that China was Polo's Cathay, and maps often placed Cathay inland. Matteo Ricci concluded between 1583 and 1598 that Cathay was simply the Mongol name for China, partly because visitors from Muslim countries whom he met in Beijing in 1598 told him they lived in the Great Cathay. The Jesuits in India doubted this, and sent Bento de Góis overland in 1603 to 1605.

He became convinced in 1605 that he was heading for China, and died in Suzhou in Gansu. In 1654 Jacobus Golius and Martino Martini matched the divisions of the Chinese day described by Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, which persuaded most European scholars that the two were the same.

In English, Cathay survived as a poetic name for China until the 19th century replaced it with China. Forms of Khitay are still the usual name for China in many Turkic and Slavic languages, among them Russian Kitai.
cathedral: The word comes from the French cathédrale, from the Latin ecclesia cathedralis and cathedra, the seat. The chair, raised above clergy and laity, marked a teacher and a presiding magistrate in the ancient world, so it symbolises the bishop's role as teacher and governor of his diocese. Strictly there could be no cathedrals before the Peace of the Church in 313, when Constantine the Great adopted Christianity, since before the 4th century bishops presided standing on a raised platform. A Christian house church buried at Dura Europos in 256 had a hall for 60 to 75 standing and a platform too low for a throne.

Four functions have remained distinctive since the first cathedrals: a regular cycle of choral prayer, a forum for civic leadership, a commitment to higher learning and the promotion of music. A secular cathedral chapter normally had four dignitaries besides the canons: the dean, precentor, chancellor and treasurer. The building is often oriented east and west with a cross-shaped plan, whose long arm is the nave, from the Latin for ship. Most cathedrals hold at least three services a day, and some, such as Aachen and Reims, were traditional coronation places of monarchs.

In the 8th century Chrodegang, Bishop of Metz, compiled a rule for cathedral clergy to live under a common roof, a modification of the Benedictine rule. Gisa, bishop of Wells from 1061 to 1088, introduced it into England, but it was not followed for long. Cathedrals did not become universal in the Western Catholic Church until the 12th century. In the English Reformation Henry VIII dissolved the monastic cathedral chapters and, except for Bath and Coventry, refounded them as chapters of canons headed by a dean. In Lutheran lands churches such as Nidaros Cathedral and Lübeck Cathedral became the seats of Protestant bishops.
cathedral-of-saint-demetrius: The cathedral was finished in 1197 and dedicated to Saint Demetrius of Thessaloniki. It was one of several large churches built by Vsevolod III, among them the much larger Cathedral of the Dormition in Vladimir, and it was originally connected directly with his palace for his personal use. The palace no longer exists. Vladimir at the end of the 12th century was a cosmopolitan artistic centre where architects and artisans from both east and west worked, and Vsevolod, whose mother was a Byzantine princess, had spent several years of his childhood in Constantinople.

The church is built of local white limestone blocks and is cubic in form, like earlier churches at Bogolyubovo, especially the Church of the Intercession on the Nerl of 1165. Four interior columns carry the drum and cupola. Each outer wall is divided into three bays, the middle one larger, each crowned by a zakomara and divided at mid-height by a horizontal arcade frieze; the windows and doors are deeply recessed and richly carved.

Shallow reliefs cover the upper half of the walls and the drum. Their sources seem to be a mixture of earlier Bogolyubovo churches, Balkan and Armenian churches and perhaps portable carvings such as Byzantine ivories. Most show plants, real and imaginary animals and ornamental patterns, which may draw on pagan beliefs, Russian folklore or Christian themes. Each zakomara holds a figural scene: King David among angels and chimeras on the west front, David with warrior saints on the south, and Solomon, Alexander the Great, Hercules, Christ, Mary and churchmen elsewhere, while the north front shows the donor, Vsevolod, with his sons. By linking the prince to ancient kings, biblical figures and military leaders, the programme reinforced his authority.

Inside, a few frescoes of the late 12th century survive above and around the west entrance. The finest faces of saints and angels in the Last Judgement are probably the work of Byzantine masters, with Russian pupils completing drapery and background. The building was renovated many times; the most extensive work, in 1832, removed structures that had joined it to the palace and replaced some outer blocks with newly carved ones. It was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1992 and is part of the Vladimir-Suzdal open-air museum.
cathedral-of-saint-tryphon: The cathedral stands on the site of an older church built in 809 by Andrija Saracenis, a citizen of Kotor, to keep the remains of Saint Tryphon, known locally as Sveti Tripun, after they were brought from Constantinople. The present building was consecrated on 19 June 1166 and became one of the largest and most ornate buildings of the city. It is one of two Roman Catholic cathedrals in Montenegro and the seat of the Diocese of Kotor, which covers the whole Bay of Kotor and the Municipality of Budva.

After the 1667 Dubrovnik earthquake the cathedral was rebuilt, but there were not enough funds for a complete reconstruction. The earthquake of April 1979, which devastated the coast of Montenegro, damaged it badly again. On 2 December 2000, after a renovation of 14 years, Josip Bozanić, Archbishop of Zagreb and President of the Croatian Bishops' Conference, blessed the restored church. The careful restoration of parts of its interior continued for some years afterwards. The building also served in the past as the city hall.

The Romanesque church holds frescoes of the 14th century, a stone ornament above the main altar showing the life of Saint Tryphon, and a relief of saints in gold and silver. Its treasury includes a silver hand and a cross decorated with ornaments and figures in relief. The saint appears on Kotor's coat of arms together with a lion and the Mount of San Giovanni, and the cathedral is the city's best-known landmark and symbol.
cathedral-of-the-holy-cross-aghtamar: King Gagik I Artsruni, who reigned from 908 to 943 or 944, chose Aghtamar island as one of his residences and founded a settlement there, of which the cathedral is the only structure still standing. The architect-monk Manuel built it of pink volcanic tuff as a palatine church; the interior measures 14.80 m by 11.5 m and the dome rises 20.40 m above the ground. Its plan follows a form developed in Armenia several centuries earlier, best known from the seventh-century Saint Hripsime Church in Echmiadzin.

In later centuries the church belonged to a monastic complex whose ruins lie to the south. From 1116 to 1895 the island was the seat of the Catholicosate of Aghtamar; its last Catholicos, Khachatur III, died in 1895. In 1915, during the Armenian genocide, the church was looted and the monastic buildings destroyed, and in July 1916 the Ottoman Empire abolished the Catholicosate. The church was then neglected and vandalised, and in the 1950s the island served as a military training ground. When the writer Yaşar Kemal visited in 1951 and found it about to be demolished, he used his contacts to stop the destruction.

Between 20 May 2005 and 21 July 2006 the Turkish Ministry of Culture restored the church at a stated cost of 2 million Turkish lira, and it reopened as a museum on 29 March 2007. Critics objected that it was not reopened for worship, that it was named Akdamar rather than Aghtamar, and that no cross was permitted; Cengiz Çandar called the handling part of a cultural genocide, while the historian Ara Sarafian called the project an important peace offering. A liturgy was held on 19 September 2010, and a cross has stood on the dome since 2 October 2010.

The reliefs of mostly biblical scenes on the outer walls have been interpreted in many ways. Some scholars see parallels with Umayyad art, such as a turbaned prince and wine imagery, and with royal Sassanian imagery such as griffins, while scenes of Eden, the serpent, Adam and Eve resemble the reliefs of the Hagia Sophia church in Trebizond.
catherine-cornaro: Catherine was born on 25 November 1454, a daughter of the Venetian Marco Cornaro, a knight of the Holy Roman Empire, and Fiorenza Crispo, whose family was of Greek descent. Her brother was Giorgio Cornaro. The Cornaro family had produced four doges and had long associations with Cyprus, where it administered sugar mills in the Episkopi area and exported Cypriot products to Venice.

After the death of King John II of Cyprus in 1458, his daughter Charlotte and his illegitimate son James disputed the succession. In 1468 Catherine was offered to James as a wife through negotiations by her father and uncle. The marriage was highly advantageous to Venice, which could then secure its commercial rights in Cyprus. They married by proxy in Venice on 30 July 1468, when she was 14, and she sailed to Cyprus in November 1472 and married him in person at Famagusta.

James died soon after the wedding after a sudden illness, and Catherine, who was pregnant, acted as regent under his will. A plot to depose the infant James III in favour of Charlotte broke out once the Venetian fleet had left, and Catherine was kept prisoner until the Venetians returned and restored order. When James III died in August 1474, probably from illness though rumour blamed Venice or Charlotte's partisans, Catherine became monarch. The kingdom had been a tributary state of the Mamluks since 1426, and under her the island was controlled by Venetian merchants.

In 1488 Venice feared an attack on Cyprus by Sultan Bayezid II and had discovered a plot to marry Catherine to Alfonso II of Naples. It recalled her to Venice and persuaded her to cede her rights, and on 14 March 1489 she was forced to abdicate. The chronicler Georgios Boustronios records that she wept as she left Nicosia for Famagusta on 15 February 1489, and the people wept with her.

Catherine kept the title of queen and was made lady of Asolo, in the Veneto, which gained a reputation as a court of literary and artistic distinction, and was the fictitious setting for Pietro Bembo's dialogues on love, Gli Asolani. She lived there until 1509, when the League of Cambrai sacked the town. She fled to Venice, where she died on 10 July 1510, and was entombed in the Church of San Salvador.
Giorgione, Gentile Bellini, Albrecht Dürer and Titian painted her. Her life was the basis of operas by Franz Lachner and Fromental Halévy in 1841 and by Gaetano Donizetti in 1844.
catherine-de-medici: Catherine was born Caterina Maria Romula de' Medici in Florence, the only child of Lorenzo de' Medici, Duke of Urbino, and Madeleine de la Tour d'Auvergne, countess of Boulogne. Her parents had married the year before at Amboise as part of an alliance between Francis I of France and Lorenzo's uncle Pope Leo X. Within a month of her birth both parents were dead. She was raised first by her grandmother Alfonsina Orsini and then by her aunt Clarice de' Medici, and from 1523 lived under the protection of her cousin Pope Clement VII. In Florence she was called duchessina, the little duchess.

Clement arranged her marriage to Henry, second son of Francis I. The wedding took place in Marseille on 28 October 1533, when both were fourteen. When Henry's elder brother died in 1536 Catherine became dauphine, and with no child for years she was told that divorce was being discussed.

As queen from 1547 she had almost no political influence: Henry gave the Château of Chenonceau, which she had wanted, to his mistress Diane de Poitiers, who stood at the centre of power. Henry's accidental death in 1559 left her the mother of the fifteen-year-old Francis II, whose reign the Guise brothers dominated. When Francis died in 1560 she became regent for the ten-year-old Charles IX and presided over his council.
