She summoned church leaders to the Colloquy of Poissy, which failed in October 1561, and in January 1562 issued the tolerant Edict of Saint-Germain.

On 1 March 1562 the Duke of Guise and his men attacked Huguenots worshipping at Vassy, killing 74; the massacre lit the fuse of the French Wars of Religion, and for thirty years France was in civil war or armed truce. Catherine at first made concessions to the Huguenots but failed to grasp the theology that drove them, and later turned to hardline policies. She was blamed for the persecutions under her sons, above all the St Bartholomew's Day massacre of 1572. After Charles IX died in 1574 she supported Henry III, her favourite son, until the last few weeks of her life.

Catherine believed in the humanist ideal of the learned prince and, once she controlled the royal purse, ran a programme of artistic patronage for three decades. An inventory after her death shows tapestries, maps, sculptures and hundreds of portraits, many by Jean Clouet and his son François Clouet.

Some historians excuse her from blame for the worst decisions of the crown, though her letters show ruthlessness. Without her, it is unlikely that her sons would have remained in power, and she has been called the most important woman in Europe in the 16th century.
catherine-jagiellon: Catherine Jagiellon was born in Kraków on 1 November 1526, the youngest daughter of King Sigismund I the Old and Bona Sforza of Milan. Italian tutors gave her a thorough Renaissance education in Latin, German and Italian, riding, dancing, singing and music. After her father's death in 1548 she moved to Masovia with her mother and sisters, and in 1556 her brother Sigismund II Augustus placed her and her sister Anna in the Palace of Vilnius to ensure a royal presence in Lithuania.

She married late for a princess because her family wanted a marriage of the highest political status for Poland, and several proposals came to nothing. In August 1560 Ivan the Terrible, recently widowed, proposed himself, but the two sides could not agree on terms and talks ended in January 1561. Her brother also wished for an alliance with Sweden against Russia over Livonia.

On 4 October 1562 Catherine married Duke John of Finland, second son of Gustav I, in the Lower Castle of Vilnius, in a Catholic ceremony. John had not obtained the permission of his half-brother, King Eric XIV. The couple set up house at Turku Castle, and when Eric sent 10,000 men to besiege it, the castle capitulated on 12 August 1563. They were imprisoned at Gripsholm Castle. Eric offered to let Catherine return to Poland, but she chose to remain with John; tradition says she pointed to the inscription in her wedding ring, Nemo nisi mors. Eric allowed her greater freedom than her husband but refused her access to Catholic priests.

She played some part in the rebellion that deposed Eric in 1568, and she entered Stockholm in a grand procession on 7 November 1568. She was crowned queen of Sweden in the spring of 1569, and kept a Catholic chapel at court, which shocked Protestants. She influenced John III in foreign policy, in his interest in Renaissance art and above all in a religious policy favouring Catholicism, negotiating with the pope and Cardinal Hosius for a Counter-Reformation. His new church order, the Red Book, brought back Catholic customs and set off a liturgical struggle that lasted twenty years. She raised her son Sigismund as a Catholic.

Catherine suffered from gout in her last years. She died in Stockholm on 16 September 1583 and was buried in the royal crypt of Uppsala Cathedral, where Willem Boy's tomb monument for her can still be seen. Her son Sigismund inherited the Polish–Lithuanian throne in 1587 and the Swedish throne in 1592 but ruled Sweden for only seven years before being deposed in 1599. He and his descendants, as Catholic kings, went on laying claim to Sweden over the following century.
catherine-of-braganza: Catherine was born on 25 November 1638 at the Ducal Palace of Vila Viçosa, the daughter of Luisa de Guzmán and the Duke of Braganza, who became John IV of Portugal on 1 December 1640. She spent most of her youth in a convent near the royal palace, and a contemporary remarked that she had hardly been ten times out of the palace in her life. Her mother led the marriage negotiations from 1656. A Marriage Treaty was signed on 23 June 1661, despite English preference for a Protestant bride and Spanish objections. A key factor was the dowry, which included Tangier and Bombay, trading privileges in Brazil and the Portuguese East Indies, and two million Portuguese crowns.

Catherine arrived at Portsmouth on 13 May 1662 and married Charles II on 21 May in two ceremonies, a secret Catholic one and a public Church of England service. Her Catholicism made her unpopular and barred her from Church of England services, so she was never crowned. She suffered at least three miscarriages and produced no heir, while Charles acknowledged many children by his mistresses. His advisers suggested divorce, but he refused. She kept out of English politics.

In the Popish Plot of 1678 Titus Oates accused her of plotting to poison the king and, on 28 November, of high treason. The House of Lords, by an overwhelming majority, refused to impeach her, and Charles's intervention lifted the threat of a trial. She is credited with popularising tea drinking in England.

After Charles's death in 1685 she lived at Somerset House. She left England in March 1692 and reached Portugal in January 1693. She served as regent for her brother Peter II in 1704 to 1705. She died at the Bemposta Palace in Lisbon on 31 December 1705 and was buried in the Pantheon of the House of Braganza. The Seven Islands of Bombay, part of her dowry, were ceded to the English Crown in 1661 and passed by Charles II to the East India Company in 1668, and Bombay became a major city of India. There is no historical evidence that Queens in New York was named for her, though it is often said to be.
catherine-of-hungary-queen-of-serbia: Catherine, born about 1256, was the second of six children of Stephen V of Hungary and his wife Elizabeth, daughter of the Cuman chieftain Seyhan; her paternal grandparents were Béla IV of Hungary and Maria Laskarina. Her sister Elizabeth also became a queen of Serbia by marrying Stefan Milutin, the brother of Catherine's husband. Béla IV had secured his southern border by placing men closely tied to the royal family in Srem and Slavonia, and dynastic marriage served the same end.

In 1268 Stephen Uroš I of Serbia failed in an attempt to conquer Macsó, and about that year Catherine was married to his son Stefan Dragutin. A Byzantine envoy who came to the Serbian court around 1268 for marriage negotiations described it with disdain: the king lived more simply than a middling official in Constantinople, and his Hungarian daughter-in-law worked at her spinning wheel in a cheap dress.

After Dragutin yielded the Serbian throne to Milutin in 1282, he held lands south of the Sava from Ladislaus IV, and it was largely through his marriage to Catherine that he received them. Late in life Dragutin turned away from his Hungarian connections, became the monk Teoktist and died in 1316; he was buried at the Đurđevi Stupovi monastery near Novi Pazar.

When Ladislaus IV died childless, Catherine's children had a claim to the Hungarian throne, but her distant cousin Andrew III inherited it instead. Her son Stefan Vladislav II of Syrmia remained a pretender to Hungary even after Andrew's death in 1301, in competition with her nephews; one of them, Charles Martel of Anjou, gave mother and son the province of Slavonia, though it was not his to give. Her other children were Elizabeth of Serbia and Urošica, who became a monk. The date of her death is not known.
catherine-of-navarre: Catherine was the younger daughter of Gaston of Foix, Prince of Viana, and Magdalena of Valois, the sister of Louis XI of France. She was born during the reign of her great-grandfather King John II, who was succeeded in 1479 by her grandmother Eleanor. Their father had already died, so when Eleanor died the same year the crown passed to Catherine's brother Francis Phoebus. She was also Duchess of Gandia, Montblanc and Peñafiel, Countess of Foix, Bigorre and Ribagorza, and Viscountess of Béarn.

The death of Francis in 1483 made Catherine queen under the regency of their mother. Her uncle John of Foix claimed the throne, appealing to the Salic Law, and began a civil war (1483–1492) that revived the old conflict of the Beaumont and Agramont parties. In 1484 Magdalena decided to marry the 15-year-old Catherine to John of Albret, from a noble family of western Gascony. The wedding took place at Lescar in 1486, but the coronation in Pamplona was deferred until 1494. When Aragon took Magdalena hostage in 1494, Catherine took control of the government herself, at twenty-six.

Ferdinand II of Aragon had allied with the Pope against France and presented claims to the royal family of Navarre. Catherine did not accept them, and Ferdinand sent Fadrique Álvarez de Toledo, 2nd Duke of Alba, who occupied Pamplona on 25 July 1512.

Catherine and John III fled to Béarn and based themselves at Pau, Orthez and Tarbes. On 23 March 1513 the Cortes of Navarre, reduced to the pro-Spanish Beaumont party, pledged allegiance to Ferdinand, and in 1515 Upper Navarre was annexed to the Crown of Castile. In 1516 John III and Pedro, Marshal of Navarre, crossed the Pyrenees to reconquer the kingdom but failed to reach its heartland. John died on 17 June 1516, and Catherine died at Mont-de-Marsan on 12 February 1517. From 1512 she was queen in fact only in parts of Lower Navarre, north of the Pyrenees. She had thirteen children, and her son Henry II of Navarre was born in 1503.
catherine-the-great: Catherine was born on 2 May 1729 as Princess Sophie Auguste Friederike von Anhalt-Zerbst-Dornburg in Stettin, now Szczecin, in the Kingdom of Prussia. Her father, Christian August, Prince of Anhalt-Zerbst, was a Prussian general and governor of Stettin, and her mother was Joanna Elisabeth of Holstein-Gottorp. At 16 she married Peter, a grandson of Peter the Great. Her choice as his wife followed the Lopukhina affair, in which Frederick the Great of Prussia took part, aiming to strengthen friendship between Prussia and Russia and weaken Austrian influence.

Peter became emperor in 1762 and reigned for seven months before he was deposed, and possibly assassinated, at the hands of Catherine, who overthrew him in a coup. She was crowned at the Assumption Cathedral in Moscow on 22 September 1762. Her reign of over 34 years extended the borders of the empire by some 520,000 square kilometres, absorbing New Russia, Crimea, the North Caucasus, Right-bank Ukraine, Belarus, Lithuania and Courland, mainly at the expense of the Ottoman Empire and the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. She installed her former lover Stanisław Poniatowski on the throne of Poland, which was eventually partitioned.

She continued Peter the Great's modernisation of Russia along Western European lines. She founded the Smolny Institute of Noble Maidens, the first state-financed higher education institution for women in Europe, and in 1795 the Imperial Public Library. The Hermitage began as her personal collection, and she had herself inoculated against smallpox in 1768. Serfdom, however, remained the basis of conscription and the economy, and the demands of the state and landowners intensified the exploitation of serf labour, one of the chief reasons for rebellions such as Pugachev's Rebellion.

According to a census of 1754 to 1762 she owned 500,000 serfs, and she gave away 100,000 in one day, 18 August 1795. She nationalised Church lands to help pay for her wars and suppressed religious dissent after the onset of the French Revolution. She died on 17 November 1796.
catholic-church: The name Catholic, from the Greek katholikos, 'universal', is first attested as an adjective for the church in the early second century. The first known use of the phrase "the catholic church" is in a letter written around 100 CE by Ignatius of Antioch to the Smyrnaeans. In 380 the emperor Theodosius I issued the edict De fide catolica when he established the state church of the Roman Empire.

The church teaches that its public ministry began at Pentecost, fifty days after the day on which Christ is believed to have risen, when the apostles are held to have received the Holy Spirit. Because Christians refused to join pagan festivals and civic rituals, some authorities feared they were angering the gods, and the resulting prosecutions lasted until Christianity was legalised in the 4th century.

The church separated from the Church of the East after the Council of Ephesus in 431 and from the Oriental Orthodox Churches after the Council of Chalcedon in 451. Its separation from the Eastern Orthodox churches developed gradually, with the Great Schism of 1054, and was solidified by the Fourth Crusade, amid disputes over papal authority.

During the Age of Discovery, Spanish, Portuguese and French explorers, conquistadors and missionaries spread Catholicism to the Americas, Asia and Oceania. Pope Alexander VI awarded sovereignty over most of the new lands to Spain and Portugal, later confirmed by the Treaty of Tordesillas. The Protestant Reformation of the 16th century prompted the Counter-Reformation. In 1798 the French general Louis-Alexandre Berthier imprisoned Pope Pius VI, who died in captivity, and Napoleon re-established the church in France through the Concordat of 1801. In the 1960s Pope John XXIII convened the Second Vatican Council.

The church follows an episcopal polity with three levels of clergy: bishops, who hold jurisdiction over a diocese or eparchy, priests, and deacons. It is led by the bishop of Rome, the pope, whose jurisdiction is called the Holy See and who is served by the Roman Curia. Of its 24 autonomous churches, the Latin Church is the largest. The church teaches that Christ instituted seven sacraments, among them baptism, the Eucharist and penance.

It is the largest non-governmental provider of education and medical services in the world, and in 2010 its Pontifical Council for Pastoral Assistance to Health Care Workers said it managed 26 per cent of health care facilities. Pope Leo XIII's encyclical Rerum novarum of 1891 laid the foundations of its social teaching.
catholicate-of-abkhazia: When the Catholicate was established is uncertain. Some scholars place it in the 9th or 10th century, when the bishoprics of Abkhazia shifted their allegiance from Constantinople to Mtskheta. Titular catholicoi of Abkhazia first appear in sources of the 11th century, though they probably did not enjoy full independence. The first written account of the Catholicate dates from 1290, and some scholars place its foundation in the 13th century, when Mongol rule had divided Georgia and the western kings of Imereti were de facto independent of the Mongol Ilkhanid dynasty.

Full independence came in the 15th century, after Georgia's political fragmentation, since the kings of Imereti wanted a church of their own while Mtskheta lay in their rivals' lands. The change is usually linked to the consecration of Archbishop Joachime of Tsaish and Bedia as catholicos by Michael IV, Patriarch of Antioch, during the reign of Bagrat VI (1463–1478); Michael's document, The Law of Faith, held that western and eastern Georgia had been converted separately. The catholicoi later took the title of patriarch, with dioceses such as Bichvinta, Kutaisi, Gelati, Tsageri, Bedia and Mokvi.

In the late 16th century Catholicos Patriarch Eudemos I moved his residence from Bichvinta to Gelati, fleeing the Ottoman advance into Abkhazia; he carried out reforms and restored communion with the Patriarchate of Georgia while keeping his independence. The catholicoi usually came from prominent noble families. The Islamization of Abkhazia, Adjara and Lower Guria under Ottoman rule dealt the church a severe blow, though Christianity revived in Guria and parts of Abkhazia in the late 18th century. Russia conquered Imereti in 1810.

The catholicoi regarded themselves as vicars of St. Andrew, who in medieval Georgian tradition had preached in western Georgia, the Colchis of classical writers, and their official style named Imereti, Odishi, Ponto-Abkhaz-Guria, Racha-Lechkhum-Svaneti, the Ossetians and the Dvals. After 1814 their dioceses remained in the Exarchate of Georgia until the unified Georgian Orthodox Church regained its autocephaly in 1917. In 2009 an Abkhazian Orthodox Church was founded as a continuation of the Catholicate; it is not recognised as canonical within the Eastern Orthodox Church.
catholicism: The word catholic comes from the Greek katholikos, meaning universal, and is first attested as a description of the church in the early second century. The first known use of the phrase the catholic church is in a letter written around 100 CE by Ignatius of Antioch to the Smyrnaeans. In 380 Theodosius I issued the edict De fide catolica when he established the state church of the Roman Empire.

The Catholic Church teaches that its public ministry began at Pentecost, and that the pope, the bishop of Rome, is the successor of Saint Peter. Scholars differ on the origin of the office. Some hold that Peter was the first bishop of Rome; others argue that the papacy does not depend on that view. Bart D. Ehrman and Raymond E. Brown note that a structure with a single bishop and several presbyters was adopted in Rome only in the mid-2nd century.

The church follows an episcopal polity with three levels of clergy: bishops, who hold jurisdiction over a diocese or eparchy; priests; and deacons. The pope's jurisdiction is called the Holy See, which governs through the Roman Curia. The church consists of 24 autonomous churches, of which the largest is the Latin Church and the other 23 are Eastern Catholic Churches, whose differing rites reflect historical and cultural diversity rather than differences in belief.

Catholic doctrine is rooted in the Nicene Creed. The church holds that revelation has two modes of transmission, Sacred Scripture and Sacred Tradition, authentically interpreted by the Magisterium, its teaching authority. It teaches that Christ instituted seven sacraments. The Eucharist, offered in the Mass, is seen as the source and summit of Christian life: Catholics believe that through consecration by a priest the bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ.

Divisions shaped the church's relations with other Christians. The Church of the East separated after the Council of Ephesus in 431 and the Oriental Orthodox Churches after the Council of Chalcedon in 451. The separation from the Eastern Orthodox churches developed gradually, in disputes especially over papal authority, and was solidified by the Fourth Crusade. The Protestant Reformation of the 16th century led to new Christian traditions and prompted the Catholic Counter‑Reformation.

Catholic social teaching, whose foundations are widely held to have been laid by Pope Leo XIII's encyclical Rerum novarum in 1891, stresses care for the poor and the sick. The church is the largest non-government provider of education and medical services in the world.
catilinarian-conspiracy: Catiline was a patrician and nobilis with strong connections to the aristocracy who had been complicit in the regime of Sulla. He was prosecuted in 65 and 64 BCE but acquitted after several former consuls spoke in his defence. He had stood for the consulship three times by 63 BCE and been rejected each time. Only after his defeat in the consular elections of 63 did he begin to plan a coup to seize by force the consulship he had been denied.

He drew into his circle senators such as Publius Cornelius Lentulus Sura and Gaius Cornelius Cethegus, along with men who had been denied advancement, and non-senators including dispossessed farmers and indebted veterans of Sulla. Scholars reject debt as the sole cause and consider the shame of unmet political ambition indispensable. The conspiracy was for the benefit of Roman citizens only, not slaves, and Catiline planned a coup, not a social revolution.

In autumn 63 BCE the consul Cicero heard rumours of a plot from a woman named Fulvia. On 18 or 19 October Marcus Licinius Crassus handed over letters describing plans to massacre prominent citizens. The senate declared a state of emergency and passed the senatus consultum ultimum. By 27 October it had reports that Gaius Manlius, a former centurion, had taken up arms near Faesulae in Etruria. After the attempts on Cicero's life failed on 7 November, he delivered his first oration against Catiline in the senate, and Catiline left the city to join Manlius. The senate declared both public enemies.

In December Cicero used envoys of the Gallic Allobroges to identify conspirators in Rome, and on 2 or 3 December five men were arrested, among them Lentulus and Cethegus. In the senate debate Julius Caesar proposed life imprisonment, but the speech of Cato the Younger carried the day, and Cicero had the five executed without trial. Early the next year Catiline's army, of at least three thousand men, was defeated near Pistoria under Marcus Petreius, and Catiline was killed.

Cicero was hailed as father of the fatherland, but the tribune Quintus Caecilius Metellus Nepos sought to prosecute him for executing citizens without trial, and in 58 BCE Publius Clodius Pulcher passed a law banishing anyone who had done so, after which Cicero went into exile. The main sources, Sallust and Cicero's orations, are both hostile to Catiline. Most classicists agree that the conspiracy occurred more or less as described, but that its threat was exaggerated, and some scholars, such as Erich Gruen, see it as not shaking the foundations of the state.
catiline: Catiline belonged to the patrician gens Sergia, which claimed descent from a Trojan companion of Aeneas, though no Sergius had been consul since 429 BCE. His father was poor by aristocratic standards. He served under Gnaeus Pompeius Strabo in the Social War and joined Sulla in 82 BCE. Ancient sources say he grew rich in Sulla's proscriptions, and Cicero accused him of killing his brother and two brothers-in-law, among them Marcus Marius Gratidianus. Some modern historians doubt his part in Gratidianus's death and see Cicero's story as political slander. He certainly profited by buying estates cheaply, and by the end of Sulla's dictatorship he was rich.

Catiline was praetor by 68 BCE and governed Africa in 67–66. On his return he was refused as a candidate for the consulship, and embassies from Africa protested his maladministration. A trial for corruption in 65 BCE ended in acquittal, with former consuls speaking for him. In the elections for 64 BCE, bankrolled by Caesar and Crassus, he lost to Cicero and Gaius Antonius Hybrida. A second prosecution for murder in the proscriptions also ended in acquittal. He stood again for 62 BCE and lost to Decimus Junius Silanus and Lucius Licinius Murena, after Cicero had presided at the elections in a cuirass and with a bodyguard.

Defeated, Catiline gathered dispossessed farmers, ruined Sullan veterans and senators whose careers had stalled, and a rising in Etruria began under Gaius Manlius. In October 63 BCE Crassus gave Cicero anonymous letters warning of a massacre, and the senate passed its emergency decree. Cicero denounced Catiline in the senate on 7 November, and Catiline left Rome, proclaimed himself consul at Faesulae, and was declared a public enemy. Cicero, with the aid of Gallic envoys, caught the conspirators who had stayed in Rome, and they were executed without trial on 5 December.

After the executions much of Catiline's army melted away, leaving perhaps just over three thousand men, and the Apennine passes to Gaul were blocked. He turned to fight at Pistoria, possibly on 3 January 62 BCE, where Marcus Petreius broke his centre. Sallust wrote that Catiline's men fell where they had stood and that he was found far ahead of them among the slain, still breathing. His name became a byword for villainy, and Sallust made him a symbol of the Republic's moral decline. The evidence is overwhelmingly Ciceronean, and some modern historians have argued that Cicero exaggerated or helped to create the conspiracy, though such defences are largely speculative.
cato-the-elder: Marcus Porcius Cato was born in the municipal town of Tusculum, like some generations of his ancestors. His family was plebeian and noted for military service, but the Tusculan Porcii had never held Roman magistracy, so at the start of his career in Rome he was regarded as a novus homo, a new man. After his father's death he inherited a small property in Sabine territory and spent his childhood overseeing the farm. Nearby stood the hut of Manius Curius Dentatus, whose simple character he admired and sought to imitate. The surname Cato comes from the Latin catus, indicating common sense that results from natural wisdom combined with experience.

Cato served in the Second Punic War, at Capua in 214, at the siege of Tarentum in 209, and, it is recorded, at the Battle of the Metaurus, where Hasdrubal Barca was slain. He was quaestor under Scipio Africanus in Sicily, where the two quarrelled over Scipio's alleged extravagance. Elected consul in 195 with his patron Lucius Valerius Flaccus, he enacted the first two of the Porcian Laws, which expanded the protection of Roman citizens against degrading or capricious punishment. In the debate over repealing the Oppian Law, which restricted women's luxury, he made an inflexible speech against repeal, but the law was repealed. In 191 he served as a legate at the Battle of Thermopylae against Antiochus III.

As censor from 184 he revised the lists of senators and knights with unsparing severity, expelling men he judged unworthy. He repaired the aqueducts, extended the sewage system and prevented private persons from drawing off public water. In addition he raised the amount paid by the publicani for tax collection and reduced contract prices for public works, which created controversy. Opposed to Hellenistic influence, he urged the dismissal of the philosophers Carneades, Diogenes and Critolaus when they came to Rome as ambassadors from Athens. He often ended his speeches by saying Carthago delenda est, Carthage must be destroyed.

Cato was the first to write history in Latin, in his Origines, a now fragmentary work on the history of Rome. His manual on running a farm, De agri cultura, written about 160, is his only work that survives complete and is the oldest extant prose in Latin. It is a miscellaneous collection of rules of husbandry and management, with sidelights on country life in the 2nd century BCE, and it assumes a farm run and staffed by slaves. Some have argued that without the impact of his writing Latin might have been supplanted by Greek as the literary language of Rome. His date of birth is deduced from conflicting reports of his age at death in 149 BCE; Cicero and Pliny give 234 BCE.
cato-the-younger: Cato was born in 95 BCE, the son of a father of the same name and of Livia, and was descended from Cato the Elder, his great-grandfather, the first of the family to be elected consul. He and his sister Porcia were orphaned, probably before he was four, and were taken in by their maternal uncle Marcus Livius Drusus. Stories of his childhood are broadly unreliable and were told to suggest that his adult character was formed early. Plutarch reports that he studied Stoicism under Antipater of Tyre. He also adopted an austere, deliberately old-fashioned public manner: he walked rather than rode, went barefoot and wore a toga without a tunic, in imitation of statues of Rome's early founders and heroes.

As an urban quaestor at the state treasury he prosecuted and dismissed a number of its clerks and was praised for his honesty. As plebeian tribune in 62 BCE he passed laws to expand the grain dole and to force generals to give up their armies before standing in elections, and he blocked a bill of Pompey's allies. In 61 BCE he refused Pompey's offer of a marriage alliance with one of his nieces. He opposed, with varying success, the legislation of Caesar's first consulship in 59 BCE. He was praised for his honest administration in Cyprus and was elected praetor for 54 BCE.

The First Triumvirate was formed to get around his obstruction. From about 52 BCE he tried to separate Pompey from Caesar and spread the view that Caesar was a tyrant in the making. Cato seems never to have advocated civil war, but he was criticised for being too uncompromising, and many scholars hold that his strategy contributed to the war that began in January 49 BCE.

In the civil war Cato joined Pompey and tried to limit the deaths of fellow citizens. In Africa he commanded Utica and strengthened its defences. Metellus Scipio rejected his advice of attrition, fought at Thapsus and was annihilated. Cato evacuated the Roman citizens who wished to flee, sent his family and allies to seek pardon and took his own life rather than accept what he saw as Caesar's tyrannical pardon.

His death produced eulogies by Cicero and Brutus; Caesar replied with an Anticato, which has not survived. Kit Morell argues that the ancient portrait of a Stoic martyr has distorted the historical Cato.
cattaraugus-reservation: The reservation stretches inland from Lake Erie along Cattaraugus Creek, on either side of New York State Route 438, and is divided among Cattaraugus, Chautauqua and Erie counties. It borders the towns of Brant, North Collins and Collins in Erie County, Perrysburg in Cattaraugus County and Hanover in Chautauqua County. Its people are mainly Seneca, with some Cayuga; both belong to the Six Nations of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy. The land is largely rural, and it is divided into communities such as Newtown, Bucktown, Pinewoods, Eleven Acres, Ozarks and Indian Hill.

The first Cattaraugus lands were reserved to the Seneca under the Treaty of Big Tree of 1797, and in 1802 the Seneca exchanged them for a tract reaching inland along Cattaraugus Creek. An agreement of 1826 purported to convey about eight square miles of the reservation to private buyers. The disputed Second Treaty of Buffalo Creek of 1838 threatened the Seneca with removal, but the Third Treaty of Buffalo Creek of 1842 left them in possession of Cattaraugus and Allegany. From 1855 to 1957 the Thomas Indian School, a boarding institution for Indigenous children, operated on the reservation.

The 2020 United States census counted 2,676 people on the reservation, which covers about 34.4 square miles (89.1 square km). The offices of the Seneca Nation government stand at its centre along Route 438. Interstate 90 crosses the reservation, and the Seneca Transit System links it with the Allegany territory, Gowanda and Salamanca.
catullus: Gaius Valerius Catullus was born into a leading equestrian family of Verona, in Cisalpine Gaul. The family was prominent enough for his father to entertain Julius Caesar when he was proconsul of both Gallic provinces. Poem 31 describes his happy homecoming to the family villa at Sirmio, on Lake Garda, and the family or Catullus also owned a villa near Tibur. No ancient biography survives, so his life has to be pieced together from scattered references and from his poems, and the dates of his birth and death are uncertain. Some scholars accept 84–54 BCE, supposing that his latest poems and the publication of his book coincided with the year of his death.

Catullus spent most of his young adult years in Rome. His friends there included the poets Licinius Calvus and Helvius Cinna and the biographer Cornelius Nepos, to whom he dedicated a libellus of poems. Cicero wrote in scorn about the new poets, a group probably to be identified with his circle. Caesar, Pompey and Cicero appear in his poems. According to Suetonius, Caesar did not deny that Catullus's lampoons left an indelible stain on his reputation, but when the poet apologised he invited him to dinner the same day. From summer 57 to summer 56 BCE Catullus was in Bithynia on the staff of the commander Gaius Memmius, and he travelled to the Troad to perform rites at his brother's tomb, which poem 101 records.

The Lesbia of his poems is usually identified with Clodia Metelli, sister of Publius Clodius Pulcher and wife of the consul of 60 BCE Quintus Caecilius Metellus Celer. The poems describe stages of the affair: initial euphoria, doubts, separation and a wrenching sense of loss. Catullus wavers between devoted love and bitter insult directed at her infidelity, as in poems 11 and 58.

His poems survive in an anthology of 116 carmina in three parts by form: about sixty short poems in varying metres, called polymetra, nine longer poems, and forty-eight epigrams in elegiac couplets. Poems 61 and 62 are traditional marriage hymns, and poem 64, his longest, is a miniature epic. Scholars do not agree whether Catullus arranged the order himself. The text used today rests on a manuscript that surfaced in Verona in 1305; it then disappeared again after two copies were made, one now in the Bodleian Library, Oxford. After the late 2nd century CE his poetry was relatively little known, though Jerome and Boethius refer to it.
catuvolcus: The Eburones were a Belgic people living between the Meuse and the Rhine, in what is now Belgium, and were ruled jointly by two kings, Catuvolcus and Ambiorix. Little is known of Catuvolcus before the Gallic Wars. Julius Caesar began his conquest of Gaul in 58 BCE, and the next year his forces occupied the lands of the Belgae, a confederation of tribes of northern Gaul to which the Eburones belonged.

His Gaulish name, Catu-uolcos, joins the stem catu-, battle, to uolcos and is rendered as war-wolf. It has an exact parallel in the Middle Welsh cadwalch, hero or warrior, both coming from a Proto-Celtic form, and is related to the name of the Volcae.

On returning from his second invasion of Britain in late 54 BCE, Caesar sent 15 cohorts under Quintus Titurius Sabinus and Lucius Aurunculeius Cotta to winter at Atuatuca among the Eburones. According to Caesar, the two kings received messages from Indutiomarus of the Treveri urging them to revolt. About a fortnight later Ambiorix attacked the Roman camp and was driven off, then met Cotta and Sabinus, claimed that his people had forced him into war and warned them that a large German force was about to cross the Rhine. When the Romans marched out, the Belgic forces ambushed them, massacring the troops and killing both commanders.

Caesar rebuilt his forces over the winter and in 53 BCE turned first on Ambiorix's allies among the Menapii, the Nervii and the Suebi, then devastated the lands of the Eburones; Lucius Minucius Basilus scattered Ambiorix's men with a cavalry attack before they could gather. Caesar claims that Catuvolcus, too old to bear the labours of war or of retreat, then took his own life by means of a yew tree, cursing Ambiorix as he did so for having started the revolt.
caucasian-war: The war was fought by the Russian Imperial Army and Cossack settlers against peoples of the North Caucasus, among them the Adyghe, Abazins, Ubykhs, Chechens and Dagestanis, who resisted subjugation as the tsars sought to expand. Other parts of the Caucasus were incorporated into the Russian Empire in the 19th century through Russian wars with Persia, and in 1801 Russia annexed the Georgian Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti. Russian control of the Georgian Military Road divided the conflict into the Russo-Circassian War in the west and the conquest of Chechnya and Dagestan in the east.

The war ran through the reigns of Alexander I, Nicholas I and Alexander II. The first period of the invasion achieved surprisingly little and ended around 1825 with the death of Alexander I and the Decembrist Revolt. Wars with Persia and Turkey then took the empire's attention until 1833. When fighting resumed it marked the beginning of what is now referred to as the Circassian genocide. Resistance was led by Ghazi Mollah, Hamzat Bek and Hadji Murad, and then by Imam Shamil, who led the mountaineers from 1834 until his capture in 1859.

In August 1843 Shamil's men converged on a Russian column at Untsukul, killing 486, and within four weeks took every Russian outpost in Avaria but one. In 1845 they withstood a major offensive led by Prince Vorontsov. A truce during the Crimean War ended in 1855. Between 1856 and 1859 an army of 250,000 under General Baryatinsky broke the mountaineers' resistance in the east, and Shamil surrendered and was exiled to central Russia. Fighting went on with the Circassians in the west until a manifesto of Alexander II declared hostilities at an end on 2 June 1864.

One of the war's most dramatic consequences was the mass forced emigration of mainly Muslim mountain peoples to the Ottoman Empire and, less so, to Persia. Land was confiscated and Cossack and Russian military colonists were settled in it. Circassians made up 40 per cent of the North Caucasus population in 1795, 30 per cent in 1835 and 25 per cent in 1858.

Exiles landed at Black Sea ports such as Trabzon, Samsun and Varna and were held in camps in conditions of overcrowding, disease and hunger. At Samsun up to 110,000 refugees were gathered, and in some phases more than 200 died each day. The Ottoman state sometimes settled the newcomers as militia on its borders. A few thousand applied to return in 1861-67.
caucasus: The Caucasus lies between the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea. The Greater Caucasus range in the north has conventionally been taken as a natural barrier between Europe and Asia, and Mount Elbrus, at 5,642 metres, stands in its western part. The Lesser Caucasus in the south includes the Armenian highlands. The region is divided into the North Caucasus and the South Caucasus. More than 50 ethnic groups live here. Three language families, the Kartvelian, Northwest Caucasian and Northeast Caucasian, are indigenous to the area, alongside Indo-European and Turkic languages.

Fossils found at Dmanisi in Georgia, dated to 1.8 million years ago, are the earliest clear evidence of early humans outside Africa. The Kura–Araxes culture, from about 4000 BCE to about 2000 BCE, spread over the southern Caucasus and beyond. The first Bronze Age states, among them Urartu, formed between the 15th and 10th centuries BCE. After the conquests of Alexander the Great, Colchis, Iberia, Armenia and Caucasian Albania were states strongly marked by Greek culture.

Rome and Parthia contested the region from the 1st century BCE, and later Rome and the Sasanian Empire. The Arsacid dynasty of Armenia adopted Christianity as a state religion in 301 CE, and Georgia and Caucasian Albania also became Christian. After the Muslim conquest of Persia large parts of the region came under Arab rule. In the 12th century the Georgian king David the Builder drove Muslim rulers out of the Caucasus, and under Queen Tamar, in 1194–1204, Georgia defeated Seljuk invasions and became the strongest Christian state in the Near East.

Russia expanded south after the Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca of 1774, annexed the Georgian Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti in 1801 and conquered the North Caucasus in the second half of the 19th century. In the Caucasian Wars the Russian military expelled the Circassians from their homeland. Georgia, Azerbaijan and Armenia became independent after the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991.

The Caucasus is shared today by Georgia, Armenia, Azerbaijan and the Russian Federation, whose republics there include Dagestan, Chechnya and North Ossetia–Alania. Georgia is predominantly Orthodox Christian, Armenia Armenian Apostolic and Azerbaijan Shia Muslim. The region is a biodiversity hotspot and holds oil, natural gas and many minerals.
caucasus-campaign: The Ottoman Empire's main objective was to recover territory in the Caucasus, including regions the Russian Empire had captured in the Russo-Turkish War of 1877–78. Its strategic goals were to retake Artvin, Ardahan, Kars and the port of Batum, and a campaign there would draw Russian forces away from the Polish and Galician fronts. Germany supplied the missing resources. War Minister Enver Pasha also hoped that success would open the route to Tiflis, with a revolt of Caucasian Muslims. Russia had about 100,000 men in its Caucasus Army under General Nikolai Yudenich, but had to redeploy almost half of them to the Prussian front, leaving 60,000, with much greater Armenian support.

The Russians crossed the frontier on 1 November 1914 and declared war on 2 November. The Ottoman 3rd Army began its offensive on 7 November, and Enver Pasha overrode its commander Hasan Izzet, who opposed attacking in harsh winter. The resulting Battle of Sarikamish was a disastrous defeat. Only 10 per cent of the army retreated to its starting position, and the whole IX Corps surrendered. By mid-January 1915 fewer than 18,000 of the 95,000 Turks who fought survived, and some 30,000 are said to have died of cold. In January 1916 Yudenich marched secretly on Erzurum, destroying an Ottoman division at Köprüköy on 10–18 January, and the fortress was abandoned on 16 February.

The Russian Revolution put a stop to Russian operations in 1917, and the army slowly disintegrated. In February 1918 Ottoman forces attacked the abandoned front and recovered the lost territories, with Erzincan taken on 13 February. The campaign between the Ottomans and Russia ended with the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk on 3 March 1918, and the Ottomans signed the Treaty of Batum with Armenia, Azerbaijan and Georgia on 4 June. Fighting went on against the Central Caspian Dictatorship, the Republic of Mountainous Armenia and the British Dunsterforce until the Armistice of Mudros on 30 October 1918.

Estimates of casualties vary. Edward J. Erickson, using Ottoman archives, counted 235,733 Ottoman battle casualties, while Russian sources report Ottoman losses of 300,000 or more, and Anton Kernosovsky gave Russian casualties of 119,000. During the campaign Ottoman Armenia was depopulated of much of its Armenian population in the Armenian genocide, which began in April 1915; the deaths are put between 600,000 and 1.5 million. After the war the borders in the Caucasus were still unsettled, and a Georgian–Armenian war in 1918 and an Armenian–Azerbaijani war from 1918 to 1920 followed.
caucasus-line-cossack-host: The host grew out of the Russian line of fortresses in the Caucasus. In 1777, when the line was extended west from Mozdok towards Azov, part of the Volga Cossacks was sent there and settled in five stanitsas between the Catherine and Alexander fortresses, over about 200 versts, forming the Volga Cossack Regiment. The local Grebensky Cossacks were reinforced by Volga and Little Russian Cossacks, and the scattered stanitsas were joined into a single line along the Terek River.

At the start of the 19th century the stanitsas of Temizhbek, Kazan, Tiflis, Ladoga and Voronezh were settled on the line. Their people, who made up the Caucasian Cossack Regiment, were recruited from the southern Russian odnodvorets of the Kursk, Voronezh and Oryol provinces, and by the middle of the century such settlers formed the backbone of the line Cossacks.

The host was formed in 1832 from five Terek regiments, the Kizlyar, Terek-Semeyny, Grebensky, Mozdok and Gorsky, stationed from the mouth of the Terek to Mozdok, and five regiments of the Azov-Mozdok line, the Volga, Caucasian, Stavropol, Khoper and Kuban. The Sunzhensky regiment, formed in 1817, and the 1st and 2nd Vladikavkaz regiments, formed in 1831, also belonged to it. With the Black Sea Cossack Host and the Separate Caucasian Corps it took part in the Caucasian War.

The Kizlyar and Terek-Family regiments were merged in 1838, the Labinsk regiment was formed in 1840 and the Urupsky in 1850. On 14 February 1845 the first statute of the host was approved. Its headquarters stood first at Pyatigorsk and then at Stavropol.

The host's lands held over 300,000 people by the middle of the 19th century. From 1846 most of its regiments were deployed as brigades, and by 1860 it consisted of nine brigades and four separate regiments. On 19 November 1860 the host was reorganised, the Khoper and Kuban regiments joining the Black Sea Cossacks in the new Kuban Cossack Host.
caupo: Caupo, also called Kaupo or Kubbe, led the Finnic-speaking Livonians by the Gulf of Riga at the beginning of the 13th century. The Chronicle of Henry of Livonia calls him quasi rex, like a king, and he is sometimes styled King of Livonia. He was most likely born in the Swedish settlement of Kaup in present-day Kaliningrad, presumably a descendant of the Varangians who took part in founding Kievan Rus'. He was the first prominent Livonian to be christened, probably around 1191, by Theoderic of Turaida, a preacher who later became abbot of Daugavgrīva Abbey.

Caupo became an ardent Christian and a friend of Albert of Buxhoeveden, Bishop of Riga. In Rome Pope Innocent III, impressed by the converted chief, gave him a Bible and a hundred gold pieces, ennobled him and gave him the name Lieven. After his return his own people rebelled, and in 1212 Caupo took part in the siege of his former fortress at Turaida. The wooden fort was rebuilt in brick and stone two years later, close to the form that survives. His son Bertold was killed in 1210 at the Battle of Ümera.

Caupo joined a crusader raid against the pagan Estonians and was killed on 21 September 1217 fighting the troops of Lembitu of Lehola. He is considered the ancestor of the Lieven family; his grandson Nicholas was the first to use the name often. Estonians, Latvians and Livonians today hold no single view of him. Baltic nationalists generally see him as a traitor to his people, a judgement some scholars dismiss as a modern view applied to a medieval chieftain, and Latvian folk tales call him Kaupo the accursed, the scourge of the Livs.
caupolican: His name means polished flint or blue quartz stone in Mapudungun. He seems to have come from a respected family, since he and his brothers were always among the leaders who planned the Mapuche campaigns. According to tradition and the writer Fernando Alegría, he was grave in manner and blind in one eye from childhood. La Araucana names his wife as Fresia, whom other authors call Gueden or Paca, and his only known child was Lemucaguin, Caupolicán the younger.

Caupolicán fought beside Lautaro at the Battle of Tucapel, where the Spanish were defeated and Pedro de Valdivia was killed; the chronicler Jerónimo de Vivar attributes Valdivia's execution to him. After Lautaro's death the Mapuche lacked a single commander and were beaten at Lagunillas on 5 September 1557 by García Hurtado de Mendoza, who had the prisoners' right hands and noses cut off. A council in the Pilmaiquen Mountains then chose Caupolicán as toqui over Paicavi, Lincoyan and Elicura; Vivar says he first had to carry a thick tree trunk on his shoulders for two days and a night. Ercilla says instead that he had been chosen earlier.

On 30 November 1557 his 15,000 warriors attacked the Spanish camp at Millarapue at dawn, but a trumpet sounded for Saint Andrew's Day made them think they had been discovered, and they were surrounded and defeated. In January 1558 he besieged the new fort at Cañete, hoping to starve it. A yanakuna named Andresillo, posing as a deserter, lured the Mapuche inside, where gunfire killed many of them.

A Spanish party under Pedro de Avendaño captured him at Antihuala as he prepared a counter-attack. Vivar tells that Fresia met the captive, rebuked him for being taken alive and threw their child at his feet. Alonso de Reinoso condemned him to impalement; Ercilla writes that he kicked the executioner off the platform and leapt onto the spike himself. His son succeeded him as war leader. Streets, theatres, parks and monuments across Chile bear his name, and Rubén Darío wrote a poem about him.
caustantin-mac-fergusa: Caustantín's parentage is not known with certainty. An older view made him and his brother Óengus sons of Fergus mac Echdach, King of Dál Riata, but it is now thought that they were kin of the earlier Pictish king Óengus mac Fergusa, perhaps his grandsons or grandnephews. The family may have come from Circin, presumed to be the modern Mearns, and had ties with the Eóganachta of Munster in Ireland. Until the Victorian era he was sometimes counted as Constantine I of Scotland, a title now generally given to Causantín mac Cináeda.

The Irish annals record little of Scotland in his time, perhaps because the annals kept at Iona and Applecross were failing, and Viking raids on Ireland and the western coasts may also account for the gap. Only two notices name him: his victory in 789 over Conall mac Taidg in a battle in Pictland, and his death in 820. Whether he was already king before that battle is not known, and the king lists, which give his reign from 35 to 45 years, cannot be relied on without other evidence.

The Dupplin Cross was long assumed to commemorate a victory of Cináed mac Ailpín, but recent analysis found part of an inscription naming Caustantín as Custantin filius Fircus[sa], so it is supposed that he commissioned the monument or that it was raised to his memory. Later chroniclers such as John of Fordun credit him with founding Dunkeld, which Andrew of Wyntoun dates to 815. He is thought to have been a patron of the céli dé, and he is commemorated with his nephew Eogán in the Liber Vitae Dunelmensis, a list of those prayed for in Northumbria.

His brother Óengus succeeded him, and his son Drest was later king; another son, Domnall, is believed to have been king of Dál Riata from around 811 until 835. A sister is said to have been the mother of Alpín mac Echdach, founder of the Alpín dynasty. His standing among later rulers may show in his name: unattested as a royal name in Scotland before him, it was borne by three kings in the century and a half after his death.
cavalry-warfare: Cavalry are soldiers or warriors who fight mounted on horseback. Forces that used other animals or platforms, such as chariots, camels or elephants, were not usually given the name. Before the Iron Age the role of cavalry on the battlefield was largely performed by light chariots, which originated with the Sintashta-Petrovka culture in Central Asia, spread through nomadic or semi-nomadic Indo-Iranians, and were adopted by settled peoples, among them the pharaohs of the New Kingdom of Egypt from 1550 BCE and the Assyrian army.

A mounted soldier had the advantages of greater height, speed and inertial mass over an opponent on foot, which were greatly valued in the ancient and medieval eras. Cavalry served as light cavalry in reconnaissance, screening and skirmishing, or as heavy cavalry for shock attacks. Some hosts were mostly cavalry, particularly in the nomadic societies of Asia, such as the Huns of Attila and the later Mongol armies. The Xiongnu, Avars, Khitans, Mongols and other Turkic peoples won substantial successes against settled agrarian and urban societies through strategic and tactical mobility.

In Europe, as heavy infantry declined with the fall of the Roman Empire, heavy cavalry became more effective and rose to dominate the battlefield; it evolved into the mounted knights of the medieval period. The Mamluks, who originated in the 9th century as Central Asian captives used as mounted auxiliaries by Arab armies, were trained as cavalry and followed al-furusiyya, a code that included tactics, horsemanship and archery. Cavalry formed the core of the Ottoman armies from the 14th to the 17th centuries, and in India it was of great importance from the Gupta period onwards. India also has the oldest evidence for toe-stirrups.

Ownership of heavy cavalry horses was a mark of wealth among settled peoples from the beginning of civilisation to the 20th century, since a horse involved considerable expense in breeding, training and equipment and had little productive use except transport. In the 17th century European cavalry discarded most of its armour, ineffective against muskets and cannon.

Cavalry was important at Blenheim in 1704, Rossbach in 1757 and Marengo in 1800. Barbed wire, machine guns and rapid-fire rifles proved deadly to horse-mounted troops on the Western Front in World War I, and by early 1915 most cavalry units no longer saw front-line action. In the interwar period many cavalry units were converted into motorised or mechanised infantry or into tank troops, and some cavalry still served in World War II. Most horse-mounted units in modern armies now serve in ceremonial roles.
cave-of-the-patriarchs: The site lies in the heart of the Old City of Hebron, 30 kilometres south of Jerusalem. The Hebrew name Me'arat haMakhpela is of uncertain meaning, perhaps cave of the double. The Talmud records two explanations: two chambers, one behind or above the other, or a cave doubled in holding couples, the four couples being Adam and Eve, Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebecca, and Jacob and Leah. The stone enclosure holds four cenotaphs, each in its own octagonal room. The caves beneath are generally not accessible, and only two entrances are known.

According to Genesis 23, Abraham asked the Hittites for a burial site for Sarah and, through Ephron the Hittite, bought the cave and its field for four hundred shekels of silver. Three of the six real estate contracts found in the Ugaritic texts were for 400 silver shekels, and their terms parallel the biblical sale. Most historians believe the Abraham, Isaac and Jacob narrative to be primarily mythological. Between 31 and 4 BCE Herod the Great built the large rectangular enclosure, the only fully surviving Herodian structure of its period.

In Byzantine times a basilica was built at the southeastern end, and the Pilgrim of Bordeaux, around 333, described a monument in which lie Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Sarah, Rebecca and Leah. In 637 the area came under Muslim control and the building was rebuilt as a roofed mosque, with two small synagogues permitted. After the Crusaders captured it in 1100 it became a church and Jews were banned from the synagogues. Saladin reconverted it into a mosque in 1188 and added minarets, two of which survive. Under the Mamluks, Jews were allowed only as close as the seventh step of a staircase.

Judaism, Christianity and Islam all hold the site holy as the burial place of the patriarchs and matriarchs. Muslims believe that Muhammad stopped at the tomb on his night journey from Mecca to Jerusalem. The building is divided between a mosque and a synagogue.
cavtat: Cavtat lies on the Adriatic coast of Croatia, in Dubrovnik-Neretva County, 15 kilometres south of Dubrovnik. It is the centre and main settlement of the municipality of Konavle. Its Italian name was Ragusa Vecchia, meaning Old Ragusa, and the modern Croatian name derives from the Latin Civitas Vetus, old city.

Greek settlers from Corinth founded the city in the 6th century BCE as Epidaurus, while the Illyrians of the surrounding area called it Zaptal. It became Epidaurum when it came under Roman rule in 228 BCE. During the Gothic War of 535–554 the emperor Justinian I sent his fleet to the town and occupied it.

The Avars and Slavs sacked and destroyed the city in the 7th century. Refugees from Epidaurum fled to the nearby island of Laus, called Ragusa, which in time grew into the city of Dubrovnik. The town was re-established in the Middle Ages as Ragusa Vecchia and after a short time came under the control of the Republic of Ragusa, its powerful neighbour.

Cavtat is a tourist destination with hotels, rented rooms, shops and restaurants along its seafront, and a ferry connects it with Mlini and Dubrovnik. The town cemetery on the hill holds the mausoleum of the Račić family, decorated by the sculptor Ivan Meštrović. The Epidaurus Festival of Music has been held there every year since 2007. Natives of the town include the painter Vlaho Bukovac (1855–1922), the jurist Baltazar Bogišić (1834–1908) and the politician Frano Supilo (1870–1917).
cavustepe: The fortress, also known as Haykaberd and Çavuştepe Kalesi, lies on a ridge on the north-eastern edge of the village of Çavuştepe in the Gürpınar district, overlooking the Gürpınar Plain on the road to Hakkâri, in a valley once known as Hayots Dzor in historic Armenia. In Armenian folklore it is the fortress built by Hayk, in legend the founder of the Armenian nation, near the place where he slew the invading Babylonian king Bel.

Its upper and lower sections held the Temple of Khaldi or Irmushini, a royal palace with a throne room, storehouses, workshops, cisterns, a kitchen and colonnaded halls, and a moat surrounded parts of it. Apart from the cyclopean wall, its blocks are smoothly finished and fit together without mortar, which led C. A. Burney to suggest it was a wealthy town of which only the acropolis remains.

Sarduri II (r. 764–735 BCE) built it at the height of Urartian power, and it is thought to be the Sardurihurda of his inscriptions. Of four cuneiform inscriptions found there, the best preserved records that Sarduri, son of Argishti, built a temple to the god Irmushini and a great fortress on solid rock, dug a canal from the Gugunaini (Hoşap), planted vineyards and founded a new city named Sardurihinili. If the identification holds, the site lay near Ulhu, which Sargon II of Assyria conquered, though Sardurihurda itself seems not to have fallen. It was destroyed in the 7th century BCE, presumably by the Scythians or Medes, and later saw a medieval occupation.

An inscription from the site was taken to Vienna in 1884 and published by D. H. Müller. Nikolai Marr and Joseph Orbeli visited in 1916 and collected objects now in the Hermitage, Carl Ferdinand Friedrich Lehmann-Haupt made the first excavations and a sketch-plan, and C. A. Burney described the site in 1956. Afif Erzen led excavations there from 1961.
caxcanes: The Caxcan are indigenous to western and north-central Mexico, in lands that correspond to present-day Zacatecas, southern Durango, Jalisco, Colima, Aguascalientes and Nayarit. Their language, most often described as an ancient variant of Nahuatl, belongs to the Uto-Aztecan family. Partly nomadic and partly settled, they lived in several city-states with elected rulers called tlatoani, and their main religious and population centres were Teul, Tlaltenango, Juchipila and Teocaltiche.

In the Mixtón Rebellion of 1540–42 the Caxcan, under their leader Tenamaztle, were allied with the Zacatecos against the Spaniards and were described as the heart and centre of the rising. Their later ceasefire with the Spaniards made them a constant target of the Zacatecos and Guachichiles. In the Chichimeca War of 1550–1590, the longest and most expensive conflict between Spaniards and indigenous peoples in the history of New Spain, they fought on the Spanish side against a confederation of Chichimeca peoples.

Warfare, disease and marriage with outsiders wore away much of Caxcan culture. During the colonial period many Spanish and some Basque settlers married or had relations with Caxcanes, so that many of their descendants were mestizos, and allied peoples and mestizos settled the Caxcan lands in Zacatecas and Jalisco.

According to the anthropologist Aleš Hrdlička, the last generation of native speakers of Caxcan came to an end in the 1890s. Anthropologists long took this to mean the end of the Caxcan people themselves, but much of their culture has persisted through oral tradition. In the 1920s Juana Belén Gutiérrez de Mendoza, a Caxcan from Durango, formed the Council of the Caxcan indigenous people and published Alto!, a book that stressed Mexican nationalism through indigenous roots.

Caxcan people live in Zacatecas and in diaspora, and the Mexican government officially recognises four communities in southern Zacatecas as Caxcan. They have sought to regain legal access to their sacred mountain, Tlachialoyantepec (El Cerro de las Ventanas), and a revival of Caxcan language, scholarship and culture has been under way.
cayenne: Cayenne stands on a former island at the mouth of the Cayenne River on the Atlantic coast, and the city occupies part of Cayenne Island. It is 268 kilometres from Saint-Laurent-du-Maroni and 64 kilometres from Kourou. Its motto is fert aurum industria, work brings wealth. The climate is tropical, with average highs of about 30 °C and lows of about 23 °C throughout the year and a very long wet season. The port of Dégrad des Cannes on the Mahury estuary has replaced Larivot and the Îles du Salut, and timber, rum and gold are exported in small quantities.

Spanish explorers who first visited the area found it too hot and did not settle it. The French founded their first settlement in 1604, but the Portuguese destroyed it, determined to enforce the Treaty of Tordesillas. French colonists returned in 1643 and founded Cayenne. An Amerindian chief named Cépérou sold them the rock on which Fort Cépérou stands, and the colonists were later forced to leave by attacks from the Indigenous population. Over the following decades the colony changed hands among the French, Dutch and English before being restored to France. Cayenne became a municipality in 1790.

In 1809 an Anglo-Portuguese force captured it, and it was administered from Brazil until 1817, when it returned to French control. It was used as a French penal colony until 1938. The Pasteur Institute has a branch in Cayenne, which studies tropical diseases. The Botanical Garden has its origin in a garden that Louis XVI established in 1786 as a storehouse and nursery for plants, to which the director Louis Claude Richard brought nutmeg trees, rattan, cardamom and black pepper vines from India.

Cayenne is the capital, prefecture and largest city of French Guiana, and the largest Francophone city on the South American continent. About 62,675 people live in the commune itself and about 153,884 in its metropolitan area, which has grown through immigration, chiefly from Haiti, Brazil and the West Indies, and a high birth rate. Its heritage includes Fort Cépérou, the Cathedral of Saint-Sauveur, built between 1825 and 1833 and registered as a historic monument, and restored Creole houses. Its carnival, held between Epiphany and Ash Wednesday, comes from Guianan Creole culture; in early colonial times enslaved people were forbidden to join the settlers' carnival and held clandestine festivals of their own.
cayor: The name, in Wolof Kajoor, comes from Waadyor, people of the joor, a fertile soil of northern Cayor. There are no written sources for its early history and few oral traditions, but its king lists reach back as far as Jolof's. Under Jolof rule it was governed by a Great Lamane of the Fall family, who led a yearly delegation to pay tribute to the Buurba. In 1549 Amary Ngone Sobel Fall, sent with the overdue tribute, defied the Buurba Léléfoulifak and routed the pursuing Jolof army at Danki, where the Buurba was killed. As damel he also ruled Baol, issued a new constitution, moved the capital to Mboul and held off Jolof for a 44-year reign.

In the late 17th century the marabout Ndiaye Sall and the former lingeer Yacine Bubu overthrew the damel, but Yacine Bubu then turned to the Buur of Saloum to stop Sall founding a theocracy. In 1693 Lat Sukaabe Fall, Teigne of Baol, took the throne, strengthened central power and clashed with the French over their trade monopoly. In 1776 the damel Amari Ngoone Ndela Kumba crushed a clerical rising and then destroyed an invading army from Futa Toro at Bunxoy, capturing the Almamy Abdul Kader.

In the 19th century Governor Louis Faidherbe encouraged the clerics to rebel. Lat Jor, enthroned by his uncle Demba War Sall, defeated the French at Mekhe on 8 July 1869 and in 1881 rose against the Dakar to Saint-Louis railway. His nephew Samba Laobe Fall, backed by the French, took power and was killed in a fight with a French lieutenant at Tivaouane on 6 October 1886; Lat Jor fell in battle soon after, and the kingdom was divided into provinces still governed by Demba War Sall's family.

A four-member council led by the Jaurin Bul, chief of the free men, chose the damel. Below the nobles, the Garmi, stood the free Jambur, then the hereditary castes of smiths, griots and other crafts, and at the bottom the enslaved, some of whom held military and political power. The lingeer commanded her own soldiers and a province's taxes. The Tyeddo, warriors drawn from the damel's slaves, raided even within Cayor, and peasants grew less food than they could so as not to attract them.
cayuga-lake: Cayuga Lake spans three counties of central New York state, Cayuga, Seneca and Tompkins. It is the second largest of the Finger Lakes in surface area, marginally smaller than Seneca Lake, and second largest in volume. Its average width is 1.7 miles (2.8 km), widening to 3.5 miles (5.6 km) near Aurora, and it is about 435 feet (133 m) deep at its deepest point, with over 95 miles (153 km) of shoreline.

Like the other Finger Lakes, it was carved by glaciers in the last Ice Age, leaving steep east and west sides and shallow ends. The water level is regulated by the Mud Lock at the north end, and the lake is linked to Lake Ontario by the Erie Canal and to Seneca Lake by the Seneca River. The marshes and mudflats of the north end, part of the Montezuma National Wildlife Refuge, are an important stopover for migratory birds. Its one small island, Frontenac, lies in the north-east near Union Springs.

Early human activity around the lake includes Late Archaic occupations of the Lamoka tradition and the Frontenac Island site, which reflects contact between Lamoka and Brewerton groups. The lake takes its name from the Cayuga people, whose name translates as People of the Great Swamp. Their territory lay between the lands of the Onondaga to the east and the Seneca to the west, two other nations of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy.

At the northern tip lies the town of Seneca Falls, site of the Seneca Falls Convention on women's rights. In the late 1960s citizens successfully opposed the building of an 830-MW nuclear power plant on the shore, and the coal-fired AES power plant on the eastern shore, which had used the lake for cooling, was shut down in August 2019. A lake source cooling system run by Cornell University, controversial while it was planned and built, began operating in 2000.

The city of Ithaca, home to Cornell University and Ithaca College, stands at the southern end, and villages such as Aurora, Union Springs and Cayuga line the east shore. The lake supplies drinking water to several communities, supports sport fishing for lake trout, smelt and smallmouth bass, and is included in an American Viticultural Area established in 1988, with over a dozen wineries.
cayuga-people: The Cayuga call themselves Gayogo̱hó꞉nǫˀ, meaning People of the Great Swamp. Their homeland lies along Cayuga Lake, between their league neighbours the Onondaga to the east and the Seneca to the west. Their relations with the British and the Thirteen Colonies during the American Revolution were complicated, with Cayuga warriors fighting on both sides and some abstaining. Most Haudenosaunee nations allied with the British, in part hoping to end colonists' encroachment on their lands.

After raids along the frontier in 1778, which the revolutionary government regarded in several cases as atrocities, George Washington appointed John Sullivan and James Clinton in 1779 to lead the Sullivan Expedition, a retaliatory campaign of 6,200 troops. It destroyed 40 to 50 Haudenosaunee villages, including the major Cayuga villages of Cayuga Castle and Chonodote, and the crops and winter stores. Survivors fled to other Haudenosaunee nations or to Upper Canada, where some were granted land by the British.

After the war the Central New York Military Tract was established for veterans' land bounties; it included a Cayuga reservation that was given up a few years later in a treaty with the state. On 11 November 1794 the Cayuga Nation signed the Pickering Treaty with the United States, ceding much land in New York and having its sovereignty recognised. New York made further treaties that the Senate never ratified and sold more than 5 million acres of former Haudenosaunee land cheaply.

Like all Haudenosaunee, the Cayuga are divided into clans of matrilineal descent, led by Clan Mothers. There are six: Wolf, Bear, Turtle, Sandpiper, Heron and Hawk. The Cayuga send ten Rotiyanehson to the Haudenosaunee Grand Council, where they belong to the Younger Brother moiety with the Oneida. Cayuga people form three bands: the Lower Cayuga and Upper Cayuga at Six Nations of the Grand River in Ontario, and in the United States the Cayuga Nation of New York and the Seneca-Cayuga Nation of Oklahoma. Some live at the Cattaraugus Reservation among the Seneca Nation of Indians.

The Cayuga Nation of New York filed a land claim on 19 November 1980, joined in 1981 by the Seneca-Cayuga Nation. In 2000 a jury found damages of about $36.9 million, and in 2001 the court awarded $247.9 million with interest. On 28 June 2005 the Second Circuit reversed the judgment on the doctrine of laches, and the Supreme Court declined review on 15 May 2006. The Nation bought 14 acres in Seneca Falls on 17 July 1996, the first land of its homeland it recovered, and in December 2005 received a 70-acre farm in Aurora, New York, as a gift.
cayuse-war: Marcus and Narcissa Whitman founded the Whitman Mission among the Cayuse at Waiilatpu, six miles west of present-day Walla Walla, Washington, in 1836. They set up schools and grist mills and introduced irrigation, but baptised no Cayuse into their church. When the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions planned to close the mission in 1842, Marcus Whitman went east to plead for it, and the following year he returned with about a thousand settlers bound for the Oregon Country.

Tensions grew with the settlers. The Cayuse held that ploughing desecrated the spirit of the Earth and expected payment from wagon trains crossing their land, while the settlers drove off the men sent to collect it as beggars. In 1847 measles killed half the Cayuse, and some suspected Whitman, a physician and religious leader, of causing it. In the attack of 29 November 1847 thirteen settlers died, every building at Waiilatpu was destroyed, and 53 women and children were held captive for several weeks.

Governor George Abernethy and the provisional legislature raised volunteers. The Oregon Rifles, fifty men under Henry A. G. Lee, formed on 8 December 1847 and bought supplies from the Hudson's Bay Company on their own credit, since the company would not lend to the government; they reached The Dalles on 21 December and built Fort Lee. In January 1848 Colonel Cornelius Gilliam led more than 500 militiamen east, reaching the mission on 4 March after a battle at Sand Hollows, and was later killed by accident in camp.

The United States Army later supported the militia. Unable to match their opponents' firepower, the Cayuse who resisted were driven into hiding in the Blue Mountains. In 1850 the tribe handed over five men, Tilaukaikt, Tomahas, Klokamas, Isaiachalkis and Kimasumpkin, who were hanged on 3 June 1850 by U.S. Marshal Joseph L. Meek; Kimasumpkin declared before his death that he was innocent. Sporadic bloodshed continued until 1855.

In 1855 the defeated Cayuse ceded most of their lands, keeping the Umatilla Indian Reservation, shared with the Umatilla and Walla Walla peoples. The war's debts strained the provisional government, which gave way to a more permanent government. The five men had been tried although their guilt and the court's jurisdiction were not fully established, and responses to the trial stayed divided for decades. It was the first of several wars in the region that led to treaties and reservations on the Columbia Plateau.
ceara: Ceará was first inhabited by peoples including the Tabajara, Potyguara, Anacés, Kariri and Tremembé, who traded with Europeans, including the French, before the Portuguese included the area in Brazil. The first Portuguese plan for settlement dates from 1534, but the earliest settlement was made near the mouth of the Ceará River in 1603 by Pero Coelho de Sousa, who built the fort of São Tiago and left a year later because of drought, a phenomenon that periodically afflicts the region.

In 1612 a military expedition under Martim Soares Moreno expelled the French from Ceará and Maranhão, and he built the fortress of São Sebastião; the Portuguese presence dates from his return in 1618.

The Dutch took the fort in 1637, allied with several Indian peoples, and held Ceará until 1644, when the Indians attacked their governor and destroyed São Sebastião. In 1649 the Dutch built Fort Schoonenborch by the Pajeú river; after they were expelled from Brazil in 1654 the Portuguese renamed it Fortaleza de Nossa Senhora de Assunção, and the Indians allied with the Dutch had to flee persecution. Ceará became a dependency of Pernambuco in 1680, and the Captaincy of Ceará became independent in 1799.

The fight for Brazilian independence in 1822 was fierce in Ceará, which was a rebel stronghold and suffered retribution from loyalists. The captaincy became a province in 1822 under Dom Pedro I. In 1824 the president of the province was deposed fifteen days after his arrival and a republic was proclaimed; after internal quarrels and the killing of the new president, the province returned to the empire. On 25 March 1884 Ceará became the first province of Brazil to abolish slavery, more than four years before the national law of 1888, passed by Princess Isabel. It became a bishopric in 1853, seated at Fortaleza.

Ceará is one of the 26 states of Brazil, in the northeast on the Atlantic coast, with an area of 148,016 km2 and its capital at Fortaleza. It is divided into 184 municipalities and has about 600 km of sandy coastline. The interior is dry, with rivers that run dry in the dry season. Drought has recurred, and the Orós Dam and the Castanhão Dam, completed in 2003, now supply much of its water. The name Ceará means sings the jandaia, though José de Alencar held it meant turquoise or green waters.
cearl-of-mercia: Cearl, also spelled Ceorl, ruled until about 626. His ancestry is unknown and he does not appear in the Mercian royal genealogy. In the 12th century Henry of Huntingdon placed him as ruling after Pybba and said that he was not Pybba's son but his kinsman. Bede, who mentions him only in passing as the father-in-law of Edwin of Deira, was a Northumbrian hostile to Mercia, and the historian Robin Fleming has speculated that the name, which means rustic in Old English, may have been a joke.

Historians read the marriage of his daughter Cwenburh to the exiled Edwin as evidence that Cearl was independent of the Northumbrian king Æthelfrith, Edwin's rival, since he would not have given his daughter to an enemy of his overlord. The Historia Brittonum credits the later king Penda with first separating the Mercians from the Northumbrians, so any subjection may have come later. D. P. Kirby suggested that Cearl was protected by the East Anglian king Raedwald, and that Edwin's later exile among the East Angles may reflect Æthelfrith's power beginning to weigh on Cearl or his successors.

It has been suggested that Cearl's kingship suffered a catastrophe between the Battle of Chester, around 616, and the appearance of his successor Penda, son of Pybba, and that he may have been involved in that conflict. Whether he reigned until Penda became king is unknown; Penda was in power by 633, and possibly by 626 if the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle is correct.

Cearl's link to Edwin may point to a rivalry with Penda, who later defeated Edwin in alliance with King Cadwallon of Gwynedd. According to Bede, Penda also executed Eadfrith, a captured son of Edwin and Cearl's grandson through Cwenburh. This is often seen as the result of pressure from the Northumbrian king Oswald, but Penda may also have judged that Eadfrith's descent from Cearl made him a threat to his own position.
ceawlin-of-wessex: Ceawlin may have been the son of Cynric of Wessex and the grandson of Cerdic, whom the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle represents as the leader of the first Saxons to come to the land that became Wessex. Whether he descended from Cerdic is debated, and the early genealogies were shaped by West Saxon efforts to trace their rulers back to him. His name has no convincing Old English etymology and seems more likely to be of British origin. Little of southern England remained in British hands by the end of his life.

The Chronicle records his first battle in 556, when he and his father fought the Britons at Beran byrg, now identified as Barbury Castle in Wiltshire. In the Chronicle's annal for 568 he and Cutha fought Æthelberht of Kent and killed two ealdormen at Wibbandun, the first recorded battle between different groups of invaders.

For 577 it records that Cuthwine and Ceawlin killed three British kings, Coinmail, Condidan and Farinmail, at Dyrham and took Gloucester, Cirencester and Bath. Reaching the Bristol Channel cut the Britons west of the Severn off from those in the south-western peninsula. His last recorded battle, in 584 at Fethan leag, probably near Stoke Lyne in Oxfordshire, saw Cutha killed, and Ceawlin turned home in anger.

The chronology is highly uncertain. The Chronicle gives his reign as 32 years, while copies of the West Saxon Genealogical Regnal List give seven or seventeen. Bede lists Ceawlin as the second of seven kings who held imperium south of the Humber, and the Chronicle later called such rulers bretwalda. Bede wrote in the eighth century, and his description of the early overlords may be coloured by the power of Mercia in his own day.

The Chronicle's entry for 592 reads in part: great slaughter at Woden's Barrow, and Ceawlin was driven out. Woden's Barrow is a tumulus now called Adam's Grave, at Alton Priors in Wiltshire. William of Malmesbury, writing about 1120, said the Angles and British had conspired together, but the successor Ceol may have been responsible. The Chronicle records that Ceawlin, Cwichelm and Crida perished in the following year.

Control may have fragmented among the West Saxons at his death, which may have helped Æthelberht of Kent rise to dominance. Some of Ceawlin's conquests were not kept: Mercia took much of the upper Thames valley, and the north-eastern towns won in 571 came under Kent and Mercia at different times.
cebu: Cebu lies east of Negros and west of Leyte and Bohol in the Central Visayas. The province consists of Cebu Island and 167 smaller islands and islets, among them Mactan, Bantayan, Malapascua, Olango and the Camotes Islands. The main island is long and narrow, stretching 196 km from north to south and 32 km across at its widest, with limestone plateaus, coastal plains and rugged mountain ranges. The climate is tropical, and little forest remains. The name is possibly derived from a hypothetical Proto-Philippine word meaning to bathe or to wade into the water.

Cebu was a native kingdom before the arrival of the Spaniards. Visayan folklore relates that it was founded by Sri Lumay, a half-Malay, half-Tamil from Sumatra, and that its capital was Singhapala, Tamil-Sanskrit for Lion City. Ferdinand Magellan left Sanlúcar de Barrameda with five ships and 250 people on 20 September 1519 and reached the Philippines on 16 March 1521. Rajah Kolambu of Mazaua told the crews to sail to Cebu, where they could trade and obtain provisions.
