In 1898 the island was ceded to the United States, and Cebu became a chartered city on 24 February 1937.

In April 1942 Japanese soldiers landed, and Cebu served as a Japanese base during the occupation. Cebuano guerrillas fought the Japanese, and the guerrilla leader James M. Cushing is credited with the Koga Papers, said to have changed American plans for retaking the Philippines. Combined Filipino and American forces landed in March 1945. Cebu later became a centre of resistance to the Marcos government, and from Fuente Osmeña circle in Cebu City the opposition relaunched its civil disobedience campaign on 22 February 1986, in the days leading up to the People Power revolution.

Cebu City, nicknamed the Queen City of the South, is the capital and largest city, and with Lapu-Lapu and Mandaue it is governed independently of the province. The province counts 53 cities and municipalities. Its population was 3,400,522 at the 2024 census, or 5,151,274 with the three independent cities. About 95 per cent of Cebuanos are Roman Catholic, and Cebuano is the main language. The Sinulog Festival is the best known of the many festivals that have earned Cebu the name Festival Island.
cecil-calvert: Cecil Calvert was born in Kent on 8 August 1605, the first son of George Calvert, then an assistant to Lord Cecil, Secretary of State to James I, after whom the boy was christened Cecilius. He entered Trinity College, Oxford, in 1621. In 1625 his father was made Baron Baltimore in the peerage of Ireland and became a Catholic, and his sons probably followed him. In 1628 the family went to the new colony in Newfoundland, which failed through disease, cold and French attacks. Cecil married Anne Arundell, daughter of Thomas Arundell, 1st Baron Arundell of Wardour; of their nine children only three reached adulthood.

He succeeded as second Baron Baltimore in April 1632 and was called to the bar at Gray's Inn in 1633. The Maryland charter, confirmed on 20 June 1632 and named for Queen Henrietta Maria, made the colony a palatinate whose proprietor could wage war, raise taxes and create a nobility, in return for a fifth of all gold and silver found and two Native American arrows delivered to Windsor each Easter. Former members of the Virginia Company fought the charter, claiming that William Claiborne's trading station on Kent Island meant the land was already settled, so Baltimore stayed in England to defend it.

The Ark and the Dove carried the first settlers, nearly equal numbers of Catholics and Protestants, with the Jesuit Andrew White among them. Baltimore's instructions stressed religious toleration. They landed on St. Clement's Island on 25 March 1634 and founded St. Mary's City two days later on land bought from the Yaocomico. During the English Civil War he named a Protestant, William Stone, as governor to keep hold of the colony.

Baltimore governed Maryland through deputies for 44 years, from his brother Leonard to his only son Charles, who succeeded him. He died in England on 30 November 1675 and is recorded as buried at St Giles-in-the-Fields in London, though the grave has not been found. After the Protestant revolution of 1689 the family lost control of the colony for a time. The counties of Calvert and Cecil bear his names, the flag of Maryland is made of the family's Calvert and Crossland arms, and the seal he had made after the first was stolen in 1645 is still in use.
cecil-rhodes: Cecil John Rhodes was born on 5 July 1853 at Bishop's Stortford in Hertfordshire, the fourth son and sixth child of the Reverend Francis William Rhodes, vicar of the town. His family sent him to Natal as a teenager in the hope that the climate would improve his poor health, and he arrived in Durban on 1 September 1870. He worked on his brother's cotton farm, and in 1871 entered the diamond trade at Kimberley. In 1873 he entered Oriel College, Oxford, but stayed one term before illness sent him back to Kimberley, and he returned to Oxford in 1876. His admiration for the Oxford tutorial system later shaped his plans for a scholarship.

With funding from Rothschild and Company, Rhodes began to buy out and consolidate diamond mines, and gained a near-complete monopoly of the world diamond market. He founded De Beers in 1888. He entered the Cape Parliament in 1881 and became prime minister of the Cape Colony in 1890. Through the Glen Grey Act he took land from black Africans, saying that they had to be driven off their land to stimulate them to labour, and the Franchise and Ballot Act tripled the wealth requirement for voting, which in effect barred black voters.

Rhodes used his wealth and that of his partner Alfred Beit to obtain mineral concessions from indigenous chiefs. The Rudd Concession, signed by Lobengula, king of the Ndebele, left out the promise that no more than ten white men would mine in Matabeleland, and when Lobengula tried to renounce it the British government ignored him. Settlers and the company's police committed widespread rape of Ndebele women in the early 1890s. The company named Rhodesia after him in 1895. He was forced to resign as prime minister in 1896 after the Jameson Raid, an unauthorised attack on Paul Kruger's South African Republic.

Rhodes died of heart failure on 26 March 1902, aged 48, at his cottage in Muizenberg. At his request he was buried at Malindidzimu in the Matopos hills, a site of great importance to Shona traditional religion, a choice interpreted as a gesture of colonial conquest. His will founded the Rhodes Scholarship at Oxford, which his estate funds, with the aim of promoting leadership and of rendering war impossible through friendship between the great powers. Critics cite his seizure of land and his promotion of false claims that Great Zimbabwe was built by European civilisations, and some historians attack him as a ruthless imperialist and white supremacist.
cecile-fatiman: Her origins are uncertain. The Haitian historian Rodney Salnave believed her father to have been a son of King Theodore of Corsica and her birth name Cécil Attiman. Aisha Khan held that she was a Muslim and that Fatiman was cognate with the name Fatima, while Aimé Césaire thought her Kongolese, a view David Patrick Geggus questions because it leaves the name unexplained. She is also believed to have been related to Marie-Louise Coidavid, later Queen of Haiti. Described as a mulatto with green eyes, she was sold with her mother from childhood, and her two brothers disappeared after being sold apart from them.

According to the historian Aisha K. Finch, Fatiman reshaped the Enlightenment ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity for the Haitian setting, upholding black women's bodily integrity and property rights, and saw spirit possession as the opposite of slavery, a moment in which the possessed became gods. At Bois Caïman, the Alligator Wood, the gathering took place in a thunderstorm in the forests of the north, and she was said to have been possessed by one of the Èzili, believed to be Dantò. Garvey F. Lundy understood the sacrifice as a Petwo rite of Vodou. Those present drank the pig's blood before swearing their oath, and during the revolution she and other manbos were credited with giving the fighters superhuman courage.

After Henri Christophe established the Kingdom of Haiti, she married Jean-Louis Pierrot, a general and a prince under the monarchy, and they had a daughter, Marie Louise Amélia Célestine. The couple later divorced; Pierrot became President of Haiti in 1845, for 10 months. She lived out her life in Le Cap, in good health to the end.

She entered the record through Antoine Dalmas, a plantation doctor who observed the ceremony, and little archival evidence of her life survives. Étienne Charlier found her in the oral history of the revolution, and family records kept by her grandson Pierre Benoit Rameau confirmed her part. Historians relying on colonial documents, such as Jean Fouchard, left her out, and Léon-François Hoffman and Franck Sylvain contested that the ceremony took place, but Carolyn Fick held it to be historical and Vodou in character. C. L. R. James rewrote her as the priestess Celestine in his play of 1934.
cedd: Almost everything known of Cedd comes from Book 3 of Bede's Ecclesiastical History of the English People. He was born in the Kingdom of Northumbria and brought up on the island of Lindisfarne by Aidan, who had come from Iona. He had three brothers, Chad of Mercia, Cynibil and Cælin, all of them priests, and Cedd and Chad both became bishops. Although the brothers were apparently Northumbrian by birth, their names are British Celtic rather than Anglo-Saxon in origin. Cedd was probably the eldest and the head of the family.

Aidan brought the practices known as the Celtic Rite, in which monasteries supported wandering missionary bishops and personal asceticism was stressed. Bede says that Cedd and Chad absorbed Aidan's example.

King Oswiu of Northumbria sent Cedd to the Middle Angles with three other priests, among them Betti and Diuma, after their sub-king, Peada of Mercia, agreed to become a Christian in return for marriage to Oswiu's daughter Alchflaed. Bede says that the pagan Penda of Mercia did not obstruct the preaching, but the mission made little headway in the wider Mercian kingdom.

Oswiu soon recalled him and sent him to the East Saxons, whose king, Sigeberht the Good, had been baptised by Bishop Finan of Lindisfarne. After Cedd's first conversions Finan ordained him bishop, and he is generally listed among the bishops of London. He excommunicated a thegn living in an unlawful marriage and denounced the king for visiting the man, and Bede presents Sigeberht's murder in 660 as the penalty. Cedd later baptised the pagan successor, Swithhelm of Essex, at the home of Æthelwold of East Anglia.
At the request of Œthelwald of Deira, Cedd founded Lastingham, keeping a 40-day fast to purify the site; when royal business called him away after 30 days, his brother Cynibil completed it.

The languages at the Synod of Whitby probably included Old Irish, Old English, Frankish and Old Welsh as well as Latin, and Cedd's skill in them likely made him a key figure. According to Bede he accepted the Roman dating of Easter. He died at Lastingham on 26 October 664. Thirty monks who came from Essex to honour him died there of the plague, all but one small boy. Chad succeeded him as abbot, and when some East Saxons returned to paganism, Wulfhere of Mercia sent Bishop Jaruman, who restored Christianity.

The Church of England commemorates Cedd on 26 October, also known as Essex Day, and in 1954 Chelmsford Cathedral was additionally dedicated to St Cedd and St Peter. The Gospel Oak at Polstead in Suffolk is one of several places where he is traditionally supposed to have preached, and a church service is held there on the first Sunday of every August.
cefalu-cathedral: The cathedral was built between 1131 and 1240 in the Norman style, after Normans conquered Sicily in 1091. By tradition, King Roger II of Sicily ordered it after a vow to the Holy Saviour, made when he escaped from a storm and reached the city's beach. The site had long been inhabited: it holds a Roman road and parts of a 6th-century polychrome mosaic showing a dove drinking, probably from an earlier Byzantine basilica, in an area that was an episcopal see until at least the 8th century.

The apse mosaics were begun in 1145, the year the sarcophagi Roger provided for himself and his wife were put in place. The church declined after 1172. In 1215 Frederick II of Hohenstaufen moved the two sarcophagi to Palermo Cathedral. Work resumed soon after, the facade was completed in 1240 and Rodolphe de Chevrières, Bishop of Albano, consecrated the church in 1267. In 1472 Ambrogio da Como added a portico between the towers.

The building has a fortress-like character and dominates the skyline of the medieval town. A terraced parvis, originally a cemetery, precedes it. The facade has two Norman towers with mullioned windows, each with a different spire, one with flame-shaped merlons said to symbolise papal authority, the other with Ghibelline merlons said to symbolise royal and temporal power. The interior is a Latin cross divided into a nave and two aisles by antique columns, fourteen of pink granite and two of cipolin.

Beyond the crossing, the church joins a Romanesque style of massive simple forms to the Gothic pointed arch, a feature also seen at Monreale Cathedral, and it has three apses. The cloister, with pointed arches resting on paired columns, was the model for later Norman cloisters in Sicily, in particular that of Monreale.

Roger II brought mosaic masters from Constantinople, who adapted Byzantine decoration to a building of northern European origin. Only the presbytery was decorated. The bust of Christ Pantokrator fills the apse semi-dome, a hand raised in blessing, and holds the Gospel of John open at the words 'I am the light of the world', in Greek and Latin. The Virgin Mary appears above, with four archangels. The work was finished before 1170 and is considered the finest Byzantine mosaic in Italy.

The cathedral is one of nine structures in the World Heritage Site Arab-Norman Palermo and the Cathedral Churches of Cefalù and Monreale. It later inspired Antonio Vandone's Mogadishu Cathedral, built from 1925 to 1928 in Italian Somaliland. From 1985 the Palermo artist Michele Canzoneri installed 72 abstract stained-glass windows, which have aroused some controversy for their style.
celali-rebellions: Banditry was rising across Anatolia by the end of the 16th century, while the Ottomans were tied down by the Ottoman–Habsburg wars and conflict with Safavid Iran. Sekban and levend soldiers formed bandit gangs on returning from campaigns. After the Battle of Keresztes a roll call found 30,000 sipahis absent, and many who lost their timar land grants in response turned to banditry. The akçe was heavily debased, the price of foodstuff rose from 182 akçes in 1585 to 631 in 1606, and taxes were raised to pay for the Long Turkish War.

The Little Ice Age hurt harvests in eastern Anatolia: a drought in 1599 brought famine in 1600, and another famine followed in 1607 and 1608. Historians explain the risings differently. Mustafa Akdağ stressed inflation and unemployed soldiers, while Karen Barkey and Halil İnalcık saw the rebels as seeking state resources and positions rather than overthrow.

Hüseyin Pasha, a former governor of Habesh, rose in Karaman at the same time as Karayazıcı, and the two joined forces, took Urfa Castle and withstood an Ottoman siege. Sultan Mehmed III made Karayazıcı governor of Amasya and Çorum after he handed Hüseyin over, but he kept up his revolt until Sokulluzade Hasan Pasha defeated him in July 1601; he died near Canik in 1602. His brother Deli Hasan, with 20,000 soldiers, killed Hasan Pasha at Tokat, besieged Ankara and was then made beylerbey of Bosnia.

The Celalis sacked Bursa, the former Ottoman capital, in 1607. In October 1607 Kuyucu Murad Pasha defeated Kalenderoğlu north of Aleppo and sent the heads of 48 Celali leaders to Constantinople. By 1608, 80,000 Celalis had been killed, and Kalenderoğlu was finally defeated near Marash that year. Later risings were also called Celali, among them that of Varvar Ali Pasha, defeated and executed in 1648.

The rebellions transformed landholding in Anatolia. Peasants who fled lost their lands to local administrators or tax farmers, the timar system was shaken to its foundations, and Janissaries turned abandoned land into animal farms despite government efforts to restore it to its owners. The populations of Amasya and Kayseri fell by half between 1580 and 1640. Armenian refugees helped make İzmir, Rodosto and Constantinople centres of Armenian life, and Ankara built walls, which it kept for over a century.
celje: Celje lies below Upper Celje Castle at the confluence of the Savinja, Hudinja, Ložnica and Voglajna rivers in the lower Savinja Valley, at the crossing of the roads connecting Ljubljana, Maribor, Velenje and the Central Sava Valley. It is a regional centre of the traditional region of Styria and is known in German as Cilli. Its name derives from the Roman Celeia; the name is of pre-Roman origin and its further etymology is unclear.

The first settlement dates from the Hallstatt era, and findings suggest that Celts coined Noric money in the region. The area was incorporated into the Roman Empire in 15 BCE as Civitas Celeia, and in 45 CE it received municipal rights as municipium Claudia Celeia under Emperor Claudius. The town was rich and densely populated, with walls, towers and multi-storied marble palaces, and a temple of Mars known across the empire. Slavic tribes razed the city in the 5th and 6th centuries, and it was rebuilt in the Early Middle Ages.

The Counts of Celje had their seat in the town from 1341 to 1456, with princely status from 1436. It received town privileges from Count Frederick II on 11 April 1451. After the counts died out in 1456 the region passed to the Habsburgs and was administered by the Duchy of Styria. The city walls and moat were built in 1473, and the town defended itself against the Turks and against peasants who had taken the Old Castle in 1515.

At the end of the 19th century Celje was a centre of German nationalism, and the 1910 census showed 66.8 percent of the population as German. In 1918 it became part of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes. Nazi Germany occupied it in April 1941. The city lost 575 people during the war, and more than 1,500 were deported. After the war the remaining German-speaking population was expelled or executed. Celje became part of independent Slovenia after the Ten-Day War in 1991.

Celje is the third-largest city in Slovenia. Its sights include a Grayfriars' monastery founded in 1241, a 16th-century palace and the 14th-century parish church with a Gothic chapel, which keeps the throne and tombs of the counts of Cilli.
cell-theory: The discovery of cells depended on the microscope. Compound microscopes first appeared in Europe around 1620. In 1665 Robert Hooke published Micrographia, whose observations included thin slices of bottle cork. He saw a multitude of tiny pores and named them cells, from the Latin cella, a small room such as monks lived in, and cellulae, the six-sided cells of a honeycomb. What he saw were the empty walls of plant tissue, and he did not think the cells alive. Soon afterwards Anton van Leeuwenhoek, using single-lens microscopes of up to 270-fold magnification, found moving organisms, which he called animalcules, and described red blood cells and bacteria.

Credit for the theory goes usually to Matthias Jakob Schleiden and Theodor Schwann. In 1839 Schleiden proposed that every structural part of a plant was made of cells or their products, and Schwann stated that animals were too. Two tenets followed: all living organisms are composed of one or more cells, and the cell is the most basic unit of life. Schleiden also held that cells formed by a crystallisation process, an idea refuted in the 1850s by Robert Remak, Rudolf Virchow and Albert Kolliker.

In 1855 Virchow added the third tenet, Omnis cellula e cellula: all cells arise only from pre-existing cells. Remak had proposed this already, and it has been suggested that Virchow plagiarised him. In 1852 Remak had published observations of cell division, holding that new animal cells arose by binary fission. With the third tenet, classical cell theory was complete.

Modern cell theory states that all known living things consist of one or more cells, that all living cells arise from pre-existing cells by division, and that the cell is the fundamental unit of structure and function. It has traditionally governed the study of life, although some biologists who count viruses as living organisms dispute its universal application. Later work on how cells control what passes in and out set a membrane theory against bulk-phase theories of protoplasm; the plasma membrane is now described as a fluid lipid bilayer with embedded proteins, following the model of Singer and Nicolson of 1972.
celle: Celle lies in the glacial valley of the river Aller, about 40 kilometres north-east of Hanover and 120 kilometres south of Hamburg. The Lachte and the Fuhse both flow into the Aller within the town. Celle is the southern gateway to the Lüneburg Heath and, apart from Lüneburg, the largest town of Lower Saxony between Hanover and Hamburg.

Celle is first mentioned in a document of 985 as Kiellu, meaning fishing bay. In the 11th century it was granted the right to mint coins, some of which were found in the Sandur hoard in the Faroes. In 1292 Duke Otto II the Strict, a Welf who ruled the Principality of Lüneburg from 1277 to 1330, left Altencelle and founded a rectangular settlement beside the existing castle, 4 kilometres to the north-west. He granted Celle town privileges in 1301 and began its town church in 1308.

From 1378 to 1705 Celle was the official residence of the Lüneburg branch of the dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg, of the House of Welf, who had been banished from their original ducal seat by its townsfolk. The Reformation came in 1524, and the castle chapel, built in 1570, was consecrated in 1585. George William, the last Heath Duke, ruled from 1665 until he died in Celle Castle in 1705. In the Middle Ages the town had only a few thousand inhabitants, and growth quickened only with industrialisation: 8,800 in 1818, 20,000 by 1900. Celle was an important garrison town in Nazi Germany, and during the pogrom of 9 and 10 November 1938 its synagogue escaped destruction only because of the risk to neighbouring buildings.

Celle is the capital of its district in Lower Saxony and has about 71,000 inhabitants. Its old town has more than 400 timber-framed houses, among them the Hoppenerhaus of 1532, and the Old City Hall of 1561 to 1579 is known for its sandstone carvings. Schloss Celle, begun in 1530 and enlarged in baroque style in the 17th century, has a theatre founded in 1674, the oldest still working in Germany. The Bergen-Belsen concentration camp, where Anne Frank died in 1945, lay in the district of Celle, and a memorial marks the site.
celtiberia: The Celtiberians were a group of Celts and Celticised peoples in the central-north-eastern Iberian Peninsula during the last centuries BCE, and several classical authors, Strabo among them, called them Celts. They spoke the Celtiberian language, a Celtic language written in an adaptation of the Iberian alphabet. Their cultural stronghold was the northern part of the central meseta, in the upper valleys of the Tagus and Douro and east to the Ebro, in the modern provinces of Soria, Guadalajara, Zaragoza and Teruel. The Ebro clearly divided them from the non-Indo-European peoples beyond it. The dominant tribe were the Arevaci, who held strongholds such as Okilis, now Medinaceli.

Celtic presence in Iberia probably dates to the 6th century BCE, when the hillforts known as castros gained stone walls and ditches. From the 3rd century BCE the clan gave way to the oppidum, a fortified city with a defined territory, as the basic political unit. These communities made and broke alliances, as surviving inscribed hospitality pacts show, and minted coins. A military aristocracy that had become a hereditary elite controlled them. Celtiberian metalwork stands out in the finds, and Polybius wrote that the Romans abandoned their traditional swords after the war with Hannibal and adopted those of the Iberians.

In the Second Punic War the Celtiberians served most often as allies or mercenaries of Carthage, until Scipio Africanus won over many tribes. Rome began conquering part of Celtiberia in 195 BCE, and uprisings followed in 195–193, 181–179, 153–151 and 143–133 BCE. Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus claimed to have destroyed over 300 Celtiberian settlements, and in 137 BCE the Celtiberians forced a 20,000-man consular army under Gaius Hostilius Mancinus to surrender.

In 134 BCE Scipio Aemilianus besieged Numantia with some 60,000 men, enclosing it with a ditch, palisade and wall. After eight months the starving town surrendered; many inhabitants killed themselves, and the survivors were sold as slaves and the town razed. The Sertorian War of 80–72 BCE was the last formal resistance of the Celtiberian cities, and by 72 BCE the whole region was under Roman rule. Hundreds of Celtic place-names remain on the map of Spain, and excavation of Numantia, published between 1914 and 1931, began the archaeological recovery of the culture.
celts: In current scholarship Celt refers primarily to a speaker of a Celtic language, not to a single ethnic group, and the links between ethnicity, language and culture in the Celtic world are debated. The Celtic languages belong to the Indo-European family. By about 400 BCE, when Celts are first mentioned in written records, they had already split into several language groups across much of western Europe, Iberia, Ireland and Britain. The name Keltoi was first recorded by Hecataeus of Miletus in 517 BCE, for a people living near Massilia, and Herodotus later placed Keltoi near the source of the Danube and in the far west.

Three theories place the origin of proto-Celtic differently. The older view held that it arose in the Urnfield culture of central Europe around 1000 BCE and spread with the Hallstatt and La Tène cultures. The Celtic from the West theory puts it earlier, along the Atlantic coast. Patrick Sims-Williams proposes that it emerged in the second millennium BCE, probably in Gaul. The earliest undisputed Celtic inscriptions are Lepontic, from the 6th century BCE.

Sources depict a pre-Christian social order based on class and kingship, with patron-client relations like those of Rome described by Caesar in Gaul. Celtic territory held tin, lead, iron, silver and gold, and smiths made weapons and jewellery for trade, particularly with the Romans. The Gauls took up coinage from the 3rd century BCE. Their religion was polytheistic and overseen by druids; the names of over two hundred deities survive, though many may be alternative names for the same deity. Art historians use Celtic art for the art of the La Tène period, with its circular forms, triskeles and spirals.

Under Caesar the Romans conquered Celtic Gaul, and from Claudius onward the empire absorbed parts of Britain. In Gaul this led to a shift to Vulgar Latin, while the Insular Celts kept their language. By about 500, Romanisation and Germanic migrations had confined Celtic culture mostly to Ireland, western and northern Britain and Brittany. The Insular Celtic communities then diversified into the Gaels, meaning the Irish, Scots and Manx, and the Britons, meaning the Welsh, Cornish and Bretons.

No group called itself Celtic from antiquity until about 1700, and the English word Celt is first attested in 1707 in the work of Edward Lhuyd. A modern Celtic identity grew out of the Romanticist Celtic Revival. Irish, Scottish Gaelic, Welsh and Breton are still spoken in parts of their former territories, and Cornish and Manx are being revived.
cen-chunxuan: Cen was born on 2 May 1861 in Xilin, Guangxi, a Zhuang Chinese and the son of Cen Yuying, Viceroy of Yunnan and Guizhou. Badly behaved in his youth, he was counted among the Three Notorious Youngsters in the Capital. He entered the civil service in 1879 and passed the imperial examination as a juren in 1885. In 1898 the Guangxu Emperor, impressed after interviewing him, made an exception and promoted him to a second-grade post in Guangdong, but a quarrel with his superior, Tan Zhonglin, had him moved to Gansu.

When the Eight-Nation Alliance attacked Beijing in 1900, Cen led troops from Gansu to protect the Guangxu Emperor and Empress Dowager Cixi on their flight to Xi'an, winning her favour. As governor of Shanxi he set up the forerunner of Shanxi University with the Welsh missionary Timothy Richard. As acting viceroy of Sichuan he set up a police force and accused more than 40 officials of corruption, earning the name Butcher of Officials. Appointed Viceroy of Guangdong and Guangxi in 1903, he urged a constitutional monarchy and the abolition of the imperial examinations, and became a leader of the Constitutional Monarchy Movement.

His attacks on corrupt officials made an enemy of Prince Qing, who with Yuan Shikai defeated him in the political struggle of dingwei: transferred to Yunnan in 1906, briefly Minister of Posts and Communications in 1907, he was accused of supporting Liang Qichao and dismissed by Cixi. In 1911 he urged the court to become a constitutional monarchy rather than crush the rebels, and resigned shortly before the Wuchang Uprising.

Under the Republic he asked Yuan Shikai in 1913 to settle his conflict with Sun Yat-sen peacefully; the revolutionaries of the Second Revolution named him their grand marshal, and after its failure he fled to Southeast Asia with a price on his head. He returned to Shanghai on 4 January 1916 to oppose Yuan's attempt to make himself emperor, and on 19 April 1916 he, Liang Qichao and Lu Rongting set up the National Protection Military Government at Zhaoqing. When the military government he led at Guangzhou from 1918 was disbanded two years later, he resigned and lived in retirement in Shanghai, where he died on 27 April 1933.
cen-yuying: Cen Yuying was of Zhuang ethnicity and was born in Xilin County, Guangxi, in 1829. He received a traditional Confucian education and first served in local militia forces, where he gained recognition for his campaigns against bandit groups. In 1856, during the Xianfeng reign, he led militia troops from Guangxi into Yunnan to help Qing forces put down the Muslim rebellion there.

The rebellion in Yunnan arose amid escalating communal violence, competition over resources and local political tensions, and one of its principal leaders, Du Wenxiu, made Dali in western Yunnan his political and military base. Cen took part in the campaigns to recover the cities and strategic positions held by the rebels, rose through the provincial administration and became Governor of Yunnan in 1868. The restoration of Qing authority came only after years of warfare and violence that inflicted severe losses on the province's population.

In 1875, while Cen was governor, the British official Augustus Raymond Margary was killed while travelling ahead of a British expedition approaching Yunnan from Burma. The Margary Affair led to a diplomatic dispute between Britain and the Qing government and contributed to the Chefoo Convention of 1876. In 1881 Cen was appointed Governor of Fujian and took part in the administration and defence of Taiwan, including measures to strengthen its infrastructure and coastal defence, before he returned to the southwest as governor-general of Yunnan and Guizhou.

In the Sino-French War he directed Qing operations on the western front in northern Vietnam, coordinating troops across the frontier in campaigns against the French, among them operations around Tuyên Quang and engagements in the region of Lào Cai.

After the war Cen remained a senior official in southwestern China, holding high provincial office and receiving further honours from the Qing court. He died in 1889 and was given the posthumous name Xiangqin. His son Cen Chunxuan became a prominent official in the last years of the Qing dynasty and the early Republic of China.
cenad: Cenad lies in the west of Timiș County, on the left bank of the Mureș River, where it serves as a customs point on the border with Hungary. It is one of the places with the oldest documented history in the Banat. People have lived there since the Neolithic, about 7,000 years ago, and finds of the Starčevo–Criș, Vinča, Tisza and Tiszapolgár cultures show long settlement. The Roman era left pottery, tools, coins and bricks stamped by military units, and a legionary camp of the Legio XIII Gemina stood on the site.

In the early Middle Ages the site served as a temporary capital for the Huns and the Avars and was later ruled by the First Bulgarian Empire. Ahtum, who resided there at the beginning of the reign of Stephen I, brought architects from Greece to build a church, a monastery and a palace. After his fall Morisena became a royal fortress and the seat of a county, and the bishop Gerard brought Italian engineers who built the fortress of Cenad on the site of the old one.

Kings of Hungary visited it often, among them Ladislaus IV in 1278, Charles I in 1322 and Sigismund several times between 1394 and 1436. It was destroyed in the Tatar invasion of 1241 and rebuilt by Bishop Bulcsú Lád. After 1526 it passed to the Eastern Hungarian Kingdom and from 1551 to Ottoman rule as the centre of the Sanjak of Çanad, until the Austrian conquest of 1716. Its fortress was demolished under the terms of the Treaty of Karlowitz, with the work directed by General Oettingen.

German colonists arrived in 1764–1765 and founded German Cenad beside Serbian Cenad, and the two later merged. In 1858 the estate passed to the Aromanian Nakó family, who built a castle there. Serbian troops occupied the village in 1918, and it passed to Romania after the Treaty of Trianon in 1920.

Cenad is a commune made up of a single village, formed in the 20th century by merging Cenadu Mare and Cenadu Vechi, with 3,537 inhabitants at the 2021 census. The ruins of the fortress and of Ahtum's monastery survive, and the neo-Gothic St. Gerard church of 1870 holds the sarcophagus of Gerard of Csanád.
cenel-conaill: The Cenél Conaill, the kindred of Conall, claim descent from Conall Gulban, son of Niall of the Nine Hostages, who is said to have been the first Irish nobleman to convert to Christianity. Their power base was at Mag Ithe in the Finn valley, and from there they gradually expanded across what are now counties Donegal and Fermanagh. They clashed regularly with their kin the Cenél nEogain, and by the 12th century had taken the latter's original seat of Ailech on the Inishowen peninsula.

The kindred was made up of branches named after descendants of Conall. The Cenél Luighdech, or Sil Lugdach, descended from Lugaid mac Sétnai, Conall's great-grandson, and held the land from Gweedore to the river Swilly; from them came the O'Donnells and O'Dohertys, the two most powerful septs of the Cenél Conaill. The Cenél Aedha, from Aedha mac Ainmirech, are said to have given their name to the barony of Tirhugh, and the Gallaghers, descended from Gallchobar, claimed to be the most senior branch of all. The Cenél Eanna, from Conall's sixth son Eanna, are listed as kings of Magh Ith, Tír Eanna and Fanad.

Smaller septs included the Cenél mBógaine, from Énna Bóguine, whose territory of Tír Boghaine O'Donovan equated with the barony of Banagh and part of Boylagh. The Laud 610 genealogies, compiled about 1000, give Énna seven sons, while O'Clery's Book of Genealogies gives a different list. Saint Crona was fifth in descent from him. The Cenél Duach took their name from Tigernach Duí, whose son Nainnid fought at Móin Daire Lothair, where the Northern Uí Néill defeated the Cruithin; Nainnid's son Baedan ruled as king of Tara for one year in 568.

The best-known member of the kindred is Saint Columba, claimed as a grandson of Conall Gulban and the founder of the monastery at Derry. The Cenél Aedha's name survives in the barony of Tirhugh, and the O'Donnells, O'Dohertys and Gallaghers trace their descent to branches of the kindred.
cenel-neogain: The Cenél nEógain, or Kinel-Owen, the kindred of Owen, were a branch of the Northern Uí Néill who claimed descent from Eógan mac Néill, son of Niall of the Nine Hostages. Their first power base was the Inishowen peninsula, with Ailech as their capital. The Cenél mBinnigh, descended from Eógan's son Eochu Binneach, were the first of the kindred to advance out of Inishowen, bypassing the Ciannachta and driving several Airgiallan clans, among them the Ui Tuirtri and Fir Li, east of the River Bann. The Cenél Feargusa followed them towards Tullyhogue and became the vanguard of the O'Neills.

Under pressure from the Cenél Conaill, the kindred spread east into what are now Tyrone and Londonderry, pushing aside the Cruithin east of the Bann and encroaching on the Airgiallan tribes west of Lough Neagh. By the 11th century their seat had moved from Ailech to Tullyhogue near Cookstown. When the Cenél Conaill took Inishowen in the 12th century it mattered little, for the Cenél nEógain had by then built the over-kingdom of Tír Eoghain, the Land of Owen, whose name survives in County Tyrone. At their height they held much of Tyrone and parts of Donegal, Fermanagh, Londonderry, Monaghan and Armagh.

The O'Neills and MacLaughlins of Clann Néill, named after Néill Caille, were the two most powerful septs, until the defeat of the MacLaughlins by the O'Neills in 1241 left the O'Neills dominant. A branch, the Clandeboye O'Neills, took its name from Aodh Buidhe O'Neill, the last king to be styled King of Ailech, and after the collapse of the Earldom of Ulster under Edward Bruce's invasion took control of most of eastern Ulster.

Many lesser septs traced themselves to Eógan's sons and grandsons. The Cenél Fearadhaigh controlled much of Tyrone by the 12th century and reached deep into Fermanagh until the Maguires broke their power there in the mid-14th century. The Clann Conchúir Magh Ithe moved into County Londonderry and ruled what became O'Cahan Country, and their offshoot the O'Cahans of the Route fought a long rivalry with the Hiberno-Norman MacQuillans. The O'Donnells forced the Cenél Moen across the River Foyle in the 14th century.
cenepa-war: The dispute between Ecuador and Peru went back to the first decades of the 19th century, when both countries emerged from the Spanish colonies. After the Ecuadorian–Peruvian War of 1941 the two signed the Rio Protocol in 1942, brokered by the United States, Brazil, Chile and Argentina, the guarantors of the settlement. Demarcation halted in 1948, when President José María Velasco Ibarra declared the Protocol impossible to implement in the Cordillera del Cóndor, and in 1960 Ecuador declared the treaty null and void. A 78 km strip of the border remained undemarcated.

Tensions rose after the Pachacútec Incident of July 1991 over a Peruvian outpost that Ecuador claimed lay on its side. From 1994 Ecuador installed outposts named Cueva de los Tayos, Base Sur and Tiwinza in the Cenepa basin on the eastern side of the range, territory Peru also claimed. In late 1994 a meeting of battalion commanders at Base Sur failed to settle the matter, and both Quito and Lima sent reinforcements.

During December the Ecuadorian Army deployed Special Forces, artillery, BM-21 rocket launchers and teams with man-portable surface-to-air missiles on the heights. On 26 January 1995 Ecuadorian Special Forces attacked Peruvian conscripts setting up a heliport behind their outposts and drove them off, and the shooting war began. Both countries ordered general mobilisation the next day, and around 140,000 men were mobilised in all. The first Peruvian ground assault came on 28 January, supported by helicopters and ground attack aircraft.

Several explanations have been offered for the course of the fighting. Peruvian reinforcements and supplies had to be flown in by helicopter from Ciro Alegría base, more than 110 km to the south. Ecuador committed Special Forces and Iwia detachments of tribal people such as the Shuar, while the Peruvian troops were at first mostly young conscripts, and Ecuadorian artillery fired from the heights of the range.

Casualty figures vary widely: official estimates give 94 dead, while the human rights organisation ALDHU put the dead of both sides at around 500. Mediation by Argentina, Brazil, Chile and the United States opened the talks that ended in the Brasilia Presidential Act of 26 October 1998. Ecuador accepted the validity of the Rio Protocol, and it received 1 km2 at Tiwinza as private property, without sovereignty, for commemorative use. The border was formally demarcated on 13 May 1999, and the observer mission MOMEP ended on 17 June 1999, closing one of the longest territorial disputes in the Western Hemisphere.
census: The word comes from the Latin censere, to assess. In the Roman Republic the census was a list of all adult males fit for military service. From the middle republic it was usually carried out every five years, and it gave a register of citizens and their property from which duties and privileges could be listed; it determined the class a citizen belonged to for both military and tax purposes. It is said to have been instituted by the king Servius Tullius in the 6th century BCE,

Other early counts served the same fiscal ends. The earliest Egyptian census counted cattle, not people, for taxation; it was taken every two years in the early Old Kingdom, and human censuses appeared in the late Middle Kingdom. In the early Achaemenid period, up to the reign of Darius the Great, a census across three continents recorded population, the wealth of the satrapies and their farmland, for finance, tax and military planning. The Han dynasty census of 2 CE registered 57,671,400 people in 12,366,470 households, counting only taxable families.

In the Middle Ages the Caliphate began regular censuses soon after its formation, starting with one ordered by the second Rashidun caliph, Umar. William I of England had the Domesday Book compiled in 1086 so that he could tax the land he had recently conquered. In 1183 a census of the crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem gauged the men and money that could be raised against an invasion by Saladin. The first national census of France, the État des paroisses et des feux of 1328, was made mostly for fiscal purposes

The Inca Empire had no written language and recorded census data on quipus, cords with values encoded in knots in a base-10 positional system. In 1577 Philip II of Spain ordered a general description of the Indies, with a questionnaire of fifty items sent to officials in New Spain and Peru.

A census is the systematic acquiring, recording and calculating of information about the members of a population. The United Nations lists its essential features as individual enumeration, universality within a defined territory, simultaneity and defined periodicity, and recommends one at least every ten years. A historical census was a house-to-house process or the product of an imperial decree, which marks the difference from the modern statistical project. Early censuses of the 19th and 20th centuries were collated by hand, so their statistics were basic.
central-africa: Central Africa is a subregion whose countries differ according to the definition used. The United Nations geoscheme, which calls it Middle Africa, lists Angola, Cameroon, the Central African Republic, Chad, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Equatorial Guinea, Gabon, the Republic of the Congo, and São Tomé and Príncipe. The African Development Bank counts seven countries. The basin of the Congo River has long been ecologically important to the peoples of the region.

Archaeological finds go back over 100,000 years, and there is evidence of iron smelting in the Central African Republic that may date to 3000-2500 BCE. Bantu migrants reached the Great Lakes region around 2500 BCE and had settled as far south as present-day Angola by the middle of the first millennium BCE. In the north, the Sao civilisation lived by the Chari River from about the 6th century BCE, and Kanem, known by that name from the 9th century CE, gave rise to the Bornu Empire, which lasted until 1900.

In the south, the Bakongo were unified by the 15th century as the Kingdom of Kongo under a ruler called the manikongo, with its capital at M'banza-Kongo. Afonso I, a Christian, took the throne in 1506, and slave trading increased with his wars of conquest. The Jaga invaded about 1568-1569, and Manikongo António I's army was destroyed by an Afro-Portuguese army at the Battle of Mbwila in the 1660s, after which the kingdom dissolved into petty polities fighting for war captives to sell. In the 1450s the Luba Ilunga Tshibinda married the Lunda queen Rweej and united the Lunda peoples; their descendants took the title Mwata Yamvo, and the empire lasted until the Chokwe, armed with guns, invaded it in the 19th century.

At the Conference of Berlin in 1884-85 Africa was divided among European colonial powers, defining boundaries largely intact today. Chad, Gabon, the Republic of the Congo, the Central African Republic and the Democratic Republic of the Congo gained independence in 1960, Equatorial Guinea in 1968, and Angola and São Tomé and Príncipe in 1975.

The main economic activities are farming, herding and fishing. Bantu languages predominate across much of the region, spoken by peoples such as the Mongo, Kongo and Luba, alongside Nilo-Saharan and Ubangian communities. Christianity and traditional faiths are the main religions, and Chad is the only country where Islam is the majority religion.
central-african-republic: The Central African Republic is a landlocked country in the interior of Africa, bordered by Cameroon, Chad, Sudan, South Sudan, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the Republic of the Congo. Much of it is a flat or rolling plateau savanna about 500 metres above sea level. Two-thirds of the country lies within the basin of the Ubangi River, a tributary of the Congo, and the remaining third within the basin of the Chari River, which flows into Lake Chad. About 36 per cent of the country is forest, with the densest forest in the south.

The name comes from the country's location in Central Africa and its republican government. During the colonial era it was called Ubangi-Shari, after the Ubangi and Chari rivers. Barthélemy Boganda, the first prime minister, favoured the name Central African Republic, reportedly because he envisioned a larger union of countries in Central Africa. From 1976 to 1979 the country was known as the Central African Empire.

The region has been inhabited since at least 8000 BCE. About 10,000 years ago desertification forced hunter-gatherer societies south into the Sahel, where some settled and began farming. Before 3000 BCE the domestication of the African oil palm improved nutrition and allowed populations to expand. The Bouar Megaliths in the west indicate an advanced level of habitation in the late Neolithic, c. 3500 to 2700 BCE, and ironwork developed in the region around 1000 BCE. The Ubangian people settled along the Ubangi River, and some Bantu people migrated from southwest Cameroon.

In the 16th and 17th centuries slave traders raided the region as part of the expansion of the Saharan and Nile slave routes, and captives were shipped to the Mediterranean coast, Europe, Arabia and the Western Hemisphere. In the 18th century the Bandia-Nzakara Azande peoples established the Bangassou Kingdom along the Ubangi. In the mid 19th century the Bobangi people became major slave traders. The borders were established by France, which began annexing portions to the French Congo in the late 19th century and in 1903 created the separate colony of Ubangi-Shari, part of French Equatorial Africa.

The Central African Republic became independent from France in 1960. Its capital and largest city is Bangui, on the southern border with the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Its people belong to about 80 ethnic groups, the largest being the Gbaya and the Banda. French and Sango, a creole based on the Ngbandi language, are the official languages. The Aka of the south-west have a vocal tradition of contrapuntal polyphony in four voices.
central-america: Central America is a subregion of North America, a tapering isthmus running from the southern extent of Mexico to the northwestern portion of South America. It has the Gulf of Mexico to the north, the Caribbean Sea to the northeast and the Pacific Ocean to the southwest. It is usually defined as consisting of seven countries: Belize, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua and Panama. The term is defined differently in different contexts. In Spanish-speaking countries the Americas are considered a single continent, América, of which Central America is a subregion.

The region has over 70 active volcanoes, and several active geological faults and the Central America Volcanic Arc make seismic activity high. The longest of its many mountain ranges are the Sierra Madre de Chiapas, the Cordillera Isabelia and the Cordillera de Talamanca. At 4,220 metres, Volcán Tajumulco is the highest peak.

Central America was formed more than 3 million years ago as part of the Isthmus of Panama. In the pre-Columbian era the northern areas were inhabited by the indigenous peoples of Mesoamerica, most notably the Maya, who built numerous cities. The cultures of eastern Honduras, Caribbean Nicaragua, most of Costa Rica and Panama were predominantly speakers of Chibchan languages at the time of European contact, and are grouped by some in the Isthmo-Colombian cultural area.

Spain began its colonisation from 1502 onward. Pedro de Alvarado began the conquest of Maya territory in 1523, arriving in Soconusco, and his forces systematically conquered most of the major Maya kingdoms, including the K'iche', Tz'utujil, Pipil and Kaqchikel. By 1528 the conquest of Guatemala was nearly complete. The last independent Maya kingdoms, the Kowoj and the Itza, were defeated in 1697. In 1609 the area became the Captaincy General of Guatemala, which encompassed most of Central America except present-day Belize and Panama.

On 24 August 1821 the Spanish viceroy Juan de O'Donojú signed the Treaty of Córdoba, which established the independence of New Spain. In 1838 Costa Rica, Guatemala, Honduras and Nicaragua became the first of the region's states to become independent countries after the dissolution of the Federal Republic of Central America, followed by El Salvador in 1841, Panama in 1903 and Belize in 1981.

Despite the dissolution of the federation, its former members preserved a Central American identity. In Spanish, Centroamérica refers to the former members of the federation, emphasising their shared culture and history, while América Central refers to the geographical area of the seven countries between Mexico and Colombia.
central-asia: Central Asia has no single definition. Alexander von Humboldt, one of the first geographers to treat it as a distinct region, defined it by latitude, while the Russian geographer Nikolaĭ Khanykov preferred a physical definition that took in all landlocked lands, including Afghanistan, Khorasan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, East Turkestan, Mongolia and Uzbekistan. The countries most commonly included are Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan.

The land is varied: high passes and mountains such as the Tian Shan, deserts such as the Kyzyl Kum and the Taklamakan, and vast treeless steppes that form, with those of Eastern Europe, the Eurasian Steppe. Much of it is too dry or too rugged for farming. Dense population and cities are found where irrigation is possible, along the eastern mountains, the Oxus and Jaxartes rivers and the north flank of the Kopet Dagh, and at oases such as Merv, Herat and Balkh.

Aridity and distance from the sea limited agriculture and trade, so few major cities developed, and for millennia the region was dominated by nomadic horse peoples of the steppe. Before about 1000 it was inhabited chiefly by Iranian peoples, among them the Bactrians, Sogdians and Chorasmians and the semi-nomadic Scythians and Dahae. Turkic migration then made it the homeland of the Kazakhs, Kyrgyz, Tatars, Turkmens, Uyghurs and Uzbeks, and Turkic languages largely replaced Iranian ones except in Tajikistan and where Tajik is spoken. The Silk Road crossed the region and gave rise to prosperous trading cities.

The Tang dynasty of China expanded west and controlled large parts of the region, directly and through Turkic vassals, until the Abbasid Caliphate defeated it at the Battle of Talas in 751. In the 13th and 14th centuries the Mongols conquered most of Central Asia, which fell largely under the Chagatai Khanate. From the mid-19th century the region was incorporated into the Russian Empire and later the Soviet Union, and Russians and other Slavs settled in it. During the Stalinist period Koreans were forcibly deported there. Historians stress that Central Asia has rarely been the seat of an empire of its own and has more often been a battleground for outside powers.

With the collapse of the Soviet Union, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan became independent. Most inhabitants speak Turkic languages, among them Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Turkmen and Uzbek, and Russian remains a lingua franca. Islam is the most common religion, mostly Sunni, and Nowruz, with Zoroastrian roots, is observed in all five states. The Aral Sea and Lake Balkhash have shrunk significantly through the diversion of the rivers that feed them.
central-bank: Government control of money is documented in the ancient Egyptian economy, 2750–2150 BCE, where goods were measured against a central unit called shat, linked to gold. Issuing paper currency is not the same as central banking: government-issued money, as in China during the Yuan dynasty, is typically not freely convertible and was occasionally followed by hyperinflation. From the twelfth century professional banks emerged, primarily in Southern Europe, which could use book money to create deposits without direct control from political authorities.

The Taula de canvi de Barcelona, established in 1401, is the first example of municipal, mostly public banks that pioneered central banking on a limited scale. The Bank of Saint George in the Republic of Genoa followed in 1407, then the Bank of Amsterdam in 1609 and the Hamburger Bank in 1619.

The Swedish central bank, known since 1866 as Sveriges Riksbank, was founded in Stockholm from the remains of the failed Stockholms Banco and answered to the Riksdag of the Estates. The Bank of England received a royal charter on 27 July 1694 through the Tonnage Act, following a 1691 proposal by William Paterson. It held the government's balances and was the only limited-liability corporation allowed to issue banknotes, though it lacked several functions of today's central banks.

Napoleon created the Banque de France in 1800 to stabilise the French economy and improve the financing of his wars, and the Bank of Finland was founded in 1812. At the start of the twentieth century about two-thirds of sovereign states had no central bank; waves of adoption followed in the interwar period and after the Second World War, and the European Central Bank was established in 1998.

A central bank manages the monetary policy of a country or monetary union. In contrast to a commercial bank, it has a monopoly on increasing the monetary base, and many also supervise commercial banks. The notion of a central bank as a separate category only fully coalesced in the twentieth century, when Montagu Norman of the United Kingdom and Benjamin Strong of the United States agreed a definition after the First World War. The expression itself appeared in the early nineteenth century, when it referred to the head office of a multi-branched bank, as in Walter Bagehot's 1873 book Lombard Street. Its primary role is usually to maintain price stability.
central-bank-of-ecuador: In the first decades of the 20th century Ecuador's finances suffered from uncontrolled issue of money by private banks, made worse by the First World War and a sharp fall in demand for cacao, its main export, in the early 1920s. The revolt of young army officers on 9 July 1925, the July Revolution, followed. Its finance minister, Luis Napoleón Dillon, first proposed a central bank, and a law for one was approved on 9 October 1925, but the bank's first board, Dillon among them, resigned in January 1926.

Under President Isidro Ayora a Central Issuance and Amortization Fund was set up on 26 June 1926, and the provisional board invited Edwin Kemmerer of Princeton University to advise. Kemmerer's commission presented the Central Bank Organic Law on 11 February 1927; Ayora approved it on 4 March, the first board under Neptalí Bonifaz was formed on 4 June, and the bank opened in the historic centre of Quito on 10 August 1927, with a branch in Guayaquil from 25 August.

The bank first tied the sucre to gold at 0.300933 grams of fine gold, a fifth of the dollar's gold value. A new organic law drawn up with the Mexican Manuel Gómez Morín took effect on 30 December 1937, and on 12 March 1948 laws proposed by Robert Triffin of the Federal Reserve made a Monetary Board, on which the government sat, its highest body. During the debt crisis of the 1980s and 1990s a law of 7 May 1992 replaced the Monetary Board with a board of directors and allowed open market operations.

The 1998 Constitution gave the bank technical autonomy, and it had a leading part in the banking crisis of 1999, which ended with the adoption of the dollar on 9 January 2000. The 2008 Constitution ended its autonomy, and the bank lent to the executive; a law approved on 22 April 2021 restored it.

The bank manages Ecuador's international reserves, acts as the state's fiscal agent, runs the central payment system, supplies dollar notes and coins in coordination with the United States Federal Reserve, publishes economic statistics and buys gold from small-scale miners. Since 4 February 1976 its emblem has been the Golden Sun of the La Tolita culture, and it keeps a Numismatic Museum in Quito and Cuenca.
central-europe: Central Europe has no agreed boundaries, and which countries belong to it often depends on the nationality and historical outlook of the author. The concept appeared in the 19th century, when it was understood as a contact zone between the southern and northern areas of Europe and later between the eastern and western. Geography fixes its borders most clearly to the north, across the Baltic Sea, and to the south, across the Alps and the Soča–Krka–Sava–Danube line, while the borders with Western and Eastern Europe are less defined.

After Roman rule fell in the 5th century, Germanic tribes, among them the Franks, Alemans and Bavarians, conquered parts of the west, while Slavic tribes lived mainly in the east. After the Holy Roman Empire was dissolved around 1800, power was consolidated in the Habsburgs and the Hohenzollerns, who cooperated at times but more often competed. At the Frankfurt Parliament of 1848 Austria proposed merging the smaller German-speaking states with the multi-ethnic Habsburg monarchy, which Prussia and others opposed. The idea of Mitteleuropa later became popular in the German Empire, founded in 1871.

After 1918 the concept shifted to the east and the countries that had reappeared on the map. Central Europe became a field for integration movements, such as the Little Entente, formed in 1921 by Czechoslovakia, Romania and the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, and the Intermarium idea, neither of which succeeded. In the Second World War Nazi Germany occupied most of the region, and the mass murder of the Jews emptied settlements that had existed for centuries. After the war much of it came under Soviet control, and the Iron Curtain divided it, although Austria, Switzerland and Yugoslavia declared neutrality.

The states most often counted as Central European are Austria, the Czech Republic, Germany, Hungary, Liechtenstein, Poland, Slovakia, Slovenia and Switzerland, and many sources add Croatia and Lithuania. The region is mostly Catholic or historically both Catholic and Protestant. The first university east of France and north of the Alps was founded in Prague in 1348 by Charles IV, Holy Roman Emperor.
central-india-agency: The agency was created in 1854 by joining the Western Malwa Agency with smaller political offices that had reported directly to the Governor-General of India. Its political agent, with his headquarters at Indore, conducted the Government of India's relations with the princely states and held influence over them on the Governor-General's behalf.

Under the agent stood several subordinate agencies and residencies. Bundelkhand Agency, between the United Provinces to the north and the Central Provinces to the south, included in 1900 nine states, among them Orchha, Panna, Datia, Charkhari, Chhatarpur and Ajaigarh, along with thirteen estates. Bagelkhand Agency was separated from it in March 1871 and covered twelve states, of which Rewa, with a hereditary salute of 17 guns, was the largest. In 1931 all its states but Rewa went back to Bundelkhand, and in 1933 Rewa passed to the Indore Residency.

Gwalior Residency, whose ruler bore the title Maharaja Scindia and a 21-gun salute, was placed under the agency in 1854 and separated from it in 1911. Bhopal Agency, of 11,653 square miles, held Bhopal, Narsinghgarh, Rajgarh and Khilchipur among others. Malwa Agency, of 8,919 square miles, with Ratlam, Jaora, Sailana and Sitamau, was joined to Bhopawar Agency in 1925; Bhopawar, which included Dhar, Alirajpur and Barwani, was renamed the Southern States Agency in 1927. Several former states had been annexed or seized by the British, among them Jhansi in 1853 and Banpur and Shahgarh in 1857.

When the British withdrew in 1947, the rulers of all the princely states of the area chose to accede to the Union of India. The eastern part, with the Bagelkhand and Bundelkhand agencies, became Vindhya Pradesh; the western part, with the Bhopal, Malwa and Bhopawar agencies and the Gwalior and Indore residencies, became Madhya Bharat; and Bhopal became a separate state. In 1956 Vindhya Pradesh, Madhya Bharat and Bhopal were merged into Madhya Pradesh, from part of which Chhattisgarh was later formed.
central-intelligence-agency: During the Second World War, American intelligence and covert operations were carried out by the Office of Strategic Services. President Harry S. Truman abolished it in 1945 and in 1946 created the Central Intelligence Group. As the Cold War intensified, the National Security Act of 1947 established the CIA, headed by a director of central intelligence. When it was proposed, its purpose was to act as a clearinghouse to collect, analyse, evaluate and disseminate foreign intelligence and to carry out covert operations. The Central Intelligence Agency Act of 1949 exempted it from most Congressional oversight and allowed the director to spend unvouchered funds. Its first training facility, the Office of Training and Education, was established in 1950.

The CIA is a civilian foreign intelligence service, headquartered in Langley, Virginia. A director, appointed by the president with Senate confirmation, heads it; since 2004 the director has reported to the director of national intelligence. Unlike the Federal Bureau of Investigation, it has no law enforcement function and focuses on intelligence gathering overseas, with only limited domestic collection. It coordinates human intelligence activities across the intelligence community.

Its work is divided among directorates. The Directorate of Analysis, long known as the Directorate of Intelligence, helps policymakers make informed decisions. The Directorate of Operations collects foreign intelligence, mainly from clandestine human sources, and conducts covert action; it was created in part to end years of rivalry with the Department of Defense. The Directorate of Science and Technology develops technical collection equipment, such as the U-2 high-altitude reconnaissance aircraft built with the United States Air Force. The Directorate of Support handles security, communications and information technology, and the newest, the Directorate of Digital Innovation, works on digital and cyber capabilities.

In the 1950s the CIA became a major instrument of American foreign policy. It used psychological operations against communist regimes and backed coups to advance American interests. Major CIA-backed operations include the 1953 coup in Iran, the 1954 coup in Guatemala, the Bay of Pigs Invasion of Cuba in 1961 and the 1973 coup in Chile.

In 1975 the Church Committee of the United States Senate revealed illegal operations such as MKUltra and CHAOS. In the 1980s the agency supported the Afghan mujahideen through Pakistan's intelligence service and the Nicaraguan Contras, and after the September 11 attacks of 2001 it played a role in the war on terrorism. The agency has been the subject of controversies, including its use of assassinations, torture, domestic wiretapping and propaganda.
central-java: Central Java lies in the middle of the island of Java. It is bordered by West Java in the west, the Indian Ocean and the Special Region of Yogyakarta in the south, East Java in the east and the Java Sea in the north. It also includes offshore islands, among them Nusakambangan in the south and the Karimun Jawa Islands in the Java Sea. The northern coastal lowland is narrow, only 4 kilometres wide at Semarang, and Mount Muria, an island at the end of the Ice Age, was fused to Java by alluvial deposits. The Bengawan Solo, at 572 kilometres the longest river on Java, rises in the Sewu Mountains and flows north through Surakarta.

Central Java is also a cultural concept that includes the Yogyakarta Special Region, administered separately since Indonesian independence. It is known as the heart of Javanese culture, and about 98 percent of its people are Javanese.

Remains of Homo erectus, known as Java Man, were found in Central Java and adjacent East Java in the 1890s by the Dutch anatomist and geologist Eugène Dubois, and are believed to be about 1.7 million years old; Sangiran is an important prehistoric site. Around 40,000 years ago peoples related to modern Australian Aboriginals and Melanesians settled there, and by about 3,000 BCE Austronesians had assimilated or replaced them, bringing pottery, outrigger canoes, domesticated animals and cultivated rice and millet.

Recorded history began in the 7th century, when writing, Hinduism and Buddhism were brought by Indians from South Asia. In 664 the Chinese monk Hui-neng visited a Javanese port he called Hēlíng, where he translated Buddhist scriptures with the Javanese monk Jñānabhadra; it is thought to lie between Semarang and Jepara.

From the late 16th century European traders frequented the ports and the Dutch established a presence through the East India Company. After Demak fell to Mataram under Sultan Agung, Mataram conquered almost all of Java by the 17th century but, through internal disputes and Dutch intervention, was partitioned: the Treaty of Giyanti of 1755 divided it into the Sultanates of Surakarta and Yogyakarta, and the Treaty of Salatiga of 1757 created the Mangkunegaran.

Central Java is a province of Indonesia with its administrative capital at Semarang and a population of 36,516,035 at the 2020 census, the third largest of any province. The standard Javanese is the Solo-Jogja or Mataram dialect, while Indonesian is the official language.

The province holds the temple of Borobudur in Magelang Regency, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, with Mendut and Pawon nearby, as well as temples of the Dieng Plateau, the Sangiran museum and the palaces of Surakarta.
central-plain-china: Zhongyuan, the Central Plain or Plains, is the part of the North China Plain around the middle and lower reaches of the Yellow River, centred on the region between Luoyang and Kaifeng. Mountains enclose it on the north, west and south, chiefly the Taihang Mountains to the north-west and the Funiu and Xionger Mountains to the west. The Yellow River crosses it from west to east. Its alluvial plains made it the centre of Chinese agrarian civilisation, known as the Breadbasket of China.

The term has not always meant the same area. It first appears in the Classic of Poetry without any exact location, and it came to denote the Central Plains region in the Spring and Autumn period (770-476 BCE). Only from the Northern and Southern dynasties (420-589 CE) was it widely accepted as a geographical term. It usually means the middle and lower Yellow River but sometimes also takes in the Yangtze and Huai valleys or the whole North China Plain.

People lived in Zhongyuan about half a million years ago. The painted pottery and stone tools of the Yangshao culture (5000 to 3000 BCE) and the Longshan culture (3000 to 1900 BCE) show that the region stood at the forefront of Chinese civilisation in the Stone Age. With the rise of the Erlitou culture the region entered the Bronze Age, and the Xia dynasty, the first in Chinese history, centred its rule there, setting the pattern for later dynasties.

The Huaxia, a confederation of tribes who lived along the Yellow River and later developed into the Han, saw Zhongyuan as the centre of the world and used the name Zhongguo, Central State, to distinguish themselves from the peoples they called barbarians. From the Xia to the fall of the Song dynasty in 1279, most legitimate dynasties placed their capitals in the region, the exceptions being the Eastern Jin and the Southern Song; in all more than 20 dynasties did so. The political centre moved only under the Yuan, who ruled from Dadu, now Beijing, and the Ming, whose Yongle Emperor moved his capital to Beijing, his power base.

The region gives its name to Central Plains Mandarin, the native tongue of about 124 million people in Henan, Shandong, Anhui, Shanxi, Shaanxi, Gansu and Hebei. In the Yuan dynasty the rime book Zhongyuan Yinyun, by Zhou Deqing, recorded the standard pronunciation of Early Mandarin, which some linguists argue rested on the Luoyang and Bianliang dialects prevalent under the Song.
central-powers: The Central Powers, also called the Central Empires or the Quadruple Alliance, were one of the two main coalitions of the First World War. The name comes from the position of the members, all four lying between the Russian Empire in the east and France and the United Kingdom in the west. The alliance began with the pact between Germany and Austria-Hungary of 1879. Italy had nominally joined that bloc in the Triple Alliance but did not fight on its side and later joined the Allies. Germany also planned a Mitteleuropa economic association with Austria-Hungary and others.

Austria-Hungary, supported by Germany, declared war on Serbia on 28 July 1914. Germany declared war on Russia and, on 3 August, on France. The Ottoman Empire, bound to Germany by a secret alliance signed on 2 August 1914, stayed formally neutral for nearly two months. It entered the war on 29 October 1914 after a raid on Russian ports by cruisers that had been transferred from Germany. Bulgaria, defeated by Serbia, Greece and Romania in July 1913, signed a treaty of defensive alliance with the Ottomans on 19 August 1914 and in October 1915 declared war on Serbia.

Other groups cooperated with the coalition. The Senussi Order, led by Ahmed Sharif as-Senussi, attacked the Italians in Libya and the British in Egypt, the Sultanate of Darfur sided with the Ottomans in 1915, and Irish nationalists launched the Easter Rising in 1916. Germany lost its colonies to the Allies; German East Africa, resisted until November 1918 by Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck, was the only one not fully conquered.

As the war lengthened, solidarity weakened. After the death of Franz Joseph, his successor Charles sought to distance Austria-Hungary from Germany, and from 1916 its leaders wanted to leave the conflict. In September 1918 a Franco-Serbian offensive under Louis Franchet d'Espèrey broke the Bulgarian front, and Bulgaria signed an armistice on 29 September 1918. The Ottoman Empire followed on 30 October, Austria and Hungary made ceasefires in the first week of November after the disintegration of the Habsburg Empire, and Germany signed on 11 November 1918. No single treaty ended the war: each of the Central Powers was dealt with in a separate treaty. The alliance dissolved in 1918.
central-provinces: The province was landlocked, made up of the mountain ranges, plateaus and river valleys of the centre of the subcontinent. Its north reached onto the Bundelkhand upland, and the Vindhya Range divided the Ganges-Yamuna basin from the valley of the Narmada, whose upper course formed the heart of the Mahakoshal region, with the railway junction of Jabalpur. South of the Satpura Range lay the Vidarbha region on the Deccan Plateau, drained by the Wainganga, Wardha and Indravati, with Nagpur. In the east the upper Mahanadi basin formed the rice-growing plain of Chhattisgarh.

The province brought together British conquests from the Marathas in central India and covered parts of the present-day states of Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and Maharashtra. It was formed by merging the Saugor and Nerbudda Territories with Nagpur Province, and the district of Nimar, until then under the Central India Agency, was added in 1864. Nagpur was the main winter capital and Pachmarhi the summer retreat. The province was almost an island among princely states such as Bhopal and Rewa to the north, the Chota Nagpur States and Kalahandi to the east, and the Nizam's Hyderabad to the south.

Censuses were held from 1866, when the population was over 9 million. It rose to 11.5 million by 1881 and nearly 13 million by 1891, after the famine of 1869 and epidemics of smallpox and cholera. The failure of the monsoon in 1897 and 1900 brought great famines, and cholera struck in seven years of that decade; the census of 1901 counted 11,873,029 people, 800,000 fewer than in 1891, part of the fall coming from emigration to Assam and other provinces.

A chief commissioner governed the province from 1861 to 1920. It had four divisions, Nerbudda, Jubbulpore, Nagpur and Chhattisgarh, with 18 districts, and 15 princely states with about 15 per cent of the people in 1901, the largest Bastar and the smallest Satki. Most people spoke forms of Hindi, chiefly Chhattisgarhi, Bundeli and Bagheli, in the Mahakoshal districts, while Marathi prevailed in Vidarbha, and the two regions never fully merged into one unit. Oriya, Telugu, Gondi, Korku and Munda languages were spoken too.
central-rada: News of the February events in Petrograd reached Kiev in March 1917, and Ukrainian organisations met at the Rodyna Club. More than 100 representatives gathered on 16 March (3 March in the old style), and the Central Council was founded the next day on the initiative of the Society of Ukrainian Progressionists, with other parties and organisations taking part. It told the new Russian Provisional Government of its creation by telegram. On 20 March Mykhailo Hrushevsky was elected its head, with Dmytro Doroshenko and Dmytro Antonovych as his deputies. After the All-Ukrainian National Congress of 19 to 21 April 1917 it became a parliament of 150 members elected from parties, professional and cultural organisations and the guberniyas.

Its four Universals led Ukraine from autonomy to sovereignty. The First, written by Volodymyr Vynnychenko and proclaimed on 23 June 1917, declared that the Ukrainian people must manage their own lives without separating from Russia, and the General Secretariat was formed on 28 June. The Second, of 16 July, enlarged the Rada with representatives of other peoples living in Ukraine. After the Bolshevik coup in Russia the Third Universal of 20 November 1917 proclaimed the Ukrainian People's Republic in federal ties with the Russian Republic. In elections to the Russian Constituent Assembly on 25 November, Ukrainian parties won 75% of the vote and the Bolsheviks 11%.

The Bolsheviks made several attempts to seize power in Ukraine. The Russian government sent an ultimatum on 17 December, which the Rada rejected, and Bolshevik troops began an offensive. Bolshevik deputies withdrew to Kharkov and formed a rival People's Secretariat on 25 December. The Fourth Universal declared the Ukrainian People's Republic a separate, free and sovereign state, and the Rada's delegation went to the peace conference with the Central Powers at Brest-Litovsk. On 29 January 1918 Bolshevik troops entered Kiev.

By the end of July 1917 the Rada formally had 822 deputies, according to Pavlo Khrystiuk, among them delegates of peasants, soldiers and workers and of Ukrainian, Russian, Jewish and Polish parties. Its executive, the Little Rada or Mala Rada, was created in April 1917 with 19 members and chaired by Hrushevsky. The general assembly met nine times and was modelled on the Russian State Duma, with party factions and inquiries. It has been judged inefficient, its sessions often given over to verbal battles between factions.

Soviet ideology described the Rada as a counter-revolutionary body of the bourgeoisie. Its members were proclaimed outlaws by the Soviet government of Ukraine in December 1917. Many went into exile, among them Vynnychenko, who died in France, while others were imprisoned or shot in the Soviet Union, and Hrushevsky died in 1934.
centre-party-finland: The party grew out of movements of citizens in the Finnish countryside. Before Finnish independence political power was centralised in the capital and the estates of the realm, which opened space for a new movement, and the older temperance movement, with overlapping membership, gave future activists experience of working in an organisation. Its ideas of humanity, education, the spirit of the land, yeomanly liberty, decentralisation, concern for poor people and progressivism are credited above all to Santeri Alkio, regarded as the party's chief ideological father.

At the dawn of independence conservative forces tried to establish a Kingdom of Finland, with a prince from the German Empire. The Agrarian League opposed monarchism fiercely, and after the Civil War, when about forty Social Democratic members of Parliament had escaped to Russia and about fifty others had been arrested, its members were the only republicans left in Parliament in 1918. In the 1919 election it became the biggest non-socialist party, with 19.7 per cent of the vote. It formed centrist minority governments with the National Progressive Party and produced its first prime ministers, Kyösti Kallio in 1922 and Juho Sunila in 1927.

The extreme right Lapua Movement grew strong in the party's rural strongholds, and many members joined it, but after the kidnapping of President Kaarlo Juho Ståhlberg in 1930 the party broke all ties. In the 1933 election it stood in the Legality Front with the Social Democrats, the Swedish People's Party and the Progressives against the Patriotic Electoral Alliance. Kallio was elected president in 1937 with the votes of the centrist and social-democratic parties, and allowed the first centre-left government.

In 1956 Urho Kekkonen, the party's candidate, was elected president after serving as prime minister several times, and held office until 1982. He continued the neutrality policy of Juho Kusti Paasikivi, the Paasikivi–Kekkonen line, under which Finland kept its independence while trading with both NATO and Warsaw Pact states. The party took the name Centre Party in 1965 and Centre Party of Finland in 1988.

Through Finland's independence the party has been the one most often in government. Twelve prime ministers and three presidents have come from it. Its influence is strongest in small and rural municipalities, and decentralisation is its most characteristic policy. It was divided over membership of the European Union: in 1992, 22 of its 55 members of Parliament voted against applying, and in June 1994 the party congress backed membership by 1,607 votes to 834 only after the prime minister, Esko Aho, threatened to resign.
