It was the largest party in Parliament from 2003 to 2011, with Matti Vanhanen as prime minister for seven years, and it has been a member of the Liberal International since 1988.
centurione-ii-zaccaria: Centurione was the son of Andronikos Asen Zaccaria and of Catherine Le Maure, daughter of Erard III, baron of Arcadia, and a grandson of Centurione I Zaccaria. The family had been established in the Morea since the lord of Chios Martino Zaccaria married the baroness Jacqueline de la Roche. In 1401 he succeeded his father in the baronies of Arkadia and Chalandritsa. His aunt Maria, widow of Prince Pedro San Superan, made him bailee when she took over the principality, but when Ladislaus of Naples demanded the ducats Pedro had once pledged for the title, Centurione secretly offered to pay if he were recognised as sole ruler, and Ladislaus accepted.

He made his brother Stephen Latin Archbishop of Patras and married a Byzantine lady of the houses of Asen-Palaiologos and Tzamblakon. His first rivals were the Toccos: in 1404 he seized the fiefs Pedro had offered Leonard Tocco, and in 1408 Leonardo and Carlo I Tocco took Glarentza, the chief sea port of the principality. Allied with the Venetians and Justinian, Lord of Chios, Centurione retook it in 1414 with the help of the Albanians under his command, and Venice arranged a three-year armistice.

In 1417 the despot Theodore II Palaiologos and Emperor John VIII invaded Achaea, took Messenia and Elis and shut Centurione in Glarentza, from which he fled by sea in the spring of 1418. That year the adventurer Oliver Franco seized the port, and Centurione had to give him a daughter in marriage with Glarentza as her dowry; Franco sold it to Carlo Tocco in 1421. In 1422 the family's offer of Patras to the Hospitallers of Rhodes was refused.

Theodore II defeated Centurione in battle and held him prisoner for a short time. In 1429 Thomas Palaiologos besieged him in Chalandritsa until he surrendered and agreed to a treaty by which his daughter Catherine would marry the despot, making him heir to Achaea. Centurione kept the barony of Arcadia, where he died in 1432, still hoping for Genoese aid; one source reports that Thomas cut off his hands and feet. In 1453, during the Morean revolt, his eldest son John Asen Zaccaria revived the title of Prince of Achaea and was recognised by Naples, Venice and the papacy.
cenwalh-of-wessex: Bede calls Cenwalh the son of King Cynegils, whom Bishop Birinus baptised, and a great-great-grandson of Cerdic, though the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle offers several ancestries for Cynegils and the family's links to later kings are uncertain. His name is of British rather than Anglo-Saxon origin. Unlike his father, Bede writes, he at first refused the Christian faith, and when he put away his wife, a sister of King Penda of Mercia, Penda drove him from his kingdom.

The dates of his exile are unclear. Bede gives it as three years, and since his host, King Anna of East Anglia, was himself driven out by Penda in 651, it cannot have begun much later than 648; if Saint Felix baptised him, as William of Malmesbury states, that happened by about 647. The break with Penda probably followed soon after Penda killed Oswald of Northumbria, protector of Cynegils's line, at Maserfeld in 642. Barbara Yorke places Cenwalh's return in 648, D. P. Kirby his exile in the 650s.

Back in power, Cenwalh tired of his bishop at Dorchester-on-Thames, the Frank Agilbert, whose language he did not understand, and set up a second see at Winchester under Wini, in the heart of the future Wessex. Mercian pressure lay behind the shift: Penda's son Wulfhere ravaged Ashdown about 661 and gave the Meon valley to Æthelwalh of the South Saxons. In 658, according to the Chronicle, Cenwalh defeated the Britons at Peonnum and drove them to the Parret, yet he is also said to have endowed the British monastery at Sherborne. In 665-668 he quarrelled with Wini, who fled to Wulfhere.

According to the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle Cenwalh died in 672 and his widow, Seaxburh, held power for about a year. No descendants of his are known in Wessex, and it is uncertain whether he ruled alone or shared power with Cenberht, father of King Caedwalla. It has been suggested that he was the Coenwalh from whom the 9th-century Mercian kings Coenwulf and Ceolwulf claimed descent.
ceolfrith: Little is known of Ceolfrith's early years. He probably entered monastic life about 660, the year his brother Cynefrid died, and his cousin Tunbert was the first abbot of Hexham. He spent four years at Gilling Abbey in what is now North Yorkshire, then left in search of a stricter house and joined the monks of Ripon under Wilfrid, later Saint Wilfrid. He was ordained priest at the age of 27 and spent some time with Abbot Botolph, who inspired in him a greater humility.

When King Ecgfrith of Northumbria granted Benedict Biscop land for a monastery at Wearmouth, Biscop sought out Ceolfrith, who became his most zealous assistant and a close friend. When the second house at Jarrow was finished, Ceolfrith became abbot of its church of St Paul, and he alone went with Biscop on his last journey to Rome. On the death of Abbot Eosterwini he became the first sole abbot of both monasteries, and after Biscop died in 690 the libraries doubled in size under his care.

Bede came into his care at the age of seven. When plague struck Northumbria and the twin monasteries in 686, master and pupil escaped it, nursed the sick and dying monks, kept up the services and then rebuilt the community. Some time after 711 Nechtan mac Der-Ilei, King of the Picts, asked Ceolfrith's advice on the reckoning of Easter, and by 716 the Picts and the clergy of Iona had adopted the pascha catholica.

Sensing that his life was ending, Ceolfrith resigned and was succeeded by Hwaetberht, then set out to carry the Codex Amiatinus to Pope Gregory II. He died at Langres in Burgundy on 29 September 716 and was buried there. The codex, modelled on the Codex Grandior of Cassiodorus, which he had obtained in Rome, is the oldest manuscript with a complete text of the Vulgate. No record shows that it reached Rome; it is said to have made its way to Florence, where the Lombard Abbot Peter, who is believed to have altered its dedication in the 9th century, presented it to the Abbazia di San Salvatore at Mount Amiata. In 1786 it moved to the Laurentian Library in Florence.
ceolred-of-mercia: At the end of the 7th century the kingdom of Mercia covered what is now the English Midlands, bordered by Northumbria, East Anglia and Wessex. Ceolred's father, Æthelred, had come to the throne in 675 on the death of his brother Wulfhere, and in 704 he abdicated and went to Rome, leaving the kingdom to his nephew Coenred, Wulfhere's son. Ceolred's mother was not Osthryth, Æthelred's only recorded wife, and he may still have been young when he became king.

The main source for the period is Bede's Ecclesiastical History of the English People, completed in about 731, but Bede appears to have had no informant in Mercia. Ceolred's own charters and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, compiled in Wessex at the end of the 9th century, add some detail.

In 709 Coenred abdicated in favour of Ceolred, went to Rome and was made a monk by Pope Constantine. Historians have generally accepted Bede's report, but Barbara Yorke has suggested that Coenred may not have given up the throne willingly, since kings were sometimes forced into holy orders to make them ineligible to rule, as Osred II of Northumbria was.

The reduced prestige of Coenred and Ceolred may have stirred unrest among the Mercian nobility, and the survival of a hostile account of Ceolred may point to wider dissatisfaction with the ruling line; much of what is said against him may reflect his treatment of the Church. Ceolred confirmed a grant to Waldhere, Bishop of London, a sign that London was firmly under Mercian overlordship, though he did not treat it as his direct possession as later Mercian kings did. Three possibly genuine charters of his survive.

Ceolred died in 716. Saint Boniface later described him dying in a crazed frenzy at a banquet, "gibbering with demons and cursing the priests of God". His successor Æthelbald belonged to another branch of the Mercian royal line. Æthelbald had been forced into exile during Ceolred's rule. Through Coenred, Ceolred was related to Saint Werburgh of Mercia, Coenred's sister.
ceolwulf-ii-of-mercia: Ceolwulf's name means ship-wolf. On the evidence of his name he is thought to belong to the C dynasty of Mercian kings, a family that claimed descent from Pybba of Mercia and may have had ties to the ruling family of the Hwicce in south-west Mercia. His immediate ancestry is unknown, but he is thought to descend from Ceolwulf I of Mercia through his daughter Ælfflæd, who married first Wigmund, son of King Wiglaf, and then Beorhtfrith, son of King Beorhtwulf.

The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle calls him an unwise king's thane who swore oaths and gave hostages to the Great Heathen Army, promising that the kingdom would be ready for them on whatever day they wanted it. The Chronicle was compiled on the orders of Alfred the Great, Burgred's brother-in-law, and its account is considered biased, written to strengthen the claims of Alfred and Edward the Elder to the overlordship of Mercia. Several thegns who had witnessed charters under Burgred witnessed them under Ceolwulf, and Mercian bishops witnessed his charters, which points to his acceptance in Mercia.

In 878 King Rhodri Mawr of Gwynedd was killed in battle against the English. Alfred was then occupied with the Vikings and Mercia traditionally claimed hegemony over Wales, so the English leader was probably Ceolwulf. In 881 Rhodri's sons defeated the Mercians at the Battle of the Conwy, which Welsh annals called the revenge of God for Rhodri; the Mercian leader by then was almost certainly Ceolwulf's successor, Æthelred. By 883 Æthelred, Lord of the Mercians, ruled Mercia with Alfred's support, and Ceolwulf is counted the last king of independent Mercia.

Three types of silver penny were issued in Ceolwulf's name. Most were minted at London and are of the Cross-and-Lozenge type that Alfred also used. Simon Keynes and the numismatist Mark Blackburn first proposed that Alfred alone was recognised in London in about 875, but a Cross-and-Lozenge penny of Ceolwulf that came to light in 1998 appears to be contemporary with Alfred's earliest coinage.

In 2015 a metal-detectorist found a hoard of coins, jewellery and silver ingots near Watlington, Oxfordshire, dating to the late 870s, with thirteen of the rare Two Emperors pennies that show Alfred and Ceolwulf seated side by side. A find near Leominster of coins of about 879, presumed buried by retreating Vikings, also depicts both kings, and some experts read them as equals. Gareth Williams of the British Museum said that these coins "enable us to reinterpret our history at a key moment in the creation of England as a single kingdom."
cephissus-boeotia: The Boeotian Cephissus, so called to distinguish it from other rivers of the same name, rises at Lilaia in Phocis on the north-western slope of Mount Parnassus. It flows east through the Boeotian plain past the towns of Amfikleia, Kato Tithorea and Orchomenos, and its drainage basin covers 1,958 square kilometres. Lake Copais, into which it emptied, was therefore also called the Cephisian Lake.

A post-glacial river, the Cephissus never carried enough water to cut a clear channel to the Gulf of Euboea. Its main flow was seasonal meltwater, which gathered in a system of three lakes in the Boeotian lowlands. Lake Copais was never more than a wetland a few feet deep. From it, water passed through katabothra, caves in the karst limestone, to Lake Yliki, the ancient Hylice, and on underground to Lake Paralimni, which hangs above the gulf; there were no surface channels between the lakes.

In Greek mythology the river god Cephissus was associated with the river. Pausanias records a Theban tradition that the river once ran under a mountain to the sea until Heracles blocked the passage and turned the water into the Orchomenian plain. He also says that on certain days the people of Lilaia threw cakes and other customary offerings into the river's spring, and that these reappeared in the Castalian Spring.

The valley links northern Greece, through the passes of Mount Oeta and Mount Kallidromo, Thermopylae among them, with southern Greece and the Gulf of Corinth. For that reason the rulers of the Duchy of Athens built a chain of forts and watchtowers along its course in the Frankish period.

Draining the lakes was a large engineering task of the 19th and early 20th centuries. Copais was turned into farmland in 1887, revealing the katabothra and Bronze Age works built to stem the flow, and an artificial outflow now leads to Lake Yliki. The opened underground paths raised Yliki enough to drown all traces of Bronze Age settlement in its valley, and in the later 20th century the waters of the two remaining lakes were taken for the Athens aqueduct.
cerball-mac-dunlainge: Cerball succeeded his father, Dúnlang (or Dúngal) mac Fergaile, as king of Osraige in 842. The kingdom of the Osraige, the Deer people, covered perhaps 2,000 square kilometres astride the River Barrow, far larger than an average túath, and lay at the eastern edge of the Eóganachta kingdom of Munster, bordering Leinster. The High King, Máel Sechnaill mac Máele Ruanaid, was married to Cerball's sister Land, and Cerball in turn married a daughter of Máel Sechnaill.

He first appears in 846, when his army besieged Viking raiders in northern Osraige for a fortnight, and in 847 he defeated a Viking force led by one Hákon. The death in 847 of Fedelmid mac Crimthainn, King of Munster, who was followed by weak kings, left him in a strong position. In 855 he slaughtered a Viking force under Rodolb, was captured by other Vikings and escaped, and then joined Danes under Horm in inflicting a heavy defeat on the Norse.

He later allied with the Norse leaders Amlaíb Conung and Ímar, campaigning with Ímar in Leinster in 858 and raiding Máel Sechnaill's lands in Mide the following year, though each time he had to submit to the high king again. After Máel Sechnaill died in 862, his successor Áed Finnliath married Land, and in 870 Cerball joined Áed's army in Leinster. Much of this comes from the Fragmentary Annals of Ireland, which were meant to magnify his deeds and break off in the early 870s.

Cerball died in 888 and was succeeded by his brother Riagan. The Annales Cambriae note his death under 887; he is the only Irish king they mention who was not an Uí Néill high king. He was the male-line ancestor of the later kings of Osraige and of the Mac Giolla Phádraig clan, and historians regard him as a patron of building and of Osraige's tradition of carved high crosses.

The Icelandic Landnámabók names him, as Kjarvalur, alongside rulers such as Alfred the Great and Harald Fairhair, and makes him the maternal grandfather of the settler Helgi the Lean. Historians treat these genealogies as unreliable; one suggestion is that the Fragmentary Annals were popular among the Norse-Gaels of 11th-century Ireland, who passed his story on to the Icelanders.
cerdanya: Cerdanya, also called La Cerdanya, is a natural comarca and historical region of the eastern Pyrenees, historically one of the counties of Catalonia. Its land area is 1,086.07 km2, divided almost evenly between Spain (50.3 percent) and France (49.7 percent). In 2001 it had about 26,500 inhabitants, of whom 53 percent lived on the Spanish side. Its only urban area is the cross-border Puigcerdà–Bourg-Madame, with 10,900 inhabitants in 2001. The area has around 3,000 hours of sunshine a year, and large solar installations have been built in French Cerdagne, among them the Mont-Louis Solar Furnace.

The first inhabitants probably spoke a language related to old Basque and Aquitanian, as many place names show. Iberians arrived from the south in the first millennium BCE and probably mixed with the natives, forming the Kerretes, whose name comes from a word for rock. Their main oppidum, Kere, stood above the modern village of Llívia. The Romans renamed it Julia Lybica. Under Rome the area was the pagus Liviensis, part of Hispania Tarraconensis, and the name Cerdanya derives from Cerretania. The Kerretes seem to have kept their language until perhaps the 8th or 9th century. The diocese of Urgell was founded in the 6th century, with Cerdanya within its limits.

Devastated by the Vandals and other Germanic tribes, Cerdanya belonged to the Visigothic kingdoms and was later conquered by the Muslims. After the Battle of Toulouse in 721 the Berber commander Uthman ibn Naissa set up a small realm there and allied with Odo the Great. Under Carolingian pressure Cerdanya became a Frankish vassal about 785. The county arose from the Spanish Marches of Charlemagne. Wilfred the Hairy, count from 870 to 897, established his youngest son Miron as Count of Cerdanya. The county later gained Capcir and Conflent, and its counts were patrons of abbeys such as Saint-Michel de Cuxa and Saint-Martin-du-Canigou, dedicated in 1009. The line died out in 1117 and the county passed to the counts of Barcelona.

The Treaty of the Pyrenees of 1659 split Cerdanya, the north becoming French and the south remaining Spanish; Llívia stayed Spanish, allegedly because the treaty ceded only villages and it counted as a city. Puigcerdà replaced Hix as capital in 1178. The Spanish side is the Catalan comarca of Baixa Cerdanya, with Puigcerdà as capital, while the French side lies in the département of Pyrénées-Orientales and has no special status. Its main towns are Bourg-Madame and the ski resort Font-Romeu. Tourism, skiing and the Yellow Train support the economy, and ties between families on both sides of the border remain close.
cerdic: Most scholars think the name Cerdic is Brittonic rather than Germanic, derived from a British name such as Caratīcos, in Old Welsh Ceretic. This may indicate that he was a native Briton whose dynasty became Anglicised over time, a view supported by the possibly non-Germanic names of descendants such as Ceawlin, Cedda and Cædwalla. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle traces his ancestry back to Woden, but Kenneth Sisam showed that the pedigree was built by borrowing and altering that of the kings of Bernicia, so it has no historical basis before Cerdic's own generation.

J. N. L. Myres noted that the Chronicle calls Cerdic and his son Cynric ealdormen in 495, a fairly junior rank, and suggested that they may have belonged to a partly British noble family entrusted with defending part of the Saxon Shore in the last days of Roman or sub-Roman authority.

According to the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, Cerdic landed in Britain in 495 with his son Cynric and five ships at Cerdic's-ore, presumably in Hampshire. In 508 he is said to have killed a British king named Natanleod and 5,000 men, and in 519 he fought another battle against the Britons at Cerdices Ford, which is associated with North Charford. The Chronicle also mentions the conquest of the Isle of Wight, later given to his kinsmen Stuf and Wihtgar.

It records that in 519 he and Cynric began to reign, which may mark their change from dependent ealdormen to independent kings. He would have been known to contemporaries as king of the Gewissae, a tribal group, and Cædwalla in a charter of 686 was the first to call himself king of the West Saxons.

The Chronicle says Cerdic died in 534 and was succeeded by Cynric, though the genealogical regnal list placed before its manuscripts puts a generation between them, making Cerdic the father of Creoda and grandfather of Cynric. The Chronicle's early history of Wessex is considered unreliable, with duplicate reports and contradictions, and the dating of Cerdic's reign was revised more than once. David Dumville showed that the earliest texts must have placed it in a different period from the one now given.

Some scholars have suggested that he never existed, but this is a minority view. The Chronicle was put together in the late ninth century, about 400 years later, and its account cannot be assumed accurate. Descent from Cerdic became a necessary qualification for later kings of Wessex, and Ecgberht was claimed as his descendant.
ceretic-guletic: Ceretic is associated with Dumbarton Castle, the fortress of Alt Clut. He appears in the Harleian genealogies of the rulers of Alt Clut, which name his father Cynloyp, his grandfather Cinhil and his great-grandfather Cluim, and present him as the great-great-great-grandfather of Rhydderch Hael, who can be dated securely to around 600. The same genealogies give his byname Guletic, land-holder. In the Book of Armagh he is called Coirthech rex Aloo, Ceretic, King of the Height of the Clyde.

His identification with Coroticus, a Brittonic warrior to whose warband Saint Patrick addressed one of his two surviving letters, rests largely on an 8th-century gloss to that letter. Ceretic's dates therefore depend on the long scholarly debate over when Patrick flourished, but a time in the 5th century is probably safe; counting twenty years for each generation back from Rhydderch Hael places him there as well.

In the letter Patrick laments that the soldiers of Coroticus had captured and enslaved newly baptised Irish Christians and sold them to non-Christians. He calls them fellow citizens of the devils rather than of the Roman saints, associates of the Scots and the apostate Picts, and announces that he has excommunicated them. The apostate Picts were the Southern Picts, converted by Saint Ninian, who had since left Christianity. It has been suggested that the letter provoked the trial Patrick mentions in his Confession.
cern: The acronym CERN originally stood for the French Conseil Européen pour la Recherche Nucléaire, European Council for Nuclear Research, a provisional council established by 12 European governments in 1952 to build the laboratory. In these early years the council worked at the University of Copenhagen under the direction of Niels Bohr before moving to its present site near Geneva. At the sixth session of the council in Paris, from 29 June to 1 July 1953, the convention establishing the organisation was signed, subject to ratification, by 12 states, and it was ratified on 29 September 1954. The founding member states were Belgium, Denmark, France, the Federal Republic of Germany, Greece, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, Switzerland, the United Kingdom and Yugoslavia.

The name changed in 1954 to Organisation européenne pour la recherche nucléaire, European Organization for Nuclear Research, but the acronym was kept. According to Lew Kowarski, a former director, the abbreviation could have become the awkward OERN, and Werner Heisenberg said that this could still be CERN even if the name was not. CERN's first president was Sir Benjamin Lockspeiser. Edoardo Amaldi was general secretary in the early stages, when operations were still provisional, and the first Director-General, in 1954, was Felix Bloch.

The organisation is based in Meyrin, a western suburb of Geneva, on the border between France and Switzerland. Its main function is to provide the particle accelerators and other infrastructure needed for high-energy physics research, and many experiments have been built there through international collaborations. Each machine in its chain of accelerators raises the energy of particle beams before passing them to experiments or to the next, more powerful accelerator. Its original linear accelerator, LINAC 1, operated from 1959 to 1992.

Several major achievements in particle physics came from experiments at CERN: the discovery of neutral currents in the Gargamelle bubble chamber in 1973, of the W and Z bosons in 1983, and of direct CP violation in 1999. In 1995 the first atoms of antihydrogen were created, and in 2000 its Heavy Ion Programme discovered a new state of matter, quark–gluon plasma. In 2012 experiments at the Large Hadron Collider, the world's largest and highest-energy particle collider, discovered a boson with a mass around 125 GeV/c2 consistent with the long-sought Higgs boson. CERN is also the birthplace of the World Wide Web. Its large computing facility at Meyrin stores and analyses experimental data, and the laboratory has historically been a major wide area network hub.
cerro-baul: The name joins the Spanish cerro, hill, and baúl, trunk, a place to store treasured things. The terraced mountain rises 2000 feet above its surroundings, and both it and the neighbouring Cerro Mejia were under Wari control. A 6.2-mile canal brought water from the Torata River through the El Paso Divide between the two hills, where it split to irrigate the terraces on their flanks, on which most of the inhabitants lived.

The public buildings and the homes of the elite stood on the summit. Two D-shaped temples in the Wari style lay in the eastern and middle sectors, with one-storey dwellings in the east that archaeologists take for the artisans' quarter. The central sector seems to have been the ceremonial core, and the two-storey houses of the elite stood in the west. Across the site ran the commonest Wari form, an enclosed plaza flanked by stone halls, which held governors' residences, offices and beer houses for state feasts.

The Wari pushed into the zone of Tiwanaku control by seizing Cerro Baúl and Cerro Mejia, and because the water of the mountain storms passed a Wari canal before reaching Tiwanaku fields, the Tiwanaku became at least partly dependent on them. Relations nonetheless seem to have been largely peaceful: there is no evidence of warfare, and a Tiwanaku-style drinking vessel was among the most sacred offerings found at the site.

Excavation began with the Asociación Contisuyo, founded in 1981 by Robert Pritzker and Michael Moseley, then of the Field Museum of Natural History, with the Southern Peru Copper Corporation. It had been thought that the Wari took the area only after the Tiwanaku, but keros and other finds in hybrid Wari and Tiwanaku styles showed that the two occupied it at the same time. After the decline of both, people of the Chiribaya culture lived in the area until the Inca conquered it.

The mountain stands near Moquegua, a city founded by the Spanish colonists that is now the capital of the Moquegua Region. It remains a place of worship for the people of the city, who offer pagapus to the Andean deities in coca, candles and chicha, and it is also visited by tourists.
cerro-rico: The mountain stands in the Andes near Potosí, in Potosí Department in the south of Bolivia, between the Porco and Sucre mines, which had been found earlier at lower altitudes. Its Quechua name, Sumaq Urqu, means beautiful or good mountain. It is largely barren, though a few plant species have colonised it and vizcachas live on its slopes. The silver was found by chance in 1545 by Diego de Huallpa, a Quechua silver miner working for the Spanish, while he was searching the mountain for an Inca shrine or burial offering.

In the early decades the mines held deposits of pure silver and silver chloride that were easy to work, but by 1565 the high-grade ores were exhausted. Extraction revived with the patio process, which used mercury to draw silver from low-grade ores known as paco for their ochre colour. The Spanish first used the forced-labour system called repartimiento, and in 1574 Viceroy Francisco de Toledo reintroduced the mita, the annual labour draft of the Inca Empire. Many workers stayed on as free wage labourers, or mingas, once their term was over.

Mercury poisoning and the harsh conditions of the mines and refining patios killed many miners, and the mountain became known as the mountain that eats men. Estimates of the dead range from about eight million to hundreds of thousands, the higher figure perhaps being the total for the whole Viceroyalty of Peru. About 85 percent of the silver produced in the central Andes in the colonial period is estimated to have come from Cerro Rico, and Potosí grew into one of the largest cities in the New World. The mountain took its present shape in the 17th century after a mountaintop removal.

Mining continues through cooperatives working underground and in the open-pit San Bartolomé mine, and in 2019 the output was mostly tin and zinc with little silver. Many miners contract silicosis. A sinkhole that opened at the summit in 2011 was filled with ultra-light cement, and in 2014 UNESCO placed Cerro Rico and Potosí on its list of endangered sites. The mountain appears on the coat of arms of Bolivia.
cersobleptes: Cersobleptes, also written Cersebleptes or Kersobleptes, inherited the throne of the Odrysians on the death of his father Cotys I in September 360 BCE. With it came a conflict with Athens and with the rebel former royal treasurer Miltokythes, and two rivals soon appeared, Berisades and Amadocus II. An inscription from Delphi dated to 355 BCE names four sons of his: Iolaus, Poseidonius, Medistas and Teres.

Despite the service of his brother-in-law, the Euboean adventurer Charidemus, Cersobleptes had to make peace with Athens and accept his rivals as rulers of their own parts of Thrace by 357 BCE. His share lay east of the rivers Tonzos and Hebrus. Charidemus led the dealings with Athens over the Thracian Chersonese, and in them Cersobleptes appears as little more than his puppet; Athens sent settlers there only in 353 BCE. When Berisades died and was followed by his sons, Cetriporis among them, the two men planned to seize their lands and win back all of Cotys's realm, and Demosthenes spoke against an Athenian decree passed in Charidemus's favour.

Around 354 or 353 BCE his envoy Apollonides negotiated with Philip II of Macedon at Maroneia, but the plan failed, and Cersobleptes instead allied with Athens, which gave up its protection of Amadocus II. He then attacked Amadocus and the Greek cities of Perinthus and Byzantium. In 352 BCE Philip invaded as their ally, defeated him and took one of his sons as a hostage to Pella.

In 347 and 346 BCE Cersobleptes again sought Athenian support, but his inclusion in the peace with Philip in 346 BCE was refused, and Philip expelled the Athenian garrisons from the Thracian coast. During Philip's larger campaign, which by early 341 BCE had passed through Cardia and Aenus and taken Cabyle, Cersobleptes and Teres III were eliminated or subjugated in circumstances that are unknown, and Philippopolis and Cabyle became Macedonian colonies. It is unclear whether his sons kept any authority. The next important Odrysian king, Seuthes III, is sometimes identified, hypothetically, as his son or brother.
certosa-di-pavia: Gian Galeazzo Visconti commissioned the Certosa from the architect Marco Solari and laid the foundation stone on 27 August 1396. The site lay midway between Milan and Pavia, at the end of the Visconti Park, which connected it to the castle of Pavia. Gian Galeazzo had deposed his uncle Bernabò in a coup in 1385, and he aspired to found a new kingdom in northern Italy. When the people of Milan decided in 1386 to rebuild their cathedral, he wished to make it a dynastic mausoleum, which met strong opposition. He chose instead to build a new church, the Certosa, as the mausoleum of the Visconti dynasty, and assigned it workers from the cathedral works.

The church was designed with a nave and two aisles, unusual for a Carthusian house. The Gothic nave was completed in 1465, and the church was consecrated in 1497. Its vaults are decorated alternately with geometrical shapes and starry skies, and it is inspired, on a reduced scale, by Milan Cathedral.

The Certosa is known for the exuberance of its architecture, in both Gothic and Renaissance styles, whereas the Carthusians were known for plain architecture. Its façade is covered with reliefs, inlaid marble and statues by sculptors including Cristoforo Mantegazza, Giovanni Antonio Amadeo and Benedetto Briosco, and is built of Carrara marble and other stones. Inside, the transept frescoes are by Ambrogio Bergognone, and an altarpiece by Pietro Perugino was commissioned in 1496 by Ludovico Sforza. Its lower panels were given in 1856 to the National Gallery in London.

The carved wooden choir, with 42 dossals of inlaid saints and biblical figures, was commissioned by Ludovico il Moro. The high altar carries a ciborium in Carrara marble, built in 1568 by Ambrogio Volpi. The Grand Cloister measures about 125 by 100 metres, with the monks' cells opening onto the central garden.

From its foundation the monks had a library, which held liturgical texts and others on scientific and humanistic subjects. A first library was set up between 1426 and 1427. The Certosa was suppressed in 1782, and its catalogue was partly divided between the libraries of Milan and Pavia, though 13 illuminated choirbooks remained in the monastery. The refectory was one of the first rooms built and served as a church in the early years of construction.

A museum in the rooms of the Ducal Palace, the summer residence of the Visconti and Sforza dynasty, holds works from the monastic complex and more than 200 casts. Gian Galeazzo Visconti and Isabella, Countess of Vertus, are among those buried there. The monument to Ludovico Sforza and his wife Beatrice d'Este is a cenotaph, since neither is buried in it.
cervera: Cervera is the capital of the comarca of Segarra, in the province of Lleida in the Autonomous Community of Catalonia, Spain. It had a population of 9,603 in 2025. The church of Sant Miquel de Tudela stands near the town. The title Comte de Cervera, formerly part of the Crown of Aragon, is a courtesy title that has been revived for Leonor, Princess of Asturias.

In 1026 three peasant families built the first settlement in Segarra, which was then uninhabited. The counts of Barcelona later granted them the lands, to establish their power in an area that was then the border between Christian and Muslim territory, and the first fortress was the castrum Cervarie. When the western border was established at Lleida in 1149, Cervera grew as terraced houses on the other side of it. The inhabitants were freed from the feudal lord's abuses, and the town became established first as a Confraria in 1182, then a Consolat, or municipal organ, in 1202, and from 1267 as a Paeria. A prosperous Jewish community lived there from the 12th century until the expulsion of the Jews in the 15th century.

Charles II, the last Spanish king of the house of Austria, died in 1700 and named Philip V as his heir. The War of the Spanish Succession began in 1702, and Cervera had supporters of both sides. In 1702 Philip V gave the town the title of city. When the war ended, Cervera had been destroyed. It sent two ambassadors to the Courts to assure Philip V's ministers of its absolute support, and among its 30 requests was a university like the one in Lleida. Philip V built the University of Cervera and closed the others, under the Nueva Planta decrees. The university gave the town an economic boost, partly because students lodged there.

In 1842 the university moved to Barcelona, a considerable economic loss. The arrival of the railway in 1860, new industries and an important wine trade then improved the local economy. When phylloxera arrived, many owners of vineyards went bankrupt, and the wine trade recovered somewhat with the creation of the Sindicat Agrícola in 1919.
cesar-milstein: César Milstein was born on 8 October 1927 in Bahía Blanca, Argentina. His parents were Máxima Vanarks and Lázaro Milstein, a Jewish Ukrainian immigrant. He graduated from the University of Buenos Aires. In 1958, funded by the British Council, he joined the Biochemistry Department at the University of Cambridge to work for a doctorate under Malcolm Dixon, and during this work he collaborated with Frederick Sanger. He later became a member of the Medical Research Council Laboratory of Molecular Biology at Cambridge and acquired British citizenship, holding dual British and Argentinian nationality.

Most of Milstein's research concerned the structure of antibodies and the way their diversity arises. In 1975 he worked with Georges Köhler, a postdoctoral fellow in his laboratory, to develop the hybridoma technique for producing monoclonal antibodies. The technique led to a great expansion in the use of antibodies in science and medicine. Milstein himself improved monoclonal antibody technology, particularly in providing markers that distinguish different cell types, and with Claudio Cuello he helped lay the foundation for using monoclonal antibodies to investigate neurological disorders. He foresaw that recombinant DNA technology could be applied to them and inspired the field of antibody engineering. He patented the production of monoclonal antibodies.

Later he used the hybridoma technique with nucleic acid sequencing to chart the changes in antibodies after an encounter with an antigen, and he showed the importance of somatic hypermutation of immunoglobulin V genes in antibody affinity maturation.

Milstein shared the 1984 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Niels Kaj Jerne and Georges Köhler. He was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1975, won the Wolf Prize in Medicine in 1980 and the Copley Medal in 1989, and became a Companion of Honour in 1995. He gave time to assisting science and scientists in less developed countries. He died on 24 March 2002 in Cambridge, aged 74, of a heart condition he had had for many years.
cesar-vallejo: César Abraham Vallejo Mendoza was born on 16 March 1892 in Santiago de Chuco, a remote village in the Peruvian Andes, the youngest of eleven children. Both his grandfathers were Spanish priests and both his grandmothers were indigenous Peruvians. Lack of money forced him to work for a time at a sugar plantation, the Roma Hacienda, where he saw the exploitation of farm workers, an experience that shaped his politics and his writing. He studied at the National University of San Marcos in Lima from 1911, worked as a schoolteacher, and took a degree in Spanish literature in 1915.

In 1920 Vallejo was accused, unjustly according to the account, of taking part in the burning of a house in Santiago de Chuco. He was held in a jail in Trujillo for 112 days, from 6 November 1920 to 26 February 1921. The lawyer Eduardo González Viaña, who studied the court papers, argues that the testimony was fabricated. The process was never closed, and in 2007 the Peruvian judiciary honoured his memory. Under threat of further imprisonment he went to Europe after publishing Trilce in 1922, and lived in poverty in Paris, apart from three trips to the USSR and about two years in Spain in the early 1930s.

He joined the Peruvian Communist Party in 1931, and wrote journalism, reportage on the USSR, plays that were not performed in his lifetime, the novel El tungsteno about a foreign-owned tungsten mine, and the children's story Paco Yunque.

Trilce, published in 1922, takes language to an extreme by inventing words, stretching syntax and using automatic writing, techniques later called surrealist, though he used them before the Surrealist movement began. It remains one of the most radically avant-garde poetry collections in Spanish.

After becoming deeply involved in the Spanish Civil War, he wrote a last burst of poems in the late 1930s. They were published after his death as Poemas humanos and España, aparta de mí este cáliz, though their titles and arrangement are still debated. He died in Paris on 15 April 1938, after an illness later understood to be a return of malaria he had had as a child.
cesare-beccaria: Cesare Beccaria was born in Milan on 15 March 1738 to an aristocrat of moderate standing. He was educated at the Jesuit college in Parma and graduated in law from the University of Pavia in 1758. Reading Montesquieu turned his attention to economics, and in 1762 he published a tract on the disorder of the currency in the Milanese states. In his mid-twenties he became close friends with Pietro and Alessandro Verri, and with other young Milanese aristocrats they formed a literary society, the Academy of Fists. Much of its talk concerned reform of criminal justice.

In 1764, encouraged by Pietro Verri, Beccaria published On Crimes and Punishments, a brief treatise that marked the high point of the Milan Enlightenment. Alessandro Verri, a Milan prison official, knew the prison's appalling conditions at first hand. The treatise protested against torture to obtain confessions, secret accusations, the arbitrary discretion of judges and capital punishment for serious and even minor offences. It was the first full work of penology. Beccaria published it anonymously, fearing a backlash, and acknowledged it only once the government's approval was clear.

He argued from the social contract and from utility. Punishment, he held, should prevent crime rather than avenge it, should be proportionate to the crime, and should be prompt. A high probability of punishment, not its severity, achieves prevention, and laws should be clear so that judges decide only whether a law has been broken. He condemned the death penalty because the state has no right to take lives and because it is neither useful nor necessary.

The treatise was translated into French and English almost at once, and Catherine the Great publicly endorsed it. Many penal reforms in the principal European nations can be traced to it, but few contemporaries accepted its argument against the death penalty. The Grand Duchy of Tuscany, the first state to abolish capital punishment, followed Beccaria's argument about its lack of utility, not about the state's lack of right. His thinking also shaped Jeremy Bentham's utilitarianism. In 1768 a chair of law and economy was founded for him in Milan. He died there on 28 November 1794, and his grandson was the novelist Alessandro Manzoni.
cesare-borgia: Cesare Borgia was born at Subiaco in the Papal States, the illegitimate son of Cardinal Rodrigo Borgia, later Pope Alexander VI, and his Italian mistress Vannozza dei Cattanei. His family came from the Kingdom of Valencia, and his great-uncle Alphonso Borgia became Pope Callixtus III in 1455. He studied law at Rome and was groomed for the Church, becoming bishop of Pamplona and archbishop of Valencia while still a youth, and a cardinal when his father was elected pope. In 1497 his brother Giovanni, the captain-general of the papal forces, was murdered in unclear circumstances. A contemporary suggested that Cesare was the killer, but his part has never been established, and he had no certain motive.

On 17 August 1498 Cesare resigned as cardinal to follow a military career, and Louis XII of France named him Duke of Valentinois. In 1499 he married Charlotte d'Albret, a sister of John III of Navarre, and accompanied Louis into Milan. With French troops and papal money, he took Imola and Forlì, which were ruled by Caterina Sforza, and then drove Giovanni Sforza from Pesaro. Rimini and Faenza followed, whose young lord Astorre III Manfredi was later drowned in the Tiber on Cesare's order. In May 1501 he was created Duke of Romagna. In 1502 he took Urbino and Camerino by treason.

His condottieri, among them Vitellozzo Vitelli and the Orsini, feared his cruelty and plotted against him. On 31 December 1502 he called for reconciliation, then imprisoned them at Senigallia and had them strangled, a deed the historian Paolo Giovio called a wonderful deceiving. In 1503 he took the Republic of San Marino. Niccolò Machiavelli, who was at his court from October 1502 to January 1503, wrote dispatches on him, and The Prince treats him as an example of the danger of gaining a principality through another's power. Leonardo da Vinci served him as military engineer in 1502 and 1503.

Machiavelli named Cesare's dependence on the goodwill of the papacy as the chief weakness of his rule. His father died in 1503, while Cesare lay ill with malarial fever. Pius III, who supported him, reigned only twenty-six days, and Giuliano Della Rovere, his deadly enemy, won his support with promises he broke once elected Pope Julius II. Cesare was captured at Naples and held in Spain, escaped from the Castle of La Mota, and reached Pamplona on 3 December 1506, where King John III welcomed him. During the siege of the castle of Viana he chased fleeing knights alone and was killed in an ambush on 12 March 1507. His remains lie outside the Church of Santa María at Viana.
cesare-maria-de-vecchi: De Vecchi was born in Casale Monferrato on 14 November 1884. After graduating in jurisprudence he worked as a lawyer in Turin. He favoured Italian intervention in the First World War and took part in its final events, ending the war as a captain with several decorations for valour. Back in Italy he joined the National Fascist Party, where he stood for its monarchical and moderate wing, led the Turin war veterans and the local Fascist squadre, and was elected to the Chamber of Deputies in 1921.

He was Commandant-General of the Blackshirt militia, tried to persuade Antonio Salandra to join Benito Mussolini's government, and served as undersecretary at the Treasury and then at the Finance Ministry. In December 1922 he inspired the squadre of Brandimarte to the Turin massacre. In Italian Somaliland he oversaw the building of the Cathedral of Mogadishu and was made Count of Val Cismon, after the battles his arditi had fought on Monte Grappa in 1918. The historian Tom Behan describes a scorched earth policy there from 1925 to 1927, and the killing of 100 civilians in Merca, counted as fascist Italy's first war crime, was committed under his leadership.

King Victor Emmanuel III made him a senator, and after the Lateran Treaty of 1929 he became the first ambassador to the Vatican. As Minister of Education from 1935 to 1936 he centralised the school system: the De Vecchi reform of 20 June 1935 put all high schools under the government, which set curricula and censored textbooks. In the Aegean Islands he enacted the Italian racial laws against the Jews. In his diary for 6 March 1940 the foreign minister, Count Ciano, called him a man of pomposity and vain illusions.

On 25 July 1943 he voted in the Grand Council of Fascism for Dino Grandi's motion deposing Mussolini. Commanding the 215th Coastal Division after the Armistice of Cassibile, he let German forces enter Piombino; when Italian sailors, soldiers and townspeople fought them off, he freed the captured Germans and surrendered his division. The Italian Social Republic condemned him to death in absentia at the Verona trial in January 1944. The Salesians of Don Bosco hid him until 1947, when he left for Argentina on a Paraguayan passport. Returning in 1949, he supported the neo-fascist Italian Social Movement without holding office, and died in Rome in 1959.
cesena: Cesena was originally an Umbrian or Etruscan town, later known as Caesena. After a brief spell under Gaulish rule it was taken over by the Romans in the 3rd century BCE, and it was destroyed in the wars between Gaius Marius and Sulla. It lay on the border that the Exarchate of Ravenna shared with the Lombards, and it was presented to the Papacy by its Frankish conqueror in 754, in the Donation of Pepin. It then passed back and forth between the popes and the archbishops of Ravenna, was briefly a communal republic from 1183 to 1198, and was long contested between popes and Holy Roman Emperors.

The brief rule of the Forlì family of the Ordelaffi was crushed in 1357 by papal troops led by Cardinal Gil de Albornoz, after a long siege endured by Cia degli Ordelaffi. The town revolted again in 1377 and was recaptured by Breton troops under the condottiere John Hawkwood and the command of Robert, Cardinal of Geneva, later the antipope Clement VII. Acting as legate of Pope Gregory XI, he directed the murder of between 2,500 and 5,000 civilians, an atrocity even by the laws of war of the time, called the Cesena Bloodbath. The following year what remained of Cesena was assigned to Galeotto I Malatesta.

From 1379 to 1465 the city recovered and prospered under the Malatesta, who rebuilt the castle, the Rocca Malatestiana. The fortress was begun by Cardinal Albornoz in 1380 and completed by the papal governor Lorenzo Zane in 1480. It is octagonal, with two main towers, the taller maschio and the shorter foemina, and Cesare Borgia later used it to imprison Caterina Sforza. Near the castle, Malatesta Novello built the Malatestiana Library, a fine example of a Renaissance library that holds many valuable manuscripts and is a UNESCO Memory of the World site.

After Novello's death in 1465 Cesena returned to the Papal States, but Cesare Borgia seized it and made it the capital of his short-lived duchy. Pope Pius VI and Pope Pius VII were born in the city and Pope Pius VIII was its bishop, which earned it the title of city of the three popes. During the Napoleonic Wars it lost numerous monasteries and churches, and some of its citizens played notable roles in the unification of Italy. In the Second World War it lay near the Gothic Line and suffered heavily from bombing.
cesis: Cēsis, in German Wenden, is a town in the Vidzeme region of Latvia, about 90 km north-east of Riga, on ridges above the valley of the Gauja. Its historic centre keeps its medieval street plan, sections of the town wall, St. John's Church of the late 13th century and the ruins of Cēsis Castle.

The earliest known fortified settlement stood on Riekstu Hill, where the Vends lived in the 11th and 12th centuries. The area came under the Livonian Brothers of the Sword in 1207, and a stone castle was begun on the neighbouring plateau, probably around 1214. Cēsis was first named as a town in 1323 and joined the Hanseatic League in the early 15th century. After the destruction of the Order's castle in Riga in 1484, Cēsis became the main residence of the Livonian Order's masters. Lutheran preaching began in 1524.

The town and castle were heavily damaged in the Livonian War, and during the siege of 1577 several hundred people sheltering in the castle killed themselves by igniting gunpowder rather than surrender to the army of Ivan the Terrible. The castle never regained its earlier importance. Swedish forces completed their conquest of the town in 1626, Russian troops occupied it in 1703, and it became a district town in 1785. The Riga-Pskov railway reached it in 1889.

After Latvia declared independence in November 1918, the Battles of Cēsis in June 1919 ended in an Estonian and Latvian victory over German forces, a major turning point in the Latvian War of Independence. In 1988 Cēsis was the first town to raise the red-white-red flag over a major public building during the national revival.

Latvians were a majority in Cēsis by the 1897 census, in a town with a substantial Baltic German community. The New Castle, converted into a manor residence in 1762, has housed the town's history museum since 1949, and a Victory Monument commemorates the battles of 1919.
cesky-krumlov: Český Krumlov lies on both banks of the Vltava in the Bohemian Forest Foothills, about 20 kilometres south-west of České Budějovice and 134 kilometres south of Prague. The area was settled from the Older Stone Age, with mass settlement in the Bronze Age, Celtic settlements about 400 BCE and the first Slavic settlement from the 6th century CE.

The castle was founded shortly before 1250 by a local branch of the noble Vítkovci family, and the town was first mentioned in a deed of 1253 as Chrumbenowe. It grew in two stages: Latrán, built spontaneously below the castle by people connected with its administration, and a newly founded Old Town. Both Czech and German nationalities were present from the start, and a Jewish community is documented from 1334.

When the Vítkovci line died out in 1302, King Wenceslaus II ceded the estate to the Rosenberg family, who made it their main residence. Peter I of Rosenberg had the upper castle built in the early 14th century, and the town reached its highest prosperity in the 15th century under Oldřich II of Rosenberg. Gold found near the town in the late 15th century brought German miners, shifting the ethnic balance further.

In 1555 William of Rosenberg joined Latrán and the Old Town into one, and later rebuilt the castle in Renaissance style. Peter Vok of Rosenberg sold Krumlov in 1602 to Emperor Rudolf II, who gave it to his illegitimate son Julius d'Austria. After the Battle of White Mountain in 1620 Emperor Ferdinand II gave it to the Eggenberg family, and it became the seat of the Duchy of Krumlov. The Schwarzenberg family held the castle from 1719 to 1947.

In 1910 the town had 8,662 inhabitants, 85 per cent of them German and 15 per cent Czech. It passed to Czechoslovakia under the Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye in 1919, was annexed by Nazi Germany under the Munich Agreement in 1938, and after the Second World War its German majority was expelled. The historic centre fell into disrepair under communist rule and has been largely restored since 1989. The castle complex, about 7 hectares with forty buildings around five courts, is one of the largest in central Europe, and the town and castle have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1992. The town has about 13,000 inhabitants.
cestius-gallus: Gaius Cestius Gallus was a Roman senator and general of the Principate, the son of Gaius Cestius Gallus, ordinary consul in 35. He was himself suffect consul in 42, holding office for the second nundinium of the year as the colleague of Gaius Caecina Largus.

At the outset of the First Jewish–Roman War, in the year 66, Gallus marched into Judaea in September with more than 30,000 men to restore order. Assembled at Antioch, his army comprised Legio XII Fulminata, detachments of the three other legions based in Syria, six cohorts of auxiliary infantry and four alae of cavalry, supported by 14,000 allied troops supplied by Agrippa II and other client rulers.

After sending detachments to occupy Galilee and the Judean coast, he turned inland against Jerusalem. He lost men from his baggage train and rearguard on the way, reached Mount Scopus and broke into the outer city, but could not take the Temple Mount. After a siege of nine days he fell back towards the coast, apparently because ambushes had cost him his siege equipment and the October rains threatened his supply lines.

The war party in Jerusalem under Shimon bar Giora pursued the retreating army as far as Antipatris. Josephus first put the Roman losses at 515, but in the rout that followed the dead numbered 5,300 infantry and 380 cavalry. The defeat fell in the month of Heshvan in the 12th year of Nero's reign and marked the beginning of the war with Rome.

Gallus returned to Syria and died before the spring of 67. According to Josephus he was broken by shame at the great and unexpected defeat. Licinius Mucianus succeeded him as governor of Syria, while the future emperor Vespasian took command of the forces gathered to crush the rising in Judaea.
cetbang: The word cetbang does not occur in Old Javanese and probably comes from the Chinese chongtong, which also gave the Korean word for a cannon. Meriam coak, from the Betawi language, means hollow cannon, after the open breech. Warastra is an Old Javanese word for a magic or powerful arrow. Bedil, the general Javanese term for any gunpowder weapon from a pistol to a siege gun, goes back to Tamil words for a gunpowder blast and saltpetre, and spread across the archipelago as bodil in Batak, badili in Makasarese, baril in Tagalog and badel among the Malays.

The eastern-style cetbang, mostly of bronze and loaded from the muzzle, fired arrow-like projectiles, some with explosive or incendiary charges, as well as round shot. It sat on a fixed mount or, as a hand cannon, on the end of a pole fitted into a socket at its rear, and served against ships and in sieges.

The western-style cetbang, of bronze or iron, was a breech-loading swivel gun with up to five chambers that could be reloaded in turn for rapid fire. Most were light enough for one man to carry. Set on a swivel yoke, the cagak, in the bulwark of a ship or the rampart of a fort, and loaded with scatter shot, it was used against men at close range in boarding fights.

Thomas Stamford Raffles wrote that by 1325 cannons were widely used in Java, and that small kingdoms seeking Majapahit's protection had to hand over theirs. The Sundanese used ship-borne bedil at the Battle of Bubat in 1357, and Ma Huan, who visited Java in 1413, saw cannons fired at weddings. The Portuguese found Javanese merchants at Malacca casting their own guns, and in 1513 a Javanese fleet under Pati Unus attacked Portuguese Malacca with artillery made in Java.

The guns stayed in use long after. When the Dutch took the Makassar fort of Somba Opu in 1669 they seized 145 breech-loading swivel guns, and Makassan sailors carried such guns, called ba'dili, on trepanging voyages to Australia, where Matthew Flinders noted them in 1803. Surviving examples are kept in the Bali Museum, the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Rijksmuseum and the Fatahillah Museum.
cetina: The Cetina has its source in the northwestern slopes of Dinara, rising from a spring at Milasevo near a small village also called Cetina, 7 kilometres north of Vrlika. It flows 101 kilometres to the Adriatic, and its basin covers 1,463 square kilometres, though the whole catchment is around 12,000 square kilometres because the river also receives water from the west Bosnian karst field by underground routes.

A large artificial lake, the Peruća Lake, begins near Vrlika. The river then passes through Sinj and Trilj, runs back westward round the mountain Mosor and enters the sea at Omiš. Its lower course begins at the Gubavica Falls, 20 kilometres from Omiš. The catchment drains mostly limestone of Cretaceous age.

The Cetina Valley and the narrow passage at Klis have always served as a principal trade route between the Croatian coast and the hinterland. The earliest evidence of agriculture is from the Early Neolithic in the upper valley. In the Early Bronze Age the Cetina culture, a widespread group with contacts across the Adriatic basin, became dominant. The river seems to have been a focus for the deliberate deposition of artefacts throughout prehistory, above all at its confluence with the Ruda at Trilj.

The area is closely associated with the heartland of the Delmatae. The legionary fortress at Tilurium (Gardun) guarded the entrance to the valley from the south and the approach to the provincial capital at Salona. In the early medieval period the valley formed a frontier between Slavic and Late Roman power, and the area around Sinj became a heartland of the Early Croatian State. It was contested until the Ottoman conquest in the early 16th century, and then lay on the frontier between the Ottoman Empire and the Republic of Venice for 150 years.

Several substantial hydroelectric power plants use the steep drop of its lower course, and its water is bottled under the name Cetina. It is the most water-rich river in Dalmatia and is home to the only known freshwater coralline alga, Pneophyllum cetinaensis, which lives nowhere else. The canyon is a destination for rafting, canyoning, kayaking and rock climbing.
cetinje: Cetinje lies in a small karst plain of about 7 square kilometres, at an average height of 671 metres, surrounded by limestone mountains that include Mount Lovćen, a mountain prominent in Montenegrin historiography. It is 12 kilometres in a straight line from the Adriatic and 15 from Skadar Lake. The town is named after the Cetina river that, according to written data, flowed down the plain until the end of the 17th century. Cetinje is first mentioned in historical documents in 1440, and rainfall there is very heavy, though the karst leaves few water sources on the surface.

Cetinje was founded in 1482, when Ivan Crnojević moved his capital from Obod, above the Crnojević River, to a more easily defended field at the foot of Mount Lovćen. He had his court built there that year and founded a monastery as a personal endowment, and the court and monastery are the first recorded Renaissance buildings in Montenegro. Because of the Ottoman invasions he also moved the seat of the Eparchy of Zeta from Vranjina to Cetinje in 1485. A printing house of the Crnojević family worked there from 1492 to 1496, and its books spread Cyrillic type among the Orthodox peoples of south-eastern Europe.

For the next two centuries Cetinje stagnated and was often attacked by Venice and the Ottomans. The court and monastery of the Crnojević dynasty were destroyed. The town began to flourish again from 1697, under the Petrović dynasty refounded by Danilo Petrović. His successors were occupied with wars of liberation and the unity of the country, and greater progress came only under Petar II Petrović Njegoš, who built his residence, the Biljarda, in 1838. New houses led to genuine urbanisation, and foreign consulates, French, Russian, British, Italian and Austro-Hungarian, put up buildings after relations with European states were established.

Podgorica is the capital of Montenegro, but Cetinje is the seat of several national institutions, among them the National Museum of Montenegro, the national library and the State Archives. The official residence of the president, the Blue Palace, is there. Its main sights include the monastery, Biljarda, the Vlaška church and the old foreign embassies. It is the seat of the Eparchy of Montenegro and the Littoral of the Serbian Orthodox Church, and the Montenegrin Orthodox Church also has its seat there. The 2023 census counted 12,460 people in the town.
cetinje-octoechos: The Cetinje Octoechos, in Serbian Cetinjski oktoih, was printed in Cetinje, then the capital of the Principality of Zeta, in present-day Montenegro. It was made under the direction of Hieromonk Makarije at the Crnojević printing house, which Đurađ Crnojević, the ruler of Zeta, had founded in 1493, so that the first volume was finished within about a year of the press's founding. It is the first incunabulum in the Serbian recension of Church Slavonic.

The book was printed in two instalments, following the eight tones of the Octoechos system of musical modes. The first volume, the Octoechos of the First Tone (Oktoih prvoglasnik), holds the hymns sung to the first four tones, and the second, the Octoechos of the Fifth Tone (Oktoih petoglasnik), those for the remaining four.

The first volume was finished on 4 January 1494. It has 270 leaves measuring 29 by 21.6 centimetres, printed cleanly in red and black with finely formed letters, and is decorated with headpieces and initials cut in wood in the spirit of the Renaissance, with traces of the older manuscript tradition. In the quality of its printing and ornament it is judged equal to the Venetian work of its time.

The Octoechos of the Fifth Tone is the first illustrated printed book in Serbian Cyrillic and the second South Slavic incunabulum. It survives only in fragments, the longest of 37 leaves, and has six woodcut illustrations whose artist fitted complex scenes with many figures into a small space. In 1987 the National Library of Montenegro, Đurđe Crnojević, in Cetinje published 600 facsimiles of the Octoechos of the First Tone.
cetshwayo: Cetshwayo kaMpande was the son of the future Zulu king Mpande kaSenzangakhona and Queen Ngqumbazi, and a half-nephew of King Shaka. In the Zulu Civil War of 1856 he led the Usuthu against his younger brother Mbuyazi, and at the Battle of Ndondakusuka on 2 December 1856 he annihilated most of Mbuyazi's Gqoza followers, among them five of his own brothers. Mpande recognised him as heir in 1861. With the advice of the trader John Robert Dunn, Cetshwayo confined the import of firearms to the Usuthu, which gave him a technological edge and weakened the military power of rivals such as his half-brother uHamu kaNzibe and Zibhebhu.

Mpande died in 1872, and his death was first concealed to ensure a smooth transition. Cetshwayo was acclaimed by his izinduna in 1873, and on 1 September 1873 Sir Theophilus Shepstone, Natal's Secretary for Native Affairs, presided over his coronation. Rival chiefs, among them uHamu, Zibhebhu and Mnyamana kaNgqengelele, declared their loyalty, which centralised Zulu military power. Cetshwayo then founded a new capital, Ulundi.

After the British annexed the Transvaal, a Boer-Zulu border dispute became a British-Zulu one, and a boundary commission of 1878 found that the Boers had no right to the land. Sir Henry Bartle Frere withheld its findings.

On 11 December 1878 Bartle Frere issued an ultimatum demanding the abolition of the Zulu military system within thirty days and payment of cattle. It could not be met, and British forces entered Zululand on 11 January 1879. Cetshwayo opposed the war and sent messengers seeking peace, whom the British imprisoned. After the Zulu victory at Isandlwana he refused to counterattack into Natal, hoping for a treaty. At the Battle of Ulundi on 4 July the British formed a hollow square with cannon and Gatling guns, routed the Zulu after about 45 minutes and burnt Ulundi. Cetshwayo was captured on 28 August and sent to Cape Town, and Zululand was divided into thirteen chiefdoms.

Bishop Colenso and Lady Florence Dixie took up his cause, and in 1882 he visited England and was received by Queen Victoria. The British returned him to Zululand in 1883, but Zibhebhu attacked his kraal at Ulundi on 22 July 1883 and wounded him. He moved to Eshowe, where he died on 8 February 1884, presumably of a heart attack, though some think he was poisoned. His son Dinuzulu was proclaimed king on 20 May 1884. Cetshwayo is remembered above all as the last independent king of the Zulu Kingdom.
ceuta: Ceuta lies on the North African coast, 17 kilometres across the Strait of Gibraltar from the Spanish mainland, and shares a land border of 6.4 kilometres with Morocco. It has an area of 18.5 square kilometres. Monte Hacho, on the La Almina Peninsula above the port, is one of the possible sites of the southern Pillar of Hercules of Greek legend; the other is Jebel Musa. The Strait of Gibraltar is an important military and commercial chokepoint, and the narrow isthmus joining the La Almina Peninsula to the African mainland made the site easy to defend.

Phoenicians established an outpost there early in the 1st millennium BCE, which continued under Roman rule as Septem Fratres. The Vandals crossed the strait around 425 CE, but lost Tingis and Septem in a series of Berber revolts. Around 533 the Byzantine general Belisarius made Septem the westernmost outpost of the Byzantine Empire, and the empire, which did not push far inland, made it their regional capital in place of Tingis. It was annexed by the early caliphates in the Islamic conquest of the Maghreb, destroyed in the Berber Revolt, and rebuilt in the ninth century. For much of the Middle Ages powers north and south of the strait vied for control of it as a key port in the so-called Battle of the Strait.

On the morning of 21 August 1415 King John I of Portugal led his sons and their forces in a surprise assault known as the Conquest of Ceuta. About 45,000 Portuguese arrived on 200 ships, caught the defenders off guard and took the town by nightfall, with only eight casualties. After the death of King Sebastian of Portugal at the Battle of Alcácer Quibir in 1578 and a succession war, Philip II of Spain was crowned Philip I of Portugal in April 1581, and Ceuta passed to the Hispanic Monarchy. On 1 January 1668 King Afonso VI of Portugal ceded it to King Carlos II of Spain by the Treaty of Lisbon.

Moroccan forces under Moulay Ismail besieged the city from 1694 to 1727, the longest siege in history, and the city lost its Portuguese character. It was besieged unsuccessfully again in 1790 and 1791, and British forces occupied it from 1810 to 1815. A dispute over the border led to the war between Spain and Morocco of 1859 to 1860, ended by the Treaty of Wad Ras.

Ceuta is an autonomous city of Spain, a status it gained through its Statute of Autonomy in March 1995; before then it was a municipality of the province of Cádiz. Spanish is its official language, and Moroccan Arabic is also widely spoken. Its population is mainly Spanish Christians and Arab Muslims, with small Sephardic Jewish and Sindhi Hindu minorities.
cevennes: The Cévennes is a cultural region and mountain range in south-central France, on the south-eastern edge of the Massif Central. It covers parts of the départements of Ardèche, Gard, Hérault and Lozère. The range runs from the Grandes Causses in the south-west to the Monts du Vivarais in the north-east, and its highest point is Mont Lozère at 1,699 metres. It forms the watershed between the Atlantic and the Mediterranean. The name comes from the Gaulish Cebenna, which probably meant ridgeline. Autumn downpours that follow when cold Atlantic air meets warm southern winds are called épisodes cévenols.

People have lived in the region for a very long time, and megaliths were erected there beginning around 2500 BCE, among them the stone rows of Bondons, the second largest megalithic site in Europe. The Celts arrived between 800 and 400 BCE. In the 3rd century BCE the Arverne Confederation used the Cévennes as a defensive barrier against the Romans, who conquered the area in 121 BCE. Julius Caesar crossed the mountains in the winter of 52 BCE, having his soldiers clear paths through up to six feet of snow, to attack the Arverni. The Visigoths took the western half of Gallia Narbonensis, known as Septimania, in 462 CE, and King Pepin the Short reconquered the whole of it in 759.

French Protestants, the Huguenots, were established in the Cévennes by the early 16th century and often worshipped in forests, caves and gullies. The Edict of Fontainebleau of October 1685 revoked the Edict of Nantes and forbade Protestant worship, and those who stayed resisted. Known as Camisards in the Cévennes, Protestants fought royal troops from 1702 to 1704, with sporadic fighting until 1715. The Edict of Versailles in 1787 and the Revolution of 1789 finally gave non-Catholics the right to practise openly. During the Second World War, families in the Cévennes organised by local Protestant pastors sheltered Jews from capture by the Nazis and protected hundreds.

Cévennes National Park was created in 1970. Parts of the region lie within the UNESCO Cévennes Biosphere Reserve and the World Heritage Site Causses and the Cévennes, Mediterranean agro-pastoral Cultural Landscape. The region still has a large community of French Protestants. The Scottish writer Robert Louis Stevenson visited in 1878 and wrote Travels with a Donkey in the Cévennes, published in 1879.
cfa-franc: The CFA franc was created on 26 December 1945, together with the CFP franc, because the French franc was weak after World War II. When France ratified the Bretton Woods Agreement in December 1945, the French franc was devalued to set a fixed rate against the US dollar. New currencies were created in the colonies to spare them the strong devaluation, which made it easier for them to import goods from France and harder to export to France. French officials presented the decision as generosity. Between 1945 and 1958 CFA stood for Colonies françaises d'Afrique, and from 1958 until independence for Communauté française d'Afrique.

The name covers two currencies that have the same value but are not interchangeable. The West African CFA franc is issued by the Central Bank of the West African States at Dakar for eight countries: Benin, Burkina Faso, Guinea-Bissau, Ivory Coast, Mali, Niger, Senegal and Togo. The Central African CFA franc is issued by the Bank of the Central African States at Yaoundé for Cameroon, the Central African Republic, Chad, Equatorial Guinea, Gabon and the Republic of the Congo. Both are guaranteed by the French Treasury.

The rate against the French franc was changed only twice. From 1945 one CFA franc was worth 1.70 French francs; from 17 October 1948 it was worth 2. On 12 January 1994 an overnight devaluation of 50 per cent halved its value. When the euro replaced the French franc on 1 January 1999 the rate became 655.957 CFA francs to the euro.

The zone has changed since independence. Guinea left in 1960 and Mali in 1962, rejoining in 1984; Madagascar and Mauritania left in 1973, and Guinea-Bissau, a former Portuguese colony, joined in 1997. Critics hold that the currency restricts the sovereignty of the member states and makes national monetary policy all but impossible, and some object that the notes are printed in France. Defenders argue that it stabilises the national currencies and eases trade with France.
chaac: Chaac, spelled Chaahk in Classic Mayan, corresponds to Tlaloc among the Aztecs and Cocijo among the Zapotecs. Like other Maya gods he is both one and manifold. Four Chaacs are tied to the cardinal directions and wear their colours: red for the east, white for the north, black for the west and yellow for the south, with green for the centre. In 16th-century Yucatán the Chaac of the east was called Chac Xib Chaac, Red Man Chaac.

In art he usually has a human body with reptilian or amphibian scales, and a non-human head with fangs and a long, pendulous nose. In the Classic style a shell serves as his ear ornament. He often carries a shield and a lightning axe, which is personified by the closely related deity K'awiil, called Bolon Dzacab in Yucatec.

Among the rituals for the rain deities, the Yucatec Ch'a Cháak ceremony asks for rain and centres on a banquet for the rain deities, with four boys, one for each cardinal point, acting and chanting as frogs. One ocellated turkey, an animal associated with the deity, is hunted and sacrificed each year, and its blood is offered to the fields.

In the Classic period the king often impersonated the rain deity or an associated rain serpent, which may have expressed his role as supreme rainmaker. More often it was the war-like fury of the deity that was stressed, and the king is shown carrying war implements and making prisoners, his acts equated with the violence of a thunderstorm. A Late Postclassic Yucatec tradition held that Chac Xib Chaac was the title of a king of Chichen Itza. A large part of the Dresden Codex is devoted to the Chaacs, and Bishop Diego de Landa combined the four Chaacs with the four Bacabs, aged deities of the subterranean waters.

Myths tell that Chaac opened with his lightning axe the mountain where maize was hidden. In a Q'eqchi' myth of the Sun and Moon he commits adultery with his brother's wife and is punished, and his tears of agony give rise to rain. Classic sources show him at the resurrection of the Maya maize god from the shell of a turtle, and with the Death God he appears to preside over an initiate's transformation into a jaguar. Chaac still matters to some Maya groups in Mexico. In 2024 a statue of the Greek god Poseidon in Progreso, Yucatán, caused controversy among locals who saw it as offensive to their beliefs in Chaac, and some of them tried to have it removed.
chabrias: Little is known of Chabrias's background beyond his father's name, Ctesippus, and his wealth: he was rich enough to bear the liturgy and served as trierarch in 377–376 BCE. He had a son, also named Ctesippus. He first appears as strategos in 390–389 BCE during the Corinthian War, when he replaced Iphicrates as commander of the Athenian garrison at Corinth. The orator Demosthenes later described him as a general who never lost a city, post, ship or soldier under his command.

In 388 BCE, sailing with ten ships and 800 peltasts to aid King Evagoras of Salamis on Cyprus, he landed by night on Aegina and ambushed its Spartan garrison, killing its commander Gorgopas. After the Peace of Antalkides he hired himself out, without Athenian sanction, to the Egyptian king Hakor, until Athens, courting Persia, recalled him. In 378 BCE, facing Agesilaos II outside Thebes, he had his men stand at ease, shields resting on the knee and spears pointing upward; Agesilaos withdrew, and Chabrias later chose that posture for his statue in the agora.

At Naxos in 376 BCE he held back from pursuit to recover the living and the dead from the water, recalling the generals condemned after Arginusae. In reward Athens freed him and his descendants from the liturgies, though he later served as trierarch and choregos all the same. In 369 BCE he defended Corinth against the Thebans. In 366 he and the politician Callistratus advised restraint over the Theban seizure of Oropos and were prosecuted, and in 362 he commanded the navy of the Egyptian king Tachos.

In the Social War, when Byzantium, Rhodes, Chios and Kos left the Athenian Confederacy, Chabrias sailed as trierarch with the fleet of Chares. Cornelius Nepos tells that at Chios he had his ship steered first into the harbour, the others did not follow, and when it was rammed and began to sink he refused to abandon it and died fighting hand to hand.
chach-nama: The work opens with a chapter on the history of Sindh just before the Arab conquest. Its body follows the Chacha dynasty from the end of the Rai dynasty and the accession of Chach of Alor down to the campaign of the Umayyad general Muhammad bin Qasim in the early 8th century. It closes with an epilogue on the tragic end of Muhammad bin Qasim and of the two daughters of Dahir, the defeated king of Sindh. It is also known as the Fateh Nama Sindh, the Story of the Conquest of Sindh.

Its author, Ali Kufi, wrote in Persian but said he was translating an Arabic book found among the possessions of the qadi of Alor, an office first filled by Muhammad bin Qasim after the conquest. The historian Yohanan Friedmann found that the battle narratives agree with Arab historians such as al-Baladhuri and may draw on works of Madāʾinī, while other parts, such as the rise of the Chach dynasty and traditions credited to Brahman elders, probably reflect a local Indian tradition.

Manan Ahmed Asif argues instead that the book is an original 13th-century work, not a translation, written to win favour at the court of Nasiruddin Qabacha. In his reading it is a romance that reshapes the far simpler accounts of al-Baladhuri and al-Biruni, turning a story in which priests and monks negotiate peace into a martial one.

Later chroniclers such as Nizamuddin Ahmad and Firishta drew their accounts of the Arab conquest from it. Western scholars including Peter Hardy, André Wink and Friedmann have questioned its authenticity, pointing to geographical errors, inconsistencies with other Persian and Arabic versions, and the absence of the Arabic tradition it claims to translate. Under British rule it shaped colonial views of how Islam came to the subcontinent and, according to Asif, a picture of age-old antagonism between Hindus and Muslims. It influenced the debate on the partition of British India and appears in the state-sanctioned history textbooks of Pakistan. H. M. Elliot and John Dowson published a partial translation in 1867, and Mirza Kalichbeg Fredunbeg a full translation from the Persian in 1900.
chaco-canyon: Chaco Canyon lies in the San Juan Basin on the Colorado Plateau, ringed by the Chuska Mountains to the west, the San Juan Mountains to the north and the San Pedro Mountains to the east. The region is arid, with about 8 inches (200 mm) of rain a year and wide swings in temperature and rainfall. Chacoans drew timber from forests of oak, piñon, ponderosa pine and juniper, and it has been suggested that even in wet periods the canyon could sustain only about 2,000 people.
