The first people in the area were Archaic and Early Basketmaker hunter-gatherers, whose more than 70 campsites have been dated to 7000–1500 BCE. By 490 CE their descendants farmed around Shabik'eshchee Village. Around 800, in the Pueblo I period, the people were building crescent-shaped stone complexes of residential suites beside subterranean kivas. A canyon-wide turquoise industry is attested from the tenth century, and the first section of Pueblo Bonito, a curved row of 50 rooms, was built about then.

The carefully planned great houses did not appear until around 1030. They averaged more than 200 rooms, some had up to 700, and they often stood four or five stories high. Pueblo Bonito covers almost 2 acres, has at least 650 rooms and walls up to 3 feet thick, and is divided by a north–south wall with a great kiva on each side. Researchers think the residential population may have been small, with larger groups gathering for annual ceremonies. About 200,000 pieces of turquoise have been excavated.

The Great North Road runs about 35 miles beyond Pueblo Alto; modern Pueblo peoples see it as an allusion to myths of their arrival from the north. Climate change is thought to have led the Chacoans to migrate and abandon the canyon. Southern Athabaskan-speaking peoples, the Apache and Navajo, succeeded the Pueblo people in the region by the 15th century.

The park lies in north-western New Mexico and is managed by the National Park Service. The Hopi and Pueblo peoples regard the sites as sacred ancestral homelands and keep oral accounts of their migration from Chaco. Fajada Butte has been closed to the public over concerns about erosion. Excavation began in earnest in 1896 with the Hyde Exploring Expedition, which sent more than 60,000 artifacts to New York. Since 1981 an approach informed by Hopi and Pueblo beliefs has replaced intrusive digging.
chaco-war: Both countries were landlocked after defeats in the nineteenth century. Paraguay lost almost half of its claimed territory to Brazil and Argentina in the War of the Triple Alliance (1864–1870) and depended on the Paraguay River, which runs through the Chaco, for its economy. Bolivia lost its Pacific coast to Chile in 1879, and the Treaty of Lima of 1929 ended hopes of a corridor to the Pacific, so access to the Atlantic by way of the Paraguay River became essential to it.

Popular memory in Bolivia holds that the war was fought to defend the oil, but the historian Stephen Cote argues that no oil deposits were known in the disputed Chaco at the time, and that Bolivia was after a river port.

On 15 June 1932 a Bolivian detachment captured and burned the Paraguayan Fortín Carlos Antonio López at Pitiantutá Lake. A month later Paraguayans drove the Bolivians from the area. Fortín Boquerón, held by 619 Bolivians, resisted a Paraguayan force of 5,000 for 22 days before falling on 29 September 1932. Bolivia then mobilised and put General Hans Kundt, a former German officer, in command of an offensive in December 1932.

Paraguay answered with encirclements. In one of them, the Bolivian regiments Loa and Ballivián, 509 men, surrendered, and President Eusebio Ayala promoted José Félix Estigarribia to general. A 20-day ceasefire began on 19 December 1933. At Ybybobó, from 28 December 1934 into January 1935, 200 Bolivians were killed and 1,200 surrendered, while the Paraguayans lost only a few dozen men.

Paraguay moved its army by river and rail and used radio messages in Guaraní, which most Bolivian soldiers did not speak. Bolivian troops came from the highlands some 800 km away, a march of 14 days against four for the Paraguayans. Thousands of non-combat casualties came from dehydration, mostly among Bolivians.

A ceasefire took effect at noon on 12 June 1935, when Paraguay controlled most of the region. A treaty signed in Buenos Aires in 1938 and approved in a referendum in Paraguay awarded Paraguay three-quarters of the Gran Chaco. Bolivia kept the remaining territory, which bordered Puerto Busch, and received navigation rights on the Paraguay and Paraná rivers.

It was the first war in South America in which machine guns, armoured vehicles and aircraft were used, and the bloodiest of the continent in the twentieth century: around 2 per cent of Bolivians and 3 per cent of Paraguayans were killed. The Bolivian writer Augusto Céspedes, a war reporter, described it in Crónicas heroicas de una guerra estúpida.
chad: Chad is a landlocked country of 1,284,000 square kilometres, bordered by Libya, Sudan, Niger, Nigeria, Cameroon and the Central African Republic. Its capital is 1,060 kilometres from the nearest seaport, Douala in Cameroon, and the distance and desert climate have led to the nickname Dead Heart of Africa. A wide basin is bounded by the Ennedi Plateau and the Tibesti Mountains, which include the dormant volcano Emi Koussi, at 3,414 metres. Lake Chad is the remains of an immense lake of 330,000 square kilometres that existed 7,000 years ago. The Sahara covers the northern third, a Sahelian belt lies in the centre, and savanna in the south.

From the 7th millennium BCE ecological conditions favoured settlement in the north, and some of Africa's most important archaeological sites are in the Borkou-Ennedi-Tibesti Region. The earliest civilisation of the Chad Basin was the Sao, known from artefacts and oral histories, which fell to the Kanem Empire. Kanem became the first and longest-lasting of the states in the Sahelian strip, its power based on the trans-Saharan trade routes. Islamisation increased from the 11th century, and by the 12th century its scribes had developed an original script style, the barnāwī.

Kanem's expansion peaked under Mai Dunama Dabbalemi, who reigned c. 1221 to 1259. Around 1396 Bulala invaders forced Mai Umar Idrismi to move the imperial centre to Bornu. The Sultanate of Bagirmi and the Wadai Sultanate arose in the 16th and 17th centuries, and Wadai's Muhammad Sharif, who reigned from 1843 to 1858, subjugated Bagirmi and resisted French colonisation. The Territoire Militaire des Pays et Protectorats du Tchad was created in 1900, and by 1920 France had secured full control and made Chad part of French Equatorial Africa.

Chad became independent in 1960 under François Tombalbaye. Resentment of his policies in the Muslim north led to a civil war that began in 1965, and rebels took the capital in 1979. Hissène Habré defeated rival commanders, and a Chadian–Libyan conflict that began in 1978 ended in 1987 with French military intervention. Idriss Déby overthrew Habré in 1990. Chad has over 200 ethnic and linguistic groups, and its official languages are French and Arabic. Islam is practised by 55.1 per cent and Christianity by 41.1 per cent.
chad-gadya: The song is a cumulative chain in which each verse adds a new figure: a little goat bought for two zuzim is eaten by a cat, the cat bitten by a dog, the dog beaten by a stick, and so on through fire, water, an ox, the slaughterer and the Angel of Death, until the Holy One, blessed be He, comes at the end. Its melody may have roots in medieval German folk music. It resembles Echad Mi Yodea (Who Knows One?), another cumulative song of the Passover Haggadah, and it is popular with children.

It is often described as wholly Aramaic, but it mixes Aramaic and Hebrew. It opens with the Aramaic had gadya and uses Aramaic words for the cat and dog, then shifts to Hebrew for the slaughterer, the Angel of Death and God, and its grammar suggests a composer with a limited grasp of Aramaic. The idea that Aramaic was chosen to hide its meaning from non-Jews is mistaken, since its first publication carried a full German translation. Versions exist in Yiddish, Ladino, Judaeo-Italian and Judaeo-Arabic.

Modern commentators have read it as an allegory of the nations that conquered the Land of Israel, the goat standing for the Jewish people and the cat, dog and stick for Assyria, Babylon and Persia. This reading was apparently first widely published in a pamphlet by Philip Nicodemus Lebrecht in Leipzig in 1731. Rabbis offered other readings: Jacob Emden saw the perils facing the soul, Jonathan Eybeschuetz a brief history of Israel, and Moses Sofer the Passover rite in the Temple of Jerusalem.

The Russian avant-garde artist El Lissitzky illustrated the song in 1917 and 1919, and art historians have read the second version, in which the Angel of Death lies dead, in the light of the October Revolution. Chava Alberstein's anti-war version drew calls for a ban on Israeli radio in 1989, and Angelo Branduardi made it popular in Italy from the 1970s as Alla fiera dell'est. In Yiddish slang the phrase is a euphemism for jail.
chadema: Chadema, in Swahili Chama cha Demokrasia na Maendeleo, is a centre-right party that campaigns for the regional autonomy of self-governing states within Tanzania. In the general election of 1995 it won 4 of the 269 seats in the National Assembly and 41 councillors across the country. In 2000 it put up no presidential candidate but won five seats, 75 councillors and the district councils of Kigoma, Karatu and Tarime.

The party grew through the following decade, especially among younger voters. In 2005 its presidential candidate, Freeman Mbowe, came third of ten candidates with 5.88% of the vote, and it won eleven seats and 103 councillors. In 2010 its secretary-general, Willibrod Slaa, took 27.1% of the presidential vote, and the party won 48 seats, becoming for the first time the second-largest party in the National Assembly, along with 467 councillors and seven district councils. Most of its seats lay in towns and cities such as Arusha, Moshi, Mwanza, Mbeya and Dar es Salaam.

For the general election of October 2015 Chadema joined the CUF, the National League for Democracy and NCCR-Mageuzi in the coalition Umoja wa Katiba ya Wananchi (UKAWA), which put forward a single presidential candidate, Edward Lowassa. In 2020, under President John Magufuli, its candidate Tundu Lissu, the MP for Singida East, received 1,933,271 votes, and the party lost 53 seats in the National Assembly, its worst defeat since its founding in 1992.

In September 2024 the police arrested Mbowe and Lissu in an effort to block protests against the government. On 22 January 2025 Lissu defeated Mbowe by 31 votes to become chairman. Days after Lissu was arrested and charged with treason following a rally at which he called for electoral reform, the National Electoral Commission disqualified the party in April 2025 for failing to sign a code of conduct due on 12 April.
chagatai-khan: Chagatai was born in late 1183 or 1184 to Börte, of the Onggirat tribe, and Temüjin, the later Genghis Khan. Because Börte had been kidnapped by the Merkit tribe before the birth of her elder son Jochi, whose paternity was never known, Chagatai was the first son definitively fathered by Temüjin. When Genghis divided his new nation after the assembly of 1206, Chagatai received territories near the Altai Mountains and either 4,000 or 8,000 subjects. He was known for his knowledge of Mongol law and custom, and chroniclers such as Juzjani noted the harshness of his temperament.

With his brothers Jochi and Ögedei he commanded the right wing in the invasion of the Jin dynasty in 1211. In the invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire in 1219 he was charged with building bridges and maintaining roads. He and Ögedei besieged Otrar, which fell in February 1220; the Mongols killed or enslaved its entire population. At the Siege of Gurganj, which fell in April 1221, the usual narrative has Chagatai and Jochi quarrel over how to conduct it until Genghis placed Ögedei over both; the historian Christopher Atwood argues that this account was a later invention meant to support Ögedei's right to rule.

Genghis thought Chagatai too strict and narrow-minded for a ruler and was troubled by his hatred of Jochi, and excluded him from the succession. After Genghis died in 1227, Chagatai held to his father's will, prevented any usurpation before the accession of Ögedei in 1229, and presided over the coronation with Tolui and their uncle Temüge. In Central Asia his capital and summer pastures were at Almaliq. He disputed jurisdiction with the imperial official Mahmud Yalavach, and when Bukhara revolted against tax demands in 1238 he left its suppression to Ögedei's armies.

After Ögedei died in December 1241, Chagatai's support made Töregene regent. He died in 1242; his wife Yesülün accused a steward named Vajir of poisoning him and had him executed. His grandson Qara Hülegü succeeded him but was displaced by Chagatai's son Yesü-Möngke between 1246 and 1250.

Chagatai upheld traditional Mongol law, which forbade elements of Islamic practice, and gained a reputation for being anti-Muslim; one contemporary Muslim writer claimed that he urged Ögedei to kill every Muslim in the empire. The historians Michael Hope and Peter Jackson think this far from the truth, pointing to the powerful Muslim officials at his court. His descendants were nonetheless far slower to convert to Islam than the rulers of the Golden Horde and the Ilkhanate.
chagatai-khanate: When Genghis Khan died in 1227, his son Chagatai Khan inherited lands that roughly matched the defunct Qara Khitai empire: the Issyk-Kul, Ili, Chu and Talas regions, Transoxania and the Tarim Basin. Chagatai was not fully independent and still received orders from Karakorum. After his death in 1242 the throne passed between young khans, regents and appointees of rival Great Khans. With the division of the Mongol Empire after 1259 the khanate became functionally separate, and at its height in the late 13th century it stretched from the Amu Darya to the Altai Mountains. It was also called the Dumdadu Mongγol Ulus, the Middle Mongolian Empire.

Under Kaidu, who dominated the khanate from 1266 to 1301, it fought both the Yuan dynasty and the Ilkhanate. After Kaidu's death Duwa recognised Yuan authority in 1303. Chagatai armies raided the Delhi Sultanate several times, with little lasting result. Tarmashirin, khan from 1326 to 1334, converted to Islam and reached Delhi, but an anti-Muslim rising of the eastern tribes brought him down.

In the 1340s the khanate split in two. In Transoxania the khans became puppets of local emirs and later of Timur, who ruled from 1369. In the east, the Dughlats enthroned Tughlugh Timur as khan of Moghulistan in 1347, and he converted to Islam in 1350. Moghulistan lasted until the late 15th century, when it divided into the Yarkent and Turpan Khanates. The last Chagatai domains lost their independence to the Dzungar Khanate in 1680.

The Chagatai Mongols remained mostly nomadic in their mode of government and did not settle in towns until the late 15th century. They treated the townspeople of Transoxiana and the Tarim Basin as dependants. The Mongol ruling groups underwent a gradual and uneven Turkification and Islamization, though Mongolian political and administrative traditions stayed important, and Mongolian was still used for official documents into the 14th century. The Kumul Khanate, governed by descendants of Chagatai Khan, was abolished in 1930, which ended the dynasty.
chagatai-language: Chagatai, also called Turki, Eastern Turkic or Chagatai Turkic, belongs to the Karluk branch of the Turkic languages and descends from Middle Turkic, which served as a lingua franca in Central Asia, with a strong infusion of Arabic and Persian words and turns of phrase. Its name relates to the Chagatai Khanate, a descendant empire of the Mongol Empire left to Genghis Khan's second son, Chagatai Khan, and many of the Turkic peoples who spoke the language claimed political descent from it.

Mehmet Fuat Köprülü divides its history into early Chagatai in the 13th and 14th centuries, a pre-classical period in the first half of the 15th, a classical one in the second half of the 15th, its continuation in the 16th and a decline from the 17th to the 19th.

Chagatai was widely spoken across Central Asia and remained the shared literary language of the region until the early 20th century, when it died out. It was used in western or Russian Turkestan, Eastern Turkestan, Crimea and the Volga–Ural region. It is written in a variant of the Perso-Arabic alphabet known as Kona Yëziq, the old script. Its basic word order is subject–object–verb, it has vowel harmony and six cases, and it has complex syntax copied from Persian. Central Asian Turkic authors regarded Persian literature as superior and deliberately imitated it in creating Chagatai literature.

The second phase of Chagatai literature began with the publication of Ali-Shir Nava'i's first divan and was its highpoint. According to Geoffrey Lewis, his writings raised Chagatai to the status of literary language of Central Asia, and the language is sometimes called Nava'i's language. In his Muhakamat al-Lughatayn he compared Chagatai with New Persian and argued for its superiority for literary purposes. The biography of Timur and the Baburnama of Babur, the Timurid founder of the Mughal Empire, are in Chagatai, as is the prose work of Muhammad Shaybani of 1507.

The 17th and 18th centuries are often seen as a period of decay, when it lost ground to Persian; Abu al-Ghazi Bahadur wrote his genealogies in it, and Magtymguly Pyragy introduced it into Turkmen literature in the second half of the 18th century.

Chagatai is the direct ancestor of Uzbek and Uyghur, and Kazakh and Turkmen were heavily influenced by it for centuries. In 1921 it was first intended as the national language of the Uzbek SSR, but it proved too archaic and a new literary language based on Uzbek dialects replaced it. In preparing the Soviet republic of Uzbekistan in 1924 it was renamed Old Uzbek, a step Edward A. Allworth argued distorted the literary history of the region.
chaghaniyan: Known in Middle Persian as Chagīnīgān and in Arabic sources as al-Saghaniyan, the region lay on the right bank of the Oxus, south of Samarkand, between Denov and Termez. After the Sasanian Empire and the First Turkic Khaganate defeated the Hephthalites in 563-567, it became a Hephthalite buffer principality and refuge under their new king Faghanish. Its coins imitated those of the Sasanian king Khusrau I. In 648-651 its chancellor Pukarzate, sent by Turantash, lord of Chaganian, visited King Varkhuman of Samarkand and appears in the Afrasiyab murals.

The Chaghan Khudah aided the Sasanians against the Rashidun Arabs, and in 652 joined other local rulers in supporting the Yabghus of Tokharistan against them. Under Ziyad ibn Abihi, al-Hakam ibn Amr al-Ghifari raided Chaghaniyan in 667. In 705 the Chaghan Khudah Tish acknowledged Umayyad authority to Qutayba ibn Muslim, chiefly to win help against the rulers of Akharun and Shuman. In 718 Tish joined Gurak of Samarkand and others in asking the Tang dynasty for aid against the Arabs, yet Chaghaniyan fought on the Arab side at the Battle of the Baggage, where its ruler was killed.

By the late 8th century the region was under direct Abbasid rule. In the 10th century the Muhtajids, perhaps descended from the Chaghan Khudahs, gained it. Their founder Abu Bakr Muhammad governed Khorasan for the Samanid Nasr II, and his son Abu 'Ali Chaghani, dismissed by Nuh I in 945, rebelled and briefly installed Nuh's uncle Ibrahim ibn Ahmad at Bukhara in 947. Nuh had Chaghaniyan ravaged and its capital sacked, but in the end let Abu 'Ali keep it in return for a son as hostage. Abu 'Ali died of plague in 955.

By the end of the 10th century the Muhtajids were vassals of the Ghaznavids, and an unnamed ruler of Chaghaniyan accompanied Mahmud of Ghazna across the Oxus in 1025. After a Karakhanid invasion no more rulers are recorded. The Seljuks soon took the region, and Alp Arslan made his brother Ilyas ibn Chaghri Beg its governor. By the 12th century the name itself had fallen out of use.
chaghri-beg: Chaghri and his brother Tughril were the sons of Mikail and the grandsons of Seljuk, the Turkic clan leader after whom the Great Seljuk Empire was named. Early in the 11th century the family left its former home and settled near the city of Jend, on the Syr Darya, where it accepted the suzerainty of the Karakhanids of Transoxania. After the Karakhanids were defeated by the Ghaznavids, the Seljuks were able to gain independence. When Seljuk Beg died in 1009, Tughril and Chaghri took over the administration of Jand, but frequent clashes with the ruler of Yengikent led them to abandon it in about 1016.
Very little is known of the brothers' lives until 1025. Both were raised by their grandfather until they were fifteen, and they fought with the Karakhanid noble Ali Tigin against Mahmud of Ghazni.

In 1025 Mahmud lured and captured Arslan Isra'il, the eldest son of Seljuk Beg, and scattered the Seljuk camps across Transoxiana. Mahmud then allowed about four thousand Seljuk families to settle near Sarakhs, Farawa and Abiward as frontier guards, but they harassed the local people, and he defeated them at the battle of Ribat-i-Farawa in 1028. Tughril and Chaghri refused to recognise the authority of Ali Tegin and began to claim power over the Seljuk tribes.

From 1035 to 1037 the brothers fought Mas'ud I of Ghazni, and Chaghri captured Merv. Between 1038 and 1040 he fought the Ghaznavids, usually by hit and run, until the major clash at Dandanaqan. Tughril was hesitant and preferred to continue the raids, but Chaghri commanded the army and favoured a direct fight, and the Seljuks defeated a numerically superior Ghaznavid force. A kurultai held after the battle divided the empire. Tughril ruled the west, and Chaghri ruled eastern Iran, Turkmenistan and Afghanistan, collectively called Greater Khorasan. He later took Balkh, conquered Kerman in 1048 and Sistan in 1056, and in 1056 married his daughter Khadija Arslan Khatun to the Abbasid caliph Al-Qa'im.

Chaghri died in Sarakhs, in north-eastern Iran. Earlier Turkic tradition let brothers share in government, and Tughril, Chaghri and other family members all took part in founding the empire. Tughril took the title sultan, but it was Chaghri's sons who continued it. He had six sons and four daughters. Alp Arslan became sultan in 1064, and all the later members of the Great Seljuk line descended from Chaghri. Kavurt became governor of Kerman, which later became fully independent, and Yaquti governor of Azerbaijan. Chaghri's daughters made marriages into the Buyid, Kakuyid and Uqaylid houses as well as the caliph's.
chagos-archipelago: The Chagos Archipelago is a group of coral atolls, reefs and submerged banks in the central Indian Ocean, at the southern end of the Chagos–Laccadive Ridge. It lies about 2,200 km north-east of Mauritius and 500 km south of the Maldives. Five atolls carry islands: Diego Garcia, Peros Banhos, the Salomon Islands, the Egmont Islands and the Great Chagos Bank, described as the world's largest atoll by area. The 55 to 59 islands are small and low, with a total land area of about 53 km2, more than half of it on Diego Garcia. The reefs are largely free of local pollution, so they serve as a scientific reference site.

Portuguese navigators probably sighted and named the islands early in the 16th century, and they appear on Portuguese charts from 1538. From the 1740s ships from Île de France, as Mauritius was then called, explored the islands, and concessions for coconut plantations followed, leading to permanent settlement. Accounts of the date differ: one dates it to a concession of February 1783, the territory's British administration dates the first French copra plantations to 1793. The plantations were worked by enslaved people brought mainly from Madagascar and Mozambique.

The United Kingdom administered the archipelago as a dependency of Mauritius until 1965, when it detached the islands to form the British Indian Ocean Territory. Between 1967 and 1973 the whole population, the Chagossians, was either prevented from returning or removed, most of them to Mauritius, and construction of a joint British–American military base on Diego Garcia began in March 1971. Mauritius says that the detachment was unlawful. In May 2025 the two governments signed a treaty on the transfer of sovereignty.

The archipelago has no permanent inhabitants. About 2,000 people, mostly military personnel and contractors, are ordinarily present on Diego Garcia. The Chagossians, also called Ilois, descend mainly from the enslaved Africans and Malagasy brought to the plantations and from labourers recruited later in Mauritius and Seychelles. By the end of the 19th century they had formed a distinct island society, mostly Roman Catholic. Their music and dance, Sega tambour Chagos, was inscribed by UNESCO in 2019 as intangible cultural heritage in need of urgent safeguarding. Their language, Chagos Kreol, is a French-lexified creole related to those of Mauritius and Seychelles.
chahar-mongols: The Chahars began as one of the estates of Kublai Khan, centred on Jingzhao, the present-day Xi'an. In the 15th century they moved from Shaanxi into the south-eastern lands of the Northern Yuan on the Mongolian Plateau. Under Dayan Khan they became one of the six tumens, and as his successors led them, they formed the personal appanage of the Northern Yuan rulers. Pressed by Altan Khan, they moved east to the Liao River under Daraisung Guden Khan in the middle of the 16th century.

Ligdan Khan died in Gansu on his way to Tibet, and his son Ejei, after submitting to the Later Jin, was made a prince; the Inner Mongolian nobility became closely tied to the Qing imperial house and married into it widely. Ejei died in 1641 and was followed by his brother Abunai. Relations stayed good until 1663, when Makata gege, a daughter of Hong Taiji married to the Chahar prince, died. Abunai showed his discontent with Qing rule and was placed under house arrest in Shenyang in 1669, and the Kangxi Emperor gave his title to his son Borni.

In 1675, during the Revolt of the Three Feudatories, Abunai and his brother Lubuzung rose against the Qing with 3,000 Chahar followers. The revolt was put down within two months, and in a battle on 20 April 1675 Abunai and his followers were killed. The title was abolished, every male of the Chahar royal house was executed, even those born to Qing princesses, and the royal women other than the princesses were sold into slavery.

After the revolt the Chahars were reorganised as the Eight Banners of Chahar, moved to the area around Zhangjiakou and placed under the emperor's direct control rather than in a league. After the fall of the Dzungar Khanate around 1758, some were resettled on the Ili River, where they mixed with the Dzungar people and the Torghut. In 1911 a hundred households under the former vice-governor Sumya fled from Xinjiang to Mongolia, and their descendants are the Tsahar of Selenge. Today the Chahars speak Chakhar Mongolian and live mainly in south-eastern Inner Mongolia.
chahar-province: The Great Wall divided Chahar from north to south. North Chahar was the larger part by area, and most of its land belonged to the north-eastern extension of the Gobi Desert. South Chahar, which held the capital, Zhangjiakou, had by far the larger population. The province bordered Xing'an to the north, Mongolia to the north and west, Suiyuan to the west and south, Shanxi and Hebei to the south, and Rehe and Liaobei to the east.

The area takes its name from the Chahar, a tribal group of the Mongols who live there. It was ruled in part or in full by the Han, Tang, Liao and Jin dynasties, and after Genghis Khan united the Mongol tribes it came under the Yuan. After the Yuan dynasty fell in 1368 it was fought over by the Ming dynasty and the Northern Yuan, and from the reign of Batumongke Dayan Khan (r. 1479-1517) the Chahar were the personal appanage of the Northern Yuan monarchs.

In the late Qing dynasty Chahar was the Zhangyuan Special Region, and Yao Xiguang proposed as early as 1908 that it become a province. In 1913 the Republic of China created the Chahar Special Administrative Region as a subdivision of Zhili Province, with six banners and eleven counties. When it became a province in 1928, five of those counties went to Suiyuan Province, and ten counties were added from Xuanhua Prefecture and the Koubei Circuit of Hebei. Its banners belonged to the Shilingol League.

On 26 May 1933 Feng Yuxiang and Ji Hongchang founded the Chahar People's Anti-Japanese Army Alliance in Kalgan. From 1937 to 1945 Japan occupied the province and made it part of Mengjiang, a Japanese-controlled region led by the Mongol prince Demchugdongrub of Shilingol. The communist government abolished the province in 1952 and divided its territory among neighbouring units.
chai-rong: Chai Rong was born in Xingzhou, the present-day Xingtai in Hebei, on 27 October 921. As a child he went to live with his aunt, a younger sister of his father Chai Shouli, and her husband Guo Wei, an officer of the Later Tang army; the couple had no sons and adopted him, and he took the name Guo Rong. He grew up skilled at mounted archery and read the classics, history and Huang-Lao philosophy, and as an adult he managed the household's affairs and travelled on business between Central China and Jiangnan.

Under the Later Han, Guo Wei rose to Commissioner of Military Affairs in 948, and in 950 Guo Rong followed him to the frontier garrison at Weizhou. That year the emperor Liu Chengyou had Guo Wei's family in the capital killed, and Guo Rong's wife, Lady Liu, and their three young sons died with them. Guo Wei rebelled, and within months the Later Han had fallen and he had founded the Later Zhou. As military governor at Chanzhou, Guo Rong suppressed armed outlaws, appointed literati to enforce the law and rebuilt public offices and housing.

The chancellor Wang Jun kept him from the capital and in 952 blocked his request to lead troops against a rebellion. Only after Wang's banishment in early 953 did he return, and in April 953 he was made Prince of Jin. By then he had married Lady Fu, a widowed daughter of the general Fu Yanqing.

A month after he took the throne, Liu Chong of the Northern Han attacked with Liao support. Against the advice of the minister Feng Dao, Chai Rong led the army himself, and at Gao Ping, after his generals Fan Aineng and He Hui fled with their troops, he broke through and routed Liu's forces, which secured his hold on power. He centralised military power and won victories over the Later Shu and the Southern Tang. He died of illness on campaign on 27 July 959, aged 38, leaving a six-year-old heir, and his generals Zhao Kuangyin and Zhao Guangyi went on to found the Northern Song. In some folk traditions he is venerated as the Wealth God of the Southern Road.
chain-mail: The earliest surviving examples of mail were found in the Carpathian Basin, in a burial at Horný Jatov in Slovakia dated to the 3rd century BCE and in a chieftain's burial at Ciumești in Romania. Its invention is commonly credited to the Celts, although Etruscan mail survives from at least the 4th century BCE, and it may have been inspired by the much earlier scale armour. The Roman Republic is believed to have first met mail in fighting the Gauls in Cisalpine Gaul, and the Roman army adopted it as the lorica hamata, a primary form of armour through the Imperial period.

Mail is made of small metal rings linked in a mesh, most often in the 4-to-1 pattern, in which each ring passes through four others. In Europe the rings were riveted closed to reduce the chance of their splitting under a thrust or an arrow. Until the 14th century European mail was made of alternating rows of round riveted rings and solid rings punched from sheet. The wire was usually wrought iron, and guild marks were often stamped on the rings. A hauberk reached the knee, a coif covered the head and chausses the legs.

Mail spread to North Africa, West Africa, the Middle East, Central Asia, India, Tibet, Southeast Asia and Japan. The Sassanid Persians adopted it from the 3rd century CE, and it passed through the Abbasid Caliphate to Central Asia and to the Delhi Sultanate. Turkish armies brought it to India in the late 12th century, and it became the armour of choice there. In China it was an imported rarity worn by high-ranking guards. In Japan mail, called kusari, was used in samurai armour at least from the Mongol invasions of the 1270s.

In Europe mail was costly to make and was often looted from the dead. By the 14th century articulated plate was commonly added to it, since plate gave better protection against windlass crossbows, bludgeoning weapons and lance charges. Mail was in use throughout Europe into the 16th century, and in Asia, Africa and the Middle East it remained in military use until the 18th century. Riveted mail resisted most cuts and thrusts, but a blow could still bruise or break bones beneath it, so a padded gambeson was worn under the hauberk.
chait-singh: Chait Singh belonged to the Narayan dynasty, a Bhumihar Brahmin family of the Gautam gotra, and was the third ruler of Benares. He succeeded his father, Maharaja Balwant Singh, in 1770. The Nawab of Awadh still wished to hold full suzerainty over Benares, but the British persuaded him to recognise Chait Singh as its ruler in 1773. Two years later the Nawab, weary of British interference, transferred the domain to the East India Company under Warren Hastings, Governor-General of Bengal.

Under the new terms Chait Singh was required to supply cavalry and to pay towards the upkeep of the Company's sepoy battalions. He refused and began a secret correspondence with the Company's enemies. The Company learned of it and in August 1781 tried to place him under house arrest pending a meeting with Hastings. His men attacked and defeated the Company's troops and killed British officers, and Hastings left Benares, an escape mocked in a popular rhyme.

Chait Singh appealed to neighbouring rulers for help, but only Raja Fateh Bahadur Shahi came to his aid, and the Raja of Gwalior, with whom he had a treaty, sent none. His troops were defeated in several battles with the Company's forces, and after the fighting he went to Gwalior with his younger brother Kunwar Sujan Singh and his family. On 14 September 1781 the Company installed his nephew Mahip Narayan Singh, son of his sister Padma Kuwar, on condition that he dispense justice and pay an annual contribution of 40 lakhs.

Chait Singh was granted a jagir of 150 villages, which was later confiscated. He died at Gwalior on 29 March 1810, leaving three sons, and his chhatri stands there; his descendants have lived in Gwalior since. Carved stone from his palace was later built into the palace of the Maharajas of Cossimbazar. The affair damaged Hastings's reputation and fed the attempt in the British Parliament to impeach him.
chaitanya-mahaprabhu: Chaitanya was born Vishvambhara Mishra at Nabadwip, in present-day West Bengal, on the evening of 18 February 1486, although some accounts give 27 February. His father, Jagannatha Mishra, was a Brahmin from Sylhet. The only sources for his life are the hagiographies of the Gaudiya tradition, which regard him as an avatar of Krishna, and the canonical account was established in the early 1600s by the Chaitanya Charitamrita of Krishnadasa Kaviraja. He began his schooling at five and mastered Sanskrit grammar and logic with great speed. At sixteen he opened a school of his own and became known as Nimai Pandit.

Around 1508 or 1509 he went to Gaya to perform funeral rites for his father and there met the ascetic Īśvara Purī, who initiated him. On returning to Nabadwip he closed his school and devoted himself to sankirtan, congregational chanting, with his associates Nityananda and Advaita Ācārya. The local Muslim ruler, the Chand Kazi, banned the chanting, and Chaitanya led thousands in a peaceful protest to his house, after which, according to the account, the ruler was won over.

In 1510, aged twenty-four, he took the vows of renunciation at Katwa and was given the name Sri Krishna Chaitanya. He made Jagannatha Puri in Odisha his headquarters, spent about two years travelling in southern India and returned in 1512. King Prataparudra arranged for him to live in a secluded room, the Gambhira, in Puri, where he spent most of his remaining years. In 1514 he set out for Vrindavan, and on the way accepted two ministers of Sultan Husain Shah as disciples, renaming them Rupa and Sanatana.

The Shikshashtaka, eight devotional verses, is the only work accepted as composed by Chaitanya. According to his associate Murari Gupta, he taught that kirtan, the chanting of God's name, is the most effective practice in the Kali Age, and he presented bhakti as the primary means of approaching Krishna. Dinesh Chandra Sen reads his teaching as centred on divine love and placing devotion above social distinction. He appointed the Goswamis to compose texts explaining this devotion, and the movement produced a large body of philosophical and literary work.
chaiya: Chaiya district lies on the Gulf of Thailand, with Cape Sui marking the northern end of the Bandon Bay, and borders districts of Surat Thani, Ranong and Chumphon provinces. The east of the district is mostly flat, low coastal land, while to the west rise the mountains of the Phuket range, including Kaeng Krung National Park. The name may come from the Malay cahaya, meaning light or gleam, and some scholars derive it from Srivijaya itself.

Laem Pho Beach in the district is thought to have been a seaport of the Srivijaya kingdom from the 7th to the 13th centuries. Tang dynasty ceramics, pottery from India and glassware from Persia have been found there. Similar finds at Ban Thung Tuek in Takua Pa district, 200 km away on the other side of the isthmus, suggest an overland route between the Gulf of Thailand and the Andaman coast that let traders avoid piracy in the narrow Strait of Malacca.

Wat Phra Borommathat is centred on a reconstructed stupa in Srivijaya style, and two more former stupas nearby are now brick mounds. Inscription 23 of Prince Damrong's Collected Inscriptions of Siam, now attributed to Wat Hua Wiang in Chaiya, is dated 697 of the Mahasakkarat era, that is 775 CE; on a stone shaped like a bai sema, it tells of the king of Srivijaya erecting three stupas there, and possibly the one at Wat Phra Borom That.

Another important temple near Chaiya is the forest temple Wat Suan Mohkha Phalaram, known by the short name Suan Mok or as Wat Than Nam Lai, the Monastery of Flowing Water. It was founded in 1932 by Phra Buddhadasa (1906–1993), a revered Buddhist teacher, and in 1959 it was relocated to its present site of 380 rai (150 acres).

Chaiya is a former capital district (amphoe mueang) of Surat Thani province, and its main town is Talat Chaiya. A branch of the National Museum near Wat Phra Borommathat displays relics of the Srivijaya period. The district lies on the southern railway line and on Asian highway AH2, and is divided into nine sub-districts and 54 villages.
chak-tok-ichaak-i: Chak Tok Ichʼaak I, also known as Great Paw and Toh Chak Ichʼak, was the son of Kʼinich Muwaan Jol and Lady Bahlam Way. He took the throne of Tikal on 7 August 360 and is one of the city's best-known kings, his name appearing on a number of ceramic pieces and stelae. Stela 39, found by archaeologists in the Mundo Perdido complex, marks the Kʼatun ending of 376 and shows him standing upon a bound captive while holding an axe decorated with jaguar markings, probably either a weapon or an instrument of sacrifice.

His name also appears on the fragmentary Stela 26 from Tikal's North Acropolis, a monument he may have dedicated himself. Both stelae were deliberately smashed soon after they were set up. A stela at the distant site of El Temblor may have been made to mark his accession, though it may instead belong to a namesake.

Stela 31 records that he died on 14 January 378, the day Siyaj Kʼakʼ, probably a war leader from Teotihuacan, entered Tikal. His death probably came at the hands of the invaders from central Mexico, in what was most likely a forcible takeover, perhaps a conquest, and his entire lineage was overthrown in favour of a new line of rulers, who took power in its place.

His palace stood in the Central Acropolis and was identified from a carved clay vessel buried under its western staircase as part of a dedication ritual. Unusually, later rulers never built over it, and it was kept in repair for centuries as what appears to have been a revered monument.
chakradhar-singh: Chakradhar Singh was born on 19 August 1905, a son of Raja Bhup Deo Singh, who died in 1917, and belonged to the Raj Gond dynasty that ruled Raigarh and held the chiefship of Bargarh. He was educated at Rajkumar College, Raipur. He succeeded his elder brother, Raja Natwar Singh, on his death in 1924, but government management of the state continued until 1927, when the raja was invested with ruling powers.

Experts of the Jaipur and Lucknow gharanas, and some of the Benares gharana, held prominent places at his court; among the Kathak masters who served there were Pandit Jaggannath Prasad of the Jaipur gharana and Guru Kalaka Prasad and his sons of the Lucknow gharana. By mixing different forms he shaped a new style, the Raigarh gharana, the youngest of the gharanas, with its own thumris, ghazals, todas and bols. He was himself a player of tabla and pakhawaj, and his name is often linked with Wajid Ali Shah of Awadh as a patron of Kathak and Hindustani classical music.

He knew Hindi, Sanskrit, Urdu and Oriya and wrote several books on music, among them Nartan Sarwasya, Raag Ratna Manjusha and Taal Toynidhi; Sanskrit scholars at his court, including Pandit Sadashiv Das and Pandit Kashi Dutt Jha, helped him translate music and dance literature in Sanskrit. In 1938 he headed the All India Music Conference at Allahabad, attending with a team of 60 artists, and at later gatherings he played tabla for Kathak performances. The Viceroy, Lord Linlithgow, gave him the title Sangit Samrat, King of Music.

He died on 7 October 1947, just after Indian independence. His son Lalit Kumar Singh succeeded him and ruled briefly before Raigarh State was merged into the Union of India on 14 December 1947; Raigarh, Jashpur, Sakti, Sarangarh and Udaipur were later united to form Raigarh district. His second son, Surendra Kumar Singh, became a politician of the Indian National Congress, and a music academy at Raigarh was established as his memorial.
chalcidice: Chalcidice, in Greek Chalkidiki, is a peninsula in the north-western Aegean Sea in coastal Macedonia, shaped like a hand with three fingers, which in Greek are often called legs. From west to east they are Kassandra, whose highest peak is 350 metres, Sithonia, whose highest peak, Mount Itamos, is 817 metres, and Athos, whose peak reaches 2,033 metres. The Toronean Gulf and the Singitic Gulf separate them. The Cholomontas mountains lie in the north-centre, and the climate is mainly Mediterranean, with cool, wet winters and hot, relatively dry summers. The peninsula is named after the Greek city of Chalcis in Euboea, which colonised it in the 8th century BCE.

The first Greek settlers came from Chalcis and Eretria, cities of Euboea, around the 8th century BCE and founded cities such as Mende, Toroni and Scione. A second wave from Andros in the 6th century BCE founded cities including Akanthos. The peninsula became an important theatre of the Peloponnesian War between Athens and Sparta. Aristotle was born at Stageira. Philip II annexed the whole peninsula to Macedon, and after the Roman conquest of Macedon a Roman colony was settled at Cassandreia in 43 BCE and resettled by Augustus in 30 BCE.

In the Byzantine period Chalkidiki belonged to the theme of Thessalonica. A chrysobull of Emperor Basil I, dated 885, proclaimed Mount Athos a place of monks, with no laymen, farmers or cattle-breeders allowed to settle there. The Great Lavra monastery was founded soon afterwards with the support of Nikephoros II Phokas, and Athos has been self-governing ever since. After a short rule by the Latin Kingdom of Thessalonica the area became Byzantine again until the Ottomans conquered it in 1430, and under them it was important for gold mining.

In 1821 the Greeks of Chalkidiki rose in the Greek War of Independence under Emmanouel Pappas, a member of the Filiki Eteria. The revolt, confined to Athos and Kassandra, ended in a decisive Ottoman victory at Kassandra, after which many villages were burnt. The peninsula joined the Greek Kingdom in 1912 to 1913, and after the exchange of populations between Greece and Turkey of 1923 refugees from East Thrace and Anatolia settled in parts of it.

The capital is Polygyros, in the centre of the peninsula, and the largest town is Nea Moudania. Athos forms an autonomous monastic region in the east, home to Orthodox monks from Greece and many other countries. The peninsula produces olive oil, honey and wine, and its beaches have made tourism the main industry.
chalcis: Chalcis, also called Chalkida, is the chief city of the island of Euboea in Greece, on the Euripus Strait at its narrowest point. The name derives from the Greek word for copper or bronze, although there is no trace of any mines in the area. In the Late Middle Ages it was known as Negroponte, an Italian name that came from the Greek phrase meaning to the Euripos, altered by folk etymology so that ponte, bridge, was read as the bridge of Chalcis to Boeotia.

Chalcis is first mentioned in the Iliad, in the same line as its rival Eretria. In the 8th and 7th centuries BCE its colonists founded thirty townships on the peninsula of Chalcidice and important cities in Magna Graecia and Sicily, among them Naxos, Rhegion, Zankle and Cumae. Pithecusae on the island of Ischia, founded around 770 BCE by Chalcidians and Eretrians, is the first recorded settlement in the West. Chalcidian trade carried its alphabet to Italy, where the Etruscans took it up.

In the late 8th century BCE Chalcis and Eretria fought the Lelantine War, one of the first major wars between Greek cities. Late in the 6th century BCE a war with Athens broke its prosperity, and the Athenians settled a cleruchy there. Aristotle came to Chalcis in 323 BCE and died there the next year.

Venice had a trading station in the 12th century and seized the town in 1209, after the Fourth Crusade. Negroponte was shared between Venice and the Veronese barons of the rest of Euboea, known as the triarchs, and became a Latin Church diocese. It was attacked by the Principality of Achaea in 1257–58, by the Catalan Company in 1317 and by the Turks in 1350–51, until the Ottoman Empire captured it in 1470 after a long siege. The Ottomans held it against a Venetian attack in 1688.

Chalkida became part of the Greek state after the Greek War of Independence, and a railway link to Athens opened in 1904. Surviving sights include the Church of Saint Paraskevi, begun about 1250 as a Dominican priory church, the Roman aqueduct, the Ottoman Karababa Fortress of 1684, and a modern cable-stayed bridge over the strait, opened in 1993.
chalcolithic: The names result from several definitions of the period. Originally the term Bronze Age meant that either copper or bronze was the chief hard substance for tools and weapons. The Hungarian scientist Ferenc Pulszky proposed a Copper Age in the 1870s, on the basis of the many large copper objects found in the Carpathian Basin, suggesting that the threefold division into Stone, Bronze and Iron Ages be divided further.

In 1881 John Evans recognised that the use of copper often preceded bronze and described a transitional Copper Age. In 1884 Gaetano Chierici named it eneo-litica in Italian, and British scholars used the translation Eneolithic. Because that word looked to untrained eyes like e-neolithic, outside the Neolithic, many writers around 1900 substituted Chalcolithic, from the Greek khalkos, copper, and líthos, stone.

The period covers early cold working of near-pure copper, as in the Old Copper complex of the North American Great Lakes, and later smelting cultures. Stone tools were still predominantly used. In Europe the transition to the Bronze Age occurred between the late 5th and the late 3rd millennium BCE.

Some regions had no well-defined Copper Age, Russia among them, and a Chalcolithic has never been defined in central and northern Europe, although copper artefacts dating from 4000 to 3300 BCE have been found in northern Germany and Denmark, from Serbian mines. Los Millares and Vila Nova de São Pedro in Iberia are examples of European Chalcolithic cultures.

In the Ancient Near East the period began in the late 5th millennium BCE and lasted about a millennium. Arsenical copper or bronze was produced around 4200 BCE at Norşuntepe and Değirmentepe in eastern Turkey. In India Chalcolithic farming communities include the Ahar or Banas, Kayatha, Malwa and Jorwe cultures, each with its own painted pottery. Independent copper smelting developed in the Aïr Mountains of Niger between 3000 and 2500 BCE, and Andean civilisations appear to have invented smelting independently.

Archaeologists study the period through mines, slag, furnaces and finished metal. A study published in 2013 reported a tin bronze foil from Pločnik dated to about 4,650 BCE and fourteen other artefacts from Bulgaria and Serbia dated before 4000 BCE, showing that early tin bronze was more common than thought and developed in Europe independently of the Near East. In Britain the period was short, between about 2,500 and 2,200 BCE, marked by the first copper and gold objects and the arrival of the Bell Beaker people, but some archaeologists do not recognise a British Chalcolithic because production was small in scale.
chalcuchimac: Chalcuchímac, originally written Challcochima or Challcuchima, was born in Quito, at the northern end of the empire, in the latter part of the 15th century. With Quizquiz and Rumiñawi he was one of the leading Inca generals of the north. When Huayna Capac died in 1527 and his intended heir Ninan Cuyochi died of smallpox, the empire divided, and as a man of the north Chalcuchímac swore allegiance to Atahualpa.

In the civil war that followed from 1529, he fought alongside Atahualpa against his half-brother Huáscar, sharing in the victory at the battle of Chimborazo, after which Huáscar's general and brother Atoc was captured, mutilated and killed. In April 1532 he and his companion defeated and captured Huáscar at the battle of Quipaipan.

After the Spaniards seized Atahualpa at the Battle of Cajamarca, Chalcuchímac was camped with an army of 35,000 in the Jauja Valley. Hernando Pizarro persuaded him that Atahualpa had summoned him to Cajamarca, and there the Spaniards arrested him, fearing that he might renew hostilities.

Once Atahualpa had been executed on 29 July 1533, Pizarro marched on Cuzco with five hundred Spaniards, taking Chalcuchímac with him. The native forces attacked the column several times with such spirit and discipline that the Spaniards suspected him of directing them in secret, and a rumour spread that he had told Quizquiz the Spanish force was divided. The suspicions were never proved, but they decided his fate: Pizarro sentenced him to be burned alive. Offered a less painful death if he became a Christian, he refused baptism and died as sentenced, protesting to the last against the injustice of his condemnation. The Spaniards later routed Quizquiz's forces and took Cuzco late in 1533.
chaldean-empire: Babylonia had been an independent state since about 1894 BCE, and under Hammurabi it briefly became a major power. It later fell to the Hittite king Mursili I, was ruled by the Kassites for almost five centuries and then by native rulers of a small rump state, before coming under Assyrian rule. Early in the reign of the Assyrian king Sinsharishkun, Nabopolassar, a southern official or general, revolted amid political instability in Assyria. In 626 BCE he seized Babylon and Nippur, and he withstood the Assyrian siege of Uruk. In November of that year he was crowned King of Babylon.

The fall of the Assyrian Empire in 612 to 609 BCE firmly established the new kingdom, the first time southern Mesopotamia had dominated the Near East since Hammurabi. Nebuchadnezzar II succeeded Nabopolassar in 605 BCE, and his reign of 43 years is described in Babylonian sources as a golden age. The biblical account tells of his campaign against the Kingdom of Judah and the siege of Jerusalem in 587 BCE, which destroyed Solomon's Temple. There is evidence that he destroyed Ashkelon in 604 BCE.

After Nebuchadnezzar the empire fell into turmoil. His son Amel-Marduk reigned two years before the courtier Neriglissar killed him in a coup. Neriglissar died in 556 BCE, and his underage son Labashi-Marduk was assassinated after nine months. The last king, Nabonidus, favoured the moon god Sîn over Babylon's patron Marduk, a policy that later served Cyrus the Great as a pretext. Cyrus defeated the Babylonian forces at the Battle of Opis, and on 12 October his soldiers entered Babylon without a battle after his engineers diverted the Euphrates. Nabonidus surrendered and was deported.

The king, called šar, took an oath of loyalty from his subjects and used the titles King of Babylon and King of Sumer and Akkad. He was the largest landowner, and other domains belonged to the royal family and high officials. Rulers followed a traditionalist policy: Akkadian remained the language of administration and culture even though Aramaic was the everyday tongue, and old artworks were preserved with near-religious care.

Local assemblies called puhru acted as courts, and slaves, mostly foreigners taken in war or trade, were costly property that owners often trained or rented out. Tribute flowed into Babylonia for the first time since the Assyrian conquest, and building projects, chiefly in Babylon, encouraged growth. Under Achaemenid rule Babylonia supplied as much as a third of the empire's tribute, and at least five rebels proclaimed themselves King of Babylon, but Babylon never regained its independence.
chaldia: The name at first meant the highlands around Gümüşhane, and in the middle Byzantine period it was extended to the coast around Trapezus. Forming the easternmost part of the Pontic Alps, Chaldia was bounded by the Black Sea to the north, Lazica to the east, Erzincan, Erzurum and Armenia Minor to the south, and western Pontus to the west. Its main cities, Kerasus and Trapezus, were old Greek colonies on the coast. The interior, Mesochaldia, was thinly settled and called inaccessible by the 6th-century historian Procopius, but rich in lead, silver and gold, which gave the town of Argyropolis its name.

Classical writers counted the Chalybes of the region among the first ironsmiths, and the Greek word for steel may derive from them; Anthony Bryer traced the name Chaldia to Ḫaldi, the Urartian sun god, a link other scholars reject. Trapezus was founded by traders from Miletus, by tradition in 756 BCE, but Greek and later Roman control stayed on the coast. Only under Emperor Justinian I were the Tzannoi of the interior subdued, Christianized and placed in the province of Armenia I Magna, with Trapezus as its capital.

In the later 7th century the region became a division of the Armeniac Theme and later a semi-distinct duchy, before becoming a theme in its own right. Arab geographers credit it with six fortified places and 4,000 troops, or, by an exaggerated count, 10,000. Its strategos drew twenty pounds of gold a year, half from the treasury and half from local taxes, among them duties on the eastern trade converging on Trapezus. Early in the 10th century its southern district, Keltzene, passed to the theme of Mesopotamia.

Under the doukes Theodore Gabras, from 1091/1095 to 1098, and Constantine Gabras, who rebelled against Emperor John II Komnenos, from 1126 to 1140, the theme was practically autonomous. Alexios Komnenos founded the Empire of Trebizond there in 1204, and by the 14th century that empire held little more than the old theme. It fell to the Ottomans in 1461, though the castle of Golacha, the last Christian stronghold in Asia Minor, held out until 1479. Many Pontic Greeks stayed until the population exchange of 1923.
chalon-sur-saone: Chalon-sur-Saône lies on the Saône in the south of the region of Bourgogne-Franche-Comté, about 55 kilometres north of Mâcon. It is the largest city of the Saône-et-Loire department, though the department's capital is the smaller Mâcon. It was once a busy port and distribution point for local wines, which were sent up and down the Saône and along the Canal du Centre, opened in 1792.

The site, ancient Cabillonum, was a capital of the Aedui, and objects of the La Tène culture have been recovered from the river bed there. Its first mention is in the Commentarii de Bello Gallico. The Roman city was already a river port and a hub of road communications, including the Via Agrippa.

In 354 CE the emperor Constantius II stationed the Roman 7th Army there for an invasion of the lands of the brother kings Gundomadus and Vadomarius, but the troops, not receiving supplies, revolted and were pacified with money by the grand chamberlain Eusebius. By Late Antiquity the city had shrunk so far that its wall enclosed fifteen hectares.

Saint Marcel is said to have been martyred there in 179. Chalon became one of the de facto capitals of the kingdom of Burgundy under Guntram, king from 561 to 592, who died there and promoted the cult of Marcel. The city was frequently attacked until the 10th century. A diocese, a suffragan of Lyon, was established in the 6th century, and a church council met there from 644 to 655. After the Concordat of 1801 the diocese was merged with that of Autun.

In the 19th century Nicéphore Niépce, born in the city in 1765, made the earliest surviving photograph; his 1807 Pyréolophore is probably the world's first internal combustion engine, and in 1818 he built a dandy horse, for which he coined the word vélocipède. Dominique Vivant Denon, who helped convert the royal palace into the Louvre museum, also lived there.

The Hôtel de Ville was completed in 1845, and in the late 19th century copper and iron works were the main industry, among them the Petit-Creusot engineering works. Saint Vincent's Cathedral dates mainly from the 12th to the 15th centuries, with elements from the eighth century and a neo-Gothic façade of the 19th. The city has a museum of photography on the Quai des Messageries, with more than two million photographs.
chalons-en-champagne: The city was a Gallic and later a Gallo-Roman settlement, named for the Catalauni, a Belgic tribe living in the region of modern Champagne. It is conjectured to have been the site of several battles, among them the Battle of Châlons in 274, fought between the Roman emperor Aurelian and Tetricus I of the Gallic Empire, and the Battle of the Catalaunian Plains in 451, which turned back Attila's westward advance.

Among its natives was Jean Talon, born in 1626, the first Intendant of New France. Nicolas Appert, born in 1749, was the inventor of appertisation, a method of preserving food. The town hall was completed in 1776, and the Porte Sainte-Croix, formerly the Porte Dauphine, was dedicated to Marie Antoinette when she passed through on her way to Paris to marry the future Louis XVI. In 1806 a national engineering school, now Arts et Métiers ParisTech, was established there.

Châlons lies in the Grand Est region and is the prefecture of the Marne department, although it has only about a quarter of the population of Reims. Formerly called Châlons-sur-Marne, it was officially renamed Châlons-en-Champagne in 1995, and should not be confused with the Burgundian city of Chalon-sur-Saône. About 22 kilometres to the north, near Mourmelon-le-Grand, lies the Camp de Mourmelon, formerly the Camp de Châlons. Napoleon III had it created, and it opened on 30 August 1857. It began as a ground for manoeuvres but quickly became a display of the Imperial Army, where citizens could watch parades.

The cathedral of Saint Étienne keeps parts of a first Romanesque cathedral of the 12th century but was mainly rebuilt in the Gothic style, with a Baroque west façade added in the 17th century. The collegiate church of Notre-Dame-en-Vaux, built between 1157 and 1217 and a place of pilgrimage in the 12th century, is part of a UNESCO World Heritage listing. Saint-Alpin, possibly the oldest church in the city, was rebuilt around 1170. The old circus of 1899 houses the Centre National des Arts du Cirque.
chalukya-dynasty: The Chalukyas ruled the Deccan for over 600 years as three related but separate dynasties: the Chalukyas of Badami, and the sibling lines of Kalyani (Western Chalukyas) and Vengi (Eastern Chalukyas). Most historians hold that the founders at Badami were natives of the modern Karnataka region. Their inscriptions call them Harithiputras of the Manavyasa gotra, the lineage of their early overlords, the Kadambas of Banavasi, whose territory they took over.

Later Chalukya court poets told that the founder sprang from the water of oblation in the palm of Brahma. An inscription of Vikramaditya VI says the family came from Ayodhya, a northern origin that Kamath and Moraes link to a common practice in the 11th century of tying southern royal lines to northern kingdoms. The Badami records themselves are silent about Ayodhya.

The dynasty was established by Pulakeshin I in 543, who took Vatapi (modern Badami) as capital. Pulakeshin II commanded the whole Deccan and halted the southward march of Harsha on the Narmada. According to the Aihole inscription of 634 he divided his empire into three Maharashtrakas of 99,000 villages each, and the Chinese traveller Xuanzang visited his court. In 642 the Pallava king Narasimhavarman attacked and temporarily occupied Badami, and Pulakeshin II is presumed to have died fighting.

Pulakeshin II had conquered the eastern Deccan in 616 and made his brother Kubja Vishnuvardhana viceroy there; after Pulakeshin's death the Vengi viceroyalty became an independent kingdom. The Rashtrakutas eclipsed the Badami line in the mid-8th century, and for two centuries the Eastern Chalukyas mostly accepted their dominance, gaining a measure of independence under Bhima I (c. 892-921). The Chalukyas revived in 973 as the Western Chalukyas, ruling from Kalyani until the end of the 12th century.

The Badami Chalukyas developed a style called Chalukyan or Karnata Dravida architecture. Nearly a hundred rock-cut and structural monuments survive in the Malaprabha basin, concentrated at Aihole, Badami, Pattadakal and Mahakuta and built of reddish-golden sandstone. Kannada took its place beside Sanskrit in inscriptions, and Ravikirti wrote the Aihole inscription as a classical poem.

Under the Western Chalukyas Vijnaneshwara wrote the Mitakshara, a work on Hindu law, and King Someshvara III compiled an encyclopaedia, the Manasollasa. The Chalukyas supported several faiths, and Jainism was prominent in the early period. The dynasty marked a golden age in the history of Karnataka and a shift from small kingdoms to large empires in South India.
chalus: Châlus is a commune in the Haute-Vienne department in the Nouvelle-Aquitaine region of western France. Its name in Occitan is Chasluç. In 1199 Richard I of England was besieging Châlus when Pierre Basile wounded him with a crossbow bolt, and Richard died of the wound.

Between 1275 and 1280 Géraud de Maumont built a second castle, Châlus Maulmont, in front of Châlus Chabrol. It was badly damaged during the French Revolution, dismantled in 1790 and then used as a prison. Its tower collapsed on 20 March 1994. In 1917 American troops were stationed at Châlus, and local tradition says that they dynamited the rock associated with Richard the Lionheart to take a piece back to the United States.

Châlus lies in the Périgord-Limousin Regional Nature Park, created in 1998. It has the Château de Châlus-Chabrol and the ruined Château de Châlus-Maulmont. Richard's entrails are still preserved in the chapel, and the town has a medieval garden and a museum dedicated to the chestnut. The inhabitants are known as Chalusiens.

T. E. Lawrence, later known as Lawrence of Arabia, marked his 20th birthday at the former Grand Hôtel du Midi on 16 August 1908, while tracing the route of Richard I on a cycling tour of France to prepare his thesis on the influence of the Crusades on European military architecture. The siege of Châlus appears in novels and in films, among them Robin and Marian of 1976, which opens on it.
chalybes: Classical authors name the Chalybes together with the Chaldoi and place both peoples in Pontus and Cappadocia in northern Anatolia. Their territory, known as Chaldia, stretched from the Halys River east to Pharnakeia and Trabzon and as far south as eastern Anatolia. The Chaldoi, Chalybes, Mossynoikoi and Tibareni were counted by classical writers among the first nations of ironsmiths. Sayce derived the Greek name from the Hittite Khaly-wa, land of the Halys River, and some scholars hold that Chalybes was less a single people than a generic Greek term for the iron-trading peoples of the Black Sea coast or for a group of specialised metalworkers.

Their identity is disputed. Apollonius of Rhodes called the Chalybes Scythians, while some modern historians argue that they were a Georgian tribe. The historian Kalistrat Salia held their Georgian origin to be beyond dispute and saw the Zans, a Kartvelian group of present-day Turkey, as their descendants.

Homer, Strabo and Xenophon are the main sources. Xenophon met them on the march of the Ten Thousand to the Black Sea and wrote in his Anabasis that they were "the most valiant of all the peoples" the Greeks passed through, ready to fight hand to hand, and that they lived in strongholds. In his Cyropaedia, Cyrus the Great helps the Armenians and the Chaldians settle a dispute over farmland.

In Roman times Plutarch mentions the Chaldaei, unrelated to the Semitic Chaldeans despite the name, and the Chalybes as settled in Pontus and Cappadocia, the part of the Roman province of Pontus known as Pontus Cappadocicus. Pliny the Elder records the Armenochalybes, a tribe living between Trebizond and Armenia. According to the 7th-century Geography of Armenia, the Chaldians called the Black Sea Kakamar, a name that may combine the Greek root kak-, ill, with an Indo-European root for sea.
chama-cha-mapinduzi: Chama Cha Mapinduzi, literally Party of the Revolution, was created on 5 February 1977 under the leadership of Julius Kambarage Nyerere, regarded as the Founding Father of Tanzania. It merged the Tanganyika African National Union, the ruling party in Tanganyika, with the Afro-Shirazi Party, the ruling party in Zanzibar. Tanganyika African National Union and its successor have dominated Tanzanian politics since the independence of Tanganyika in 1961. Through the merger the party also became the ruling party in Zanzibar, where its hold has been more contested since the mid-1990s by the Civic United Front and later the Alliance for Change and Transparency.

From 1977 until 1992 it was the only legally permitted party. Every five years its national chairman was automatically elected president, confirmed by referendum, while voters chose between two party candidates for each seat in the National Assembly. This changed on 1 July 1992, when amendments to the Constitution and laws allowing more than one party were enacted.

Originally a champion of African socialism and of the collectivised agriculture known as Ujamaa, firmly oriented to the left, the party later espoused a more mixed economic approach, with a focus on economic diplomacy abroad. Under John Magufuli, president from 2015 until his death in 2021, it moved in a left-conservative direction. It was admitted to the Socialist International as a full member in February 2013.

The party has won every presidential election under the multi-party system, in 1995, 2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, 2020 and 2025, and has kept a supermajority in the legislature. In 2005 Jakaya Kikwete won the presidency with 80.28 percent of the vote and the party took 206 of 232 directly elected seats.

In 2015 Magufuli won with 58 percent, the lowest share claimed by the party or its predecessors. In 2020 he won with over 84 percent, and the party took 256 of 264 constituencies. Critics have described Magufuli's presidency as marked by attacks on the opposition, civil society and the press. Research suggests that nostalgia for the party that brought independence and kept relative peace is a major source of its support, which is strong among subsistence farmers.
chamar: Between the 1830s and the 1950s the Chamars of the United Provinces, especially around Kanpur, prospered through the British leather trade. Around 1910 U. B. S. Raghuvanshi published the Shri Chanvar Purana in Kanpur, claiming that the Chamars had once been Kshatriya rulers whose king, Chamunda Rai, was cursed by Vishnu and promised a rise in the Kaliyuga after a new sage, whom Raghuvanshi identified as Ravidas. Another section claimed descent from Krishna as Jatavs; the Jatav Veer Mahasabha, founded in 1917, spread this claim and discriminated against lower-status Chamars such as the Guliyas.

The most influential Chamar leader of the early 20th century was Swami Achutanand, whose anti-Brahmanical Adi Hindu movement portrayed the lower castes as India's original inhabitants, enslaved by Aryan invaders. In the 1940s the Indian National Congress promoted the Chamar politician Jagjivan Ram to counter the influence of B. R. Ambedkar. The 1st Chamar Regiment, raised by the British on 1 March 1943, fought at the Battle of Kohima and was disbanded soon after the Second World War.

Chamars live mainly in northern India and also in Bangladesh, Pakistan and Nepal. The Jatavs, a sub-caste, made up 54% of the 22,496,047 Scheduled Caste people of Uttar Pradesh in the 2011 census, and Nepal's census of the same year counted 335,893 Chamars, 1.3% of the population. In Punjab the Ad-Dharmi and the Ravidassia, who worship Guru Ravidass, form communities of their own: the Ad-Dharm name spread after Chamar converts to Sikhism met discrimination. Chamars who moved from leatherwork to weaving took the identity of Julaha Chamar.

In villages of Rohtas and Bhojpur districts in Bihar, Rajput landlords forced women of the Chamar, Musahar and Dusadh communities into sexual relations, raped those who refused, brought false cases against their men and barred them from Rajput paths and wells. Peasant organisations such as the Kisan Samiti are said to have ended these practices in the 1970s, though conflict over wages continued.

In Uttar Pradesh the Ambedkarite Republican Party of India remained dominated by Chamars and Jatavs, and after its decline in the 1970s the Bahujan Samaj Party drew their votes; Mayawati became Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh. Other Dalit communities, such as the Bhangis, complained that Chamars monopolised state benefits, while the party also brought together old rivals such as the Pasis. A large diaspora lives in the United Kingdom, Canada, the United States, Italy, Mauritius and Fiji, where Ravidassia Chamars from Doaba founded a gurdwara at Nasinu in 1939.
chamavi: The origin of the name is uncertain but generally thought to be Germanic, formed like the names of the neighbouring Batavi and Frisiavones. Proposals link it to a verb meaning to hem in, to Old English hamm, an enclosed piece of land, or to the word for shirt. When the Ampsivarii asked the Roman authorities in about 58 CE to settle a buffer zone on the north bank of the Rhine, they said the fields had once belonged to the Chamavi, which suggests the people had lived by the Rhine before 12 BCE and later moved away. Pliny the Elder, writing around 70 CE, counted them among the Hermiones.

In the third and fourth centuries Roman writers listed the Chamavi at times as Franks, at times as Saxons, and sometimes apart from both. In about 293 or 294 Constantius Chlorus won victories in the Scheldt and Rhine delta, and a panegyric of 297 claims that Chamavus and Frisius now ploughed his land. Many resettled Chamavi became Roman soldiers, and a district of the Jura in France, the Comté d'Amaous, was named after a settlement of them. Constantine the Great fought them, probably in 310, 313 or 314, and the Peutinger map notes Hamavi who are Franks.

In the spring of 358 Julian, not yet emperor, attacked the Salians and the Chamavi, who were pressing into Roman territory around the Rhine-Meuse delta, because he needed safe passage for 600 grain ships coming from Britain. He used the warrior Charietto against their raiding, captured the son of their king and took captives and cattle, but still had to reach an agreement with them. In 392 the general Arbogast crossed the Rhine and devastated the lands of the Bructeri and then of the Chamavi, who did not confront him.

In the early Middle Ages a Frankish district called Hamaland, between the IJssel and the Rhine and including Deventer, Doesburg, Zutphen and Elten, is believed to have taken its name from them. A Frankish law code of Charlemagne's time, known today as the Lex Chamavorum Francorum, was given that name by its 1855 editor, though it is not clear that it refers to the Chamavi.
chambal-river: The Chambal is a tributary of the Yamuna and so part of the Ganges drainage system. It is 1,024 km long and rises at the Bhadakla Falls in the Janapav Hills, on the northern slopes of the Vindhyan escarpment, at about 843 metres, 67.5 km south-west of Mhow. It flows north through Madhya Pradesh for about 376 km, north-east through Rajasthan for 249 km, then for 216 km between Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan and for 150 km between Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh, before joining the Yamuna in Jalaun District.

Its basin drains 144,591 square kilometres and is rainfed, bounded by the Vindhyan ranges and the Aravallis. Badland topography is characteristic of the valley, with undulating floodplain, gullies and ravines. Tributaries include the Shipra, Kalisindh, Banas and Parbati. The river is much older than the Yamuna and the Ganges, into which it flows.

In the Vedic era the river's name was Charmanvati, meaning the river on whose banks leather is dried. The Mahabharata calls it Charmanyavati and says it arose from the blood of thousands of animals sacrificed by King Rantideva. The epic places the Chambal area in the kingdom of Shakuni, and tradition holds that Draupadi, after the attempt to disrobe her, cursed anyone who would drink its water. It is believed that this curse has kept the river unpolluted and its animals largely undisturbed.

Four works known as the Chambal Valley Projects were built on the river. Gandhi Sagar Dam, a masonry gravity dam 64 metres high on the Rajasthan-Madhya Pradesh border, was completed in 1960. Rana Pratap Sagar Dam followed in 1970 and Jawahar Sagar Dam, upstream of Kota, in 1972. The Kota Barrage, completed in 1960, diverts the water released after power generation for irrigation by canals in Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh.

The region lies in the semi-arid zone of north-western India, at the border of Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh. Its vegetation is ravine and thorn forest, with sparse ground cover along severely eroded banks, and over a thousand flowering plants have been reported, among them Tectona grandis, the teak. The Chambal is regarded as one of the most pristine rivers of India.
chamber-of-rhetoric: Because of their close ties with local civic leaders, the chambers' public plays served the cities as an early form of public relations. In Holland they were an important part of the literary scene of the Dutch Golden Age and experimented with poetic form and structure. At the start of the 16th century Antwerp had three societies, the Violieren, the Olijftak and the Goudbloem, while Brussels and Ghent each had four. The building that now houses the Frans Hals Museum in Haarlem was paid for by a lottery in which chambers from all over the country took part, and the Haarlem society Trou moet Blycken, which hosted it, still keeps many of the blazons from that lottery.

During the Protestant Reformation De Egelantier sided with the reformers against Amsterdam's city government and enjoyed its most flourishing period, although it received very little official funding. Since most rederijkers were amateurs, the literary quality of their work was often low, and in the 18th century some chambers were spoken of with contempt.

Besides providing recitations, plays and performances at civic festivities and keeping up literary contacts between cities, the chambers had many of the social functions of a guild, a confraternity, the Puy or the Meistersingers. They attended the funerals of members, held collections for sick or impoverished members and gave wedding presents to members who married.

By the 17th century many chambers relied on semi-professional actors called personagiën. These did not pay membership fees; in return for their work they received free food and drink after rehearsals and performances and were exempted from other civic obligations.
chambery: Chambéry was founded at a crossroads of ancient routes between the Dauphiné, Switzerland and Italy, in a wide valley between the Bauges and Chartreuse massifs on the Leysse River. It lies 214 kilometres from Turin, 100 from Lyon and 85 from Geneva, and is a railway and road junction. Its surroundings run from the vineyard slopes of the Combe de Savoie almost to the shores of the Lac du Bourget, the largest natural lake in France.

The history of Chambéry is closely linked to the House of Savoy. It was the Savoyard capital from 1295 to 1563, when Savoy stretched from Bourg-en-Bresse across the Alps to Turin, north to Geneva and south to Nice. The Château des ducs de Savoie, a fortified castle dating from the 11th century, was settled by the first counts of Savoy in 1285 and expanded in the early 14th century as residence, seat of administration and stronghold. It soon became obsolete as a defence against a siege, and constant French hostilities led Duke Emmanuel Philibert to move his capital to Turin in 1563.

The château remained an administrative centre until Christine Marie of France, Duchess of Savoy, returned to hold court there in 1640. In 1684 it saw the marriage of Victor Amadeus II and Anne Marie d'Orléans, a niece of Louis XIV. Victor Amadeus III added a Royal Wing in 1786. France annexed the lands of the duchy west of the Alps in 1792, but returned them to the House of Savoy in Turin in 1815 after Napoleon's defeat. Chambéry was ceded to France by Piedmont in 1860, under Napoleon III, and its Hôtel de Ville opened in 1867.

Chambéry is the prefecture and largest city of the Savoie department, with 60,251 inhabitants in 2022. The château now houses the departmental administration. The Fontaine des Éléphants, built in 1838 to honour Benoît de Boigne's feats in India, is its best-known landmark. The Cistercian Abbey of Hautecombe, founded in 1135, is one of the burial places of the rulers of Savoy, and the cathedral of Saint Francis of Sales has the largest trompe-l'oeil paintings in Europe. The Sisters of St Joseph, an order founded at Chambéry in 1812, work in teaching and charity.
chameria: Chameria, also spelled Çameria, lies along the Ionian coast in south-western Albania and north-western Greece and is traditionally associated with the Albanian subgroup of the Chams. In the Middle Ages the area was known as Vagenetia. The name is of uncertain etymology and may derive from the ancient name of the Thyamis river, called Cham in Albanian.
