It appears in European travel reports from the beginning of the 19th century, but the Ottomans did not use it in administration before the 20th century, when in 1909 they combined three kazas into the Çamlik sancak.

Its extent has been defined differently by different writers. Many scholars equate it with the Greek prefecture of Thesprotia plus a small area around Konispol in Albania, while others, among them the Ottoman intellectual Sami Frashëri, drew a far larger region covering much of southern Epirus.

A Venetian document of 1210 records Albanians opposite Corfu, and Byzantine sources show them in the Despotate of Epirus in sizable numbers from 1337, as nomads. After Stefan Uroš IV Dušan conquered Epirus in the 1340s, Albanian chieftains defeated Nikephoros II Orsini in 1358 and founded the Despotate of Arta and the Principality of Gjirokastër. These fell to the Tocco family, who gave way to the Ottomans, who took Ioannina in 1430, Arta in 1449 and Vonitsa in 1479.

Under Ottoman rule the region belonged to the Vilayet of Ioannina and then the Pashalik of Yanina. About 25 villages were converted to Islam in 1739, often by force. Ali Pasha Tepelena, governor of Ioannina from 1788, conquered the Souli area in 1803. Epirus was divided at the London Peace Conference in 1913, and most of Chameria came under Greece. The Greek census counted Muslim Chams separately, and in the 1930s the region had about 70,000 people, of whom 18,000 to 20,000 were Albanian-speaking Muslims. In 1936 Greece created Thesprotia prefecture to control the Muslim Albanian minority more closely.

During the Axis occupation of Greece from 1941 to 1944 large parts of the Muslim Cham community collaborated with Italian and German forces. At the end of World War II, Cham Albanians were cleansed from the region by guerrillas of the National Republican Greek League under Napoleon Zervas, in mass assaults on Cham villages.

Most of Chameria is divided between the Greek regional units of Thesprotia, Preveza and Ioannina, with Konispol at its southern extremity in Albania. The name is used mostly by Albanians and is obsolete in Greek, and in Albania it has also acquired irredentist connotations. The Greek census of 1951 counted 127 Muslim Chams in Epirus. Orthodox Albanian speakers, who call themselves Arvanites in Greek, identify as Greeks and speak Arvanitika, though some have kept a distinct Albanian identity.
chamorro-people: The Chamorro are commonly believed to have reached the Mariana Islands from the Philippines about 1,500 BCE. They are most closely related to other Austronesian-speaking peoples of the Philippines, eastern Indonesia, Taiwan and the Caroline Islands. DNA testing of ancient remains from the Unai and Latte periods has traced the lineage to eastern Indonesia, most likely Sulawesi, with no direct prehistoric connection to the Philippines. The Chamorro language belongs to the Malayo-Polynesian subgroup of the Austronesian family, and has taken many loanwords from Spanish.

Early Chamorros were expert seafarers and skilled in weaving and pottery. They used the latte stone, a stone pillar topped with a hemispherical capstone, as a building foundation. Society was based on a matrilineal clan in which the mother's brother played the chief paternal role. Before the Spanish arrived there were two main castes.

The Chamori were divided into the ruling Matua and the Achoti, and the Manachang below them were born and died in their station. Early Chamorros venerated ancestors without worshipping deities, and spirits called taotaomo'na are still believed in by some. According to creation legend, the twins Puntan and Fu'uña made the world from Puntan's body, and from a rock into which Fu'uña transformed herself all human beings emerged. Core values include inafa'maolek, doing good for each other.

Ferdinand Magellan's crew met the islanders on 6 March 1521. Spain converted the people to Catholicism, the caste system faded under Spanish rule, and all the inhabitants came to be called by the Spanish name Chamorro. The Spanish colonial era ran from 1521 to 1898.

The United States captured Guam on 21 June 1898, and Spain ceded it by the Treaty of Paris, effective 11 April 1899. Japanese forces invaded Guam on 8 December 1941. During the occupation of two and a half years, Chamorros were subjected to forced labour, incarceration, torture and execution, and American forces retook the island on 21 July 1944, the date commemorated as Liberation Day.

The Guam Organic Act of 1950 made Guam an unincorporated organised territory of the United States and granted its people citizenship. Chamorro people today live in Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands and in several US states. The 2020 census counted about 63,035 people with Chamorro ancestry in Guam and 17,163 in the Northern Marianas. Public schools on both Guam and the Northern Marianas are required by law to teach the Chamorro language, and many institutions on Guam prefer the spelling CHamoru.
champa: Champa was a collection of independent Cham polities along the coast of what is now central and southern Vietnam, from about the 2nd century CE until 1832. According to the earliest sources the first Cham polities arose in the 2nd and 3rd centuries, after Khu Liên's rebellion against the Eastern Han. They grew out of the seafaring Austronesian Sa Huỳnh culture. Scholars disagree about how far Champa was ever united: older writers saw one kingdom, while others argue that it was mostly a confederation of kingdoms and city-states.

Wars with the neighbouring kingdom of Funan in the 4th century brought Indian culture into Cham society, and Hinduism became the state religion. The Đông Yên Châu inscription, of about 350, is the oldest known text in a native Southeast Asian language. King Vikrantavarman I, who reigned from 653 to 686, had many sanctuaries built at Mỹ Sơn and sent regular embassies to the Tang court. Champa reached its height in the 9th and 10th centuries, and its trade linked the Indian Ocean and East Asia until the 17th century.

In 1471 Champa suffered serious defeats by the Vietnamese state of Đại Việt, in which 120,000 people were captured or killed, among them the king, Tra Toan, who died in captivity on the way north. What remained was a small enclave near Nha Trang and Phan Rang, and many Chams fled to Cambodia. In 1832 the emperor Minh Mạng annexed the last Cham territory. Islam began to spread among the Chams after the 10th century, and by the 17th century the royal families had adopted it.

The Cham, Rade and Jarai peoples of Vietnam and Cambodia speak Chamic languages, and many Cham today are Muslim, while the Bacam keep a form of Hinduism. Cham red brick temples survive in many places. Mỹ Sơn, a former religious centre, and Hội An are World Heritage Sites, and the largest collection of Cham sculpture is in the museum at Da Nang, founded in 1915.
champaner: Champaner lies in Panchmahal district, 47 kilometres from the city of Vadodara, below Pavagadh fort, which stands on a precipitous hillside above the town. At an early period it was the seat of a Bhil dynasty, and the town is named after a man called Champa, though accounts differ on who he was. By the later 15th century the Khichi Chauhan Rajputs held the fort above the town.

The young Sultan of Gujarat, Mahmud Begada, set out against Champaner with his army on 4 December 1482. After defeating the army of Champaner he besieged Pavagadh, where King Jayasimha had taken refuge, and took the fort on 21 November 1484 after a siege of 20 months. He then spent 23 years rebuilding and adorning the town, which he renamed Muhammadabad, before moving his capital there from Ahmedabad. His Jama Masjid ranks among the finest buildings of Gujarat. It stands on a high plinth, with a central dome, two minarets 30 metres high, 172 pillars, seven mihrabs and carved entrance gates with latticed stone windows called jalis.

In 1535, after driving out Bahadur Shah, Humayun led 300 Mughals up spikes driven into the rock and stonework of a remote, unguarded part of the citadel. They took great heaps of gold, silver and jewels, though Bahadur Shah escaped to Diu with much of his treasure.

The town is the site of the Champaner-Pavagadh Archaeological Park. Among its monuments are the Jama Masjid, the Bawaman Masjid, Saat Kaman, the citadel of Mahmud Begada, the Hissar I Khas, a stepwell, a Jain temple, the tomb of Sikandar Shah and the temples of Mahakali Mata and Bhadrakali Mata. The mausoleum of Syed Khundmir is also there.
champawat: Champawat lies in the south-east of Uttarakhand, in the eastern part of the Kumaon Himalayas, at an average elevation of 1,615 metres. Its historical name is said to be Champavati, after the Champavati stream on whose banks it stands. The valley of the stream holds seven ancient temples: Baleshwar, Kranteshwar, Tadkeshwar, Rishneshwar, Dikteshwar, Mallareshwar and Maneshwar. Of these the Baleshwar temple is considered the most important. According to a local epic, the Gurupaduka, Champavati, the sister of the Nagas, did penance near it, and a temple in her memory stands inside the Baleshwar complex.

Champawat was the original residence of the Rajas of Kumaon before they moved their capital to Almora in the mid-16th century, and it was formerly the capital of the Chand rulers. The Baleshwar temple, built by the Chand rulers in the 12th century, is noted for its stone carving. To the west of the town stood a fort called Donkot, where the local Rawat kings lived. According to the Vayu Purana, Champavati was the capital of nine kings of the Puri Naga dynasty.

Local tradition tied to the Skanda Purana holds that a mound near the old fort is the Kurmachal, the spot where Vishnu appeared in his Kurma, or tortoise, incarnation. The name Kumaon is widely believed to be a corruption of Kurmachal, and the region around Champawat became known as Kali Kumaon to distinguish it from the rest of the territory.

After the British occupation a cantonment was first set up at Champawat, but in 1815 it was moved six miles north to Lohaghat because the valley's climate was judged unhealthy. The Champawat Tiger, a man-eating tigress that killed more than four hundred people in the surrounding area, was shot by Jim Corbett in 1907, the first man-eater of his long career.

Champawat is a town and municipal board and the administrative headquarters of Champawat district, which was carved out of Pithoragarh district in 1997. It had a population of 4,801 at the 2011 census and lies on National Highway 9. Among its religious sites are the Kranteshwar temple, dedicated to Shiva, and a temple to Ghatotkacha, whose head is believed to have fallen here after he died in the battle of the Mahabharata.
champoeg: The town site lies on the south bank of the Willamette River in northern Marion County, on French Prairie, about 5 miles south-east of Newberg and halfway between Oregon City and Salem. The name comes from a Kalapuyan word that may be a shortened form of a phrase referring to the edible root yampa. Most of the town stood on the Donation Land Claims of Robert Newell and André Longtain.

On 7 February 1841 settlers of the Willamette Valley met at Champoeg for the first time, chose the missionary Jason Lee as chairman and discussed the wolves menacing their settlements. These Wolf Meetings laid the basis for civil codes. As the United States and the United Kingdom disputed the Oregon Country, the meeting of 2 May 1843 named nine representatives to create a provisional government with Champoeg as its capital. William Gilpin, who had helped draft a petition to Congress, carried it east, spreading Oregon fever on the way, and presented it in 1845. The Oregon Treaty settled the dispute in 1846, but when the Oregon Territory was organised in 1848 Champoeg was not chosen as its capital.

By about 1852 the town had a ferry, a steamboat landing, a warehouse of Francis Pettygrove and Alanson Beers, a Hudson's Bay Company granary and a stagecoach office, with ten streets running north to south and six east to west. On 2 December 1861 the Willamette rose 55 feet above its summer level and covered the town in seven feet of water. Only two saloons survived; residents sheltered in the Newell House on its hill, and Robert Newell nearly went bankrupt caring for them. The town was never rebuilt.

The site is an Oregon state park, Champoeg State Heritage Area, where a monument of 1901 lists the 52 settlers who voted for the provisional government. It holds Robert Newell's restored house of 1852 as a museum, the Pioneer Mothers Memorial Cabin Museum and the Historic Butteville Store, founded in 1863. Its archaeological district was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1984 and includes what appears to be Newell's first homesite.
chamunda: Ramakrishna Gopal Bhandarkar claims that Chamunda was originally a tribal goddess worshipped by the tribes of the Vindhya mountains in central India, who offered animal and human sacrifices and liquor to goddesses. These methods, he says, were retained in Tantric worship of Chamunda after her assimilation into mainstream Hinduism, and the fierce nature of the goddess is due to her association with Rudra, or Shiva. Wangu also supports the theory of tribal origins. Chamunda is also counted among the chief Yoginis, the sixty-four or eighty-one Tantric goddesses.

In the Devi Mahatmya, Chamunda emerged from between the eyebrows of the goddess Kaushiki, who was created from the sheath of Durga, and was charged with killing the demons Chanda and Munda, servants of the demon kings Shumbha and Nishumbha. Another legend has her appear from the frown of Parvati.

In a later episode of the Devi Mahatmya, Durga creates the Matrikas, and Kali, who sucks the blood of the demon Raktabija, is given the epithet Chamunda. The Varaha Purana, by contrast, names Chamunda and Kali as separate goddesses, and in the Matsya Purana she and the other Matrikas help Shiva kill the demon Andhakasura by drinking his blood.

She is one of the seven Matrikas, fearsome mothers who were emblems of childhood pestilence, fever and disease. She is always shown last in the group, is sometimes called its leader, and is the only Matrika who is a Shakti of the great goddess rather than of a male god and the only one who is worshipped independently.

In art she is a skeletal old woman with sunken eyes and sagging breasts, black or red, with up to twelve arms holding a drum, trident, sword, snake and skull-bowl, wearing a garland of skulls, and seated on a corpse. This appearance symbolises the inevitability of old age, death and decay.

A South Indian inscription describes sacrifices of sheep to Chamunda, and animal sacrifice has become less common with Vaishnavite influences. Chamunda puja is part of the Sandhi Puja, a key ritual of Durga Puja. Temples include the Chamunda Devi Temple near Palampur in Kangra, the Chamundeshwari Temple on Chamundi Hill, Mysore, and the shrine on a hilltop at Dewas. The Chamunda Mataji temple in Mehrangarh Fort, Jodhpur, was established in 1460 when the ruler Jodha moved the idol from Mandore. In Jain legend the monk Ratnaprabhasuri persuaded her to accept vegetarian offerings at Osian.
chan-chan: Chan Chan lies at the mouth of the Moche Valley in La Libertad, about five kilometres west of Trujillo, in a particularly arid part of the northern Peruvian coastal desert. With no rain, the main fresh water came from rivers carrying runoff from the Andes, which allowed the control of land and water by irrigation. The city first relied on wells about 15 metres deep. A network of canals diverting water from the Moche River, some reported as running up to 20 miles, later extended the farmland around it. The name Chan Chan is unexplained: linguists agree it is not Mochica, but they dispute whether it comes from Quingnam or from a Quechua word meaning fenced place.

Chan Chan was the capital of Chimor, a conquest state that developed from the Chimú culture of the Peruvian coast. It is believed to have held 40,000 to 60,000 people. Its society was strongly stratified, with rulers and deities at the top and servants at the bottom, and its craftsmen were known for pottery and textiles. The Chimú are said to have held that the sun made three eggs, of gold for the ruler and elite, of silver for the rulers' spouses and of copper for everyone else. Many canals to the north were destroyed by a catastrophic flood around 1100, which turned the Chimú towards an economy based on outside resources.

The Incas conquered the Chimú around 1470 and dispersed Chimú civilians to lands they had recently conquered. It is reported that they cut off the irrigation system. Chan Chan declined, and after Francisco Pizarro founded Trujillo in 1535 the Spaniards looted its tombs, one sixteenth-century list recording a treasure equal to 80,000 pesos of gold.

The site covers about 20 square kilometres, with a dense urban centre of six, and is considered the largest adobe city in the Americas. It has ten walled compounds, called ciudadelas, which contained courts, storerooms, temples, reservoirs and burial platforms for rulers, with high walls carved in relief with fish, birds, waves and nets.

The walls of the Tschudi compound rise up to twelve metres and are wider at the base, which suits an earthquake zone. Ordinary housing took the form of small irregular rooms that doubled as workshops. UNESCO designated Chan Chan a World Heritage Site on 28 November 1986. Excavations by Michael Moseley and Carol J. Mackey began in 1969, and rain and floods from El Niño threaten the adobe walls.
chanakya: No documented historical information about Chanakya survives. Narratives about him come from tales preserved in traditions dating from the 4th to the 11th century CE. Thomas Trautmann distinguishes four accounts of the legend of Chanakya and Chandragupta: a Buddhist version in the Mahavamsa and its commentary, a Jain version in the Parishishtaparvan of Hemachandra, a Kashmiri version in the Kathasaritsagara of Somadeva and the Brihat-Katha-Manjari of Ksemendra, and the Sanskrit play Mudrarakshasa by Vishakhadatta, which he regards as largely fictional.

The versions differ on his origins. In the Buddhist account Chanakya was a Brahmin from Takshashila, learned in the three Vedas and in politics, with an ugly appearance. In the Jain account he was born to lay Jain parents in the village of Chanaka, and Hemachandra calls him a Dramila, implying a native of South India. Both say he was born with a full set of teeth, taken as a sign that he would become a king, and that a parent broke them to prevent his arrogance.

In all four versions Chanakya is insulted by the Nanda king and vows to destroy him. In the Buddhist account the emperor Dhana Nanda has him thrown out of an alms-giving ceremony for Brahmins at Pataliputra. Chanakya breaks his sacred thread in anger, curses the emperor and escapes in the disguise of an Ajivika. In the Jain account he sits on the emperor's throne and is kicked off it by a servant. In the Kashmiri version he unties his topknot and vows not to retie it until the emperor is destroyed, and in the play he makes the same vow, which fits the removal from the first seat of the empire.

After dethroning the Nanda, Chanakya installs Chandragupta as king. According to these narratives he served as chief adviser and prime minister to both Chandragupta Maurya and his son Bindusara. In the play, Chanakya engineers an alliance between Chandragupta and the king Parvata, whose army of Bahlika, Kirata, Parasika, Kamboja, Shaka and Yavana soldiers invades Pataliputra and defeats the Nandas. The Nanda minister Rakshasa continues to resist, and Chanakya foils each of his plots by cunning and the use of spies.

Chanakya has conventionally been identified with Kautilya, also called Vishnugupta, to whom the ancient Indian treatise on politics and economics, the Arthashastra, is attributed. Its composition and the date of its attribution to Chanakya remain matters of scholarly debate. In India he is regarded as a great thinker and diplomat, and many Indian nationalists regard him as one of the earliest people to envision a united India spanning the entire subcontinent.
chanarcillo: Chañarcillo lies in the Atacama Desert of Copiapó Province, near Vallenar and 60 km from Copiapó. Its water holes include Ña Justa and Yerbas Buenas, and the expedition of Diego de Almagro is said to have filled its water supply at Ña Justa in 1536 on its way south. The mines sit on the south flank of a dome, the Sierra de Chañarcillo, where silver ore runs in nearly vertical veins along fractures and faults in beds of limestone and tuff. Above the water table the ores are oxidised; below it they are enriched with sulphides such as proustite, polybasite and pyrargyrite, and large crystals of proustite, stephanite and chlorargyrite have been found there.

Juan Godoy found the silver on 16 May 1832, and the town grew up around the mine as the Chilean silver rush took hold. It rose in importance through the 19th century to become one of the mines that mattered most to the Chilean economy, and it was linked by railway before 1862. Up to 20 mines worked an area of only a third of a square mile, and the district produced at least $100 million in silver, 2,500,000 kg of it between 1860 and 1885.

In 1870 some 1,570 miners worked there. The mines were exhausted by 1874, and mining largely ended in 1888 after they were accidentally flooded; afterwards only small amounts were won by removing pillars in the mines or from the waste dumps. Chañarcillo was nonetheless the most productive mining district of 19th-century Chile, and the settlement is now largely in ruins.
chand-bibi: Chand Bibi was the daughter of Hussain Nizam Shah I of Ahmednagar and the sister of Burhan Nizam Shah II, the sultan of Ahmednagar. She knew Arabic, Persian, Turkish, Marathi and Kannada, played the setar and painted flowers. Under a policy of alliance she was married to Ali Adil Shah I of the Bijapur Sultanate, and a stepwell near Bijapur's eastern boundary, built by her husband, was named Chand Bawdi after her.

After Ali Adil Shah died in 1580, Shi'a nobles proclaimed his nine-year-old nephew Ibrahim Adil Shah II. The Deccani general Kamal Khan seized power as regent, and Chand Bibi plotted with another general, Haji Kishvar Khan, against him; Kamal Khan was captured and beheaded. Kishvar Khan then became regent, but a quarrel over captured elephants and a failed conspiracy ended with Chand Bibi imprisoned at Satara fort. Ikhlas Khan and other Habshi generals drove him out. Dilavar Khan held the regency from 1582 to 1591, and when order returned Chand Bibi went back to Ahmednagar.

In 1591 Akbar asked the four Deccan sultanates to acknowledge his supremacy, and all evaded. In 1595 the ruler of Ahmednagar was killed in battle against Ibrahim Adil Shah II, and Chand Bibi accepted the regency for her infant great-nephew Bahadur Shah. The minister Miyan Manju had invited the Mughal prince Murad to march on the city, and when the Mughals invaded in November 1595 Chand Bibi led the defence of the fort. On 23 February 1596, with her troops suffering famine, she made peace by ceding Berar to Murad, who retreated. Troops from Bijapur and Golconda then joined the Ahmednagar forces, but the Mughals won a battle on the Godavari on 8-9 February 1597.

In 1599 Akbar sent Prince Daniyal, Mirza Yusuf Khan and Abdul Rahim Khan-I-Khana, and Daniyal reached Ahmednagar by an alternative route and laid siege to the fort. Chand Bibi again defended it, but decided to negotiate terms. Hamid Khan spread the false news that she was in league with the Mughals; in another version it was her eunuch valet Jita Khan who did so. She was killed by an enraged mob of her own troops. After a siege of four months and four days the Mughals captured Ahmednagar on 18 August 1600. She is the subject of two Indian films, from 1931 and 1937, and a tomb in the city is wrongly called her palace.
chand-dynasty: The traditional genealogical lists of the Chand kings, the vamshavalis, were compiled in the mid-19th century and are not completely reliable. They place Som Chand in the 7th century, and a British report of 1849 accordingly dated the start of Chand rule to 685 CE. Historians dispute this, because the Katyuri kingdom is known to have ruled Kumaon until the third quarter of the 10th century.

Tradition makes Som Chand an immigrant from Jhusi and a relative of the king of Kannauj. The historian Krishna Pal Singh suggests that he came to Kumaon during the upheaval of the Ghaznavid invasion of Kannauj in 1018–1019, and dates the beginning of Chand rule to 1019–1021. By the early 13th century the Chands appear to have ruled as feudatories: the Baleshwar Temple inscription of 1223, set up by Krachalla Deva, a conqueror from present-day Nepal, lists men whose names suggest that they belonged to the family.

Rudra Chand (1565–1597) seized Sira in 1581 and made the first of several attacks on the Garhwal Kingdom, all of which were repulsed. In 1587 he visited the Mughal emperor Akbar at Lahore as a mark of obeisance, and the Ain-e-Akbari lists a Sarkar of Kumaon. Baz Bahadur Chand (1638–78), one of the most powerful of the line, joined Shahjahan in an attack on Garhwal in 1655 that captured the Terai region including Dehradun, and extended his territory east to the Karnali river. In 1672 he began a poll tax whose revenue was sent to Delhi as tribute.

In 1744 the Rohilla leader Ali Mohammed Khan sent a force that took Almora against weak resistance. The Rohillas stayed seven months and left after a payment of three lakh rupees; a second attack was defeated at Barakheri. Hill troops under Dip Chand later fought beside the Rohillas at the Third Battle of Panipat in 1761. Internal strife over the following thirty years cost the kings most of the land they had held in the plains.

The Gurkhas invaded early in 1790, crossing the Kali River, and the Chands were driven to the Bhabhar and finally expelled. Nepalese rule lasted twenty-four years. During the Anglo-Nepalese War Harak Deo Joshi, minister of the last Chand raja, sided with the British, who captured Almora on 26 April 1815; with the Treaty of Sugauli, ratified on 4 March 1816, Kumaon passed to British rule. Champawat, the first capital, keeps a medieval fort and the Baleshwar and Nagnath temples, and Chand kings also built temples at Bageshwar, Bhimtal and Almora.
chand-sultan: Chand Sultan, styled Maharaja Chand Sultan Shah, was the eldest son and successor of Bakht Buland Shah of Deogarh and belonged to the Rajgond dynasty. He came to the throne of Deogarh in 1706 and moved his capital from Deogarh to Nagpur. He carried out further reforms, planned the layout of the new city, and extended his territory considerably to the east of the river Wainganga. His people remembered him as a kind ruler, and the kingdom prospered under him.

He built the Jumma Talao, now known as Shukrawari Lake, a reservoir with steps built into it that also supplied water to Nagpur. He enclosed the whole city in a wall almost 3 miles long with five solid gates, and built his fortress at Mahal, the oldest part of Nagpur, inside a wall of its own. One of the city's gates, the Jumma Gate, still stands under the name Gandhi Gate.

After his death in 1739 the throne was seized by Wali Shah, an illegitimate son of Chand Sultan by a woman who was not a Gond. Chand Sultan's widow called on the Maratha leader Raghoji Bhonsle of Berar to support her sons Akbar Shah and Burhan Shah. Wali Shah was put to death and the heirs placed on the throne, and Raghoji Bhonsle returned to Berar with a rich reward, which convinced him that Nagpur was a wealthy country.

The brothers soon quarrelled, and Burhan Shah again asked for Raghoji Bhonsle's help. Akbar Shah was driven into exile and later poisoned at Hyderabad. This time the Maratha leader stayed, declaring himself protector of the Gond king, and in 1743 Burhan Shah became in effect a state pensioner while real power passed to the Bhonsle rulers of Nagpur. Burhan Shah was followed by Rahman Shah and then by Rahman Shah's nephew and adopted son Suleiman Shah, who was loyal to the British government and died on 15 April 1885.
chanda-sahib: Chanda Sahib was born Husayn Dost Khan. He served as dewan under Dost Ali Khan, Nawab of the Carnatic at Arcot, who was the Mughal representative in the region; between them stood the Nizam of Hyderabad, in theory subordinate to the emperor and superior to the Nawab. In 1734 Dost Ali Khan sent an expedition under his son Safdar Ali Khan and Chanda Sahib to exact tribute from the kingdoms of the far south. The invaders stormed Tanjore and reached Madurai, where the widowed Queen-Regent Meenakshi was fighting Vangaru Tirumala, father of her adopted son, for the throne.

Safdar Ali Khan took 30,000 gold and silver coins to declare Vangaru Tirumala king and left Chanda Sahib to enforce the award, but Meenakshi paid him 100,000 to recognise her instead, made him swear on the Quran, and admitted him to the fort of Trichinopoly. Returning in 1736, he defeated Vangaru Tirumala at Ammaya Nayakkanur and Dindigul and occupied the southern provinces of the Madurai Nayaks. He made his two brothers governors of Dindigul and Madurai, subdued the king of Tanjore and forced him to cede Karaikal, which became a French colony on 14 February 1739.

Tanjore and Vangaru Tirumala called in the Marathas, who in 1740 defeated and killed Dost Ali Khan in the pass of Damalcheruvu, and in 1741 the general Raghuji Bhonsle captured Chanda Sahib at Tiruchirappalli and imprisoned him. During the Second Carnatic War he plotted against the Nawab Anwaruddin Muhammed Khan and, backed by Joseph François Dupleix, became Nawab, driving Anwaruddin's son Muhammad Ali Khan Wallajah, whom the British supported, into the rock-fort of Tiruchirappalli.

With French help Chanda Sahib besieged Tiruchirappalli in 1751–1752. A British diversion of 300 soldiers against Arcot drew off 10,000 men under his son Raza Sahib, who was defeated there and at Kaveripakkam by a British force made up mostly of Indian soldiers. Chanda Sahib fled to Tanjore, was captured by its Maratha army and was beheaded by the Tanjore raja Pratap Singh of Thanjavur on 12 June 1752. The British installed Wallajah as Nawab of Arcot in 1754, and most of Chanda Sahib's forces went over to them.
chandannagar: Chandannagar came into being in colonial times, since no medieval Bengali text such as the Chandimangal mentions it. Historians think the French created the town by joining several localities, notably the villages of Gondalpara, Boro and Khalisani. The first Frenchman to hold land there was Du Plessis, who bought 13 arpents at Boro Kishanganj for 401 taka in 1673-74. In 1688 the director of the French East India Company, Boureau-Deslandes, paid 40,000 coins to the Mughal subahdar to gain control of the area and build a factory. The name Chandernagor first appears in a letter of 1696.

Joseph François Dupleix became governor in 1730, and more than two thousand brick houses were built during his administration. From his time until 1756 Chandannagar was the main centre of European commerce in Bengal, trading in opium, indigo, silk, rice, rope and sugar, and its fine cloths were exported to Europe. The prosperous merchant Indranarayan Chaudhari, who built the Nandadulal Temple in 1740, made a great fortune there.

War between France and Great Britain began in 1756, and on 23 March 1757 Colonel Robert Clive and Admiral Charles Watson bombarded and captured Chandannagar. Its fortifications and many houses were demolished, and its commercial importance passed to Calcutta downriver. It was restored to France in 1763, retaken by the British in 1794 during the Napoleonic Wars and returned in 1816 with a 3 square mile enclave. It was governed as part of French India from Pondicherry until 1950. By 1900 it was a quiet suburb of Calcutta with 25,000 people.

A municipality was created on 1 August 1880 with Charles Dumaine as first mayor. Citizens could elect a representative to each French parliamentary house. The guillotine was last used in the town on 22 July 1895.

After Indian independence, France recognised the right of self-determination of its Indian settlements in 1948. A referendum on 19 June 1949 found that 98.5 per cent of Chandannagar's residents wished to join India. On 2 May 1950 the French allowed the Indian government to assume de facto control, and on 2 October 1954 the city was integrated into West Bengal. The inhabitants could keep French nationality.

The city on the Hooghly retains Indo-French buildings, among them the Strand promenade with Fort d'Orleans, the Sacred Heart Church inaugurated in 1884, a gate of 1937 marking Bastille Day, and a museum founded in 1961. Jagaddhatri Puja, held ten days after Diwali, is held across the city with a large procession.
chandra-shekhar-azad: Chandra Shekhar Tiwari was born on 23 July 1906 in Bhabhra village in the princely state of Alirajpur, into a Kanyakubja Brahmin family whose forefathers came from Badarka village in Unnao district. He was sent to study at Kashi Vidyapeeth in Banaras.

In 1921, at the height of the Non-Cooperation Movement, he joined it as a student of 15 and was arrested on 24 December. Brought before the magistrate two weeks later, he gave his name as Azad, meaning the Free, his father's name as Swatantrata, or Independence, and his residence as Jail. The angered magistrate punished him with 15 blows.

After Mahatma Gandhi suspended the non-cooperation movement in 1922, Azad was disappointed. Manmath Nath Gupta introduced him to Ram Prasad Bismil, founder of the revolutionary Hindustan Republican Association (HRA), and he began to collect funds for it, mostly through robberies of government property. He took part in the Kakori Train Robbery of 1925. Afterwards the British suppressed the revolutionaries, and Bismil, Ashfaqulla Khan, Roshan Singh and Rajendra Nath Lahiri were sentenced to death, while Azad evaded capture.

In September 1928 he and Bhagat Singh reorganised the HRA as the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA), with the aim of an independent socialist India. On 17 December 1928 the group shot John P. Saunders, an assistant superintendent of police, at Lahore, mistaking him for James A. Scott, whom they meant to kill to avenge the death of Lala Lajpat Rai. In 1929 he took part in an attempt to blow up the train of the Viceroy of India.

On 27 February 1931 the CID chief at Allahabad, J. R. H. Nott-Bower, was told that Azad was at Alfred Park talking with a companion, Sukhdev Raj Shukla. The police surrounded the park and a shootout began. Azad killed three policemen and was badly wounded, and he covered Raj's escape. Behind a jamun tree he shot Nott-Bower in the wrist. Holding to his pledge never to be captured alive, he shot himself in the head with his last bullet. The body was cremated at Rasulabad Ghat without informing the public, and when the news spread, crowds surrounded the park chanting against British rule.

Jawaharlal Nehru wrote in his autobiography that Azad had visited him weeks before his death. Schools, colleges and roads across India are named after Azad, and he has been portrayed in many films and a television series.
chandra-shumsher-jang-bahadur-rana: Chandra Shumsher was born on 8 July 1863, the sixth of the seventeen sons of Dhir Shumsher Rana, the youngest brother of Jung Bahadur Rana, founder of the Rana dynasty. He was educated in Kolkata and became the first Nepalese prime minister to have passed the matriculation examination. In 1884 the Vice Chancellor of Calcutta University praised him as a man who could handle the pen as well as the sword.

With his brothers Khadga Shumsher and Bhim Shumsher he arranged the murder of his uncle, the prime minister Ranodip Singh, to move up the line of succession. After the death of his eldest brother Bir Shamsher in March 1901 he became commander in chief under his brother Dev Shamsher, a liberal, and in June 1901 he seized power in a coup. He kept firm control of domestic and foreign policy, and with his adviser Ram Mani Acharya Dixit he grew rich from deals with the British over the recruitment of Gurkha soldiers.

He was the second Nepalese prime minister, after Jung Bahadur Rana, to visit Britain, where he was received by Edward VII and given an honorary Doctor of Civil Laws by the University of Oxford. After this tour, embarrassed by his country's backwardness, he is said to have made reforms: he abolished sati, made it illegal to kill a person for witchcraft, paid for the end of slavery from the treasury of the Pashupatinath temple, founded Tri-Chandra College, built canals in the Terai and hospitals, and saw the opening of the Nepal Government Railway from Raxaul to Amlekhganj. He gave money and troops to Britain in the First World War.

He suffered from tuberculosis and lived on rice and black lentils alone, so that he was very thin. Generally he is seen as despotic and conservative, and his reforms as made mostly for his family's benefit. He built Singha Durbar, then the largest palace in Asia with over 1,200 rooms, and Chandra Nahar in Saptari, the oldest canal of Nepal. On 26 November 1929 he died, and his son Mohan Shamsher later became the 9th Rana Maharaja, in whose time the century-old oligarchy of the Ranas came to an end.
chandrabhanu: According to inscription no.24 found at Wat Hua-wieng in Chaiya, near Nakhon Si Thammaraj, Chandrabhanu was a ruler of Tambralinga of the Padmavamsa, the lotus dynasty. He built the Phrae Boromadhatu, a Buddhist stupa in Nakhon Si Thammaraj, to hold a relic of the Buddha. Sri Lankan sources call him a Javaka chieftain and a sea pirate from Tambralinga.

The Mahawamsa, the historical chronicle of Sri Lanka, records that he invaded the island in 1247, ostensibly to acquire the Buddha's relic that Sri Lanka already held. King Parakramabahu II of Dambadeniya sent his nephew Prince Veerabahu against the unexpected invasion, and Chandrabhanu was defeated. His forces, using poison darts, then occupied the Jaffna kingdom in the north of the island, where he secured the Tamil throne around 1255. In 1258 Jatavarman Sundara Pandyan I of the Pandyan Dynasty intervened and made him submit to Pandyan rule, with an annual tribute of precious jewels and elephants.

When Chandrabhanu attacked the south again from the north, Prince Jatavarman Veera Pandyan, brother of the emperor Jatavarman Sundara Pandyan, intervened, and Chandrabhanu was killed in the fighting. Veera Pandyan planted the Pandyan bull victory flag at the Koneswaram temple at Konamalai.

His son Savakanmaindan inherited the northern throne and submitted to Pandyan rule. Marco Polo, landing at Trincomalee, described the people of the Jaffna kingdom under King Sendemain as eating rice and meat, and the land as rich in rubies and other precious stones. When Savakanmaindan stopped paying tribute and invaded the south, the Pandyans under Maravarman Kulasekara Pandyan I defeated him in the late 1270s, and later installed Kulasekara Cinkaiariyan, an Aryacakravarti, as king. Place names of the Jaffna peninsula still recall the episode: Chavakacheri means a Javanese settlement and Chavahakottai a Javanese fort.
chandragiri: The fort of Chandragiri was built in the 11th century by Immadi Narasimha Yadava Raya. Its walls enclose the Raja Mahal, or royal palace, the Rani Mahal, eight ruined temples of the Saivite and Vaishnavite pantheons and other ruined structures. The palace, an example of the architecture of the Vijayanagar period, was built of stone, brick and lime mortar without timber, and its crowning towers carry Hindu architectural elements.

Chandragiri was under the rule of Vijayanagar from 1367 and rose to prominence under Saluva Narasimha Raya. It became the fourth capital of the Vijayanagara Empire when the Rayas moved their seat here after the sultans of Golconda attacked Penukonda. In 1646 the fort was annexed to the territory of Golconda.

After the decline of Vijayanagara, the King of Mysore ordered Bisaya Nayaka, a palaygara of Harapanayakanahalli, the present Mulbagal in Karnataka, to make war on the Sultan of Chandragiri. His army was reported to have killed everyone inside the fort. With the Sultan's death Chandragiri fell under Mysore suzerainty, and from 1792 onward it sank into obscurity.

Chandragiri lies in Tirupati district of Andhra Pradesh and is the headquarters of Chandragiri mandal, within the limits of the Tirupati Urban Development Authority. The Raja Mahal is now an archaeological museum, and the fort and palace are in the care of the Archaeological Survey of India. Next to Chandragiri stands the Kalyana Venkateswara Temple at Srinivasamangapuram, from which the stone footpaths of the Srivari Mettu lead up to Tirumala.
chandragupta-i: Chandragupta was the son of the Gupta king Ghatotkacha and grandson of the dynasty's founder, Gupta. The Allahabad Pillar inscription calls both of these earlier rulers Maharaja, 'great king'. Chandragupta took the higher title Maharajadhiraja, 'great king of kings', and issued gold coins, which suggests that he was the first imperial ruler of the dynasty.

He certainly reigned in the first quarter of the 4th century, but the exact period is uncertain. V. A. Smith and P. L. Gupta date his accession to 319-320, the supposed start of the Gupta era, though this is an assumption. D. C. Sircar and R. C. Majumdar think the era marks the coronation of his son Samudragupta. He probably reigned long, since he appears to have named his son successor in old age.

Little is known of Chandragupta beyond his ancestry, his marriage and the expansion of Gupta power implied by his title. He married the Lichchhavi princess Kumaradevi. The Lichchhavis were an ancient clan whose seat had been Vaishali in present-day Bihar, though which Lichchhavi kingdom she came from is uncertain. Samudragupta is called Lichchhavi-dauhitra, 'Lichchhavi daughter's son', in Gupta inscriptions, which suggests the family thought the marriage important.

Most historians accept that the marriage helped Chandragupta extend his power. Because Samudragupta's inscription lists the kings he defeated, scholars infer that his father's kingdom did not reach far beyond Prayaga in the west and excluded southern Bengal. R. C. Majumdar thought it may have covered the whole of present-day Bihar and parts of Uttar Pradesh and Bengal. Ashvini Agarwal holds that it included central and eastern Uttar Pradesh and Bihar but not Bengal.

Gold coins found at Mathura, Ayodhya, Varanasi, Bayana and Hajipur show portraits of Chandragupta and Kumaradevi with the legend Lichchhavayah, 'the Lichchhavis', and a goddess seated on a lion on the reverse. Scholars disagree whether Chandragupta, Samudragupta or the Lichchhavis issued them. The goddess is variously identified as Durga or Lakshmi.

The Allahabad Pillar inscription and the Eran inscription of Samudragupta state that Chandragupta chose his son as the next king, and the former suggests he gave up the throne in old age. Some coins of a Gupta ruler named Kacha raise a debate: Kacha may be another name for Samudragupta or an elder brother who succeeded first. Samudragupta further expanded the empire.
chandragupta-ii: Chandragupta II was a son of Samudragupta and queen Dattadevi, as his own inscriptions attest. The official Gupta genealogy has him succeed his father directly. The Sanskrit play Devichandraguptam, read with other evidence, suggests that an elder brother named Ramagupta reigned first. In the play Ramagupta agrees to surrender his queen Dhruvadevi to a Shaka enemy when besieged, but Chandragupta goes to the enemy camp disguised as the queen and kills him, and later dethrones Ramagupta. Historians debate whether this narrative rests on real events or is fiction.

The Udayagiri inscription of his foreign minister Virasena shows that Chandragupta had a distinguished military career, and places his empire from the mouth of the Indus and northern Pakistan in the west to Bengal in the east, and from the Himalayan foothills to the Narmada River in the south. Inscriptions of c. 401 to 413 found in central India, together with the Western Kshatrapa coinage that ends abruptly in the last decade of the 4th century, point to his conquest of the Western Kshatrapas. Modern scholars generally identify him with King Chandra of the Delhi iron pillar inscription, though not with complete certainty.

He also built power through marriage. He married Kuvera-naga, apparently a princess of the Naga dynasty, and their daughter Prabhavatigupta married the Vakataka king Rudrasena II. After her husband's death in c. 390 she acted as regent for her minor sons for about twenty years, and some historians regard the Vakataka kingdom as practically part of the Gupta empire in that time. His queen Dhruvadevi was the mother of his successor Kumaragupta I.

Chandragupta's coins and inscriptions call him a devotee of Vishnu, yet his officers built a temple to Shiva at Udayagiri and made donations to a Buddhist monastery at Sanchi. The Chinese pilgrim Faxian spent about six years in the Gupta kingdom during his reign. He recorded no name for the king, but his description of a peaceful and prosperous land is generally taken to be true, though idealised.

A later tradition places nine scholars, the Navaratnas, at the court of Vikramaditya. The text that names them is considered a later forgery, and there is no evidence that they were contemporaries. Several scholars nevertheless think the poet Kalidasa may have been a court poet of Chandragupta.
chandragupta-maurya: There are no historical facts about Chandragupta's origins and early life, only legends, and the narrative of his reign is deduced mainly from a few fragments in Greek and Roman sources and a few Indian religious texts, all written centuries after his death. Plutarch says that in his youth he saw Alexander the Great during the invasion of India, which led one scholar to propose a birth after 350 BCE. The Sanskrit play Mudrarakshasa calls him Vrishala, a word that one later commentator read as meaning a shudra, while the historian Radha Kumud Mukherjee argued that it means the best of kings.

He rose in the unrest after Alexander's death in 323 BCE, in Magadha, a region then ruled by the unpopular Nanda dynasty. The exact chronology remains debated. His conquest of Magadha is generally dated to about 322 to 319 BCE and his expansion into the Punjab to about 317 to 312 BCE, though some scholars think he first consolidated in the Punjab, and an alternative chronology places these events in about 311 to 305 BCE. According to Mudrarakshasa, his mentor Chanakya assisted him and later became his minister. The Roman writer Justin says Chandragupta led the people in killing Alexander's Greek governors, and then oppressed those he had freed.

Seleucus I Nicator, who had established the Seleucid Empire at Babylon, confronted him between about 305 and 303 BCE, intending to retake the former Persian satrapies along the Indus. The two formed a dynastic marriage alliance, with Seleucus receiving five hundred elephants and Chandragupta gaining control of the regions bordering the Indus. The administration was decentralised, with provinces, local governments and a council of ministers.

Digambara Jain accounts say that Chandragupta abdicated in favour of his son Bindusara and became a monk under Bhadrabahu at Shravanabelagola in Karnataka, where he fasted to death. These legends developed about 900 years later; contemporary Greek evidence says he drank wine, hunted and performed Vedic sacrifices, and no contemporary source supports his conversion to Jainism.

His reign is called the sheet anchor of Indian chronology, because in 1793 Sir William Jones identified him with the Sandracottus of Greek and Roman writers, allowing Indian and Greek history to be dated together. The empire he founded reached its peak under his grandson Ashoka. Western and Indian historians differ in their views of him, the latter often presenting him as the founder of the first Indian nation.
chandrapur: Chandrapur, earlier called Chanda, the official name until 1964, is a city and municipal corporation in Chandrapur district, Maharashtra, at the confluence of the Erai and Zarpat rivers. By tradition the place was once called Lokapura, then Indpur, and finally Chandrapur. According to the founding legend, the Gond king Khandkya Ballal Sah, afflicted with tumours, found a healing spring on the dry bed of the Zarpat River. The Achaleshwar Temple was raised there after the deity appeared to him in a dream, and he later founded the fortified city.

The area lies on terrain rich in coal and is called a geological museum for its variety of rocks, minerals and fossils. There are many Stone Age sites in the district, and signs of pottery suggest settlement in Neolithic times.

The area passed through many hands. Between 322 BCE and 187 BCE it belonged to the Maurya Empire, then to the Shunga Empire until 78 BCE and to the Satavahana Empire from the 1st century BCE to the 2nd century CE. The Vakataka dynasty ruled from the mid-3rd century CE to 550, followed by the Kalachuri dynasty in the 6th and 7th centuries, the Rashtrakuta dynasty between the 7th and 10th centuries and the Chalukya dynasty to the 12th century. The Seuna (Yadava) dynasty of Devagiri held a kingdom including the area from about 850 to 1334.

The Gond kings built the city's walled fort, with strong walls 15 to 20 feet high and four main gates, and the Mahakali temple, built around the 16th century by Dhundya Ram Sah. The Bhonsles of Nagpur took Chandrapur in 1751 during the Maratha period. When the last Bhonsle ruler, Raghuji Bhonsle III, died in 1853 without issue, it was annexed to British India under the Doctrine of Lapse. In 1956 the district was transferred to Bombay state, and in May 1960 it became part of Maharashtra.

Chandrapur had a population of about 518,000 at the 2011 census, and Marathi is spoken by most people, with Gondi spoken by most of the Gonds. It is a centre of coal mining. The old city, with the fort and the Anchaleshwar Temple, where the Gond kings' samadhi stands, lies at the river confluence.

The Tadoba Andhari Tiger Reserve lies about 30 kilometres north of the city. The Chandrapur Super Thermal Power Station, whose foundation stone was laid in 1977, supplies a large share of the state's electricity.
chandrayaan-3: Chandrayaan-3 is the third mission of the Chandrayaan programme, a series of lunar-exploration missions developed by ISRO. Its name comes from the Sanskrit chandra, Moon, and yana, craft. ISRO had earlier launched Chandrayaan-2, with an orbiter, a lander and a rover. Its lander lost contact with mission control, deviated from its intended trajectory while attempting to land near the lunar south pole, and crashed. Chandrayaan-3 consisted of a lander, Vikram, and a rover, Pragyan, as replacements for those of Chandrayaan-2, together with a propulsion module. The mission aimed to land safely and softly on the Moon, to show the rover driving there, and to carry out experiments on the lunar surface materials.

Chandrayaan-3 was launched on 14 July 2023 aboard an LVM3 M4 rocket from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh. It entered lunar orbit on 5 August, and on 17 August the Vikram lander separated from the propulsion module, which had carried it to a lunar orbit of 100 kilometres.

On 23 August 2023 the lander fired its four engines as a braking manoeuvre at 30 kilometres above the Moon. It then rotated from a horizontal to a vertical position using eight smaller thrusters. It slowed to roughly 150 metres, where it hovered for about 30 seconds to find a good landing spot, and touched down near the lunar south pole, at 69 degrees south, at 12:33 UTC.

The rover's laser-induced breakdown spectroscope reported sulfur near the south pole, and ISRO released temperature profiles from the top 10 centimetres of the lunar surface, in which a high range of 70 °C near the surface was not expected. The lander also made a short hop of about 40 centimetres. The lander and rover were built to operate for one lunar daylight period, or 14 Earth days, and not to endure the night temperatures of minus 120 °C. The rover was put into sleep mode on 3 September, and neither responded to wake-up calls later in September.

With the landing, ISRO became the fourth national space agency to land successfully on the Moon, after the Soviet space programme, NASA and CNSA, and the first to make a soft landing near the lunar south pole. The Prime Minister of India, Narendra Modi, named the touchdown point Station Shiv Shakti and declared 23 August National Space Day. The live stream of the landing on ISRO's YouTube channel had eight million concurrent viewers, the highest on YouTube for a live video. ISRO chairman S. Somanath said that the agency had learnt a lot from its failure and corrected it.
changan: The site south of the Wei River in central Xi'an has been inhabited since Neolithic times. The Yangshao culture had a major centre at Banpo to its south from around 5000 to around 4300 BCE. Fenghao, the twin capitals of the Western Zhou, lay to its southwest, and the Qin had their capital at nearby Xianyang, north of the Wei. Chang'an itself was only a small village under the Qin. When Liu Bang founded the Han dynasty he first ruled from Luoyang, but he accepted the advice of the soldier Lou Jing and the general Zhang Liang that the Guanzhong Region, the Zhou and Qin heartland, could support a larger core population and offered much greater natural protection.

Liu Bang moved his court to the Changle Palace in 200 BCE. The neighbouring Weiyang Palace served as the imperial palace of many later dynasties and became the largest palace ever built, covering 4.8 km2, before its destruction under the early Tang. Chang'an was the Western Jin capital from 312 to 316, then capital of the Han-Zhao, the Former Qin and the Later Qin. Under the Later Qin ruler Yao Xing it became an important hub for Buddhism in China.

In 582 Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty built a new capital southeast of the ruined Han city and named it Daxing. It was renamed Chang'an in 618, when Li Yuan proclaimed himself Emperor Gaozu of Tang. Along with Constantinople and Baghdad, Tang Chang'an was one of the largest cities in the world. Most modern estimates put the population within its walls at around 800,000 to 1,000,000. In 904 the warlord Zhu Wen forcibly moved most of the remaining population to Luoyang. The city lost importance, became a regional centre again under the Northern Song, and was renamed Xi'an under the Ming, who built walls around the former Sui and Tang palace district, about an eighth of the medieval city's size.

Tang Chang'an was laid out as a rectangle of about 78 km2 inside walls 5.5 m high, divided by eight avenues into nine districts and 160 walled wards. It had a Palace City reserved for the emperor, an Imperial City for administrators and an Outer City with about 110 wards, two markets and religious institutions. Grain for the residents came from the surrounding region and from granaries supplied by canals. The site lies in the modern city of Xi'an, in Shaanxi Province.
changchub-gyaltsen: Under the Sakya regime, whose regents or ponchen ruled Tibet under Mongol Yuan overlordship, Central Tibet was divided into thirteen myriarchies. One was Phagmodru, centred on the palace of Nêdong and headed by a lord of the noble Lang Family, which also ruled the monastery of Thel. Changchub Gyaltsen was born into this lineage in 1302, the son of Rinchen Kyab and his second wife Tramon Bumkyi. Ordained a monk at nine, he went to the Sakya monastery at fourteen, where his tutor persuaded him that he would make an excellent administrator.

In 1322 he replaced his deposed uncle Gyaltsen Kyab as lord of Phagmodru, receiving a seal with a tiger's head from the great khan Sidibala. He enlarged and walled the Nêdong palace and ruled by Buddhist principles. His claim to the estate of Yazang angered the Sakya: the official Wangtson seized him at a banquet in 1336 and held him for three months, and after fresh fighting in 1346 the ponchen Gyalwa Zangpo captured him at a parley and had him tortured. Pelted with mud on entering Sakya, he reportedly said, "Now I eat the mud of Sakya – soon I will be eating Sakya itself".

A shift of alliances freed him, and his outnumbered troops beat back the Sakya. By 1349 he held most of Ü, including Lhasa; a coalition attack failed in 1353, and in 1354 his army under Rinchen Zangpo brought most of Tsang under his authority, though taking power was a longer process than the date suggests. After a conference he convened at Sakya in 1358, forces from Lhatse under Wangtson were quickly defeated; Wangtson was imprisoned and 464 of his men were blinded.

Changchub Gyaltsen declined royal titles and took the Tibetan title desi, regent, while accepting the title Tai Situ from the great khan in 1357. He revived the dress of the old Tibetan court, kept Mongols and mongolised Tibetans out of authority and set the tax at one sixth of the produce. His law code in 15 chapters was milder than Mongol law but divided society into nine classes. A patron of religion, he had many copies of the Kangyur made and in 1351 or 1352 founded the monastery of Tsetang. He died on 21 November 1364 and was succeeded by his nephew Jamyang Shakya Gyaltsen; his successors governed Tibet independently for over eighty years.
changchun: Changchun lies in the middle portion of the Northeast China Plain at a moderate elevation of 250 to 350 metres, with a small area of low mountains in the east, the highest being Laodaodong Mountain at 711 metres. It has a humid continental climate, with long, cold, windy but dry winters from November to March and hot, humid summers. Its name means long spring in Chinese. The municipality is administered as a sub-provincial city of Jilin province.

Changchun began as a small trading post and frontier village, dealing mainly in furs and other natural products. In 1800 the Jiaqing Emperor selected a village on the east bank of the Yitong River and named it Changchun Ting. At the end of the eighteenth century peasants from overpopulated provinces such as Shandong and Hebei began to settle in the region, and in 1889 the village was promoted to a city known as Changchun Fu. In May 1898 it received its first railway station, at Kuancheng, on the southern branch of the Chinese Eastern Railway built by the Russian Empire between Harbin and Lüshun.

After Russia lost the southern section of this line in the Russo-Japanese War of 1904–1905, the Kuancheng station became the last Russian station on the branch. The next station to the south, the new Japanese Changchun station, became the first of the South Manchuria Railway. The Treaty of Portsmouth transferred the railway between Changchun and Port Arthur to Japan in 1906, and the Japanese government sent planners and engineers to choose the best site for a new station.

On 10 March 1932 the capital of Manchukuo, a Japan-controlled puppet state in Manchuria, was established in Changchun, and on 13 March it was renamed Hsinking, meaning new capital. The Emperor Puyi lived in the Imperial Palace, now a museum. The region experienced harsh suppression, forced conscription and labour and brutal warfare on the civilian population, and at the same time rapid industrialisation and militarisation. On 20 August 1945 the Soviet Red Army captured the city and renamed it Changchun; Soviet forces remained until 1946.

Changchun became the capital of Jilin in 1954. Construction of the First Automobile Works began in 1953, with Soviet technical support, and production of the Jiefang CA-10 truck, based on the Soviet ZIS-150, started in 1956. In 1958 it introduced the Hongqi limousines. The city is known as China's City of Automobiles and is home to Jilin University and Northeast Normal University. Among its sights are the Badabu, the group of buildings of the former eight Manchukuo ministries, the Museum of the Manchu State Imperial Palace and the Jilin Provincial Museum.
changnyeong-county: The name Changnyeong means prosperous peace, from the Sino-Korean roots chang, prosperity, and nyeong, peace. The Nakdong River flows through the county, and part of its basin is occupied by the Upo wetland, the largest wetland in Korea, estimated to have formed about 140 million years ago. It covers more than 2,310,000 square metres across the townships of Yueo, Ibang, Daehap and Daeji and holds over 340 species of endangered plants, among them Euryale ferox, as well as 62 kinds of wild birds and 28 of fish.

In the early Three Kingdoms period Changnyeong was the seat of Bihwa Gaya, a member of the Gaya confederacy later conquered by Silla. The territory of Yeongsan was established in 1631, and Changnyeong joined it in 1637. On 24 May 1895 Changnyeong and Yeongsan became separate counties under Daegu, and on 4 August 1896 they passed to South Gyeongsang Province. On 1 April 1914 the two counties were merged and divided into 15 townships; Changnyeong township became a town in 1960 and Namji in 1963.

The Upo wetland was designated a natural monument in 1933, under Japanese occupation, and after the Cultural Properties Protection Law of 3 December 1962 it was listed as the Changnyeong swan habitat. That status was cancelled in 1973 when migratory birds were found to have declined, and the wetland was protected again as a natural preserve after a new survey in 2001.

The county covers 532.72 square kilometres in two towns and 12 townships, with 61,789 people in 2011, and its government sits in Changnyeong Town, the largest town. The Bugok hot springs under Deokam Mountain, found in 1973, were made a national tourist attraction in 1977.
changsha: Changsha lies in northeastern Hunan, in the lower reaches of the Xiang River and the western part of the Changliu Basin. Most of the rivers in the area belong to the Xiang system, and fifteen tributaries flow into the Xiang. The city has a humid subtropical climate with distinct seasons, long and very hot summers, and a mean January temperature of 5.3 °C. It forms a metropolitan region with Zhuzhou and Xiangtan, known as the Changzhutan City Cluster. The name means long sandy place and is attested as early as the eleventh century BCE, when a vassal lord sent King Cheng of Zhou a gift described as a Changsha softshell turtle.

Settlement is said to have begun around 3000 BCE with the proliferation of the Longshan culture, although there is no firm evidence of such a link; people certainly lived in the area during the Bronze Age. The name appears in the Yi Zhou Shu, written before the Qin, and the Qin set up the Changsha Commandery. In the Western Han dynasty the Changsha Kingdom was established. The historian Ying Shao wrote in the second century that the Qin use of the name for the area continued its old name. In the Tang dynasty the Tongguan Kiln in Changsha produced the world's earliest underglaze porcelain, which was exported to Western Asia, Africa and Europe.

During the period of the Five Dynasties Changsha was the capital of Southern Chu. In the Northern Song dynasty the Yuelu Academy, later Hunan University, was one of the four major private academies of the last thousand years. Under the Qing, Changsha was the capital of Hunan and prospered as one of China's chief rice markets. During the Taiping Rebellion rebels besieged the city for three months, in 1852 or 1854, but it never fell. The rebels moved on to Wuhan, and Changsha became the principal base for the government's suppression of the rebellion.

Changsha is the capital of Hunan and among the first cities designated a National Historical and Cultural City in China. It has a history of more than 2,400 years of urban construction. Its main industries include construction machinery and new materials, and it is home to the Hunan Broadcasting System. Sights include the Yuelu Academy and the statue of the young Mao Zedong on Orange Isle. Changshanese, a kind of Xiang Chinese, is spoken in the downtown area, and Hunan cuisine, hot and spicy, remains the most popular.
changu-narayan-temple: The temple stands on the hill of Changu, also called Dolagiri, about 12 km east of Kathmandu and a few miles north of Bhaktapur, with the Manohara River flowing beside it. It was built in the 4th century and is one of the oldest Hindu temples in Nepal. The hilltop was once surrounded by a forest of champak trees and a small village. According to tradition a Kashmiri king gave his daughter Champak in marriage to the prince of Bhaktapur, and the temple is considered to be named after her.

The Sanskrit inscription on its pillar was made by King Manadeva of the Lichhavi dynasty, who reigned from 464 to 505. Georg Buhler and Bhagawanla Indraji first transcribed and published it in 1885 in Twenty-three Inscriptions from Nepal. In 1899 Sylvain Lévi was allowed to do research in Nepal with the help of the Rana prime minister Bhim Shamshere, but the priests refused him entry to the compound, so he published the text and a translation in Le Népal from rubbings. Later readings were made by Gnoli, Naraharinath, Vajracharya, Joshi and Khanal.

The temple has suffered repeated thefts: statues of Krishna in 1975, Kileswor Mahadev in 1977 and Surya in 1980, the main image in 1981, and in September 2001 three images, among them the gilded metal statue of King Bhupalendra Malla that stood with one of his wife Bhuvan Laxmi at the main gate. The 2015 earthquake destroyed the temple, which was rebuilt with Chinese support over five years.

The two-tiered pagoda rises from a plinth about four feet high that spreads its load like a mat foundation, with walls of sun-dried brick inside and fired brick outside. Since 1979 it has been one of the seven monument zones of the Kathmandu Valley World Heritage Site, and a museum nearby shows objects such as a rhino-skin shield and a raincoat made of leaves.
channel-islands: The Channel Islands are an archipelago in the English Channel, to the west of the Cotentin Peninsula and off the Normandy coast. Channel Islands is a geographical term, not a political unit, first used around 1830, possibly by the Royal Navy. The two major islands, Jersey and Guernsey, make up 99 per cent of the population and 92 per cent of the area. The highest point is Les Platons in Jersey at 143 metres.

Humans lived on what is now Jersey at least 250,000 to 200,000 years ago, as La Cotte de St Brelade shows Neanderthal occupation when the island was connected to the mainland. Rising sea levels detached the islands in the Mesolithic period. Dolmens, the burial mound of La Hougue Bie in Jersey and the statue menhirs of Guernsey show a population large and organised enough for constructions of considerable size. In the sixth century Christian missionaries visited, and saints such as Samson of Dol and Helier are associated with the islands.

In 933 Raoul, King of Western Francia, granted the islands to William Longsword, and they were annexed to the Duchy of Normandy. When King John lost mainland Normandy to King Philip II of France, he kept control of the islands, and by the Treaty of Paris of 1259 Henry III surrendered his claim to the duchy while retaining them. Since around 1290 they have been split into two bailiwicks. In the Wars of the Three Kingdoms Jersey held out for the Royalist cause and gave refuge to Charles, Prince of Wales, while Presbyterian Guernsey favoured Parliament. Charles II rewarded George Carteret, bailiff and governor of Jersey, with a grant of land in America, which he named New Jersey.

The islands form two self-governing Crown Dependencies, the Bailiwick of Jersey and the Bailiwick of Guernsey, which includes Alderney, Sark and Herm. Neither is part of the United Kingdom, which is responsible for their defence and international relations. Each has its own laws, elections and representative bodies. The capitals are Saint Helier and Saint Peter Port. German forces occupied the islands in the Second World War: the British government demilitarised them in June 1940, and 6,600 of 50,000 people left Jersey and 17,000 of 42,000 left Guernsey, among them thousands of children evacuated with their schools.
chanyu: Chanyu, also written Shanyu, was the title of the supreme rulers of the Inner Asian nomads for eight centuries, until it was superseded by the title Khagan in 402 CE. It is short for Chengli Gutu Chanyu. The ruling Luandi clan of the Xiongnu used it most widely, in the time of the Qin dynasty (221 to 206 BCE) and the Han dynasty (206 BCE to 220 CE). The Chinese later also used it, infrequently, as a name for Tujue leaders. The Book of Han explains the words. According to it, the Xiongnu called heaven chengli and a child gutu, while chanyu meant a vast and great appearance.

Scholars have proposed other origins for the title. L. Rogers and Edwin G. Pulleyblank argue that chanyu may be equivalent to the later title tarkhan, with an original Chinese pronunciation approximating the sound darxan. Bailey derives it from a Proto-Iranian root meaning to speak or command, and compares a Saka title in which the meaning shifted in the same way. Related forms that have been compared include the Khotanese ttarkana and the Ossetian tærxon.

Alexander Vovin tentatively proposes a Yeniseian origin for the full title, built from four roots meaning heaven, son or child, north or the lower reaches of the Yenisei, and prince, so that the whole would mean Son of Heaven, Ruler of the North. Dybo instead derives it from a Turkic root meaning vast as the sky, and compares the Old Uyghur words tarkan and tarkar. Her Old Uyghur tarkan is not listed in Wilkens (2021), and Caferoğlu (1968) glosses it as to feel embarrassed or to get tired of, so that this comparison is disputed.
chanyuan-treaty: Relations between the Song, founded in 960, and the Liao were at first cordial while the Song conquered the southern states. In 979 the Song destroyed Northern Han, a Shatuo Turk state under Liao protection, but what concerned them more was Liao's hold on the Sixteen Prefectures, which included modern Beijing. Emperor Taizong's march on them ended in rout at the Battle of Gaoliang River, and a second attempt in three columns in 986 was defeated on every front. From 999 Emperor Shengzong of Liao attacked the Song every year.

In 1004 Shengzong led a campaign in person and camped about 160 kilometres north of the Song capital, Bianjing. Emperor Zhenzong reluctantly marched north to Chan Prefecture, the first large town beyond the Yellow River, whose defences had been prepared by the planner Kou Zhun. The emperor's arrival lifted Song morale, and late in 1004 a Song crossbow killed the Liao general Xiao Talin, crippling the Khitan offensive. Wang Jizhong, a Song officer captured in 1003 and given rank by the Liao, urged peace on Empress Dowager Xiao, who held power at the Liao court.

A ceasefire was reached in January 1005, and the envoy Cao Liyong concluded the agreement with Empress Dowager Xiao. The Song were to send 200,000 bolts of raw silk and 100,000 taels of silver every year. Existing moats and city walls could be repaired, but no new ones built. The two states became sibling nations: Shengzong called Zhenzong his elder brother, and Zhenzong called the Empress Dowager his aunt. Wang Jizhong had persuaded her to give up territorial claims.

The treaty brought about a century of relative peace, which lasted until the Song and the Jurchen Jin agreed in the Alliance Conducted at Sea to invade Liao together. Liao used the payments to build its central capital, Zhongjing, and a wide trade network, while the Song kept disputed territory for a burden far smaller than its military spending, though the treaty also admitted the loss of the Sixteen Prefectures. Under pressure from Liao and Western Xia, the Song raised the payments in 1042 to 300,000 bolts and 200,000 taels. The framework shaped Song relations with Western Xia and Jin and was copied in East Asia until the Mongol Empire, and for the first time two Sons of Heaven recognised each other.
chao-cuo: Chao Cuo was born in Yuzhou, Henan. While a junior official in the Ministry of Ceremonies he was sent by Emperor Wen to study with Fu Sheng, an academician of the Qin dynasty who had hidden and partly recovered a copy of the Classic of History during the Qin purge of literature. His appointment in 155 BCE as Imperial Secretary in Chang'an made him one of the three most senior officials of the central government, known for his knowledge of warfare, agriculture, economics and frontier management.

His thinking drew on Legalist writers such as Shang Yang and Shen Buhai, and the essays of his preserved in the Book of Han show no influence of Confucian ethics. He was among the first ministers to urge Emperor Wen to build up cavalry to match the Xiongnu, and advised using surrendered Xiongnu horsemen in Han armies. Like Jia Yi he argued for ending the heqin marriage and tribute treaty, but on practical grounds, since the Xiongnu had broken it again and again; it was abandoned only after the Battle of Mayi in 133 BCE.

In his memorandum Guard the Frontiers and Protect the Borders he judged the Xiongnu better on rough ground and at mounted archery, but weaker on level plains against Han iron armour, crossbows and infantry. His frontier towns were to hold at least a thousand households, with double walls 150 paces apart and sandy fields to show intruders' footprints, settled first by convicts, then by slaves and volunteers, with houses, tools, food and rewards. The plan influenced Emperor Wu's colonisation of the Hexi Corridor. He also wrote of peasant families driven by sudden taxes to borrow at two hundred per cent interest and sell their land to merchants.

Chao Cuo helped lead the court's efforts to reduce the subordinate kingdoms. When the kings of seven kingdoms plotted rebellion, his enemies at court, among them Yuan Ang, persuaded Emperor Jing that his death would appease them. After his execution the emperor soon saw that the claims were false, as Liu Bi, King of Wu, and his allies rose in open revolt. The historian Nishijima Sadao later cited Chao's account of farmers and merchants as evidence of the contrast between their lives in the Former Han.
chao-phraya-river: The Chao Phraya begins at the confluence of the Ping and Nan rivers at Nakhon Sawan and flows south for 372 kilometres to Bangkok and the Gulf of Thailand. At Chai Nat it splits off the Tha Chin River, which runs parallel and reaches the gulf at Samut Sakhon. Its watershed, 157,924 square kilometres, is the largest in Thailand.

The plain falls only about 80 metres over 500 kilometres from the hills to the sea, so the rivers run sluggishly and boats could be poled or paddled upstream for most of the year, which made water the most convenient transport before the modern era. The delta took its present form late: the coast reached the site of Bangkok between 3000 and 1000 BCE and settled near its present position by 500 CE.

The basin saw the rise of some of the earliest civilisations of Southeast Asia, notably Dvaravati from the 7th to the 11th century. The river was crucial to the Lavo kingdom and to its successors, and formed the basis of the Ayodhya Kingdom, incorporated into the Ayutthaya Kingdom in the 14th century. Rice growing intensified from the 13th century under Sukhothai and Ayutthaya with the introduction of floating rice from Bengal.
During the Ayutthaya period shortcut canals were dug across river loops, the first in 1538 on the order of King Chairachathirat, and the river's course has since followed many of them.

Rattanakosin, now Bangkok, was founded in 1782 on the east bank, a position that protected it from Burmese invasions from the west. Canalisation and cultivation of the southern swamps followed, and Thailand began to export rice in 1855. The name Chao Phraya is documented in writing only from the reign of King Mongkut in the 19th century; earlier maps usually called the river the Menam. It probably comes from Bang Chao Phraya, the settlement now called Samut Prakan, recorded from about 1660.

The provinces along the river, from Nakhon Sawan to Samut Prakan, include Ayutthaya, Nonthaburi and Bangkok, among the most historically significant and densely populated in Thailand. Its many canals, called khlong, irrigate the rice paddies of the plain, and in Bangkok the river is a major transport artery for ferries and long-tail boats. The original swamp forests of the lowlands have almost entirely been cleared for farming and cities.
chaonians: The name is first attested indirectly in fragments of Hecataeus of Miletus, about 500 BCE, and directly by Thucydides around 429 BCE; its etymology is uncertain. How the Chaonians formed remains unsolved, as archaeology shows a sharper break between Bronze Age tumulus burials and later settlements in Chaonia than in other parts of Epirus. There is today a broad consensus that they spoke the North-West Doric dialect of Greek, and their inscriptions, all in Greek, begin around 329 BCE. They traced their descent to the Trojan prince Helenus and Andromache, a genealogy whose core scholars such as Dakaris and Hammond date to the 6th century BCE.

In the 5th century BCE the Chaonians were a tribal state living in a collection of villages rather than a city, though they called their community a polis. Thucydides says their leaders were chosen each year and names two, Photius and Nikanor, of the ruling lineage; in the 4th century the leader was called prostates. Most people lived in rural settlements until Phoenice developed in the late 4th century BCE, with Bouthroton as its harbour. Pastoral life was prominent, and Roman poets such as Virgil made Chaonia a model of the bucolic. The Chaonians worshipped Zeus, Athena, Artemis, Asclepius, Pan and Poseidon, and built their own treasury at the sanctuary of Dodona.

An account in Strabo, probably going back to Theopompus of Chios, says the Chaonians were the most powerful people of the region before the Molossians, which may preserve the memory of an early Chaonian expansion. Molossian growth brought them into a unified Epirote state between about 340 and 295 BCE; Pyrrhus of Epirus founded Antigonia in the Drino valley around 296 or 295 BCE, and elite Chaonian warriors fought in his Italian campaign of 280 to 275 BCE. In the Third Macedonian War they fought as allies of Rome while the Molossians and most Thesprotians opposed it, so Chaonia escaped the destruction and enslavement that followed Rome's annexation of Epirus.
chaoyang-liaoning: Chaoyang is a prefecture-level city in western Liaoning, bordering Hebei province and the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region on the west. Its land area is almost 20,000 square kilometres, the largest of any prefecture-level city in Liaoning, and its total population is about three million. The name means morning sun and comes from a poem in the Shijing, one of the oldest collections of Chinese poetry in which a fenghuang bird sings towards the morning sun. A mountain in the east has been called Fenghuang Mountain since ancient times, and in 1778 it was linked with the poem and the city given its present name.

The over five-thousand-year-old Niuheliang ruins of the Hongshan culture have made Chaoyang known as one of the birthplaces of ancient Chinese culture. The area first appears in Chinese records as Liucheng County in the early Han period.
