In 342 Murong Huang, king of the Former Yan, made it his capital under the name Longcheng, the Dragon City, and it remained the capital through the Later Yan and Northern Yan periods. The building of the Longxiang temple in 345 began Buddhist culture in Northeast China.

Under the Sui and Tang dynasties Liucheng was the seat of Ying Prefecture, a prosperous multi-cultural city whose people included Khitans, Kumo Xi, Mohe, Shiwei, Goguryeo, Göktürks and Sogdians. The Khitan general Li Guangbi, who did much to put down the An Lushan rebels, was born there. The city declined after that rebellion; the Liao dynasty established Ba Prefecture there, later renamed Xingzhong, and it was abandoned under the Yuan.

Under the Qing, Mongol banners held the region, and Chinese peasants settled in Mongol lands despite an official prohibition. Chaoyang County was established in 1778. In 1891 the secret society Jindandao rose in rebellion, massacring tens of thousands of Mongols and forcing the survivors to flee northward. The People's Republic of China placed Chaoyang in Liaoning in 1955, and it became a prefecture-level city in 1984.

Chaoyang is called China's fossil city. Many palaeontological discoveries have been made there, among them the early birds Longipteryx and Sapeornis, named after the city, and the feathered dinosaur Microraptor, all in the Early Cretaceous Jiufotang Formation. Discoveries in the 1990s contributed to understanding of the origin of birds. Agriculture is the backbone of the local economy, and the city has an airport.
chapel-of-the-holy-shroud: Duke Carlo Emanuele I of Savoy commissioned a chapel for the Shroud from Ascanio Vitozzi and Carlo di Castellamonte in 1610 and 1611, but work stopped in 1624 with only the foundations laid. Charles Emmanuel II revived the project in 1657, urged by Cardinal Maurizio di Savoia, who remembered the fire of 1532 at Chambery that had damaged the Shroud. Amedeo di Castellamonte and the Swiss sculptor Bernardino Quadri designed a chapel raised 6–7 metres above the floor of the cathedral, reached by two staircases from its aisles and by a portal from the palace. Structural problems halted the work, and Quadri was removed in 1666.

Guarino Guarini took over in 1668, strengthened the thin walls, decorated the pilasters with symbols of the Passion and reshaped the plan around three vestibules. He replaced the planned hemispherical dome with great arches that spread the weight, a drum of six arched windows and six niches, and six levels of six small arches set on a hexagonal plan, each level smaller and turned against the one below. A twelve-pointed star with the dove of the Holy Spirit crowns the lantern. The dome was completed on 27 October 1679, and Guarini said the inaugural mass on 15 May 1680. After his death in 1683, Antonio Bertola finished the black marble altar, where the Shroud was placed in 1694.

The chapel is regarded as one of the masterpieces of Baroque architecture, and features such as its ribbed dome derive from Islamic architecture. It was closed in 1990 after a piece of marble fell. On the night of 11 to 12 April 1997 a short circuit started a fire that badly damaged it; firefighters broke the glass case and saved the Shroud. Marble was found in 2007 at the original quarries of Frabosa Soprana, and the dome was taken apart and rebuilt. The chapel reopened on 27 September 2018, at a cost of over 30 million euros, and won a European Heritage Award in 2019.
chapultepec-castle: The castle stands at the entrance to Chapultepec Park, at a height of 2,325 metres above sea level. Chapultepec is the Nahuatl word chapoltepēc, meaning on the hill of the grasshopper, and the hill was a sacred place for the Aztecs. In August 1785 Viceroy Bernardo de Gálvez ordered a stately home built for himself at its highest point, to a plan by the engineer Francisco Bambitelli. Captain Manuel Agustín Mascaró took over the work, and was later accused of building a fortress from which to rebel against the Spanish Crown.

Gálvez died suddenly on 8 November 1786, which fuelled speculation that he was poisoned, though no evidence supports it. The Crown ordered the unfinished building auctioned, but no buyer came, and a later plan to house the General Archive of New Spain was not carried out. In 1803 Alexander von Humboldt condemned the sale of its windows to raise money, and in 1806 the municipal government of Mexico City bought it.

The building was abandoned during the Mexican War of Independence and for years afterwards. It became the Military College in 1833, and on 13 September 1847 the Niños Héroes died defending it when United States forces took it in the Mexican-American War. A mural above the main entrance honours them. The United States Marine Corps remembers the battle in the first line of its hymn, From the Halls of Montezuma, though the castle was built long after Montezuma's time.

When Maximilian von Hapsburg came to establish the Second Mexican Empire, the castle, then called Castillo de Miravalle, became the residence of the emperor and Empress Carlota in 1864. European and Mexican architects renovated it in a neoclassical style, a roof garden was made, and Maximilian had a straight boulevard laid to the city centre, which after the republic's return in 1867 became the Paseo de la Reforma. An observatory opened there in 1878 but lasted five years. In 1882 President Manuel González made the castle the presidential residence, and most later presidents lived there until Lázaro Cárdenas moved to Los Pinos in 1934.

In February 1939 Cárdenas established the castle as the National Museum of History, holding the collections of the former National Museum of Archaeology, History and Ethnography. The museum opened on 27 September 1944. With Iturbide Palace, it is one of only two royal palaces in North America to have been inhabited by monarchs. Its design was the model for the 13th Regiment Armory in Brooklyn, and it appears in films including Vera Cruz (1954) and Romeo + Juliet (1996).
chapultepec-peace-accords: The Salvadoran Civil War began with the coup of 15 October 1979 against President Carlos Humberto Romero. In October 1980 five left-wing groups joined to form the Farabundo Martí National Liberation Front (FMLN). The war killed between 70,000 and 80,000 people, and after ten years more than a million had been displaced. Talks between President José Napoleón Duarte's government and the guerrillas, with Archbishop Arturo Rivera y Damas as mediator, were held at La Palma in October 1984, at Ayagualo in November 1984, at Sesori in 1986 and in San Salvador in October 1987, without ending the war.

In 1989 the government of President Alfredo Cristiani and the FMLN asked UN Secretary-General Javier Pérez de Cuéllar to mediate, and Álvaro de Soto was named his special representative. The FMLN's offensive of November 1989 ended in a stalemate with 2,500 dead. An agreement at Geneva on 4 April 1990 set the rules of negotiation, and a meeting at Caracas on 21 May 1990 the agenda. A preliminary agreement was initialled on 31 December 1991.

The accords had nine chapters. The armed forces were to be purged of officers implicated in human rights abuses, made subordinate to civil authority and stripped of their intelligence service, and a Truth Commission was to investigate the worst violence of the war. The new police was to take 20 per cent of its members from the FMLN, 20 per cent from the old National Police and 60 per cent from neither. A Procurator for the Defense of Human Rights and a Supreme Electoral Tribunal were created, and land in conflict zones was to go to demobilised fighters.

Fighting ended on 1 February 1992, after the Legislative Assembly passed a National Reconciliation Law granting an amnesty on 23 January. Land distribution and the legalisation of the FMLN were delayed, and the end of the armed conflict was officially marked on 15 December 1992. In 1997 Boutros Boutros-Ghali closed the UN's peace process, judging compliance acceptable though incomplete. A Monument to the Reconciliation inaugurated in 2017 was demolished in January 2024.
char-bouba-war: After the disintegration of the Sanhaja Berber confederation, which had helped to found the Almoravid dynasty, its weaker clans paid tribute to stronger ones and turned to Islamic learning and piety; they became known as the Zawaya, or maraboutic tribes. In the 15th century the Arab Banu Maghfar, part of the larger Beni Hassan coalition, arrived in the south-western Sahara and extorted payment from the Zawaya in return for a protection they often failed to give.

Some historians, following a thesis first put forward by Boubacar Barry, link the war to the French trading post founded at Saint-Louis in 1659, which competed with the nomads for slaves and for the grain of the Senegal River valley; others point out that the caravan trade remained strong. South of the river the Atlantic slave trade had made wars and raids more frequent, and many Wolof and Fula, among them the Torodbe scholars of Futa Toro, turned to Islam as a counterweight to their rulers.

The scholar Awbek b. Ashfaga, who took the title Nasr al-Din, protector of the faith, called for an Islamic state modelled on the society of the early Caliphs. In early 1673 he entered Futa Toro preaching toubenan, repentance, and an end to slave raids; the population rose and the Silatigi Sire Sawa Laamu fled. The movement went on to take Jolof, Cayor and Waalo, and it blocked almost all French trade, since the marabouts refused to sell Muslims to Christians as slaves.

When Nasr al-Din tried to impose the zakat on the warrior tribes north of the river, a tributary named Bubba persuaded his chief to call on Haddi b. Ahmad b. Daman of the Trarza, and war broke out. Nasr al-Din's forces won three battles, but he was killed at Tirtilass in 1674. His successors quarrelled, the French and the restored Wolof and Fula rulers struck back, and in 1677 the last emir, al-Mukhtar Agd 'Abdullah, was cornered at Amadir and chose martyrdom rather than retreat.

The defeated Zawaya gave up all political and military claims and paid tribute to the Hassan: Hassani warriors could drink the milk of Zawaya herds, take a third of the water of their wells and be lodged for three days. A famine that began in 1676 lasted several years, and whole families sold themselves into slavery rather than starve. The war's militant preaching endured, and the first Fula jihads, in Futa Jallon and Futa Toro, were modelled directly on Nasr al-Din's movement.
charaideo: Charaideo lies in Charaideo district of Assam, about 30 km from the town of Sivasagar. Its name comes from the Tai-Ahom Che Rai Doi, the shining city on the hills, which became Charaideo or Charai-khorong in Assamese; the place was earlier called Che-Tam-Doi-Phi, the city of the sacred hill. Before the arrival of the first Ahom king, Chaolung Sukaphaa, it was a place of worship for local peoples such as the Moran and the Borahi.

Charaideo was Sukaphaa's permanent settlement, and according to the Tai-Bailung-Mohong Buranji, a manuscript in Tai, he was buried in his capital Che-Rai-Doi. Although later Ahom kings moved their capital many times, Charaideo remained the symbolic centre of their power and the place of the ancestral gods of the Ahoms. Kings and queens were buried there after long royal rituals, in maidams whose mounds on the hillocks have been likened to pyramids and which show the skill of the masons and sculptors of medieval Assam.

There were once more than 150 maidams. Some were plundered under British rule: the largest of those now unprotected, the Bali Maidam near Nimonagarh, is said to take its name from the excess sand, bali, around it, which hampered the British when they plundered it.

Charaideo is now known above all for its many maidams, the burial mounds of Ahom kings and members of the royal family. Only 30 maidams are protected by the Archaeological Survey of India and the Assam State Archaeology Department, and many of the others have been encroached on and damaged. The maidams were chosen for nomination by Prime Minister Narendra Modi in 2023 and formally recognised as a World Heritage Site on 26 July 2024.
charax-spasinou: The name Charax, probably from the Greek for a palisaded fort, was given to several fortified Seleucid towns; the city was also called Alexandria and Antiochia in Susiana. It stood on a large mound, Jabal Khuyabir at Naysān, near the meeting of the Karkheh, the ancient Eulaios, with the Tigris. Pliny the Elder described it on an artificial rise between the rivers, once about 1.9 kilometres from the sea with its own harbour, but by his time far inland as river silt pushed the coast back.

Alexander the Great founded the city in 324 BCE in place of a small Persian settlement, Durine, and settled Macedonian veterans in a quarter called Pella. After floods destroyed it, it was rebuilt with an embankment against floods almost four and a half kilometres long. Amid the instability that followed the Parthian conquest of most of the Seleucid Empire, Hyspaosines made Characene an independent state in 127 BCE, and Charax remained its capital for 282 years. Its coins point to a multi-ethnic, Hellenised city. Trajan annexed it in 116 CE and watched ships leave for India, wishing he were young enough to follow Alexander; independence returned fifteen years later under Mithridates, a son of the Parthian king Pacoros.

Ships came from Gerrha, Egypt and India; Strabo called the city an emporium, and Pliny names it as a market for rare perfumes and a centre of pearl diving. It was the start of the overland route to Petra and Palmyra. The Chinese envoy Gan Ying reached it in 97 CE, and the geographer Isidore of Charax came from it. Later Arab histories say that Ardašēr, satrap of Fars and founder of the Sasanian Empire, killed the last ruler of Characene and renamed the town Astarābād-Ardašīr. As Maysan it had governors through the fifth century and a Church of the East in the sixth, and its mint struck coins as late as 715.

Persistent flooding and falling trade with the West led to the city's abandonment in the 9th century. The mound now lies about a kilometre south of the rivers' confluence, which moved during a storm in 1837. Excavations began in 2016 and found a grid of housing blocks measuring 185 by 85 metres, among the largest known in the ancient world.
charcoal: Charcoal is a lightweight black residue of carbon, made by strongly heating wood or other plant and animal material in minimal oxygen so that all water and volatile constituents are driven off. In the traditional process, called charcoal burning, part of the starting material is itself burnt to supply the heat, with a limited supply of air. The properties of the product depend on the material charred and on the temperature: charcoal made at about 300 degrees Celsius is brown, soft and friable, while charcoal made at higher temperatures is hard and brittle.

Wood charcoal has been made since ancient times wherever wood was abundant. Billets of wood were stacked on end in a conical pile, with openings at the bottom to admit air and a central shaft serving as a flue. The pile was covered with turf or moistened clay and lit at the bottom of the flue, and the fire spread slowly outward and upward. In the clamp used in Britain, logs leaned against a chimney of four stakes and were covered with soil and straw, and burned into charcoal over about five days.

The skill lay in controlling the combustion, so the work was left to professional charcoal burners, or colliers, who often lived alone in small huts to tend their piles. In the Harz Mountains of Germany they lived in conical huts called Köten, which still exist.

Charcoal has served for art, medicine, pigment and as a constituent of black powder, but its most important use has been as a metallurgical fuel. It burns at more than 1,100 degrees Celsius, and its heat can be moderated by controlling the flow of air, so it remains the traditional fuel of the blacksmith's forge. It has been used to make iron and steel, where it also supplies carbon, since at least 2000 BCE, with remains found in Proto-Hittite layers at Kaman-Kalehöyük.

The demand was great enough that charcoal making became a major cause of deforestation, especially in Central Europe, where at its height it employed hundreds of thousands of people. In the 16th century England passed laws to keep the country from being stripped of trees by iron production, and many woods were managed as coppices, cut and regrown in cycles. Growing scarcity of wood helped drive the move to coal, and in the 19th century coke largely replaced charcoal in steelmaking.
charente-maritime: Charente-Maritime lies on the west coast of France, named after the river Charente, with an area of 6,864 square kilometres. It was created by a decree of the Constituent Assembly of 22 December 1789, which took effect on 4 March 1790, as one of the 83 original departments of the French Revolution. It encompasses most of the former province of Saintonge, nearly all of Aunis and the Pays d'Aulnay from Poitou. Initially named Charente-Inférieure after the lower course of the river, it was renamed on 4 September 1941, reflecting its Atlantic coast identity. Saintes, the capital of Saintonge, was the prefecture from 1790 until Napoleon decreed its transfer to La Rochelle in 1810.

Human settlement dates to the Lower Paleolithic, and a Neanderthal skeleton found at Roche à Pierrot in Saint-Césaire in 1979, dated to about 36,300 years ago, confirmed an overlap with Cro-Magnons. The Santoni made the oppidum at Pons their political and trading hub in the La Tène period, and after the Gallic War Mediolanum Santonum, now Saintes, became the first capital of the Roman province of Aquitaine under Augustus. It was burned by the Alamanni in 276. In 418 the Visigoths settled in the region, and Clovis ousted them after defeating Alaric at Vouillé in 507.

La Rochelle grew in the twelfth century under the Dukes of Aquitaine and received a communal charter from Henry II in 1175. Eleanor of Aquitaine's marriage to Henry Plantagenet in 1152 tied the region to England, and the Hundred Years' War devastated it until the French recaptured Montguyon in 1451. La Rochelle became a Protestant stronghold in the Wars of Religion. In 1627 Cardinal Richelieu began a siege of the city, with a dike blocking its access to the sea, and famine and disease reduced the population from 28,000 to 5,000 before it surrendered on 28 October 1628. Explorers Pierre Dugua de Mons and Samuel de Champlain, from Saintonge, founded Québec in 1608.

The nineteenth century brought prosperity under the Second Empire, driven by cognac, until the phylloxera crisis. German forces occupied the department in the Second World War and built sea defences, including pillboxes on Oléron. Royan was nearly destroyed by an RAF raid on 5 January 1945, and La Rochelle was freed on 9 May 1945.

The prefecture is La Rochelle, and the department lies in the region of Nouvelle-Aquitaine. The islands of Ré and Oléron belong to it. The Paléosite centre at Saint-Césaire, opened in 2005, presents the Neanderthal find, and Saintes keeps Roman monuments such as a votive arch and an amphitheatre.
chares-of-athens: Chares first appears in the records in 367 BCE, when he was sent to relieve the city of Phlius, hard pressed by the Arcadians and Argives with help from the Theban commander at Sicyon, and his forces relieved it. In 361 BCE he succeeded the admiral Leosthenes after Leosthenes' defeat by Alexander of Pherae. At Corcyra he backed the oligarchic party, which took control only after much bloodshed, and the island was lost to Athens when the Social War broke out.

In the Social War he shared command with Iphicrates and Timotheus after the death of Chabrias. According to Diodorus his colleagues refused to fight in a storm and Chares reported them to Athens; Cornelius Nepos held that Chares attacked, was defeated and then accused them to protect himself. Either way they were recalled and tried. Left in sole command and short of funds, he took service with Artabazus, the rebel satrap of Hellespontine Phrygia, until complaints from Artaxerxes III made Athens order him to stop.

In 353 BCE he took Sestus, massacred the men and sold the women and children as slaves. He commanded mercenaries in the Olynthian War of 349 BCE with little result, and in 346 BCE, while Philip II of Macedon marched against Cersobleptes, Athens had to send a squadron to find out where its general was. At Byzantium in 340 BCE the citizens distrusted him and refused to receive him, and he was replaced by Phocion. In 338 BCE, sent to aid Amphissa, he was defeated by Philip together with the Theban general Proxenus. After the defeat at Chaeronea he escaped prosecution, while his colleague Lysicles was condemned to death.

Arrian lists Chares among the Athenians whose surrender Alexander demanded in 335 BCE, though Plutarch omits him. He later lived at Sigeion, met Alexander on his way to Troy, and then commanded mercenaries for Darius Codomannus at Mytilene, which Pharnabazus and Autophradates had captured in 333 BCE and which he was compelled to surrender the next year. He probably ended his days at Sigeion. He has been charged with rashness, profligacy and rapacity, and his bad faith became proverbial, though he was for much of his career perhaps the best commander Athens had.
charibael: The Periplus calls him the lawful king of the Homerites and of their neighbours the Sabaites. Through a vassal-chief named Cholaebus (Kula'ib) he controlled the towns of Muza (Mocha) and Saua (Taiz) in Mapharitis, and from the Roman merchants calling at Mocha he required tribute of horses and pack mules, vessels of gold and polished silver, finely woven clothing and copper vessels. His realm included Ocelis at the Bab-el-Mandeb and the ruins at Eudaemon Arabia but reached little further, and the text credits him, through his vassals at Mocha, with indirect dominion over the ports of Azania on the Somali and Swahili coasts.

He is also probably the king who destroyed the port of Eudaemon Arabia (Aden), likely on behalf of his allies at Mocha, its commercial rivals, although this requires revising the text, whose manuscripts name a Caesar. In the 19th century Müller and Dittrich read Elisar, the king Eleazus named elsewhere in the text, which South Arabian inscriptions do not support. Others thought of the invasion of Arabia by the Egyptian prefect Aelius Gallus in 26 BCE, but that campaign came decades before the Periplus and went overland, never reaching the southern ports.

The two Greek manuscripts give the name as Kharibaḗl and Kharibaḗla, latinised as Charibael. Scholars now widely agree that it renders the Sabaic krbʾl, Karibʾīl, meaning blessed by God or following God, a regnal name shared by many South Arabian rulers rather than a title. Since Glaser's work on the inscriptions in the 19th century he has usually been identified with Karibʾīl Watar Yuhan'im, who ruled Himyar some time between 40 and 70 CE.

The matter is unsettled because the rulers of both Himyar and Saba used the title king of Saba and Dhu Raydan, which Hadhramauti invaders also took, and the word lawful in the Periplus probably sets him apart from weaker rivals. The inscriptions also show five different Karibʾīls in the 1st century, so some identify him instead with Karibʾīl Bayān, son of Dhamarʿalī Dharib and king of Saba in the 80s.
charibert-i: Charibert was the second-eldest son of King Chlothar I and his first wife Ingund; his elder brother Gunthar died before their father. In 556 Chlothar sent Charibert and his brother Guntram against their stepmother, called Chunna, and their half-brother Chramn, who were in revolt. Chramn was hiding on Black Mountain in the Limousin. During negotiations a thunderstorm prevented a battle, and Chramn sent forged letters falsely reporting the death of Chlothar. Charibert and Guntram returned at once to Burgundy to secure their positions.

After Chlothar died in 561 the Frankish kingdom was divided among his sons, each of whom ruled a realm named after the city he ruled from, which need not be geographically coherent. Charibert received the old kingdom of Childebert I: Neustria, the region between the Somme and the Loire, with Aquitaine and Novempopulana, and Paris as his capital. His other chief cities were Rouen, Tours, Poitiers, Limoges, Bordeaux, Toulouse, Cahors and Albi. Guntram received Burgundy, Sigebert Austrasia with its capital at Metz, and Chilperic a compact kingdom around Soissons.

Charibert married Ingoberga, and their daughter Bertha married Æthelberht, the pagan King of Kent. She took Bishop Liudhard with her as her private confessor, and her influence at the Kentish court was important to the success of the mission of St. Augustine of Canterbury in 597, which converted the first Anglo-Saxon ruler.

Gregory of Tours found Charibert eloquent and learned in the law but one of the most dissolute of the early Merovingians. He kept four wives at once, two of them sisters, and Germanus excommunicated him, the first excommunication of a Merovingian king. He was buried in disgrace at Blavia castellum, a stronghold in the Tractus Armoricanus.

After his death his brothers divided his realm, agreeing at first to hold Paris in common. His surviving queen, Theudechild, proposed a marriage with Guntram, though a council at Paris had outlawed such matches as incestuous. Guntram, unwillingly, had her housed in a nunnery at Arles. Charibert of Hesbaye, said to be his son, received nothing. The main source for his life is Gregory of Tours' History of the Franks, and from the English side Bede's Ecclesiastic History of the English People.
charilaos-trikoupis: Charilaos Trikoupis was born on 11 July 1832 in Nafplio, the son of Spyridon Trikoupis, briefly Prime Minister of Greece in 1833, and Ekaterini Mavrokordatou, sister of the later Prime Minister Alexandros Mavrokordatos. After studying law and literature at the University of Athens and in Paris, where he obtained a doctorate, he was sent to London in 1852 as an attaché of the Greek legation, and by 1863 was chargé d'affaires. His family had supported the English Party, and with his reserved nature this earned him the nickname The Englishman. After negotiating the cession of the Ionian Islands by the United Kingdom to Greece he returned to Athens in 1865, was elected to Parliament and the next year became Minister for Foreign Affairs at thirty-four.

In 1872 he founded the Fifth Party on a reformist programme. On 29 June 1874 he published in the daily Kairoi a manifesto, Who's to Blame?, naming King George I as the cause of public distrust, because the king bypassed election results in choosing prime ministers and produced weak minority governments. It briefly landed him in jail but boosted his popularity. On 8 May 1875 he mustered a parliamentary majority and George I reluctantly named him Prime Minister. His first acts included electoral reform and the dedilomeni principle, which obliged the king to appoint the leader of the majority as prime minister and was later incorporated into all Greek constitutions.

Short governments followed until 15 March 1882, when he became prime minister for the third time. His government lasted more than three years and pursued roads, railways and harbours, attracting foreign investment, and the digging of the Corinth Canal. He also envisioned a bridge across the Gulf of Corinth, beyond the means of the young kingdom; it was completed in 2004 as the Charilaos Trikoupis Bridge. Military spending after the union of Bulgaria and Eastern Rumelia added to his difficulties, and in his sixth term, from 22 June 1892 to 15 May 1893, he told parliament: Unfortunately, we are bankrupt. Servicing of foreign loans was suspended and non-essential spending cut.

His last term ran from 11 November 1893 to 24 January 1895, during which he was persuaded to host the 1896 Olympic Games despite fearing the cost. His tax proposals aroused hostility and he resigned. At the election four months later Theodoros Deligiannis defeated him and he lost his own seat, after which he left politics for Cannes. He was elected in the elections of 17 March 1896 but never returned to take his seat, and he died in Cannes on 30 March 1896. He was buried in Athens. He is considered one of the leading modern Greek politicians for his reforms, and roads in major Greek cities bear his name.
chariot: The critical invention that allowed light, horse-drawn chariots was the spoked wheel. Chariots emerged in the early 2nd millennium BCE. The oldest known come from burials of the Sintashta culture in present-day Russia, dated to about 1950 to 1880 BCE, although some scholars classify those finds as carts rather than true chariots. Cylinder seals from Kültepe in central Anatolia of about 1900 BCE also depict them. The first certain attestation of chariots in the Hittite empire dates to the late 17th century BCE, and they reached Egypt around 1650 BCE during the Hyksos invasion. The Hittites developed a lighter design with four-spoked wheels, wide enough for a driver, an archer and a shield-bearer.

A chariot was a fast, light, open, two-wheeled vehicle drawn by two or more horses harnessed side by side, little more than a floor with a waist-high guard at the front and sides. Greek chariots had no seat and no suspension. Egyptian chariots served as mobile archery platforms with two men, and the best preserved examples are the four found in the tomb of Tutankhamun. By the 7th century BCE the Neo-Assyrian Empire used heavy chariots with a crew of four. In Roman usage a two-horse chariot was a biga, a three-horse chariot a triga and a four-horse chariot a quadriga.

Chariots were of great importance in Late Bronze Age warfare, including the Battle of Kadesh, fought about 1274 BCE between the Hittites and the Egyptian Empire. The Mycenaean Greeks, who most probably adopted them from the Hittites, recorded large inventories of them on Linear B tablets. In China the earliest evidence is a burial at Hougang, Anyang, from about 1250 BCE, and their use there peaked from the 8th to the 5th centuries BCE. Massed chariot warfare became all but obsolete after the Warring States period, as crossbows, long halberds and cavalry took over.

Elsewhere cavalry likewise replaced them, though chariots remained in use for travel, processions, games and races. British chariots were described by Julius Caesar, and the last mention of chariots in battle seems to be at the Battle of Mons Graupius in 84 CE. In the Roman Empire they were used in racing at the Circus Maximus and in triumphal processions.
charioteer-of-delphi: The Charioteer of Delphi, also called Heniokhos, the rein-holder, was part of a larger group that included a chariot, at least four horses and possibly two grooms. It was set up at the Sanctuary of Apollo at Delphi to commemorate a victory by the tyrant Polyzalus of Gela in the Pythian Games, of either 478 or 474 BCE. An inscription on the limestone base, in hexameter, reads in reconstruction: Polyzalus dedicated me. Make him prosper, honoured Apollo.

The sculptor is unknown. The work has been linked to Pythagoras of Rhegion, who worked in Sicily, and to Calamis, but it is thought unlikely to come from Sicily. In style it resembles statues cast in Athens, such as the Piraeus Apollo.

The statue is 1.8 metres tall and shows a young man, as his soft side-curls indicate, wearing the champion's headband. He is dressed in the long sleeved tunic called the xystis, belted high above the waist, with two bands, the analavos, crossing on the back to keep the garment from billowing in the wind during the race. His head turns slightly to the right, and his long fingers are still curled round the reins and a riding crop. He does not appear to be racing; his movement lacks intensity, and he seems to be making his victory lap.

Unusually for the period the figure is clothed from head to foot, whereas most athletes of the time competed and were shown nude. This suggests a status lower than that of his master Polyzalus, and it has been speculated that he was a household slave whom it was not appropriate to show nude. His eyes are inlaid glass, which is rare in surviving Greek bronzes. Stylistically the work belongs to the Early Classical or Severe style. It is more naturalistic than the kouroi of the Archaic period, and its introverted expression shows none of the Archaic smile.

The Charioteer survived because it was buried under a rock fall that destroyed part of the site in 373 BCE. It was found in 1896 during excavations at Delphi, in three pieces: the head and upper torso, the lower torso and the right arm. Its left forearm and some details of the head are lost. It had a blue patina when found, which has turned green except on the lower torso. It is now in the Delphi Archaeological Museum.
charites: The Charites, called the Graces in English and the Gratiae in Latin, personify beauty and grace. In Hesiod's Theogony they are the three daughters of Zeus and the Oceanid Eurynome: Aglaia, Euphrosyne and Thalia. Accounts differ, however, in names, number and parentage. Homer mentions Pasithea as one of the younger Graces, and Pausanias reports that the Athenians worshipped two Charites, Auxo and Hegemone, and the Spartans two, Cleta and Phaenna, while by Boeotian tradition Eteocles, king of Orchomenus, fixed the number at three.

They have little independent mythology and mostly attend the Olympian gods, above all Aphrodite, whom they bathed and anointed at Paphos. Pindar says they arranged feasts and dances for the Olympians and danced with Apollo and the Muses. One of them was the wife of the smith god Hephaestus: Hesiod calls her Aglaia, and in the Iliad she is called Charis.

Their cult is very old, and their name appears to be pre-Greek in origin. Its purpose seems to have resembled that of the nymphs, concerned with fertility and nature and with springs and rivers. An inscription of the sixth century BCE on Thera records a cult, and dance was strongly linked with it. At least four temples were dedicated to them alone, at Orchomenus, Hermione, Sparta and Elis. The most important was at Orchomenus in Boeotia, where the cult was thought to have begun. There the goddesses were worshipped at a very ancient site with a trio of stones and received a share of the produce of the rich plain, and Strabo says that Eteocles founded their temple.

In Greek art of the Archaic and Classical periods the Charites were dressed and shown in a line as dancers. The Roman and later pose, a nude interlaced group, developed later; Pausanias says he could not find who first showed them naked. The earliest known image is from a temple of Apollo at Thermon, of the seventh or sixth century BCE. A Classical relief of the Charites and Hermes at the entrance to the Acropolis was popularly ascribed to Socrates. In the Renaissance the nude group allowed pagan beauty to appear in art, and the Graces were painted by Botticelli in Primavera and sculpted by Antonio Canova and Bertel Thorvaldsen.
charlemagne: Charlemagne was the eldest son of Pepin the Short and Bertrada of Laon. His year of birth is uncertain, and the biographer Einhard reports him as 72 at his death. He was probably functionally bilingual in Germanic and Romance dialects from an early age, also spoke Latin and, according to Einhard, could understand and perhaps speak some Greek. After Pepin's death in 768 he and his brother Carloman I became kings of the Franks, and he became sole ruler three years later.

Charlemagne continued his father's policy of protecting the papacy and removed the Lombards from power in northern Italy in 774. His first war against the Saxons began what became over thirty years of nearly continuous warfare. After a defeat in 782 the annals record that he had 4,500 Saxon prisoners beheaded in the massacre of Verden, a figure historians think may be exaggerated although the event itself is not in doubt. The Capitulatio de partibus Saxoniae, with the death penalty for pagan practices, has been described as a programme for forced conversion. His campaigns of the 790s were more destructive still, and his court settled at Aachen, where he built a palace and a chapel. His forces also brought down the kingdom of the Avars.

Pope Leo III was attacked by his enemies in April 799 and fled to Charlemagne. After an assembly in Rome at which Leo swore an oath of innocence, Leo crowned Charlemagne emperor of the Romans at St Peter's Basilica on Christmas Day 800. He was the first reigning emperor in the west since 476, and historians debate the significance of the coronation. From 801 he ruled more from Aachen and rarely led armies in person. He sought recognition of his title from Constantinople, which Emperor Michael I finally confirmed after a peace in 810.

In September 813 Charlemagne crowned his only surviving son, Louis, as co-emperor at Aachen. He died in 814 and was buried in the Palatine Chapel at Aachen. His reign inspired the cultural revival known as the Carolingian Renaissance, for which he promoted learning to create a more effective clergy. He held 23 synods and required the Rule of St Benedict in monasteries. After Louis's death the Treaty of Verdun divided the empire among his sons, and Carolingians ruled in East Francia until 911 and in West Francia until 987. Otto the Great was crowned emperor in 962, founding or re-establishing the Holy Roman Empire, which lasted until 1806.
charlemagne-peralte: François Borgia Charlemagne Péralte was born in Hinche, the son of the Haitian army general Remi Masséna Péralte and the seamstress Anne-Marie Claude Emmanuel. He grew up in a middle-class family of the rural bourgeoisie and attended the Saint-Louis Gonzague School in Port-au-Prince. From 1908 to 1915 he held several government posts, among them mayor of Hinche, justice of the peace in Mirebalais and commander of the Port-de-Paix region, where he oversaw both political and military affairs.

The United States invaded Haiti in July 1915, officially to protect American lives after a period in which seven presidents held office between 1912 and 1915. After defeating the Cacos in the First Caco War that November, American forces set up the Gendarmerie of Haiti under the supervision of the United States Marine Corps. Péralte left government service, farmed at Hinche and joined a Revolutionary Committee that sought to negotiate with Colonel Littleton Waller, the Marine commander.

In October 1917 he took part in a failed raid on a Gendarmerie payroll and was sentenced to five years in prison early in 1918. He escaped in September and led Cacos raids on Gendarmerie targets, vowing to drive the invaders into the sea. By mid-1919 his force had grown to 5,000, too large for the Gendarmerie to put down. On 6 October 1919 a raid he led on Port-au-Prince was repelled within minutes, with 30 Cacos killed, though he escaped.

Marine Sergeant Herman H. Hanneken planned his killing. For $2,000 a former police chief of Grande-Rivière-du-Nord, Jean-Baptiste Conzé, revealed that Péralte was at Fort Capois near Sainte-Suzanne and staged a false revolt to win his trust. On the evening of 31 October 1919 Hanneken and Corporal William R. Button, disguised as Cacos, passed six outposts with Conzé's band, and Hanneken shot Péralte twice in the chest. US forces spread a photograph of his body tied to a door to deter resistance, but its likeness to a crucifixion made him a martyr, later shown on Haitian stamps and coins. Leadership of the Cacos passed to Benoît Batraville.
charles-albert-of-sardinia: Charles Albert was born on 2 October 1798 at the Palazzo Carignano in Turin, the son of Charles Emmanuel, Prince of Carignano, and Maria Cristina of Saxony. The Carignano line was a junior branch of the House of Savoy, so his chances of succeeding to the kingdom were slim at his birth. His father, sympathetic to liberalism, joined the French cause after the invasion of 1796, and the family was sent to Paris and kept under surveillance. Charles Albert grew up there and received a liberal education.

In March 1821 young liberal officers met him as they planned to force a constitution on Victor Emmanuel I. When the king abdicated, Charles Albert was made regent, but he left Turin secretly on the night of 21 March, and Charles Felix ordered him to Tuscany. To show his penitence he joined the French expedition against the Spanish liberals in 1823.

Charles Albert became king on 27 April 1831, when Charles Felix died without an heir and the direct line of Savoy came to an end. Alarmed by the July Revolution in France, he made an alliance with Austria, signed on 23 July 1831. His rule was conservative at first, yet he set up a Council of State, abolished torture and had new codes drawn up: a civil code in 1837, a criminal code in 1839, and commercial and procedural codes in 1842.

In 1848, as revolutions spread across Europe, he granted the Albertine Statute, which remained in force until 1947. On 23 March 1848 he issued a proclamation to the people of Lombardy and Veneto and sent his troops against the Austrians in the First Italian War of Independence. Pope Pius IX and Ferdinand II of the Two Sicilies abandoned the cause, and he was defeated at Novara in 1849.

After the defeat Charles Albert abdicated in favour of his son Victor Emmanuel II. He left Novara just after midnight on 23 March 1849; stopped at an Austrian roadblock, he gave his name as the Count of Barge, a title he held, and was allowed to pass. He reached Porto in Portugal, where his health failed, and he died there on 28 July 1849.

He was nicknamed the Hesitant King, because he hesitated between constitutional monarchy and absolute rule, and the Italian Hamlet by Giosuè Carducci. His war was the first attempt by the House of Savoy to alter the settlement of the Congress of Vienna, and his son carried it to success in 1861.
charles-alexander-grand-duke-of-saxe-wei: Charles Alexander, in German Karl Alexander August Johann, was born in Weimar on 24 June 1818, the second but eldest surviving son of Karl Frederick, Grand Duke of Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach, and Grand Duchess Maria Pavlovna of Russia. His mother engaged the Swiss scholar Frédéric Soret as his tutor, and Soret became a close acquaintance of Johann Wolfgang von Goethe. Charles Alexander later remembered Goethe on his deathbed.

On 8 October 1842, at Kneuterdijk Palace in The Hague, he married his first cousin, Princess Sophie of the Netherlands, daughter of William II and of Grand Duchess Anna Pavlovna of Russia, his mother's sister. They had four children, among them the Hereditary Grand Duke Karl August, who died in 1894. As Hereditary Grand Duke he formed a close friendship with Fanny Lewald and the Danish writer Hans Christian Andersen. The friendship with Andersen broke off in 1849 over the First Schleswig War against Denmark; in 1997, 173 letters between the two, spanning 32 years, were published.

His father died on 8 July 1853, but Charles Alexander postponed his constitutional accession until Goethe's birthday, 28 August 1853. He renovated Wartburg Castle and left his mark on many places in Eisenach. He was a protector of Richard Wagner and Franz Liszt, kept up the tradition of Weimar's classical period, and gave the old part of Weimar a new appearance with the Herder monument and the double monument to Goethe and Schiller.

In 1860 he founded the Grand-Ducal Saxon Art School in Weimar, with Arnold Böcklin, Franz von Lenbach and the sculptor Reinhold Begas. As grand duke he was also rector of the University of Jena, where he supported its collections, among them the Oriental Coin Cabinet. In the Franco-Prussian War of 1870 to 1871 he took part only in relief work for the wounded.

In November 1900 the Weimar Congress of the Goethe Federation, which opposed the Lex Heinze, described his government as the Silver Age of Weimar. He fell ill with influenza in late December 1900, his condition worsened with inflammation of the lungs, and he died at Weimar on 5 January 1901. His only son having died before him, he was succeeded by his grandson Wilhelm Ernst. Prince Gabriel Constantinovich of Russia recalled in his memoirs that his mediation was said to have helped reconcile Emperor Alexander II and Emperor Franz Joseph.
charles-alexander-margrave-of-brandenbur: Christian Frederick Charles Alexander was born on 24 February 1736, the son of Charles William Frederick, Margrave of Brandenburg-Ansbach, and Friederike Luise of Prussia, a sister of Frederick II of Prussia. He became heir when his elder brother Carl Frederick August died suddenly on 9 May 1737. He studied at Utrecht and travelled to Turin and Savoy as the young Count of Sayn, and on 22 November 1754 in Coburg he married Princess Frederica Caroline of Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld.

He succeeded his father on 3 August 1757. He preferred his hunting seat at Triesdorf to the Residenz at Ansbach and built or renovated villas there for himself and his mistresses, among them the actress Hippolyte Clairon and Elizabeth, Baroness Craven. In 1758 he founded a porcelain factory at Ansbach and imported sheep, and in 1780 he set up his own bank, the Hofbanco, from which the Bayerische Hypotheken- und Wechselbank later grew. He seems to have wanted to keep his revenues in his own hands rather than rely on the Jewish banking houses that managed his finances.

For the American Revolutionary War he hired out to George III a force of 1,644 men, of whom only about 1,183 came home in 1783, and he leased further troops to Holland. With this income he cut the principality's debt from 5,000,000 guilders when he inherited to 1,500,000 by his abdication. On 16 January 1791 he sold the margraviate to Prussia in a contract arranged by Karl August von Hardenberg, in return for 300,000 guilders a year, and he signed his formal abdication at Bordeaux on 2 December.

His first wife died in February 1791, and that autumn in Lisbon he married Elizabeth Craven, widow of William Craven, 6th Baron Craven. In England the couple bred horses, living at Brandenburgh House in Fulham and, from 1798, at Benham Park near Newbury. He died there of lung disease on 5 January 1806 and is commemorated in St Mary's Church at Speen. His lands passed from Prussia to France and then to Bavaria.
charles-alexandre-de-calonne: Charles Alexandre de Calonne was born on 20 January 1734 in Douai into an upper-class family. He entered the legal profession and became a lawyer to the general council of Artois, procureur to the parlement of Douai and Master of Requests, then intendant of Metz in 1768 and of Lille in 1774. He seems to have had notable business abilities and an entrepreneurial spirit. He owed his appointment as Controller-General of Finances, which he took up on 3 November 1783, to the Comte de Vergennes, who supported him for over three years.

On taking office Calonne found that the nation had debts of 110 million livres, partly incurred through France's involvement in the American Revolution. At first he tried to maintain confidence through loans and through building projects and spending, reissued gold coinage in October 1785 and developed the Caisse d'Escompte. He presented Louis XVI with a larger plan on 20 August 1786. Its heart was a new land value tax to replace the old vingtième taxes and sweep away the fiscal exemptions of the privileged orders, to be run through provincial assemblies elected by property owners. It also proposed free trade in grain and the abolition of internal customs barriers.

Knowing that the Parlement of Paris would reject such a tax, Calonne persuaded the king to call a hand-picked Assembly of Notables, which met at Versailles in February 1787. The notables balked at the size of the deficit and suspected the controller-general of being responsible for it. Protests against him followed, and effigies of him were burned. Louis XVI dismissed him on 8 April 1787 and exiled him to Lorraine, and in Paris he was known as Monsieur Déficit. Loménie de Brienne replaced him.

Calonne went to Great Britain. In 1789 he crossed to Flanders hoping to stand for election to the Estates-General but was forbidden to enter France, and he joined the émigrés at Coblenz. He was with the Count of Artois at Pillnitz in August 1791. Napoleon Bonaparte allowed him to return to France in 1802, and he died about a month after his arrival, on 30 October 1802.

Historians judge him differently. Munro Price considers his reputation for the financial crisis unfair, while Eugene White stresses that he continued a venal system of financial administration. His fall revealed the monarchy's financial instability and the lack of public scrutiny of its accounts.
charles-algernon-parsons: Parsons belonged to an aristocratic Anglo-Irish family whose seat is Birr Castle in County Offaly, Ireland. The town of Birr was called Parsonstown, after the family, from 1620 to 1901. With his three brothers he was educated at home by private tutors, among them John Purser and Sir Robert Ball, who also acted as practical assistants to the Earl in his astronomical work.

He read mathematics at Trinity College Dublin and then at St. John's College, Cambridge, graduating in 1877 with a first-class honours degree. He then joined the Newcastle engineering firm of W. G. Armstrong as an apprentice, an unusual step for an earl's son. Later he moved to Kitsons in Leeds, where he worked on rocket-powered torpedoes.

At Clarke, Chapman and Co. Parsons became head of electrical-equipment development and used Regnault's collection of steam data to develop his turbine. Another turbine of the time, Gustaf de Laval's, was an impulse design that exposed the machine to great centrifugal forces and limited its output. In his Rede Lecture of 1911 Parsons explained that he had split the fall in steam pressure into small expansions across a large number of turbines in series, so that the steam velocity nowhere became great. In 1890 Forth Banks Power Station, run by his Newcastle and District Electric Lighting Company, became the first power station in the world to generate electricity with turbo generators.

On 26 June 1897 the Turbinia appeared unannounced at the fleet review for Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee at Spithead, before the Prince of Wales and the Lords of the Admiralty. It ran at 34 knots, while the fastest Royal Navy ships reached 27. Within two years the destroyers HMS Viper and Cobra had Parsons's turbines, followed by the passenger steamer TS King Edward in 1901, the transatlantic liners Victorian and Virginian in 1905, and HMS Dreadnought in 1906.

Parsons was elected to the Royal Society in 1898 and received its Copley Medal in 1928. He was president of the British Association for the Advancement of Science from 1916 to 1919 and became a member of the Order of Merit in 1927.

He died on 11 February 1931 on board the steamship Duchess of Richmond, on a cruise with his wife, of neuritis. A memorial service was held at Westminster Abbey on 3 March, and he was buried at St Bartholomew's church in Kirkwhelpington, Northumberland. The Parsons turbine company survives in Heaton, Newcastle, as part of Siemens.
charles-augustus-grand-duke-of-saxe-weim: Karl August, also called Charles Augustus, was born in Weimar on 3 September 1757, the eldest son of Duke Ernst August II and Duchess Anna Amalia of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel. His father died when he was nine months old, and his mother supervised his upbringing as regent. Count Johann Eustach von Görtz was his governor, and in 1771 Christoph Martin Wieland became his tutor. On a journey to Paris in 1774 he met the young Johann Wolfgang von Goethe at Frankfurt through the poet Karl Ludwig von Knebel. After he returned to Weimar and took over the government, he married Luise Auguste of Hesse-Darmstadt on 3 October 1775.

One of his first acts was to summon Goethe to Weimar, and Goethe joined the privy council in 1776. The duke funded the Weimar Free Drawing School, encouraged Weimar Classicism and summoned Herder to reform education, while the University of Jena reached the height of its fame. By his own account his aim was to educate his people to independence of judgment. Weimar became the intellectual centre of Germany.

In the affairs of Germany he worked for unity. He was the prime mover of the league of princes of 1785, which under Frederick the Great frustrated the plans of Emperor Joseph II, and he refused the offer of the Hungarian crown. From 1788 he served in the Prussian army, and he was present with Goethe at the Battle of Valmy in 1792. After the sack of Weimar following the battle of Jena in 1806 he was forced to join the Confederation of the Rhine, and his contingent fought on the French side until after the Moscow campaign of 1812. In 1813 he joined the Sixth Coalition.

At the Congress of Vienna in 1815 he protested against the powers' neglect of the rights of the people, and he received more territory and the title of grand duke. On 5 May 1816 he granted his state a liberal constitution under Article XIII of the Act of Confederation, and he allowed liberty of the press. Metternich mocked him for patronising the Burschenschaften, and the festival held at the Wartburg with his permission in 1817 angered Prussia, Austria and Russia, so that the press was restricted again.

Karl August died at Graditz, near Torgau, on 14 June 1828. Goethe wrote that he had the gift of discriminating intellects and characters and setting each in its place. His correspondence with Goethe was published at Weimar in 1863. He left two surviving sons, Karl Frederick, who succeeded him, and Karl Bernhard, a soldier.
charles-babbage: Babbage's birthplace is disputed, but the Oxford Dictionary of National Biography holds that he was most likely born at 44 Crosby Row, Walworth Road, London. His obituary in The Times gave 26 December 1792, but a nephew wrote that he was born a year earlier, and the parish register records his baptism on 6 January 1792, which supports 1791. He arrived at Trinity College, Cambridge, in October 1810, already self-taught in parts of contemporary mathematics, and was disappointed by the instruction there. In 1812 he, John Herschel, George Peacock and friends formed the Analytical Society.

He was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1816. He helped found the Astronomical Society of London, later the Royal Astronomical Society, in 1820 and won its Gold Medal in 1824 for his invention of an engine for calculating tables. As Lucasian Professor of Mathematics at Cambridge he was inattentive to teaching and never gave a lecture. His Reflections on the Decline of Science in England (1830) led to the formation in 1831 of the British Association for the Advancement of Science, and his On the Economy of Machinery and Manufactures (1832) was an influential early work of operational research.

In 1838 he invented the cow-catcher, the metal frame on the front of locomotives that clears the track. He made notable advances in cryptography that stayed unknown long after his death, and campaigned against street music.

Babbage began in 1822 with the difference engine, made to compute polynomial values by the method of finite differences. Joseph Clement built a prototype from 1823, but he and Babbage fell out over costs around 1831. After the attempt fell through Babbage designed the more complex Analytical Engine, which marks the transition from mechanised arithmetic to general-purpose computation. Its architecture resembled a modern computer, with separate program and data memory, conditional jumps and a separate input and output unit.

Ada Lovelace is credited with an algorithm for calculating Bernoulli numbers on it, though some scholars dispute how far the ideas were hers. Babbage received about £17,000 in government funding before the Treasury lost confidence in him, and clashes with George Biddell Airy also hampered the work. He died at Marylebone on 18 October 1871, aged 79, having declined both a knighthood and a baronetcy.
charles-baudelaire: Baudelaire was born in Paris on 9 April 1821. His father, Joseph-François Baudelaire, a senior civil servant and amateur artist, was 34 years older than his mother, Caroline Dufaÿs, and died in 1827. The next year Caroline married Lieutenant Colonel Jacques Aupick, later a French ambassador. Baudelaire wrote to his mother that "There was in my childhood a period of passionate love for you."

He studied law in Paris and began to run up debts. After gaining his degree in 1839 he told his brother, "I don't feel I have a vocation for anything." In 1841 his stepfather sent him on a voyage to Calcutta to end his dissolute habits, but he left the ship after a few weeks on Mauritius and Réunion. At 21 he received a sizable inheritance, which he squandered, and his family placed his property in trust.

His first published work, under the pseudonym Baudelaire Dufaÿs, was the art review "Salon of 1845"; in 1846 he wrote a second, championing Eugène Delacroix as the foremost Romantic painter. He took part in the Revolutions of 1848 and wrote for a revolutionary newspaper, though he later noted that his interest in politics was passing. From 1847 until 1865 he was largely occupied with translating Edgar Allan Poe, and the translations were widely praised.

Les Fleurs du mal appeared in 1857. Théodore de Banville described its effect on fellow artists as "immense, prodigious, unexpected", and Gustave Flaubert wrote that Baudelaire had found a way to rejuvenate Romanticism, while J. Habas wrote in Le Figaro that everything in it not hideous was incomprehensible. A second edition without the six condemned poems but with considerable additions appeared in 1861, and the six were printed in Brussels in 1866 as Les Épaves.

In 1864 Baudelaire left for Belgium, hoping to sell the rights to his works and give lectures. He suffered a massive stroke in 1866 and spent his last year semi-paralysed in nursing homes in Brussels and Paris, where he died on 31 August 1867. A few dozen people attended his funeral, and he is buried in the Cimetière du Montparnasse.

Four years after his death Arthur Rimbaud called him "the king of poets, a true God". In 1895 Stéphane Mallarmé published a sonnet in his memory. T. S. Eliot said he had learnt his art "under the aegis of Baudelaire", and Walter Benjamin made him the focus of his Das Passagenwerk.
charles-belgrave: Sir Charles Dalrymple Belgrave was educated at Bedford School and Lincoln College, Oxford. In the First World War he served with the Imperial Camel Corps in Sudan, Egypt and Palestine, and took part in the Darfur Expedition of 1916. He then worked for the frontier districts administration at the Siwa Oasis and in 1924-25 was an Administrative Officer in Tanganyika Territory.

In 1923 the British had induced Shaikh Isa ibn Ali Al Khalifa, nearly 80, to hand power to his son Shaikh Hamad, who agreed to employ a personal adviser of his own to help modernise the state. The post was advertised in The Times in August 1925, and Belgrave, appointed at £720 a year, studied Arabic at the School of Oriental and African Studies and reached Bahrain in March 1926.

Known in Bahrain as Al Mustashar, the Adviser, Belgrave served Shaikh Hamad and then his son Shaikh Salman. He established civil and criminal courts, a trained police service, widely available education and municipal authorities, and gave political support to the search for oil, which made Bahrain in 1932 the first Gulf state to discover it. He promoted the building of the Bab Al Bahrain at the entrance to the market, and his wife Marjorie Belgrave founded schools for girls, which some traditionalists opposed.

In March 1956 a general strike of an estimated 30,000 people, 9,000 of them oil workers, demanded his removal. Riots on 11 March left at least 11 people reported dead, a figure later lowered to 5, and days earlier stones were thrown at the car of the British foreign secretary Selwyn Lloyd amid shouts against Belgrave. Shaikh Salman cut his powers sharply but would not dismiss him, and allowed the National Union Committee, the first legal political party. Some held that Gamal Abdel Nasser had helped to stir the unrest.

In December 1956 five men of the National Union Committee were found guilty of plotting to destroy the royal palace and kill the royal family and Belgrave, and he left Bahrain within months. His office, the Advisory, later housed Bahrain's courts. According to Philip L. Kohl, Mara Kozelsky and Nachman Ben-Yehuda, he was the first Westerner to use and advocate the name Arabian Gulf, in the journal Sawt al-Bahrain in 1955. He died on 28 February 1969.
charles-borromeo: Charles Borromeo was born in the castle of Arona on Lake Maggiore on 2 October 1538. His father, Gilbert, was Count of Arona, and his mother, Margaret, belonged to the Milanese branch of the House of Medici. The Borromeo family was one of the oldest and wealthiest in Lombardy. Charles received the tonsure at about twelve and, when given the income of a rich Benedictine abbey, told his father that whatever exceeded the cost of his preparation for the church belonged to the poor. He studied law at the University of Pavia and took his doctorate on 6 December 1559.

When his uncle was elected Pope Pius IV on 25 December 1559, he summoned Borromeo to Rome and made him a cardinal on 31 January 1560. He organised the third and last session of the Council of Trent in 1562 and 1563 and had a large share in the Tridentine Catechism. The death of his brother Federico in November 1562, and his contacts with the Jesuits and Theatines, led him to a stricter life and to put into practice a bishop's duties as the Council set them out. He was formally appointed archbishop of Milan in 1564 and entered the city in September 1565.

Milan was the largest archdiocese in Italy, with over 3,000 clergy and 800,000 people, and no archbishop had been present for about 80 years. Borromeo found indulgences and offices sold and monasteries in disorder. He made pastoral visits and, believing that abuses arose from ignorant clergy, founded seminaries and colleges, the Oblates of St Ambrose and the first Sunday school classes. Some members of the Humiliati, an order that opposed him, plotted against his life, and a shot fired at him in his chapel missed.

In 1576 famine struck Milan, followed by plague, and the governor and many nobles fled. Borromeo stayed, tried to feed 60,000 to 70,000 people daily and went into debt to do so. In 1583, as apostolic visitor to the Swiss cantons, he repressed Protestantism in the valleys. In the Valle Mesolcina 150 people were arrested for witchcraft, and the civil authorities condemned eleven women and the provost of Roveredo to be burned alive.

Borromeo's uncompromising stance brought him into conflict with secular leaders, priests and even the pope. He fell ill in 1584 and died in Milan on 3 November, aged 46. Paul V canonised him on 1 November 1610, and he is the patron saint of bishops, catechists and seminarians.
charles-bridge: The bridge replaced the Judith Bridge, built between 1158 and 1172 and severely damaged by a flood in 1342. Czech legend holds that Charles IV himself laid the first stone at 5:31 in the morning of 9 July 1357, chosen because the figures, 1357, 9/7, 5:31, form a palindrome, a numerical bridge in the eyes of an emperor who believed in numerology. The bridge was completed in 1402. It was originally called the Stone Bridge or the Prague Bridge and has been called Charles Bridge only since 1870. Until 1841 it was the only way across the Vltava, which made Prague important on the trade route between Eastern and Western Europe.

The bridge is 516 metres long and nearly 10 metres wide. Following the example of the Stone Bridge at Regensburg, it was built as a bow bridge with 16 arches shielded by ice guards. Three towers protect it, two on the Lesser Quarter side and the Old Town Bridge Tower on the other. An avenue of 30 statues stands along the balustrade, mostly Baroque and mostly erected between 1683 and 1714, among them John of Nepomuk. Since 1965 all have been replaced by replicas, and the originals are shown in the Lapidarium of the National Museum.

The bridge has survived floods and wars. A flood in 1432 damaged three pillars, and in 1496 the third arch broke down. After the Battle of White Mountain the heads of leaders of the anti-Habsburg revolt, executed on 21 June 1621, were displayed on the Old Town Bridge Tower. In 1648 the heaviest fighting for the Old Town took place on the bridge, as the Swedes advanced from the west bank. A flood on 2-5 September 1890 tore down three arches and two pillars, and the bridge reopened on 19 November 1892. A capital repair from 1965 to 1978 secured the pillars, and all vehicles have been excluded since then.
charles-brooke-rajah-of-sarawak: Charles Anthoni Johnson was born on 3 June 1829 at Berrow Vicarage, Burnham, Somerset, in England, the son of the Reverend Francis Charles Johnson and Emma Frances Johnson, née Brooke, the younger sister of James Brooke. He was educated at Crewkerne Grammar School and entered the Royal Navy. In 1852 he joined his uncle's service in Sarawak, took the name Brooke and began as Resident at the Lundu station.

In the rebellion of 1857 against the White Rajah, led by Liu Shan Bang, Charles helped his uncle put it down with a force of Ibans and local Bidayuh. His Iban forces pursued the remaining rebels to Bau, where they massacred 3,000 villagers, among them women, children and the elderly. He resigned his commission in the Royal Navy in 1861, and in 1865 James named him as his successor.

As rajah from 3 August 1868 he carried on his uncle's work, suppressing piracy, slavery and head-hunting, encouraging trade and extending his borders as opportunities arose. In 1891 he established the Sarawak Museum, the first museum in Borneo, and in 1903 he founded the Government Lay School, where Malays could be taught in the Malay language; it was the forerunner of SMK Green Road. He was made a Knight Grand Cross of the Order of St Michael and St George in 1888.

He married Margaret Alice Lili de Windt at Highworth, Wiltshire, on 28 October 1869, and she was made Ranee of Sarawak the same day. Of their six children three survived infancy. He also had a son, Esca Brooke, from an earlier marriage with a Malay woman known as Dayang Mastiah. By the time Brooke died on 17 May 1917, Sarawak had a parliamentary government, a railway and oil had been found there. His son Charles Vyner Brooke succeeded him as the third and last White Rajah, and all three rajahs are buried at St Leonard's Church in Sheepstor on Dartmoor, Devon.
charles-canning-1st-earl-canning: Charles John Canning was born on 14 December 1812 at Gloucester Lodge, Brompton, near London, the youngest child of George and Joan Canning. His father was a Tory Member of Parliament who served in the ministries of William Pitt the Younger and the Duke of Portland, was Foreign Secretary from 1807 to 1809 and again from 1822 to 1827, and was Prime Minister for a few months before his death in 1827. His mother was made Viscountess Canning in her own right, largely in tribute to her husband. Charles was educated at Christ Church, Oxford, where he graduated in 1833 with a first class in classics and a second in mathematics.

In 1836 he entered Parliament as the member for Warwick, but on his mother's death in 1837 he succeeded to the peerage and moved to the House of Lords. He was Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs under Sir Robert Peel from 1841 to January 1846, and Postmaster General from January 1853 until July 1855, when Lord Palmerston chose him to succeed Lord Dalhousie as Governor-General of India. He took up the office at the end of February 1856.

The Indian Rebellion of 1857 broke out in his first year. Canning is credited with keeping the administration and most departments working normally, and he took major decisions at the height of the rebellion, among them the founding of the first three modern universities in India, at Calcutta, Madras and Bombay.

A resolution of 31 July 1857 distinguished sepoys from regiments that had mutinied and killed their officers and European civilians from those who had disbanded and gone home without violence. It earned him the derisive nickname Clemency at a time when British opinion favoured collective reprisals, but it was later seen as humane and sensible. In 1858 he became the first Viceroy of India, presiding over the transfer of government from the East India Company to the Crown.

In April 1859 Canning received the thanks of both Houses of Parliament and was made an earl. The Indian Penal Code, drafted from Macaulay's code, came into force in 1862. He and his wife Charlotte had begun a photographic survey of Indian people, later made an official study and published in eight volumes as The People of India between 1868 and 1875. Strain and the death of his wife damaged his health. He left India, reached England in April 1862 and died in London on 17 June 1862. As he left no children, his titles became extinct. Canning Town in London and Fort Canning Hill in Singapore are named after him.
charles-cornwallis-1st-marquess-cornwall: Charles Cornwallis was born in Grosvenor Square, London, on 31 December 1738, the eldest son of the 5th Baron Cornwallis. His mother was a niece of Sir Robert Walpole, and his uncle Frederick was Archbishop of Canterbury. The family had been established at Brome Hall, near Eye in Suffolk, since the 14th century. He was educated at Eton College and Clare College, Cambridge, and received his first commission as an ensign in the 1st Foot Guards in December 1757. He then studied at the military academy of Turin and served as a staff officer in the Seven Years' War.

On the outbreak of war in North America he put his misgivings aside and sought active service. He fought under Sir Henry Clinton at the failed siege of Charleston in 1776, led the advance at the Battle of Long Island and chased George Washington across New Jersey. In 1780 he defeated the Continental Army at the Battle of Camden, and in March 1781 he won a costly victory at Guilford Court House. His campaign through the southern colonies was marked by quarrels with Clinton. He surrendered his army at Yorktown in October 1781. The surrender did not end the war, but it ended major fighting in North America.

He kept the confidence of George III and later governments. In 1786 he became Governor-General and commander-in-chief in India, having refused the post until it carried military command. He ended the East India Company's practice of letting its employees trade on their own account, raised their salaries, and introduced advancement by merit. He enacted the Cornwallis Code, which included the Permanent Settlement, and led the Third Anglo-Mysore War from 1789 to 1792 against Tipu Sultan.

After a spell as Master-General of the Ordnance he became Lord Lieutenant of Ireland in June 1798, in response to the Irish Rebellion. He oversaw the defeat of the rebels and of a French force under General Jean Humbert, and helped to bring about the Union of Great Britain and Ireland. On 25 March 1802 he signed the Treaty of Amiens for the United Kingdom.

Reappointed Governor-General of India in 1805 to curb the expansionist policy of Lord Wellesley, he arrived in July and died of a fever at Gauspur, near Ghazipur, on 5 October 1805. He was buried there above the Ganges, and his tomb is a protected monument. A memorial to him stands in St Paul's Cathedral. His son Charles became the 2nd Marquess, and the marquessate ended with him.
charles-d-b-king: Charles Dunbar Burgess King, born on 12 March 1875, was of Americo-Liberian and Sierra Leone Creole descent. He belonged to the True Whig Party, which ruled Liberia from 1878 until 1980. He was Attorney General from 1904 until 1912 and Secretary of State from 1912 until his election as president in 1919. In that capacity he attended the 1919 Paris Peace Conference and the First Pan-African Congress that accompanied it, and Liberia had become a charter member of the League of Nations in 1919. King was a moderate supporter of reform who continued to support the patronage machine of the True Whig Party.

King became president in 1920 and served for ten years. In 1929 he helped to found the Booker Washington Institute in Kakata. Liberia's finances were in crisis, and in March 1921 he led a commission to the United States to seek reorganisation of the country's debt. The State Department favoured a loan of 5 million dollars, and the House of Representatives approved it by 148 votes to 139, but the Senate rejected it by 42 to 32, to the disappointment of Liberian officials, who feared that British and French designs on their country might now prove unstoppable. The Firestone Rubber Company later agreed with his government on a 99-year lease of 1,000,000 acres for rubber growing, on which the Liberian economy came to depend.

King's challenger in the 1927 election, Thomas J. R. Faulkner, lost to him by an official count of 234,000 votes in a country with 15,000 registered voters, and King was later listed in the Guinness Book of World Records for the most fraudulent reported election in history. Faulkner then accused members of the government of recruiting contract labour and selling it as slaves.

The League of Nations sent a commission under the British zoologist Cuthbert Christy, and President Herbert Hoover briefly suspended relations to press Liberia to comply. The Christy Report of 1930 supported many of the allegations and implicated officials including Vice President Allen Yancy, who it found had approved forced labour for public works such as roads and for the shipment of goods abroad. King, Yancy and other implicated leaders resigned. His administration has been described as marked by patronage, nepotism and corruption. From 1947 to 1952 King served as Liberia's minister, and then ambassador, in the United States.
charles-darwin: Charles Robert Darwin was born on 12 February 1809 at The Mount, his family's home in Shrewsbury, Shropshire, the fifth of six children of the wealthy doctor and financier Robert Darwin and Susannah Darwin, née Wedgwood. His grandfathers Erasmus Darwin and Josiah Wedgwood were both prominent abolitionists, and Erasmus had praised general concepts of evolution and common descent in his Zoonomia (1794). His mother died in July 1817. In October 1825 he entered the University of Edinburgh Medical School, found lectures dull and surgery distressing, and neglected his studies. He assisted Robert Edmond Grant's research on marine invertebrates, then studied at Christ's College, Cambridge, from 1828 to 1831.

His five-year voyage on HMS Beagle, from 1831 to 1836, established him as an eminent geologist, and his observations supported Charles Lyell's concept of gradual geological change. The Voyage of the Beagle (1839) made him a popular author. Puzzled by the distribution of the wildlife and fossils he had collected, he devised his theory of natural selection in 1838, but he needed time for extensive research and his geological work had priority.

In 1858 Alfred Russel Wallace sent him an essay outlining the same idea, which led to a joint submission to the Linnean Society of London. Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859, and later The Descent of Man (1871), on human evolution and sexual selection. His final book was The Formation of Vegetable Mould, through the Actions of Worms (1881). He and his wife and cousin Emma Wedgwood had ten children, two of whom died in infancy.

Darwin died on 19 April 1882 and was buried in Westminster Abbey. By the 1870s the scientific community and most of the educated public accepted evolution as a fact, though many favoured explanations that gave natural selection only a minor role. A broad consensus that natural selection is the basic mechanism came with the modern evolutionary synthesis of the 1930s to the 1950s. Later movements, among them eugenics and Social Darwinism, invoked his name, sometimes against his own comments; he insisted that social policy should not be guided simply by concepts of struggle and selection.
charles-de-foucauld: Charles Eugène, vicomte de Foucauld de Pontbriand, was born in Strasbourg on 15 September 1858 into an old noble family from Périgord. His parents died within months of each other in 1864, and he and his sister were brought up in Strasbourg by their maternal grandfather, Colonel Beaudet de Morlet. In 1870 the family fled the Franco-Prussian War and later settled in Nancy. At 15 he lost his faith and for twelve years believed, in his later words, nothing. He entered the Saint-Cyr Military Academy in 1876, graduating 333rd of 386, and led an extravagant life after inheriting his grandfather's fortune.

Posted to the 4th Regiment of Chasseurs d'Afrique in Algeria, he grew bored with garrison service and travelled in Morocco in 1883–84, the Sahara in 1885 and Palestine in 1888–89. His research on the geography and culture of Algeria and Morocco won the gold medal of the Société de Géographie de Paris in 1885, and he published an account of his Moroccan journey in 1888. On 14 January 1890 he entered the Trappist monastery of Notre-Dame des Neiges. He was later sent to Akbès on the Syrian-Turkish border, and left the order in 1897 after seven years, working as a servant near a convent of Poor Clares in Nazareth.

He was ordained a priest on 9 June 1901 and settled at Béni Abbès in the Algerian Sahara, building a hermitage for adoration and hospitality, though nobody joined him. He then moved to Tamanghasset among the Tuareg and spent ten years studying their language and traditions, using the Assekrem as a place of retreat. His Tuareg dictionary, published after his death in four volumes, is known to specialists for its rich and apt descriptions, and he also collected Tuareg poetry.

On 1 December 1916 a group of tribal bandits dragged de Foucauld from his bordj at Tamanrasset, intending to kidnap him. Interrupted by two soldiers of the French Camel Corps, a startled 15-year-old shot him dead, and the soldiers were also killed. The Tuareg buried him the next morning. His remains were moved in April 1929 to El Meniaa. René Bazin's biography made him widely known, and the Little Brothers of Jesus, the Little Sisters of Jesus and many other congregations and fraternities draw on his life and writings. He was beatified on 13 November 2005 and canonised on 15 May 2022.
charles-de-gaulle: Charles André Joseph Marie de Gaulle was born on 22 November 1890 in Lille, the third of five children. He was raised in a devoutly Roman Catholic, conservative and monarchist family. His father, Henri de Gaulle, was a professor of history and literature at a Jesuit college and later founded his own school.

In 1909 he won a place at the military academy of Saint-Cyr, finishing 119th out of 221. Before entering he served a year in the ranks in the 33rd Infantry Regiment at Arras. His company commander declined to make him a sergeant at first, remarking that the young man evidently thought nothing less than Constable of France good enough for him.

In the First World War he was wounded in the knee at the Battle of Dinant on 15 August 1914 and later taken prisoner by the German Empire. After the armistice he served on the French military mission to Poland and won the Polish Virtuti Militari. In the interwar years he advocated mobile armoured divisions.
