When the German invasion came in May 1940 he led an armoured division in a counterattack and was appointed Undersecretary for War. Refusing his government's armistice with Germany, he went to Britain and urged the French to fight on in his Appeal of 18 June. He led the Free French Forces and in June 1944 became head of the Provisional Government of the French Republic. He resigned in 1946 and withdrew to Colombey-les-Deux-Églises to write his War Memoirs.

During the May 1958 crisis, as the Algerian War threatened the Fourth Republic, the National Assembly brought him back to power. He commissioned a new constitution and was elected President of France on 21 December 1958. He withdrew France from NATO's integrated military command and launched an independent nuclear force, and on 22 January 1963 he signed the Élysée Treaty with Chancellor Konrad Adenauer. He resigned in late April 1969 after losing a referendum on decentralisation.

De Gaulle died suddenly on 9 November 1970 from an abdominal aortic aneurysm while watching television. His successor Georges Pompidou announced his death by saying simply, "General de Gaulle is dead. France is a widow." French political parties and leaders claim a Gaullist legacy, and streets and monuments in France and elsewhere bear his name.
charles-de-menou-daulnay: D'Aulnay was born at the Château de Charnizay in Touraine, the son of a high-ranking official of Louis XIII. A member of the French nobility, he served at different times as a sea captain and as a lieutenant in the French navy under his cousin Isaac de Razilly. When Razilly became governor of Acadia in 1632, d'Aulnay helped him borrow money, hire ships and recruit men for the crossings made for the Compagnie des Cent-Associés and the private company Razilly-Condonnier. In 1635 he held Fort Pentagouet on Penobscot Bay against a force from Plymouth, letting the attackers spend their ammunition before sending them home.

After Razilly's death in 1635 the king appointed his brother Claude de Launay-Razilly, who stayed in France and named d'Aulnay his lieutenant in Acadia. D'Aulnay built a new fort at Port Royal, moved the colonists of La Hève there and sent to France for twenty more families, making Port Royal the colony's main settlement.

His rival Charles La Tour, at the mouth of the Saint John River, held a commission much like his own. Through his influence at court d'Aulnay obtained a royal order of 13 February 1641 for La Tour's arrest, but their forces were too evenly matched for him to carry it out. A siege of Fort La Tour with 500 men was broken by help from New England, and a later attempt, made while La Tour was in Quebec, was beaten off by Madame La Tour.

On the third attack a treacherous sentry let him in; he offered terms promising the garrison their lives, then broke them and hanged every member, forcing Madame La Tour to watch with a rope around her neck. She died a few weeks later.

With all of Acadia under his control, d'Aulnay had marshes diked, mills built and shipbuilding begun, and in 1647 he was commissioned governor and lieutenant-general. He died in 1650 after a boating accident. La Tour then won his own title back in France and succeeded him, and on 24 February 1653 he married d'Aulnay's widow, Jeanne Motin.
charles-de-sales: Charles de Sales was born in 1625 at the Château de Sales, in what is today Thorens-Glières in Haute-Savoie. His father, Louis, comte de Sales, was a noble of the Duchy of Savoy and a brother of Saint Francis de Sales. Charles became a chevalier of the Order of Saint John of Jerusalem in 1643, fought in several of the order's campaigns against the Turks, and took part in the defence of Crete in 1650.

In 1651 the bankrupt Compagnie des Îles de l'Amérique sold the French part of Saint Christopher Island, with Saint Barthélemy, Saint Martin and Saint Croix, to the order for 120,000 écus, at the urging of Philippe de Longvilliers de Poincy and with the agreement of the grand master Jean-Paul Lascaris-Castellar. King Louis XIV kept sovereignty. In 1657, on the death of the Chevalier Charles de Montmagny, the order sent de Sales to govern alongside Poincy.

In 1659 de Sales and Governor Charles Houël du Petit Pré of Guadeloupe signed for the French an offensive and defensive league with the English governors Roger Osborne of Montserrat and James Russell of Nevis against the Island Caribs of the Leeward Islands. When Poincy died in 1660 the order, which had still not paid the whole purchase price, made de Sales governor, and he took office on 11 April 1660. Under pressure from Jean-Baptiste Colbert the Hospitallers gave up the islands in 1665, and in February 1665 the new French West India Company confirmed de Sales in his post.

As war between France and England grew likely, de Sales agreed with William Watts, governor of the English part of the island, in January 1666 that each side would warn the other when it heard war had been declared and wait three days before attacking. A mission he sent to the English governor general Francis Willoughby in Barbados received only evasive answers.

Fighting on Saint Christopher began on 21 April 1666, before the declaration of war reached the island, and two days later the French routed the larger English force. De Sales was killed on 22 April, and Watts also died in the fighting. Claude de Roux de Saint-Laurent then became governor of the whole island.
charles-de-thierry: De Thierry came of a French family that had fled to England after the Revolution. He claimed to have been born in 1793 while his parents were in flight, probably at Grave in the Netherlands, and on reaching England his father, Charles Antoine de Thierry, claimed the title of Baron Nasher. He was enrolled at Magdalen College, Oxford, and claimed to have moved on to a college of the University of Cambridge.

At Cambridge he met Hongi Hika, the Ngāpuhi chief then visiting England, and the missionary Thomas Kendall, through whom he arranged the purchase of 40,000 acres (16,000 ha) at Hokianga, in Northland, for the price of 36 axes. After travels in North America and the Caribbean he came to the Pacific in 1835. In the Marquesas Islands he proclaimed himself King of Nuku Hiva, and he wrote to James Busby of a kingdom that would embrace free trade and medicine and share its occasional bounties with local chiefs.

In Sydney in 1837 he recruited followers, but when he reached Hokianga the rangatira Tāmati Wāka Nene and Eruera Maihi Patuone repudiated his claims. Nene and Te Taonui allowed him to settle a smaller plot of 800 acres. His followers rioted and abandoned him, and he came to depend on Māori charity. He went on exaggerating his successes to France and agitating for a French colony under his own leadership, a hope finally ended by the Treaty of Waitangi between the British Crown and the Māori chiefs in 1840. He later moved to Auckland, where he worked as a piano teacher until his sudden death on 8 July 1864.
charles-debbas: Charles Debbas was born in Beirut to a prominent Greek Orthodox family, the son of Gerges Khalil Debbas and Marie Salim Jbeili. He studied at the Collège des Jésuites, took his baccalaureate at fourteen and a half and read law in Montpellier and then in Paris, where he met Marcelle Burgart, a nurse. The couple settled in Beirut, where he worked as an attorney, and they married at Neuilly-sur-Seine on 24 October 1919.

In Beirut he joined the nationalist circles that had grown more active in Ottoman Syria since the Young Turk Revolution, writing for the French-language newspaper La Liberté. An article of 3 June 1909 was judged subversive by the wali of Beirut, Edhem Bey; Debbas answered in the press that he stood by it and that the wali should take the matter to court. He went to Paris in 1913 as secretary of the Arab Congress and joined the Central Syrian Committee during the First World War.

On 20 October 1920 Robert de Caix, Secretary General of the High Commissioner, appointed him Director of Judicial Services of Greater Lebanon. On 26 May 1926, three days after the constitution was adopted, both chambers meeting in congress elected him president for three years. According to Dib, he let Bechara al-Khouri and Emile Eddé take turns as prime minister. The Chamber of Deputies re-elected him on 23 March 1929 by 42 votes out of 44. When High Commissioner Henri Ponsot suspended the constitution on 9 May 1932, citing a budget crisis and the chance that a Muslim, Muhammad al-Jisr, might win the presidency, he extended Debbas's term by a year.

Debbas resigned on 2 January 1934 and was replaced by Habib Pacha Saad. A few days later he became Speaker of the Chamber of Deputies, serving until October. He sailed to France in April 1935 and died in Paris on 22 August that year. After a service at the Greek Orthodox Church of Saint Stephen, attended by Henri Gouraud, his body was taken to Beirut and buried in the Mar Mitr cemetery. His presidency introduced the compulsory baccalaureate for the liberal professions.
charles-denis-bourbaki: Bourbaki was born at Pau on 22 April 1816, the son of the Greek colonel Constantin Denis Bourbaki, who died in the Greek War of Independence in 1827. He was educated at the Prytanée National Militaire and at Saint-Cyr, joined the Zouaves in 1836, became a lieutenant of the Foreign Legion in 1838 and served as aide-de-camp to King Louis Philippe.

He rose in the campaigns in Africa: captain in the Zouaves in 1842, colonel of the Turcos in 1847 and brigadier-general in 1854. In the Crimean War he commanded part of the Algerian troops at the Alma, Inkerman and Sevastopol. Made general of division in 1857, he took command at Lyon in 1859 and did well in the war in Italy, second only to MacMahon. In 1862 he was proposed for the vacant Greek throne but declined it.

Commanding the Imperial Guard around Metz in 1870, he was criticised for refusing to commit its reserves at the Battle of Gravelotte. During the siege of Metz a businessman, Edmond Régnier, told Marshal Bazaine on the empress's alleged authority that peace was near and that Bourbaki or Marshal Canrobert should go to Hastings. Bourbaki went, with Prussian connivance, only to learn from the empress Eugénie that he had been tricked, and he was then refused re-entry to Metz on a technicality.

He offered his services to Léon Gambetta and, after a short command of the Northern Army, led the Army of the East. Its attempt on Belfort began with victory at the Battle of Villersexel and ended in defeat in the three-day battle of the Lisaine. Pressed by Field Marshal Edwin Freiherr von Manteuffel, short of food and reduced from 150,000 men, the army crossed into Switzerland at Les Verrières, Sainte-Croix, Vallorbe and the Vallée de Joux, and was held for six weeks before being repatriated in March.

On 26 January 1871 Bourbaki handed his command to General Justin Clinchant and, rather than face surrender, shot himself in the forehead that night; he survived, was carried into Switzerland and recovered. In July 1871 he again took command at Lyon, later becoming its military governor. He was retired in 1881 for his political opinions, failed to win a seat in the Senate in 1885, and died at Bayonne on 22 September 1897. The Bourbaki group of 20th-century French mathematicians took his surname as their collective pseudonym.
charles-dickens: Charles John Huffam Dickens was born on 7 February 1812 at Landport in Portsea Island (Portsmouth), the second of eight children of Elizabeth and John Dickens, a clerk in the Royal Navy Pay Office. He spent his formative years at Chatham in Kent, reading widely, including Tobias Smollett, Henry Fielding and The Arabian Nights. At 12 he left school to work in a boot-blacking factory when his father was imprisoned for debt, and after three years he returned to school.

Dickens began as a political journalist, reporting Parliamentary debates and election campaigns. His journalism in periodicals formed Sketches by Boz in 1836, Boz being a family nickname. His literary success began with the serial publication of The Pickwick Papers in 1836, and within a few years he was an international celebrity. In December 1845 he became editor of the Daily News but resigned after ten weeks.

On 9 June 1865, returning from Paris with Ellen Ternan, he was in the Staplehurst rail crash in Kent, in which ten passengers were killed. He tended the wounded until rescuers came and went back for the manuscript of Our Mutual Friend.

Dickens wrote 15 major novels, several novellas and many short stories. Most were published in weekly or monthly instalments, which became the dominant Victorian mode, and let him judge his audience's reaction and sometimes change his plot. Among his works are A Christmas Carol (1843), David Copperfield (1849 to 1850) and Bleak House (1852 to 1853), a satire on the judicial system that helped support a reformist movement leading to the legal reform of the 1870s. His works have never gone out of print.
charles-duke-of-lower-lorraine: Charles was born at Reims in the summer of 953, the son of Louis IV of France and Gerberga of Saxony and the younger brother of King Lothair. He was a sixth-generation descendant of Charlemagne. When his father was captured by the Normans, both sons were demanded as ransom, but Queen Gerberga would send only Charles, and his father was released into the custody of Hugh Capet.

In or before 976 Charles accused Lothair's wife Emma, daughter of Lothair II of Italy, of infidelity with Adalberon, Bishop of Laon. The council of Sainte-Macre at Fismes exonerated both, but Charles kept up his claim and was driven from the kingdom. He took refuge with his cousin, the emperor Otto II, who promised to crown him once Lothair was out of the way. Charles paid Otto homage and received Lower Lorraine.

In August 978 Lothair invaded Germany and captured Aachen but failed to take either Otto or Charles. In October the emperor and Charles invaded France in turn and devastated the land around Reims, Soissons and Laon, where Theodoric I, Bishop of Metz, crowned Charles. Lothair fled to Paris and was besieged, but a relief army under Hugh Capet forced Otto and Charles to lift the siege on 30 November, and Lothair and Hugh retook Laon. Around 979 Charles moved the relics of Saint Gudula to Saint-Géry Island near Brussels and built the city's first permanent fortification there.

Because Charles was also Lothair's vassal, his acts for Otto were treated as treason and he was excluded from the throne. The magnates elected Lothair's son Louis V in 986 and, on his death in 987, Hugh Capet. Charles's unexceptional marriage and lack of wealth were further reasons he was denied the crown. He made war on Hugh and took Reims and Laon, but on Maundy Thursday, 26 March 991, he was captured through the treachery of Bishop Adalberon and imprisoned by Hugh at Orléans. His son Otto succeeded him as duke.

The date and place of Charles's death are uncertain. The necrology of the diocese of Liège gives 22 June without a year, and two documents of January 992 imply that he was still alive. He was dead by 995, when Adalberon and Count Odo of Blois tried to put his son Louis on the throne. In 1666 a lead sarcophagus bearing the date 1001 was found in the Basilica of Saint Servatius in Maastricht; the date seems to mark his reburial, probably arranged by his son Otto. The Historia Francorum Senonensis, written between 1015 and 1034, held that Charles had been the rightful king in 987 and Hugh a usurper.
charles-edward-duke-of-saxe-coburg-and-g: Charles Edward was born in Surrey, England, on 19 July 1884, several months after his father Prince Leopold, Duke of Albany, the youngest son of Queen Victoria, died after slipping and hitting his head. His mother was Princess Helen of Waldeck and Pyrmont. He succeeded to his father's titles at birth and grew up as a British prince, a sickly child, and was educated privately, including at Eton College. In 1899 he was selected to succeed his uncle Duke Alfred, because he was young enough to be re-educated as a German, and at fifteen he moved to Germany, where his cousin Emperor Wilhelm II took control of his education.

Charles Edward inherited the duchy at sixteen, on Alfred's death in July 1900, and reigned through a regency under Prince Ernst of Hohenlohe-Langenburg until he came of age on 19 July 1905. He married Princess Victoria Adelaide of Schleswig-Holstein-Sonderburg-Glücksburg on 11 October 1905, a bride chosen by Wilhelm, and they had five children. He joined patriotic groups and stressed his loyalty to Germany with Christmas festivities and folk costumes, yet he never won much popularity. People in Gotha thought him absolutist, and in Coburg they disliked his foreignness and his English accent.

At the outbreak of the First World War he was in England to receive an honorary degree from Oxford. He told his sister that he wanted to fight for Great Britain but felt obliged to return to his duchy, where he did on 9 July, and he sided with the German Empire. Britain removed his titles under the Titles Deprivation Act of 1917, effective 28 March 1919, and he was deposed like the other German princes, ending his rule on 14 November 1918.

In the 1920s he described himself as a monarchist but supported violent far-right paramilitary groups. From 1929 he gave financial support to the Nazi Party, attracted by its militarism and anti-communism, and he joined it in March 1933 and became an Obergruppenführer in the Sturmabteilung. On 1 December 1933 he became head of the German Red Cross, where control passed largely to his deputy Paul Hocheisen in 1934. He served the regime as an informal diplomat, touring Japan in 1934.

American authorities interned him from 1945 to 1946, and a denazification court gave him a minor conviction. He died of cancer in Coburg on 6 March 1954. His sister Alice minimised his role in her memoirs, but the historian Karina Urbach argued that the book is misleading and selective.
charles-edward-stuart: Charles Edward Louis John Sylvester Maria Casimir Stuart was born on 31 December 1720 at the Palazzo Muti in Rome, where his father had been given a residence by Pope Clement XI. His mother was Maria Clementina Sobieska, a Polish noblewoman and granddaughter of John III Sobieski. His grandfather James II and VII had been deposed in the Revolution of 1688, and the Jacobite cause aimed to restore the Stuarts to the thrones of England and Scotland.

In 1734, aged thirteen, he went with his cousin the Duke of Liria to the siege of Gaeta, his first experience of war. His mother died in January 1735. A tour of Italian cities from 1737 shocked him: most courts, wishing not to antagonise Britain, would receive him only as the Duke of Albany, and Venice was the exception.

Charles went to France in 1744 to join a planned invasion that storms partly wrecked. Encouraged by Irish and Scottish exiles, he borrowed some 180,000 livres from Paris bankers, using the Sobieski crown jewels as security, and fitted out two ships. He landed on the west coast of Scotland, won the support of Donald Cameron of Lochiel, and raised his father's standard at Glenfinnan on 19 August 1745. Lord George Murray joined him at Perth on 4 September.

The Jacobites won at Prestonpans in September 1745, and Charles held court at Holyrood Palace. A Prince's Council of senior leaders was formed, and he resented it as an imposition on his divinely appointed monarch. The council agreed to invade England by way of Carlisle. After a victory at Falkirk Muir in January 1746 the siege of Stirling Castle was abandoned and the army moved north to Inverness, pursued by the Duke of Cumberland. Defeat at Culloden in April 1746 effectively ended the Stuart cause, and Charles landed back in France on 10 October 1746.

The French received him warmly but gave no further help. He was arrested at the opera in December 1748 and expelled under the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle. After his father's death in 1766 he lived mostly in Rome and Florence, and he married Princess Louise of Stolberg-Gedern in 1772. His health declined and he was said to be an alcoholic. He died in Rome of a stroke on 30 January 1788; his brother, Cardinal Henry, had the record read as 31 January, since 30 January was the anniversary of the execution of Charles I.

He was buried at Frascati and in 1807 his remains were moved to the crypt of St Peter's Basilica. His escape from Scotland made him a romantic figure of heroic failure, and songs such as The Skye Boat Song and Mo Ghile Mear commemorate his flight.
charles-edzard-prince-of-east-frisia: Charles Edzard was born on 18 June 1716 in the castle at Aurich, the fourth child of the reigning prince George Albert and Princess Christine Louise of Nassau-Idstein. All his siblings died in their first year, and his father, fearing the end of the male line of the Cirksena, gave him a harsh education in an atmosphere of ascetic piety, in which every hour, even his riding and walking, followed a fixed timetable.

He was taught Roman law, medieval history and French, and though his father made him colonel and chief of the small princely militia at the age of ten, he never received military training. His world was limited to the court at Aurich, the hunting lodge at Sandhorst and Berum Castle. He never visited Emden, the largest city of his territory, though he once looked at it from a distance.

When George Albert, long ill, suffered a stroke, a marriage was hastily arranged, probably by Charles Edzard's stepmother. On 25 May 1734 at Berum Castle he married his sixteen-year-old cousin, Princess Sophie Wilhelmine of Brandenburg-Kulmbach-Bayreuth. Three weeks later, on 12 June 1734, his father died and he became ruler without being prepared for the task. Years of conflict between the princely house and the estates had left the prince with little prestige, and Emden and other rebellious estates refused to pay him homage. Whether he took any part in governing is doubtful; his decisions were probably made by others.

His only child to be born alive, Elisabeth Sophie Magdalena, died in 1742 at the age of one. Charles Edzard died unexpectedly at Aurich on 25 May 1744, aged 28, four days after his wife miscarried in her second pregnancy; whether his death was natural can no longer be established. Under the Emden Convention, concluded on 14 March 1744 between the city of Emden and Frederick II of Prussia, Frederick was able to march into East Frisia without resistance.
charles-eliot-diplomat: Charles Norton Edgcumbe Eliot was born on 8 January 1862 in the village of Sibford Gower near Banbury, Oxfordshire. He was educated at Cheltenham College and Balliol College, Oxford, where he took a double first in classical moderations and Greats and won the Craven, Ireland and Hertford scholarships, as well as the Boden Sanskrit Scholarship and the Houghton Syriac prize. He knew 16 languages fully and could converse in 20 more.

Eliot served in diplomatic posts in Russia from 1885, Morocco, Turkey and Washington, D.C., and as British Commissioner in Samoa, and was knighted on 1 January 1900. In East Africa he hosted the colonial secretary Joseph Chamberlain in December 1902. When hundreds of would-be settlers, chiefly from South Africa, arrived in 1903, he wrote in the Natal Witness that the Maasai and many other peoples must go under, a prospect he said he viewed with equanimity.

Lord Lansdowne, the Foreign Secretary, decided to lease 500 square miles to the East Africa Syndicate but refused Eliot leave to grant 50 square miles each to two South African applicants. Eliot refused to carry out instructions he called unjust and impolitic, and resigned by a public telegram from Mombasa dated 21 June 1904. In 1905 he became the first Vice-Chancellor of the University of Sheffield, and in 1912 the first Vice-Chancellor of the University of Hong Kong, until he was made high commissioner in Siberia in August 1918. As ambassador to Japan he regretted the decision to end the Anglo-Japanese alliance.

After his post in Japan ended he stayed there to study the practice of Buddhism. Taken ill with influenza on the voyage home, he died on 16 March 1931 and was buried at sea in the Straits of Malacca; he never married. Besides The East Africa Protectorate, Turkey in Europe and the three volumes of Hinduism and Buddhism, he wrote A Finnish Grammar. He was also a marine biologist who described many sea slugs, among them Chelidonura varians; the World Register of Marine Species lists 119 taxa named by him, and the nudibranch genus Eliotia bears his name.
charles-emmanuel-i-duke-of-savoy: Charles Emmanuel was born on 12 January 1562 in the Castle of Rivoli in Piedmont, the only child of Emmanuel Philibert, Duke of Savoy, and Margaret of France, Duchess of Berry. He succeeded his father on 30 August 1580. He spoke Italian, French, Spanish and Latin and proved an able warrior, though short and hunchbacked. He was nicknamed Testa di Fuoco, or Hothead, for his aggressive and rash military character, and was also a patron of the arts and a writer.

In the autumn of 1588, with France weakened by civil war, he occupied the Marquisate of Saluzzo, a French possession since 1548. Henry IV demanded its return, Charles Emmanuel refused, and war followed. Geneva and the Swiss cantons joined the French coalition, but their offensive was repelled in April 1589 and Bern signed a truce that October. The Peace of Vervins of 2 May 1598 left Saluzzo unsettled; the Treaty of Lyon of 17 January 1601 finally gave it to Savoy.

He then attacked Geneva. On the night of 11 December his troops reached the walls by two in the morning, and his cuirassiers were ordered to dismount and climb them in full armour. A night watchman raised the alarm and the city's militia rose to meet the invaders. Fifty-four Savoyards were killed, many were captured, and the prisoners were executed. The defence is still marked each year at the festival of L'Escalade, and the Treaty of St. Julien of July 1603 restored occupied territories on both sides.

Later wars set him against Spain, France and Venice by turns. After the death in 1612 of Duke Francesco IV Gonzaga of Mantua he assaulted Montferrat, which arrayed the Venetians, Tuscany, the Empire and Spain against him and forced him to give up his conquest. In 1619 his son Victor Amadeus married Christine Marie, sister of Louis XIII of France.

In 1628 he allied with Spain, annexed Trino and Alba and defeated a French army at Sampeyre, but when Cardinal Richelieu invaded Piedmont he changed sides again, and then declared himself neutral. In 1630 a French army entered Savoy to end that neutrality and occupied Pinerolo and Avigliana. The duke died suddenly of a stroke at Savigliano in late July, aged 68. His son Victor Amadeus made peace, which confirmed the annexation of Trino and Alba and the loss of Pinerolo.

His campaigns against Spanish influence stirred early Italian patriotic feeling. Alessandro Tassoni published two Filippiche urging the Italian nobles to join Savoy in ridding Italy of Spanish hegemony, and the poet Fulvio Testi dedicated a collection of poems to him.
charles-emmanuel-ii-duke-of-savoy: Charles Emmanuel was born in Turin on 20 June 1634, the son of Victor Amadeus I, Duke of Savoy, and Christine of France, whose parents were Henry IV of France and Marie de' Medici. In 1638, on the death of his elder brother Francis Hyacinth, Duke of Savoy, he succeeded to the duchy at the age of four. His mother governed in his place until he came of age in 1648, and he then invited her to continue to rule while he lived a life of pleasure far from the affairs of state.

He was notorious for his persecution of the Vaudois, or Waldensians, which culminated in the massacre of 1655 known as the Piedmontese Easter. John Milton wrote the sonnet On the Late Massacre in Piedmont in response. Oliver Cromwell, Lord Protector, called a general fast in England, proposed to send the navy if the killing was not stopped and raised funds for the Waldensians, with Sir Samuel Morland commissioned to carry out the task. The massacre began the Savoyard–Waldensian wars (1655–1690), in which Waldensian rebels used guerrilla tactics against ducal campaigns to enforce Roman Catholicism on the whole population.

Charles Emmanuel took real power only after his mother's death in 1663. He failed to win a passage to the sea at the expense of Genoa in the Second Genoese–Savoyard War of 1672–1673 and struggled to keep his influence against France. He did improve commerce, developed the port of Nice and built a road through the Alps towards France. He replaced the mercenary army with five Piedmontese regiments, recreated the cavalry, introduced uniforms and restored fortifications, and he built many buildings in Turin, among them the Palazzo Reale.

His first marriage, on 3 April 1663, was to Françoise Madeleine d'Orléans and produced no children; his mother had favoured it over his wish to marry Marie Jeanne of Savoy. His first wife died at the start of 1664, and on 20 May 1665 he married Marie Jeanne, who bore his son Victor Amadeus II. In 1672 he allowed Hortense Mancini, Duchess of Mazarin, to take refuge in Chambéry, which led to tension at court. He died on 12 June 1675 and was buried in Turin Cathedral, leaving his wife as regent for their nine-year-old son.
charles-emmanuel-iii-of-sardinia: Charles Emmanuel was born in Turin to Victor Amadeus II of Savoy and his first wife Anne Marie d'Orléans. As Duke of Aosta he was not at first the heir, but his older brother died in 1715. His father had been made king of Sicily in 1713 under the Treaty of Utrecht and was forced to exchange Sicily for the less important Kingdom of Sardinia in 1720.

On 3 September 1730 Victor Amadeus abdicated. His son, whom he had not favoured and whose education he had neglected except in military matters, became king. Victor Amadeus soon reclaimed the throne, accusing his son of incompetence, and settled at Moncalieri. Charles Emmanuel had him arrested by the Crown Council to prevent an attack on Milan that might have brought an invasion of Piedmont. The old king was confined at the Castle of Rivoli, where he died without further interference.

In the War of the Polish Succession Charles Emmanuel sided with the French-backed King Stanislaw I and, after an alliance signed at Turin on 28 October 1733, marched on Milan and occupied Lombardy. He refused to let Spain take Milan and Mantua, which would have restored Spanish domination in Italy, and voluntarily thwarted the expedition against Mantua. His army was victorious at Crocetta and Guastalla, but when Austria and France made peace he had to leave Lombardy and received instead Langhe, Tortona and Novara.

In the War of the Austrian Succession he sided with Maria Theresa, with financial and naval support from Great Britain and the Dutch Republic. A Franco-Spanish invasion took Savoy and the County of Nice, and in 1744 he defended Cuneo against besiegers. In 1745, with some 20,000 men against armies totalling some 60,000, he lost Alessandria, Asti and Casale; with Austrian reinforcements he recaptured Alessandria and Asti in 1746, and in 1747 he won a crushing victory over the French at the Battle of Assietta. At the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle he regained Nice and Savoy and obtained Vigevano and other lands in the Po plain.

Charles Emmanuel declined to take part in the Seven Years' War and concentrated on administrative reforms, a well-disciplined army and stronger fortresses. To improve the condition of Sardinia he restored the universities of Sassari and Cagliari. He added many paintings to the collection he inherited, which came to hold the largest collection in Italy of 16th and 17th-century Flemish and Dutch paintings in the Sabauda Gallery, and he founded a tapestry workshop in Turin in 1731. Charles Emmanuel married three times, and all three wives died young. He died in Turin in 1773 and was buried in the Basilica of Superga. He was the paternal grandfather of the last three mainline kings of Sardinia.
charles-emmanuel-iv-of-sardinia: Charles Emmanuel was born in Turin on 24 May 1751, the eldest son of Victor Amadeus III and Infanta Maria Antonia Ferdinanda of Spain. Until 1796 he was styled Prince of Piedmont. After his father became king of Sardinia in 1773, a political marriage was arranged for him, and on 6 September 1775 he married Clotilde of France, a sister of Louis XVI, at Chambéry. The union was arranged for political reasons, but the couple became devoted to each other and shared a strict and sober Catholic faith. They had no children.

The French Revolution affected him deeply, especially the execution of his brother-in-law Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette in 1793. From 1794 troops of the French First Republic raided the Savoyard domains, and he sought solace in his faith, joining the Third Order of Saint Dominic that year.

He succeeded his father on 16 October 1796. The kingdom held the island of Sardinia and large territories in north-western Italy, including all of Piedmont. In March 1796 Sardinia had been forced to accept the disadvantageous Treaty of Paris, which gave the French army free passage through Piedmont. The treasury was empty, the army disorganised and revolutionary feeling strong; two conspiracies against the monarchy were foiled between 1796 and 1798 and the conspirators condemned to death.

On 6 December 1798 French troops under Joubert occupied Turin and forced the king to give up his mainland territories. He went to Parma and Florence, and in February 1799 security concerns drove him to Sardinia. There he protested against the confiscation of his mainland lands, announced reforms for the island and closed its ports to the English fleet. After a Russian army freed Turin, he returned to Livorno on 22 September 1799, only to find that the Russian army had left Piedmont in Austrian hands and that the Austrian side was not inclined to support his restoration.

From 1800 to 1802 he and his wife stayed in Rome, Frascati, Naples and Caserta. Clotilde died on 7 March 1802, and he was so moved by her death that he abdicated on 4 June 1802 in favour of his brother Victor Emmanuel I, keeping the personal title of king. In 1815, aged sixty-four, he took simple vows in the Society of Jesus and lived the rest of his life at the Jesuit novitiate in Rome, never ordained a priest. He died at the Palazzo Colonna in Rome on 6 October 1819 and is buried in the Church of Sant'Andrea al Quirinale.

When his cousin Henry Benedict Stuart died in 1807 he became heir-general of Charles I of England and so inherited the Jacobite claim to the British thrones, which neither he nor his successors ever pressed.
charles-fourier: François Marie Charles Fourier was born in Besançon on 7 April 1772, the son of a small businessman. He cared more for architecture than for his father's trade and as a boy was most interested in geography. When his father died in 1781 he received two-fifths of an estate valued at more than 200,000 francs, which allowed him to travel through Europe. From 1791 to 1816 he worked in Paris, Rouen, Lyon, Marseille and Bordeaux as a travelling salesman and correspondence clerk, complaining of serving the knavery of merchants. He wrote most of his works between 1816 and 1821 and died in Paris on 10 October 1837.

His first book, the Theory of the Four Movements and the General Destinies, appeared anonymously in Lyon in 1808 and sold few copies. Fourier held that cooperation is the key to social success. People would live in communities called phalanxes, housed in phalanstères, four-storey apartment complexes where the richest had the upper floors. Jobs would be assigned by interest and desire, with higher pay for unattractive work. He counted 12 common passions and 810 types of character, so that an ideal phalanx would have 1,620 people. The phalanstères remained concepts, since he never obtained the money to build them.

Fourier argued that important jobs should be open to women by skill, and he never married. He saw poverty rather than inequality as the chief cause of disorder. He also wrote of Jews as the ruin of the body politic, called trade, which he associated with them, the source of all evil, and proposed that Jews be made to farm in the phalansteries. John K. Roth and Richard L. Rubenstein see his antisemitism as economic and religious, not the racial kind that emerged later.

Fourier's proposals inspired intentional communities in the United States, among them Utopia in Ohio, the North American Phalanx in New Jersey and Brook Farm in Massachusetts, and the Familistery of Guise in France. His follower Victor Considerant carried his ideas into the 1848 Revolution and the Paris Commune. Friedrich Engels named him one of three major utopian socialists, and Peter Kropotkin saw him as founder of the libertarian branch of socialism.
charles-frederick-duke-of-holstein-gotto: Charles Frederick was born in Sweden on 30 April 1700, the son of Frederick IV of Schleswig-Holstein-Gottorp and Hedvig Sophia, daughter of King Charles XI of Sweden and sister of Charles XII. His father died at the Battle of Kliszów in 1702, and he became duke in infancy, with his mother as regent. She died in 1708, and his great-grandmother Hedwig Eleonora of Schleswig-Holstein-Gottorp, who reportedly spoiled him, raised him. His guardians sided with Sweden in the Great Northern War, and in 1713 Danish troops conquered the northern portions of the Gottorp share of the duchies, including Gottorp castle.

Charles Frederick met Charles XII for the first time in 1716 and was declared of age in 1717. When Charles XII died in 1718 the duke was presented as a claimant to the Swedish throne, but his aunt Ulrika Eleonora took it, arguing that her elder sister had not obtained the consent of the Estates for her marriage to his father. The duke's party held that Sweden's absolute monarchy made that clause irrelevant. Arvid Horn forced him to greet her as queen, and he left Sweden in 1719.

He settled in Russia and in May 1725 married Anna Petrovna, elder daughter of Peter the Great, who saw the match as politically useful. After Peter's death Catherine I gave him a place in the council, a court, a palace and an income. As commander of the palace guard in St Petersburg he tried to secure his wife's succession on Catherine's death in 1727, but failed. They then moved to Kiel Castle, where Anna died after the birth of their son in 1728.

In the Treaty of Frederiksborg of 1720 Sweden pledged to cease its support of the house of Holstein-Gottorp, which made regaining the lost share of Schleswig virtually impossible; the duke opposed it. Sweden later excluded him and his heirs from the succession because of their Russian ties, and his cousin Adolph Frederick was elected crown prince. Charles Frederick died in 1739 at Rohlfshagen and is buried at Bordesholm. His son Charles Peter Ulrich became Russian tsar as Peter III in 1762, and so Charles Frederick is the patrilineal ancestor of the Russian emperors from Peter III onward.
charles-frederick-grand-duke-of-baden: Charles Frederick was born at Karlsruhe on 22 November 1728, the son of Hereditary Prince Frederick of Baden-Durlach and Amalia of Nassau-Dietz. He succeeded his grandfather as Margrave of Baden-Durlach in 1738 and ruled personally from 1746. On 28 January 1751 he married Caroline Louise of Hesse-Darmstadt, and they had five children, of whom three survived infancy. In 1747 he was elected a fellow of the Royal Society.

In 1771 Charles Frederick inherited the Margraviate of Baden-Baden from the Catholic line of his family, which reunited the original land of Baden. It made him the Protestant ruler of a state that was overwhelmingly Catholic, but the Imperial Diet allowed it, because the Elector of Saxony had converted from Lutheranism to Catholicism and had been permitted to keep control of the Protestant body of the Diet.

He was regarded as a good example of an enlightened despot, supporting schools, universities, jurisprudence, the civil service, the economy, culture and urban development. He outlawed torture in 1767 and serfdom in 1783. With his architect Friedrich Weinbrenner he built the classical buildings that distinguish Karlsruhe.

In 1803 he became Elector of Baden and in 1806 the first Grand Duke. Through the policy of his minister Sigismund von Reitzenstein, Baden acquired the Bishopric of Constance, the right-bank Rhine territories of the bishoprics of Basel, Strassburg and Speyer, and also the Breisgau and Ortenau. In 1806 Baden joined the Confederation of the Rhine.

Charles Frederick died at Karlsruhe on 10 June 1811, one of the few German rulers to die during the Napoleonic era. His grandson Charles succeeded him. In 1787 he had made a second, morganatic marriage to Louise Caroline Geyer von Geyersberg, whose children could not succeed. By 1817 his descendants by the first marriage were dying out, and to keep Baden from passing to the king of Bavaria, Grand Duke Charles changed the succession law to give the Hochberg family full rights. The constitution of 1818 and the Treaty of Frankfurt of 1819 confirmed this, and the descendants of his son Leopold ruled Baden until 1918.
charles-george-gordon: Charles George Gordon was born at Woolwich on 28 January 1833, the son of Major General Henry William Gordon. The men of the family had been army officers for four generations, and all of his brothers also became officers. He grew up in England, Ireland, Scotland and the Ionian Islands as his father was posted from place to place, and was educated at Taunton School and the Royal Military Academy at Woolwich. In the Crimean War he arrived at Balaklava in January 1855, after writing several letters to the War Office asking to be sent there.

Gordon volunteered for service in China in 1860 and arrived at Hong Kong too late for the fighting of the Second Opium War. In March 1863 he took command of the Ever Victorious Army, a force of Chinese soldiers led by European officers, at Songjiang. He moved his men and supplies by the canals and rivers, treated prisoners well, and enlisted many former Taipings. After he took Suzhou in November 1863 he guaranteed humane treatment for any rebel who laid down arms, but Imperial forces executed the Taiping prisoners, which enraged him. He disbanded the army in June 1864, having won thirty-three battles in succession at a cost of about 1,000 of his 3,500 soldiers killed or wounded.

In 1871 he was British representative on the commission for navigation of the mouth of the Danube. He entered the service of the Khedive of Egypt in 1873, with the approval of the British government, and later became Governor-General of the Sudan, where he worked to end the slave trade and abolished torture and public floggings. Corrupt officials ignored many of his orders against the trade. He left the Sudan and returned to Europe in 1880.

A revolt had broken out in the Sudan under Muhammad Ahmad, who proclaimed himself the Mahdi. In early 1884 Gordon was sent to Khartoum to arrange the evacuation of loyal soldiers and civilians. He removed about 2,500 civilians but stayed, and the siege by Mahdist forces began on 18 March 1884. He held out for almost a year, which won him the admiration of the British public but not of the government, which had decided to abandon the Sudan. A relief force under General Wolseley reached Khartoum two days after the city fell, and Gordon was killed in January 1885.

How he died is uncertain. The popular account, in which he met the Ansar unarmed in his dress uniform, was promoted by the British press and by George William Joy's painting of 1893. Public grief in Britain was great, and the Gordon Boys Home, now Gordon's School at Woking, was founded as his memorial.
charles-grant-1st-baron-glenelg: Grant was born on 26 October 1778 at Kidderpore in the Bengal Presidency, the eldest son of Charles Grant, chairman of the directors of the British East India Company. His brother, Sir Robert Grant, also became an MP and was Governor of Bombay. Charles was educated at Magdalene College, Cambridge, became a fellow in 1802 and was called to the bar in 1807.

Grant entered the House of Commons in 1811 as Member of Parliament for Inverness Burghs and sat for Inverness-shire from 1818. He became a Lord of the Treasury in December 1813; having failed to retake the parliamentary oaths in the prescribed manner at his ministerial by-election, he needed a private act, Mr. Grant's Indemnity Act 1814, to escape the penalties. He was Chief Secretary for Ireland and a Privy Counsellor from August 1819, Vice-President of the Board of Trade from 1823, and President of the Board of Trade and Treasurer of the Navy from September 1827 to June 1828.

Breaking with the Tories over Reform, he joined the Whigs by way of the Canningites and was President of the Board of Control under Lord Grey and Lord Melbourne from November 1830 to November 1834, chiefly responsible for the Government of India Act 1833. Created Baron Glenelg when he became Colonial Secretary in April 1835, he had serious differences with Sir Benjamin d'Urban, Governor of Cape Colony, and graver ones with King William IV and others over Canada. After the rebellion of 1837 his policy was fiercely attacked in Parliament, he quarrelled with Lord Durham, and even cabinet colleagues favoured replacing him; he resigned in February 1839.

Glenelg died at Cannes, France, on 23 April 1866, aged 87, and the barony became extinct with him. He has been called the last of the Canningites. A ship named the Lord Glenelg after him sailed from Britain to Australia in 1841.
charles-i-count-palatine-of-birkenfeld: Charles was born in Neuburg on 4 September 1560, a member of the House of Wittelsbach and the youngest son of Wolfgang, Count Palatine of Zweibrücken, and his wife Anna of Hesse, a daughter of Philip I, Landgrave of Hesse. His titles were Count Palatine of the Rhine, Duke in Bavaria, and Count of Veldenz and Sponheim.

When the brothers partitioned their father's lands after his death in 1569, Charles, as the youngest, received only the Palatine share of the Rear County of Sponheim, a small territory around Birkenfeld. He ruled it as Duke of Zweibrücken-Birkenfeld from 1569 until 1600. His state was of little weight, and his chief fame rests on his descendants.

On 23 February 1590 he married Duchess Dorothea of Brunswick-Lüneburg (1570-1649), a member of the House of Welf and a daughter of William VI, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg, and Princess Dorothea of Denmark. They had four children: George William (1591-1669), Sophie (1593-1676), who married Crato VII of Hohenlohe-Neuenstein, Frederick (1594-1626) and Christian (1598-1654).

Charles died in Birkenfeld on 16 December 1600, aged 40. He was buried in the Schlosskirche at Meisenheim, where his wife was later laid beside him. As the founder of the House of Palatinate-Birkenfeld, he is the ancestor from whom the later dukes and kings of Bavaria descended. His eldest son, George William, was born on 6 August 1591 and lived until 25 December 1669.
charles-i-of-anjou: Charles was the youngest child of King Louis VIII of France and Blanche of Castile, and the first Capetian to be named for Charlemagne. The late king willed that his youngest sons be prepared for a career in the Church, and Charles was destined for it until the early 1240s. He received a good education and had a documented passion for poetry, medicine and law. In December 1244 Louis IX took a vow to lead a crusade, and Charles took the cross too, despite his mother's opposition. The crusaders took Damietta in 1249, and the brothers were captured on 6 April 1250 and released for a ransom. Charles returned to France in October 1250.

Charles held Provence and Forcalquier through his wife's inheritance. After returning from Egypt he put down a rebellion in Provence: Arles surrendered in April 1251, Avignon in May, and Marseille, the last to resist, made peace in July 1252. In 1263 he accepted the Holy See's offer of the Kingdom of Sicily, called the Regno. He was crowned in Rome on 5 January 1266, annihilated Manfred's army and occupied the Regno almost without resistance. His victory over Conradin at Tagliacozzo in 1268 secured his rule. In 1272 he took the title King of Albania, in 1277 he purchased a claim to the Kingdom of Jerusalem, and in 1278 he became Prince of Achaea.

His rule in the Regno rested on heavy taxation, notably the subventio generalis, which the popes called illegal. In 1281 Pope Martin IV authorised a crusade against the Byzantine Empire. The Sicilian Vespers rebellion of 30 March 1282 ended his rule on the island, and Peter III of Aragon was declared king of Sicily at Palermo on 4 September.

Charles prepared a campaign to regain Sicily, but fell seriously ill, made his will on 6 January 1285 and died on 7 January. His body was buried in Naples, and his heart was placed at the Couvent Saint-Jacques in Paris. Two realms, each ruled by a king styled of Sicily, then coexisted for more than a century. The chroniclers Bartholomaeus of Neocastro and Saba Malaspina strongly influenced modern views of Charles, though both were biased: the first called him a tyrant to justify the Vespers. He gave estates in the kingdom to about 700 noblemen from France or Provence.
charles-i-of-england: Charles was born at Dunfermline Palace on 19 November 1600, the second son of King James VI of Scotland and Anne of Denmark, and was created Duke of Albany. He was a weak and sickly infant and stayed in Scotland when his family went to England in 1603 after James inherited the English throne. He became heir apparent in 1612 on the death of his elder brother Henry Frederick. An unpopular attempt to marry him to the Spanish Infanta Maria Anna ended with a visit to Spain in 1623, and on 1 May 1625 he married the French princess Henrietta Maria by proxy.

Charles believed in the divine right of kings and was determined to govern according to his own conscience. He quarrelled with the English Parliament, and many subjects opposed his levying of taxes without its consent. In January 1629 MPs held the Speaker down in his chair so that resolutions against Catholicism, Arminianism and tonnage and poundage could be read. Charles dissolved Parliament and imprisoned nine leaders, among them Sir John Eliot. To raise money he revived the Distraint of Knighthood, a law unused for over a century, and fined men who had not attended his coronation in 1626.

His religious policies and his Catholic marriage made Puritans and Scottish Covenanters distrust him. His attempts to make the Church of Scotland adopt high Anglican practices led to the Bishops' Wars, the first beginning in 1639. The Long Parliament assembled on 3 November 1640 and began proceedings against his leading counsellors. In mid-1642 both sides armed, and Charles raised the royal standard at Nottingham on 22 August 1642, setting up his court at Oxford.

After defeat in 1645 by the New Model Army he surrendered to a Scottish force and was handed over to the Long Parliament. He escaped from Hampton Court on 11 November 1647 but was confined at Carisbrooke Castle. In January 1649 the Rump Parliament's House of Commons indicted him for treason, though the House of Lords rejected the charge, and the Chief Justices of the three common law courts opposed the indictment as unlawful. He was executed on 30 January 1649. The monarchy was abolished and the Commonwealth of England established; the monarchy was restored in 1660 under his son Charles II.

A memoir purportedly by him, the Eikon Basilike, went on sale ten days after his death and proved effective royalist propaganda. King Charles the Martyr was added to the Church of England's calendar in 1660.
charles-i-of-hungary: Charles was born in 1288 as Caroberto, the only son of Charles Martel, Prince of Salerno, and Clemence of Austria. His grandmother Mary, daughter of Stephen V of Hungary, claimed Hungary after her brother Ladislaus IV died in 1290, though the lords and prelates chose Andrew III instead. She passed the claim to her son and, after his death in 1295, to the seven-year-old Charles. His grandfather Charles II of Naples preferred his third son, Robert, and in 1296 gave him the rights of a firstborn, which excluded Charles from Naples.

In August 1300 the twelve-year-old Charles landed at Split, invited by the Croatian lord Paul Šubić. After Andrew III died on 14 January 1301 he was crowned with a provisional crown at Esztergom, but most Hungarians held the coronation unlawful and elected Wenceslaus of Bohemia.

Charles was elected king in Pest on 27 November 1308 and crowned with the Holy Crown at Székesfehérvár on 27 August 1310, his third coronation, yet his rule stayed nominal over most of the kingdom, which had broken into about a dozen provinces under oligarchs. He won his first decisive victory at Rozgony on 15 June 1312 against the Aba family and Matthew Csák. By 1323 he had taken full possession of his kingdom and moved his capital to Visegrád. Croatia kept its autonomous status.

Charles introduced a system of office fiefs, under which officials enjoyed revenues only while they held a royal office, and founded the Order of Saint George, the first secular order of knights. He promoted new gold mines, and the first Hungarian gold coins were minted in his reign. In 1330 his army was ambushed by the Wallachians at Posada, and Wallachia became independent. At the congress of Visegrád in 1335 he mediated between John of Bohemia and Casimir III of Poland.

Charles died at Visegrád on 16 July 1342 and was buried in the Székesfehérvár Basilica. He married several times: historians disagree about his first wife, Mary of Bytom or Mary of Galicia, and he then married Beatrice of Luxembourg and, in 1320, Elisabeth, daughter of Władysław I of Poland. His son Louis the Great succeeded him.

He declared that his aim was the restoration of the ancient good conditions of the kingdom. He left his son a full treasury and an effective system of taxation, according to Bryan Cartledge, but Louis's achievements overshadowed his reputation. The only contemporary record of his deeds was written by a hostile Franciscan friar, who dwelt on his cruel revenge against the family of Felician Záh and called the defeat at Posada a punishment from God.
charles-ii-archduke-of-austria: Charles II Francis was born in Vienna on 3 June 1540, the third son of Ferdinand I, Holy Roman Emperor, and Anne of Bohemia and Hungary. He belonged to the House of Habsburg. In 1559 and again from 1564 to 1568 he was proposed as a husband for Elizabeth I of England. Ferdinand I expected her to promise that Charles, as her widower, would succeed her if she died childless. Elizabeth decided against the match because he was a Catholic and her authority rested on a coalition that demanded the succession follow the Norman-Anglo-Saxon lineage. In 1563 he was also a suitor of Mary, Queen of Scots, but she disagreed, as did his older brother Maximilian.

From 1564 he ruled Inner Austria, comprising Styria, Carniola, Carinthia and Gorizia. Unlike his brother, Emperor Maximilian II, he was a devout Catholic and promoted the Counter-Reformation, inviting the Jesuits into his lands. Yet in 1572, in the Religious Pacification of Graz, and again in the Libellum of Bruck in 1578, he made significant concessions to the Inner Austrian Estates, which in practice meant tolerance towards Protestantism.

The Inner Austrian line bore the major burden of the wars against the Ottoman Empire, and in 1579 the fortress of Karlovac in Croatia was founded to guard against Ottoman invasions and named after him. He was a benefactor of the arts and sciences, and the composer Orlando di Lasso and the music theorist Lodovico Zacconi were among his protégés. He founded the Akademisches Gymnasium in Graz, the oldest secondary school in Styria, in 1573, and a stud for horses of Andalusian origin at Lipica in Slovenia in 1580, which gave him a leading part in the creation of the Lipizzan breed.

In 1585 he founded the University of Graz, which bears his name as the Karl-Franzens-Universität. On 26 August 1571 he had married his niece Maria Anna of Bavaria in Vienna; they had fifteen children, twelve of whom lived to adulthood. He died at Graz on 10 July 1590. His mausoleum in Seckau Abbey, where other members of the House of Habsburg are also buried, was begun in 1587 by Alessandro de Verda and completed by Sebastiano Carlone by 1612; it is one of the most important buildings of the early Baroque in the south-eastern Alps.
charles-ii-count-of-hohenzollern-sigmari: Charles was the fifth but second surviving son of Count Charles I of Hohenzollern and of Anna, daughter of Ernest, Margrave of Baden-Durlach. He was educated in Vienna and then in Freiburg im Breisgau with his elder brother Eitel Friedrich. At the Aulic Council in Vienna, where his father was president, he won the trust of Ferdinand II, Archduke of Further Austria, and entered his service in Tyrol. In 1570 he was appointed Supreme Captain and Governor in Alsace, and two years later he became guardian of Count Jakob of Geroldseck.

Under Charles I the county of Zollern, made up of the districts of Sigmaringen, Böhringen, Haigerloch and Wehrstein, was still united. In 1576 his three eldest sons agreed on a pact of inheritance by which each received an economically equal share, founding the lines of Hohenzollern-Hechingen, Hohenzollern-Haigerloch and Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen. Charles received Sigmaringen with the monasteries of Hedingen and Inzigkofen and the County of Veringen, but the inheritance carried heavy taxes owed to the Holy Roman Empire, and in 1588 the Reichskammergericht ruled that Sigmaringen was an imperial fief, a finding questioned until 1806.

He made Sigmaringen his main residence and rebuilt its castle, adding a vault and a church. In 1589 he acquired Ratzenhofen Castle in the village of Sigmaringendorf, and in 1595 he bought the district of Krauchenwies, which remained closely tied to Sigmaringen until 1850, when the region was annexed by Prussia.

In Munich on 18 January 1569 he married Euphrosyne, daughter of Frederick V, Count of Oettingen-Wallerstein, who bore him fifteen children before her death in 1590. On 13 May 1591 he married Elisabeth, daughter of Floris, Freiherr of Palant, and widow of James III, Margrave of Baden-Hachberg, with whom he had ten more; many of the children died young. Charles died on 8 April 1606. His son Johann became the first Prince of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen in 1623, and another son, Eitel Friedrich, became a cardinal in 1621 and Bishop of Osnabrück.
charles-ii-duke-of-brunswick: Charles was born in Brunswick on 30 October 1804, the eldest son of Frederick William, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg. His mother, Princess Marie of Baden, died in April 1808 after giving birth to a stillborn daughter. Charles and his younger brother William lived with their maternal grandmother in Glückstadt while their father raised the Black Brunswickers to fight Napoleon. After the duke escaped to Britain in 1809, the boys joined their paternal grandmother, Princess Augusta of Great Britain, at Blackheath and later at Vauxhall.

During his minority Charles was under the guardianship of George, prince regent of the United Kingdom and of Hanover. A dispute over his age of majority, which Charles put at 18 and George at 21, ended in a compromise at 19. Hanover meanwhile introduced a new constitution that limited his powers and income. On 10 May 1827 Charles declared it invalid in an edict that called Hanover a usurper, and when the German Confederation ordered him to accept it, he ignored the order and governed without countersigned decrees.

The press turned opinion against him, and his administration was attacked as corrupt and misguided. When the July Revolution broke out in 1830 he was in Paris. He hurried home promising to crush revolutionary tendencies, but on 6 September stone throwers attacked him on his way back from the theatre, and the next day a mob tried to break into the palace. He fled on 7 September. On 2 December the German Diet declared him incapable of governing.

Charles tried in vain to depose his brother by diplomacy and by force, and kept filing protests, including against Prussia's annexation of Hanover after the Austro-Prussian War of 1866. He lived mostly in Paris and London, where he feuded with the publisher Barnard Gregory over articles in The Satirist. In 1849 he won a libel case against The Weekly Dispatch, Brunswick v Harmer, which set a precedent in English defamation law on new publication of an old libel. He also lost to Paul Morphy in the chess game known as the Opera Game.

After war broke out between France and Germany he moved to Geneva, where he died at the Beau-Rivage Hotel on 18 August 1873. He left his estate of 24 million Swiss francs to the city on condition that it build him a mausoleum in the style of the Scaliger Tombs in Verona. The Brunswick Monument on the Quai du Mont-Blanc was unveiled on 14 October 1879, and the rest of the money paid for public buildings such as the Grand Théâtre.
charles-ii-duke-of-guelders: Charles was the son of Adolf of Egmond and Catherine of Bourbon, born either at Arnhem or at Grave. He grew up at the Burgundian court of Charles the Bold, who had bought the duchy of Guelders from Adolf in 1473. As a young man Charles fought in several battles against the armies of Charles VIII of France, until he was captured at the Battle of Béthune in 1487. Meanwhile King Maximilian acquired the Burgundian lands for the Habsburgs by marriage.

In 1492 the citizens of Guelders, disenchanted with Maximilian's rule, ransomed Charles and recognised him as their duke and Count of Zutphen, with his aunt Catherine as regent. Backed by the French king, he lost Guelders in 1505 to Maximilian's son Philip the Handsome and was made to accompany Philip to Spain for his coronation as King of Castile, but escaped at Antwerp. Philip died soon afterwards, and by July 1513 Charles held the whole duchy again.

In his struggle with the Habsburgs he was a major force behind the Frisian peasant rebellion, at first paying the rebel leader Pier Gerlofs Donia, then changing sides with his commander Maarten van Rossum when the rebels' fortunes turned. In the Treaty of Gorinchem of 1528 Emperor Charles, Philip's son, offered to recognise him on condition of inheriting the duchy if Charles died without issue; after further fighting the clause was removed. The Treaty of Grave brought peace with Burgundy in 1536.

In 1531 Charles turned on his former ally, the County of East Frisia. Balthasar Oomkens, lord of Esens, Stedesdorf and Wittmund, driven out by Enno II of East Frisia, ceded his lands to the Catholic duke in exchange for help, and the Guelderian Feud began when the commander Meindert von Hamme invaded East Frisia. The Lutheran counts accepted defeat in 1534. In 1519 Charles had married the young Elisabeth of Brunswick-Lüneburg; the marriage was childless, though he fathered several illegitimate children. He died at Arnhem on 30 June 1538 and was buried in the St. Eusebius Church there.
charles-ii-duke-of-lorraine: Charles, called the Bold (le Hardi), was the elder son of John I, Duke of Lorraine, and Sophie, daughter of Eberhard II, Count of Württemberg. His father had drawn away from the French court, and in his youth Charles was close to Philip II, Duke of Burgundy, beside whom he fought on several occasions. He was hostile to Louis I, Duke of Orléans, who had backed the citizens of Neufchâteau against his father.

He took part in some of the last crusading movements. He joined the Barbary Crusade of Louis II, Duke of Bourbon, in 1390, fought at the disastrous Battle of Nicopolis in 1396 in the company of John the Fearless, then Count of Nevers, and in 1399 aided the Teutonic Knights in Livonia. In 1393 he married Margaret of the Palatinate, daughter of Rupert, who replaced the deposed Wenceslaus as King of the Romans in 1400.

When France split between the Armagnacs and the Burgundians of John the Fearless, Charles supported the Burgundians, but he kept out of the Hundred Years' War itself; his brother Frederick I, Count of Vaudémont, was killed at the Battle of Agincourt in 1415. Queen Isabeau of Bavaria nevertheless made him Constable of France in 1418, an office he gave up in 1425, saying the burden was too great for him.

After John the Fearless was murdered in 1419, Charles changed course. The new duke, Philip III, held wide lands in the Low Countries, and only Lorraine and Champagne separated them from Burgundy, so Charles turned away from so dangerous a neighbour. Through his French connections he gained the support of King Charles VII against Burgundy and married his daughter Isabella to the Angevin René, later king of Naples.

His last years were troubled. His nephew Anthony of Vaudémont claimed part of the inheritance, and in 1425 Charles went to war against him without much success. Early in 1429 Joan of Arc, on a pilgrimage to Saint-Nicolas-de-Port, counselled him to leave his mistress Alison du May; he ignored the advice but gave Joan an escort and sent her on to Chinon. Charles died at his capital, Nancy, on 25 January 1431, the day Alison du May was murdered there. Of his legitimate children only two daughters survived, Isabella, who became duchess in her own right, and Catherine, who married Jacob, Margrave of Baden.
charles-ii-duke-of-parma: Charles Louis was born on 22 December 1799 at the Royal Palace of Madrid, the son of Louis, Prince of Piacenza, and Infanta Maria Luisa of Spain, and appears in Francisco de Goya's portrait of the family of Charles IV, in his mother's arms. After his father's death in 1803 he succeeded as King of Etruria, aged three. In 1807 Napoleon dissolved the kingdom and had him and his mother brought to France.

A plan to give him a Kingdom of Northern Lusitania in northern Portugal came to nothing. His mother was arrested in 1811 and shut in a convent in Rome, while the boy lived until 1815 in the household of his grandfather, the deposed Charles IV. The Congress of Vienna gave Lucca to his mother, with him as heir, and promised him Parma on the death of the Empress Marie Louise.

In 1820 he married Princess Maria Teresa of Savoy. They lived largely apart, and had two children, of whom only Charles III survived. On his mother's death on 13 March 1824 he became Duke of Lucca, but showed little interest in ruling. He travelled across Italy and Germany and left the government to his minister Ascanio Mansi, of whom it was said that while Charles Louis was the Duke, Mansi was king. In 1833 he returned and granted a general amnesty.

He studied biblical and liturgical texts, built a Greek Orthodox chapel at Marlia and was said to have flirted with Protestantism. Short of money, he sold the paintings of the Palatine Gallery in 1841. Under Austrian pressure he agreed in the Treaty of Florence of 1844 to cede Guastalla to Modena. Riots in 1847 led him to abdicate Lucca on 4 October in favour of the Grand Duke of Tuscany, for a pension.

When Marie Louise died on 17 December 1847 he took up Parma as Charles II. He was coldly received, and in the revolution of 1848 he granted a regency and then fled to Saxony. Austrian troops later occupied Parma and he took control of the government under their protection, but he soon abdicated for good in favour of his son.

As Count of Villafranca he lived in Paris, Nice and Saxony. His son Charles III was assassinated on 27 March 1854, and his grandson Robert I was deposed in March 1860. Unlike other dethroned Italian monarchs, he welcomed Italian unification as a positive development. He died at Nice on 16 April 1883, aged 83, and was buried at Viareggio.
charles-ii-elector-palatine: Charles II was born in Heidelberg on 10 April 1651, the son of Charles I Louis, Elector Palatine, of the House of Wittelsbach, and Charlotte of Hesse-Kassel. His parents separated after years of a turbulent marriage and his mother retired to Kassel, so that he grew up without her under the eye of an authoritarian father. His younger sister Elizabeth Charlotte, known as Liselotte, married Philippe I, Duke of Orléans, the brother of Louis XIV, in 1671. The scholars Samuel von Pufendorf and Ezekiel Spanheim directed his education. On a tour to Switzerland and France in 1670 he caught smallpox, which permanently disfigured his face.

In 1671, through the mediation of his aunt Sophia of Hanover, he married Princess Wilhelmine Ernestine of Denmark, a daughter of King Frederick III of Denmark. The marriage was unhappy and remained childless.

His short reign was not glamorous. He made his former tutor Paul Hachenberg, described as incompetent, his chief minister, and he left his half-siblings, the Raugraves, out of favour. He brought his mother back from Kassel and paid her large debts. He was a strict Calvinist, and after Hachenberg's death the court preacher Johann Ludwig Langhanns became senior minister. His character was weak and timid, marked by his childhood, and his enthusiasm for military life was superficial.

The state's finances worsened under the cost of oversized households, hunting, the theatre and military spending, which tax increases could no longer cover. In 1682 Charles pledged Germersheim to France for twenty years. He liked to stage expensive theatrical re-enactments of battles with sieges and ships, and within a few years he wasted the treasury that his father had saved over many years.

Charles died in Heidelberg on 26 May 1685. He was the last Elector Palatine of the Protestant Reformed House of Palatinate-Simmern, and the electorate passed to the Catholic branch of Palatinate-Neuburg. The rival claims to the Palatinate of his sister Elizabeth Charlotte, the Duchess of Orléans and Louis XIV's sister-in-law, served as the pretext for the French invasion of the Palatinate in 1688, which began the Nine Years War.
charles-ii-grand-duke-of-mecklenburg-str: Charles Louis Frederick of Mecklenburg was born in Mirow on 10 October 1741, the second son of Duke Charles Louis Frederick of Mecklenburg and Princess Elisabeth Albertine of Saxe-Hildburghausen. When his uncle Adolphus Frederick III died on 11 December 1752 and his older brother succeeded as Adolphus Frederick IV, Charles was taken with the rest of the family from Mirow to the capital, Strelitz. From the age of four he was set on a career in Hanoverian service, with a captain's commission.

His sister Charlotte married the Elector of Hanover, King George III of the United Kingdom, on 8 September 1761. Charles often visited her in Great Britain and entered his brother-in-law's service, with a chief military appointment at Hanover after service in Spain under Count Lippe.

In the autumn of 1776 George III appointed him governor-general of Hanover, where he effectively held all the powers of a sovereign ruler, since the king, thoroughly English, had no wish to live in Germany. After being widowed for a second time in December 1785, Charles asked to retire and resign the governorship. The king granted the request, promoted him to field marshal and gave him a pension. He then travelled and settled in Darmstadt as President of the Imperial Credit Commission.

His childless older brother Adolphus Frederick IV died on 2 June 1794, and Charles succeeded him as Duke of Mecklenburg-Strelitz. He encouraged new agricultural methods, set up a new police force and introduced compulsory education. In 1806 his duchy joined the Confederation of the Rhine, and after the Congress of Vienna he was raised to grand duke on 28 June 1815.

Charles fell ill with inflammation of the lungs after a tour in the summer of 1816 and died in Neustrelitz on 6 November 1816, following a fit of apoplexy. His eldest son George succeeded him. He had married Princess Friederike of Hesse-Darmstadt on 18 September 1768, and ten children were born, of whom five survived to adulthood. They included Louise, who married Frederick William III of Prussia, and Frederica, who married three times, the third time to Ernest Augustus, King of Hanover. After Friederike died in 1782 he married her sister Charlotte in 1784; she died in December 1785 shortly after the birth of a son.
charles-ii-margrave-of-baden-durlach: Charles was born in Pforzheim on 24 July 1529, the son of Margrave Ernest of Baden-Durlach and his second wife, Ursula of Rosenfeld. Because the marriage was morganatic, his right to succeed was disputed. He nevertheless began to govern Upper Baden in his father's name in September 1552. His half-brother Bernard IV, twelve years older, died on 20 January 1553 and his father two weeks later, on 6 February, leaving Charles the whole territory, then called Baden-Pforzheim.

Like his cousin Margrave Philibert of Baden-Baden, Charles supported the Peace of Augsburg in the Reichstag, and at the urging of Duke Christopher of Württemberg he adopted a new Church Order on 1 June 1556. A commission chaired by the chancellor Martin Achtsynit, with the theologian Jacob Andreae of Tübingen among its members, chose for political reasons to copy most of the Württemberg church order drafted by Johannes Brenz. Charles himself became bishop of the Evangelical Church, many Catholic priests were expelled, and the people called him the Pious.

The reform led to the prelate controversy. Catholic monasteries that held rights of patronage refused to pay for Lutheran pastors, citing Habsburg claims to the Upper Baden lordships, and Charles seized their estates. A compromise mediated by Johann Ulrich Zasius returned the estates but let Baden-Durlach keep the funds for the pastors; after the Austrian authorities in Innsbruck rejected it, the treaty of Neuenburg am Rhein of 24 April 1561 reached essentially the same result. That year he avowed the unchanged Augsburg Confession at Naumburg, and he sent auxiliary troops to help King Charles IX of France against the Huguenots.

The move of his residence from Liebeneck Castle in Pforzheim was allegedly set off by a quarrel with the townspeople, who refused to serve as drivers in a hunt, though Durlach was also more central within Lower Baden. He had the hunting lodge of Karlsburg enlarged into a castle and paid the workers himself from a shoulder bag of money, which earned him the nickname Charles with the Bag. A mint followed in 1571.

Charles died in Durlach on 23 March 1577. His widow, Anna of Veldenz, governed as regent for seven years, and the margraviate was then divided among his three sons, Ernest Frederick, James III and George Frederick. Ernest Frederick became a Calvinist and James a Catholic, but George Frederick, who outlived his brothers and remained a Lutheran, kept Baden-Durlach Lutheran.
charles-ii-of-england: Charles was born on 29 May 1630 at St James's Palace, the eldest surviving son of Charles I and Henrietta Maria of France. At or around his eighth birthday he was designated Prince of Wales, though he was never formally invested. After his father's execution on 30 January 1649 the Parliament of Scotland proclaimed him king on 5 February, while England became a republic. Oliver Cromwell defeated him at the Battle of Worcester on 3 September 1651, and Charles spent the next nine years in exile in France, the Dutch Republic and the Spanish Netherlands.

After Cromwell's death in 1658 the unrest that followed his son Richard's resignation led George Monck, the Governor of Scotland, to march into London and restore the excluded members of the Long Parliament. A general election followed, and Charles was invited to return; he was received in London on 29 May 1660, his thirtieth birthday. The royalist and Anglican Cavalier Parliament passed the acts later called the Clarendon Code, which secured the position of the Church of England against nonconformists. Charles accepted them although he favoured religious tolerance.

In 1665 the Great Plague of London peaked at up to 7,000 deaths a week, and the court withdrew to Salisbury. The Great Fire of London began on 2 September 1666 in Pudding Lane and destroyed about 13,200 houses and 87 churches, including St Paul's Cathedral; Charles and his brother James helped direct the firefighting. In 1670 he made the Treaty of Dover with Louis XIV of France, and in 1672 issued a Declaration of Indulgence for Catholics and dissenters, which Parliament forced him to withdraw. The Test Act followed, and by 1674 the Third Anglo-Dutch War had gained England nothing.

The Popish Plot of 1679 and the Catholicism of his heir James, Duke of York, produced the Exclusion Crisis, from which the Whig and Tory parties took their names. Charles sided with the Tories, dissolved Parliament several times, and after 1681 ruled without it. He had a lasting interest in the navy and in science, and revived public festivities after the Puritan rule of Cromwell. His marriage to Catherine of Braganza produced no surviving children, but he acknowledged at least 12 illegitimate children.

He suffered an apoplectic fit on 2 February 1685 and died four days later at Whitehall, aged 54. Suspicion of poison arose at the time; a modern analysis points instead to symptoms resembling uraemia, though the cause remains unproven. His brother succeeded him as James II.
charles-ii-of-naples: Charles was the son of Charles I of Anjou and Beatrice of Provence, and the sole heir to his father's wide dominion, which included Provence and Forcalquier, Anjou and Maine, and the Kingdom of Sicily. In 1272 his father made him Prince of Salerno. After the Sicilian Vespers, the uprising against Angevin rule that began in Palermo on 30 March 1282, Peter III of Aragon was declared king of the island on 4 September 1282. In 1283 Charles I made his son regent of the mainland territories. Charles held a general assembly that abolished unpopular taxes and confirmed the liberties of nobles and clergy.

Against his father's orders, Charles sailed against the Aragonese on Nisida on 5 June 1284, and the Aragonese galleys surrounded and defeated his fleet. He was taken to Messina, where the crowd demanded his execution; to save his life Constance of Sicily imprisoned him at Cefalù. His father died on 7 January 1285 while he was still a prisoner. By the treaty of Canfranc in October 1288 Charles was released for a ransom of 50,000 marks of silver, leaving his sons as hostages. Pope Nicholas IV crowned him king at Rieti on Whit Sunday 1289. Charles ordered the expulsion of Jews from Anjou and Maine, forced many Jews of southern Italy to convert and introduced the Inquisition in the Regno.

Treaties at Senlis in 1290 and Brignoles in 1291 made peace with France and Aragon, and Charles Martel, his eldest son, was granted a claim to Hungary by the pope in 1292. Frederick was crowned king of Sicily on 12 December 1295 after the Sicilians refused the Treaty of Anagni, and the long war ended with the Peace of Caltabellotta in 1302, in which Charles gave up all rights to Sicily and agreed to the marriage of his daughter Eleanor to King Frederick.

Charles spent his last years quietly in Naples, which he improved and embellished. He died there in May 1309 and was succeeded by his son Robert the Wise, while his eldest grandson Charles I of Hungary was excluded from the Neapolitan succession. With his wife Maria of Hungary, daughter of Stephen V of Hungary, he had fourteen children. They included Saint Louis of Toulouse and Philip I of Taranto.
charles-ii-of-navarre: Charles was born at Évreux on 10 October 1332, the son of Philip III of Navarre, count of Évreux, and Joan II of Navarre, the only daughter of Louis X of France.
