His mother had received extensive lands in Normandy as compensation for resigning her claims to France, Champagne and Brie in 1328, so that Charles held Évreux, Mortain, parts of the Vexin and a portion of the Cotentin as well as Navarre. He was raised in France and was declared king at 17. He spent most of his reign there, regarding Navarre chiefly as a source of manpower for his designs on the French throne, to which he hoped for recognition as heir-general of Philip IV through his mother.

In 1352 Charles married Joan of Valois, daughter of King John II of France. Jealous of the Constable of France, Charles de la Cerda, he arranged his murder at l'Aigle on 8 January 1354 and made no secret of it. He then intrigued with the English, which led John II to make peace in the Treaty of Mantes on 22 February 1354 on terms that enlarged Charles's possessions. This became his pattern: he used the threat of an English alliance to wring concessions from the French king, as again in the Treaty of Valognes of 10 September 1355.

After John II was captured at Poitiers, Charles was freed from prison on 9 November 1357 and entered Paris to a hero's welcome. He allied with Étienne Marcel against the Dauphin, but in 1358 he led the suppression of the Jacquerie at the Battle of Mello on 10 June. His bid to become Captain of Paris failed, and on 19 August 1359 he renounced his demands. In 1361 he claimed the Duchy of Burgundy, which John II took instead. When war resumed in 1369 he again offered alliances to both Charles V of France and Edward III of England, but paid homage to Charles V in March 1371.

Charles died at Pamplona on 1 January 1387, aged 54. His death was known all over Europe and was often cited by moralists. Versions of the story vary in detail. In Francis Blagdon's account of 1803, a physician had him wrapped in linen soaked in brandy, and a servant sewing the cloth closed used a candle to burn off the thread; the cloth caught fire and he was burned alive. His children included Charles III of Navarre.
charles-ii-of-spain: Charles was born on 6 November 1661, the only surviving son of Philip IV of Spain and Mariana of Austria, his second wife and niece. The Spanish and Austrian Habsburgs married within the family to an unusual extent, and the causes of Charles's lifelong ill health remain disputed. He survived measles, chickenpox, rubella and smallpox in childhood, and rickets left him unable to walk unaided until he was four. The suggestion that he went uneducated is incorrect: he had tutors from the age of six, and records of his government and reports of foreign diplomats indicate that his mental capacities remained intact.

Philip IV died on 17 September 1665, and Mariana ruled as Queen Regent through a valido, first the Austrian Juan Everardo Nithard. Reform was hampered by her rivalry with Charles's illegitimate half-brother Don Juan, who took control of the government in January 1678 and made peace with France in the Treaties of Nijmegen. In 1679 Charles married Marie Louise of Orléans, a niece of Louis XIV.

The state finances were in perpetual crisis, and the Crown had declared bankruptcy nine times between 1557 and 1666. Castile's population fell from 6.5 million in 1600 to fewer than 5 million in 1680, and in the 1680s drastic deflationary decrees revalued the coinage, disrupting commerce before the currency was stabilised in 1686.

Marie Louise died in February 1689, and Charles married Maria Anna of Neuburg, who also had no children. The autopsy suggested that Charles was incapable of fathering any. The succession then dominated European diplomacy. Treaties in 1698 and 1700 tried to divide the Spanish possessions among claimants, but the Spanish government refused any division. In September 1700 he fell gravely ill, and Luis Manuel Fernández de Portocarrero persuaded him to name Philip of Anjou, Louis XIV's grandson, as heir. Charles died on 1 November 1700, aged 38.

Philip was proclaimed king on 16 November 1700, and the War of the Spanish Succession formally began on 9 July 1701. Charles's reign has traditionally been viewed as one of decline, a foreign ambassador remarking in 1691 that it was incomprehensible how the monarchy survived. More recent studies call the myth of decline and an incapable king simplistic, and argue that Bourbon propaganda shaped the older view. The monarchy remained largely intact at his death, and some of the commercial policies begun in his reign formed the basis for Bourbon reforms. Universities approved by decrees in his name, such as San Carlos in Guatemala, still exist.
charles-iii-duke-of-bourbon: Charles de Bourbon, born on 17 February 1490, was the son of Gilbert de Bourbon, Count of Montpensier, and Clara Gonzaga, and belonged to a junior branch of the royal house. Both his parents were dead by 1503, and he was raised at the Bourbon court of Moulins beside his future wife, Suzanne de Bourbon, with a humanist and courtly education. His elder brother's death in 1501 made him Count of Montpensier.

On 26 February 1505 he contracted to marry Suzanne, heiress of the senior Bourbon line, and after their marriage on 10 May 1505 he took the title of Duke of Bourbon. His domains included the duchies of Bourbon, Auvergne and Châtellerault and many counties, and he could raise soldiers and employ his own fiscal and judicial officers. The historian David-Chapy calls him the last feudatory able to oppose royal power.

He fought for Louis XII at Genoa in 1507 and at Agnadello on 14 May 1509, was made governor of Languedoc in 1512, and fought the Spanish in Navarre and the English in Picardy. Francis I made him Constable of France after 1515, and he led the vanguard to victory at Marignano, then governed Milan until May 1516.

In 1521 he was denied the command of the vanguard that was his by right, and Suzanne died that year. She had willed him her inheritance, but Francis and his mother, Louise, disputed it. In July 1523 Bourbon made a treaty with Charles V, and in August all the disputed lands were sequestered from him. He fled France and joined the imperial commanders in Italy.

He led an invasion of Provence that stalled before Marseille, and he fought at Pavia, where the French king was taken prisoner. Bourbon hoped to marry the emperor's sister Eleanor, recover his French lands as a sovereign lord and become count of Provence.

In the spring of 1527 his army, unpaid, mutinied in March and ransacked his pavilion, and he advanced on Rome with no artillery to speak of. Assaults on the city began on the morning of 6 May 1527, in fog. While climbing the walls in white, he was hit by an arquebus bullet, supposedly fired by the sculptor Benvenuto Cellini. The Prince of Orange succeeded him as head of the army.

By the end of the day Rome was open to the imperial troops, who sacked it for eight days: thousands were murdered, many raped, and the city pillaged and burned by soldiers angry at their lack of pay. Cloulas estimates the loot at 1,000,000 ducats. Pope Clement VII fled into the Castel Sant'Angelo and capitulated on 6 June, remaining a prisoner until November.
charles-iii-of-naples: Charles was the only child of Louis of Durazzo and Margaret of Sanseverino. In the spring of 1360 Louis rebelled against his cousins, Queen Joanna I of Naples and her husband Louis of Taranto, and was defeated. The child Charles was sent to Joanna's court as a hostage. After his father died in prison in the summer of 1362, Joanna ordered that he be treated with all honours due to the royal household.

King Louis I of Hungary, who had no son, invited Charles to Hungary, where he arrived in 1364 or 1365. Louis proposed that he marry his cousin Margaret of Durazzo, over the opposition of Queen Joanna, and the marriage took place in Naples on 24 January 1370. In 1371 Louis made Charles governor of Slavonia, Croatia and Dalmatia with the title of duke.

The schism in the papacy decided Charles's fortunes. Joanna recognised the antipope Clement VII in 1378. Pope Urban VI excommunicated her in 1379 and, as feudal overlord of the kingdom, declared her deprived of it in favour of Charles and Margaret. Charles marched on Naples with a Croatian army, defeated Joanna's husband Otto, Duke of Brunswick-Grubenhagen, at San Germano and besieged the queen in the Castel dell'Ovo. He captured her and imprisoned her at San Fele. When news came that her adopted heir, Louis I of Anjou, was preparing an expedition, Charles had her strangled in 1382 and took the crown.

Louis of Anjou's force numbered some 40,000 men. Charles relied on the mercenary companies of John Hawkwood, about 14,000 men in all, and harassed the invaders with guerrilla tactics. Louis died at Bisceglie on 20 September 1384. Charles's relations with Urban VI then broke down. In January 1385 the pope had six cardinals arrested, and one revealed under torture that Charles was party to a conspiracy. Urban excommunicated him and laid the kingdom under interdict.

When Louis I of Hungary died, Charles left Naples and claimed the Hungarian throne as the senior male of the Angevin line. In December 1385 he ousted Louis's daughter Mary, helped by Croatian lords and by contacts made while he was duke of Croatia and Dalmatia. Louis's widow, Elizabeth of Bosnia, then arranged his assassination. He was attacked on 7 February 1386 and died of his wounds on 24 February. Because his excommunication still stood, he was buried without a religious ceremony.

His son Ladislaus of Naples succeeded him in Naples, while Mary's regents restored her in Hungary. Ladislaus later tried to win the Hungarian crown himself. Charles had also founded the chivalric Order of the Ship in 1381.
charles-iii-of-navarre: Charles was born on 22 July 1361 at Mantes, the heart of his father's lands in northern France, the firstborn son of King Charles II of Navarre and the French princess Joan of Valois. The House of Évreux was a cadet branch of the French royal House of Capet. As a young man he was often sent by his father as envoy to France. On 27 May 1375, at Soria in Castile, he married Eleanor, daughter of King Henry II of Castile, which sealed the peace between their fathers.

In 1378 an embassy to King Charles V of France ended in his arrest. During interrogation he revealed his father's plan to seize the town of Logroño, and Castile invaded Navarre and forced the Treaty of Briones. Eleanor helped secure his release in 1381.

Charles became king on 1 January 1387 and the same year recovered from Castile the last occupied parts of Navarre. His early reign was marked by a breach with Eleanor, who returned to Castile with their daughters and stayed away for seven years. The historian Elena Woodacre suggests the cause was his illegitimate children, since Eleanor found four mistresses and six such children at court. The couple were reunited in November 1394 at Tudela.

Charles was an effective diplomat. In 1393 he secured the return of Cherbourg from the English. Through the marriages of his sisters and legitimate daughters to Iberian and southern French rulers and nobles, and of his illegitimate children into the Navarrese nobility, he built alliances that kept the peace. Until 1406 he took an active part in French affairs, after which he turned towards the Iberian Peninsula. In 1416 he stopped recognising Benedict XIII at Avignon and accepted Gregory XII at Rome.

Both of Charles's sons died in 1402, and his eldest daughter Joan died in 1413, so his third daughter Blanche became heir. In October 1419 she married John, son of the king of Aragon, after Charles promised not to remarry and father sons who might displace her. On 8 September 1425 Charles collapsed suddenly, died the same day in Blanche's arms and was buried in the Cathedral of Pamplona beside Eleanor, who had died in 1416. Historians debate whether he saw himself chiefly as a French prince or an Iberian king, but agree that Navarre became steadily more Iberian under him. He earned the name the Noble in contrast to his father, Charles the Bad.
charles-iii-of-spain: Charles was born on 20 January 1716, the fourth son of Philip V of Spain and the eldest son of Philip's second wife, Elisabeth Farnese. His mother, who hoped he would have a kingdom of his own, made him heir to the Italian duchies of Parma and Piacenza, and in 1731, at fifteen, he became their duke. At eighteen he led Spanish troops down Italy in an almost bloodless march to take the Kingdom of Naples and the Kingdom of Sicily, entering Naples on 10 May 1734. The Treaty of Vienna of 1738 confirmed him in both kingdoms. In Naples his chief minister, Bernardo Tanucci, pursued a regalist policy that limited the privileges of the clergy, whose lands were exempt from tax.

Charles became King of Spain on the death of his childless half-brother Ferdinand VI on 10 August 1759, and gave up the thrones of Naples and Sicily. He ruled as an enlightened absolutist and relied on capable ministers, among them the Marquess of Esquilache, the Count of Campomanes, the Count of Aranda and the Count of Floridablanca. He widened trade, modernised agriculture and land tenure, promoted science and university research, and strengthened the army and navy.

Spain joined France in the Family Compact of 15 August 1761, and the British captured Havana and Manila in 1762–63, though both were returned in the peace of 1763. To pay for a standing army and fortified ports, the sales tax, the alcabala, was raised from 2% to 5%. Bread riots in 1766, the Esquilache Riots, drove out the minister, and in 1767 Charles expelled the Jesuits from Spain and its empire, confiscating their haciendas and closing their colleges.

The Bourbon Reforms sought to bring the overseas territories under firmer control. The Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata, set up in 1776, took Upper Peru and what is now Argentina from the Viceroyalty of Peru, so that the silver of Potosí flowed towards Buenos Aires. In 1780 an indigenous rising led by Túpac Amaru II broke out against colonial rule in the Viceroyalty of Peru.

Charles died on 14 December 1788, months before the French Revolution began. The historian Stanley Payne judged him probably the most successful European ruler of his generation. His reforms mostly raised revenue and extended state power, though he never gained complete control of the finances. His reign has been called the apogee of empire, which was not sustained after him: his son Charles IV continued some of his policies, but was forced to abdicate by his own son Ferdinand VII and was imprisoned by Napoleon Bonaparte, who invaded Spain in 1808.
charles-iii-philip-elector-palatine: Charles Philip was born in Neuburg an der Donau on 4 November 1661, the seventh of seventeen children of Philip William, Elector Palatine, and Elisabeth Amalie of Hesse-Darmstadt. He became a cleric at Cologne at the age of fourteen, in 1677, and again at Salzburg and Mainz in 1679, but he was not ordained. In 1684 he began a military career, joined the Habsburg war against the Turks from 1691 to 1694 and was promoted to imperial field marshal. In 1712 he was appointed Governor of Further Austria at Innsbruck.

Charles Philip succeeded his brother Johann Wilhelm as Elector Palatine in 1716, and with the electorate held Neuburg and the duchies of Jülich and Berg; until 1728 he was also Count of Megen. In 1720 he moved the capital of the Palatinate from Heidelberg to the new city of Mannheim, but not before putting his favourite court jester, Perkeo of Heidelberg, in charge of the castle's wine stocks. At Mannheim he and his successor Charles IV Theodore built up what was commonly regarded as the finest orchestra in Europe. Under musicians such as Johann Stamitz and Carlo Grua, the orchestra of the Kapelle was praised by Leopold and Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart.

To strengthen the union of the lines of the Wittelsbach dynasty he arranged a wedding on 17 January 1742, at which his granddaughter Elisabeth Auguste married Charles Theodore of Palatinate-Sulzbach and her sister Maria Anna married the Bavarian prince Clement. A few days later, in the imperial election, he voted for his Bavarian cousin, the Elector Charles Albert.

Charles Philip married three times. His first wife was Ludwika Karolina Radziwiłł, a wealthy heiress in Lithuania, whom he married in Berlin in 1688; only one of their four children, Elisabeth Auguste, lived to adulthood. In 1701 he married Teresa Lubomirska, heiress of Ostróg, in Kraków, and their two daughters died before the age of three. His third marriage, in 1728, to Countess Violente Maria Theresia of Thurn und Taxis, was childless and considered morganatic.

He died in Mannheim on 31 December 1742. The Palatinate-Neuburg line became extinct, and the electorate, with Neuburg, Jülich and Berg, passed to Charles Theodore of the Palatinate-Sulzbach line of the Wittelsbach family.
charles-iii-prince-of-monaco: Charles Honoré Grimaldi was born in Paris on 8 December 1818, the only son of Florestan, Prince of Monaco, and Caroline Gibert de Lametz. While he was Hereditary Prince he married Countess Antoinette de Mérode-Westerloo in Brussels on 28 September 1846. He succeeded his father in 1856 and was Prince of Monaco and Duke of Valentinois from 20 June 1856 until his death.

During his reign the towns of Menton and Roquebrune, which made up some 80 percent of Monegasque territory, were formally ceded to France. This made formal French recognition of Monaco's independence possible. Rebellions in these towns, aided by the Kingdom of Sardinia, had exhausted Monaco's military resources for decades.

The principality was in dire need of money, and Charles and his mother, Princess Caroline, had the idea of building a casino. The Monte Carlo Casino was designed to the prince's liking in the German style and placed on the site of Les Spélugues. Monte Carlo, or Mount Charles, takes its name from him. He set up a business to run the casino, which became the Société des bains de mer de Monaco. His name in Monegasque and Italian was Carlo III.

Monaco also increased its diplomatic activity. In 1864 Charles concluded a Treaty of Friendship with the Bey of Tunis, Muhammad III as-Sadiq, which also regulated trade and maritime questions. He instituted the Order of Saint-Charles on 15 March 1858, and received many foreign honours, among them the Grand Cross of the Order of the Red Eagle from Prussia in 1869.

His sight weakened in his middle years, and in the last decade of his life he was almost totally blind. Dr Thomas Henry Pickering wrote in 1882 that Charles had lost his eyesight as far back as 1860. He died at the Château de Marchais on 10 September 1889 and was succeeded by his son Albert I of Monaco.

Monaco issued a silver 10 franc coin in 1966 with his portrait, for the hundredth anniversary of Monte Carlo, and on 1 June 2016 fifteen thousand 2 euro coins marking its 150th anniversary. The British politician Sir Charles Wentworth Dilke made him a character in a satire, The Fall of Prince Florestan of Monaco, in which a radical republican nephew who comes to the throne tries to democratise Monaco and fails.
charles-iii-william-margrave-of-baden-du: Charles William was born in Durlach, the son of Margrave Frederick Magnus of Baden-Durlach and Augusta Maria of Schleswig-Holstein-Gottorp. His older brother had died aged about one month, so he was born hereditary prince. After studies in Utrecht, Geneva and Lausanne he travelled to England, Sweden and Italy, and began his military career in the Imperial Army in the summer of 1694, serving under his uncle Margrave Louis William of Baden-Baden, known as Türkenlouis.

In the War of the Spanish Succession he was a senior officer from 1702 to 1709. He was wounded at the siege of Landau in 1702, fought at Friedlingen that year, helped cover the retreat at Höchstädt in 1703 and fought under Prince Eugene of Savoy at Blenheim in 1704, where he narrowly escaped death. He was promoted Generalfeldzeugmeister in 1705 and in 1715 imperial Generalfeldmarschall.

When he succeeded in 1709 his territory measured about 75 square kilometres and held about 70,000 people, with only two significant towns, Pforzheim and Durlach. The Estates had been removed from power in 1668, and the war left the administration in poor order. Charles William therefore met little resistance in centring government on himself. He held a weekly audience open to all subjects and issued regulations in 1709 and 1710 demanding absolute obedience from officials, and he fought corruption with harsh penalties, needing five regulations against bribery during his reign.

He inherited a heavily indebted country and followed the mercantilist theories of his time, introducing monopolies on iron, salt and tobacco. A rigorous fiscal programme began in 1732, and he is credited with reducing the debt by about 1 million florins in the first fifteen years of his reign, laying the basis for the reforms of his grandson Charles Frederick. He also kept a large garden: a catalogue of 1713 lists 2,121 varieties of flowers, 1,163 of them tulips, and he left at least 6,000 watercolours of his plants.

Dissatisfied with Durlach, he had the foundation stone of a new palace laid in the Hardtwald forest on 17 June 1715. Thirty-two avenues radiated from its central Lead Tower, a plan that still shapes Karlsruhe. A decree of 24 September 1715 granted settlers legal, religious and financial privileges, the court moved by 1718, and the town had 2,000 inhabitants in 1719. Its wooden houses, painted red, earned it the name Red City.

Charles William died in Karlsruhe in 1738, reportedly of a stroke while working in his tulip bed. His son Frederick had died in 1732, so his grandson Charles Frederick, aged ten, succeeded him under a regency.
charles-la-trobe: La Trobe was born in London on 20 March 1801, the son of Christian Ignatius Latrobe, a leader of the Moravian Church from a family of French Huguenot descent; the architect Benjamin Henry Latrobe was his uncle. Educated in England, he spent time in Switzerland, climbed in the Alps in 1824-26 and wrote travel books on the Alps and the Tyrol.

In 1832 he went to the United States as companion to Count Albert Pourtales on a Grand Tour, travelling for six months with Washington Irving and then with Henry Leavitt Ellsworth to the lands claimed for the relocation of displaced Native nations. In 1834 he went on to Mexico. His The Rambler in North America (1835) was praised by John Stuart Mill, though it described Native Americans as a "degenerate race". On 16 September 1835 he married Sophie de Montmollin in Berne.

From 1837 he inspected the Negro Education Grant in the West Indies, and on 4 February 1839 he was appointed superintendent at Port Phillip, though he had little administrative experience. He reached Melbourne, a town of around 3,000, on 1 October, began work on its streets and sanitation, and worked well with Gipps, the head of New South Wales, who had to approve land sales and appointments. In 1842 he offered to underwrite the costs of the Native Police Corps, armed and mounted Aboriginal police under white officers, who conducted indiscriminate raids and punitive expeditions against Aboriginal people on the frontier.

He acted as lieutenant-governor of Van Diemen's Land for four months in 1846-47. Criticised for his inexperience in the gold rush, when officials came to be called joes after his nickname Charley Joe, he resigned in December 1852 but had to wait for his successor, Charles Hotham.

His wife died in Europe on 30 January 1854. In 1855 he married her sister, Rose Isabelle de Meuron, a marriage then illegal in English law, and received no further appointments. He went blind in his last years and died on 4 December 1875. Melbourne owes much of its ring of parks to the land he reserved, and La Trobe University, the Latrobe River and the Latrobe Valley bear his name.
charles-lienard-de-lolive: Charles Liénard, sieur de l'Olive, was born about 1601, the son of Pierre Lienart and Françoise Bonnart of Chinon. The French colony on Saint Christopher (Saint Kitts) had been founded under a company formed in 1626 with the support of Cardinal Richelieu; its settlers suffered famine, were driven out by the Spanish admiral Fadrique de Toledo in 1629 and returned in 1630. In 1631 l'Olive became lieutenant governor there to Pierre Belain d'Esnambuc, and he sent his young assistant Guillaume d'Orange to visit Guadeloupe, Dominica and Martinique, of which d'Orange judged Guadeloupe the most promising.

In late 1634 l'Olive and d'Orange sailed to France, where Jean du Plessis d'Ossonville, a relative of Richelieu who owned a sturdy ship, joined the project. Their contract with the Compagnie des Îles de l'Amérique, signed on 14 February 1635, bound them to take 200 men to settle Dominica, Martinique or Guadeloupe and to have settled at least 800 within ten years, in return for arms, ammunition and protection, and Dieppe merchants were brought in for a share of the profits. That year l'Olive married Marie Philibert in Chinon. The expedition left Dieppe on 25 May 1635 with 554 people, among them four Dominican missionaries, 40 Norman peasant families and 400 hired labourers bound to work for three years.

Underfunded and with food for only two months, the settlers landed near Pointe-Allègre, where l'Olive built Fort Saint-Pierre on what became the Vieux-Fort river. The Caribs were at first friendly, but the French distrusted them, and as famine killed many settlers l'Olive let them take over the gardens of the Caribs, steal their food and attack them. Du Plessis, who broke with his more brutal partner, left for France late in 1635 and died on 4 December. Between 1635 and 1641 l'Olive massacred the Caribs of Basse-Terre, while Carib reprisals and yellow fever struck the colonists.

According to the missionary Jacques du Tetre, l'Olive was stricken by blindness and insanity for his sins. Jean Aubert was named governor in his place on 25 November 1640, and l'Olive died in 1643. In 1875 a street in La Chapelle, then a separate municipality of Paris, was renamed Rue L'Olive in his honour; in October 2011 the Paris council renamed it Rue de L'Olive to remove the reference to colonialism.
charles-magoon: Magoon was born in Owatonna, Minnesota, on 5 December 1861, and his family moved to Nebraska while he was a small child. He studied at the University of Nebraska from 1876, left in 1879 to read law with a prominent firm, was admitted to the bar in 1882 and became a partner in Lincoln. As judge advocate of the Nebraska National Guard he took the title of Judge, which he kept for the rest of his career.

In 1899 he joined the law office of the War Department's new Division of Customs and Insular Affairs. A report he prepared for Secretary Russell A. Alger in May 1899 held that the Constitution follows the flag into the territories taken after the Spanish-American War; under Elihu Root a second report, of 12 February 1900, reached the opposite conclusion, a view the Supreme Court largely adopted in the Insular Cases from 1901. A leak of the first report during the debate on the Puerto Rico Tariff Act became the Magoon Incident. His reports, published as a book in 1902, were long considered the standard work on the subject.

In June 1904 Theodore Roosevelt made him general counsel of the Isthmian Canal Commission, and in 1905 governor of the Panama Canal Zone, a member of the commission and, from 2 July, also Minister to Panama, drawing two salaries. He came to accept that mosquitoes carried yellow fever and malaria and set out to drain the swamps that bred them. After Congress barred a diplomat from holding another post, he was named governor of Cuba instead.

Magoon took office in Cuba on 13 October 1906 without an inauguration, declaring that he would preserve Cuban independence. Under him about two hundred kilometres of highway were built and he called for a formal Cuban army and the removal of the wreck of the USS Maine from Havana harbour. On 28 January 1909 Cuban government was restored under José Miguel Gómez. Admired in the United States and commended by President Taft, he was bitterly criticised by Cuban writers: the bibliographer Carlos Manuel Trelles wrote that he had deeply corrupted the nation, though no explicit evidence of his corruption ever surfaced. He retired from public life and died in Washington, D.C., on 14 January 1920 after surgery for appendicitis.
charles-margrave-of-burgau: Charles was born on 22 November 1560 at Křivoklát Castle in Bohemia, the brother of Andrew of Austria. He pursued a military career, leading a Spanish regiment without success in the war against the Netherlands. In the Long War against the Ottoman Empire he recorded some successes, at the expense of his soldiers, who were hungry and unpaid and some of whom deserted, and he was promoted to Field Marshal.

When his father died in 1595, Charles was amply compensated with money and lands. Besides Burgau he held the Landgraviate of Nellenburg and the County of Hohenberg, and contemporary sources describe the court he kept at his residence, Günzburg Castle. He was unpopular with his subjects, whom he forbade to drink wheat beer, and with the powers within his margraviate, among them the Bishop of Augsburg, the Counts of Fugger and the free imperial cities of Ulm and Augsburg, with whom he quarrelled over tax increases and their sovereign rights.

His rule left its mark on Günzburg. In 1615 or 1616 he founded a Capuchin monastery there, whose church would later receive his body, and in 1617 he expelled the Jews from the town, ordering them to leave within a year.

In 1601 Charles married Sibylle, daughter of Duke William of Jülich-Cleves-Berg; the marriage was childless. He had several children outside marriage: with Chiara Elisa Isabella di Ferrero a daughter, Anna Elisabeth, Baroness of Hohenberg, who married Pietro Francesco di Ferrero, Marchese della Marmora, and with an unknown woman two sons, Charles, Baron of Hohenberg, and Ferdinand, Baron of Hohenberg. He died at Überlingen on 30 October 1618. In 1619 his body was moved to the church of the Capuchin monastery in Günzburg, where his widow was also buried in 1627, and when the monastery was demolished in 1806 both were transferred to St. Martin's church.
charles-marie-david-de-mayrena: Marie-Charles David de Mayréna was born in Toulon on 31 January 1842. In June 1883 he fled Paris for Java, fearing prosecution for embezzlement, and the next year he was expelled from the Dutch East Indies. Back in Paris he organised an arms shipment to Aceh, and on his way back to the East Indies he stopped in Vietnam and started a plantation.

In 1888, as the King of Siam began claiming territory west of French territory, the Governor-General of French Indochina accepted Mayréna's proposal to lead an expedition into the interior to negotiate treaties with the peoples there. Instead he persuaded tribal chiefs to form a kingdom of their own, he and his supporters arguing that the tribes were not vassals of the Annamese emperor. On 3 June 1888, in the village of Kon Gung, the chiefs of the Bahnar, Rengao and Sedang elected him king, and he took the style Marie the First, King of Sedang.

He declared Catholicism the official religion without forcing his subjects to convert, designed a national flag and created the Order of Marie the First, whose insignia he had cast by goldsmiths in Hong Kong. Seeking recognition, he offered to cede the kingdom to France in exchange for monopoly rights, hinting that the Prussians were interested if the French were not. Rebuffed by the English in Hong Kong in 1889, he went to Belgium, where a financier named Somsy offered arms and money in exchange for mineral rights.

The French Navy blockaded the Vietnamese ports to prevent his return, and his arms were seized as contraband at Singapore. Mayréna retired to British Malaya and died on Tioman Island on 11 November 1890 in mysterious circumstances, which reports variously put down to poisoning, snakebite or a duel. The Sedang were afterwards conquered by France and its protectorate of Annam. The French writer and statesman André Malraux wrote an unpublished novel about him.
charles-martel: Charles was a son of the Frankish statesman Pepin of Herstal and a noblewoman named Alpaida, who was his mistress and possibly his second wife. Older writing calls him illegitimate, but the line between wives and concubines was not clear-cut in 8th-century Francia, and the charge probably comes from the wish of Pepin's first wife Plectrude to see her own line as heirs. By his lifetime the Merovingian kings had ceded power to the mayors of the palace, who controlled the treasury and granted land in the name of a figurehead king.

When Pepin died in December 714, Plectrude had designated his young grandson Theudoald as sole heir and imprisoned Charles in Cologne. Charles escaped in 715 and was acclaimed mayor of the palace over Austrasia. In the civil war that followed he suffered his only defeat, near Cologne in 716, against the Neustrians and Radbod, King of the Frisians. He then won at Amblève in April 716 and at Vinchy on 21 March 717, took Cologne, and defeated Chilperic II and Odo, duke of Aquitaine, at Soissons in 718. Between 718 and 732 he campaigned against the Saxons, the Frisians, Bavaria and the Alemanni, and he appointed the Merovingian kings himself.

In 731 he crossed the Loire into Aquitaine. An army under Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi then marched north and was defeated by Charles at the Battle of Tours, between Tours and Poitiers, in 732. The historian Paul Fouracre suggests the Arab campaign was a long-distance raid rather than the start of a war, and Arabic sources of the period give the battle little prominence. Charles did not gain full control of Aquitaine, and Odo remained duke until 735. After the death of King Theuderic IV in 737 he appointed no successor, and the throne stayed vacant until his own death.

Charles died on 22 October 741 at Quierzy-sur-Oise and was buried at Saint Denis. A year earlier he had divided his lands between his sons Carloman and Pepin the Younger. Many historians see him as laying the foundations for Pepin's rise to the Frankish throne in 751 and for Charlemagne's imperial acclamation in 800, although Fouracre notes that his career ended with unfinished business.

His reputation has varied. Early authors praised his victories, while a 9th-century text portrayed him suffering in hell for taking church lands. Edward Gibbon and later writers made him the saviour of Christian Europe at Tours, a view that more recent historians such as Alessandro Barbero call overstated.
charles-maurice-de-talleyrand: Charles-Maurice de Talleyrand-Périgord was born in Paris on 2 February 1754 into an ancient but not wealthy aristocratic family. From childhood he walked with a limp, which later gave him the nickname le diable boiteux, the lame devil. In his Memoirs he blamed an accident at the age of four, but recent research has shown the condition was congenital. It barred him from inheriting his father's title despite being the eldest surviving son, so his parents chose a career in the Church for him.

He studied theology at the Sorbonne, read Montesquieu and Voltaire and other writers who were beginning to question the authority of the ancien régime, was ordained a priest on 19 December 1779, and in 1780 became Agent-General of the Clergy. In 1789, just before the French Revolution, he became Bishop of Autun.

Talleyrand sat in the Estates-General of 1789 for the clergy and supported the revolutionaries' anti-clericalism. With Mirabeau he promoted the appropriation of Church property, helped write the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, and proposed the Civil Constitution of the Clergy. Few bishops followed him in obeying the new decree, and much of the clergy came to regard him as schismatic.

He helped bring about the coup of 18 Brumaire in 1799 and was soon made foreign minister by Napoleon, though he rarely agreed with his foreign policy. The Pope released him from excommunication in the Concordat of 1801. He worked for peace, helped complete the Treaty of Amiens in 1802. After resigning as foreign minister in 1807 he kept a seat on the Council of State, and at the Congress of Erfurt in 1808 he secretly counselled Tsar Alexander I against Napoleon's proposals.

In April 1814, as Louis XVIII succeeded Napoleon, Talleyrand was a key agent of the Bourbon Restoration. He signed the Treaty of Paris, whose terms were lenient towards France, and was the chief French negotiator at the Congress of Vienna. There he won admission for France to the inner decisions, and on 3 January 1815 signed a secret defensive treaty with Austria's Metternich and Britain's Castlereagh against Russia and Prussia. He served under Louis XVIII, Charles X and Louis Philippe I.

He died on 17 May 1838. He left no legitimate children. Opinion remains divided: some see one of the most skilled diplomats in European history with a realistic view of the French national interest, others a serial turncoat who betrayed the ancien régime, the Revolution and Napoleon in turn for his own advantage.
charles-of-blois: Charles was born in Blois, the son of Guy de Châtillon, count of Blois, and Margaret of Valois, a sister of King Philip VI of France. Devout from an early age, he was drawn to religious books, which his father forbade him to read as unfitting for a knight. As he grew older he mortified his flesh: he is said to have put pebbles in his shoes, slept on straw, confessed every night and worn a hair shirt under his armour. On 4 June 1337, in Paris, he married Joan, heiress and niece of John III, Duke of Brittany.

With Joan he fought the House of Montfort in the Breton War of Succession, which began in 1341, with the support of the crown of France. He was an able commander who inspired loyalty by his religious fervour, but his piety did not restrain him in war: he ordered the massacre of 1,400 civilians after the siege of Quimper and of thousands after the siege of Guerande. His official captor in 1347 was Thomas Dagworth.

In captivity in England he visited graveyards to pray and recite Psalm 130; when he asked his squire to join him, the young man refused, saying that the men buried there had killed his parents and friends and burned their houses. Released in 1356 for a ransom of about half a million écus, he walked barefoot in winter from La Roche-Derrien to Tréguier Cathedral in devotion to Saint Ivo of Kermartin, and could not walk for 15 weeks afterwards. He then resumed the war.

Charles died fighting at Auray on 29 September 1364. The battle and the second treaty of Guerande of 1381 ended the war as a victory for the Montforts. He was buried at Guingamp, where the Franciscans promoted an unapproved cult of him as saint and martyr. In 1368 Duke John IV of Brittany persuaded Pope Urban V to order the Breton bishops to stop it, without effect. Pressed by Charles V of France, Urban allowed a commission to examine his cause, which met at Angers in 1371, but it lapsed after Pope Gregory XI left Avignon and was revived only in 1894. He was beatified on 14 December 1904, and his feast day is 30 September.
charles-ohara: Charles O'Hara was born in Lisbon, the illegitimate son of James O'Hara, 2nd Baron Tyrawley, and his Portuguese mistress. After Westminster School he was commissioned a cornet in the 3rd (King's Own) Regiment of Dragoons on 23 December 1752 and moved to the Coldstream Guards in 1756. In the Seven Years' War he served in Germany as aide-de-camp to John Manners, Marquess of Granby, and in 1762 he served under his father against the Spanish invasion of Portugal.

As the first governor of the Province of Senegambia he backed the Emirate of Trarza in its wars with the kingdom of Waalo and sold captives taken on his own expeditions around Saint-Louis. A petition sent to London on 22 August 1775 accused him of trying to abolish the Catholic Church there, of sentencing house slaves and free people of colour to be sold into the Atlantic slave trade, and of seizing property. Few British settlers ever came, and France captured the province in May 1779.

In America from July 1778, he was made brigadier in October 1780 and commanded the Brigade of Guards as second-in-command and friend of Charles Cornwallis. He distinguished himself at Cowan's Ford on 1 February 1781 and led the counterattack at the Battle of Guilford Courthouse on 15 March 1781, where he was severely wounded. At Yorktown on 19 October 1781 he offered his sword to the Comte de Rochambeau, who deferred to George Washington, who in turn deferred to Benjamin Lincoln.

In 1793 O'Hara was captured at Toulon while leading a sortie, and Napoleon, who directed the operation, accepted his formal surrender. Held in the Luxembourg Prison and threatened with the guillotine, he befriended Thomas Paine, and he was exchanged for Rochambeau in August 1795. He was thus the only man taken prisoner by both Washington and Napoleon. Named governor of Gibraltar again on 30 December 1795, he broke off his engagement to the writer Mary Berry, quarrelled with John Jervis, 1st Earl of St Vincent, over the naval yard, and built the folly of O'Hara's Tower. He died in Gibraltar in February 1802 of complications from his old wounds.
charles-prince-of-viana: Charles was born on 29 May 1421, the eldest son of King John II of Aragon and Queen Blanche I of Navarre. His mother was the daughter and heiress of Charles III of Navarre and ruled the kingdom from 1425 to 1441. Both his grandfather and his mother bequeathed the kingdom to him, and the Cortes recognised his right, but when Blanche died in 1441 her husband seized Navarre and excluded his son.

On 30 September 1439 Charles married Agnes of Cleves, who died childless on 6 April 1448. He later took a mistress, Brianda de Vaca, and had an illegitimate son, and a match with Catherine of Portugal was agreed but had not taken place when he died. He left three illegitimate children by three mistresses.

The ill feeling between father and son grew when John married Juana Enriquez in 1447. She soon bore a son, the future Ferdinand II of Aragon, and regarded her stepson as an interloper. When she began to interfere in the internal affairs of Navarre, a civil war broke out. In 1452 Charles, aided by King John II of Castile, was defeated and taken prisoner. He was released on promising not to take the royal title until after his father's death, and after another unsuccessful appeal to arms took refuge in Naples with King Alfonso V of Aragon.

Alfonso died in 1458 and John became king of Aragon. Charles was offered the crowns of Naples and Sicily but declined, and having been reconciled with his father he returned to Navarre in 1459. When he aspired to marry Isabella of Castile, his father imprisoned him, and the Catalans rose in his favour. The insurrection became general, and John released his son, recognising him as perpetual governor of Catalonia and as heir to the kingdom.

Charles died at Barcelona on 23 September 1461, amid a suspicion that his stepmother, Juana Enriquez, had poisoned him. He is described as a cultured and amiable prince, fond of music and literature. He translated Aristotle's Ethics into Aragonese, a work first published at Zaragoza in 1509, and wrote a chronicle of the kings of Navarre, the Cronica de los reyes de Navarra.
charles-rigault-de-genouilly: Pierre-Louis-Charles Rigault de Genouilly was born on 12 April 1807 in Rochefort, Charente-Maritime, into a family with naval connections: his father was a naval engineer, and his mother was the niece and adopted daughter of Claude Mithon de Genouilly, a naval commander in the American War of Independence. He entered the École Polytechnique in 1825 and the navy as a midshipman in 1827, serving in the Morea expedition of the Greek War of Independence and against pirates in the Greek archipelago.

He took part in the French invasion of Algiers and the forcing of the Tagus in 1831. In 1843 he took command of the corvette Victorieuse on the China and India Seas station, and on 25 April 1847 she and Gloire, sent to Da Nang to seek the release of two French missionaries, destroyed the Vietnamese vessels that attacked them. Between 1849 and 1851 he commanded Charlemagne, the first French battleship converted from sail to screw, and tested her at length.

In the Crimean War he was flag-captain of Ville de Paris at the bombardment of Odessa on 22 April 1854 and, as a rear admiral, commanded the French marines at the siege of Sebastopol. In the Second Opium War he led the French naval division, captured Canton and served at the capture of the Hai River forts.

In Vietnam the allies found themselves besieged at Da Nang by an army under Nguyen Tri Phuong, and disease took a heavy toll. After taking Saigon the allies blew up its citadel on 8 March 1859, and on 8 May he led an attack on the siege lines at Da Nang that failed to break the siege. Criticised in France, he was replaced by Admiral François Page in October 1859.

From 1862 to 1864 he commanded the French squadron of evolutions in the Mediterranean, and in 1869 he was briefly Minister of War as well. He refused a fleet command in the Franco-Prussian War, sent naval personnel and gunboats to the Siege of Paris and resigned at the fall of the Second Empire. He retired to Spain and died in Barcelona on 4 May 1873. A square in Saigon bore his name and statue until the statue was removed in 1945 and the square renamed Mê Linh Square in 1955.
charles-riviere-herard: Charles Rivière-Hérard, also known as Charles Hérard aîné, the eldest, was born in Port-Salut on 16 February 1789. Little is known of his early life beyond his service with the revolutionaries against the French and his command, probably later in his career, of a battalion of black troops. He was an officer under Alexandre Pétion in Pétion's struggles against Henri Christophe, and he became the leading figure among the conspirators who removed Jean-Pierre Boyer in the Reform Revolution.

Hérard was declared president on 4 April 1843, with the army's loyalty behind him. On 30 December a provisional parliament enacted a new constitution, apparently without his approval. On 27 February 1844 Dominican rebels led by Francisco del Rosario Sánchez and Matías Ramón Mella occupied the city of Santo Domingo and the next day declared independence. In March two Haitian corps of more than 10,000 men invaded. Hérard's western army met General Pedro Santana's force of about 3,000 at Azua on 19 March and was beaten, with more than 1,000 Haitians left dead against two Dominicans killed, and it could advance no further.

The northern army under General Pierrot was repulsed near Santiago de los Caballeros on 30 March and harassed in its retreat. Hérard's army withdrew from Azua to Port-au-Prince, burning the town's houses as it left, and Dominican gunboats bombarded Haitian coastal towns in reprisal. Facing growing opposition at home, Hérard dissolved the constitution and the parliament on 30 March 1844.

While he was campaigning in the east, peasants and farmers known as piquets, after their long pikes, gathered near Les Cayes under General Jean-Jacques Acaau as the Army of the Sufferers. In April they defeated a government army, though their advance on the capital was checked at Aquin. A second revolt, backed by his opponents in the government, broke out in the north. Hérard gave up the presidency on 3 May 1844, went into exile on 2 June and settled in Jamaica, where he died on 31 August 1850.
charles-robin: Robin was born in Saint Brélade, Jersey, and by 1763 was captain of a ship in the Newfoundland cod trade. In 1765 he formed a firm with his two brothers and two others to work the fishing grounds off Cape Breton Island and the Gaspé. The coast was then thinly settled: in 1765 the Baie des Chaleurs had 209 people, and the census of 1777 counted 874 permanent and seasonal inhabitants between Gaspé and Tracadigaiche. Robin brought exiled Acadians from France to work for him on Cape Breton Island and around Chaleur Bay.

The firm sold dried cod to Portugal and Spain and salmon, furs and timber to England and Quebec, and beat rivals from Guernsey and Jersey through a truck system. American forces did it much damage during the American Revolution, and after the destruction of his ship Robin gave up in despair, returning in 1783 as partner in a new firm under his own name. It advanced goods to fishermen against future catches, which kept them bound to it by debt and lowered its costs, and his connections with the government in Quebec won him the best beaches for curing fish.

His operations reached around the Gulf of St. Lawrence, above all at Paspébiac and at Arichat in Nova Scotia, where the fishermen of Isle Madame sold him all their fish and he set the price. From 1790 he built 200-ton merchant ships at Paspébiac. He sat as a judge of the Court of Common Pleas from 1788 to 1792, was a justice of the peace and served on the land board of the District of Gaspé.

When Robin left Paspébiac for good on 28 September 1802, his company had stores and fishing stations along the whole Gaspé coast and shipped some 15,000 to 17,000 quintals of dry cod a year to Spain, Portugal, Italy and South America. He retired to Jersey and died unmarried at Saint Aubin, leaving about £22,500. His nephews Philip and James took over, and the firm, later Robin, Jones and Whitman, still had dozens of stores in Quebec, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia around 1940.
charles-stewart-parnell: Charles Stewart Parnell was born at Avondale House in County Wicklow, the third son and seventh child of the Anglo-Irish Anglican landowner John Henry Parnell and his American wife Delia Tudor Stewart, daughter of the naval officer Admiral Charles Stewart. He was one of eleven children. He was first elected to the House of Commons on 17 April 1875 in a County Meath by-election as a Home Rule League member, and from 1880 he sat for Cork City.

On 21 October 1879 Parnell was elected president of Michael Davitt's new Irish National Land League, joining the mass movement to the parliamentary agitation. He toured North America from December 1879 to raise funds and support, addressing the United States House of Representatives on 2 February 1880; Timothy Healy called him the uncrowned king of Ireland. Arrested on 13 October 1881, he was held in Kilmainham Gaol, where the No Rent Manifesto was issued. In April 1882 he agreed a deal with the government, the Kilmainham Treaty, negotiated through Captain William O'Shea.

That October he refounded the suppressed Land League as the Irish National League and reformed the Home Rule League as the Irish Parliamentary Party, which he controlled closely as Britain's first disciplined democratic party. After the 1885 general election his party held the balance between Gladstone's Liberals and Lord Salisbury's Conservative Party. In 1887 The Times published letters linking him to the Phoenix Park murders of 1882; they were shown to be forged by Richard Pigott. Parnell met Gladstone at Hawarden on 18–19 December 1889, the high point of his career.

In 1890 Captain O'Shea's divorce case named Parnell as co-respondent. Gladstone made clear that the Liberals could not work with him, and at a meeting in committee room 15 on 1 December the party split; Parnell refused to withdraw. His candidates lost the by-elections in North Kilkenny and North Sligo, and he married Katharine O'Shea on 25 June 1891, the day the Catholic hierarchy condemned him. He died of pneumonia at Hove on 6 October 1891, aged 45. More than 200,000 people attended his funeral at Glasnevin Cemetery in Dublin on 11 October, and his gravestone of unhewn Wicklow granite reads only Parnell.
charles-the-bald: Charles was born on 13 June 823 in Frankfurt, the youngest son of Louis the Pious by his second wife, Judith. His elder brothers were already adults with sub-kingdoms of their own, and his father's attempts to give him one, first Alemannia and then the country between the Meuse and the Pyrenees, failed in the face of rebellions by Lothair, Pepin I of Aquitaine and Louis the German. At a diet in Aachen in 837 Louis the Pious had the nobles do homage to Charles as heir to all that was once Gaul. When Louis died in 840 war broke out between his sons.

Charles allied with Louis the German against the new Emperor Lothair I, and they defeated Lothair at Fontenoy-en-Puisaye on 25 June 841. In 842 the brothers confirmed their alliance by the Oaths of Strasbourg, and the war ended with the Treaty of Verdun in August 843, which gave Charles the western kingdom, roughly modern France as far as the Meuse, the Saône and the Rhône, with the Spanish March as far as the Ebro. His reign was troubled. The Bretons under Nomenoë and Erispoë defeated him at Ballon in 845 and Jengland in 851 and gained de facto independence.

Vikings devastated the Seine and Loire valleys, and after they sacked Paris in 845 Charles had to buy their retreat at a heavy price. By the Edict of Pistres of 864 he gave the army a cavalry element and ordered fortified bridges built across rivers; two of them saved Paris during the siege of 885 to 886. After the death of his nephew Lothair II in 869 he had himself consecrated king of Lotharingia at Metz, but under pressure from Louis he agreed in 870 to partition it.

After the death of Emperor Louis II, Charles travelled south with the support of Pope John VIII, was crowned king at Pavia, and received the imperial insignia in Rome on 25 December 875. He was beaten by Louis the German's forces at Andernach on 8 October 876, and a second expedition at the pope's call found little support among the nobles. Ill, he turned back and died at Brides-les-Bains on 6 October 877.

His son Louis succeeded him. His nickname may have been ironic, for contemporary images show him with a full head of hair; one suggestion links it to his early lack of a kingdom. His seal as emperor bore the words renovatio imperii Romani et Francorum, renewal of the empire of the Romans and Franks.
charles-the-bold: Charles Martin was born on 10 November 1433 in Dijon, the only child of Philip the Good and his third wife, Isabella of Portugal, to survive infancy. His father made him a knight of the Golden Fleece and count of Charolais. From 1454 to 1464 Philip excluded him from power. In his youth Charles was known for his chivalric ambitions and his admiration for Alexander the Great. He developed an intense rivalry with Louis XI of France, who became king on 22 July 1461, and in 1465 formed the League of the Public Weal, a coalition of French feudal lords, and led them in a war against the king.

Philip the Good died on 15 June 1467, and Charles formally became duke fourteen days later. His joyous entry into Ghent provoked unrest, and the following January he forced the mayors to ask his pardon and abolished the city's governmental rights. He inherited a vast but fragmented collection of territories from the Low Countries to the borders of Switzerland and wanted to turn them into an independent kingdom.

At Trier in October 1473 he met the Holy Roman Emperor Frederick III, hoping to be recognised as king of the Romans and to betroth his daughter Mary to the emperor's son Maximilian. He married Margaret of York to secure an English alliance. A patron of illuminated manuscripts, he kept a court noted for its chivalric culture and etiquette. Between 1468 and 1473 he issued military ordinances, creating in 1471 a standing army of 1,250 lances fournies with archers, handgunners and pikemen.

Charles fought the Burgundian Wars against an alliance of Swiss, German and Alsatian powers. His siege of Neuss lasted from July 1474 to June 1475 and cost him heavily. In 1476 he was defeated by the Swiss at Grandson and at Morat. When René II of Lorraine retook Nancy on 6 October 1476, Charles besieged it through the winter. On 5 January 1477, in the Battle of Nancy, the Count of Campobasso's Italian mercenaries having deserted to René, Charles was killed. His body was found two days later on the frozen river, and René had him buried in the Saint-George collegiate church. In Artois some refused to believe he was dead.

Three weeks later Louis XI invaded Burgundian territory, Ghent rebelled, and Liège and Guelders sought independence. His death led to the collapse of the Burgundian State, since he had no legitimate male heir, and he was succeeded by his only child, Mary. His German enemies called him the Grand Turk of the West.
charles-the-child: Charles the Child, also called Charles the Young or Charles III, was born at Frankfurt am Main in 847 or 848. He was the second son of Charles the Bald and brother of Louis the Stammerer. His father had himself ruled as King of Aquitaine from 838, and appointed the younger Charles as a sop to Aquitainian separatism.

The Aquitainians had rebelled against Charles the Bald and asked Louis the German to send one of his sons to rule them. Louis sent his second son, Louis the Younger, and Charles the Bald released the rival claimant Pippin II. Pippin rallied the nobles and drove out Louis the Younger, but by October 855 had lost popularity, and Charles the Bald appointed Charles the Child as king. He was anointed at Limoges. Within a year the Aquitainians had replaced him with Pippin II, but then deposed Pippin and restored Charles the Child. Pippin was captured in 864 and imprisoned at Senlis, after which he disappears from history.

Unlike earlier sub-kings of Aquitaine, Charles the Child had no real authority. He had no chancery, could issue no instruments and could not bestow privileges, endow religious establishments or dispose of royal property. All the rights of the region were invested in Charles the Bald, and in his absence the nobles gathered power. As he grew older, Charles exercised what little personal authority he could. In 862 he chose and married a wife against his father's will, a widow of a count named Humbert whose own name is unknown. In 863 his father reasserted power over him and forced him to put her away and be loyal.

A year later Charles was struck in the head with a sword by a member of his own hunting party, in a mock combat. Ado of Vienne remarked that he was dishonoured by having suffered it. The blow left him mentally incapacitated until his death on 29 September 866. He died childless at Buzançais and was buried at Bourges.
charles-the-fat: Charles was the youngest of the three sons of Louis the German, first King of East Francia, and Hemma, of the House of Welf, and a great-grandson of Charlemagne. The nickname Carolus Crassus is not contemporary: it first appears with the Saxon Annalist in the twelfth century, and no contemporary source mentions his size. He was made Count of the Breisgau in 859 and, when Louis the German's lands were divided in 865, received Alemannia. After Louis died in 876, Charles ruled there. In 879 his brother Carloman, incapacitated by a stroke, divided his domains, and Italy passed to Charles, who spent most of his time there until 886.

Pope John VIII, begging his help against Guy II of Spoleto, crowned Charles emperor on 12 February 881. Charles did little against Guy, though hopes of a revival had been raised. His brother Louis the Younger died on 20 January 882, leaving him the whole of East Francia, and on the death of Carloman II on 12 December 884 the nobles of West Francia invited him to rule there too, reuniting the Carolingian Empire. He built a palace at Sélestat in Alsace on the model of Charlemagne's at Aachen. His rule in the west was distant, and he left daily business to the higher nobility.

Against the Vikings he preferred negotiation. In 882 he besieged their camp at Asselt, then made terms: Godfrid accepted Christianity and became his vassal, and Sigfred was bribed off. In 885 Charles had Godfrid executed at a conference at Spijk. When a large fleet under Sigfred besieged Paris in 885 and 886, Charles brought a large army but did not fight; he sent the attackers up the Seine to ravage rebellious Burgundy and paid the 700 pounds of silver promised, and his prestige in France was greatly diminished.

Charles had no legitimate children and failed to have his illegitimate son Bernard recognised as heir, against opposition from several bishops; he then adopted Louis of Provence. In November 887 his nephew Arnulf of Carinthia led a rising of Bavarians and Slavs, and Charles's support in East Francia collapsed within a week. By 17 November he was out of power. He was given estates at Naudingen (Donaueschingen) and died there, of natural causes, on 13 January 888, and was buried at Reichenau.

The empire then split into separate kingdoms: Arnulf took East Francia, the French elected Odo, Berengar was acclaimed in Italy, and Louis was crowned in Provence. Contemporary opinion of Charles was kinder than later accounts, and the Annales Fuldenses praise his piety. A modern suggestion is that his poor record owed much to constant illness; he is believed to have had epilepsy.
charles-the-good: Charles was born in Denmark, the only son among the three children of King Canute IV and Adela of Flanders. His father was assassinated in Odense Cathedral in 1086, and Adela fled to Flanders with the very young Charles, leaving her twin daughters Ingeborg and Cecilia in Denmark. Charles grew up at the court of his grandfather Robert I of Flanders and his uncle Robert II of Flanders.

He travelled to the Holy Land in 1107 or 1108 with a fleet of English, Danish and Flemish crusaders. In 1124 a faction of nobles opposed to King Baldwin II offered him the crown of the Kingdom of Jerusalem, and according to Galbert of Bruges he refused at the urging of advisers who feared that his departure would leave Flanders at the mercy of the Erembald clan.

When Robert II died in 1111, Charles's cousin Baldwin VII became count, and Charles was a close adviser. Wounded at the Battle of Bures-en-Brai in September 1118, the childless Baldwin designated Charles as successor before dying on 17 July 1119.

In 1125 Charles was also considered a candidate for King of the Romans after the death of Henry V but rejected the offer. During the famine of that year he had legumes planted on his own estates and given away, distributed bread to the poor, and, according to Galbert, said it was better for the rich of Flanders to drink only water than for a single poor person to die of hunger. He cracked down on the hoarding of grain to raise prices, and expelled the Jews from Flanders, attributing such practices to Jewish merchants. At the urging of his advisers he also began legal proceedings to reduce the wealthy Erembald family to serfdom.

Bertulf, head of the Erembald family, a priest and provost of the Church of St. Donatian, organised a conspiracy to kill Charles and replace him with William of Ypres. On the morning of 2 March 1127 Charles knelt in prayer in St. Donatian's, his hand full of coins to give alms. During Mass knights answering to the Erembalds entered and hacked him to death with broadswords. The murder provoked widespread outrage, and he was almost at once regarded as a martyr and saint, though not formally beatified until 1882 by Pope Leo XIII.

The Erembalds were besieged in the comital castle of Bruges by nobles and commoners of Bruges and Ghent, and all the conspirators were captured and tortured to death. King Louis VI of France, who had supported the uprising, then used his influence to have William Clito of the House of Normandy chosen as the next count.
charles-the-simple: Charles was born on 17 September 879, the third and posthumous son of King Louis the Stammerer and his second wife, Adelaide of Paris. He was a child of five when his half-brother, King Carloman II, died on 6 December 884, and the Frankish nobles asked their cousin, Emperor Charles the Fat, to take the crown instead. After Charles the Fat was deposed in 887, the nobility again passed over the young prince and elected Odo, Count of Paris, the hero of the siege of Paris of 885 to 886, as king. Charles was put under the protection of Ranulf II, Duke of Aquitaine.

In 893, aged 14, Charles was crowned at Reims Cathedral by a faction opposed to Odo, aided by Archbishop Fulk of Reims. By 897 he ruled only the city of Laon. He became king of West Francia in 898, when Odo on his deathbed designated him as his successor. He soon showed ambition to conquer Lotharingia, the homeland of the Carolingian dynasty, and invaded in 898 at the call of Count Reginar of Hainaut.

In 911 a band of Vikings led by Rollo besieged Paris and Chartres. After a victory near Chartres on 26 August, Charles negotiated with Rollo, and the Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte created the Duchy of Normandy. The Vikings received the land between the river Epte and the sea, and Rollo agreed to be baptised and to marry Charles's daughter Gisela. Also in 911, Louis the Child, the last Carolingian king of East Francia, died, and the Lotharingian nobles under Reginar declared Charles their king, in preference to Conrad I, whom East Francia had elected. Charles defended Lotharingia against two attacks by Conrad.

Charles's favouritism towards Hagano, a petty nobleman and a relative of his first wife Frederuna, turned the aristocracy against him. He gave Hagano monasteries that were already the benefices of other barons. The nobles seized him in 920, and Archbishop Herveus of Reims negotiated his release. In 922 the nobles revolted again under Robert of Neustria, Odo's brother, who was crowned king, and Charles fled to Lotharingia. Returning in 923 with a Norman army, he was defeated by Robert's forces at the Battle of Soissons on 15 June, and Rudolph of Burgundy, Robert's son-in-law, was elected king. Charles was captured by Herbert II of Vermandois and imprisoned, finally at Péronne.

He died in prison on 7 October 929 and was buried in the monastery of Saint-Fursy. His son Louis by his second wife Eadgifu of Wessex was crowned in 936 as Louis IV of France, with the support of Hugh the Great.
charles-the-younger: Charles the Younger was born in 772 or 773 to the Frankish king Charlemagne and his wife Hildegard. He had an older half-brother, Pepin the Hunchback, the son of Himiltrude, whose precise relationship with Charlemagne was unclear. All of Charlemagne's children were educated in the liberal arts, and his sons were trained in riding, combat and hunting.

By the 780s Pepin was seen as illegitimate. Charles was his father's deputy on campaigns, while Pepin received no such commands, and after a grant of lands in Maine Charles began to be described as primogenitus, or first-born. In 792 Pepin conspired with Bavarian nobles to kill Charlemagne, Charles and Louis at Regensburg and make himself king. The plot was discovered, Pepin was sent to a monastery and many of his co-conspirators were executed.

Charles received his first command in 784, leading an army in Westphalia during the Saxon Wars, and thereafter held army commands in Saxony. In 789 Charlemagne granted him rule of the kingdom west of the Seine, corresponding to the Duchy of Maine in Neustria. On Christmas Day, 25 December 800, in Rome, Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne emperor and anointed Charles as a king. Frankish annals record his successful campaigns against the Bohemians, Sorbs and other Slavic groups in 805 and 806, and in 808 he led the armies that met the Danish king Gudfred.

In 806 the Divisio Regnorum set out Charlemagne's plans for his inheritance. Charles received the largest share, Francia proper with Saxony, Nordgau and parts of Alemannia, while Louis and the younger Pepin kept Aquitaine and Italy and gained further lands. The Divisio did not address the imperial title.

Pepin of Italy, his sister Rotrude, his aunt Gisela, Abbess of Chelles, and Pepin the Hunchback died in quick succession in 810 and 811, and Charles followed them on 4 December 811. All may have been victims of an epidemic that spread from cattle in 810. His place of death and burial are unknown. Charlemagne then named Pepin's son Bernard ruler of Italy and his only surviving son, Louis, heir to the rest of the empire. Louis was crowned emperor in 813 and succeeded fully in 814.
charles-theodore-elector-of-bavaria: Charles Theodore was born on 11 December 1724 at Drogenbos near Brussels into the Sulzbach branch of the House of Wittelsbach and was educated in Mannheim. His father was Johann Christian. He became Margrave of Bergen op Zoom in 1728 and Count Palatine of Sulzbach on his father's death in 1733.

In 1742 the death of his cousin Charles III Philip, Elector Palatine, gave him the Electoral Palatinate and the duchies of Jülich and Berg. To bind the Wittelsbach lines together, Charles III Philip had arranged a double wedding on 17 January 1742, in which Charles Theodore married his granddaughter Elizabeth Augusta. Their only child lived one day in June 1761, and Elizabeth Augusta died in 1794.

As elector of the Palatinate he founded an academy of science, built up museum collections and supported the arts. When Maximilian III Joseph of Bavaria died in 1777 he also became elector and duke of Bavaria and moved to Munich. He had several mistresses and many illegitimate children, who could not inherit either electorate, and he wanted territory that he could bequeath to them. On 3 January 1778 he agreed with Emperor Joseph II to exchange southern Bavaria for part of the Austrian Netherlands.

The plan was opposed by Maria Anna Sophia of Saxony, the widow of Maximilian Joseph, and by his cousin Charles II August, Duke of Zweibrücken, the next heir, who were supported by Frederick II of Prussia and most of the smaller German states. The crisis led to the War of the Bavarian Succession, ended by the Peace of Teschen in 1779. Charles Theodore kept Bavaria but accepted that his illegitimate descendants could not inherit it, and Austria gained the Innviertel. Charles Theodore never became popular in Bavaria. In 1785 he disbanded Adam Weishaupt's order of the Illuminati and appointed the American Loyalist Benjamin Thompson, later Count von Rumford, as aide-de-camp and chamberlain.

French revolutionary armies occupied Jülich in 1794, invaded the Palatinate in 1795 and marched towards Bavaria in 1796. Charles Theodore died of a stroke in Munich in 1799 and is buried in the crypt of the Theatinerkirche. Bavaria and the Palatinate passed to his cousin Max Joseph, Duke of Zweibrücken.

His court at Mannheim kept an orchestra regarded as one of the finest of its day, and the Mannheim School of Christian Cannabich and Johann Stamitz did work that later composers drew on. In 1780 he commissioned Mozart's Idomeneo. His architect Nicolas de Pigage completed the Mannheim Palace and designed the gardens at Schwetzingen. In Munich the English Garden was laid out in his reign, and the old fortifications were taken down; Karlsplatz bears his name.
charles-town-jamaica: Charles Town lies on the Buff Bay River in Portland Parish and is one of the four official towns of the Jamaican Maroons. With Moore Town and Scott's Hall it belongs to the eastern or Windward Maroons, while Accompong Town is the only official town of the western or Leeward Maroons.

The largest Windward Maroon town had been Crawford's Town, high in the Blue Mountains, until a leadership conflict between Quao and Edward Crawford destroyed it in 1754. The governor, Sir Charles Knowles, 1st Baronet, moved Crawford's supporters to a new village three miles to the north, first called New Crawford Town, while Quao's followers went to Scott's Hall. Crawford's people reportedly renamed it Charles Town after Knowles in gratitude for his support.

White superintendents soon controlled the town, and its Maroon officers reported to them. In 1781 Charles Town Maroons, among them Samuel Grant, took part in hunting down Three Fingered Jack, leader of a community of runaway slaves. During the Second Maroon War of 1795–6 the Windward Maroons stayed neutral; when the governor, Alexander Lindsay, 6th Earl of Balcarres, summoned Grant's men to Kingston, Grant suspected a plan to deport them and led them home, and Balcarres later admitted he had intended it.

The population rose from 226 in 1770 to 391 in 1831. Under the superintendent Alexander Fyffe the Maroons helped to suppress the Christmas Rebellion of 1831–2, led by Samuel Sharpe. In the 19th century the town embraced the Anglican Church, and by the 1850s Revival and Pentecostal traditions had grown from the merging of West African religions with Christianity; the colonial authorities abolished the post of superintendent in the same decade.

The Charles Town Maroon Museum, opened in 2003 by Colonel Frank Lumsden and Kenneth Douglas, stands beside a library on Maroon heritage, and the Asafu Ground hosts the annual Charles Town Maroon celebrations. Unlike Moore Town and Accompong Town, a significant share of the inhabitants are not Maroons.
charles-university: Holy Roman Emperor Charles IV asked his friend and ally Pope Clement VI to create a university in Prague. The papal bull, modelled on the University of Paris, established all four faculties, including theology, and Charles, as king of Bohemia and later as king of the Romans, confirmed its privileges and immunities from secular power by Golden Bull. Archbishop Arnošt of Pardubice took part in the foundation and became chancellor. The first graduate was promoted in 1359, and lectures were held in colleges, the oldest of them the Carolinum of 1366.

In 1402 Jerome of Prague copied works of John Wycliffe at Oxford, and Jan Hus, dean of the philosophical faculty, translated the Trialogus into Czech. The university forbade its members to follow Wycliffe in 1403, but his doctrine spread. In the Western Schism the Bohemian nation backed King Wenceslaus and the Council of Pisa, while the other three nations supported Pope Gregory XII. By the Decree of Kutná Hora on 18 January 1409 the king gave the Bohemian masters three votes and left one for all the other nations together. Foreign, mostly German, professors and students left and founded the University of Leipzig in May 1409. Hus became rector of the Czech-dominated university that autumn, and it became a bastion of the Hussite movement.

The faculties of theology and law disappeared by 1419, and the faculty of arts became the chief doctrinal authority of the Utraquists. In 1654 Ferdinand III merged the Carolinum and Clementinum as the Charles-Ferdinand University.

German replaced Latin as the language of instruction on 29 July 1784, and Protestants and then Jews were admitted. After disputes between Czechs and Germans, an act sanctioned by Emperor Franz Joseph on 28 February 1882 divided it into a German and a Czech university of equal status.

In 1920 a law made the Czech university the successor of the original and named it Charles University. In 1939, after German occupation, Czech universities were closed on 17 November after the funeral demonstration for the student Jan Opletal; nine student leaders were executed and about 1,200 students were interned in Sachsenhausen. The German university was dissolved at the end of the war. After the communist coup of 1948 the university suffered purges for four decades, and students and faculty played a large part in the Velvet Revolution of 1989. Today it is the largest university in the Czech Republic, with 17 faculties.
charles-v-holy-roman-emperor: Charles was born on 24 February 1500 in the Prinsenhof of Ghent, in the Habsburg Netherlands. His father was Philip the Handsome, son of Maximilian I and Mary of Burgundy, and his mother was Joanna of Castile, a daughter of Ferdinand II of Aragon and Isabella I of Castile. After Philip died in 1506 Charles became Lord of the Netherlands, and his aunt Margaret of Austria acted as regent until 1515. She oversaw his education, with Adrian of Utrecht, later Pope Adrian VI, as his tutor. He was raised speaking French, which stayed his most natural language, and later learned some Dutch, Spanish and German.

After Ferdinand II died on 23 January 1516, Charles was proclaimed king of Castile and Aragon jointly with his mother and reached Spain in the autumn of 1517. On the death of Maximilian in 1519 he inherited the Austrian lands and, on 28 June, was elected emperor over Francis I of France, Henry VIII of England and Frederick III of Saxony. Some say the electors were bribed; others hold that Frederick's refusal and his speech urging a strong leader against the Ottomans decided it. Charles was crowned at Aachen on 23 October 1520 and by Pope Clement VII at Bologna on 24 February 1530, the last emperor to receive a papal coronation.

He had no fixed capital. He made 40 journeys through his realms, naming regents to govern in his absence. At the Diet of Worms in 1521 he declared Martin Luther an outlaw. His wars with France brought the capture of Francis I at the Battle of Pavia in 1525, and in 1527 his mutinous soldiers sacked Rome. He captured Tunis in 1535, but lost Buda and failed at Algiers in the early 1540s. Having agreed on the Council of Trent with Pope Paul III, he defeated the Lutheran Schmalkaldic League in the war that followed. Loans from German and Italian bankers, the wealth of the Low Countries and silver from New Spain and Peru financed these campaigns.

Between 1554 and 1556 Charles divided his lands between a Spanish line under his son Philip II and an Austrian line under his brother Ferdinand. He abdicated Naples, Sicily and Milan in favour of Philip on 25 July 1554 and sailed to Spain in September 1556. At the Monastery of Yuste in Extremadura he lived secluded, suffering from severe gout, and he died there in 1558. Historians differ over him: some see a great ruler, others a tragic political failure, though most now judge him a capable politician and an effective military leader whose vision and finances are open to question.
charles-vane: Little is known of Vane's early life. He lived in Port Royal before becoming a pirate but was most likely not born there, and neither A General History of the Pyrates nor his trial transcript says where he was born. He worked with Henry Jennings in the attack on the salvage camp of the wrecked Spanish 1715 Treasure Fleet, first operated as an independent captain in the summer of 1717, and by that winter was one of the leaders of the pirates at Nassau.

When King George I offered a pardon to pirates who surrendered, Vane led those who opposed it, among them many with Jacobite leanings. On 23 February 1718 Captain Vincent Pearse arrived at Nassau in HMS Phoenix and captured Vane's sloop Lark, but released him at the urging of Benjamin Hornigold and others, and Vane declared that he would take the pardon. On 21 March he and his men, including Edward England, turned pirate again and captured a Jamaican sloop. He left Nassau on 4 April, raided ships around the Bahamas and gained a reputation for cruelty, beating captured sailors or torturing them with matches to make them give up their valuables.

Vane was back at Nassau on 22 July 1718 when Woodes Rogers arrived to take office as governor, and Rogers's ships trapped him in the harbour. That night he set his large French prize on fire and sailed it towards Rogers's fleet, forcing the ships to pull away, and escaped through the smaller entrance in a sloop, the Katherine. In August he took eight ships off Charleston. In October he met Blackbeard at Ocracoke Inlet, and the two crews feasted for several days before parting.
