On 23 November a large frigate that he took for a prize raised a French naval ensign and opened fire, and Vane ordered a retreat. His crew saw this as cowardice and voted him out of command, and he and sixteen supporters were put on a sloop.

In February 1719 Vane and his first mate Robert Deal were caught in a hurricane and separated, and Vane was wrecked on an uninhabited island. When English ships arrived for water he tried to join a crew under a false name, but an old acquaintance recognised him and he was arrested. He was held for months in Spanish Town, Jamaica, tried on 22 March 1721 and found guilty. He was hanged on 29 March at Gallows Point in Port Royal, and his body was hung in chains at Gun Cay. He appears in the television series Black Sails and the video game Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag.
charles-vi-holy-roman-emperor: Archduke Charles was born on 1 October 1685, the second son of Emperor Leopold I and his third wife, Eleonore Magdalene of Neuburg. After the death of Charles II of Spain in 1700 without a direct heir, he declared himself King of Spain, and the War of the Spanish Succession lasted almost 14 years against Louis XIV's grandson Philip, Duke of Anjou. Portugal, England, Scotland, Ireland and most of the Holy Roman Empire backed Charles, and in Spain his supporters were concentrated in the Crown of Aragon.
He landed in Spain in 1705 and held power only in Catalonia until the death of his brother Joseph I called him to Vienna. In 1708 he married Elisabeth Christine of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel.

Britain, unwilling to see Austria and Spain united again, withdrew its support, and the Treaties of Utrecht, Rastatt and Baden recognised Philip as king of Spain while ceding Naples, Milan, the Austrian Netherlands and Sardinia to Austria. In the Austro-Turkish War of 1716 to 1718 he added the Banat to Hungary and established direct Austrian rule over Serbia and Oltenia. The War of the Polish Succession ended in 1738 with Charles giving Naples and Sicily to Don Carlos in exchange for Parma and Tuscany. His last Turkish war, begun in 1737 with Russia, ended with the Treaty of Belgrade in 1739, in which he gave up central Serbia and Oltenia.

Charles was a devout Catholic who supported the restoration of Catholic church structures in lands freed from Ottoman rule, and he confirmed older privileges of his Orthodox subjects. Having no surviving son, he issued the Pragmatic Sanction of 19 April 1713, abolishing male-only succession and declaring Habsburg lands indivisible, although the Diet of Hungary approved it only in 1723. He spent the rest of his reign seeking recognition from other powers, and agreed to close the Ostend Company, which he had founded in 1722, to win Britain's assent.

Charles fell ill after a hunting trip in October 1740 and died on 20 October in the Hofburg; Voltaire wrote that he died after eating death cap mushrooms. His daughter Maria Theresa had to defend her inheritance in the War of the Austrian Succession against a coalition of states, among them Prussia, Bavaria and France, that had all been parties to the sanction. She kept her crown and most of her lands but lost Silesia to Prussia and Parma to Spain. At his death the Habsburg lands were deeply in debt, the exchequer held only 100,000 florins, and the Habsburg male line was extinct.
charles-vi-of-france: Charles VI was born in Paris, in the Hôtel Saint-Pol, on 3 December 1368, the son of Charles V and Joanna of Bourbon. His father died on 16 September 1380, leaving a favourable military situation, and Charles was crowned at Reims on 4 November, aged eleven. His uncles ruled as regents: Philip the Bold, Duke of Burgundy, Louis I, Duke of Anjou, John, Duke of Berry, and Louis II, Duke of Bourbon. Philip took the dominant role.

During the regency the treasury built up by Charles V was squandered for the dukes' profit, and the reimposition of unpopular taxes led to revolts known as the Harelle. In 1388 Charles stripped his uncles of their positions and restored his father's advisers, the Marmousets.

In 1392, leading an expedition against the Duchy of Brittany, Charles suffered his first attack of delirium in the forest near Le Mans, and killed several of his own men. From then until his death he alternated between mental instability and lucidity. The cause of his illness is unknown; theories include schizophrenia, manic-depressive psychosis, porphyria and typhus-induced encephalopathy. He believed at times that he was made of glass, and in one episode he claimed to be Saint George.
On 29 January 1393 the Bal des Ardents, a masked ball in which his costume was set alight by a torch, left four dancers dead. In September 1394 he ordered that no Jew should dwell in his domains.

Queen Isabeau and the grandees governed in his name. The enmity between his brother Louis I, Duke of Orléans, and Philip's son John the Fearless led to the murder of Orléans in 1407 and to the Armagnac–Burgundian Civil War, which lasted until 1435. John the Fearless was himself killed on 10 September 1419 at Montereau, in a meeting with the Dauphin, and his son Philip the Good then sided with the English.

Henry V of England invaded and defeated the French army at Agincourt on 25 October 1415. By the Treaty of Troyes of 21 May 1420 Henry was named Charles's successor, the Dauphin was disinherited, and Charles's daughter Catherine of Valois was betrothed to Henry. Charles died on 21 October 1422 at the Hôtel Saint-Pol and was buried at Saint-Denis. Henry V had died a few weeks earlier, so the infant Henry VI of England became king of France under the treaty. The disinherited Dauphin, with Joan of Arc's help, was crowned Charles VII at Reims on 17 July 1429, and the war ended in 1453 with a Valois victory.
charles-vii-holy-roman-emperor: Charles Albert was born in Brussels on 6 August 1697, the eldest son of Maximilian II Emanuel, Elector of Bavaria, and Theresa Kunegunda Sobieska, a daughter of King John III Sobieski of Poland. The family was divided by the War of the Spanish Succession. His father was defeated at Blenheim in 1704 and put under an imperial ban, his mother was forced into exile for ten years, and Charles spent many years under house arrest in Austria. The family was reconciled only in 1715. On 5 October 1722 he married Archduchess Maria Amalia, the youngest daughter of Emperor Joseph I.

Charles became elector on 26 February 1726 after his father's death. When Charles VI died, he rejected the Pragmatic Sanction of 1713 and claimed the Habsburg German lands against Maria Theresa. By the Treaty of Nymphenburg in July 1741 he allied with France and Spain. His French allies took Prague in November 1741, and he was crowned king of Bohemia on 19 December. He was elected king of Germany on 24 January 1742 and crowned emperor on 12 February 1742.

Soon after, the Austrians overran most of his lands and occupied Bavaria, and he lived for almost three years in Frankfurt. Most of Bohemia was lost in December 1742. He was mocked as an emperor who controlled neither his realm nor the empire, and a Latin saying called him et Caesar et nihil, both emperor and nothing. In October 1744 he regained Munich for good.

Suffering badly from gout, Charles died at Nymphenburg Palace on 20 January 1745 and was buried in the crypt of the Theatinerkirche in Munich. His son Maximilian III Joseph made peace with Austria, and in the Treaty of Füssen Austria recognised the legitimacy of his father's election. His reign was the height of the Bavarian rococo: Nymphenburg Palace was completed, and the architect François de Cuvilliés built the Amalienburg hunting lodge.
charles-vii-of-france: Charles was born at the Hôtel Saint-Pol in Paris on 22 February 1403, the eleventh child and fifth son of Charles VI of France and Isabeau of Bavaria. His four elder brothers each held the title of Dauphin and all died childless. After the Burgundians seized Paris in 1418 the fifteen-year-old Charles became the Armagnac leader and set up his court at Bourges. His men killed John the Fearless, Duke of Burgundy, on the bridge at Montereau during a meeting meant to reconcile them; how far Charles was involved has remained uncertain. Under the Treaty of Troyes of 1420 Charles VI recognised Henry V of England as his heir.

In October 1422 northern France, including Paris, was ruled for the infant Henry VI of England by the Duke of Bedford. Charles, mockingly called the King of Bourges, kept an itinerant court in the Loire Valley. Joan of Arc reached him at Chinon on 23 February 1429, the siege of Orléans was lifted on 8 May, the French won at Patay on 18 June, and Charles was crowned at Reims on 17 July 1429. Joan was captured by Burgundian troops in 1430 and burnt at the stake on 30 May 1431; Charles took no action to save her.

By the Treaty of Arras of 5 August 1435 Philip the Good of Burgundy abandoned the English alliance. Charles entered Paris on 13 April 1436. He took royal control of church appointments through the Pragmatic Sanction of Bourges in 1438 and, between 1445 and 1448, formed a cavalry force 12,000 strong, followed by conscripted infantry archers. After a truce at Tours in 1444 he resumed the war in 1449. The French won at Formigny on 15 April 1450 and Castillon on 17 July 1453, leaving only Calais in English hands.

Charles's last years were spoiled by conflict with his heir, the future Louis XI, whom he banished to the Dauphiné in 1446 and who fled to Philip the Good in 1456. Ill from 1458, Charles became convinced that traitors surrounded him, and died at Mehun-sur-Yèvre on 22 July 1461. His reputation has long been overshadowed by Joan of Arc, but he achieved what four generations of his predecessors had not, the expulsion of the English apart from Calais. He also founded the University of Poitiers in 1432.
charles-viii-of-france: Charles was born on 30 June 1470 at the Château d'Amboise, the only surviving son of Louis XI and Charlotte of Savoy. He succeeded on 30 August 1483 at the age of 13. His health was poor, and contemporaries thought him pleasant but unsuited to the business of state. As Louis XI wished, the regency went to his elder sister Anne, whom her father called the least foolish woman in France, and her husband Peter of Bourbon, until 1491. In the Mad War of 1485 to 1488 the great lords rebelled against royal centralisation, and the royal government won.

Charles had been betrothed in 1483 to the three-year-old Margaret of Austria, daughter of Maximilian of Austria. When Francis II, Duke of Brittany, died in 1488, his daughter Anne, aged 11, inherited the duchy and in 1490 married Maximilian by proxy. The regents refused a Habsburg on a second French border, and the French army invaded Brittany while Maximilian was preoccupied with Hungary. Anne of Brittany was forced to renounce Maximilian and marry Charles at Langeais in December 1491. Margaret went home in 1493 with her dowry, though Burgundy was retained under the Treaty of Senlis.

Charles bought the neutrality of England, Aragon and Maximilian by the treaties of Étaples, Barcelona and Senlis in 1492 and 1493, and built a large army with one of Europe's first siege trains. He invaded Italy in September 1494 with 25,000 men, 8,000 of them Swiss mercenaries, took Naples without a pitched battle on 22 February 1495 and was crowned King of Naples on 20 May. The Italian rulers, Spain and the Empire formed the League of Venice on 31 March 1495, but could not stop him at Fornovo in July from marching home, and Aragonese forces soon subdued his garrisons in Naples.

Charles died at Amboise in 1498. By the usual account he struck his head on a door lintel on the way to a game of real tennis and died nine hours later; a study of 2021 held that such a blow would cause only minor injury. All his children died before him, so he was the last of the elder branch of the House of Valois, and Louis XII succeeded him. He left France in debt, but his expedition strengthened cultural ties with Italy and energised French art and literature.
charles-vyner-brooke: Charles Vyner de Windt Brooke was born in London on 26 September 1874, the son of Charles Brooke and Margaret de Windt, and was educated at Clevedon, Winchester College and Magdalene College, Cambridge. He served his father as aide-de-camp and then rose through the Sarawak service as district officer of Simanggang, Resident of Mukah and Oya and of the Third Division, and President of the Law Courts from 1904 to 1911. In 1911 he married Sylvia Brett, daughter of Reginald Brett, Viscount Esher. In the First World War he served incognito as a rating in a naval anti-aircraft unit and as a fitter in an aircraft works at Shoreditch.

He succeeded his father on 17 May 1917, was proclaimed Rajah at Kuching a week later and took the oath before the Council Negri on 22 July 1918. As his father had wished, he shared the work with his younger brother Bertram. A boom in rubber and oil let him modernise Sarawak's institutions, including the public service, and in 1924 he introduced a penal code based on that of British India. His administration was hands-off and fairly popular; it kept out Christian missionaries and encouraged indigenous traditions, though headhunting stayed banned.

In 1941 he took £200,000 from the treasury for his personal use in exchange for the new constitution. When Japanese forces landed at Miri on 16 December 1941, he and his family were in Sydney, where he stayed for the rest of the war.

Vyner returned on 15 April 1946 and resumed power briefly before ceding Sarawak to Britain on 1 July 1946, ending a century of Brooke rule. His nephew Anthony Brooke, heir since 1937 because Vyner had three daughters and no son, opposed the cession, as did most native members of the Council Negri. In 1948 the governor Duncan Stewart was assassinated in Sibu by the young nationalist Rosli Dhobi; documents released later showed that Anthony had no part in it. Vyner died in London on 9 May 1963, four months before Sarawak joined Malaysia, and is buried at Sheepstor on Dartmoor.
charles-warren: Warren was born in Bangor, Wales, on 7 February 1840, the son of Major-General Sir Charles Warren, and after Cheltenham College, Sandhurst and the Royal Military Academy at Woolwich he was commissioned in the Royal Engineers on 27 December 1857. From 1861 to 1865 he surveyed Gibraltar and made two detailed models of the Rock, one of which survives in the Gibraltar Museum. In 1867 the Palestine Exploration Fund sent him to Jerusalem, where he dug shafts down to the lower courses of the Temple Mount walls, found the water shaft now named Warren's Shaft and made the first excavations at Tell es-Sultan, the site of Jericho.

In South Africa he surveyed the boundary of Griqualand West and the Orange Free State in 1876, was badly wounded at Perie Bush in the Transkei War and became Administrator of Griqualand West in 1879. In 1882 the Admiralty sent him to Sinai to learn the fate of Professor Edward Henry Palmer's expedition; he found that its members had been robbed and murdered and brought the killers to justice. His Bechuanaland expedition of 4,000 men, which carried the British Army's first observation balloons in the field, reached its aims without bloodshed, and he then lost the Sheffield Hallam election as an independent Liberal by 690 votes.

As Commissioner of Police he quarrelled with the Home Secretary Henry Matthews and with James Monro, head of the detectives. The radical press turned against him after Bloody Sunday, 13 November 1887, when police and troops broke up a demonstration in Trafalgar Square. During the Ripper murders he was blamed for the failure to find the killer, often unfairly, and censured for publishing an article on the police without permission. He resigned just before the killing of Mary Jane Kelly on 9 November 1888 and stayed in post until 1 December.

After commanding in Singapore and the Thames District, Warren led the 5th Division in the Second Boer War and had operational command at the Battle of Spion Kop on 23-24 January 1900, where his delay and indecision led to disaster; Redvers Buller called him a duffer. Recalled in August 1900, he never commanded troops again. He later helped Baden-Powell found the Boy Scout movement, and he died of pneumonia at Weston-super-Mare on 21 January 1927.
charles-wheler: Charles Wheler was born around 1620, the only son of William Wheler of Martin Husingtree in Worcestershire and Nantwich in Cheshire, and his wife Eleanor, daughter of Edward Polkston of Allington in county Denbigh. He was a student at Cambridge in 1638 and became a Fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge, and an M.A. of the university. At the start of the English Civil War he was among those entrusted with carrying the university's plate to Charles I to help pay for the Royalist cause, and he was ejected from his fellowship on 18 April 1644.

Wheler served as a major in a Royalist cavalry regiment from early in the war until 1644, then in a regiment of foot until early 1646, when he surrendered to Parliament and was allowed to go into exile. In 1656 he was commissioned as a captain in Charles II's Guards, then a regiment of the Spanish army, which fought at the Battle of the Dunes in 1658.

After the Restoration he was a Gentleman of the Privy Chamber from 1660 and a captain in the 1st Foot Guards from 1661 to 1672, and held commands in the Duke of Richmond's Horse and Prince Rupert's Horse. He succeeded his first cousin Sir William Wheler as 2nd Baronet on 6 August 1666, though without the first baronet's estates. He was Member of Parliament for the University of Cambridge from 1667 to 1679 and governed the Leeward Islands in 1671–1672. In 1678–1679 he was colonel of a regiment that later became the 7th Regiment of Foot.

In 1676 he inherited the estate of Sir Thomas Trevor, 1st Baronet, his mother's first cousin, at Leamington Hastings in Warwickshire. He had married Dorothy, daughter of Sir Francis Bindlosse of Borwick-Hall in Lancashire, on 7 August 1648. Their eldest son Trevor died in 1678, a major in his father's regiment, and another son, Sir Francis Wheler, became an admiral and drowned in a wreck on the rocks of Scilly. Sir Charles died on 26 August 1683, was buried at Leamington Hastings and was succeeded by his son Sir William Wheler, 3rd Baronet.
charles-woodford: Woodford was born in Gravesend, Kent, on 30 October 1852, the first son of Henry Pack Woodford, a wine merchant. At Tonbridge School the headmaster introduced him to natural history. In the early 1880s he worked for a time for the colonial government in Fiji, and he made three journeys to the Solomons as a naturalist, learning several local languages. Between 1885 and 1886 he tried three times without success to reach the centre of Guadalcanal from his base on Bara Island to collect specimens for the British Museum. In A Naturalist Among the Head-Hunters (1890) he deplored the lawlessness he blamed on contact with labour recruiters and called for firm and paternal government.

Britain declared a protectorate over the islands in 1893 but set up no government, and the Colonial Office insisted the Solomons pay for themselves. Woodford worked in the office of the High Commissioner for the Western Pacific, Sir John Bates Thurston, and won his support for a resident commissioner funded by a small salary, an imperial grant of £600 a year and licences on traders and recruiters. In 1896 he toured the islands aboard HMS Pylades and on 29 September bought the island of Tulagi as the site for the administrative centre. He was formally appointed Resident Commissioner on 17 February 1897, with orders to curb blackbirding, the coercive recruitment of labour, and the illegal trade in firearms.

He returned in 1897 with six Fijian policemen, a whaleboat and about six pence in reserve. A smallpox outbreak at the Anglican mission of Siota won him an assistant, Arthur Mahaffy, who was based at Gizo from 1898 and charged with suppressing headhunting in New Georgia. For serious trouble Woodford relied on the Royal Navy, appealing for HMS Torch to make a punitive raid on Malaita. Rent from land sold in 1905 to Lever's Pacific Plantations let the government expand, and a district office opened at Auki on Malaita in 1909.

By the time Woodford left, headhunting had nearly died out, though New Georgia and Malaita remained troubled, and much of his progress was undone after his departure. He was made a Companion of the Order of St Michael and St George in 1912 and died on 4 October 1927. Several animals of the Solomons bear his name, among them Woodford's rail and the bird genus Woodfordia, as do two lizards and an orchid.
charles-x-gustav: Charles Gustav was born on 8 November 1622, the son of John Casimir, Count Palatine of Zweibrücken-Kleeburg, and Catherine of Sweden, a daughter of King Charles IX. His parents fled the Thirty Years' War and never returned to Germany, and he was raised at the Swedish court alongside his cousin Queen Christina. He learned war under Lennart Torstenson and was present at the second Battle of Breitenfeld in 1642. Christina, who refused to marry him, declared him her successor in 1649 despite the opposition of the Privy Council under Axel Oxenstierna. He became king when she abdicated in June 1654.

In 1654 Charles married Hedwig Eleonora of Holstein-Gottorp, hoping for an ally against Denmark. In 1655 he led Sweden into the Second Northern War, invading Poland-Lithuania with 50,000 men. His forces took Warsaw and Kraków, but the defence of the fortress-monastery of Częstochowa and a national rising turned opinion against him. He gained the elector of Brandenburg, Frederick William I, as an ally by the treaties of Königsberg, Marienburg and Labiau, the last of which gave Frederick William sovereignty in East Prussia.

When Denmark-Norway declared war on 1 June 1657, he attacked from the south and overran Jutland. In the winter of 1658 the Little Belt froze, and on 30 January he led his army across the ice to Funen. On the advice of his engineer Erik Dahlberg he then crossed by way of Langeland, Lolland and Falster and reached Zealand on 11 February. Denmark-Norway accepted the Treaty of Taastrup and then the Treaty of Roskilde of 26 February 1658, giving up a great part of its territory. Charles renewed the war in July and besieged Copenhagen, but a Dutch fleet defeated the Swedish fleet in the Battle of the Sound on 29 October 1658.
At the Riksdag of 1655 he began a land reduction to recover estates that Christina had granted to the nobility. It only partly eased the state's finances, and his son used the same decrees later.

In December 1659 Charles summoned the estates to Gothenburg for fresh subsidies. Soon after they opened on 4 January 1660 he fell ill, and his physician mistook his pneumonia for scurvy and treated it with bloodletting and laxatives. On 12 February he signed his testament, naming a regency of six relatives and friends for his minor son, Charles XI, and he died the next day aged 37.
charles-xi-of-sweden: Charles was born in November 1655, the only son of Charles X Gustav and Hedwig Eleonora of Holstein-Gottorp. His father died in February 1660, and a regency led by his mother governed until Charles came of age on 18 December 1672. As an adolescent he devoted himself to sport and bear-hunting and was considered poorly educated. His difficulties are now seen as signs of dyslexia, which was poorly understood then.

Sweden joined the French war against the Dutch in 1674, and after the Swedish defeat at Fehrbellin Denmark declared war in September 1675, beginning the Scanian War. Charles took command in Scania. He won the Battle of Halmstad on 17 August 1676 and fought the Battle of Lund on 4 December, one of the bloodiest battles of its time, in which about 8,000 of over 20,000 combatants died. Louis XIV dictated peace in 1679, which left the Swedish empire practically intact.

The remaining twenty years of his reign were the longest peacetime of the Swedish Empire. At the Riksdag of October 1680 he pushed through the reduction, which recovered crown lands and lordships that had been lent or given away. It ruined some nobles and readjusted the nation's finances. The Estates also told him that he was bound by no one but himself, which formally established absolute monarchy. In 1682 he proposed the army reform in which two farms supported one soldier, and in 1680 he founded the naval base at Karlskrona.

Charles married Ulrika Eleonora of Denmark on 6 May 1680. She died in July 1693, and he never fully recovered. He complained of stomach pains from 1694 and died on 5 April 1697, aged 41, of cancer that had spread through his abdomen. Opinion of him has varied, and a 2003 biography by Rystad describes a strong-willed shaper of Sweden through economic reforms and military strength. His son Charles XII used the well-trained army he left in battles throughout Europe.
charles-xii-of-sweden: Charles was born on 17 June 1682 (Old Style) in the royal castle of Tre Kronor in Stockholm, the first son of King Charles XI and the Danish princess Ulrika Eleonora. Four younger brothers died in infancy, and a younger sister, Ulrika Eleonora, later succeeded him. After his mother died in 1693 his father took him on inspections and official business, and he received an excellent education. Charles XI died in April 1697, and the Riksdag of the Estates recognised the fifteen-year-old's majority in November 1697. He was the first and last Swedish ruler to inherit absolute monarchical authority from his predecessor.

In 1700 Denmark–Norway, Saxony–Poland–Lithuania and Russia allied against Sweden, largely through the efforts of the Livonian nobleman Johann Reinhold Patkul, who had turned against the crown after the great reduction of 1680 stripped much of the nobility of its lands. Charles invaded Zealand with 8,000 men and 43 ships and forced Denmark–Norway to accept the Peace of Travendal in August 1700. He then turned on Russia and Saxony, and by 1706 had forced all his enemies except Russia to submit. His ally Stanisław Leszczyński was crowned in Poland.

Meanwhile Peter the Great reformed the Russian army and founded Saint Petersburg in Ingria. In late 1707 Charles set out for the Russian heartland with some 35,000 men, allied with the Ukrainian Cossack hetman Ivan Mazepa. The campaign ended in the defeat at Poltava. Charles spent the following years in the Ottoman Empire, at Bender, where a village called Karlstad was built for the Swedes. He then rode across Europe in fifteen days to Stralsund and, after five years away, found Sweden at war with Russia, Saxony, Hannover, Great Britain and Denmark.

On 30 November 1718 (11 December New Style) Charles was struck in the head by a projectile in the trenches before the fortress of Fredriksten and died instantly. Where and when he was hit, and whether the shot came from the enemy or his own side, is not known, and no one saw the moment. He never married and had no known children, and his sister Ulrika Eleonora succeeded him. His death came as most of the Swedish Empire lay under foreign occupation. The Treaty of Nystad later formalised the loss, and the absolute monarchy gave way to a parliamentary government that lasted half a century, until Gustav III restored royal autocracy. Voltaire wrote a biography of Charles in 1731.
charles-xiii-of-sweden: Charles was born on 7 October 1748, the second son of King Adolf Frederick of Sweden and Louisa Ulrika of Prussia, a sister of Frederick the Great, and the younger brother of the future Gustav III. He was appointed grand admiral when only a few days old. As heir after his brother he was early seen by the Caps party as a tool against Gustav, but Gustav took care to keep him from being used, and in the December Crisis of 1768 Charles did not let himself be used by the Caps.

In the Revolution of 1772 Charles helped his brother by neutralising the Caps through his connections there and securing the southern provinces with the army, and Gustav III rewarded him with the title Duke of Södermanland. In 1774 he married his cousin Hedvig Elisabeth Charlotte of Holstein-Gottorp, then 15. Their two children, born in 1797 and 1798, did not survive infancy. He took part in secret societies and Freemasonry, was interested in mysticism, and in 1811 founded the Order of Charles XIII, which was limited to 33 knights who had to be Freemasons.

In 1788 he served with distinction as admiral of the fleet in the Russo-Swedish War, notably at the battles of Hogland and Öland. When Gustav III was assassinated in 1792, Charles acted as regent for his nephew Gustav IV Adolf until 1796, after successfully contesting a will that would have restricted his powers. He left government to his favourite, Gustaf Adolf Reuterholm, and the years have been called an Age of Lead in Swedish history. In 1794 the discovery of the Armfelt Conspiracy exposed the opposition of the Gustavian party.

He is presumed to have been aware of the plans to depose Gustav IV Adolf in 1809, and he kept passive during the coup. On 13 March 1809 the victorious party appointed him regent, and the Riksdag of the Estates then elected him king. He was 60 and in poor health, and he suffered a heart attack in November 1809. The new constitution, together with his indecision, also limited his role.

A search for an heir followed. The Danish prince Christian August was adopted as Charles August but died within months of arriving in Sweden. The marshal Jean-Baptiste Bernadotte was then chosen, and on landing in 1810 he took over the government. After a stroke in 1812 Charles lost his memory and the ability to communicate, and he sat as a silent witness in councils chaired by the crown prince. By the union of Sweden and Norway on 4 November 1814 he became king of Norway, as Charles II. He died childless on 5 February 1818, and Bernadotte succeeded him as Charles XIV John.
charles-xiv-john: Jean-Baptiste Bernadotte was born on 26 January 1763 in Pau, the capital of Béarn, the youngest of five children of Jean Henri Bernadotte, a prosecutor at Pau. At fourteen he was apprenticed to a local attorney, but his father's death when he was seventeen turned him away from the law. He joined the Régiment Royal–La Marine as a private on 3 September 1780 and reached the rank of sergeant in August 1785. He was nicknamed Sergeant Belle-Jambe for his smart appearance.

After the outbreak of the French Revolution Bernadotte rose quickly. By 1794 he was a brigadier, and after Jourdan's victory at Fleurus on 26 June 1794 he became a divisional general. When the First French Empire was proclaimed he became one of its eighteen Marshals. From June 1804 to September 1805 he governed Hanover, gaining a reputation for independence, incorruptibility and moderation. He was made Prince of Pontecorvo after Austerlitz, and his wife Désirée Clary was the sister-in-law of Joseph Bonaparte.

In 1810, as he was about to take up the governorship of Rome, he was unexpectedly elected Crown Prince of Sweden, since King Charles XIII was 61, in poor health and childless. Bernadotte entered Stockholm on 2 November 1810, was adopted as Charles John, and converted from Roman Catholicism to Lutheranism.

As Crown Prince he was the de facto head of state. After the French invasion of Swedish Pomerania in 1812 he allied with Alexander I of Russia and helped bring Russia and Britain together in the Sixth Coalition. He commanded the Allied Army of the North, which defeated two French attempts to take Berlin, and made the decisive attack on the last day at Leipzig. He then invaded Denmark, and King Frederick VI signed the Treaty of Kiel on 15 January 1814, ceding Norway to Sweden. Norway was defeated in nineteen days, and the union lasted until its peaceful dissolution in 1905.

Charles John became king on 5 February 1818. His foreign policy sought balance among the Great Powers and avoided conflicts outside Scandinavia, and he kept his kingdoms at peace from 1814 until his death. In 1834 he proclaimed neutrality in advance of a crisis between Britain and Russia, which is pointed to as the origin of Swedish neutrality. He died on 8 March 1844 after a stroke and was succeeded by his only son, Oscar I.
charlesfort: Charlesfort stood on present-day Parris Island, on Port Royal Sound in South Carolina. The expedition that built it was organised by the Huguenot leader Admiral Gaspard de Coligny and led by the Norman navigator Jean Ribault, who landed first on the May River in May 1562 before moving north to the sound. There Ribault left twenty-eight men to build a settlement and sailed for France to arrange supplies, but he was arrested in England after becoming caught up in the unrest of the French Wars of Religion, and could not return.

In his absence most of the settlers' stores were burned, and Captain Albert de la Pierria died in a mutiny, possibly provoked by his harsh discipline. Without supplies or leadership, and facing the hostility of the native population, all but one of the colonists built a boat and crossed the Atlantic without a compass. On the long voyage they were reduced to cannibalism, killing and eating a crew member named La Chère, before an English ship rescued the survivors in English waters.

A Spanish force from Cuba under Hernando de Manrique de Rojas then destroyed Charlesfort and took captive the one Frenchman who had stayed. In 1566 the Spanish founded Santa Elena, the first capital of Spanish Florida, on the same ground, and built Fort San Felipe directly on top of the old French fort. Santa Elena was abandoned in 1576, reoccupied the next year and finally given up in 1587; at its height it had about sixty dwellings and an estimated 400 to 450 people. A second French party, wrecked in the sound in January 1577 under Nicholas Strozzi, was killed or captured, and the Spanish hanged almost all of the captives.

Amateurs recognised the area's importance in the mid-19th century. In the 1920s Major George Osterhout excavated it and concluded that it was Charlesfort, and a memorial marker was placed there, but by the 1950s archaeologists agreed that the remains were Spanish. Only excavations from the 1970s to the 1990s located the French fort, through the restricted spread of distinctively French artefacts and the evidence of several moats dug around the site of the first Fort San Marcos. Finds include the only known early Spanish pottery kiln on the continent. The site became a National Historic Landmark in 2001.
charleston-south-carolina: Charleston lies just south of the midpoint of South Carolina's coastline on Charleston Harbor, an inlet of the Atlantic formed where the Ashley, Cooper and Wando rivers meet. Before colonial settlement the area was inhabited by the Cusabo people, including sub-tribes such as the Kiawah, and by the Ittiwan, whom the colonists called Settlement Indians. The old downtown stands on a peninsula between the Ashley and the Cooper.

Charles II granted the Province of Carolina to eight Lords Proprietors on 24 March 1663. In 1670 Governor William Sayle arranged for shiploads of settlers from Bermuda and Barbados, who founded Charles Town at Albemarle Point on the west bank of the Ashley River. It was the first comprehensively planned town in the Thirteen Colonies, laid out under a scheme called the Grand Model that John Locke prepared for the Proprietors. Because the Fundamental Constitutions of Carolina were never ratified, the town was never incorporated in the colonial period. In 1680 the settlement moved to its present site, and by the 1690s it was the fifth-largest city in North America.

Charleston was central to the Atlantic slave trade. Local merchants, among them Joseph Wragg, helped break the monopoly of the Royal African Company, and almost half of the enslaved people imported into what became the United States arrived there. The state legislature incorporated the city as Charleston on 13 August 1783. The capital moved to Columbia in 1788, yet Charleston stayed among the ten largest American cities until 1840. Cotton brought great wealth to a small part of society and funded fine architecture, but it also raised the economic importance of slavery and brought ever tighter restrictions on Black Charlestonians.

The Civil War began in Charleston Harbor in 1861, and it ended months after United States soldiers retook the city in 1865. Reconstruction followed: the African American population rose from 17,000 in 1860 to over 27,000 in 1880. Free people of colour, 3,785 at the war's outset, became leaders of South Carolina's Republican Party. In the 20th century the city languished economically, helped by a large federal military presence, and tourism grew after the 1920s.

Charleston is the most populous city in South Carolina, with 150,227 people at the 2020 census, and is the seat of Charleston County. Its economy rests on tourism, the port, aerospace and information technology. It is known for preserved architecture, including the Battery and Rainbow Row, for Fort Sumter National Monument, and for Gullah heritage, and it hosts the Spoleto Festival USA, founded in 1977 by Gian Carlo Menotti.
charlestown-saint-kitts-and-nevis: Charlestown was originally called Bath Bay, after Bath Stream, a stream noted for its curative waters. It became the chief town of Nevis after Jamestown, the island's first settlement, was inundated by a tidal wave in 1680. In the late 18th century it was both a naval base and a resort known for its mineral waters. At the northern end of the town stood the Bath Hotel and Spring House, which was a tourist hotel and spa during the 18th century, and whose main building was for a while occupied by government offices. In colonial times the town was protected by Fort Charles to the south and Fort Black Rocks to the north. Fire almost destroyed it in 1873.

Many of the oldest two-storey stone buildings were badly damaged over time by earthquakes, which tended to make the upper storey collapse into the lower one. This design flaw led to the common practice of building a wooden upper floor above a stone ground floor.

Charlestown lies on the leeward side of Nevis, near the southern end of Pinney's Beach, in the Leeward Islands of the West Indies. It has a population of about 1,500 and is the main administrative and commercial centre of the island and its most concentrated residential area. It is also the hub of much of the island's transport, with a modern port where the ferries from St Kitts load and unload passengers, though it has no commercial airport. Its main industry has been sugar milling.

Hamilton House, where Alexander Hamilton, later a Founding Father of the United States, was born, stands in the town. Hamilton was born and spent his childhood there, and the restored stone building now holds the Museum of Nevis History on the ground floor and the Nevis Island Administration Assembly Room above. There are also the Nelson Museum and the Nevis Sport Museum. Nearby are the ruins of Montpelier Estate, where the naval commander Horatio Nelson was married. Memorial Square commemorates the Nevisian soldiers who died in the two World Wars.
charlotte-grand-duchess-of-luxembourg: Charlotte was born on 23 January 1896 at Berg Castle, the second daughter of Grand Duke William IV and Marie Anne of Portugal. Her older sister Marie-Adélaïde had succeeded their father, but her actions during the German occupation of Luxembourg in the First World War were controversial. She was seen as sympathetic to the occupier, there were calls in parliament for her abdication, and she was forced to abdicate in favour of Charlotte on 14 January 1919.

Luxembourg adopted a new constitution that year. In a referendum on 28 September 1919, 77.8 per cent voted to keep the monarchy with Charlotte as head of state. The constitution severely restricted the monarch's powers, codifying actual practice since the end of the personal union with the Netherlands in 1890. On 6 November 1919 she married Prince Felix of Bourbon-Parma; they had six children.

By 1935 she had sold the former ducal palaces of Biebrich and Weilburg in Germany to Prussia. Luxembourg's neutrality was violated on 9 May 1940, when she was at Colmar-Berg. She and her ministers placed themselves under French protection, then went on through Spain to Portugal after the French capitulation. The Germans proposed to restore her functions, but she refused, mindful of her sister's experience. By 29 August 1940 she was in London, where she began broadcasting to her homeland on the BBC.

She travelled to the United States and Canada and met President Roosevelt several times. In 1943 she and the government established themselves in London, where her more regular broadcasts made her a focus for resistance in Luxembourg. Her eldest son, Jean, served from 1942 in the Irish Guards. She returned to Luxembourg in April 1945, and in the postwar years received heads of state and raised the country's profile abroad.

Charlotte abdicated on 12 November 1964 in favour of her son Jean. Her reign is the longest of any Luxembourgish monarch since the country became a grand duchy in 1815. She died of cancer at Fischbach Castle on 9 July 1985 and was interred in the Ducal Crypt of Notre-Dame Cathedral in Luxembourg.

She was the last agnatic member of the House of Nassau and the last personal recipient of the Golden Rose, an honour that in modern times the Pope has awarded only to churches and shrines. A statue of her stands in the Place Clarefontaine in Luxembourg city.
charlotte-of-mecklenburg-strelitz: Charlotte was born on 19 May 1744, the youngest daughter of Duke Charles Louis Frederick of Mecklenburg, Prince of Mirow. Mecklenburg-Strelitz was a small north-German duchy in the Holy Roman Empire. She was taught literature, botany, natural history, French, Italian and Latin, and played the harpsichord, though diplomatic reports at the time of her engagement called her education very mediocre.

George III, unmarried when he succeeded in 1760, needed a wife, and the Hanoverian minister in London suggested Charlotte. At 17 she appealed partly because a girl raised in an insignificant duchy would probably have no interest in party politics, and George told her soon after the wedding not to meddle. They married on 8 September 1761. They had 15 children, the first of them the future George IV, born on 12 August 1762, and all but two survived to adulthood. She had a strained relationship with her mother-in-law, Augusta, and turned to German companions.

She was a music lover and an amateur botanist who enlarged the collections at Kew Gardens, and the bird of paradise flower was named Strelitzia reginae for her. The eight-year-old Mozart played before her in 1764. George III fell ill from October 1788 until March 1789, which distressed her greatly, and after his illness became permanent in 1811 she was made his guardian while her son governed as Prince Regent.

Charlotte died on 17 November 1818 at Kew Palace and was buried at St George's Chapel, Windsor Castle. She had been queen consort for 57 years and 70 days, the longest of any British queen consort. Places named for her include Charlotte in North Carolina, Charlottesville in Virginia, Charlottetown and the Queen Charlotte Islands, now Haida Gwaii. Her funding kept the General Lying-in Hospital in London open, and it is now Queen Charlotte's and Chelsea Hospital.
charlotte-stanley-countess-of-derby: Charlotte de La Trémoille was born at the chateau of Thouars in Poitou, the daughter of Claude de La Trémoille, 2nd Duke of Thouars, and Countess Charlotte Brabantina of Nassau. Her maternal grandparents were William I, Prince of Orange, and Charlotte de Bourbon. She married James Stanley on 26 June 1626 and was naturalised as an English subject by Act of Parliament in February 1629. The couple had four daughters and six sons, of whom only five appear to have reached marriageable age, among them Charles Stanley, 8th Earl of Derby.

While her husband, a Royalist commander, was away, she was left in charge of Lathom House, which became the last Royalist stronghold in Lancashire. After the fall of Warrington she refused to acknowledge Parliament's authority and surrender the house, saying it would dishonour her husband, but offered to confine herself to defending her home, which delayed an attack. In February 1644 the forces of Sir Thomas Fairfax laid siege. She had fortified the house against bombardment and gathered a militia of seasoned marksmen whose sniping caused heavy losses, and she refused repeated offers of surrender until Prince Rupert relieved the siege on 27 May 1644.

She and her household were then evacuated to the Isle of Man, of which her husband was Lord. Her attempt to barter the island for his freedom after his capture provoked a revolt led by Illiam Dhone. With the Royalist army destroyed at the Battle of Worcester and her husband beheaded at Bolton, she held Castle Rushen at Castletown until it yielded to Colonel Duckenfield in October 1651.

David Hume wrote that she kept the glory of being the last person in the three kingdoms to submit to the victorious rebels, though the claim is incorrect: the last holdout against Cromwellian forces was the island of Inishbofin in County Galway, in 1653. Her defence of Lathom House was commemorated by Letitia Elizabeth Landon in a poem of 1833 written for a portrait of Lord and Lady Derby after van Dyck.
charlottetown-conference: Britain encouraged a Maritime Union of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, hoping the colonies would grow less dependent on the Crown and stronger economically and militarily in the light of the American Civil War. When the Province of Canada, made up of present-day Ontario and Quebec, heard of the planned meeting, it asked that the agenda be widened to a union including itself.

A circus was in Charlottetown at the same time, the first on the island in over 20 years, and it drew far more interest from the townspeople. With accommodation scarce, many Canadian delegates stayed aboard their steamship. No one was working at the public wharf when they arrived, so William Henry Pope of Prince Edward Island rowed out to greet them himself.

The conference opened on Thursday 1 September with a banquet, and most of its sessions were held in Province House, the colony's legislative building; dinners and banquets followed each evening at venues including Government House. No formal transcript was kept, and historians rely on private sources such as delegates' letters home. The Canadians dominated the meetings: four of the first five days were spent setting out their position, and George Brown spent two days on the details of a proposed constitution that would keep Canada within the British Empire. The Maritime delegates put their own plans forward only on 6 and 7 September, and largely set aside the idea of a Maritime Union.

Most Maritime delegates came to believe that the wider union would benefit them, and that it could be achieved within a few years; Prince Edward Island remained unsure and largely opposed. The delegates met again in Halifax on 10 and 12 September 1864 and then at Quebec City from 10 to 27 October, where the Quebec Conference produced a draft constitution. Canada was founded on 1 July 1867. Some historians believe Confederation was a pre-emptive step against the annexation of northern and western territories by the United States, whose army had grown greatly during the Civil War.
charminar: Construction began in 1589 and was completed in two years, at a cost of 9 lakh rupees, about 2 lakh gold huns. Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah, the fifth ruler of the Qutb Shahi dynasty, built it after moving his capital from Golconda to the newly founded Hyderabad. Accounts of its purpose differ. The Archaeological Survey of India records that it is widely accepted to have been built at the centre of the city to commemorate the end of a plague. The 17th-century French traveller Jean de Thévenot, whose narration was complemented with Persian texts, says it marked the beginning of the second Islamic millennium, the year 1000 AH.

The monument stood at the crossing of the trade route that linked the city to the port of Machilipatnam, and the Old City was laid out around it in four quadrants. Architects from Persia were invited to help plan the city.

The building is in the Indo-Islamic style with Persian elements and was intended as a mosque and madrasa. Its square body is 20 metres on each side, and each side opens in a grand arch facing a cardinal direction. The four fluted minarets, each with a double balcony and a bulbous dome, are built into the main structure, unlike the free-standing minarets of the Taj Mahal. A flight of 149 winding steps leads to the upper floor. The structure is of granite, limestone, mortar and pulverised marble, and is known for its stucco decoration.

The mosque occupies the top floor of the four-storey building. Its main gallery has 45 covered prayer spaces, and the rest of the roof served as a royal court in Qutb Shahi times. Clocks on the four sides were added in 1889.

A minaret fell after being struck by lightning in 1670 and was repaired, and in 1820 Sikandar Jah paid for the renovation of part of the building. The Charminar remained the tallest structure in Hyderabad for 396 years, until 1987. To the south-west stands the Makkah Masjid, whose central arch Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah is said to have built with bricks made from soil brought from Mecca. The Laad Bazaar around the monument is known for jewellery, especially bangles, and in its heyday the Charminar market had some 14,000 shops.

The Charminar appears on the coins and banknotes of the Hyderabad rupee and on the emblem of Telangana. With the Golconda Fort and the Qutb Shahi Tombs it was submitted to the UNESCO World Heritage Site tentative list on 10 September 2010.
charter-oath: The first draft was written in January 1868 by the junior councillor Yuri Kimimasa, in progressive language that spoke to the frustrations of radical but modestly born Meiji leaders. In February his colleague Fukuoka Takachika moderated it to be less alarming, and Kido Takayoshi prepared the final form, using language broad enough to embrace both readings. The Oath was meant both as a statement of policy for the government that followed the Tokugawa shogunate and as an offer of inclusion to pro-Tokugawa domains, to keep them from joining the Tokugawa remnant in the Boshin War.

The Oath was promulgated on 6 April 1868 in the Kyoto Imperial Palace. Its five clauses promised that deliberative assemblies would be widely established and all matters decided by open discussion, that all classes would be united in carrying out the affairs of state, and that commoners, like officials, could pursue their own calling. Evil customs of the past were to be broken off and everything based on the just laws of Nature, and knowledge was to be sought throughout the world to strengthen imperial rule. Sanjō Sanetomi read it aloud before the Emperor and more than 400 officials, and 767 people signed in all.

The promised reforms were at first unfulfilled. A parliament with real power was not established until 1890, and the oligarchy from Satsuma, Chōshū, Tosa and Hizen kept political and military control well into the 20th century. The wording was deliberately broad, a promise of gradualism and equity: the reference to all classes implied that classes would continue, and only the search for knowledge pointed clearly to change, and that was to be selective and purposeful.

The Oath was repeated as the first article of the constitution of June 1868 and remained influential, more as inspiration than as a means of government. It can be considered the first constitution of modern Japan. After the Second World War Emperor Shōwa paid homage to it in his Imperial Rescript on National Revitalization.
charter-of-kortenberg: The charter was signed and sealed in the abbey of Kortenberg by the duke and representatives of the towns, and it applied to the whole duchy of Brabant. The duke agreed that no demands or taxes would be raised beyond the three feudal cases: the knighting of his son, the marriage of his daughter and his own ransom if he were taken captive. Taxes were to be reasonable, justice honourable for rich and poor alike, and the freedom of the good towns recognised.

The council had four knights or nobles and ten townsmen: three from Leuven, three from Brussels and one each from Antwerp, 's-Hertogenbosch, Tienen and Zoutleeuw. It was to see that the financial, judicial and municipal prerogatives were kept and to introduce improvements to the administration of the land. Members who died were to be replaced, and every member swore on the Gospel to pursue the best interests of the public.

The Council of Kortenberg, an early kind of parliament and a forerunner of the later Estate assembly, met at the abbey and elsewhere, with ups and downs, until 1375. In the financial commission of August 1314 there were two nobles and twelve representatives of eight towns. From 1332 the council had sixteen lords, Antwerp gaining a second member and the Walloon Brabant town of Nivelles one. By 1340 it sealed documents with a common seal showing a tree on a small hill.

Historians see the charter as the start of what they call Brabant's constitutionalism, in which inhabitants without power claimed rights and had them put in writing, rights somewhat comparable to the civil and political rights of later centuries. It has been judged more democratic than Magna Carta, which benefited the barons and was to be enforced by a council of 25 barons, whereas the Kortenberg charter expressly named the rich and the poor, riken ende armen.

A line of continuity has been drawn from it through the Joyous Entries of new dukes into Flemish and Brabantian towns and the Act of Abjuration of 1581 to the Seven United Provinces, where some of the Mayflower Pilgrim Fathers lived in Leiden for two decades before leaving for America.
chartism: Chartism grew out of disappointment after the Reform Act 1832, which failed to extend the vote beyond those owning property. Working-class leaders spoke of a great act of betrayal, a feeling strengthened by the Whig governments of the 1830s, notably through the Poor Law Amendment of 1834, which deprived working people of outdoor relief and drove the poor into workhouses, where families were separated. In 1837 six Members of Parliament and six working men, including William Lovett of the London Working Men's Association, formed a committee, and in 1838 they published the People's Charter. None of its demands was new, but it became a widely known political manifesto of 19th-century Britain.

The movement was launched in 1838 by large meetings in Birmingham, Glasgow and the north of England, among them a mass meeting on Kersal Moor near Salford on 24 September 1838. There Joseph Rayner Stephens called Chartism a knife and fork, a bread and cheese question. Support was strongest in northern England, the East Midlands, the Staffordshire Potteries, the Black Country and the South Wales Valleys, where working people depended on single industries. The strategy relied on the scale of petitions and mass meetings, though some Chartists took part in insurrection, notably in South Wales and Yorkshire.

The Northern Star, published from 1837 to 1852 and owned by Feargus O'Connor, was in 1839 the best-selling provincial newspaper in Britain, with a circulation of 50,000, and was often read aloud in workplaces and in the open air. From 1843 O'Connor proposed land as the answer to workers' problems, and the Chartist Co-operative Land Company bought five estates between 1844 and 1848 before Parliament ordered it shut. In 1848, after news of revolution in Paris, a demonstration was called for 10 April on Kennington Common, and 100,000 special constables were recruited. O'Connor cancelled the planned procession to Parliament, and the movement declined rapidly.

Chartism did not directly generate any reforms, but after 1848 its demands appeared less threatening and were gradually enacted by others. The Reform Act 1867 admitted part of the urban working men to the franchise, secret voting came in 1872, payment of Members of Parliament in 1911 and full manhood suffrage in 1918. Annual elections remain the only demand never implemented. The historian Malcolm Chase argues that Chartism was a movement characterised by many small victories, since Chartism collapsed but Chartists did not. Many learned to speak in public and became journalists, poets, ministers and councillors.
chartres: Chartres is built on a hill on the left bank of the River Eure, about 90 km south-west of Paris. The cathedral stands at the top of the hill, and its two spires can be seen from a long way across the flat country. To the south-east lies the fertile plain of Beauce, called the granary of France, for which Chartres is the commercial centre.

Chartres was one of the principal towns of the Carnutes, a Celtic tribe in Gaul. In the Gallo-Roman period it was called Autricum and afterwards civitas Carnutum, the city of the Carnutes, from which its present name comes. The Norsemen raided and burned it in 858 and besieged it unsuccessfully in 911. In the Middle Ages it gave its name to a county held by the counts of Blois and of Champagne and then by the House of Châtillon, one of whom sold it to the Crown in 1286.

The English held it from 1417 to 1432 during the Hundred Years' War, and Francis I raised it to a duchy in 1528. Royal troops of Henry IV took it on 19 April 1591, and on 27 February 1594 Henry was crowned in its cathedral after his conversion to the Catholic faith, the only king of France whose coronation was not held at Reims. In 1674 Louis XIV made it a duchy peerage for his nephew Philippe II of Orléans, and the title of Duke of Chartres passed to the eldest son of each Duke of Orléans.

In 1944 Allied bombs destroyed part of the old town, including most of the library of the School of Chartres. The cathedral was spared when Colonel Welborn Barton Griffith Jr. questioned the order to destroy it on 16 August and confirmed that it held no Germans. He was killed later that day, and American divisions liberated the town on 18 August.

Chartres is the prefecture of the Eure-et-Loir department and the seat of a bishopric. Its Gothic cathedral, Notre-Dame de Chartres, is regarded as one of the finest and best preserved in Europe and is a World Heritage Site. It replaced a Romanesque cathedral destroyed by fire in 1194, and its stained glass was paid for by guilds of merchants and craftsmen and by wealthy noblemen. Chartres has been a place of Catholic pilgrimage since the Middle Ages.
charyapada: The manuscript, also called the Caryācaryāviniścaya, holds 47 padas, or verses, with a Sanskrit commentary by Munidatta. They were composed by 22 of the Mahasiddhas, or Siddhacharyas, whose names stand at the head of each pada except the first, together with the raga to which it was to be sung; some of these ragas are now extinct. The Sanskrit names of the poets were probably given by Munidatta. The title page, the colophon and several pages, holding padas 24, 25 and 48, are missing.

Haraprasad Shastri, following Munidatta's commentary, called the enigmatic language of the verses twilight language, Sandhya-bhasha, half expressed and half concealed. Vidhushekhara Shastri later named it, from other Buddhist texts, intentional language, Sandha-bhasha.

Shastri published the palm-leaf manuscript through the Bangiya Sahitya Parishad in 1916 in his Hajar Bacharer Purano Bangala Bhasay Bauddhagan O Doha; it is now kept at the National Archives of Nepal. Prabodhchandra Bagchi later published a Tibetan translation of 50 verses, which supplies the missing padas, including pada 25 by Tantripāda. The Tibetan text names Munidatta as the commentator and says the songs were translated by Shilachari and the commentary by Chandrakirti or Kirtichandra.

Scholars disagree on its date. Shastri placed it in the 10th century, Suniti Kumar Chatterji and Prabodh Chandra Bagchi between the 10th and 12th, and Sukumar Sen allowed for the 11th to 14th, while Muhammad Shahidullah argued for the 7th to 11th and Rahul Sankrityayan for the 8th to 11th.

Because its poets came from different regions, scholars of several languages find their own features in it. Luipa came from Kamarupa and Sarahapa is said to have come from Rani, near present-day Guwahati, and grammatical forms such as the negative placed before the verb are shared with Assamese. Many of the Siddhacharyas were from Bengal. Sankrityayan held that most were from Bihar and wrote an early Magahi, and the historian K. P. Jayaswal saw the poems as early Maithili, while Odia poetry is traced to the same Charya literature.
chasseurs-d-afrique: The corps was formed shortly after the French occupation of Algiers by transfers from the chasseurs à cheval, other metropolitan cavalry regiments and some infantry units. At first about 40 men of each squadron were indigenous horsemen recruited locally, but in 1836 the Arab and Berber troopers were moved to the newly organised Spahis, the other main cavalry of the Armée d'Afrique. Two more regiments were raised in 1832 and 1833, and the Chasseurs became the mounted equivalent of the Zouave infantry.

Besides many North African campaigns, the regiments served in the Second Italian War of Independence, Indochina, Dahomey (1892) and Madagascar (1895). In the Crimea the 1st and 4th regiments secured the flank of Lord Cardigan during the Charge of the Light Brigade, advancing rapidly in open order. On 5 May 1863 the 1st regiment fought Mexican lancers at the Battle of San Pablo del Monte, and its flag became the first of any French cavalry regiment to be decorated with the Cross of the Legion of Honour. All four regiments then in existence fought in the Franco-Prussian War and lost heavily in charges at Sedan.

Seven regiments, three of them marching regiments, went to France during the First World War, and squadrons fought at Gallipoli, in the Balkans and against the Turks in the Middle East. Conversion to mechanised units began in 1933 with White TBC and White-Laffly 50 AM armoured cars and was completed during the Second World War. In 1941 the new 6th and 7th regiments fought Allied forces in Syria and Lebanon during Operation Exporter, and the 5th, with M4 Sherman and M5 light tanks, landed in Provence in August 1944 and fought through Toulon, the Rhone valley, Burgundy and Alsace into the Black Forest.

Until 1914 the troopers wore light blue tunics with yellow facings, tucked into a red sash, with red breeches and the taconnet, a light blue and red shako; the blue tunics reportedly earned them the nickname Blue Butchers among some opponents. After the corps ended through disbandments and transfers between 1962 and 1964, the 1st Chasseurs d'Afrique Regiment was re-established in 1998 to preserve its traditions. Stationed at Canjuers, it is a mechanised unit of the French Army that keeps 5 May as its day and has brought back the red sash, and at times the fez, for parade.
chastana: Chashtana's name is attested in Greek as Siastansas, the form written in the corrupted Greek of his coins, and as Tiastanēs in Ptolemy, in Brahmi as Caṣṭana and in Kharosthi as Chaṭhaṇa, forms derived from a Saka name meaning master. The bards called him Tisman, a spelling closer to the Greek. His coins name his father as Ysamotika.

Ptolemy's Geographia, which classes the Western Satraps as Indo-Scythians, describes Chashtana's territory as reaching from Patalene in the west to his capital Ujjain, Ozene, in the east, and beyond Barygaza in the south. According to Ptolemy he ruled Ujjain directly, while Paithan, Pratisthana, was held by Siristolemaios, identified with Sri Pulumayi, son of Gautamiputra Satakarni; his rule thus fell in the reign of the Satavahana king Vasisthiputra Sri Pulamavi. A statue found at Mathura together with statues of the Kushan kings Kanishka and Vima Taktu, bearing the name Shastana, is often attributed to him.

His coins carry his portrait with a corrupted Greek legend, a rendering of the Prakrit for King and Satrap Chashtana. The reverse bears a Brahmi legend, Of the Rajah, the Great Satrap, son of Ysamotika, Chashtana, around a symbol of three hills and a river with the sun and two moons, sometimes followed by his name in Kharosthi.

Chashtana founded the Kardamaka, or Bhadramukha, line, one of the two major Saka satrap dynasties of north-western India. The other, the short-lived Kshaharatas, included Bhumaka and Nahapana. His grandson Rudradaman I became the great conqueror among the Western Satraps. Ptolemy still knew Chashtana as Tiastanēs, ruling a large area of western India into the 2nd century CE, especially the area around Ujjain.
chateau-gaillard: The castle stands on a limestone promontory 90 m above Les Andelys and a bend of the River Seine, about 95 kilometres north-west of Paris. Richard the Lionheart built it in defiance of the Treaty of Louviers of January 1196, which barred both kings from fortifying the site, and seized the manor of Andeli from Walter de Coutances, Archbishop of Rouen, who placed Normandy under an interdict until Richard bought peace with lands and the port of Dieppe. The town of Petit Andely was built at the same time.

The work cost an estimated £12,000 between 1196 and 1198, more than Richard spent on all his castles in England. The castle has three baileys separated by rock-cut ditches, with a keep in the innermost. It was among the first castles in Europe to use machicolations, and the inner bailey's wall of semicircular projections, built on the principle of concentric defence, has no parallel.

In his last years the castle was Richard's favourite residence, but he died on 6 April 1199. During the siege by Philip II, the castellan Roger de Lacy expelled the civilians who had taken refuge inside. The last group, at least 400 people, was refused passage by the French and shut out by the garrison, and more than half died of exposure and starvation at the foot of the walls before Philip ordered the survivors fed and released in February 1204. The French undermined the outer tower and entered by the chapel, and the garrison of 20 knights and 120 soldiers surrendered on 6 March 1204.

In 1314 it held Margaret and Blanche of Burgundy, convicted of adultery in the Tour de Nesle Affair, and after the Scottish defeat at the Battle of Halidon Hill in 1333 Philip VI granted it to the child-king David II of Scotland, who lived there until 1341. In the Hundred Years' War it changed hands several times until the French took it for the last time in 1449.

Henry IV ordered the ruin demolished in 1599, and the work ended in 1611. The site was classified as a monument historique in 1862. Its inner bailey is open to the public from March to November and the outer baileys all year.
chateaubriant: Châteaubriant lies in the north of the Loire-Atlantique department, in the middle of a triangle between Nantes, Angers and Rennes, about 350 km south-west of Paris. It stands in the small drainage basin of the river Chère, among hills of the Armorican massif, and is not on any of the roads linking the three cities. Its name means 'Briant's castle' and refers to Brient, who founded the castle and the town.

The town began in the 11th century, when Brient, an envoy of the Count of Rennes, built a castle on a motte beside the Chère and Rollard rivers and later founded the priory of Saint-Sauveur-de-Béré and a fair. The fortress belonged to the Marches of Brittany, the defensive line facing the French kingdom, with Vitré, Fougères, Ancenis and Clisson. Louis IX of France besieged it in 1235, and walls were built in the 13th century and completed in the 15th.

In 1486 the baroness, Françoise de Dinan, signed the Châteaubriant treaty, in which Breton barons asked the King of France to settle an internal dispute. It undermined the authority of Francis II of Brittany and was one reason for the Mad War, and the town surrendered in 1488 after a week's siege. Jean de Laval, governor of Brittany from 1531 to 1542, built a Renaissance palace inside the old castle for his wife, Françoise de Foix. The barony later passed to Anne de Montmorency and, in the 17th century, to the House of Condé.

A concentration camp opened at Choisel in 1940 and held first prisoners of war and later political activists, mostly Communists, treated as hostages. After the German Feldkommandant Karl Hotz was killed by Resistance members, 27 hostages were shot in a quarry outside the town on 22 October 1941. They included Guy Môquet, aged 17, who became a symbol of the French Resistance.

Châteaubriant is a sous-préfecture of Loire-Atlantique. The château combines a medieval castle, with walls and towers mostly of the 13th century and a 14th-century keep, and a Renaissance palace. The town also has half-timbered houses mostly of the 15th century and the church of Saint-Jean-de-Béré, built about 1100. The fair of Béré, held each September since 1050, is one of the oldest in Europe, and the quarry of the 1941 shootings is now a memorial.
chattahoochee-river: The Chattahoochee is about 430 miles (690 km) long. Its source lies in Jacks Gap, at the southeastern foot of Jacks Knob in Union County, in the southern Blue Ridge Mountains. From there it flows southwest to Atlanta and its suburbs, then turns due south to form the southern half of the Georgia and Alabama border. At Columbus, Georgia, it crosses the Fall Line of the eastern United States, and it also forms part of the boundary between Florida and Georgia.

The name is thought to come from a Muskogee word meaning rocks-marked or painted, from chato (rock) and huchi (marked), possibly referring to the coloured granite outcroppings along its northeast-to-southwest stretch. Its present course has a geological history of at least 100 million years.
Indigenous peoples lived near the river from at least 1000 BCE. The Kolomoki Mounds near Blakely in Early County, built between 350 CE and 650 CE, form the largest mound complex in Georgia.

During the Atlanta campaign of the American Civil War the river was of considerable strategic importance to Union General William Tecumseh Sherman. In early July 1864 the Confederate Army held a defensive line designed by Brigadier General Francis A. Shoup and later called Johnston's River Line, after General Joseph E. Johnston. It consisted of 36 small earth and wooden triangular forts, the Shoupades, set in a sawtooth pattern to maximise crossfire. Sherman avoided them by crossing the river to the northeast. Nine survive. Two of the last battles of the war, at West Point and Columbus, were fought at crossings of the river.

In the nineteenth century the river carried trade and passengers. Congress passed legislation in 1944 and 1945 to improve navigation and to create hydroelectric power and recreation on a series of reservoirs. Most of the lakes were complete by 1963, and they covered many historic and prehistoric sites, among them the largely Native American settlement of Oketeyeconne, Georgia, flooded by Walter F. George Lake.

The Chattahoochee, the Flint and the Apalachicola together make up the Apalachicola-Chattahoochee-Flint River Basin, and the Chattahoochee forms its largest part. The river flows past Atlanta, Columbus and Fort Benning, and its upper course lies within Chattahoochee National Forest. Georgia, Alabama and Florida have disputed rights to its water since the late twentieth century, since withdrawals for metropolitan Atlanta affect flows downstream, including the oyster beds of Apalachicola Bay. Between 2010 and 2013 two dams at Columbus were breached to form a whitewater course 2.5 miles long.
chattuarii: The Chattuarii, also spelled Attuarii, lived east of the Rhine delta and north of the Lippe, outside the Roman Empire but close to it, near what is now the border between Germany and the Netherlands. Their name, reconstructed by Günter Neumann as *Chattwarijiz, is generally read as inhabitants of the Chatti lands, formed like the names of the Ampsivarii, the dwellers on the Ems, or the Baiuvarii and Boructuarii, who lived where the Boii and Bructeri once had.

Wagner and Rübekeil note that the name is always spelled with -tt-, unlike that of the Chatti, and propose that the Chattuarii were newcomers who spoke a Germanic language, probably Suebi. Petrikovits instead saw the name as evidence that the Chatti had themselves once lived further north.

According to Velleius Paterculus, the emperor Tiberius crossed the Rhine in 4 CE and attacked them after a people of the modern Netherlands and before the Bructeri. Strabo, writing about 23 CE, counts them among the tribes allied under the Cherusci and made poor after their defeat by Germanicus, and they appear among the peoples shown at his triumph in 17 CE. The Laterculus Veronensis records that in the reign of Gallienus, from 260 to 268, the Romans lost five communities beyond the Rhine, among them the Gallovari, generally believed to be the Chattuarii.

In 360 they appear again as Franks living near the Rhine. Ammianus Marcellinus tells how the emperor Julian crossed the river from Xanten into the district of the Attuarii, a turbulent people then plundering Gaul, and surprised them where they felt safe behind their rugged roads.

Under the Franks their name passed to two early medieval gaus on either side of the Rhine, north of the Ripuarian Franks of Cologne: one near the Ruhr, the other near the Niers between the Maas and the Rhine, named in the Treaty of Meerssen of 870. Some were settled in France as laeti, giving their name to the pagus attuariorum south of Langres. They may be the Hetwaras of the Old English poem Beowulf, allied with the Frisians against the Geats of Hygelac.
chaturbhuj-temple-gwalior: The temple, also called the Temple of Zero, is cut into a rock face of Gwalior Fort. Its shrine is a square of 12 feet (3.7 m) on each side, entered through a portico on four carved pillars whose reliefs show figures meditating in yoga postures and amorous couples. To the right of the portico stands a covered pillared mandapa. Figures of the river goddesses Ganga and Yamuna flank the doorway into the rock.

The ceiling is a low square pyramid, like that of the Dhamnar temple, and the tower above is a shikhara in the North Indian Nagara style, curving gently over a square plan and carved, like the rest, from the single rock. Inside are wall reliefs of Varaha, the boar avatar of Vishnu, of a four-armed Vishnu and of a four-armed Lakshmi; the temple's name may come from these four-armed figures. Much of the interior carving is lost and every face has been removed. The tower has been restored, and a steel gate now closes the entrance.

The dedicatory inscription opens with praise of Vishnu, then of Shiva and of nine Durgas, and dates the excavation to Samvat 933. Another inscription records that the community planted a garden of 187 by 270 hastas, a hasta being about 1.5 feet, which supplied the temple with 50 garlands every day. The last digits of both 270 and 50 are written as a small circle.

This makes it the earliest known stone inscription to use the circular sign for zero. Indian and other texts speak of zero much earlier, and the Bakhshali manuscript is held to be an older surviving use of it, but the Gwalior inscription is the earliest dated epigraphic evidence of the concept in use.
chatusadom: The four ministries already existed in early Ayutthaya before King Trailokanat's reform: each was called a krom and led by an official of the rank of khun, under a chancellor called the senabodi. In his Palatine Law Trailokanat raised the four ministers to the rank of phraya and gave the ministries Sanskrit-derived names; together they were called Wiang-Wang-Khlang-Na. The original law is lost, and the system is known mainly from the version King Rama I enacted in the Three Seals Law. In the late Ayutthaya and Bangkok periods the ministers rose to the rank of chaophraya.

Later kings added departments as needs arose. King Ramathibodi II created the Registration Department in 1518 to keep the census of manpower for levies and conscription, and after a trade treaty with the Portuguese in 1511 a Royal Warehouse was set up within the treasury to handle foreign trade, a royal monopoly. As trade with Western nations grew in the seventeenth century the Krommatha, once a department of the treasury, rose in importance. King Prasat Thong moved the cavalry and elephant regiments from the Samuhakalahom to the Samuhanayok, and King Narai preferred to leave both posts empty.

The largest reform came under King Phetracha, who, after rebellions in Nakhon Ratchasima and Nakhon Si Thammarat, extended the system to the regions: the Samuhanayok became minister for northern Siam and the Samuhakalahom for the south, while the coastal ports went to the Krommatha, so that the division became regional rather than functional. King Borommakot, who came to the throne in 1733 after a civil war, transferred the southern cities to the Krommatha and left the Samuhakalahom powerless, until Rama I restored them to him in 1782.

After the fall of Ayutthaya in 1767 the Thonburi and Rattanakosin kingdoms inherited the whole apparatus. Rama I, himself a former Samuhanayok, founded the Chakri dynasty. King Chulalongkorn and Prince Damrong then turned the old ministries into ministries in the Western sense, beginning in 1875 by dividing the Phraklang into a Ministry of Finance and a Ministry of Foreign Affairs. When the cabinet of twelve ministries was established on 1 April 1892, the Krom Mahatthai became the Ministry of Interior and the Krom Kalahom the Ministry of Defence.
chaulukya-dynasty: The dynasty called itself Chaulukya in almost all its records; Solanki is the vernacular form of the name. The word is thought to be a variant of Chalukya, but unlike the Chalukyas of Kalyani and Vengi the Gujarat house never claimed descent from the Chalukyas of Vatapi. It shared their myth that Brahma created the founding hero from his chuluka, a pot or cupped palm filled with Ganges water, a story of no historical value. Colonial-era historians read the Agnikula fire-pit legend as a sign of foreign Gurjara origin, but the Chaulukyas themselves linked that legend to the Paramaras, and the theory has been weakened.

The Chaulukyas rose as the Gurjara-Pratihara and Rashtrakuta empires declined. Their founder Mularaja supplanted Samantasimha, the last Chavda king, in the mid-10th century, and his successors fought the Chudasamas, the Paramaras and the Chahamanas of Shakambhari. In 1024–1025 the Ghaznavid ruler Mahmud entered the kingdom unopposed and sacked the Somnath temple while Bhima I fled to Kanthkot; Bhima restored his rule afterwards and, by accounts that are partly legend, joined the Kalachuri king Lakshmi-Karna in bringing down the Paramara king Bhoja around 1055.

Jayasimha Siddharaja (r. c. 1092–1142) annexed Malwa in 1135–1136 and pushed east to the Chandela kingdom. Under his relative Kumarapala the realm stretched from Chittor and Jaisalmer to the Vindhyas and the Tapti river, with Kachchha and Saurashtra. In 1178 a Chaulukya army defeated Muhammad of Ghor at Kasahrada. Under the young Bhima II provincial governors rebelled, and on 4 February 1197 Qutb al-Din Aibak dealt the Chaulukyas a heavy defeat at Anahilapataka. Their Vaghela generals Lavanaprasada and Viradhavala saved the kingdom more than once and took royal titles, and after Tribhuvanapala they seized the throne.
