The Māru-Gurjara or Chaulukya style of temple architecture arose in Gujarat and Rajasthan under the dynasty in the 11th to 13th centuries and, mainly through Jain patronage, later spread across India. Most of the rulers were Shaivaite but also patronised Jainism: the earliest of the Dilwara Temples were built under Bhima I, whose queen Udayamati is traditionally credited with the Queen's step-well, and Jain accounts remember Kumarapala as the last great royal patron of their faith. The kings also endowed mosques to keep good relations with Muslim traders. The Vaghelas claimed descent from a sister of Kumarapala, and Solanki princely houses such as the rulers of Lunavada claimed descent from the dynasty.
chauri-chaura-incident: From 1920 Indians led by Mohandas Gandhi had taken part in the nationwide Non-cooperation movement, organised by the Indian National Congress with the non-violent civil disobedience known as Satyagraha, against measures such as the Rowlatt Act and with Swaraj, home rule, as its goal. On 2 February 1922 volunteers led by Bhagwan Ahir, a retired soldier of the British Indian Army, protested against high food prices and liquor sales at Gauri Bazaar. The police under the local inspector, Gupteshwar Singh, beat them back and locked several leaders up at the Chauri Chaura police station.

On 4 February some 2,000 to 2,500 protesters marched to picket the liquor shop at Gauri Bazaar, shouting anti-British slogans. Warning shots fired into the air only angered the crowd, which threw stones, and the sub-inspector Prithvi Pal ordered the police to fire, killing three and wounding others. The outnumbered police fell back to the chowki, the police station, which the crowd set alight. Most of those inside burned to death; some appear to have been killed at the entrance and thrown back into the fire. One constable, Raghuvir Singh, declared dead, was found alive months later and became the sole witness in court.

The authorities declared martial law around Chauri Chaura and arrested hundreds. Gandhi fasted for five days as penance, judging that he had urged revolt without preparing people for ahimsa, non-violence; Jawaharlal Nehru and most Congress workers, then in prison, thought his halt hasty and wrong. Gandhi was sentenced to six years' imprisonment and released in February 1924 because of ill health.

Of 225 people tried at the Gorakhpur Sessions Court of Judge H. E. Holmes, 170 were sentenced on 9 January 1923 to hang, verdicts the communist leader M. N. Roy called legalised murder. On appeal the High Court of Allahabad, on 30 April 1923, confirmed 19 death sentences, and those men were hanged between 2 and 11 July 1923. A memorial to the dead policemen was raised in 1923; after independence local people and the Government of India built memorials to the men who were hanged.
chausath-yogini-temple-jabalpur: The temple, also called the Golaki Math or circular lodge, stands on a hilltop above the Narmada at Bhedaghat, some 5 km from Jabalpur in Madhya Pradesh. The town was formerly called Bhairavaghat. Some 125 feet across, it is the largest of the circular yogini temples, and the scholar Shaman Hatley calls it the most imposing and perhaps best known of them. A covered walkway runs round the inside of its circular wall with cells for the yoginis, and three openings, two to the west and one to the south-east, serve as entrances.

Exceptionally, it has shrines for 81 yoginis rather than the usual 64, though scholars still count it among the 64-yogini temples. A group of 81 is a mark of royalty and implies a royal founder. Scholars credit the building to King Yuvaraja II of the Kalachuris of Tripuri, who lived around 975 to 1025; Tripuri lay four miles away across the river, and David Gordon White judges it the dynasty's largest building project. In 1155 the temple was adapted as a Gauri-Shankar temple with a new building in the courtyard, and the central deities, Bhairava or a dancing Shiva, were moved.

Each yogini is carved on a rectangular slab with a throne, flying deities above and smaller figures below, and a label is cut into the base. The figures are rather over life-size, with haloes and from 4 to 18 arms. The art historian Vidya Dehejia describes them as a statuesque seated group whose regal presence suggests acolytes or aspects of Devi, the Great Goddess. The scenes on the bases show cremation grounds with jackals, birds and human yoginis, many of them eating severed limbs. Among the images are eight older Matrikas, mother goddesses, one of them Chandika riding a corpse.

Most of the images have been vandalised, their faces broken and some surviving only from the waist down; only the horse-faced yogini Erudi is in perfect condition. Three niches now hold male gods, a dancing Ganesh and two images of Shiva, probably from the original central shrine. The set of 81 follows the Mula Chakra of the Sri Matottara Tantra, preserved in manuscript in Nepal, which arranges nine Matrikas each at the head of eight further yoginis.
chavda-dynasty: The Chavdas are connected with the Chapas of Bhinmal and of Wadhwan, and a grant of the Chapa king Dharanivaraha of 914 CE traces the line to the bow of Shiva, a common practice of the time. They began as minor rulers and forest-dwelling thieves. A small Chavda chiefship centred at Panchasar existed in the 7th century, and a Navsari copperplate of 738-39 CE names the Chavotakas among the dynasties defeated by the Arabs. Most of what is known comes from works written under their successors, the Chaulukyas, above all the Prabandhachintamani and a list of kings by the Jain author Merutunga.

According to the Ratnamala, Jayaśekhara, the Chavda king of Panchasar, was killed in battle, and his pregnant wife Rupasundari, sent into the forest, gave birth to Vanaraja, who grew up under his uncle Surapala, an outlaw. Historians doubt the tradition, and the story that a Jain monk raised the boy seems invented by Jain writers. Merutunga says Vanaraja waylaid a deputation from Kanyakubja and took its money and horses, raised an army and made himself king. A shepherd named Anahila is said to have shown him the site of his capital, which bore his name. Vanaraja gave rich merchants administrative posts, among them his chief minister Jamba.

The lists of his successors, Yogaraja, Kshemaraja, Bhuyada and others, vary so much in names, order and lengths of reign that little trust can be placed in them. The Prabandhachintamani tells that Yogaraja mounted the funeral pyre after his sons seized the treasure of storm-bound ships at Somanatha, saying it renewed the old stain of a nation of thieves.

Merutunga credits Vanaraja with the Vanrajavihara and a temple of Kanteshwari, later the patron goddess of the Chaulukya kings, and Bhuyada with the Bhuyadeshwara temple at Patan in the late 9th century. Surviving temples of the period include the Roda group. Around 942 a queen of Samantasimha fled with her infant son Ahipata to Jaisalmer; he became an outlaw who conquered villages in Kutch and ruled from Morgadh. Under the British Raj the small princely states of Varsoda and Mansa remained in the hands of claimed descendants of the dynasty until 1947.
chavundaraya: In his own writing Chavundaraya claims descent from the Brahmakshatriya line, Brahmins who had taken Kshatriya status. The 10th-century Algodu and Arani inscriptions name him as the grandson of Govindamayya and the son of Mabalayya, a subordinate of King Marasimha II; the family's political position under that king is believed to have led to its gradual adoption of Kshatriya status. He was a devotee of the Jain teachers Nemichandra and Ajitasena Bhattaraka, and a eulogy of him is inscribed on the Tyagada Brahmadeva Pillar at Shravanabelagola, whose base shows him with his guru Nemichandra.

The Western Gangas were feudatories of the Rashtrakutas, and as their commander Chavundaraya fought many battles for those overlords, beginning in the days of the Rashtrakuta king Khottiga Amoghavarsha. In the last years of Rashtrakuta rule the Gangas were threatened by civil war and by invasions of the Chola dynasty. When civil war broke out in 975 he supported Prince Rachamalla IV and installed him on the throne.

In the same year he suppressed a rebellion by Panchaldeva Mahasamanta, and in the battle of Bageyur he killed Mudurachayya, avenging the death of his own brother Nagavarma. His exploits earned him titles such as Samara Parashurama and Vira Martanda. He remained influential into the reign of Rachamalla V, who ruled from 986 to 999.

The Chavundaraya Purana, also known as the Trishashtishalaka Mahapurana, is the second oldest existing prose work in Kannada. It is based on two Sanskrit works, the Adipurana of Jinasena and the Uttarapurana of Gunabhadra, and tells the legends of sixty-three figures of Jain tradition: twenty-four tirthankaras, twelve chakravartis, nine balabhadras, nine narayanas and nine pratinarayanas. It was meant mainly for ordinary readers and avoided the complicated elements of Jain doctrine. He also wrote the Charitrasara in Sanskrit, and he patronised the Kannada grammarians Gunavarma and Nagavarma I and the poet Ranna.

The statue of Bahubali that he commissioned stands on the Indragiri hill, also called Vindhyagiri. Carved from fine-grained white granite, it is 60 feet tall, with a face measuring 6.5 feet, and has no support up to the thighs. The Chavundaraya basadi on the Chandragiri hill is credited to him by some scholars and to his son Jinadevana by others; another view holds that it was consecrated in the 11th century in his memory.
che-guevara: Ernesto Guevara was born on 14 May 1928 in Rosario, Argentina, the eldest of five children of Ernesto Guevara Lynch and Celia de la Serna y Llosa, in an upper-class family of Spanish, Basque and Irish ancestry. The family had leftist leanings. As a medical student Guevara travelled through South America and was appalled by the poverty, hunger and disease he saw.

After completing his medical degree he set out on 7 July 1953 through Bolivia, Peru, Ecuador, Panama, Costa Rica, Nicaragua, Honduras and El Salvador. In December he arrived in Guatemala, where President Jacobo Árbenz headed a democratically elected government attempting to end the latifundia system. Árbenz's overthrow, assisted by the CIA at the behest of the United Fruit Company, solidified Guevara's political ideology.

In Mexico City Guevara met Raúl and Fidel Castro and joined the 26th of July Movement. They sailed for Cuba aboard the Granma on 25 November 1956. Batista's military attacked soon after landing, and many of the 82 men were killed or executed on capture; only 22 found each other afterwards. Guevara, who had put down his medical supplies to pick up a box of ammunition, rose to second-in-command in the two-year guerrilla campaign that deposed Fulgencio Batista.

After the revolution he reviewed appeals and death sentences of those convicted as war criminals in the revolutionary tribunals, a procedure the Cuban Ministry of Justice said most of the population supported and likened to the Nuremberg trials. He instituted agrarian land reform as minister of industries, served as president of the National Bank and travelled as a diplomat. Critics point to half-completed or empty factories left from his short tenure as minister of industries, and to the internment of people labelled anti-social in labour camps between 1965 and 1968 under the ideal of the socialist new man.

In late 1966 he went to Bolivia. He arrived in La Paz on 3 November under the false name Adolfo Mena González. His first base camp was in the remote Ñancahuazú region, where training proved hazardous and little was accomplished in building an army.

Guevara was killed in Bolivia on 9 October 1967. According to the account of his last minutes, he told the soldier guarding him that he was thinking about the immortality of the revolution, and Sergeant Terán shot him. He remains a revered and reviled figure. Admirers see a martyr and an icon of leftist movements; critics accuse him of promoting authoritarianism and endorsing violence against opponents. A photograph of him by Alberto Korda, Guerrillero Heroico, was cited by the Maryland Institute College of Art as the most widely known in the world.
chechens: The Chechens are a Northeast Caucasian people of the Nakh group, native to the North Caucasus, who call themselves Nokhchiy. The Nakh peoples have lived in the highlands of the North Caucasus since prehistory, and there is archaeological evidence of continuity from 3000 BCE. The only three surviving Nakh peoples are the Chechens, the Ingush and the Bats. The ancestors of the Chechens and Ingush were known as Durdzuks, and the state of Durdzuketi has been recorded since the 4th century BCE.

In the Middle Ages the lowlands were dominated first by the Khazars and then by the Alans, and some Chechens adopted Eastern Orthodox Christianity. Islam spread gradually, while the Chechens' pagan religion stayed strong until the 19th century. The Mongol invasions of the 13th century and those of Tamerlane in the 14th devastated Chechnya. The Chechens never really fell under the rule of the Ottoman or Persian empires.

In the Caucasian War Russia began a full-scale conquest. General Yermolov used scorched earth and deportations and founded the fort of Grozny in 1818. Resistance peaked under Imam Shamil and ended in defeat after decades of war, in which the Chechens lost most of their population.

In 1944 Stalin ordered all Chechens deported to the Kazakh and Kirghiz republics, and their republic was abolished. At least a quarter, and perhaps half, of the population died. They were rehabilitated in 1956 and allowed to return the next year. Attempts to regain independence after the fall of the Soviet Union led to two wars with Russia, beginning in 1994.

Chechen society is largely egalitarian. It is organised around about 130 teips, local clans, grouped in loose confederations called tukkhums. The social code is nokhchallah, loosely Chechen character. Chechens remember their history through the illesh, a collection of epic poems and stories. Their language belongs to the Nakh branch of the Northeast Caucasian family. Most Chechens are Sunni Muslims, and about half belong to Sufi brotherhoods.
chechnya: Chechnya lies in the eastern part of the North Caucasus. It borders Dagestan to the east, Ingushetia and North Ossetia-Alania to the west, Stavropol Krai to the northwest and Georgia to the south. It is divided between flatter country north of the Terek river and highlands to the south, and the Terek, Sunzha and Argun are its main rivers. Traces of human settlement dating back to 40,000 BCE have been found near Lake Kezenoyam, and cave paintings and artefacts indicate continuous habitation for some 8,000 years. Georgian tradition, in the chronicle of Leonti Mroveli, names a forefather of the Vainakhs, the ancestors of the Chechens and Ingush, as Kavkas, from whom the word Caucasus was said to derive.

In the 14th and 15th centuries the Chechens fought repeatedly with Tamerlane and Tokhtamysh. In the mid-14th century a Chechen princedom called Simsim arose under Khour II, who defeated the warlord Mamai at the Battle of Tatar-tup in 1362. Khour II later allied himself with Tokhtamysh, and Timur invaded Simsim in 1395 to punish the highlanders. Chechen tribes built fortresses, castles and defensive walls in the mountains. Peter the Great sought to extend Russian influence in the Caucasus in the Russo-Persian War of 1722–1723.

Under the Soviet Union Chechnya and Ingushetia were joined as the Checheno-Ingush Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic. In 1944, near the end of the Second World War, the Chechens and Ingush were accused of supporting Nazi Germany, an accusation described as false, and whole nations were deported to the Kazakh SSR in Operation Lentil; over 60 percent of the Chechen and Ingush populations are said to have died.

After the dissolution of the Soviet Union the republic split into Ingushetia and the Chechen Republic, which proclaimed itself the independent Chechen Republic of Ichkeria. In the First Chechen War of 1994–1996 Russian forces failed to establish permanent control of the mountains. Its president, Dzhokhar Dudayev, was killed in April 1996, and after Aslan Maskhadov's forces retook Grozny, Boris Yeltsin declared a ceasefire and signed a peace treaty a year later. Federal control was restored in the Second Chechen War of 1999–2009. A constitution that kept Chechnya within Russia with limited autonomy was put to a referendum on 23 March 2003.

Chechnya is a republic of the Russian Federation with its capital at Grozny, and about 1.5 million inhabitants, nearly all of them Chechens. The languages in use are Chechen, which belongs to the Vainakh branch of the Caucasian languages together with Ingush, and Russian. Most of the people are Sunni Muslims who follow the Shafi'i or Hanafi schools of jurisprudence, and many belong to the Qadiri or Naqshbandi Sufi orders.
cheddi-jagan: Cheddi Berret Jagan was born on 22 March 1918 at Port Mourant in the county of Berbice, the eldest of eleven children. His parents were Hindus of the Kurmi caste who had come from British India as children to work as indentured labourers in British Guiana, and the family lived in rural poverty. After Queen's College in Georgetown, Jagan was sent by his father to the United States with $500, the family's savings, to study dentistry. He studied at Howard University and Northwestern University, graduating in 1942, and returned to British Guiana in October 1943.

Jagan opened a dental practice in Georgetown and became active in the sugar workers' unions. In 1946 he co-founded the Political Affairs Committee with his wife Janet, and in November 1947 he was elected to the Legislative Council. The People's Progressive Party was founded on 1 January 1950 with Jagan as leader and Forbes Burnham as chairman. In the election of 27 April 1953 the party won 18 of 24 seats, and Jagan became Chief Minister. Winston Churchill voiced fears that he was a Marxist-Leninist.

On 8 October 1953 his government passed a Labour Relations Act, and the next day the British suspended the constitution, landed troops and dismissed Jagan after 133 days. Burnham split from him in 1955, and the party divided along largely racial lines. After the elections of 1957 Burnham founded the People's National Congress, and Jagan served as minister of trade and industry. He became Premier after the August 1961 elections and served until 1964. The CIA helped fund strikes and protests against him, and in December 1964 his party won 46 percent of the vote, but Burnham's party and the United Force formed the government.

He was Leader of the Opposition from 1966 to 1973 and again from 1976 until 1992. The election of 5 October 1992 gave his party about 54 percent of the vote, and he became president. He governed as a democratic socialist, sought foreign investment and invested in sea defences, irrigation, roads and health.

He suffered a heart attack on 15 February 1997 and died in Washington on 6 March 1997. More than 200,000 mourners attended his funeral, and he was cremated at Port Mourant on 12 March. The Red House in Georgetown, his residence from 1961 to 1964, holds the Cheddi Jagan Research Centre.
chedworth-roman-villa: The villa lies in a sheltered spot above the River Coln in the Cotswold Hills, just off the Roman road known as the Fosse Way and 8 miles (13 km) north of Corinium Dobunnorum, the civitas capital at Cirencester. It was one of about fifty villas in the Cotswolds and one of nine within 5 miles. It was built beside a natural spring, which supplied all its water and around which an apsidal shrine to the water-nymphs, a nymphaeum, was later raised. A Christian chi-rho was found scratched on the rim of its octagonal pool.

Founded about 120 as a working farm of separate buildings around three sides of a rectangle, the villa went through at least six stages of building. After a fire in the early 3rd century the west and south wings were rebuilt. In the early 4th century the wings were joined by a covered portico around an inner garden, the dining-room received its mosaics, and a second bath suite was made in the west wing; the north baths were soon rebuilt for dry heat. At least 15 rooms had mosaic floors, and a new dining-room was added late in the century.

Work in 2017 showed that the mosaic and walls of room 28 were laid after 424, after the end of Roman rule in Britain: the first evidence that such wealth paid for a Roman way of life there some fifty years later than had been thought. Historians have debated whether the site was a villa rustica or a religious sanctuary with a hostel; most now hold it was the home of a very wealthy Romano-Briton. A temple stood about 800 metres to the south-east.

The gamekeeper Thomas Margetts found the villa while digging for a ferret, and James Farrer excavated it in 1865-7 for the landowner, the Earl of Eldon, recording little. Ian Richmond dug there from 1957 to 1965 but died without publishing. The villa is a scheduled monument, and a new cover building over the west wing's mosaics was provided in 2011, part of a project designed by Feilden Clegg Bradley Studios and completed in March 2012.
chefchaouen: Chefchaouen stands about 600 metres above sea level in the foothills of the Kaʻala mountain in the western Rif range, between Tétouan and Ouazzane. The name is of Arabic and Berber origin: chef comes from the Arabic word for look, and echaouen is a Berber word for horns, used for mountain peaks, so that it means look at the horns, referring to the two peaks above the town. The city consists of the walled Medina and a newer town outside the old walls.

The city was founded in 1471 as a small kasbah by Ali ibn Rashid al-Alami, a descendant of Idris I, to defend the area against Portuguese attacks on northern Morocco. Ali went to the Emirate of Granada in 1460 and fought Christian forces, and settled in Chefchaouen c. 1465. His daughter Aisha al-Hurra, known as Sayyida al-Hurra, married the emir of Tétouan and ruled Chefchaouen through a period of rapid growth.

The fall of Granada in 1492 drove many Muslims and Jews from Spain and Portugal to Morocco over several centuries; the last Moriscos were expelled from Spain by Philip III in 1609. Some settled in Chefchaouen, building quarters in the Andalusi style, very like those of Granada, and within a few decades the fortress had become a prosperous city with walls, about ten gates and several mosques, including the Great Mosque.

In October 1920 General Dámaso Berenguer occupied the city for the Spanish protectorate. From 1924 to 1926 it was part of the Republic of the Rif led by Abd el-Krim, and the Spanish army retook it in 1926. Spain ceded it in 1956, when Morocco became independent.

Blue and white paint dominates the walls and houses of the Medina, which gives the city the nickname the Blue City. Several theories explain the colour; one holds that it keeps mosquitoes away, and some locals say the walls were ordered painted blue in the 1970s to attract tourists. The heart of the Medina is Uta Hammam Square, with the Kasbah, now a museum, the Great Mosque and a caravanserai. The municipality had 46,168 inhabitants in the 2024 census.
cheitharol-kumbaba: The keeping of the chronicle began in the reign of King Kiyamba, in 1485. The record up to the reign of King Kyampa (1467–1508) was redrafted under Ching-Thang Khomba, also called Bhagyachandra, because those leaves were said to be lost, presumably from oral sources or scattered written records. The title reflects the Meitei way of counting: sticks (chei) were placed (thapa) to represent a base number, kum signifies a period of time, and paba means to read or reckon, so the name connotes reckoning the years by placing sticks.

The chronicle is the main source for the list of pre-modern kings of Manipur and the primary source for its ancient and medieval history. It traces the Ningthouja dynasty back to Nongda Lairen Pakhangba, said to have ruled for more than a century, from 33 to 154 CE. It is to the Meitei what the Buranji is to the Assamese and the Yazawin to the Burmese.

The early part is particularly unreliable: its kings are given implausible reigns and little objective information. The scholar Saroj Nalini Parratt suggests that many of them were borrowed from the cultural pantheon, and she and Gangmumei Kamei suspect that the scribes reached the starting date of 33 CE by astrological calculation. The early sections chiefly tell of the Meitei, originally the Ningthouja clan, expanding across the valley of Manipur. The chronicle uses three eras, the Kalyabda, the Saka era and the Chandrabda or Kangleipak era, and from 1666 it names the days of the week.

Pundit Thongam Madhob Singh transliterated it into Bengali script around 1940, and an edition by L. Ibungohal Singh and Pundit N. Khelchandra Singh was published by the Manipuri Sahitya Parishad in 1967; followers of Sanamahi reject this Hindu-oriented version for the Sanskrit and Hindi words it adds. In 1891 Major Maxwell, the Political Agent of Manipur, had the court translate it into English through a Bengali clerk named Mamacharan; L. Joychandra Singh published that translation in 1995 as The Lost Kingdom. Parratt's English version with a facsimile of the manuscript followed in 2005, Rajkumar Somorjit Sana's dated edition in 2010 and Nepram Bihari's translation in 2012.
cheka: In the first weeks after the October Revolution the task of suppressing resistance fell to the Petrograd Military Revolutionary Committee, a temporary body. On 6 December 1917 the Council of People's Commissars decided that a special commission was needed to apply the most energetically revolutionary measures. It was established on 20 December 1917 (7 December Old Style), with Felix Dzerzhinsky as its head. Its official name was the All-Russian Extraordinary Commission for Combating Counter-Revolution and Sabotage, shortened to VChK or Cheka, and its members were called Chekists.

In its first months the Cheka had only 40 officials, with a regiment of soldiers and a group of Red Guards, and worked mainly in Petrograd. It soon had sections for railways and branches in every guberniya and uyezd. By the end of the Civil War it had at least 200,000 personnel. Although it was created to protect the revolution from class enemies such as the bourgeoisie and the clergy, within a month it had extended its repression to all political opponents of the Bolshevik government, including anarchists. On 11 and 12 April 1918 it attacked 26 anarchist centres in Moscow, killing forty anarchists and arresting about 500.

At Vladimir Lenin's direction it carried out mass arrests, imprisonments and executions without trial in what came to be known as the Red Terror, which Dzerzhinsky implemented on 5 September 1918. Its special punitive troops fought desertion from the Red Army, which had more than three million deserters in 1919 and 1920, and took and shot hostages to force compliance. It also policed labour camps, requisitioned food and put down worker and peasant rebellions.

Estimates of its executions vary widely. Its own officer Martyn Latsis gave 12,733 for 1918 to 1920, a figure that historians generally regard as far too low. Estimates run from at least 50,000 to as many as 200,000, and many put the total at about 100,000. The Cheka was dissolved in February 1922 and succeeded by the State Political Directorate, the GPU. It was the first of a long succession of Soviet secret police bodies, and the name Chekists long remained a name for their members.
chellah: Whether the Phoenicians settled on the site has been debated by archaeologists. Jean Boube, who led some of the modern excavations, found neo-Punic artefacts from as early as the 3rd century BCE, suggesting a small trading post, and the settlement's name, Shalat, appears to come from the Punic word for rock. In the 1st century BCE an urban centre grew on hill terraces above the Bou Regreg valley under the Kingdom of Mauretania, whose client kings Juba II and Ptolemy may have used it as a dynastic sanctuary; portrait statues of both have been found there.

After Ptolemy's death in 40 CE the region was annexed by Rome as the province of Mauretania Tingitana. Sala Colonia became a port city with a forum, a triumphal arch and a main road, the decumanus maximus, and inscriptions show it held the status of a municipium around the mid-2nd century. It was one of the province's two main naval outposts on the Atlantic, with Lixus. Sala began to be abandoned in the 5th century and was largely in ruins when the Muslim Arabs arrived in the 7th century.

The Marinid enclosure is roughly pentagonal and smaller than the Roman city. Its rammed-earth walls have three gates and square towers; the main gate in the north-west, of brick and cut stone with a Kufic inscription recording its construction, shows the influence of Almohad gates such as Bab er-Rouah. Inside lies the khalwa, a religious complex with a mosque, a madrasa and a garden cemetery of domed tombs, among them those of Sultan Abu Sa'id, who died in 1331, and Shams al-Duha, who died in 1349. Sultans Abu Ya'qub Yusuf and Abu Thabit 'Amir were buried there in 1307 and 1308. A hammam, a pool fed by the spring of 'Ayn al-Janna and later Sufi shrines complete the site.

After the Marinid period the necropolis declined. It was first pillaged by Ahmad al-Lihyani, a pretender to the Marinid throne, and many of its buildings were ruined by the 1755 Lisbon earthquake. In 1790 Sultan Moulay Yazid ordered the governor of Salé to remove the Sabbah tribe, who had taken over the enclosure, and the site was looted again.

Excavations in the 20th century uncovered about 1.2 hectares of the Roman town around its forum. Since 2012 the site has formed part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and finds from it, including Marinid tombstones, are kept in the Museum of History and Civilizations in Rabat.
chelm: Chełm lies in the Lublin Voivodeship in eastern Poland, south-east of Lublin and about 25 kilometres from the Ukrainian border. Its name is most often derived from the Proto-Slavic word for a hill, in reference to the fortified settlement on Wysoka Górka. Its landmarks are Castle Hill with the Baroque Basilica of the Birth of the Virgin Mary and the Chełm Chalk Tunnels, which run for about 15 kilometres under the city.

Settlement in the area dates from at least the 9th century, and in the 10th a fortified town served first as a centre of pagan worship. In 981 the Kievan Rus' annexed it from Poland. In 1235 Daniel of Galicia granted the town a city charter, and after the Mongols destroyed Halych in 1240 and 1241 he moved the capital of his domain to Chełm, where it stayed until 1272. He built a new castle on the hill in 1237, one of the few Ruthenian castles to withstand Mongol attacks, and set up an Orthodox eparchy at the basilica. In 1366 Casimir III the Great of Poland took control of the region.

The city prospered in the 15th and 16th centuries, when Catholics, Orthodox Christians, Protestants and Jews lived there, and declined in the 17th through wars that ravaged Poland. After the Third Partition it passed to Austria, and in 1815 the Congress of Vienna awarded it to Russia. Poles liberated the city from Austrian rule on 2 November 1918, nine days before Poland officially regained independence.

In September 1939 about 18,000 of the city's people, 60 per cent, were Jews. German forces occupied the city in October. On 1 December 1939 around 2,000 Jewish men were driven on a death march to Hrubieszów, and perhaps 400 survived. In 1942 the Jews of Chełm were deported to the Sobibór extermination camp or killed in the city, and only an estimated 60 survived the Holocaust.

Chełm is a city of mostly industrial character with 60,231 inhabitants. From 1975 to 1998 it was the capital of its own voivodeship. Its Jewish past lives on in folklore: Chełm became the setting of Yiddish stories of foolish wise men, retold by writers such as Isaac Bashevis Singer.
chelmno: Chełmno is a town near the Vistula in northern Poland. Its name comes from chelm, an old Polish word for hill. Because of its regional importance in the Middle Ages it gave its name to Chełmno Land, to the local Catholic diocese and to the Kulm law, used by over 180 cities and towns in Central Europe, among them Warsaw, Gdańsk, Toruń, Königsberg and Klaipėda. Its population was mixed, Poles and Germans, with Poles two thirds in the second half of the 19th century.

The first written mention is in a document allegedly issued in 1065. In 1226 Duke Konrad I of Masovia invited the Teutonic Knights to Chełmno Land, and in 1233 the town received the city rights known as Kulm law, renewed in 1251. In 1243 it became the nominal see of the Diocese of Chełmno, though the cathedral was at neighbouring Chełmża. A member of the Hanseatic League, it grew prosperous. In 1440 it was a founder of the Prussian Confederation against the Order's rule, and after the Thirteen Years' War the Order recognised it as part of Poland. In 1692 the local gymnasium became the Chełmno Academy.

Prussia annexed the town in 1772 and called it Kulm. The Prussians expelled the Kraków professors, abolished the Polish academy and closed Catholic monasteries. The surgeon Ludwik Rydygier opened a clinic in 1878 and performed pioneering operations. Polish troops entered the town on 22 January 1920. In 1939 the German authorities murdered 5,000 Polish civilians in the territory, and the rest of the Polish population was expelled to the General Government.

Chełmno keeps a well-preserved medieval centre with five Gothic churches, a Renaissance town hall in the market square, rebuilt in 1567–1572, and city walls surviving almost whole. The Old Town was designated one of Poland's official Historic Monuments on 20 April 2005.
chelmno-extermination-camp: Following the invasion of Poland in 1939, Germany annexed the area into the new territory of Reichsgau Wartheland, and the village of Chełmno nad Nerem was renamed Kulmhof. The camp was set up by SS-Sturmbannführer Herbert Lange after gas van experiments in which he murdered 1,558 Polish prisoners of the Soldau concentration camp. In October 1941 he chose the site because of an estate with a large manor house that could be adapted for mass admissions of prisoners.

Arthur Greiser, the governor of the Wartheland, initiated its use for the mass murder of Jews deported to the Łódź Ghetto. In a letter to Himmler of 30 May 1942 he referred to an authorisation for the murder of 100,000 Polish Jews, about one third of the Jewish population of the Wartheland.

The camp consisted of the manor estate in the village, known as the Schlosslager, and a forest clearing about 4 km to the north-west, the Waldlager. Victims were told they were to be disinfected and bathe, undressed in the manor house and were put into gas vans, in which the engine exhaust was directed into a sealed compartment. They died of suffocation on the way to the forest. Killing began on 8 December 1941. The first victims were the Jewish and Romani populations of Koło County; before February 1942 some 3,830 Jews and about 4,000 Romani were gassed. Victims later came from the Łódź Ghetto and from as far away as Hungary, Germany and Austria.

The camp operated until 11 April 1943. On 23 June 1944 the SS resumed gassing in the forest to destroy the remaining 70,000 Jews of the Łódź Ghetto; about 25,000 were murdered in this final phase. A Jewish detachment was then made to exhume and burn the bodies, and about half of its 80 men were shot in October 1944.

The camp's last phase ended on 18 January 1945, when the remaining Jewish workers were executed. Red Army troops captured the town on 17 January 1945, and no prisoners were left. At the very minimum 152,000 people were murdered at Chełmno; West German prosecutors charged at least 180,000 deaths, the Kulmhof Museum of Martyrdom gives around 200,000, and early Polish postwar estimates ran up to 340,000. Only a few prisoners survived, among them Simon Srebnik. The first trial of three SS men took place in Łódź in 1945, and four further trials were held in Bonn and Cologne from 1962 to 1965.
chelmno-land: The region runs along the right bank of the Vistula from the mouth of the Drwęca in the south to the Osa in the north, with Lubawa Land to the east. Its largest city is Toruń, and Grudziądz is another major town. Depending on the period and the interpretation it has been counted as part of Mazovia, Pomerania or Prussia; Polish usage today places it in Vistula Pomerania, mostly within the Kuyavian-Pomeranian Voivodeship. It was not inhabited by the Old Prussians but by Slavic Lechites, who became part of the emerging Polish state in the 10th century.

Chełmno is first recorded in 1065, in a tax privilege of Bolesław II of Poland. Christianised in the 11th century, the land passed to the Duchy of Masovia after the death of Bolesław III Wrymouth in 1138. Pagan Prussians sacked Chełmno in 1216 and repeatedly devastated the province. The Teutonic Knights kept the region despite papal verdicts for its return to Poland, and local nobles formed the secret anti-Teutonic Lizard Union in 1397. Toruń, Chełmno, Grudziądz and Brodnica were among the founders of the Prussian Confederation in 1440, which rose against the order in 1454 and asked King Casimir IV Jagiellon to join the region to Poland, starting the Thirteen Years' War.

Afterwards the land formed the Chełmno Voivodeship in Royal Prussia. Nicolaus Copernicus was born in Toruń in 1473, and the Chełmno Academy became a branch of the Jagiellonian University in 1756. Prussia seized the land in the First Partition of 1772, Toruń following in 1793. After a spell in the Duchy of Warsaw from 1807 to 1815 it returned to Prussia, whose Germanisation policies met Polish resistance, and it came back to Poland in January 1920. Under German occupation from 1939 the Polish population suffered mass arrests, deportations and murder, including the Intelligenzaktion against its elites; about 23,000 Poles of the Pomeranian Voivodeship were killed in the autumn of 1939 alone. The Red Army took the region in January 1945.

About 650,000 people live in its 14 towns. The Medieval Town of Toruń has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1997, and the Old Town of Chełmno and the Grudziądz Granaries are Historic Monuments of Poland.
chelmno-law: The law was issued on 28 December 1233 in the Monastic State of the Teutonic Knights by Grand Master Hermann von Salza and Hermann Balk, when Toruń (Thorn) and Chełmno (Kulm) received German town law as a modification of the Magdeburg rights. The charter, the Kulmer Handfeste, was named after the town where it was signed. The original was lost in 1244, when the town hall of Chełmno burned during an attack by Świętopełk II, Duke of Pomerania. A renewed charter of 1 October 1251 was based on a copy kept in Toruń, but with reduced rights.

Compared with Magdeburg rights the law gave residents several advantages, among them the right to elect the local judge and inheritance by descendants of both sexes. It was granted mostly by the Teutonic Order to towns of its state and by the neighbouring Duchy of Masovia, but also elsewhere in Poland and Lithuania, and from the 13th to the 18th century at least 224 towns received it. The town hall of Chełmno was the seat of the higher court of the law until 1458. Independently of the Knights, the law was also expanded into a larger collection known as the Alter Kulm.

The towns founded under the law now lie mostly in northern and central Poland, in Dobrzyń Land, Kuyavia, Masuria, Mazovia, Pomerania and Warmia among other regions, with some in Lesser Poland, Lithuania and Russia's Kaliningrad Oblast. The largest are Warsaw, the Vistula cities of Płock, Toruń and Grudziądz, the ports of Gdańsk, Kaliningrad and Klaipėda, and Olsztyn.

During World War II the German occupiers stole the charter of 1251 from the Old Town City Hall in Toruń, but it was returned to Poland after the war and has been held in the State Archive in Toruń since 1959. It is on the Polish National List of the Memory of the World Register. The historic centres of Toruń and Warsaw are UNESCO World Heritage Sites, and those of Chełmno, Gdańsk and Tykocin are among the Historic Monuments of Poland.
chelmza: Chełmża is a town in the Toruń County of the Kuyavian-Pomeranian Voivodeship and one of the historic centres of Chełmno Land. It lies on Lake Chełmża, which covers 2.71 square kilometres and once gave the town its German name Culmsee. The first signs of settlement date to about 10,000 BCE, when reindeer hunters visited the area, and about 4500 BCE the first agricultural settlements were founded. Around the 7th century the Slavic Lechitic tribe of the Goplans arrived.

In the time of the first Piasts the settlement of Łoza, now Chełmża, was part of the Chełmno castellany. In the 13th century the ruler Konrad I brought the missionary Bishop Christian of Oliva to Christianize the Old Prussians, and the bishop received lands that included Łoza. The Teutonic Knights, granted local lands to support him, in time took over his diocese and divided the area into four dioceses in 1243, among them that of Chełmno. At the end of 1245 Heidenreich became its bishop and chose Łoza as his place of stay. In 1251 he granted it city rights and renamed it Culmsee, and a cathedral was begun in 1254. Jutta von Sangerhausen was buried in it in 1260, and her shrine drew pilgrims.

The Old Prussians besieged the town in 1268 and 1273. In 1454 it joined the Prussian Confederation, and Casimir IV Jagiellon re-incorporated it into Poland that year, confirmed in 1466 after the Thirteen Years' War. The Swedish invasions of 1626–29 and 1655–60, a plague in 1708–1710 and a fire in 1762 almost destroyed it. After the First Partition in 1772 it passed to Prussia with only 600 inhabitants, belonged to the Duchy of Warsaw from 1807 to 1815 and then to Prussia again.

Railway and an agricultural plant completed in 1882 brought growth: the population rose from 3,400 in 1880 to 10,600 in 1910. Under the Treaty of Versailles Chełmża became part of Poland again, and its population rose from 10,700 in 1921 to 13,000 in 1939. After the German invasion in September 1939 the town was occupied, and local Poles were executed, and many teachers massacred in the Barbarka forest, in the Intelligenzaktion. The Red Army took the town in January 1945, and by 1980 it had 15,000 inhabitants. The best-known sports clubs are the football club Legia Chełmża and the rowing club Chełmżyńskie Towarzystwo Wioślarskie 1927.
chemical-weapons: A chemical weapon is a munition that uses chemicals formulated to inflict death or harm on humans. The Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons defines it as a chemical compound intended as a weapon, or its precursor, that can cause death, injury, temporary incapacitation or sensory irritation through its chemical action. Lethal agents include nerve agents such as sarin and VX and blister agents, chiefly mustard gas; non-lethal ones include tear gases. Toxic agents used for another property, such as the herbicide Agent Orange or incendiary white phosphorus, are not chemical weapons under this definition. Lethal chemical weapons are counted among weapons of mass destruction with biological, radiological and nuclear weapons.

Simple chemical weapons were used sporadically in antiquity and into the industrial age. In the First World War most major powers used them on a large scale, including mustard gas, phosgene and chlorine, which caused lung scarring, blindness and death. Between the wars, European colonial forces used them to put down rebellions. In the Second World War the Allies never used them and the Axis only sparingly; Nazi Germany discovered nerve agents but did not use them. Japan used mustard gas and lewisite in China. Nazi Germany used Zyklon B in gas chambers to commit genocide against Jews and other peoples, the largest death toll from chemical weapons in history.

After the war, about 100,000 Iranian troops became casualties of Iraqi chemical weapons in the Iran–Iraq War, and Iraq used mustard gas and nerve agents against its own civilians in the Halabja attack of 1988. In the Cold War the Soviet and United States programmes became the largest in history.

The First Hague Conference of 1899 prohibited employing poison and poisoned arms. The Geneva Protocol, signed on 17 June 1925 and in force from 8 February 1928, prohibited the use of chemical and biological weapons in international armed conflicts, though not their production or storage. The Chemical Weapons Convention of 1993 outlaws the development, production, stockpiling and use of chemical weapons and is administered by the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons, based in The Hague. After the Second World War the Allies dumped large quantities of captured German chemical weapons into the Baltic Sea, mostly in wooden crates.
chemirocha: Chemirocha is a series of three field recordings made in 1950 by the ethnomusicologist Hugh Tracey among the Kipsigis people. Tracey had moved to the region to help his brother on a tobacco farm, and on the side he travelled with a reel-to-reel recorder, collecting traditional African songs. In the town of Kapkatet the district chief Arapsang gathered singers for him, and Tracey recorded three songs that he titled Chemirocha I, Chemirocha II and Chemirocha III.

Chemirocha was the Kipsigis pronunciation of the name of Jimmie Rodgers, whom they pictured as a faun, half man and half antelope. Chemirocha III was sung by young girls with high voices as they danced, accompanied by a stringed instrument called the kibugandet, and was credited to Chemutoi Ketienya with Kipsigis girls. Its words said that the being's songs made the villagers so happy that their clothes would fall off.

Chemirocha I and II were sung by men and expressed the Kipsigis' love for their land and their lament that colonisation had taken it. The word was also used for something strange and new. Tracey misread the place of Rodgers' music among the Kipsigis as a kind of cargo cult, describing Rodgers as the spirit to whom young Kipsigis women appealed as they invited him to dance.

In 1954 Tracey founded the International Library of African Music to keep the 40,000 recordings he made among many peoples, and he released Chemirocha III on his 1972 album The Music of Africa: Musical Instruments 1: Strings. After his death in 1977 his son Andrew Tracey led the library until 2005, when Diane Thram became curator. She began to digitise the collection and worked with the label Ketebul Music to take the recordings back to the villages where they were made; in 2014 the library returned to Kapkatet to present the songs.

In 2015 the team found Cheriyot Arap Kuri, one of the original singers of Chemirocha I, who said he had not known what Tracey was doing and that the Kipsigis had sung to entertain him. Villagers explained the word as slow, nice music, and Josiah, son of chief Arapsang, said that the mistreatment of the Kipsigis by the colonial government had led them to think of the newcomers as man-eaters.
chemnitz: Chemnitz lies in the Ore Mountain Basin, with the Ore Mountains to the south and the Central Saxon Hill Country to the north, on the Chemnitz River, which is formed by the confluence of the Zwönitz and the Würschnitz. The name of the city and of the river is of Slavic origin, derived from the root for stone (Upper Sorbian kamjeń), so that the river's name means stony brook.

The area was sparsely settled by Slavic tribes related to the modern Sorbs. The first recorded mention of Chemnitz comes in 1143, when King Conrad III of Germany confirmed the rights of a Benedictine monastery, including permission to hold a royal public market, and a town grew around the market. It passed to the Margraviate of Meissen in 1307 and to the Electorate of Saxony in 1356. After it received the bleaching privilege in 1357 it became a regional centre of weaving, linen manufacture and textile trade, employing more than a third of its people. The scholar Georgius Agricola, author of De re metallica, was city physician from 1533 and died there in 1555.

By the early 19th century the city was an industrial centre, called the Saxon Manchester. Its population was 320,000 in 1913, and Auto Union was founded there in 1932. Allied bombing in the Second World War destroyed 41 percent of its built-up area, and Soviet troops occupied the city on 8 May 1945. On 10 May 1953 the East German government renamed it Karl-Marx-Stadt. In a referendum on 23 April 1990, 76 percent voted for the old name, and Chemnitz was officially restored on 1 June 1990.

Chemnitz is the third-largest city in Saxony, after Leipzig and Dresden, and is home to Chemnitz University of Technology. Mechanical engineering, metal processing and vehicle manufacturing are its main industries. The red tower, built in the late 12th or early 13th century as part of the city wall, is its most conspicuous landmark, and the Karl Marx Monument by Lev Kerbel, nicknamed Nischel by locals, stands in the centre. The city was a European Capital of Culture in 2025.
chemosh: In Moabite the god's name was pronounced Kamōš, a form better kept by the Septuagint's Khamōs and the Vulgate's Chamos than by the Hebrew Kəmōš, which was vowelled after a word meaning stench. Its origin is uncertain. He may be the same as Kamiš, a god of Ebla attested around 2300 BCE, but the long gap before the 9th-century Moabite evidence makes that link very doubtful; other proposals connect the name with an epithet of the Mesopotamian god Nergal or with words meaning conqueror or subduer. In the 9th century BCE Chemosh was also identified with ʿAštar, a Moabite form of the North Arabian god of the planet Venus, as ʿAštar-Kamōš.

Mesha called Chemosh the subduer of the enemies of Moab, and the Moabites believed that his anger brought subjection and his favour independence and victory. Mesha waged his war on Israel as a holy war in the god's honour: after taking the Gadite city of Ataroth he killed all its people to fulfil a vow to Chemosh, and after taking Nebo he sacrificed its whole Israelite population to ʿAštar-Chemosh and offered the lambs of Yahweh's sanctuary there to his own god. He also built a high place for Chemosh in the citadel of the capital, Ḏaybān. The main sanctuary was probably at Qerīyōt, and the god's name forms many Moabite personal names, such as Kamōš-nātān, Chemosh has given.

His worship outlived the kingdom of Moab: people of Moabite descent in Egypt and Babylonia bore his name, and an Aramaic inscription of the 3rd century BCE from Al-Karak mentions him. Under Hellenistic and Roman rule he was identified with Ares, so that Rabbat Mōʾāb was called Areopolis. The Hebrew Bible names him the abomination of Moab and says that Josiah destroyed the high places that Solomon had built for him, while the Books of Kings tell that Mesha sacrificed his own son to Chemosh, a claim no Moabite inscription confirms.
chen-gongbo: Chen Gongbo was born in Nanhai, Foshan, in Guangdong, to a Hakka peasant family that had migrated from Shanghang in Fujian; his father was an official in the Qing administration. As a student at Peking University he took part in the May Fourth Movement and studied Marxism under Chen Duxiu. He attended the First Congress of the Chinese Communist Party in Shanghai in July 1921, but was expelled the next year for supporting Chen Jiongming in the June 16 Incident of 1922. He then went to the United States and took a master's degree in economics at Columbia University in 1925.

Back in China he joined the Kuomintang and headed its Department of Peasants and Workers under Liao Zhongkai. He belonged to the party's left with Wang Jingwei, with whom he formed a close political and personal bond. Although he did much in Chiang Kai-shek's Northern Expedition, he and Wang strongly opposed Chiang as he took dictatorial power, and Chen thought it particularly unfair that Chiang had displaced Wang through a military coup in 1926.

During a period of cooperation between Chiang and Wang, Chen served as Minister of Industry from 1932 to 1936, and some of the economic policies he helped set remained in use under various Chinese regimes until the 1970s. As director of the Sichuan branch he helped organise the government's evacuation to Chongqing after the Second Sino-Japanese War began. When Wang broke with the Kuomintang and set up the collaborationist government in Nanjing, Chen followed despite his initial opposition and became speaker of the Legislative Yuan. After Japan handed nominal rule over Shanghai to the Nanjing government in November 1940, he was appointed its mayor. In mid-1944, when Wang went to Japan for medical treatment, Chen was left in charge of the government.

At the end of the Second World War Chen fled to Japan. On 9 September 1945 China's representative, He Yingqin, asked Japan's representative, Yasuji Okamura, to hand him over for trial, the American occupation forces granted the request, and Chen was escorted back to China on 3 October. At his trial he defended himself vigorously, insisting that he had refused to cooperate with the Japanese in several significant matters and had acted only out of loyalty to his friend Wang Jingwei. Convicted and sentenced to death, he took his fate calmly, saying that "soon I will be reunited with Wang Jingwei in the next world". He was shot by firing squad at Suzhou, Jiangsu, on 3 June 1946.
chen-jiongming: Chen was born on 18 January 1878 in Haifeng, Guangdong, to a landlord family of moderate means. He took the name Jiongming on gaining the xiucai degree in 1899, and in 1908 graduated at the top of his class from the Academy of Law and Political Science in Canton. Zou Rong's The Revolutionary Army, with its call for a republic on the American model, left him with a lifelong ideal of a federated China.

Elected to the Guangdong Provincial Assembly in 1909, he led the campaign that ended legal gambling in 1911. He likely joined the Tongmenghui around 1909, sponsored the anarchist-inspired Chinese Assassination Corps, and in November 1911 led the Xun Army's rising at Huizhou, after which Guangdong declared independence and he became vice military governor.

From 1918 to 1920 Chen governed twenty-six counties of southern Fujian from Zhangzhou, where his reforms earned it the name of a Little Model China. In 1920 he declined arms offered by an envoy of Vladimir Lenin. After his Guangdong Army took Canton, he became civil governor: he banned gambling and opium, made Chen Duxiu head of a provincial education committee, founded the University of Guangdong, and issued a charter for Canton in December 1920 and a provincial constitution in 1921.

He opposed Sun Yat-sen's election as President-Extraordinary in April 1921 and his expedition north to reunify China by force. Sun dismissed him in April 1922. At 3:00 am on 16 June 1922 a detachment of the Guangdong Army moved against Sun's Presidential Palace; Sun had escaped to the warship Yongfeng, and the next day he had Canton shelled from it, killing over a hundred civilians. Most scholars conclude that Chen did not plan the coup. In February 1925 Whampoa forces under Chiang Kai-shek began the First East River Campaign against his army.

From Hong Kong Chen led the China Zhi Gong Party, formed in San Francisco in 1925, and in 1927 published A Proposal for the Unification of China. He died poor in Hong Kong on 22 September 1933 and was buried on Ziwei Hill in Huizhou in 1935. Both Nationalist and Communist historians long portrayed him as a counter-revolutionary warlord, but since the late 20th century many scholars have reassessed him as a democrat and federalist.
chen-sheng: Chen Sheng, also known by his courtesy name Chen She, was born in Yangcheng, in present-day Fangcheng County, Henan. In August or September 209 BCE, during the reign of the Second Qin Emperor, he and Wu Guang were military captains ordered to lead 900 soldiers to Yuyang, near present-day Beijing, to defend the northern border against the Xiongnu. Storms made it clear they would miss the deadline, and the law punished late arrival with death.

Believing themselves doomed, the two captains led their men into revolt. They claimed that the Qin crown prince Fusu, who had been forced to commit suicide, and the Chu general Xiang Yan, who had killed himself after the Qin conquest of Chu, were alive and joining them, and they declared Chu restored. People who felt oppressed by the Qin joined quickly, and more than 20,000 men rallied. Against the advice of Zhang Er and Chen Yu, Chen Sheng declared himself King of Rising Chu, with his capital at Chen County.

He sent generals out in all directions: Wu Guang as acting King of Chu, Zhou Wen west towards Qin proper, his friend Wu Chen north to the old lands of Zhao, and Zhou Fu north-east towards Wei. None returned. Qin forces regrouped under general Zhang Han; Wu Guang was murdered by his own officers, Zhou Wen was defeated, and Zhou Fu set up a descendant of the Wei royal house. Chen Sheng executed generals at any rumour of disloyalty, and his followers fell away. While leading a force to gather reinforcements he was assassinated by Zhuang Jia, about five months after the rising began.

His defiance provided the spark that eventually led to the fall of the Qin dynasty, and later Chinese histories often idealised him as a leader of peasants against oppression. The Song dynasty historian Sima Guang, in the Zizhi Tongjian, described how Chen slighted his father-in-law, executed old friends who talked of his humble youth and let his officials Zhou Fang and Hu Wu arrest returning generals, so that the generals had no affection for him. According to the Shiji he coined the proverb about a little songbird that cannot understand the ambitions of a grand swan. He was posthumously known as King Yin and sometimes appears as a door god, usually paired with Wu Guang.
chen-shubao: Chen Shubao was born at Jiangling, the eldest son of Chen Xu, then a mid-level official of Emperor Yuan of Liang, and his second wife Liu Jingyan. When the Western Wei took Jiangling in 554, his father was carried off to Chang'an while mother and son were left at Rang City. After Chen Xu's uncle founded the Chen dynasty, the family was brought back by 562, and when Chen Xu seized power and took the throne as Emperor Xuan in 569, Chen Shubao became crown prince.

As heir he was known for his love of literature and feasting, and his father removed the official Jiang Zong from his household after the two feasted too much together. When Emperor Xuan died in 582, Chen Shubao's brother Chen Shuling stabbed him in the neck as he mourned beside the casket. Chen Shuling's coup failed, and three days later the severely wounded prince took the throne.

In 584 he built three luxurious pavilions in the palace and spent his days feasting with Consort Zhang Lihua, Consort Kong and literary officials such as Jiang Zong, whom he made prime minister. Traditional historians say he let Consort Zhang rule on petitions from his lap. Taxes were raised to pay for his building, even on soldiers and officials, and at the urging of Kong Fan much military command passed to civilians, angering the generals. In 587 he accepted the surrender of Western Liang officials with the people of Jiangling, which Emperor Wen of Sui treated as provocation.

Sui attacked in 588 on three fronts under Yang Guang, Yang Jun and Yang Su, while the official Shi Wenqing kept reports of the danger from the emperor. In spring 589 Heruo Bi and Han Qinhu crossed the Yangtze and closed on Jiankang. Chen Shubao panicked, and after Heruo defeated Xiao Mohe the Chen army collapsed. He hid in a well with Consorts Zhang and Kong but was captured, and Gao Jiong had Consort Zhang executed.

Taken to the Sui capital, he was treated kindly by Emperor Wen, who allowed his heavy drinking, and in 594 he was given supplies to sacrifice to his ancestors. He died in December 604, early in the reign of Emperor Yang, who made him Duke of Changcheng and gave him the posthumous name Yang. He is remembered as Houzhu, the Last Ruler of Chen.
chen-yonghua: Chen Yonghua, courtesy name Fufu, was born in 1634 in the region near modern-day Jiaomei, close to Quanzhou. In 1648 his father was forced to commit suicide by the invading army of the Qing dynasty. Chen took refuge with Koxinga and became tutor to Koxinga's son Zheng Jing.

After Koxinga's death in 1662 a struggle broke out between Zheng Jing and Koxinga's fifth son, Zheng Xi, whose claim was backed by officials led by Huang Zhao and Xiao Gongchen. Chen led an army against Huang Zhao in Tainan; Huang was defeated and killed, and Zheng Xi was put under house arrest. Zheng Jing, now ruler of Tungning, made Chen his chief minister.

Chen introduced a Chinese bureaucracy and a method of making high-quality salt by evaporation along the coast, which made Tungning self-sufficient. He is credited with storing water for the dry season and growing sugar cane as a cash crop, and with policies for agriculture, education, finance, industry and trade; his tax system was harsh. When Zheng Jing lost a campaign against the Qing in 1664 and many people left for the mainland, he thought of surrendering, but Chen told him that those who had gone over were slaves and merchants who had lied to the Qing.

Chen also built the Tainan Confucian Temple, the first Confucian temple on the island, together with an academy. In 1674 his daughter married the crown prince, Zheng Kezang, and Chen was left in charge of the kingdom while Zheng Jing went on another campaign against the Qing.

When Zheng Jing came back from a failed campaign in 1680, Feng Xifan and Liu Guoxuan, out of jealousy, ousted Chen from power. He died in July 1680 and was buried in the mountains near Tainan. In Jin Yong's wuxia novel The Deer and the Cauldron, Chen Jinnan, master of martial arts and leader of the Tiandi Society, is believed to be based on him; in the novel Chen Jinnan is killed by Zheng Keshuang and his master Feng Xifan.
chen-youliang: Chen was born in the village of Huangpengshan, in present-day Honghu, in Yusha County of Mianyang Prefecture, a district known since the Song dynasty as a land of fish and rice. He grew up poor in a family of fishermen. Some accounts say he was born with the surname Xie: the scholar Tong Chengxu wrote that his grandfather Chen Qianyi had married into a Chen family and taken its name. He served as a district official before becoming a general under Ni Wenjun in the Red Turban Rebellion.

When Ni Wenjun planned to assassinate the Red Turban leader Xu Shouhui, Chen killed Ni first. He went on to capture Anqing and to conquer large parts of Fujian and Jiangxi. After Zhu Yuanzhang sent him a bribed former retainer of his general Zhao Pusheng, and rumours spread that Zhao meant to defect to Wu, Chen had Zhao put to death and proclaimed himself King of Han. In the spring of 1360 he declared himself emperor of Da Han, Great Han, with Zou Pusheng as Grand Preceptor and Zhang Bixian as chancellor.

From 1359 to 1363 his fleet was the strongest on the upper Yangtze, and his power was at least equal to that of Wu under Zhu Yuanzhang. The long war between Han and Wu culminated at the Battle of Lake Poyang, where the Wu fleet narrowly defeated the larger Han fleet after three days of fighting and then blockaded it. A month later Chen tried to break out and was killed by an arrow that struck his head.

His crown prince Chen Shan had been captured, so his second son Chen Li, who had escaped to Wuchang with Zhang Dingbian, succeeded him and surrendered in March 1364; fighting in Hubei, Hunan and Jiangxi went on until April 1365. The Ming later granted his father and brothers titles, and sent Chen Li to Goryeo in 1372. Chen was buried on the southern slope of Sheshan in present-day Wuhan. He is remembered as a rebel who helped end Yuan rule; the historian Wu Han called him a hero who opposed the Mongolian and Han landlord classes.
chenani-nashri-tunnel: The tunnel was built to bypass an old section of the highway full of hairpin bends, with places such as Patnitop, Kud and Batote prone to snow and avalanches, which blocked the road every winter and left long queues of vehicles, sometimes for days. The foundation was laid in July 2011 by the Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Omar Abdullah with the Union Health Minister Ghulam Nabi Azad, under the UPA government. The project then stalled for some years amid funding difficulties, and its cost rose from an estimated ₹2,520 crore to ₹3,720 crore.

Completion was planned for May 2016 and then July 2016, but a dispute between the workers and the executing agency held up the work. Snowfall in early 2017 cut the electricity needed for testing, and the independent engineers reported that the demonetisation of 8 November 2016 had left contractors unable to pay their labourers. Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurated the tunnel on 2 April 2017. Nearly 1,500 engineers, geologists and labourers worked on it.

The tunnel carries two lanes of National Highway 44 at an altitude of about 1,200 metres in the lower Himalaya, from about 2 kilometres from Chenani, south of Patnitop, to Nashri village north of it. It has two parallel tubes, a main traffic tube 13 metres across and an escape tube 6 metres across, joined by 29 cross passages every 300 metres. Fresh air enters the main tube every 8 metres and is drawn out into the escape tube every 100 metres, making it India's first road tunnel with transverse ventilation and the country's first with a fully integrated tunnel control system.

A control room outside the tunnel watches 124 cameras and a linear heat detection system. SOS boxes stand every 150 metres, the lighting is graded to ease the change of light at the portals, and in a fire the supply of fresh air stops while fans draw the smoke away and emergency vehicles use the escape tube. The tunnel bypasses 44 avalanche and landslide-prone spots and cuts travel time between Jammu and Srinagar by two hours.
chengdu: Chengdu lies in central Sichuan on a vast plain with an elevation of 450 to 720 metres, crossed by the Jin River. The Chengdu Plain is known as the Country of Heaven and the Land of Abundance, a phrase the Shu Han minister Zhuge Liang used of the region. The Qin Mountains far to the north shield the city from cold Siberian winds, so its winters are milder than those of the lower Yangtze.

Archaeological finds at Sanxingdui and the Jinsha Site show that the surrounding area was inhabited more than four thousand years ago. In the time of the Xia, Shang and Zhou dynasties it formed a separate bronze-working culture that, after partial sinification, became known to the Chinese as Shu. The city is said to have been founded by the Kingdom of Shu in the 4th century BCE. Qin conquered Shu in 316 BCE, and the settlement was re-founded by the Qin general Zhang Yi.

The name Chengdu is attested from the Warring States period, and the city has been called the only major Chinese city to keep both its location and its name through the imperial, republican and communist eras, although it was briefly known as Xijing in the 17th century.

Under the Han, Chengdu brocade became fashionable throughout China, and a Brocade Official was appointed to oversee its production and trade. After the fall of the Eastern Han, Liu Bei ruled Shu Han from Chengdu. Under the Tang it was considered the second most prosperous city in China after Yangzhou, and the poets Li Bai and Du Fu lived there; Du Fu's thatched cottage of 760 is commemorated by the Caotang, built in 1078.

In 1911 Chengdu's branch of the Railway Protection Movement helped trigger the Wuchang Uprising. During the Second World War refugees from eastern China fleeing the Japanese settled there, and after the war the city was briefly the capital of the Nationalist government before it withdrew to Taipei. A railway to Chongqing was built in 1952.

Chengdu is the capital of Sichuan province, with 20,937,757 inhabitants at the 2020 census. The nearby Dujiangyan irrigation system and Mount Qingcheng, an important Taoist site, are World Heritage Sites. Among its landmarks are the Wuhou Shrine, built to honour Zhuge Liang, the Jinsha Site museum and the Daci Temple, where the monk Xuanzang was initiated. UNESCO recognised it in 2011 as a city of gastronomy.
chennai: Chennai lies on the Eastern Coastal Plains, a flat stretch of clay soil on the Bay of Bengal, at an average elevation of 6.7 m. It receives most of its rain from the northeast monsoon, and cyclones are common in that season. The name derives from Chennappa Nayaka, a Nayak ruler who served as a general under Venkata Raya of the Vijayanagara Empire and from whom the East India Company took the town on lease in 1639. The first official use of the name was in August 1639, in a sale deed to Francis Day of the Company.

Stone Age implements have been found near Pallavaram. In the 2nd century CE the region was part of Tondaimandalam, ruled by the Early Cholas, and the Pallavas of Kanchi ruled it independently from the 3rd to the 9th century. The Later Cholas under Aditya I defeated the Pallavas in 879, Jatavarman Sundara Pandyan brought the region under Pandya rule in 1264, and the Vijayanagara Empire held influence over it in the 15th century.

In 1639 the East India Company obtained a grant of coastal land containing the fishing village of Madrasapattinam and built Fort St George, the first British fortress in India. The Corporation of Madras was established on 29 September 1688. In the 18th century the British and the French fought for control of the city, and by the late 18th century the British had conquered most of the region and made Madras the capital of the Madras Presidency. The idea of the Indian National Congress was conceived there after a Theosophical convention in December 1884. After 1947 Madras became capital of Madras State, the predecessor of Tamil Nadu.

Chennai is the capital and largest city of Tamil Nadu, officially renamed from Madras in 1996. The 2011 census counted 4,646,732 people within the city's 174 km2, and Tamil is the language of most residents. Its oldest surviving buildings date from the 6th to 8th centuries CE, among them the Kapaleeshwarar Temple in Mylapore and the Parthasarathy Temple in Triplicane. The Madras Music Season, begun by the Madras Music Academy in 1927, brings Carnatic music performances each December.
chennakeshava-temple-belur: Belur, called Beluhur, Velur or Velapura in old inscriptions, stands on the Yagachi River and was an early capital of the Hoysala kings, who called it an earthly Vaikuntha, the abode of Vishnu. Vishnuvardhana, who came to power in 1110, commissioned the temple to the god Vijayanarayana; the scholar Dhaky sees in it his devotion to the Sri Vaishnavism of Ramanujacharya. His queen Santala Devi sponsored the smaller Chennigaraya temple beside it at the same time. The complex continued to grow for more than a century, and the temple has remained in worship ever since, unlike the other great Hoysala temples.

The main temple is a single shrine of soapstone, which is soft when quarried and hardens with time, set on a jagati platform for walking around the sanctum. It combines North Indian Nagara and South Indian Karnata elements and drew on the Western Chalukyan tradition of Aihole, Badami and Pattadakal. Bands of carving run round the walls: elephants at the base, then horsemen, dancers and musicians, scenes from the Ramayana and the Mahabharata, and scenes of daily life, courtship and festivals. There are 80 large reliefs of deities, 38 surviving madanakai bracket figures, and a Jina of Jainism among the images.

Inside, the navaranga hall, the largest of any Hoysala temple, has forty eight pillars, among them the Narasimha and Mohini pillars, under a domed ceiling about 10 feet across. The sanctum holds a four-armed image of Keshava about 6 feet high, its halo carved with the ten avatars of Vishnu. Artists signed some of their work: Ruvari Mallitamma is credited with more than 40 sculptures, and Dasoja and his son Chavana with several madanikas.

Delhi Sultanate armies plundered Belur in the 14th century, and a raid under the general Salar, serving Muhammed bin Tughlaq, burnt the gateway. The Vijayanagara Empire repaired the temple under Harihara II, adding four granite pillars in 1381 and a seven-storey gopuram in 1397. Further repairs followed in 1709 and 1774. In the late 19th century the collapsing tower over the sanctum was removed and never replaced, and in 1935 the Mysore government restored parts of the complex. In 2023 it became part of the Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas World Heritage Site.
chennakeshava-temple-somanathapura: Somanatha, called Someya Dandanayaka in some inscriptions, founded the town while serving King Narasimha III. He created an agrahara, land granted to Brahmins with resources set aside to build and maintain temples, and the settlement took his name as Somanatha-pura. In its middle he built the Kesava temple, consecrating it in 1258. He also consecrated the Shaiva Panchalinga, or five-linga, temple at the edge of the grant and walled the land. Inscriptions say he built further temples in the region, but all except the ruined Lakshminarasimha temple disappeared after wars between Hindu kingdoms and Muslim sultanates.

The temple faces east inside a walled courtyard, before whose main gate stands a tall pillar that once carried a statue of Garuda. A corridor round the courtyard holds 64 small shrines for Vedic and Puranic deities, whose statues were defaced. The temple is carved from soapstone, a green-grey chloritic schist that is soft in the quarry and hardens in air; it is not found locally. The platform, about 3 feet high, is a path for walking clockwise round the temple, and of the 15 stone elephants that stood at its points, 11 survive in a damaged state.

The outer walls carry bands of carving: elephants, armed horsemen with camels in places, which suggests that the Hoysala army had adopted them, a scroll of nature, and friezes of the Ramayana, the Bhagavata Purana and the Mahabharata, read in order by walking clockwise. Higher up, about 90 larger reliefs show mostly Vishnu with Lakshmi, beside Shiva, Brahma, Saraswati and others, and some panels are signed by their carvers. The image of Keshava is lost, while those of Janardhana and of Krishna as Venugopala, playing the flute, each 4.5 feet high, remain, framed by the ten avatars of Vishnu.

It is one of some 1,500 Hindu and Jain temples built by the Hoysala kings, and the author George Michell calls it the climax of the Hoysala temple style, though also unique in many ways. Inscriptions of 1497 and 1550 record damage and repairs. The emperors of the Vijayanagara Empire paid for repairs in the 16th century, visible in the different colour and quality of stone in the veranda and parts of the northern tower and platform. Damaged again in the 19th century, it was repaired in the early 20th century by the colonial-era Mysore government.
chenqiao-mutiny: After Huang Chao's rebellion broke the Tang court's hold on the provinces, northern China was ruled by the Five Dynasties, each supplanting the last by usurpation or war. The Later Zhou, founded in 951, was the last of them. Its emperors Guo Wei and Chai Rong curbed the regional military governors, centralised the army and won territory from the Later Shu, the Southern Tang and the Liao dynasty. Zhao Kuangyin, son of the general Zhao Hongyin, helped Guo Wei seize power, distinguished himself in Chai Rong's campaigns and became inspector-general of the Palace Command, which let him build up his troops' personal loyalty.

Chai Rong died in 959 and was succeeded by his five-year-old son, Guo Zongxun. When a joint invasion by the Liao and the Northern Han was reported early in 960, the court sent Zhao against it despite warnings about his influence. He crossed the Yellow River on 1 February and camped at Chenqiao, a village north-east of Kaifeng.

That night his officers agreed to make him emperor, with the support of his younger brother Zhao Kuangyi and his adviser Zhao Pu. According to the History of Song, at dawn on 2 February they burst into his room and draped him in a yellow imperial robe, and he agreed to lead them back to Kaifeng only if they swore loyalty and did not loot the capital.

Traditional accounts present Zhao as an unwilling victim of circumstance, and later works added portents such as a second sun seen by the astrologer Miao Xun. Most modern historians, among them Deng Guangming, Chen Dengyuan and Wang Boqin, hold that Zhao, his brother and key advisers engineered the mutiny; the yellow robe was probably a later addition.

Han Tong, the only serious opponent in the capital, was killed, and the child emperor abdicated and was exiled. The handover was so peaceful that the street markets kept trading. Revolts by Li Yun and Li Chongjin were each defeated in under two months. In 971, according to the Sushui Jiwen, Zhao persuaded his top generals to give up their commands in exchange for marriages into the royal family. His brother completed the reunification of China with the conquest of the Northern Han in 979.
cheomseongdae: Cheomseongdae, whose name means star-gazing tower, stands 9.17 m high and has three parts: a base, a curved cylindrical body and a square top. When seen from above it resembles the Korean character jeong, meaning well. The square base is 5.7 m wide and built from a single layer of 12 rectangular stones. The body is built from 365 pieces of cut granite in 27 tiers, a number said to symbolise the days of the year. Documents report different counts, and a survey of 1962 found 366 blocks, a difference that may come from a slab inside the top that cannot be seen from outside.

A square opening on the south side, between the 13th and 15th tiers, is believed to have been an entrance reached by an external ladder, while a ladder inside may have given access to the top. There, two tiers of well-shaped stones form a frame, and it is presumed that an observation device was placed on it. The opening divides the body into 12 layers above and 12 below, which have been taken to stand for the 12 months and the 24 solar terms. The 12 stones of the base may also refer to the months. The tower's construction style parallels that of the Bunhwangsa in Gyeongju.

Cheomseongdae was built in the Silla period, in the reign of Queen Seondeok (r. 632 to 647). It was designated the country's 31st national treasure on 20 December 1962 and is part of the Gyeongju Historic Areas, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Its shape has remained unchanged for over 1,300 years, though it now tilts slightly to the north-east. The National Research Institute of Cultural Heritage has inspected it regularly since 1981, and since 2007 a system has measured its condition every hour, watching for cracks and movements of the foundation stones. The government of South Korea owns it, and the Gyeongju municipal government manages it.
cheonghaejin: Cheonghaejin, clear sea headquarters, lies at Jangjwa-ri in Wando County, South Jeolla Province. From it a maritime trading route was held that dominated the seas off three sides of the Korean Peninsula.
