The Godae, a high point on the castle wall south of the base, overlooked the passage leading inland from the sea, from which merchant ships and pirates offshore could easily be watched.

General Chang Pogo asked King Heungdeok to establish a military complex to protect Silla's merchant fleets and coastal residents from pirates, and in 828, the third year of the king's reign, he was granted permission and 10,000 troops. He built a small castle and a military base at Garipo. The base kept strong commercial ties with Chinese and Japanese ports, and Chang sent envoys called Hoyeoksa for trade and cultural exchange.

Silla noblemen of small maritime communities resented the base, since they lost the profits of their private trade, and they sent an assassin, Yŏm Chang, to kill Chang. Yŏm Chang held the base afterwards, but its residents, mourning Chang, left for other parts of Silla, and some for China or Japan. The Samguk Sagi records that the central government closed Cheonghaejin in February 851, and the remaining residents were relocated to Byeokgolgun.

The remains include a wooden fence of oak posts 331 m long, radiocarbon dated to the mid-9th century, a castle of rammed earth stretching 890 m, outer and inner gates, and a well 5.8 m deep that yielded earthenware flasks, iron pots and bronze bottles. Nearby lies the site of the Buddhist temple Beobhwasa, reportedly built in imitation of the Beobhwawon that Chang founded in Shandong. A stele commemorates the move of the residents to Byeokgolgun.
cheongju: Cheongju is the largest city of North Chungcheong Province as well as its capital. The Geum River runs through its centre, and the tributaries Musim and Miho join in the north of the city, with the mountains of Wuam and Bumo to the east and west. The climate is temperate, with four seasons. On 1 July 2014 Cheongju and Cheongwon County were unified, and the city is now divided into four districts: Heungdeok, Seowon, Sangdang and Cheongwon.

Cheongju has been an important provincial town since ancient times. Ruins from the Old Stone Age to the Bronze Age have been found in the Cheongju Mountains, and the Durubong Cave Site is associated with the Paleolithic. After Silla unified the Three Kingdoms in 676, Buddhism spread through the region. Under King Gwangjong of Goryeo several Buddhist monuments were made, among them the Cheoldanggan, an iron flagpole of twenty cylinders, 13.1 metres tall, raised in 962 near the remains of Yongdu Temple to hang the flag that honours the Buddha. It was designated a National Treasure in 1962. Under the Joseon dynasty the region took up Confucianism as its main faith, and temples in Cheongju played a part in the advance of Korean printing.

In 1593, during Hideyoshi's invasions of Korea, the Battle of Cheongju was fought between Japanese forces and Joseon, and more than 8,000 Korean warrior monks took part. The fortress of Sangdangsanseong linked the northern and southern provinces after the Japanese invasion of 1592.

The provincial government moved to Cheongju from Chungju in 1908. Under Japanese colonial rule Cheongju County and Munui County were merged in 1914, and the opening of the Chungbuk line in 1926 spurred regional development. Cheongju and Cheongwon County were separated in 1946, and Cheongju was made a city in 1949. Its population almost quadrupled, from 147,000 in 1970 to 582,158 in 2000.

Sangdangsanseong lies on the slopes of Mount Uam within the city. Its wall, 3 to 4 metres high and 4.2 kilometres around, dates in its present form to a restoration in 1716. Cheongju National Museum, near the mountain, holds artefacts of the region. The Early Printing Museum on the site of Heungdeoksa Temple is dedicated to the history of printing and to the Jikji. Chojeonghaenggung, a temporary palace where King Sejong stayed for treatment of an eye disease, is said to be where he completed the creation of Hangul. Cheongju is also a seat of several universities.
cheonmachong: Cheonmachong, formerly Tomb No. 155, is a tumulus inside the Daereungwon tomb complex in Gyeongju. In the typical Silla style it has a wood-lined chamber running east to west, covered by a mound of boulders and earth, a type said to follow the pattern of a Scytho-Iranian tomb at Pazyryk in Russia. The mound is 47 metres in diameter, 157 metres round and 12.7 metres high.

The chamber held a lacquered wooden coffin with burial goods placed around it, and a chest of further goods: the painted saddle flaps, iron kettles, pottery, bronze vessels, lacquerware, saddles and a sword 98 centimetres long. The burial of horse trappings and of a sacrificed horse with the king points to the importance of horse culture in Silla society and to the king's place at the centre of its shamanism.

Excavation began on 16 April 1973, and 11,500 artefacts were recovered. The king buried there is unknown, though a strong view holds that it is the tomb of King Jijeung; the dead man is estimated to have been about 160 centimetres tall. The gold crown, gold girdle, gold bracelets and gold rings for every finger mark a royal burial, as do the girdle's likeness to one from the Gold Crown Tomb and dragon motifs matching the treasures of King Muryeong of Baekje.

The horse on the saddle flap, a Cheonma or flying horse, has eight legs and wings on its feet, and the painting shows strong influence from the Goguryeo kingdom; the other side of the flaps shows horsemen and a phoenix. The crown, counted among the most valuable of Silla, has three branch-shaped and two antler-shaped ornaments hung with jade and spangles, and is thought to have been set on a hat of birch bark.
cheontae: The Chinese Tiantai school was founded in 594 by the monk Zhiyi under the Sui dynasty. Its teachings reached Korea earlier, but Cheontae became an independent school only in the Goryeo period, through Daegak Guksa Uicheon (1055–1101), a royal prince and Buddhist scholar, who promoted it to bridge the gap between the doctrinal Gyo schools and the meditative Seon schools.

Cheontae holds the Lotus Sutra to be the culmination of the Buddha's teaching. Its doctrine rests on three insights: that all phenomena are fundamentally empty, that they have a provisional or conventional existence, and that all things are at once empty and provisionally real. Everyday sensory experience is therefore an expression of the Dharma and a path to enlightenment, a view reflected in the colourful Dancheong painting of Korean temples, which contrasts with the minimalist style of Japanese Zen.

Under Goryeo, Cheontae gained institutional recognition alongside the Jogye school, and Buddhism was organised under the Five Orders and Two Schools, the two schools being the Jogye and Cheontae sects. Its influence waned under the Joseon dynasty, whose rulers sought to reunify the Buddhist schools: by 1424 Cheontae had been absorbed into the Chongnam sect, and later into the Seon-dominated structure known as Seon-Gyo Yangjong, the Two Schools of Seon and Doctrinal Buddhism.

In the modern period Park Sangwol, also known as Sangwol Wongak Daejo, founded the present Korean Buddhist Cheontae Order, which regards Zhiyi, Uicheon and Park Sangwol as its spiritual forebears. Its headquarters are at Guinsa Temple near Danyang in Chungcheongbuk-do, built of concrete unlike the usual Buddhist temples, and the order runs Geumgang University. A foundation of the order was established on 16 April 1991 to carry on its education, the care of its temples, translation and welfare work.
chepni: The Chepni are counted among the 24 Oghuz Turkic tribes. In the legend of Oghuz Qaghan they appear as one of the clans of the tribe of Gök Han, together with the Pecheneg, the Bayandur and the Chowdur, within the Üç-Oklar branch of the Oghuz Turks. The Dīwān Lughāt al-Turk of Mahmud al-Kashgari lists them as the 21st of 22 Oghuz tribes.

The Chepni converted to Islam, and they are Sunni, Shia or Alevi. The Turkish historian Faruk Sümer suggested that the first murids, or disciples, of Haji Bektash Veli may have been Chepni living at Suluca Kara Üyük, now a town of Nevşehir Province in Central Anatolia, and some Turkish historians claim that Haji Bektash Veli himself may have been of Chepni origin.

In the 1330s groups of Turkmens appeared in the coastal regions of the Pontus. Some of these nomads seem to have wandered through Trapezuntine territory as subjects of the Grand Komnenoi, and there is a recorded case of Christian Chepni. Linguistic evidence points the same way: according to the scholar Brendemoen, a group of Pontic Chepni nomads was bilingual in Turkic and Greek by the 14th century.

The earliest Turkic dialect of the Pontos was based on the Aq Qoyunlu dialect, shaped by the influence of Pontic Greek, and the historian Michael Meeker considers the linguistic Hellenization of some Turks who settled in the region not altogether improbable.

Giresun and the country around it were known in history as the Chepni province. Besides the Black Sea provinces of Giresun and Ordu, where most Chepni live, communities are found in Gaziantep, Trabzon and Balıkesir. In Turkmenistan the Chepni are a clan of the Geklen Turkmens in the west of the country.
chepstow-castle: The castle stands on a narrow ridge between the limestone river cliff and a valley known locally as the Dell, overlooking an important crossing of the River Wye on the routes inland to Monmouth and Hereford. Its four baileys, added one after another, record its building history rather than make it strong: it has neither a strong keep nor a concentric plan. It was first called Striguil, from the Welsh ystraigl, river bend, and with its Marcher lordship took the name of the neighbouring market town of Chepstow from the late 14th century.

The Great Tower, probably finished by about 1090, was built in stone from the start, partly with blocks reused from the Roman ruins at Caerwent. In the 12th century the castle served the conquest of Gwent, the first independent Welsh kingdom the Normans conquered. William Marshal, Earl of Pembroke, built the present main gatehouse from the 1190s and strengthened the Middle Bailey with round towers. Roger Bigod, 5th Earl of Norfolk, who inherited it in 1270, added a new range in the Lower Bailey, the town's Port Wall around 1274–78, and the tower later called Marten's Tower.

Its defensive value declined after the wars between England and Wales ended. Garrisoned with twenty men-at-arms and sixty archers against Owain Glyndŵr in 1403, it was not attacked. Sir Charles Somerset, later Earl of Worcester, who received it in 1508, remodelled it as a residence. In the English Civil War the Royalist garrison was besieged in 1645 and 1648, and the castle fell to Parliament on 25 May 1648; Sir Nicholas Kemeys, who led the defence, was killed after refusing to surrender. It then served as an artillery fort, barracks and political prison, where Henry Marten, a signatory of the death warrant of Charles I, was held until his death in 1680.

The garrison was disbanded in 1685 and the buildings left to decay, used in part as a farmyard and a glass factory. By the late 18th century the ruins were a stop on the Wye tour, and J. M. W. Turner painted the castle in 1794. The film Ivanhoe was made in its grounds in 1913, and the following year the businessman William Royse Lysaght bought it and began conservation.

The ruins were listed Grade I on 6 December 1950, and the Lysaght family placed the castle in the care of the Ministry of Works in 1953. Since 1984 it has been looked after by Cadw, the Welsh government's heritage body, and it is open to the public.
chera-dynasty: The Cheras, also called Keralaputra, are documented from the third century BCE, when the edicts of the Maurya emperor Asoka name them Kedalaputo. Pliny the Elder, Ptolemy and the Periplus Maris Erythraei also name them. The Cheras of the early historic period, from about the second century BCE to the third or fifth century CE, had their capital at Vanchi-Karuvur (Karur) in the Kongu country, with ports at Muchiri-Vanchi (Muziris) and Thondi. They also controlled the Palakkad Gap and the Noyyal valley, the main route between the Malabar Coast and eastern Tamil Nadu. Their emblem was the bow and arrow.

The main sources are the Sangam poems, among them the Pathitrupattu, in which each Chera ruler is praised in ten songs by a court poet, and Graeco-Roman accounts. Their date rests on the Gajabahu-Chenguttuvan synchronism: the epic Silappathikaram says that Gajabahu, identified with a second-century ruler of Sri Lanka, attended the consecration of a temple for Pattini by the Chera ruler Chenguttuvan. Another ruler, Yanaikatchai Mantharam Cheral Irumporai, c. 215 CE, was captured by the Pandya king Nedum Chezhian II but escaped and regained his lands.

The Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas were the three crowned kings, the Vendars, over lesser Velir chieftains who were likely required to pay tribute. Scholars disagree about whether these were states or, as R. Champakalakshmi argues, kinship-based chiefdoms living on tribute and plunder. Most people probably followed native Dravidian beliefs, such as the worship of departed heroes and trees, and migrants brought Jainism and Buddhism from about the third century BCE. Poets and bards were held in high regard and richly rewarded.

The economy rested on agriculture, fishing and cattle rearing, and on Indian Ocean trade. According to the Periplus, Muziris abounded with large ships of Romans, Arabs and Greeks. Pepper and other spices, ivory, timber, pearls and gems went west, and Roman gold came back in exchange, as hoards of Roman coins in Kerala and Tamil Nadu show. The trade dwindled with the decline of the Roman empire in the third and fourth centuries.

After about the fifth century Chera influence declined, and the region saw the rise of the Kalabhras and then Chalukya, Pallava, Pandya, Rashtrakuta and Chola dominance. By around the ninth century central Kerala had separated to form the medieval Chera kingdom of Mahodayapuram. In the early eleventh century the Cholas forced it into submission, mainly to break its monopoly on the pepper trade, and it was dissolved in the early 12th century. The Kulasekharas of Venad were also called the Chera dynasty from the 12th century.
chera-perumals-of-makotai: The medieval Cheras claimed descent from the early historic Cheras of pre-Pallava south India, a lineage tied to the prestige of Sangam literature, and they are often described as members of the Surya Vamsa, the Solar Race. Present-day central Kerala probably broke away from a larger Kongu Chera or Kerala kingdom around the 8th or 9th century. At first the dynasty's influence seems to have reached only from present-day Kollam to Koyilandy, but it later extended north to the Chandragiri river and south to Nagercoil.

Most royal revenue came from the Indian Ocean spice trade with the Middle East, with Nambudiri-Brahmin settlements on the fertile wetlands as another main support. Sthanu Ravi, the earliest recorded ruler, helped the Cholas conquer the western Tamil country in the late 9th century, but the kingdom was later subdued under the Chola emperor Rajaraja I, and firm Chola control followed under Rajendra I. Merchant guilds such as manigramam and anjuvannam were active, West Asian Muslims settled as traders, and the earliest inscriptional Malayalam is tentatively dated to this period.

In the early 12th century the kingdom dissolved into local powers, a collapse in which the gradual change of land relations is thought to have played a crucial part. Besides Venad in the south, the chieftains of Kolathunad and the future rulers of Kozhikode and Kochi emerged as successors.

Older Kerala historiography called the state a centralised Second Chera Empire or Kulasekhara Empire. Research of the late 1960s and early 1970s rejected this, finding that only two kings, Sthanu Ravi Kulasekhara and Rama Kulasekhara, are known to have used that regnal name. Some historians since the early 2000s, such as M. G. S. Narayanan, see the king's power as largely ritual and confined to the capital, with real power held by local chieftains, the udaiyavar, and a Brahmin oligarchy.

The chiefdoms, or nadus, owed the king service in war and dues collected by a royal prince, the Koyil Adhikarikal. The managers of four Brahmin temples around the capital, the Nalu Thali, likely served as his council, and the Ayiram, a thousand Nair warriors, formed his guard.
cheraman-perumal-nayanar: His name means "Chera king the Nayanar", and Cheraman Perumal is itself a title, "the Chera ruler". According to tradition he was born into the royal family of Malai-nadu, whose capital was Kodunkolur or Makotai by the Ocean. When the reigning king, Chenkor Poraiyan, abdicated, his ministers persuaded the young prince, also known as Perumakkotaiyar or Kalarirrarivar, "the One who knows [all] Languages", to take up the kingdom. He was then meditating at the Tiruvanchaikkalam Temple, and they convinced him only with great difficulty.

The legend tells that the king learned of the singer Sundarar through a vision of the Nataraja of Chidambaram. He left his capital, travelled through the Kongu country to Chidambaram and went on to Tiruvarur, where he met Sundarar in person. The two became close companions and made a long pilgrimage across south India, visiting Madurai, Tirunelveli, Ramesvaram, Tiruvaiyyaru and many other shrines. Years later Sundarar stayed in Kodunkolur as the king's guest. When messengers of Shiva came to call Sundarar back to Mount Kailasa, he rose there on a white elephant, and the Cheraman Perumal followed him on horseback.

He is credited with the Ponvannattandadi, hymns in praise of the Lord of Chidambaram; the Thiruvarur Mummanikkovai, dedicated to the deity of Thiruvarur; and the Adiyula, also called the Thirukkailayajnana Ula, the first of the ulas, in honour of Shiva. Historians tentatively identify the saint with Rama Rajasekhara, a 9th-century ruler of the Chera state of Kerala.

The legend of the king and Sundarar appears to have begun in pre-Chola times, but its surviving forms took shape at the Chola courts between the late 10th and the 12th century. It is told in the Periyapuranam, composed in the mid-12th century by Chekkizhar, a courtier of the Chola ruler Kulottunga II, which drew on an earlier compilation by Nambiyandar Nambi. The Thiruvanchikulam Shiva Temple in Kodungallur, on the Malabar Coast, is closely associated with both saints.
cherchell: Iol was probably established around 600 BCE, and the oldest remains found there date from the 5th century BCE. In the 3rd century BCE it was fortified and began issuing the first coins of Numidia. After the Punic Wars it was given to Micipsa, king of Numidia, who made it a royal court, and it was the main capital of Bocchus I and II. It was annexed to Rome in 33 BCE. In 25 BCE Augustus made Juba II king of Mauretania and gave him the city as his capital.

Juba and his wife Cleopatra, daughter of Mark Antony and Cleopatra of Egypt, rebuilt it on a lavish scale, with a grid of roads, a theatre, an art gallery and a lighthouse modelled on the Pharos of Alexandria. Their son Ptolemy was assassinated by Caligula in 40 CE, and Claudius sent legions to complete the conquest of Mauretania. By 44 most resistance had ended and the kingdom was divided into two provinces, one of them Mauretania Caesariensis, governed from Caesarea. The city became a Roman colony and reached a population of over 20,000, possibly 30,000.

It was the harbour of the Mauretanian Fleet, set up as a permanent force after Berber raids in the early 170s, and it had a hippodrome, an amphitheatre, temples and a basilica. Macrinus, a native of the city, became emperor in 217. A Berber revolt sacked the city in 371 and 372, and the Vandals ravaged it after 429. Its schools produced the grammarian Priscian. Byzantine forces under Belisarius brought it back under imperial rule after 533, but it declined. It fell to Umayyad forces in the late 7th century, and by the ninth century much of its defences were beyond repair. Hayreddin Barbarossa captured it in 1520, and the French took it in 1840 after a siege.

Cherchell, 89 kilometres west of Algiers, is the seat of Cherchell District in Tipaza Province. Its name is the French transcription of a Berber word meaning waterfall. It has industries in marble, plaster quarries and iron mines. The local museum displays ancient Greek and Roman antiquities, and the Mosque of the Hundred Columns, now a hospital, contains 89 diorite columns. Many statues found there are in the Museum of Antiquities in Algiers. The writer and film director Assia Djebar was born in Cherchell.
chernigov: Chernigov, in Ukrainian Chernihiv, stands on the upper right bank of the Desna River, about 150 kilometres north-north-east of Kyiv. Its name begins with the Slavic root for black; the medievalist Martin Dimnik connects it with the worship of a black god, Chernibog.

The city was a tribal centre of the Siverians and is first mentioned in the Rus'–Byzantine Treaty of 907, though the time of its founding is unknown. From the early 11th century it was the seat of the Principality of Chernigov, the largest in Kievan Rus, which reached Murom, Ryazan and Tmutarakan; its rulers at times vied with the Kievan grand princes and often took the seat at Kiev for themselves. The city's population peaked at about 25,000 before Batu Khan's hordes sacked it in 1239, and it then entered a long period of obscurity.

The area fell under the Grand Duchy of Lithuania in 1353. The Crimean khan Meñli I Giray burned the city in 1482 and 1497, and in the 15th to 17th centuries it passed several times between Lithuania, Muscovy and the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, which held it from 1618 to 1648. It received Magdeburg rights in 1623. After the Khmelnytsky Uprising it rose again as the base of a regiment of the Hetman State, and the Treaty of Andrusovo of 1667 ceded suzerainty over the area to the Tsardom of Russia.

After the Hetmanate was abolished, Chernigov became a provincial capital of the Russian Empire, as a governorate from 1808. In 1897 it had 27,006 inhabitants, 11,000 of them Jews. Under Soviet rule it industrialised, and it was severely damaged in the Second World War, during which the German army occupied it from 9 September 1941 to 21 September 1943.

Chernihiv is the administrative centre of Chernihiv Oblast, with 282,747 people. Its monuments record two flourishing periods, that of Kievan Rus in the 11th and 12th centuries and that of the Cossack Hetmanate in the late 17th and early 18th centuries. They include the Transfiguration Cathedral, commissioned in the early 1030s by Mstislav the Bold and one of the oldest churches in Ukraine. The historic centre has been on UNESCO's Tentative List since 1989.
chernobyl-disaster: Reactor 4 of the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant, near Pripyat in the Ukrainian SSR, was an RBMK reactor cooled by water circulated by electrically driven main pumps. More than 6% of the heat comes from radioactive decay, which goes on after fission stops, so cooling must continue to prevent the core from overheating.

The accident happened during a test meant to simulate the cooling of the reactor in a serious accident with a blackout. The operators carried out the test after an accidental drop in reactor power. Four of the eight main circulating pumps were to run on power from the coasting turbine. As the turbine slowed, the water flow fell and steam voids formed in the coolant.

The test began at 01:23:04 on 26 April 1986. The reactor was shut down in an unstable condition, and underlying design flaws led to a huge, uncontrollable power surge. The reactor components ruptured and lost coolant, and steam explosions and a meltdown destroyed the reactor building, followed by a core fire that spread radioactive contaminants across the Soviet Union and Europe. The explosion killed two engineers and severely burned two others.

Of 237 workers hospitalised, 134 showed symptoms of acute radiation syndrome, and 28 of them died within three months. Pripyat was not evacuated at once and its people were not warned during the night. An exclusion zone with a 10-kilometre radius was set up 36 hours after the accident and about 49,000 people were evacuated. It was later extended to 30 kilometres, and about 68,000 more people left. The Soviet government did not acknowledge the disaster until two days after the explosion.

The response involved more than 500,000 personnel. Workers removed an estimated 100 tonnes of debris from the roof, using about 60 remote-controlled robots designed mainly for lunar exploration or policing work, and the concrete sarcophagus was completed in December 1986. Pripyat was abandoned and replaced by the purpose-built city of Slavutych.

Estimates of the long-term toll vary: the United Nations puts deaths at up to 4,000 in Ukraine, Belarus and Russia, and other estimates reach 16,000 across Europe. By 2005 about 6,000 cases of childhood thyroid cancer had occurred in the affected populations, 15 of them fatal. The International Nuclear Safety Advisory Group blamed the operators' actions in its first report, in 1986, and the reactor's design in its revised report of 1992.
chernorizets-hrabar: Hrabar worked at the Preslav Literary School of the First Bulgarian Empire at the end of the 9th and the beginning of the 10th century. Chernorizets, literally a wearer of the black robe, was the lowest rank of the monastic hierarchy, and Hrabar is taken to be his given name, though it is sometimes translated as a nickname, the Brave. His identity and the authorship of his work have long been debated: the name has been explained as a pseudonym of another man of letters, such as Constantine, John the Exarch, Clement of Ohrid or even Tsar Simeon I of Bulgaria.

On the Letters, written in Old Church Slavonic, is the only work credited to him. Partly based on Greek scholia and grammatical treatises, it sets out the origin of the Glagolitic alphabet and of the Slavic translation of the Bible. It says that the pagan Slavs had read and divined by strokes and incisions, then after their baptism wrote their speech with Roman and Greek letters without any system, until God sent Constantine the Philosopher, called Cyril, who made them thirty-eight letters, some after the Greek and some for Slavic sounds.

The mention of strokes and incisions is important evidence for Slavonic palaeography; it may refer to a runic script, but no authentic example survives. Most scholars read the treatise as a defence of Slavonic against Greek criticism, while others see it as a defence of Glagolitic against Cyrillic.

The treatise survives in 79 copies in seven families of texts, plus four abridgements, probably all going back to a lost Glagolitic original that was changed as it was copied into Cyrillic. The families give the alphabet 38 letters, although the original Glagolitic alphabet had 36, as the acrostic of Constantine of Preslav attests. The oldest copy, in Lavrentiy's Miscellany, was made in 1348 by the monk Laurentius for Tsar Ivan Alexander of Bulgaria. Printed at Vilnius, Moscow, Saint Petersburg and Supraśl, it is the earliest printed work of an early Bulgarian author, included in a 1578 primer printed for East Slav readers. Hrabar Nunatak on Greenwich Island in Antarctica is named after him.
chernozem: Chernozem is a black soil containing a high percentage of humus, between 4% and 16%, and high percentages of phosphorus and ammonia compounds. Its name comes from the Russian words for black and for soil or earth. It is very fertile and, with its high capacity to store moisture, gives high agricultural yields, but prolonged farming depletes its nutrients as the humus decreases, so it still needs fertilisers.

Chernozem covers about 230 million hectares in two main belts. One is the Eurasian Steppe, which includes the Pontic-Caspian, Kazakh and Mongolian-Manchurian steppes. The other runs from the Canadian Prairies in Manitoba through the Great Plains of the United States as far south as Kansas. Its layer varies from a few centimetres to 1.5 metres thick.

Several explanations for its formation were proposed. Mikhail Lomonosov suggested in 1763 that it came from the decomposition of plants and animals; Sir Roderick Murchison argued in 1840 that it weathered from Jurassic marine shales, and Karl Eichwald in 1850 that it was lake sediment. In 1866 Franz Josef Ruprecht proposed decomposed steppe grasses, in 1929 Otto Schlüter proposed that it was man-made, and in 1999 Michael W. I. Schmidt proposed Neolithic burning of biomass.

No single reconstruction of past climate could explain the variations in chemistry found in the chernozems of central Europe. Charcoal is a prominent component of grassland soils in the Russian Steppe, the Great Plains and the Pampa, and burning of vegetation could account for chernozem's high magnetic susceptibility. The term therefore covers black soils of the same appearance but different histories of formation.

In 1883 the geologist Vasily Dokuchaev studied the steppe soils of the Poltava region in the Russian Empire. He found that the peasants named soils by colour, and he adopted such names. He was the first to describe the chernozem of the European part of the Russian Empire and to recognise its fertility, and he published Russian Chernozem, a complete study of the soil, in that year. It shares many chemical and physical properties with the terra preta of the Amazon rainforest, though it is classified separately.
chernyakhov-culture: The culture takes its name from Chernyakhov (Cherniakhiv), a site near Kyiv, and from Sântana de Mureș, a cemetery in Transylvania, the dual name reflecting the preferences of Soviet and Romanian scholarship. It replaced the Zarubintsy culture in the same territory; both were discovered by the Czech-Ukrainian archaeologist Vikentiy Khvoyka. In the 20th century its ethnic identity was fiercely debated. Soviet scholars such as Boris Rybakov saw in it the Proto-Slavs, while German historians and Polish archaeologists attributed it to the Goths. Scholars now see it as the meeting of many peoples, mostly those already in the region, such as the Sarmatians and Getae-Dacians.

Peter Heather argues that it reflects Gothic domination of the Pontic area, pointing to influences from the Wielbark culture near the Baltic and to Jordanes' tale of a Gothic migration under Filimer. Guy Halsall and Michael Kulikowski dispute the Wielbark link; Kulikowski holds that the Goths formed in place, as a product of the Roman frontier.

Its people were mainly settled farmers who grew wheat, barley and millet with ploughshares, sickles and scythes. Cattle were the chief livestock, horse breeding appears to have been limited to the open steppe, and metalworking was widespread, with local smiths making most tools. Pottery was mostly local, wheel-made from finer clay in forms recalling Sarmatian types refined by Roman and La Tène influence; Roman amphorae point to trade with the Roman world.

Both inhumation and cremation were practised. The dead were usually laid north to south with pottery, iron tools, bone combs, brooches, belt buckles and glass drinking vessels, but seldom weapons. Women were often buried with a brooch on each shoulder, as in the Wielbark culture. Over time burials moved towards inhumation without grave goods, which may reflect Christian influence or changing beliefs about the afterlife.

Its end is attributed to the arrival of the Huns. Around 370 the presence of the Huns on its eastern edge culminated in the death of Ermanaric, leader of the Gothic confederation, and his successor Athanaric took refuge south of the Danube with most of the Gothic population. Recent theories explain the collapse as the breakdown of the political hierarchy that held the culture together rather than as a displacement of people. It was followed by the Penkovka culture, and some local elements spread further after the Gothic elite fell, a change associated with the expansion of the early Slavs. A genetic study of 2019 suggested that three individuals tested represent its Gothic component.
cherokee: The Cherokee, who call themselves Aniyvwiya, meaning Principal People, are one of the Indigenous peoples of the Southeastern Woodlands. Before the 18th century they lived in towns along river valleys in what is now southwestern North Carolina, southeastern Tennessee, southwestern Virginia, parts of western South Carolina, northern Georgia and northeastern Alabama, with hunting grounds reaching into Kentucky, together about 40,000 square miles. Their language belongs to the Iroquoian family.

Scholars hold two main views of their origins. One is that they migrated to Southern Appalachia from the Great Lakes region in late prehistoric times, which the Cherokee oral tradition also supports. The other is that they had been in the Southeast for thousands of years and that proto-Iroquoian developed there. A Spanish expedition led by Hernando de Soto in 1540–1541 recorded a people called Chalaque around the Keowee River.

From 1710 to 1715 the Cherokee and Chickasaw allied with the British and fought the Shawnee, who were allied with the French, forcing them to move north. After the Cherokee–American wars the Cherokee lands between the Tennessee and Chattahoochee rivers remained independent, but the deerskin trade could no longer support the people on their reduced lands. Ravaged by smallpox and pressed by settlers, they adopted a representative government modelled on that of the United States, with an elected principal chief, senate and house of representatives, and the Cherokee Supreme Court was established by the 1820s. In the 1810s Sequoyah invented a syllabary for the language. Between 1898 and 1906 the federal government dissolved the former Cherokee Nation to make way for the state of Oklahoma.

The Cherokee were mainly farmers living in permanent towns. John Howard Payne, visiting in the 1830s, recorded elders' account of a society with a hereditary, priestly white organisation of elders representing the seven clans, and a red organisation of younger men responsible for warfare, which the Cherokee considered polluting. Women made decisions for the clan and kept its sacred knowledge. Slavery existed before European colonisation, mostly of enemy captives taken in raids, and was seen as a temporary status.

Today three Cherokee tribes are federally recognised: the Cherokee Nation and the United Keetoowah Band, both headquartered in Tahlequah, Oklahoma, and the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians, based on the Qualla Boundary in North Carolina.
cherokee-phoenix: In the mid-1820s the Cherokee were under pressure from the United States government, and from Georgia in particular, to move west of the Mississippi River or to give up their tribal government and territory. The General Council of the Cherokee Nation founded the paper to keep its people united and informed, working with the missionary Samuel Worcester, who cast the type for the syllabary. The council chose as editor Elias Boudinot, born Galagina Oowatie at Oothcaloga in 1804 and educated at the Foreign Mission School in Cornwall, Connecticut; he named the paper after the mythical bird reborn from the ashes of fire, as a symbol of renewal.

The first issue, of 21 February 1828, had four pages of five columns each; because translation was slow, only three columns a week were at first to be in Cherokee. Worcester wrote in praise of Sequoyah's invention of the syllabary, and Boudinot's first editorial criticised white settlers who wanted Cherokee land. According to Langguth, readers of Cherokee alone received the paper free, while English readers paid $2.50 a year in advance or $3.50 if they waited a year. A fund-raising and publicity tour drew subscribers from almost all of the United States and Europe, and Boudinot came to publish mostly in English.

In 1829 he renamed the paper the Cherokee Phoenix and Indians' Advocate, reflecting his wish to reach a wider audience, and covered the issues of assimilation and removal that Indians faced across the country, the debates over Indian removal and the Supreme Court cases that affected Indian life.

Boudinot came to think removal inevitable and, with Major Ridge, favoured protecting Cherokee rights by treaty. Most Cherokee, including Principal Chief John Ross, opposed him, and Ross forbade pro-removal arguments in a paper meant to express the leadership's positions; Boudinot resigned in protest in the spring of 1832, and Ross's brother-in-law Elijah Hicks replaced him. The paper ceased when the federal government failed to pay the Cherokee annuity in 1834, and in August 1835 the Georgia Guard took the press. It appeared intermittently after removal to Indian Territory and has been revived by the Cherokee Nation at Tahlequah, Oklahoma, in print and online.
cherrapunji: Cherrapunji, also called Sohra, stands at an average elevation of 1,430 metres on a plateau in the southern part of the Khasi Hills, facing the plains of Bangladesh. Rain comes from the Bay of Bengal arm of the Indian summer monsoon. The clouds cross about 400 km of plain and then meet the hills, which rise abruptly to about 1,370 metres within 2 to 5 km. Deep valleys funnel the low, moisture-laden clouds together over Sohra, and the steep slopes force them upward, so that the vapour cools and condenses. Sohra holds the record for the most rainfall in a calendar month, 9,300 millimetres in July 1861, and for the most in a year, between August 1860 and July 1861.

The history of the Khasi people, the native inhabitants of Sohra, can be traced from the early 16th century. Between the 16th and 18th centuries they were ruled by their tribal chiefs, the Syiems of Khyriem, and Sohra was the traditional capital of the Khasi kingdom of ka hima Sohra. Khasi society is matrilineal, and children take their mother's surname. The Khasi Hills came under British authority in 1833, when Tirot Sing Syiem, the last of the important Syiems, submitted. The 19th-century British mispronounced the name Sohra as Cherra, and people from the plains later added the Bengali suffix punjee, 'a cluster of villages'. The town has since been officially renamed Sohra.

Sohra is a sub-divisional town in the East Khasi Hills district of Meghalaya. Despite its rainfall it has long had a shortage of drinking water, since heavy rain washes the topsoil from the deforested plateau. Tourism is its main economic activity. The villages near the town are known for living root bridges, which people have grown from the roots of trees over hundreds of years. Each takes 10 to 15 years to grow, and the oldest still in use is over 500 years old.
chertsey-abbey: The abbey was dedicated to St Peter. Its founder, Saint Erkenwald, was its first abbot and from 675 Bishop of London, and at the same time he founded Barking Abbey on the Thames east of London, where his sister Saint Ethelburga was the first abbess. When the Danes attacked Chertsey in the 9th century many monks were killed; the abbot then, Beocca, and those slain with him were remembered as Saint Beocca, Saint Ethor and the Martyrs of Chertsey, and William of Malmesbury recorded their deaths.

King Edgar of England refounded the monastery from Abingdon Abbey in 964. In the eleventh century the monks dug the Abbey River as an offshoot of the River Thames to drive the abbey's watermill. In the late Middle Ages the abbey became known as the burial place of King Henry VI, whose body was later moved to St George's Chapel, Windsor; William Shakespeare recalls it in Richard III, where Lady Anne says, "Come now towards Chertsey with your holy load". Among the abbots were John de Rutherwyk, abbot 1307–46, and John Corderoy in 1537.

After the commissioners of King Henry VIII dissolved the house in 1537, the community moved to Bisham Abbey in Berkshire. The site went to Sir William Fitzwilliam, and in 1602 Dr John Hammond, physician to the royal household under James I, bought it. His son Thomas Hammond, a lieutenant colonel of the New Model Army, sat as a commissioner at the trial of Charles I but did not sign the death warrant. In the mid-19th century the architect and archaeologist Samuel Angell excavated the site and in 1862 published an account with a ground plan of the abbey church.

Only slight traces remain among later buildings, but local names such as Abbey River, Monk's Walk and Abbey Fields keep its memory. Fine medieval tiles from the abbey, some showing the legend of Tristan and Iseult, are in the British Museum. Individual letter tiles of the second half of the 13th century, set together to form religious inscriptions on the floor, have been seen as a forerunner of printing with movable type.

A bell cast at Wokingham around 1380, weighing just over half a ton, still rings as the fifth of eight at St Peter's church, Chertsey. A stained glass panel with the abbey's arms is in the Burrell Collection near Glasgow, the crossed keys of Saint Peter from those arms appear on the banner of Surrey County Council, and the Chertsey Breviary of about 1300 is in the Bodleian Library at Oxford.
cherven-towns: The name comes from the gord of Cherven, the region's main town, which historians identify with the stronghold beside the village of Czermno in Tomaszów Lubelski County, in easternmost Poland. Cherven is derived from the Slavic word for worm, after the larvae of the insect Porphyrophora polonica, from which a valued red dye was made for export to Byzantium. The name was later read as the word for red, which gave rise to the names Red Towns and Red Ruthenia.

The extent of the region is not entirely clear. Written sources name only the strongholds of Przemyśl and Cherven. The name probably first meant a territory between the Bug and Wieprz rivers, west of the Bug and east of the Kraków region, and it may have included the lands of Chełm.

Before the Rus' conquest the borderland lay between several powers. Cosmas of Prague relates that the Přemyslid rulers of Bohemia controlled the land of Kraków until 999, and the traveller Abraham ben Jacob wrote in 965 that Boleslaus II of Bohemia ruled from Prague to Kraków. Historians assume that Mieszko I of Poland took over the region in the 970s. Polish and Ukrainian-Russian historiography dispute the tribe of its people, West Slavic or East Slavic, and their independence of both Poland and Rus'; the historian Leontii Voitovych has speculated that they may have formed an independent tribal union with some vassalage to Bohemia.

The towns were taken by the Polish prince Bolesław I the Brave in 1018. In the campaign of 1031 that won them back for Grand Prince Yaroslav the Wise, Harald, chief of Yaroslav's bodyguard, fought in his army, and between 1034 and 1039 Yaroslav most likely founded the gord of Sutiejsk to guard the border with Poland. In 1085 the region became the Principality of Peremyshl under the lordship of Rus'.

In 1240 the region was conquered by the Golden Horde, and the Cherven Cities appear in written sources for the last time in 1289. King Casimir III the Great acquired the territory for the Kingdom of Poland in 1340. From the 15th century the term Red Ruthenia, taken from the misread name of the towns, was used for the new Ruthenian Voivodeship, which took in the Chełm and Przemyśl regions as well as those of Lviv and Halych.
chesapeake-bay: The Chesapeake Bay lies in the Mid-Atlantic region, separated from the Atlantic Ocean mainly by the Delmarva Peninsula. Its mouth is between Cape Henry and Cape Charles. More than 150 major rivers and streams flow through its drainage basin, which covers parts of six states and all of Washington, D.C. The bay is 2.8 miles (4.5 km) wide at its narrowest and 30 miles (48 km) at its widest, and its average depth is 21 feet (6.4 m). It is the drowned valley of the Susquehanna River, where the river once flowed when sea level was lower. The name comes from an Algonquian word, Chesepiooc, referring to a village at a big river.

Paleoindians may have lived around the bay 11,000 years ago. For thousands of years Native American societies lived in villages of wooden longhouses near the water, where they fished and farmed beans, corn, tobacco and squash. Later, communities formed confederations such as the Powhatan, the Piscataway and the Nanticoke, each led by a central chief.

Giovanni da Verrazzano sailed past the bay in 1524 in the service of the French crown. Spanish Jesuits founded the short-lived Ajacan Mission on a Chesapeake tributary in 1570. In 1781 the bay was the site of the Battle of the Chesapeake, or Battle of the Capes, in which a French fleet defeated the Royal Navy in the decisive naval battle of the American Revolutionary War. The victory allowed George Washington and the Comte de Rochambeau to trap Lord Cornwallis's army at Yorktown, Virginia.

The bay forms a link in the Intracoastal Waterway, joined to the Delaware River by the Chesapeake and Delaware Canal. A shipping channel, dredged by the US Army Corps of Engineers since the 1850s, serves the Port of Baltimore. Two bridges span the bay, the Chesapeake Bay Bridge in Maryland and the Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel in Virginia. It is known for blue crabs, clams and oysters. In the 1970s it was found to contain one of the first identified marine dead zones, and a report of 1983 called it an ecosystem in decline. More than 1,800 wrecks of ships and boats lie on its bed.
cheshire: Cheshire covers 905 square miles (2,344 km2), between Merseyside, Greater Manchester, Derbyshire, Staffordshire, Shropshire and the Welsh counties of Flintshire and Wrexham, with a short coastline on the Dee Estuary. The Cheshire Plain, flat land of glacial till left by the retreat of a Quaternary ice sheet, is dotted with meres, the water-filled kettle holes. To the east the land rises to the Pennines and part of the Peak District. The bedrock is almost entirely red Triassic sandstone, quarried at Runcorn and used for Liverpool Cathedral, Chester Cathedral and Beeston Castle.

The name was first recorded in 980 as Legeceasterscir in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, 'the shire of the city of legions', after Chester; the county is thought to have been created by Edward the Elder around 920. After 1066 local resistance was put down in 1069 as part of the Harrying of the North, and the lands of landowners such as Earl Edwin of Mercia were given to Norman barons. William I made Cheshire a county palatine. Hugh d'Avranches, nicknamed Hugh Lupus, became Earl of Chester about 1070, with autonomous powers on the Welsh Marches. Magna Carta did not apply to the shire, so the earl issued his own Chester Charter.

In 1397 Richard II added lands in the Welsh march and raised Cheshire to a principality, in reward for the support of the Cheshire Guard, his standing force of about 500 men. It lost the rank on his fall in 1399.

Cheshire is a ceremonial county of North West England with a population of 1,139,884 in 2024; its largest settlement is Warrington and the city of Chester lies in the west. Four unitary authorities carry out local government: Cheshire East, Cheshire West and Chester, Halton and Warrington. The county council was abolished on 1 April 2009. The county is known for Cheshire cheese, salt and silk, and its farming is based mainly on dairying. Iron Age hill forts and the Roman fortress and walls of Chester survive, and Lewis Carroll named the Cheshire Cat after the county.
chester: Chester lies on the River Dee, very close to the England-Wales border, at the southern end of a two-mile sandstone ridge that rises to 42 metres within a natural S-bend of the river. The eastern and northern parts of the area were heathland and forest, and the western side towards the Dee Estuary was marsh. It is the historic county town of Cheshire.

The Roman Legio II Adiutrix founded Chester in the 70s CE, during the reign of Vespasian, as a fort named Deva Victrix, on land of the Celtic Cornovii. Deva was named for the goddess of the Dee or from the British name of the river, and Victrix came from the Legio XX Valeria Victrix, based there. Its four main roads, Eastgate, Northgate, Watergate and Bridge Street, follow routes laid out then.

After the Romans withdrew, Chester is thought to have become part of the kingdom of Powys. In 689 King Æthelred of Mercia founded the Minster Church of West Mercia, later Chester's first cathedral, and the Angles strengthened the walls against the Danes. It was one of the last cities in England to fall to the Normans, and William the Conqueror ordered a castle built there. It received city status in 1541, and in 1643 the Parliamentarians subdued it in the Civil War.

The city walls of Chester are the most complete in Britain. The circuit measures nearly two miles and is broken only in the south-west, and the walls have Grade I listed status. A footpath runs along the top, and above Eastgate stands Eastgate Clock. Many of the black-and-white buildings are Victorian restorations of the Black-and-white Revival. The Grosvenor Museum holds a collection of Roman tombstones.
chester-le-street: Chester-le-Street is a market town in County Durham, about 6 miles north of Durham and 9 miles south of Newcastle upon Tyne. The Romans built a fort there, named Concangis, around 100 CE, alongside the Roman road later known as Cade's Road and close to the River Wear. It was occupied until the Romans left Britain in 410. The Chester of the town's name comes from the Latin castra, and the Street from the paved Roman road that ran north to south through the town.

In 883 a group of monks driven out of Lindisfarne seven years earlier chose a base at Chester-le-Street, having been given a church by the Danish king Guthred. They built a shrine to St Cuthbert, whose body they had carried with them, and the church became the seat of the Bishop of Lindisfarne. The body remained for 112 years, until the community left in 995 for a safer home at Durham. In the 10th century Aldred the Scribe, provost of Chester-le-Street, added an Old English translation of the Gospels as a word-for-word gloss between the lines of the Latin Vulgate text.

The church was rebuilt in stone in 1054. In 1080 most of the huts in the town were burned and many people killed in retaliation for the death of Walcher, the first prince-bishop, at the hands of an English mob. The town is not recorded in the Domesday Book of 1086. Cade's Road lay beneath the later Great North Road, the main route from London to Newcastle and Edinburgh, and inns sprang up to serve travellers. The coaching trade peaked in the early 19th century, and coal was dug in increasing quantities from the late 17th century. The population in 1841 was 2,599. On 5 October 1936 the Jarrow marchers stopped in the town after their first day's walk.

The parish church of St Mary and St Cuthbert has a rare surviving 14th-century anchorage, occupied by six anchorites from 1383 to about 1538, and now a museum. Lumley Castle, built in 1389, overlooks the town from the east bank of the Wear. The Chester Burn viaduct, completed in 1868 for the North Eastern Railway, has 11 arches, and the railway station on the East Coast Main Line opened in the same year. The 2021 census recorded a population of 23,555.
chetniks: Small-scale guerrilla warfare has a long history in the South Slav lands that were under Ottoman rule. Bandit companies took part in the First Serbian Uprising, which began in 1804. Chetnik veterans of the fighting since 1904 became leading Serbian patriotic groups in the new Yugoslav state, and in 1921 they organised the Chetnik Association for the Freedom and Honor of the Fatherland in Belgrade.

In April 1940 the Yugoslav General Staff set up a Chetnik Command of six battalions. After the Axis invasion of April 1941, Draža Mihailović began his own movement in May, and its ideology was set out in a series of documents. Stevan Moljević's memorandum Homogeneous Serbia of June 1941 proposed a Greater Serbia of 65 to 70 per cent of Yugoslav territory, with large-scale population transfers.

The Chetniks took part in the uprising in German-occupied Serbia from July to December 1941. The Germans then applied a ratio of 100 hostages executed for every soldier killed, and in October 1941 massacres at Kraljevo and Kragujevac killed over 4,500 civilians, mostly Serbs. Mihailović concluded that attacks on German troops would only bring more deaths, scaled them back and waited for an Allied landing.

The movement drifted into collaboration with the Axis: first with the puppet government in Serbia, then with the Italians in Dalmatia and Montenegro, and after the Italian capitulation in September 1943 with the Germans directly. The Chetniks called this using the enemy. They also fought the Yugoslav Partisans, and the Western Allies eventually withdrew their support.

Chetnik units used terror against Croats, against Muslims in Bosnia, Herzegovina and Sandžak, and against the Partisans. Estimates of the deaths they caused in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina range from 50,000 to 68,000, and about 300 villages and small towns were destroyed. Several historians regard these acts as genocide. Mihailović disapproved of some of them but lacked control over local commanders.

In April and May 1945 many Chetniks retreated towards Italy and Austria. Some were returned by British forces or killed in the Bleiburg repatriations, and many captured members were tried or executed. Mihailović was captured, tried in Belgrade and executed in July 1946. Small Chetnik groups continued an insurgency against the Communist regime until 1950.
cheyenne: The Cheyenne are made up of two tribes, the Tsitsistas and the Suhtai, which merged in the early 19th century; the Suhtai, whose speech and customs differed slightly, travelled with the Tsitsistas and joined them after 1832. The name Cheyenne comes from a Lakota word, Šahíyena, 'little Šahíya', whose meaning is uncertain. Their earliest written record dates from the mid-17th century, when a group visited the French Fort Crevecoeur, near present-day Peoria, Illinois. They then lived between the Mississippi River and Mille Lacs Lake in Minnesota, collecting wild rice and hunting bison. Tribal history says the Assiniboine drove them to Minnesota and North Dakota, where they built villages such as Biesterfeldt on the Sheyenne River. They first reached the Missouri River in 1676.

Pushed west by the Lakota, the Cheyenne formally allied with the Arapaho around 1811, and the alliance helped them expand their territory over much of the central Plains. By 1820 traders reported them at present-day Denver and on the Arkansas River. After Bent's Fort was built, a large part of the tribe moved south and became the Southern Cheyenne, while the rest stayed on the North Platte and Yellowstone headwaters as the Northern Cheyenne. Emigrant traffic along the trails from the 1840s increased competition for water and game, and cholera in 1849 killed about 2,000 Cheyenne, one-half to two-thirds of their population.

The Cheyenne fought the United States Army for over two decades from 1856. With the Arapaho and Lakota they fought in Red Cloud's War and the Great Sioux War of 1876, and a peaceful encampment of mostly women, children and elderly was massacred by US soldiers at Sand Creek. A reservation on the Tongue River, now the Northern Cheyenne Indian Reservation, was created by executive order on 16 November 1884 and extended in 1900. Along with the Lakota and Apache, the Cheyenne were among the last nations forced onto reservations.

Today the Cheyenne are two federally recognised nations: the Northern Cheyenne in Montana and the Southern Cheyenne, who form the Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes in Oklahoma with the Southern Arapaho. Historical figures include Black Kettle, Dull Knife, Little Wolf, Roman Nose and Two Moons, and the historian George Bent. The Southern Cheyenne artist Oakerhater is a canonised saint of the Episcopal Church.

The Cheyenne were a horse and warrior people. A warrior was also a protector, provider and leader, and men gained rank by counting coups, acts of bravery in battle. Their government was centred on the Arrow Keeper and the Council of Forty-Four, with four delegates from each of ten principal bands; the council also regulated the military societies. Women tanned hides and made lodges and clothing, and gathered roots and berries. The Cheyenne language belongs to the Algonquian family.
chhatrasal: Chhatrasal was born on 4 May 1649 at Kachar Kachnai in Tikamgarh, into a Bundela Rajput family, the son of Champat Rai and Sarandha and a descendant of Rudra Pratap Singh of Orchha. He was 12 when the Mughals killed his father, Champat Rai of Mahoba, in the reign of Aurangzeb. He wished to join Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj in Maharashtra, but Shivaji encouraged him to fight for independence in Bundelkhand instead.

In 1671, at the age of 22, Chhatrasal raised the banner of revolt in Bundelkhand with an army of 5 horsemen and 25 swordsmen. He was known as Maharaja of Panna, or of Bundelkhand, from 1675. He held out against the Mughals until Muhammad Khan Bangash attacked him in December 1728. At 79 he led his army against Bangash, was defeated after a hard battle and retreated to his fort at Jaitpur, where the Mughals besieged him and took most of his lands.

He appealed several times to the Peshwa Baji Rao I, writing that he was like the elephant caught by the crocodile and that his race was close to extinction. In March 1729 Baji Rao led his army into Bundelkhand and cut the Mughal supplies with his cavalry. Refused help by the emperor, Bangash negotiated and was allowed to withdraw on condition that he never again attack Bundelkhand. Chhatrasal rewarded the Peshwa with lands and diamond mines that opened Central and North India to the Marathas. Baji Rao's second wife, Mastani, was Chhatrasal's daughter by his concubine Ruhani Begum.

Chhatrasal was a patron of poets, whose eulogies by Kavi Bhushan, Lal Kavi, Bakhshi Hansaraj and others spread his fame, and he contributed to the Jain temples of Kundalpur. Before his death on 20 December 1731 he divided his kingdom: Baji Rao received a third, worth 30 lakhs of revenue, his eldest son Harde Sah of Panna lands worth 38 lakhs, and his second son Jagat Raj of Banda lands worth 30 lakhs, with smaller grants to the younger sons. The town and district of Chhatarpur in Madhya Pradesh are named after him, as are the Chhatrasal Stadium in Delhi and a museum, and he is the subject of the film Veer Chhatrasal of 1971.
chhattisgarh: In ancient times the region was known as Dakshina Kosala, South Kosala, the native place of Rama's mother Kausalya. In the post-Vedic period the Pulinda tribe dominated part of it. The Sitabenga Caves, among the earliest examples of theatre architecture in India, are dated to the Mauryan period of the 3rd century BCE. From the 6th to the 12th centuries the region was split between rival dynasties, and parts of it were briefly under the Chola dynasty in the 11th century. Most of it was then consolidated under the Haihaiyavansi kingdom, whose rule lasted about 700 years until it came under the suzerainty of the Maratha Empire in the 1740s.

The name Chhattisgarh was popularised under the Maratha Empire and was first used in an official document in 1795. The Bhonsles of Nagpur ruled the region until 1845, when the East India Company annexed it. It was then administered until 1947 as the Chhattisgarh Division of the Central Provinces, and Raipur gained prominence over the earlier capital Ratanpur. Some areas that make up the present state were princely states, later merged into Madhya Pradesh.

The States Reorganisation Act of 1956 placed Chhattisgarh in Madhya Pradesh, where it remained for 44 years. A demand for a separate state was first raised in the 1920s, by the Raipur Congress unit in 1924, and was discussed at the Indian Congress at Tripuri. It was put to the States Reorganisation Commission in 1954 and rejected. No well-organised movement was ever started, and the campaigns took the form of petitions, public meetings, seminars, rallies and strikes. Chhattisgarh was granted statehood on 1 November 2000, with Raipur as its capital.

Chhattisgarh is a landlocked state in east-central India with a population of roughly 30 million. Its northern and southern parts are hilly and the centre is a fertile plain, with forests covering a large share of the state. Hindi and Chhattisgarhi are its official languages, and Scheduled Tribes such as the Gond, Halba and Oraon make up about 30 percent of the population, mainly in the forests of Bastar. The state is known as the rice bowl of India and holds large coal reserves, including the open-cast mines at Korba.
chhau-dance: Chhau, also spelled Chhou, is a semi-classical dance with martial and folk traditions. It may be a syncretic form that emerged from a fusion of classical Hindu dances and the traditions of ancient regional tribes. Its name may derive from the Sanskrit chaya, meaning shadow, image or mask, or from chadma, disguise. Sitakant Mahapatra suggests instead the Odia chhauni, meaning military camp, armour or stealth. The precursors of the Purulia style were the Paika and Natua traditions, and the Nachni dance also shaped it, giving Chhau its female gaits and movements, while the vigorous male movement is attributed to the tandava style of Shiva.

The dance is traditionally performed by all-male troupes, at night in an open space called an akhada or asar, to folk music played on the reed pipes mohuri and shehnai, with drums such as the dhol and the large kettle drum dhumsa. Its themes include local legends, folklore and episodes from the Ramayana, the Mahabharata and the Puranas.

The two masked styles blend dance with martial practice, using mock combat called khel, stylised gaits of birds and animals called chalis and topkas, and movements based on the chores of village housewives called uflis. Mohan Khokar states that this form has no ritual meaning and is community celebration and entertainment. Knowledge of dance, music and mask-making is passed on orally.

The three styles are named after the places where they are performed. Seraikella Chhau developed in Seraikela, in Jharkhand, and its technique and repertoire were shaped by the local nobility, who were both its performers and choreographers. Purulia Chhau, in West Bengal, uses large masks shaped like the character, so that a lion has a lion's face and walks on all fours, and Mayurbhanj Chhau, in Odisha, uses none, though technically it is similar to Seraikella. Dancers in the northern Odisha style do wear masks when they first appear to introduce themselves.

Purulia masks are made by the Sutradhar community from layers of paper and glue on a clay mould, then coloured and decorated, and the Purulia mask is registered as a Geographical Indication. Chhau was inscribed in UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2010. The Government of Odisha founded the Government Chhau Dance Centre at Seraikella in 1960 and the Mayurbhanj Chhau Nritya Pratisthan at Baripada in 1962, and the Sangeet Natak Akademi has set up a National Centre for Chhau Dance at Baripada.
chhindwara-district: Chhindwara district lies in the south-west of the Satpura Range, in the south of Madhya Pradesh, and is part of the Jabalpur division. It borders Nagpur district in Maharashtra and Pandhurna district to the south, Narmadapuram and Narsinghpur districts to the north, Betul district to the west and Seoni district to the east. Its altitude runs from about 470 to 1,160 metres. The Kanhan, the Pench, the Jam and other rivers cross it. The name comes from chhind, the local name of a common tree. The climate is subtropical, with a hot dry summer, monsoon rains from July to September and a cool winter.

The early history of the district is poorly documented. Copper-plate inscriptions suggest that the Vakatakas held power until the third century CE, and the south was ruled for several centuries by the Rashtrakutas. The Gond dynasties emerged in the fourteenth century. According to legend, Jatba, founder of the Gond dynasty, killed the Gauli chiefs Ransur and Ghamsur during a temple festival and so established Gond rule. Deogarh, on the Chhindwara plateau, is believed to have been the last seat of Gauli power, and for a time its kingdom was the most powerful of the four Gond states. It later became a tribute-paying sarkar under the Mughal administration of the Berar subah.

King Bakht Buland, one of its most powerful rulers, adopted Islam in the reign of Aurangzeb and conquered extensive territory from Mandla and Chanda. After a succession dispute the Marathas took Deogarh into the territories of the Bhonsles of Nagpur. On 17 September 1803 the British East India Company defeated Raghoji II Bhonsle, and in 1853 the territory was annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse. The district was formed on 1 November 1956, when Maharashtra was created and took Nagpur.

Chhindwara town is the district headquarters. At the 2011 census the district had 2,090,922 people, of whom 36.82 percent belonged to Scheduled Tribes. Hindi is the main language, while Gondi and Korku, spoken by shrinking minorities, are highly endangered, as is the little-known Bhariati language of Patalkot. Notable sites include the Tamia Hills and Deogarh Fort.
chiang-ching-kuo: Chiang was born on 27 April 1910 at Fenghua in Zhejiang, the eldest son of Chiang Kai-shek. In 1925, when the Kuomintang and the Communist Party were allied, he was sent to Moscow Sun Yat-sen University, where he was placed in a study group with Deng Xiaoping. After his father broke with the Communists in 1927, he publicly denounced him. The Soviet authorities then refused his repeated requests to return home, and he worked in an electrical plant and at the Uralmash heavy machinery plant, where in 1935 he married Faina Vakhreva. Stalin allowed him to return to China in 1937.

In 1948 he was sent to Shanghai to enforce price controls during the gold yuan currency reform, which failed, and he resigned. In 1949 he moved to Taiwan when the Kuomintang lost the Chinese Civil War. He directed the Taiwan Garrison Command, the military secret police, which used arbitrary arrests and torture during the White Terror. He became minister of defence in 1965, premier in 1972 and chairman of the Kuomintang after his father's death in 1975. The National Assembly elected him president on 21 March 1978.

He is credited with the Ten Major Construction Projects, an anti-corruption campaign and the promotion of native Taiwanese into government. After a pro-democracy rally at Kaohsiung on 10 December 1979 turned violent, opposition leaders were tried by a military court. When the Democratic Progressive Party was founded on 28 September 1986, he did not dissolve it. He ended martial law on 15 July 1987 after 39 years, and in the same year lifted the ban on travel to the mainland.

Chiang died of a heart attack on 13 January 1988, aged 77, and Lee Teng-hui succeeded him. Assessments differ. Some credit him with democratising Taiwan and with economic growth. Others point to the White Terror, the Kaohsiung Incident and the 1984 murder in California of the journalist Henry Liu by Taiwanese military intelligence operatives, and argue that his late reforms came mainly under pressure from Taiwanese citizens, the United States and diplomatic setbacks.
chiang-kai-shek: Chiang was born on 31 October 1887 in Xikou, then a small village about 48 km south of Ningbo, into a family of merchants. His father ran the family salt business, and his mother was a devout Buddhist, the daughter of a Buddhist monk. He received a military education in China and Japan, settling in Tokyo for its reputation as the centre of Japanese military science and for its exiled Chinese revolutionaries. There he became close to Chen Qimei, who recommended him for the Tongmenghui; he swore allegiance to the Three Principles of the People in 1908.

In 1920 Sun Yat-sen appointed Chiang chief of staff of the Second Guangdong Army, and from 1924 he was commandant of the Whampoa Military Academy. After Sun died on 12 March 1925, Chiang became one of the principal figures in a struggle for the succession in Guangzhou. He was appointed commander-in-chief of the Northern Expedition in June 1926, and by the end of October its army had occupied Wuhan. On 12 April troops and armed Green Gang groups attacked Communist-aligned workers' organisations in Shanghai, killing resisters and arresting many. Chiang proclaimed a rival Nationalist government at Nanjing on 18 April.

The Xi'an Incident of 1936 forced him into a Second United Front with the Communists. When the Second Sino-Japanese War broke out in July 1937 he sent 600,000 of his best soldiers to defend Shanghai, losing over 200,000 men. Nanjing fell in December, and he moved the government inland, first to Wuhan and later to Chongqing. In 1949 his Kuomintang was defeated by Mao Zedong's Communists and retreated to Taiwan, where he resumed his duties as president on 1 March 1950.

On Taiwan Chiang imposed martial law and a White Terror, which lasted until 1987 and 1992 respectively. He remained president of the Republic of China until his death on 5 April 1975, presiding over land reform and economic growth. Supporters credit him with unifying the nation and leading the resistance against Japan. Critics fault him for early appeasement of Japan, the deliberate flooding of the Yellow River, corruption and authoritarian rule on both the mainland and Taiwan.
chiang-rai: Chiang Rai lies on the flat alluvial plain of the Kok River, a tributary of the Mekong, between the Daen Lao Range in the north and the Phi Pan Nam Range in the south. The Kok flows along the north side of the city and joins the Mekong about 40 kilometres to the north-east. The Lao River, a tributary of the Kok, runs south of the city. Limestone hills rise to the west and north-west, and most of the region's hill peoples, such as the Karen, Akha, Lisu, Miao and Hmong, have their villages in that direction. The Golden Triangle, where the borders of Thailand, Laos and Myanmar meet, is 55 kilometres to the north-east.

King Mangrai founded the city in 1262 as a capital, and it became the seat of the Mangrai Dynasty. Chiang means city, so the name means the city of Mangrai. It was later conquered by Burma and stayed under Burmese rule for several hundred years. In 1786 it became a vassal of Siam. Siam annexed the Kingdom of Chiang Mai in 1893 as a Monthon, which Chiang Rai joined in 1910, and Chiang Rai became a full province of Thailand in 1933.

In 1432, in the reign of King Sam Fang Kaen (1402 to 1441), the Emerald Buddha, the most revered Buddha statue in Thailand, was found at Chiang Rai. According to one account an earthquake split the chedi at Wat Phra Kaeo and revealed a jade figure inside. Another telling says the statue had been hastily covered in mud just before marauders came to pillage, and that the earthquake broke off a piece of the clay. In 1992 the city pillar was moved from Wat Klang Wiang to Wat Phra That Doi Chom Thong, where it is known as Sadue Mueang, the navel of the city.

Chiang Rai is the capital and business centre of Chiang Rai Province and the northernmost major city of Thailand. It lies about 860 kilometres north of Bangkok and about 200 kilometres north-east of Chiang Mai, and Route 1 links it with Mae Sai on the border with Myanmar. Its temples include Wat Phra Kaeo, Wat Phra Sing and Wat Phra That Doi Chom Thong, and the modern Wat Rong Khun, built since 1998 by the artist Chalermchai Kositpipat. Mae Fah Luang University has a campus there. Chiang Rai is recognised as a Design City by the UNESCO Creative Cities Network.
chiang-saen: Chiang Saen, capital of the Chiang Saen district in the north of Chiang Rai province, lies about 60 kilometres north-east of the provincial capital, Chiang Rai. It stands on the west bank of the Mekong, opposite Laos, in the plain of the lower Kok River, which joins the Mekong about five kilometres to the south. Finds shown in the Chiang Saen National Museum prove the area was inhabited in prehistoric times.

Chronicles describe Ngoenyang, probably the first major city of the area, on a trade route from northern Thailand to Yunnan. Its ruler made a marriage alliance with Chiang Hung, now Jinghong, and into this family Mangrai, later king of Lan Na, was born in 1239. Ngoenyang no longer exists, though its name is still used interchangeably with Chiang Saen.

The city was founded in 1329 by Saenphu, a grandson of Mangrai, and first called Mueang Roi. An irregular rectangle of about 3,000 by 1,400 metres, it had the Mekong on one side and a moat and earth wall on the other three, with five gates and eight watchtowers. Saenphu made his son Khamfu governor of Chiang Mai, retired to the new city, which has borne his name since, and died there in 1334.

During Burmese rule over Lan Na from 1558 to 1774 the Burmese built a fort at Chiang Saen, which became their military and political centre in the 18th century and the seat of a governor, the myowun. In 1804 Siamese troops, with the armies of King Kawila of Chiang Mai and Prince Atthawarapanyo of Nan, took it for King Rama I, who had the city destroyed except for its religious sites and its Tai Yuan people deported as forced labourers to the central plain.

The British surveyor Holt Samuel Hallett found the city deserted in 1876; it was refounded in 1881 under King Rama V with families from Lamphun, Lampang and Chiang Mai. Only part of the old town is inhabited, and of its five gates only the Chiang Saen Gate has been restored. Its monuments include the chedi of Wat Pa Sak, in the Mon style, and the 88-metre octagonal chedi of Wat Phra That Chedi Luang.
chiapas: Chiapas is the southernmost state of Mexico. It borders Oaxaca, Veracruz and Tabasco and, to the east and south-east, Guatemala, and it has a long Pacific coastline. Its climate is humid and tropical but is moderated by altitude, and several parallel mountain ranges run through the centre, with cloud forests such as that of the El Triunfo biosphere reserve. The state is among the larger in Mexico, with a territory of 74,415 km2. Its capital and largest city is Tuxtla Gutiérrez.

Hunter-gatherers began to occupy the central valley around 7000 BCE, and agricultural villages appeared across the state between 1800 BCE and 300 CE. The coastal Soconusco region holds the oldest sites, including the Mokaya culture, described as the oldest ceramic culture of Mesoamerica, and Paso de la Amada, with the oldest Mesoamerican ballcourt. Later the Maya built Palenque, Yaxchilán, Bonampak and Toniná. The Bonampak murals are the only Mesoamerican murals preserved for over 1,500 years.

The Spanish found Maya and non-Maya peoples, the latter dominated by the Zoques and the Chiapanecas. Hernán Cortés sent tax collectors in 1522, and Luis Marín led the first military incursion in 1523. Many Tzotzils resisted fiercely in the highlands, and under Diego de Mazariegos many natives preferred suicide to submission, as at the Battle of Tepetchia, where some jumped into the Sumidero Canyon. The diocese was founded in 1538, and Bartolomé de las Casas was its best-known bishop. Because it lacked mineral wealth and was remote and rugged, Chiapas was spared the battles of independence.

In the late 19th century Governor Emilio Rabasa took on the regional caciques and in 1892 moved the capital from San Cristóbal de las Casas to Tuxtla. Estates grew coffee and other cash crops, and recruiters used a debt practice called enganche that trapped workers in a kind of indentured servitude. In January 1994 the Zapatista Army of National Liberation began an armed struggle, rooted in rural poverty and in opposition to Mexico's economic liberalisation.

Chiapas is one of the 32 federal entities of Mexico. It has one of the largest indigenous populations in the country, with twelve federally recognised ethnicities. Its rivers supply a large share of Mexican hydroelectric power, and it is a major producer of coffee and cacao. The marimba is its most important instrument, and its Maya sites draw visitors.
chiaramonte-family: The family's rise began in the 13th century with the marriage of Manfredi I Chiaramonte, also called Manfredi il Vecchio, to Isabella Mosca, which united the two Sicilian counties of Modica and Ragusa. Around 1307–1320 the couple built the family seat in Palermo, the Palazzo Chiaramonte. By tradition the direct male descendants of Manfredi are called Pietro, Ugo or Flavio: Pietro for the foundation stone, Ugo for the king of Sicily and Flavio for Sicily's bright yellow sun.

The Chiaramonte became the most powerful and wealthy family in Sicily, holding the united counties of Modica and Ragusa as well as their seat in Palermo. Their power lasted until Andrea Chiaramonte, 8th Count of Modica, held Palermo as its last defender against Martin I of Aragon, whom the family's side regarded as an illegitimate pretender. Andrea was executed outside the Palazzo Chiaramonte, the house his forebears had built, on 1 June 1392, and the family's great power ended with him.

After the family's fall their palace became known as the Palazzo Steri. It was the residence of Martin I of Aragon and Blanche de Navarre, then of the Spanish viceroys, and later a prison of the Inquisition. Its much copied and distinctive form of Norman Gothic architecture is known in Sicily as the Chiaramontan style.

The family's name survives in many Sicilian place names: the town of Chiaramonte Gulfi in the province of Ragusa and Palma di Montechiaro in the province of Agrigento are both named after it. Near Palma di Montechiaro still stands the stronghold that Federico III Chiaramonte built in 1358. The family's descendants use the surname Cardone.
chiavenna: Chiavenna is a comune in the Province of Sondrio and the centre of the Alpine Valchiavenna. It lies about 100 kilometres north of Milan on the right bank of the river Mera, some 16 kilometres north of Lake Como. The Valle Spluga leads north to the Splügen Pass and the road to Chur, and the Val Bregaglia leads east. The name was long explained as coming from the Latin clavis, key, for its position on the passes, but it comes from a much older pre-Latin word, klava, meaning fallen rocks of a mountain slip.

Clavenna was conquered in 16 BCE by the troops of Augustus during his Alpine campaigns. The Romans built two roads from it: one up the Valle Spluga to the Splügen Pass, and another up the Val Bregaglia and across the Septimer Pass to Chur. After the fall of the Western Roman Empire the town marked the northern limit of the Ostrogothic Kingdom in Italy, and it was retaken by the Byzantine Empire in the mid-6th century, avoiding capture by the Lombard kingdom until the 7th century. The bishops of Como gave the citizens town privileges in 1030, and counts ruled the valley until 1194, when the district passed to the bishops of Chur. The Visconti of Milan acquired the town and the Valtellina in 1335.

In 1486 the forces of the Three Leagues set Chiavenna ablaze in their fight with the Sforza, and Ludovico Sforza fortified it two years later. The town came under the Three Leagues during the War of the League of Cambrai and became a bailiwick governed by them. A first Protestant parish arose in 1542, and Chiavenna became a centre of the Reformation, sheltering religious refugees from Italy such as Camillo Renato, Bernardino Ochino and Girolamo Zanchi.
