Three Leagues rule lasted, apart from a loss during the Bündner Wirren of 1620–39, until 1797, when French revolutionaries merged the town into the Cisalpine Republic. From 1815 to 1859 it belonged with Lombardy to the House of Habsburg, and then followed Lombardy into the Kingdom of Italy.

Chiavenna is the chief town of its district. It is crowned by a ruined castle and is a member of the Cittaslow movement. A statue commemorates Peter de Salis, governor of the Valtellina in the 18th century.
chibinda-ilunga: In the oral tradition he is a son, or in some versions a grandson, of Ilunga Mbili, who came from east of the Lualaba river, commanded the army of King Kongolo and helped him found the Luba Kingdom. His mother Bulanda and her sister Mabela, the mother of his elder brother Kalala Ilunga, were both sisters of Kongolo and wives of Ilunga Mbili, so the brothers were Kongolo's nephews. When their father returned to his homeland, the prophet Mujibu raised them at the royal court.

The story makes Chibinda the great hunter and Kalala the warrior. Jealous of their fame, Kongolo plotted their deaths, once through a mutiny against Kalala and once with a pit of spears dug where Kalala had to dance before him. The brothers fled with their father's princely insignia, returned at the head of his army, and killed Kongolo, after which Kalala was proclaimed Mulopwe of the Luba. Chibinda then led an army westward.

Among the Lunda, who lived south-west of the Luba, the ruler Yala Mwaku had quarrelled with his sons Kinguri and Kinyama and given his bracelet of power, the rukan, to his daughter Lueji A'Nkonde; the brothers went into exile, Kinguri to rule the Kasanje Kingdom and Kinyama the Luvale. Lueji married the foreign prince, who brought Luba rituals, culture and religion that the Lunda adopted. While she kept law and order, his army conquered neighbouring peoples, among them the Chokwe. When illness kept her from ruling, she passed him the rukan, and he took the title Mukalenge, bringing the principle of sacred kingship and rule by council; his powers gave him the standing of a god-king linked with the sun.

Lueji had no children and agreed to his taking a second wife, who bore an heir, Yav Ilunga. On Chibinda's death this son succeeded as the first Mwata Yamvo, a title the Lunda rulers in the Democratic Republic of the Congo still hold. Descendants of his are said to have founded the Kingdom of the Bakwa Dishi in Kasai-Oriental. Chokwe carvers often portray him with an elaborate headdress, a medicine horn for his mystical knowledge and a staff of rule.
chicago-boys: The group's training grew out of the Chile Project, organised in the 1950s by the United States State Department under the Point Four Program and funded by the Ford Foundation and the Rockefeller Foundation, with the aim of reshaping Chilean economic thought. Between 1955 and 1973, one hundred twenty-six selected Chilean students were trained first in Chile and then in postgraduate studies at Chicago, under teachers such as Milton Friedman, Arnold Harberger and Larry Sjaastad. The first wave, from 1955 to 1964, was set up by the United States Agency for International Development, and the second, from 1965 to 1973, was funded by the Ford Foundation. The name Chicago Boys itself emerged in the 1980s.

Their ideas remained marginal in Chilean politics until the early 1970s. A group of them wrote a 189-page economic programme, El ladrillo (the brick), for Jorge Alessandri's unsuccessful presidential campaign of 1969; Alessandri rejected it, but it was revived after the 1973 coup that brought General Augusto Pinochet to power. In 1975, with inflation still high and a world recession pushing Chile into depression, Pinochet appointed several of them to powerful posts. Members included the finance ministers Jorge Cauas, Sergio de Castro and Hernán Büchi, and José Piñera, minister of labour and pensions.

Their programme, often called shock therapy, combined severe austerity, deep cuts in government spending, deregulation, privatisation of state-owned enterprises and the dismantling of protectionist barriers to trade. By 1982 Chile's GDP had contracted by about 15 per cent, and the reforms widened income inequality. The junta presented them as a corrective to the socialist policies before it and a bulwark against communism during the Cold War.

The Chilean Miracle, as supporters called the results, gave the regime a degree of international legitimacy that helped offset criticism of its human rights record, and it influenced the turn to free-market policy under Ronald Reagan in the United States and Margaret Thatcher in the United Kingdom. Critics point to the social costs and to the policies being imposed under a repressive dictatorship. After the return to democracy in 1990 the group lost direct political power, though the core of its economic model remained in place, and Chicago graduates also shaped policy in Mexico, Argentina and Brazil.
chicago-pile-1: The concept of a nuclear chain reaction was first hypothesised by the Hungarian scientist Leo Szilard on 12 September 1933. The discovery of nuclear fission by Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann in 1938 opened the possibility of a chain reaction with uranium. Szilard and Walter Zinn found significant neutron multiplication in natural uranium. A letter drafted by Szilard and signed by Albert Einstein in August 1939 warned President Franklin D. Roosevelt of a German nuclear weapon project and led to the formation of an Advisory Committee on Uranium.

In April 1941 a special project headed by Arthur Compton at the University of Chicago was created to report on the uranium programme. The pursuit of a reactor was touched off by concern that Nazi Germany held a substantial scientific lead. The Army Corps of Engineers took control of the programme in June 1942, and it became part of the Manhattan Project.

Samuel K. Allison found a suitable space under the west stands of Stagg Field, originally a rackets court. Between 15 September and 15 November 1942 groups under Herbert Anderson and Walter Zinn built 16 experimental piles there. Stacking of the final pile began on the morning of 16 November 1942, in twelve-hour shifts. The workers machined 45,000 graphite blocks, enclosing 19,000 pieces of uranium metal and oxide. The pile was enclosed in a balloon so that the air could be replaced by carbon dioxide.

On 2 December 1942, 49 scientists assembled for the experiment. The startup began at 09:54. Fermi announced that the pile had gone critical at 15:25. After 28 minutes the alarm bells sounded because the neutron flux had passed the preset safety level, and Fermi ordered the emergency rod released. The pile had run for about 4.5 minutes at about 0.5 watts. Compton telephoned Conant in an impromptu code: the Italian navigator had landed in the New World, and the natives were very friendly.

CP-1 was operated until 28 February 1943, then dismantled and moved to Site A, near Chicago, where its materials were used to build Chicago Pile-2, which was operated for research until 1954. Its success showed that a reactor was feasible and that the neutron multiplication factor was larger than originally thought, which removed objections to cooling by air or water. It led to the X-10 Graphite Reactor at Oak Ridge and the production reactors at the Hanford Site.

A commemorative plaque was unveiled at Stagg Field on 2 December 1952, and the West Stands were demolished in August 1957. The site was designated a National Historic Landmark on 18 February 1965 and a Chicago Landmark on 27 October 1971.
chichen-itza: The Maya name means At the mouth of the well of the Itzá. The northern Yucatán Peninsula is karst, and its rivers run underground, so water comes from sinkholes called cenotes. Four visible cenotes could have supplied water all year at Chichen Itza, of which the Sacred Cenote is the best known. According to sources written after the Spanish conquest, in Maya and Spanish, the Maya threw objects and human beings into it as worship of the rain god Chaac. Edward Herbert Thompson dredged it from 1904 to 1910 and recovered gold, jade, pottery and incense, as well as human remains with wounds consistent with sacrifice.

The city's core took shape between 750 and 900, and its final layout dates from after 900. The earliest hieroglyphic date found there corresponds to 832 and the last, in the Osario temple, to 998. The city was founded by local Maya of northern Yucatán. The Itza, a Maya group of debated origins, began arriving around 800. Chichen Itza rose as the major centres of the southern lowlands declined, and in the 10th century it appears to have contributed to the collapse of Yaxuna and Coba. Between 900 and 1050 it was a powerful regional capital, trading by sea through its port of Isla Cerritos, obtaining obsidian from central Mexico and gold from southern Central America, and taking wealth as tribute from cities it conquered.

Archaeologists in the late 1980s proposed that it was ruled by a council of elite lineages, a system called multepal, but that idea has since been questioned. Colonial Maya sources such as the Book of Chilam Balam of Chumayel say that Hunac Ceel, ruler of Mayapan, conquered it in the 13th century. Archaeological data indicate instead that it had declined by 1100, before Mayapan rose.

In 1526 Francisco de Montejo obtained a charter to conquer Yucatán. His son Francisco Montejo the Younger reached Chichen Itza, renamed it Ciudad Real and divided the land among his soldiers. The Maya besieged the Spanish among the ruins, and an assault lost Montejo 150 of his remaining troops. He abandoned the city in 1534, and by 1535 the Spanish had been driven from the peninsula.

The site core covers at least 5 square kilometres and has over 80 causeways, called sacbeob. The Temple of Kukulcán, about 30 m high with nine terraces, was built over an older temple found in the 1930s. The buildings were once painted in red, green, blue and purple. John Lloyd Stephens's book of 1843 made the city known, and Mexico's national anthropology institute now cares for the ruins.
chichester: Chichester stands on the River Lavant, a winterbourne, south of its gap through the South Downs. Many ancient routeways converge there, which made it a good site for settlement. The oldest part lies within the medieval walls, which are built on Roman foundations, and the plan of the city, with its North, South, East and West streets radiating from a central market cross, is inherited from the Romans. It is the county town of West Sussex and its only city.

There is no recorded evidence of a settlement of any size before the Romans. The area is believed to have played a significant part in the Roman invasion of 43, and military storage structures have been found near Fishbourne Roman Palace. The city centre stands on the foundations of Noviomagus Reginorum, capital of the Civitas Reginorum. Stane Street ran from its east gate to London, and an amphitheatre was built outside the walls around 80.

The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle says Ælle of Sussex and his three sons annexed the area late in the fifth century and that the city was renamed after his son Cissa. Historians regard this as a myth, since no evidence shows reoccupation before the 9th century. Alfred the Great rebuilt Chichester as a burh, probably in 878 or 879, and it was one of the larger burhs, rated at 1500 hides in the Burghal Hidage.

After the Norman Conquest the cathedral founded at Selsey in 681 was moved to Chichester after the Norman Council of London of 1075 decreed that sees should be centred in cities. Domesday Book of 1086 records 300 dwellings and a population of 1,500. Roger de Mongomerie, 1st Earl of Shrewsbury, received the town and built Chichester Castle soon after 1066. The city was besieged at Christmas 1642 during the First English Civil War.

Chichester Cathedral, the Cathedral Church of the Holy Trinity, is the seat of the Anglican Bishop of Chichester and has a separate bell tower, unusual in Britain. It holds a shrine to Saint Richard of Chichester, and Leonard Bernstein's Chichester Psalms were commissioned for it. Chichester Cross, built in 1501 as a covered marketplace, stands where the four main streets meet. The Novium museum, opened in 2012, preserves the Roman baths.
chichimeca: Chichimeca is the name that the Nahua peoples of Mexico generically applied to nomadic and semi-nomadic peoples established in the present-day Bajío region. The Nahuatl name Chīchīmēcah means inhabitants of Chichiman, a word meaning area of milk. It is sometimes said to be related to chichi, dog, but the vowel lengths differ, and vowel length changes the meaning in Nahuatl. The name carried the same meaning as the Roman term barbarian, and the Spanish Empire adopted it in that pejorative sense.

To the Spanish the Chichimeca were wild people who had no fixed dwelling places and lived by hunting. In fact it was a broad term used by outsiders, Spanish and Nahuatl speakers alike, for many different peoples whose cultures ranged from hunter-gatherers to sedentary agriculturalists with sophisticated political organisation.

In the late 16th century Gonzalo de las Casas, who had received an encomienda near Durango and fought in the wars against the Chichimec peoples, wrote the Report of the Chichimeca and the Justness of the War Against Them. He named the Pame, Guachichil, Guamare and Zacateco, who lived in the area then known as La Gran Chichimeca, and wrote that they covered only their genitals, painted their bodies and ate only game, roots and berries. To the Spanish they were wild people north of the Valley of Mexico who fiercely resisted intrusion into land that contained silver mines.

In the long Chichimeca War, from 1550 to 1590, Chichimeca raids, ambushes of critical economic routes and pillaging proved effective. The Spanish at first tried to defeat them in a war of fire and blood, but eventually sought peace, since they could not win. To end the war they adopted a Purchase for Peace programme, providing food, tools, livestock and land, sending Spanish to teach agriculture and converting the Chichimeca to Catholicism.

Within a century the Spanish and Chichimeca had assimilated. The interaction brought a drastic fall in the population of all the peoples known collectively as Chichimecas, and their eventual disappearance as peoples, except for the Pames of San Luis Potosí and the related Chichimeca-Jonaz of the Sierra Gorda in eastern Guanajuato. Today only one ethnic group is customarily called Chichimec, the Chichimeca Jonaz, a few thousand of whom live in the state of Guanajuato.
chichimeca-war: On 8 September 1546 natives near the Cerro de la Bufa showed the Spaniard Juan de Tolosa silver-rich ore, and Spaniards soon crowded into what became Zacatecas, followed by mining towns such as Fresnillo, Sombrerete and Mazapil. Spanish soldiers raided for slaves for the mines, and the new roads from Querétaro and Jalisco carried caravans across Chichimeca land. The war began eight years after the Mixtón War of 1540–1542, and is sometimes seen as its continuation. The Chichimecas, perhaps 30,000 to 60,000 people, lived mostly by hunting and gathering; their four main nations were the Guachichiles, Pames, Guamares and Zacatecos, skilled archers whose obsidian-tipped arrows could pierce Spanish mail.

Fighting began in late 1550, when Zacatecos attacked supply routes of the Purépecha and then Spanish settlements south of Zacatecas. In 1551 the Guachichiles and Guamares killed 15 soldiers at San Miguel de Allende and forced its abandonment. Wagon trains were destroyed in 1553 and 1554 with goods worth 32,000 and 40,000 pesos, and by the end of 1561 more than 4,000 Spaniards and native allies were estimated to have been killed. The Chichimecas raided in groups of 40 to 50 warriors, learned to fight on horseback and used spies and lookouts.

In 1567 Spain declared a war of fire and blood, promising death, enslavement or mutilation. It built a dozen presidios, beginning at San Miguel and San Felipe in 1562 and Nombre de Dios in 1563, and settled towns that grew into Celaya, León, Aguascalientes and San Luis Potosí, with Caxcan, Purépecha and Otomi allies. Yet attacks grew from 1575 to 1585, and in 1581 the viceroy, Conde de Coruna, wrote to Felipe II that many mines in Zacatecas had closed. Soldiers' slave raiding kept the hostility alive.

In 1574 the Dominicans declared the war unjust and caused by Spanish aggression. The Bishop of Guadalajara proposed new towns with priests in 1584, and from 1586 the viceroy Alvaro Manrique de Zuniga withdrew soldiers and offered tools, food, clothing and land, with the help of Miguel Caldera, a captain of Spanish and Guachichile descent. In 1591 Luis de Velasco persuaded 400 Tlaxcalan families to found eight settlements, in return for land, freedom from taxes and the right to bear arms. This purchase for peace shaped Spanish frontier policy for nearly three centuries. The Wixárika are believed to descend from the Guachichiles, and Pame and Chichimeca Jonaz speakers live on.
chickamauga-cherokee: The Chickamauga were followers of the war chief Dragging Canoe from the Overhill Cherokee towns on the landward side of the Appalachian continental divide, close to the Muscogee. While most Cherokee on the Atlantic seaboard, surrounded by settlers, made peace with the Americans in 1776–1777 after the Second Cherokee War, Dragging Canoe accused the elderly chiefs of endangering the survival of their people and never met with whites to negotiate a treaty again.

In the winter of 1776–77 his followers moved down the Tennessee River and settled where the Great Indian Warpath crossed Chickamauga Creek. American settlers named the band after the town of Chickamauga there; Wilma Mankiller, a former Principal Chief of the Cherokee Nation, called them Chickamaugans.

Shawnees, Muscogees and exiles from other nations joined them, as did escaped slaves and British loyalists. After militias destroyed their towns, Dragging Canoe sent his brother Little Owl to ask the Muscogee chief Alexander McGillivray for land, and five new towns were founded in Muscogee territory, among them Running Water, Nickajack, Long Island, Crow Town and Lookout Mountain; from then on the band was often called the Lower Cherokee. From Running Water Dragging Canoe led attacks across the Southeast, and his warriors raided as far as Indiana, Kentucky and Virginia alongside the Northwestern Confederacy, which they helped establish.

After Dragging Canoe's death in 1792 his chosen successor, John Watts, known as Young Tassel, moved the base to Willstown, nearer his Muscogee allies, and concluded a treaty at Pensacola with the Spanish governor of West Florida, Arturo O'Neill de Tyrone, for arms and supplies. The war ended with the Treaty of Tellico Blockhouse in late 1794.

Former warriors of the Lower Towns then dominated Cherokee affairs: the first three Principal Chiefs, Little Turkey, Black Fox and Pathkiller, had all fought under Dragging Canoe. Asked in 1799 what kind of people the Chickamauga were, the former warrior Richard Fields laughed and replied, "They are Cherokee, and we know no difference." Later, Lower Towns leaders such as Sequoyah moved west to Arkansas Territory, founding what became the Cherokee Nation West.
chickasaw-wars: The Province of Louisiana stretched from Illinois to New Orleans, and the French needed safe communications along the Mississippi River. The Chickasaw, living in northern Mississippi and western Tennessee, lay across that route and traded with the British. Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville, governor of Louisiana and founder of New Orleans, set out to stop that trade, and in 1721 he incited the Choctaw to raid Chickasaw villages and ambush pack trains on the Trader's Path to Charleston. The Chickasaw drew their villages closer together, founded Savannah Town in South Carolina in 1723 to secure British guns, and blocked French traffic from Chickasaw Bluff near present-day Memphis.

Over the following years the French repeatedly revived the Choctaw war. Choctaw raiders ambushed hunting parties, killed traders' horses, ruined crops and killed peace envoys, and the Illini and Iroquois sometimes joined from the north. This war of attrition wore the Chickasaw down, bringing them to a crisis in the late 1730s and early 1740s.

Bienville, back in Louisiana from 1734, mounted campaigns in the European style. In 1736 a northern force of French and Illini under Pierre D'Artaguiette, coming from Fort de Chartres, was crushed on 25 March at Ogoula Tchetoka, and D'Artaguiette was killed. Unaware of this, Bienville attacked the fortified village of Ackia on 26 May with 1,200 French and Choctaw and was repulsed. In 1739 he gathered a larger army with siege guns at Fort de l'Assumption on the Fourth Chickasaw Bluff, with troops from Canada under Charles Le Moyne de Longueuil and Pierre-Joseph Céloron de Blainville, but disease and the impossibility of moving artillery through the wilderness ended in terms without battle.

The Marquis de Vaudreuil, who replaced Bienville in 1742, kept up the Choctaw raids. Many sources describe a further French expedition in 1752, but Dawson A. Phelps concluded that it never took place, although a strong Choctaw attack backed by the French did. The Chickasaw held their fortified villages at great cost to their numbers and way of life, and the French never defeated them, to the eventual advantage of the British and the later United States. The Illini and the Chickasaw remained enemies long afterwards.
chidambaram: Chidambaram, also known as Thillai, is a major town and municipality in Cuddalore district in Tamil Nadu. It lies on the Vellar River where it meets the Bay of Bengal, and is the headquarters of the Chidambaram taluk. The name is linked to the groves of thillai trees, a mangrove species, that once surrounded the town and temple. The Sanskrit chit ambara is said to mean the ether of consciousness or the atmosphere of wisdom, in association with Shiva Nataraja, the cosmic dancer.

According to Hindu legend, sages in the Thillai forest believed that rituals and mantras could control the gods. Shiva came as a mendicant, followed by Vishnu as Mohini, and the sages created serpents, a tiger and an elephant to attack him. He wore the serpents and the tiger's skin, then invoked the demon Muyalakan, stepped on his back and performed the dance of eternal bliss, showing his true form, and the sages surrendered.

The town is believed to be of great antiquity. It was ruled at different times by the Pallavas until the ninth century, the medieval Cholas, later Cholas, later Pandyas, the Vijayanagara Empire, the Thanjavur Nayakas, the Marathas and the British. Sangam literature of the first to fifth centuries refers to the temple or the town. The Thevaram hymns, by the seventh-century poet-saints Thirugnana Sambanthar, Thirunavukkarasar and Sundaramoorthy Nayanar, praise Nataraja here. These hymns, the Thirumurai, were stored on palm leaf in the temple and recovered by the Chola king Rajaraja Chola under the guidance of Nambiandarnambi.

Most inscriptions in the temple date from the Cholas, from Rajaraja Chola I (985 to 1014) to Rajaraja Chola III (1216 to 1256), with others from Pandya, Pallava and Vijayanagara kings. The Chola king Parantaka I (907 to 950) laid the golden roof of the Chitrambalam, and Rajaraja Chola I and Kulothunga Chola I (1070 to 1120) made significant donations. Court historians of the Delhi Sultanate state that in 1311 the general Malik Kafur raided Chidambaram, Madurai, Srirangam and other temple towns and destroyed temples that held gold and jewels. The temple complex covers about 40 acres.

The Thillai Nataraja Temple complex holds shrines to Shivakami Amman, Ganesh, Murugan and Vishnu as Govindaraja Perumal, one of the Divya Desams. Its main festivals are the Marghazhi Thiruvaadhirai in December and January and the Aani Thirumanjanam in June and July, when the festival deity is taken out in a procession with a temple car. Natyanjali, a festival of bharatanatyam dancers, takes place each February. Annamalai University, founded in 1929, stands in the town, and the 2011 census counted 62,153 people in the municipality.
chief-joseph: Chief Joseph was born on 3 March 1840 in the Wallowa Valley of north-eastern Oregon and was known as Young Joseph because his father, Tuekakas, had been baptised with the same Christian name. In 1855 Tuekakas and other Nez Perce chiefs signed the Treaty of Walla Walla, which set aside a reservation of 7,700,000 acres that kept the Wallowa Valley.

In 1863, after a gold rush brought new settlers, the government asked the Nez Perce to accept a reservation of 760,000 acres around Lapwai in Idaho that excluded the valley. Chief Lawyer signed, but Joseph the Elder and several other chiefs refused. Joseph the Younger succeeded his father as leader of the Wallowa band in 1871, charged never to sell the bones of his parents.

Joseph allowed no violence against the settlers and prospectors who wronged his people. In 1873 he negotiated to keep the valley, but in 1877 the government reversed its policy, and General Oliver O. Howard gave the band 30 days to move. In June 1877 a young man whose father had been killed announced that he and others had killed four settlers, and Joseph and other leaders began moving people away from Idaho.

About 750 Nez Perce and a small band of Palouse were pursued for more than three months across present-day Oregon, Washington, Idaho, Wyoming and Montana in what became the Nez Perce War. At White Bird Canyon on 17 June 1877 they killed 34 soldiers. General Nelson Miles intercepted them at Bear Paw, about 40 miles from the Canadian border, and after a five-day siege in freezing weather Joseph surrendered on 5 October 1877. A speech ending 'I will fight no more forever' is attributed to him, but Mark Herbert Brown writes that the story of the surrender speech has not a word of truth. Several historians hold that Joseph was not a war chief and did not command the retreat.

General William T. Sherman overruled the terms Joseph had negotiated. About 400 followers were taken to Fort Leavenworth, held for eight months, and then sent to a reservation in Indian Territory, where many died of epidemic disease. Joseph met President Rutherford B. Hayes in Washington in 1879 to plead for a return home. In 1885 the survivors were moved to the Colville Reservation in Washington, far from the Wallowa Valley. Joseph died on 21 September 1904 at Nespelem, and his doctor said it was of a broken heart. The Chief Joseph band on the Colville Reservation bears his name.
chief-pleas: For most of its history the Chief Pleas was not elected. It consisted of the hereditary Seigneur, the Seneschal, who was then appointed by the Seigneur, and the owners of the island's forty tenements. It met only now and then to hear the pleas of its members, and this gave the assembly its name.

In 1922 the assembly was enlarged to include 12 Deputies chosen by popular vote, for which only those who were not tenants could stand. In 1957, after residents appealed to the Lieutenant Governor of Guernsey, 12 People's Deputies were introduced.

Sark was the last jurisdiction to abolish its feudal regime. In 2006 the Chief Pleas voted by 25 to 15 to reform itself, cutting its membership from 52 to 28, with 14 landowners and 14 residents to be elected. The Privy Council endorsed the law in 2008, and Sark held its first democratic election to the Chief Pleas on 10 December 2008.

A further reform, decided in 2010 and in force from 2013, split the office of Seneschal, who until then had been both president of the Chief Pleas and the island's chief judge, after concerns that the double role did not comply with human rights law. From 2013 the assembly had presidents of its own, and from 2017 a Speaker.

The Chief Pleas is a non-partisan assembly of 20 members: 18 directly elected Conseillers, the Speaker, whom the Conseillers elect, and the Seigneur, the last two without a vote. Conseillers serve four years, and half the seats are contested every two years. The island's administration is run through committees of Conseillers, some with members from outside the assembly, covering such matters as agriculture and sea fisheries, harbours and shipping, education, medical and emergency services, and policy and finance.
chief-seattle: His name is an anglicisation of the Lushootseed siʔaɬ, also spelled Si'ahl or Sealth. He was born around 1780 to Schweabe, a Suquamish leader, and Sholeetsa, a Duwamish woman. His birthplace is disputed: Suquamish tradition and Seattle himself said Blake Island, while the Duwamish say his mother's village on the Black River. In his youth he received the thunderbird as a spirit power in a vision quest. In 1792, when he was about six, he met the ships of George Vancouver. He had two wives and seven children. The best known was Kikisoblu, also called Princess Angeline.

Seattle gained a reputation as a strong warrior. Around 1810 he led an ambush on raiders coming down the Green River, in which the occupants of three of five canoes were killed or enslaved, and like many of his contemporaries he enslaved captives. In 1847 he helped lead the Suquamish war against the Chemakum, who were nearly wiped out. One of his sons was killed in it, and Seattle then sought baptism in the Catholic Church, taking the name Noah.

He afterwards cooperated with American settlers, guiding them, supplying labour to sawmills and farms and befriending Doc Maynard. As first signatory for the Suquamish he signed the 1855 Treaty of Point Elliot, ceding roughly 2.5 million acres to the United States, though it has been argued that he had no authority to sign for the upriver peoples. The unpopular treaty led many Duwamish to renounce his leadership. In the Puget Sound War he supported the Americans and afterwards sought clemency for Native leaders such as Leschi. In 1865 the town of Seattle banned Native Americans unless housed and employed by a settler, and he moved to the Suquamish reservation.

Seattle died on 7 June 1866 on the Port Madison Reservation and was buried with both Catholic and Suquamish rites. A speech given in 1854 to Isaac Stevens has been attributed to him. It is known only from a text reconstructed in 1887 from notes taken by Henry A. Smith; the historian Walt Crowley says it was filtered and embellished, and there is no corroboration for the exact words. Later versions added text and influenced environmentalists and Native American rights activists in the 1960s. The Suquamish hold Chief Seattle Days each August.
chieti: Chieti is a city and comune in Abruzzo, 200 kilometres east of Rome, and the capital of the province of Chieti. It lies about 10 kilometres from the Adriatic Sea, with the Majella and Gran Sasso mountains in the background. The old town, Chieti Alta, stands on a hill surrounded by the Pescara and Alento rivers. Its inhabitants are called teatini, and the English form of that name survives in the Theatines, a Catholic religious order.

Legend says the city was founded by the companions of Achilles and named for his mother Thetis, and according to Strabo it was founded by Arcadians as Thegeate. Around the 10th century BCE the Marrucini, an Italic tribe probably from Sabina, took the territory from the Osci, and Teate Marrucinorum was their chief town. After defeat by Rome the Marrucini became loyal allies. They received Roman citizenship and municipal status after the Social War, in which the Teate general Herius Asinius was killed. Teate flourished in the first century BCE as a municipium.

In 801 Pepin of Italy, son of Charlemagne, destroyed the town, which remained a fief of the Duchy of Spoleto for two centuries. In the 16th century Venice opened a consulate there in 1555, and Gian Pietro Carafa, the future Pope Paul IV, was bishop and archbishop. In 1861 it became part of the Kingdom of Italy.

Chieti has Roman remains: three temples, a theatre, baths with mosaics, underground cisterns, and a citadel with an amphitheatre of the first century CE. The National Archaeology Museum of Abruzzo houses the Warrior of Capestrano. The cathedral, dedicated to Saint Justin, was probably founded in the 8th century and keeps parts of a Romanesque crypt. Its Good Friday procession is held by some historians to have taken place since 842.
chigils: Scholars disagree about the origin of the name. The sinologist Yu. A. Zuev held that Chinese historians wrote it as Chuyue, a tribe of mixed Yueban and Western Turkic origin, and saw a first mention in the Book of Sui; others have proposed a Turkic word for land or country, or for raw clay. Mahmud Kashgari told a folk story that traced the name to Alexander the Great, who was said to have cried out in Persian at the mud of Talas.

According to Kashgari, the Oghuz Turks called all the Turks between the Oxus and northern China Chigils. He placed one group of nomad Chigil near the township of Quyās beyond Barsghān, another in the township of Chigil near Ṭarāz, and a third in villages of that name near Kāshgar. In the middle of the 7th century the Western Turkic yabgu Ashina Helu drew the Chigils, Chumuls and Karluks into his uprising against the Tang.

From at least the 9th century the Chigils, the Yagma and the Tuhsi belonged to the Karluk tribal union. The Hudud al-'Ālam, compiled in 982–3, places them in the Karluk Yabghu state around Issyk Kul and describes them as very rich, with a king of their own people. Power in the Kara-Khanid state was shared between the nobility of the Chigils and the Yagma: the senior, eastern khagan, with his courts at Kashgar and Balasagun, came from the Chigil tribe and bore the title Arslan Kara-Hakan.

In the 11th century the Chigils became independent, in three branches according to Kashgari. After the Mongol invasion of Turkestan they and their neighbours gave up their lands to nomads from the east and moved into Transoxania and Kashgharia; four villages called Chigil in Turkey suggest that some went on to Asia Minor. Medieval sources name settlements after them, among them Chigil-kant and Chigil-balyk in Xinjiang, and the city of Yar on the southern shore of Issyk Kul, whose name survives as Chal.

The earliest accounts describe the Chigils as Manichaeans and later ones as Nestorian Christians, while the Hudud al-'Ālam says that some worshipped the sun and the stars. The Arab writer Abū Dulaf found only a few Christians among them, most worshipping the stars, Sirius above all. Their symbol was the lion, a central image of Manichaeism. A Turkic Manichaean book, the Iki jïltïz nom, found at Kara-Khoja in the Turpan oasis in 1907 by Albert von Le Coq, was dedicated to a ruler of the Chigil-Arslan tribe and completed at Talas, which had four Manichaean cloisters.
chihuahua-city: The city began with nearby silver. The Spanish captain Diego del Castillo founded the mining settlement of Santa Eulalia in 1652, but the climate and constant attacks by indigenous people halted work. Rich discoveries in 1707 brought immediate settlement. On 12 October 1709 Blas Cano de los Rios and Antonio Deza y Ulloa founded El Real de Minas de San Francisco de Cuéllar.

It became a villa in 1718 (some sources say 1715) as San Felipe el Real de Chihuahua, for Philip V of Spain, and the name was shortened in 1823. A tax on Santa Eulalia's silver paid for the parish church that is now the cathedral. The meaning of the name is variously given as between two waters, place of the holed rock and, in Rarámuri, dry and sandy place.

News of Mexico's independence movement was slow to reach Chihuahua, and royalists chose it for the trial of the insurgents seized at Acatita de Baján. Ignacio Allende, Mariano Jiménez, Juan Aldama and Manuel Santamaría were shot on 26 June, and Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla on 30 July.

Benito Juárez briefly made it capital of Mexico in 1864, during the second French intervention. In the Mexican Revolution it was a centre of the Madero movement and of Villismo, with figures including Abraham González, Pascual Orozco and Francisco Villa.

Chihuahua is the capital of the Mexican state of the same name, with 925,762 inhabitants in 2020, and its economy rests mainly on industry. Much colonial building was destroyed in the 1970s to widen streets, but the Temple of San Francisco, begun in 1717 and completed in 1789, survives, and the former Federal Palace, now a museum, holds Hidalgo's jail cell.
chikka-devaraja-wodeyar: Chikka Devaraja was born on 22 September 1645, the eldest son of Maharani Amrit Ammani and Dodda Deva Raja, elder brother of Devaraja Wodeyar I and governor of a town of the kingdom. He succeeded his uncle, who died on 11 February 1673, and was installed on the Mysore throne on 28 February 1673 as the fourteenth maharaja.

He took Maddagiri, which brought Mysore up to the Carnatic-Bijapur-Balaghat province held by Venkoji, the Raja of Tanjore and half-brother of Shivaji. In his first decade he imposed many petty taxes on the peasants, from which his soldiers were exempt, and the burden provoked wide protests among the ryots, backed by the Jangama priests of the Virasaiva monasteries. Accounts say the king invited over 400 priests to a feast at Nanjanagudu and had his wrestlers strangle each as he left through a narrow lane, which ended the protests.

After the Mughals under Aurangzeb made Carnatic-Bijapur-Balaghat part of their province of Sira, Chikka Devaraja cultivated an alliance with Aurangzeb through Qasim Khan, the Mughal faujdar of Sira. He annexed Baramahal and Salem below the Eastern Ghats, extended his lands west to the Baba Budan Mountains in 1694, and two years later attacked the Naiks of Madura and besieged Trichinopoly, a siege abandoned as his alliances began to break.

After Qasim Khan's death he sent an embassy to Aurangzeb at Ahmadnagar, and in 1700 the emperor sent him a signet ring bearing the title Jug Deo Raj, leave to sit on an ivory throne and a sword from his own regalia. The embassy also meant formal subordination to the Mughals and an annual tribute, and his new administration is said to have imitated what the envoys had seen at the Mughal court.

When he died on 16 November 1704 his lands reached from Medigeshi in the north to Palni and Anaimalai in the south. Subrahmanyam judged the state he left at once strong and weak, its growth resting on alliances that undermined its stability. A devout Śrīvaiṣṇava, he wrote the Gītagōpālam, a musical work on the life of Kṛṣṇa, and the Cikadēvarāya Binnapaṃ, a theological work in verse.
chikka-vira-rajendra: He was a son of Linga Rajendra II. His own name was Vira Rajendra, which had also been the name of his uncle, another ruler of Kodagu, so the prefix Chikka, meaning younger in Kannada and Kodava Takk, tells the two apart. He was drawn to literature and general knowledge and composed poems himself. He was proficient in Kannada and Persian and could also speak Hindi, Tulu, English and Urdu.

His own account of his fall, published in London in 1853, traced it to a quarrel over his brother-in-law Chen Busawah, who fled to Mysore in 1830 against the family and killed some officers on the way. The East India Company refused to hand him over, saying he had sought its protection. Some time later the raja detained a Company messenger travelling from Malabar to Mysore, and when the man was not released the Company took the palace by force, with possessions he valued at £160,000. On 24 April 1834 he was deposed and exiled, and his kingdom became a separate chief commissionership of British India.

He lived at Benares for 14 years on an annual allowance of £12,000, and there in December 1850 his daughter Muddama became the third wife of Jung Bahadur Rana. He sailed to England on the Euxine with two wives and his favourite daughter Gouramma, reaching Southampton on 12 May 1852, to plead for his kingdom. In a letter to the London Standard of 18 November 1853 he recalled that his uncle had helped the Company in its campaign against Tipoo Sultan in 1799 and rejected the picture of him as a tyrant in Thornton's History of British India. He died on 24 September 1859 at Maida Hill and was buried in Kensal Green Cemetery.

The Kannada writer Masti Venkatesha Iyengar, who won the Jnanpith Award in 1983, made his life the subject of the novel Chikavira Rajendra, noted for treating him neither as a villain nor as a victim of the British. A television series based on it, Anthimaraju, was to be broadcast by Doordarshan in 1992 but was withdrawn after protests from the Veerashaiva community and Kodavas at its portrayal of the king.
chikugo-province: Chikugo bordered Chikuzen to the north and east, Bungo to the east, Higo to the south-east and Hizen to the west. Its short name, Chikushū, it shared with Chikuzen, and it was also called Chikuin. Under the Gokishichidō system it belonged to the Saikaidō circuit, and the Engishiki classed it as one of the superior countries in importance and one of the far countries in distance from the capital. In the early Meiji period it counted 789 villages with a total assessed yield of 536,851 koku.

The province was carved out of ancient Tsukushi Province, a major centre of power in the Yayoi period with contacts with the Asian mainland, which may have been the site of the Kingdom of Yamatai named in Chinese histories. In the Kofun period many burial mounds were raised there and the area was ruled by a clan holding the title Tsukushi no kuni no miyatsuko. The Iwai Rebellion of 527 broke out there. After the Taika Reforms and the Ritsuryō system of 701, Tsukushi was divided into Chikuzen and Chikugo. The provincial capital stood in what is now Kurume, where its ruins are a National Historic Site, as are those of the Chikugo Kokubun-ji; the province's chief shrine, Kōra taisha, is also in Kurume.

In the Muromachi period the Ashikaga won the Battle of Chikugo River in 1359, and in 1361 imperial forces under Kikuchi Takemitsu captured Dazaifu. In the Sengoku period the Otomo clan held the office of shugo, but in practice the province was in the hands of some 15 petty warlords of the Kamachi, Tajiri, Kuroki and other clans.

After the Boshin War and the Meiji restoration, the former shogunal lands went to Hita Prefecture in October 1868, and in November Shimotedo Domain moved its seat to Chikugo and restored Miike Domain. When the domains were abolished on 25 December 1871, Kurume, Yanagawa and Miike became prefectures, soon united as Mizuma Prefecture, which was merged into Fukuoka Prefecture on 21 August 1876.
chikunda: From the 16th century the Portuguese Crown leased crown lands in the Zambezi valley as prazos da coroa, nominally for three lives, to holders who were to administer justice, collect taxes and maintain enough armed retainers to keep the peace. By the mid-18th century the name chikunda, probably from a Bantu word kunda, to conquer, was reserved for these armed clients. They came from diverse backgrounds, often from areas of conflict or famine, offering themselves as unfree dependents in return for protection and advancement, and swore lifelong loyalty to the prazo holder in a ritual. In the mid-18th century their total in Zambezia was estimated at 50,000.

The chikunda usually lived in small fortified villages near the margins of the larger prazos, each headed by the owner's deputy, the capitão; the villages grew their own food and paid a contribution to their master. Under a strong owner they defended and policed the estate and collected tribute, but under a weak one or in famine they could become little more than bandits.

In the 19th century they set themselves apart from the people among whom they were quartered by living in separate villages and speaking a mixed language drawn from Shona, Mang'anja, Sena, Tonga and Portuguese. They disdained farming, observed patrilineal descent, venerated the spirits of former chikunda rather than their own ancestors, and marked themselves out with facial tattoos, filed teeth and imported calico.

The drought of 1794 to 1802 and later droughts and smallpox epidemics into the 1830s destroyed the prazo economy. By the 1840s five powerful families, mostly of Goan origin, ruled the middle Zambezi as virtually independent states built on the slave and ivory trades, with chikunda in their thousands, European firearms and fortified towns called aringas. The da Cruz of Massangano defeated four Portuguese expeditions between 1867 and 1869, executing the governor of Tete, Miguel Gouveia.

After the Berlin Conference demanded effective occupation, the Mozambique Company took control of the area between 1891 and 1902, and its armed police took over the chikunda's roles. As many as 15,000 former chikunda revolted against the Portuguese in Barue in 1917, a rising largely broken by the end of that year, and their descendants' identity as chikunda survives in communities around the confluence of the Zambezi and Luangwa rivers.
chikuzen-province: Chikuzen bordered Hizen Province to the west, Buzen to the east and Bungo to the south-east. Its short name, Chikushū, it shared with neighbouring Chikugo Province, and it was also called Chikuyō. Under the Gokishichidō system it belonged to the Saikaidō circuit, and the Engishiki classed it as a superior country in importance and a far country in distance from the capital. Its provincial capital is believed to have stood in what is now the city of Dazaifu, though its exact site has not been found; the ruins of the Chikuzen Kokubun-ji nearby are a National Historic Site.

The area belonged to ancient Tsukushi Province, a major centre of the Yayoi period with contacts with the Asian mainland, which may have been the site of the Kingdom of Yamatai named in Chinese histories. In the Kofun period many burial mounds were raised and a powerful clan ruled with the title Tsukushi no kuni no miyatsuko. Tradition places a palace of Emperor Chūai, the 14th ruler of Japan in the traditional list, at the present Kashii-gū shrine and makes the area the starting point of Empress Jingū's purported conquest of Korea. Many Toraijin immigrants, such as the Hata clan, settled there, and in 527 it saw the Iwai Rebellion.

After the Yamato defeat by Silla and Tang China at the Battle of Hakusonko in 663, the government founded Dazaifu as a regional military and civil centre. Following the Taika Reforms and the Ritsuryō system of 701, Tsukushi was divided into Chikuzen and Chikugo. At the end of the 13th century a Mongol invasion force landed in Chikuzen, but its main force was destroyed by a typhoon later called kamikaze. In April 1336 Kikuchi Taketoshi attacked the Shoni clan's stronghold at Dazaifu; the Shoni, allies of Ashikaga Takauji, were defeated, and their leader Shoni Sadatsune took his own life.

In the Edo period almost all of Chikuzen lay in the Fukuoka Domain of the Kuroda clan. An early Meiji survey counted 862 villages with a total assessed yield of 633,434 koku. The provinces were later replaced by prefectures, but the name survives in railway lines and stations such as Chikuzen Habu and Chikuzen Ueki.
chilarai: Chilarai, popularly called Bir Chilarai, was the third son of Biswa Singha, founder of the Koch dynasty of the Kamata kingdom, and a younger brother of Nara Narayan, its second king. Under his brother he was both commander-in-chief and finance minister, or dewan, of the kingdom. The name Chilarai came from the speed of his troop movements, compared to that of a chila, a kite or eagle.

Told of the war between the Koch and the Ahoms, King Ripu Singha of Manipur surrendered to Chilarai's forces without a fight, paying twenty thousand silver rupees, a thousand gold coins and forty elephants, and accepting an annual tribute. The king of Jaintia, between the Jaintia Hills and the Barak River, chose to resist and was killed in battle; his son submitted, giving a thousand horses, silver and gold coins and a hundred Jaintia swords called khanga, and agreed to a yearly tribute.

According to the Vamshavali, Chilarai then marched on the Tripura Kingdom with 40,000 soldiers. In a battle at Langai, on the southern border of Kachar, the king of Tripura was killed and, the sources say, 18,000 of his soldiers were put to death; the king's brother was placed on the throne on condition of an annual tribute. Chilarai next invaded Sylhet, held for Sulaiman Khan Karrani of Bengal by a governor named Amil. After two days of fighting he beheaded Amil, whose brother submitted and paid three lakhs of silver rupees. On the way home he defeated the small chiefdom of Dimrua and imprisoned its king, Panteshwar, before releasing him.

Chilarai's patronage is credited with allowing Sankardeva to establish the ekasarana-namadharma in Assam. Tradition holds that he never treated unarmed common people with brutality, that he respected kings who surrendered, and that he and his brother collected tribute from the defeated rather than annexing their lands, even giving prisoners land to settle. Since 2005 the Government of Assam has marked his birth anniversary every year as Bir Chilaray Diwas, a state holiday falling on the full moon of the month of Magh, and its Directorate of Cultural Affairs has given a Bir Chilaray award.
childebert-i: Childebert was the third of the four sons of Clovis I and was born at Reims. When the kingdom of the Franks was divided on his father's death in 511, he received Paris, the country to the north as far as the Somme, the land to the west as far as the English Channel, and Brittany. His brothers ruled elsewhere: Theuderic I at Metz, Chlodomer at Orléans and Chlothar I at Soissons.

In 523 Childebert joined his brothers in a war against Godomar of Burgundy, in which Chlodomer died in 524. According to tradition, Childebert and Chlothar then sent scissors and a sword to their mother Clotilde, giving her the choice of seeing Chlodomer's sons shorn of their long hair, a symbol of royal power, or killed. The two elder boys were murdered, the youngest, Clodoald, escaped to a monastic life, and Childebert annexed Chartres and Orléans. In 534 he conquered Burgundy with Chlothar and Theuderic's son Theudebert I and received Mâcon, Geneva and Lyons, and Arles and Marseille were guaranteed to him when Provence was ceded to the Franks in 535.

In 531 his sister Chrotilda, a Catholic married to the Arian king Amalaric of Hispania, appealed to him against her husband's mistreatment. Childebert defeated Amalaric, who was assassinated at Barcelona. In 542 he took Pamplona and besieged Zaragoza but had to retreat.

From Spain he brought back to Paris the tunic of Saint Vincent, and in its honour built the monastery later known as St-Germain-des-Prés. He died in December 558 and was buried there, and the abbey remained the royal necropolis of the Neustrian kings until 675. He left two daughters by his wife Ultragotha. He fought in more foreign wars than any of his brothers, in Burgundy, Spain and Provence, and was an acquisitive king.
childeric-i: Childeric was a Frankish ruler in what is now northern France, in the period when this part of Roman Gaul was cut off from the central Roman government in 461 and the last emperor based in Italy was deposed in 476. Gregory of Tours, writing in the 6th century, names his father as Merovech, after whom the Merovingian dynasty was named. Medieval sources disagree about his ancestry.

Gregory is the only near-contemporary source and mentions him twice. One passage tells a story of exile: Childeric dishonoured the daughters of his fellow Franks, was driven out and stayed in Thuringia with King Basinus and his wife Basina. After eight years he received a signal to return, and Basina left her husband to come with him. Modern scholars are sceptical of the claim that the Franks chose the Roman commander Aegidius as king meanwhile, though some think it preserves a memory of real events.

Childeric is called a king, rex, on the seal ring buried with him, though scholars interpret the term differently for northern Gaul at this time. Modern scholars generally assume he was allied with Aegidius, Roman military commander in Gaul from around 457, though there is little evidence of it. Gregory's second passage gives a compressed account of conflicts near the Loire, where the Visigoths were expanding. It places Childeric at a battle at Orléans, usually equated with the battle of about 463 in which Frederic, brother of the Visigothic king Theoderic II, was killed fighting Aegidius and the Franks, though other sources do not name Childeric.

Gregory also reports that Odovacrius allied with Childeric and that they subdued the Alamanni. Many scholars take this as an alliance with Odoacer, who ruled Italy after 476, but others dispute it. The Life of Saint Genevieve shows Childeric holding military control of the countryside around Paris.

He is generally considered to have died in 481 or 482, because Gregory says Clovis had ruled thirty years when he died about 511. Clovis I, his son, went on to unite much of Roman Gaul under Frankish rule.

His tomb was found in 1653 near the church of Saint-Brice in Tournai, now in Belgium. It held gold and garnet jewels, gold coins, a ring with the king's name and some 300 golden winged insects, usually viewed as bees or cicadas, laid on his cloak. The treasure was stolen from the royal library on the night of 5–6 November 1831 and melted down; a few pieces, including two bees, were recovered from the Seine. Napoleon later adopted the bees as a symbol of the French Empire.
chile: Stone tool evidence suggests humans visited the Monte Verde valley sporadically as far back as 18,500 years ago, and about 10,000 years ago Indigenous peoples settled the fertile valleys and coasts. The Mapuche, now the largest Indigenous group in South America with nearly two million people, lived mainly in scattered farming villages led by chiefs whose authority was limited to their own village. They resisted both the Inca and the Spanish, reorganised and formed alliances in the 16th century, and kept a level of autonomy until Chile subdued their territory in the late 19th century.

Ferdinand Magellan reached the strait that bears his name in 1520, and Diego de Almagro came from Peru with Spanish conquistadors in 1535, seeking gold. After Napoleon made his brother Joseph King of Spain in 1808, a national junta in the name of Ferdinand was formed on 18 September 1810; Chile still keeps that date as its National Day. Chile won the War of the Confederation against the Peru–Bolivian Confederation (1836–39), and the War of the Pacific (1879–83) added considerable territory.

Chile settled its remaining borders early in the 20th century: with Argentina through British arbitration in 1902 and a settlement over the Puna de Atacama the following year, and with Bolivia in the Treaty of Peace and Friendship of 1904. A constitution of 1925 separated church and state, after liberal lay laws of the late 19th century had reduced the clergy's influence.

The present constitution was drafted by Jaime Guzmán and approved in a plebiscite in September 1980 under Augusto Pinochet; it took effect in March 1981 and was amended after Pinochet lost the 1988 plebiscite. Amendments signed by President Ricardo Lagos in September 2005 ended appointed and life senators and cut the presidential term from six years to four. Michelle Bachelet became the first woman elected president in January 2006.

Chile stretches more than 4,300 kilometres from north to south but averages only 175 kilometres in width. The capital and largest city is Santiago, Spanish is the official language, and the 2024 census counted 18,480,432 people. The country has 16 regions. Its World Heritage Sites include Rapa Nui National Park, the Churches of Chiloé, the historic quarter of Valparaíso, the Humberstone and Santa Laura saltpetre works and the mining city of Sewell. Gabriela Mistral and Pablo Neruda won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1945 and 1971.
chilean-civil-code: The code, also called the Code of Bello, was the result of several years of Andrés Bello's own work, though it was officially presented as the work of several commissions of Congress. Bello delivered the complete draft on 22 November 1855, and President Manuel Montt sent it to Congress with a foreword by Bello. Congress passed it into law on 14 December 1855 and it came into force on 1 January 1857. It has been altered many times but has remained in force ever since.

A preliminary title (articles 1 to 53) deals with law in general. Like the French code, it allows a law to be applied only once it has been duly promulgated and officially published, with allowances for delays in communication, so that no secret laws were possible; it forbids laws that apply to events before their passage and bars judges from issuing general rulings with the force of legislation.

Book I (articles 54 to 564) covers persons: birth and death, marriage and paternity, and legal persons. Book II (565 to 950) covers kinds of goods, ownership, possession and other rights in property; Book III (951 to 1436) succession, wills and donations; and Book IV (1437 to 2524) obligations and contracts, including torts. Books I and III were later heavily amended to end discrimination between children of married and unmarried parents. A final article set the date of entry into force and repealed earlier laws on the same matters.

The code is regarded as original in plan and content when set against the French code. It was adopted whole by Ecuador in 1858, El Salvador in 1859, Venezuela in 1862 (for that year only), Nicaragua in 1867, Honduras in 1880 (until 1899 and again from 1906), Colombia in 1887 and Panama after its separation from Colombia in 1903. Augusto Teixeira de Freitas, author of the Esboço de un Código Civil para Brasil, and Dalmacio Vélez Sársfield, the main author of the Argentine Civil Code, considered it the most important legal achievement of Latin America.
chilean-civil-war-of-1829-1830: After Bernardo O'Higgins resigned and went into exile in 1823, Chile went through the years of the so-called constitutional essays: Juan Egaña's Moralist constitution of 1823, which abolished slavery, José Miguel Infante's federalist scheme of 1826, never formally adopted, and the liberal constitution of 1828 drafted by José Joaquín de Mora with Melchor Santiago Concha. Presidents rose and fell quickly. The pelucones, heirs of O'Higgins and of the colonial aristocracy, wanted strong central government and support for the Catholic Church; the pipiolos, followers of José Miguel Carrera, wanted a freer government without the Church's interference. The estanqueros of Diego Portales and Infante's federalists stood beside them.

President Francisco Antonio Pinto alienated the federalists and his own liberals with the constitution of 1828, and angered the aristocracy by abolishing estates inherited by primogeniture. In the election of 1829 he won clearly, but the liberal Congress, arguing that no vice-presidential candidate had a majority, passed over the conservatives Francisco Ruiz-Tagle and José Joaquín Prieto and chose Joaquín Vicuña, who had only 48 electoral votes. That gave the conservatives their pretext.

Pinto resigned on 14 July, handing power to the President of the Senate, Francisco Ramón Vicuña. On 7 December 1829 Prieto's army, raised largely by his cousin Manuel Bulnes, approached Santiago from the south; the government fled to Valparaíso and then Coquimbo, and on 14 December Prieto defeated Francisco de la Lastra at the Battle of Ochagavía. A junta under the neutral José Tomás Ovalle ruled from 24 December. Once the conservative convention named Ruiz-Tagle acting president, the liberal generals Manuel Borgoño, Lastra and Juan Gregorio de las Heras were struck from the army rolls, and fighting resumed. Ruiz-Tagle resigned on 1 April 1830 and Ovalle took over as vice president.

After Lircay, near Talca, Ramón Freire was exiled first to Peru and then to Tahiti; he later returned but never took part in politics again. With nobody willing to serve, Ovalle made Portales universal minister, and his ideas shaped Chile for the rest of the century. The liberals signed the Treaty of Cuz-Cuz, which ended the anarchy and their dominance, and the constitution of 1833 remained in force until 1925.
chilean-war-of-independence: The war grew out of the crisis of the Spanish monarchy after Napoleonic forces captured King Ferdinand VII in 1808. In Chile, one of the smallest and poorest colonies of the Spanish Empire, Governor Francisco García Carrasco alienated the criollo elite with his harsh manner, a corruption case known as the Scorpion scandal and the arrest without due process of prominent citizens suspected of favouring a junta. He was forced to resign on 16 July 1810, and his successor, the 82-year-old criollo Mateo de Toro Zambrano, called an open cabildo in Santiago for 18 September 1810, which set up the First Junta, sworn loyal to Ferdinand VII.

Chilean historians divide the period into the Patria Vieja (1810-1814), the Reconquista (1814-1817) and the Patria Nueva (1817-1823). The fighting itself began in 1812. José Miguel Carrera, a veteran of the Peninsular War, took power in two coups at the end of 1811, issued the provisional Constitution of 1812 and founded the Instituto Nacional and the National Library. The Viceroy of Peru, José Fernando de Abascal, sent expeditions south, and on 1 and 2 October 1814 the royalists under Mariano Osorio crushed the patriots at Rancagua, where only 500 of 5,000 survived.

The persecution that followed, led by Vicente San Bruno, persuaded even moderates that only independence would do. Exiles gathered in Mendoza, while the lawyer Manuel Rodríguez waged a guerrilla campaign. After Chacabuco on 12 February 1817, O'Higgins became Supreme Director. A royalist force surprised the patriots at the Second Battle of Cancha Rayada on 18 March 1818, but San Martín's victory at Maipú on 5 April ended the threat to Santiago. A merciless irregular war in the south, the Guerra a muerte, lasted until the band of Vicente Benavides was destroyed in 1822.

O'Higgins built a navy under Lord Cochrane, who took the fortifications of Valdivia in 1820 and carried San Martín's expedition to Peru, whose independence was secured at Ayacucho on 9 December 1824. Chiloé fell in 1826 under Ramón Freire, the last royalists in Araucanía in 1827, and Spain recognised Chilean independence in 1844. The wars damaged the wheat trade, and a London loan of 1822 left a debt that was not regularised until the 1840s.
chilehaus: The Chilehaus was designed by the architect Fritz Höger and built between 1922 and 1924 for the shipping magnate Henry B. Sloman, who made his fortune trading saltpeter from Chile, which gave the building its name. The cost of construction is difficult to determine, because the building went up during the hyperinflation that struck Germany in the early 1920s. It is estimated to have been more than 10 million reichsmark. The building is an example of the 1920s Brick Expressionism style and stands in the Kontorhaus District of Hamburg. The large angular block stands on a site of about 6,000 square metres and spans the street Fischertwiete.

The building is known for its top, which recalls a ship's prow, and for facades that meet at a very sharp angle at the corner of the Pumpen- and Niedernstrasse. The best view is from the east. Accentuated vertical elements, recessed upper storeys and a curved facade on the Pumpenstraße give the building, despite its size, a touch of lightness. The sculptor Richard Kuöhl made the sculptural elements on the staircases and the facade.

The structure is reinforced concrete, faced with 4.8 million dark Oldenburg bricks. The ground was difficult, so the building rests on reinforced-concrete pilings 16 metres deep. Because of the nearby Elbe, the cellar was specially sealed, and the heating equipment was built in a caisson that can float within the building, so that a flood cannot damage it. The building had two sets of paternoster lifts until it was modernised in 1991. As part of the Kontorhaus District it was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2015.
chiloe: The Chiloé Archipelago lies in the Los Lagos Region of Chile, separated from the mainland by the 2-kilometre-wide Chacao Channel in the north, the Sea of Chiloé in the east and the Gulf of Corcovado in the southeast. Chiloé Island, at 8,394 square kilometres, is by far the largest island. Its southwestern half is a wilderness of forests, wetlands and low mountains, none higher than 800 metres, while the northeast has rolling hills of pasture and fields. The original vegetation is Valdivian temperate rainforest. The name comes from a Mapuche word, chillwe, meaning seagull place.

The first identifiable inhabitants are believed to be the Chonos, a seafaring people, though the Huilliche language was the main one when the Spanish arrived. Francisco de Ulloa first reached the main island in 1553, and in 1567 Captain Martín Ruiz de Gamboa conquered it with an expedition of 110 Spaniards and founded Castro. The Jesuits arrived in 1608 and built a circular mission of chapels reached by travelling in dalcas; by 1767, when the Society of Jesus was suppressed, there were 79 chapels.

Ancud replaced Castro as capital in 1767, and in 1784 the island became a direct dependency of the viceroyalty of Peru. A large Huilliche rebellion affected it in 1712. Chiloé never joined the Patria Vieja and gave Spain wide support: from 1812 its men were enlisted to fight for the royalist cause in Chile, Bolivia and Peru. In December 1817 it became, with Valdivia, the last stronghold of the royalists. Chilean expeditions failed at the Battle of Agüi and, in 1824, at the Battle of Mocopulli.

On 15 January 1826 Antonio de Quintanilla negotiated a surrender to a force led by Ramón Freire, and the island joined the Republic of Chile. Charles Darwin stayed there for six months from 28 June 1834. In the 19th century expeditions to the Straits of Magellan and the colonisation of Patagonia set out from Chiloé, and thousands of Chilotes migrated to work on the mainland. The great earthquake of 1960 destroyed Ancud's cathedral and badly damaged Castro.

The archipelago forms Chiloé Province, whose capital is Castro, with Ancud as the seat of the Catholic bishopric. Its people are called Chilotes, and its culture mixes Huilliche, Spanish and Chono influences. Wooden churches built by the Spanish and the Jesuits, roofed and clad in shingles, are among its best-known buildings, and some are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Stilt houses called palafitos stand in towns such as Castro and Chonchi. Salmon farming, fishing, tourism and agriculture are the mainstays of the economy, and Chiloé is a centre of diversity of the potato.
chilperic-i: On the death of his father Chlothar I in 561, Chilperic tried to take the whole kingdom, seized the treasure at Berny and entered Paris. His brothers compelled him to divide it. Soissons, with Amiens, Arras, Cambrai, Thérouanne, Tournai and Boulogne, fell to him, while Charibert received Paris, Guntram Burgundy and Sigebert Austrasia. When Charibert died in 567 the brothers divided his kingdom and agreed to share Paris and the territory around it.

Chilperic soon went to war with Sigebert. While Sigebert was away fighting the Avars, Chilperic attacked Reims and took it, but Sigebert returned, retook the city, defeated him at Soissons and imprisoned his eldest son Theudebert. The war flared again in 567 and in 573, when Guntram first allied with Chilperic and then changed sides, and Chilperic lost both times.

Sigebert married Brunhilda, daughter of the Visigothic king Athanagild. Chilperic, who had repudiated his first wife Audovera and taken a serving-woman, Fredegund, as concubine, dismissed Fredegund and married Brunhilda's sister Galswintha. She was soon found strangled in her bed, and a few days later Chilperic married Fredegund.

The murder led to long wars between the brothers. In December 575 two assassins working for Fredegund killed Sigebert, when he had Chilperic at his mercy. Chilperic then took Tours, Poitiers and places in Aquitaine from Austrasia and encouraged discord there during the minority of Childebert II.

In 578 he sent an army against the Breton ruler Waroch II of the Bro-Wened, who submitted after three days of fighting, did homage for Vannes, gave his son as hostage and agreed to pay tribute. He later broke his oath, but Chilperic's dominion over the Bretons was relatively secure.

Most of what is known of Chilperic comes from the History of the Franks by Gregory of Tours, who detested him, calling him the Nero and Herod of his time. He had provoked Gregory by taking Tours from Austrasia, seizing church property and appointing as bishops counts of the palace who were not clerics. Gregory also objected to his attempts to teach a new doctrine of the Trinity, although some scholars dispute how far Gregory disliked him, and he reports a forced conversion of Jews. His reign in Neustria saw the introduction of the Byzantine punishment of eye-gouging.

Chilperic was also a musician of some talent, wrote verse modelled on that of Sedulius, tried to reform the Frankish alphabet, and worked to reduce the worst effects of Salic law upon women. He was stabbed to death by an unknown assailant on his return from hunting at Chelles and buried in the Saint Vincent Basilica of Paris. His son Chlothar II succeeded him in Neustria and later became sole king of the Franks.
chimalpahin: Chimalpahin, also called Chimalpain, bore Nahuatl names that mean Runs Swiftly with a Shield and Rising Eagle. He claimed descent from the lords of Tenango-Amecameca-Chalco. His grandfather, Don Domingo Hernández Ayopochtzin, a seventh-generation descendant of the founding king of the polity, was learned and esteemed, above all for his education and his skill at keeping records in the ancient tradition. Chimalpahin died in Mexico City in 1660.

He wrote on the history of Mexico and of neighbouring nations in Nahuatl and Spanish. The most important of his surviving works, the Relaciones or Anales, was compiled in Nahuatl in the early seventeenth century from the testimony of indigenous people. It covers the years 1589 to 1615, but also deals with events before the conquest and gives lists of indigenous kings and lords and of Spanish viceroys, archbishops of Mexico and inquisitors.

Among the events he recorded are the visits to Mexico of Japanese delegations in 1610 and 1614, led by Tanaka Shōsuke and Hasekura Tsunenaga, and brawls between the Japanese and Spaniards, in one of which the Spanish ambassador Sebastián Vizcaíno was severely wounded at Acapulco in 1614.

His Diferentes historias originales, also called Relaciones originales, gathers the claims and proofs of nobility put forward by the indigenous leaders of Chalco-Amequemecan. Written as a judicial guide for the viceregal authorities when they granted privileges and offices to members of the indigenous nobility, it comprises eight relaciones, all holding ethnographic, social and chronological information of great value to historians. His manuscripts later came into the possession of Carlos de Sigüenza y Góngora.
chimalpopoca: Chimalpopoca, whose name means smoking shield in Classical Nahuatl, was born in 1397, the son of the ruler Huitzilihuitl and Queen Ayauhcihuatl. Some sources instead make him a son of Acamapichtli, the first ruler of Tenochtitlan, and so a brother of Huitzilihuitl, and the friar Gerónimo de Mendieta, noting the discrepancy, concluded that Huitzilihuitl, Chimalpopoca and Itzcoatl must have been brothers. He was a grandson of both Acamapichtli and Tezozomoc, ruler of Azcapotzalco, and a half-brother of Moctezuma I.

He was crowned at about 20 years old, in 1417 by most accounts, though some sources give 1416 or 1418. The bond with his grandfather was strengthened by Tenochtitlan's loyalty in Tezozomoc's war of 1418 against Ixtlilxochitl I of Texcoco, after which the conquered city was granted to Tenochtitlan as a tributary. Chimalpopoca interceded with Tezozomoc for Nezahualcoyotl, the displaced prince of Texcoco, who was then allowed to live in Tenochtitlan under his protection.

With Tezozomoc's help he built a wooden aqueduct from the high ground of Chapultepec to Tenochtitlan in 1426, and he had a causeway built to Tlacopan with openings spanned by wooden bridges that were taken up at night. He dedicated a sacrificial stone in the Tlacocomoco quarter, and the conquest of Tequizquiac is attributed to him. He had many wives, among them his cousin Matlalatzin, and his son Tezozomoc became king of Ecatepec.

When Tezozomoc died in 1426 his son Tayauh succeeded him, but another son, Maxtla, ruler of Coyoacan, seized the throne. Chimalpopoca had sided with Tayauh, and Maxtla had him killed, though the details are unclear, and raised the tribute demanded of Tenochtitlan. Itzcoatl, who followed him as tlatoani, allied with Nezahualcoyotl of Texcoco and Totoquihuatzin of Tlacopan, and together they brought down Maxtla.
chimborazo: Chimborazo stands in the Cordillera Occidental of the Andes, in the Chimborazo Province, 150 km south-southwest of Quito, and rises about 2,500 metres above the surrounding highlands. It is a double volcano with four summits, of which Whymper (6,263 m) is the highest. In Quechua, chimba means on the other side and razu means ice or snow, one proposed origin of the name. Its glaciers supply water to people in the Bolívar and Chimborazo provinces, and local ice-gatherers, the hieleros, have sold its ice in the markets of Guaranda and Riobamba.

About 35,000 years ago a collapse produced a debris avalanche that underlies the city of Riobamba. The volcano erupted several times in the Holocene, the last about 550 CE, give or take 150 years. Until the early 19th century Chimborazo was thought the highest mountain on Earth, which drew many attempts on its summit. In 1746 French academicians of the French Geodesic Mission explored it. In June 1802 Alexander von Humboldt, with Aimé Bonpland and Carlos Montúfar, was forced back by altitude sickness at 5,875 m, higher than any European had recorded. On 4 January 1880 the English climber Edward Whymper reached the summit, and when critics doubted it he climbed it again later that year by another route with David Beltrán and Francisco Campaña.

At 6,263 m Chimborazo is the highest mountain in Ecuador. Because the Earth bulges at the Equator, its summit, one degree south of the line, is widely reported to be the farthest point on the surface from the Earth's centre, about 2.1 km farther than the summit of Mount Everest, though Everest is higher above sea level. A faunal reserve for vicuña, llama and alpaca surrounds it, and it appears on the coat of arms of Ecuador. Simón Bolívar's poem Mi delirio sobre el Chimborazo was inspired by it, and Frederick Edwin Church painted it in 1864.
chimera-of-arezzo: The Chimera of Arezzo is cast entirely in bronze and measures 78.5 cm in height and 129 cm in length. It was originally part of a larger group showing the fight between the Chimera and the Greek hero Bellerophon. According to Greek myth, the Chimera was a fire-breathing hybrid of Lycia in Anatolia, the offspring of Typhon and Echidna, which Bellerophon killed on his winged horse Pegasus. A round hole on the left rump may mark where his spear struck.
The statue shows the beast contorted in pain, with its mouth open, and was probably meant to be seen from all sides. Like Hellenistic sculpture, it conveys movement and the tension of the muscles.

The statue was probably commissioned by an aristocratic clan or a prosperous community and set up in a sanctuary near Arezzo about 400 BCE. Historians generally agree that Italiote craftsmen, the Greek-speaking people of southern Italy, made it in the last decades of the fifth century BCE or the early fourth. The art historian A. Maggiani compares it with works from Metaponto and Kaulonia. An Etruscan inscription on the right foreleg is now thought to read tinscvil, offering belonging to Tinia. The statue was one of a hoard of bronzes that had been carefully buried for safety.

Workers found it on 15 November 1553 near the San Lorentino gate of Arezzo. Cosimo I de' Medici claimed it and placed it in the hall of Leo X in the Palazzo Vecchio, and he kept the smaller bronzes from the hoard in his studiolo at the Palazzo Pitti, where, Benvenuto Cellini reported, he cleaned them himself. The statue lacked the snake and two paws and was first taken for a lion, until Giorgio Vasari identified the subject by comparing coins. A sculptor, Francesco Carradori or his teacher Innocenzo Spinazzi, replaced the tail in 1785 but set the serpent to bite the goat's horn, which is unlikely.

It moved to the Uffizi in 1718 and has belonged to the National Archaeological Museum in Florence since 1870. The art historian David Ekserdjian called it the supreme masterpiece of Etruscan bronze-casting.
china: China covers 9.6 million square kilometres, the third largest country by area, with a dry and mountainous west and both mountains and wide river valleys in the east. Chinese civilisation was traditionally centred in the lowlands around the two longest rivers, the Yangtze and the Yellow River, both of which originate on the Tibetan Plateau. Mount Everest, the world's highest point, lies on the border with Nepal. The climate is dominated by dry seasons and wet monsoons, and the Yellow River's perennial floods have devastated the surrounding plains throughout recorded history.

Modern Homo sapiens are attested in China from around 50,000 years ago, and pottery-making Neolithic cultures emerged after about 8,000 BCE. After 2000 BCE the Erlitou culture emerged in the Central Plain, controversially identified with the Xia, the traditionally accepted first dynasty; no written records confirm this. The Shang dynasty purportedly succeeded the Xia around 1600 BCE, and its late phase is attested by oracle bone script, the earliest known writing in China. The Zhou overthrew the Shang c. 1046 BCE, and centralised authority collapsed in 771 BCE. The Eastern Zhou saw the Spring and Autumn period and then the seven Warring States, and schools of thought such as Confucianism and Daoism.

In 221 BCE the Qin ruler Qin Shi Huang proclaimed himself the first emperor, but the dynasty lasted only fifteen years. It was followed by the Han dynasty, and two millennia of imperial rule across periods of unity and division followed. The empire was succeeded by the Republic of China after the 1911 Revolution. The Warlord Era and the Chinese Civil War followed, interrupted by the Second Sino-Japanese War. In 1949 the Chinese Communist Party proclaimed the People's Republic of China, and the Republic of China retreated to Taiwan; both sides still claim political legitimacy. The party's attempts to advance its political program faltered through famine and political turmoil, and the reform and opening-up that began in 1978 moved China towards a socialist market economy.

The 2020 census recorded a population of 1,411,778,724, and Beijing is the capital. China is a unitary state with the Chinese Communist Party as its sole ruling party. It maintained a one-child policy from 1979 to 2015.

The Han are the dominant ethnicity, and 55 minorities are recognised, including the Hui, Mongols, Tibetans, Uyghurs and Zhuang. It has 60 World Heritage Sites, including the Great Wall and the Grand Canal.
chinampa: The word chinampa comes from the Nahuatl chināmitl, meaning a square made of canes, with the locative pan.
