The plots were built on the shallow lake beds of the Valley of Mexico, chiefly in Lakes Xochimilco and Chalco, near the springs along the south shore. The earliest fields that have been securely dated belong to the Middle Postclassic period, 1150-1350.

The Aztecs did not invent the technique but were the first to develop it to large-scale cultivation. Before the Aztec Triple Alliance formed, farmers kept small chinampas beside their households and communities, and the conquest of southern basin cities such as Xochimilco was one of the first strategies of imperial expansion.

Often called floating gardens, chinampas did not float. They were artificial islands made by interweaving reeds with stakes beneath the lake's surface to form underwater fences, which were filled with mud, lake sediment and decaying vegetation until the top layer rose above the water. Willows and cypresses were often planted at the corners to secure the plot. One scholar, using the Codex Vergara, found that chinampas usually measured about 30 m by 2.5 m, and in Tenochtitlan they ranged from 90 m by 5 m to 90 m by 10 m.

Channels wide enough for a canoe separated them, and mud dug from the ditches was spread on top as fertiliser. The ditches gave plants continuous access to water, so the crops did not depend on rainfall, and the beds gave up to seven harvests a year. Crops included maize, beans, squash, amaranth, tomatoes, chili peppers and flowers.

Chinampa farms ringed Tenochtitlan, which the Aztecs built on an island around 1325 and which kept growing, so that more food was needed. According to some researchers the Aztecs undertook significant state-led efforts to expand the chinampas, the so-called hydraulic hypothesis. The argument rests on the manpower needed and on the assumption that dikes were needed to keep the saline water of Lake Texcoco from the freshwater zone, though the chinampas worked before the dike was built.

The extent to which Tenochtitlan relied on them for fresh food has been much studied. When dams and sluice gates were destroyed during the Spanish conquest, many fields were abandoned, but cultivation was labour-intensive and unattractive to Spaniards, so many lakeshore towns kept their chinampas to the end of the colonial period.

Remnants survive at Xochimilco, San Gregorio, San Luis, Tláhuac and Mixquic, where some plots grow vegetables and flowers. The United Nations designated the system a Globally Important Agricultural Heritage System in 2018. Drained lakes, the earthquake of 1985, pollution and urban sprawl are among the challenges to it.
chincha-islands-war: Under Isabella II, Spain greatly increased its military spending and became one of the larger naval powers, active in Morocco, the Philippines, Mexico and the Dominican Republic. At the end of 1862 it sent a scientific expedition to South American waters under Admiral Luis Hernández-Pinzón Álvarez, with the covert aim of backing the claims of Spanish citizens there. On 4 August 1863 a fight at the Talambo hacienda in Lambayeque, Peru, left one Spaniard dead and four injured. Pinzón demanded an apology and reparations, which Peru refused as an internal police matter, and Madrid added a demand for debts from the War of Independence.

Its envoy, Eusebio Salazar y Mazarredo, arrived in March 1864 with the title of Royal Commissary, a colonial office rather than an ambassador's, which Peru took as an insult. On 14 April 1864 the Spanish seized the islands, which produced almost 60% of the Peruvian government's annual revenue, arrested their governor and landed 400 marines.

Vice Admiral José Manuel Pareja, sent to replace Pinzón, signed the Vivanco-Pareja Treaty on 27 January 1865, but Peruvian opinion saw it as a blow to national honour, and President Juan Antonio Pezet fell on 7 November. When Chile refused coal to Spanish ships, Pareja demanded a 21-gun salute at Valparaíso on 17 September 1865; Chile refused and war was declared on 24 September. After the Chilean corvette Esmeralda captured the Spanish schooner Covadonga at the Battle of Papudo on 26 November, Pareja took his own life, and Casto Méndez Núñez took command.

Under General Mariano Ignacio Prado, Peru allied with Chile on 5 December 1865 and declared war on 14 January 1866; Ecuador followed on 30 January and Bolivia on 22 March, closing every Pacific port south of Colombia to the Spanish. An exchange of fire at Abtao on 7 February ended indecisively. On 31 March the Spanish shelled and burned Valparaíso, sinking or burning 33 vessels, and on 2 May they attacked Callao, where both sides claimed victory.

Without ports for coal and supplies, the Spanish fleet left the Chincha Islands and returned home by way of the Philippines, completing a circumnavigation. Whether Spain planned to recover its former colonies is unknown. Prado presented the war as a national victory and ordered the ironclads Independencia and Huáscar, the first armoured ships in Latin America, while in Chile Federico Errázuriz Zañartu, secretary of war during the conflict, later worked to modernise the army.
chinchaysuyu: Chinchay Suyu, in Spanish Chinchaysuyo, was one of the suyus or quarters, the largest divisions of Tawantin Suyu, the Inca Empire. Together with Antisuyu it formed the Hanan Suyukuna, the Upper Quarters of the empire. Its name comes from the Chincha culture, a trading kingdom in what is now the Ica Region. In Quechua chinchay is the tigrillo, an animal present in the imagery of some cultures of the region, such as the Chavín culture, through Amazonian influence.

Each suyu was divided into wamani, or provinces. Those of Chinchay Suyu included Cajamarca, Casma, Chachapoya, Chancay, Chimu, also called Moche, Chincha, Huánuco, Jauja, Lambayeque, whose people spoke Mochica, Piura, Tarma and Tumbes. Lima or Rimaq was a large province of perhaps 150,000 inhabitants, and Lurin was home to the Oracle at Pachacamac. The name of the province of Virú, or Wanapu, is likely the origin of the word Perú.

Before the Inca Civil War, Atahualpa, a son of the dead emperor Huayna Capac, ruled most of Chinchay Suyu from his capital at Quito, supported by his father's veteran generals and soldiers. Huayna Capac had ordered that his heart and organs be buried in an urn in Quito, the city he loved, and his mummified body taken to Cuzco to lie beside his royal ancestors. Spanish chroniclers called Atahualpa's realm the Kingdom of Quito.

Huascar, the eldest son of Huayna Capac, ruled the rest of the empire from Cuzco and resented Atahualpa's position, but could do little while the best soldiers of the empire were sworn to his brother. After four or five years of peace the nobles and Huascar's mother, Rava Ocllo, urged him to reconquer the north. He sent Atahualpa an ultimatum demanding submission, and when Atahualpa refused, the young general Atoc was sent to invade the Kingdom of Quito.
chindwin-river: The Chindwin, also called the Ningthi, is a river of Myanmar and the largest tributary of the Irrawaddy. The Tanai leaves the Hukawng valley through the Taron or Turong valley and a sharp defile, and below that it takes the name Chindwin and keeps a generally southerly course. It passes Singkaling Hkamti and Homalin on its left bank. Its course is generally south-westerly as far as Mingin, after which it turns south-eastwards into the broad central plain and passes Monywa, forming the boundary between the Sagaing and Magway regions.

The Uyu is its largest tributary, joining below Homalin; the jade mines of Hpakant lie in its headwaters. The Myittha, which drains the Kale valley, joins from the right at Kalewa, and the Tizu comes down from central Nagaland in northeast India. The river reaches the Irrawaddy through several outlets about 35 kilometres apart, with long low islands between them. By tradition the lowest mouth is a channel cut by one of the kings of Bagan, which silted up and was reopened by an exceptional flood in 1824.

The mountains west of the Chindwin are hard to cross but have not stopped armies. The Kabaw valley saw many invasions by the kingdom of Manipur, most notably under King Garibaniwaj (1709–1748), whose army crossed the Chindwin and the Mu, took Myedu and reached Sagaing, opposite the capital Ava. The positions reversed in 1758, when Alaungpaya came to the Burmese throne: Burmese armies crossed the western ranges, occupied Manipur and Assam and even pressed on British India.

In World War II, after the Japanese cut off the sea route, British and other Allied forces under General Joseph Stilwell retreated on foot across the same mountains to India, with heavy losses from disease and hunger. The Ledo Road was built across the Hukawng valley to supply China. The Chindwin was a major barrier both for the Japanese trying to invade India and for the Allied forces seeking to retake Burma.

Much of the river runs through mountain and forest that is hard to reach, and large parts remain unspoilt. Regular river vessels serve it as far as Homalin. Teak forests in its basin have been a valuable resource since ancient times, and the Hukawng valley is known for Burmese amber. Hpakant, in the headwaters of the Uyu, is described as the only place where the finest jadeite, called imperial jade, is found.
chinese-civil-war: After the 1911 Revolution China fell into a power struggle following Yuan Shikai's death in 1916. Sun Yat-sen's Kuomintang (KMT) set up a government in Guangzhou to rival the warlords. When Western countries ignored his requests for aid, Sun turned to the Soviet Union, and in 1923 the Sun–Joffe Manifesto pledged Soviet assistance. In 1926 and 1927 the KMT and the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), allied in the First United Front, carried out the Northern Expedition against the warlords. After the Shanghai massacre of 1927 the CCP launched an uprising at Nanchang on 1 August 1927, the date from which armed conflict continued intermittently.

The first phase lasted from 1927 to 1937. In October 1934 the CCP broke out of the ring of blockhouses that encircled it, beginning the Long March, which lasted a year. When Japan invaded Manchuria in 1931, Chiang Kai-shek held to a policy of 'first internal pacification, then external resistance'. From 1937, when Japan launched its full-scale invasion, hostilities were mostly put on hold under the Second United Front, though cooperation was minimal and clashes remained common.

As Japan's defeat approached, both sides rushed to take over occupied areas. In 1945 the Communists had 1.2 million troops with 2 million militia, and Soviet forces handed them Northeast China and captured Japanese weapons. On 20 July 1946 Chiang launched a large assault on Communist territory in the north with 113 brigades. The CCP gave up territory to preserve its forces, and after a year the balance had shifted. The Liaoshen, Huaihai and Pingjin campaigns ended in Communist victory in January 1949.

The Communists proclaimed the People's Republic of China in October 1949, and the Republic of China government retreated to Taiwan on 7 December 1949. Historians explain the Communist victory by the hyperinflation, corruption and loss of trust under the Nationalist government, and by the CCP's land reform, which won peasant support. Both sides committed atrocities in which millions of non-combatants were killed. After 1927 the Kuomintang killed between 300,000 and one million people, mainly peasants, in the White Terror, and the Communists executed 2,000 to 3,000 members of the Futian battalion in December 1930. After 1949, official figures of 1954 give at least 2.6 million arrested and 712,000 executed in the Campaign to Suppress Counterrevolutionaries.
chinese-communist-party: The October Revolution and Marxist theory inspired the founding of the party. Chen Duxiu and Li Dazhao were among the first to support Leninism and world revolution in public, and both regarded the October Revolution as heralding a new era for oppressed countries. In 1921 they founded the party with the help of the Far Eastern Bureau of the Russian Communist Party and that of the Communist International. In its first years it was aligned with the Kuomintang. The rise of the Kuomintang's right wing under Chiang Kai-shek, and massacres of tens of thousands of party members, led to a split and a prolonged civil war.

On 15 July 1927 the Wuhan government of the Kuomintang expelled all communists. The party answered by founding the Workers' and Peasants' Red Army of China, and a battalion under General Zhu De took the city of Nanchang on 1 August 1927 in the Nanchang uprising. During about ten years of guerrilla warfare Mao Zedong became the most influential figure in the party, which built a strong base among the rural peasantry with its land reform policies.

Support continued to grow during the Second Sino-Japanese War, and after the Japanese surrender in 1945 the party defeated the Nationalist government. Mao proclaimed the People's Republic of China before a large crowd at Tiananmen Square on 1 October 1949, and the remnants of the Nationalist government retreated to Taiwan.

Mao remained the most influential member until his death in 1976. Under him the party completed its land reform, launched five-year plans and split with the Soviet Union, and in the Cultural Revolution he tried to purge the party of elements deemed capitalist or reactionary. After his death Hua Guofeng removed the Gang of Four from power, and Deng Xiaoping won a power struggle with Hua to become paramount leader in 1978. Deng, with Hu Yaobang and Zhao Ziyang, led the policies of reform and opening up, and argued that a socialist state could use a market economy without itself being capitalist.

The party seeks officially to adapt Marxism–Leninism to Chinese conditions, a process it calls socialism with Chinese characteristics. It is organised on democratic centralism, which allows open discussion of policy on condition of unity once a decision is made. Its highest body is the National Congress, convened every five years. When the Congress is not in session the Central Committee is the highest body, but because it usually meets only once a year, most duties lie with the Politburo and its Standing Committee. The party's leader holds the office of general secretary, and also chairs the Central Military Commission.
chinese-new-year: A poem in the Classic of Poetry, written in the Western Zhou period (1046 to 771 BCE), describes the celebration of the tenth month of the ancient solar calendar, when people cleaned millet stacks, offered rice wine to guests and toasted their master with wishes for longevity, and this is believed to be one prototype of the New Year. The Lüshi Chunqiu records that in the state of Qin an exorcism called the Big Nuo was held on the last day of the year. After Qin unified China it spread and evolved into the practice of cleaning the house. Legend says the festival began in the struggle against the Nian, a beast that ate villagers and feared red and loud noises.

The first day falls on the new moon between 21 January and 20 February, in more than 96 percent of years the new moon nearest the beginning of spring. Yuan Shikai, then interim president of the Republic of China, first proposed the name Spring Festival in 1914. Families gather for a reunion dinner on New Year's Eve, which traditionally includes fish that is not eaten completely, since the phrase for surpluses every year sounds like fish every year. The second day is for married daughters to visit their birth families, the fifth is the birthday of the God of Wealth and the ninth is the birthday of the Jade Emperor. The fifteenth is the Lantern Festival.

Red envelopes are given by married couples and the elderly to unmarried juniors and children, and are also called yasuiqian, from a phrase meaning money to suppress evil spirits. In 1967, during the Cultural Revolution, official celebrations were banned in China, and they were reinstated when it ended. The festival has influenced the Losar of Tibet, the Tết of Vietnam and the Seollal of Korea, and is a public holiday in several countries with large Chinese populations. UNESCO added it to the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity list in 2024.
chinese-peoples-political-consultative-c: The conference has roots before the People's Republic. During negotiations between the Chinese Communist Party and the Kuomintang in 1945, the two parties agreed in the Double Tenth Agreement to open multiparty talks on post-war political reforms through a Political Consultative Conference. The National Government of the Republic of China organised the first one at Chongqing from 10 to 31 January 1946, with representatives of the Kuomintang, the Communist Party and other parties. It ended in failure, and the Communist Party withdrew. On 1 May 1948, after major successes in the civil war, the party invited other parties, popular organisations and community leaders to form a new conference to discuss a new state and a new coalition government.

In September 1949, with the Communist Party in control of most of mainland China, the new conference met with delegates from friendly parties and was renamed the People's Political Consultative Conference. On 29 September 1949 its first plenary session unanimously adopted the Common Program as the basic political programme of the country. It approved the new national anthem, flag, capital city and state name, and elected the first government of the People's Republic of China. From 1949 to 1954 it acted as the de facto legislature and issued nearly 3,500 laws; the Constitution of 1954 transferred legislative functions to the National People's Congress.

During the Hundred Flowers Campaign of 1956–1957 Mao Zedong encouraged members to speak about the party's shortcomings, but those who did faced heavy criticism or imprisonment in labour camps in the Anti-Rightist Campaign that followed. Like most institutions, the conference was effectively decimated in the Cultural Revolution. It was revived at the first session of its 5th National Committee, from 24 February to 8 March 1974, when Deng Xiaoping was elected chairman. Rules issued in 1983 limited Communist Party members to 40 percent of its membership.

The conference consists of a National Committee and regional committees at the provincial, prefecture and county levels. Its members come from the Communist Party and its people's organisations, from eight other parties, and from nominally independent members, with seats also reserved for overseas delegates and for deputies from Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan. National Committee members serve five-year terms. The National Committee normally meets in March, at the same time as the National People's Congress, and the two meetings are together called the Two Sessions. The conference advises government bodies and submits proposals but has no legislative power.
chinese-red-army: The First United Front between the Communists and the Kuomintang, held together by the prestige of Sun Yat-sen, broke after his death in 1925 and Chiang Kai-shek's violent purge of communists in 1927. On 1 August 1927 about 25,000 Communist insurgents seized Nanchang in the Nanchang Uprising, but on their march south to Guangdong heat, hunger, illness and desertion wore them down, and they failed before Chaozhou, Shantou and Tangkeng. Zhu De and Chen Yi led the survivors into guerrilla war on the borders of Guangdong, Jiangxi and Hunan, and in April 1928 led over 10,000 troops from an uprising in southern Hunan into the mountains, where they joined Mao Zedong to form the 4th Army.

By the summer of 1930 the Red Army had more than 100,000 soldiers and several base areas, Jiangxi the largest, and in 1931 it beat back three large Nationalist offensives. Purges took a heavy toll: suspecting spies, the First Red Army executed about 4,000 men in 1931, and Zhang Guotao killed more than 2,500 officers of the Fourth Red Army who had come from the Nationalist forces. In 1934 a fifth offensive, armed with new German weapons, cost the First Red Army more than 50,000 men and drove it out of Jiangxi on the Long March; it reached northern Shaanxi in the autumn of 1935 with only 6,000. A Fourth Red Army force that struck into Gansu in 1936 was destroyed by Ma Bufang.

After the Marco Polo Bridge Incident of 7 July 1937 the three main armies became the 115th, 120th and 129th Divisions, 45,000 soldiers in all, while 10,000 men in the south fought on as guerrillas. The army grew rapidly during the war against Japan and ended it with 900,000 regular troops and 2 million militia. Its veterans were later honoured in the People's Republic and set apart from those who joined after 1937.

The Red Army had no ranks. Officers were at first elected by their soldiers, and at every level from regiment to army a commander, political commissar, chief of staff and director of the political department shared command, the commissar holding most power. Mao held that its main task was to mobilise the masses, fighting being only a means, and the Gutian Congress of 1929 set out party leadership of the army. Coerced recruitment was forbidden; villages competed to supply recruits, and local red guards gave logistical support. Almost all its weapons were captured, and rifles were short: in the winter of 1934 the First Red Army's twelve divisions had 72,300 soldiers and 25,300 rifles.
chingiz-aitmatov: Chinghiz Torekulovich Aitmatov was born on 12 December 1928 to a Kyrgyz father and a Tatar mother, both civil servants in Sheker. He grew up as Kyrgyzstan was transformed from one of the most remote lands of the Russian Empire into a republic of the USSR. In 1937 his father was charged in Moscow with bourgeois nationalism, and he was arrested and executed in 1938. Aitmatov worked from an early age, as assistant to the secretary of the village soviet at fourteen and later as a tax collector and a loader. He studied animal husbandry at Frunze, then literature at the Maxim Gorky Literature Institute in Moscow.

His first publications appeared in 1952, in Russian, and his first work in Kyrgyz, White Rain, in 1954. The novella Jamila, published in 1958, proved his talent: seen through the eyes of an adolescent boy, it tells of a village girl, separated from her soldier husband by the war, who falls in love with a disabled former soldier. He received the Lenin Prize in 1963 for the collection Tales of the Mountains and Steppes. Later works include Farewell, Gyulsary!, The Day Lasts More Than a Hundred Years of 1980 and The Place of the Skull of 1987.

His writing draws on folklore, recreating oral tales in contemporary settings, and nearly every story refers to a myth, legend or folktale. In The Day Lasts More Than a Hundred Years a legend of a young captive turned into a mankurt serves as a tragic allegory. He also wrote of the closeness of people to animals, such as a man and his stallion in Farewell, Gyulsary!. Most of his early works were in Kyrgyz, but from 1966 he wrote in Russian, which he said was as much a native language for him as Kyrgyz.

Aitmatov worked for Pravda for eight years, joined the Soviet Communist Party in 1959 and endorsed Mikhail Gorbachev's glasnost. From 1990 to 1993 he was Soviet ambassador to Luxembourg, then accredited by Russia, and from 2000 to 2008 he represented Kyrgyzstan to the European Union, NATO, UNESCO and the Benelux countries. He died of pneumonia on 10 June 2008 in a hospital in Nuremberg, aged 79.
chinguetti: Chinguetti is a ksar and medieval trading centre in northern Mauritania, on the Adrar Plateau east of Atar. A wadi divides it into an old sector and a new one. The region was once a broad savannah, and rock paintings at Agrour Amogjar in the nearby Amogjar Pass show giraffes, cows and people in a green landscape. The older houses are built of reddish dry-stone and mud-brick with flat roofs timbered from palms, and many have hand-hewn doors cut from ancient acacia trees that have long disappeared from the area. Narrow streets lead to the central mosque.

The name means spring of horses in the Azer dialect, an extinct dialect of Soninke heavily mixed with Berber. By the 11th century the town was a trading centre for the Sanhaja, a confederation of Berber tribes that merged with the Almoravids, who spread the Malikite rite of Sunni Islam across the western Maghreb. The town's stark architecture is said to reflect their strict beliefs.

After two centuries of decline the town was effectively re-founded in the 13th century as a fortified trading centre for nomadic trans-Saharan caravans, connecting the Mediterranean with Sub-Saharan Africa. The walls have disappeared, but many buildings in the old sector date from this period. For centuries it was a gathering place for pilgrims of the Maghreb on their way to Mecca and was regarded as a holy city in its own right. Its schools taught rhetoric, law, astronomy, mathematics and medicine, and for many centuries all of Mauritania was commonly known in the Arab world as Bilad Shinqit, the land of Chinguetti.

UNESCO designated Chinguetti, with Ouadane, Tichitt and Oualata, a World Heritage Site in 1996. The Friday Mosque, a dry-stone building of the 13th and 14th centuries with a square minaret topped by five ostrich egg finials, is widely considered by Mauritanians to be the national symbol. The old quarter has five important manuscript libraries of scientific and Qur'anic texts, many from the later Middle Ages. The desert threatens the town: high dunes mark its western edge and several houses have been abandoned to the sand.
chinon: Chinon is a commune in the Indre-et-Loire department of the Centre-Val de Loire region, 47 kilometres south-west of Tours. It lies on both banks of the river Vienne, about 10 kilometres from where the Vienne joins the Loire, with the historic town mainly on the northern bank at the foot of the medieval castle. Rivers were the main trade routes in the Middle Ages, and the Vienne links the fertile Poitou and the city of Limoges to the Loire. The rocky outcrop above the town gave both a natural fort and protection from floods.

Settlement dates from prehistoric times, and by the 5th century a Gallo-Roman castrum stood on the site. About the middle of that century Saint Mexme, a disciple of Saint Martin, founded a hermitage and then a monastery east of the town. Chinon grew especially under Henry II, Count of Anjou and, from 1154, King of England, who rebuilt the castle as his administrative centre and favourite residence. He died there in 1189, and it passed to Richard I and then to John, who lost it in 1205 in a siege by Philip II of France.

In 1307 Jacques de Molay, Grand Master of the Knights Templar, and other dignitaries of the order were held in the castle before their trial. During the Hundred Years' War the heir apparent, the future Charles VII, installed his court at Chinon in 1425. In 1429 the seventeen-year-old Joan of Arc came there to meet him, and after she was questioned and given men and arms she broke the siege of Orléans, and Charles was crowned at Reims. François Rabelais was born in the commune. From the 16th century Chinon was no longer a royal residence, and its fortifications were pulled down in the 1820s.

Chinon is known for its castle, its historic town and its Cabernet Franc-based red wines, kept in caves cut into the banks of the Vienne. The historic centre, a conservation area since 1968, has half-timbered houses of the 14th and 15th centuries and town houses of local tufa stone with slate roofs. The Romanesque collegiate church of Saint-Mexme keeps a nave and first façade from about the year 1000. This part of the Loire Valley has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2000.
chinvat-bridge: The Avestan name, Cinvatô Peretûm, is rendered as bridge of judgement or as beam-shaped bridge; other forms of the name are Chinwad, Cinvat, Chinvar and Chinavat. How the bridge appears depends on the asha, the righteousness, of the soul that comes to it. Three divinities are thought to be its guardians: Sraosha, who stands for conscience, Mithra, for covenant, and Rashnu, for justice. Believers hold that the souls that cross successfully are united with Ahura Mazda. The Yasna describes the bridge in its 71st chapter and the Vendidad in its nineteenth fargard.

The bridge has often been identified with the rainbow or with the Milky Way, as in C. P. Tiele's History of Religion. Other scholars, among them C. F. Keary and Ferdinand Justi, reject this reading, citing descriptions of the bridge as rising straight upward and not in a curve.

Cyrus Niknam, a mobad and writer on ancient Iranian culture, denies that Zoroaster taught a bridge at all. In his reading the phrase in the hymns means a passage concerned with how to live, a questioning of the conscience, with no material crossing for the soul. He holds that the priests of the Sasanian era adapted beliefs about heaven, hell and the afterlife from other cultures that had reached Iran, and that the picture of a bridge wide for the righteous and thin as a hair for sinners belongs to that later development, as does the Book of Arda Viraf, and not to the Gathas.

The most notable of the Sogdian depictions is on the east wall of the funerary couch of the sabao Wirkak, excavated at Xi'an; a fragmentary one is on the couch in the Miho Museum. As-Sirat in Islam is a similar idea. In Yazidism the Silat Bridge at Lalish leads to the holiest Yazidi shrine, marks the passage from the profane world to the sacred, and is held to play a part at the end of times as well. In modern literature Charles Olson refers to the bridge in The Maximus Poems, and Dimitris Lyacos alludes to it in With the People from the Bridge.
chioggia: Chioggia lies on a small island at the southern entrance to the Venetian Lagoon, about 25 kilometres south of Venice. Causeways connect it to the mainland and to its quarter of Sottomarina. It is a comune of the Metropolitan City of Venice in the Veneto region. It is often called Little Venice because of its few canals, chief among them the Canale Vena, and its narrow streets, known as calli.

Chioggia and Sottomarina were not prominent in antiquity. Pliny mentions the place as the fossa Clodia, and a local legend attributes the name to a founder called Clodius, though the origin of the belief is not known. The name later appears as Clugia, Chiozza and finally Chioggia. The oldest documents naming it date from the 6th century, when it was part of the Byzantine Empire. King Pippin of Italy destroyed it in the 9th century, and it was rebuilt around a new industry based on salt pans. In the Middle Ages the town proper was Clugia major, while Clugia minor was a sand bar about 600 metres further into the Adriatic.

A free commune and an episcopal see from 1110, Chioggia played an important part in the War of Chioggia between Genoa and Venice. Genoa conquered it in 1378 and Venice took it finally in June 1380. The town remained largely autonomous but was always afterwards subordinate to Venice. On 14 March 1381 it made an alliance with Zadar and Trogir against Venice. The town's churches were much reworked in the 16th and 17th centuries, the period of its highest prosperity. The cathedral of Santa Maria Assunta, founded in the eleventh century, became a cathedral in 1110 and was rebuilt from 1623 by Baldassare Longhena.

Fishing has historically been the livelihood of the port and remains a significant economic sector, alongside textiles, brick-making and steel, while Sottomarina is largely given over to seafront tourism. The bell tower of the Church of Sant'Andrea, dating from the 11th or 12th century, is said to hold the oldest functioning tower clock in the world. Chioggia is known for bobbin lace and was the setting of Carlo Goldoni's play Le baruffe chiozzotte. It also gives its name to a variety of beetroot and of radicchio. Its most common surname is Zennaro, and the comune officially records the nicknames known as detto that distinguish branches of one family.
chipata: Chipata lies on the Great East Road about 570 kilometres east of Lusaka and about 150 kilometres west of Lilongwe, the capital of Malawi, at an elevation of 1,181 metres. The name comes from the Chewa word Chimpata, meaning large space, which refers to the town's position in a shallow valley between hills; Kapata, the original centre of the town, takes its name from a Chewa word for small space. The climate is tropical savanna, with a wet season from November to March, and the main vegetation is miombo woodland. Four major streams flow from the area into the Luangwa River.

The town was formerly Fort Jameson, informally Fort Jimmy, named after Sir Leander Starr Jameson, the British politician and adventurer known above all for the Jameson Raid. Even in the colonial period few thought him fully deserving of the honour. It was called a fort, like Fort Manning and Fort Rosebery, because the local government offices, the boma, were once fortified. Fort Jameson was the capital of the British protectorate of North-Eastern Rhodesia between 1900 and 1911.

In 1941 eighty Polish refugees who had escaped German- and Soviet-occupied Poland were admitted to Fort Jameson. Chipata is the regional seat of the Ngoni of Zambia, who adopted the languages of the peoples they conquered, so that Chewa and Nsenga are the principal languages, with Tumbuka and English widely spoken. Each year, usually at the end of February, the Ngoni hold the Nc'wala first-fruits ceremony at Mutenguleni on the edge of the town.

Chipata is the administrative centre of Zambia's Eastern Province and of Chipata District, and in 2017 it was declared the fifth city of the country. The city had 193,288 inhabitants in 2022. The main groups are the Chewa, Tumbuka, Ngoni and Nsenga, and a large number of Zambian Indians live there and run many of the shops.

It is the main transport hub for trade between Zambia and Malawi. A rail link of about 35 kilometres to Mchinji in Malawi, opened in August 2011, gives a through route to the Indian Ocean port of Nacala in Mozambique. The town is also a common gateway to South Luangwa National Park, about 100 kilometres to the north-west.
chippenham: Chippenham lies in north-west Wiltshire, 13 miles north-east of Bath and 86 miles west of London, at a prominent crossing of the River Avon. It is set between the Marlborough Downs to the east, the southern Cotswolds to the north and west, and Salisbury Plain to the south-east. Some form of settlement is believed to have existed there since before Roman times, and remains of Romano-British settlements are visible in a wall behind the former magistrates' court.

The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records the town as Cippanhamme. The name may refer to a person called Cippa who had his hamm, an enclosure in a river meadow, or it may come from the Old English word ceap, meaning market. The name is recorded as Cippanhamm in 878, Cepen in 1042, Cheppeham in 1155 and Chippenham in 1227. The town was a royal vill, probably a royal hunting lodge, under Alfred the Great. In Norman times the royal properties were divided into the manors of Sheldon, Rowden and Lowden, and the town expanded into Langstret, now the Causeway, from 1245 and into Le Newstret from 1406.

The A4 through the town incorporates parts of a 14th-century road linking London to Bristol, which was important for the cloth trade and was maintained partly with money from Bristol cloth merchants. The wool industry took off in the 16th century, partly because of the river. Plague struck in 1611 and 1636, and a recession in woollen cloth and poor corn harvests in 1622 and 1623 caused hardship. In 1747 a bribery scandal involving two of the town's members of parliament contributed to the fall of Sir Robert Walpole's government.

A branch of the Wilts and Berks Canal reached Chippenham in 1798, ending at a wharf near the market place, and the Great Western Railway arrived in 1841, attracting new businesses and bringing house building north of the line. The railway station has arches and other buildings engineered by Isambard Kingdom Brunel. The original Buttercross, of about 1570, was moved in 1889 to Castle Combe and re-erected in the town in 1995. Markets are held in the town centre each Friday and Saturday, and the museum in the Market Place tells the story of the town from Neolithic times. At the 2021 census the parish had 36,548 inhabitants.
chirmiri: Chirmiri, also spelled Chirimiri, lies at an altitude of 579 metres above sea level on the bank of the Hasdeo River, one of the prominent tributaries of the Mahanadi. The surrounding region has dense forests and a pleasant climate through the year. It was part of Koriya district until the separate Manendragarh-Chirmiri-Bharatpur district was created, and it is a municipal corporation, a status the Chhattisgarh government granted in 2008. The town is divided into 40 wards and nine zones, which hills and forest physically separate from each other.

The coal mines were at first privately owned. Dadu Lehri is said to have been the founder of Chirimiri, and the Tata Iron and Steel Company began prospecting for coal but carried out no mining. The Chirimiri colliery opened in 1930 and began production in 1932. New Chirimiri colliery followed in 1942, Pure Chirimiri in 1945 and North Chirimiri in 1946, and later the New Chirimiri Pondi Hills, West Chirimiri, Duman Hill and Korea collieries began work.

Coal production rose from 264,000 tonnes in 1933 to 3,162,500 tonnes in 1980. The collieries belonged to several companies and owners, among them the Chirimiri Colliery Company, Dababhoy's New Chirimiri Ponri Hill Company, United Collieries Limited, K. N. Dhady and Indra Singh and Sons. All were nationalised in 1973.

Coal remains the basis of the economy. The South Eastern Coalfields Limited, the largest coal-producing company in India, operates in the region, and Chirmiri is one of the 13 administrative areas of the coal industry. The railway station is used mainly to carry coal away. The census of 2001 recorded a population of 91,312.

The Lord Jagannath Temple, built by workers from Puri as a replica of the Jagannath Temple at Puri, was a gift to the town from the Odia community of the region. Other places visited by pilgrims and picnickers nearby include the Kalibadi temple at Haldibadi, the Amrit Dhara Falls at Barbaspur, about 17 kilometres away, and the banks of the Hasdeo River. The Maha Maya Temple at Ratanpur, said to have been built by the Kalachuri king Ratnadeva in the 12th or 13th century, is one of the 52 Shakthi Peeths in India.
chisinau: Chișinău stands on the river Bâc, a tributary of the Dniester, in the middle of Moldova, on a relatively level landscape with very fertile ground. It is roughly equidistant between the borders with Romania, 58 km away, and Ukraine, 54 km away, and very close to the geographic centre of the country. The city proper covers 120 km2 and the municipality 635 km2. Its climate is humid continental, with hot summers and cold, windy winters.

The origin of the name is unclear. One theory derives it from the archaic Romanian chișla, meaning spring or source of water, and nouă, new, because the town grew around a small spring. Another, attributed to the historian Ștefan Ciobanu, holds that it was formed like the name of Chișineu in western Romania, from the Hungarian kis, small, and Jenő, one of the seven Hungarian tribes. A third, by the linguist Kiss Lajos, derives it from a Cuman word for a grave or kurgan.

Chișinău was founded in 1436 as a monastery village and belonged to the Principality of Moldavia, which from the 16th century was a vassal state of the Ottoman Empire while retaining its autonomy. At the beginning of the 19th century it was a small town of 7,000 inhabitants. In 1812, after the Russo-Turkish War of 1806-1812, the Ottomans ceded the eastern half of Moldavia to the Russian Empire. The new territory became known as Bessarabia, and Chișinău became the capital of its oblast.

A generous development plan gave the city broad, long roads by 1834 and divided it roughly into an old part with irregular buildings and a newer centre and station. Between 1830 and 1836 the architect Avraam Melnikov built the Nativity Cathedral with a bell tower, and in 1840 the Triumphal Arch, planned by Luca Zaushkevich, was completed. The belfry was demolished in Soviet times and rebuilt in 1997. After the Russian Empire the city belonged to the Moldavian Democratic Republic in 1917-1918, to the Kingdom of Romania in 1918-1940 and 1941-1944, and to the Soviet Union in 1940-1941 and 1944-1991.

Chișinău has been the capital of Moldova since 1991. It is the country's main industrial and commercial centre and its largest transport hub, and the municipality holds nearly a third of the population. The city was significantly damaged in the Second World War and by earthquakes. The architect Alexander Bernardazzi designed many buildings, including the City Hall and the Church of Saint Theodore, and much of the city is built of limestone quarried at Cricova. The house where Alexander Pushkin lived in exile is now a museum.
chithira-thirunal-balarama-varma: He was born on 7 November 1912, on Deepavali and on his mother's sixteenth birthday, the eldest son of Sethu Parvathi Bayi, Junior Maharani of Travancore, and Ravi Varma Kochu Koyi Thampuran of the Royal House of Kilimanoor, a Sanskrit scholar and great-nephew of the painter Raja Ravi Varma. Under the matrilineal traditions of the royal family he was heir apparent from birth. From the age of six he was taught by tutors chosen by Maharaja Sree Moolam Thirunal, and he succeeded him at the age of 11, on 7 August 1924, under a regency.

Rumours that he was mentally unfit delayed his full powers until Sir C. P. Ramaswami Iyer, a family friend, put his case to the Viceroy, who insisted that Sir C. P. become his adviser; he assumed full ruling powers on 6 November 1931. In 1932 he created a bicameral legislature, the Sree Chitra State Council and the Sree Moolam Assembly, which began work on 1 January 1933, and the Jenmi-Kudiyaan Regulation freed tenants from the interference of landlords. His government founded about twenty industries, among them Fertilisers and Chemicals Travancore and Punalur Paper Mills, and in 1939 the Sri Swathi Thirunal Music Academy.

His reign also saw severe unrest. From 1938 the Travancore State Congress campaigned for responsible government, and the Dewan, Sir C. P., banned meetings, arrested its leaders and cancelled the licences of newspapers. Government action against the Communist Punnapra-Vayalar uprising after the Second World War led to the deaths of hundreds of Communist Party workers. In 1947 Travancore at first declared that it would stay independent, and the first public election came in 1948.

After the Constitutional Amendment of 1971 he lost his political powers and his privy purse. He kept control of the Sree Padmanabhaswamy Temple, supporting it from his own funds, and on 31 March 1991 led its Arattu procession barefoot despite his weakened health. He died on 20 July 1991 after a stroke. The Sree Chitra Thirunal Institute of Medical Sciences and Technology and other trusts were founded with his funds, land and buildings, and he paid for the higher education of K. R. Narayanan, later the 10th President of India.
chitpavan-brahmins: The Chitpavans, also called Kokanastha Brahmins, explain their name through a legend in the Sahyadrikhanda of the Skanda Purana: Parashurama, finding no Brahmins in the Konkan, purified sixty fishermen gathered by a funeral pyre, so that the name was read as purified at the pyre. The community prefers the reading pure of mind. Historians such as Jadunath Sarkar have argued for a non-Indian origin, while the Bene Israel of the Konkan claim a shared descent. Maureen L. P. Patterson writes that the Chitpavans were apparently the last major group to arrive in the region and settled around Ratnagiri, its least fertile part.

Very little is known of them before 1707. Balaji Vishwanath Bhat, a Chitpavan from Ratnagiri, won the favour of Chhatrapati Shahu and was appointed Peshwa in 1713, and his family held the office until the fall of the Maratha Empire. Chitpavans then moved in large numbers to Pune, where they received offices, tax relief and land; a document of 1763-64 shows at least 67% of clerks were Chitpavans. Until then the older Deshastha Brahmins had looked down on them as newcomers. Jayant Lele argues that their influence under the Peshwas and the British has been greatly exaggerated.

After 1818 they lost their political dominance and many turned to English education. The community produced reformers such as Dhondo Keshav Karve and Mahadev Govind Ranade, the Gandhian politicians Gopal Krishna Gokhale and Vinoba Bhave, and also Vinayak Damodar Savarkar, the founder of Hindutva. After the assassination of Mahatma Gandhi by Nathuram Godse, a Chitpavan, Brahmins in Maharashtra were attacked, mostly by members of the Maratha caste, and the violence in Sangli, ruled by the Patwardhan family, hastened the integration of the Patwardhan states into the Bombay Province by March 1948.

In the Konkan their main occupation was farming. Chitpavans are traditionally vegetarian, with rice as their staple, and they speak Marathi; the Marathi of Pune's Chitpavans is the standard form used across Maharashtra. Some families perform bodan after a birth or marriage, a rite in which invited women mix a meal around an idol of the goddess Annapurna and feed it to a cow. Families publish genealogies called Kulavruttantas. Relations with the Deshastha Brahmins have improved since the 20th century through social mixing and intermarriage.
chitradurga: Chitradurga lies in the valley of the Vedavati river in central Karnataka and is the headquarters of Chitradurga district. It is a place of bold rock hills and valleys with towering boulders, and the boulders on which much of the city stands belong to the oldest rock formation in India. Its names in Kannada include Kallina Kote, the stone fortress, Ukkina Kote, the steel fort, and Yelusuttina Kote, the fort of seven circles. In the British period its official name was Chittaldrug. By legend from the Mahabharatha, a man-eating rakshasa named Hidimba lived on the hill until Bhima killed him in a duel and married his sister Hidimbi.

Timmanna Nayaka, a chieftain under the Vijayanagara Empire, was made governor of Chitradurga as a reward for military service, which began the rule of the Nayakas of Chitradurga. His son Obana Nayaka was known as Madakari Nayaka. Later rulers included Kasturi Rangappa, who consolidated the kingdom, and Bharamappa Nayaka, who came to the throne in 1689 after the Dalawayis overthrew Madakari Nayaka III. Several brief reigns followed. The last ruler, Madakari Nayaka V (1758–1779), lost the fort to a siege by Hyder Ali, after which the city came under Hyder Ali and his son Tipu Sultan and then, after Tipu's defeat by the British, under the royal family of Mysore.

The fort was built between the 10th and 18th centuries by successive dynasties, the Rashtrakutas, Kalyana Chalukyas, Hoysalas, Vijayanagara and the Nayakas. It has seven enclosing walls, 19 gateways, 38 posterns, a palace, a mosque added under Hyder Ali, granaries, oil pits and many tanks that collected rainwater. In the upper part stand eighteen temples, of which the Hidambeshwara temple is the oldest.

The 2011 census counted 1,25,170 people in Chitradurga. The city is administered by a municipal council, and wind farms with a total installed capacity of 49.7 MW stand on the surrounding hills. The Chandravalli cave complex lies between three hills, with stone steps leading to underground rooms, and the pillow lava near the village of Maradihalli is a National Geological Monument of India.

Local legend celebrates Onake Obavva. When Hyder Ali's soldiers were found entering the fort through an opening in the rocks, while the guard had gone home for lunch, she killed them one by one with an onake, a wooden club for pounding rice, as they emerged. The opening and the well she was going to, the Tanniru doni, survive.
chittagong: Chittagong lies in south-eastern Bangladesh, between the Chittagong Hill Tracts and the Bay of Bengal, on the banks of the Karnaphuli River, which enters the bay through an estuary 12 kilometres west of the city centre. The city straddles the coastal foothills of the hill tracts. The highest peak in the district is Mount Sitakunda, at 351 metres. Several lakes were created under Mughal rule. The etymology of the name is uncertain, and the city has been known as Chatigaon, Chattagrama, Islamabad and Porto Grande de Bengala.

Stone Age fossils and tools show that the region has been inhabited since Neolithic times, and the port has a recorded history reaching back to the 4th century BCE. Its harbour appears on Ptolemy's world map of the 2nd century. The region belonged to the ancient Bengali kingdoms of Samatata and Harikela. In the 7th century the Chinese traveller Xuanzang described the area as a sleeping beauty rising from mist and water. In the 9th century merchants from the Abbasid Caliphate established a trading post there, and the port fell to the Muslim conquest of Bengal in the 14th century. A royal mint stood there under the Delhi Sultanate, the Bengal Sultanate and the Mughal Empire.

Between the 15th and 17th centuries Chittagong was also a centre of administrative, literary, commercial and maritime activity in Arakan, a strip of land along the eastern coast of the Bay of Bengal that was under strong Bengali influence for 350 years. In the 16th century the port became a Portuguese trading post. The Mughal Empire expelled the Portuguese and the Arakanese in 1666. The port was later reorganised, in 1887, and declared a Major Port of British India in 1928.

During the Second World War Chittagong was a critical base for the Allied forces in the Burma Campaign. The Partition of British India in 1947 made it the chief port of East Pakistan, and in 1971 it was the site of the Bangladeshi declaration of independence.

Chittagong, officially Chattogram, is the second-largest city of Bangladesh after Dhaka and the seat of the Chittagong Division. Its port is the busiest in Bangladesh and in the Bay of Bengal. The city is also the business capital of Bangladesh, and the Chittagong Stock Exchange and the Chittagong Tea Auction are based there. The Anderkilla Shahi Jame Mosque is a well-known Mughal property.
chittor-fort: The fort stands on a hill that rises abruptly 180 m above the plains on the right bank of the Berach River, a tributary of the Banas. Its walls run for 13 km round a fish-shaped plateau about 5 km long. Seven gates built by Rana Kumbha, who ruled Mewar from 1433 to 1468, lead up the slope from the Paidal Pol at the base to the Ram Pol, the main gate. The fort once held 84 water bodies, of which 22 remain, and their storage was said to meet the needs of an army of 50,000 for four years.

Tradition holds that the fort was first called Chitrakut and was built by a Mori ruler, Chitrangada Mori. The Guhila ruler Bappa Rawal is said to have taken it in 728 or 734, though some historians doubt that the Guhilas held Chittor before the reign of Allata. In 1303 Alauddin Khalji took the fort after a siege of eight months, and his courtier Amir Khusrow wrote that he ordered a massacre of 30,000 local Hindus. Most modern historians reject the later legends that he came for the queen Padmini. Rajput rule was restored under Hammir Singh, from whom the Sisodia line took its name, and the fort was at its most powerful under Rana Kumbha and Rana Sanga, who ruled from 1509 until January 1528.

Bahadur Shah, Sultan of Gujarat, besieged the fort in 1535, and tradition says Rani Karnavati led 13,000 women in the jauhar while 3,200 warriors rode out to die. Akbar camped before the fort on 20 October 1567, after Rana Udai Singh II had withdrawn to Gogunda, leaving Jaimal and Patta with 8,000 soldiers. The siege lasted four months. Jaimal was killed by a musket shot on 22 February 1568, and the next day the defenders rushed out. They died with 20,000 to 25,000 civilians. Jahangir returned the fort to Amar Singh in 1615.

The fort holds 65 historic structures, among them four palace complexes, 19 main temples and four memorials. The Vijaya Stambha, a nine-storey tower of 37.2 m, was raised by Rana Kumbha between 1458 and 1468 for his victory over Mahmud Shah I Khalji of Malwa in 1440. The older Kirti Stambha, probably of the 12th century, is dedicated to the Jain teacher Adinath. In 2013 the fort was inscribed with five other hill forts of Rajasthan as a World Heritage Site.
chivalry: Before the code of chivalry there was an uncodified standard of noble conduct centred on the preudomme, a wise, honest and sensible man. David Crouch argues that this habitus was recognised as courtoisie, superior conduct suited to the aristocratic hall, and that it existed long before 1100. He explains the rise of chivalry through a more exclusive definition of nobility in the late 12th century, which raised the status of the knight, and places the tipping point in the household of Henry the Young King, who died in 1183. The first known work to treat the knight as a moral exemplar, the De Re Militari of Ralph Niger of about 1187, was written by the Young King's former chaplain.

In literature chivalry falls into three overlapping areas: duties to countrymen and fellow Christians, including mercy and protection of the weak; duties to God; and duties to women, including courtly love. Different emphases gave warrior chivalry, as in Sir Gawain, religious chivalry, as with Galahad in the Grail legends, and courtly love chivalry, as with Lancelot. The code also included pledging loyalty to an overlord and refraining from attacking a defenceless opponent. The Peace and Truce of God in the 10th century placed limits on knights.

Léon Gautier compiled what he called the Ten Commandments of chivalry in 1884, but there is no such medieval list: he abstracted it from his reading of 12th and 13th century romances. Jean Charles Léonard de Sismondi wrote that chivalry should not be confused with the feudal system, being the ideal world as it existed in the imaginations of romance writers.

Jean Froissart's Chronicles described how the French armoured nobility, charging in the face of arrows, were defeated by largely common archers at Crécy and Poitiers. Richard W. Kaeuper argues that knights played an ambivalent, problematic role in public order, and that chivalry's ideals were often contradictory. Elizabeth I ended the tradition that any knight could create another, and Christopher Wilkins holds that Sir Edward Woodville, who died in 1488, was the last knight errant.

Don Quixote burlesqued the medieval chivalric romance, giving rise to the term Quixotism, and Romanticism revived medieval ideals in the late 18th and early 19th century. Orders of chivalry continued to be founded, among them the Order of Saint Louis in 1693.
chlodio: Very little is known about Chlodio, who is also called Cloio or Chlogio, and he is mentioned only briefly in a small number of records. His name is a short form of Frankish names such as Hlodowig and Hlodhari, from a Germanic root hlod-. A popular proposal among modern scholars makes him a descendant of the Salian Franks whom the Romans allowed to settle in Texandria in the 4th century.

In his time northern Gaul was changing from a Roman border province into an area where several powers lived side by side. It was formally Roman, but the empire largely let the region go, and the general Flavius Aëtius campaigned there mainly through negotiation, temporary garrisons and allies among the Huns.

The poet Sidonius Apollinaris, in a panegyric for the emperor Majorian, describes Franks overrunning the Atrebates under Cloio while Aëtius commanded in Gaul, and tells how Majorian fought under Aëtius in an attack on a Frankish wedding at Vicus Helena. Gregory of Tours, writing much later, says Chlodio attacked from a fort called Dispargum, sent spies to Cambrai, crushed the Romans and captured the town, then occupied the country up to the Somme. Its location is uncertain: Duisburg, a place of that name near Brussels, and Diest have all been proposed.

The Liber Historiae Francorum, a later and generally unreliable work, adds that he pushed west through the Silva Carbonaria and took Tournai before moving south to Cambrai. One study suggests the conquest of Tournai and Cambrai probably happened between 445 and 450. His advance carried Frankish rule deeper into the empire, far from the Rhine border where the Franks had long been established.

Gregory of Tours reports that some people said Merovech, father of Childeric, was descended from Chlodio, and in his own time it was believed that the Merovingian dynasty descended from him somehow. Later chronicles give conflicting parentage, naming Pharamond or Theudemer as his father, and these pedigrees are considered unreliable. No contemporary records mention Merovech, so modern scholars find the link difficult to judge. Childeric was buried in Tournai, which later writers associated with Chlodio, and Childeric's son Clovis I first took power in the same area.
chlodomer: Chlodomer, also spelled Clodomir or Clodomer, was one of the four sons of Clovis I and his wife Clotilde. On his father's death in 511 he divided the kingdom of the Franks with his brothers Theuderic I, Childebert I and Chlothar I, and became king at Orléans. His kingdom included the bishoprics of Tours, Poitiers and Orléans. He married Guntheuc, and they had three sons: Theodebald, Gunthar and Clodoald.

In 523 and 524 Chlodomer and his brothers invaded Burgundy, possibly at the instigation of his mother Clotilde, who wished to avenge the death of her parents, allegedly murdered by her uncle Gundobad, the father of Sigismund of Burgundy. Gregory of Tours tells this story of Clotilde's revenge, but it is assumed to be apocryphal. After capturing Sigismund, Chlodomer returned to Orléans and had Sigismund and his sons Gisald and Gondebaud killed in May 524. Sigismund's brother Gondomar then returned in triumph at the head of troops sent by his ally, the Ostrogothic king Theodoric the Great, and massacred the garrison the Franks had left behind. Chlodomer led a second expedition and was killed in June 524 at the Battle of Vézeronce.

After his death his kingdom was divided: Chlothar I received Touraine and Poitou, and Childebert I the lands on both banks of the Loire with Orléans. His widow married Chlothar, and Chlodomer's three sons were taken to Paris and entrusted to their grandmother Clotilde. Two of them, Theodebald, aged ten, and Gunthar, aged seven, were murdered so that they would not claim a share of their father's inheritance. Only the youngest, Clodoald, was saved by a few loyal followers. Better known as Saint Cloud, he gave up his hair, the symbol of Frankish royalty, rather than his life, and later became abbot of Nogent.
chlodwig-zu-hohenlohe-schillingsfurst: Chlodwig Carl Viktor of Hohenlohe-Schillingsfürst was born on 31 March 1819 at Rotenburg an der Fulda, in Hesse, the second of six sons. His father was a Catholic and his mother a Lutheran, and the sons were brought up as Catholics according to the custom of the time. As the younger son of a cadet line he needed a profession. He considered a commission in the British army through his aunt, a half-sister of Queen Victoria, but chose the Prussian civil service. The years of training confirmed his liberalism: he favoured a free press and German unity under Prussia, but opposed the Prussification of Germany.

After the Austro-Prussian War of 1866 he argued for closer union with Prussia. On 31 December 1866 he was appointed minister of the royal house and of foreign affairs and president of the council of ministers of Bavaria, reportedly at the urging of Richard Wagner. He reorganised the Bavarian army on the Prussian model, brought about a military union of the southern states and became a vice-president of the customs parliament in 1868. He opposed the ultramontane party over the First Vatican Council, and the combination of ultramontanes and Bavarian patriots forced him to resign on 7 March 1870.

He was elected to the Reichstag in 1871 and became its vice-president. He helped found the Imperial Liberal Party and supported Bismarck's Kulturkampf. Bismarck made him ambassador in Paris in 1873, and in 1880 he served briefly as head of the Foreign Office in Berlin. As governor of Alsace-Lorraine from 1885 he carried out the coercive measures of 1887 and 1888, though he largely disapproved of them, and his conciliatory manner did much to reconcile the population to German rule.

In October 1894 Emperor Wilhelm II, at his urgent request, made the aged Hohenlohe Imperial Chancellor in succession to Leo von Caprivi. He rarely appeared in the Prussian or German parliaments and left great independence to his secretaries of state, among them Bernhard von Bülow. Wilhelm's reshuffles of 1897, which brought Bülow to the Foreign Office and Alfred von Tirpitz to the Naval Office, in effect disempowered him.

He could not halt the turn to imperialist world policy and naval armament. He attempted a reform of the Prussian Military Law in 1898 and a Law on Associations in 1899, and the Bürgerliches Gesetzbuch was adopted in 1896. He resigned on 17 October 1900, was succeeded by Bülow, and died on 6 July 1901 at Bad Ragaz, aged 82.
chlothar-i: Chlothar was one of the four sons of Clovis I who inherited shares of their father's kingdom in 511. His brothers were Theuderic, Chlodomer and Childebert I. Chlothar received Soissons, which he made his capital, with Laon, Noyon, Cambrai, Maastricht and the lower Meuse, and a second part in Aquitaine. Merovingian custom divided an inheritance evenly among sons, so the kingdom was often split. Chlothar had five wives, more from political expediency than personal motive, among them Radegund, a Thuringian princess later canonised, and Ingund, by whom he had most of his sons. He was a less than enthusiastic Christian and introduced taxes on church property.

Chlothar spent most of his life expanding his territory at the expense of relatives and neighbours, while his brothers avoided open war with him by joining his attacks and sharing the spoils. In 524 Chlodomer was killed at the Battle of Vézeronce. Chlothar and Childebert then took Chlodomer's kingdom of Orléans, and two of Chlodomer's young sons, Theodebald and Gunthar, were killed, according to the account given, by Chlothar himself. A third, Clodoald, escaped and became a monk. With Theuderic he conquered Thuringia, and in 534, with Childebert and Theudebert, he overran the Burgundian kingdom, which was divided among the three.

When Theudebald died childless in 555, Chlothar took Metz, and he put down a Saxon revolt. On 23 December 558 Childebert died without heirs, and Chlothar reunited the whole Frankish kingdom. His son Chram, who had set himself against him with Childebert's encouragement, was captured and put to death with his wife and daughters.

Chlothar died at the end of 561, at the age of 64, of acute pneumonia, and was buried at Soissons. His kingdom then covered all of Gaul except Septimania and part of present-day Germany. It was divided again among his four surviving sons: Charibert received Paris, Guntram Burgundy, Sigebert the kingdom of Metz and Chilperic Soissons.
chlothar-ii: Chlothar was born in May or June 584, the son of Chilperic I and Fredegund. His parents, who suspected that their four older sons had been murdered, raised him in secret at Vitry-en-Artois. In September 584 Chilperic was murdered after a hunt near Chelles, and Fredegund asked King Guntram of Burgundy to adopt the child and protect him. A meeting of Greater Neustria recognised the boy, though some doubted his paternity, and named him Clothar; he was baptised on 23 October 585 with Guntram as godfather.

He took power on Fredegund's death in 597. His realm was rich but one of the smallest in Francia, and in 599 his nephews Theuderic II of Burgundy and Theudebert II of Austrasia defeated him at Dormelles and reduced it to the regions of Beauvais, Amiens and Rouen.

The brothers soon fought each other, and Theuderic died of dysentery at Metz in 613 while preparing to invade Neustria. The mayors of the palace Warnachar and Rado abandoned his heir's cause and nobles deserted the army of the old queen Brunhilda and her great-grandson Sigebert II. Chlothar's soldiers caught them near Lake Neuchâtel, and he had Brunhilda tried and put to death by being dragged behind a horse. Sigebert and his brother Corbo were executed too. Chlothar was sole ruler of the Franks.

In 614 he issued the Edict of Paris, which reserved many rights to the nobles, required officials to come from the region they administer, and excluded Jews from civil employment for the Crown. Historians interpret it in different ways. In 617 he made the office of mayor of the palace a lifetime appointment. In 623 he gave Austrasia to his son Dagobert I, repaying the support of Bishop Arnulf of Metz and Pepin I, who were in effect granted semi-autonomy.

Chlothar died in 629, aged 45, and was buried in the Saint Vincent Basilica of Paris. Dagobert succeeded him in Neustria and Burgundy, and Charibert became king of Aquitaine. Unusually for a Merovingian he practised monogamy, though early deaths meant he had three wives, and he was generally an ally of the church. His reign was long but saw royal power erode in favour of the nobility and the church.
cho-man-sik: Cho Man-sik, also known by his art name Godang, was born on 1 February 1883 in Kangsŏ-gun, South P'yŏngan Province, into the Changnyeong Jo clan. Raised in the Confucian tradition, he converted to Protestantism and became a church elder. From 1908 to 1913 he studied law at Meiji University in Tokyo, where he met Gandhi's ideas of non-violence and self-sufficiency; he also admired the teachings of Jesus and the writings of Leo Tolstoy.

After Japan annexed Korea in 1910, Cho joined the independence movement. He was imprisoned for helping to organise the March First Movement and publicly rejected the policy pressing Koreans to take Japanese surnames. In 1922 he founded the Korean Products Promotion Society, meant to be a national movement of all religious and social groups, which with his example of non-violent resistance earned him the name Gandhi of Korea. His encouragement of Korean students to enlist in the Imperial Japanese Armed Forces gave him a mixed reputation among some nationalists.

In August 1945 the Japanese governor of Pyongyang asked him to keep order, and on 17 August he formed the Provisional People's Committee for the Five Provinces, mostly right-wing nationalists. Soviet officers urged him to head the new northern administration, but Cho disliked communism and asked for wide autonomy, which they refused. On 3 November 1945 he founded the Democratic Party of Korea, whose deputy chairman, Choi Yong-kun, was a secret communist placed to control it, as Andrei Lankov later found in Soviet archives.

Cho refused to back the five-year four-power trusteeship proposed at the Moscow Conference of 1945, and on 5 January 1946 Soviet soldiers arrested him and held him at the Koryo Hotel. In June 1950 the two Korean governments tentatively agreed to exchange him and his son for the jailed South Korean Workers' Party leaders Kim Sam-yong and Yu Ju-ha, but the exchange failed. He is generally believed to have been executed early in the war, though a CIA report of 1962 had him alive in a prison camp in December 1953. In 1970 South Korea awarded him the Order of Merit for National Foundation.
choco-department: The Chocó Department lies in the west of Colombia and is the only Colombian department with coastlines on both the Pacific Ocean and the Atlantic. It contains all of Colombia's border with Panama and makes up most of the ecoregion known as El Chocó, which extends from Panama to Ecuador. The Baudó Mountains on the coast and the inland Cordillera Occidental are cut by low valleys, under 1,000 metres in altitude, that form most of the territory, and most of the land is thick rainforest. Three large rivers drain it: the Atrato, the San Juan and the Baudó.

The first city founded by conquistadors on the American mainland, Santa María la Antigua del Darién, was established by Vasco Núñez de Balboa in 1510 and disestablished in 1524. Spanish colonisers brought enslaved Africans to the area, and their descendants make up most of the department's population today. In the late 19th century the Chocó's gold drew miners from many countries. The department was created in 1944.

Its low population, mountainous and inhospitable terrain and distance from Bogotá meant that it received little attention from the Colombian government. Under the military dictator Gustavo Rojas Pinilla, his administration proposed to abolish the Chocó and divide its territory between the departments of Antioquia and Valle del Cauca. The coup of 1957 by General Gabriel París Gordillo overthrew Rojas Pinilla and ended these plans.

Quibdó is the capital and largest city. The department produces much of Colombia's platinum and is its top gold-producing region, and much of the wood used inside the country is harvested there. Afro-Colombians form the large majority of its people, followed by the Embera, an Indigenous people more than half of whose Colombian population lives in the Chocó. Its rainforests are a Key Biodiversity Area, with a high proportion of endemic plant and bird species.
choe-chung-heon: Ch'oe Ch'unghŏn was the son of Supreme General Ch'oe Wŏnho and Lady Yu, and is thought to have been born in Gaeseong or Gyeongju. His family descended from the Confucian scholar Ch'oe Ch'iwŏn, but became the Ubong Ch'oe clan when his father was given Ubong as an ancestral seat. Like his father he entered the military. He first held a minor post in the Agency for Royal Liquors, came to notice fighting Cho Wich'ong's rebellion in 1174, and later served as royal inspector of Gyeongsang Jinju Province until an impeachment stalled his career for several years.

His chance came in April 1196, when Yi Chiyŏng, a son of the military ruler Yi Ŭimin, took a pet pigeon from Ch'oe's younger brother Ch'oe Ch'ungsu. The brothers, with their nephew Pak Chinjae and others, beheaded Yi Ŭimin while he was away at Mount Mita, won over General Paek Chonyu in the capital, and killed or exiled Yi's followers among the officials. To justify the coup they presented the king with a ten-point reform programme, the Bongsasipjo, which called for fair taxes, fewer officials, frugality and curbs on monks and temples.

In 1197 Ch'oe confined King Myeongjong to Changrak Palace and set Sinjong on the throne. When Sinjong fell ill in 1204 Ch'oe chose his son Huijong, deposed him after a plot against his own life in 1211, and installed Gangjong and then Gojong. He had his brother Ch'oe Ch'ungsu beheaded in a struggle over a royal marriage, crushed a revolt by Pak Chinjae in 1207, a Silla restoration movement around Gyeongju and a rising of slaves led by Manjeok, and based his power on a private guard, the Tobang, and on the Directorate-General for Policy Formulation, set up in 1209 to hunt down conspirators.

Ch'oe named his elder son, Ch'oe U, as successor after U defeated his brother Ch'oe Hyang in a sword fight, and retired. He died on 29 October 1219, a year after a stroke, and his funeral was recorded as like a king's. The system he built passed to Ch'oe U, Ch'oe Hang and Ch'oe Ŭi. Unlike earlier military rulers he drew Confucian scholars such as Yi Kyubo into government, though his regime is judged essentially a continuation of the military regimes before it. Its private army, the Sambyeolcho, rebelled after the regime fell and was defeated by a Mongol-Goryeo army.
choe-je-u: Ch'oe Cheu was born on 18 December 1824 at Kajong-ni, a village near Gyeongju, into a yangban family; his birth name was Ch'oe Chesŏn, and his disciples later called him Suun. His father, Ch'oe Ok, a scholar who had never gained a government post, married the widow Han late in life, and as the son of a remarried widow he was barred by the Neo-Confucian order from the civil examinations. He nonetheless received a strong education in Neo-Confucianism.

His mother died when he was six and his father when he was sixteen. He married Madam Park of Ulsan, led a wandering life and settled in Ulsan in 1854. Though trained as a Confucian, he took part in Buddhist practice, and in 1856 and again the next year he made 49-day retreats. After losing his house in bankruptcy in 1858 he returned to his father's household, where he prayed and meditated, troubled by disorder in Korea, the spread of Christianity and Western power over East Asia.

On 25 May 1860, at his father's Yongdam Pavilion on Mount Gumi, he experienced an encounter with Sangje, the Lord of Heaven, and received a talisman, drawn on paper, burned and swallowed in water, and an incantation to be chanted, rites believed to restore body and spirit. He wrote songs in vernacular Korean in the four-beat gasa style, which reached commoners and women, and essays in classical Chinese. Scholars differ on Donghak: So Jeong Park calls it an original school of thought, while Susan Shin stresses its continuity with the spiritual Neo-Confucianism of Wang Yangming.

Suspected of Catholicism, he hid in Jeolla province from June 1861 to March 1862, where he wrote parts of his scripture. By his arrest in December 1863 he had assemblies in at least twelve villages and towns. He was beheaded on 15 April 1864. Choe Sihyeong carried on the movement and published his works in 1880 and 1881. Donghak's followers led the Donghak Peasant Revolution of 1894, and in 1905 Son Byong-Hi renamed the movement Cheondogyo, which played a major part in the March First Movement of 1919.
choe-mu-seon: Ch'oe Musŏn was born into a wealthy family in Yeongcheon, in Gyeongsang Province, where his father was an official, and qualified as a military officer through the civil service examination. As a child at the royal palace with his father he saw fireworks made by Mongols and Chinese. He grew up as the Goryeo government lost control of the country and wokou pirates crossing the Korean Strait plundered the coasts and, in the south, raided deep inland, which the generals Yi Sŏnggye and Ch'oe Yŏng could not prevent.

Ch'oe travelled to China under the Yuan dynasty, where the making of gunpowder was kept secret, and learned that it needed sulfur, fine coal and potassium nitrate, but not how to obtain niter or prepare the powder. After repeated failures he bribed Li Yuan, a Chinese merchant visiting Goryeo on business, for the recipe, against Mongol and Chinese law, and Korea began making its own gunpowder between 1374 and 1376. After he demonstrated its power before King U, the government gave him an official laboratory and factory.

There he developed cannons, hand cannons and other firearms, among them the singijeon and the hwacha, a launcher that has been likened to the first modern multiple rocket launcher. He was one of the commanders at the Battle of Jinpo, which the Korean forces won with the help of their gunpowder weapons, and he began building warships to drive off the pirates. Two works on gunpowder and guns, the Hwayaksuryeonbeop and the Hwapobeop, are attributed to him.

His inventions brought him promotion and a part in politics, but he was already old, and soon after the founding of the Joseon dynasty he retired from military and political affairs. He died in 1395, and King Taejo gave him the honorary title of vice-premier. His son Ch'oe Haesan was also a military officer. In Korea he is remembered as a patriot and a model for scientists.
choe-yeong: Ch'oe Yŏng was born in Hongseong or Cheorwon into the Cheorwon Ch'oe noble clan, the son of Ch'oe Wŏn-jik and a fifth-generation descendant of the scholar Ch'oe Yu-ch'ŏng. He was raised to an austere life and kept it after he rose to success, scorning fine clothes and men who desired costly things. His father's maxim, to regard gold as nothing but rocks, became his motto.

He won the trust of his men and the king in fighting the Japanese pirates who began raiding the coast around 1350, and in 1352 became a national hero by putting down Cho Il-sin's rebellion. Goryeo was then a tributary of the Mongol Yuan dynasty, and in 1354 he led 2,000 mounted archers to northern China to help suppress the Red Turban Rebellion. Back home he told King Gongmin of the Yuan's troubles, he fought to recover towns west of the Yalu River, and in 1356 he received the surrender of Ssangseong, whose darughachi was Yi Cha-ch'un, father of Yi Sŏng-gye.

He defeated the Red Turban invaders in 1360, rescued the king from an assassination attempt by Kim Yong in 1363, and in 1364 defeated Prince Deokheung and 10,000 Mongol cavalry. In 1370 he took Oro Mountain Fortress and Liaoyang. Accused by the monk Sin Ton, he spent six years in exile until Gongmin restored him after Sin Ton's death. In 1374 he led 314 ships and 25,605 troops to crush the Mongol horse herders' revolt on Tamna, and in 1376 he and Yi Sŏng-gye drove Japanese pirates from Gongju.

In 1388 Yi Sŏng-gye objected to the invasion of Liaodong, arguing among other things that a small nation should not attack a large one and that summer rains would spoil the army's composite bows. Ch'oe ordered it nevertheless, backed by the young King U. Yi's turn back to the capital, Gaegyeong, became known as the Wihwado Retreat. Ch'oe defended the palace but was overwhelmed, banished to Goyang and later beheaded. He is said to have predicted that grass would never grow on his grave, which became known as Jeokbun, the red grave, for its bare red soil.
chogha-zanbil: Chogha Zanbil, typically translated as 'basket mound', is an Elamite complex in the Khuzestan province of Iran, about 30 km southeast of Susa. Its construction date is unclear because the chronology of the reign of Untash-Napirisha is uncertain, but it falls in the 14th or 13th century BCE. Its original name was Dur Untash, 'town of Untash', and it was built mainly to honour the great god Inshushinak. It is unlikely that many people besides priests and servants ever lived there. Some scholars infer from its many temples that Untash-Napirisha tried to create a new religious centre, possibly meant to replace Susa, uniting the gods of highland and lowland Elam.

Three concentric walls protect the complex. Inscriptions record that the outer wall had seven gates, of which only two have been found. Between the outer and middle walls stood a temple shared by Napirisha and Inshushinak, the middle area held eleven temples for other gods, and the outer area royal palaces and a funerary palace with five subterranean royal tombs. Most of the innermost area is taken up by the great ziggurat, which originally measured 105.2 metres on each side and about 53 metres in height, in five levels, and was crowned with a temple. It has a mud-brick core faced with baked bricks, many inscribed with the names of deities in Elamite and Akkadian. It now stands 24.75 metres high.

Building continued after Untash-Napirisha's death, and the site was occupied until the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal destroyed it in about 645 BCE, though some researchers place the end of occupation in the late 12th century BCE. A geologist doing oil exploration found an inscribed brick and took it to the excavators at Susa.
