Roland de Mecquenem excavated the site from 1935, and Roman Ghirshman excavated it in six seasons between 1951 and 1962. In all 5,257 inscribed bricks were found, most in Elamite. In 1979 Chogha Zanbil became the first Iranian site inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List, and UNESCO considers its ziggurat the best preserved example of the stepped pyramidal monument.
choiseul-island: Choiseul Island, whose native name is Lauru, is the largest island, at 2,971 square kilometres, of Choiseul Province in the Solomon Islands. The provincial headquarters is the town of Taro, on Taro Island. The islanders speak Austronesian languages, among them Vaghua, Varisi, Ririo and Central Eastern Choiseul. In the centre lies the Mount Maetambe to Kolombangara River Important Bird Area, 78,398 hectares of intact forest reaching 800 metres. BirdLife International identified it for its threatened or endemic birds, and it holds the best example of karst limestone forest in the Solomons, with caves and subterranean rivers. Mount Maetambae is an extinct volcano.

In 1768 the French explorer Louis Antoine de Bougainville named the island after Étienne François, duc de Choiseul, then French foreign minister. The first recorded European sighting was by the Spanish expedition of Álvaro de Mendaña in April 1568, from the brigantine Santiago, commanded by Pedro Ortega Valencia; they charted it as San Marcos. In the nineteenth century the islanders suffered attacks from blackbirding, the often brutal recruitment or kidnapping of labourers for the sugar plantations of Queensland and Fiji.

The German Empire declared a protectorate over the North Solomon Islands, including Choiseul. Under the Treaty of Berlin, signed on 14 November 1899, Germany transferred them, except Bougainville and its surrounding islands, to the British Solomon Islands Protectorate in 1900, in exchange for the British giving up all claims to Samoa. Missionaries converted most of the population to Christianity, and British and Australian firms began large-scale coconut planting. The Austrian anthropologist Hugo Bernatzik visited in 1932 and documented some of the few remaining ancestral customs. Japanese forces occupied the island in 1942, and US Marines raided it in October and November 1943. Since independence in July 1978 it has been part of Choiseul Province.
chol-people: Spanish forces first invaded the Lacandon jungle, home of the Lakandon Chʼol and other Indigenous groups, in 1554. At the end of the 1550s the Spanish forced Chʼol and other Maya groups into settlements called reducciones. When these were split up, Chʼol were sent north to Palenque, Tilá and Tumbalá, and those sent there were the ancestors of today's Chʼol. They were forced to work on encomiendas until the Spanish crown granted them, in documents called cédulas reales, the land they had worked for generations.

In the 19th century President Benito Juarez set up a system of agrarian ejidos and took land from Indigenous peoples such as the Chʼol to establish it. The ejidos did not provide enough to support them, and Chʼol began to move into the Lacandon Jungle, which has brought conflict with the Lacandon-Yucatec speakers who claim that land as their own.

The Chʼol call their language Lak tyʼañ, our speech. It has three branches, Sabanilla, Tilá and Tumbalá, which some linguists treat as separate languages but which are usually counted as dialects of one language; speakers of Tilá and Tumbalá can usually understand each other. Chʼol who speak Spanish use a variety called Castia, which keeps archaisms such as cuartia, fanego and libra, uses vos in the second person singular, and uses lo even beside a masculine or feminine article.

The Chʼol practise Christianity with many Maya traditions incorporated. Local curers alternate between churches and caves to gain their powers, and cave ceremonies have continued since the conversion, the earth owner, the Maya cave god, having been reconciled with Christ. Staple foods are corn, beans, squash, bananas, greens and other fruits, with chickens and turkeys; some Chʼol sell livestock and fruit to buy soap, medicine and other necessities.

Children are taught in Chʼol until fourth grade, when instruction turns to Spanish. Contact with Spanish speakers has raised the demand for education and work, and has stigmatised the native language. Secondary schools exist in some rural villages, but higher education usually means travelling to another town, and many students, especially girls, leave school around the sixth grade because of early marriage and financial difficulties.
chola-dynasty: There is very little written evidence for the Cholas before the 7th century CE. The main sources on the early dynasty are Sangam literature, oral traditions, religious texts and temple and copperplate inscriptions. The Ashokan edicts name the Cholas among the neighbours of the Mauryan empire to the south, not subject to Ashoka but on friendly terms with him. They are also mentioned in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea and by the geographer Ptolemy.

Sangam literature records early kings, among them Karikala and Kocengannan, but the order of their succession cannot be settled. Uraiyur was their oldest capital. Around three centuries followed in which the Kalabhras invaded the Tamil country and the Pallavas and Pandyas came to dominate it, and little is known of the Cholas then. A branch can be traced in the Telugu country, where Telugu Chola families ruled as chieftains of the Pallavas.

The Chola Empire was founded in 848 by Vijayalaya, a descendant of the early Cholas. His successor Aditya I defeated the Pallavas and Pandyas, and Parantaka I defeated the Rashtrakuta dynasty at the battle of Vallala. Rajaraja I and Rajendra I carried the dynasty to its imperial state in the 11th century. Rajendra I conquered Odisha, reached the Ganges, and built a new capital, Gangaikonda Cholapuram, for his northern victories.

In 1025 Rajendra I launched naval raids on the ports of Srivijaya, and a Chola inscription says he captured or plundered 14 places, among them Palembang and Kedah. The raids did not lead to direct administration, but they weakened Srivijayan hegemony and increased the influence of Tamil guilds on the Malay Peninsula and the north coast of Sumatra.

The Later Chola dynasty began in 1070, when Kulothunga Chola I took the throne after Athirajendra was assassinated in a civil disturbance. The empire stayed stable until 1215, when Maravarman Sundara Pandiyan II defeated Kulothunga Chola III. The Cholas were then absorbed by the Pandyan empire and ceased to exist by 1279.

Under the Cholas the Tamil country reached new heights in art, religion, music and literature, with monumental temples and sculpture in stone and bronze, among them the Brihadeeswarar Temple. The poet Kamban flourished under Kulothunga III. The Cholas were followers of Hinduism. Hindu cultural influence in Southeast Asia owes much to them, and the Malay chronicle Sejarah Melayu says the rulers of the Malacca sultanate claimed descent from the Chola kings.
chola-empire: The Imperial Cholas were founded by Vijayalaya, a descendant of the Early Cholas, who about 850 used a conflict between the Pandyas and the Pallavas to take Thanjavur from the Muttarayar; Thanjavur became the capital. Under Aditya I the Cholas, with the Pallavas, defeated the Pandyas of Madurai in 885 and later took Tondaimandalam from the Pallavas. His son Parantaka I conquered Sri Lanka in 925, but was defeated by the Rashtrakutas under Krishna III at the Battle of Takkolam, where the heir Rajaditya was killed and Tondaimandalam was lost. The Cholas recovered under Parantaka II.

Under Rajaraja I and Rajendra I the empire reached its height, stretching from northern Sri Lanka to the Godavari–Krishna basin, the Konkan coast at Bhatkal, the Malabar Coast, Lakshadweep and the Maldives. Rajaraja bound the empire into a tight administrative grid, conducted a land survey in 1000 and commissioned the Brihadisvara Temple at Thanjavur in 1010. Chola armies reached the Ganges and Chola embassies went repeatedly to Song China.

Marriages linked the Cholas with the Eastern Chalukyas, and in 1070, after Athirajendra Chola was killed in a civil disturbance, Kulothunga Chola I, son of the Eastern Chalukya prince Rajaraja Narendra and a Chola princess, took the throne and began the Later Chola line. About that time the Cholas lost almost all their overseas territories; they kept parts of southern India until 1279, declining from the early 13th century as the Pandyas rose.

The empire was divided into provinces called mandalams, subdivided into valanadus and kottams, and every village governed itself. Some historians call the system feudal, while others, among them Burton Stein, reject the term. Land revenue and trade taxes were the main income; cotton cloth was the chief export, and the Manigramam and Ayyavole merchant guilds followed Chola armies overseas. Canals of the Kaveri and great tanks such as Rajendra's at Gangaikonda Cholapuram served a large agrarian expansion. Temples were also centres of lending, and Chola bronzes were cast by the lost-wax process. The poet Kambar wrote the Ramavataram under Kulothunga III.
chola-invasion-of-srivijaya: Relations between Srivijaya and the Chola dynasty had been cordial under Rajaraja I. In 1006 the Srivijayan Maharaja Maravijayattungavarman, of the Sailendra dynasty, built the Chudamani Vihara in the Chola port of Nagapattinam. Srivijaya controlled the Malacca Strait and the Sunda Strait, holding Kedah and Pannai at the northwest opening and Malayu and Palembang at the southeast, and it compelled passing ships to call at its ports or risk being plundered.

The reasons for the expedition are unclear. The historian Nilakanta Sastri suggested that Srivijaya may have obstructed Chola trade with China, or that Rajendra I wished to carry his digvijaya, or world conquest, across the sea. Another view points to diplomacy: King Suryavarman I of the Khmer Empire sought Chola help against the Tambralinga kingdom, which turned to the Srivijayan king Sangrama Vijayatunggavarman.

Instead of entering the Malacca Strait from the north, the Chola fleet crossed the Indian Ocean to the west coast of Sumatra, took on supplies at Barus, a port controlled by Tamil trade guilds, and sailed south into the Sunda Strait. The Srivijayan navy, stationed at Kedah, did not see it coming. Palembang, the capital, was attacked first and its Kadatuan royal palace and monasteries were plundered. The Thanjavur inscription records that Rajendra captured the king and seized treasures, among them the Vidhyadara Torana, a jewelled war gate. The Cholas moved swiftly from port to port, probably with the monsoon winds, raiding rather than holding the cities.

With its king imprisoned, the Srivijaya mandala fell into confusion and the Sailendra dynasty came to an end. A Srivijayan princess who escaped Palembang reached the court of King Airlangga in East Java, brokered peace with the kingdom of Kahuripan and became his queen, Dharmaprasadottungadevi. Kingdoms based on agriculture, Kahuripan and later Kediri, grew in Java. No Srivijayan envoys reached China between 1028 and 1077.

Chinese chronicles name a Chola country of Sanfoqi, probably Kedah, which sent missions to China between 1077 and 1090. Tamil presence in the Malacca Straits seems to have lasted about a century, leaving inscriptions in northern Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula, and the expedition helped Tamil merchant associations such as the Manigramam and Ayyavole spread into Southeast Asia.
chollima-movement: The movement was meant to lift North Korea out of the rubble of the Korean War. The five-year plan of 1957–61 aimed to complete the socialist transformation of industry, to nationalise industry and agriculture entirely and to make the country largely self-sufficient in food, clothing and housing. At a meeting of the Workers' Party of Korea in December 1956 Kim Il Sung urged: "Let us produce more, practice economy, and overfulfill the five-year plan ahead of schedule!" In the legend no mortal could ride the Chollima, which accomplished the hardest tasks and led heroes to victory.

Its first success was reported in 1957, when Kim Il Sung asked a steel works in Kangdong County, near Pyongyang, with a capacity of 60,000 tons, for an extra 10,000 tons; it produced 120,000, a result credited with lighting the torch of the movement. Under the slogan "Let us dash forward in the spirit of Chollima" successes were reported across the economy, with annual industrial growth of 36.6 percent during the plan, and a slogan of drink no soup was meant to keep workers from leaving their posts.

The Chollima Work Team Movement was initiated by Chin Ung-won, who organised his team to produce far beyond its quota and became the ideal Korean worker. Teams that set a target high enough to stand out in the whole nation and met it won the title of Chollima Work Team, with banners, flags and notebooks embossed with the horse. The movement had 178,000 members less than a year and a half after it began.

By 1961 the labour force was exhausted and output had begun to fall, and in the mid-1960s North Korea stopped publishing economic statistics other than percentage increases over earlier periods. Kim Il Sung had no economists willing or able to tell him that his plans needed to change, and Kim Jong Il gave speeches praising Chollima until his death. In the late 1990s, during massive energy shortages and severe famine, the government called for a second Chollima movement.

The 46-meter Chollima Statue on Mansu Hill carries a worker holding high the Red Letter of the Central Committee of the Workers' Party of Korea and a young peasant woman with a sheaf of rice. The horse has appeared on North Korean currency since 1978 and on postage stamps. The hero of the 1960 short story A Letter from Haeju-Hasong is an exemplary Chollima Rider, and the song Chollima on the Wing was written to rally support for the movement.
chongzhen-emperor: Zhu Youjian was born on 6 February 1611, the fifth son of Zhu Changluo, the Taichang Emperor, and a low-ranking concubine, Lady Liu. When he was four his father had his mother executed, for reasons unknown, and she was buried in secret. He was raised by his father's other concubines in a lonely but quiet environment. All the Taichang Emperor's sons but two died before adulthood, and after his father's death in 1620 his elder brother Zhu Youjiao became the Tianqi Emperor and made him Prince of Xin.

The Tianqi Emperor died in October 1627 without a surviving heir, and Zhu Youjian, about sixteen years old, took the throne as the Chongzhen Emperor, helped by Empress Zhang. He quickly eliminated Wei Zhongxian and Madam Ke and others held to belong to the Wei-Ke conspiracy, and tried to stem the dynasty's decline, concentrating his reforms on the top ranks of the civil and military establishment. Corruption and an empty treasury left few capable ministers, and he was suspicious of his officials and feared factions. He executed dozens of field commanders, among them Yuan Chonghuan, who had directed the northern defence against the Manchu.

Drought and famine drove two great uprisings, led by Zhang Xianzhong and Li Zicheng, both poor men from Shaanxi. Meanwhile Hong Taiji, whose father Nurhaci had united the Manchu tribes, declared himself emperor of the Qing dynasty in 1636. From 1633 to 1644 the Great Plague of Jingshi devastated northern China. Li Zicheng took Luoyang in 1641 and Kaifeng the next year, and on the lunar New Year of 1644 he proclaimed himself king of the Shun dynasty. The emperor refused repeated proposals to move the court south to Nanjing.

Li Zicheng's forces attacked Beijing on 24 April 1644. Rather than face capture, the emperor gathered the imperial household, killed Consort Yuan and Princess Zhaoren with his sword and severed the arm of Princess Changping. On 25 April he is said to have gone to the hill of Meishan, in present-day Jingshan Park, where he took his own life. Accounts differ on whether he left a note.

The Qing declared their aim to be avenging the emperor and defeated Li Zicheng at the Battle of Shanhai Pass. Because the emperor had not moved the court south, they took over a largely intact Beijing bureaucracy. A Southern Ming court was set up at Nanjing, and its last emperor was executed in 1662. A modern account holds that the Chongzhen Emperor was not especially incompetent by the standards of the later Ming, but that his suspicion, impatience and stubbornness doomed a dynasty already far gone.
chormaqan: Chormaqan, also called Chormagan or Chormaqan Noyan, belonged to the Sunud tribe and served in the keshik, the imperial guard of the Mongol Empire under Genghis Khan and Ögedei Khan. He is mentioned many times in The Secret History of the Mongols. As a quiver bearer he is often called Qurchi in the sources. He probably took part in the Mongol campaigns in northern China and later in the expedition of Subutai and Jebe through the Caucasus and the Russian steppes.

In the winter of 1230 Ögedei sent him to renew the Mongol conquests in Persia, which had stalled after Genghis Khan's assault on the Khwarezmid Empire between 1218 and 1223. His army is said to have numbered some 30,000 to 50,000 men, and the small Khwarezmid band under Jalal ad-Din was swept away at its approach. From the steppes of Azerbaijan around Tabriz, his campaigns in the mid-1230s made the Kingdom of Georgia and the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia vassals of the Mongols, perhaps to secure communications for the westward attack under Batu that soon followed.

Local rulers came over to him. Buraq Hajib of the Qutlugkhanids of Kerman sent his son Rukn al-Din Mubarak Khwaja to Ögedei's court, and the Salghurid atabeg Abu Bakr sent his brother or nephew Tahamtan to Karakorum. Isfahan refused to submit, and he besieged it in 1236. After the Georgian and Armenian lords submitted, he divided Georgia into eight tumens. His authority weakened in 1239, when Ögedei gave fiscal administration to Chinqai and Korguz in Khorasan.

Chormaqan died around 1241. His wife Altani, who held considerable influence in his ordo, proposed his lieutenant Baiju as his successor, and Baiju was appointed. His son Shiramun later served the Il-khans Hulagu and Abaqa, while another son, Bora, was executed under Hulagu. His daughter Esukan married King David VII of Georgia, and the Armenian prince Hasan Jalal offered him his daughter Ruzanna in marriage.
choshu-domain: The Chōshū Domain, also called the Hagi Domain, was a han of the Tokugawa Shogunate from 1600 to 1871. It was based at Hagi Castle in Nagato Province and ruled throughout by the tozama daimyō of the Mōri family. Its rulers descended from the warlord Mōri Motonari, who had extended his power over all of Chūgoku and held territory worth 1,200,000 koku.

Motonari's grandson Mōri Terumoto allied with Toyotomi Hideyoshi and, after Hideyoshi's death, was chosen titular head of the Toyotomi forces at the Battle of Sekigahara. His cousin Kikkawa Hiroie secretly made a deal with Tokugawa Ieyasu that left 15,000 Mōri soldiers inactive. After assurances from Ieyasu, Terumoto gave up Osaka Castle without a fight. The Mōri were moved from Aki to Nagato, and their holdings were cut to 369,000 koku.

The reduction left a large shortfall for military upkeep, though the domain remained the seventh largest in Japan outside the shogunate's own lands. To restore its finances the Mōri cut all retainers' fiefs, paid some in rice instead of land, and encouraged some to take up farming. A land survey found hidden mountain farms and taxed them, and the domain controlled the trade in paper, rice, salt and wax. These measures strengthened the daimyō's control but angered peasants and displaced samurai, and revolts were frequent.

The Mōri created four subordinate domains, Iwakuni, Chōfū, Tokuyama and Kiyosue, ruled by branches of the family. The main line died out in 1707, and heirs were then adopted from the Chōfū branch, which itself died out in 1751, after which the family continued through the Kiyosue branch. The daimyō governed with the help of karō, domain elders, some of whom held the rank by heredity and some, such as the reformer Murata Seifū, for life as men of talent.

Chōshū later became a centre of anti-Tokugawa activity. According to tradition, each New Year the elders asked the daimyō whether the time had come to overthrow the shogunate, and he replied that it had not, since the shogunate was still too strong. About 260 years after Sekigahara the domain joined Satsuma and sympathetic court nobles in the Satchō Alliance. In 1865 it bought the warship Union in Satsuma's name. In the Boshin War its forces fought the armies of the former shōgun, and its forces of 1867 to 1869 formed the foundation of the Imperial Japanese Army. The domain was dissolved in 1871 and absorbed into Yamaguchi Prefecture.
chosokabe-morichika: Morichika, a samurai of the Azuchi–Momoyama and early Edo periods whose childhood name was Senkumamaru, was the fourth son of Chōsokabe Motochika and Lady Motochika, who died in 1583. He was named heir to the Chōsokabe after the death of his elder brother Chōsokabe Nobuchika in 1587, and he married Nobuchika's daughter. He fought in the Siege of Odawara in 1590 and in the first of the Korean campaigns, in 1592–93. His father died in 1599.

In 1600 Morichika sided with Ishida Mitsunari and commanded 6,600 men at the Battle of Sekigahara, where his troops faced those of Ikeda Terumasa. Through failures of communication, the positions they held and the betrayal of neighbouring armies, his forces stood idle and saw almost no action before the Western Army collapsed. That same year he ordered the execution of his elder brother Tsuno Chikatada, who had questioned his right to succeed Motochika as ruler of Tosa Province. Although he sent an apology to Tokugawa Ieyasu, he was deprived of his fief.

In 1614 Morichika went to join the defenders of Osaka Castle against the Tokugawa, arriving on the same day as Sanada Yukimura, and his Chōsokabe contingent fought very well in both the Winter and the Summer campaigns of Osaka. After the defeat of the Toyotomi and Chōsokabe forces at the Battle of Tennōji and the fall of Osaka, he tried to flee but was caught at Hachiman-yama by men of the Hachisuka. He and his sons were beheaded on 11 May 1615. His four sons, Moritaka, Morisada, Morinobu and Moritsune, all died that year, as did Moritsune's son Moritane.
chosokabe-motochika: Motochika, the 21st chief of the Chōsokabe clan, was the son and heir of Chōsokabe Kunichika and a daughter of the Saitō clan of Mino Province; his childhood name was Yasaburō. He is said to have been born in Okō Castle in the Nagaoka district of Tosa. Tall, fair-skinned and quiet, he is said to have worried his father with his gentle nature, which earned him the nickname Himewako, Little Princess, until he proved a brave warrior at his first battle, near Nagahama castle in 1560.

He defeated Motoyama Shigetoki at Asakura castle in 1562 and built a power base on the Kōchi plain through alliances with local families. In 1569 he marched on the Aki clan of east Tosa with 7,000 men, defeated Aki Kunitora at the Battle of Yanagare and took Aki Castle. Outwardly loyal to the Ichijō family until then, he attacked their headquarters at Nakamura in 1573, driving Ichijō Kanesada to flee to Bungo, and finished the Ichijō at the Battle of Shimantogawa in 1575.

He then turned on Iyo, where his general Kumu Yorinobu was defeated and killed at the Battle of Mimaomote in 1579, before Motochika himself led some 30,000 men there and forced Kōno Michinao to flee. Oda Nobunaga, once his ally, grew suspicious of his advance. In 1582 Motochika defeated the Miyoshi clan at the Battle of Nakatomigawa and Sengoku Hidehisa at Hiketa. In 1585 Toyotomi Hideyoshi sent 113,000 men against his 40,000, and after the 26-day siege of Ichinomiya Castle he surrendered Awa, Sanuki and Iyo.

In Hideyoshi's service he joined the invasion of Kyūshū in 1587, where his son Nobuchika was killed at the Battle of Hetsugigawa, led a fleet at the sieges of Shimoda and Odawara in 1590, and fought in the invasion of Korea in 1592. When the Spanish ship San Felipe was wrecked in his territory in 1596, he seized its cargo, and the affair led to the crucifixion of 26 Christians in Nagasaki, the first lethal persecution of Christians by the state in Japan.

Motochika died at his mansion in Fushimi in 1599, aged 60, and was succeeded by his son Chōsokabe Morichika. He is remembered for his 100-Article Code of the Chōsokabe and for his efforts to found an economically strong castle town, moving his seat from Oko to Otazaka and then to Urado. Nobunaga is said to have called him the bat who refuses to fly away from its home.
chosroid-dynasty: The Chosroids, also called the Iberian Mihranids, were a branch of the Mihranids, one of the Seven Great Houses of Iran and distant kin of the Sasanians; other branches were placed on the thrones of Gogarene and Gardman. Their rise to the thrones of Caucasia marked the Sasanian victory over what remained there of the Arsacid dynasty of Parthia. According to the Georgian Chronicles, Mirian III was installed in Iberia by his father, called Chosroes, Great King of Iran, through his marriage to Abeshura, daughter of the last Arsacid king Aspacures I; another chronicle, the Conversion of Kartli, makes him the son of an otherwise unattested King Lev.

Mirian fought for Iran against Rome, but after the Peace of Nisibis of 298 he drew close to Rome, and the missionary Nino converted him, his wife Nana and his household. Iran and Rome then contested Iberia: the Sasanians deposed Sauromaces II in 361, the Roman emperor Valens restored him in 370, and by 380 Iran had reunited the kingdom under Aspacures III and taken tribute. Resistance to Iranian influence and Zoroastrianism by the church and part of the nobility left the Georgian alphabet as its chief cultural legacy.

The kings stayed generally loyal to Iran until Vakhtang I Gorgasali turned towards Byzantium in 482 and, allied with the Armenian prince Vahan Mamikonian, waged an unsuccessful revolt until his death in 522. The family then declined, an Iranian viceroy in Tbilisi governing with the local princes. After the kingship was abolished, the senior line held Kakheti and the junior Guaramids held Klarjeti and Javakheti. In 588 Guaram I revolted, received the Byzantine dignity of curopalates and restored Iberia as a presiding principate.

His son Stephanus I went over to Iran, and in 627 the Byzantine emperor Heraclius, allied with the Khazars, took Tbilisi, had Stephanus flayed alive and gave his office to the Chosroid Adarnase I of Kakheti. Stephanus II had to accept tribute to the Arab Caliphate. Archil, a saint of the Georgian Orthodox Church, was martyred by the Arabs in 786. With the death of his son Juansher around 807 the line died out; its lands in Kakheti passed to local noble families, and the Bagratids took the throne of Iberia.
chota-nagpur-plateau: The Chota Nagpur Plateau covers about 65,000 square kilometres of eastern India. The Indo-Gangetic Plain lies to its north and east and the basin of the Mahanadi River to its south. It is a continental plateau of Precambrian rocks, raised by continental uplift in the Cenozoic, and part of the Deccan Plate.

It rises in three steps. The highest, in the west, holds the flat-topped plateaus called pats, 910 to 1,070 metres above sea level, and the highest point is 1,164 metres. The middle step includes the Ranchi and Hazaribagh plateaus at around 610 metres, and the lowest, around 300 metres, covers Manbhum and Singhbhum, where the Parasnath Hills reach 1,370 metres. The Damodar River flows through a trough between the Ranchi and Hazaribagh plateaus, whose coalfields it preserved.

The name Nagpur probably comes from the Nagavanshis, who ruled this part of the country. Colonial writers such as Dalton and Blochmann thought Chhota, small, was a mistaken form of Chutia, a village near Ranchi with the remains of a Nagavanshi fort; Ambrish Gautam calls this weak and speculative, and argues from Walter Hamilton's writings that British officials added the prefix in the late 18th and 19th centuries to tell the plateau from the larger Nagpur ruled by the Bhonsle Marathas.

Human habitation dates back to the Mesolithic and Chalcolithic periods, and stone tools show activity in the Mesolithic and Neolithic. Cave paintings at Isko in Hazaribagh district date to the Meso-Chalcolithic period, 9000 to 5000 BCE. The region is home to Adivasi peoples such as the Santhal, Munda, Oraon and Ho, alongside non-tribal groups, with festivals such as Sarhul and Karam celebrating harvests and nature.

The plateau is rich in minerals: mica, bauxite, copper, limestone, iron ore and coal. The Damodar valley is the prime centre of coking coal in the country, and the main coalfields include Jharia, Raniganj and Bokaro. The Chota Nagpur dry deciduous forests, an ecoregion of about 122,100 square kilometres, cover the plateau, with sal forest predominant, and the Palamau Tiger Reserve protects part of them. Rice, maize and pulses are staple crops, and its waterfalls include Hundru Falls, 75 metres on the Subarnarekha River near Ranchi.
chouf: The Chouf, in Arabic Jabal ash-Shuf, is both a historic region of Lebanon and an administrative district of the Mount Lebanon governorate. It runs from a narrow coastal strip, where the Christian town of Damour stands, up the valleys and mountains of the western slopes of Jabal Barouk, as the local part of the Mount Lebanon massif is called. These slopes carry the largest forest of Cedars of Lebanon, and the mountains are high enough to receive snow in winter.

The emirs of Mount Lebanon lived in the Chouf. The best known, the Druze emir Fakhr al-Din II, won considerable power and autonomy from the Ottoman Empire in the 17th century, with influence reaching into parts of Palestine and Syria, and he is often called the founder of modern Lebanon. In the first half of the 19th century Emir Bachir Chehab II built the palace of Beiteddine, close to the older town of Deir al-Qamar, whose name means the monastery of the Moon.

Druze and Christians long lived side by side in the region, and in the early 18th century the two communities were at peace. Fighting broke out between them in 1848 and 1860, and again in 1983 and 1984 during the Lebanese Civil War, in what is called the Mountain War, when an estimated 300,000 Christians fled their homes.

At the end of January 1989 the Druze leader Walid Jumblatt, who lived in the family palace at Moukhtara, proposed a plan for their return, supported by Dany Chamoun. It was shelved in March after General Michel Aoun blockaded the Druze port at Jieh, shelled Souq El Gharb and one of Jumblatt's aides was assassinated. Reconciliation came on 8 August 2001, when the Maronite Patriarch, Cardinal Nasrallah Boutros Sfeir, visited the Chouf and met Jumblatt.
chremonidean-war: The war is poorly documented and known mostly from fragmentary accounts by the later historians Pausanias and Justin. Athens and Sparta wanted their former independence back from Antigonid Macedonia. At the same time the ambitions of Ptolemy II Philadelphus of Egypt in the Aegean were threatened by the fleet of Antigonus II Gonatas, so Ptolemy built an anti-Macedonian coalition among the Greek city-states and courted Athens by supplying it with grain. In Athens the anti-Macedonian faction led by Chremonides, a Stoic statesman and general, took power and declared war on Macedon, possibly as early as the autumn of 268 BCE.

The first year brought only minor clashes, which generally went the coalition's way. The campaign of 266 BCE, in which a Ptolemaic fleet under Patroclus assisted Athens, was indecisive. After that the war turned against the Greek cities. With their main ally beaten outside Corinth and too weak to face the Antigonids alone, the Athenians stayed behind their walls, hoping that the Ptolemies would send help before the siege began.

Ptolemy II could not mount a major expedition until after Athens had been starved into surrender, in either 262 or 261 BCE. When the Ptolemies did send reinforcements, their fleet was defeated off Cos, probably in 261 BCE; the Battle of Cos also figures in accounts of the Second Syrian War, with a strong alternative date of 258 or 255 BCE.

The Macedonian victory confirmed Antigonid control over Greece, and Athens lost the last of the political independence it had kept from before the Hellenistic age. Historians regard the war as a key event of Hellenistic Greece, since it was the last credible attempt by the Greek city-states to regain their independence.
chretien-de-troyes: Little is known of Chrétien's life, but he seems to have come from Troyes or to have been closely tied to it. Between 1160 and 1172 he served at the court of Marie of France, Countess of Champagne, a daughter of King Louis VII and Eleanor of Aquitaine, who married Count Henry I of Champagne in 1164. Gaston Paris speculated that he may have served as a herald-at-arms. Later he served at the court of Philippe d'Alsace, Count of Flanders. His name means literally Christian from Troyes, and Urban T. Holmes, Jr., proposed that it might be a pen name of a convert from Judaism to Christianity, also known as Crestien li Gois.

Chrétien wrote five major poems in rhyming eight-syllable couplets, in vernacular Old French marked by the regional Champenois dialect. Four are complete: Erec and Enide (c. 1170), Cligès (c. 1176), and Yvain, the Knight of the Lion and Lancelot, the Knight of the Cart, written together between 1177 and 1181. Yvain is generally considered his most masterful work. The fifth, Perceval, the Story of the Grail, was written between 1181 and 1190 and dedicated to Philip of Flanders. He completed only about 9,000 lines; four successors added 54,000 more in the Four Continuations. The last thousand lines of Lancelot were written by Godefroi de Leigni, apparently by arrangement with Chrétien.

Among his lesser works is Philomela, the only one of four poems based on Ovid's Metamorphoses to survive. In the introduction to Cligès he mentions a treatment of King Mark and Iseult, presumably related to the Tristan legend, which he says was not well received and has not survived. His immediate sources are uncertain, since he speaks of them only vaguely; Geoffrey of Monmouth or Wace may have supplied some names, and Lancelot makes repeated use of the customary law of his day.

Chrétien was the first writer to mention the Holy Grail, in Perceval, and Camelot and the love affair of Queen Guinevere and Lancelot, in Lancelot. His romances survive in many copies and were adapted widely: Wolfram von Eschenbach's Parzival and Hartmann von Aue's Erec and Iwein follow Perceval, Erec and Yvain, and the Welsh romances Peredur, Geraint and Enid, and Owain derive from the same three, though not directly. Karl Uitti argues that Yvain, with its clear beginning, middle and end, helped initiate the vernacular novel.
chris-hani: Hani was born Martin Thembisile Hani on 28 June 1942 in a Xhosa village at Cofimvaba in the Transkei, the fifth of six children. His father, Gilbert Hani, was a mine union worker and political activist who went into exile in 1962 and returned to South Africa in 1991. At 12 he wished to join the African National Congress (ANC) after hearing his father explain apartheid, but was too young. At Lovedale school he joined the ANC Youth League at 15, though political activity was forbidden at black schools. In 1959 he went to the University of Fort Hare in Alice, where he studied English, Latin and literature.

As a student Hani took part in protests against the Bantu Education Act. In 1961 he joined a communist party, where he began to read about Marxism, and he then joined Umkhonto we Sizwe (MK), the ANC's armed wing. After his arrest under the Suppression of Communism Act he went into exile in Lesotho in 1963 and took the first name Chris while in hiding. He trained in the Soviet Union and served in the Luthuli Detachment operation in the Rhodesian Bush War. In 1969 he co-signed the Hani Memorandum, which criticised the leadership of Joe Modise and Moses Kotane and called for the movement to radicalise.

He organised MK guerrilla operations from Lesotho and later moved to the ANC's headquarters in Lusaka. As head of MK he was responsible for suppressing a mutiny in detention camps, though he denied any role in abuses. After the ANC was unbanned in 1990 he returned to South Africa and on 8 December 1991 succeeded Joe Slovo as head of the South African Communist Party. He supported suspending the armed struggle in favour of negotiations.

Hani was shot on 10 April 1993 outside his home in Dawn Park, Boksburg, by Janusz Waluś, a Polish immigrant. A neighbour and a housewife, Margareta Harmse, helped identify him, and Clive Derby-Lewis, a Conservative Party MP who had lent the pistol, was also arrested. Both were convicted in October 1993 and sentenced to death; the sentences became life imprisonment after the death penalty was abolished in 1995. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission refused them amnesty, ruling that they had not acted under orders. Riots followed the killing. Negotiators nonetheless agreed that elections would be held on 27 April 1994. At his death Hani was the most popular ANC leader after Nelson Mandela and was seen as a possible successor.
christ-church-cathedral-dublin: The cathedral was founded probably some time after 1028, when King Sitric Silkenbeard of Dublin made a pilgrimage to Rome. Its first bishop was Dúnán, or Donat, and the new diocese was a small island of land within the much larger Diocese of Glendalough.

The church stood on high ground overlooking the Viking settlement at Wood Quay, and Sitric gave it the lands of Baldoyle, Raheny and Portrane for its maintenance. It was first staffed by secular clergy. In 1163 the second Archbishop of Dublin, Laurence O'Toole, converted it to a priory of Augustinian canons. The Priory of the Holy Trinity became the wealthiest religious house in Ireland.

Henry II attended the Christmas service in 1171. In the 1180s Strongbow and other Norman magnates helped to fund a rebuilding in stone, with choir, transepts, crypt and chapels. Much of the nave dates from the 1230s and was built of oolitic limestone from Dundry by craftsmen from the same area of Somerset. In 1300 an agreement, the Pacis Compositio, acknowledged both Christ Church and St Patrick's as cathedrals of Dublin, and it remained in force until 1870. In 1487 the cathedral was the setting of the purported coronation of the pretender Lambert Simnel.

Henry VIII abolished the priory by royal warrant on 12 December 1539, and its prior and canons became the dean and chapter. In 1562 the nave's foundations, resting in peat, slipped and brought down the south wall and the stone roof.

Neglect followed, and when the Irish Church was disestablished in 1869 the building was in such a poor state that handing it to the Roman Catholics was seriously considered. From 1871 to 1878 the architect George Edmund Street rebuilt it at the expense of the whiskey distiller Henry Roe. He demolished the 14th-century choir, rebuilt the tower and added flying buttresses and the covered footbridge to the Synod Hall.

Christ Church is the cathedral of the United Dioceses of Dublin and Glendalough in the Church of Ireland. Its crypt, built in 1172 and 1173, is 63.4 metres long and is the largest cathedral crypt in Britain or Ireland. The tomb called Strongbow's stands in the nave. Its bells include 19 swinging bells, the highest number of change-ringing bells in the world. The former Synod Hall now houses the Dublinia exhibition on medieval Dublin. In March 2012 the heart of Saint Laurence O'Toole was stolen from the cathedral, and it was recovered in Phoenix Park in April 2018.
christchurch: Christchurch lies near the centre of the east coast of the South Island, east of the Canterbury Plains and near the southern end of Pegasus Bay. The Pacific Ocean bounds it to the east and the ancient volcanic complex of Banks Peninsula to the south. Apart from the Port Hills, the city is flat, on average about 20 metres above sea level. The Avon River, Ōtākaro, winds through the centre, with a large urban park along its banks. Gravel layers beneath the plains form an artesian aquifer. It feeds numerous spring-fed streams, including the Avon and the Heathcote. The city has a reputation as an English city; its nickname is the Garden City.

Before European settlement the land was swampland, with marsh, grassland, scrub and patches of tall forest of kahikatea, mataī and tōtara. The Māori iwi Waitaha first inhabited the area in the mid-thirteenth century. Kāti Māmoe invaded in the sixteenth century, and Kāi Tahu absorbed the Waitaha a century later. Ōtautahi was inhabited seasonally, and a major trading centre was established at Kaiapoi Pā.

European settlement was influenced by the brothers William and John Deans, who farmed at Riccarton Bush from 1843 and showed that the swampy ground could be farmed. The name Christchurch was adopted at the first meeting of the Canterbury Association on 27 March 1848, most likely after Christ Church, Oxford, the college of some of its members. The First Four Ships chartered by the association brought the Canterbury Pilgrims to Lyttelton Harbour in 1850, and the plan of the central city, with its grid of streets, squares and parkland, was laid out by 1850. Christchurch became a city by letters patent on 31 July 1856, the first in New Zealand, and from 1853 to 1876 it was the seat of the Province of Canterbury.

Between 1871 and 1876 nearly 20,000 immigrants arrived in Canterbury, and in the 1880s frozen meat joined wool as a main export. Many Gothic Revival stone buildings by the provincial architect Benjamin Mountfort date from the period. In the early twentieth century the city grew with industry and state housing, and it has been recognised as an Antarctic gateway since 1901. It hosted the 1974 British Commonwealth Games.

Christchurch is the largest city of the South Island and the second largest in New Zealand by urban area, with an urban population of 407,800. It is home to the University of Canterbury. A magnitude 7.1 earthquake struck the region on 4 September 2010. The most destructive of the following earthquakes, on 22 February 2011, killed 185 people and brought down many central buildings. On 15 March 2019 two mosques in the city were the target of the deadliest terrorist attack in New Zealand history.
christchurch-call: The initiative began as the Christchurch Call to Action Summit, held in Paris on 15 May 2019, two months after the Christchurch mosque shootings of 15 March 2019. It was proposed by Jacinda Ardern, then Prime Minister of New Zealand, and co-chaired by her and President Emmanuel Macron of France. Its stated aim was to bring countries and technology companies together to end the use of social media to organise and promote terrorism and violent extremism.

The pledge is a non-binding agreement in three parts: commitments for governments, commitments for online service providers, and ways in which the two can work together. Seventeen countries signed it at first and another 31 followed on 24 September 2019. Signatories include the European Commission, the Council of Europe and UNESCO. Amazon, Dailymotion, Facebook, Google, Microsoft, Qwant, Twitter and YouTube signed as members of the Global Internet Forum to Counter Terrorism.

The government of President Trump declined to attend in 2019, citing concerns that compliance could conflict with free-speech protections in the United States Constitution, though it supported the summit's overarching message. On 7 May 2021 the White House press secretary, Jen Psaki, announced that the United States under President Biden would join, taking part in a virtual summit on 14 May 2021.

On 4 April 2023 Prime Minister Chris Hipkins appointed Ardern Special Envoy for the Christchurch Call, an unpaid role reporting to him. On 14 May 2024 Prime Minister Christopher Luxon and Macron agreed that the Call would continue as a charity rather than as part of New Zealand's Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, and announced a new non-governmental body, the Christchurch Call Foundation, to coordinate its work.

Reactions to the summit were divided. InternetNZ's chief executive Jordan Carter called it a vital first step, and Jillian York of the Electronic Frontier Foundation welcomed its call for transparency about moderation while questioning how governments define terrorism and violent extremism. Tom Rogan in the Washington Examiner argued that it would breach Americans' First Amendment rights, and Nick Gillespie of Reason objected to governments and corporations deciding together what speech was acceptable.
christiaan-huygens: Christiaan Huygens, Lord of Zeelhem, was born in The Hague on 14 April 1629, the second son of Constantijn Huygens, a diplomat and adviser to the House of Orange who was also a poet and musician. Constantijn corresponded with Galileo Galilei, Marin Mersenne and René Descartes. Christiaan was educated at home until sixteen, studying languages, music, history, geography, mathematics, logic and rhetoric, alongside dancing, fencing and horse riding. From 1645 to 1647 he studied law and mathematics at Leiden University, where Frans van Schooten taught him the work of Viète, Descartes and Fermat. Mersenne compared him to Archimedes in a letter of 3 January 1647.

Between 1651 and 1657 Huygens published works showing his mastery of classical and analytical geometry, beginning with Theoremata de Quadratura Hyperboles, Ellipsis et Circuli in 1651. He questioned Descartes's laws of collision, which were largely wrong, and derived the correct ones; his De Motu Corporum ex Percussione, completed in 1656, was published only in 1703. In 1655 he began grinding lenses with his brother Constantijn to build refracting telescopes, discovered Titan, and explained Saturn's appearance as due to a thin, flat ring, nowhere touching, inclined to the ecliptic. He patented the pendulum clock, manufactured in Paris by Isaac II Thuret, and analysed pendular motion in Horologium Oscillatorium (1673).

In 1666 Huygens moved to Paris on an invitation to a leadership position at Louis XIV's new Académie des sciences, with Jean-Baptiste Colbert as his patron. After serious depressive illness he moved back to The Hague in 1681. He could not return to France in 1685 because of the revocation of the Edict of Nantes. On his third visit to England he met Isaac Newton on 12 June 1689. He died in The Hague on 8 July 1695, never having married, and was buried in an unmarked grave at the Grote Kerk.

Huygens described his wave theory of light in the Traité de la Lumière (1690). It was initially rejected in favour of Newton's corpuscular theory until Augustin-Jean Fresnel adapted Huygens's principle in 1821, and it is now known as the Huygens–Fresnel principle. In 1659 he derived the formula for centrifugal force, a decade before Newton. In 1662 he developed the Huygenian eyepiece. His work on games of chance, published in Latin in 1657, used expected values and later inspired Jacob Bernoulli's work on probability theory. He had no taste for grand philosophical systems and was the leading European natural philosopher between Descartes and Newton.
christiaan-snouck-hurgronje: Snouck Hurgronje was born in Oosterhout on 8 February 1857 and began studying theology at Leiden University in 1874. He took his doctorate there in 1880 with a dissertation on the festivities of Mecca, Het Mekkaansche Feest, and from 1881 taught at the Leiden school for colonial civil servants. He arrived in Jeddah on 28 August 1884, won the confidence of the Ottoman governor and an examining delegation of Meccan scholars, and on 21 January 1885 was allowed to enter Mecca under the name Abdul Ghaffar.

In Mecca he lived as a student of Islamic learning and studied the daily life of the city and its many foreign residents, above all the pilgrims from Aceh and Java whose links with Meccan scholars the Dutch government feared. He photographed the Kaaba and the city and made what is considered the first known recording of a Qur'an recitation. His two-volume Mekka appeared in German in 1888 and 1889. In a letter of 18 February 1886 to his friend Carl Bezold he admitted that he had only pretended to be a Muslim, and some critics have called his stay treachery.

In 1889 he became professor of Malay at Leiden and adviser to the government, and moved to the Dutch East Indies, where he married the daughter of a nobleman of Ciamis in West Java in 1890. After travelling in Aceh in 1891 and 1892 he opposed military terror tactics and urged systematic espionage and the winning of the aristocratic elites, while holding that certain radical ulama would yield only to force. From 1898 he was the closest adviser of J. B. van Heutsz in the last phase of the Aceh War, which cost between 50,000 and 100,000 Acehnese lives by varying estimates. Disappointed that his ideas for an ethical administration were not carried out, he returned to the Netherlands in 1906.

At Leiden he held chairs including Arabic and Acehnese and was widely consulted as an authority on Islam. In 1915 he blamed Germany and its orientalists for the Ottoman declaration of jihad. In 1923 he called for vigorous reform of the constitution of the Indies, an end to the idea of native inferiority and representative bodies with wide autonomy. He retired in 1927 and died in Leiden on 26 June 1936. Historians still debate whether he was chiefly a scholar or a spy and architect of colonial policy.
christian-august-of-saxe-zeitz: Christian August was born at Moritzburg on 9 October 1666, the third son, and the second to survive, of Maurice, Duke of Saxe-Zeitz, and his second wife, Dorothea Maria of Saxe-Weimar. As a younger son of the House of Wettin he entered the Teutonic Order as a knight. In 1696 he converted to Catholicism, and in the same year he became Provost of Cologne and Bishop of Raab, offices he kept until his death in 1725.

Soon after his conversion he was given a delicate task. The law then required the king of Poland to be a Catholic, and Christian August was chosen to bring his kinsman, the King-Elector August the Strong, into the Catholic Church. He instructed him in secret and baptised him privately on 1 June 1697 in the court chapel at Baden bei Wien, and then publicly and solemnly at Piekar in Oppeln. When the conversion was formalised he issued the king a certificate, authenticated by the papal nuncio. Pope Clement XI later created him a cardinal.

As Archbishop of Esztergom he also served the emperor as Principal Commissioner, the imperial deputy, at the Perpetual Imperial Diet of Regensburg. Besides crowning Charles VI, he crowned the emperor's wife, Elisabeth Christine of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, in St. Martin's Cathedral on 18 October 1714. After the victory over the Turks at Belgrade in 1717 he organised a celebration at the Imperial Diet on the emperor's behalf, during which the Order of St. Emmeram was created in the knights' hall on 26 October.

When his brother Maurice Wilhelm, Duke of Saxe-Zeitz, died on 15 November 1718 without surviving male issue, Christian August became heir to the duchy. Because he had taken monastic vows, and the next heir, his nephew Maurice Adolf, was also a priest, Saxe-Zeitz was merged into the Electorate of Saxony in accordance with the will of Elector Johann Georg I. Christian August died at Regensburg on 23 August 1725 and was buried in the crypts of St. Martin's Cathedral in Bratislava, now the capital of Slovakia.
christian-august-prince-of-anhalt-zerbst: Christian Augustus was born at Dornburg on 29 November 1690, the third son of John Louis I, Prince of Anhalt-Dornburg, of the House of Ascania, and Christine Eleonore of Zeutsch. When his father died in 1704 he inherited Anhalt-Dornburg jointly with his brothers. On 8 November 1727, at Vechelde, he married Johanna Elisabeth of Holstein-Gottorp, a sister of the future King Adolf Frederick of Sweden. They had five children, of whom the eldest, Sophie Auguste Fredericka, born on 2 May 1729, became Catherine II of Russia; two of the others died in infancy.

On 11 February 1709 he joined the Anhalt-Zerbst infantry regiment, stationed in Stettin, in Prussian service. He received the Order De la Générosité, later renamed Pour le Mérite, in 1711, was made lieutenant-colonel on 1 March 1713, and took part in several campaigns of the War of the Spanish Succession in the Spanish Netherlands. In 1714 he became chief of the regiment, and he rose to colonel in 1716 and major-general in 1721.

He was made a knight of the Order of the Black Eagle in 1725 and became commander of Stettin on 22 January 1729. Promoted lieutenant-general in 1732 and general of infantry in 1741, he was named Governor of Stettin on 5 June 1741. On 16 May 1742 Frederick the Great gave him the highest military rank, Generalfeldmarschall.

About six months later his cousin John Augustus, Prince of Anhalt-Zerbst, died without children, and Christian Augustus and his only surviving brother, John Louis II, inherited the principality as co-rulers. Christian Augustus stayed in Stettin while his brother governed. When John Louis II died, unmarried and childless, Christian Augustus left Stettin for Zerbst, but he ruled alone for only four months before his own death there on 16 March 1747.
christian-democracy-italy: The party was founded on 15 December 1943 in the Italian Social Republic, as the nominal successor of the Italian People's Party, which had the same symbol, a crusader shield. That party was created in 1919 by the priest Luigi Sturzo and won over 20 per cent of the votes in the 1919 and 1921 general elections, but the Fascist dictatorship declared it illegal in 1926. Its doctrine drew on Catholic social teaching, the thought of Romolo Murri and Sturzo, and the encyclicals Rerum novarum of 1891 and Quadragesimo anno of 1931. It was a catch-all party that sought to represent both right-wing and left-wing Catholics under the principle of the political unity of Catholics.

As the war ended, the Christian Democrats helped organise post-Fascist Italy in coalition with all the other mainstream parties, including the Communists and Socialists. Alcide De Gasperi became prime minister in December 1945, and in the 1946 election the party won 35.2 per cent of the vote. In May 1947 De Gasperi broke with his Communist and Socialist partners under pressure from President Harry Truman. In 1948 the party won 48.5 per cent, its best result ever, with the support of the Catholic Church and the United States. Under De Gasperi land reforms were carried out in poorer rural regions, a national health service was established and low-cost housing was begun in major cities. He served until 1953 and died a year later.

From 1954 progressive leaders such as Amintore Fanfani and Aldo Moro led the party, and in 1963 Moro formed a coalition with the Socialists. From 1976 to 1979 the party governed with the external support of the Communists in the Historic Compromise, until Moro, who had inspired it, was abducted and murdered by the Red Brigades. In 1981 Giovanni Spadolini of the Republican Party became the first non-Christian Democrat to lead a government since 1944, and the five-party Pentapartito coalitions governed almost continuously until 1993.

In 1992 the Mani pulite investigation began in Milan and uncovered the Tangentopoli corruption scandals. The party received 29.7 per cent in the 1992 election, helped by the rise of Lega Nord, and it was disbanded in 1994 under its last secretary, Mino Martinazzoli, who renamed it the Italian People's Party. Pier Ferdinando Casini launched the Christian Democratic Centre and allied with Silvio Berlusconi's Forza Italia, which became the party with the most former members. The left-wing factions remained in the People's Party, which joined the Olive Tree alliance in 1996. It later merged into the Democratic Party, formed in 2007.
christian-i-duke-of-saxe-merseburg: Christian was born on 27 October 1615, the sixth son, and third to survive, of John George I, Elector of Saxony, and his second wife Magdalene Sibylle of Prussia, and a member of the House of Wettin. With little prospect of inheriting the electorate, he received in 1650 the administration of the former Bishopric of Merseburg, confiscated after the Reformation, and was also elected by its cathedral chapter. On 19 November 1650 in Dresden he married Christiana, daughter of Philip, Duke of Schleswig-Holstein-Sonderburg-Glücksburg, in a double wedding at which his brother Maurice married her sister Sophie Hedwig.

His father's testament of 20 July 1652 divided the Albertine lands, and in 1653 Christian moved to Merseburg and set up his own household, whose court soon numbered 150 people. Under the will he received Merseburg with Bad Lauchstädt, Schkeuditz, Lützen and Zwenkau, half of Brehna, Zörbig and Finsterwalde, and the Margraviate of Lower Lusatia with Lübben, Guben, Luckau and other towns. When the House of Biberstein died out on 9 January 1668 he also gained Forst. In 1659 he allowed Protestant refugees from Silesia to settle at Neudorf, which they renamed Christiansdorf in his honour, and in 1655 he was admitted to the Fruitbearing Society.

His elder brother, Elector John George II, resented a will that broke the principle of primogeniture and tried to recover his brothers' lands, and after long discussions Christian reluctantly accepted the Elector's overlordship. When John George III annulled the earlier agreements on his accession in 1680, Christian lived for the rest of his reign under the threat of open conflict with his nephew.

Christian died on 18 October 1691. He and Christiana had eleven children, several of whom died young. His son Christian II succeeded him, August inherited Zörbig, Philipp, who held Lauchstädt, was killed at Fleurus in 1690, and Heinrich, who held Spremberg, inherited Merseburg in 1731 and died in 1738.
christian-i-of-denmark: Christian was born in February 1426 in Oldenburg in northern Germany, the eldest son of Count Dietrich of Oldenburg and his second wife, Hedvig of Holstein. The House of Oldenburg was a comital family established since the 12th century west of the River Weser, which had gradually extended its rule over the neighbouring Frisian tribes. When Dietrich died in 1440 Christian and his brothers jointly succeeded him as counts of Oldenburg and Delmenhorst. Christian was raised by his childless uncle Adolphus, who wished him to be his heir and had him elected his successor in the Duchy of Schleswig.

In January 1448 King Christopher of Denmark, Sweden and Norway died without heirs. The Council of the Realm offered the Danish throne first to Duke Adolphus, who declined and recommended Christian. Christian had to promise to obey the Constitutio Valdemariana, which barred one person from ruling both Schleswig and Denmark, and to marry the dowager queen Dorothea of Brandenburg. He was elected at Viborg on 1 September 1448 and crowned at Copenhagen on 28 October 1449, when his marriage was also held.

In Norway the Council of the Realm was divided between Christian and Karl Knutsson, whom Sweden had elected in June 1448. In 1450 the Swedish Council forced Karl to give up his Norwegian claim, and Christian was crowned at Trondheim on 2 August. A treaty signed at Bergen on 29 August made Denmark and Norway elective monarchies sharing one king in perpetuity. Karl was driven into exile in 1457, and Christian was elected king of Sweden, restoring the Kalmar Union for a short time. His reign there ended in 1464, and his attempt to regain Sweden ended in defeat by the regent Sten Sture the Elder at the Battle of Brunkeberg in October 1471.

In 1460, after Adolphus's death, Christian became Duke of Schleswig and Count of Holstein-Rendsburg, his succession confirmed by the estates at Ribe on 5 March 1460. Emperor Frederick III raised him to Duke of Holstein in 1474. Many parts of his realm sought to govern themselves, and there were constant struggles. With the permission of Pope Sixtus IV given in 1475, he inaugurated the University of Copenhagen on 1 June 1479.

Christian died at Copenhagen Castle on 21 May 1481, aged 55, and was buried at Roskilde Cathedral in the Chapel of the Magi. The dynasty he founded went on to rule Denmark, and it held the throne of Norway until 1818 and again from 1905.
christian-i-prince-of-anhalt-bernburg: Christian was born in Bernburg on 11 May 1568, the second son of Joachim Ernest, Prince of Anhalt, of the House of Ascania, and his first wife Agnes, daughter of Wolfgang I, Count of Barby-Mühlingen. He was taught Latin, Italian and French in Dessau by Caspar Gottschalk, and as a child took part in diplomatic missions, among them one to Constantinople. In early 1586 he went to Dresden, where he spent several years as the closest friend of his namesake, Christian I, Elector of Saxony, whose Calvinist sympathies he shared; his heavy drinking at the electoral court is recorded.

A committed Calvinist, he became adviser to Frederick IV, Elector Palatine. In 1591 he led the Palatine army in support of the French king Henry IV, and in the Bishops' War over the bishopric of Strasbourg, which broke out in 1592, he backed Brandenburg against Lorraine. In 1595 Frederick IV made him Governor of the Upper Palatinate, and he settled in Amberg. That year, at Lohrbach, he married Anna of Bentheim-Tecklenburg, with whom he had sixteen children; their son Christian II succeeded him in Bernburg.

By the division of 1603 he revived the principality of Bernburg, extinct since 1468. As a diplomat he played an important part in founding the Protestant Union in 1608. He went on to serve Frederick V, and when the Bohemian nobles elected Frederick their king in 1619 he was given command of the Protestant forces defending Bohemia against Emperor Ferdinand II. The same year he was admitted to the Fruitbearing Society.

After the defeat at White Mountain in 1620 he advised Frederick not to make a stand in Prague. In 1621 he was placed under the imperial ban, which made him an outlaw in the Holy Roman Empire and stripped him of his lands. He fled first to Sweden and then to the court of King Christian IV of Denmark-Norway. In 1624 he appealed to Ferdinand for mercy and was allowed to return to his principality, where he died on 17 April 1630. His son Ernest, a cavalry colonel in Saxon service, was fatally wounded at the Battle of Lützen in 1632.
christian-ii-of-denmark: Christian was born at Nyborg Castle on 1 July 1481, the son of King John of Denmark and Christina of Saxony. He took part in his father's conquest of Sweden in 1497 and in the Dano-Swedish War of 1501–1512. In 1506 he became viceroy of Norway, where he kept control but quarrelled with the privy council by trying to reduce the nobility's traditional influence.

He succeeded his father in 1513. In 1515 he married Isabella of Austria, a granddaughter of the Holy Roman Emperor Maximilian I. His mistress Dyveke Sigbritsdatter remained with him until her death in 1517, and her mother, Sigbrit Willoms, became his chief counsellor.

Believing that the magnate Torben Oxe had poisoned Dyveke, Christian had him tried by a common jury, not the Council of State, and executed in November 1517, which deepened the division between king and aristocracy. His attempts to take Sweden from the regent Sten Sture the Younger failed in 1517 and 1518 but succeeded in 1520 with French, German and Scottish mercenaries. Christian was crowned king of Sweden in November.

On 8 and 9 November the Stockholm Bloodbath took place: after an ecclesiastical court condemned Sture's followers for heresy, they were executed at Stockholm castle, among them the bishops of Skara and Strängnäs. The killings provoked a rising led by Gustav Vasa, and Sweden left the Kalmar Union. In Denmark Christian issued a Town Law and a Land Law in 1521, strengthening tradesmen and peasants at the nobility's expense and allowing clergy to marry. Nobles and bishops saw them as a threat, and after rebellion began in Jutland the crown was offered on 20 January 1523 to his uncle Frederick.

Christian left Denmark in April 1523 and lived in exile at Lier in the Netherlands, where he corresponded with Martin Luther and for a time became a Lutheran. By 1531 he was Catholic again and sailed to Norway, but failed to take Akershus Castle and accepted a promise of safe conduct from Frederick I. It was broken, and he was held for 27 years, first at Sønderborg and from 1549 at Kalundborg, where he was treated as a nobleman. His supporters were defeated in the Count's Feud of 1536. He died at Kalundborg in January 1559 and is remembered in Sweden as Christian the Tyrant.
christian-iii-count-palatine-of-zweibruc: Christian was born in Strasbourg on 7 November 1674, the son of Christian II of Zweibrücken-Birkenfeld and Katharina Agathe, Countess of Rappoltstein. He was the only son of his father to survive into adulthood, and a member of the House of Palatinate-Zweibrücken-Birkenfeld, a cadet branch of the House of Wittelsbach. In 1699 he inherited the County of Rappoltstein from his mother, a title he kept until his death.

He made his career in the French army, which he entered in 1697, taking over the Alsatian regiment. He became a field marshal in 1702 and was promoted to lieutenant general in 1704, and he distinguished himself at the Battle of Oudenaarde in 1708. When his father died in 1717 he left the army and took over the administration of Zweibrücken-Birkenfeld, a small part of the County of Sponheim, which he governed as count palatine until 1731.

In 1719, at Château de Lorentzen, he married Caroline of Nassau-Saarbrücken, with whom he had four children. In 1731 Count Palatine Gustavus Samuel Leopold of Zweibrücken died childless, and Christian inherited his sovereign duchy of Palatine Zweibrücken, becoming Count Palatine and Duke of Zweibrücken. His relatives contested the inheritance, and it was settled only by a treaty with Elector Palatine Charles III Philip, concluded in Mannheim on 24 December 1733, which confirmed that Christian would receive Palatine Zweibrücken.

Christian died in Zweibrücken on 3 February 1735, less than four years after coming into the duchy. He was buried in the crypt of Alexander's Church in Zweibrücken, beside other counts and dukes of his line, in the church built in 1493 by his ancestor Alexander, Count Palatine of Zweibrücken. His widow, Caroline of Nassau-Saarbrücken, lived until 1774, and the duchy he had secured by the Mannheim treaty passed to his descendants of the Birkenfeld line.
christian-iii-of-denmark: Christian was born on 12 August 1503 at Gottorf Castle in Schleswig, the eldest son of the future Frederick I of Denmark and Anna of Brandenburg. After his father was elected king in 1523 he was made stadtholder of Holstein and Schleswig in 1526 and viceroy of Norway in 1529, and showed considerable administrative ability. His teachers Wolfgang von Utenhof and Johann Rantzau were zealous reformers. In 1521 he travelled to the Diet of Worms to hear Martin Luther speak, and he made no secret of his Lutheran views, which brought him into conflict with the State Council. In 1528 he made the Lutheran Church the state church of Schleswig-Holstein by a Church Ordinance.

After Frederick I died in 1533, Christian was proclaimed king at an assembly in Rye in 1534. The Rigsraad, dominated by Catholic bishops and nobles, refused to accept him and turned to Count Christopher of Oldenburg to restore Christian II, which led to the two-year civil war known as the Count's Feud. Christian found his support among the nobles of Jutland. When peasants under Skipper Clement rose in northern Jutland, Christian sent Johan Rantzau north with Protestant German mercenaries, who stormed Aalborg. Gustav Vasa of Sweden sent armies to Scania and Halland. Count Christopher's forces held out in Malmø and Copenhagen until they surrendered in July 1536.

On 12 August 1536 Christian had three bishops of the State Council arrested, and some Catholic bishops were later executed. On 30 October 1536 the reconstituted council adopted the Lutheran Ordinances designed by Johannes Bugenhagen, making Lutheranism the Danish national church. Monasteries, nunneries and priories were closed and their property taken by the crown, which helped pay his large debt from the war. In 1537 he made Lutheranism the state religion of Norway as well, which remained joined to Denmark until 1814. In Iceland the suppression of the Catholic Church disrupted poor relief.

The first six years of his reign were a contest between the Danish Rigsraad and German counsellors, who had led his armies. He declared war on Charles V in 1542 and allied with German Protestant princes and France. In 1544 he and his half-brothers John the Elder and Adolf partitioned Holstein and Schleswig. He built Landskrona Citadel from 1549 and rebuilt Sønderborg Castle in Renaissance style between 1549 and 1557. Christian died at Koldinghus on 1 January 1559 and was buried in Roskilde Cathedral. His son Frederick II succeeded him.
christian-iv-of-denmark: Christian was born at Frederiksborg Castle on 12 April 1577, the eldest son of King Frederick II and Sofie of Mecklenburg-Schwerin. Denmark was then an elective monarchy, so he was not automatically heir, but in 1580 his father had him elected prince and successor. He was ten when his father died on 4 April 1588, and a regency council led by the chancellor Niels Kaas governed until he came of age. On 17 August 1596 he signed his haandfæstning, a curtailment of the monarch's power comparable to Magna Carta, and he was crowned in Copenhagen on 29 August 1596.

Christian pursued domestic reforms and rearmament. Dutch engineers directed the building of new fortresses, and the navy grew from twenty-two vessels in 1596 to sixty in 1610. He relied mainly on hired mercenaries for his army. Until the early 1620s the economy profited from boom conditions in Europe, and he expanded overseas trade, founding merchant cities such as Christianstad in 1614, Glückstadt in 1617 and Kongsberg in 1624. He rebuilt the Norwegian capital Oslo as Christiania, a name used until 1925. In 1620 a treaty with the Nayak of Tanjore gave Denmark the village of Tranquebar in India.

In 1611 he went to war with Sweden for supremacy of the Baltic, which ended in the Treaty of Knäred of 20 January 1613 with no decisive gains. He entered the Thirty Years' War as war leader of the Lower Saxon Circle, a war that devastated much of Germany, undermined the Danish economy and cost Denmark–Norway some of its conquered territories. In 1643 Sweden attacked again in the Torstenson War, and by the end of January 1644 all of Jutland was in Swedish hands. Christian spent more time in Norway than any other Oldenburg monarch, and founded four cities there.

His last years were embittered by quarrels with his sons-in-law, especially Corfitz Ulfeldt. His obsession with witchcraft led to public executions, among them the burning of Maren Spliid at Ribe on 9 November 1641. He died in Copenhagen on 28 February 1648 and was buried in Roskilde Cathedral. His reign of 59 years and 330 days made him the longest-reigning monarch in Scandinavian history, and he remains popular in both Denmark and Norway.
christian-knorr-von-rosenroth: Knorr von Rosenroth was born on 15 or 16 July 1636 at Alt-Raudten, today Stara Rudna, in Silesia. After his studies at the universities of Wittenberg and Leipzig he travelled through the Netherlands, France and England. At Amsterdam he came to know an Armenian prince, the chief rabbi Meier Stern, John Lightfoot and Henry More, and under their influence studied Oriental languages, chemistry and the cabalistic sciences. On his return he settled at Sulzbach in the service of Christian Augustus, Count Palatine of Sulzbach, and devoted himself to the study of Hebrew. He died on 4 May 1689.

He studied the Kabbalah in the belief that it held proofs of Christian doctrine: for him the Adam Kadmon of the cabalists was Jesus, and the three highest sefirot represented the Trinity. He intended a Latin translation of the Zohar and the Tiḳḳunim, and as preliminary studies published at Sulzbach in 1677–78 the first two volumes of the Kabbala Denudata. They contain a cabalistic nomenclature, the Idra Rabbah, the Idra Zuṭa and the Sifra di-Ẓeni'uta, and cabalistic essays of Naphtali Herz ben Jacob Elhanan. Two further volumes, published at Frankfurt in 1684, contain the Sha'ar ha-Shamayim of Abraham Cohen de Herrera and several writings of Isaac Luria.

At the request of Franciscus Mercurius van Helmont he helped translate, edit and publish in Latin the writings of Jan van Helmont on chemistry. He also translated into German Thomas Browne's Pseudodoxia Epidemica, a work of over 200,000 words, completing it in 1680 for publication in Frankfurt and Leipzig. He wrote hymns, among them Morgenglanz der Ewigkeit, sung in English as Come, Thou Bright and Morning Star. The Emperor Leopold I created him a baron. A partial English translation of the Kabbala Denudata by S. L. MacGregor Mathers appeared in 1887 as The Kabbalah Unveiled.
christian-social-party-austria: The Christian Social Party emerged before the 1891 elections to the Imperial Council under the populist Vienna politician Karl Lueger. It drew on the ideas of the Christian Social movement of Karl von Vogelsang and the Christian Social Club of Workers, and it was oriented towards the petite bourgeoisie and the Catholic clergy. Many priests belonged to it, among them the later chancellor Ignaz Seipel, and this brought in many votes from the tradition-bound rural population. As a social conservative counterweight to the Social Democrats, whom it called godless, the party gained mass support through Lueger's anti-liberal and antisemitic slogans. Its backing of Austro-Hungarian cohesion and the House of Habsburg also gave it popularity among the nobility.
The party was affiliated with an Austrian nationalism that sought to keep Catholic Austria out of the German state founded in 1871, which it viewed as Protestant and dominated by Prussia.

When universal male suffrage was introduced under minister-president Max Wladimir von Beck, the party won a plurality in the 1907 elections and became the largest group in the lower house, but it lost that position to the Social Democrats in 1911. It backed the government in the First World War. In October 1918, as the monarchy dissolved, its 65 deputies voted for the Republic of German-Austria and its accession to Germany, though party members soon began to oppose annexation.

The party formed a grand coalition with the Social Democrats under the Social Democrat state chancellor Karl Renner, took 35.9 per cent in the 1919 constituent assembly election, and supported the Habsburg Law. The coalition broke up in 1920. In the election that year the party won 41.8 per cent and became the strongest, entering a coalition with the Greater German People's Party under Michael Mayr. Every chancellor of the First Republic from 1920 belonged to it, as did President Wilhelm Miklas, who succeeded Hainisch in 1928. Seipel, party chairman since 1921, became chancellor on 31 May 1922. The Social Democrats stayed in opposition and concentrated on Red Vienna, and politics grew more polarised.

On 20 May 1933 Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuß, in setting up what is called the Austro-fascist dictatorship, founded the Fatherland Front by merging the party with the Landbund, the Heimwehr and other conservative groups. The party was dissolved when the May Constitution of 1934 came into force and the Federal State of Austria was founded. Its members included Dollfuß, Seipel, Lueger, Kurt von Schuschnigg and the later chancellor Julius Raab.
christian-social-union-in-bavaria: The Christian Social Union in Bavaria, founded in 1945, is regarded as the de facto successor of the Catholic Bavarian People's Party of the Weimar period. It is a Christian democratic and conservative party with a regionalist identity, and it operates only in Bavaria, while its larger counterpart, the Christian Democratic Union, operates in the other states. The CSU has led the Bavarian state government since 1946, except from 1954 to 1957, when the Social Democrat Wilhelm Hoegner formed a coalition government. The separatist Bavaria Party had at first competed for the same voters, since both saw themselves as successors to the Bavarian People's Party; the CSU won this contest, and in 1966 the Bavaria Party left the state parliament.

Franz Josef Strauß left the strongest legacy. He led the party from 1961 until his death in 1988, held four federal ministerial posts between 1953 and 1969, and was Minister-President of Bavaria from 1978. In 1980 he was the first CSU leader to stand for the chancellorship, but lost to the incumbent Helmut Schmidt. No chancellor has ever come from the CSU. Edmund Stoiber, leader from 1999, ran for chancellor in 2002 and also lost.

Before 2008 the CSU regularly won absolute majorities in Bavaria, a dominance unique among the German states. In 2003 it won 60.7 per cent of the vote and 124 of 180 seats, the first two-thirds majority in a German state parliament. It lost its majority in 2008, when its share fell to 43.4 per cent, and governed in coalition with the Free Democratic Party.

In the Bundestag the CSU forms a common group with the Christian Democratic Union, known as the Union. Below the federal level the two parties are entirely independent. The CSU and the state of Bavaria did not sign the Grundgesetz of the Federal Republic, as they could not agree with the division of Germany into two states after the Second World War. The party is divided into ten district associations, 105 county associations and almost 3,000 local associations.
christian-the-younger-of-brunswick: Christian was born on 20 September 1599 at Gröningen Priory near Halberstadt, the third son of Duke Henry Julius of Brunswick-Lüneburg, of the House of Welf, and his second wife Elizabeth, a daughter of King Frederick II of Denmark. After his father's death he was brought up by his uncle, King Christian IV of Denmark, and studied at the University of Helmstedt. In 1616, at 17, he was elected Lutheran administrator of Halberstadt after his brother Rudolf. Neither the emperor nor the Catholic Church confirmed him, but the post gave him the money for a military career, and he became known as der tolle Halberstädter, the daredevil from Halberstadt.

In 1620 he joined the army of Prince Maurice of Orange in the Netherlands, and in 1621 he raised his own army for Frederick V, Elector Palatine, declaring a chivalric love for Frederick's wife Elizabeth. By the end of that year he had 10,000 men, wintered in Westphalia and took great sums from the dioceses of Münster and Paderborn. Beaten by Johan t'Serclaes, Count of Tilly, at Höchst on 22 June 1622, he escaped with much of his army and joined Ernst von Mansfeld, with whom he quarrelled so badly that they nearly fought a duel.

At the Battle of Fleurus on 29 August 1622 he led five cavalry charges against the Spanish under Fernández de Córdoba before breaking through to help relieve Bergen op Zoom, at the cost of most of his infantry and one arm; he then took the motto Altera restat, the other remains.
