In 1623 a plan with Mansfeld and Bethlen Gabor, Prince of Transylvania, to retake Bohemia failed, and on 6 August Tilly caught him short of the Dutch border at Stadtlohn, where his army of 15,000 was reduced to 2,000.

Three days after Stadtlohn, Frederick V signed an armistice with Emperor Ferdinand II, closing the Palatine phase of the Thirty Years' War. When Denmark-Norway, the Dutch Republic and England entered the war in 1625, Christian received new funds and was ordered to the Rhineland, but was checked by Tilly in Hesse and withdrew. Ill from the start of the campaign, he died at Wolfenbüttel on 16 June 1626, aged 26. The historian Herfried Münkler holds that he was driven less by Protestant conviction than by a love of adventure and a romantic view of himself as a knight.
christian-thomasius: Christian Thomasius was born in Leipzig on 1 January 1655 and was educated by his father Jakob Thomasius, then a junior lecturer at Leipzig University and later its dean and rector and head master of the Thomasschule. His father's lectures introduced him to the political philosophy of Hugo Grotius and Samuel Pufendorf. He studied law at the University of Frankfurt (Oder) from 1675 and took his doctorate in 1679. In 1680 he married Anna Christine Heyland and began a legal practice in Leipzig, and the next year he started teaching at the university's law school.

In 1684 Thomasius became professor of natural law. In 1685 he published a provocative dissertation, De crimine bigamiae, arguing that bigamy is permissible under natural law. In 1687 he lectured in German instead of Latin, on how the French way of life should be emulated, pointing to the French use of their own language in scholarship; the scholar Klaus Luig dates the real beginning of the German Enlightenment to this event. From 1688 he published a monthly periodical that ridiculed the pedantry of the learned, took the side of the Pietists against the orthodox and defended marriages between Lutherans and Calvinists.

On 10 May 1690 he was denounced from the pulpits, forbidden to lecture or write, and ordered arrested. He escaped to Berlin, and the elector Frederick III offered him refuge in Halle, with a salary of 500 thaler and leave to lecture. He helped found the University of Halle in 1694, became its second and then first professor of law, and was rector in 1710. In 1709 he was appointed to the privy council. He died in Halle in 1728.

Thomasius aimed to free politics and jurisprudence from the control of theology and fought for freedom of thought and speech in religious matters. He taught that the state may interfere only with legal or public duties, not moral or private ones. He would not have atheists punished, though they should be expelled from the country, and he opposed the prosecution of witches and the use of torture. He was not a deist but held that revealed religion is necessary for salvation, and he came strongly under Pietist influence, especially that of Spener.

In law he tried to show that rules of Roman law contrary to his natural law had never been truly received, and he presented his own principles as common law with Germanic foundations, which helped create a scholarship of private law separate from Roman law. His main works in German include the monthly periodical, the Einleitung zur Vernunftlehre of 1691 and the Kurze Lehrsätze von dem Laster der Zauberei of 1704. His Latin works include the Institutiones iurisprudentiae divinae of 1688 and the Fundamenta juris naturae et gentium of 1705.
christian-viii-of-denmark: Prince Christian Frederick was born on 18 September 1786 at Christiansborg Palace in Copenhagen, the eldest son of Hereditary Prince Frederick and Duchess Sophia Frederica of Mecklenburg-Schwerin. His mother died in 1794. He was raised conservatively under the minister Ove Høegh-Guldberg, with a broad education, and a love of science and art stayed with him all his life.

In 1806 he married his cousin Charlotte Frederica of Mecklenburg-Schwerin. Their son, the future Frederick VII, was born in 1808, the year Christian Frederick became heir presumptive to his cousin Frederick VI, who had no sons. He divorced her in 1810 after her alleged affair with her singing teacher. In 1815 he married Caroline Amalie of Schleswig-Holstein-Sonderburg-Augustenburg; they had no children.

In May 1813 he was sent to Norway as governor-general to strengthen loyalty to the House of Oldenburg. When the Treaty of Kiel forced the king to cede Norway to Sweden, he placed himself at the head of the Norwegian party of independence. An assembly of notables elected him regent on 16 February 1814, and after the Constituent Assembly at Eidsvoll he was unanimously elected king of Norway on 17 May, when the constitution was signed. He failed to win the great powers to Norway's cause.

A short campaign followed in which the Swedish crown prince Charles John defeated the Norwegian army. By the Convention of Moss of 14 August 1814 Christian transferred executive power to the Storting, abdicated and returned to Denmark. On 4 November the Storting elected Charles XIII of Sweden king of Norway.

Christian became king of Denmark on 3 December 1839. The Liberal party had high hopes of him as the giver of constitutions, but he had grown conservative and rejected every Liberal project, promising only administrative reform. On the national unrest in Schleswig and Holstein he often seemed hesitant, and not until 1846 did he clearly support the idea of Schleswig as a Danish area. In 1845 the last remnants of Danish India, Tranquebar and Serampore, were sold to the British. He died of sepsis at Amalienborg Palace in 1848 and was buried at Roskilde Cathedral. Some historians believe he would have given Denmark a free constitution had he lived longer.
christiansted: Christiansted is the largest town on Saint Croix, one of the main islands of the United States Virgin Islands. Its name is Danish for Christian's Place, after King Christian VI of Denmark. The streets run at right angles to the waterfront, and the commercial area centres on King and Company streets, beside the Christiansted National Historic Site. The residential area, which includes parts first settled by free Black people, extends inland and uphill.

Captain Frederik Moth founded the town after he became governor of St. Croix in 1733. His party, which set out from St. Thomas, had cleared a space for Fort Christianswærn by 5 September. On 8 January 1734, in a ceremony beside the fort, the French formally handed the island over to the Danes in the person of the Danish West India and Guinea Company. The island was to be divided into 300 plantations, 215 for sugar and the rest for cotton, and the company also set up a sugar refinery and distillery. The fort was finished by 1740.

The 1742 census listed 120 sugar plantations, 122 cotton plantations, 1,906 enslaved people, about 300 Englishmen and 60 Danes. By 1745 the enslaved population had grown to 2,878, and by 1754 it numbered 7,566. The 83 white inhabitants of the town in that year each owned between one and sixty-six enslaved people. The town was built by African slaves, which is why its design carries African as well as Danish influences. Later residents included Alexander Hamilton in 1765 and, from 1887 to 1905, the fireburn leader Mary Thomas, who was imprisoned there.

Christiansted keeps 18th-century Danish-style stone buildings in pastel colours with red tile roofs along cobblestone pavements. It was a capital of the Danish West Indies. Tourism supports its economy, and Henry E. Rohlsen Airport serves it.
christina-of-lorraine: Christina was born in Nancy, the daughter of Charles III of Lorraine and Claude of Valois, and was named after her paternal grandmother, Christina of Denmark. Catherine de' Medici saw to her scholarly education. In 1584 Mary, Queen of Scots, wrote to Catherine hoping that Christina might marry her son, King James VI, as a useful ally, but nothing came of the plan.

When Francesco I de' Medici died in 1587 without a legitimate male heir, his brother Ferdinando declared himself the third Grand Duke of Tuscany. Seeking a marriage that would preserve his political independence, he chose his distant cousin Christina, the favourite granddaughter of Catherine, who had influenced her towards a match that would re-align the Medici with France rather than Spain.

The wedding festivities of 1589 in Florence were designed to impress the royal houses of Europe. A ceremony in Florence Cathedral was followed by public events, banquets, balls, comedies, musical interludes and a mock sea battle in the flooded courtyard of the Palazzo Pitti. These entertainments influenced theatrical practice in European courts through the 17th century. Ferdinando died in early 1609, and their son Cosimo II took power at 19. In 1610 the Venetian ambassador Giacomo Vendramin wrote that the grand duchess wanted to govern everything absolutely. She commissioned a biography of Cosimo I and Jacques Callot's engravings of the life of her husband.

Her son Cosimo II died in February 1621, leaving his ten-year-old son Ferdinando II as grand duke. Christina and her daughter-in-law Maria Maddalena of Austria acted as regents, a period known as the Tutrici. Maria Maddalena took the public political role, while Christina dealt with the Florentine religious establishment. In 1623 the co-regents abolished a century-old law so that patricians could take part in the government of Florence, a move meant to weaken Roman aristocrats there. The historian Jacopo Riguccio Galluzzi judged that everything began to decline with Cosimo II's death and criticised the admission of clergy to administrative posts.

Christina invited Galileo Galilei in 1605 to tutor her son Cosimo. In December 1613, at a breakfast in Pisa, the philosopher Cosimo Boscaglia argued against Galileo's reading of the moons of Jupiter by appeal to Scripture, and Christina asked Galileo's former student Benedetto Castelli for his opinion. Galileo answered in his Letter to Grand Duchess Christina, arguing that Scripture conveys the message of salvation rather than natural philosophy. She was also a patron of Florentine convents, above all Santa Croce, known as La Crocetta.
christina-queen-of-sweden: Christina was born on 18 December 1626 in the royal castle Tre Kronor, the daughter of Gustavus Adolphus and his German wife Maria Eleonora. When Gustavus Adolphus left for Germany in June 1630 to defend Protestantism in the Thirty Years' War, he secured her right to inherit the throne and ordered that she receive the education normally given only to boys. She succeeded him at five, after his death at the Battle of Lützen, but began to rule only in 1644, when she was declared an adult at eighteen.

Chancellor Axel Oxenstierna soon found that her political views differed from his. At the Peace Congress in Osnabrück in 1645 his son argued against peace with the Holy Roman Empire, while Christina, who wanted peace at any cost, sent her own delegate. She patronised scholars and artists and founded the newspaper Ordinari Post Tijdender in 1645. The philosopher René Descartes arrived at her invitation on 4 October 1649, but the two did not get on. She was crowned on 22 October 1650. On 26 February 1649 she had announced that she would not marry and named her cousin Charles Gustav as heir.

In the summer of 1654 she left Sweden in men's clothing and travelled through Denmark as Count Dohna. She entered Rome on 20 December in a sedan chair designed by Bernini, was confirmed by the pope and settled in the Palazzo Farnese, where she opened the Academy of Arcadia on 24 January 1656.

At Fontainebleau in 1657 Christina had her master of the horse, Gian Rinaldo Monaldeschi, whom she suspected of betraying her, stabbed to death by her servants. The act cost her popularity. In 1660, after Charles X Gustav's death, she returned to Sweden hoping to regain the throne if his young son died, but as a Catholic she could not, and she submitted to a second renunciation. She died on 19 April 1689 in the Palazzo Corsini and is one of the few women buried in the Vatican Grottoes. Her life inspired Strindberg's play Kristina (1901) and the film Queen Christina (1933). Historians still discuss her unconventional dress and her letters to Ebba Sparre.
christine-de-pizan: Christine was born in September 1364 in the Republic of Venice, the daughter of Tommaso di Benvenuto da Pizzano, a physician and councillor of the Republic, whose family came from the village of Pizzano, south-east of Bologna. When she was four, in 1368, her father was appointed court astrologer to King Charles V of France. In 1379, aged fifteen, she married the notary and royal secretary Etienne du Castel, and they had three children. Her husband died of the plague in 1389, a year after her father. Left to support her mother and her children, she faced complicated lawsuits over salaries still owed to her husband.

By 1393 she was writing love ballads that caught the attention of wealthy patrons at court, and she is called the first professional woman of letters in Europe. In 1402 she questioned the literary merits of Jean de Meun's Romance of the Rose, which depicted women as seducers, in the Querelle du Roman de la Rose.

In 1404 she wrote the life of Charles V, commissioned by Philip the Bold, and by 1405 she had completed The Book of the City of Ladies and The Book of Three Virtues, known as The Treasure of the City of Ladies. In The Book of the City of Ladies she built a symbolic city defended by the allegorical figures Reason, Justice and Rectitude, in which only female voices supply evidence. After John the Fearless had Louis of Orléans assassinated in 1407, she wrote the Livre de la paix in 1413 for the dauphin, urging peace.

Historians assume that she spent her last ten years in the Dominican convent of Poissy, where her daughter had become a nun in 1397. In 1429, a few days after the coronation of Charles VII, she published the Ditié de Jehanne d'Arc, casting Joan of Arc as the fulfilment of prophecies. She published 41 known pieces and was known across Europe.

William Caxton translated her Book of Feats of Arms and of Chivalry for Henry VII in 1489, and The Book of the City of Ladies appeared in English in 1521. By the early nineteenth century she was nearly forgotten, and Mathilde Laigle and Marie-Josephe Pinet revived her work. Judy Chicago's The Dinner Party of 1979 has a place setting for her, and she was one of ten women honoured by statues at the opening ceremony of the 2024 Summer Olympics in Paris.
christine-of-france: Christine was born in the Palais du Louvre in Paris on 10 February 1606, the third child and second daughter of King Henry IV of France and his second wife Marie de' Medici. As a daughter of the king she was a Daughter of France, and she was a younger sister of Louis XIII and Elisabeth of France and an older sister of Gaston, Duke of Orléans, and Henrietta Maria. She was raised under the royal governess Françoise de Montglat. After Elisabeth's marriage in 1615, Christine took the honorary title Madame Royale, which marked the eldest unmarried daughter at her brother's court.

She married Victor Amadeus I, Duke of Savoy, on 10 February 1619, and was known as Princess of Piedmont until he succeeded his father on 26 July 1630. Reputedly she was volatile and frivolous. She brought French culture to Savoy, had the Palazzo Madama rebuilt and drove the reconstruction of the Castello del Valentino. Her aim was a court that rivalled her sister Henrietta Maria's, and she hoped to turn the minor Duchy of Savoy into a little France. When Victor Amadeus died in 1637 she became regent for her son Francis Hyacinth, and after his death in 1638 she kept the regency for her second son Charles Emmanuel II.

Her brothers-in-law Prince Maurice and Prince Thomas of Savoy disputed her power and that of her French entourage. After Francis Hyacinth died they began the Piedmontese Civil War with Spanish support. Their followers were called principisti, and hers madamisti, supporters of Madama Reale. After four years of fighting she won with French military backing, kept the duchy for her son and prevented France from gaining too much power in it. When peace was made in 1642 Maurice married his fourteen-year-old niece Louise Christine and gave up the title of cardinal. Her formal regency ended in 1648, but she stayed in control at her son's invitation until she died.

She encouraged her son to marry her niece Françoise Madeleine d'Orléans, and they married on 3 April 1663. Christine died at the Palazzo Madama in Turin on 27 December 1663, aged 57, and was buried at the Basilica of Sant'Andrea. She had outlived four of her seven children. She kept up a close correspondence with Henrietta Maria, to whom the exiled queen wrote about the English Civil War. Through her granddaughter Marie Anne Christine Victoire of Bavaria and her second son Philip V of Spain, she is a direct ancestress of the Spanish branch of the House of Bourbon.
christmas: The English word is a shortened form of Christ's Mass, recorded as Crīstesmæsse in 1038. The Anglo-Saxons called the season midwinter or Gēola, Yule. Early church records of the 2nd century show Christians remembering the birth of Jesus, though without agreeing on a date, and Christmas is missing from the festival lists of Irenaeus and Tertullian. Towards the end of the 4th century John Chrysostom, Augustine of Hippo and Jerome attested 25 December as its date.

Several theories explain that choice. Liturgical historians agree, according to the theologian Susan Roll, that it was linked in some way with the sun, the winter solstice and solar worship in the later Roman Empire. Writers of the 2nd and 3rd centuries called 25 December the birthday of the Sun, and the early church called Jesus the true Sun. Thomas J. Talley holds that the Emperor Aurelian placed his rival festival on 25 December to compete with a church already celebrating Christmas on that date.

Two Gospels give the accounts of the birth. In Luke, Joseph and Mary travel from Nazareth to Bethlehem to be counted in a census, and Jesus is born there and laid in a manger, with angels proclaiming him to shepherds. In Matthew, magi follow a star to Bethlehem to bring gifts. Preparation begins on the first Sunday of Advent, and in the West Christmastide lasts twelve days, ending on Twelfth Night.

Customs include gift-giving, carols, cards, church services and a special meal. Nativity scenes are known from 10th-century Rome and were popularised by Francis of Assisi from 1223, when he assembled one outside his church at Greccio. The earliest surviving Christmas hymns date from 4th-century Rome, among them Ambrose's Veni redemptor gentium, and English carols appear in a work of 1426 by John Awdlay. The first commercial Christmas card was produced in London in 1843 by Sir Henry Cole.

Christmas has often been disputed. The Parliament of Scotland, dominated by Presbyterians, passed acts against its observance between 1637 and 1690, and Christmas Day did not become a public holiday in Scotland until 1871. Puritans outlawed it in Colonial New England in 1659, arguing that Scripture does not mention it. Some Eastern Orthodox jurisdictions, among them those of Russia, Georgia and Serbia, still mark feasts by the Julian calendar, so that they keep Christmas on what the civil calendar calls 7 January.
christmas-battles: The advance of the German 8th Army had been stopped near Riga in October 1915, and the Germans at once fortified their positions. Across the Tīreļpurvs, or Tīrelis bog, between Lake Babīte and Jelgava, they built the German Wall, about 30 kilometres of sand and timber that separated the two armies for more than a year. The Russian 12th Army of the Northern Front, commanded by Radko Dimitriev, was ordered to attack after the failure of the 1916 campaigns in Romania, to draw German reserves away.

A heavy frost in mid-December froze the bog and made an assault on Jelgava possible. Its main force, the Babīte group, had 48 battalions and 208 guns against 19 German battalions of the 6th Landwehr Brigade. At its core was the 6th Siberian Rifle Corps with both Latvian Riflemen brigades.

The attack began early on 23 December 1916 by the Julian calendar, 5 January by the Gregorian, and surprised the Germans, who expected the Russians to be celebrating Christmas. In white camouflage, the Latvians cut through the barbed wire and took the first line without artillery support. On 25 December the 3rd and 7th Latvian Regiments, the 53rd Siberian Regiment and the 2nd Latvian Brigade took the fortified hill later called Ložmetējkalns, Machine-gun Hill, with about 1,000 prisoners, opening a gap more than 7 kilometres wide. The 17th Siberian Regiment and men of other Siberian units refused to fight, and the army commander could not exploit the breakthrough.

The Germans brought fresh divisions to Jelgava and counter-attacked on 23 January after a heavy barrage. In three days of fighting, at temperatures falling to -38°C, they regained about 80 per cent of the lost positions, but Machine-gun Hill stayed in Russian hands.

The Russians had tested a new breakthrough tactic and drawn part of the German forces away from the Romanian front. The command punished the Siberian units that had refused to fight: 92 men were sentenced to death by a war tribunal and several hundred sent back to Siberia. The mutiny is seen as a sign of the Russian Revolution to come. Tīrelis bog and the nearby forests are now the Museum of the Christmas Battles, a branch of the Latvian War Museum, where many old trenches can still be seen.
christmas-carol: The term noel has sometimes been used, especially for carols of French origin. The first Christmas hymns, such as Veni redemptor gentium by Ambrose, Archbishop of Milan, were austere statements of the doctrine of the Incarnation against Arianism, and Corde natus ex Parentis by the Spanish poet Prudentius is still sung in some churches. In the 9th and 10th centuries the Christmas sequence emerged in monasteries of northern Europe, and in the 12th century the Parisian monk Adam of Saint Victor began to add melodic elements from popular songs.

The songs now called carols were originally communal festival songs of seasonal celebrations such as harvesttide, and only later were adopted for church use. It is not clear whether the word carol comes from the French carole or the Latin carula, meaning a circular dance.

Many carols were printed in Piae Cantiones, a collection of late-medieval Latin songs first published in 1582, which includes early Latin forms of Good King Wenceslas. Almost all the well-known carols were not sung in church until the second half of the 19th century, when Hymns Ancient and Modern included several. How All the Welkin Rings became Hark! the Herald Angels Sing, set to a tune from Felix Mendelssohn's cantata Festgesang of 1840, adapted by William H. Cummings.

Silent Night was first performed in the Nikolauskirche in Oberndorf on 24 December 1818, with words by Joseph Mohr from 1816 and a melody and guitar accompaniment by Franz Xaver Gruber. Some carols can be traced to the Middle Ages, among them Personent hodie, Good King Wenceslas and The Holly and the Ivy.

During the Puritan ban on Christmas in England, carols were sung privately despite official restrictions. In the 19th century William Sandys's collection of 1833 included God Rest Ye Merry, Gentlemen, The First Noel and I Saw Three Ships, and Christmas Carols, New and Old by Henry Ramsden Bramley and John Stainer, published in 1871, contributed to a revival in Victorian Britain. The Oxford Book of Carols, first published in 1928 and edited by Martin Shaw, Ralph Vaughan Williams and Percy Dearmer, was widely used by choirs and congregations.

Some songs called carols are not religious: A Bone, God Wot! appears to be a wassailing song, and Greensleeves took Christmas words in 1865 as What Child is This?. A sociological study of caroling in Finland in the early 21st century found that the sources of songs are often misunderstood and that caroling also reinforces diverse national customs and local family traditions.
christmas-tree: Modern Christmas trees originated in Central Europe and the Baltic lands, particularly Germany and Livonia, during the Renaissance. The first evidence of decorated trees tied to Christmas comes from guildhalls, where trees were hung with sweets for apprentices and children. In 1441, 1442, 1510 and 1514 the Brotherhood of Blackheads put up a tree in its guild houses in Reval, now Tallinn, and in Riga, and on the last night of the celebrations it was taken to the Town Hall Square, where the members danced around it. A Bremen guild chronicle of 1570 describes a tree hung with apples, nuts, dates, pretzels and paper flowers.

Some researchers see forerunners in the paradise trees of medieval mystery plays given on 24 December, the name day of Adam and Eve, when a fir hung with apples, for the fruit of the tree of knowledge, and round white wafers, for the Eucharist, served as a prop. The earliest firmly dated representation of a Christmas tree is on a keystone of a private house in Turckheim in Alsace, dated 1576. A tree was placed in the Cathedral of Strasbourg in 1539 under the reformer Martin Bucer, and the Moravian Christians put lighted candles on such trees.

After the Reformation decorated trees appear in the homes of upper-class Protestant families as a counterpart to the Catholic cribs. In the early 19th century the custom became popular among the nobility and reached royal courts as far as Russia. It came to Vienna in 1814 during the Congress of Vienna, and in France the first tree was introduced in 1840 by the duchesse d'Orléans. Glass baubles were first made in Lauscha in 1847. In 1935 the Soviet Union, which had banned Christmas, introduced a secular New Year spruce. Pope John Paul II introduced a tree to the Vatican in 1982.
christmas-truce: By November 1914 the armies on the Western Front had built continuous trench lines from the North Sea to the Swiss frontier. Fraternisation, peaceful contact between opposing forces, was already common in quiet sectors, and truces between British and German units can be dated to early November, when both sides paused to collect rations after dusk. Officers often resisted it: Lieutenant Charles de Gaulle wrote of the lamentable desire of French infantrymen to leave the enemy in peace. Before Christmas there were peace initiatives, among them an Open Christmas Letter signed by 101 British women.

The Germans placed candles on their trenches and on Christmas trees and sang carols, and the British answered with carols of their own. Greetings were shouted across, and men crossed no man's land to exchange food, tobacco, alcohol, buttons and hats. The artillery fell silent, burial parties brought in the dead, and joint services were held. In many sectors the truce lasted through Christmas night, and in others until New Year's Day. Many accounts mention football matches, the earliest in a letter from a Rifle Brigade doctor published in The Times on 1 January 1915. Hostilities went on in other sectors.

The truces went unreported for a week, until The New York Times broke an unofficial press embargo on 31 December. A German order of 29 December 1914 forbade fraternisation, and in December 1915 Allied commanders ordered raids and barrages to prevent a repeat. The historian Tony Ashworth sets the Christmas truces within a wider live and let live system of local agreements along the front. A memorial was unveiled at Frelinghien on 11 November 2008. The last known participant, Alfred Anderson of the Black Watch, died on 21 November 2005, aged 109.
christmas-uprising: Several historians hold that most Montenegrins favoured union with the other South Slavs after the First World War, but many wanted Montenegro to enter the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes as an autonomous unit, not to be absorbed into a centralised Serbian kingdom. At the Podgorica Assembly the unionist Whites outnumbered the Greens after a questionable selection of candidates. The historian Ivo Banac suggested that the Greens had wider support but were poorly organised and divided, some seeking full independence and King Nikola's return, others only an equal place in a union.

The military leader of the rising was Krsto Popović and its political leader Jovan Plamenac. Their plan, delivered to the Italian ethnographer Antonio Baldacci on 14 December 1918, was for three columns to take Nikšić, Podgorica and the country around Lake Skadar and then attack Cetinje together, with food and arms asked of the government in exile at Neuilly-sur-Seine.

The rising broke out first around Podgorica, where the rebels were surrounded and disarmed by unionist youth and the Bjelopavlići without a battle. Nikšić was besieged from 3 January 1919 until reinforcements relieved it, and several rebel leaders were captured, among them Marko Đukanović, once minister of defence. At Virpazar, Plamenac agreed to send his men home, then rallied them again and finally crossed the Bojana to the Italian troops in Albania. The siege of Rijeka Crnojevića ended when the rebels found themselves outnumbered.

Cetinje, surrounded by 2 January, was the centre of the rising. Its defenders under Colonel Dragutin Milutinović were rearmed from the garrison at Tivat, while the rebels held serdar Janko Vukotić captive at Bajice and demanded new elections. On 6 January about 250 Serbian troops and 850 Montenegrin volunteers fought some 1,500 to 2,000 Greens there; the rebels, divided among themselves, were defeated.

Participants were tried and imprisoned, some fled to Italy, and others kept up a guerrilla war as the Montenegrin Army in exile until 1929, its best-known leader being Savo Raspopović. An Inter-Allied Commission of Investigation concluded from interviewing prisoners that the rising had been caused by King Nicholas's agents and supported by emissaries from Italy. The rising later became a theme of Montenegrin nationalism: in 2008, on its 90th anniversary, Prime Minister Milo Đukanović unveiled a memorial to the Greens killed in it.
christoph-bernhard-von-galen: Christoph Bernhard von Galen was born on 12 October 1606 to Lutheran parents of the noble Westphalian von Galen family. His father, Dietrich von Galen, held estates in the Baltic region and the title of Marshal of Courland. On 15 February 1607, during a state assembly in Münster, Dietrich killed the hereditary marshal of Münster, Gerd Morrien zu Nordkirchen, and spent twelve years in detention at Bevergern Castle, where his wife joined him of her own accord.

In 1616 the boy was placed with his uncle Heinrich von Galen, a canon of Münster, who had him educated as a Catholic by the Jesuits at the Paulinum. He began working for the cathedral chapter at 13, completed his Jesuit schooling in Cologne and Mainz, travelled to Bourges and Bordeaux, and returned to Münster in July 1627. He became treasurer of the cathedral in 1630 and a spiritual adviser in 1634, and was sent on many diplomatic missions, among them negotiations with the imperial generals in Westphalia during the Thirty Years' War.

Left poor by the loss of his father's inheritance, he took holy orders, yet fought for Emperor Ferdinand III in the last stages of the war. In 1650 he succeeded Ferdinand of Bavaria as prince-bishop. Ruling the largest ecclesiastical principality of the Holy Roman Empire with a strong army, he became an important figure in Europe. In 1664 he was chosen one of the directors of the imperial army raised against the Turks, though his troops arrived too late to fight. His war on the Dutch on the side of Charles II of England ended when Louis XIV and Frederick William, Elector of Brandenburg, forced a disadvantageous peace at Cleve in 1666.

In the Franco-Dutch War his troops, helped by Louis XIV, took Groenlo, Deventer and Coevorden, but stalled before Groningen when deliberate flooding made the fields and marshes almost impassable. In October 1674 he withdrew and gave up his attempt to restore Catholicism in the eastern provinces. In 1675 he changed sides to fight for Emperor Leopold I and, with Brandenburg and Denmark–Norway, conquered the Duchy of Bremen from Charles XI of Sweden.

Galen died at Ahaus on 19 September 1678. He sought to reform the church, but his main energies went into his own power and prestige, and he rid Westphalia of the foreign armies that had occupied it since 1648. In the Netherlands he is remembered as Bommen Berend, and Groningen still celebrates the breaking of his siege every 28 August.
christoph-duke-of-wurttemberg: Christoph was born on 12 May 1515, the son of Ulrich, Duke of Württemberg, and Sabina of Bavaria. In November of that year his mother fled to her parents' court in Munich, and he stayed in Stuttgart with his father and his elder sister Anna. When the Swabian League raised troops against Ulrich, the children were taken to Castle Hohentübingen, and after the castle surrendered in 1519 Ulrich was banished and Württemberg came under Austrian rule.

Christoph was sent to the court of Emperor Maximilian I at Innsbruck, where he grew up under Habsburg tutelage and gained political experience, and Maximilian's successor Charles V took him on his travels through Europe.

After Ulrich won back Württemberg from the Austrians in 1534, Christoph went to the French court and was drawn into France's wars against the Habsburgs. At the end of the 1530s he became a Protestant. The Treaty of Reichenweier of 1542 made him governor of Montbéliard, a Württemberg possession, and in 1544 he married Anna Maria, daughter of George, Margrave of Brandenburg-Ansbach, with whom he had twelve children.

When he succeeded his father in 1550 he had to make heavy payments to Ferdinand I to avoid charges of treason. In the following years he reorganised the whole administration of church and state and reformed and supported the schools. He gave Amandenhof castle near Urach to Hans von Ungnad, who made it the seat of the South Slavic Bible Institute.

Christoph died on 28 December 1568. His eldest son Eberhard had died in May of that year, and he was succeeded by his son Ludwig I. His daughters married into many Protestant princely houses: Hedwig and Sabine to the landgraves of Hesse-Marburg and Hesse-Kassel, Dorothea Maria to Otto Heinrich, Count Palatine of Sulzbach, and Sophie to Friedrich Wilhelm I, Duke of Saxe-Weimar.
christoph-froschauer: Froschauer was born in Neuburg near Oettingen in Bavaria. He learned the printer's trade from his uncle, Hans Froschauer, in Augsburg, and came to Zürich in 1515. There he worked for one Hans Rüegger and built a printing press. When Rüegger died in 1517, Froschauer married his widow and took over the press, and in 1519 he gained the citizenship of Zürich. His arrest in 1522, in the dispute over fasting during Lent, brought Zwingli into open conflict with the clerical establishment.

Froschauer was the first printer in Zürich. Besides the works of Zwingli he printed those of Erasmus and Luther, and religious writings by Leo Jud, Heinrich Bullinger and Rudolf Gwalther. He also published scientific works, among them Joachim Vadian's atlas of 1534, the chronicle of Johannes Stumpf of 1547/48 and Conrad Gessner's Historia animalium of 1551–1558. Between 1520 and 1564 about 700 titles, in close to a million copies, left his four presses, printed on paper from the city's mill on the Limmat, which he also ran.

His best-known work was the Froschauer Bible, a complete German Bible translated from the original Hebrew and Greek texts, which began to appear in 1524. The translation is credited to Luther, Zwingli and Jud, and its final volume, with the Apocrypha, came out some years before Luther's own translation of the full Bible in 1534. The workshop stood at Brunngass 18, on the northern edge of the Froschau quarter, facing the Zähringerplatz.

After his wife died in 1550 he married Dorothea Locher. Froschauer died of plague in Zürich in 1564, and his nephew, Christoph Froschauer the Younger (1532–1585), took over the shop. The workshop is the nucleus of the Orell Füssli publishing house, and the Froschau quarter of Zürich, by the present Froschaugasse, is named after him. The name Froschauer means man from the frog meadow, and the family used a drawing of a frog as its printing mark. In 2020 a frog, Stumpffia froschaueri, was named after him.
christoph-martin-wieland: Wieland was born on 5 September 1733 at Oberholzheim, half of which belonged to the Free Imperial City of Biberach an der Riss and half to Gutenzell Abbey. His father was a pastor, first at Oberholzheim and then at Biberach, and took great pains with his son's education. At twelve Wieland went to the Kloster Berge gymnasium near Magdeburg, and by 1749 he was widely read in the Latin classics and the leading French writers. In 1750 he went to the University of Tübingen to study law, but gave most of his time to literature.

The Swiss reformer J. J. Bodmer invited him to Zürich in 1752, but the two soon parted. Wieland stayed in Switzerland until 1760, spending the last year as a private tutor in Bern. He then returned to Biberach as director of the chancery, where the library of Count Stadion at Warthausen gave him access to French and English literature.

He married Anna Dorothea von Hillenbrand on 21 October 1765, and they had 14 children. Between 1769 and 1772 he was professor of philosophy at the University of Erfurt. His pedagogic work Der goldene Spiegel (1772) drew the attention of Duchess Anna Amalia of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, who appointed him tutor to her sons Karl August and Constantin at Weimar, which remained his home until his death.

In 1773 he founded Der teutsche Merkur, which under his editorship until 1789 became the most influential literary review in Germany. Goethe attacked him in the satire Götter, Helden und Wieland, and Wieland answered with good nature. Goethe and Herder were soon drawn to Weimar, where Anna Amalia formed a circle later joined by Schiller. Wieland died in Weimar on 20 January 1813.

Geschichte des Agathon (1766 to 1767) is regarded as the first Bildungsroman. Under the guise of a Greek fiction it describes his own spiritual and intellectual growth. He translated twenty-two of Shakespeare's plays into prose (1762 to 1766), the first attempt to present Shakespeare to the German public in something close to full. His light verse romances, such as Musarion (1768) and Der neue Amadis (1771), served as an antidote to the sentimental excesses of Sturm und Drang.

Die Abderiten (1774) satirises German provinciality, and his poetic masterpiece, the romantic epic Oberon (1780), became the basis of operas by Friederike Sophie Seyler and Carl Maria von Weber. Politically he was a moderate liberal who advocated constitutional monarchy and a free press, and his thought was cosmopolitan: only a true cosmopolitan, he remarked, can be a good citizen.
christoph-willibald-gluck: Gluck was born in the Upper Palatinate, probably on 2 July 1714, the date he himself gave on a document requested from Paris in 1785, and was baptised on 4 July. His father Alexander was a forester. In 1727 the family moved to Eisenberg in Bohemia, where Alexander became head forester to Prince Philipp Hyazinth von Lobkowitz. About 1727 or 1728 Gluck went to Prague, left without a degree, and probably reached Vienna in 1734. In 1737 he arrived in Milan and studied with Giovanni Battista Sammartini. His first opera, Artaserse, was performed on 26 December 1741, and he went on to write for Milan, Turin and Venice, mostly to texts by Metastasio.

After posts in London and with touring companies, Gluck married Maria Anna Bergin on 15 September 1750 and settled in Vienna as Kapellmeister. Pope Benedict XIV made him a Knight of the Golden Spur in 1756. With the choreographer Gasparo Angiolini he wrote the ballet Don Juan (1761). Orfeo ed Euridice, first performed on 5 October 1762 to a libretto by Ranieri de' Calzabigi, subordinated star singers to drama and did away with dry recitative. The preface to Alceste (1767) set out the principles: no da capo arias, no virtuoso display, simpler melodic lines and an overture linked to the action.

Under the patronage of Marie Antoinette he wrote eight operas for Paris. Iphigénie en Aulide, premiered on 19 April 1774, set off a quarrel between Gluckists and supporters of the Italian composer Niccolò Piccinni. Iphigénie en Tauride (1779) was a great success, but Echo et Narcisse failed after twelve performances, and he returned to Vienna.

Gluck died on 15 November 1787, a few hours after a heart arrhythmia struck while he lunched with friends, at the age of 73. Only half of his work survived a fire in 1809. It includes about 35 full-length operas and numerous ballets and instrumental works. His reforms influenced Mozart, particularly Idomeneo (1781), and left a school of disciples in Paris, among them Antonio Salieri, Cherubini, Méhul and Spontini. Berlioz was his most devoted French admirer, and his example influenced Weber and Wagner.
christophe-plantin: Plantin was born in France, probably in Saint-Avertin, near Tours, to a family that was not wealthy; his mother died while he was young. He apprenticed as a bookbinder in Caen, where he also married. In 1545 he and his wife, Joanna Rivière, set up shop in Paris, but after three years they moved to Antwerp, where he became a free citizen and a member of the Guild of St Luke, the guild of painters, sculptors, engravers and printers. His bookbinding brought him into contact with nobility and wealth.

A wound to his arm, received when he was mistakenly attacked while delivering a prestigious commission, ended his work as a bookbinder and turned him to printing. By 1555 he had his own print shop; the first book he is known to have printed was La Institutione di una fanciulla nata nobilmente, by Giovanni Michele Bruto.

In 1561 the Spanish governor ordered a raid on his workshop on suspicion of heretical works, and in 1562 his presses and goods were seized and sold after his workmen printed a heretical pamphlet while he was in Paris. With the help of four Antwerp merchants he re-established the business and acquired a house in the Hoogstraat named De Gulden Passer, the Golden Compasses. His printer's mark showed compasses held by a hand from the clouds, with the motto Labore et Constantia.

His most important work was the Biblia Regia, or Plantin Polyglot, with parallel texts in Latin, Greek, Syriac, Aramaic and Hebrew. Philip II of Spain encouraged it and sent Benito Arias Montano to lead the editing. Plantin mortgaged his business to pay for it, and it took thirteen presses and fifty-three men and earned little profit. In return Philip granted him the privilege of printing Roman Catholic liturgical books for the states he ruled and the title Architypographus Regii. By 1575 the firm had more than 20 presses and 73 workmen.

After the Spanish sack of Antwerp in November 1576 he paid a heavy ransom to protect his works, and in 1583 he moved temporarily to Leiden, leaving the Antwerp business to his sons-in-law Jan Moretus and Frans van Ravelinghen. He returned after the city surrendered in 1585 and worked there until his death on 1 July 1589. The Moretus family left the workshop untouched, and in 1877 the city of Antwerp opened it as the Musée Plantin. The Christophe Plantin Prize was created in his memory in 1968.
christopher-columbus: Scholars agree that Columbus was born in the Republic of Genoa, between 25 August and 31 October 1451; theories placing his origin in Aragon or Portugal are discounted by most of them. His father, Domenico Colombo, was a wool weaver who worked in Genoa and Savona and owned a cheese stand where the boy worked. His mother was Susanna Fontanarossa. In 1470 the family moved to Savona, where Domenico took over a tavern. Columbus wrote that he went to sea at the age of 14, and he later settled in Lisbon, where his brother Bartholomew ran a cartography workshop.

After Constantinople fell to the Ottoman Empire in 1453, the Silk Road was closed to Christian traders. In 1474 the Florentine astronomer Paolo dal Pozzo Toscanelli suggested to King Afonso V of Portugal that sailing west across the Atlantic would reach Asia faster than the route around Africa, but the king rejected the idea. Columbus and his brother proposed such a plan in the 1480s, and Bartolomeu Dias's rounding of the Cape of Good Hope in 1488 complicated it. After the Granada War and years of lobbying, Queen Isabella I and King Ferdinand II of Spain agreed to sponsor the voyage.

Columbus left the Port of Palos in August 1492 with three ships and made landfall on 12 October on an island in the Bahamas known to its inhabitants as Guanahani. He then visited Cuba and Hispaniola, where he founded the short-lived fort of La Navidad, and returned to Castile in early 1493 with captured American Indians. Three further voyages took him to the Lesser Antilles in 1493, to Trinidad and the northern coast of South America in 1498, and to the east coast of Central America in 1502. He never clearly renounced his belief that he had reached the Far East, and he called the people he met indios.

As colonial governor Columbus was accused by some contemporaries of significant brutality, and he was arrested and removed from Hispaniola in 1500. He afterwards demanded the tenth of the new lands' wealth promised in the Capitulations of Santa Fe, and after his death his heirs pursued the claim in the protracted lawsuits known as the pleitos colombinos. His remains were moved several times, between Valladolid, Seville, Santo Domingo and perhaps Havana, and DNA tests on those in Seville in 2003 led researchers to conclude that they are his.

His voyages began lasting contact between the two hemispheres and the Columbian exchange of plants, animals, diseases and ideas. Diseases and warfare introduced from the Old World contributed to the decline of Hispaniola's American Indians, who were also enslaved and mistreated under Columbus's government. Once idealised as a heroic discoverer, he is now examined more critically.
christopher-ii-of-denmark: Christopher was a younger son of Eric V and the brother of King Eric VI, who reigned from 1286 until 1319, which made him a possible heir. As a young man, with the title Duke of Estonia, he supported his brother's policies and arrested Archbishop Jens Grand in 1294. Later he joined the opposition and went into exile at Eric's death in 1319.

The magnates wanted a weak royal power, and in January 1320 they elected Christopher king. In return he signed a håndfæstning, the first time such a document was used as a coronation charter. He received a bankrupt estate in which entire regions were mortgaged to German and Danish magnates. The charter limited his ability to levy taxes and required the consent of the nobility and bishops for any decision about the realm. It also extended the privileges of nobles and church. This shift of power away from the king lasted until 1660.

Christopher ruled as if the charter did not exist. Unable to tax the church or nobles, he taxed the German territories and peasants heavily, and he revived Eric's wars against the duchies, counties and cities of northern Germany. This brought new mortgages and taxes, and conflict with the church and the magnates. In 1326 an alliance of Danish magnates with Gerhard III, Count of Holstein-Rendsburg, and John I, Count of Holstein-Kiel, overthrew him in a rebellion.

Christopher lived in exile until 1329, when the chaos of the magnates' republic gave him another chance. He was restored with the cooperation of Count John, but as a puppet. Jutland was mortgaged for 100,000 silver marks that had to be paid at once, and Gerhard took it as his own property, while John took Funen and Zealand. A military defeat at Dannevirke in 1331 left him king in title only. He was imprisoned at Ålholm Castle on Lolland, where he died the next year, and was buried at Sorø Abbey.

Historians have judged him very harshly, as the king who mortgaged Denmark to the Germans, but he largely continued his predecessor's policy, and mortgaging land was common practice among nobles and kings. The power of the Danish and German high nobility and the church undermined his freedom of action.
christopher-marlowe: Christopher Marlowe was the second of nine children of the Canterbury shoemaker John Marlowe and his wife Katherine, daughter of William Arthur of Dover. He was baptised at St George's Church, Canterbury, on 26 February 1564, and was probably born a few days earlier, about two months before William Shakespeare. Little is known of his adult life beyond legal records. In 1587 the Privy Council ordered Cambridge to award him his Master of Arts, denying rumours that he meant to go to the English Catholic college at Rheims and saying he had been engaged in matters touching the benefit of his country. Some writers conclude that he was a government spy, though that is speculation.

Six dramas have been attributed to Marlowe, alone or in collaboration: Dido, Queen of Carthage, Tamburlaine, The Jew of Malta, Doctor Faustus, Edward the Second and The Massacre at Paris. Tamburlaine, first performed on a regular London stage in 1587, was the first English play in blank verse and, with Thomas Kyd's The Spanish Tragedy, is seen as the start of the mature phase of Elizabethan theatre. His plays formed the foundation of the repertoire of the Admiral's Men, and the haughty roles of Tamburlaine, Faustus and Barabas were probably written for the tall actor Edward Alleyn. Doctor Faustus is the first dramatised version of the Faust legend, and its hero is carried off by demons.

His poetry includes The Passionate Shepherd to His Love and the unfinished Hero and Leander, completed by George Chapman and printed in 1598, as well as translations of Ovid's Amores and of the first book of Lucan's Pharsalia. In 1599 the Ovid translation was banned and copies were publicly burned.

In May 1593 bills threatening Protestant refugees were posted in London, one signed Tamburlaine. The next day Thomas Kyd was arrested, and a heretical tract found in his lodgings was said by Kyd, under torture, to be Marlowe's. A warrant for Marlowe's arrest was issued on 18 May, and he presented himself on 20 May. He was killed on 30 May 1593, and scholars still dispute the circumstances. George Peele called him the Muses' darling, and Ben Jonson wrote of Marlowe's mighty line.
christopher-soames: Arthur Christopher John Soames was born in Penn, Buckinghamshire, the son of Captain Arthur Granville Soames, brother of Olave Baden-Powell, the World Chief Guide, and of Hope Mary Woodbine Parish. He was educated at West Downs School, Eton College and the Royal Military College at Sandhurst and was commissioned in the Coldstream Guards just before the Second World War. He served in France, Italy and North Africa and won the French Croix de Guerre at the Second Battle of El Alamein in 1942. On 11 February 1947 he married Mary Churchill, the youngest child of Winston and Clementine Churchill; they had five children.

After serving as Assistant Military Attaché in Paris, Soames was Conservative MP for Bedford from 1950 to 1966. He was Under-Secretary of State for Air under Anthony Eden, Secretary of State for War under Harold Macmillan from 1958 to 1960, and Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food in the cabinets of Macmillan and Alec Douglas-Home from 1960 to 1964. He lost his seat in 1966.

Harold Wilson made him Ambassador to France in 1968. In February 1969 the Soames affair followed a private meeting at which President Charles de Gaulle offered bilateral talks on a partnership for Britain in a larger and looser European union; the British government refused, and Franco-British relations were strained for a time. He was a Vice-President of the European Commission from 1973 to 1976 and became a life peer in 1978.

As governor he arrived in Salisbury on 12 December 1979, lifted the ban on ZANU-PF and the Zimbabwe African People's Union, granted a general amnesty and oversaw about 1,200 Commonwealth monitoring troops. The elections of February 1980 were held amid widespread violence and allegations of intimidation, and his decision not to disqualify ZANU-PF was controversial. His governorship ended after 129 days, on 18 April 1980. He was also Lord President of the Council and Leader of the House of Lords under Margaret Thatcher from 1979 to 1981.

Lord Soames died of cancer at his home in Odiham on 16 September 1987, and his ashes were buried in the Churchill plot at St Martin's Church, Bladon. Among his children were Nicholas Soames, a Conservative MP and later a member of the House of Lords, and Emma Soames, editor of Saga magazine.
christopher-wren: Wren was the only surviving son of Christopher Wren the Elder, rector of East Knoyle and later Dean of Windsor, and of Mary Cox, whose inheritance made the family well off. He was a sickly child who seemed consumptive, yet lived into robust old age.

After taking his master's degree in 1653 he became a fellow of All Souls College, Oxford, and began experiments, among them what is recognised as the first injection of fluids into the bloodstream of a live animal under laboratory conditions. In 1657 he became Professor of Astronomy at Gresham College, London, and the weekly meetings of men who attended his lectures, begun formally in 1660, grew into the Royal Society.

His first architectural work was a chapel for Pembroke College, Cambridge, designed in the winter of 1662 or 1663 for his uncle Matthew Wren, Bishop of Ely, and completed in 1665. His design for the New Theatre at Oxford, financed by Gilbert Sheldon and completed in 1669, met a lukewarm reception. In July 1665 he made his only trip abroad, to Paris, where he met Gian Lorenzo Bernini. A week after his dome design for St Paul's was accepted in principle on 27 August 1666, the Great Fire destroyed two-thirds of the City.

He became King's Surveyor of Works in 1669 and was knighted on 14 November 1673. His later works include the Monument, the Royal Observatory, the Wren Library at Trinity College, Cambridge, the Chelsea Hospital, Kensington Palace and Hampton Court. In his study of Old St Paul's and Ely he challenged the view that Gothic architecture was invented by the Goths, preferring to call it Saracen, a theory since disputed.

Wren married Faith Coghill in 1669; she died of smallpox in 1675. He married Jane Fitzwilliam in 1677 and she died in 1680. His son Christopher the Younger supervised the topping out of St Paul's in 1710 and wrote the Parentalia. Wren was given a lease at Hampton Court in lieu of salary arrears for building St Paul's.

He was buried in the crypt of St Paul's, where the inscription ends: Reader, if you seek his monument, look around you. His close friend Robert Hooke wrote that scarcely since Archimedes had so mechanical a hand and so philosophical a mind met in one man. UNESCO inscribed his Greenwich Hospital on the World Heritage list in 1997.
chrodegang-of-metz: Chrodegang was born early in the 8th century in Hesbaye, around the old Roman civitas of Tongeren, into a noble Frankish family. He was possibly the son of Sigramnus, Count of Hesbaye, and of Landrada, a sister of Rotrude of Hesbaye, the first wife of Charles Martel. He was educated at the abbey of Saint-Trond and at the cathedral school of Metz, and he is claimed as a forebear of the Frankish dynasty of the Robertians.

At the court of his kinsman Charles Martel he became referendary, then chancellor, and in 737 prime minister, and he kept his civil office after he succeeded Sigibald as bishop of Metz. In 753 he met and escorted Pope Stephen II, who had come to seek help against Lombard incursions; as apostolic delegate he took part in the coronation of Pepin in 754 and the defeat of the Lombard king Aistulf. After the death of Saint Boniface the pope gave him the pallium, making him an archbishop without raising the see of Metz.

He founded Gorze Abbey near Metz in 748 and St. Peter's Abbey on the Moselle, helped the abbeys of Gengenbach and Lorsch, and is said to have obtained relics of Saint Nazarius for Lorsch and of Saint Gorgonius for Gorze. Around 755 he wrote the Regula Canonicorum, a rule of thirty-four chapters based on the Rule of Saint Benedict but adapted to canons who served the faithful. In 762, during a dangerous illness, he set up among his priests a confraternity of prayer, the League of Attigny.

Chrodegang died at Metz on 6 March 766 and was buried at Gorze, the site of his principal shrine. The historian M. A. Claussen holds that his work lay at the foundation of the Carolingian spiritual revival. His rule spread community life among the secular clergy, was partly taken into the Council of Aachen's rule for canons in 816, and gave way only in the eleventh and twelfth centuries to rules based on Augustine. It was probably carried to Ireland, where the Rule of the Céli Dé is analogous to it. He is venerated as a saint in the Catholic and Orthodox churches.
chronicle-of-fredegar: No surviving manuscript names the author. The name Fredegar was first applied in 1579 by Claude Fauchet. In 1883 Bruno Krusch proposed three authors, a view later accepted by Theodor Mommsen, Wilhelm Levison and J. M. Wallace-Hadrill, and in 1934 Siegmund Hellmann proposed two. In 1963 Walter Goffart renewed the case for a single author, which is now generally accepted. The author is usually taken to have been a Burgundian from the region of Avenches, who knew the annals of many Burgundian churches and could apparently interview Lombard, Visigoth and Slavic ambassadors.

Krusch's edition has four books. The first three rest on earlier writings and run from the creation of the world to 584, drawing on Jerome's version of Eusebius, the Chronicle of Hydatius and the Decem Libri Historiarum of Gregory of Tours. The author also quotes unacknowledged sources, condenses others heavily and inserts passages of unknown origin, some of which weave a legend of a Trojan origin for the Franks.

Book IV, in 90 chapters, treats events at the Burgundian court and ends abruptly with the Battle of Autun in 642. Chapters 24 to 39 contain witness accounts of events between 603 and 613. Historians have studied it most, as it holds information found in no other medieval source.

The original is lost. It survives in an uncial copy made in 715 by a Burgundian monk named Lucerius, now in the Bibliothèque nationale de France, and in more than thirty manuscripts in all. Matthias Flacius Illyricus printed it at Basel in 1568 as an appendix to Gregory's History of the Franks.

One group of manuscripts adds Continuations carrying the narrative to 768. A colophon says that Count Childebrand, uncle of King Pippin, had the history recorded, and that his son Count Nibelung authorised what follows. Roger Collins has argued that this version is a separate work, which he would call the Historia vel Gesta Francorum. The chronicle is one of the few sources for the Merovingian dynasty after 591.
chronicle-of-the-morea: The Chronicle runs to more than 9,000 lines and tells how the crusaders who settled in the Peloponnese after the Fourth Crusade established feudalism there, covering the years from 1204 to 1292 or later, depending on the version. It opens with a prologue of 1302 verses, and its account of the administrative laws and practices of the Principality of Achaia, and of life in a feudal community, makes it a major source for the Frankish period in Greece despite its historical inaccuracies.

The original text is lost, and there is no agreed view on whether the Greek or the French version came first. The Greek is the only verse version, in unrhymed fifteen-syllable political verse in the spoken Greek of the time, with French loanwords. It survives in two parallel texts in five manuscripts: the older Copenhagen text, of 9219 verses, which runs to 1292, and a later Paris text that is plainer in language and drops several remarks hostile to the Greeks. The French prose text reaches 1304, the Italian is a later summary with several mistakes, and the Aragonese was compiled in 1393 for Jean Fernandez de Heredia, Grand Master of the Knights of St. John.

The author appears to have been a Frank or a gasmoule, the child of a mixed French and Greek marriage. He admired the crusaders and showed contempt for the local population and for the Roman Empire, though he still called the Byzantine Greeks Romans. According to the scholar Polet, this hostility is why the work did not pass into popular culture once the Franks had left the Peloponnese.

The Chronicle's language reflects the rapid change from medieval to modern Greek, and the work is counted, with the Ptochoprodromic poems and the acritic songs, among the beginnings of modern Greek literature. J. A. Buchon printed the Paris text in 1840 and the Copenhagen text in 1845, John Schmitt set the two side by side in 1889, and Harold E. Lurier published a translation of the Greek text in 1964.
chronicon-terrae-prussiae: The chronicle was completed some 100 years after the crusaders first came into the Baltic region, and it is the first major chronicle of the Teutonic Order in Prussia. It is divided into four volumes. The first gives the background of the Order and its crusades in Outremer, the second tells how the Order came to the Prussian land, and the third describes its wars with the Old Prussians and other Baltic tribes. The fourth sets these events beside other events of the time elsewhere in the world.

An addendum of another 20 chapters covers the years 1326 to 1330 and may also be the work of Peter of Dusburg. Peter drew on local monastery annals, chronicles, reports and oral accounts that he considered reliable, used the archive of the Grand Masters at Marienburg, and witnessed some of the events himself.

The work is written to glorify the Order's mission. Many chapters take the form of religious visions, miracles and lives of saints; the war against the pagans is presented as sacred, and every knight who falls in it goes to heaven. As a priest, Peter also wrote to teach his readers: the pagan Prussians and Lithuanians are shown as pious in their own way, an example that should shame sinful and disobedient Christians.

The chronicle preserves some ethnographic information about the Old Prussians, such as their sacred forests, fields and waters, where, as the Descriptiones terrarum of 1253 also records, no one was allowed to cut trees, plough or fish. It describes minor raids and clashes in great detail but takes no interest in the Order's domestic policy, saying nothing of its towns, trade or colonisation. Historians regard its accounts of events and battles as mostly reliable, while its chronology is at times wrong and its ethnographic material is ideologically charged.
chrysocheir: His name, also written Chrysocheres, Chrysocheris or Chrysocheiros, means goldhand. According to Peter the Sicilian he was the nephew and son-in-law of Karbeas, which indicates that he had married his first cousin, a practice the Byzantine Church strongly condemned. After the campaign against the Paulicians launched in 843 by the Empress-regent Theodora, Karbeas and many of his followers had fled to the Muslim border emirates and set up an independent principality centred on Tephrike, from which he fought Byzantium on the side of the Muslims. Nothing is known of Chrysocheir's life before he succeeded his uncle. Like Karbeas, he may have served in the Byzantine army in his youth.

Chrysocheir raided deep into Byzantine territory, as far as the western coasts of Asia Minor and the neighbourhood of Nicaea, Nicomedia and Ephesus, where he is reported to have stabled his horses in the Church of Saint John the Evangelist. When Emperor Basil I the Macedonian sent envoys to offer peace in 869/70, Chrysocheir is said to have demanded that the emperor first give up the eastern half of his lands in Asia Minor. Peter the Sicilian reports spending nine months in Tephrike at about this time to arrange the release of high-ranking prisoners; some scholars think he led the embassy, others do not.
In 871 Basil himself attacked Tephrike but failed to take it. In 872/3 the Domestic of the Schools Christopher won a decisive victory over the Paulicians at the Battle of Bathys Ryax.

Chrysocheir was killed in the battle by a common soldier called Poullades. His head was sent to Constantinople, where Basil reportedly shot three arrows into it with his bow. Tephrike itself fell to the Byzantines only six years later, ending the Paulician principality, and some modern scholars place Chrysocheir's defeat and death in the same year as the city's fall. His memory is commonly thought to survive in the Byzantine epic Digenes Akritas as Chrysoberges, the Muslim paternal grandfather of its hero.
chu-ci: The Chu Ci takes its name from a form of poetry that began in the State of Chu, in what is now central China, then on the southern fringe of the Chinese cultural area. Chu blended the culture of the Central Plain with influences associated with the south, and a Chinese form of shamanism was prominent there. Many of the verses describe spirit journeys, encounters with fragrant plants, spirits and deities, and travel to the heavens, the ends of the earth, Bactria and the mythical Mount Kunlun.

Qu Yuan is the central figure of the collection. According to common tradition he was an official at the court of King Huai of Chu who urged an alliance against the Qin, was slandered and exiled, and drowned himself in the Miluo River when the Qin general Bo Qi sacked the Chu capital Ying in 278 BCE. Dragon boat races are traditionally said to commemorate his death. His name appears in no text before the Han dynasty.

The standard version has seventeen main sections. It opens with the Li Sao, a poem of 373 verses that critics have often read as political allegory, though it also has religious and mythological aspects. The Jiu Ge, or Nine Songs, in fact has eleven parts and seems to reflect shamanistic drama of the Yangzi River valley, with the invocation of divine beings through a process of courtship. The Tian Wen, or Heavenly Questions, consists of 172 questions on myth and ancient religious belief, with few answers.

Some pieces follow the four-syllable lines of the Classic of Poetry, others the long lines of the sao style, which imitates the Li Sao. The poems are a major source for the myths of Nüwa and the Great Flood and the Xiang River goddesses.

Wang Yi, a librarian of the 2nd century CE under Emperor Shun of Han, gave the anthology its present contents and added a commentary and his own Nine Longings as the last section. Liu Xiang had apparently compiled the poems earlier, probably from a compilation by Liu An. The traditional view held that Qu Yuan wrote about half the pieces, but modern scholars have no consensus on which are his. The Chu Ci never became a canonical work like the Classic of Poetry, but it influenced poets including Jia Yi, Du Fu, Han Yu and Su Shi.
chu-han-contention: After the death of the First Emperor in 210 BCE, the eunuch Zhao Gao and the chancellor Li Si placed Prince Huhai on the throne and forced the heir, Prince Fusu, to kill himself. Revolts followed, beginning with the rising of Chen Sheng and Wu Guang at Dazexiang in 209 BCE. While the main Qin forces fought Xiang Yu at Julu, Liu Bang entered the Guanzhong region through the Wu Pass. The last Qin ruler, Ziying, surrendered the capital Xianyang, and Liu Bang forbade looting and abolished the harsh Qin laws except those against murder, harm and theft.

Xiang Yu, the hegemon among the rebels, then divided the empire into the Eighteen Kingdoms. His awards were seen as favouritism: he gave Guanzhong, which should have gone to Liu Bang, to three surrendered Qin generals, and left many rebel leaders with little or nothing.

Within six months Tian Rong rose in Qi, and Chen Yu took Zhao. While Xiang Yu marched north, Liu Bang's commander Han Xin feigned repairs to the burnt gallery roads, then struck through Chencang and conquered the Three Qins. Liu Bang accused Xiang Yu of the murder of Emperor Yi, but after his defeat at Pengcheng in 205 BCE his family was taken hostage and many allies changed sides.

Han Xin then won the northern front: he took Wei Bao at Anyi, defeated a Zhao army of 200,000 at Jingxing Pass by seizing its camp with 2,000 horsemen, and conquered Qi. Besieged at Xingyang, Liu Bang bribed Xiang Yu's men with 40,000 catties of gold to spread rumours that turned Xiang Yu against his adviser Fan Zeng.

In 203 BCE, on the advice of Zhang Liang and Chen Ping, Liu Bang broke the Treaty of Hong Canal and attacked the retreating Chu army. In December 203 BCE he, Han Xin and Peng Yue surrounded Xiang Yu at Gaixia, where Han troops sang Chu songs to break his army's morale. Xiang Yu fought a last stand by the Yangtze at Wujiang with 28 horsemen and took his own life.

The remaining Chu forces surrendered. Liu Bang made Peng Yue King of Liang, Ying Bu King of Huainan and Han Xin King of Chu, and months later declared himself emperor, with his wife Lü Zhi as empress. The capital was first at Luoyang and later moved to Chang'an. The war left a mark on Chinese culture: the river across the middle of the xiangqi board is called the Chu river and Han border, the Beijing opera Farewell My Concubine depicts Xiang Yu's defeat, and the idiom breaking cauldrons and sinking boats recalls his orders at Julu.
chu-nom: Chinese characters reached Vietnam after the Han dynasty conquered Nanyue in 111 BCE. Independence followed the Battle of Bạch Đằng in 938, and Literary Chinese was adopted for official purposes in 1010. Vietnamese scholars, thoroughly familiar with Chinese writing, applied its structural principles to record their own language. The oldest surviving inscription with Vietnamese names is on a stele at the Báo Ân pagoda in Tháp Miếu village, re-engraved in the 18th century from an original of 1209; it is written in Chinese but includes the names of 21 people and villages in an early form of Nôm. Trần Nhân Tông (r. 1278–1293) ordered that Nôm be used for his proclamations to the people.

Nôm used unchanged Chinese characters in three ways: for Sino-Vietnamese words, for native words of similar meaning, and for native words of similar sound. Scribes also invented thousands of new characters. The commonest kind was the phono-semantic compound, with one part suggesting the meaning and the other the sound: ba, three, combines a phonetic part with the character for three. A smaller group joined two characters of similar meaning, as in the character for the sky, which pairs those for sky and upper.

The script was never standardised, so one word could be written several ways, and it was complex and required prior knowledge of Chinese. Fewer than five percent of Vietnamese could use it. As an analytic language, Vietnamese suited a character script better than Japanese or Korean, but the literati regarded Chinese as the proper medium of civilised writing, so no phonetic system for the public developed until Europeans arrived.

Nôm became the official script only briefly, under the Hồ dynasty (1400–1407) and the Tây Sơn (1778–1802), and both times the change was reversed. During the Ming occupation of 1407–1427 Nôm printing blocks, texts and inscriptions were destroyed, so the earliest surviving texts post-date it. Under the Lê dynasty it served as a medium of social protest and was banned in 1663, 1718 and 1760. In the 19th century it reached a golden period, producing novels, plays and manuals, among them Nguyễn Du's The Tale of Kiều and the poetry of Hồ Xuân Hương. Nearly every village had someone who could read Nôm aloud.

French colonial authorities promoted the Vietnamese alphabet from the later 19th century. The traditional civil service examination was given for the last time in 1919, and after the First World War Nôm gradually died out. Its main research centre is the Institute of Hán-Nôm Studies in Hanoi.
chu-silk-manuscript: Like many illicit antiquities, the manuscript has an uncertain history. Grave robbers took it from a tomb at Zidanku, literally bullet storehouse, east of Changsha; archaeologists later found the tomb and dated it to around 300 BCE. In 1946 it belonged to the collector Cai Jixiang, and John Hadley Cox then took it to the United States. How Cox obtained it is disputed: Cai said Cox had only been asked to help scan it, and Cai's efforts to have it returned lasted until the late 1970s without success. Arthur M. Sackler bought it in 1965.

The sheet is 47 cm long and 38 cm wide, with worn edges and folds, and light has darkened parts of it; infrared photography has helped read some of them. The brush-written characters are hard to interpret, some illegible or lost and some, in Barnard's phrase, descendantless graphs that may reflect the Chu way of writing. Barnard published the first English translation in 1973, and Li and Cook another in 1999. The manuscript is roughly contemporary with the Tsinghua Bamboo Slips and Guodian Chu Slips and earlier than the Mawangdui Silk Texts of 168 BCE.

Its 926 characters fall into three sections, each concerned with the lunisolar calendar. Two blocks in the middle are written facing opposite ways: one, of thirteen lines, warns that if the months are miscounted the seasons and heavenly bodies will go astray and calamity will follow; the other, of eight lines set upside down, tells how Bao Xi and Nü Tian's four children separated heaven and earth and fixed the four seasons, and how Gong Gong knocked down a pillar of heaven. The scholar Jao Tsung-I suggests the inversion reflects a time when heaven was in disarray.

Round the margins are four coloured trees at the corners, taken to be the pillars holding up the heavens, and twelve masked figures with notes saying what may and may not be done in each month. Loewe thinks they may be guardian spirits of the months or masked shamans, and Li Xueqin matched them with the month names of the Erya.

The layout follows the shi or divination board, a model of the cosmos with a round board for heaven turning above a square board for earth, several of which have been found in Han tombs and which preceded the feng shui compass. Li Ling classes the manuscript as the oldest example of shushu, the arts of astronomy, calendar and divination.
chufut-kale: Chufut-Kale is a medieval city-fortress in the Crimean Mountains, now in ruins, 3 kilometres east of Bakhchysarai. It is a national monument of Crimean Karaite culture. Its name is Crimean Tatar and Turkish for Jewish fortress, while the Crimean Karaites call it simply the Fortress, and in Hebrew it was Sela ha-Yehudim, Rock of the Jews. In the Middle Ages it was Qırq Yer, Place of Forty, and the Crimean Tatars used several forms of that name in the Crimean Khanate. Legend says the name comes from forty Karaite families brought there by Meñli Giray or Tokhtamysh.

Researchers do not agree on when the town appeared. It may have been a fortified settlement in the 5th or 6th century on the edge of the Byzantine Empire, or it may date from the 10th or 11th. Early on it was populated mainly by Alans, who spoke an Eastern Iranian language and adopted Christianity. Written sources mention it in the 13th century as Kyrk-Or. In 1299 Nogai Khan's Golden Horde forces raided Crimea. The Byzantine garrison resisted a direct assault, but the Tatars played loud music for three days and nights, and on the fourth morning the exhausted defenders fell to a massacre.

At the turn of the 15th century the Tatars settled Karaite craftsmen in front of the eastern fortifications and built a second wall for them. After the fall of Constantinople in 1453 many Karaite Jews, who still spoke Greek, migrated to Crimea, especially to the Principality of Theodoro and Chufut-Kale. In the 15th century the first Crimean Khan, Hacı I Giray, turned the old part into his fortified residence. Later Meñli I Giray moved the capital to Bakhchysarai, and the old town became a citadel and a place of imprisonment for aristocratic prisoners.

In the mid-17th century the Tatars left. Only Karaites and a few Krymchak families remained, because anti-Jewish restrictions barred them from staying in other towns of the Khanate, and the name Chufut-Kale gradually took hold, in a scornful sense. After the Russian annexation of the Crimean Khanate in 1783 the inhabitants were free to live anywhere in Crimea, and the town was deserted. By the mid-19th century it had ceased to exist.

The Karaite scholar Abraham Firkovich claimed to have found tombstones in its cemetery dating from the year 6 of the common era. According to Harkavy, no epitaph there is earlier than 1203, and the tombs belong to Rabbinite Krymchaks, not Karaites. Adam Mickiewicz wrote a sonnet about the place, published in 1826.
chugoku-region: The Chūgoku region, also called the San'in-San'yō region, is the westernmost region of Honshū. It consists of the prefectures of Hiroshima, Yamaguchi, Shimane, Tottori and Okayama, and neighbours Kyūshū, Shikoku and Kansai. The land is characterised by irregular rolling hills and limited plains, and mountains running east and west divide it in two. San'in, the yin of the mountains, is the northern part facing the Sea of Japan, and San'yō, the yang of the mountains, the southern part facing the Seto Inland Sea.

Chūgoku literally means middle country, but the origin of the name is unclear. Japan was divided into provinces called koku, classified by distance from the administrative centre in Kansai into near, middle and far countries. One explanation is that Chūgoku first referred to the middle countries west of the capital, but only five of the provinces normally counted in the region were so classified. An alternative is that it meant the provinces between Kansai and Kyūshū, historically the link between Japan and mainland Asia. Historically the name covered the 16 provinces of the San'indō and San'yōdō, though some of the easternmost were later absorbed into prefectures based in Kansai.

Hiroshima, regarded as the capital of the region, was rebuilt after being destroyed by an atomic bomb in 1945 and is now an industrial city of more than one million people. Okayama is the other large centre. The San'yō coast is a zone of heavy industry, while the San'in is less industrialised, with an agricultural economy.
chulalongkorn: Chulalongkorn was born on 20 September 1853, a son of King Mongkut and Queen Debsirindra, and was made heir presumptive as the first son born to Debsirindra. He learned Buddhism, Pali, chronicles and royal ritual, and also science, English and French from Western teachers, among them Anna Leonowens. In 1868 he went with his father to observe a solar eclipse; both caught malaria, and Mongkut died on 1 October 1868. A council headed by Chuang Bunnag chose the fifteen-year-old Chulalongkorn, and Chuang acted as regent. After visits to Singapore, Java and British India he was crowned in his own right on 16 November 1873.

His first reform, in 1873, was an Auditory Office to take tax collection from nobles such as the Bunnag family. After armed Front Palace troops came to a palace fire in December 1874, reducing the nobility's power became a chief aim, and he abolished the Front Palace, the seat of a second king, in 1885.
