He founded a military academy in 1887, replaced the old government with ministries in 1888–1892, introduced a Western legal code with the Belgian adviser Gustave Rolin-Jaequemyns, and set up the monthon system of provinces in 1897, which ended the power of local dynasties. Rebellions against it in 1901 were crushed in 1902.

He abolished slavery by steps, wishing to avoid the bloodshed he associated with abolition in the United States. A law of 1874 freed at twenty-one those born as household slaves after 1867, and the Slave Abolition Act of 1905 ended slavery in all forms. The first railway, from Bangkok to Korat, opened in 1901.

In 1893 French demands for Lao lands east of the Mekong led to the Franco-Siamese crisis: French gunboats entered the Chao Phraya, Siam refused an ultimatum, and the matter ended with the cession of Laos. In 1906 France also received Inner Cambodia, and in 1909 four Malay sultanates came under British influence. Chulalongkorn visited Europe in 1897 and 1907, the first Siamese monarch to do so.

He died of kidney disease on 23 October 1910 and was succeeded by his son Vajiravudh. His reforms aimed to secure Siam's independence against Western encroachment, and he is honoured as Phra Piya Maharat, the Great Beloved King. Chulalongkorn University, founded in 1917, bears his name.
chungin: The chungin were petty bureaucrats and skilled, highly educated workers whose technical and administrative work allowed the yangban and the royal family to govern. The highest-ranking among them were local functionaries, who in the countryside administered the control that the aristocracy held over the sangmin. They were the smallest social class of dynastic Korea, and their traditions and habits are regarded as forerunners of the administrative systems of both North and South Korea.

Because the chungin could enter the palace as royal servants, a daughter of a family with a clean reputation or good connections could become a royal consort. Jang Ok-jeong, Royal Noble Consort Hui of the Indong Jang clan, was a consort of King Sukjong of Joseon and the mother of Gyeongjong, and she was queen of Joseon from 1689 until she was deposed in 1694.

Though as well educated as the yangban, the chungin never shared their standing and met discrimination. Seeking recognition, they formed poetry groups, whose work survives in the books Okgyeiseungcheop and Okgyecheongyucheop. They published a first collection of their poems, Sodaepungyo, and a new collection every 60 years after it. Yangban admirers helped some of them into print, and Remaining Pearls of Korea was compiled by a chungin at a yangban's encouragement. The Songsogwon Poetry Society brought the two classes into closer contact, yet poetic fame did not raise a writer's place in society.

Kim Ch'ŏnt'aek, a constable in the reign of King Sukjong, was a noted author of sijo and a singer whose performances were said to move people to tears. He compiled the collection Ch'ŏngguyŏngŏn and knew hundreds of works from the Sigyeong by heart. Unable to advance because of his class, he chose a life close to nature, a choice he expressed in a sijo about a white seagull.

The chungin became prominent in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, when many of them looked to Western institutions and ideas to modernise Korea. Among the best known were Yu Dae-chi, also called Yu Hong-gi, Oh Gyeong-sok and his son Oh Se-chang, Byeon Su, Kim Kyu-sik and Choe Nam-seon.
chungnyeol-of-goryeo: Chungnyeol, personal name Wang Kŏ, was born on 3 April 1236, the son of King Wonjong, and became Crown Prince Sim in 1260. In 1271 he proposed to marry a daughter of Kublai Khan, who agreed. For more than 80 years afterwards Goryeo kings married into the Mongol royal family, and heirs were given Mongol names and raised in Dadu. He was also the first Goryeo ruler remembered by the title wang, king, since Kublai forbade the temple names ending in jo or jong that had been reserved for emperors.

He came to the throne on Wonjong's death in 1274. Within the limits of vassal status he worked to keep Goryeo's autonomy: he recovered Dongnyeong and Tamna Prefectures by negotiation, insisted on Goryeo's right to keep its customs, and on a visit to the Yuan in 1278 had the Mongol darughachis and troops withdrawn. He revived the Censorate of Household and Land Inspection to seize illegally held property and promoted Confucian learning, with Confucian temples and, on the proposal of the scholar An Hyang, the Sunkyungam, predecessor of Sungkyunkwan.

Goryeo had to build the fleets and send troops for Kublai's invasions of Japan, which ruined the economy and the people's livelihoods. Chungnyeol chose the general Kim Pang-gyŏng, one of the expedition's few competent commanders. When the Mongol rebel Kadaan invaded in 1290, the king was said to have feasted indifferently and was criticised even by the Yuan general Naimandai; Korean forces won at Chi'ak Fortress and Yeongi, aided by ten thousand Yuan troops under Naimandai, but many local people were killed.

In 1298, after Crown Prince Chang returned from Mongolia, Chungnyeol gave up the throne to him, but factional strife over his son's reforms brought him back eight months later. In 1306 he tried to block his son's return by having him divorced from his Mongol wife, but the accession of Külüg Khan, her brother, defeated the plot. The prince was crowned as King Chungseon in 1307, and Chungnyeol, held for a time at a temple in Dadu, came home without power. He spent his last days hunting and drinking and died at Shinhyo Temple in July 1308, said to regret the devastation of the country and the quarrels within the royal house.
chupan: Chupan came from the Suldus clan and descended from Chilaun, son of Sorqan Shira, one of Genghis Khan's four great companions. His grandfather Tudaun went west with Hulagu, governed Diyar Bakr and died at the Battle of Elbistan in 1277, and his father Malek took part in the Siege of Baghdad in 1258. In his twenties Chupan fought against Nogai of the Golden Horde in 1289. He supported Gaykhatu's bid for the throne and in 1295 changed sides to join Ghazan against Baydu.

Under Ghazan he served as a senior commander in three campaigns against Syria, then ruled by the Mamelukes, and after the defeat at Marj al-Saffar in 1303 he stayed with the army when its commander Qutlugh Shah fled. In 1307 he led one of four armies against the rebellious province of Gilan and persuaded the rulers of Astara and Gaskareh to surrender. When Qutlugh Shah was killed there, Öljeitü made Chupan Amir of the Ulus, his chief military commander, and he married Öljeitü's daughter Dowlandi Khatun on 30 September 1307.

Under Abu Sa'id he turned on the vizier Rashid-al-Din Hamadani, who was put to death in July 1318. In 1319 he drove back an invasion by Öz-Beg of the Blue Horde and defeated a conspiracy led by Abu Sa'id's uncle Irinjin near Mianeh. His sons Timurtash, Shaikh Mahmud, Hasan and Demasq Kaja then received Anatolia, Georgia, Khorasan and Azerbaijan, and Chupan married Abu Sa'id's sister Sati Beg. In November 1325 he made the Hajj, repairing the water system of Mecca and founding a bath and madrasa in Medina.

The extravagance of Demasq Kaja, the hostility of viziers such as Chupan's protégé Rukn al-Din Sa'in, and Chupan's refusal to let Abu Sa'id marry his daughter Baghdad Khatun, wife of Hasan Buzurg, turned the ruler against him. On 25 August 1327 Abu Sa'id had Demasq Kaja killed. Chupan marched west for revenge, but near Ray most of his army deserted, and he withdrew east. The Kartid ruler of Herat, Ghiyath ud-Din, received him as a friend and then had him strangled on Abu Sa'id's orders, sending one of his fingers as proof. Baghdad Khatun had him buried in the Baqi cemetery at Medina. Sources describe him as a devout Muslim who rebuilt mosques in Tabriz and demolished churches, yet protected Mar Yahballaha III.
chupanids: The Chupanids came from a Mongol family of the Suldus clan. Amir Chupan served three successive Ilkhans in the early 14th century, beginning with Ghazan Mahmud, and as a military commander of note he gained great influence over them and married several women of the line of Hulagu Khan. His power bred resentment among the nobility, whose conspiracy of 1319 failed, but the Ilkhan Abu Sa'id also came to dislike his influence and drove him from court. Chupan fled to Herat in 1327, where the Kartids executed him, and several of his sons fled to the Golden Horde or to the Mamluks of Egypt while others were killed.

The family kept a foothold through Chupan's daughter Baghdad Khatun. Divorced by Hasan Buzurg, the future founder of the Jalayirids, she married Abu Sa'id and gained wide influence over him. Some believed she caused his death in 1335, an allegation never proven, and his successor Arpa Ke'un had her executed.

In the strife that followed, members of the family took different sides. Chupan's granddaughter Delsad Khatun married Hasan Buzurg, but another grandson, Hasan Kucek, rallied most of the Chupanids, defeated the Jalayirids in 1338 and built a realm around Tabriz. That year he raised Sati Beg, sister of Abu Sa'id and widow of Chupan, to the Ilkhanid throne and made her marry his puppet Suleiman Khan. In the south, Pir Husayn Chubani governed Fars and Isfahan from 1339 until the Injuid Abu Ishaq Inju took Isfahan in 1342. Hasan Kucek fought the Jalayirids and quarrelling relatives until his death in 1343.

His brother Malek Ashraf eliminated his uncles and by the end of 1344 controlled the Chupanid lands, ruling behind puppet khans such as Anūshīrwān. He failed to take Baghdad from the Jalayirids in 1347 and Fars from the Injuids in 1350, and his growing cruelty turned his subjects against him. When forces of the Golden Horde captured Tabriz in 1357, few mourned the dynasty's fall. Malek Ashraf was executed, his family was taken north to the Golden Horde, and his descendants were later killed in Persia, ending the Chupanids as a power.
chuquicamata: Chuquicamata lies just outside Calama in the north of Chile, at 2,850 metres above sea level, 215 km north-east of Antofagasta and 1,240 km north of Santiago. Its open pit is 4.3 km long, 3 km wide and over 900 metres deep. The deposit is a porphyry copper system that formed in the Eocene-Oligocene, and the mine is also a significant producer of molybdenum. The meaning of the name is disputed: one version takes it to mean the limit of the land of the Chuqui, another a metal-tipped wooden spear, another summit of gold in Aymara.

Copper was mined here for centuries: a mummy found in 1899 in an ancient shaft, the Copper Man, is dated to about 550 CE, and the men of Diego de Almagro are said to have obtained copper horseshoes from local people in 1536. Mining stayed small until the War of the Pacific (1879-1883), when Chile annexed the area and the Red Gold Fever drew miners. The camp was disorderly, its title claims uncertain, and the army had to be sent in to keep order as late as 1918.

The modern mine began when an American engineer named Bradley developed a way to process low-grade oxidised ores. The Guggenheim Brothers organised the Chile Exploration Company in January 1912, and production started on 18 May 1915 with steam shovels bought from the Panama Canal. Output rose from 4,345 tonnes in the first year to 50,400 tonnes in 1920. Writers such as Laura Jorquera denounced the conditions of workers, women and children, among them air pollution from sulphuric acid gases.

The Guggenheims sold the mine to Anaconda Copper in 1923, and production reached 135,890 tonnes by 1929. Under Anaconda, housing and sanitary conditions improved and mortality fell. When the oxidised ore was nearly exhausted in 1951, the company built a mill, flotation plant and smelter. In 1971 the mine was nationalised under President Salvador Allende and passed to the state company Codelco; after the military overthrow of Allende in 1973 the new government paid Anaconda 250 million dollars in compensation.

Chuquicamata is part of Codelco's Codelco Norte division, with the Radomiro Tomic and Ministro Hales mines. In April 2019 it began to extract ore from a new underground mine, starting its change into an underground operation, though above-ground mining was still in place in May 2021 because the expansion was delayed. Copper became Chile's most consistent export after the collapse of the nitrate market that followed the First World War.
chur: Chur lies in the Grisonian Rhine Valley, where the Rhine turns north, on the right bank of the Plessur at 594 m above sea level, almost entirely surrounded by the Alps. It is reputedly the oldest town in Switzerland, with settlement going back to the Pfyn culture. It stands where the roads from several Alpine passes, among them the Lukmanier, Splügen and San Bernardino, come together and continue down the Rhine.

Rome conquered the area in 15 BCE as the province of Raetia. In the late 3rd century Curia Raetorum, later Chur, became the capital of Raetia prima. In the 4th century it became the seat of the first Christian bishopric north of the Alps, and the first known bishop is Asinio in 451. Otto I granted the right to collect tolls in 952, and in 1170 the bishop became a prince-bishop. The League of the House of God was formed in Chur in 1367 to resist the bishopric and the House of Habsburg. After a fire in 1464, Emperor Frederick III freed the city from the bishop's power, and in 1465 the citizens gave all government to the guilds.

The League joined the Grey League and the League of the Ten Jurisdictions in 1471 to form the Three Leagues. From 1523 Johannes Comander preached the Reformation in St Martin's Church, and by 1525 the bishop had fled. The Ilanz Articles of 1524 and 1526 allowed each resident of the Three Leagues to choose a religion and sharply reduced the bishop's power. The Three Leagues became the canton of Graubünden in 1803, with Chur as its capital.

Chur is the capital and largest town of the canton of Graubünden, or Grisons, and lies 120 km by rail from Zürich. German is the main language, with Italian and Romansh also spoken. The cathedral of the Assumption was built between 1154 and 1270 on the site of a church of the first half of the 5th century. The church of St Luzi, first recorded in 821, became a Premonstratensian monastery in 1149.
church-building: The English word church comes from Old English cirice, from the Common Germanic kirika, probably borrowed via Gothic from the Greek kyriakon doma, "the Lord's house". Kyriakon was used of Christian houses of worship from about 300 CE, especially in the East, though less commonly than ekklesia or basilike. Many of the first purpose-built halls, called aula ecclesiae, were destroyed early in the fourth century in the Diocletianic Persecution.

Between 1000 and 1200 the Romanesque style spread across Europe, with large, bulky buildings, circular arches and a cruciform plan. The Gothic style emerged about 1140 in Île-de-France. Pointed arches, rib vaults and buttresses reduced the need for thick walls and allowed larger windows and brighter interiors; several towers collapsed when their designs exceeded what was sound. Cologne Cathedral, begun in 1248, was halted in 1473 and not resumed until 1842.

Many churches are cross-shaped, often with a dome or vaulted space representing the heavens. The altar often faces east, or toward the sunrise, a tradition that began in Byzantium in the fourth century and became prevalent in the West in the eighth and ninth. The old Roman custom of an altar at the west end was sometimes followed as late as the eleventh century, as at Bamberg and Hildesheim cathedrals.

A basilica was first a Roman public building; after the Empire became officially Christian the word came to mean a large church with special ceremonial rights given by the Pope. A cathedral houses the seat, or cathedra, of a bishop and need not be large. Other types include chapels, collegiate churches served by a college of canons, conventual churches of monasteries, parish churches and pilgrimage churches.

Besides worship the medieval cathedral or parish church was frequently the community's general gathering place, hosting guild meetings, banquets, mystery plays and fairs, and its grounds and buildings were used to thresh and store grain.

The Renaissance and Reformation produced a simplified Gothic and favoured hall churches. In Protestant churches the line of sight leads to the pulpit. The Baroque style, first used in Italy about 1575, treated a church as a single work of art and used buildings to show wealth, authority and influence; its ornament lasted until about 1720, in the Rococo era.
church-fathers: The Fathers are usually grouped by language and region. The Apostolic Fathers, of whom Clement of Rome, Ignatius of Antioch and Polycarp of Smyrna are counted the chief, were believed to have known some of the Twelve Apostles or to have been shaped by them. Their writings were popular in early Christianity but were not included in the canon of the New Testament once it took its final form. Ignatius, the third bishop of Antioch, wrote a series of letters on his way to martyrdom in Rome, dealing with the sacraments, the role of bishops and the incarnation of Christ.

Those who wrote in Greek are the Greek Fathers: Justin Martyr, Irenaeus of Lyons, Clement of Alexandria, Origen of Alexandria, Athanasius of Alexandria, the Cappadocians Basil of Caesarea, Gregory of Nazianzus and Gregory of Nyssa, John Chrysostom, Cyril of Alexandria and John of Damascus among them. In the Catholic tradition four Latin Fathers, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine of Hippo and Pope Gregory I, are called the Great Church Fathers. A smaller group wrote in Syriac, among them Aphrahat, who worked within the Persian Empire, and Ephrem the Syrian. The Desert Fathers, early monastics in the Egyptian desert such as Anthony the Great and Pachomius, wrote less, but their sayings were gathered in the Apophthegmata Patrum and they are credited with forming the basis of monasticism.

Churches differ on where the age of the Fathers ends. In the Catholic Church the patristic era is believed to have passed, with John of Damascus and Bernard of Clairvaux among those considered the last Fathers, though the Church grants the similar title of Doctor of the Church to later saints. The Eastern Orthodox Church does not consider the age over and includes influential writers up to the present day. Its doctrine rests on the consensus of the Holy Fathers, the points on which they agree, rather than on any one of them being infallible.

The Lutheran Augsburg Confession of 1530 and the Formula of Concord of 1576 to 1584 both begin with the doctrine professed by the Fathers of the First Council of Nicaea, and the first Protestant reformers, like the Catholic and Orthodox churches, used the Fathers' interpretations of scripture. The academic study of the Fathers is called patristics. Their works before Nicaea were translated into English in the nineteenth-century collection Ante-Nicene Fathers, and later ones in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers.
church-of-england: The Church of England traces its history to the Christian hierarchy recorded in Roman Britain by the 3rd century and to the Gregorian mission to Kent. In 597 Pope Gregory I sent missionaries led by Augustine, who became the first archbishop of Canterbury, and the church counts 597 as the start of its formal history. In Northumbria Celtic and Roman missionaries disagreed over the date of Easter and the monks' tonsure. King Oswiu summoned the Synod of Whitby in 664 and decided that Northumbria would follow the Roman tradition.

In 1527 Henry VIII asked Pope Clement VII to annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon. When the Pope refused, Henry used Parliament to assert royal authority over the church. The Act in Restraint of Appeals of 1533 allowed the Archbishop of Canterbury to annul the marriage without reference to Rome, and in November 1534 the Act of Supremacy declared Henry Supreme Head of the Church of England. Archbishop Thomas Cranmer shaped its doctrine and developed the Book of Common Prayer. Papal authority was briefly restored under Mary I, and Elizabeth I renewed the breach. The Elizabethan Settlement of 1559-1563 concluded the English Reformation.
Struggles over the church under James I and Charles I led to the First English Civil War in 1642, and the Puritans abolished the Book of Common Prayer and episcopacy until 1660.

The monarch is Supreme Governor. The church is organised in dioceses under bishops, with parishes within each, and its legislative body is the General Synod. Its doctrine rests on scripture, informed by the Church Fathers and the creeds, and is expressed in the Thirty-Nine Articles, the Book of Common Prayer and the Ordinal. James I ordered the translation published in 1611 as the King James Version. The church describes itself as a via media between Lutheranism and Calvinism, with Anglo-Catholic, high church, central church and low church strands.
church-of-ireland: The Church of Ireland sees itself as the part of the Irish Church that was influenced by the Reformation, with its origins in the early Celtic Church of Saint Patrick. It therefore regards itself as both catholic, as the inheritor of a continuous tradition, and protestant, since it rejects the authority of Rome. Christianity in Ireland is generally dated to the mid to late 5th century, when the Romano-British cleric Saint Patrick began his mission, although the exact dates are disputed.

Before the 12th-century reforms the Irish church was part of the Latin Church and in communion with Rome, though major monasteries held considerable authority. After the Synod of Ráth Breasail in 1111 and the Synod of Kells in 1152 it was organised by dioceses and parishes, and the Primacy of Ireland went to the Archdiocese of Armagh.

At the beginning of the 17th century most native Irish were Catholic, while Protestant settlers in Ulster established an independent Presbyterian church. The most important figure in the Church's development was the Dublin-born theologian and historian James Ussher, Archbishop of Armagh from 1625 to 1656. In 1615 the Church drew up its own confession of faith, similar to the English one but more detailed and often explicitly Calvinist. The Thirty-Nine Articles were formally adopted in 1634 and soon superseded the Irish Articles.

In 1704 the Test Act was extended to Ireland, which restricted public office to members of the Church of Ireland until the Catholic Relief Act of 1829. It is estimated that fewer than 15 to 20 per cent of the population were nominally members. After the Act of Union 1800 the Church was united with the Church of England, and one archbishop and three bishops from Ireland, chosen by rotation, sat in the House of Lords.

The Church of Ireland did not divide when Ireland was partitioned in the 1920s and is still governed on an all-Ireland basis. Its head is, ex officio, the Archbishop of Armagh. Its polity is episcopal, with parishes grouped into dioceses; there are now eleven dioceses or united dioceses in two provinces. On its disestablishment it adopted synodical government, the second province of the Anglican Communion after the Anglican Church of New Zealand to do so.

It has two cathedrals in Dublin, Christ Church Cathedral and Saint Patrick's Cathedral, the latter designated the National Cathedral for Ireland in 1870. It began ordaining women to the priesthood in 1990, and in 2013 appointed its first female bishop, Pat Storey. The first translation of the Book of Common Prayer into Irish was published in 1606.
church-of-jesus-christ-of-latter-day-sai: The church arose during the Second Great Awakening. Joseph Smith formally organised it as the Church of Christ on 6 April 1830 in western New York. Early converts were drawn in part by the newly published Book of Mormon, a self-described chronicle of Indigenous American prophets that Smith said he had translated from golden plates. After Smith's death, Brigham Young and the largest body of his followers incorporated the church in 1851 under the name The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. Members hold that after the death of Jesus and his apostles the authority of the original church was lost, and that it was restored through Smith.

Under Smith the church's headquarters moved to Ohio, Missouri and Illinois. In Missouri fear of its political and military power led to the Mormon War of 1838 and Governor Lilburn Boggs's Mormon Extermination Order. In 1844 the Nauvoo Expositor criticised plural marriage and other doctrines. Smith took a leading part in destroying its press, was charged with treason and jailed, and was shot dead by a mob that stormed the jail. After the succession crisis most followers sided with Brigham Young, who led them to Nebraska and in 1847 to what later became the Utah Territory. About 80,000 settlers arrived between 1847 and 1869. Plural marriage, announced publicly in 1852, was curtailed in 1890 and officially rescinded in 1904.

The church is led by a president, regarded by members as a prophet, seer and revelator, over a hierarchy of areas, stakes and wards led by volunteer bishops. Its canon consists of the Bible, the Book of Mormon, the Doctrine and Covenants and the Pearl of Great Price. Members believe in Jesus Christ as the Son of God but reject the ecumenical creeds and the Trinity, holding that God the Father, Jesus and the Holy Ghost are three distinct beings united in purpose. Members observe the Word of Wisdom, which forbids alcohol, coffee, tea and tobacco, and give a tenth of their income. Young men are expected to serve a two-year mission.
church-of-scotland: According to traditional Scottish historiography, the first Christians in Scotland were converted by Saint Ninian around 400, and Saint Columba founded a mission at Iona about two centuries later. In 1192 the papal bull Cum universi separated the Scottish church from the Archbishopric of York, making it an independent national church with no higher authority than the Pope. The Church of Scotland in its present form traces its origins to the Reformation of 1560, when many in the church in Scotland broke with Rome in a Protestant reform led by John Knox, who had been exposed to the principles of John Calvin while living in Geneva.

An assembly of nobles, lairds, burgesses and some churchmen, claiming in defiance of the queen to be a Scottish Parliament, abolished papal jurisdiction and approved the Scots Confession in 1560. Mary I, a Catholic, refused to ratify the settlement, and the acts were finally approved in 1572 by the young James VI. The Concordat of Leith let the crown appoint bishops, and in response a Presbyterian party emerged under Andrew Melville, author of the Second Book of Discipline.

Charles I and William Laud tried to bring Scottish worship closer to English practice, and the Scottish Prayer Book of 1637 caused rioting at St Giles Cathedral in Edinburgh. The National Covenant was signed in early 1638, and in November the General Assembly in Glasgow declared the Prayer Book unlawful and abolished the office of bishop.

The Covenanters later made common cause with the English parliamentarians, and the Westminster Confession of Faith, agreed by both, remains the church's subordinate standard. Episcopacy returned after the Restoration, but in 1690, after the Glorious Revolution, the Scots Parliament guaranteed Presbyterian governance of the church. Later disputes over patronage led to the secession of 1733 and the Disruption of 1843, when a large part of the church formed the Free Church of Scotland.

The church is Presbyterian in polity and Reformed in theology. It has no bishops and no single head, since it holds that role to belong to God. Elders and ministers, called presbyters, sit in a series of courts: each congregation is led by a Session, which answers to a regional presbytery, and the supreme body is the General Assembly, which meets each May in Edinburgh and is chaired by a Moderator elected for a year. It celebrates two sacraments, baptism and the Lord's Supper. Since 1968 all ministries and offices have been open to women and men equally, and Alison Elliot became the first woman Moderator in 2004.
church-of-st-trophime: The church stands on the site of the 5th-century basilica of Arles, dedicated to St. Stephen. When it was built, Arles was the second-largest city in Provence, with between 15,000 and 20,000 people, a busy port on the Rhône and many religious orders. The apse and transept were probably built first, and the nave and bell tower were finished in the second quarter of the 12th century. On 29 September 1152 Raimon de Montredon had the relics of St. Trophimus brought from the Alyscamps necropolis to the new cathedral.

Frederick Barbarossa was crowned there by the archbishop of Arles on 30 July 1178, and on 4 June 1365 Emperor Charles IV followed his precedent and was crowned king of Arles. Between 1445 and 1465 a Gothic choir replaced the Romanesque apse.

The Romanesque church has a central nave 20 metres high with lower aisles, a transept carrying a square bell tower and small windows set high in the nave. Its west portal shows Christ in majesty among the symbols of the Evangelists, the Apostles below, the chosen led to heaven on one side and sinners cast into hell on the other, with statues of saints connected with Arles on the lower level.

The cloister was built for the canons, who under a papal reform were to live like monks. Its northern and eastern galleries were finished around 1210-1220; then work stopped as the city declined, and the southern and western galleries were added only in the late 14th century in the Gothic style of the popes at Avignon. The capitals tell the Easter story, the childhood and Passion of Christ and the legends of St. Trophimus.

When the bishopric moved to Aix-en-Provence in 1801, St. Trophime became a parish church, and Pope Leo XIII made it a minor basilica in 1882. It holds Late Roman sarcophagi, reliquaries, Baroque paintings including three by Louis Finson, and a set of ten tapestries on the Life of the Virgin, many brought from churches dispersed in the French Revolution. In 1981 it was listed as a World Heritage Site within the Arles, Roman and Romanesque Monuments group.
church-of-the-east: The Church of the East, also called the East Syriac Church, the Persian Church or the Nestorian Church, arose in Mesopotamia under the Parthian Empire, where Christian communities were forming as early as the 1st century. It traced its origins to Thaddeus of Edessa, Mari and Thomas the Apostle. Sasanian rule from 266 brought significant communities in Upper Mesopotamia, Elam and Fars.

In 315 Papa bar Aggai, bishop of Seleucia-Ctesiphon, imposed the primacy of his see and took the title of Catholicos. The Council of Seleucia-Ctesiphon of 410 organised the church as the national church of the Sasanian Empire, and in 424 it declared itself independent of the state church of the Roman Empire.

The church shared communion with the Roman Empire's churches until the Council of Ephesus condemned Nestorius in 431. The Church of the East refused to condemn him and was therefore called Nestorian by the Roman church, a name that scholars have since called a misnomer. After 431 the Roman authorities suppressed Nestorianism, a reason for Christians in Persia to favour it. After the Muslim conquest of the Sasanian Empire in 644, the church became a dhimmi minority under the Patriarch of the East, restricted but protected, and its missionaries were allowed to work elsewhere.

Missionaries reached India, where the Saint Thomas Christians kept a long association with the church, and Central Asia. The Nestorian Stele, set up on 7 January 781 in Chang'an, credits a mission under the Persian cleric Alopen in 635 with introducing Christianity to China. Under the Mongols the church reached its widest extent in the late 13th century, and Genghis Khan's sons took wives from the Christian Kerait clan. Decline followed: there were 68 cities with resident bishops in 1000, 24 in 1238 and only seven at the death of Timur in 1405.

From the middle of the 16th century a series of schisms produced rival patriarchates, some of them uniting with the Catholic Church. The traditionalist branch became the Assyrian Church of the East, and the groups united with Rome became the Chaldean Catholic Church. In the later 20th century the traditionalist patriarchate itself divided into the Assyrian Church of the East and the Ancient Church of the East. The Syro-Malabar Church in India also claims the heritage of the Church of the East.
church-of-the-holy-sepulchre: After the siege of Jerusalem in 70 the city lay in ruins. In 130 the emperor Hadrian began building the Roman colony of Aelia Capitolina, and about 135 he ordered a cave containing a rock-cut tomb to be filled in as a flat foundation for a temple of Venus or Aphrodite. When Constantine the Great began to favour Christianity, Bishop Macarius of Jerusalem asked permission to dig for the tomb. With the help of Eusebius, three crosses were found near a tomb, and one that was said to have cured the dying was taken to be the True Cross.

The church, planned by the architect Zenobius, was built as two separate structures: a rotunda called the Anastasis, or Resurrection, over the tomb, and the great basilica known as the Martyrium, across a colonnaded courtyard to the east, with the traditional site of Calvary in one corner. The New Testament places the tomb outside the city wall.

After Jerusalem came under Islamic rule the early Muslim rulers protected its Christian sites. On 18 October 1009 the Fatimid caliph al-Hakim ordered its complete destruction, as part of a wider campaign against Christian and Jewish places of worship, and Christian Europe reacted with shock. His son allowed Emperor Constantine IX Monomachos to rebuild it, and the work was completed in 1048.

The knights of the First Crusade took the church on 15 July 1099, and it was modified into a structure that departs greatly from the original. It was lost to Saladin in 1187, though the treaty after the Third Crusade allowed Christian pilgrims to visit. Emperor Frederick II regained it by treaty in the 13th century, and the Khwarezmians and Ayyubids captured it in 1244. An Ottoman decree of 1757 helped establish the Status Quo, confirmed by a firman of Sultan Abdülmecid I in 1852 and 1853.

The church is the seat of the Armenian, Greek Orthodox and Latin Catholic patriarchates of Jerusalem, and it has been a major pilgrimage site since the fourth century. The main communities sharing it are the Roman Catholic, Greek Orthodox, Armenian Apostolic, Coptic, Syriac and Ethiopian Orthodox. Inside lie the last four stations of the Cross and Calvary, and the tomb is enclosed in the Aedicule, a 19th-century shrine. Disputes between the communities have at times led to violence: in 1902, 18 friars were hospitalised after a dispute over who could clean a step.
church-of-the-holy-spirit-heidelberg: A manuscript of 1239 mentions a Romanesque chapel of the Holy Ghost in the centre of Heidelberg, and an aisleless Gothic church, the Chapel of the Holy Spirit, stood on the site from around 1300. King Rupert commissioned the present building, the third church there, as the burial place of the Electors of the Palatinate and the chief church of their seat. Its cornerstone was laid in 1398, the choir was consecrated in 1411 and the nave finished in 1441. Arnold Rype, a former mayor, is named as its master builder, a term then meaning the man who paid for it.

The church changed confession more than ten times between the 16th and 20th centuries. The first Protestant service was held there in 1546; Elector Otto Henry made it a Lutheran parish church in 1557, and his successor Friedrich III turned it to Calvinism and commissioned the Heidelberg Catechism. When Elector Karl III Philipp had soldiers tear down the dividing wall in 1719, pressure from other states and the Holy Roman Empire forced him to rebuild it. The wall was removed in 1886, put up again during the Kulturkampf, and finally taken down on 24 June 1936; the church has been solely Protestant since.

The galleries, chosen for their light, held the Bibliotheca Palatina, which gathered the libraries of the university, the castle and several monasteries. In 1622, during the Thirty Years War, the Count of Tilly took it as loot and presented it to the Pope; some 54 oxcarts of books reportedly went to Rome. After the Congress of Vienna, 847 German manuscripts returned to Heidelberg in 1816. French troops raided the church in 1693, during the Palatine War of Succession, and a fire destroyed the electors' tombs and the tower, which was rebuilt in baroque style in 1709.

Only the tomb of the founder, Rupert III, survives. A vault of the nave keeps a fresco of around 1440 showing eight angels with instruments, restored in 1950. The medieval glass was lost in 1693. Of 22 windows commissioned from Johannes Schreiter in 1977, only the Physics Window, installed in 1984 with Einstein's E=mc2 and the date of the Hiroshima bombing, was made before protests ended the project in 1986; Hella Santarossa's five windows of broken coloured glass were later placed in the north nave. The church is now a parish church of the Evangelical Church of Heidelberg.
church-of-the-intercession-on-the-nerl: The church was commissioned by Andrei Bogolyubsky, grand prince of Vladimir. According to Janet L. B. Martin, he ordered it in 1165 to commemorate a victory over the Volga Bulgars and the death of one of his sons in the battle. A source of 1702 says it was built in a single season in memory of his son Izyaslav Andreyevich, who died of wounds after a campaign in Volga Bulgaria. The craftsmen were probably brought from western Russia. It stands at the confluence of the Nerl and the Klyazma, where trade routes crossed, as the forward element of the princely ensemble at Bogolyubovo.

The building is of white stone, with one dome and four columns inside. Its proportions are deliberately elongated to make it look slimmer, which restricts its use for services. It is one of the oldest and best-preserved single-domed churches in Russia. In spring the meadow floods and the church seems to float on the water. The walls still carry 12th-century stone carvings. Apart from a slight change to the dome, it has not been substantially altered.

The church began as the cathedral of a small fortified monastery, abolished in 1764. In 1784 permission was obtained to dismantle the church for building material, but a lack of funds prevented it. An onion-shaped dome was placed over the old dome in 1803 and was removed in the late 1980s restoration.

It was unknown even to professional historians until the 1850s, and Igor Grabar's measurements in the early 20th century brought it into full art-historical circulation. It was closed in 1923, became part of the Vladimir-Suzdal Museum-Reserve and in 1992 was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List with the White Monuments of Vladimir and Suzdal. It was returned to believers in 1993.
church-of-the-transfiguration-on-ilyina-: A church stood on the site from at least the 12th century, and the icon of Our Lady of the Sign was first kept there. According to legend, during a siege of Novgorod by the Suzdalians in 1169 Archbishop Ilya carried the icon across the Volkhov River to the Detinets, and it saved the city. The icon and the episode came to stand for Novgorod and its independence and were depicted in several icons of the battle.

In the late 17th century the Church of Our Lady of the Sign was built next door to house the icon. It was kept in a museum in the Soviet period and now stands in the Saint Sophia Cathedral, in front of the main iconostasis.

The church stood just inside the city's eastern gates, on Ilyina (Elijah) Street, one of the first buildings a traveller reached on the way to the Marketplace and the great bridge into the Detinets. The chronicles record that Novgorodians often met their archbishop there on his return from Moscow, after his consecration or other journeys, and received visiting dignitaries such as the metropolitan in the same place. Clergy and people, carrying icons and crosses, then went in procession with him through the market and over the bridge to the cathedral and the archbishop's palace.

The present building, of 1374, is no longer a working church but a museum of the Novgorod State Museum-Preserve. Substantial parts of the frescoes Theophanes the Greek painted in 1378 survive, among them the Christ Pantocrator in the dome, a group of saints inside the south entrance and The Old Testament Trinity in the western vestry.
chuson-ji: Chūson-ji is the head temple of the Tendai sect in the Tōhoku region. The temple claims that Ennin, the sect's third chief abbot, founded it in 850, while the historian George Sansom states that Fujiwara no Kiyohira founded it in 1095. Kiyohira, who had lost his family in the fighting, built it to placate the souls of all who died in the Former Nine Years War and the Latter Three Years' War, hoping to bring peace to the region through the Buddha's teachings. According to the Azuma Kagami, it held more than 40 halls and pagodas and over 300 monks' residences.

The Konjiki-dō is one of two buildings left from the original complex, the other being a sutra repository. Five and a half metres on each side and eight metres tall, it is gilded inside and out and decorated with mother-of-pearl inlay, woodwork, metalwork, lacquer and paintings of the late Heian period. Its three altars, one for each of the first three Fujiwara lords, each held a seated Amida Nyōrai with attendant figures. The mummies were last examined in 1950: Fujiwara no Motohira's lay under the north-west altar, Fujiwara no Hidehira's under the south-west, beside a casket with the head of his son Fujiwara no Yasuhira, beheaded in 1189.

Hiraizumi flourished for nearly a hundred years until the forces of Minamoto no Yoritomo destroyed it in 1189. Chūson-ji survived but declined, and a fire in 1337 destroyed much of it, though more than 3,000 National Treasures and Important Cultural Properties were saved. The Konjiki-dō was given a wooden cover in 1288; it now stands behind acrylic glass in a concrete building of 1965, and was rebuilt from 1962 to 1968.

In the Edo period the Date clan of Sendai Domain partly rebuilt the temple, which became a subsidiary of Kan'ei-ji in Edo, and Matsuo Bashō visited it on the travels of the Oku no Hosomichi. The Konjiki-dō was the first structure designated a National Treasure of Japan, and the temple became a Special Historic Site in 1979.
chutia-people: The origin of the name Chutia is not known; the chronicles written in the Ahom language called the kingdom Tiora, while those in Assamese used Chutia. The historic Chutias are thought to have had some Shan admixture, and their ruling families are estimated to have been originally matrilineal or not entirely patrilineal. They worshipped a primordial male deity and a primordial female deity, Kechaikhati, whose worship was conducted by a priestly section identified today as the Deori people. The settlement of Brahmins in the kingdom led to the Hinduisation of its rulers, and inscriptions of the late 14th century suggest that the kings then followed the Vaishnava tradition.

After the annexation the capital region became a frontier province of the Ahom kingdom under an officer called the Sadiya-khowa Gohain, and the Chutia nobles were widely dispersed in Upper Assam. Those Chutias who had not been Hinduised were initiated in the 17th century into the Ekasarana dharma under the Mayamara Satra by Aniruddhadev. After the fall of the kingdom a new Hindu lineage was constructed, tracing the Chutias to the legendary King Bhishmaka of Vidarbha.

The community divided into several groups. The Hindu Chutias were a large section. The Ahom Chutias intermarried with the Ahoms, held high offices in the Ahom administration and were mostly absorbed. The Borahi Chutias had religious rites of their own, and the Miri Chutias fled to the Miri hills and intermarried with the Mishing. According to one chronicle, the Ahom court adopted muga silk by employing a thousand producers and weavers from the Chutia community.

Most Chutias live in Upper Assam, mostly in the interior on the banks of rivers, in villages of about 60 to 140 families. They generally live in joint families headed by the father, which at times exceeded one hundred members. Their original Tibeto-Burman language has disappeared; a British colonial officer of the 19th century wrongly identified it with the Deori language, but the Deori community is not related to the Chutias ethnically or linguistically.

Their rituals have a tribal and tantric base influenced by Hinduism and Vaishnavism. Those called Kesa-ponthi accept restrictions on meat and alcohol in their rites, while the Poka-ponthi keep the older customs. The Government of India recognises the Chutias as an Other Backward Class, and there is a political movement to include them in the list of scheduled tribes.
chutu-dynasty: The name Chutu-kula, the Chutu family, is found in contemporary inscriptions, and the coins attributed to the family carry legends naming kings such as Mulananda and Sivalananda; the numismatist Michael Mitchiner read these as matronymics marking the queen's gotra. The emblem of the cobra hood on Chutu inscriptions suggests that Chutu meant cobra crest, linking the family to the Naga tribes of the Nagara Khanda region around Banavasi. Historians variously see the Chutus as a branch of the Satavahanas, as descendants of Satavahana princesses, or simply as their successors in the southern Deccan.

Mitchiner also speculated that they were of Indo-Scythian origin, pointing to coin designs copied from Indo-Scythian coins and to a legend that he and V. V. Mirashi read as naming a chief commander Saka Mana of the Chutu family; D. C. Sircar disputed that reading. In Mitchiner's view they became Satavahana feudatories after Gautamiputra Satakarni defeated Nahapana around 125 CE.

The Chutus were probably among the dynasties the Puranas call Andhra-bhritya, servants of the Satavahanas. Coins place them beside two other feudatory families, the Kuras of Kolhapur and the Sadakana Maharathis of Chandravalli, with whom they seem to have intermarried. By the last quarter of the 2nd century the Satavahanas appear to have tightened their control over all three, but when Satavahana power declined in the first half of the 3rd century only the Chutus kept their authority at Banavasi. An Ikshvaku record says that the Maharaja of Vanavasa married a daughter of the Ikshvaku king Vira-purusha-datta.

Apart from the edicts of Asoka, the Chutu inscriptions are the oldest documents found in the northern part of present-day Karnataka. At Banavasi, King Haritiputra Visnukada Chutukulananda Satakarni gave a Nagashilpa, a tank and a vihara, and a grant recorded at Malavalli gave the village of Belgame to Hindu priests, who made it a centre of learning that the Kadambas later expanded. Mitchiner thought the coin designs suggest the Chutus may have been Buddhists, though they also patronised Hinduism. The Chalukyas of Badami claimed descent from a son of Hariti, a genealogy taken from the Kadambas, who had taken it from the Chutus.
chuuk-lagoon: Chuuk Lagoon lies in the central Pacific Ocean, about 1,800 kilometres northeast of New Guinea. A protective reef 225 kilometres around encloses a natural harbour 79 by 50 kilometres, with an area of 2,130 square kilometres. The atoll has eleven major islands and 46 smaller ones within the lagoon, plus 41 on the fringing reef. Chuuk means mountain in the Chuukese language, and the lagoon was known mainly as Truk, a mispronunciation of Ruk, until 1990.

Archaeological evidence shows that the islands of Feefen and Wééné had human settlements in the first and second century BCE, and widespread settlement appeared in the 14th century CE. The Spanish navigator Álvaro de Saavedra made the first recorded European sighting in 1528. Spain claimed the islands but its control was nominal, and tribal warfare continued until the German colonial era after the Caroline Islands were sold to the German Empire in 1899. Japan seized the German possessions in October 1914, and Chuuk became Japanese under the South Seas Mandate.

In the Second World War Truk was the main forward anchorage of the Imperial Japanese Navy in the South Pacific, nicknamed the Gibraltar of the Pacific, though it was in fact lightly fortified. The Japanese built roads, bunkers, five airstrips, seaplane bases and a radar station, and the battleships Yamato and Musashi were stationed there for months around 1943. The garrison numbered 27,856 naval and 16,737 army men.

Warned a week ahead, the Japanese withdrew their larger warships to Palau. On 17 February 1944 American carrier aircraft began Operation Hailstone, which lasted three days. They sank 12 smaller warships and 32 merchant ships and destroyed 275 aircraft, mainly on the ground. British forces attacked again in June 1945 in Operation Inmate.

Chuuk Lagoon is part of Chuuk State in the Federated States of Micronesia. Weno city, on Weno Island, is the capital of the atoll and of the state. Diving on the wrecks is the main industry, following Jacques Cousteau's 1971 television documentary. The Truk Lagoon Underwater Fleet was added to the US National Register of Historic Places in 1976, and the ships are classed as a Japanese war grave.
chuvash-people: There is no universally accepted etymology of the name Chuvash. One theory derives it from Common Turkic jăvaş, 'friendly' or 'peaceful'; another from Tabghach, the name of the Xianbei clan that founded the Northern Wei dynasty, which Gerard Clauson showed could become Chuvash through regular sound changes. Two schools place the people's origin differently: a mixing of the Sabir tribes with Finno-Ugrians, or descent from the Volga Bulgars. After Old Bulgaria broke up in the second half of the 7th century, the Sabirs and other Oghuric tribes migrated to the Volga-Kama region and founded Volga Bulgaria.

The Mongols destroyed Volga Bulgaria in 1236, and the Golden Horde and then the Kazan Khanate ruled the Chuvash. The modern name appears in records from the sixteenth century. Russia conquered the Kazan Khanate in 1552; the Chuvash had to pay yasak and gradually lost much of their land, and many farmers became bonded laborers in the timber industry or worked on barges. Most were not converted to Orthodox Christianity until the mid-19th century.

A written script was created in 1871. The Chuvash Autonomous Region was established on 24 June 1920 and became a Soviet republic on 21 April 1925. Soviet authorities redrew its borders, leaving many Chuvash in neighbouring republics, and the language vanished from education and public use for most of the Soviet period. A cultural revival began in 1989.

Chuvash is the only surviving member of the Oghur branch of Turkic, marked by r for Common Turkic z and l for š. It was first thought a Turkified Finno-Ugric language until August Ahlqvist's fieldwork of 1856. UNESCO considers it endangered. Most Chuvash are Eastern Orthodox Christians; a minority are Sunni Muslims or follow Vattisen Yaly, a revival of the ethnic religion. Some pre-Christian traditions survive, including prayer and goose sacrifice at shrines called keremet, and distinctive embroidery on traditional clothing. A 2017 genome study found a largely Finno-Ugric genetic component beside a Turkic one shared with the Bashkirs and Volga Tatars.
chuzan-seikan: King Shō Shitsu commissioned the history from his sessei, Shō Sei Kin Wōji Chōtei, and members of the sanshikan, who gathered a team of former bureaucrats specialised in ancient studies; Haneji Chōshū edited their findings into genealogical trees. Both Chōtei and Chōshū were close to the Shimazu clan, whose political ideas shaped the text, and a copy of the Shimazu genealogy given to Chōtei in 1638 probably served as its model. Its sources included commemorative steles in the kingdom and Chinese texts, above all the chronicle of the embassy to Ryūkyū by the Chinese ambassador Chen Kan, who had come in 1534.

The word seikan in the title comes from the maxim inkan tookarazu, which holds that a government should learn from the mistakes of its direct predecessors; the saying refers to the Shang dynasty, which was advised not to repeat the mistakes of the Xia dynasty before it. The title carries the hope that the book would give future kings a source of reflection on the actions of their ancestors.

A preface and general introduction written in Chinese precede five volumes that mix Chinese characters with katakana and use only Chinese era names. They run from the founding myths and the Tenson and Shunten dynasties to the reign of Shō Sei (r. 1527-1555), leaving out that of his predecessor Shō Shin, and describe in detail the thirty-six islands of the kingdom. The style borrows from Japanese war tales such as the Tale of Hōgen, and legend mixes with history: Shunten appears as the son of the warrior Minamoto no Tametomo, and the life of King Satto is told through the legends of a heavenly maiden and a charcoal burner.

The book lacks stylistic unity and has many flaws as history, but it became the basis of every later history written in the kingdom, and its account of Shunten's descent from Tametomo was taken up in all later official histories. Sai Taku used it as a source for the Chūzan Seifu of 1701, which his son Sai On completed in 1725, and its myths fed Kyokutei Bakin's novel Chinsetsu yumiharizuki, published between 1807 and 1811. An original copy stolen during the Second World War was returned in 1953 and is kept at the Okinawa Prefectural Museum; another is held by the National Archives of Japan.
chwezi: In the traditions of Kitara the Chwezi formed the second ruling dynasty of the kingdom. The dynasty is said to have been founded by an Iru, or commoner, named Karubumbi, and is traced back to Isimbwa, son of Isaza. Isimbwa is said to have married Nyabiryo, a woman of the underworld, before leaving it to hunt and coming to Kitara, then ruled by Bukuku. The accounts recorded by John Nyakatura and Ruth Alice Fisher differ in detail, but agree that Isimbwa climbed by a ladder into the house of Bukuku's daughter Nyinamwiru, stayed for months, and left; she then bore Karubumbi.

The first Chwezi capital is placed at Mubende, the second 40 miles to the south at Bigo bya Mugenyi. The Chwezi are remembered as skilled blacksmiths, and nine of them, sons or grandsons of Isimbwa, are especially well known, nine being a special number in Nyoro culture.

Scholars have looked for the roots of the Chwezi spirits beyond the kingdom itself. John Sutton notes that the spirits share a common Bantu root, suggesting a concept much older than Kitara. Okot P'Bitek places them in a time before all dynasties, when gods were believed to roam the earth. Peter Schmidt traces their worship to the earliest iron smelters around 500 BCE, in the Urewe period, and suggests that the displacement of Chwezi blacksmiths from power in places such as Buhaya may explain why Chwezi spirit mediums opposed later royal dynasties and colonial rule. Their links with iron tools and anvils appear on more recent shrines.

The Rutara people venerate the Chwezi as ancestor spirits. Oral traditions contrast them with later rulers such as the Biito clan, who favoured cattle herding and imposed new hierarchies. Under the racist Hamitic hypothesis, writers assumed without evidence that the Bahima, called Bahuma in Kitara, were the Bachwezi because of their appearance. Kitara tradition, however, keeps the two apart, saying the Bachwezi had Bahuma servants, and the Bahuma claim no descent from them. Historians have concluded that the Bachwezi were a local Bantu aristocracy.
chyhyryn: Chyhyryn lies on the banks of the Tiasmyn river, not far from where it enters the Dnieper, in central Ukraine. Its name appears in Polish as Czehryń. From 1320 to 1569 the area was part of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, and it passed to the Kingdom of Poland before the Union of Lublin.

In 1589 King Sigismund III of Poland allowed Aleksander Wiśniowiecki, starosta of Cherkasy, to found a town and build a castle on a deserted site called Czehryn. The castle stood on a hill surrounded by the Tiasmyn, and in 1592 the town received Magdeburg rights and a coat of arms with three arrows. Cossacks settled there from the start, and in 1638 the Polish Sejm created the Chyhyryn Regiment of registered Cossacks.

After Bohdan Khmelnytsky's Cossack rebels defeated Crown forces, he chose Chyhyryn as his main seat. From 1648 to 1669 it was the hetman's residence, and after the Ruthenian Orthodox metropolitan see was forcibly moved from Kyiv in 1658 it became a full capital of the Cossack Hetmanate. Petro Doroshenko took it about 1665 and accepted Turkish protection; he was given a small principality there, but the land was devastated and Chyhyryn became a Tatar slave market.

In 1676 Russian and Cossack forces besieged the city and Doroshenko surrendered. A Turkish siege in August 1677 was repelled by the Russians, but another a year later, led by Kara Mustafa, succeeded: the Turks destroyed the city and dismantled the fortress. Under a Polish-Russian treaty of 1686 the land around it was to stay uninhabited, so it was not rebuilt. People returned after peace in 1714, and Russia annexed the town in 1793.

Since the 17th century Chyhyryn has shrunk to a semi-rural settlement. The Trinity Monastery, built near it in 1627, was destroyed by the Soviet authorities, together with the town hall and Khmelnytsky's palace. After Ukraine regained independence the hetman's residence was restored and became a museum.
ciamis: The name Galuh comes from a Sanskrit word for gemstone. In the history drawn up for the regency, the kingdom was founded by Wretikkandayun, youngest son of Kandiawan, who ruled the Kendan kingdom for 15 years (597–612) before becoming a hermit at Layungwatang. Based at Medangjati, Wretikkandayun founded a new centre named Galuh, near the present village of Karangkamulyan, to free himself from Tarumanagara, long the dominant power. He sought good relations with the Kalingga kingdom in Central Java, arranging the marriage of his youngest son to Parwati, eldest daughter of Maharanissima, and was crowned on a date reckoned as about 23 March 612.

In 1970 the regency's council set up a committee, advised by historians of IKIP Bandung led by Said Raksanegara, to fix the regency's founding date. The candidates included the founding of Galuh in 612, the move of the seat of Galuh Regency from Garatengah near Cineam to Barunay, now Imbanagara, on 12 June 1642, its move from Imbanagara to Cibatu, the present Ciamis, under the regent Wiradikusumah on 15 January 1815, and the renaming of Galuh Regency as Ciamis by the regent Tumenggung Sastra Winata in 1916. The historians chose 12 June 1642, and the council confirmed it on 17 May 1972.

Ciamis Regency is bordered by Majalengka and Kuningan regencies to the north, Tasikmalaya to the west, Banjar City and Central Java Province to the east and Pangandaran Regency to the south, and the national road between West and Central Java crosses it. Its land runs from flat to hilly and mountainous. The main river is the Tanduy, which rises on Mount Cakrabuana in Tasikmalaya Regency and empties into Sagara Anakan in Central Java, and most of the regency lies within its watershed. The climate is tropical rainforest, with substantial to heavy rain all year.

Ciamis is a district and town and the seat of Ciamis Regency, covering 33.80 square kilometres and divided into twelve villages, with 102,059 people in the official estimate for mid-2024. The regency lost Banjar City as a separate authority in December 2002 and its southern part, which became Pangandaran Regency, in October 2012.
ciaran-of-saighir: The martyrologies, among them the Félire Óengusso, and the medieval genealogies name his father as Lugna, a nobleman of the Dál Birn rulers of Osraige, and his mother as Liadán of the Corcu Loígde. According to the legend, Liadán dreamt before his conception that a star fell into her mouth, and the druids told her that her son's fame would reach the end of the world. Cape Clear Island, south-west of County Cork, is regarded as his birthplace. His biography is full of obscurities, but it is commonly said that he was already a Christian when he left Ireland to study at Tours and Rome.

By one account Patrick sent Ciarán ahead of him with a little bell that would not ring until he reached the well where he was to build his monastery. Ciarán settled as a hermit at Saighir near the Slieve Bloom Mountains, and all four of his Lives describe him dressed in skins with the animals of the forest as his first pupils, an image that recalls John the Baptist as forerunner. Disciples gathered, and his mother is said to have joined him with a community of women. Saighir became the chief church of Osraige and a wealthy industrial community, later superseded by Saint Canice's foundation at Aghaboe.

The dating of his life is a long-standing matter of academic disagreement. Plummer, Hogan and Kenny accept a mission before Patrick, which would place his birth near the end of the 4th century, while Baring-Gould, Sharpe, O'Riain and Sperber move his life into the 5th or 6th century. It seems more likely that he was one of the twelve men Patrick consecrated as helpers on his arrival.

His Lives credit him with many miracles: healing a bird taken by a kite, blessing a well whose water tasted of wine or honey, and keeping a fox, a badger and a wolf as monks who cut wood and built huts. He is thought to have died at an advanced age of natural causes. The ruins of his monastery remain, and there are old church ruins and a well on Cape Clear. He is venerated on 5 March in England, Brittany, Wales and Scotland, a feast he shares with Liadán and his successor Carthach the Elder, and St. Kieran's College, founded in 1782, bears his name. Pádraig Ó Riain considers his identification with Saint Piran groundless.
ciaruteun-inscription: The inscription, also known as the Ciampea inscription, lies in the village of Ciaruteun Ilir in the Cibungbulang district of Bogor Regency, about 19 kilometres north-west of the centre of Bogor. The spot is a small hill, locally a pasir, where three rivers meet: the Cisadane, the Cianten and the Ciaruteun. Until the 19th century it was counted part of Pasir Muara, within the private estate of Tjampéa. The text is cut into a huge natural river boulder weighing eight tonnes and measuring 200 by 150 centimetres. It is the earliest inscription that clearly names the kingdom of Tarumanagara.

The text is a Sanskrit sloka of four lines in the anustubh metre. It speaks of the powerful, illustrious and brave King Purnawarman, lord of Tarumanagara, whose foot soles are like those of Vishnu. At its end are the prints of a pair of feet and characters in the shell script known as sankha lipi.

The footprints are read as a sign of the king's authority over the land where the stone lies, probably serving much as a seal, a signature or a mark of ownership would. The comparison with Vishnu suggests that he was the chief god Purnawarman revered, and likens the king's rule to Vishnu's as ruler and protector of the people.

The boulder was noticed in 1863, in the Dutch East Indies, on the bed of the Tjiaroeteun river near Tjampea, not far from Buitenzorg, as Bogor was then called, and the find was reported the same year to the learned society in Batavia whose collections became the National Museum of Indonesia. A great flood in 1893 carried the stone several metres and tilted it, and in 1903 it was put back in place.

In 1981 the Directorate of Protection and Development of Heritage and Antiquities, part of the Ministry of Education and Culture, moved it from the riverbed to higher ground close by. A roofed pendopo structure now protects it from weathering and vandalism. Replicas are shown in the National Museum of Indonesia and the Jakarta History Museum in Jakarta and in the Sri Baduga Museum in Bandung.
cibao: The name comes from the Taino Ciba-o, stone mountain, from ciba, rock or stone, and o, mountain. It was an Indigenous name for the island, which the Spanish used during their conquest for the rich valley between the Central and Septentrional ranges. The region occupies the centre and north of the Dominican Republic, with the Atlantic Ocean to the north and east, Haiti to the west and the Central Range to the south.

The Cordillera Central holds Pico Duarte, the highest peak in the Caribbean, and the region is drained by the Yaque del Norte, the country's largest river, and the Yuna. Chains of dams on both rivers supply water for irrigation and hydroelectric power. Rice, coffee and cacao are the main crops, and the mountains are mined for gold, iron and nickel.

The speech of the Cibao mixes two dialects: that of the Portuguese colonists who settled the valley in the 16th and 17th centuries and that of the Canarian settlers of the 18th century. Merengue, played on the güira, tambora and accordion, originated in the Cibao; its original folk form, known as perico ripiao or típico, is still played by local groups. The carnival of La Vega, held in late January and February, dates back to the first European settlements and began as a religious celebration of the season before Lent.

Many Dominican patriots came from the region, among them the generals José Desiderio Valverde and José Antonio Salcedo, who were responsible for the restoration of the Republic in the later decades of the 1800s. Under the Trujillo dictatorship the Mirabal sisters organised clandestine resistance; they were murdered in 1960 and are remembered as martyrs of the nation.

The Cibao is a cultural and administrative region and is regarded as the cultural heartland of the Dominican Republic. Most of its people live in the centre of the region, where Santiago de los Caballeros is the regional centre.
cicero: Marcus Tullius Cicero was born on 3 January 106 BCE in Arpinum, a hill town 100 kilometres south-east of Rome, into a wealthy family of the equestrian order. His father was in poor health and could not enter public life, so he studied extensively to compensate. The cognomen Cicero comes from the Latin for chickpea, cicer. Plutarch explains that it was first given to an ancestor with a cleft in the tip of his nose resembling a chickpea, and says that Cicero refused to change the name when he entered politics.

His first major appearance in the courts came in 81 BCE, at 26. In 80 BCE he defended Sextus Roscius of Ameria on a charge of parricide in Pro Roscio Amerino, his first criminal case. He accused Chrysogonus, a freedman of the dictator Sulla, of fabricating the proscription of Roscius's father to obtain the family's property, while tactfully avoiding any charge against Sulla himself. He won and gained a good reputation as an orator.

Cicero was elected consul for 63 BCE with the support of every unit of the centuriate assembly. He suppressed the Catilinarian conspiracy, but because he had executed five of the conspirators without trial he was exiled in 58 BCE and recalled the next year. In 60 BCE he refused Julius Caesar's invitation to join the partnership of Caesar, Pompey and Marcus Licinius Crassus, fearing it would undermine the Republic.

In 51 BCE he reluctantly took the proconsulship of Cilicia, where he restored calm by mild government and recovered public property embezzled by previous governors. In Caesar's civil war he favoured Pompey and followed the Pompeian forces to Pharsalus, but after Caesar's victory there on 9 August 48 BCE he refused to take command and returned to Rome in 47 BCE.

After Caesar's assassination in 44 BCE Cicero opposed Mark Antony in a series of speeches called the Philippics, and he praised Caesar's heir Octavian to play him against Antony. When Octavian and Antony joined with Lepidus in the Second Triumvirate, Cicero was proscribed and executed in late 43 BCE, on 7 December, while trying to escape Italy. On Antony's order his head and hands were displayed on the Rostra.

Cicero is considered the master of Latin prose. He coined much of Latin's philosophical vocabulary. Of his speeches 88 were recorded and 52 survive. Petrarch's rediscovery of his letters is often credited with starting the 14th-century Renaissance, and his authority peaked in the 18th-century Enlightenment.
cicones: In Homer the stronghold of the Cicones was Ismara, or Ismarus, at the foot of Mount Ismara on the south coast of Thrace. Book two of the Iliad lists them among the allies of the Trojans, led by Euphemus. In book nine of the Odyssey, Odysseus and his men take the town by surprise, kill most of the men they find and carry off the women as slaves, then linger on the shore drinking and slaughtering cattle.

The Cicones of the town call on their kin inland, who are more numerous and skilled at fighting both from chariots and on foot. In the words of one translation they come "as thick as leaves and bloom in summer", fight the Achaeans by the ships through the day and, as the sun goes down, drive them off, killing six men from each of Odysseus's ships.
In historical times the Cicones fade from view. Herodotus, in the 5th century BCE, mentions their land as one that the army of Xerxes passed. The tribe itself is thought to have disappeared early.

The Cicones remained a name in later Greek and Roman myth. Ovid's Metamorphoses mentions them twice: in book VI, when the north wind Boreas carries off Orithyia to the northern lands and the city of the Cicones, and in book XV, which tells of a river in their country whose water turns flesh to stone.

Ciconian women were also said to have torn apart Orpheus, the Thracian lyre-player who had sought Eurydice in the underworld, after he rejected their advances. In one telling he was reborn as a swan; in Ovid's, his head floated on the sea to the island of Lesbos, where it went on speaking and uttering prophecies.
cidade-velha: Cidade Velha lies on the south coast of Santiago, at the mouth of the river Ribeira Grande de Santiago, 10 kilometres west of Praia. Abundant water from the river gave the site an advantage over the other settlement on the island, Alcatrazes. The Portuguese changed the name from Ribeira Grande to Cidade Velha, old city, in the late 18th century after relocating the capital to Praia.

The island of Santiago was discovered in 1460 by António da Noli, a Genoese in Portuguese service, who settled at Ribeira Grande in 1462 with family members and colonists from the Algarve and Alentejo. The settlement became a key port of call for Portuguese colonisation in Africa and South America, and in the 16th and 17th centuries a centre of maritime trade. Its closeness to the African coast made it an essential platform for the trade in enslaved Africans. Vasco da Gama called there in 1497, Christopher Columbus in 1498 and Ferdinand Magellan's expedition in 1522. In 1533 it became the seat of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Santiago de Cabo Verde.

Privateers attacked it, among them Sir Francis Drake in 1585 and Jacques Cassard in 1712. The fort Forte Real de São Filipe, built in 1587-93, did not end its vulnerability, and the town declined. The capital was moved to Praia in 1770.

Restoration began in the 1960s, and in 2009 Cidade Velha was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Surviving parts of the original planned layout include the royal fortress, a 16th-century town square, and Nossa Senhora do Rosário, built in 1495 and described as the oldest colonial church in the world. The pillory in the main square, erected in 1512 or 1520, was where rebellious enslaved people were publicly punished.
cielito-lindo: In an article titled ¡Hasta que me cayó el veinte!, the researcher Ortega traced the first verse to Spain in the early 17th century, when armed bandits took refuge in the Sierra Morena and travellers feared for their lives crossing the range. The words appeared in a song of that time that hinted at this fear. Over time the verse was romanticised, so that the face of the beloved became the Sierra Morena and her eyes the thieves who lived there. The verse was set to other melodies before Quirino Mendoza adapted it to his own.

Some debate whether the words refer to the Sierra Morena in southern Spain or to the Sierra de Morones in the Mexican state of Zacatecas. Most Mexicans, however, read the line as la Sierra, Morena, morena being a common term of endearment, so that the singer addresses the woman directly rather than naming a place. The song should not be confused with Cielito lindo huasteco, a Son Huasteco or Huapango from La Huasteca with quite different music, though its stanzas share the metre and the fillers cielito lindo and ay ay ay ay. Mariachis sometimes combine the two.

Mariachi bands commonly play the song, and it has been recorded in Spanish, English and other languages. A recording by the Mexican Tipica Orchestra for Victor is dated 26 November 1926, and Carl Sandburg printed it with a piano arrangement in The American Songbag of 1927. Pedro Infante sang it in the 1947 film Los tres García, Carmen Costa released a Portuguese version in 1942, and José Feliciano's version of 1989 won the Grammy Award for Best Latin Pop Performance. An adaptation was used in the finale of Shostakovich's 6th Symphony.

The tune travelled far from Mexico. In Nazi-occupied Poland street musicians and the resistance sang it as the chant Teraz jest wojna, Now there is war. An advertisement for Fritos in which the Frito Bandito character sang a version with new words was considered by many Mexican nationals a racist insult to their culture. The song is widely sung by Mexicans abroad and at international events such as the Olympic Games and the FIFA World Cup.
cieszyn: Cieszyn stands on the east bank of the Olza River, a tributary of the Oder, in the western Silesian Foothills north of the Silesian Beskids. It lies in the historical region of Cieszyn Silesia, the south-easternmost part of Upper Silesia. Because of several major fires and later rebuilding, the last in the late 18th century, its old town combines Polish and Old Austrian styles and is sometimes called Little Vienna.

West Slavic peoples have lived in the area since at least the 7th century, and it became part of the emerging Polish state in the 10th century. According to legend, three sons of a prince, Bolko, Leszko and Cieszko, met here in 810 and founded a settlement, naming it from the words cieszym się, 'we are happy'. Cieszyn was the capital of the Duchy of Cieszyn from 1290. The Piast dynasty ruled the duchy until 1653 and the Habsburg dynasty until 1918. In May 1779 Maria Theresa and Frederick II signed the Peace of Teschen there, ending the War of the Bavarian Succession.

In July 1920 the Spa Conference divided the town. Its smaller western suburbs became Český Těšín in Czechoslovakia, and the larger part joined Poland as Cieszyn. Poland annexed the Trans-Olza area together with Český Těšín in October 1938. Germany occupied the town from 1939 to 1945. In 1939 and 1940 the Germans arrested local Poles in the Intelligenzaktion campaign and imprisoned them in a new Nazi prison, and many teachers, priests and activists were deported to concentration camps and murdered. Almost the entire Jewish community was murdered. After the war the 1920 border was restored.

Cieszyn is a border town in southern Poland and the seat of Cieszyn County. Three bridges connect it to Český Těšín. Its sites include a Romanesque rotunda of St Nicholas from the 11th century, a Piast castle tower mostly of the 14th century and the Gothic Church of St Mary Magdalene, the burial site of the Cieszyn line of the Piast dynasty. The Museum of Cieszyn Silesia is housed in the former Larisch palace.
cilento: The Cilento is a mountain range of the Lucan Apennines that gives its name to a region in the central and southern part of the province of Salerno. It lies south of the Sele plain, north of Basilicata and west of the Alburni mountains and the Vallo di Diano. Its main peaks are Mount Stella (1,131 metres), Mount Gelbison (1,705), Mount Cervati (1,899) and Mount Bulgheria (1,225).

The area is sparsely inhabited, with most villages at high altitude and forests covering much of the land. The coast on the Tyrrhenian Sea runs from Paestum to the Gulf of Policastro near Sapri. The name comes from the Latin Cis Alentum, meaning on this side of the Alento, which the Lombards gave it.

In antiquity the Cilento belonged to Lucania and was inhabited by the Lucanians, an Italic people; excavations have been made at the Lucanian sites of Roscigno, Roccagloriosa and Caselle in Pittari. Greek colonies stood on the coast: Velia, ancient Elea, and Paestum, ancient Poseidonia. Velia was the seat of the Eleatics, the pre-Socratic school of Parmenides, Zeno of Elea and Melissus of Samos. The Romans founded new cities mainly in the Vallo di Diano and the Eremita-Marzano mountains, such as Volcei, because of their position on the road from Capua to Regio.

After the Lombard conquest the area belonged to the Principality of Salerno as a gastaldato of Lucania, divided into the counties of Capaccio and Magliano. The Normans created the baronies of Rocca Cilento and Novi Velia, which became the main centres of the region. Because the Cilento lay on the border with the Byzantine area, many Greek rite monasteries were founded there. Its nobles often rebelled against their sovereigns, including Frederick II of Swabia and Ferrante of Aragon, and the Angevins and Aragonese fought there during the War of the Vespers. Continuous battles with Ottoman pirates at the end of the Middle Ages led to the building of the many castles that mark the area.

The Cilento and Vallo di Diano National Park was instituted in 1991 to preserve the landscape and promote tourism, and in 1998 it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The archaeological site of Paestum lies at the northern end of the coast. The local dialect shows Neapolitan influence in the north and similarities to Sicilian in the south. Proposals in the 1990s to make the Cilento a sixth province of Campania were never carried out. The area gives its name to the Cilento DOC wines, whose reds are based on Aglianico and whites on Fiano.
cilicia: Cilicia lies on the southern coast of Anatolia. It historically extended from Coracesium or the river Melas in the west to the Amanus Mountains in the east, and was bounded on the north by the Taurus Mountains, passable in very few places such as the Cilician Gates. The name derives from the Akkadian Ḫilakku, used by the Neo-Assyrian Empire for the western part. Rough Cilicia in the west is a rugged mountain district whose small harbours made the coast a string of havens for pirates in classical times. Plain Cilicia in the east has a large coastal plain of rich soil, praised by Xenophon, and formed an important link between Syria and the Anatolian highlands.

Plain Cilicia has been intensively settled since the Neolithic. After the Bronze Age Collapse ended Kizzuwatna, two main states emerged: Ḫiyawa in the east, called Que in Neo-Assyrian sources, and Ḫilakku in the west. The ancient inhabitants were largely Luwian speakers. Alexander the Great entered through the Cilician Gates unopposed after the Battle of Issus.
