In 102 BCE the Roman Republic set up a command there against the Cilician pirates, and between 78 and 74 BCE Publius Servilius Vatia Isauricus conquered Rough Cilicia, which made a lasting Roman presence possible.

The Muslim Arabs invaded in the 7th century, and under the Abbasid Caliphate Cilicia became a fortified frontier zone, with Tarsus, rebuilt in 787/788, as its largest settlement. In 1080 Ruben, a relative of the last king of Ani, founded a small principality in the Cilician Taurus that grew into the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia, a Christian state that lasted about 300 years and supported the Crusaders. The Mamluks took the whole region by 1375, and Selim I incorporated the Ramadanid beylik into the Ottoman Empire in 1516.

Modern Cilicia, in Turkey, includes the provinces of Mersin, Adana, Osmaniye and Hatay, and its population is concentrated mostly on the Cilician plain, Çukurova. The Armistice of Mudros in 1918 gave Cilicia to France, and the region became part of the Republic of Turkey in 1921 with the Treaty of Ankara. Among its sites are Kizkalesi, a fort built in the early 12th century by the Armenian kings of the Rubeniyan dynasty, and the Roman town of Soloi-Pompeiopolis.
ciliwung-river: The Ciliwung is 119 km long, with a catchment area of 476 km2. It rises at Mandalawangi in Bogor Regency and flows north past the volcanoes Mount Salak, Mount Kendeng and Mount Halimun, through the cities of Bogor and Jakarta, into the Java Sea at Jakarta Bay. The initial syllable ci means river; the rest of the name may mean the whirlpool or the meandering one, or may come from Prabu Haliwungan, an epithet of the Sunda king Sri Baduga Maharaja. Its steep upper course and heavy rainfall make it prone to flooding parts of Jakarta.

The basin has been settled since at least the 4th century. On its upper course near Bogor stood the kingdoms of Tarumanegara, whose king Purnawarman is known from the inscription at Ciaruteun, and later of Sunda. To protect Sunda Kelapa from the Sultanate of Cirebon and Demak, Prabu Surawisesa, on the king's instruction, made a treaty with the Portuguese, trading pepper for leave to build a fort at the port; the pact was recorded on a padrão of 1522. The Portuguese failed to build the fort that year. The padrão was later found by Fatahillah, commander of the Sultanate of Demak, and fell into the river, to be found again only in 1918.

From 1619 the Dutch used the harbour, built a fort on the east bank of the estuary and founded Batavia. They turned the river into canals in the Dutch manner, with moats around the walled city and a central canal, the Kali Besar or Grote Rivier. Silting made the channels shallow by the 1630s and worse after the earthquake of January 1699, and by 1740 the canals were fouled with rubbish and hospital waste, spreading dysentery and cholera among the townspeople, who still drew drinking water from the river.

The natural estuary has been lost to the canals, which divide the river into western and eastern branches through Jakarta, and since 1922 the Banjir canal has carried flood water west of the city. The river's banks in Jakarta are crowded with informal settlements and its water is heavily polluted. The Sundanese live along its southern course and the Betawi along its northern reaches.
cimbri: Ancient authors described the Cimbri variously as a Celtic-Gaulish, Germanic or even Cimmerian people. Several ancient sources place them in Jutland, which some classical texts call the Cimbrian peninsula. Augustus's Res gestae records that his fleet sailed east from the mouth of the Rhine to the lands of the Cimbri, who sent envoys seeking his friendship. Archaeologists, however, have found no clear sign of a mass migration from Jutland in the early Iron Age. There is no direct evidence for their language: their chiefs bore Celtic names such as Boiorix and Lugius, while northern Jutland has only Germanic place names.

Some time before 100 BCE many of the Cimbri, with the Teutons and Ambrones, migrated south-east and appeared about 113 BCE in Noricum, where they invaded the lands of the Taurisci, a Roman ally. At the Battle of Noreia they defeated the Romans under Gnaeus Papirius Carbo, saved from annihilation only by a storm. They turned west into Gaul, defeating Roman armies in 109 and 107 BCE. In 105 BCE discord between the proconsul Quintus Servilius Caepio and the consul Gnaeus Mallius Maximus let them rout the Romans at the Battle of Arausio, where Livy reports as many as 80,000 Romans lost.

Rome was in panic, and Gaius Marius was elected consul five years in a row, from 104 to 100 BCE. The Cimbri pillaged the Iberian Peninsula until Celtiberians confronted them. In 101 BCE Marius and Quintus Lutatius Catulus destroyed them at Vercellae.

At Vercellae the chieftains Lugius and Boiorix died, Caesorix and Claodicus were captured, and the women killed themselves and their children to avoid slavery. Some captives may have had sons among the rebel gladiators of the Third Servile War. Julius Caesar held that the Belgic Atuatuci descended from the Cimbri and Teutones. The people of Himmerland in Denmark claim to be their heirs, and the Danish author Johannes V. Jensen told their story in 1922.
cimbrian-war: The Cimbri were Germanic and Celtic tribes who, with the Teutones, Ambrones and Tigurini, migrated from the Jutland peninsula into Roman-controlled territory. According to some Roman accounts the Cimbri left their lands around the North Sea because of flooding, though Strabo thought this unlikely. The Teutones joined them, and in 113 BCE they reached Noricum on the Danube, home to the Roman-allied Taurisci, who asked Rome for aid. The war was the first time since the Second Punic War that Italia and Rome itself had been seriously threatened.

The following year the consul Gnaeus Papirius Carbo demanded that the Cimbri leave Noricum. They began to comply but found that Carbo had laid an ambush, and at the Battle of Noreia they annihilated his army. They then moved west into Gaul and defeated Roman armies in 109 and 107 BCE, the latter at Burdigala, where the consul Lucius Cassius Longinus Ravalla was killed.

In 105 BCE the consul Gnaeus Mallius Maximus and the proconsul Quintus Servilius Caepio gathered more than 80,000 men. They distrusted each other and camped on opposite banks of the Rhône near Orange. Caepio attacked without support and his legions were wiped out, after which Maximus's troops were defeated too. Only a few hundred Romans escaped. Arausio was the costliest defeat Rome had suffered since Cannae.

Gaius Marius was elected consul for five years running from 104 BCE and rebuilt the army. In 102 BCE he routed the Teutones at Aquae Sextiae, using five cohorts hidden in a wood, and captured their king, Teutobod. In 101 BCE the Cimbri crossed the Alps into northern Italy, and Marius and Quintus Lutatius Catulus defeated them at Vercellae. Their leaders Boiorix and Lugius fell, and the women killed themselves and their children to avoid slavery.

Some surviving captives are reported to have been among the gladiators in the Third Servile War. The war marked the start of the rivalry between Marius and Sulla, which led to the first of Rome's great civil wars. After Vercellae Marius granted Roman citizenship to two cohorts of allied Italian soldiers without asking the Senate. According to traditional historiography the Italian allies then demanded a larger say in Roman policy, leading to the Social War. The putative Marian reforms of the legions are now contested by modern historians.
cimmerians: The Cimmerians were an Eastern Iranic equestrian nomadic people from the Pontic-Caspian steppe. They were culturally Scythian and related to the Scythians, but ethnically distinct, and the Scythians later displaced and replaced them. The Cimmerians left no written records. Most information comes from Neo-Assyrian records of the 8th to 7th centuries BCE and from Greek and Roman authors from the 5th century BCE onward.

Their early homeland lay in the Caspian and Ciscaucasian steppes, north and west of the Caspian Sea, with the Volga as the eastern border separating them from the Scythians and the Kerch Strait at the west. The early Scythians began to arrive from Central Asia in the 9th century BCE, driven west by the Massagetae or the Issedones.

In the second half of the 8th century BCE and the 7th century BCE the Cimmerians moved south into West Asia, crossing the Caucasus by the Alagir, Darial and Klukhor passes. Mesopotamian sources call their first land in Transcaucasia māt Gamir, near the Kuros river, north of Lake Sevan. They later became active in the Iranian Plateau and Anatolia, and split into a western horde in Anatolia and an eastern horde that moved into Mannai and later Media.

Three kings are recorded: Teušpâ, who ruled until 679 BCE, Dugdammî, from 679 to 640 BCE, and Sandakšatru, from 640 to about the 630s BCE. The inroads of the Cimmerians and the Scythians upset the balance between Assyria, Urartu and Phrygia, and contributed to the decline of several of them and the rise of the Medes and the Lydians.

The Cimmerians were a tribal confederation, possibly ethnically mixed under an Iranic aristocracy, ruled by a supreme king whose power passed within a single dynasty. Military assemblies could be convened by the king, and warlords could rebel against him. They lived as mounted pastoralists like the Scythians, with the same weapons, horse harness and Animal Style art.

The western Cimmerians in Anatolia became settled, in fortified and other settlements, with a capital called Ḫarzallē. There they adopted chariot warfare and infantry, and appear to have taken up the worship of the Anatolian god Šanta. Homer's Odyssey gives the first mention of the Cimmerians in Greek literature, placing them in a misty land at the entrance of Hades.
cimon: Cimon was born into the Athenian nobility, a member of the Philaidae clan from the deme of Laciadae. His grandfather, Cimon Coalemos, won three Olympic victories with his four-horse chariot and was assassinated by the sons of Peisistratus. His mother was Hegesipyle, daughter of the Thracian king Olorus. When his father Miltiades was fined 50 talents after an accusation of treason, he could not pay and died in prison in 489 BCE. Cimon inherited the debt. As head of the household he also had charge of his sister or half-sister Elpinice, and in his youth he had a reputation as a hard drinker, blunt and unrefined.

Cimon distinguished himself at the Battle of Salamis and was a member of an embassy to Sparta in 479 BCE. When the Delian League was formed, he was agreed to be its principal commander, and he directed most of its operations until 463 BCE. He captured Eion on the Strymon from the Persian general Boges, conquered Scyros and drove out the pirates based there, and brought back to Athens the bones said to be those of Theseus. Around 466 BCE he defeated the Persians at the Eurymedon in Pamphylia, capturing their camp and destroying or taking a fleet of 200 triremes. He founded Amphipolis in 465 BCE with 10,000 settlers.

Between 465 and 463 BCE he besieged Thasos, which had left the League over a trade rivalry and the ownership of a gold mine. He was then prosecuted by Pericles for allegedly taking bribes from Alexander I of Macedon, and was acquitted. As Sparta's proxenos at Athens, he persuaded the Assembly in 462 BCE to send 4,000 hoplites to help Sparta against its rebellious helots. The Spartans, fearing that the Athenians would side with the helots, sent them home. The snub ended his popularity, and he was ostracised for ten years from 461 BCE.

In his absence Ephialtes, with the support of Pericles, reduced the power of the Council of the Areopagus, and some of Cimon's policies were reversed. Cimon returned around 451 BCE and negotiated a five-year truce with Sparta. He then proposed an expedition against the Persians on Cyprus and sailed with two hundred triremes. He besieged Citium and died during or soon after the failed siege in 450 BCE, of unrecorded causes. His death was kept secret from the army, which won a victory at Salamis-in-Cyprus. He was buried in Athens.

He had also paid for building in Athens, including the expansion of the Acropolis and the city walls. His domestic policy was consistently antidemocratic and failed, but his foreign policy rested on continued resistance to Persia and on Athens as the leading sea power and Sparta the leading land power. That arrangement probably delayed the outbreak of the Peloponnesian War.
cincinnatus: Lucius Quinctius Cincinnatus belonged to the rich patrician clan Quinctia. His cognomen means 'the curly haired'. In the late 460s BCE Rome was fending off raids by the Aequi, while the tribune Gaius Terentilius Harsa pressed from 462 BCE for a written code of laws to check the near-regal power of the patrician consuls. According to tradition, Cincinnatus's son Caeso led patrician gangs against the plebeians, was charged with a capital offence in 461 BCE and fled to the Etruscans. Modern historians reject the story that his father was fined into poverty as a later invention.

In 460 BCE Appius Herdonius seized the Capitoline Hill and the consul Publius Valerius Poplicola was killed in its recovery. Cincinnatus, probably illegally, became suffect consul for the rest of the year and violently opposed the plebeian proposal, which made no progress. In 458 BCE the Aequi broke their treaty and besieged the army of the consul Lucius Minucius Esquilinus Augurinus at Mount Algidus. The Senate fell into panic and named Cincinnatus dictator. Senators sent to him are said to have found him ploughing his farm.

He named Lucius Tarquitius his master of the horse and ordered every man of military age to the Campus Martius with twelve times the usual number of stakes. At Mount Algidus the Romans used the stakes to besiege the besiegers. Cincinnatus accepted the Aequi's pleas for mercy, requiring that three principal offenders be executed and their leaders delivered in chains, and made the army pass under a yoke of three spears. He then disbanded his army and returned to his farm. Modern historians question particulars, and some consider the military account fictional, noting parallels with later episodes of 380 BCE and 217 BCE.

He may have been dictator a second time in 439 BCE, against the alleged plot of Spurius Maelius, who was killed by Cincinnatus's master of the horse, Gaius Servilius Ahala. That story may be linked to the earlier dictator only by the clan name.

Cincinnatus became a Roman model of civic virtue, a leader who held supreme power no longer than necessary. His story was later invoked for George Washington, who gave up command of the Continental Army and retired to his farm at Mount Vernon. The Society of the Cincinnati was founded by Henry Knox in 1783, and Cincinnati, Ohio, was named in his honour.
cinekoy-inscription: The inscription stands on a monument to the storm god Tarhunza. Its author is the ruler called Urikki in Assyrian texts, War(a)ika in Luwian, a vassal king of the land the Assyrians named Quwê, modern Cilicia. Whether he is the same person as the Awariku of the Karatepe inscription remains debated. Like Karatepe, the text traces the kings of ancient Adana to the house of Mopsos, a king of ancient legend given in Luwian as Muksa and in Phoenician as mps.

The king describes his bond with his Assyrian overlords: in the Phoenician version the king of Assyria and the whole House of Assyria were for him a father and a mother, and his people and the Assyrians were a single House. The Luwian version says that Hiyawa and Assyria were made a single House. In the Phoenician text Awariku also claims to have built 15 fortresses in his kingdom, a sentence the Luwian version has been misread as describing their destruction.

The stone was uncovered in 1997 near the village of Çine, some 30 km south of Adana. The find was first reported and described in 1999, the first edition appeared in 2000, and important additions to its reading were made in 2007, 2012, 2015 and 2017.

The text bears on the origin of the name Syria, debated since Theodor Nöldeke proposed in 1871 that it derives from Assyria. Where the Phoenician version writes ʾŠR for Ashur and ʾŠRYM for the Assyrians, the Luwian version uses su+ra/i-, Syria, for the same words. In 2006 the historian Robert Rollinger argued that this gives conclusive evidence that Syria was first used as another name for Assyria, and scholars now broadly agree on that reading.
cinematograph: Soon after photography was introduced in 1839, people saw that its images could be combined with the principle of the phenakistiscope, but real-time recording of motion took several decades. Eadweard Muybridge's chronophotography of 1878 inspired many attempts, and in 1887 Ottomar Anschütz introduced his Elektrische Schnellseher, which showed chronophotographic sequences on a small glass screen to paying audiences.

Léon Bouly took the name Cinématographe from the Greek for writing in movement. Turning a handle made a padded pressure plate stop the film intermittently as a rotating cylinder carried it. At least three Bouly cinematographs were built, but his patents lapsed at the end of 1894 because the annual fees were paid only once, and he seems to have abandoned the project.

The Lumière brothers wanted a machine as simple and economical as a common photographic camera, since many of their customers were amateur photographers. Their Cinématographe weighed only 16 lb (7.3 kg), unlike the bulky, electrically powered Kinetoscope. The same device took pictures, printed positives from the negative and projected them. A common magic lantern made by Alfred Molteni served for the projections of 1895. The film was 35 mm, with one perforation on each side of each frame, and the Lumières advocated 15 frames per second, usually recording about 50 seconds of action in 800 pictures.

Louis Lumière decided by February 1896 on a fixed shutter and a lens diaphragm after noticing that perfectly sharp pictures looked jerky in sudden movement, and in 1897 the Lumières added a glass flask of water as condenser, which also protected the flammable film.

Louis Lumière presented his first film, Workers Leaving the Lumière Factory, on 22 March 1895 in Paris to a few dozen invited guests, who were more enthusiastic about it than about the colour slides expected to be the main item. The first Lumière public show was on 28 December 1895 at the Salon Indien du Grand Café, with ten short films each about 17 metres long. The first commercial public screening had in fact been held on 20 May 1895 in New York with the Eidoloscope of Woodville Latham and Eugene Lauste.

The Cinématographe became a popular attraction for people of all classes. It was shown in nickelodeons, at fairs and in vaudeville houses, and the Lumières took it to China and India. Its reversibility was abandoned after a few years, because few amateurs made films and theatrical screenings grew popular, so specialised cameras and projectors were wanted.
cinnamon: Cinnamon is obtained from the inner bark of several tree species of the genus Cinnamomum. Cinnamomum verum, known as Ceylon cinnamon after its origin in Sri Lanka, is considered true cinnamon, but most cinnamon in international commerce comes from four other species, more correctly called cassia. The stems are processed while the inner bark is still wet: the outer bark is scraped off and the inner bark pried off in long rolls, which curl into quills as they dry. Ceylon cinnamon is lighter and finer than the thicker, harder cassia.

The English word comes through Latin and medieval French from the Greek kinnámōmon, which was borrowed from a Phoenician word similar to the Hebrew qinnāmōn. Cinnamon was imported to Egypt as early as 2000 BCE, and it was so prized that it was regarded as a gift fit for monarchs. Its source was kept a trade secret in the Mediterranean world for centuries by traders protecting their monopoly. In Ancient Egypt it was used to embalm mummies. Herodotus and Aristotle named Arabia as its source and recounted that giant cinnamon birds gathered the sticks for their nests; Pliny the Elder called this a traders' fiction made up to raise prices.

According to Pliny, a Roman pound of cassia or cinnamon cost up to 1,500 denarii, the wage of fifty months' labour. Through the Middle Ages the cinnamon-based cameline sauce was among the most common at tables in Western Europe, though the origin of the spice remained a mystery. The first mention that it grew in Sri Lanka is in al-Qazwini about 1270. Venetian traders held a monopoly in Europe, distributing it from Alexandria, and the disruption of this trade by the Mamluk sultans and the Ottoman Empire was one of many factors that led Europeans to search for other routes to Asia.

The Portuguese controlled Sri Lankan cinnamon in the 1500s. Dutch traders established a trading post on the island in 1638, took control of the manufactories by 1640 and expelled the remaining Portuguese by 1658. The British seized control of Ceylon from the Dutch in 1796.
cipollino-marble: Cipollino marble, also known as Karystian marble, is a variety of silicate marble. It has a white-green base crossed by thick wavy green bands, which are held between thin bands of mica, and its base and grain grow darker the further north the quarry lies. It is a metamorphic rock with crystals between 0.2 and 0.6 mm and veins coloured by epidote and chlorite.

The ancient quarries lay at several places on the south-west coast of Euboea, between the modern towns of Styra and Karystos, and some of them survive with a mine-face of over 100 metres. A marble of similar appearance was also mined in the Iberian peninsula at the Anasol mines, in the Alpi Apuane, in north-west Greece and in present-day Serbia.

First used in ancient Greece, the stone was exported to Rome from the 1st century BCE. Pliny the Elder, in his Natural History, records columns of it in the house of the eques Claudius Mamurra, who had served Julius Caesar as an engineer in the Gallic Wars. The quarries at Karystos became imperial property in 17 CE, and in the imperial period cipollino became common throughout Rome.

It served above all for column shafts, many of them large and mostly smooth, as in the pronaos of the Temple of Antoninus and Faustina in the Forum. It was also carved: a crocodile in the Canopus of the Villa Adriana at Tivoli used its colour to imitate the animal's skin. Roman builders used it in the Basilica Aemilia, the Domus Augustana, the Villa Gordiani and the forums of Augustus, Vespasian, Domitian and Trajan, and in rebuilding the Temple of Zeus at Cyrene between 172 and 175. Septimius Severus closed the quarries in 206.

The quarries were used again in the Byzantine period. Cipollino went into the Basilica of Gaza in the 4th century, the Church of Saint Demetrius in 412, the Basilica of Saint Apollinare in Ravenna in 504, the rebuilt Hagia Sophia in 537, the Church of the Holy Apostles in 546 and the Monastery of Saint Loukas between 920 and 945. It was also used for Westminster Abbey in London in the middle of the 11th century and for Saint Mark's Basilica in Venice in 1094.
cippus-perusinus: The cippus is a stone tablet discovered on the hill of San Marco in Perugia. Its 46 incised lines run over the front and one side of the stone. It seems to have been a border stone, and its text records a legal contract between the Velthina family of Perugia and the Afuna family of Chiusi on the sharing or use of a property, including its water rights, on which stood a tomb belonging to the noble Velthinas. It is kept in the National Archeological Museum of Perugia.

In the tentative translation of van der Meer, following Facchetti and others, the text opens by naming Lart Rezul, son of Lart, as arbitrator, and records an oath taken by the Velthina family together with a member of the Afuna family. It assigns the Velthina 12 measures of land according to Etruscan law, deals with the drawing of water acquired by Larth Afuna, declares the tomb the Velthina family's own, and allows Afuna to keep three measures. The side ends with an accord on the water rights, closing with the word ziχuχe, meaning was written.

The meaning of many words is still uncertain, and the readings given for them are marked as tentative. The scholar Wylin points out that the three words acilune, turune and ścune probably correspond to the Latin legal phrase facere, dare, praestare, to do, to give and to make good, which was used of personal obligations rather than legal rights.

The stone was found in 1822, and its date is placed in the 3rd or 2nd century BCE. The scholar F. Roncalli has argued that the original lines of the text were distorted when they were copied onto this stone, and the text is now arranged according to his theory. The original has no capital letters, and the spacing between words is mostly hypothetical. Other scholars, among them van Heems, have identified and partly translated individual phrases, and the form fulumχva in the text has been compared with pulumχva in the Pyrgi Tablets and pulum in the inscription of the Golini Tomb.
cipriano-castro: José Cipriano Castro Ruiz was born on 12 October 1858 in Capacho Viejo, in the Andean state of Táchira, the only son of a mid-level farmer. He studied at a seminary in Pamplona, Colombia, then worked for a trading company and as a cowboy.

In 1886 he returned to Táchira as a soldier in a regional autonomy rising, defeated government forces at Capacho Viejo and Rubio, and was made a general; at a funeral he met Juan Vicente Gómez, his later ally. After he failed to carry a campaign against the government to Caracas in 1892, he spent seven years in Colombia, amassing a fortune in illegal cattle trading and recruiting a private army.

In October 1899 Castro marched on Caracas in the Restorative Liberal Revolution and seized power, naming Gómez his vice-president. His rule was marked by frequent rebellions, the murder or exile of opponents and disputes with the United States and European powers. In 1901 the banker Manuel Antonio Matos led the Liberating Revolution, backed by foreign companies, which brought the government close to collapse; Castro's troops broke the Siege of La Victoria in November 1902.

Within weeks, Britain, Germany and Italy blockaded Venezuelan ports over unpaid debts and damages to their citizens. Castro assumed the Monroe Doctrine would restrain them, but Theodore Roosevelt's government let the action go ahead. After two Venezuelan ships were sunk and the coast bombarded, the United States pressed for a settlement, and an agreement signed in Washington on 13 February 1903 lifted the blockade and committed 30 per cent of customs duties to claims.

On 22 February 1904 the Permanent Court of Arbitration at The Hague held that the blockading powers were entitled to preferential treatment, a decision that helped produce the Roosevelt Corollary. In 1908 a dispute with the Netherlands led to a Dutch naval blockade.

Seriously ill with a kidney problem, Castro left for Paris for treatment in December 1908. On 19 December Gómez seized power himself and ended the war with the Netherlands. Castro spent years in exile in Europe, Trinidad, Cuba and the United States, trying repeatedly to raise a force to return, and settled in Santurce, Puerto Rico, in 1918. He died there on 4 December 1924. He was the first Venezuelan from the Andes to rule the country and the first of four military strongmen from Táchira to do so over the next 46 years.
circassians: The Circassians, also called the Cherkess or the Adyghe, are a Northwest Caucasian people native to Circassia in the North Caucasus. Dolmens in the northwest Caucasus point to a megalithic culture. Feudalism began to emerge among them by the 4th century. Christianity spread through the Caucasus between the 3rd and 5th centuries, and the Circassians, then known as Kassogs, began to accept it without abandoning every older belief. They founded several states, among them the medieval kingdom of Zichia, but could not achieve political unity. Around the end of the first millennium they were integrated into the Kingdom of Alania. In the 17th century, under Crimean Tatar and Ottoman influence, large numbers converted to Islam, and most Circassians are now Sunni Muslim.

In 1714 Peter I drew up a plan to occupy the Caucasus, and Catherine II began to carry it out. Circassian resistance lasted until 1864, in the Russo-Circassian War. Most Circassians were then exiled to the Ottoman Empire, in what is described as the Circassian genocide; the Russian and Ottoman governments negotiated the process, and the Circassians were moved or pressed to the Black Sea coast, from where Ottoman boats took them to Anatolia. In the 1860s and 1870s the Ottoman government settled them in what are now Turkey, Syria, Jordan, Lebanon, Israel, Iraq and parts of the Balkans.

Circassians had lived outside the Caucasus since the Middle Ages. Most leaders of the Burji Mamluk dynasty of Egypt (1382–1517) were of Circassian origin, and Qaitbay was sultan from 1468 to 1496. In Jordan, Circassian refugees founded Amman in 1878. About 800,000 Circassians live in historical Circassia, in Adygea, Kabardino-Balkaria, Karachay-Cherkessia and Krasnodar Krai, and some 4,500,000 live elsewhere, mostly in Turkey.

Before the Russian conquest Circassian society was highly stratified, with a caste of princes, then lesser nobility, commoners, serfs and slaves, though a few mountain tribes were fairly egalitarian. Custom was governed by Adyghe khabze. The people are divided into twelve tribes, among them the Abzakh, Besleney, Kabardians, Shapsugh and Ubykh, which the twelve stars of the Circassian flag represent. They speak two mutually intelligible languages, Adyghe, or West Circassian, and Kabardian. The Ubykh language became extinct in 1992 with the death of its last speaker.
circe: In Greek mythology Circe is a witch and goddess, in most accounts a daughter of the sun god Helios and the Oceanid Perse; the Orphic Argonautica names her mother Asterope instead. Some sources call her a nymph. Her brother was Aeëtes, keeper of the Golden Fleece and father of Medea, and Pasiphaë, wife of King Minos, is sometimes listed as her sister. Dionysius Scytobrachion and Diodorus Siculus make her and Medea daughters of Hecate, whom they treat as a mortal woman who discovered drugs. She was known for her knowledge of potions and herbs, and with these and a wand or staff she changed her enemies, or those who offended her, into animals. Her Homeric epithet is polypharmakos, knowing many drugs or charms.

In Homer's Odyssey, Circe lives in a palace in a dense wood on her island of Aeaea, where strangely docile lions and wolves prowl. She lures visitors with her singing as she weaves, then drugs them and changes their shape. When Odysseus visits her on the way home from the Trojan War she turns most of his crew into swine, but he persuades her to restore them, and he stays with her for a year. Hesiod's Theogony says she bore him three sons, Agrius, Latinus and Telegonus. In the lost Telegony she gave Telegonus a poisoned spear, and he killed his father unknowingly, after which Circe made Penelope and Telemachus immortal.

In the Argonautica, Apollonius has her purify Jason and Medea of the murder of Absyrtus with the blood of a piglet and send them away. Other tales say she turned the Italian king Picus into a woodpecker for resisting her advances, and that she poisoned the water where the nymph Scylla bathed, out of jealousy over the sea-god Glaucus, turning her into a monster. Circe was venerated at a tomb-shrine on one of the Pharmacussae islands and at Mount Circeo in Italy, which was said to be named for her. The gens Mamilia of Latium claimed descent from her.

Early philosophers asked whether being changed from a reasoning human into a beast might be preferable, a debate that affected the Renaissance; Giovan Battista Gelli's La Circe of 1549 gave it dialogue form. Socrates had explained the transformation as gluttony overcoming self-control, while Andrea Alciato's Emblemata of 1546 made Circe a type of the prostitute. Renaissance epics gave her heirs in the sorceresses Alcina, Armida and Acrasia. Later Christian opinion saw her as an abominable witch.

She is common in ancient vase painting, usually stirring a potion or threatened by Odysseus. Stradella's cantata La Circe was first performed in 1667, and Martha Graham's ballet Circe appeared in 1963.
circipanians: Their territory, Circipania, was enclosed roughly by the upper Recknitz, Trebel and Peene rivers, with its western border east of Güstrow, and its main burghs were Teterow, Malchin and Demmin. The Slavic name joins a prefix meaning across, the name of the Peene, a word for foam, and a suffix for the dwellers of a place. The region took shape in the 10th and 11th centuries, when the Circipanes were one of the four tribes of the Lutici federation centred on Rethra.

Circipania was incorporated into the Billung March of the Holy Roman Empire in 936, but the Lutici threw off the empire's overlordship in a successful uprising in 983. In the 1050s the federation broke apart: the Circipanes and Kessinians, struggling for more influence, were opposed by the Redarians and Tollensians, who allied with the Obodrites, and it dissolved in 1057. The Obodrites then invaded Circipania and made it a province of their realm.

Weakened by these struggles, the land became a target of the Wendish Crusade of 1147 and of a raid by Denmark in 1170. In the late 12th century the Duchy of Pomerania subdued it and joined it to Pomerania-Demmin. Mecklenburg, under Borwin III of Rostock, conquered the last of the territory in the early 1230s, leaving it divided: Mecklenburg held the larger western part with Güstrow and Teterow, and Pomerania the smaller eastern part around Demmin.

The name Circipania fell out of political use once the Mecklenburg part was divided between Mecklenburg-Rostock and Mecklenburg-Werle, but it stayed on Roman Catholic ecclesiastical maps as the Pomeranian province of the Diocese of Cammin, whose borders matched the old territory. The Circipanes, whose numbers had already dwindled in the wars, were assimilated by German settlers called in by Wartislaw III, Duke of Pomerania, and by Mecklenburg knights during the Ostsiedlung.
circus-maximus: The Circus Maximus was sited on level ground in the Valley of Murcia between the Aventine and Palatine hills. In Rome's early days the valley would have been rich farmland, prone to flooding from the Tiber and from a stream dividing it lengthwise. The earliest races were probably held in that landscape with little more than turning posts and banks for spectators. In Livy's account the first Etruscan king, Lucius Tarquinius Priscus, built raised wooden seating for the equites and patricians, and his grandson Tarquinius Superbus added seating for the plebs.

Permanent starting stalls were built in 329 BCE. By the late Republic there were twelve stalls, allocated by lottery, with teams identified by colours, chiefly the Blues and the Greens, and seven laps to a race. Julius Caesar's development from about 50 BCE extended the seating almost round the whole circuit. Augustus brought an obelisk from Heliopolis and set it on the central barrier. A fire in 64 CE swept through the stands and shops, and the Circus was rebuilt to the same plan. Trajan rebuilt it in stone, giving it its definitive form. By the late Republic ludi were held on 57 days of the year, and eventually on 135.

With the advent of Christianity as the official religion of the empire, ludi gradually fell out of favour. The last known beast-hunt at the Circus took place in 523, and the last known races, held by Totila, in 549. The site is now a public park in Rome, Italy, in the valley between the Aventine and Palatine hills.
cirebon: Cirebon is the only coastal city of West Java, about 40 km west of the provincial border with Central Java and about 297 km east of Jakarta. Because it lies on the border of the Sundanese and Javanese cultural regions, many residents speak a dialect mixing the two, known as Jawareh, and linguists treat Cirebonese as a language area of its own. The name may derive from the Javanese word caruban, meaning mixed, a reference to the city's blend of Sundanese, Javanese, Chinese and Arabic elements, or from the Sundanese ci, water, and rebon, shrimp.

According to the manuscript Purwaka Caruban Nagari, Cirebon began in the 15th century as a small fishing village named Muara Jati that attracted foreign traders. Its port master, Ki Gedeng Alang-Alang, was appointed by the king of Galuh and later moved the port to Lemahwungkuk. A prince of Pajajaran, Walangsungsang, converted to Islam, became duke of Cirebon with the title Cakrabumi, and declared independence from Sunda and Galuh. This marked the first Islamic rule in western Java. Under Sunan Gunungjati in the early 16th century the sultanate was independent, and Tomé Pires named Cirebon around 1513 as one of the trade centres of Java.

After the Sunda kingdom collapsed, Banten and Mataram fought over Cirebon, which declared its allegiance to Sultan Agung of Mataram. His grandson Amangkurat II ceded the city to the Dutch in 1677, the year the sultanate split into four royal houses, each with its own palace. In 1705 a treaty made the area west of the Cisanggarung River a Dutch protectorate jointly administered by three sultans. Under the Dutch Culture System, trade in cash crops attracted Chinese entrepreneurs, and a famine struck in 1844 after drought and the shift from subsistence farming to indigo and sugarcane.

Cirebon had 333,303 inhabitants at the 2020 census, and a large ethnic Chinese community that dates from immigration since the 17th century. Four palaces of the former sultanate remain as cultural institutions: Kasepuhan, Kanoman, Kaprabonan and Kacirebonan. The city is known for batik, whose Megamendung pattern resembles Chinese cloud imagery, for glass painting and for the Topeng Cirebon mask dance. The Sunan Gunung Jati complex lies about 24 km west of the city centre.
cirencester: Cirencester lies in the Cotswold District of Gloucestershire on the lower dip slopes of the Cotswold Hills, an outcrop of oolitic limestone. The River Churn, a tributary of the Thames, flows through its eastern side, and the Thames itself rises a few miles to the west. The Roman name Corinium is first attested by Ptolemy around 150 CE, and its origin is unknown; the same name lies behind that of the Churn. The later forms ending in ceaster come from the Old English word for a fort.

Around 49 CE the Romans built a fort where the Fosse Way crossed the Churn, and Dobunni from nearby Bagendon were drawn to a civil settlement beside it. When the frontier moved north after the conquest of Wales the fort was closed and levelled, around the year 70, but the town persisted as Corinium. A large forum and basilica were built over the fort. The defensive wall of the late 2nd century enclosed 240 acres, making it the second-largest city by area in Roman Britain, and it is generally thought to have been the capital of Britannia Prima after the reforms of about 296. The amphitheatre survives, only partly excavated.

The town was fortified in the 5th or 6th century, and in 628 the Mercian king Penda fought the West Saxon kings Cynegils and Cwichelm there. Henry I founded Cirencester Abbey in 1117 and its church was dedicated in 1176; the manor was granted to the abbey in 1189. The abbots obtained charters for fairs in 1215 and 1253, and the wool trade gave them great importance. For centuries the townsmen struggled with the abbots for borough rights, and in 1477 parliament declared that Cirencester was not corporate. The abbey buildings were demolished after 1539, and only the Norman Arch and parts of the precinct wall remain.

Wealth from wool paid for the rebuilding of the parish church's nave in 1515-1530, creating the large building sometimes called the Cathedral of the Cotswolds. In February 1643, during the Civil War, Royalists and Parliamentarians fought in the streets, over 300 were killed and 1,200 prisoners were held in the church. The Thames and Severn Canal's Cirencester arm opened in 1789 and a branch railway in 1841.

Cirencester is the largest town within the Cotswolds, with a population of 20,229 in 2021. It is home to the Royal Agricultural University, founded in 1840 and the oldest agricultural college in the English-speaking world. The Corinium Museum holds an extensive Roman collection, and the Grade I listed Church of St John the Baptist is noted for its Perpendicular Gothic porch, fan vaults and merchants' tombs. Cirencester Park, a landscape garden laid out by Allen Bathurst after 1714, lies to the west.
cirta: The Punic name krṭn, probably pronounced Kirthan, is thought to render an existing Berber place name rather than the Punic word for town; it became Cirta in Latin, and Greek historians and geographers wrote it Kirta. The city's port was Russicada. As capital of Numidia it was a political, economic and military centre west of Carthage, and the Battle of Cirta in 203 BCE was a decisive victory for Scipio Africanus in the Second Punic War. A large corpus of Punic inscriptions, the Cirta steles, has been found in the area.

After King Micipsa died in 118 BCE, his natural son Adherbal and adopted son Jugurtha fought over the kingdom, and Jugurtha besieged Cirta and killed Adherbal and the Romans who defended him, bringing on the Jugurthine War. Rebuilt in the 1st century BCE, the city held Numidians, Carthaginian refugees and Greek, Roman and Italian merchants and veterans. It came under direct Roman rule in 46 BCE, when Julius Caesar gave its lands to Publius Sittius and his Campanian legionaries, and with Rusicade, Milevum and Chullu it formed an autonomous confederation. By the end of the 2nd century it may have had nearly 50,000 inhabitants.

Records of Christians martyred at Cirta exist from the mid-3rd century, and a council held there around 305 to elect a bishop helped set off the Donatist movement. In 303 Diocletian made it capital of the province of Numidia Cirtensis. The city was destroyed after a siege by Rufius Volusianus, prefect of Maxentius, who defeated the claimant Domitius Alexander in 310; Constantine rebuilt it after 312 and made it the capital of all Roman Numidia. Augustine oversaw a second council there in 412.

Under Justinian I the walls were strengthened, and the city belonged to Byzantine Africa from 534 to 697. The Berber queen Kahina defended it without success during the Muslim conquest, after which it was known as Qusantina and kept a small Christian community until the 10th century. The modern city of Constantine stands on the site and is again the seat of a diocese.
cis-sutlej-states: The region lay between the Sutlej River to the north, the Himalayas to the east, the Yamuna River and Delhi District to the south and Sirsa District to the west. Many chiefs held it under the Mughal Empire, and as Mughal and Afghan power declined they ruled in practice on their own; Ala Singh, founder of Patiala, was conquering territory from about 1730. At the Battle of Sirhind on 13–14 January 1764 the Buddha Dal and Taruna Dal of the Dal Khalsa killed the Afghan governor, Zain Khan Sirhindi, ending Afghan rule. Lepel Henry Griffin wrote that most of the leading families were descendants of the conquerors.

A treaty of 10 May 1785 with Mahadji Sindhia, regent of the Mughal Empire, made the small states an autonomous protectorate of the Maratha Scindia dynasty, though the chiefs did not keep its terms, and the Marathas lost their influence in the Second Anglo-Maratha War of 1803–1805. Ranjit Singh of the Sikh Empire then crossed the Sutlej three times, in 1806, 1807 and 1808, using a quarrel between Nabha and Patiala as his pretext; he took Ludhiana and later Ambala and Faridkot, but stopped short of Patiala. The chiefs of the Sirhind region asked for British protection, Charles Metcalfe was sent to Lahore, and David Ochterlony warned on 9 February 1809 that further incursions would be resisted.

By the treaty of 25 April 1809 Ranjit Singh kept the lands he had taken before his third expedition but gave up Ambala and Faridkot, agreed to station only the troops needed to govern his holdings south of the river, and promised never to dispossess the local chiefs. A British decree of 22 August 1811 forbade the states to seize one another. A political officer at Umballa, styled agent of the Governor-General for the Cis-Sutlej states, supervised them, and after the First Anglo-Sikh War the treaty of 9 March 1846 gave the British the Sikh Empire's lands south of the Sutlej. Several states were taken under the doctrine of lapse.

When the Punjab was annexed in 1849, the Cis-Sutlej commissionership of Ambala, Ferozepore, Ludhiana, Thanesar and Simla joined the new Punjab Province; the name lasted until 1862, when the remaining tract became the Ambala Division. Patiala, Jind and Nabha formed a separate political agency from 1901. After Indian independence every state except Kaithal joined PEPSU.
cisalpine-gaul: Cisalpine means on this side of the Alps from the Roman point of view, as opposed to Transalpine Gaul beyond them. The region was also called Gallia Citerior, Hither Gaul, and Gallia Togata, toga-wearing Gaul, a name that points to its early Romanization. It was divided into Gallia Cispadana, south of the Po, and Gallia Transpadana, north of it, and the Roman province of the 1st century BCE ran from the Alps to the Apennines, the Rubicon and the Adriatic Sea.

The Canegrate culture of the 13th century BCE may represent a first migration of proto-Celtic people over the Alps into the western Po valley, bringing cremation. It later merged with the native Ligurians to give rise to the Golasecca culture. According to Livy, a group led by Bellovesus occupied the area between Milan and Cremona in the time of Tarquinius Priscus, and Milan itself was presumably founded by Gauls in the early 6th century BCE.

In 391 BCE, according to Diodorus Siculus, Celts from beyond the Alps seized the land between the Apennines and the Alps, and the Senones sacked Rome in 390 BCE. A Celtic army was crushed at the Battle of Telamon in 225 BCE. In the Second Punic War the Boii and Insubres allied with the Carthaginians, and after Hannibal's victories all the Gauls except the Cenomani joined the revolt; Rome withdrew until Carthage was defeated in 202 BCE. Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica completed the conquest of the Boii in 191 BCE, and the Ligurians were finally subdued in 155 BCE.

The province was probably established about 81 BCE and governed from Mutina, where in 73 BCE forces under Spartacus defeated the governor's legion. In 49 BCE all its people received Roman citizenship, and Julius Caesar's crossing of the Rubicon that year began the civil war. It was merged into Italia about 42 BCE. Virgil, Catullus and Livy were born there.
ciskei: Ciskei, meaning on this side of the river Kei, covered about 7,700 square kilometres in the south-east of South Africa, almost surrounded by the Cape Province, with a small Indian Ocean coastline. The name was given by Europeans to distinguish the area from the Transkei, north of the Kei; at the end of the 19th century the area between the Fish and Kei rivers, British Kaffraria, had been set aside for black people. The Native Lands Act of 1913 demarcated reserves, and the Native Trust and Land Act of 1936 ended the right of Cape black people to buy land outside them. By the 1970s the government had consolidated the territory by joining reserves and buying the white-owned land between them.

Ciskei became a separate administrative region in 1961 and self-governing in 1972, under Chief Justice Mabandla and then Lennox Sebe. It became a single-party state in 1978 and, after a referendum in 1980, was declared independent in 1981, the fourth homeland to be so declared. Its residents lost their South African citizenship. The apartheid authorities forcibly relocated black people from white areas to resettlement camps there. A 1983 Rhodes University study found that 40% of the children in one camp suffered from wasting caused by malnutrition. The government imposed collective punishment on communities that opposed it.

In 1986 and 1987 Transkei raided Ciskei, including an attack on Sebe's compound. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission later heard that South African security forces had planned a union of the two homelands as part of Operation Katzen. In 1990 Brigadier Oupa Gqozo deposed Sebe. On 7 September 1992 the Ciskei Defence Force fired into a crowd of African National Congress members demanding reincorporation, killing 28 people outside the stadium in Bisho. In March 1994 government workers struck and the police mutinied, and Gqozo resigned on 22 March. Ciskei was reincorporated on 27 April 1994 and joined Transkei in the new Eastern Cape Province.

Ciskei had a succession of capitals: Zwelitsha first, then Bisho. Its elected headmen and relatively educated working class, who often worked in East London, Queenstown and King Williams Town, differed from the hereditary chiefs of the Transkei. According to the historian Quinn Slobodian, an economist group led by Leon Louw suggested running it as a de facto export processing zone. The textile industry, with a mostly female workforce, depended on Taiwanese and Hong Kong investors, who received generous incentives and faced repression of the labour movement.
cisleithania: Cisleithania, officially the Kingdoms and Lands Represented in the Imperial Council, was the northern and western part of Austria-Hungary. Its capital was Vienna, the residence of the Emperor of Austria, and in 1910 it had a population of about 28.6 million. It reached from Vorarlberg in the west to Galicia and Bukovina in the east, and from Bohemia in the north to Dalmatia in the south. Its name comes from the Leitha River, a tributary of the Danube that formed the historical boundary between the Archduchy of Austria and the Kingdom of Hungary. The official name was used by politicians and officials but had no official status until 1915, and the public usually just called the lands Austria.

Cisleithania consisted of 15 crown lands, each with a regional assembly, the Landtag, that made laws on matters of mostly minor importance. The Reichsrat in Vienna was its parliament. From 1873 its lower house was directly elected on a four-class franchise, and equal and universal suffrage for men came only with the reform of 1907. The government handled everything except the common army, navy and foreign ministry. German-speaking deputies dominated at first, but as the franchise widened the Slavs gained a majority, and conflict between German and Slavic politicians, notably over the Czech National Revival, often paralysed politics. After 1893 no government could rely on a parliamentary majority, and the emperor sometimes ruled by decree.

The December Constitution of 1867 declared all languages equal, but German kept a privileged position in administration, courts, army and education and never became the legal state language. In April 1897 Minister-President Kasimir Felix Badeni issued ordinances making Czech equal to German in Bohemia and Moravia. German deputies answered with a filibuster, there were street demonstrations, and on 28 November 1897 Emperor Franz Joseph dismissed Badeni. Riots followed in German and Czech towns, and martial law ended four days of rioting in Prague. The ordinances were withdrawn in 1899. The Reichsrat was prorogued in March 1914 and did not meet again until May 1917.

Cisleithania covered the present territory of Austria except Burgenland, most of the Czech Republic and Slovenia, southern Poland, and parts of Italy, Croatia, Montenegro, Romania and Ukraine. Roman Catholics made up about 79 per cent of its population, and almost 60 per cent were ethnically Slavic. Its economic growth after the Compromise was significantly faster than in the preceding half-century.
cisplatine-war: The dispute over the Banda Oriental was inherited from the Portuguese and Spanish empires, whose borders in the River Plate basin had never been settled. Portugal founded Colônia do Sacramento in 1680 opposite Buenos Aires, and Spain founded Montevideo in 1724 and created the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata in 1776. In 1816 the United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves invaded the Banda Oriental, defeated the resistance led by José Gervasio Artigas and annexed it as Cisplatina. In 1821 the Montevideo cabildo approved its incorporation into the United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves, and Cisplatina stayed in Brazil after independence in 1822. A diplomatic mission from the United Provinces in 1823 failed to win a Brazilian withdrawal.

In 1825 a group known as the Thirty-Three Orientals, led by Juan Antonio Lavalleja and supported by the Argentine government, rebelled against Brazil. On 25 August they declared Cisplatina's independence and union with the United Provinces in the Congress of Florida, and after victories at Rincón and Sarandí the Argentine Congress proclaimed it reintegrated on 25 October. Brazil declared war on 10 December 1825 and blockaded the River Plate.

The United Provinces occupied the Uruguayan countryside with local insurgents but never took Montevideo or Colonia del Sacramento. The Brazilians could not retake the countryside either, and the largest battle, at Ituzaingó, was indecisive. At sea the Brazilian Navy, with 96 warships, did better, and the small fleet of the Irish-born admiral William Brown was largely destroyed. Both navies relied heavily on British officers and sailors.

The blockade, the stalemate and public pressure in Brazil led both sides to seek peace, and Britain, whose trade was threatened, pressed them to negotiate. In 1827 the Argentine envoy Manuel José García, exceeding his instructions, signed a treaty renouncing Argentine claims, which President Bernardino Rivadavia rejected and which contributed to his resignation. Under British mediation, a Preliminary Peace Convention signed on 27 August 1828 made Cisplatina an independent state, and the treaty also guaranteed free navigation of the River Plate.

In Brazil the cost of the war and the loss of Cisplatina added to the disputes around Emperor Pedro I, who abdicated in 1831 in favour of his five-year-old son Pedro II. In Argentina the national authorities were dissolved, and tensions between Federalists and Unitarians grew. Uruguayans honour the Thirty-Three Orientals as national heroes, and Argentines regard William Brown as the father of their navy. In Brazil the war has drawn little interest.
cistercians: In 1098 Robert of Molesme left Molesme Abbey in Burgundy with around twenty supporters, who felt that the Cluniac communities had abandoned the rigour and simplicity of the Rule of Saint Benedict. They founded Cîteaux Abbey near Dijon, whose Latin name, Cistercium, gave the order its name. The first three abbots were Robert, Alberic and Stephen Harding, a monk from England. The Cistercians are also called White Monks, after the colour of their cowl, in contrast to the black cowl of the Benedictines.

Their life returned to literal observance of the Rule, including manual labour and especially work in the fields, and at times went beyond it in austerity. Bernard entered Cîteaux in the early 1110s, and his charisma greatly enlarged the order. In 1115 Count Hugh of Champagne gave the order forested land east of Troyes, where Bernard founded the Abbey of Clairvaux with twelve other monks.

By the end of the 12th century the order had spread through most of Europe. Houses included Waverley Abbey in Surrey (1128), Rein Abbey in Styria (1129), Mellifont Abbey in County Louth (1142) and Alcobaça Monastery in Portugal (1153). The first community of nuns, Tart, was founded in 1125. In the early 13th century there were about five hundred abbeys.

For a hundred years, until the first quarter of the 13th century, the Cistercians were the most powerful order and chief religious influence in western Europe, replacing Cluny. Bernard became mentor to popes and kings, and in 1145 one of his monks was elected Pope Eugene III. Afterwards the initiative passed to the mendicant orders. Henry VIII's Dissolution of the Monasteries confiscated every monastery in England, while in Germany abbeys such as Loccum and Amelungsborn adopted the Lutheran faith. A reform at La Trappe Abbey in 17th-century France produced the Trappists.

The Cistercians were the main force in spreading technology in fields such as agriculture and hydraulic engineering. They developed an organised system for selling produce, cattle and horses, and encouraged the wool and cloth trade. Their architecture avoided decoration as a sign of poverty and simplicity, yet the order helped to spread Gothic construction across Europe. The abbeys of Fontenay, Fountains, Alcobaça, Poblet and Maulbronn are recognised as UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
citadelle-laferriere: The Citadelle was built as part of a system of fortifications to deter foreign invaders, especially the French. Haiti had been under French rule until 1803, when the Haitians defeated the French. When the fortress was planned Henri Christophe was a general in the Haitian army and chief administrator of the northern regions, and in 1811, after a power struggle with Alexandre Pétion, he declared himself king of Northern Haiti.

The fortress proved unneeded, since Napoleon, occupied with his European campaigns, never tried to regain Haiti. It stands on the 900-metre Bonnet à l'Evêque mountain, about 8 kilometres uphill from Milot and 27 kilometres south of Cap-Haïtien, a vantage point from which Haitian forces could watch the valleys and the coast.

Construction involved up to 20,000 workers, of whom about 10 percent are believed to have died. The walls rise 40 metres from the mountaintop. Foundation stones were laid directly into the rock with a mortar of quicklime, molasses, the blood of cows and goats, and cows' hooves cooked to a glue. The Haitians equipped the fortress with 365 cannons of various sizes assembled from munitions left by earlier European forces, and stacks of cannonballs still stand at the foot of the walls.

Large cisterns and storehouses were designed to feed and supply 5,000 defenders for up to a year. It also had palace quarters for the king and his family, dungeons, bathing quarters and bakery ovens. Some of its angles were set to deflect cannonballs. Christophe planned, in an invasion, to burn the crops and food stocks along the coast and retreat to the fortress, setting ambushes along the single mountain path.

Christophe suffered a stroke in 1820 and some of his troops mutinied. Shortly afterwards he killed himself, according to legend with a silver bullet, and loyal followers covered his body in quicklime and entombed it in a courtyard of the Citadelle to prevent others mutilating it. The fortress was eventually abandoned. UNESCO designated it a World Heritage Site in 1982 together with the Sans-Souci Palace.

It is one of the largest fortresses in the New World, appears on Haitian currency and stamps, and is a symbol of Haitian independence. It has been repaired several times, including in the 1980s with the help of UNESCO and the World Monuments Fund. On 11 April 2026 at least 30 people were crushed to death in a stampede at the fortress, according to initial reports.
citania-de-briteiros: The site lies on Monte de São Romão, a small promontory about 15 km north-west of Guimarães, above the Ave River and an early north-south route between the Douro and Minho valleys. Four lines of walls enclose a roughly oval plan whose main platform measures 250 by 150 metres, within a site of about 24 hectares. The walls, of dry stone, are 1 to 3 metres thick. Unusually for a castro, its streets form a rough grid, with around 100 family compounds on the acropolis, each holding one to three circular stone houses around a paved courtyard. Estimates put the population at around 625 on the acropolis and perhaps 1,500 in all.

Monte de São Romão was a favoured place for rock engravings of the Atlantic Bronze Age early in the first millennium BCE, and many engraved boulders were later cut up to build ramparts and houses. Pottery shows the settlement was already fortified in the early Iron Age, but most of the visible ruins date from the last two centuries BCE. Coins, chiefly of Augustus and Tiberius, record the expansion of the Roman Empire into the region, though Roman influence on the buildings is slight. Occupation declined from the 1st century CE, few people lived within the ramparts by the 2nd century, and in the High Middle Ages a chapel and graveyard were built on the acropolis.

Martins Sarmento bought the land, reconstructed a pair of dwellings and bequeathed the site and his papers to the Sociedade Martins Sarmento. From the 1930s to the 1960s Mário Cardozo uncovered much of the eastern slope, and further surveys followed in the 1970s and in 2002, 2005 and 2006.

The site was classified as a Portuguese National Monument in 1910, and about 7 of its 24 hectares can be visited. Its bath, found by chance during road work in the 1930s, is the best-preserved building of its kind in northern Portugal and Galicia. Since 2004 the University of Minho and the Sociedade Martins Sarmento have worked together on its study and conservation.
citarum-river: The Citarum River, more correctly the Tarum River since the prefix Ci simply means river, is the longest and largest river in West Java and the third longest on the island after the Bengawan Solo and the Brantas. It plays an important part in the life of the people of West Java.

Its basin covers 6,929 square kilometres and holds about five million people. The river flows through a tropical monsoon climate: the annual average temperature is 24 °C, with April the warmest month at around 26 °C and January the coldest at 22 °C, and average annual rainfall is 2,646 mm, January being the wettest month and September the driest.

In Indonesian history the Citarum is linked with the Tarumanagara kingdom of the 4th century. The kingdom and the river share an etymology, from tarum, the Sundanese word for the indigo plant. Earlier still, the prehistoric Buni clay pottery-making culture of the 4th century BCE flourished near the river's mouth. Stone inscriptions, Chinese sources and archaeological sites such as Batujaya and Cibuaya suggest that people lived and civilisation grew in the estuaries and river valleys from the 4th century and probably earlier.

Three hydroelectric dams stand on the river, Saguling, Cirata and Ir. H. Djuanda, also called Jatiluhur, supplying electricity to the Bandung and Greater Jakarta areas. Their waters irrigate the rice paddies of Karawang and Bekasi, which makes the northern lowlands of West Java one of the most productive rice-farming areas. The Jatiluhur Dam holds 3 billion cubic metres, forming the largest reservoir in Indonesia, a freshwater lake of 83 square kilometres. The river supplies around 80 per cent of the surface water available to the people who use it.

Industrial waste, in particular from textile factories in Bandung and Cimahi, has heavily polluted the river. In December 2008 the Asian Development Bank approved a loan of 500 million dollars for cleaning it. A revitalisation programme began in November 2011, and in February 2018 President Joko Widodo launched a seven-year plan to clean the whole river, ordering 7,000 soldiers to clean allocated sections.
citeaux-abbey: Cîteaux Abbey stands in Saint-Nicolas-lès-Cîteaux, south of Dijon. When the monks arrived the site was wooded and swampy, in a sparsely populated area. The place name is older than the abbey and its origin is uncertain. One theory derives it from the Latin cis tertium, this side of the third milestone, on the Roman road linking Langres and Chalons sur Saône; another from cisternae, which in Middle Latin could mean the stagnant pools of a swamp.

The abbey was founded on 21 March 1098, Saint Benedict's Day, by monks of Molesme Abbey led by Robert of Molesme, its first abbot. Renaud, Vicomte de Beaune, and Odo I, Duke of Burgundy, supported it. The second abbot was Alberic and the third Stephen Harding, who wrote the Carta Caritatis describing the organisation of the order.

In 1111 the monastery produced the illuminated manuscript known as the Cîteaux Moralia in Job. Bernard of Clairvaux, a monk of Cîteaux, was sent in 1115 to found Clairvaux Abbey and became its first abbot. His influence helped the order grow rapidly. By the early 13th century it had more than 500 houses.

The great church, begun about 1140 and finished in 1193, became the burial place of the Dukes of Burgundy. As head of the order the abbey had to house the delegates of the annual chapter and the ducal family, which shaped its buildings. During the Hundred Years' War it was pillaged in 1360, 1365, 1434 and 1438. Soldiers looted it in 1589, reportedly carrying off three hundred wagonloads of booty, and monastic life was not firmly re-established until about 1610.

In 1790, after the French Revolution, the monks were offered pensions to return to civilian life. Fourteen refused and twenty-nine accepted. The government seized and sold the abbey, and the local population looted what remained. From 1846 an agricultural penitentiary colony for minors, run by Father Joseph Rey, occupied the site, and an 1888 scandal over its conditions was raised in the National Assembly. Trappist monks, the first four from Sept-Fons arriving on 2 October 1898, resumed monastic life.

Cîteaux belongs to the Trappists, also called the Cistercians of the Strict Observance, and has about 35 monks. The community makes a cheese under the abbey's name, as well as caramels and honey-based candies. Three old buildings survive: the library of 1509, the Définitoire and the Lenoir building of 1771, classified as historic monuments by decree of 28 December 1978. The ninth centenary of the founding in 1998 was marked by the renovation of the church.
ciudad-bolivar: Ciudad Bolívar lies where the Orinoco River narrows to about 1 mile (1.6 km) in width. It is the site of the first bridge across the river and a major river port for the eastern regions of Venezuela. Moriche palms and scrub oaks grow on the shores of the river, and the local fauna include capybaras, turtles, herons, parrots and iguanas. The climate is tropical savanna, with a dry season from December to April and a wet season from May to early November.

The settlement began as a Spanish fortified port called Santo Tomé de Guayana, which had to be moved on three occasions because Carib peoples and European rivals, such as the Dutch and English, kept attacking it. The first settlements lay downstream from the present city. Dutch forces destroyed the town in 1579. A second settlement was founded in 1595 by Don Antonio de Berrío. One of Walter Raleigh's expeditions sacked it in 1617, and Raleigh's son Watt died in the fighting. Fernando de Berrío refounded the town in 1620, but English and Dutch pirates destroyed it in 1629 and the Dutch burned it again in 1637.

The fourth and present city was officially founded in 1764 by Don Joaquín Moreno de Mendoza, with names that included San Tomé de Angostura, after its diocese and its position at the first narrows of the Orinoco. Angostura became the capital of Guayana Province and the seat of the Congress of Angostura from 1819 to 1821, which was responsible for the creation of Gran Colombia. Angostura bitters were invented in the city in 1824, although the company that made them later moved to Trinidad and Tobago. The city took the name Ciudad Bolívar in 1846, in honour of Simon Bolívar.

Ciudad Bolívar is the capital of Bolívar State. Its well-preserved historic centre has a cathedral and other colonial buildings around the Plaza Bolívar. The Jesús Soto Museum of Modern Art, designed by the Venezuelan architect Carlos Raúl Villanueva and opened in 1973, honours the sculptor and painter Jesús Soto, a native of the city. The guitarist and composer Antonio Lauro was also born there. The state economy rests on agriculture and animal husbandry, and the city has several universities, among them the Universidad de Oriente's Bolívar campus, created in 1960.
ciudad-perdida: Ciudad Perdida lies in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta and is also called Teyuna and Buritaca-200. In 1972 a family of treasure looters, Los Sepúlvedas, found it when a bird they had shot fell on a series of stone steps rising up the mountainside. Gold figures and ceramic urns soon appeared on the black market, which alerted archaeologists, and a team from the Instituto Colombiano de Antropología reached the site in 1976. It was reconstructed between 1976 and 1982. Members of local peoples, notably the Kogi, say they visited regularly before it was widely reported. They call it Teyuna and hold that it was the heart of a network of villages of their forebears, the Tairona.

The city is believed to have been founded about 800 CE, some 650 years before Machu Picchu, and was built by the Tairona. It has 169 terraces cut into the mountainside, a network of tiled roads and several small circular plazas, and the entrance can be reached only by climbing 1,200 stone steps through dense jungle. It was most likely the political and manufacturing centre of the region on the Buritaca River and may have housed 2,000 to 8,000 people. The Tairona were forced to leave it sometime in the 16th century, after years of trade and conflict.

The area was affected by the Colombian armed conflict, and in September 2003 the ELN kidnapped eight foreign tourists there, releasing the last three months later. Tourist hikes resumed in 2005. Colombia's national parks service and the Colombian Institute of Anthropology and History manage the area with Indigenous communities, who take part in decisions about the territory. Since 2009 the Global Heritage Fund has worked to protect the site from climate, vegetation, looting and unsustainable tourism.
ciudad-real: Ciudad Real lies in the southern half of the Inner Plateau, in the centre of the Iberian Peninsula, at about 625 metres above sea level. It belongs to the Campo de Calatrava, a transitional region between the Montes and La Mancha that is unusual in the peninsula for its volcanic origin; the Plaza del Pilar is built at the centre of a shallow volcanic maar. No major river passes through the city, which lies between the Guadiana to the north and its tributary the Jabalón to the south. It stands at the crossroads of the Madrid–Andalusia and Levante–Portugal routes but did not particularly prosper from this.

Villa Real, the Royal Town, was founded in 1255 under Alfonso X as a royal demesne town, with a charter modelled on that of Cuenca, over the hamlet of Pozuelo de San Gil. As an independent royal enclave within the dominion of the Order of Calatrava, it struggled at first to attract settlers, and the Order set up a rival market at nearby Miguelturra. Friction reached its climax about 1323 in armed conflict. A middle-sized jewry was documented by 1290, and the local aljama was largely dismantled in the pogroms of 1391. The town hosted the Cortes of Castile in 1346.

Juan II of Castile made it a city in 1420, with probably no more than 2,000 inhabitants. It became capital of the province of La Mancha in 1691, and many of the buildings that followed were destroyed by the Lisbon earthquake of 1755. French troops occupied it in 1809. After the territorial division of 1833, Almagro and Manzanares challenged its status as provincial capital without success. Much of the centre was destroyed in the Spanish Civil War.

Ciudad Real is the capital of its province in Castile–La Mancha. Only two parts of the medieval wall stand, including the Toledo Gate. The Church of Santiago dates from the end of the 13th century and the Church of San Pedro from the 14th and 15th centuries. The cathedral, built in the 16th century, has the second-largest nave in Spain.
ciudad-vieja: Jorge de Alvarado founded the city for the Captaincy General of Guatemala after the earlier capital at Tecpán Guatemala became untenable. Its exact first site was already disputed in 1818, when the historian Domingo Juarros noted that some authors placed it at Almolonga and others on the old court of King Sinacam in the Tzacualpa valley. Either way, the cabildo settled the city on the edge of the plain at the foot of the south-west slope of the Volcán de Agua, and it was declared the capital of the province and quickly grew in importance.

Beatriz de la Cueva had been appointed governor by the city council after the death of her husband, the adelantado Pedro de Alvarado. Grieving, she signed the council's documents on 9 September 1541 as la sin ventura, the hapless one. After the disaster the survivors met in permanent session on 17 and 18 September and named Bishop Francisco Marroquín and her brother Francisco de la Cueva interim governors. On 27 September a commission of two auxiliary majors and eleven civilians set out to inspect the surrounding land and recommended the Tianguecillo valley, but the engineer Juan Bautista Antonelli advised the Panchoy valley instead, which the volcanoes could never flood, which hills guarded to the north and which had plenty of water and flat ground.

The chroniclers ascribed the disaster to the bursting of a lake in the crater of the Volcán de Agua, along with supernatural signs. Anne Cary Maudslay, who visited the region in 1895 with her husband, the archaeologist Alfred Percival Maudslay, and climbed the volcano, judged this improbable in her book A Glimpse at Guatemala: the break in the crater wall faces the other way, and no water flowing from it could have reached the town. She suggested that heavy rain dammed in one of the deep gullies on the slope, followed by a landslip, would account for the damage. The Guatemalan writer José Milla y Vidaurre set his novel La hija del Adelantado in the months before the city's destruction.

Ciudad Vieja is a town and municipality of the department of Sacatepéquez. The 2018 census counted 32,802 people in the town and 33,405 in the municipality, and the district holding the ruins of the old capital is now called San Miguel Escobar.
cius: Cius stood at the head of the Gulf of Cius, the Cianus Sinus, on the Propontis, at the foot of Mount Arganthonius, on the borders of Bithynia and Mysia; Herodotus and Xenophon both placed it in Mysia. Pliny the Elder called it a Milesian colony. Its position made it the port for the inland country, and Pomponius Mela called it the most convenient emporium of Phrygia. The river Cius may have been the channel by which Lake Ascania, now Lake Iznik, drained into the gulf.

Ancient writers gave the city a mythical founding. Strabo named its founder as an Argonaut returning from Colchis, at the place where the nymphs carried off Hylas, the companion of Herakles, and in his day the people held a festival in which they marched into the forests calling Hylas. Apollonius of Rhodes said instead that the city took its name from a nearby river and was founded by the Argonaut Polyphemus.

During the Ionian Revolt of 499 to 493 BCE the Persian general Hymaees captured Cius, and the city later belonged to the Delian League. During the Cretan War of 205 to 200 BCE, when Cius was a member of the Aetolian League, Philip V of Macedon besieged and razed it with the help of Prusias I of Bithynia, who restored it under the name Prusias. According to the numismatist Katja Sommer, under Roman rule the city went back to the name Cius by the reign of Claudius, possibly to gain autonomy, and became Prusias again in the Flavian period.

Cius became an early Christian bishopric. Its bishop Cyrillus took part in the First Council of Nicaea in 325, and Theosebius attended the Council of Ephesus. First a suffragan of Nicomedia, it became an autocephalous archdiocese and is listed as such from the 7th century; the Catholic Church now lists it as a titular see.

Few remains of the ancient town and its harbour survive, and the town of Gemlik in Bursa Province lies a little to the west. After the population exchange of 1923 Greek refugees from Cius founded Nea Kios in Argolis and the village of Paralia in Pieria.
ciutadella-de-roses: The citadel lies in the municipality of Roses, in the Alt Empordà comarca of the Province of Girona, on the Gulf of Roses. Near it stand the Castell de la Trinitat and the monastery of Santa Maria de Roses, the earliest known example there of the Lombard architectural style. Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor, ordered the present citadel and the Castell de la Trinitat built to protect the town from pirates and from the French, making the citadel the centre of the defences of the whole gulf.

The site goes back to the 4th century BCE, when Greeks from Massalia set up a trading centre on the gulf that had to be defended from the Iberians. Over the following century it minted coins inscribed ΡΟΔΗΤΩΝ, with the head of Arethusa on one side and a rose on the other. The Romans, under Marcus Porcius Cato, sacked the city, and the Roman colony founded afterwards lasted almost to the end of the Roman Empire. In the second half of the 1st century CE Roses was made a town, with a temple to Minerva inside the walls and one to Venus in the nearby mountains.

In the 7th century the Visigoths built a fort on one of the Puig Rom peaks, used until the early 8th century. After a short Arab occupation Roses came under the county of Empúries. Benedictine monks founded the Monastery of Santa Maria in 960, and it soon became an important abbey with its own fishing rights; the name Roses was granted to the settlement only in 1362. After the French burned the town, Roger of Lauria's Aragonese fleet defeated a French fleet in the bay and freed it in 1285, and walls followed in 1402.

Once the Habsburg Empire was formed, the port linked the Spanish and Italian parts of the empire. After an epidemic in 1588 the monks left, the monastery was attached by papal order to Santa Maria de Amer in 1592, its last occupants abandoned it in 1792, and French troops destroyed it the following year.
civic-forum: Civic Forum set out to unite the dissident forces of Czechoslovakia and bring down the Communist regime, which gave up power in November 1989 after only ten days of protests. The playwright Václav Havel, its founder and leader, was elected president on 29 December 1989. The movement had a very loose structure, and most of its self-appointed leaders were Prague members of the Charter 77 dissident movement.

In the first free elections in Czechoslovakia since 1946, Civic Forum won 36 percent of the vote, the highest share any Czechoslovak party ever obtained in a free election. Its 68 seats in the Chamber of Deputies, with the 19 of Public Against Violence, gave it a strong majority, although it had no clear political strategy beyond the elections. Jan Urban, chairman after Havel became president, resigned in June 1990, saying he did not want a rift between the movement and the president.

On 16 October 1990 Václav Klaus was elected chairman. His policies were opposed by other leading figures, and the movement already held distinct wings: the Interparliamentary Club of the Democratic Right under Klaus, the centrist Liberal Club, and a Social Democratic Club led by Rudolf Battěk, which became the Association of Social Democrats.
