At its congress in January 1991 the movement divided. The right wing formed the Civic Democratic Party, with a clearer free-market programme, and elected Klaus its chairman in February 1991. The centrists, led by the federal foreign minister Jiří Dienstbier, formed the Civic Movement. Klaus said the two would govern as a coalition until 1992, but in July 1991 he declared the cooperation over. In the elections of 1992 the Civic Democratic Party won, while the Civic Movement fell short of the five percent threshold and later disappeared.
civic-united-front: The Civic United Front, in Swahili Chama Cha Wananchi, the Party of Citizens, is a liberal party. It was formed on 28 May 1992 by the merger of KAMAHURU, a pressure group for democratisation in Zanzibar, and the Civic Movement, a human rights organisation on the mainland. Many of its leaders were former stalwarts of the ruling Chama Cha Mapinduzi (CCM), some expelled over disputes about party and government policy. The party received full recognition on 21 January 1993.

In 1995 its candidate Ibrahim Lipumba came third in the presidential election with 6.43% of the vote, and the party won 24 of 232 elective seats, becoming the largest opposition party in the National Assembly. In Zanzibar, Seif Shariff Hamad took 49.76% of the vote against 50.24% for CCM's Salmin Amour, and the CUF won 24 of 50 elective seats in the House of Representatives. Observers at home and abroad sharply criticised the conduct of the Zanzibar polls, and the CUF boycotted the House and refused to recognise the island government. In November 1997 eighteen of its leaders were arrested and charged with treason; the charges were later dropped.

In the election of 29 October 2000 Lipumba came second to Benjamin Mkapa with 16.26%, and the CUF remained the largest opposition party with 17 seats. In Zanzibar, Hamad took 32.96% against 67.04% for Amani Abeid Karume. Observers judged the mainland vote largely free and fair but noted serious irregularities in Zanzibar, and when the electoral commission annulled the results in only 16 constituencies, the CUF boycotted the new polls of 5 November 2000.

On 30 October 2005 Hamad again came second to Karume in Zanzibar, with 46.07%, and the party won 19 seats in the House of Representatives. In the national elections of 14 December 2005 Lipumba finished a distant second to Jakaya Kikwete with 11.68%, and the CUF won 19 of the directly elected seats in the National Assembly.
cividale-del-friuli: Cividale del Friuli, in Friulian Cividât and in Slovene Čedad, lies in the Friuli-Venezia Giulia region of north-eastern Italy, 135 metres above sea level in the foothills of the eastern Alps and close to the Slovenian border. It stands on the river Natisone, which forms a picturesque ravine and splits the town in two. In the Iron Age the area was settled by Veneti and Celts.

Because of its strategic position on the north-eastern frontier of Roman Italy, the Romans founded a castrum there in 50 BCE, which Julius Caesar transformed into a forum named Forum Iulii. After Aquileia was destroyed in 452, Forum Iulii became the chief town of the district, which took its name from it. In 568 it was the first major centre occupied by Alboin's Lombard invasion of Italy, and Alboin gave it to his nephew Gisulf as capital of the Lombard Duchy of Friuli. After the Franks defeated the Lombards in 774, the town was renamed Civitas Austriae, Charlemagne's City of the East.

The patriarchs of Aquileia resided there from 773 to 1031, and it became the capital of the Patriarchal State of Friuli when that was founded in 1077. When the patriarchs moved on to Udine in 1238, a rivalry began between the two towns that ended only when they surrendered to Venice, Cividale in 1419 or 1420. A church council held there in 1409 by Pope Gregory XII was poorly attended and achieved nothing. After the Napoleonic Wars Cividale became part of the Kingdom of Lombardy–Venetia, and it passed to the Kingdom of Italy in 1866.

Cividale is a quiet small town that attracts visitors with its medieval centre, which holds the National Archaeological Museum and the Duomo, built in the 15th century over an 8th-century building. A silver altarpiece of Patriarch Pellegrino II, made between 1195 and 1204, is inscribed with individual letter punches. The Oratorio di Santa Maria in Valle, also called the Lombard Temple, shows strong Byzantine influence. The part of the historical centre dating from Lombard times was added to the UNESCO list in 2011.
civil-disobedience: The practice is older than the term. An early depiction is in Sophocles' play Antigone, in which Antigone defies King Creon of Thebes, who forbids her to give her brother Polynices a proper burial, and says she must obey her conscience rather than human law. The earliest recorded collective incident took place under the Roman Empire, when unarmed Jews gathered in the streets to prevent the installation of pagan images in the Temple in Jerusalem. Conrad Grebel and the Anabaptists advocated civil disobedience to oppression, and Étienne de La Boétie, in his Discours de la servitude volontaire of 1552, was one of the first to propose non-cooperation as an effective weapon.

Henry David Thoreau's essay Resistance to Civil Government, first published in 1849 and published after his death in 1866 as Civil Disobedience, popularised the term in the United States. Mahatma Gandhi wrote in 1935 that he had not drawn the idea from Thoreau, since resistance to authority in South Africa was well advanced before he read the essay, and that he came to prefer the phrase civil resistance.

Civil disobedience is the active and professed refusal of a citizen to obey certain laws, demands or orders of a government or other authority. Some definitions require it to be nonviolent, as Black's Law Dictionary does, while others, such as that of Christian Bay, require only carefully chosen and legitimate means. Howard Zinn noted that some campaigns classed as nonviolent, such as the Birmingham campaign, included elements of violence. Writers also distinguish revolutionary from non-revolutionary disobedience, and collective from solitary acts such as Thoreau's.

It concerns a citizen's relation to the state, not a conflict between two public bodies. Those who practise it can expect arrest, charge and punishment. Martin Luther King Jr. held that a person who breaks a law that conscience tells him is unjust, and accepts the penalty, expresses the highest respect for law. Acts that avoid punishment by concealment or flight, or a test case brought only to challenge a law's constitutionality, are generally not counted.

Governments have generally not recognised civil disobedience as legitimate. The law usually distinguishes criminal motive from criminal intent, so a protester with admirable motives may still have a criminal intent, and the saying goes that any justification must come from outside the legal system. It has been used by many movements: Susan B. Anthony in the late 19th century, Saad Zaghloul in the 1910s, Gandhi in 1920s British India, and the civil rights movement in the United States in the 1960s, in which King and James Bevel led protests. The term has also been stretched; in Marshall Cohen's words it has been used to describe everything from bringing a test case in court to taking aim at a federal official.
civil-rights-act-of-1964: In the Civil Rights Cases of 1883 the Supreme Court ruled that Congress had no power to prohibit discrimination in the private sector, which stripped the Civil Rights Act of 1875 of much of its force. The Civil Rights Act of 1957, signed by President Dwight D. Eisenhower on 9 September 1957, was the first federal civil rights law since 1875. Televised events such as the Little Rock Crisis of 1957 and the attack on protestors in the 1963 Birmingham campaign put pressure on the executive branch, and President John F. Kennedy proposed a bill in June 1963.

The House Judiciary Committee, chaired by Emanuel Celler, strengthened the bill with bans on employment discrimination and the desegregation of all publicly owned facilities. After Kennedy was assassinated on 22 November 1963, President Lyndon B. Johnson pressed for passage. The House passed it on 10 February 1964 by 290 to 130. The prohibition on sex discrimination was added by Howard W. Smith, a Virginia Democrat who strongly opposed the bill; historians debate whether he meant to defeat it or to broaden it. The Senate passed it on 19 June 1964, by 73 to 27, after a 72-day filibuster, and Johnson signed it on 2 July 1964.

Title II outlawed discrimination in hotels, restaurants, theatres and other public accommodations engaged in interstate commerce, Title IV enforced the desegregation of public schools, and Title VII prohibited employment discrimination by covered employers. Title I did not end literacy tests; the Voting Rights Act of 1965 later addressed voting qualifications. The act divided both parties: Johnson won the 1964 election by one of the largest landslides in American history, but five Southern states swung Republican. In Heart of Atlanta Motel v. United States (1964) the Supreme Court held that Congress drew its authority from the Commerce Clause.
civil-war-era-in-norway: Co-rule had long been the usual answer when two or more worthy candidates existed, and the main test of a claim was descent from Harald Fairhair in the male line, legitimate or not. In the late 1120s Harald Gille arrived from Ireland claiming to be a son of King Magnus Barefoot, proved it by ordeal of fire and swore not to claim the title while King Sigurd the Crusader or his son Magnus lived. When Sigurd died in 1130 he broke the oath, and some two dozen kings and pretenders would fight over the throne in the following century.

Harald captured Magnus in Bergen in 1135 and had him blinded and mutilated; Sigurd Slembe, another claimant, murdered Harald in 1136 and was defeated at Holmengrå in 1139. Harald's sons later fell out: Inge Crouchback's men killed Sigurd Munn in 1155, and Øystein Haraldsson was murdered in 1157. His followers then chose a ten-year-old figurehead, Håkon the Broadshouldered, a sign that factions now outlived their leaders. Inge's party answered in 1161 with the five-year-old Magnus Erlingsson, whose father Erling Skakke allied with the Church; Magnus became the first crowned king of Norway in 1163, under a written law favouring the eldest legitimate son.

From 1174 the Birkebeiner, named for the birch bark some wore as footwear, rose against Magnus. Under Sverre Sigurdsson, whose royal descent most historians doubt, they killed Erling at Kalvskinnet in 1179 and Magnus at Fimreite in 1184. The Church opposed Sverre, and in 1198 Pope Innocent III placed Norway under interdict. In 1197 his opponents formed the Bagler, named after the bishop's crosier. A settlement at Kvitsøy in 1208 left their king Philippus in the east, and in 1217 the Bagler dissolved their party and swore fealty to Håkon Håkonsson.

Contemporaries saw the era as exceptional. Theodoricus the Monk, writing about 1180, ended his history in 1130 rather than record the crimes that followed, and William of Newburgh noted around 1200 that for over a century no king of Norway had died of age or sickness.

The sagas present the wars as personal struggles made dangerous by unclear succession and shared kingship. Narve Bjørgo argued that the push towards a unitary kingdom itself triggered them, and Edvard Bull stressed regional rivalries. Older views of a contest between king and aristocracy, and later readings as a class struggle, have lost ground for lack of support in the sources. Knut Helle emphasises the steady growth of royal power, so that the wars can be seen as the final phase of Norway's unification.
civilista-party: The party arose as a counterweight to the growing power of the military in the first half of Peru's republican history, with the single purpose of establishing civilian rule, though in its early years it still made alliances with soldiers. Economic growth, some political stability and a new era of international trade and finance in the 1870s created the conditions for the country's first political party, and some held that the age needed the managerial skills of an educated, professional elite, which they saw in Manuel Pardo. Pardo was its first candidate and was elected on 2 August 1872.

Its first members were mostly newly rich merchants, planters and businesspeople, many of whom had profited from the exports of the Guano Boom. They held that the military was corrupt and fit to serve the country as soldiers rather than to rule it. Under Pardo the civilistas pursued fiscal and administrative reform, expanded public education, founded a college for the bureaucracy and a school for naval officers, and set up a National Guard with promotion by merit.

The political scientist Luis Schenoni describes the original civilista project of building the state as the clearest casualty of the War of the Pacific, since defeat weakened the national state and strengthened regional elites. After the war, and a revolution that again removed the military from power, the party played a key part in rebuilding the country, reviving its anti-military and pro-export programme. Most of its members belonged to the economic and social elite of Lima.

Most Peruvian presidents of the Aristocratic Republic, a name Peruvians gave to the period after the social elite that governed them, were civilistas. Elections in those years were limited by strict property and literacy qualifications and were often manipulated by the civilista government in office. The party ceased to be a major political force during the oncenio, the eleven years of Augusto B. Leguía's second term in power.
civita-castellana: Civita Castellana is a town and comune in the province of Viterbo, 65 kilometres north of Rome. Mount Soracte lies about 10 kilometres to the south-east. The site was settled in the Iron Age by the Italic Falisci, who called it Falerii.

After the Faliscan defeat by the Romans, the Romans built a new city about 5 kilometres away, Falerii Novi. The abandoned city was repopulated from the early Middle Ages and took the name Civita Castellana, meaning City of the Castle, first mentioned in 994. In the following centuries it was a flourishing independent commune, often disputed between the Pope and the Holy Roman Empire. Emperor Otto III died on 23 January 1002 at the castle of Paterno, whose ruins survive.

Pope Paschal II captured the city at the beginning of the 12th century, and it was later given as a fief to the Savelli by Pope Gregory XIV. Pope Sixtus IV assigned it to Cardinal Rodrigo Borgia, the future Pope Alexander VI, who began the Rocca, the citadel, designed by Antonio da Sangallo the Elder. It was completed under Pope Julius II and enlarged under him and Pope Leo X.

The town became an important road hub with its connection to the Via Flaminia in 1606 and with the Ponte Clementino, built after the Battle of Civita Castellana. In that battle, on 5 December 1798, a French army defeated a Neapolitan army while the town was part of the Roman Republic of 1798 to 1799.

The cathedral of Santa Maria Maggiore has a Cosmatesque portico erected in 1210 by Laurentius Romanus, his son Jacobus and his grandson Cosmas, with ancient columns and mosaic decoration. Its interior was modernised in the 18th century, and the high altar is made from a Paleo-Christian sarcophagus of the 3rd or 4th century. The church of Santa Chiara has a Renaissance portal of 1529, and the belltower of Santa Maria del Carmine, of the 12th century, incorporates ancient Roman spolia. The National Museum of the Faliscan Countryside houses finds from ancient Falerii and the surrounding area.
cizre: Cizre lies on the Tigris by the Syria–Turkey border, in the historical region of Upper Mesopotamia. It was founded in the 9th century as Jazirat Ibn ʿUmar by Al-Hasan ibn Umar, Emir of Mosul, on a manmade island in the river, and the name means island of the son of Umar. Its position as a river crossing and port, at the end of an old Roman road to the Mediterranean, made it an important commercial and strategic centre.

By the 12th century the town had an intellectual and religious role, with Christian and Jewish communities, four Shafi'i madrasas and two Sufi lodges outside the walls. Badr al-Din Lu'lu' acknowledged Mongol suzerainty as early as 1252. The town suffered several sackings in the 15th century, and the Aq Qoyunlu leader Uzun Hasan took it in 1456. After the Ottoman victory at Chaldiran in 1514, Idris Bitlisi persuaded the emir of Bohtan to submit to Sultan Selim I, and in 1515 Bohtan became an autonomous territory in the province of Diyarbekir.

In 1836 an Ottoman army retook the town from Muhammad Pasha of Rawanduz and replaced the emir of Bohtan with Bedir Khan Beg, who reportedly set up a munitions factory there. By the end of the 19th century Cizre had shrunk to a small district centre dominated by ruins. Its Christian population was destroyed in 1915 in the Armenian genocide and the Sayfo, and its Jews left for Israel in 1951.

Cizre is a city in Şırnak Province in Turkey, in the cultural region of Turkish Kurdistan, and is predominantly inhabited by Kurds. It received electricity and running water in the mid-1950s, and its population grew greatly from 1984 as people fled the Kurdish–Turkish conflict. As the capital of the Bohtan emirate, it was an important Kurdish cultural centre in which music, poetry and science flourished under the emirs' protection.
clan-donald: The Norse-Gaelic Clan Donald traces its descent from Dòmhnall Mac Raghnuill, who died around 1250, son of Ranald, styled King of the Isles, and grandson of Somerled, who was killed at the Battle of Renfrew in 1164. It shares that descent with Clan MacDougall. Medieval Gaelic historians traced Somerled's line back to the High Kings of Ireland, Colla Uais and Conn of the Hundred Battles, but a DNA study of 2005 found that his male line was of Norse descent.

After Alexander III of Scotland defeated Haakon IV of Norway at the Battle of Largs in 1263, the chief Aonghas Mor passed from Norwegian to Scottish overlordship. His son Aonghus Óg of Islay supported Robert the Bruce at Bannockburn in 1314. Donald of Islay married Mariota, Countess of Ross, claimed the Earldom of Ross through her and fought the Battle of Harlaw on 24 July 1411. His son Alexander of Islay was confirmed as Earl of Ross in 1437, but James III forfeited the earldom in 1475, which in many ways ended the Lordship as a power.

Attempts to restore the Lordship had all failed by 1545, and the Crown kept the branches divided by granting each its own charters. The clan's attempts to regain control destabilised the west for generations. In 1644 Alasdair Mac Colla of the Dunnyveg branch landed with 1500 Irish troops and joined Montrose's Royalist campaign. In the Massacre of Glencoe in 1692, 38 unarmed MacDonalds of Glencoe were murdered after their chief MacIain was late in swearing allegiance to William III. Several branches fought as Jacobites in 1715 and 1745, at Sheriffmuir, Prestonpans, Falkirk Muir and Culloden, while the Sleat branch raised two companies for the government in 1745.

The Lord Lyon King of Arms recognises a High Chief of Clan Donald and the chiefs of several branches, among them Sleat, Clanranald, Keppoch, Glencoe, Glengarry and MacAlister; the MacDonnells of Antrim have a chief recognised in Ireland. In 1947 Alexander Godfrey Macdonald, 7th Lord Macdonald, became the first High Chief. The Lords of the Isles had their seat at Finlaggan on Islay, and Armadale Castle on Skye, begun in 1815, now houses the Clan Donald Centre and the Museum of the Isles.
clan-douglas: The family took its name from the village of Douglas in Lanarkshire, a name modern writers derive from the Gaelic dubh, dark or black, and glas, stream. A tradition that the first chief was Sholto Douglas, who helped a king of Scotland win a battle in 767, is unsubstantiated and likely pseudohistory. The first certain record of the name is William Douglas, Lord of Douglas in 1179, who witnessed a charter of the Bishop of Glasgow to the monks of Kelso. Two sons of his grandson fought against the Norsemen at the Battle of Largs in 1263.

In the Wars of Scottish Independence Sir William Douglas le Hardi, governor of Berwick-upon-Tweed, was captured when the English besieged the town, later joined William Wallace, and died a prisoner in the Tower of London in 1298. His son James, the Good Sir James, shared Robert the Bruce's defeats at Methven and Dalrigh in 1306, then waged the guerrilla warfare the Scots called secret war, recaptured Roxburgh Castle in 1313 and fought at Bannockburn in 1314.

Archibald Douglas, 3rd Earl of Douglas, defended Edinburgh Castle against Henry IV of England in 1400. His son, the 4th Earl, was taken prisoner at the Battle of Shrewsbury in 1403, became one of the regents for the young James I of Scotland, led 10,000 Scots to the aid of Charles VII of France in 1423, was made Duke of Touraine and was killed at the Battle of Verneuil on 17 August 1424. Of the Red Douglases, two sons of Archibald Douglas, 5th Earl of Angus, fell at Flodden in 1513, and the 6th Earl married Margaret Tudor and won the Battle of Ancrum Moor in 1545.

In 1660 William Douglas, brother of the second Marquess of Douglas, became Duke of Hamilton through marriage, and the titles of Marquess of Douglas and Earl of Angus later passed to the Dukes of Hamilton. Because their surname is Douglas-Hamilton, the Lord Lyon does not recognise them as chiefs, and the clan has no recognised chief. A Swedish branch descends from Robert Douglas, who went to Sweden in 1627 as an officer in the Thirty Years' War, was made a count in 1654 and built Stjärnorp Castle in Östergötland from 1655.
clan-macdougall: The clan takes its name from Dougall (Dubgall), whose Gaelic name means dark foreigner. After his father Somerled died at the Battle of Renfrew in 1164, Dougall held most of Argyll and the islands of Mull, Lismore, Jura, Tiree and Coll, and was styled King of the South Isles and Lord of Lorne, his royal descent acknowledged by the king of Norway. His son Duncan and grandson Ewan built castles at Dunstaffnage, Dunollie and Duntrune on the mainland and Aros and Cairnburgh on the islands, and Duncan founded Ardchattan Priory, where the chiefs were buried until 1737.

Ewan held his islands from the king of Norway and his mainland lands from the king of Scotland. When King Haakon IV of Norway arrived off Oban with a fleet in 1263, Ewan refused to join him and fought on the Scottish side at the Battle of Largs. In 1294 John MacDougall of Argyll led the clan against the Campbells at the Battle of Red Ford, where Sir Colin Campbell was killed. The killing of John Comyn III, a kinsman by marriage, by Robert the Bruce in 1306 set the clan against Bruce, whom they defeated at the Battle of Dalrigh.

After Bruce's victory at the Pass of Brander the king gave their lands to the Campbells. John's grandson, John Gallda MacDougall, came back from England in the mid-14th century, married a niece of David II, King of Scotland, and regained most of the mainland lands by royal charter, though the lordship of Lorne later passed to the Stewarts. The clan fought the Stewarts of Appin at the Battle of Stalc in 1468, sided with the royalists in the civil war of the 17th century and fought for the Jacobites at Sheriffmuir; some clansmen fought at Culloden in 1746.

Dunollie Castle near Oban, a site fortified since the days of the kings of Dál Riata, was sacked and burnt by a Covenanter army under David Leslie in 1647 and abandoned after Dunollie House was built nearby in 1746; it still belongs to the MacDougalls. Bruce made Dunstaffnage Castle a royal castle with the Campbells as keepers, and it is now in the care of Historic Scotland. Robert the Bruce lost the Brooch of Lorne at Dalrigh, and it became one of the clan's great treasures. The chief, recognised by the Lord Lyon King of Arms, represents the senior line of Somerled's descendants.
clan-sinclair: The name, de Sancto Claro in French and Sanctus Clarus in Latin, derives from the hermit St. Clare and from St. Clair-sur-Epte near Paris. No certain record exists, but the family probably came from Saint-Clair in Normandy and reached England with William the Conqueror; Richard and Brittel of Saint-Clair appear in the Domesday Book. William of Saint-Clair is said to have escorted Saint Margaret to Scotland in 1068 and to have been granted the barony of Roslin in return.

William St. Clair commanded a wing of Alexander III's army against Haakon IV of Norway at the Battle of Largs in 1263. In the Wars of Scottish Independence Sir William Sinclair of Rosslyn was captured at Dunbar in 1296, while Henry Sinclair of Rosslyn helped defeat the English at Roslin in 1303 and, with Robert the Bruce, at Loudoun Hill in 1307. The clan fought for Bruce at Bannockburn in 1314, and Sir William Sinclair was among the Scots killed with Sir James Douglas at Teba in 1330.

William Sinclair, 1st Earl of Caithness, High Chancellor of Scotland from 1454 to 1458, received Caithness in 1455 and divided the family lands, passing over his eldest son, William the Waster, who became Lord Sinclair. William Sinclair, 2nd Earl of Caithness, was killed at the Battle of Flodden in 1513 with 300 Sinclairs, and in the 16th century the clan feuded with the Clan Sutherland. A dispute with Sir John Campbell of Glenorchy over the earldom led to the Battle of Altimarlach, but in 1681 Parliament restored it to the Sinclairs.

The clan supported the Jacobites in 1715. In 1745 many Sinclairs had Jacobite sympathies, but their chief, the Earl of Caithness, backed the government; only about thirty men under Sinclair of Scotscalder answered the call of the Jacobite Lord MacLeod, and Sir James Sinclair of Rosslyn commanded the Royal Scots for the government at Culloden in 1746.

Besides Rosslyn Chapel, the Sinclairs built or held Roslin Castle, their earliest seat in Scotland, Castle Sinclair Girnigoe near Wick, the Castle of Mey, sold in 1952 to Queen Elizabeth The Queen Mother, and Ravenscraig Castle in Kirkcaldy, one of the first in Britain built for artillery. The Sinclairs of Roslin claimed to be hereditary Grand Master Masons of Scotland, and William St Clair became the first elected Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Scotland.
clann-ruaidhri: The kindred was a branch of Clann Somhairle, alongside Clann Dubhghaill and Clann Domhnaill. Its eponym, Ruaidhrí mac Raghnaill, Lord of Argyll, was a son of Raghnall mac Somhairle and a grandson of Somhairle mac Giolla Brighde, King of the Isles, whose death in battle in 1164 left his descendants to split into rival segments. Ruaidhrí, styled Lord of Kintyre, raided Derry with Thomas fitz Roland, Earl of Atholl, in 1213/1214 and seems to have arranged marriages with the Crovan dynasty, before being driven from Kintyre by Alexander II, King of Scotland, in the early 1220s.

Ruaidhrí's son Dubhghall killed Jordan d'Exeter, the English Sheriff of Connacht, in 1258, and the next year gave a daughter in marriage to Aodh na nGall Ó Conchobhair with a tocher of one hundred and sixty gallowglass warriors led by his brother Ailéan, among the earliest known warriors of that kind. Dubhghall sought the kingship of the Isles from Hákon Hákonarson, King of Norway, fought in Hákon's campaign of 1263, and refused to submit to the Scots until Norway ceded the Isles to Scotland in 1266.

Ailéan then served the Scottish Crown, commanding in the invasion of Mann in 1275 and attending the council at Scone in 1284 that named Margaret as heir. His sons Lachlann and Ruaidhrí fought the Earl of Ross and Clann Domhnaill for Skye and Lewis, and his daughter Cairistíona is said to have sheltered Robert I when he was a fugitive after seizing the throne. After she resigned her claims, Ruaidhrí received a lordship of Moidart, Arisaig, Morar, Knoydart, Rhum, Eigg, Barra, St Kilda and Uist, comparable to an earldom; he probably fell at the Battle of Faughart in 1318.

Clann Ruaidhrí gallowglasses fought for Irish kings into the 14th century; the last of their captains on record was killed in 1342. Ruaidhrí's son Ranald MacRuairi, confirmed in the lordship by David II in 1343 and granted Kintail by William III, Earl of Ross, was murdered by the earl's men at Elcho Priory in October 1346. The lands passed through his sister Amy to John of Islay, and their son Raghnall Mac Domhnaill, apparently named after his uncle, became the ancestor of Clann Raghnaill.
clara-schumann: Clara Josephine Wieck was born in Leipzig on 13 September 1819 to Friedrich Wieck and Mariane, born Tromlitz, who sang and played piano at the Gewandhaus. Her parents divorced in 1825, and five-year-old Clara stayed with her father. After her mother left he taught her daily in piano, violin, singing, theory, harmony, composition and counterpoint, followed by two hours of practice, to the detriment of her general education. She began touring at eleven and succeeded in Paris and Vienna, among other cities.

Robert Schumann, a little more than nine years older, proposed in 1837. Friedrich Wieck refused his permission, so the couple sued him, and the judge allowed the marriage, which took place on 12 September 1840, the day before her 21st birthday. They had eight children. Clara premiered many of Robert's works and earned money by giving concerts, and the burden of family duties narrowed her scope as a composer. After his early death she toured Europe for decades, often with the violinist Joseph Joachim, and gave sixteen winter-spring tours of England between 1865 and 1888. From 1878 she taught piano at Dr. Hoch's Konservatorium in Frankfurt and edited her husband's works.

More than 1,300 programmes of her concerts between 1831 and 1889 survive. Her early repertoire, chosen by her father, was showy; later she played Scarlatti and Bach, and above all contemporaries such as Chopin, Mendelssohn, her husband and Johannes Brahms. Her Op. 1, the Quatre Polonaises, dates from 1831, and she wrote her Piano Concerto in A minor at fourteen. After marriage she turned to songs and choral works, and published one joint work with Robert in 1841, settings of Friedrich Rückert. She died on 20 May 1896 after a stroke and was buried in Bonn beside her husband, as she wished. Interest in her compositions revived in the late 20th century.
clara-zetkin: Clara Josephine Eißner was born in July 1857 in Wiederau, a peasant village in Saxony, the eldest of three children of a schoolmaster and church organist and a highly educated mother of French roots. The family moved to Leipzig in 1872, and she was educated at the Leipzig Teachers' College for Women, where she made contact with the young Social Democratic Party. Socialist activity was banned in Germany in 1878. She left for Zürich in 1882 and then went into exile in Paris, where she took the name of her partner Ossip Zetkin. After his death in June 1889 she moved to Stuttgart.

Zetkin edited the party's women's newspaper Die Gleichheit until 1917 and in 1907 became leader of its Women's Office. She rejected what she called bourgeois feminism and argued that the emancipation of women could be solved only by a complete social transformation. In August 1910 she, Käte Duncker and others proposed at the International Women's Conference in Copenhagen an annual women's day, first marked on 19 March 1911 by over a million people in Austria, Denmark, Germany and Switzerland. About 1898 she began a twenty-year friendship with Rosa Luxemburg.

She rejected the party's wartime truce, organised an anti-war conference of socialist women in Berlin in 1915 and was arrested several times. She co-founded the Spartacist League in 1916 and joined the Communist Party of Germany after its founding in January 1919, representing it in the Reichstag from 1920 to 1933. The conference of Communist women that she chaired in Moscow in June 1921 changed the date of International Women's Day to 8 March. In December 1928 she was one of only three members of the Comintern executive to vote against Stalin's plan to split the Communist trade unions from the main federation.

In August 1932, as the oldest deputy, she opened the new Reichstag with a call for a united front against fascism. After the Reichstag fire and the ban on the Communist Party in 1933 she went into exile in the Soviet Union and died at Arkhangelskoye, near Moscow, aged nearly 76. Her ashes were placed in the Kremlin Wall Necropolis. After 1949 she was honoured in East Germany, where every major city had a street named after her.
claros: Claros lay on the coast of Ionia, twelve kilometres south of Colophon, one of the twelve cities of the Ionian League, and two kilometres north of the coastal city of Notion. Apollo was honoured there as Apollo Clarius, and the Claria games were held in his honour every fifth year. A sacred cave near the temple, important in Hellenistic and Roman times, points to an early cult of Cybele. In the 1st century BCE, as the hinterland was deforested, the site was buried in silt from the small river beside it.

In the founding myth the seer Manto, daughter of Teiresias, was sent by Apollo from Delphi to Ionia with captive Thebans; the Cretan Rhacius married her and let them found Claros, and their heir was the seer Mopsus, who defeated Calchas in a contest of divination. Excavation has found a religious area around a spring of fresh water from the 9th century BCE, a round altar of the later 7th century and, by the mid-6th century, a marble temple of Apollo and a precinct of Artemis.

A new temple of Apollo was begun in the 3rd century BCE, with a dark crypt-like adyton from which the oracle spoke. By legend the oracle advised the people of Smyrna to move to Mount Pagos. Pliny the Elder wrote that drinking from the pool in the Clarian cave gave the power of prophecy but shortened life, and the oracle was said to have hinted at an early doom to Germanicus, who visited in 18 CE. Fifty tons of marble columns from Proconnesos, bound for Claros, were recovered from a late Hellenistic wreck off Kizilburun found in 1993.

T. Macridy uncovered the monumental entrance in 1905 and returned with Charles Picard in 1913. Louis Robert excavated from 1950 to 1961, revealing the Doric Temple of Apollo and Roman monuments, and the Sacred Way was cleared under J. de La Genière in 1988.

The ruins lie north of Ahmetbeyli in the Menderes district of İzmir Province. The adyton's narrow vaulted corridors survive, with fragments of a colossal seated Apollo with Leto and Artemis, over seven metres high. Its inscriptions form the largest surviving assembly of Greek inscriptions, and rows of iron rings show how a hundred victims could be sacrificed at once.
classic-maya-collapse: The Maya often dated their monuments, and the count of these dates traces the decline. Around ten dated monuments a year were raised in 514, twenty a year by 672 and forty by about 750; the number then fell quickly, to ten by 800 and to none by 900. No new buildings were put up in the central Maya area after 830. Among the cities of the southern lowlands that declined and were then abandoned were Palenque, Copán, Tikal and Calakmul.

King lists tell the same story. Altar Q at Copán records a line of kings from 426 to 763, followed by Ukit Took, probably a usurper, after whom the dynasty seems to have ended. At Quirigua the last king, Jade Sky, began his rule between 795 and 800. Obsidian hydration dating in the Copán Valley gives a population of about twenty-eight thousand at its peak in 400 to 450, a steady decline from 750 to 800, about fifteen thousand by 900 and fewer than 1,000 by 1200.

The collapse did not end Maya civilisation but moved its centre away from the southern lowlands. Northern Yucatán prospered with new styles and far less hieroglyphic writing; Chichén Itzá built an empire that briefly united much of the region, Mayapán and Uxmal flourished, as did the highland states of the Kʼicheʼ and Kaqchikel. Independent Maya rule lasted until the Spanish conquest of Nojpetén in 1697. Many scholars therefore prefer to speak of a rupture or transformation; the archaeologist David Stuart sees such ruptures as a regular part of Maya history.

More than 80 explanations have been proposed, among them foreign invasion, the loss of trade, epidemic disease, ecological decline and the growing costs of social complexity, a view developed by the anthropologist Joseph Tainter. Drought has gained ground in the 21st century as the leading explanation: a study of lake gypsum published in Science in 2018 found that yearly rainfall fell by 41 to 54 percent. Critics such as David Webster note that much of the evidence of drought comes from northern Yucatán, where many centres survived, rather than from the south, where Classic civilisation had flourished.
classic-of-poetry: The collection holds the oldest chronologically authenticated Chinese poems. Most date to the Western Zhou period, 1046 to 771 BCE, and the latest song was dated by Zheng Xuan to about 700 BCE. It falls into the Airs of the States and the Hymns and Eulogies. The Airs are shorter lyrics in simple language, generally ancient folk songs on love, soldiers on campaign, farming and political satire. The Hymns and Eulogies are longer ritual songs, courtly praise and dynastic hymns for the founders of the Zhou dynasty. About 95 per cent of the lines have four syllables.

Tradition says officials collected verses current in the various states so that the king could understand the condition of the common people. Tradition also says Confucius selected the 300 songs that best conformed to ritual propriety from some 3,000. The Han historian Sima Qian was the first to attribute the work to Confucius directly, and the view is now generally discredited, since the Zuo Zhuan records the Classic of Poetry already existing in definitive form when Confucius was a child. The Analects does record Confucius telling his son that without studying the Odes there was nothing to say to him.

The Odes became a classic in the canonical sense when the Han dynasty adopted Confucianism officially. Three versions had chairs at the Imperial Academy under Emperor Wu, but the Mao tradition became dominant in the Eastern Han, and by the 5th century it alone survived as the received text. Scholars long read the songs as moral and political allegory, a tradition first doubted by Zheng Qiao in the 12th century. Since the Qing dynasty the rhymes have been studied to reconstruct Old Chinese pronunciation, and the Odes remain a source of four-character idioms still used in Chinese.
classical-antiquity: The earliest period of classical antiquity followed the Late Bronze Age collapse and the Greek Dark Ages. The 8th and 7th centuries BCE are still largely protohistorical, with the earliest Greek alphabetic inscriptions appearing in the first half of the 8th century. The poet Homer is usually assumed to have lived in the 8th or 7th century BCE, and the traditional date for the founding of the Olympic Games is 776 BCE. During the Archaic period Greeks founded colonies across the Mediterranean and the Black Sea, many of which became independent city-states, and the Phoenicians, who founded Carthage in 814 BCE, dominated Mediterranean trade. According to legend Rome was founded on 21 April 753 BCE, and the monarchy was expelled in 510 BCE.

The span covers several periods. Classical Greece runs from the end of the Athenian tyranny in 510 BCE to the death of Alexander the Great in 323 BCE, and includes the Greco-Persian Wars (499–449 BCE) and the Peloponnesian War (431–404 BCE). The Hellenistic period, from 323 to 146 BCE, ended with the Roman conquest of Greece, and Greek became a common language far beyond Greece. The Roman Republic began about 509 BCE and gave way over the 1st century BCE to the Roman Empire, which reached its widest extent under Trajan in 117 CE.

Late antiquity, from the 4th to the 6th century CE, saw Christianity displace the imperial cult through the Theodosian decrees of 393. Writers have proposed several endings: the deposition of the last Western emperor in 476, the closing of the Platonic Academy in Athens by Justinian I in 529, and the Muslim conquests of 634 to 718. The change to medieval society was slow and that no single date marks it.

The Greco-Roman foundation influenced the language, politics, law, education, philosophy, science, literature and art of the Western world. The coronation of Charlemagne as Roman Emperor in 800 led to the Holy Roman Empire, which ruled central Europe until 1806. In Constantinople the Byzantines called themselves Romans, and refugees from its fall in 1453 helped begin the Renaissance. Reverence for Roman republicanism was strong among the Founding Fathers of the United States, who gave their government a Senate and a President, and in Revolutionary France. Latin epic poetry was still written in the 19th century, and the philosophy of Thomas Aquinas drew largely on Aristotle.
classical-greece: Classical Greece is a period of around 200 years, the 5th and 4th centuries BCE. It is marked by much of the eastern Aegean and northern Greek regions, such as Ionia and Macedonia, gaining autonomy from the Persian Empire, by the peak of democratic Athens, by the Peloponnesian Wars, by the Spartan and then Theban hegemonies, and by the expansion of Macedonia under Philip II. Much of the early defining mathematics, science, architecture, sculpture, theatre, literature, philosophy and politics of Western civilisation derives from it. In the history of Greek art it follows the Archaic period and is succeeded by the Hellenistic period.

The Athenian democracy grew out of the reforms of Cleisthenes, which made the deme the basic civic unit and gave power to an assembly of citizens headed by a council of 500 chosen at random. Only men were citizens. The Ionian Greeks rose against Persia in 499 BCE, and in 490 BCE an Athenian army of 9,000 hoplites and 1,000 Plataeans defeated the Persians at Marathon. After Thermopylae the Persians were beaten at Plataea in 479 BCE. In 477 BCE Athens became leader of the Delian League, which became a front for Athenian hegemony in the Aegean.

War broke out between Athens and Sparta in 431 BCE. Plague killed many in besieged Athens, including Pericles, and the Peace of Nicias in 421 BCE brought a pause. Athens was decisively defeated in 404 BCE. The Treaty of Antalcidas in 387 BCE handed the Greek cities of Ionia and Cyprus to Persia. Thebes under Epaminondas won at Leuctra in 371 BCE, and Philip II of Macedon was drawn into Greek affairs in 346 BCE.

In 334 BCE Alexander the Great crossed the Hellespont and conquered the Achaemenid empire in less than a decade. He died in Babylon in 323 BCE, and the period conventionally ends there, as his empire was divided among the Diadochi. Post-Renaissance European elites saw themselves as the spiritual heirs of Greece, and Will Durant wrote in 1939 that, excepting machinery, there is hardly anything secular in our culture that does not come from Greece.
claude-auguste-court: Court was born at Saint-Cézaire-sur-Siagne, near Grasse, the son of Andre Ambroise Court, a captain in the French army, and Marguerite Diaque. He studied at the École Spéciale Militaire de Saint-Cyr and joined the 15th régiment de Ligne as a sub-lieutenant on 30 January 1813. He fought in the campaigns of 1813-1814, at Bautzen, Leipzig, Hanau, Champaubert and Vauchamps among other engagements, and was wounded in the left leg. Dismissed after Napoleon's defeat at Waterloo, he left France in 1818 for Baghdad and joined the Persian forces trained at Kermanshah by former officers of Napoleon, among them Jean-Baptiste Ventura.

Court, Ventura and Paolo Avitabile travelled on to Lahore, where Maharaja Ranjit Singh put Court in charge of training artillerymen, organising batteries and setting up arsenals and magazines on European lines. As director of the foundries he worked with Sardar Lehna Singh Majithia, and the Maharaja rewarded him with Rs 30,000 for the first shell cast at Lahore and Rs 5,000 for the first fuse. He drew Rs 2,500 a month besides a jagir.

His brigade joined the units raised by Jean-François Allard and Ventura, called the French Legion by British intelligence, which grew to 15,000 troops. In 1834 Court, commanding two brigades, annexed Peshawar, and he fought at Jamrud in 1837. He became a general in 1836 and around then married a Kashmiri Muslim woman, Fezli Azam Joo. After the death of Nau Nihal Singh in 1840 he backed Sher Singh, whose assassination in September 1843 led him to flee to Firozpur and return to France with his family.

Court settled between Paris and Marseille, where he was buried after his death in Paris on 21 January 1880. He made the first archaeological surveys and maps of the Punjab and the north-west as far as Kabul, was the first to excavate and record Buddhist sites there, and collected the coins of South Asia from 1829. His collection disappeared after his death; three albums of 627 coin rubbings, found at a sale in 1994, are now in the British Museum, and many of the coins passed through Alexander Cunningham's collection.
claude-dabbeville: Claude d'Abbeville was one of a mission of four friars sent under a patent letter of 1611 from the regent Marie de Médicis, together with Father Yves D'Evreux. The colonial enterprise of France Équinoxiale was led by Daniel de la Tousche, sieur de la Ravardière, and François de Razilly, and one of its aims was to establish a trade in brazilwood and tobacco. The French reached the island in August 1612, and their outpost later became the city of São Luís do Maranhão.

The Tupinambá were allied with the French in order to resist Portuguese encroachment. Claude d'Abbeville and Yves D'Evreux learned the Tupinambá language and wrote about their experience. The enterprise followed earlier Protestant attempts at a colony in South America, above all the short-lived France Antarctique, and reflected the recent dominance of the Catholic faith over Protestantism in France.

The mission sent Tupinambá from Maragnan to the court of Louis XIII, where they caused a sensation; only three of the six who set out had survived by the time they were baptised in the Church of the Capuchins. Claude wrote: "Who would have thought that Paris, used to the strange and the exotic, would go so wild over these Indians?" His Histoire de la mission des pères Capucins en l'isle de Maragnan et terres circonvoisines was published in Paris by F. Huby in 1614.

When France and Spain, which then ruled Portugal in the Iberian Union, became allies through the marriage of Louis XIII and Anne of Austria in 1615, support for the colony ended and the colonists were abandoned. The Portuguese soon expelled the French. Claude's book was removed from circulation, and a similar work by Yves D'Evreux and Francois Huby was destroyed.
claude-debussy: Debussy was the eldest of five children of Manuel-Achille Debussy and Victorine, née Manoury. His father ran a china shop that closed in 1864, after which the family moved to Paris, first living with Victorine's mother in Clichy and from 1868 in their own apartment in the Rue Saint-Honoré; his father then worked in a printing factory. At the end of 1880, while still a student, he became accompanist for Marie Moreau-Sainti's singing class. One of its members, Marie Vasnier, inspired him to compose 27 songs dedicated to her during their seven-year relationship. His cantata L'enfant prodigue won the Prix de Rome in 1884, and a friend remarked that in it he admirably imitated Massenet's turns of phrase.

Returning to Paris in 1887, Debussy heard the first act of Wagner's Tristan und Isolde and attended the Bayreuth festivals of 1888 and 1889. He was briefly influenced, but concluded there was no future in developing Wagner's style; in 1903 he called Wagner "a beautiful sunset that was mistaken for a dawn". At the Paris Exposition Universelle of 1889 he first heard Javanese gamelan music, whose echoes appear in "Pagodes" in Estampes, and he attended two concerts of Rimsky-Korsakov's music.

In December 1894 the Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune, based on a poem by Stéphane Mallarmé, was premiered at the Société Nationale; Pierre Boulez later observed that "Modern music was awakened" by it. He completed the first draft of Pelléas et Mélisande the following year and in 1903 was appointed a Chevalier of the Légion d'honneur. In 1904 he left his wife Lilly for Emma Bardac. Lilly attempted suicide on 14 October and survived, and the ensuing scandal cost him friends including Dukas and André Messager.

Debussy admired the painter Turner and drew inspiration from Whistler; he described the orchestral Nocturnes as a study in the combinations obtainable from one colour, like a study in grey in painting. He read widely and was friendly with Symbolist poets such as Mallarmé, setting many of their works. In 1904 he played piano accompaniment for Mary Garden in recordings of four of his songs, and in 1913 he made piano rolls for the Welte-Mignon company.

He died of cancer at his home in Paris on 25 March 1918. Béla Bartók said that Debussy's great service was to reawaken among musicians an awareness of harmony and its possibilities, and Igor Stravinsky wrote his Symphonies of Wind Instruments (1920) as a memorial. Roger Nichols observes that a list of twentieth-century composers influenced by Debussy is practically a list of twentieth-century composers, leaving aside Schoenberg.
claude-lorrain: He was the third of five sons of Jean Gellée and Anne Padose, born at Chamagne in the Duchy of Lorraine. The early biographers disagree about his youth. Baldinucci has him orphaned at twelve and taught drawing by an elder brother before he went to Naples and then to Agostino Tassi in Rome. Sandrart says he was apprenticed to a pastry baker and reached Rome as a servant and cook to Tassi, who made him an apprentice. Modern scholars generally prefer Sandrart or combine the two. Most agree that he trained with Goffredo Wals around 1620 to 1622 and with Tassi from about 1622 or 1623 to 1625, and by 1627 he had settled in Rome near the Spanish Steps for life.

Sandrart reported that in the late 1620s he already sketched outdoors, especially at dawn and dusk. His first dated painting is of 1629. Commissions came from the French ambassador in Rome in 1633 and from Philip IV of Spain, and Cardinal Guido Bentivoglio recommended him to Pope Urban VIII, who ordered four pictures. By the end of the 1630s he was the leading landscapist in Italy. About 1636 he began the Liber Veritatis, a book of drawings of his finished pictures with the purchasers' names on the back, whose 195 drawings are now in the British Museum. He died in Rome on 23 November 1682.

His landscapes grew larger, with fewer figures. He was not generally an innovator, except in placing the sun and its streaming light in many paintings, which had been rare before. His grand temples and palaces are mostly imagined from real buildings, and his harbour scenes show up-to-date merchant ships whatever the period of the subject. Figures were his weak point, and according to Baldinucci he joked that he charged for the landscape and gave the figures for free. After his death he became very popular with English collectors, and the UK still holds many of his works. The Claude glass, a tinted mirror used by tourists to frame views, was named after him.
claude-maxwell-macdonald: Claude Maxwell MacDonald was born on 12 June 1852, the son of Major-General James Dawson MacDonald and Mary Ellen MacDonald. He was educated at Uppingham School and Sandhurst and commissioned into the 74th Foot in 1872, and he later thought of himself as a soldier-outsider in the Foreign Office. He served in the Anglo-Egyptian War of 1882, was military attaché to Sir Evelyn Baring from 1884 to 1887 and acting agent and consul-general at Zanzibar from 1887 to 1889. In the Oil Rivers he observed the rebellion of King Koko of Nembe in 1895, and he retired from the army in 1896.

In 1896 MacDonald was appointed minister in China, and until 1898 he was also British minister to the Empire of Korea. He obtained a lease at Weihaiwei and railway contracts for British syndicates, and he was instrumental in securing the Second Peking Convention, by which China leased the New Territories of Hong Kong to Britain. He settled for a 99-year lease because he thought it as good as forever, which later complicated the negotiations for the Sino-British Joint Declaration of 1984. In 1899 his note proposed a boundary between Jammu and Kashmir and Chinese Turkestan, the Macartney–MacDonald Line, to which the Qing never replied.

During the Boxer Rebellion of 1900 he led the defence of the besieged legations, working closely with the Japanese colonel Shiba Gorō. In October 1900 he exchanged posts with Sir Ernest Satow and went to Tokyo, where he headed the British legation through the Anglo-Japanese Alliance of 30 January 1902 and its renewals in 1905 and 1911. When the legation was raised to an embassy in 1905, he became Britain's first ambassador to Japan, and he was made a Privy Councillor in 1906.

MacDonald died of heart failure at his London residence on 10 September 1915 and is buried with his wife in Brookwood Cemetery. In 1892 he had married Ethel Armstrong, who received the Royal Red Cross for tending the sick and wounded during the siege of the Peking legations and was made a Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 1935. The boundary line he proposed is still seen by scholars as relevant to the border disputes between China and India.
claude-mckay: Festus Claudius McKay was born on 15 September 1890 at Nairne Castle near James Hill in Clarendon Parish, Jamaica, the youngest of eight children of Thomas Francis McKay and Hannah Ann Elizabeth Edwards, farmers with enough property to vote. His parents were active and respected members of the Baptist faith. His father was of Ashanti descent and his mother traced her ancestry to Madagascar. His elder brother and tutor Uriah Theodore introduced him to British Fabian socialism in his teens.

McKay left for the United States in 1912 to attend Tuskegee Institute, shocked by the racism he met on arriving in Charleston, which inspired him to write more poetry. He disliked Tuskegee and moved to Kansas State Agricultural College, where he read W. E. B. Du Bois's The Souls of Black Folk. In 1914 he moved to New York City and married Eulalie Imelda Lewars, who returned to Jamaica after six months, where their daughter was born; McKay never met her.

McKay worked as a restaurant manager and a waiter, and in autumn 1919 joined the Industrial Workers of the World. He became a co-editor of The Liberator and clashed with its editor Mike Gold. In London he moved in socialist circles and wrote for Sylvia Pankhurst's Workers' Dreadnought. His poetry collection Harlem Shadows (1922) was among the first books of the Harlem Renaissance, and in 1919 he wrote the sonnet If We Must Die in response to the riots and lynchings that followed the First World War.

In November 1922 he travelled to Russia for the Fourth Congress of the Communist International and was warmly received. He concluded that the party was using him, and, critical of the regime's authoritarian bent, left for Western Europe in 1923. He spent eleven years around Europe and North Africa, publishing Home to Harlem (1928), a best-seller that won the Harmon Gold Award for Literature, then Banjo (1929) and Banana Bottom (1933). Some critics, including Du Bois, first disliked Home to Harlem's portrayal of lower-class Harlem. After returning to Harlem in 1934 he quarrelled with the Stalinist Communist Party, and became an American citizen in 1940.

In ill health in the mid-1940s, McKay joined Catholic activists, moved to Chicago in April 1944 and was baptised there in October. He died of heart failure in 1948. His Selected Poems appeared in 1953, and his Complete Poems in 2004. Unpublished novels, Harlem Glory and Amiable With Big Teeth, appeared in 1990 and 2017. In 1977 Jamaica named him its national poet and awarded him the Order of Jamaica, and his work influenced writers such as James Baldwin and Richard Wright.
claude-monet: Monet was born in Paris on 14 November 1840 and baptised Oscar-Claude. His family moved to Le Havre in 1845, where his mother, a singer, supported his wish to become an artist. In 1862 he joined the studio of Charles Gleyre, where he met Frédéric Bazille, who became his closest friend.

He married Camille on 28 June 1870, shortly before the Franco-Prussian War, and lived in London and the Netherlands to avoid conscription. In London he met the dealer Paul Durand-Ruel, an encounter decisive for his career, and admired the works of John Constable and J. M. W. Turner. Back in France he joined Renoir, Pissarro, Sisley, Paul Cézanne, Edgar Degas and Berthe Morisot in exhibiting independently as the Anonymous Society of Painters, Sculptors and Engravers. At their first exhibition in 1874 he showed Impression, Sunrise, The Luncheon and Boulevard des Capucines, and the critic Louis Leroy's hostile review coined the term Impressionism. In 1883 Monet and his family rented a house and gardens at Giverny.

Monet made light the central subject of his paintings. He sometimes finished a canvas in one sitting, often without preparation, and wished to show how light alters colour and perception. He believed his only merit lay in having painted directly in front of nature, seeking to render the most fleeting effects, and he wanted to paint the air. His method of painting a scene many times produced the haystacks of 1890 to 1891 and the paintings of Rouen Cathedral of 1892 to 1894.

In his garden at Giverny the water lilies, the pond and the Japanese bridge became his chief subject. An exhibition of 1909 showed 42 canvases of the Water Lilies, and he eventually made over 250 paintings of them. Around 1905 he began to abandon the pond's edge, and by the mid-1910s his style had become fluid and nearly abstract. In his later years the first signs of cataracts appeared, and they darkened his later paintings and altered his perception of colour.

Monet died of lung cancer on 5 December 1926, aged 86, and is buried in the church cemetery at Giverny. At his funeral Clemenceau removed the black cloth from the coffin, saying: No black for Monet. His Giverny paintings are said to link Impressionism with twentieth-century art and modern abstraction, and he is now the best known of the Impressionists.
claude-of-france: Claude was born on 13 October 1499 at Romorantin-Lanthenay and named after Claudius of Besançon, a saint her mother had invoked on a pilgrimage so that she might bear a living child. Of Anne of Brittany's at least fourteen pregnancies, only Claude and her sister Renée, born in 1510, survived to adulthood. Because Anne had no surviving sons, Claude was heir presumptive to Brittany, while the French crown could pass only through male heirs under Salic Law.

Queen Anne sought to keep Brittany separate from the crown by marrying Claude to the future Emperor Charles V, and the contract was signed at Lyon on 10 August 1501. The first Treaty of Blois of 1504 gave Claude a large dowry if her father died without male heirs, including Brittany, Milan, Burgundy, Blois and Asti. In 1505 the ailing Louis XII cancelled the engagement at the Estates General of Tours, after Louise of Savoy had obtained a secret promise that Claude would marry her son.

Claude became Duchess of Brittany on 9 January 1514, when her mother died, and on 18 May, at fourteen, she married her cousin Francis. Louis XII died on 1 January 1515, less than three months after marrying Mary of England, and Francis and Claude became king and queen. She was crowned at the Basilica of St Denis on 10 May 1517.

She never ruled Brittany: in 1515 she gave its government to her husband in perpetuity. She refused his repeated suggestion that Brittany be incorporated into France and named her eldest son, Francis, heir to the duchy. At court she was eclipsed by her mother-in-law, Louise of Savoy, and had little interest in politics, preferring religion. Anne Boleyn was in her household until late 1521. She spent almost all her marriage in annual pregnancies.

Claude died on 26 July 1524 at the Château de Blois, aged twenty-four, and was buried at St Denis. Sources disagree on the cause: childbirth or miscarriage, exhaustion after many pregnancies, or bone tuberculosis, as her mother had. Her eldest son, Francis, succeeded her as Duke of Brittany, with his father as guardian, and after his death in 1536 her second son, Henry, became Dauphin and Duke of Brittany. He later became King of France as Henry II.
claudia-gens: According to legend the founder of the house, Attius Clausus, led a Sabine faction that wanted peace with Rome; when his efforts failed he went over to the Romans, bringing, by the account of Dionysius, no fewer than five hundred men able to bear arms. He took the Latin name Appius Claudius, was enrolled among the patricians and given a seat in the Senate. His descendants received a burial site at the foot of the Capitoline Hill, and his followers land beyond the Anio, which became the core of the Old Claudian tribe. Appius Claudius Sabinus Regillensis was the first of the family to be consul, in 495 BCE.

Suetonius, in his life of Tiberius, counted for the gens twenty-eight consulships, five dictatorships, seven censorships, six triumphs and two ovations. The early Claudii favoured the first names Appius, Gaius and Publius and, by Suetonius's account, avoided Lucius because two early bearers had disgraced the family. Its patrician branches included the Pulchri, Centhones and Nerones, many descended from the sons of Appius Claudius Caecus. Publius Claudius Pulcher, ignoring the auguries, was defeated by the Carthaginian fleet at Drepana in 249 BCE, and Gaius Claudius Nero triumphed over Hasdrubal at the Battle of the Metaurus in 207 BCE.

Plebeian Claudii appear early, probably descendants of members who passed to the plebs or of the family's freedmen. Their branches bore the surnames Asellus, Canina, Centumalus, Cicero, Flamen, Glaber and Marcellus, and among the Claudii Marcelli Marcus Claudius Marcellus, consul five times between 222 and 208 BCE, was a hero of the Second Punic War. In the late Republic one patrician member voluntarily became a plebeian and adopted the spelling Clodius.

The patrician Claudii were noted for pride and for hatred of the common people, and the historian Niebuhr judged that the house produced several very eminent men but few great ones. No patrician Claudius adopted a member of another gens during the Republic; the emperor Claudius broke the custom by adopting the future emperor Nero. Claudius also appealed to the family's Sabine origin in arguing before the Senate for admitting Gauls to it, and Virgil flattered the family in the Aeneid by making Attius Clausus a companion of Aeneas.
claudio-monteverdi: Monteverdi was baptised in Cremona on 15 May 1567, the first child of the apothecary Baldassare Monteverdi. There is no clear record of his early training. His first published work, the three-voice motets Sacrae cantiunculae, was issued in Venice in 1582 when he was fifteen, and in it he calls himself the pupil of Marc'Antonio Ingegneri, maestro di cappella at Cremona Cathedral, who by one account gave him a solid grounding in counterpoint and composition.

In 1590 or 1591 Monteverdi entered the service of Duke Vincenzo I Gonzaga of Mantua as a player of the vivuola, working beside the maestro di cappella Giaches de Wert. He married the court singer Claudia de Cattaneis in 1599. In his last five years at Mantua he completed L'Orfeo (1607) and L'Arianna (1608), and wrote the Messa in illo tempore and the Vespro della Beata Vergine (both 1610). In 1613 he became maestro di cappella of San Marco in Venice, where he found the choir neglected and had to recruit and manage about 30 singers and six instrumentalists. Much of his Mantuan stage music is lost, perhaps in the wars of 1630. His last years were largely given to opera for Venice.

He published nine books of madrigals between 1587 and 1638, moving from the style of his teacher to more expressive settings influenced by Wert. He defended novel techniques as a seconda pratica, as against the older prima pratica, and used the basso continuo of the Baroque. In Il ritorno d'Ulisse in patria and L'incoronazione di Poppea (1643) he helped turn opera from a private entertainment of the nobility into a commercial genre; how much of the surviving Poppea is his is debated. He died on 29 November 1643 and was given a funeral of royal pomp at the Frari. After the 1650s his name faded, and his music was largely forgotten until its rediscovery around the beginning of the twentieth century.
claudius: Claudius was born on 1 August 10 BCE at Lugdunum in Roman Gaul, where his father Nero Claudius Drusus was stationed as a military legate, and so was the first Roman emperor born outside Italy. His mother was Antonia Minor, a granddaughter of Octavia Minor, the sister of Augustus, and his elder brother was Germanicus. Because of a limp, a stammer and a tremor, which he suffered after an illness in youth, his family kept him from public office until his consulship with his nephew Caligula in 37. His infirmity probably saved him from the purges of Tiberius and Caligula. He also wrote history, including a work on the Civil Wars that offended Augustus's circle and a twenty-book Etruscan history.

Caligula was assassinated on 24 January 41 in a conspiracy involving the tribune Cassius Chaerea and several senators. Claudius, the last adult male of his family, was declared emperor by the Praetorian Guard. He took pains to please the Senate, allowing it to issue its own bronze coinage and returning Macedonia and Achaea to it as senatorial provinces. He relied heavily on freedmen, dividing the secretariat into bureaus led by Narcissus (correspondence), Pallas (the treasury) and Callistus (justice).

In his reign the Empire began its conquest of Britain. A census in 48 counted 5,984,072 adult male citizens. He finished the Aqua Claudia and the Aqua Anio Novus and built Portus, a new harbour near Ostia, which reduced flooding in Rome. He sat in judgment on many cases, and ancient writers complained that he was easily swayed. Several plots against him led to the deaths of many senators. He married four times, last to his niece Agrippina the Younger.

Ancient historians agree that Claudius was poisoned and died in the early hours of the 13th of October in the year 54, and nearly all blame Agrippina, who wished to secure the throne for her son Nero before Claudius's own son Britannicus could gain power. Nero and the Senate deified him almost at once, though many of his edicts were later disregarded. The Flavians later contrasted him favourably with Nero. Tacitus, Suetonius and Cassius Dio, who favoured the Senate, painted a poor picture of him, and more recent historians have revised that view.
claudius-florimund-mercy: Mercy was born at Longwy in Lorraine, now in France, a grandson of the Bavarian field marshal Franz Freiherr von Mercy. He entered the Austrian army as a volunteer in 1682 and won his commission at the Battle of Vienna the following year. During seven years of campaigning in Hungary he rose to Rittmeister, and a wound received there permanently damaged his sight. He served in the Italian campaigns until 1697, when Prince Eugene of Savoy recalled him to Hungary, and at the Battle of Zenta he won two grades of promotion.

In the first campaigns of the War of the Spanish Succession in Italy he was twice captured in close fighting. For his conduct at the surprise of Cremona on 31 January 1702 he received the thanks of the Holy Roman Emperor Leopold I and the colonelcy of a newly raised cuirassier regiment. He fought in the Rhine campaign of 1703 and at the Battle of Friedlingen, and early in 1704 was sent to harry the lands of Maximilian II Emanuel, Elector of Bavaria. As Generalfeldwachtmeister he fought at the Battle of Schellenberg on 2 July 1704, and by the end of the war he was general of the cavalry.

He distinguished himself at the Battle of Peterwardein in 1716, and at the Battle of Belgrade in 1717 he led the second line of the left wing cavalry in a decisive charge that drove the Ottoman forces back to their trenches. In southern Italy he fought the Battle of Francavilla on 20 June 1719, took Messina and besieged Palermo, before returning to administer the Banat, which had come out of more than 150 years of Ottoman rule.

Made a general field marshal in 1733, he and the Irish-born Major General Baron Francis Patrick O'Neillan assembled 50,000 men at Mantua to recover what the Austrians had lost in Italy to the Franco-Spanish forces. He was killed on 29 June 1734 at the Battle of Parma while leading his troops in person. He left no children; his name passed to Count Argenteau, from whom came the Mercy-Argenteau family, and he was the foster father of Florimund Count de Mercy d'Argenteau. A bust of him was unveiled in Central Park, Timișoara, on 3 August 2009.
claudius-gothicus: Marcus Aurelius Claudius was born on 10 May 214, according to most historians, though some suggest 219 or 220. His birthplace is unknown; he may have been born near the Danube. The only source for his early life is the Historia Augusta, which is full of fabrications and flattery. In the 4th century he was declared a relative of Constantius Chlorus, the father of Constantine the Great; historians regard this as a genealogical fabrication meant to connect Constantine's family with a respected emperor. Before coming to power he served in the army and reached the highest military posts.

In the 260s the empire was split into the core Roman Empire, the Gallic Empire and the Palmyrene Empire. In the summer of 268, probably between July and October, the emperor Gallienus was killed in a conspiracy of senior officials, and the army outside Milan chose Claudius to succeed him. Accounts differ on whether he took part in the plot. He asked the Senate to spare Gallienus's family and supporters and had the dead emperor deified. He was the first of a series of tough soldier emperors who eventually restored the empire after the crisis of the third century.

The most pressing threat was a Gothic invasion of Illyricum and Pannonia. At the Battle of Naissus Claudius and his legions, with his cavalry commander, the future emperor Aurelian, routed a huge Gothic army, took thousands of prisoners and destroyed the Gothic cavalry as a force. The victory earned him the surname Gothicus, and the Goths did not pose a serious threat again for nearly a century. He also routed the Alamanni at the Battle of Lake Benacus in the late autumn of 268, and won victories against the Gallic Empire, regaining Hispania and the Rhône valley.

Claudius went to Sirmium late in 269 to prepare for war against the Vandals, who were raiding Pannonia. He fell victim to the plague, possibly the Plague of Cyprian, and died in 270; historians date his death to January, April, August or September, as the sources conflict. He is thought to have named Aurelian as his successor, though his brother Quintillus briefly seized power. The Senate deified him as Divus Claudius Gothicus.

His victories made him a hero in Latin tradition. A medieval legend links him to Saint Valentine, said to have refused to deny Christ before an Emperor Claudius and to have been beheaded; historians agree that the accounts cannot be verified.
claudius-ptolemy: Ptolemy's date and place of birth are both unknown. A 14th-century astronomer, Theodore Meliteniotes, gave his birthplace as Ptolemais Hermiou in the Thebaid, but the testimony is late and nothing supports it. He lived in or around Alexandria in the Roman province of Egypt and died there. His Latin name Claudius is generally taken to mean that he was a Roman citizen. He wrote in Koine Greek and used Babylonian observations and lunar theory. Later Arabic sources often called him the Upper Egyptian.

Astronomy took most of his effort. The Almagest, originally the Mathematical Treatise, is the only surviving comprehensive ancient treatise on astronomy. Following Hipparchus, Ptolemy derived geometrical models for the Sun, Moon and planets from observations, and supplied tables for computing their positions. It also contains a star catalogue with forty-eight constellations. The planetary models were geocentric and almost universally accepted until heliocentric models reappeared in the Scientific Revolution. Robert R. Newton argued in 1977 that Ptolemy fabricated data, a charge that Owen Gingerich and others rejected.

His Geography is a handbook on drawing maps from coordinates, based on earlier work by Marinus of Tyre. Its second part catalogues some 8,000 localities, of which about 6,300 have coordinates. He also wrote the Tetrabiblos, an astrological treatise, and the Harmonics, on the mathematics of musical scales.

For over a thousand years the Almagest was the authoritative text on astronomy across Europe, the Middle East and North Africa. It was preserved in Arabic manuscripts and translated twice into Latin in the 12th century, once in Sicily and once in Spain. Plato of Tivoli first translated the Tetrabiblos from Arabic into Latin in 1138. Many abridged introductions to his astronomy circulated among Arabs and Byzantines, which suggests that few truly mastered the mathematics.
claus-sluter: The name Claes de Slutere van Herlam is inscribed in the register of the Corporation of Stonemasons and Sculptors of Brussels around 1379 and 1380. Sluter then moved to Dijon, the Burgundian capital. From 1385 to 1389 he was assistant to Jean de Marville, court sculptor to Philip the Bold, Duke of Burgundy.

From 1389 until his death he held the post himself, with the rank of valet de chambre. His nephew Claus de Werve succeeded him. He was the most important northern European sculptor of his age and is considered a pioneer of the northern realism that came into full flower in Early Netherlandish painting with Jan van Eyck and others of the next generation.

His most significant work is the Well of Moses, also called the Great Cross, made between 1395 and 1403 for the Carthusian monastery of Champmol, which Philip the Bold founded outside Dijon in 1383. Life-sized figures of the Old Testament prophets and kings Moses, David, Daniel, Jeremiah, Zachariah and Isaiah stand around the base, holding phylacteries and books inscribed with verses from their texts.

In the Middle Ages these were read as prefigurations of the sacrifice of Christ, and the structure, with the Old Testament figures supporting those of the New, makes that reading literal. The pedestal rises over a hexagonal fountain, and the monument is of limestone from Tonnerre and Asnières. The cross itself was destroyed at some point between 1736 and 1789, probably when the roof of the building protecting it collapsed. Fragments are kept in the Musée Archéologique de Dijon.

The portal of the former mortuary chapel of Champmol stands a few feet away. It holds three sculptural groups by Sluter: a standing Madonna and Child at the central post, the duke with his patron Saint John at the left, and the duchess with her patron Saint Catherine at the right.

He also did the main part of the work on Philip's tomb, now restored and partly reconstructed in the Museum of Fine Arts in the former ducal palace in Dijon, and was one of the sculptors of the mourners in niches below the tombs of Philip the Bold, his wife Margaret and John the Fearless.
claus-von-stauffenberg: Claus Philipp Maria Justinian Schenk Graf von Stauffenberg was born on 15 November 1907 at Stauffenberg Castle in Jettingen, the third of four sons of Alfred Schenk Graf von Stauffenberg, the last Oberhofmarschall of the Kingdom of Württemberg. He married Nina von Lerchenfeld on 26 September 1933, and they had five children. Though he did not join the Nazi Party, in 1932 he voiced tentative support for Hitler. His views wavered, and the Night of the Long Knives and Kristallnacht led him further from the party.

Stauffenberg served in the invasion of Poland, on the general staff of the 6th Panzer Division in the Battle of France and in Tunisia in 1943 with the 10th Panzer Division. On 7 April 1943 he was wounded near Mezzouna and lost his left eye, his right hand and two fingers of his left hand. In September 1943 the conspirators brought him to the Replacement Army headquarters on the Bendlerstrasse in Berlin, where Friedrich Olbricht was one of his superiors. The Replacement Army was to carry out Operation Valkyrie, a contingency plan that was secretly changed to sweep the Nazi regime from power if Hitler died.

With Henning von Tresckow on the Eastern Front, Stauffenberg became the driving force of the plot. He knew that under German law he was committing high treason. After General Hellmuth Stieff declined to act on 7 July 1944, he decided to kill Hitler himself and also run the coup in Berlin.

On 20 July 1944 at the Wolf's Lair, Stauffenberg armed one of two small bombs in a briefcase and left it under the conference table. Four people were killed, but Hitler, shielded by the table leg, was only slightly wounded. After Goebbels announced on the radio that Hitler had survived, the coup in Berlin failed. General Friedrich Fromm held an impromptu court martial, and Stauffenberg, Werner von Haeften, Olbricht and Albrecht Mertz von Quirnheim were shot in the Bendlerblock courtyard before 1:00 on 21 July.

His brother Berthold was executed at Plötzensee on 10 August. More than 200 were condemned in show trials, and over 20,000 Germans were killed or sent to concentration camps in the purge. The Bendlerblock now houses the Memorial to the German Resistance.
clausthal-zellerfeld: Clausthal-Zellerfeld lies on the Upper Harz Plateau in the south-western part of the Harz mountains, at an altitude between 390 and 821 metres. The surrounding area is less mountainous than most of the Harz, with less woodland and more pasture. Numerous dams and streams of the Upper Harz Water Regale are scattered in and around the town. A depression between Clausthal and Zellerfeld marks a natural borderline between them. Its population is about 15,000, and it is the largest town in the area that lies in the mountains rather than at their edge.

The town originally consisted of two towns, Clausthal and Zellerfeld, which were merged in 1924 into one administrative unit. Mining in the area began in the 16th century. The German mining engineer Wilhelm Albert invented modern wire rope between 1831 and 1834 for use in the Harz mines at Clausthal. It proved superior to ropes of hemp or metal chains and soon found wide application, notably in suspension bridges. The Clausthal mint operated from 1617 to 1849. A railway, the Innerste Valley Railway, was opened in 1877 and extended to Altenau in 1914, and it closed in 1976.

The Clausthal University of Technology was established in 1775 to educate mining engineers. An air raid on 7 October 1944 destroyed the large station building and 70 other buildings, and 92 people died. Mining halted in 1930 because the ore deposits were exhausted.

The university is now a technical university teaching engineering, natural science, computer science and business studies, and it is of great importance to the town.
