The rebuilt station of 1961 to 1963 houses the tourist information and the municipal library. Among the surviving buildings are the Market Church in Clausthal, begun in 1639, which is the largest wooden church in Germany with 2,200 seats, the Bergapotheke of 1674 in Zellerfeld, the Salvator Church, also begun in 1674, and the Oberbergamt building. The microbiologist Robert Koch was born in the town, and the Upper Harz Mining Museum and the university's GeoMuseum are open to visitors.
clayton-bulwer-treaty: The treaty was negotiated amid growing tension over Central America, where British influence was traditionally strong but American expansion was increasing, and over American plans for a canal through Nicaragua joining the Pacific and the Atlantic. Britain had indefinite territorial claims in British Honduras, Mosquitia and the Bay Islands. The United States made no claims but held in reserve treaties with Nicaragua and Honduras that gave it a diplomatic counterweight. As agreement on territory proved impossible, the negotiators put the canal first.

Signed on 19 April 1850, the treaty bound both parties not to obtain or maintain exclusive control of the proposed canal or unequal advantage in its use, guaranteed its neutrality, and extended their protection to any other practicable route across the isthmus, by canal or railway. Neither would occupy, fortify, colonise or exercise dominion over Nicaragua, Costa Rica, the Mosquito Coast or any part of Central America, nor use a protectorate or alliance to that end.

Before ratifications were exchanged, Lord Palmerston had Bulwer declare on 8 June that Britain did not take the treaty to apply to its settlement at Honduras or its dependencies. Clayton's counter-declaration accepted the exception only for British Honduras and the small islands near it, held that the treaty covered all the Central American states within their just limits, and stated that the declarations, not put before the Senate, did not affect its legality.

Britain held that the Bay Islands were a dependency of Belize and that it need not give up its protectorate over the Mosquito Coast; the United States denied both, and in 1852 Britain broke the treaty by making the Bay Islands a colony. Treaties of 1859 and 1860 settled the questions nearly in accord with the American contentions: Britain ceded the Bay Islands and the northern Mosquito Coast to Honduras by the Treaty of Comayagua and the rest of the coast to Nicaragua by the Treaty of Managua.

In 1880–1884 the United States advanced reasons for repudiating the treaty at will, among them that circumstances had changed fundamentally since it was signed, the first time its government invoked that principle in international law. It returned to its traditional policy in 1885, and the canal was never built under the treaty.
clear-script: The Clear Script belongs to the family of Mongolian scripts. Its closest forebear is the vertical Mongolian script, which had itself been derived from the Uyghur alphabet. Zaya Pandita designed it as a better way of writing the speech of the western Mongolian groups, the Oirats and the Kalmyks, and also to make it easier to transcribe Sanskrit and the Tibetic languages.

The older script left much of the spoken language ambiguous. The Clear Script gave each symbol kept from traditional Mongolian a single fixed meaning and added new symbols and diacritics to mark vowels, vowel length and the difference between voiced and unvoiced consonants. Some marks even drew distinctions that did not matter for Oirat words but helped in writing foreign words and names, such as the difference between ši and si.

Like its parent, the Clear Script is written vertically. Letters and diacritics stand along a central axis; strokes to the right of the axis generally slant upwards and those to the left slant downwards. The only signs that break this rule are the horizontal signs for S, Š and part of Ö. Words are separated by a space and by the different shapes letters take. Most letters have a single form, but some change according to whether they stand at the beginning, in the middle or at the end of a word.

The script has an alphabetical order of its own, which differs from that of traditional Mongolian. It begins with the seven vowels a, e, i, o, u, ö and ü, followed by the consonants, starting with n, b, x, ɣ and g.

The script was used by the Oirats and neighbouring Mongols, mostly in the late 17th and early 18th centuries. Its creator and others used it widely to translate Buddhist works, above all from Tibetan, so that the religion could spread through western Mongolia. It also served for everyday writing, as some letters surviving from the late 1690s show. In the 19th and early 20th centuries some Altaians in Russia learned to read and write it through their contacts with Mongolian Buddhists.

The Kalmyks of Russia went on using the script until 1924, when the Cyrillic script took its place. In Xinjiang the Oirats still write it, although Mongolian education throughout China now takes place in Chakhar Mongolian.
cleisthenes: Historians estimate that Cleisthenes was born around 570 BCE. He belonged to the aristocratic Alcmaeonid clan and was the younger son of Megacles and Agariste, which made him the maternal grandson of the tyrant Cleisthenes of Sicyon. When Pisistratus took power in Athens as a tyrant, he exiled his opponents and the Alcmaeonidae. After Pisistratus died in 527 BCE, Cleisthenes returned and became the eponymous archon, but Pisistratus's successors Hipparchus and Hippias exiled him again. He then turned to the Oracle of Delphi, which accepted his plea for help against the tyranny because his family had earlier helped rebuild the sanctuary after a fire.

With Spartan help and the support of his clan, Cleisthenes took part in overthrowing Hippias in 510 BCE. He then rivalled Isagoras, who gained the upper hand by appealing to the Spartan king Cleomenes I, and Cleisthenes went into exile. Isagoras tried to dissolve the Boule, the council of citizens that ran the city's daily affairs. The council resisted and the people backed it. Isagoras and his partisans were besieged on the Acropolis and left the city on the third day. Cleisthenes and the exiles were recalled, and he took the lead in Athens.

He replaced the four traditional tribes, based on family ties, with ten tribes drawn from residence in demes. The demes, perhaps 139 in number though this is debated, were grouped in thirds called trittyes, one each from the city, coastal and inland regions. He had citizens named by their deme rather than by their father's name, and he reorganised the Boule from 400 members to 500, fifty from each tribe. Appointment to office by lot is also credited to him. Cleisthenes called his reforms isonomia, equality before the law, rather than demokratia.

Cleisthenes may also have introduced ostracism, first used in 487 BCE, by which a vote of at least 6,000 citizens could exile a man for ten years. In 507 BCE, probably at his instigation, Athens sent envoys to Artaphernes, the Persian satrap at Sardis, seeking help against Sparta. According to Herodotus, the envoys agreed to give earth and water as a sign of submission and were censured on their return. No ancient text mentions Cleisthenes after his reforms, and his later life is unknown. Historians call him the father of Athenian democracy.
clemens-august-of-bavaria: Clemens August was born in Brussels on 17 August 1700, the son of Elector Maximilian II Emanuel of Bavaria and Theresa Kunegunda Sobieska, and a grandson of King John III Sobieski of Poland. The War of the Spanish Succession split the family, which spent many years under house arrest in Austria and was reunited only in 1715. His uncle Joseph Clemens, Elector and Archbishop of Cologne, secured him early posts at Altötting, in the Diocese of Regensburg and at the Prince-Provostry of Berchtesgaden, and he soon received papal confirmation as Bishop of Regensburg and later of Cologne.

In the War of the Austrian Succession he crowned his brother Charles VII emperor at Frankfurt in 1742, and after Charles's death in 1745 he leaned again towards Austria; over the years he changed sides between Austria and France more and more often, swayed by his changing first ministers and by large payments. The biographer Jan Swafford judged him uninterested in governing and devoted at Bonn to women, music, dancing and building. Beethoven's Flemish grandfather became a musician in Bonn during his reign. With his mistress Mechthild Brion he had a daughter, Anna Marie zu Löwenfeld.

He died at Schloss Philippsburg below the fortress of Ehrenbreitstein on 6 February 1761. Pope Clement XIII then refused the succession of his brother Cardinal John Theodore of Bavaria, doubting his moral conduct, which ended 178 years of unbroken Wittelsbach rule in Cologne. Of his buildings, the palaces of Augustusburg and Falkenlust at Brühl are on the UNESCO World Heritage list, and he also had the church of St Michael in Berg am Laim in Munich built; others, such as Schloss Arnsberg and Schloss Herzogsfreude, are lost.
clemens-brentano: Clemens Brentano was born on 9 September 1778 into a wealthy merchant family in Frankfurt, the son of Peter Anton Brentano and Maximiliane von La Roche. His maternal grandmother was the writer Sophie von La Roche, and his sister Bettina von Arnim corresponded with Goethe as a young girl and published the letters in 1835. He studied in Halle and Jena and lived afterwards at Heidelberg, Vienna and Berlin. He was close to Wieland, Herder, Goethe, Friedrich Schlegel, Fichte and Tieck.

From 1798 to 1800 he lived in Jena, the first centre of the Romantic movement, and in 1801 he moved to Göttingen, where he befriended Achim von Arnim. In 1804 he moved to Heidelberg and worked with Arnim on Des Knaben Wunderhorn, a collection of folk songs published from 1805 to 1808 on which Gustav Mahler later drew. In 1818 he returned to the practice of the Catholic faith and withdrew to Dülmen, where he became secretary to the visionary nun Anne Catherine Emmerich, copying her dictation until her death in 1824.

He then prepared an index of her visions, The Dolorous Passion of Our Lord Jesus Christ, published in 1833. Investigations in 1923 and 1928 made it uncertain how much of the books he attributed to her was his own creation. He spent his later years in Regensburg, Frankfurt and Munich, promoting the Catholic faith.

Brentano belonged to the Heidelberg group of German Romantic writers, and his works are marked by fantastic imagery and abrupt, bizarre modes of expression. His first publications were Satiren und poetische Spiele (1800) and the romance Godwi (1801). His finest work is generally held to be the Romanzen vom Rosenkranz, published posthumously in 1852, and his short story Geschichte vom braven Kasperl und dem schönen Annerl (1817) was very popular. His collected works, edited by his brother Christian, appeared in nine volumes from 1851 to 1855. He died in Aschaffenburg.
clemens-wenceslaus-of-saxony: Clemens Wenceslaus was born on 28 September 1739, a prince of the House of Wettin and the ninth child of Augustus III of Saxony, who was Prince-Elector of Saxony and King of Poland. In 1760 he went to Vienna and entered the Austrian army as a field marshal, and he was present at the Battle of Torgau on 3 November 1760. He decided that warfare was not for him and entered the church instead. In April 1763 he was elected Bishop of Freising and Bishop of Regensburg.

From 1764 he served as coadjutor of Trier and Augsburg, and in 1768 he gave up Freising and Regensburg, becoming Archbishop-Elector of Trier in February and Prince-Bishop of Augsburg in August. In Trier he did much for public education, founded several non-profit bodies for education and the general welfare, and in 1783 issued an edict of tolerance. In church matters he took a mixed course: he let the Jesuits remain in Trier after their order was abolished, protested against the radical reforms of his cousin, Emperor Joseph II, and banned several processions and holidays.

Though a modest man who lived simply, he rebuilt Ehrenbreitstein as a palace and lived there. He founded the theatre in Coblenz, encouraged music in the archdiocese and built a hunting lodge at Kärlich, while opposing several inhumane ways of hunting.

The French Revolution alarmed him. He halted his reforms and began to rule strictly, offered refuge at Schönbornslust palace to members of the French royal family, to which his nephew King Louis XVI belonged, and allowed Coblenz to become a centre of French monarchism. By the Treaty of Lunéville in 1801 he lost all the electorate's lands west of the Rhine, keeping only a few small territories belonging to Trier itself.

In 1803 he lost those too, along with the Prince-Bishopric of Augsburg and the Prince-Provostry of Ellwangen Abbey, which were secularised and annexed by the princes of Nassau-Weilburg, the Elector of Bavaria and the Duke of Württemberg. With a pension of 100,000 guldens he retired to Augsburg. He died at the episcopal summer residence in Marktoberdorf in the Allgäu on 27 July 1812 and was buried there. His grandniece Archduchess Maria Clementina of Austria was named after him.
clement-attlee: Clement Richard Attlee was born on 3 January 1883 at Putney, then in Surrey, the seventh of eight children of Henry Attlee, a solicitor, and Ellen Bravery Watson. He attended Haileybury College and the University of Oxford and became a barrister. From 1906 he volunteered at Haileybury House, a charitable club for working-class boys in Stepney. The poverty he saw there convinced him that only direct action by the state would help, and he joined the Independent Labour Party in 1908. He served in the First World War in the South Lancashire Regiment at Gallipoli, became mayor of Stepney in 1919 and was elected Member of Parliament for Limehouse in 1922.

Attlee was Under-Secretary of State for War in the first Labour government of 1924. At the 1931 election Labour lost over 200 seats, and he kept Limehouse by 551 votes and became deputy to George Lansbury. When Lansbury resigned on 8 October 1935, Attlee became interim leader and then leader. He took Labour into Winston Churchill's coalition in May 1940, as Lord Privy Seal and from 1942 as deputy prime minister.

Labour won a landslide at the 1945 election. The government aimed to maintain full employment, a mixed economy and an enlarged system of social services. It nationalised public utilities and major industries, passed the National Insurance Act 1946 and the National Assistance Act 1948, and formed the National Health Service in 1948. It oversaw the partition of India in 1947, the independence of Burma and Ceylon and the end of the British mandate in Palestine, and Attlee and Ernest Bevin supported the Marshall Plan and in 1949 promoted NATO. Shortages of food, housing and resources persisted, and the 1950 election cut Labour's majority to five seats. The Conservatives took power in 1951, although Labour won the most votes.

Attlee stayed on as leader until 1955, in years marked by quarrels between Hugh Gaitskell's right wing and Aneurin Bevan's left. He then became Earl Attlee. In 1958 he helped to found the Homosexual Law Reform Society. He died on 8 October 1967 at Westminster Hospital, and his ashes were buried at Westminster Abbey. He remains the longest-serving Labour leader.
clement-of-alexandria: Titus Flavius Clemens, known as Clement of Alexandria, was born to pagan parents, and neither his birthdate nor his birthplace is certain. Epiphanius of Salamis says Athens, but there is also a tradition of an Alexandrian birth. He rejected paganism as a young man because of its perceived moral corruption and travelled in Greece, Asia Minor, Palestine and Egypt, a journey that was mainly religious. He met an Ionian theologian in Greece, identified as Athenagoras of Athens, and in the east he was taught by an Assyrian, sometimes identified with Tatian, and by a Jew, possibly Theophilus of Caesarea.

Around 180 he reached Alexandria and met Pantaenus, who taught at the Catechetical School. Clement studied under him and was ordained to the priesthood by Pope Julian before 189. Little else is known of his life in Alexandria.

Three major works survive in full, as a trilogy: the Protrepticus, an exhortation to the Greeks to adopt Christianity, written around 195; the Paedagogus, or Tutor, written around 198; and the Stromata, or Miscellanies, written between about 198 and 203. His Salvation for the Rich, written around 203, argues that Jesus's words about the rich are not to be taken literally and that wealth is not wrong in itself if it is used charitably.

Clement was influenced by Hellenistic philosophy, especially Plato and the Stoics, more than any other Christian thinker of his time. He held that philosophy was a preparation for Christianity among the Greeks and sought to harmonise its insights with biblical teaching. Faith, in his view, was the basis of salvation and of gnosis, spiritual knowledge, a word he took from the Gnostics he opposed. He is often regarded as one of the first Christian universalists.

Clement died around 215. Eusebius gave the first account of his life and works, and Jerome called him the most learned of men. He is usually regarded as a Church Father and is venerated as a saint in Coptic Christianity, Eastern Catholicism, Ethiopian Christianity and Anglicanism. In the West he was revered until his name was removed from the Roman Martyrology in 1586 on the advice of Baronius.
clement-of-ohrid: The date and place of Clement's birth are unknown. Most scholars think he was a Slav from southern Macedonia, perhaps from the area of Thessaloniki, because his hagiographer Theophylact of Ohrid says he knew the life of Methodius like no other; Theophylact calls him 'the first bishop in the Bulgarian language'. He joined Methodius as a young man, following him to the monastery on Mysian Olympus, and took part in the mission of Cyril and Methodius to Great Moravia. In 867 or 868 he was ordained a priest in Rome by the bishops Formosus and Gauderic, together with two other disciples, Gorazd and Naum.

After the death of Methodius in 885, Clement and Gorazd led the struggle against the German clergy in Great Moravia. He spent some time in jail and was then expelled, reaching Belgrade, then within Bulgaria, in 885 or 886 with Naum of Preslav and Angelarius. Clement and Naum were sent to the capital Pliska, where Boris I commissioned them to instruct the future clergy in the Slavonic language. Since the adoption of Christianity in 865 services had been conducted in Greek by clergy from the Byzantine Empire, and Boris saw Old Slavonic as a way to preserve Bulgaria's independence.

Clement was sent to the south-west, to the region then called Kutmichevitsa, where he founded the Ohrid Literary School. For seven years, between 886 and 893, he taught some 3,500 disciples in Slavonic and the Glagolitic alphabet, and he and his co-workers translated Christian literature into Old Church Slavonic. Naum meanwhile worked on the school at Pliska, which was moved to Preslav in 893.

In 893 Clement was ordained to the bishopric of Drembica, Velika. He died in 916 and was buried in his monastery of Saint Panteleimon in Ohrid, and was soon canonised by the Bulgarian Orthodox Church. He was one of the most prolific writers in Old Church Slavonic. He is credited with the Panonic Hagiography of Saint Cyril and Saint Methodius, translated the Flower Triode, and is believed to be the author of the oldest service dedicated to Cyril and Methodius. The invention of the Cyrillic alphabet is usually ascribed to him, although it was most likely developed at the Preslav school early in the 10th century. Sofia University, founded in 1888, is named after him.
clements-kadalie: He was born Lameck Koniwaka Kadali Muwamba in the village of Chifira near the Bandawe Mission Station in Nkhata Bay District, the second son of Musa Kadalie Muwamba and grandson of Chiweyu, a paramount chief of the Tonga of Nyasaland. Educated by Church of Scotland missionaries, he completed teacher training at Livingstonia in 1913 and taught briefly in a primary school before joining the stream of Nyasalanders seeking work in South Africa in early 1915.

He settled in Cape Town in 1918 and befriended Arthur F. Batty, an emerging trade unionist and political activist, on whose advice he founded the Industrial and Commercial Union, later renamed the Industrial and Commercial Workers' Union of Africa, to protest against unfair labour laws and protect workers' rights. In December 1919 a dockworkers' strike of 2,000 men lasting fourteen days stopped all exports through Cape Town harbour and made him known across the country. By 1927 the union could claim a membership of one hundred thousand.

On 24 November 1924 he was arrested and served with a deportation order naming him a prohibited immigrant and ordering him to leave South Africa within three days. In May 1927 he represented the union at the international labour conference in Geneva. Internal fighting followed, and William G. Ballinger removed him with the full backing of the executive committee. In May 1928 he and six other union leaders were arrested under the Native Administration Act, which made it a criminal offence to arouse racial animosity towards the white population.

After forming his independent union in East London he was also a provincial organiser of the African National Congress. In 1921 he had married Johanna Davidson, a widow with two children, with whom he had four children; he later lived in East London with his second wife, Eva, and their son, Victor. He never returned to his homeland and died in 1951. His granddaughter Rhoda Kadalie (1953–2022) became an academic, columnist and director of the Impumelelo Social Innovations Centre.
cleomenean-war: Cleomenes III came to the Spartan throne in 236 or 235 BCE after deposing his father, Leonidas II, who had executed the reforming king Agis IV. In 229 BCE Cleomenes took Tegea, Mantineia, Caphyae and Orchomenus in Arcadia, by treachery according to Polybius, at their own request according to other historians. When the ephors then sent him to seize the Athenaeum near Belbina, a border point disputed with Megalopolis, the Achaean League declared war. Ptolemy III of Egypt soon shifted his financial support from the Achaeans to Sparta, judging it the more useful ally against Macedon.

Cleomenes routed the Achaean army of Aratus of Sicyon near Mount Lycaeum in 227 BCE and defeated another at Ladoceia, where Lydiadas of Megalopolis was killed. He then had four of the five ephors killed, divided the land into equal lots, made some perioeci citizens, trained 4,000 hoplites and armed them with the Macedonian sarissa. In 226 BCE he crushed the Achaeans at Dyme, and later took Argos during the Nemean Games and won the surrender of Corinth. Aratus allied with Antigonus III Doson, who demanded the citadel of Acrocorinth.

Antigonus came south with 20,000 infantry and 1,300 cavalry. After a revolt at Argos Cleomenes abandoned his lines at the Isthmus, and in 223 BCE Antigonus took Tegea, Orchomenus, Mantinea and Heraea, confining him to Laconia. When Ptolemy withdrew his money, Cleomenes freed helots who could pay five minae, and he surprised and burned Megalopolis. In the summer of 222 BCE Antigonus, with 29,200 men by Polybius's count, attacked the Spartans holding the hills of Evas and Olympus at Sellasia. Eucleidas, the king's brother, was killed, and of 6,000 Spartans who fought only 200 survived.

Cleomenes fled by ship from Gythium to Egypt. Antigonus entered Sparta as its first foreign conqueror, treated the people generously, revoked the reforms and restored the ephors, but did not restore the kings, and within three days left to deal with a Dardani invasion of Macedon. Sparta's power collapsed and it fell to a series of tyrants. In Alexandria Ptolemy III promised Cleomenes an army, but died; under Ptolemy IV he was put under house arrest, and in 219 BCE, after a failed attempt to raise the city, he and his friends killed themselves.
cleomenes-i: Cleomenes was the son of Anaxandridas II of the Agiad dynasty. When Anaxandridas's first wife bore him no son, the ephors forced him to take a second wife without divorcing the first, an unprecedented case of bigamy in Sparta. Cleomenes was born of the second marriage, after which his father had three more sons with the first wife: Dorieus, Leonidas and Cleombrotus. When Anaxandridas died, Dorieus contested the succession on the ground of his superior manly virtue, but Cleomenes, as eldest son, had the stronger claim and became king. Dorieus left for colonial ventures in Libya and Sicily.

Cleomenes first acted against the Peisistratid tyranny at Athens, after the exiled Alcmaeonid family bribed the oracle at Delphi to tell the Spartans to remove it. A first Spartan expedition under Anchimolus was defeated by Hippias around 511. In 510 Cleomenes went by land, defeated Hippias's Thessalian mercenaries and besieged him on the Acropolis, where he surrendered after the Spartans captured his sons. In 507 Cleomenes returned at the request of Isagoras, expelled 700 families linked to Cleisthenes and tried to dissolve the council.

The Athenians rose and besieged him on the Acropolis, where he answered the priestess barring him from the temple: Woman, I am not Dorian but Achaean. On the third day he surrendered. His expedition of 506 collapsed at Eleusis when the Corinthians went home and the other king, Demaratus, took the allies with him. In 494 Cleomenes defeated the Argives at the Battle of Sepeia, near Tiryns, after ferrying his army across the Argolic Gulf; the Argive army was wiped out, perhaps as many as 6,000 men.

He burned the sacred grove where survivors had fled, and made Tiryns and Mycenae independent of Argos. On his return he was accused of bribery for sparing Argos but was acquitted. In 491 he bribed the oracle at Delphi to announce that deposing Demaratus was the divine will, and replaced him with Leotychidas.

Around 490 Cleomenes fled when the plot against Demaratus was discovered, and in Arcadia he tried to unite the Arcadians under an oath to follow him. Fearing a combined revolt of Arcadia and the helots of Messenia, the ephors recalled him, but Herodotus says he was thought insane, and his half-brothers had him chained in prison.

He was found dead, his shins, thighs and belly slashed, and the Spartan authorities called it suicide. Herodotus records four explanations of his madness, among them divine retribution for the bribed oracle. Some modern scholars suspect he was murdered by Leonidas, who succeeded him and married his daughter Gorgo. Most of what is known comes from Herodotus, whose account is biased against him and rests on the testimony of his opponents.
cleomenes-iii: Cleomenes was the son of the future Agiad king Leonidas II and his wife Cratesicleia. Around 242 BCE Leonidas was exiled after opposing the reforms of the Eurypontid king Agis IV, but he returned, removed Cleombrotus and had Agis arrested and executed. Cleomenes, then about eighteen, was forced by his father to marry Agis's widow, the wealthy heiress Agiatis. According to legend he was hunting when his father summoned him and learned of the wedding only on reaching the city; he was reportedly doubtful about the marriage because his father had had her husband executed. He came to be inspired by Agis, as told to him by his lover Xenares.

Cleomenes took the throne in 235 BCE on his father's death. In 229 BCE Tegea, Mantinea, Caphyae and Orchomenus joined Sparta; Polybius and William Smith say he took them by treachery, while Richard Talbert says they asked. The Achaean League under Aratus of Sicyon then declared war. Cleomenes defeated the Achaeans near Mount Lycaeum and again at Leuctra, and, confident of his position, sent followers who killed four of the ephors. He then began his reforms, giving his land to the state and dividing all land into equal lots for some 4,000 citizens, half of them old citizens and half new, largely mercenaries. He restored the agoge and the austere communal life and armed his troops with the Macedonian sarissa, a five-metre pike.

In 226 BCE he removed the Achaean garrison from Mantinea, routed the Achaeans at Dyme and later took Corinth. Oligarchies across the Peloponnese opposed his reforms. Aratus turned to Antigonus III Doson of Macedon, whose army forced Cleomenes back, and in 222 BCE the Macedonian phalanx overwhelmed the Spartans at the Battle of Sellasia.

After Sellasia, Cleomenes advised the Spartans to submit to Antigonus and fled to Alexandria, hoping for help from Ptolemy Euergetes. His successor Ptolemy Philopator neglected him and put him under house arrest. In 219 BCE he and his friends escaped and tried to start a revolt, but found no support, and they killed themselves. Panteus died last, over the king's body. William Smith described Cleomenes as the last truly great man of Sparta and, perhaps with Philopoemen, of all Greece.
cleon: Cleon was the son of Cleaenetus, a wealthy tanner, and was among the first prominent Athenian politicians of the 5th century BCE to gain power from outside the established elite. He made his name in the late 430s BCE by opposing the strategy of Pericles, in particular his policy of avoiding battle with the invading Peloponnesian League in 431 BCE. In 430 BCE he led the opposition to Pericles and accused him of mismanaging public funds; Pericles was removed from office but quickly reinstated.

After Pericles died of the plague in 429 BCE, Cleon rose quickly, and by 428 BCE, according to Thucydides, he was the most persuasive speaker in the Athenian Assembly. He won support among poorer citizens by raising the pay for jury service, on which many lived, and by using the courts against rivals. In 424 BCE he was elected one of the ten strategoi.

After Mytilene revolted in 428 BCE and surrendered, Cleon proposed putting to death all its adult men and enslaving the women and children. Diodotus spoke against him and narrowly won, though about 1,000 of the rebellion's leaders were still executed. In the spring of 425 BCE an Athenian fleet defeated a Spartan one at Pylos and trapped 400 Spartan soldiers on the island of Sphacteria. Spurred on by Cleon, the Athenians turned down Spartan peace offers. When the blockade dragged on, the general Nicias offered to give up his command, and Cleon accepted, promising to take the island in 20 days. He did so at the Battle of Sphacteria, although the general Demosthenes is often credited with the tactical success.

In 422 BCE Cleon led a force to retake Amphipolis, which had been lost to the Spartans. He was outmanoeuvred by the Spartan general Brasidas at the Battle of Amphipolis and killed by a peltast as his army was routed. Brasidas also died in the battle, removing the chief opponents of peace on both sides, and the Peace of Nicias was signed in 421 BCE.

The two main contemporary sources, Thucydides and Aristophanes, portray him harshly, often as a demagogue. Aristophanes had a grievance, since Cleon is said to have complained about his lost play Babylonians, and Thucydides was exiled after failing to hold Amphipolis. Some modern scholars see bias in both writers, while others argue that the portrait was less shaped by personal dislike than once believed.
cleopatra-selene-ii: Cleopatra Selene was raised and educated in Alexandria as a Ptolemaic princess. Her second name means "moon" in Greek, matching that of her twin Alexander Helios, "sun". Mark Antony acknowledged the twins in 37 BCE, and in 34 BCE, at the Donations of Alexandria, he bestowed kingdoms on the children before huge crowds. Selene was made ruler of Cyrenaica and Libya, though she was too young to rule.

After the defeat at Actium in 31 BCE her parents sent the children away, but Roman soldiers captured them on the road to Thebes, and their parents killed themselves as Octavian invaded Egypt. Octavian paraded the twins in his triumph in golden chains so heavy that they could not walk in them, which drew sympathy from onlookers. Augustus gave them to his sister Octavia to be raised on the Palatine Hill. Selene is the only known surviving member of the Ptolemaic dynasty, and her brothers are not recorded again.

Octavia arranged her marriage to Juba II, a learned prince raised in Octavian's household. It likely took place in 25 BCE, when Augustus made the couple co-rulers of the client kingdom of Mauretania, and they renamed their capital Caesarea, now Cherchell in Algeria, in the emperor's honour. Selene is said to have had great influence on Juba's policies. She brought scholars and artists from Alexandria, introduced the cult of Isis to Caesarea and imported sculptures from Egypt.

The kingdom exported fish, grapes, pearls, figs, grain, wooden furniture and a purple dye from shellfish to Spain and Italy. Selene minted coins in her own name as Queen Cleopatra, and the couple also issued a joint coinage. Building at Caesarea and Volubilis mixed Egyptian, Greek and Roman styles and included a lighthouse like the Pharos of Alexandria and a seafront palace.

The couple had a son, Ptolemy of Mauretania, born in 10 BCE and named for her dynasty and her younger brother, who succeeded Juba, and probably a daughter whose name has not survived. Selene's death is placed about 5 BCE, and the country became extremely wealthy during the couple's reign.
cleopatra-vii: Cleopatra VII was born in Alexandria in early 69 BCE, the daughter of Ptolemy XII Auletes and an uncertain mother, presumably his wife Cleopatra V Tryphaena. She belonged to the Macedonian Greek Ptolemaic dynasty, descended from Ptolemy I Soter, a general and companion of Alexander the Great. Earlier Ptolemaic rulers refused to learn Egyptian; she was the first known to have done so, and Plutarch implies that she spoke several other languages as well.

Her father tried to ward off Roman annexation by lavish gifts to statesmen such as Pompey and Julius Caesar, which bankrupted him, and in 58 BCE he was exiled from Egypt. Before he died, some time before 22 March 51 BCE, he named her his heir.

Cleopatra began to reign alongside her brother Ptolemy XIII. Her first act as queen was installing a sacred Buchis bull at Hermonthis, and she faced famine caused by drought and a low Nile flood. A falling-out with her brother led to civil war. When Pompey fled to Egypt after losing at Pharsalus in 48 BCE, Ptolemy XIII had him ambushed and killed, and Caesar then occupied Alexandria and was besieged with Cleopatra in the palace. After Ptolemy XIII drowned in the Nile, Caesar made Cleopatra and her brother Ptolemy XIV joint rulers; her son Caesarion was born of her affair with Caesar. After Caesar's assassination she named Caesarion co-ruler.

In the civil war of 43–42 BCE she sided with the Second Triumvirate of Octavian, Mark Antony and Marcus Aemilius Lepidus. After meeting Antony at Tarsos in 41 BCE she had three children with him, and he came to rely on her for funds and military aid. The Donations of Alexandria declared their children rulers of territories under his authority, and Octavian presented this as treason and declared war on Cleopatra. She ruled as an absolute monarch and chief religious authority.

After Octavian defeated the fleet of Antony and Cleopatra at Actium in 31 BCE, his forces invaded Egypt in 30 BCE and Antony killed himself. Cleopatra reportedly killed herself too, probably by poison, to avoid being paraded in a Roman triumph. Her three surviving children were sent to Rome in the care of Octavian's sister Octavia.

Plutarch's Life of Antonius gives the fullest surviving account and draws on eyewitness sources as well as the Augustan view. Roman historiography and Latin poetry produced a generally critical view of the queen that shaped medieval and Renaissance literature.
clermont-ferrand: Clermont-Ferrand lies on the plain of Limagne in the Massif Central, surrounded by the chain of volcanoes called the Chaîne des Puys, which includes the dormant Puy de Dôme, 10 kilometres away. The mountains put the city in a rain shadow, so it has one of the driest climates in metropolitan France outside the Mediterranean coast, with cold winters and hot summers. The old part of Clermont follows the line of the ramparts as they stood at the end of the Middle Ages, and the city's cathedral is built of black lava stone.

The first known mention is by Strabo, who called it the metropolis of the Arverni, then named Nemessos, a Gaulish word for a sacred forest, on the mound where the cathedral now stands. Vercingetorix was born somewhere near it around 72 BCE and repulsed the Roman assault at Gergovia in 52 BCE. After the Roman conquest it was Augustonemetum, Latin for sanctuary of Augustus. It became a bishop's seat in the 5th century under Namatius, and the emperor Julius Nepos ceded it to the Visigoths in 475. The Franks took it a generation after the Visigoths lost it in 507. Vikings ravaged it in 862 and 864 and again around 898.

The castle of Clarus Mons gave its name to the town in 848. Pope Urban II called the First Crusade at the Council of Clermont in 1095. In 1120 the counts of Auvergne founded the rival town of Montferrand next to Clermont's walls to counter the bishops' power. Clermont became a royal town in 1551, and the Edict of Troyes of 1630 joined the two towns, confirmed in 1731 by Louis XV. Montferrand demanded independence three times, in 1789, 1848 and 1863.

The Michelin factories and the city gardens built in the 20th century united the two towns, though two distinct downtowns survive and Montferrand keeps a strong identity. Clermont-Ferrand is the prefecture of Puy-de-Dôme and had a population of 146,351 in 2023. It is the headquarters of Michelin and hosts an international short film festival. Its Romanesque church of Notre-Dame du Port was nominated as a World Heritage Site in 1998, and the cathedral, in Gothic style, was built between the 13th and 19th centuries.
cleruchy: The word comes from the Greek klēroukhos, lot-holder. Greek colonies were normally independent of their mother city, but a cleruchy was given local institutions on Athenian models, such as the council on Samos. The first cleruchy is thought to have been Salamis, taken from Megara in the 6th century BCE. Others followed on the Thracian Chersonese after its recapture from the Persian Empire and at Chalcis after its defeat by Athens, and many more under the Delian League and the Second Athenian League, reaching as far as Amisos on the Black Sea.

The lots were a significant source of private wealth: according to Thucydides the 3,000 lots on Lesbos yielded 100 talents a year. The network was lost at the end of the Peloponnesian War and never reached that extent again, although some cleruchies, such as those of Lemnos and Samos, were re-established in the 4th century BCE.

The Ptolemaic, Seleucid and Attalid kingdoms also used the system. In Egypt Greeks recruited into the army received land grants, klēroi, on which they lived in peacetime, forming a reserve that could be called up at any time. They were often given marginal land that they had to cultivate, which helped reclaim the Faiyum. The first were Ptolemy I's roughly 6,500 Macedonian soldiers, and after the Battle of Gaza in 312 BCE Ptolemy settled 8,000 prisoners as reservists.

Plot sizes followed rank. In the 3rd century BCE native Egyptian machimoi received 5 arouras, infantrymen 30 and cavalrymen 100, and a soldier could be called a 100-aroura man. As grants spread to phylakitai, ephodoi and others, plots shrank and lost their tax advantages, while native soldiers gained land, especially after the machimoi proved themselves at the Battle of Raphia in 217 BCE.

Cleruchs also formed ethnic communities, politeumata, of Cilicians, Boeotians, Cretans, Jews, Idumaeans and Phrygians. Their descendants, the epigonoi, intermarried with Egyptians and adopted Egyptian religious beliefs, so that by the Roman period much of the Greek population of the Faiyum was made up of Hellenized Egyptians or people of mixed Egyptian-Greek origins. The Roman authorities regarded them as Egyptians, though a group called the 6,475 katoikoi of the Greek men of the Arsinoite nome kept a privileged tax status. The Fayum mummy portraits, blending Egyptian and Greek traditions, come from this society.
click-go-the-shears: The tune is that of the American Civil War song "Ring the Bell, Watchman" by Henry Clay Work, and the first verse closely parodies Work's words. In June 2013 the folklorist Mark Gregory found the earliest known printing, in the regional Victorian newspaper the Bacchus Marsh Express in 1891, under the title "The Bare Belled Ewe" and set to Work's tune. It was signed "C. C. Eynesbury, Nov. 20, 1891", Eynesbury being a rural property near Bacchus Marsh, and C.C. may have been the author. Its appearance in the year of a shearers' strike would have struck a chord with readers.

The song follows a day in the shearing shed and its people: the ringer, the boss of the board, the colonial experience man and the tar boy. The chorus pictures the old shearer working fast while the ringer, beaten by a blow, curses him and his bare-bellied ewe. When the day's shearing is done the old shearer takes his cheque to the local pub to drink. The words vary widely between versions: the dialect yoe of the bare-bellied yoe often becomes joe, or the ewe blue-bellied, and a crude line about the colonial experience man is often softened or rewritten.

After the 1891 printing the song appeared in two Australian newspapers in 1939, and in 1946 the musicologist the Reverend Dr Percy Jones published it as a traditional song he had collected and arranged. Burl Ives recorded it in 1952 for his album Australian Folk Songs, A. L. Lloyd in 1956 and William Clauson in 1958. Its tune carried the jingle for the change to decimal currency on 14 February 1966, and it was played along the route of Prime Minister Gough Whitlam's motorcade from Peking airport during his visit to China in 1973.
cliff-palace: The Ancestral Puebloans who built Cliff Palace and the other cliff dwellings of Mesa Verde are thought to have been driven to these defensible places by increasing competition amid changing climatic conditions. The sandstone was shaped with harder stones and set in a mortar of soil, water and ash, with chinking stones to fill gaps, and the walls were coated with thin plaster in yellow, white and red, of which some traces remain. The small doorways reflect the people's height: the average man stood about 1.68 m and the average woman about 1.5 m. The tallest of its towers, 7.9 m high with four levels, almost reaches the roof of the alcove.

Most kivas, round sunken ceremonial rooms, have six stone pilasters supporting the roof, a central firepit, a ventilation opening and a sipapu, a small hole believed to symbolise the way by which souls come into this world. The two southernmost kivas are joined by a tunnel, perhaps for appearances during rituals. With a room-to-kiva ratio of 9 to 1, against 12 to 1 elsewhere at Mesa Verde, archaeologists suggest it may have been a social, administrative and ceremonial centre for nearby communities. Twenty-five living rooms, mostly about 6 by 8 feet, are blackened by soot; nine granaries high in the alcove were reached by ladders. The site was abandoned by 1300, perhaps because megadroughts disrupted food production, though the cause is debated.

Richard Wetherill and Charlie Mason also found Spruce Tree House and Square Tower House, and they gathered artifacts from Cliff Palace over the years, keeping a detailed record; Wetherill took the first collection to Durango on 2 March 1889. Jesse Walter Fewkes of the Smithsonian Institution excavated the site in 1906 and repaired its crumbling walls. Though he found it almost completely rifled, he recovered pots, yucca sandals, cloth of feathers, yucca and cotton, tools and weapons, and remains of corn, squash, beans and gourds. Today visitors can enter only on ranger-guided tours.
clifford-dupont: Dupont, of Huguenot ancestry, was born in London to Alfred Walter and Winifred Mary Dupont; his father's firm dealt largely in the rag trade. He was educated at Bishop's Stortford College and read law at Clare College, Cambridge, qualified as a solicitor in 1929 and set up his own firm in 1933. In the Second World War he served in the Royal Artillery as adjutant of a light anti-aircraft battalion in North Africa, was on General Eisenhower's staff during the liberation of Europe in 1944, and ended the war at the War Office.

After a visit to Southern Rhodesia in 1947 he bought land at Featherstone, south of Salisbury, and turned it into a cattle ranch, emigrating for good in the early 1950s. His second wife died in 1957, and in 1958 his son and daughter were killed in an air crash. That year he won the Fort Victoria federal seat for the Dominion Party, and four years later he took Charter for the Rhodesian Front and became Minister for Justice.

With Desmond Lardner-Burke he worked to replace Prime Minister Winston Field with Ian Smith. In October 1964 he resigned his seat to fight Sir Roy Welensky at a by-election in Arundel and beat him by 1079 votes to 633. As Smith's deputy he held External Affairs and, from June 1965, Defence.

Dupont was the second to sign the Unilateral Declaration of Independence on 11 November 1965. Smith's government still professed loyalty to Elizabeth II as Queen of Rhodesia but no longer recognised the governor, Sir Humphrey Gibbs. On 2 December Smith asked the Queen to appoint Dupont governor-general; Buckingham Palace replied that she could not entertain such advice, and the United Kingdom held Gibbs to be the only lawful authority. Opponents of UDI such as Ahrn Palley refused to recognise Dupont's office.

After a predominantly white electorate approved a republican constitution in a referendum on 24 June 1969, Dupont signed the proclamation of the republic on 2 March 1970 and became interim president. Parliament elected him president on 14 April. The office was largely ceremonial, real power remaining with Smith and his cabinet. He suffered long bouts of ill health, and he died on 28 June 1978 while undergoing radium treatment for what was believed to be cancer.
cloaca-maxima: The name Cloaca Maxima is related to that of Cloacina, a Roman goddess. It was built in either the Roman Kingdom or the early Republic to drain the local marshes and carry waste to the Tiber. According to tradition, the king Tarquinius Priscus ordered it, using Etruscan workers and plebeians. He and his son Tarquinius Superbus first turned the land by the Forum from a swamp into solid building ground, reclaiming the Velabrum.

At first the drain consisted of open channels lined with bricks. It may also have begun as streams from three neighbouring hills, channelled through the Forum to the Tiber and gradually built over as building space became more valuable. The Romans seem to have valued it as sacred, and a small sanctuary to Venus Cloacina, Venus of the Drain, stood in the Forum Romanum.

By the late Republic it was the city's main storm drain, a system 1,600 metres long. Pliny the Elder described the early sewer as large enough for a wagon loaded with hay to pass. From 31 BCE to 192 CE manholes gave access, decorated with marble reliefs. Agrippa renovated much of it, and by the 1st century CE all eleven aqueducts supplying Rome were connected to it, so that running water helped keep it clear. Its outfall was by the Ponte Rotto and the Ponte Palatino. Draining marshy ground reduced the mosquitoes that spread malaria, though some of its water was polluted.

Livy described it as a work whose like the splendour of later days had scarcely matched, and Pliny called it an engineering marvel because it withstood floods for centuries. After the fall of the Roman Empire it stayed in use, and in the 1600s the Cardinal Chamberlain taxed the residents of Rome to pay for its upkeep. By the 1800s it was a tourist attraction, and Henry James said it gave him the deepest and grimmest impression of antiquity he had ever received. In 1890 the archaeologist Otto Ludwig Richter mapped it. Parts of it still drain rainwater from the centre of Rome. Roman sewers were widely imitated, and part of the one at Eboracum (York) survives.
clodius-albinus: Albinus was born at Hadrumetum in the province of Africa, to an aristocratic Roman family. The unreliable Historia Augusta gives his parents' names, which modern historians doubt. He entered the army young and served with distinction, especially in 175 during the rebellion of Avidius Cassius against Marcus Aurelius, who is said to have written that without Albinus the legions in Bithynia would have gone over to Cassius and that he intended to have him made consul.

Commodus gave Albinus commands in Gallia Belgica and then in Britain. When a false rumour spread that Commodus had died, Albinus denounced him before his soldiers as a tyrant and argued that the Empire would benefit from restoring the Senate's ancient dignity and power. The Senate was pleased, the emperor was not, and he sent Junius Severus to relieve Albinus of his command. Albinus kept it until after the murders of Commodus and Pertinax in 193.

In the Year of the Five Emperors the legions in Syria proclaimed Pescennius Niger, those in Illyricum and Pannonia proclaimed Septimius Severus, and the armies in Britain and Gaul proclaimed Albinus. Albinus first allied with Severus, who had taken Rome. He added the name Septimius to his own, accepted the title of Caesar. With three British legions and one Spanish, he remained effective ruler of much of the western Empire. After Severus defeated and killed Niger in 194 and took Byzantium in 196, he resolved to be absolute master of the Empire.

In autumn 196 Albinus heard that Severus had named his elder son Caracalla as successor with the title of Caesar and had persuaded the Senate to declare Albinus an enemy of Rome. He proclaimed himself emperor, crossed from Britain to Gaul with a large part of the British garrison and defeated Severus's legate Virius Lupus. He made Lugdunum his headquarters, but he could not win over the Rhine legions.

On 19 February 197 Albinus met the army of Severus at the Battle of Lugdunum, where according to Cassius Dio 150,000 troops stood on each side. Albinus was defeated and died. Severus had the naked body laid out so that he could ride his horse over it. Albinus's wife and two sons were at first pardoned and then beheaded, and their bodies and his headless body were thrown into the Rhône. Severus sent the head to Rome with a letter mocking the Senate for its loyalty to Albinus. Lugdunum was plundered, and Albinus's adherents were persecuted.
clodoald: Clodoald was a grandson of Clovis I and the son of King Chlodomer of Orléans and his wife Guntheuc. After Chlodomer was killed at the Battle of Vézeronce on 25 June 524, fighting the Burgundians, Clodoald and his two brothers were raised in Paris by their grandmother, the queen dowager Clotilde. Their uncles Childebert I, king of Paris, and Clotaire I, king of Soissons wanted the kingdom of Orléans for themselves.

By one account the uncles asked Clotilde to send them the boys so that they could be proclaimed their father's successors, and then had them killed; some say they killed the older two, Thibault and Gonthaire, aged ten and seven, with their own hands. Another account has them ask Clotilde whether the boys should be shorn of their long hair, the sign of Frankish nobility, or killed. Clodoald was saved by a few faithful followers and found refuge with Remigius, the Bishop of Rheims.

Renouncing the throne, he became a disciple of the hermit Séverin of Paris. At about twenty the Bishop of Paris cut his long hair, and his uncles, no longer seeing him as a threat, gave him some of his inheritance. After Séverin's death he lived for eleven years in Provence, where people came to him for healing, then returned to his first hermitage. Bishop Eusebius of Paris ordained him a priest in 551. Seeking to escape the honours that followed, he retired to Novigentum on the Seine, two leagues below Paris, where he built a church dedicated to Martin of Tours and, according to tradition, a monastery endowed with his uncles' gifts.

According to legend he foretold his death, and miracles followed at his tomb, which drew crowds of pilgrims; Novigentum took the name Sanctus Clodoaldus in his honour. Gregory of Tours wrote that he despised an earthly kingdom, cut his hair with his own hand and died a priest. His relics are kept in the Église Saint-Clodoald, and his feast day is 7 September. He is venerated in both the Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches, and St. Cloud in Minnesota, Florida and Wisconsin are named after the French town.
cloistered-rule: The ritsuryo system allowed retired emperors some limited powers, and early examples include Empress Jitō, Emperor Shōmu and Emperor Uda in the 7th, 8th and 9th centuries. By the end of the 10th century the Hokke family of the Fujiwara clan held power through the office of Imperial Regent, and the emperor was increasingly a figurehead. In 1068 Emperor Go-Sanjō became the first emperor in almost 200 years unrelated to the Hokke family by marriage or blood.

While the Fujiwara were occupied with internal conflicts he issued several laws, most notably the Enkyū Shōen Regulation Decree, and so weakened the regency. In 1072 he fell ill and abdicated in favour of Emperor Shirakawa, and died the following year, too soon to exert power after his abdication, but he had made cloistered rule possible.

Retired emperors were called Daijō Tennō or Jōkō, and one who entered a Buddhist monastic community became a Cloistered Emperor, Daijō Hōō. In 1086 Shirakawa abdicated in favour of his four-year-old son, Emperor Horikawa. His aim appeared to be to protect his son from his younger brother, who threatened to become a pretender, but after his retirement he used his own power to set the system in motion.

Separate imperial courts, the In no Chō, grew up round the retired emperors, and their will was carried out through documents called Inzen and In no Chō Kudashi Bumi. The cloistered emperors also had their own troops, the Hokumen no Bushi.

These military units eventually led to the rise of the Taira clan, who used their membership to gather political and economic power. The end of the Heian period saw a rapid succession of cloistered emperors, so that several retired emperors lived at once. The Hōgen Rebellion, after the death of Emperor Toba, was a direct clash between an emperor and an emperor emeritus. The end of the reign of Emperor Go-Shirakawa was marked by the Genpei War and the rise of Minamoto no Yoritomo as the first Kamakura shōgun.

The system was not abandoned at once. When Go-Toba, a grandson of Go-Shirakawa, tried to overthrow the Kamakura shogunate, his forces were defeated in the Jōkyū War, and the shogunate then reduced the power and finances of the retired emperors. Cloistered rule continued formally for another 200 years, a retired emperor presiding as head of the Kyoto court with the approval of the shogunate. The last person to use the title Daijō Hōō was Emperor Reigen, in 1687.
clonakilty: The Irish name, Cloich na Coillte, means stone castle of the woods. In the 14th century a ten-mile strip of woodland called Tuath na gCoillte divided the baronies of Ibane and Barryroe and reached the sea at Clonakilty Bay, and a castle there, Coyltes Castell, appears in a plea roll of 1378. The area has ancient sites such as the Lios na gCon ringfort, and Norman settlers built castles around it. In 1292 Thomas De Roach received a charter for a Monday market at nearby Kilgarriffe. The hinterland is used mainly for dairy farming.

The charter of 1613, obtained from James I by Richard Boyle, 1st Earl of Cork, let the borough return two members to the Irish House of Commons until it was disfranchised by the Act of Union in 1801. The Earls of Shannon, another branch of the Boyle dynasty, were the town's main landlords from the 18th to the early 20th century. In the rebellion of 1641 Protestant settlers fled to Bandon and Catholic rebels burned much of the town. Lord Forbes retook it in October 1642; when rebels attacked his garrison, two Scottish companies were killed to a man, and the rebels later driven out fled towards Inchydoney, where about six hundred drowned at high tide.

A battle was fought at the town in 1691 during the Williamite War, and in 1798 Shannonvale nearby saw the Battle of the Big Cross. Michael Collins attended the local boys' national school and lived in Emmet Square from 1903 to 1905; he later gave orations from O'Donovan's Hotel. The West Cork Railway served the town from 1886 until the station closed on 1 April 1961.

Clonakilty is a market and tourism town of 5,112 people at the 2022 census. A statue of Collins was put up on Emmet Square in 2002, and his former house there has been a museum since 2016. The Church of the Immaculate Conception, designed by George Ashlin, was built in 1880, and the town is known for its black pudding, made to a family recipe since the 1880s.
clonard-abbey: Clonard stood on the River Boyne in County Meath; its Irish name, Cluain Ioraird, means Erard's Meadow. It lay on the Esker Riada, the main east-west road of early medieval Ireland, which added to its standing, but also on the border between the kingdoms of Leinster and Meath, which were at times at war. Very little of the site remains today, though from the air the outlines of some wall boundaries and other earthworks can be seen.

Finnian founded the monastery in about 520, at first building a single cell; the first site may have been nearby Ard Relec. Medieval chronicles say an angel led him there, and he modelled the house on his training at Tours and Llancarfan. He was buried there after his death in about 549. From the eighth century rival dynasties controlled Clonard, and by the mid-ninth century it was the leading church of the Irish midlands, its abbot leading their clergy as the abbot of Armagh led those of the north.

A hymn in Finnian's honour claimed that its school held 3,000 pupils at a time. Much of the abbey burned in 764, and it suffered repeatedly in the Viking age: Danes destroyed it and killed the clergy in 838 and returned in 888, and Ceallachan, King of Cashel, plundered it with the Danes of Waterford in 939. It was pillaged and burnt again in 970, plundered by Connor, King of Munster, in 1113, and in 1143 a fire consumed much of the abbey and all its library.

From the Synod of Ráth Breasail in 1111 Clonard was the seat of a diocese that took in the bishoprics of Trim, Ardbraccan, Dunshaughlin and Slane, as the Synod of Kells confirmed in 1152. It was burnt in 1170 by M'Murcha with Earl Strongbow and the English, and again in 1175, when Walter, son of Hugh de Lacy, built an Augustinian monastery, probably on the ruins of the old abbey. In 1202 the Norman bishop de Rochfort moved the see to Trim in the new Diocese of Meath.
clonmacnoise: The monastery stands south of Athlone, in the ancient territory of Uí Maine, where the main east-west route through the bogs of central Ireland, along the Eiscir Riada, crossed the River Shannon. Saint Ciarán, a young man from Rathcroghan in County Roscommon, came there with seven companions and, with Diarmait mac Cerbaill, later the first Christian High King of Ireland, built a small wooden church. Ciarán died of plague in September 549, not yet thirty-three, and is said to have been buried under it. The name means Meadow of the Sons of Nós.

Its position made Clonmacnoise a centre of religion, learning, craftsmanship and trade by the 9th century, visited by scholars from across Europe. It was tied to the kings of Connacht until the 9th century and then to the kings of Meath, and many high kings were buried there. Between the 8th and 12th centuries its community grew from fewer than ten men to perhaps 1,500 to 2,000, and it was attacked at least 27 times by the Irish, 7 by the Vikings and 6 by the Normans. Its craftsmen made the Clonmacnoise Crozier and the Cross of the Scriptures, and the Book of the Dun Cow was written there in the 12th century.

From the late 12th century the rise of Athlone drew away its people and support, the new continental orders set up rival houses, and the shift from monasteries to dioceses left it the seat of a small, poor diocese. After the English garrison of Athlone wrecked it in 1552 it lay in ruins. Rory O'Connor, the last High King of Ireland, had been buried near the altar of its cathedral in 1198.

The site holds the ruins of a cathedral, seven churches, two round towers, three high crosses and many early Christian grave slabs, among them Temple Ciarán of 909, held to be the oldest dated stone church surviving in Ireland. The Church of Ireland handed it to the state in 1955, and the original crosses are kept in the visitors' centre opened in 1993.
clos-de-vougeot: The vineyard takes its name from the River Vouge, in fact a stream between the village of Vougeot and Chambolle-Musigny. The Cistercians of Cîteaux, the order's mother abbey, bought or were given its land between the 12th and early 14th centuries, beginning with donations of 1109 to 1115, and by 1336 the vineyard was complete and walled. It was the order's flagship vineyard. The monks made separate cuvées from different parts of the slope and blended them, using the top and middle and only sometimes the bottom, to give a wine of consistent quality. The château inside the wall was added in 1551 by rebuilding and enlarging a small chapel and other buildings.

In the French Revolution the state took the vineyard from the church and sold it. Julien-Jules Ouvrard bought the château and vineyards in 1818, and after his death his three heirs kept them as one property until 1889, when six Burgundy wine merchants bought them, dividing the vineyard for the first time in more than 700 years; inheritance and sales have split it further since. One of the buyers, Léonce Bocquet, also bought the château. Etienne Camuzet, who owned it from 1920, made it available to the Confrérie des Chevaliers du Tastevin and on 29 November 1944 sold it to the Société civile des Amis du Château du Clos de Vougeot, which gave the Confrérie a 99-year lease.

The roughly rectangular vineyard slopes gently from its north-west corner, where the château stands, down to the south and east. The best wines are thought to come from the light chalky and gravelly soils on oolitic limestone near the château, bordering Musigny and Grands Échezeaux. The middle has softer limestone with clay, and the almost flat bottom, by the N74 road, has alluvial clay with poor drainage. No other grand cru of the Côte de Nuits reaches down to that road, so wines from the lower plots, all entitled to the grand cru name, vary widely in quality.

Clos de Vougeot is an appellation d'origine contrôlée for red wine made from Pinot noir, with up to 15 percent of Pinot blanc, Pinot gris or Chardonnay allowed. Of its 50.6 hectares, 47.3 are in production, and it is the largest single vineyard of the Côte de Nuits with grand cru status. The château has been the headquarters of the Confrérie des Chevaliers du Tastevin since 1945.
clotilda-slave-ship: Timothy Meaher had the Clotilda built in 1855 or 1856 as a copper-sheathed schooner 86 feet long, designed for the lumber trade. He had learned that West African peoples were at war and that the King of Dahomey was willing to sell prisoners, brought from raids in the interior to the slave market at Ouidah. Meaher was said to have wagered a wealthy man from New Orleans that he could smuggle Africans into the country despite the Act Prohibiting Importation of Slaves of 1807. The schooner was refitted with a false deck, and William Foster carried papers falsely stating that he was delivering lumber.

Foster sailed from Mobile on 4 March 1860 with a crew of 12, including himself, and reached Whydah on 15 May. A hurricane off Bermuda had damaged the ship on the way, and the crew, who had found the hidden deck, were promised double pay, which Foster never gave them. He offered 100 dollars each for 125 captives, chosen from about four thousand held in a warehouse, but seeing two steamers off the port he left with 110 on board. Research in the 21st century suggests that many were Takpa or Tapa, the northern Yoruba name for the Nupe people of present-day Nigeria.

On the voyage back the schooner escaped a man o' war in a squall and was disguised as a coastal trader. Foster brought it into the Port of Mobile at night, transferred the captives to a river steamboat and burned the Clotilda before sinking it. Meaher kept 30 of the captives, and the rest went to the venture's financial backers or were sold further away.

In 1861 the federal government prosecuted Meaher and Foster in Mobile for illegal importation, but the case was dismissed for lack of evidence, perhaps also because of the outbreak of the Civil War. After emancipation the community of Africatown kept Yoruba and its own customs into the 1950s; Kossola lived until 1935, Redoshi (Sally Smith) until 1937 and Matilda McCrear until 1940. The reporter Ben Raines and a team from the University of Southern Mississippi surveyed the 12 Mile Island section of the Mobile River in 2018, and the Alabama Historical Commission announced the find on 22 May 2019. Zora Neale Hurston's Barracoon, an account of Kossola's life completed in 1931, was published in 2018.
cloves: Cloves are the aromatic flower buds of Syzygium aromaticum, an evergreen tree of the family Myrtaceae that grows up to 8 to 12 metres tall, with large leaves and crimson flowers grouped in terminal clusters. The buds are pale at first, turn green and then bright red when ready for harvest, and are picked at 1.5 to 2 centimetres in length. The tree is native to the Maluku Islands, or Moluccas, in Indonesia. The word clove first appears in English in the 15th century and derives, through Old French clou de girofle, from the Latin clavus, meaning nail. A major component of the taste is the chemical eugenol, which makes up 72 to 90 per cent of the essential oil.

Until the colonial era cloves grew only on a few islands in the Moluccas, historically called the Spice Islands, among them Bacan, Makian, Moti, Ternate and Tidore. They were first traded by the Austronesian peoples in their maritime trade network, which began around 1500 BCE and later became the Maritime Silk Road and part of the Spice Trade. The archaeologist Giorgio Buccellati found cloves at Terqa in Syria, in a burned house dated to 1720 BCE, the first evidence of their use in the west before Roman times. They reached Rome by the first century CE.

A Chinese book of about 200 BCE, the Han Guan Yi, says that ministers should suck cloves to sweeten their breath before speaking to the emperor. During the Song dynasty private ventures imported cloves from Austronesian polities such as Java, Srivijaya, Champa and Butuan, and during the Yuan dynasty Chinese merchants began sending ships directly to the Moluccas. Some early mentions of cloves in China, South Asia and the Middle East from before Southeast Asian maritime trade are thought to be misidentifications of other plants such as cassia buds, cinnamon or nutmeg.

Cloves flavour meats, curries, marinades, fruit and hot drinks, and are common in spice blends such as the Malay rempah empat beradik. They are added to betel quids, and in Indonesia they are used in a type of cigarette called kretek. Clove oil is used in traditional medicine as an anodyne, chiefly for dental emergencies. In Europe cloves were used in burial and embalming practices from the late Middle Ages. The earliest known macro-botanical cloves in northwest Europe come from the wreck of the Danish-Norwegian flagship Gribshunden, which sank in June 1495.

In the 17th century the Dutch East India Company sought a monopoly in cloves as it had in nutmeg. In 1770, on the instruction of Pierre Poivre, seedlings of an old tree on Ternate were taken to the Isle de France, now Mauritius, and the Seychelles, and later spread to Martinique and Saint-Domingue. Indonesia is today the largest producer.
clovis-i: Clovis was the son of Childeric I, a king of the Salian Franks, and Basina, a Thuringian princess. The dynasty he founded is named after his supposed grandfather Merovech. Historians believe that Childeric and Clovis were both commanders of the Roman military in the province of Belgica Secunda. Childeric died in 481 and Clovis succeeded him, aged fifteen. Imperial power in Gaul had declined since the death of Aetius in 454, and the lands held by Syagrius, son of Aegidius, formed the Kingdom of Soissons.

In 486 Clovis allied with his relative Ragnachar of Cambrai and another Frankish king, Chararic, and defeated Syagrius at Soissons, ending the last remnant of the Western Roman Empire outside Italy. Clovis made Paris his capital and married Clotilde, a Burgundian Catholic princess, to win the clergy's support. In 496 he narrowly defeated the Alamanni at Tolbiac. In 507 he defeated the Visigothic kingdom of Toulouse at Vouillé, where King Alaric II died.

Clovis was born a pagan. Clotilde persuaded him to accept Catholic Christianity, and he was baptised on Christmas Day near the later abbey of Saint-Remi at Reims; scholars debate the year. After Vouillé he removed the other Frankish kings, among them Chararic and Ragnachar. Under him Salian Frankish law was first written down.

Shortly before his death Clovis called the First Council of Orléans, which passed decrees establishing equality between Franks and Romans. He died in 511 and was buried at the Abbey of Saint Genevieve in Paris. His kingdom was divided among his four sons, a practice that led to disunity until the Merovingian dynasty ended in 751. Many French people regard him as the founder of the French state. In later centuries he was venerated as a saint in France, though never formally canonised.
clovis-point: A Clovis point is lenticular or nearly oval in cross-section and usually widest at or just below the middle, which often gives it a long sharp tip. Most are 75 to 110 mm long, 25 to 50 mm wide and 5 to 10 mm thick, and weigh roughly 25 to 35 grams. The flutes usually run 30% to 50% of the point's length, and the lower edges and base are ground smooth. Points were made of flint, chert, jasper, chalcedony and other stone of conchoidal fracture; those of quartz crystal tend to be smaller.

Few points survive in their original condition: most were reworked to resharpen or repair them, which can make their tradition hard to identify. They vary even at a single site, the eight found at Naco ranging from 2 to 4 inches. Around 10,000 years before present Clovis points disappeared from the continental United States and the Folsom point, mostly shorter and with longer flutes, took their place.

Of the around 6000 points classified as Clovis in the United States, most were found east of the Mississippi, especially in the Southeast, though some researchers think many eastern points are misclassified. Finds reach, less commonly, as far south as Venezuela, and since sea level is now about 50 meters higher than in the Paleoindian period, coastal sites may lie under water. Major sites include the Blackwater Draw type site in New Mexico, the Anzick site in Montana and the Gault site in Texas. Fraudulent points, some with false documentation, have also reached the market.

Clovis points have been identified in over two dozen caches with other stone and bone or ivory tools, from the Mississippi River to the Rocky Mountains. Most seem to be material stored at strategic places on the Pleistocene landscape, though the Anzick cache accompanied a child burial.

Whether the technology arose in the Americas, in response to the hunting of megafauna, or came from elsewhere is an open question. No antecedents have been found in northeast Asia, the homeland of the first Americans in the current consensus. The Solutrean hypothesis, drawing on similarities with points of the Solutrean culture of Iberia, holds that hunters crossed the Atlantic ice-shelf, but it is not well accepted: the two technologies are distinct, Indigenous North Americans show no genetic evidence of European ancestry, and the route was likely unsuitable.
clunia: The remains of Clunia lie on Alto de Castro, more than 1,000 metres above sea level, between the villages of Peñalba de Castro and Coruña del Conde, 2 km from the latter. The city stood on the road from Caesaraugusta (Zaragoza) to Asturica Augusta (Astorga) and was the capital of the Conventus Cluniensis in the province of Hispania Tarraconensis. Its name is of Arevacian origin: a Celtiberian settlement called Cluniaco, or Kolounioukou, stood a short distance from the mount on which the city was founded.

According to Livy, Pompey besieged the place in 75 BCE in his war against Sertorius and was forced to leave, partly because of the weather, before destroying it in 72 BCE. The city was formally founded anew under the emperor Tiberius, as part of the plan to pacify the region after the Cantabrian Wars. As a municipium it minted small coins, asses and dupondi, naming the local quattuorviri in charge of the mint. In 68 CE Sulpicius Galba, governor of Hispania, took refuge at Clunia during the revolt against Nero, received there the news of his elevation by the Senate, and travelled from it to Rome.

The city flourished in the 1st and 2nd centuries CE and at its height is calculated to have had about 30,000 inhabitants. It lost people during the crisis of the 3rd century and was burned by invading tribes towards its end. Limited rebuilding took place under Diocletian and Constantine, but large parts lay empty by the Visigothic era. Troops of the Berber general Tariq ibn-Ziyad took the area in 713, and Christian settlers in 912 built their town on the site of present-day Coruña del Conde.

Excavations began in 1915 and resumed in 1931 and 1958, revealing a city of about 1.2 square kilometres: a theatre cut into the rock for 10,000 spectators, the forum with a basilica and a macellum, houses with mosaics and underfloor heating, large baths and a great drain. Finds such as an effigy of Isis and a torso of Dionysus are kept in the National Archaeological Museum of Spain and the museum of Burgos.
cluny-abbey: William I, Duke of Aquitaine, founded the abbey in 910 on a modest scale as the motherhouse of the Congregation of Cluny and chose as its first abbot Berno, abbot of Baume and of Gigny. The deed of gift stipulated that the monastery would be free from local authorities, lay or ecclesiastical, and subject only to the pope, who could not appoint an abbot without the consent of the monks. William gave up his hunting preserve in Burgundy and released the abbey from all obligations to him and his family other than prayer, whereas patrons normally kept a proprietary interest and installed their kinsmen as abbots.

Odo, abbot from 926, travelled from monastery to monastery to consolidate the reform, and in 931 obtained the right to reform other abbeys. Majolus directed Cluny from 954 until 994 and was nicknamed the arbiter of kings. Odilo, abbot for 55 years from 994, supported the Peace and Truce of God, and at his death the order had 70 houses. Under Hugh of Semur, abbot from 1049, it extended into Spain, Italy and England and numbered 10,000 monks.

Cluny III was financed largely by the annual payment set by Ferdinand I of León, which Alfonso VI doubled in 1090. When payments in gold later lapsed, the Order fell into a financial crisis. The foundation of the more austere Cîteaux Abbey in 1098 challenged Cluny's supremacy, and the Cistercians and the Mendicants later weakened its standing. With the Concordat of Bologna in 1516 the king of France gained the power to appoint the abbot. The order was suppressed in France in 1790, the library and archives were burned in 1793, and the monastery was mostly demolished in 1810.

Cluny created a highly centralised federated order, foreign to Benedictine tradition, in which the heads of subsidiary houses, styled priors, answered to the abbot of Cluny and met at Cluny once a year. By the twelfth century 314 monasteries paid allegiance to it. Its central work was the liturgy: monks recited 138 psalms each day, rising to 215 in Lent, and hired workers did the labour that monks had traditionally done.

Cluny was not known for the severity of its discipline, and its monks ate well and used silver candelabras and gold chalices set with gems. Four monks of Cluny became popes: Gregory VII, Urban II, Paschal II and Urban V. Little remains of the buildings, only about 10 per cent of the floor space of Cluny III.
clynnog-fawr: Clynnog Fawr, often simply Clynnog, is a village and community in the historic county of Caernarfonshire, lying on the A499 road between Caernarfon and Pwllheli, between the coast and a mountainous area that includes Bwlch Mawr. The community, which includes Pant Glas, covers 4,551 hectares. Its name means the place of the holly-trees, Celynnog in Middle Welsh, and can be compared with the Breton Quelneuc and the Gaelic Cuilneach.

The site of St Beuno's Church is said to be that of a Celtic monastery founded by Beuno. It grew into an important foundation, and some Welsh law manuscripts state that the Abbot of Clynnog was entitled to a seat at the court of the king of Gwynedd. The church is recorded as having been burnt by the Vikings in 978 and later by the Normans. By the end of the 15th century it was a collegiate church, one of only six in Wales.

Pilgrims bound for Bardsey Island left alms in Cyff Beuno, an ancient chest hollowed from a single piece of ash that the church still holds, and Maen Beuno, Beuno's Stone, bears marks said to be those of the saint's fingers. In the churchyard stands a canonical sundial dated between the late 10th and the early 12th century. Two battles were fought in the area: at Bron yr Erw in 1075 Trahaearn ap Caradog defeated Gruffudd ap Cynan's first bid for the kingship of Gwynedd, and at Bryn Derwin in 1255 Llywelyn ap Gruffudd defeated his brothers Owain and Dafydd to become sole ruler of Gwynedd.

The church, far larger than a village of its size would lead one to expect, is a major stop on the North Wales Pilgrims Way, and Ffynnon Beuno, St Beuno's Well, at the south-west end of the village, is a Grade II* listed structure. The community had 997 inhabitants at the 2011 census, when 73.2% could speak Welsh. The poet Ebenezer Thomas, Eben Fardd, lived in the village opposite the church from 1827.
cnut-the-great: Cnut was a son of Swein Forkbeard and came from a line of Scandinavian rulers central to the unification of Denmark. His grandfather Harald Bluetooth was king at the time of the Christianization of Denmark. Neither the place nor the date of his birth is known. He was already a Christian before he was king, and was named Lambert at his baptism. In September 1015 he landed at Sandwich, sailed round Kent to Wessex and harried Dorset, Wiltshire and Somerset, beginning a campaign of an intensity not seen since the days of Alfred the Great.

On 18 October 1016 Cnut's army defeated Edmund Ironside's at the Battle of Assandun in Essex, where Eadric Streona withdrew his forces and brought about a decisive English defeat.
