Cnut ruled England for nearly two decades. He quickly eliminated possible challengers from the Wessex dynasty: Eadwig Ætheling was killed on his orders, and Edmund Ironside's sons fled abroad. In July 1017 he married Queen Emma, widow of Æthelred. In 1018 he collected a Danegeld of £72,000, with another £10,500 from London, paid off his army and kept 40 ships as a standing force.

When Harald II died in 1018, Cnut went to Denmark to secure the throne. At Easter 1027 he attended the coronation of the Holy Roman Emperor Conrad II in Rome, where he sought lower costs for the pallium of English archbishops and better conditions for pilgrims. On the way back he wrote that he was king of all England and Denmark and the Norwegians and of some of the Swedes. He claimed the crown of Norway at Trondheim in 1028. He repaired churches and monasteries that Viking raids had plundered and was a patron of monastic communities, though his marriage to Emma while he was married to Ælfgifu of Northampton conflicted with Church teaching.

Cnut died on 12 November 1035 at Shaftesbury in Dorset and was buried in the Old Minster at Winchester. His son Harthacnut succeeded him in Denmark, while Harold Harefoot, his son by Ælfgifu, became regent in England and claimed the throne in 1037. The medieval historian Norman Cantor called Cnut the most effective king in Anglo-Saxon history. Henry of Huntingdon, in the early twelfth century, first recorded the story of Cnut commanding the tide not to wet him, which has become the best-known story about him. In modern readings he is usually a wise man who knew from the start that he could not control the waves.
co-loa-citadel: Cổ Loa lies in Hanoi's Đông Anh District, about 17 kilometres north of the city centre, on the upper plain north of the Red River. Its name is the Sino-Vietnamese reading of characters meaning ancient spiral; the chronicle Đại Việt Sử Ký Toàn Thư describes the city as shaped like a snail. Two outer ramparts enclose a rectangular inner citadel, and the outer embankment covered some 600 hectares. Streams such as the Hoàng Giang River and a network of lakes served as moats and waterways. Relics of the Bronze Age Phùng Nguyên and Đông Sơn cultures have been found there, and it may have been the first political centre of Vietnamese civilisation.

Tradition holds that An Dương Vương had the city built after he defeated the Hùng king of Văn Lang. In the legend of the Golden Turtle, spirits led by a thousand-year-old white chicken undid each day's work until the giant turtle Kim Quy rose from the water to protect the king, leaving him a claw to serve as the trigger of an invincible crossbow made by Cao Lỗ.

In the legend of Trọng Thủy and Mị Châu, the king's daughter gave away the crossbow's secret to her husband, a prince of Nam Việt, and the fortress fell to that kingdom. Ngô Quyền was enthroned at Cổ Loa in 939, and it remained the capital until it was sacked in 965 during the Anarchy of the 12 Warlords.

The outer rampart runs for 8 km, was lined with guard towers and still stands up to 12 m high and 25 m wide at the base. A cut through the inner rampart was dated to 400 to 350 BCE, which suggests it was built by a local society before Han rule; archaeologists estimate that over two million cubic metres of material were moved. In 1970 Đông Sơn sherds were found beneath the outer wall, and an excavation of 2007 to 2008 through the middle wall showed three periods and five major phases of construction.

A bronze drum found by chance outside the inner wall in the 1980s weighs 72 kg and held around 200 bronze pieces: 96 ploughshares, 32 socketed axes, sixteen spearheads, six hoes, eight arrowheads, a chisel and a dagger. One spearhead has an iron blade in a bronze socket.
coahuila: Coahuila borders Nuevo León to the east, Zacatecas to the south and Durango and Chihuahua to the west. To the north it holds a 512 km stretch of the border with the United States, along the Rio Grande opposite Texas. With an area of 151,563 km2 it is the third-largest state in Mexico. The Sierra Madre Oriental crosses it from north-west to south-east, and west of the range the land lies in the Chihuahuan Desert. The state is largely arid or semi-arid, but its rivers support irrigated farming, especially of cotton, and the Parras district produces wine and brandy.

The Spanish explored the north some decades after their victory over the Aztecs, and the harsher climate and the absence of gold delayed them. The first Spanish settlement in the region was at Minas de la Trinidad in 1577, and Saltillo was settled in 1586 as part of the province of Nueva Vizcaya in New Spain. Tlaxcalan settlers founded a community beside Saltillo, San Esteban de Nueva Tlaxcala.

Under the Constitution of 1824 Coahuila y Tejas became a state of independent Mexico, first with Nuevo León, which was detached later that year, and with Texas, which stayed until it seceded in 1836. Monclova was the capital from 1833 to 1835. In 1840 Coahuila was briefly part of the Republic of the Rio Grande. In the mid-19th century the Sánchez Navarro family owned a ranch of 6,700,000 hectares, mostly in Coahuila, the largest privately owned property in the Americas, and Comanche raiders attacked the state often in the 1840s and 1850s. On 19 February 1856 Santiago Vidaurri annexed Coahuila to Nuevo León, and it regained separate status in 1868. In the Mexican Revolution Francisco Villa attacked Torreón.

Coahuila de Zaragoza, named for General Ignacio Zaragoza, who was born there, is one of the 31 states of Mexico. Its capital is Saltillo, and its other main cities are Torreón, Monclova, Piedras Negras and Ciudad Acuña. The state has two biosphere reserves, Maderas del Carmen and the Cuatro Ciénegas Basin. Venustiano Carranza and Francisco I. Madero, both presidents of Mexico, came from Coahuila.
coal: The word coal took the form col in Old English, from a reconstructed Proto-Germanic root meaning live coal, and has cognates in Old Norse kol, Dutch kool and German Kohle. The oldest intentional use of black coal documented is at Ostrava, Petřkovice, in an Old Stone Age settlement on the top of Landek Hill. Radiocarbon dating places the site between 25,000 and 23,000 BCE. Coal has been known and used for thousands of years, but its use was limited until the Industrial Revolution, and with the invention of the steam engine consumption increased.

Coal is a combustible black or brownish-black sedimentary rock that forms in layers called coal seams. It is mostly carbon, with variable amounts of hydrogen, sulfur, oxygen and nitrogen. It formed when plants decayed into peat, which the heat and pressure of deep burial over millions of years converted into coal. Vast deposits formed from wetlands, the coal forests that covered much of the tropics during the late Carboniferous and early Permian. The process is called coalification: dead plant matter was protected from oxidation, usually by mud or acidic water, and became peat, which was then buried by sediments and lost water, methane and carbon dioxide, so that its proportion of carbon rose.

The grade of coal depends on the maximum pressure and temperature reached. Lignite, or brown coal, forms under relatively mild conditions and is the lowest rank. Sub-bituminous coal, bituminous coal and anthracite follow with increasing temperature and pressure. Bituminous coal is the more abundant of the two main black coals, and anthracite has the highest percentage of carbon; some anthracite deposits contain pure carbon in the form of graphite.

Most coal is used as fuel. Bituminous coal, known as steam coal in the UK, was historically used to raise steam in locomotives and ships, and coal later fired power stations, where it is burned in a furnace to make the steam that turns turbines. Coke is made by baking metallurgical coal in an oven without oxygen at temperatures as high as 1,000 °C, and it serves in blast furnaces as a fuel and as the agent that reduces iron ore to iron.

Chemicals have been made from coal since the 1940s, mainly by gasification to produce syngas, from which methanol, hydrogen, ammonia, urea and many other products derive. Coal can also be converted into synthetic fuels equivalent to gasoline or diesel; the chemical company Sasol of South Africa used gasification combined with the Fischer–Tropsch process to make chemicals and motor fuels from coal. The deadly London smog was caused chiefly by the heavy use of coal.
coatzacoalcos-river: The Coatzacoalcos rises in the Sierra de Niltepec and crosses the state of Oaxaca in the region of the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, flowing for 325 kilometres to the Gulf of Mexico and feeding mainly the south of Veracruz. Its tributaries include the El Corte, Sarabia, Jaltepec, Chalchijalpa, El Chiquito, Uxpanapa and Calzadas, and together they give it one of the largest flows in the region. Two-thirds of its streams are navigable.
By legend the god Quetzalcoatl sailed away on a raft of serpent skin until he was lost on the horizon, and the river has since borne the Nahuatl name Coatzacoalcos, the place where the serpent hides.

The expedition of Juan de Grijalva reached the river in 1518, and Hernán Cortés later sent Diego de Ordaz to explore it as a possible port. The oldest known map of the river was drawn by Francisco Gali in 1580. Unlike most maps made in New Spain in the last quarter of the sixteenth century, it is wholly European in style, somewhat like a nautical chart, and its errors of distance and many corrections suggest it was made in haste.

Gali seems to have been most interested in the possibility of joining the North Sea and the South Sea across the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, and the map was probably drawn to show that the river could serve as an interoceanic passage.

The city of Coatzacoalcos at the river's mouth is a commercial and industrial port serving the farming, forestry and trade of the isthmus. The river is heavily polluted, partly for lack of laws protecting public water; the Mexican Center of Environmental Law names the petrochemical industry of Pemex as the largest polluter.
cobbold-commission: The commission was to establish whether the people of North Borneo, now Sabah, and Sarawak supported a federation of Malaya, Brunei, Singapore, North Borneo and Sarawak. Its chairman was Lord Cobbold, former Governor of the Bank of England, and its members were Wong Pow Nee, Chief Minister of Penang; Ghazali Shafie, Permanent Secretary to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs; Anthony Abell, former Governor of Sarawak; and David Watherston, former Chief Secretary of Malaya.

The commission released its report on 1 August 1962 and concluded that Malaysia should be formed, with all parties entering as equal partners. It judged the project better than continued British rule, early independence or a federation of the Borneo territories alone, provided they received special positions in view of their different racial composition, their distance from Malaya and their political immaturity compared with Malaya and Singapore. Abell and Watherston also argued that Malaysia would check a Communist takeover of Singapore, which might spread to Sarawak and North Borneo.

Cobbold reported that about a third of each territory's people strongly favoured early federation, a third asked for conditions and safeguards, and the rest wanted independence first or British rule for some years more; a hard core of opponents might amount to near 20 per cent in Sarawak and somewhat less in North Borneo. In a letter of 21 June 1962 to Harold Macmillan, not disclosed in the report, he wrote that he supported Malaysia on the assumption that Singapore also joined.

The commission recommended that Sarawak and North Borneo keep their identity through a high level of local autonomy and a quota of seats in the federal parliament. It accepted Islam as the religion of the federation without endangering the freedom of other faiths, allowed Malay, English and indigenous languages in the Borneo assemblies for ten years, gave the Borneo states control over entry from other states of Malaysia, and recommended no right of secession, for fear of political and racial division.
coburg: Coburg lies on the River Itz at the foot of the Thuringian Highlands, about 90 kilometres south of Erfurt and 100 kilometres north of Nuremberg. During the Cold War, as part of West Germany, it bordered East German Thuringia on three sides. The origin of the name is unclear; the first element may be the German kuh, cow, giving a literal meaning of cow borough.

Coburg was first mentioned in a monastic document of 1056, although a settlement called Trufalistat already stood there. The name at first referred to a property centred on the hill where Veste Coburg was later built. The castle passed to the House of Henneberg in 1248 and to the House of Wettin in 1353. During the Diet of Augsburg in 1530 Martin Luther spent six months there, since his lord John, Elector of Saxony, feared he would be imprisoned and burned as a heretic if he attended, and he continued his translation of the Bible into German. In 1547 the princely residence moved to the Ehrenburg, a former monastery rebuilt as a Renaissance palace.

Coburg became capital of the Duchy of Saxe-Coburg in 1596 and of Saxe-Coburg-Gotha from 1826 to 1918. Dynastic marriages tied the ducal family to the royal houses of Belgium, Bulgaria, Portugal and Britain. Leopold of Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld became King of Belgium in 1831, and Prince Albert married Queen Victoria in 1840. The last duke, Charles Edward, abdicated in November 1918. The Free State of Coburg then voted by an 88 per cent majority to join Bavaria rather than Thuringia, and the merger took place on 1 July 1920.

Coburg is in Upper Franconia, Bavaria, with a population close to 41,500. It was not much damaged in the Second World War and keeps many historic buildings. Veste Coburg is one of Germany's largest castles, and its museum includes the collection of copperplate engravings begun by the duke in the early 19th century.
cochabamba-water-war: After hyperinflation reached an annual rate of 25000% in 1985, successive Bolivian governments followed the World Bank's provisions to qualify for loans, and a condition of one loan was to privatise the water utilities of La Paz and Cochabamba. Aguas del Tunari was the only bidder for SEMAPA, the city's state water agency, and the government of President Hugo Banzer signed a 40-year concession guaranteeing the consortium a minimum annual return of 15%. The contract bound it to finish the stalled Misicuni dam, a project backed by the mayor, Manfred Reyes Villa. Law 2029, passed to secure the deal, led many to fear that communal and irrigation water would also be taken over.

The company raised rates by an average of 35% to about 20 dollars a month, when many customers earned about 100 dollars a month. Irrigators of the Federación Departamental Cochabambina de Regantes under Omar Fernandez and factory workers' unions under Oscar Olivera formed the Coordinadora, which led protests from January 2000. A general strike shut the city for four days, and clashes on 4 February left 70 protesters and 51 policemen injured. In March the Coordinadora held its own referendum, in which 96% of fifty thousand votes demanded the contract be cancelled.

In April protesters took the central plaza again, the Coordinadora's leaders were arrested, and roadblocks spread across Bolivia. Banzer declared a state of siege on 8 April, suspending some constitutional guarantees and curtailing the press. After an army captain, Robinson Iriarte de la Fuente, was filmed firing into a crowd and killing the student Víctor Hugo Daza, the consortium's executives fled to Santa Cruz. The government declared the contract revoked, and Law 2029 was changed in a special session on 11 April 2000.

Aguas del Tunari filed a claim at the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes; in a settlement of 19 January 2006 its shareholders withdrew their claims. A military tribunal acquitted Iriarte in March 2002. Water prices returned to their earlier levels under a restored SEMAPA, but as late as 2005 half of the city's 600,000 people had no water connection. The struggle raised the profile of Evo Morales, elected president in 2005, and won anti-globalisation groups' support; it was later drawn on by films including Even the Rain and Quantum of Solace.
cochasqui: Cochasquí lies on the slopes of Mojanda, an inactive volcano, 52 km north of Quito and 3,040 metres above sea level. Its builders, the Caranqui, lived between the Chota river in the north and the Guayllabamba river in the south. They were farmers living in scattered villages grouped into chiefdoms under a cacique, and Cochasquí is thought to have been one of the most powerful, beside Otavalo, Cayambe and Caranqui. Such complexes are common in the northern highlands; the largest, at Hacienda Zuleta, has 148 mounds and pyramids.

The first settlers, of the phase archaeologists call Cochasquí I, arrived around 950 but built no mounds. The pyramids came in the next phase and were raised over a long time, some enlarged in several stages. They were made of earth packed between retaining walls of cangahua, a soft volcanic rock, and faced with cangahua blocks covered in mud; nine have ramps giving them a T shaped plan. They are thought to have been temples, and a Caranqui clay model shows a round hut and an enclosing wall on top. Among the burial mounds, mound a held a woman with three vases and seven deformed human skulls; no gold has been found.

After the Inca conquest Inca pottery reached the site, which became a tambo on the Inca roads. A legend tells that Quilago, Queen of Cochasquí, resisted Huayna Capac for two years, was captured and forced to marry him, and was executed after plotting to kill him. Under Spanish rule Cochasquí became an encomienda of Antón Diez by 1561, was slowly abandoned, and in 1655 became an hacienda. On 20 March 1740 the astronomer Pierre Bouguer of the French Geodesic Mission took measurements from the top of a pyramid.

Max Uhle, aged 76, made the first excavation in 1932, funded by Jacinto Jijón y Caamaño, and archaeologists of Bonn University under Udo Oberem continued it in 1964–1965. The Cochasquí Archaeological Park was created in 1981, and nearby indigenous communities gather there for festivals such as the Inti Raymi.
cochinchina-campaign: French missionaries had worked in Vietnam since the 17th century, and by the mid-19th century Bishop Pellerin counted 600,000 Catholic converts in Annam and Tonkin, led mostly by French and Spanish clergy whom many Vietnamese distrusted. The persecution of missionaries under the emperors Minh Mạng and Thiệu Trị in the 1840s drew only sporadic French responses. In 1857, however, the execution of two Spanish missionaries approved by Emperor Tự Đức coincided with a French expedition to China in the Second Opium War, and in November Napoleon III authorised Admiral Charles Rigault de Genouilly to lead a punitive expedition.

In September 1858 a French and Spanish force captured Tourane (Da Nang), but the Vietnamese Christians did not rise as Pellerin had predicted, and an army under Nguyễn Tri Phương pinned the allies down in a siege of nearly three years in which disease caused heavy losses. Rigault de Genouilly turned south and took Saigon on 17 February 1859, demolishing its citadel and burning its rice granaries on 8 March. A garrison of about 1,000 men was then besieged in Saigon from March 1860 to February 1861, while Tourane was evacuated.

With the war in China over, Admiral Léonard Charner brought 70 ships and 3,500 soldiers to Saigon and broke the siege lines at the Battle of Ky Hoa on 24 and 25 February 1861. Mỹ Tho fell on 12 April without a shot. Tự Đức turned to guerrilla warfare, and French units roving the countryside fanned resistance by their brutality towards suspected insurgents. Admiral Louis Adolphe Bonard took Biên Hòa on 16 December 1861 and Vĩnh Long on 23 March 1862, after which Tự Đức sued for peace.

Tự Đức's minister Phan Thanh Giản signed the treaty with Bonard and the Spanish representative, Colonel Carlos Palanca Gutiérrez, on 5 June 1862. Besides the provinces of Biên Hòa, Gia Định and Định Tường, Vietnam ceded the islands of Poulo Condore, legalised Catholic worship, opened the Mekong and three ports to French trade and agreed to pay one million dollars over ten years.

In 1867 Admiral Pierre de la Grandière forced the cession of Châu Đốc, Hà Tiên and Vĩnh Long, which Tự Đức recognised only in the 1874 Treaty of Saigon. Spain, the junior partner, gained a share of the indemnity but no territory and withdrew its last troops in 1863. Peace also freed Tự Đức to crush a rising in Tonkin led by the Catholic nobleman Le Bao Phung, who was captured, tortured and put to death.
cocijoeza: The king, whose name is also written Guxi Chikoeza or Kosi'ioeza, bore a Zapotec name meaning storm or time of obsidian knives; the Aztecs called him Huizquiauitl. He was born around 1450 and took the throne of Zaachila as coquitao, or king, in 1487. His kingdom lay on the route between the highlands of the Valley of Mexico and the Maya lands of present-day Chiapas and Guatemala, and it had important industries of salt production, goldsmithing and cochineal dye, which drew the interest of the Aztec Empire.

To counter the Aztec threat, in 1494 the king ordered the Aztec spies in his territory killed. The Aztec ruler Ahuitzotl took the killings as a cause for war and invaded. Huaxyacac was the first city attacked and destroyed, followed by Mitla, the Isthmus of Tehuantepec and Soconusco. The king asked for help from the Mixtec king Dzahuindanda, who sent 24,000 warriors to join the 36,000 of Zaachila's army, and the allies drove the Aztecs out.

Ahuitzotl attacked the Zapotec and Mixtec kingdoms a second time and sent his general, the Tlacateccatl, against the stronghold of Guiengola, a city the king had built. The siege lasted seven months. Ahuitzotl then proposed a peace treaty that included the hand of his daughter, Princess Xilabela.
Two princes were born of the marriage with Xilabela, one of them named Pinopiaa. The king died in 1529 and was buried in Zaachila, where it was the custom to bury the Zapotec sovereigns.
cockacoeske: The death of Opechancanough in 1646 broke up the confederacy his brother Powhatan had built. Cockacoeske, herself a descendant of Opechancanough, was the wife of Totopotomoi, who became leader in 1649 but whom the English called only "king of the Pamunkeys". He was killed in what was later called the Battle of Bloody Run, fighting alongside the Virginia militia against the migrating Westo. The colony then recognised Cockacoeske as "Queen" of the Pamunkey, who lived between the Pamunkey and Mattaponi rivers on land later designated the Pamunkey Indian Reservation.

During Bacon's Rebellion Governor Berkeley's faction asked the Pamunkey for warriors. Cockacoeske came to the statehouse at Jamestown in wampum and a fringed deerskin mantle, with an interpreter and retainers including her son. In the historian Martha McCartney's words, she gave the council "a reminder ... that it was in identical circumstances that her husband and a hundred of his bowmen had lost their lives, for which sacrifice there had been no compensation", and offered only a few men. Nathaniel Bacon's followers attacked the Pamunkey first and drove them into the Dragon Swamp, killing an attendant who led them astray.

She signed the Treaty of Middle Plantation with Governor Jeffreys on 29 May 1677, after negotiations begun on 5 May, as its first signatory, and King Charles II had a medal made for her. Article 12 gave every Indian king and queen equal power over their own people except the Queen of Pamunkey, to whom "several scattered Indian Nations doe now againe owne their antient subjection", probably meaning the Chickahominys and Rappahannocks. They soon refused her tribute, complaining that she had executed some Chickahominys, and her appeals to colonial arbitration in 1678 seem to have failed.

Colonial records name one child, John West, born around 1656–57 and "reputed the son of an English colonel", who signed the treaty as "Cap't John West, sonne to the Queen of Pamunkey"; Pamunkey tradition names others, such as Susannah. She died in 1686 and, in a matrilineal society, was succeeded by her niece Betty. In 2004 the Library of Virginia honoured her among its Virginia Women in History.
cockburn-town: Cockburn Town stands on Grand Turk, the largest island in the Turks Islands archipelago, and spreads across most of it. Historic Bermudian architecture of the 18th and 19th centuries lines Duke and Front Streets, and the town is known for its long, narrow streets and old street lamps. The nearest anchorage is Hawk's Nest Anchorage, which is sheltered but should be entered only in good light because of reefs near the entrance.

Cockburn Town was the first permanent settlement on any of the islands, founded in 1681 by salt collectors. It is supposed to lie where Juan Ponce de León first landed on the island. It has been the seat of government ever since 1766, and it is named for Francis Cockburn, a former Governor of the Bahamas. It reportedly has ties to the Burrowes family, whose proclivity aided the naming of the town.

Her Majesty's Prison on Pond Street was built in the 1830s and stayed in operation until 1994. It has a main cell block, offices for prison officials and a bell tower, and today it hosts its own museum.

Cockburn Town is the capital of the Turks and Caicos Islands. The Turks & Caicos National Museum is in Guinep House on Front Street, a colonial-era house believed to be over 180 years old, built largely from the timber of local shipwrecks, including a ship's mast that is one of its main supports. The museum's collections include the Molasses Reef Wreck, dated 1505, the oldest known European shipwreck in the Americas, and exhibits on the Lucayans, slavery and the slave trade, and the sisal and salt industries.
code-noir: Before the code, slavery in the French Antilles had no statute of its own. The Edict of May 1664 founding the French West India Company did not mention slaves, and the Sovereign Council of Martinique filled the gap with its own rulings: in 1652, at the request of Jesuit missionaries, it held that slaves should not work on Sundays, and in 1664 that they must be baptised and attend catechism. In 1681 the king had Jean-Baptiste Colbert prepare a statute, drawing on memoranda from the intendants Jean-Baptiste Patoulet and Michel Bégon and the governor general Charles de Courbon de Blénac, as well as local custom and the Council's rulings.

In 60 articles the code treated the slave as property, though criminally liable. Its first article ordered all Jews out of the colonies within three months, aimed chiefly at the Jewish community of Martinique, whose first synagogue the Da Costa family had founded in 1676. Slaves could practise no religion but Catholicism, could marry only with their master's permission, and a child took the status of its mother. Slaves of different masters were forbidden to gather, on pain of whipping and branding. A fugitive absent for a month was to lose his ears and be branded, after a second month his hamstring was cut, and a third flight meant death.

Masters had to feed and clothe their slaves, including the sick and old, and might chain and beat them but not torture or mutilate them; in practice masters were very rarely convicted of killing or torturing slaves. Married slaves and their young children were not to be separated by sale. Owners of 20 could free their slaves, and freed people became French subjects with the rights of colonial subjects, though bound to show special respect to their former master.

The title Code noir first appeared during the regency of Philippe II, Duke of Orléans. Louis XV ratified versions for the Mascarene Islands in December 1723 and for Louisiana, registered in New Orleans on 10 September 1724; both had 54 articles and were far more racialist and segregationist, and the Louisiana code forbade marriage between whites and blacks. The British kept the Mascarene text after annexing Mauritius. The historian Tyler Stovall called the code one of the most extensive official documents on race, slavery and freedom ever drawn up in Europe.
code-of-hammurabi: The Code is a Babylonian legal text in the Old Babylonian dialect of Akkadian, purportedly by Hammurabi, sixth king of the Amorite First Dynasty of Babylon, who ruled from around 1792 to around 1750 BCE by the middle chronology. When he inherited the throne Babylon held little sway, and the local power was Rim-Sin of Larsa. Hammurabi conquered his territory in one campaign. His letters suggest an interest in law and justice, and he often calls himself his people's shepherd. The Code was not the first Mesopotamian law collection: the Code of Ur-Nammu, the Code of Lipit-Ishtar and the Laws of Eshnunna are earlier, and they too claim a ruler as author.

The main copy is a basalt stele 2.25 m tall, with a relief at the top of Hammurabi with Shamash, the sun god and god of justice. Below are about 4,130 lines of cuneiform, one fifth a poetic prologue and epilogue and four fifths the laws. In the prologue Hammurabi says the gods chose him to rule in order to prevent the strong from oppressing the weak. The laws are conditional sentences, if one thing happens then another follows, and cover criminal, family, property and commercial law, including rules on medical treatment. They apply the principle of lex talionis: law 196 prescribes an eye for an eye, and law 229 requires the death of a builder whose house collapses and kills its owner.

Nobles had greater protection than commoners and enslaved people. Scholars dispute what the text was. Some treat it as legislation, others as a law report of past cases, and others as an abstract work of jurisprudence, a view that has gained support among Assyriologists.

The stele was found in 1901 at Susa in present-day Iran, where it had been taken as plunder about 600 years after it was made. It was found in three large fragments and now stands in the Louvre. Seven columns near the bottom were polished away in antiquity, but over 50 manuscripts of the laws are known, from Susa, Babylon, Nineveh, Assur and other sites, and they fill in most of the erased text. Scribes copied the text for over a millennium. Father Jean-Vincent Scheil published the first edition in 1902, and editions in German, English and Italian followed. Scholars compared its provisions with the Mosaic Law, but the consensus is that the similarities come from shared traditions and not direct borrowing.
code-of-justinian: Soon after he became emperor in 527, Justinian decided that the legal system needed repair. Three codices of imperial laws existed, together with individual laws, many of which conflicted or were out of date. The Codex Gregorianus and the Codex Hermogenianus were unofficial compilations, and the Codex Theodosianus was ordered by Theodosius II. The constitution Hac quae necessario told the commission to eliminate everything unnecessary or obsolete, make changes as it saw fit, and produce a single compilation of laws in force. The commission finished in 14 months.

The first compilation did not remove all conflicts in Roman jurisprudence, and its constitutions were to be used alongside the opinions of ancient jurists. Justinian tried to harmonise these through his Fifty Decisions and new laws, so the Code no longer reflected the latest imperial law, and he ordered a new compilation. No copy of the first edition survives; only a fragment of an index on an Egyptian papyrus remains.

The second edition, the Codex Repetitae Praelectionis, was published on 16 November 534 and took effect on 30 December. Book 1 concerns ecclesiastical law, the sources of law and the duties of higher offices; books 2 to 8 cover private law; book 9 deals with crimes; books 10 to 12 contain administrative law.

In the West the Codex was largely lost, or in many places never present. The only manuscript known to have held the whole Latin text is a Veronese palimpsest of the 6th or 7th century, now only fragments. In the empire it was translated into Greek and adapted in the 9th century as the Basilika. Substantially complete Latin versions were restored around the end of the 12th century, and Paul Krüger produced the modern standard version in 1877. No English translation was made before the 20th century; Samuel Parsons Scott's of 1932 was criticised for using the edition of the Kriegel brothers, and a new one from Cambridge University Press appeared in October 2016.
code-of-ur-nammu: The first copy of the code, a tablet known as Ni 3191, is an Old Babylonian period copy in two fragments found at Nippur, in what is now Iraq. Samuel Kramer translated it in 1952; the fragments are held at the Istanbul Archaeology Museums. Because of its poor preservation only the long prologue and five of the laws could be read.

Two further Old Babylonian fragments, found at Ur and now in the Iraq Museum in Baghdad, were translated in 1965 and allowed about 30 of the 57 laws to be reconstructed. Two copies from Sippar, one in Istanbul and one in the British Museum, carry the prologue and laws and part of the concluding formula. A clay cylinder of unknown origin in the Schoyen Collection has been dated to the Ur III period.

The prologue invokes the deities Nanna and Utu for Ur-Nammu's kingship and decrees equity in the land. It credits the king with fixing the bronze sila measure and standard weights, and states that the orphan was not delivered up to the rich man, nor the widow to the mighty man. The preface credits the laws to Ur-Nammu, though some scholars have attributed them to his son Shulgi.

The laws are arranged in the form of IF (offence) THEN (penalty), a pattern followed in nearly all later codes. They set monetary compensation for bodily injury rather than the later principle of an eye for an eye: a man who knocked out another's tooth paid two shekels of silver, and one who cut off a foot paid ten. Murder, robbery, adultery and rape were capital offences. A man accused of sorcery had to undergo ordeal by water, though the translation is disputed.

The code shows a society with two basic strata beneath the king, the free person and the slave, with rules for the marriage of slaves and for divorce. It is about three centuries older than the Code of Hammurabi, and earlier law codes such as that of Urukagina are known to have existed but do not survive. Ur-Nammu's laws and reforms have been seen as some of the earliest documented regard for widows, orphans and the poor in the Fertile Crescent.
codelco: The company grew out of the Copper Office, created by Law 11,828 of 5 May 1955 under President Carlos Ibáñez del Campo. Under President Eduardo Frei Montalva, Law 16,425 of 25 January 1966 turned the office into the Copper Corporation of Chile. The constitutional reform of 11 July 1971, under President Salvador Allende, transferred full ownership of all the country's copper mines to the corporation, and its present form was set by a decree of 1 April 1976 under the dictatorship of Augusto Pinochet. Its symbol is based on the alchemical sign for copper.

Copper had been mined at Chuquicamata for centuries, as the Copper Man, a mummy of about 550 found in an ancient shaft in 1898, shows. The modern mine began when the Guggenheim brothers formed the Chile Exploration Company in January 1912; production started on 18 May 1915. Anaconda Copper took control in 1923, the Chilean state bought a 51% holding in the 1960s, and the mine was nationalised in 1971. For many years Chuquicamata and its smelter were known for pollution, and people in the mine camp and Calama had serious amounts of arsenic in their blood; the camp was closed and its inhabitants moved to Calama.

At El Teniente, once worked by the Jesuits, the American William Braden began a mine in 1905, and Kennecott ran it from 1915 until 1971. Its old camp, Sewell, the city of stairs founded in 1906 with some 15,000 people at its peak, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Andina mine, discovered in 1920, was brought into production in 1970 by the Cerro de Pasco Corporation. From the late 1980s it dumped waste rock on rock glaciers, affecting 2.1 km2 of them.

Its headquarters are in Santiago. A seven-member board appointed by the President of the Republic is chaired by the Minister of Mining and includes the Minister of Finance and representatives of the Copper Workers Federation and the National Association of Copper Supervisors. Its operating divisions are Codelco Norte, Salvador, Andina, Ventanas and El Teniente, and all excess profits go to the state; in 2007 it paid US$7.394 billion to the Treasury. Besides cathode copper it produces molybdenum, rhenium and small amounts of gold and silver. Production in 2023 was 72% of that of 2004, largely because of geomechanical problems at El Teniente, Chuquicamata and Ministro Hales, and from 2025 it entered lithium mining with SQM and Rio Tinto.
codex: The word codex comes from the Latin caudex, meaning a trunk of a tree, a block of wood or a book. The Romans used reusable wax-covered wooden tablets for notes, and two polyptychs excavated at Herculaneum used a connecting system that anticipates the later sewing of leaves with thongs or cords. Around the turn of the 1st century CE a folded parchment notebook called pugillares membranei became common in the Roman Empire.

Martial described three of the books he sent as Saturnalia gifts as codices, praising their compactness and their convenience on a journey. In another poem he advertised an edition of his works as a codex that took less space than a scroll and was easier to hold in one hand.

A codex is a stack of pages bound at one edge. Sheets of papyrus or parchment were folded, gathered into quires, most often of four folded sheets making sixteen pages, and sewn through the fold, so that both sides of each leaf could be used. Scribes pricked the parchment and ruled lines to guide the text.

The form was compact and sturdy and allowed a reader to turn to any page at once, where a scroll had to be read in sequence. Used parchment could be scraped and written on again, producing a palimpsest in which the older text can often be recovered.

There is evidence that by the early 2nd century a codex, usually of papyrus, was the preferred format among Christians. The evidence cannot settle the matter: they may have led its development, or adopted it to distinguish themselves from Jews. The earliest surviving fragments come from Egypt and include the Rylands Library Papyrus P52, containing part of the Gospel of John, perhaps from between 125 and 160.

The codex reached numerical parity with the scroll around 300 CE and had replaced it by the 6th century. Many works not copied from scroll to codex between the 4th century and the 8th were lost. Maya and Aztec codices were long strips folded like a concertina, and in China folded-leaf books developed from the 9th century. Judaism still keeps the Torah scroll for ceremonial use.
codex-amiatinus: The manuscript is a single immense volume about 49 cm high, 34 cm wide and 18 cm thick, weighing over 34 kg. It holds 1,040 leaves of vellum arranged in quires of four sheets, written in large, regular uncial script in two columns of 43 or 44 lines. There is no punctuation; the text is set out instead in sense lines, cola et commata, a layout thought to be modelled on the Codex Grandior of Cassiodorus, which the monastery owned. Its two full-page miniatures show little of the Insular style of Northumbrian art and were copied from late antique originals.

Designated A or am in critical editions, it is commonly considered the most reliable witness to Jerome's Vulgate for the New Testament and most of the Old. The Psalms are given in Jerome's translation from the Hebrew, though in a weaker text taken from an Irish psalter. As in all Vulgate Bibles before the 9th century, the Book of Baruch and the Letter of Jeremiah are absent.

Abbot Ceolfrith commissioned the three Bibles in 692, a date fixed by the monastery's grant of extra land to raise the 2,000 cattle needed for the vellum, and Bede was most likely involved in the work. After Ceolfrith died at Langres on 29 September 716, the book reappears in the 9th century at the Abbazia di San Salvatore on Monte Amiata, where a list of relics of 1036 described it as written in the hand of Pope Gregory. It passed to the Laurentian Library in 1786.

Its dedication page had been altered, and the librarian Angelo Maria Bandini attributed it to Servandus at Monte Cassino around the 540s, a claim accepted for a century. In 1888 Giovanni Battista de Rossi showed that it was one of the Bibles mentioned by Bede.

During the Counter-Reformation the codex mattered to Catholics because its Latin text was older than any Hebrew manuscript then known. In 1587 Pope Sixtus V had it sent to Rome for the Sixtine Vulgate, though its editors made little or no use of its readings. It became a primary source of the Oxford critical edition of the Vulgate New Testament proposed by John Wordsworth and published between 1889 and 1954, and of the Benedictine edition commissioned by Pope Pius X in 1907, both of which took their layout from it.
codex-argenteus: The Codex Argenteus, Latin for Silver Book, contained the Gospels in the Gothic translation of the Christian Bible traditionally attributed to the Gothic bishop Wulfila and made in the 4th century. It was probably written for the Ostrogothic king Theodoric the Great, either at his royal seat in Ravenna or in the Po valley or at Brescia, in gold and silver ink on thin vellum stained purple, with an ornate treasure binding. After Theodoric's death in 526 it is not mentioned in inventories or book lists for a thousand years. In 1998 carbon-14 analysis dated it to the 6th century.

It is written in an uncial script in the Gothic alphabet, reportedly created by Ulfilas. Two hands have been identified. Decoration is limited to a few large framed initials and, at the foot of each page, a silver arcade enclosing the monograms of the four evangelists.

Of the original 336 folios, 187 leaves are preserved. The manuscript was discovered at Werden, a former Benedictine abbey near Essen, in the 16th century, and part of it was in the library of Emperor Rudolf II in Prague. After the Battle of Prague at the end of the Thirty Years' War it was taken as war booty to Stockholm in 1648, to the library of Queen Christina of Sweden. In 1654 it went to the Netherlands among the property of her former librarian Isaac Vossius. In the 1660s Count Magnus Gabriel De la Gardie bought it and took it to Uppsala University, and he provided its present decorated binding.

The final leaf, folio 336, was found in October 1970 in Speyer Cathedral, in a box of non-authentic relics walled up in 1859. It holds the end of the Gospel of Mark. Bonaventura Vulcanius, a professor of Greek at Leiden, published four fragments in 1597, the first publication of a Gothic text, and named it Codex argenteus. The standard edition is Wilhelm Streitberg's Die Gotische Bibel of 1910.

The codex remains at Uppsala University Library in the Carolina Rediviva building, where it is displayed under the name Silverbibeln. Parts on display were stolen on 5 April 1995 and recovered a month later in a storage box at Stockholm Central Station. It has been on UNESCO's Memory of the World Register since 2011. It contains parts of Matthew, John, Luke and Mark.
codex-aureus-of-st-emmeram: The book was made at the court workshop of Charles the Bald, often called his Palace School. Where that workshop was based is uncertain and much discussed: its earlier home, St Martin's Abbey in Tours, had been destroyed in 853, and by the time of the Codex Aureus it had probably moved to the Basilica of St Denis outside Paris. The manuscript passed to Arnulf of Carinthia, who gave it to Saint Emmeram's Abbey in Regensburg, then under abbot Tuto. It is catalogued in Munich as Clm 14000.

The text was written out by the monks Liuthard and Beringer in golden uncial letters, each page framed. The book measures 420 by 330 mm and has 126 vellum folios. Seven full-page miniatures show the four evangelists, Charles the Bald enthroned, the Adoration of the Lamb and a Christ in Majesty, and there are twelve canon tables, ten illuminated initials and incipits.

The gold cover is set with sapphires, emeralds and pearls. At its centre a repoussé Christ in Majesty sits on the globe of the world, holding a book inscribed: I am the way, and the truth, and the life. Around him are the four evangelists, each with a scene from his Gospel: Christ and the Adulterous Woman, the Expulsion of the Money-lenders from the Temple, the Healing of the Blind Man and the Healing of the Leper. Each gem stands in a raised setting whose claws are formed as acanthus leaves, where earlier jewelled metalwork mostly used plain claws.

The cover is one of very few treasure bindings of its date to survive. Scholars group it with three other works of the same workshop: the upper cover of the Lindau Gospels, which differs in style, the Arnulf Ciborium, a miniature architectural ciborium now in the Munich Residenz, and the frame of an antique serpentine dish in the Louvre. Recent scholars tend to see the Lindau Gospels and the Arnulf Ciborium as closer to each other than either is to the Codex Aureus.
codex-bodley: The codex is also called the Codex Ñuu Tnoo, after the Mixtec name of Tilantongo, meaning Black Town-Temple of Heaven. It is painted in a variant of the Mixteca-Puebla style. Its content and style place its completion before the Spanish conquest of 1521. Because it describes the Tilantongo dynasty before turning to the house that ruled Tlaxiaco, and resembles the Codex Selden, it is presumed to come from that part of Oaxaca, though this cannot be proved.

Its history before it reached the Bodleian at the start of the 17th century is unknown. It may have been used in lawsuits by descendants of the Tilantongo rulers to prove their nobility and then sent to Seville. The archaeologist J. Eric Thompson suggested that it had belonged to Bishop Jerónimo Osório of Faro before Robert Devereux, 2nd Earl of Essex, looted it and gave it to his friend Thomas Bodley.

The deerskin is 6.7 metres long, folded like an accordion, coated white and divided by red lines into five bands on the obverse and four on the reverse. It is read from right to left: the obverse runs from page 1 to page 20 and ends with Lord Eight Deer as the latest lord of Tilantongo, and the reverse runs from page 40 back to page 21, where Lord Eight Grass appears as the last king of Tlaxiaco. The reverse is the more complex, with some bands carrying notes to the story told in the others.

The obverse tells of the War of Heaven and the career of Eight Deer, who defeats the Sun God and Venus God at a ball game, founds a kingdom on the Pacific coast, receives a turquoise nose plug from the Toltec king Cē Ācatl Topiltzin and takes the throne of Tilantongo, until Four Wind kills him. The reverse follows the rival house of the Red and White Bundle and the lords of Tlaxiaco. The two sides place the origin of the royal houses at Achiutla and at Apoala.

The pages have long been numbered after the facsimile in Lord Kingsborough's Antiquities of Mexico, whose artist Agostino Aglio seems to have copied them before greens and yellows faded to ochre and brown. In 1949 Alfonso Caso concluded that the genealogy traced the descent of Tilantongo and its links with Teozacoalco. The ethnohistorian Wigberto Jiménez Moreno identified Eight Grass, tentatively, with the Lord Malinalli whom the Aztecs defeated in 1503–1504.
codex-cumanicus: The Codex Cumanicus is a linguistic manual of the Middle Ages, designed to help Catholic missionaries communicate with the Cumans, a nomadic Turkic people. It likely developed over time and consists of a number of independent works combined into one. Mercantile, political and religious leaders, particularly in Hungary, sought effective communication with the Cumans as early as the mid-11th century. When Italian city-states such as the Republic of Genoa established trade posts and colonies along the Black Sea coast, the need for tools to learn Cuman rose sharply. The earliest parts are believed to date from the 12th or 13th century, with substantial additions made later. The copy in Venice is dated 11 July 1303 on folio 1r.

The first part is a dictionary in Latin, Persian and Cuman written in the Latin alphabet, with a column of Cuman verbs, names and pronouns glossed in Latin. It was written for the practical purpose of learning the language. The second part holds a Cuman-German dictionary and information on Cuman grammar. It was written to spread Christianity among the Cumans, with quotations from religious books given in Cuman translation, together with words, phrases and sentences, stories about the lives and work of religious leaders, and about 50 riddles. The codex itself calls the language Tatar (tatar til).

The Cuman riddles are a crucial source for the study of early Turkic folklore. Andreas Tietze called them the earliest variants of riddle types that form a common heritage of the Turkic nations. One runs: The white yurt has no mouth; that is the egg. Another describes a place where the speaker sits as hilly and where he treads as a copper bowl; the answer is the stirrup.

The codex is considered one of the oldest attestations of the Crimean Tatar language and is of great importance for the history of the Kipchak and Oghuz languages, which are directly related to the Kipchaks of the Black Sea steppes, particularly Crimea. It is kept in the Library of St Mark in Venice as BNM ms Lat. Z. 549.
codex-justinianus: Shortly after becoming emperor in 527, Justinian I decided that the legal system needed repair. Three codices of imperial laws existed beside individual laws, many in conflict or out of date: the Codex Gregorianus and Codex Hermogenianus were unofficial, the Codex Theodosianus an official compilation ordered by Theodosius II. In February 528 Justinian created a ten-man commission to review them, remove what was obsolete and produce a single compilation of imperial laws in force. It was headed by the praetorian prefect John the Cappadocian and included Tribonian, who later led the other Corpus Juris Civilis projects. It finished in 14 months, and the compilation was promulgated in April 529.

The first Code did not remove every conflict in Roman jurisprudence, and its constitutions were to be used beside the opinions of the ancient jurists. Justinian's Fifty Decisions and new laws meant it no longer reflected the latest imperial law, so he ordered a new compilation to replace it. No copy of the first edition survives, only a fragment of an index on an Egyptian papyrus.

The second edition, the Codex Repetitae Praelectionis, was published on 16 November 534 and took effect on 30 December. Its twelve books cover ecclesiastical law, the sources of law and the duties of higher offices (book 1), private law (books 2 to 8), crimes (book 9) and administrative law (books 10 to 12).

In the West the Codex was largely lost, or in many places never present. The only manuscript known to have held the whole Latin Codex is a Veronese palimpsest of the 6th or 7th century, now only fragments. In the East the code was translated into Greek and adapted in the 9th century as the Basilika.

Substantially complete versions were restored around the end of the 12th century, and 16th-century humanists added the laws originally promulgated in Greek. Paul Krüger created the modern standard version in 1877. No English translation appeared until the 20th century: Samuel Parsons Scott's translation of the whole Corpus Juris Civilis (1932) was severely criticised, and Fred H. Blume's translation was published online in 2005 and, revised, by Cambridge University Press in October 2016.
codex-manesse: The Codex Manesse is also known as the Große Heidelberger Liederhandschrift or the Pariser Handschrift. It is an anthology of Minnesang, with some fables and didactic poems called Spruchdichtung, by minnesingers of the mid 12th to early 14th century. For each poet a portrait is followed by the text of the works. The entries are ordered roughly by social status, starting with the Holy Roman Emperor Henry VI and Kings Conradin and Wenceslaus II, and passing through dukes, counts and knights to the commoners.

The oldest poets had been dead for more than a century when the book was compiled, while others were contemporaries. Some nobles are shown in full armour with their heraldic colours, often jousting or in single combat. Some images draw on the poet's biography, some on his name, so that Dietmar is shown riding a mule, and others on his lyrics: Walther von der Vogelweide sits in the thoughtful pose he describes in one of his songs.

The codex was produced in Zürich for the Manesse family and was presumably commissioned by Rüdiger II Manesse, born before 1252 and dead after 1304. The main part was written and illustrated first, and addenda followed. The poet Johannes Hadlaub of Zürich, active around 1300, is possibly the redactor of the codex. The family declined in the late 14th century and sold its castle in 1393.

The fate of the manuscript in the 15th century is unknown. By the 1590s it belonged to Baron Johann Philipp of Hohensax, two of whose forebears are portrayed in it, and in 1604 Melchior Goldast published excerpts of its didactic texts. After 1657 it was in the French royal library and then the Bibliothèque Nationale, where Jacob Grimm studied it in 1815. In 1888, after long bargaining and a public subscription headed by William I and Otto von Bismarck, it was sold to the Bibliotheca Palatina of Heidelberg.

The first critical editions appeared in the early 19th century. Scholars of Minnesang usually refer to the codex as C, an abbreviation introduced by Karl Lachmann, who used A and B for the two main earlier songbooks. Gottfried Keller made the question of the compiler the subject of the novella Hadlaub in 1878. In 2023 the codex was admitted to UNESCO's Memory of the World register.
codex-mendoza: The viceroy of New Spain, Don Antonio de Mendoza, knew that the conquest had destroyed many native works and the crafts that made them. When the Spanish crown ordered him to provide evidence of the Aztec political and tribute system, he brought skilled artists and scribes trained at the Franciscan college in Tlatelolco into a workshop under Spanish priests to make the document. The codex must date from after 6 July 1529, since it calls Hernán Cortés marques del Valle, and from before 1553.

Its last page apologises for the rough Spanish interpretation, explaining that the interpreter received the history only ten days before the fleet sailed, because the Indians came to agreement late. The conquistador Jerónimo López recalled, probably in 1547, seeing such a book in the house of Francisco Gualpuyogualcal, master of the painters, made at the viceroy's command. Silvio Zavala identified it with the codex, though H. B. Nicholson pointed out that the description is not an exact fit.

The codex has seventy-one folios of Spanish paper, 20.6 by 30.6 centimetres, drawn in the native style but bound in the European way. Section I tells the history of the Aztec people from 1325 to 1521, from the founding of Tenochtitlan to the Spanish conquest. Section II lists the towns conquered by the Triple Alliance and their tribute, and was probably copied from the Matrícula de Tributos, although it includes five provinces the Matrícula lacks, probably from pages since lost. The daily life of the Aztecs is depicted in Section III.

According to Samuel Purchas, writing in 1625, French privateers seized the fleet carrying the codex and took it to France. It certainly belonged to André Thevet, cosmographer to King Henry II of France, who wrote his name on it, twice with the date 1553. It then passed to Richard Hakluyt, who by Purchas's account paid 20 French francs for it, to Purchas himself and his son, and to John Selden. It entered the Bodleian Library in 1659, five years after Selden's death, and stayed little known until Viscount Kingsborough brought it to scholars' attention in 1831.
coele-syria: Coele-Syria, in Greek Koílē Syría, was a region of Syria in classical antiquity, and its name means hollow Syria. The term originally referred to the hollow Beqaa Valley between the Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon mountain ranges, but it was sometimes applied to a broader area. The region is now part of modern-day Syria and Lebanon. The Greek word for hollow is thought to be a folk-etymological reinterpretation of the Aramaic kul, meaning all or the entire, so that the term originally identified all of Syria, between the Euphrates, the Mediterranean and the Taurus.

Writers used it in different senses. Pliny, Arrian, Ptolemy and Diodorus Siculus used it for all Syria or all Syria except Phoenicia, and Diodorus stretched it at least as far south as Joppa. Polybius placed the border between Egypt and Coele-Syria between Rhinocolara and Raphia. Strabo defined Coele-Syria Proper by the parallel ranges of Libanus and Anti-Libanus. Under the Romans the name was confined to this narrower area, and could include the district about Damascus and part of the land east of the Jordan.

The first and only official use of the term was under Seleucid rule, from about 200 BCE to 64 BCE, when Coele-Syria and Phoenicia, or Coele-Syria, could mean the former Ptolemaic territory south of the river Eleutherus. According to Polybius, Ptolemy Thrasea, who had fought at the Battle of Raphia in 217 BCE, defected to the Seleucid king Antiochus III the Great, who gave him the title strategos and archiereus of Coele-Syria and Phoenicia.

The region was disputed in the Wars of the Successors and then in the Syrian Wars. Ptolemy first occupied it in 318 BCE, and later withdrew several times. After the Battle of Ipsus in 301 BCE the victors assigned it to Seleucus I Nicator, who did not take it by force, remembering that Ptolemy had helped him regain Babylonia. Later Seleucids were less forbearing, and a century of Syrian Wars followed. The Battle of Panium in 200 BCE, in the Fifth Syrian War, ended Ptolemaic control. Antiochus IV Epiphanes and Ptolemy VI Philometor fought over the region again from 171 to 168 BCE.

Seleucid control of Judea began to fade with the Maccabean Revolt in 165 BCE, and Judea secured its independence by 140 BCE. Pompey's conquests in 64 BCE were a decisive blow to the Seleucids, and Syria became part of the Roman Republic. About 125 CE the emperor Hadrian promoted Damascus to Metropolis of Coele-Syria. Septimius Severus later divided Syria in two, and the northern half, with two legions, was called Coele-Syria.

The region lies in modern Syria and Lebanon, and the name no longer has an official use. Eunapius, writing about 350 CE, gave Antioch as the capital of Coele-Syria, a city founded by Seleucus Nicator.
coenwulf-of-mercia: Coenwulf was a descendant of King Pybba, who ruled Mercia in the early 7th century. His family was powerful but not of recent Mercian royal lineage, and he is recorded witnessing charters under Offa. Offa died in July 796 and was succeeded by his son Ecgfrith, who reigned for less than five months before Coenwulf took the throne. The scholar Alcuin of York regarded him as a tyrant. His early reign saw a breakdown of Mercian control in the south: in East Anglia a king named Eadwald issued his own coins, and in Kent an uprising was led by Eadberht Præn, who had been an exile at Charlemagne's court and probably had Carolingian support.

Coenwulf would not act in Kent without word from Pope Leo III that Eadberht was a pretender, because Eadberht had reportedly been a priest. The pope's authorisation came in 798. The Mercians captured Eadberht, put out his eyes and cut off his hands. By 801 Coenwulf had placed his brother Cuthred on the throne of Kent, and when Cuthred died in 807 he took the kingdom himself, styling himself in 809 King of the Mercians and the Province of Kent. His own coinage in East Anglia began by about 805, so he probably restored Mercian control there by force. Wessex stayed independent under Egbert, so he never held Offa's overlordship over the southern English.

He fought the Welsh, killing Caradog ap Meirion of Gwynedd by 798, and later ravaged Snowdonia and devastated Dyfed. He quarrelled with Archbishop Wulfred of Canterbury over lay control of religious houses, and by 821 he was threatening to exile him unless he surrendered an estate of 300 hides.

Coenwulf died in 821 at Basingwerk, probably while preparing a campaign against the Welsh, and was buried at Winchcombe. His brother Ceolwulf succeeded him but was deposed within two years, and the kingship passed permanently out of his family. A gold mancus bearing his name, found at Biggleswade in 2001, was bought by the British Museum in 2006. He was the last Mercian king to exercise substantial dominance over other Anglo-Saxon kingdoms, and the rise of Wessex under Egbert began within a decade of his death.
cog-ship: The earliest ancestors of the cog are believed to be logboats from northern Germany, which developed into larger craft of the same shape with planking in place of hollowed logs. After Roman power collapsed, Frisians carried trade on the estuaries and the Wadden Sea in flat-bottomed vessels that were precursors of the cog. The seagoing cog seems to have evolved on the Frisian coast during the 12th century, although the name is recorded as early as the 9th.

Archaeology points to the Frisian coast or western Jutland as its birthplace. The Limfjord in northern Jutland, a sheltered passage between the North Sea and the Baltic, was blocked by sand by the early 12th century, and larger ships had to sail round Cape Skagen. This led to modifications in ship structure and a boom in small cogs, which became the workhorse of the Hanseatic League.

Cogs had clinker-built sides and a flush-planked bottom built shell-first, mostly of oak, with one mast and a single square sail. Typical seagoing cogs were 15 to 25 metres long and 5 to 8 metres wide. Around 1200 a central rudder on a sternpost replaced the earlier side rudder. From the 13th century cogs were decked and larger ones had a stern castle, which left more cargo space below. Compared with Mediterranean carvel-built ships a cog was costly and needed specialist shipwrights, but its simple rig needed only half the crew of a similar ship with lateen sails.

Cogs carried bulk trade in north-west Europe and were also used in war. They replaced Viking-type ships such as the knarr in northern waters during the 13th century, since they carried more cargo, were cheaper to build and steered more easily. Their flat bottoms let them settle level in harbour or be beached at low tide where there were no quays, and their high sides made them harder for pirates to board. By about the 14th century the cog had reached its structural limits, and larger vessels were of another type, the hulk.

The first wreck identified as a cog was found in 1944 near Emmeloord, with wood dated to 1339. The best known is the Bremen cog, found in 1962 and dated to the 1380s. Before that the cog was known mainly from texts and seals, the oldest depiction being the Lübeck seal of 1223. Other finds include a cog in the Pärnu River estuary in Estonia, dated to 1300, and one at Kampen in the Netherlands.
cohen-plan: Presidential elections were due in January 1938, and Getúlio Vargas had no successor he liked and no legal way to extend his term. With Benedito Valadares and General Eurico Gaspar Dutra, his Minister of War, he came to plan a coup that would only work if it looked like a national necessity. Since the National Security Law of 4 April 1935 and the failed Communist Uprising of that year, anti-communism had become institutionalised in Brazil, and conservative currents had joined it to the myth of a Jewish-communist conspiracy.

Captain Olímpio Mourão Filho was then chief of staff of the Brazilian Integralist Action's militia and of its secret service, and edited the party's bulletin. Plínio Salgado asked him to write a text showing that the communist threat was still alive. The signature recalled the Hungarian communist leader Béla Kun: first Béla Kun, then Bela Cohen, an Integralist joke, and finally Cohen alone through a typing error, chosen also for its Jewish sound. Scholars note its many parallels with The Protocols of the Elders of Zion, which the Integralist leader Gustavo Barroso had translated into Portuguese.

General Pedro Aurélio de Góis Monteiro, chief of the Army's General Staff, sent the document to the leading military authorities and presented it at a meeting as if it had been seized by the armed forces. Released on 30 September 1937, it contained only the second chapter; the first, which said the plan was hypothetical, a text for debate, was left out. It described a rising in a large city with a general strike, the burning of public buildings, looting, and the arrest and possible murder of ministers and the heads of the courts and Congress. Amid the outcry Vargas pressed Congress to declare a state of war, and forty days later the Estado Novo began.

No authority of the Estado Novo questioned the document in public, though officers such as Eduardo Gomes are reported to have doubted it. In 1945, conspiring against Vargas, Góis Monteiro revealed the fraud and blamed Mourão, who confirmed his authorship but said he had written a mere simulation that Góis Monteiro had misused. Their mutual accusations made it hard to fix each man's share of blame, and no action was taken against the forgers. The plan has been linked to the rooting of anti-communism in the identity of the Brazilian military and compared with the scare campaign before the 1964 coup.
cohong: Its predecessor was the Baoshang system, set up in 1738, which licensed a number of Chinese merchants to trade with Westerners on condition that they helped to collect duties from them, so tying the merchants' interests to the government's revenue. Accounts of the guild's own foundation differ: the historian Immanuel C. Y. Hsu dates it to 1738, while John Phipps, author of the 19th-century Practical Treatise on the China and Eastern Trade, credited the merchant Poankeequa with founding it in the 1790s. The Chinese merchants were known as hangshang and their foreign counterparts as yanghang.

Membership varied between five and 26 merchants authorised by the Qing government to trade with the West, above all in tea and silk, from offices called hangs. They worked under a revenue official known to the British as the Hoppo, a corruption of hubu, who held great power over their appointment and finances. Because of the low social status of merchants in the Confucian social hierarchy, a member was forced to pay bribes, levies and gifts to his superiors throughout his three-year term. Even so, the members' fortunes were among the largest in the Qing realm, and they worked to keep Canton the sole site of official trade with the West.

From 1781 the guild ran the Consoo Fund, a pool raised by a levy of 3% on the value of goods, which covered the debts of any bankrupt hong at the year's end and the exactions of officials. The levy at first applied only to tea but by the late 18th century covered 69 products.

Western silver from the New World paid for porcelain, silk and tea, but when the British needed a substitute for silver they turned to opium from British India. Despite the opium prohibition edicts of the Daoguang Emperor, the trade through Canton came to centre on the drug. The Cohong did not distribute it within China, but its merchants arranged the small smuggling boats, called fast crabs or shifting dragons, that carried opium from Lintin Island to the warehouses of Canton. The British victory in the First Opium War ended both the guild and the Canton System.
coimbra: Coimbra stands on a hill beside the Mondego River in central Portugal. It lay historically at a junction between Braga and Lisbon, and the river gave a route between the interior and coastal towns such as Figueira da Foz, 40 km to the west. Lisbon is 197 km and Porto 116 km away.

In Roman times the city was Aeminium. The Romans founded its civitas at the time of Augustus, and it came under the protection of nearby Conímbriga. Its walls followed an orthogonal plan, with the main streets crossing at the forum, and it had an aqueduct. When the Sueves and Visigoths sacked Conímbriga in the 460s and it was abandoned, Aeminium became the seat of the bishopric in its place. Coimbra capitulated to the Muslim commander Musa bin Nusair in 714, and as Qulumriyah in Al-Andalus it was the largest settlement along the northern Tagus valley, with a walled enclosure of 10 hectares and between 3,000 and 5,000 inhabitants.

Ferdinand I of León and Castile reconquered it in 1064. In 1096 Alfonso VI placed the counties of Portucale and Coimbra under Henry of Burgundy, who married his daughter Theresa. Their son Afonso Henriques made his home at Coimbra. The city was the capital of Portugal from 1131 to 1255, and Afonso Henriques and Sancho I are buried in the Santa Cruz Monastery.

After it lost its political role Coimbra became a cultural centre, and the first Portuguese university, founded at Lisbon in 1290, is the oldest academic institution in the Portuguese-speaking world. In the 15th and 16th centuries Manuel I and the local bishops patronised artists who left Manueline and Renaissance works. In 1772 the Marquis of Pombal reformed the university and strengthened the sciences, but his plans led to the demolition of the medieval walls and castle.

Coimbra is the largest city of its district and of Portugal's Central Region. UNESCO classified the university's historical buildings as a World Heritage site in 2013. The old and new cathedrals, the Roman aqueduct and cryptoporticus survive, and Coimbra fado is a distinct form of the music that grew there.
colchester: Colchester lies on the River Colne in north-eastern Essex, about 80 kilometres north-east of London. The gravel hill on which it stands was formed in the Middle Pleistocene, and Palaeolithic flint tools, including at least six Acheulian handaxes, have been found there, along with Mesolithic tools and many sherds of Neolithic, Bronze Age and early Iron Age pottery. It is surrounded by Neolithic and Bronze Age monuments, among them a henge at Tendring and large barrow cemeteries at Dedham, Langham and Brightlingsea.

Colchester is said to be the oldest recorded town in Britain because Pliny the Elder, who died in 79, mentioned it. Its Celtic name, Camulodunon, meaning the fortress of the war god Camulos, appears on coins minted by the chieftain Tasciovanus in 20–10 BCE. Before the Roman conquest it was a centre of power for Cunobelin, king of the Catuvellauni, known to Shakespeare as Cymbeline, who minted coins there. Roman writers called him king of the Britons.

Soon after the conquest of 43 a legionary fortress, the first in Britain, was set up there. When the twentieth legion moved west around 49, Camulodunum became a colonia, named in a second-century inscription as Colonia Victricensis. It had a large Temple to the Divine Claudius, the largest classical-style temple in Britain. Tacitus describes how the settlement of ex-soldiers was burned in the Iceni rebellion. Its walls, built between 65 and 80, shortly after Boudicca destroyed the undefended colonia, stayed in use until after the Siege of Colchester in 1648. The Balkerne Gate is the earliest and most complete Roman gateway in the United Kingdom.

Colchester Castle, an 11th-century Norman keep, was built on the vaults of the old Roman temple. In 1648, during the Second English Civil War, a Royalist army under Lord Goring was surrounded by Thomas Fairfax and Henry Ireton for eleven and a half weeks from 13 June. After the surrender on 27 August, Charles Lucas and George Lisle were executed in the castle grounds.

Colchester has been an important military base since Roman times. The Castle Museum has an extensive exhibit on Roman Colchester, and the town also has the ruins of St Botolph's Priory and the gateway of St John's Abbey. Colchester claims to be Britain's first city, as the site of Camulodunum, the first major city and first capital of Roman Britain.
cold-war: Animosity between the Allies of the Second World War predated its end. After the death of Franklin D. Roosevelt in April 1945, the administration of Harry Truman took a harder line, and diplomats disputed how to read the Yalta agreements, the composition of the Polish government and the running of the United Nations. In February 1946 George F. Kennan's Long Telegram from Moscow helped shape American strategy, and on 5 March Winston Churchill gave his Iron Curtain speech at Fulton. The term itself was used by George Orwell in 1945 and applied to the confrontation by Bernard Baruch on 16 April 1947.

The United States declared the Truman Doctrine of containment in 1947, launched the Marshall Plan in 1948 and founded NATO in 1949; the Soviet-led Warsaw Pact followed in 1955. Early confrontations were the Berlin Blockade of 1948 to 1949 and the Korean War of 1950 to 1953, which ended in a stalemate. The Soviet Union tested its first nuclear weapon in 1949. After Joseph Stalin died in 1953, Nikita Khrushchev denounced him in 1956, the year the Soviet Union crushed the Hungarian Revolution. The Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962 is widely considered the closest the war came to nuclear conflict.

Both powers courted the newly decolonised states, and the Vietnam War of 1955 to 1975 ended in a North Vietnamese victory. In Indonesia from 1965 to 1966 the military, with the aid of the United States and other Western governments, led the mass killing of more than 500,000 members and sympathisers of the Indonesian Communist Party. The Soviet Union invaded Czechoslovakia with the Warsaw Pact in 1968, and a period of détente in the 1970s brought treaties limiting nuclear arsenals. The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979 renewed tensions.

Mikhail Gorbachev became leader of the Soviet Union in 1985. In June 1987 he announced perestroika, an agenda of economic restructuring, and introduced glasnost, or openness. These reforms contributed to the revolutions of 1989 in the Eastern Bloc and to the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991, which ended the Cold War.

By 1989 the United States had military alliances with 50 countries and 526,000 troops stationed abroad. Nearly 100,000 Americans died in the Korean and Vietnam Wars, and millions died in the proxy wars around the globe, most of all in eastern Asia. Historians have disagreed over who was responsible for the breakdown of relations: orthodox accounts blame the Soviet Union, revisionists place more responsibility on the United States, and post-revisionists see a more nuanced pattern.
colebrooke-cameron-commission: After the British conquest of the Kandyan kingdom in 1815 the whole island of Ceylon became a British colony. By 1828 government spending had far outrun revenue, in part because the island was run as two separate parts, the upcountry and the low country, and because of the cost of salaries and facilities for officers sent from Britain. The British government had to meet the deficit itself, and the Colonial Secretary sent a Royal Commission of Eastern Inquiry to examine the administration and propose administrative, financial, economic and judicial reforms.

According to Sir Charles Jeffries, by the time the commission reached Ceylon most of its members had fallen away, leaving Major William Colebrooke, later Sir William. Charles Hay Cameron, the other commissioner, was in charge of investigating the judicial system.

The commission's proposals of 1833 were radical for their time, and only some of them were adopted. They called for an Executive Council and a Legislative Council, the amalgamation of the Kandyan and Maritime provinces under a single government by the Governor in Council, the admission of Ceylonese to the Ceylon Civil Service and the abolition of rajakariya, the compulsory personal service owed in the Kandyan provinces. They also proposed a commission to manage education and a principal public school on the British model for English education and teacher training, which became the Colombo Academy.

The reforms gave Ceylon its first form of constitutional government and of modern central administration, the first steps in modernising its economic system, and the beginnings of a uniform system of justice, education and civil service. The two councils later became the foundation of a representative legislature, education passed from the church to the government, and rajakariya was abolished soon after.

The constitution also met protest. European planters in the upcountry, who wanted the Legislative Council to fund roads and posts near their estates, objected that its three unofficial members were outnumbered by officials and that it had too little power, and in 1856 they formed the Planters' Association of Ceylon.
coleraine: Coleraine is a market town and civil parish near the mouth of the River Bann, the county town of County Londonderry in Northern Ireland. It lies 55 miles north-west of Belfast and 30 miles east of Derry. The town stands at the lowest bridgeable point of the Bann, where the river is 90 metres wide. Its name comes from the Irish Cúil Raithin, meaning nook of the ferns. The 9th-century Tripartite Life of Saint Patrick says that when Patrick arrived, the local chieftain Nadslua offered him ground for a church beside the river, where boys were burning ferns.

Coleraine has some of the oldest evidence of human settlement in Ireland, at Mount Sandel, east of the town, where wooden houses were uncovered. An Iron Age souterrain and an Ogham stone lie just south-west of the town at Dunalis. At the start of the 17th century the town was one of two urban communities developed by the London Companies in County Londonderry in the Plantation of Ulster. The Honourable the Irish Society was made responsible for much of Coleraine, and the slightly skewed street pattern of the town centre and traces of the ramparts are the legacy of that planning.

During the War of the Two Kings (1689–91) Coleraine was a centre of Protestant resistance to James II. Richard Hamilton's Irish Army tried to seize it and was repulsed, but the Protestants soon withdrew to Derry. Later in 1689 the Jacobite garrison under Sir Charles Carney fled, and the Williamites held the town for the rest of the war. In the 19th century the river port, the railway and industry, including a substantial distillery producing Coleraine Whiskey, doubled the population. The New University of Ulster opened there in 1968 and became a major employer.

During the Troubles 11 people were killed in or near Coleraine before 1998. On 12 June 1973 an IRA car bomb on Railway Road killed six Protestant civilians, all in their sixties and seventies. A van bomb on 13 November 1992 damaged the town centre, and Coleraine Town Hall did not reopen until August 1995.

Coleraine had 24,483 residents at the 2021 census. The town square is called the Diamond, and the town is part of the Causeway Coast and Glens district. The Coleraine campus of the University of Ulster is the original site of the New University of Ulster.
