The town is a base for visiting the Giant's Causeway, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the nearby resorts of Portrush and Portstewart.
coles-creek-culture: Coles Creek was an indigenous development of the Lower Mississippi Valley between the end of the Woodland period and the Plaquemine culture. The archaeologist James A. Ford defined it by the distinctive decoration of its grog-tempered pottery after his work at the Mazique Archeological Site; he had studied both Mazique and Coles Creek and nearly named the culture after Mazique, but chose the site with the less involved history. Its area is divided into Coles Creek proper, in the interior of the valley to the north, and Coastal Coles Creek, along the Gulf coast roughly south of the latitude of modern Baton Rouge.

Its platform mounds were pyramids with flat tops and ramps, usually raised over successive years in many layers, with a temple or other building of wattle and daub on the summit. In late Coles Creek times site plans were often enlarged with up to three more mounds; Mount Nebo, Holly Bluff, Kings Crossing and Lake Agnes are typical sites. Researchers suggest that by building over older burial mounds the emerging elites were appropriating dead ancestors to project their own authority, though many classic traits of chiefdoms had not yet appeared.

Exotic goods are rare at Coles Creek sites, so long-distance trade seems to have been slight. Besides acorns, people ate persimmons, palmetto and starchy seeds such as maygrass, part of the Eastern Agricultural Complex, and they may have loosely managed some plants to make the food supply more dependable. The atlatl stayed in use beside the new bow and arrow.

Potters made more durable wares for more varied uses, tempering wet clay with particles of dry clay so that it would not crack in firing. Most pots were decorated only on the upper half, with incised lines or impressed tool marks, in tan, black, brown and grey, and red pots and effigy pots are rare.
colin-renfrew: Andrew Colin Renfrew was born on 25 July 1937 and educated at St Albans School in Hertfordshire. From 1956 to 1958 he did National Service in the Royal Air Force. He then went up to St John's College, Cambridge, where he read first Natural Sciences and then Archaeology and Anthropology, graduating in 1962. He was elected president of the Cambridge Union in 1961. In 1965 he completed his doctoral thesis, Neolithic and Bronze Age cultures of the Cyclades and their external relations, and married Jane M. Ewbank in the same year.

In 1965 Renfrew became a lecturer at the University of Sheffield, and between 1968 and 1970 he directed excavations at Sitagroi in Greece, where he also worked with Marija Gimbutas. In 1972 he became Professor of Archaeology at the University of Southampton, succeeding Barry Cunliffe, and directed excavations at Quanterness in Orkney and at Phylakopi on the island of Milos. He was elected a Fellow of the British Academy in 1980 and in 1981 became Disney Professor of Archaeology at Cambridge, a post he held until he retired in 2004.

He was Master of Jesus College from 1986 to 1997 and in 1990 became the founding Director of the McDonald Institute for Archaeological Research. In 1991 he was made a life peer as Baron Renfrew of Kaimsthorn, and he received the Balzan Prize in Prehistoric Archaeology for 2004. He directed new excavations on the Cycladic island of Keros from 2006 to 2008 and died on 24 November 2024, aged 87.

In Before Civilisation (1973) Renfrew used radiocarbon dating to challenge the assumption that prehistoric cultural innovation began in the Near East and spread to Europe. In Archaeology and Language (1987) he proposed the Anatolian hypothesis: that Proto-Indo-European, the reconstructed ancestor of the Indo-European languages, originated about 9,000 years ago in Anatolia and spread with farming across the Mediterranean and into central and northern Europe. This contradicted Marija Gimbutas's Kurgan hypothesis, in which a migration of peoples from the Pontic–Caspian steppe about 6,000 years ago spread the language.

His use of the archaeological record to understand the ancient mind was foundational to evolutionary cognitive archaeology, and with his student Lambros Malafouris he coined the term neuroarchaeology. In 1996 he formulated the sapient paradox: why there was such a long gap between the emergence of anatomically and genetically modern humans and the development of complex behaviours. He also wrote on the ethics of looting in archaeology, in Loot, Legitimacy and Ownership (2000).
collasuyu: Qullasuyu, also written Collasuyu or Kholla Suyu and in Spanish Collasuyo, was the largest in area of the four suyus, or quarters, into which the Inca Empire was divided. Its name joins the Quechua qulla, which means south and is also the name of a people, with suyu, a region or quarter, giving the sense of the southern region.

The quarter took in the Bolivian Altiplano and much of the southern Andes, ran down into north-western Argentina and reached as far south as the Maule river near present-day Santiago, Chile. Together with Kuntisuyu it formed the Hurin Suyukuna, the Lower Quarters of the empire.

Most of the Aymara territories that now lie within northern Chile, Peru, Bolivia and the Argentine Northwest were conquered during the reign of the Sapa Inca Huayna Cápac in the sixteenth century. Like every suyu, Qullasuyu was divided into provinces called wamani. Among them were Arica, Cana, Canche, Caranga, Chicha, Cochabamba, Collagua, Lipe, Lupaqa, Moquegua, Pacajes, Sama, Tarata and Yampará. The people of the province of Cavina were counted as Incas by privilege.

The first large Spanish incursion into Qullasuyu was the expedition of Diego de Almagro to Chile in 1535. A large force passed through present-day Bolivia and the Argentine Northwest before it entered Chile.

The modern demonym Colla, used for the people of western Bolivia, comes from the name Qullasuyu. In recent times the office of the Apu Mallku and the parliament of the Qullana have proposed a Greater Qullasuyu, or Qullana Suyu Marka, which would take in a territory similar in extent to the former Inca Empire, Tawantinsuyu.
collective-farming: Collective farming has older forms. Under the Aztec Empire central Mexico was divided into calpulli, local units that owned land and granted families the right to farm parts of it. The Wendat held land communally and let any person clear and farm it while they kept it in use. In Imperial Russia the obshchina or mir was a peasant community, as opposed to individual farmsteads. In Mexico a constitution of 1917 offered the development of ejidos, communal farms formed on land bought from large estates.

The Soviet Union introduced collective farming in its republics between 1927 and 1933, and the Baltic states and most of the Eastern Bloc, except Poland, adopted it after the Second World War. Leon Trotsky and the opposition had advocated voluntary cooperatives, and scholars distinguish his programme from the forced collectivisation Stalin carried out after 1928. In Hungary collectivisation was attempted several times between 1948 and 1956, with police pressure, and succeeded only in the early 1960s under János Kádár; by the early 1950s only a quarter of peasants had joined. Romania's began in 1948 and was virtually complete in 1962, with force used at times. Polish collectivisation stopped in 1956.

In China, rural collectivisation began after the Party's 1953 "general line for the transition to socialism" and passed in six years through mutual aid groups, cooperatives and people's communes. Lin Chun notes that researchers agree it proceeded on a largely voluntary basis, without the violence of the Soviet case. In North Vietnam by 1960, 85 per cent of farmers and 70 per cent of farmland were collectivised. In Tanzania, Julius Nyerere's ujamaa began voluntarily and from 1973 to 1975 became forced villagisation. North Korea's system collapsed in the late 1990s under drought, and estimates of deaths from starvation ran into the millions.

Voluntary forms continue. Israel's kibbutzim began in 1909 as a combination of Zionism and socialism, and in 2006 there were 267 kibbutzim and 40 moshavim shitufi'im, in which production is collective but consumption left to households. The Anabaptist Hutterites have farmed communally since the 16th century and now live mostly on the Canadian Prairies and the northern Great Plains. In the European Union farmers generally keep their land privately and cooperate in processing and marketing; in the Netherlands cooperatives hold about 70 per cent of the market.
collectivity-of-saint-martin: The Collectivity of Saint Martin occupies the northern 60% of the island of Saint Martin in the Leeward Islands, together with smaller islands, the largest of which is Tintamarre. Its land area is 53.2 km2. The southern 40% of the island is Sint Maarten, so this is the only place in the world where France borders the Netherlands. The terrain is generally hilly, with Pic Paradis, at 424 m, the highest point on the island.

Archaeological evidence shows that Amerindian peoples lived on the island from as early as 2000 BCE. Saladoid people from the Orinoco basin arrived around 550 BCE and brought agriculture and pottery, and the Kalinago arrived around 1300 to 1400 CE and began to displace the earlier Arawak inhabitants. Christopher Columbus is commonly said to have named the island after Saint Martin of Tours on 11 November 1493, but he gave that name to the island now called Nevis, and confusion among the poorly charted Leeward Islands moved it to this one.

The island was nominally Spanish and was contested by France and the United Provinces, while the Amerindian population fell sharply from diseases brought by Europeans. In 1631 the Dutch built Fort Amsterdam, and the Spanish captured the island in 1633. When the Eighty Years' War ended in 1648 the island lost its value to Spain, which left. The French and Dutch then agreed in the Treaty of Concordia to divide it, and the boundary settled in its present position by 1817.

In the 18th century cotton, tobacco and sugar plantations brought many African slaves, who came to outnumber the European settlers. France abolished slavery on 28 May 1848, and the Dutch did so on 1 July 1863. The French part was merged into the Guadeloupe colony in 1763 and became an arrondissement of Guadeloupe in 1946, and tourism grew from the 1960s. In 2007 it was detached from Guadeloupe and became an overseas collectivity.

The capital of the collectivity is Marigot, and French is the official language, although English is widely spoken. It uses the euro and remains an outermost region of the European Union. Tourism is its main economic activity.
collectivization-in-the-soviet-union: During the Russian Civil War the policy of prodrazvyorstka obliged peasants to surrender their surplus produce at a fixed price. After the war the New Economic Policy replaced it with a less drastic food tax. From 1927 a crisis in grain deliveries developed, which grew more serious as the Soviet Union pressed ahead with industrialisation and needed more food for its cities. Leon Trotsky and the Opposition had advocated industrialisation with voluntary agricultural cooperatives and collective farms. Some scholars hold that Stalin took over the Left Opposition's position, while others argue that Trotsky's programme differed from the forced collectivisation that Stalin carried out after 1928, because of the brutality of its enforcement.

In 1928 the Soviet Union fell 2 million tons short in the grain it bought from neighbouring markets. Stalin claimed that the grain had been produced but was being hoarded by kulaks, and the Politburo, instead of raising the price, ordered the requisition of 2.5 million tons. Much of it was taken from middle peasants, and resistance spread in 1929, with violent incidents and hoarding.

Between September and December 1929 the share of collectivised households rose from 7.4 per cent to 15 per cent, and in the first two months of 1930 eleven million households joined, taking the total to nearly 60 per cent. The Party sent 25,000 industrial workers, the twenty-five-thousanders, to the countryside to help. On 2 March 1930 Pravda published Stalin's article Dizzy with Success, which called for a pause and blamed overzealous officials. Peasants began to leave the farms, but pressure resumed, and decrees of March 1931 forbade peasants to leave the collective farms. By 1936 about 90 per cent of Soviet agriculture was collectivised.

Peasants resisted with protests, armed revolt and the slaughter of livestock. Many saw the kolkhoz as a second serfdom, since entry was forced, leaving needed permission and the state took most of the crop at low prices. The closing of churches and the arrest of priests gave further cause for revolt, and in 1929 the Red Army put down a revolt in Buryatia.

The immediate effect was often a fall in output and the halving of livestock herds. The number of horses fell from 36.1 million in 1928 to 21.0 million in 1941. In Kazakhstan livestock fell sharply, 1.5 million people fled to China and as many as a million of those who stayed died in famine.

Most historians agree that the disruption and the peasants' resistance contributed greatly to the great famine of 1932–1933, above all in Ukraine, where it is called the Holodomor. Information about the disaster was suppressed, and Ukrainian villages were blacklisted and penalised for supposed sabotage. Only in the late 1950s did Soviet livestock stocks approach their 1928 levels.
college-of-cardinals: The word cardinal comes from the Latin cardo, meaning hinge. The office evolved slowly during the first millennium from the clergy of Rome. The term first appears in the Liber Pontificalis in the biography of Pope Stephen III, where a Roman synod of 769 decided that the pope should be elected from among the cardinal priests and deacons.

The three classes of the College began to form under Pope Stephen V (816-817), who bound the cardinal bishops to sing Mass in rotation at the high altar of St. Peter's Basilica. In 845 the Council of Meaux-Paris required bishops to establish cardinal titles or parishes in their towns, and the popes began using cardinal priests as legates and special envoys.

The College gained its weight through the Gregorian Reform. Before the mid-11th century the papacy was fought over by Roman aristocratic families such as the Theophylacti and Colonna, and the Holy Roman Emperor held a special power to appoint the pope.

After the death of Henry III in 1056 left a child on the throne, reformers took advantage of the king's weakness, and in 1059 Pope Nicholas II reserved papal elections to the clergy of Rome by the bull In nomine Domini. This was part of the wider Investiture Controversy. From the start of the 12th century the three orders met as one College. The last non-cardinal to be elected pope was Urban VI, who died in 1389.

Its size was a recurring dispute. From the 13th to the 15th centuries it never exceeded thirty, and John XXII (1316-1334) limited it to twenty. Popes also enlarged the College to raise money, win allies or dilute its strength as a counterweight to papal supremacy: in 1517 Leo X added 31 cardinals, bringing the total to 65. In 1586 Sixtus V fixed the number at 70.

The College advises the pope when he summons it to a consistory and has no ruling power except during a papal vacancy, when its powers are limited by law. The dean and vice-dean are chosen from the cardinal bishops, with papal confirmation, and act as first among equals. Paul VI barred cardinals over 80 from voting in conclaves from 1971 and set the number of electors at 120 in 1975.
college-of-justice: Before the college, civil justice in Scotland lay with local feudal courts, established by 1153, and with barons and lords of regality sitting with the king's authority. Parties often found these courts ineffectual, and appeals went to the king and the Lords of Council or to the Parliament of Scotland, which struggled with the burden. A bull of Pope Clement VII of 15 September 1531 provided 10,000 gold ducats from the Scottish bishoprics and monasteries to maintain the college's members, half of whom were to be churchmen.

The College of Justice Act of 17 May 1532 created a college of 14 members, half spiritual and half temporal, with a president and the Lord Chancellor, and it first met in the royal presence on 27 May 1532.

The first Lord Chancellor of the college was Gavin Dunbar, Archbishop of Glasgow, and its first Lord President Alexander Myln, Abbot of Cambuskenneth. The 14 ordinary lords, called senators, were joined by an indefinite number of extraordinary lords. The college dealt only with civil law: criminal justice stayed with the king's justiciars until the High Court of Justiciary was brought into the college in 1672. At first there was little legal literature beyond the acts of Parliament, the books of the Old Law and Roman and canon law texts, until judges began noting their decisions in books of practicks.

The Treaty of Union of 1707 with England preserved the Scottish legal system, providing in Article XIX that the Court of Session or College of Justice should remain within Scotland in all time coming. The court has sat at Parliament House in Edinburgh since 1707.

The college today includes the Court of Session, the High Court of Justiciary, the Office of the Accountant of Court and the Auditor of the Court of Session, together with the Faculty of Advocates, the Society of Writers to His Majesty's Signet and the Society of Solicitors in the Supreme Courts of Scotland. It is headed by the Lord President of the Court of Session, who is also Lord Justice General of the High Court of Justiciary; the judges of the two courts are now the same people.
college-of-william-and-mary: A school of higher education for Native American young men and the sons of colonists was among the earliest aims of the leaders of the Colony of Virginia. Plans dating from 1618 at Henrico were thwarted by the attack of 1622, the end of the Virginia Company's charter in 1624, events connected with the English Civil War and Bacon's Rebellion.

The royal charter was granted on 8 February 1693 under King William III and Queen Mary II, to found a place of universal study and a perpetual college of divinity, philosophy, languages and other arts and sciences. Construction of the College Building, now called the Sir Christopher Wren Building, began in 1695. The charter named James Blair first president, a post he held until his death in 1743. The college was founded as an Anglican institution.

C. Society, popularly the Flat Hat Club, in 1750 and Phi Beta Kappa in 1776. In 1779, under James Madison and with reformers including Thomas Jefferson, the college abolished its Divinity School and Indian School, established what is described as the first American university-affiliated law school and introduced the first elective system of study and an honour system.

At the outset of the American Civil War enlistments depleted the student body, and on 10 May 1861 the faculty voted to close the college for the duration. The College Building served as a Confederate barracks and then as a hospital, and in September 1862 drunken soldiers of the 5th Pennsylvania Cavalry set it on fire.

Benjamin Stoddert Ewell reopened the college in 1869 with his own funds, and it closed again in 1882 for lack of funding. It resumed in 1888 as a teacher-training institution after Virginia appropriated $10,000. In 1906 the Virginia General Assembly took over the grounds, and the college has been publicly supported since. In 1918 it was one of the first universities in Virginia to admit women. In 1926 the college's W. A. R. Goodwin persuaded John D. Rockefeller Jr. to begin the restoration of Williamsburg, which led to Colonial Williamsburg, and the Wren Building was restored in 1928–1931.

William & Mary is a public university in Williamsburg, Virginia, on a campus of 1,200 acres bordering the colonial town. Its alumni include the presidents Thomas Jefferson, James Monroe and John Tyler, Chief Justice John Marshall and Speaker Henry Clay. George Washington received his surveyor's license from the college in 1749 and later served as its first American chancellor. The Wren Building, designated a National Historic Landmark, is described as the oldest college building in the United States.
collegium-trilingue: Hieronymus van Busleyden (c. 1470–1517), of an influential Luxembourg family, studied law at Louvain, Orléans and Padua, befriended Erasmus and served Philip I of Castile as a diplomat. He died in August 1517 after falling ill on a mission to Spain, and the date of his will, 22 June 1517, is taken as the college's foundation. It provided ten scholarships for poor students, fees for the high-born and three paid professors, one for each language, who were to teach publicly and free of charge.

The executors wished to join it to an existing college of the university, but the Arts Faculty, which taught Latin, opposed the competition. In April 1519 they bought buildings near the Vismarkt, inaugurated in October 1520 with a chapel, lecture halls, rooms and a library for Busleyden's books and manuscripts. Teaching had begun earlier: Matthaeus Adrianus in Hebrew in March 1518, Hadrianus Barlandus in Latin and Rutger Rescius in Greek that September.

Louvain theologians attacked the college and Erasmus, accusing him of Lutheran sympathies and calling language study useless or harmful; Jacobus Latomus set out their case in a dialogue of 1519. The college followed the method of Lorenzo Valla and Erasmus, ad fontes: theology should rest on a critical reading of scripture in Latin, Greek and Hebrew. Hundreds of students came, and its alumni included Mercator, Lipsius, Dodoens and Vesalius.

That prosperity ended in the last quarter of the 16th century, when Spanish troops occupied Louvain in the Eighty Years' War and most teaching stopped. The college revived under its president Adrianus Baecx from 1606, with Valerius Andreas teaching Hebrew and Erycius Puteanus holding the Latin chair for nearly forty years, but later declined. Its Latin chair stood vacant after 1768; after its suspension its buildings were sold, and it was not revived when the university was reinstated in 1834.

The college was the model for the Collège de France, founded in 1530. Later plans to make its buildings a centre of humanist studies again, by the rector Paulin Ladeuze in the early 20th century and once more in the 1970s, came to nothing; meanwhile the buildings served as a social house, printing works, ice factory and fish smokehouse.
colln: Cölln lay on the Fisher Island part of the Spree Island, facing Old Berlin across the river, to which it was joined by the Mühlendamm causeway. The trade route from Magdeburg to Frankfurt (Oder) crossed the twin town, and inland waterways passed through it, so Cölln and Berlin grew prosperous quickly. The deed of 1237 that first names it records a priest, Symeon of Cölln, of Saint Peter's Church as a witness; Old Berlin is not mentioned before 1244, and places now within Greater Berlin such as Spandau and Köpenick are older still.

In 1307 a second crossing, the Lange Brücke, now the Rathausbrücke, was built with a common town hall in the middle, and the same year the twin towns joined Brandenburg an der Havel, Frankfurt (Oder) and Salzwedel in an alliance to defend their rights against the sovereign. Elector Frederick II Irontooth of Brandenburg ended their autonomy and made the twin town his residence in 1451. When King Frederick I of Prussia merged them in 1710 into the capital of Prussia, Old Berlin was twice the size of Cölln, so the new city took its name.

Saint Peter's Church, built about 1230 and named for the many inhabitants who lived by fishing, was badly damaged in the air raids and the Battle of Berlin in 1945 and demolished in 1964; the Petriplatz marks its site. The Brüderstraße took its name from a Dominican monastery founded in 1297.

The site of Cölln is the historic core of Berlin-Mitte. Survivors of the old town include the Ribbeckhaus of 1624 on Breite Straße, one of Berlin's oldest homes, the Nicolaihaus, where the bookseller Christoph Friedrich Nicolai lived from 1787 to 1811, and the Galgenhaus of about 1688. The Jungfernbrücke of 1798 is the city's oldest bridge. The name survives in the district and borough of Neukölln.
colmar: Colmar lies 64 km south-south-west of Strasbourg, on the River Lauch, a tributary of the Ill, immediately east of the Vosges and linked by canal to the Rhine. The mountains hold back moisture from the west, so the city is one of the driest in France, a sunny setting for the vineyards of Alsace. Colmar sits on the Alsatian Wine Route and calls itself the capital of Alsatian wine.

Colmar was first mentioned in the 9th century, and the Carolingian emperor Charles the Fat held a diet there in 884. Frederick II made it a free imperial city in 1226, and in 1354 it joined the Décapole, a league of Alsatian cities. It adopted the Protestant Reformation in 1575, long after Strasbourg and Sélestat to the north. In the Thirty Years' War the Swedish army took it in 1632 and held it for two years, and in 1635 imperial forces spoiled its harvest while the townspeople shot at them from the walls.

Louis XIV conquered the city in 1673, and the Treaties of Nijmegen formally ceded it in 1679. It kept a distinct German character because of its location, language and culture. A cholera epidemic killed many people in 1854, and the Franco-Prussian War brought Colmar, with the rest of Alsace, to the new German Empire in 1871, in the province of Alsace-Lorraine. It returned to France under the Treaty of Versailles in 1919, was annexed by Nazi Germany in 1940, and was again French after the battle of the Colmar Pocket in 1945. A hoard of precious objects hidden by Jews during the Black Death, the Colmar Treasure, was found in the city in 1863.

Colmar is the seat of the prefecture of the Haut-Rhin department and the third-largest commune of Alsace. Its old town was largely spared by the French Revolution and the wars of 1870 to 1871, 1914 to 1918 and 1939 to 1945, and its buildings show eight centuries of German and French architecture in timber framing and Vosges sandstone. The area of canals along the Lauch is called Little Venice. The Unterlinden Museum holds the Isenheim Altarpiece. The sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi, creator of the Statue of Liberty, was born there, and the Municipal Library owns more than 2,300 incunabula, many from monasteries dissolved during the Revolution.
cologne: Cologne is centred on the left bank of the Rhine, about 35 kilometres south-east of Düsseldorf and 22 kilometres north-west of Bonn, in the Cologne Lowland of the central Rhineland. The city's highest point is 118 metres above sea level and its lowest 37.5 metres. It is regularly affected by flooding from the Rhine, and its flood control system was redesigned after a flood in 1993 that caused heavy damage.

The first urban settlement on the site was the Oppidum Ubiorum, founded in 38 BCE by the Ubii, a Germanic tribe. In 50 CE the Romans founded Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensium, named after Emperor Claudius and his wife Agrippina the Younger, who was born here. It became capital of the province of Germania Inferior in 85, and from 260 to 271 was the capital of the Gallic Empire under Postumus, Marius and Victorinus. Emperor Constantine I had a bridge built over the Rhine at Cologne in 310. The Franks occupied the city in 462. Its population is put at about 40,000 in 100–200 CE, 20,000 in 1000 and 50,000 in 1200.

Cunibert, made bishop of Cologne in 623, advised the Merovingian King Dagobert I. In 795 Charlemagne's bishop Hildebold was promoted to archbishop, and the Treaty of Verdun of 843 placed the city in Lothair I's Middle Francia.

Its position on major trade routes between eastern and western Europe made it a free imperial city of the Holy Roman Empire and a major member of the Hanseatic League, and one of the largest European cities of the medieval and Renaissance periods. French forces occupied it in 1794, and the Treaty of Lunéville of 1801 made the left bank of the Rhine part of the French Republic. The Napoleonic Code, introduced under French rule, remained in use there until 1900. In 1815 the Congress of Vienna gave Cologne to the Kingdom of Prussia.

Cologne is the fourth-most populous city of Germany and the largest city of North Rhine-Westphalia, with over one million inhabitants. It was one of the most heavily bombed cities in Germany during the Second World War, which reduced its population by 93%, mainly through evacuation, and destroyed around 80% of the old city centre. Most major historic landmarks were restored, among them Cologne Cathedral, built to house the Shrine of the Three Kings and the world's tallest building from 1880 to 1890, and the Romanesque churches. Eau de Cologne has been produced in the city since 1709.
colombia: The territory served as a corridor of early human movement between Mesoamerica, the Caribbean, the Andes and the Amazon basin. The oldest finds, at Pubenza and El Totumo in the Magdalena Valley, date from the Paleoindian period (18,000–8000 BCE), and the oldest pottery found in the Americas, at San Jacinto, dates to 5000–4000 BCE. The earliest gold craftsmanship is attributed to the Tumaco people of the Pacific coast, about 325 BCE, and the San Agustín culture raised ceremonial centres and stone monoliths between about 200 BCE and 800 CE.

Alonso de Ojeda reached the Guajira Peninsula in 1499, and Rodrigo de Bastidas explored the Caribbean coast in 1500. Santa María la Antigua del Darién, founded in 1510, was the first stable settlement on the continent; Santa Marta followed in 1525 and Cartagena in 1533. Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada led an expedition into the interior in April 1536 and named the region the New Kingdom of Granada. In August 1538 he founded its capital, Santa Fe, near the Muisca cacicazgo of Muyquytá, which became Santa Fe de Bogotá. The search for El Dorado drew Sebastián de Belalcázar, who founded Cali and Popayán, and Nikolaus Federmann.

The Declaration of Independence was issued on 20 July 1810, now Independence Day, following the example of Saint-Domingue's independence in 1804. Simón Bolívar became a leader of the movement, and Francisco de Paula Santander played a decisive part. The name Colombia, derived from Christopher Columbus and intended to refer to the whole New World, was adopted by the Republic of 1819, formed from the territories of the Viceroyalty of New Granada.

United States efforts to control the route of the Panama Canal contributed to Panama's secession in 1903. In 1921 the United States paid Colombia $25,000,000 under the Thomson–Urrutia Treaty, and Colombia recognised Panama. A war with Peru over territory in the Amazon basin ended with a peace deal brokered by the League of Nations, which awarded the disputed area to Colombia in June 1934. An armed conflict among governments, paramilitaries and guerrillas such as the FARC and the ELN began in the mid-1960s.

Colombia is a presidential republic under the Constitution of 1991, divided into 32 departments and the Capital District of Bogotá, its largest city. It covers 1,141,748 square kilometres and has a population of around 52 million. Spanish is the official language, with 65 Amerindian languages also used. The country spans the Andes, the Pacific and Caribbean coasts, the Llanos plains and part of the Amazon rainforest.
colombia-peru-war: The boundary treaty of 24 March 1922 had given Colombia the Leticia district and access to the Amazon, but most of its people were Peruvian, and heavy tariffs on sugar added to the grievance. On 27 August 1932 Peruvian civilians led by Oscar Ordoñez and Juan La Rosa Guevara founded the Patriotic Junta of Loreto, whose Leticia Plan denounced the treaty and called for a peaceful recovery of the port by civilians alone. A force of 48 gathered at the border town of Caballococha, and after the seizure on 1 September Colombian officials and police fled to Brazil.

Colombia's government took notice only on 17 September, when Peruvian forces on the Putumayo began stopping trade ships bound for Leticia. Laureano Gómez, head of the Senate minority, called for war on the border, El Tiempo reported more than 10,000 letters demanding it, and the Senate voted 10 million dollars for a fleet under General Alfredo Vásquez Cobo.

President Luis Miguel Sánchez Cerro believed Colombia, without Amazon roads or a proper navy, could not respond. Yet by December 1932 Vásquez Cobo had reached the Amazon with old gunboats and new British destroyers, and German aviators of SCADTA, the airline that later became Avianca, fitted their planes as a temporary air force. President Enrique Olaya Herrera at first held back, hoping for a diplomatic settlement, and commanders quarrelled before Olaya named Vásquez Cobo Minister of War and pressed an attack on Tarapacá.

The Colombians struck Tarapacá first, as a softer target than Leticia. On 13 March 1933 a landing at Puerto Hilario was driven off by Peruvian troops and aircraft, ending an attempt to threaten Leticia from behind, but Colombian troops occupied Gueppi on 26 March and in May took the Peruvian seaplane base on the Algodón River. On 26 May ten Colombian soldiers, unaware that a suspension of hostilities had been agreed at Geneva the day before, captured four Peruvian officers and 77 soldiers at La Zoila.

Peru's forces in Leticia were never driven out. Sánchez Cerro was shot dead on 30 April 1933, and 15 days later his successor, Óscar Benavides, met Alfonso López Pumarejo, head of the Colombian Liberal Party, to agree that Leticia be handed to a League of Nations commission. In the Rio de Janeiro Protocol of 1934, which reaffirmed the Salomón–Lozano Treaty, Peru declared that it sincerely deplored the events that began in September 1932.
colombo: Colombo lies on the west coast of Sri Lanka. It is the most populous city of the country and its financial centre, with 752,993 inhabitants within the municipal limits. The name was introduced by the Portuguese in 1505 and is believed to come from the classical Sinhala Kolon thota, port on the river Kelani. Another belief derives it from Kola-amba-thota, harbour with leafy mango trees.

The traveller Ibn Battuta, who visited the island in the 14th century, called it Kalanpu. Arabs began to settle in Colombo around the eighth century, mostly because the port helped them control much of the trade between the Sinhalese kingdoms and the outside world. Portuguese explorers led by Dom Lourenço de Almeida arrived in Sri Lanka in 1505 and made a treaty with Parakramabahu VIII, King of Kotte, which let them trade in cinnamon and establish a trading post. Within a short time they expelled the Muslim inhabitants of Colombo and began to build a fort in 1517.

The Dutch captured Colombo in 1656 after a long siege, at the end of which 93 Portuguese survivors were given safe conduct out of the fort. It served as capital of the Dutch maritime provinces under the Dutch East India Company until 1796. The British captured it in 1796, but it remained a military outpost until the Kandyan Kingdom was ceded to them in 1815, when they made it the capital of the crown colony of British Ceylon and built houses and civilian structures around the fort. Ceylon became independent in 1948.

Colombo is Sri Lanka's executive and judicial capital and its commercial capital, since plans of the 1980s moved Parliament and several ministries to Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte, though the move was never completed. Its harbour is the largest and one of the busiest ports in Sri Lanka. The Fort area keeps the name of the old fortifications, whose ramparts the British demolished in the late 19th century. Few buildings survive from the Dutch period, among them the former Dutch Hospital.
colombo-plan: In the winter of 1949 to 1950 the United States, the United Kingdom and other Commonwealth members discussed ideas for economic development in South and Southeast Asia. The key meeting was the Commonwealth Conference on Foreign Affairs, held in Colombo, Ceylon, in January 1950 and attended by ministers of Australia, the United Kingdom, Canada, Ceylon, Pakistan and New Zealand and by the prime ministers of Ceylon and India. The Colombo Plan began operations on 1 July 1951. Canada and the United Kingdom were founding members in 1950, and South Vietnam and Cambodia joined in 1951.

The organisation's main focus has been the development of human resources in South and Southeast Asia. Aid to education from 1950 to 1983 came to 72 billion dollars, of which 41 billion came from the United States. Its Long-Term Scholarships Programme dates from 1951 and its Drug Advisory Programme from 1973.

In 1995 it was restructured: the Colombo Plan Bureau became a Secretariat headed by a Secretary-General rather than a Director, the first being Dr Kim Hak-su of Korea, and programmes for private sector development and public administration began. After the restructuring its work rested on cooperation among developing member countries, and by 2010 it had provided 16,082 scholarships to 23 member countries.

The Colombo Plan has a host country agreement with the government of Sri Lanka, set out in a memorandum of understanding granting privileges and immunities, and its work is funded by voluntary contributions from members and international agencies. Later programmes covered gender affairs from 2014 and environment and climate change from 2016. The Colombo Plan Staff College for Technician Education in Manila trains mid-level technicians. Notable scholars include Dr Sanduk Ruit of Nepal, founder of the Tilganga Eye Hospital in Kathmandu, and Ong Teng Cheong, a later President of Singapore. In January 2026 the United States was ordered to withdraw, among 66 international organisations.
colon-panama: Colón lies beside the Caribbean Sea near the Atlantic entrance to the Panama Canal. The city proper stands on the Manzanillo Peninsula, a former island surrounded by Limon Bay, Manzanillo Bay and the Folks River. It was founded on the western end of a marshy islet, Manzanillo Island, which was joined to the mainland by a causeway built for the railroad, with part of the island drained for permanent buildings.

The city was founded in 1850 as the Atlantic terminal of the Panama Railroad, built to meet the demand during the California Gold Rush for a fast route to California. For some years the community of emigrants from the United States called the town Aspinwall, after the railroad's promoter William Henry Aspinwall, while Hispanic residents called it Colón in honour of Christopher Columbus. Its population grew from 3,001 in 1900 to 31,203 by 1920 with the building of the canal.

Fires destroyed much of the city in 1885, during the Colombian Civil War, in 1915, and on 13–14 April 1940, when one third of it burned. A boundary treaty of 1914 made Colón an exclave surrounded by the Canal Zone, and the Hull–Alfaro Treaty of 1936 ceded a strip, the Colón Corridor, for a road linking it to the rest of Panama. In 1948 part of Manzanillo Island was designated the Colón Free Trade Zone. Riots in the 1960s destroyed the municipal palace and began a decline.

Colón is the capital of Colón Province and has traditionally been known as Panama's second city, with around 204,000 people in 2000. Most are of West Indian or mixed mestizo ancestry. The Panama Canal Railway and Enrique Adolfo Jiménez Airport serve it. Henryk Sienkiewicz's novella Latarnik is set in the lighthouse at Aspinwall.
colonia-claudia-ara-agrippinensium: After Julius Caesar wiped out the Eburones in a war of reprisal, the Roman general Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa resettled the Ubii from the right bank of the Rhine in the Cologne Lowland in 38 BCE. Their settlement, probably called Oppidum Ubiorum, stood on a flood-free rise between today's Heumarkt and Alter Markt and already had a Roman grid of streets. Under Augustus the Altar of the Ubii was built there, perhaps meant as the centre of worship for a larger Germanic province, a plan largely given up after the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest in 9 CE. Germanicus had his headquarters there from 13 to 17 CE.

The colony's name joined the emperor, the empress's compatriots, whom she named Agrippinenses, and the altar on the forum. From 70 CE the city had a strong wall about 8 metres high, and in 80 CE the Eifel Aqueduct began to bring it 20,000 cubic metres of water a day. In the civil war after Nero's death in 68, the legions stationed there proclaimed their commander Aulus Vitellius emperor; during the Batavian revolt the townspeople, still mostly Ubii, at first sided with the rebels, then returned to Rome when told to tear down their wall. The governor resided in the Praetorium, rebuilt in 184 or 185 under Didius Julianus.

In 260 Postumus made the city the capital of the Gallic Empire, which lasted fourteen years. Constantine I built a bridge over the Rhine in 310, guarded by the fort of Divitia, and a letter of his of 321 documents Jews in the city. In December 355 the city was abandoned after a long siege by the Franks and lay in ruins; it fell finally to the Ripuarian Franks in 459. Cologne stayed inhabited within its Roman layout, with about 3,000 people around 700, and the Praetorium served as a palace of the Merovingian kings.

The Roman grid survives in Cologne's street plan: Hohe Straße follows the cardo maximus and Schildergasse the decumanus maximus. Remains include the northwest Roman Tower of the wall, the foundations of the Praetorium under the city hall and the late Roman core of St. Gereon's Basilica, standing up to 16.50 metres high. St. Mary in the Capitol stands on the site of the Capitoline temple. The Romano-Germanic Museum keeps the gate arch inscribed CCAA, the Dionysus mosaic and a large collection of the city's Roman glass.
colonial-office: Before 1768 colonial affairs belonged to the Secretary of State for the Southern Department and the Board of Trade and Plantations, a committee of the Privy Council. A separate American or Colonial Department was set up in 1768 to deal with British America, but after the loss of the Thirteen Colonies it was abolished in 1782 and its work passed to the Home Office. In 1801, in the lead-up to the Napoleonic Wars, colonial business moved to the War Office, renamed the War and Colonial Office, under a Secretary of State for War and the Colonies.

An Under-Secretary of State for the Colonies was created in 1825, first held by Robert William Hay. From 1824 the empire outside India was divided into departments for North America, the West Indies, the Mediterranean and Africa, the Australian colonies and the eastern colonies of Ceylon and Mauritius.

In 1854 the War and Colonial Office was split into the War Office and a new Colonial Office under the Secretary of State for the Colonies. It never ran all British possessions: from 1858 the India Office governed the British Raj and nearby territories, and informal protectorates such as the Khedivate of Egypt were left to the Foreign Office. The growing independence of the Dominions after the 1907 Imperial Conference led to a Dominion Division inside the office, and from 1925 there was a separate Secretary of State for Dominion Affairs.

After the Cairo Conference of March 1921 the Colonial Office took over the administration of the Palestine Mandate from the Foreign Office. On 16 April 1947 the Irgun planted a bomb at the office that failed to explode. In 1966 the Colonial Office and the Commonwealth Relations Office were merged as the Commonwealth Office, which two years later joined the Foreign Office as the Foreign and Commonwealth Office.

From 1862 the office published historical and statistical information on the colonies in The Colonial Office List, called The Dominions Office and Colonial Office List between 1926 and 1940 and later the Commonwealth Relations Office Year Book and Commonwealth Office Year Book. An edited version was also printed by Waterlow and Sons, and the two can be hard to tell apart in library catalogues. The office worked from what is now the Foreign and Commonwealth Office Main Building in Whitehall.
colonna-family: According to tradition, the Colonna are a branch of the Counts of Tusculum, taking their name from the Columna Castle in the Alban Hills, held by Peter de Columna, lord of Colonna, Monteporzio, Zagarolo and Gallicano. From the 14th century the family claimed descent from the Julio-Claudian dynasty. The first cardinal certainly of the family was Giovanni Colonna di Carbognano, appointed in 1206; an earlier cardinal long counted as a Colonna was shown by modern scholars to have been included on false information from the early 16th century. A rivalry with the pro-papal Orsini, leaders of the Guelph faction, began in this period and reinforced the Colonna's Ghibelline, pro-imperial course.

In 1297 Cardinal Jacopo Colonna disinherited his brothers, who appealed to Pope Boniface VIII. When Jacopo refused to return the land and surrender the family strongholds, Boniface removed him from the College of Cardinals and excommunicated him and his followers. The Colonna declared that Boniface had been elected illegally after the abdication of Celestine V. By the end of 1298 Landolfo Colonna, commanding the papal army, had razed Colonna, Palestrina and other towns, and the rest of the family fled Italy.

The exiles allied with Philip IV of France. In September 1303 Sciarra Colonna and Guillaume de Nogaret led a small force into Anagni to arrest Boniface; Sciarra reportedly slapped the pope, an event called the Outrage of Anagni. Locals freed Boniface, who died on 11 October. In 1328 Sciarra Colonna crowned Louis IV of Germany as Holy Roman Emperor when John XXII refused, and the family received the right to place the imperial pointed crown above its arms. The poet Petrarch was a friend of the family, especially of Giovanni Colonna, and wrote sonnets for it.

At the Council of Constance, Oddone Colonna was elected on 14 November 1417 as Martin V and reigned until 20 February 1431. The feud with the Orsini was settled by Pope Julius II's bull Pax Romana in 1511, and in 1571 the heads of both houses married nieces of Pope Sixtus V.

The family supplied one pope and 23 cardinals. Marcantonio II Colonna led the papal fleet at the Battle of Lepanto on 7 October 1571 and was Viceroy of Sicily from 1577 to 1584. Vittoria Colonna, a sixteenth-century poet, was a friend of Michelangelo, and Costanza Colonna was patron and protector of Caravaggio. The Colonna were Prince Assistants to the Papal Throne, and the Palazzo Colonna in Rome is open to the public.
colony-of-natal: In 1823 Francis Farewell, a former naval lieutenant, and other Cape Town merchants formed a company to trade on the south-east coast. In August 1824 Farewell and Henry Francis Fynn obtained from Shaka a document ceding land including the port of Natal, and Farewell declared the territory a British possession. In 1835 the settlers, about 50 in number, laid out a town and named it Durban after Benjamin D'Urban, governor of the Cape Colony.

Voortrekkers fleeing British rule in the Cape took control of the port in May 1838 and founded the Natalia Republic, which suffered from disorganised government and poor relations with the Zulus. In December 1841 Sir George Napier, governor of the Cape, announced that British forces would reoccupy Port Natal. On 8 August 1843 the Natal volksraad agreed to British terms, and many Boers trekked over the Drakensberg.

Natal was proclaimed a British colony in 1843, administered from the Cape, and in 1856 became a separate colony with a legislative council of sixteen. Settlers arrived from the United Kingdom in numbers around 1850, and John Colenso came as bishop in 1854. Sugar was introduced from 1852; because Africans did not volunteer in sufficient numbers, the first Indian indentured labourers arrived in 1860, and by 1904 Indians outnumbered whites in the colony. Mohandas Gandhi, who reached Durban in 1893, helped found the Natal Indian Congress in 1894.

Responsible government was established in 1893, with John Robinson as first premier, under an electoral law framed to keep all but a very few Africans from the vote. In 1873 colonial forces broke up the Hlubi people of Chief Langalibalele, who had not enforced the registration of firearms; women and children were killed and survivors were apprenticed to colonists. Zululand was annexed to Natal in 1897. During the Second Boer War the Siege of Ladysmith lasted until 28 February 1900, and districts of the Transvaal were added to Natal.

In 1906 the Bambatha Rebellion broke out, ostensibly over a poll tax of £1, and it was suppressed by colonial forces. On 31 May 1910 the colony became Natal Province, one of the founding provinces of the Union of South Africa.
colorado: Colorado is a landlocked state in the Mountain West. It shares the Four Corners region with Arizona, New Mexico and Utah, and is bordered by Wyoming to the north, Nebraska to the northeast, Kansas to the east and Oklahoma to the southeast. It takes in most of the Southern Rocky Mountains, the northeastern portion of the Colorado Plateau and the western edge of the Great Plains, and its landscape includes alpine mountains, high plains, deserts with huge sand dunes and deep canyons.

In 1861 the United States Congress defined the boundaries of the new Territory of Colorado exclusively by lines of latitude and longitude, from 37°N to 41°N and from 102°02′48″W to 109°02′48″W. After 165 years of government surveys the borders were officially defined by 697 boundary markers and 697 straight lines. Colorado, Wyoming and Utah are the only states whose borders are defined solely by straight lines with no natural features. The Four Corners Monument is the only place in the United States where four states meet.

The region has been inhabited by Native Americans and their Paleo-Indian ancestors for at least 13,500 years and possibly more than 37,000. The Lindenmeier site contains artifacts dating from approximately 8720 BCE. The Ancient Pueblo peoples lived in the valleys and mesas of the Colorado Plateau in the far southwest, and the Ute Nation inhabited the mountain valleys of the Rocky Mountains. The Apache and Comanche lived in the east and southeast. In the 17th century the Arapaho and Cheyenne moved west from the Great Lakes region to hunt across the High Plains.

The United States acquired the territorial claim to the eastern Rocky Mountains with the Louisiana Purchase from France in 1803. In 1806 Zebulon Pike led an army reconnaissance expedition into the disputed region. Spanish cavalry arrested him and his troops in the San Luis Valley the following February, took them to Chihuahua and expelled them from Mexico in July.

In 1848 much of the Nuevo México region was annexed to the United States by the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo. The Pike's Peak Gold Rush of 1858-1862 brought an influx of settlers. On 28 February 1861 President James Buchanan signed the act creating the Territory of Colorado, and on 1 August 1876 President Ulysses S. Grant signed Proclamation 230, admitting Colorado as the 38th state.

Denver is the capital, the most populous city and the centre of the Front Range Urban Corridor. Colorado Springs is the second-most populous city. The state is the eighth-largest by area. Its economy rests on government and defence, mining, agriculture, tourism and manufacturing.
colorado-party-uruguay: The party's origin is bound up with Fructuoso Rivera, a caudillo and leader of the independence process, who was the first president of Uruguay from 1830 to 1834. In 1836 he led a revolt against the second president, Manuel Oribe. The feud had more to do with personal influence than with ideology: Oribe had eliminated a government post from which Rivera exercised patronage over the countryside, and his administration had accused Rivera's cabinet of gross corruption. The battle between their followers in September 1836 produced the Colorado (Red) Party and the Blanco (White) Party, named for the colours each side wore. The Blanco tradition later merged with other tendencies to form the National Party.

The confrontation was the first of many armed clashes between the two parties through the 19th century. Because Uruguay was a new nation with fragile autonomy, the quarrel became international: the Argentine caudillo Juan Manuel de Rosas and his Federalists supported Oribe, while Rivera's Colorados had the Unitarians, Britain and France, all enemies of Rosas. The resulting civil war, the Guerra Grande, kept the country divided for almost a decade, with Rivera and his followers confined for most of the 1840s in the walled city of Montevideo, besieged by Oribe's Blancos and the armies of Rosas. The Colorado Party was afterwards the dominant party of government almost without exception during the stabilisation of the republic.

The party has traditionally been ideologically diverse, seeking to unite moderate and liberal groups, with Krausism, liberal conservatism and pragmatism among its tendencies. A study of the 1950s noted that the liberal position the Colorados took up under Batlle pushed the Blancos towards a relatively more conservative one, though both parties had conservatives and liberals.

From 1942 to 1994 the Ley de Lemas allowed each party up to three presidential candidates, and a referendum in 1996 limited each to one from the 1999 elections. By then the leftist Broad Front, formed in the early 1970s, had become the most-voted force, and the Colorado Party lost its traditional dominance.
colosseum: The site was a flat area on the floor of a low valley between the Caelian, Esquiline and Palatine Hills, crossed by a canalised stream and an artificial lake or marsh. After the Great Fire of Rome in 64, Nero seized much of the area and built the Domus Aurea there, with an artificial lake and a gigantic bronze Colossus of himself nearby. Much of the Domus Aurea was torn down and the lake filled in for the Flavian Amphitheatre. Vespasian's decision can be seen as a populist gesture, returning to the people an area Nero had appropriated. The name Colosseum is believed to derive from the colossal statue of Nero, which Hadrian moved beside the amphitheatre.

The Colosseum is entirely free-standing, unlike Roman theatres built into hillsides, and is elliptical in plan, 189 metres long and 156 metres wide, with an outer wall 48 metres high. The outer wall required over 100,000 cubic metres of travertine, set without mortar and held by about 300 tons of iron clamps. Seating reflected the stratification of Roman society: boxes for the emperor and the Vestal Virgins, a podium for senators, then tiers for knights, citizens and, in a gallery added under Domitian, the poor, slaves and women. The arena floor was wood covered by sand, and the hypogeum beneath it, ordered by Domitian, held tunnels and cages with eighty vertical shafts giving access to the arena.

The shows, called munera, were always given by private individuals rather than the state. The animal hunt, the venatio, used wild beasts imported mainly from Africa and the Middle East, among them elephants, giraffes, lions and crocodiles. Trajan is said to have marked his victories in Dacia in 107 with contests involving 11,000 animals and 10,000 gladiators over 123 days.

By the late 6th century a small chapel had been built into the structure, the arena became a cemetery, and the arcades were rented as housing and workshops as late as the 12th century. Around 1200 the Frangipani family fortified it. The earthquake of 1349 collapsed the outer south side, and much stone was reused elsewhere in Rome. In 1749 Pope Benedict XIV consecrated it to the Passion of Christ, a view for which no historical evidence exists. The arena substructure was fully exposed in the 1930s.
colossus-of-rhodes: In the late fourth century BCE Rhodes, allied with Ptolemy I of Egypt, resisted an invasion by Antigonus I Monophthalmus. His son Demetrius I of Macedon besieged the city for a year, and in 304 BCE a relief force sent by Ptolemy arrived and he abandoned the siege, leaving most of his equipment. The Rhodians sold it for 300 talents and decided to build a colossal statue of their patron god Helios. Chares of Lindos directed the work, which began in 292 BCE. His teacher Lysippos had made a 22-metre bronze statue of Zeus at Tarentum.

Most descriptions give the statue a height of about 70 cubits. It stood on a white marble pedestal near the harbour entrance, though other sources place it on a breakwater. Accounts describe an iron frame with bronze plates as a skin, filled with stone blocks as work proceeded. Philo of Byzantium wrote that Chares cast it in horizontal courses, burying each section in earth. The image of the statue straddling the harbour mouth is a medieval invention, and engineering analysis indicates that a bronze statue with legs apart would have collapsed. Its true location remains in dispute.

The statue stood for 54 years. An earthquake in 226 BCE snapped it at the knees. Ptolemy III offered to pay for rebuilding, but the Oracle of Delphi led the Rhodians to fear they had offended Helios, and they declined. The remains lay for over 800 years and drew visitors. Strabo called it the best of the city's votive offerings, and Pliny the Elder wrote that few men could clasp its thumb in their arms. Theophanes the Confessor records that in 653 an Arab force sold its bronze to a Jewish merchant, who loaded it on 900 camels; he is the only source, and L. I. Conrad considers the story likely propaganda.
coluccio-salutati: Coluccio Salutati was born on 16 February 1331 at Stignano, a small commune near Buggiano in Tuscany. His father lived in exile in Bologna after a Ghibelline coup in Buggiano, and Salutati studied there before the family returned to Buggiano, which had become more securely part of the Republic of Florence. He worked there as a notary, pursued literary studies and came into contact with the Florentine humanists Boccaccio and Francesco Nelli.

The classical Latin of his letters earned him the nickname Ape of Cicero. In 1367 he became chancellor of Todi in the Papal States, and from 1368 to 1370 he assisted the papal secretary Francesco Bruni at the curia of Pope Urban V in Rome. In 1370 he became chancellor of Lucca but soon lost the post in internal struggles.

In 1374 Salutati received an appointment in Florence, and the next year he became Chancellor, the most important post in the Florentine bureaucracy. He was responsible for the official correspondence with other states, confidential instructions to ambassadors, diplomacy and treaties. Florence was at once at war with the papacy, and although he could not prevent it he became the most best-known chancellor in Italy.

Gian Galeazzo Visconti, Duke of Milan, the city's chief adversary, remarked that one of his letters could cause more damage than a thousand Florentine horsemen. Not every letter worked as intended: when he urged the people of Ancona in 1376 to revolt against the pope's governor, his remarks on the evils Italy had suffered from the French reached the King of France, and Salutati wrote a conciliatory letter. He held the office until his death on 4 May 1406, and Florence paid 250 florins for his funeral.

Salutati built a prose style on the Latin of Virgil and Cicero, writing that he imitated antiquity to produce something new, and not simply to reproduce it. He spent much of his salary on a collection of 800 books and found Cicero's lost Letters to his Friends, which showed Cicero as a defender of republican liberty.

His studies tied Florence's origin to the Roman Republic rather than the Empire. He promoted younger humanists including Poggio Bracciolini, Niccolò de' Niccoli, Leonardo Bruni and Pier Paolo Vergerio. In 1397 he brought the Byzantine scholar Manuel Chrysoloras to Florence to teach one of the first courses in Greek since the end of the Roman Empire, which let Bruni and Vergerio read Aristotle and Plato in the original.

His writings include a large collection of public and private letters, De seculo et religione, which defends active civic life as compatible with Christian devotion, De tyranno (1400), De fato et fortuna (1396–1397) and the unfinished De laboribus Herculis.
columba: Columba was born to Fedlimid and Eithne of the Cenél Conaill at Gartan, in Tír Chonaill, mainly modern County Donegal. His name in Irish, Colmcille, means dove. He studied at the monastic school of Movilla and then at Clonard, where he was one of twelve students of Finnian of Clonard known as the Twelve Apostles of Ireland. He became a monk and was ordained priest. Several important monasteries are attributed to him in the following years, among them Derry, Durrow, Kells and Swords.

Traditions link him with a quarrel over a psalter and with the Battle of Cúl Dreimhne in 561, though Richard Sharpe warns against accepting the many references that connect the battle with his leaving Ireland. One account says that a synod threatened him with excommunication and that he resolved to expiate his sense of offence by leaving Ireland, a departure described as exile or, more often, as pilgrimage.

In 563 he crossed to Scotland with twelve companions in a currach of wicker covered with leather. The island of Iona was given to him by his kinsman Conall mac Comgaill, king of Dál Riata, who perhaps invited him. The Ulster Gaels had lived on the Scottish west coast for a couple of centuries, so he was in a sense not leaving his own people. Iona was the only centre of literacy in the region, and his reputation as a holy man gave him a role as a diplomat among the tribes. He visited the pagan King Bridei of Fortriu at Inverness and won his respect but, according to Adomnán, not his conversion.

Columba founded several churches in the Hebrides and turned Iona into a school for missionaries. He is credited with transcribing 300 books, and two Latin hymns, Altus Prosator and Adiutor Laborantium, are attributed to him.

According to traditional sources he died on Iona on Sunday, 9 June 597, and was buried by his monks. His relics were removed in 849 and divided between Scotland and Ireland. The main source for his life is the Life of Columba by Adomnán, one of his successors at Iona. He is one of the patron saints of Ireland with Patrick and Brigid, and patron of Derry, and was venerated by both the Gaels of Dál Riata and the Picts.
columbanus: Columbanus, the Latinised form of Colmán, meaning little dove, was born in the Kingdom of Leinster in Ireland. He was first educated under Abbot Sinell of Cluaninis, whose monastery stood on an island of the River Erne in modern County Fermanagh, and under Sinell he composed a commentary on the Psalms. He then moved to Bangor Abbey to study as a teacher of the Bible, learning grammar, rhetoric and geometry, and Abbot Comgall taught him Greek and Latin. He stayed at Bangor until about 590, when Comgall reluctantly allowed him to travel to the continent.

Columbanus sailed with twelve companions, among them Gallus, and landed at Saint-Malo in Brittany. In Burgundy King Guntram welcomed them and granted land in the Vosges Mountains, where they turned a ruined Roman fortress into a school. It drew so many students that they moved to Luxeuil and founded a second school at Fontaines, all under his authority and following the Celtic tradition in which he had been educated. In 603 he and his followers quarrelled with the Frankish bishops over the date of Easter, since the Irish used their own calculation, and the bishops also objected to the Irish tonsure.

In 611 he reached the court of Theudebert II at Metz and travelled up the Rhine to preach to the Suebi and Alemanni, settling at Bregenz on Lake Constance, where Gallus preached and a monastery was founded. When war in 612 gave Theuderic II control of Austrasia and some of his students were murdered, he crossed the Alps. In Milan he was welcomed by King Agilulf and Queen Theodelinda of the Lombards and wrote against Arianism. In 614 Agilulf gave him land at Bobbio. At the king's request he also wrote to Pope Boniface IV about the controversy over the Three Chapters.

In his last year King Chlothar II invited him to return to Burgundy, but he declined and asked the king to protect his monks at Luxeuil. He retired to a cave above the Trebbia river and died at Bobbio on 21 November 615. His Rule set down the customs of Bangor and other Irish monasteries and was much shorter than the Rule of Saint Benedict, with ten chapters beginning with absolute obedience. His teaching on penance stressed private confession to a priest, followed by penances imposed in reparation. Gallus stayed in the Alps until his death, and the Abbey of Saint Gall was founded at the site of his cell about seventy years later.
columbia-university: Columbia University is a private university in New York City. Its main campus lies in the Upper Manhattan neighbourhood of Morningside Heights, on more than six city blocks, about 32 acres. It was designed on Beaux-Arts principles by the architects McKim, Mead and White, following the vision of Seth Low, a campus where all disciplines could be taught in one place. In 2007 the university bought most of a 17-acre site in Manhattanville for a second campus.

Classes began in July 1754 under the first president, Samuel Johnson, and the college was officially founded on 31 October 1754 as King's College by royal charter of George II, on the grounds of Trinity Church in Manhattan. After the American Revolution it was renamed Columbia College in 1784, and in 1787 it was placed under a private board of trustees headed by Alexander Hamilton and John Jay. In 1857 it moved to a Gothic Revival campus at 49th Street and Madison Avenue. Barnard College was created in 1889 in response to the refusal to admit women. In 1896 President Seth Low moved the campus to Morningside Heights, and the name became Columbia University.

Columbia is organised into 17 schools, with two affiliated colleges, Barnard College and Teachers College, and two seminaries. It is a member of the Ivy League and was the first school in the United States to grant the MD degree. Scientists there took part in the first nuclear fission reaction in North America and in the invention of the laser and of FM radio. The university administers the Pulitzer Prize and the Bancroft Prize in history, and a prize for the translation of Japanese literature, the oldest of its kind.
columbian-exchange: The term was first used in 1972 by the American historian Alfred W. Crosby in his book The Columbian Exchange, which mapped the biological and cultural transfers between the Old and New Worlds and was rapidly adopted by other historians. Before 1492 there is little evidence of contact between the two hemispheres. The Norse visits to Greenland, Newfoundland and Vinland in the late 10th and 11th centuries had no known impact on the Americas, and many scientists accept that contact between Polynesians and coastal South Americans around 1200 explains the sweet potato in Polynesia. The exchange began with the first voyage of Christopher Columbus in 1492.

Plants moved in both directions. Potatoes, grown only in South America before 1500, were widely eaten in Europe by the 18th century and are estimated to have contributed 12 to 25 per cent of the population growth in Afro-Eurasia between 1700 and 1900. The Portuguese brought cassava to Africa in the 16th century, and it gradually replaced sorghum and millet as the most important food crop there. Spanish colonisers brought maize and sweet potatoes to Asia, and the Portuguese took chili peppers to India. In the other direction rice, wheat, sugar cane, citrus fruits and coffee became important in the Americas, and enslaved Africans brought rice-growing skills to Georgia, South Carolina, Cuba and Puerto Rico.

Horses, donkeys, mules, pigs, cattle, sheep, goats, chickens and bees were rapidly adopted by native peoples; the Plains Indians used horses for hunting and the Mapuche adopted them in the Arauco War. The turkey and the Muscovy duck went to Europe. Diseases were far deadlier toward the Americas. Hispaniola's pre-contact population was probably at least 500,000, and fewer than 500 remained by 1526. Smallpox, first recorded in the Americas in 1518, is estimated to have killed 40 per cent of the 200,000 people of Tenochtitlan in 1520.

An estimated 80 to 95 per cent of the Native American population died in epidemics within 100 to 150 years of 1492. The Mexican population fell from an estimated 20 million to barely more than a million in the 16th century. The need for labour and the decline of Indigenous peoples was linked to the Atlantic slave trade, which brought 11.7 million Africans to the Americas, far more than the about 3.4 million Europeans who migrated between 1492 and 1840. The Old World also gained from the discovery of quinine, the first effective treatment for malaria. Syphilis may have been carried to Europe by Columbus's crew, though historians debate its origin.
colwyn-bay: Colwyn Bay (Welsh: Bae Colwyn) lies on the north coast of Wales, overlooking the Irish Sea, about halfway along the coast between the sea and the Pwllycrochan Woods on the hillside above. It lies within the historic county boundaries of Denbighshire. The western part of the bay, Rhos-on-Sea, has historic sites associated with St Trillo and with Ednyfed Fychan, the 13th-century general and councillor to Llywelyn the Great. King Richard II was ambushed in Old Colwyn in 1399 by supporters of Henry Bolingbroke as he returned to England from Ireland.

Colwyn Bay railway station opened in 1849 on the Chester and Holyhead Railway, at first under the name Colwyn, and was renamed in 1876. As at nearby Llandudno and Rhyl, the railway brought rapid growth, and the place became a seaside holiday town within easy reach of the large towns of north-west England. From 1875 the Pwllycrochan Estate sold building plots round the station. In 1890 the Reverend William Hughes, a missionary pastor and friend of Henry Morton Stanley, founded the African Training Institute in the town. He had brought two Congolese children to Colwyn Bay in 1885 to train them as missionaries. It trained 87 students in 23 years.

A local government district, Colwyn Bay and Colwyn, was created in 1887, became an urban district, was renamed Colwyn Bay in 1926 and became a municipal borough in 1934. The borough was abolished in 1974, and the modern county borough of Conwy was created in 1996. Britain's first milk bar branch of the National Milk Bar company opened in the town in 1933. In the Second World War the Colwyn Bay Hotel was the headquarters of the Ministry of Food until 1953, and the town became a significant centre for diamond cutting and polishing, which helped fund the war effort.

At the 2021 census the community had a population of 10,576 and the built-up area 29,275. The town's economy is dominated by tourism, and its sandy beach, 4.8 kilometres long, has been enhanced with millions of tonnes of sand. Colwyn Bay hosted the National Eisteddfod in 1910 and 1947. The Victoria Pier, closed in 2009 and partly collapsed in 2017, was demolished in May 2018. The Welsh Mountain Zoo is nearby, and the ruined medieval manor house Llys Euryn stands on Bryn Euryn. Colwyn Bay is the birthplace of the actors Terry Jones and Timothy Dalton and of the priest and martyr William Davies, born at Groes yn Eirias in 1555 and beatified in 1987.
comana-pontica: Comana lay on a natural hill just south of the village of Gümenek, on the west bank of the Yeşilırmak, the ancient Iris, 9 km northeast of Tokat on the road to Niksar, ancient Neocaesareia. Strabo placed it upstream from the plain of Dazimonitis. The fertile land around the hill must have been central to the economy of the temple state, and a bridge, now lost, probably joined the temple to the far bank of the river.

Under the Kingdom of Pontus, from 281 BCE until Pompey defeated Mithridates VI in 63 BCE, Comana was a large temple state. The kings ceded large tracts of land to the temple of Ma, which kept the profits of their cultivation, and the chief priest ranked second only to the king. Strabo, who visited the temple, as did Julius Caesar, described it as a replica of the temple in Cappadocia, with the same rites.

Pompey added two schoeni to the temple land, and Caesar or Antony four more; under Augustus the territory reached the size of the region's city-states. The city was known as both Hierocaesareia and Komana until the time of Titus, and Ma appeared on its coins from the reign of Caligula. As the temple declined, Christianity spread: Basiliscus of Comana, its bishop, was executed around 310, and John Chrysostom died there in 407. The city disappears from Byzantine records, but a place called Komada is recorded in 1347, and the Turkish form Qōmanāt gave the modern name Gümenek.

J. G. C. Anderson, travelling through Pontus in 1899, found a mound near a bridge over the Iris with an inscription naming Comana. The site was located with ground radar in 2009, and excavations led by the Middle East Technical University in Ankara have found remains of Greek, Roman, Byzantine and Ottoman times. Eight grey columns in the Ali Pasha Mosque in Tokat may come from the temple. Modern irrigation channels and a new highway have damaged the site.
comanche: The Comanche call themselves Nʉmʉnʉʉ, 'the people'. Their language is a Numic language of the Uto-Aztecan family, closely related to Shoshone. It was originally a Shoshone dialect but diverged after the Comanche adopted a nomadic horse culture in the early 18th century. The movement of Proto-Comanche groups onto the Plains was part of the wider Shoshonean expansion, and the Kotsoteka were probably among the first. Contact with the Shoshone of Wyoming lasted until the 1830s, when advancing Cheyennes broke it. The name Comanche comes from the Ute word kɨmantsi, 'enemy', which the Spanish adopted. It is first recorded in 1706.

After the Pueblo Revolt of 1680 various Plains peoples acquired horses. The horse made hunting, war and moving camp easier, a man's wealth was measured by his herd, and the Comanche came to be regarded as among the finest light cavalry in history. They built a vast territory across what is now north-western Texas, eastern New Mexico, south-eastern Colorado, south-western Kansas and western Oklahoma, which colonists called Comanchería. It was not a centralised state, but a set of politically autonomous divisions linked by kinship. At its peak their language was the lingua franca of the southern Great Plains.

Their large raids of the 1840s and 1850s reached hundreds of miles into Mexico, where they took livestock that they mostly sold in Texas. They also took many captives, whom they used as slaves, sold to the Spanish and later to Mexican settlers, or adopted. In 1844 Sam Houston, president of the Republic of Texas, almost reached a peace treaty at Tehuacana Creek, but in 1845 the Texas Legislature refused to fix a boundary with Comancheria. Epidemics, the destruction of the bison herds and warfare and massacres by the United States Army forced the Comanche onto reservations in Indian Territory in the mid-1870s.

Bison supplied most of the Comanche's tools, household goods and weapons, and nearly 200 utilitarian items were made from its horn, hide and bone. They moved so often that they used no pottery. Men hunted bison, elk, pronghorn and deer, and hunting was a main source of prestige.

In the later 19th century Quanah Parker, appointed paramount chief by the United States government, argued for better terms for his people and became a wealthy cattleman. He also campaigned for the right to practise the rites of the Native American Church. Many Comanche children were placed in boarding schools, where they were discouraged from speaking their language. The Comanche Nation today is headquartered in Lawton, Oklahoma.
comayagua: Comayagua lies in a valley 80 km north-west of Tegucigalpa on the highway to San Pedro Sula, 594 metres above sea level, and is the capital of the Comayagua department. Hondurans call it La Antañona, the old one, because it keeps much of its colonial architecture. The name is indigenous: most agree it combines the Lenca words koma, a huge amount of land, and jawa, water, meaning abundant land of water. The Spaniards called the place Valladolid and the Country of the Fig Trees. The Lenca people have lived in the valley since approximately 1,000 BCE, as remains at Yarumela and Tenampúa show.

Captain Alonso de Cáceres founded the city in 1537, on the instructions of Francisco de Montejo, to find a site for a city between the two oceans. It was first called Santa María de la Concepción de Comayagua. King Philip II granted it the title of city in 1557, and in 1561 the episcopal see moved there from Trujillo because of its central position and its closeness to the gold and silver mining regions. It remained the capital of Honduras throughout the colonial period, and in 1788 it became an intendancy that absorbed Tegucigalpa, which had grown as a mining centre. This fed a rivalry between the two cities.

Honduras became part of the United Provinces of Central America in 1823, and Comayagua stayed its capital. On 4 April 1827 federal troops under Colonel Justo Milla laid siege to the city to overthrow the head of state, Dionisio de Herrera, and much of it was burned and looted. A decree of June 1849 to move the capital to Tegucigalpa was not carried out. On 30 October 1880 President Marco Aurelio Soto decided to transfer it, after which the population, commerce and importance of Comayagua fell notably, though it remained the seat of the diocese of Honduras.

Comayagua has some of the oldest buildings in Central America, among them the churches of La Merced, San Francisco and San Sebastián, built in the 16th century. The cathedral of the Immaculate Conception, built in the colonial period, holds a clock that is said to be the oldest in the Americas. The Caxa Real, built between 1739 and 1741, stored the tribute and the silver and gold of the Spanish crown. Museums cover colonial religious art, the Lenca and the republican period.
combat-of-the-thirty: The War of the Breton Succession between the House of Montfort and the House of Blois was absorbed into the Hundred Years' War, with England backing the Montforts and France the Blois. By 1351 it had become a stalemate of rival strongholds. Jean de Beaumanoir, captain of Josselin, challenged Robert Bemborough of Ploërmel to single combat, and according to Froissart, Bemborough proposed a fight of twenty or thirty on each side instead.

Jean le Bel and Froissart present it as a matter of honour for the two ladies then leading the factions, Joan of Penthièvre and Joan of Flanders. A ballad by a Blois supporter cast Bemborough's men as plunderers of the local people and Beaumanoir as their defender.

The fight was held like a tournament at the Halfway Oak, with refreshments and many spectators. Beaumanoir led thirty Bretons; Bemborough had twenty Englishmen, among them Robert Knolles and Hugh Calveley, six German mercenaries and four Breton Montfortists. They fought with swords, daggers, spears and axes, mounted or on foot. After several hours, with four dead on the French side and two on the English, both sides paused for refreshments and to bind wounds.
