When the wounded Beaumanoir asked for water, Geoffroy du Bois is said to have told him: "Drink thy blood, Beaumanoir; thy thirst will pass."

When fighting resumed Bemborough was killed, apparently by du Bois, and his men formed a tight defensive body, rallied by a German soldier called Croquart. The squire Guillaume de Montauban then mounted his horse, rode into the English line and broke it, overthrowing seven champions; the rest surrendered. Nine of the Anglo-Breton side were killed.

The combat had no effect on the outcome of the war, but contemporaries saw it as chivalry at its finest. King Charles V of France commissioned a tapestry of it, and twenty years later Froissart saw a scarred survivor, Yves Charruel, honoured above all others at the king's table. The ballad's version later entered French nationalist accounts as a moral victory over foreigners: an obelisk ordered by Napoleon in 1811 was erected in 1819 under Louis XVIII. English writers, among them Edward Smedley and Arthur Conan Doyle in his novel Sir Nigel, presented Montauban's charge as treachery.
comecon: Comecon was founded in 1949 by the Soviet Union, Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Poland and Romania. It was the Eastern Bloc's response to the Marshall Plan and the Organisation for European Economic Co-operation in Western Europe. Czechoslovakia, Hungary and Poland had remained interested in Marshall aid, but its conditions of a convertible currency and market economies would have tied them more closely to free European markets than to the Soviet Union. In July 1947 Joseph Stalin ordered these governments to withdraw from the Paris Conference on the European Recovery Programme.

After Stalin's death in 1953 the members began again to discuss complementary specialisation, and in 1956 ten permanent standing committees were set up. The Soviet Union began to trade oil for goods made in Comecon countries. A charter modelled on the 1957 Treaty of Rome followed in 1959. Until 1967 Comecon worked only by unanimous agreement, which usually meant failure. That year it adopted the interested party principle, under which any country could opt out of a project while the others still used Comecon's machinery. This was aimed partly at letting Romania chart its own economic course without leaving.

From the early 1970s Soviet oil and gas were transferred within Comecon at below-market rates, which many Western commentators saw as a politically motivated subsidy. In the 1980s, under Mikhail Gorbachev, Soviet influence grew and there were attempts to give Comecon some supranational authority. East Germany withdrew on 2 October 1990, after reunification.

Comecon's official hierarchy had a Session, an executive committee, a Secretariat, four council committees and twenty-four standing commissions. The Session was the highest organ and usually met in a member's capital each year. Each country had one vote, and the charter of 1959 proclaimed the sovereign equality of members. In practice the Soviet Union dominated, holding about 90 per cent of the members' land and energy resources and 70 per cent of their population, and many committees had their headquarters in Moscow. Members traded by barter, using world prices as a reference but keeping prices stable for years, which suited central planning. Albania stopped taking part in 1961, and Yugoslavia had associate status from 1964.
comilla: Comilla, officially spelled Cumilla, lies on the banks of the Gumti River in the east of Bangladesh. It is the seat of Comilla District and the second largest city in Chittagong Division. The district is bounded by Tripura to the north, and the rivers that pass through it include the Gomati and the Little Feni. Comilla was one of the cities of ancient Bengal and was once the capital of the Tripura kingdom. Its city corporation covers 53.04 square kilometres.

In ancient times the region was under Gangaridai and Samatata. In the 9th century CE it came under the kings of Harikela, and Lalmai Mainamati was ruled by the Deva dynasty in the 8th century and by the Chandra dynasty in the 10th and mid-11th centuries. In 1732 the area became the centre of the Bengal-backed domain of Jagat Manikya. A peasants' movement against the king of Tripura, led by Shamsher Gazi, rose in 1764, and in 1765 the area came under the East India Company. It was made the Tripura district in 1790 and renamed Comilla in 1960.

Under British rule Comilla saw unrest during the partition of Bengal in 1905, and on 21 November 1921 Kazi Nazrul Islam composed patriotic songs there to protest the visit of the Prince of Wales. The Avay Ashram was a revolutionary institution of this time, and Rabindranath Tagore and Mahatma Gandhi visited the town. In 1931 about 4,000 peasants at Mohini village in Chauddagram revolted against a land revenue tax, and Gurkha soldiers fired on the crowd, killing four; in 1932 police fired at a peasant gathering at Hasnabad, killing two.

Comilla Cantonment, the oldest military base in East Bengal, was widely used by the British Indian Army in the Second World War and was the headquarters of the British 14th Army. The Maynamati War Cemetery, kept by the Commonwealth War Graves Commission, commemorates Allied soldiers who died in both world wars and also holds Japanese graves. In the war of 1971 Pakistan formed an ad hoc division in mid-November to hold the Comilla and Noakhali districts, and its forces surrendered on 16 December 1971, a day commemorated in Bangladesh as Bijoy Dibos.

Comilla Victoria Government College in the city is named after Queen Victoria. Archaeological finds from the district, especially of the 7th and 8th centuries, are kept in the Mainamati Museum. The professional cricket team Comilla Victorians is based in the city.
commander-of-the-faithful: The Arabic title Amir al-Mu'minin combines amir, meaning commander or leader, with al-mu'minin, the believers, and so denotes authority that is military, administrative, judicial and moral at once. The word amir was used for Muslim military commanders during the lifetime of Muhammad, and a commander bore it at the Battle of al-Qadisiyya. The second caliph, Umar, adopted the title on his accession in 634, probably not for its military sense but because of a Quranic injunction to obey God, the Apostle and those invested with command.

According to Fred M. Donner, the adoption of the title marked a step in the centralisation of the early Muslim state, since the Amir al-Mu'minin appointed and dismissed generals and governors, took major political decisions and kept the diwan, the list of Muslims entitled to a share of the spoils of conquest. It appears to have been the chief title of the early caliphs; the word caliph itself does not seem to have been adopted until the reign of the Umayyad Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan (685-705), after the Second Fitna.

Among Sunnis, taking the title became almost the same as claiming the caliphate, and the Umayyads, Abbasids and Fatimids used it for a universal claim. Later regional rulers, especially in the west of the Muslim world, adopted it to stress their own independence: the Umayyads of Cordoba in 928, the Hafsids of Ifriqiya from 1253, then the Marinids and later Moroccan dynasties. The title also kept a sense of command in jihad. The early Ottoman sultans used it in that sense, as did Aurangzeb, Timur, Muhammad Umar Khan of the Kokand Khanate, Abdelkader El Djezairi from 1834 and Dost Mohammad Khan, who proclaimed a jihad against the Sikh Empire in 1836.

Shia and other traditions understand the title differently. Twelver Shias apply it only to Ali, regarded as the first Imam. The Ismaili Fatimid caliphs used it, and among the Nizari Ismailis it belongs to the Imam of the Time. Among the Zaydis it was the right of any rightful Imam who claimed leadership by force of arms, and the Ibadis did not use it except for the Rustamid dynasty.

In the late twentieth century the title was taken up again. A Taliban-convened assembly of Afghan ulama conferred it on Muhammad Umar at Kandahar in April 1996, and the Islamic State of Iraq's leaders adopted it from 2005 and 2006. Morocco's constitution still names it as the principal title of the King of Morocco.
commentarii-de-bello-gallico: Caesar's victories in Gaul had increased the alarm and hostility of his aristocratic enemies at Rome, the optimates, who intended to prosecute him for abuse of his authority once he laid down his imperium. A conviction would have stripped him of wealth and citizenship and undone the laws he had passed as consul. The Commentaries are understood as an effort to address the plebeians and the Tribunes of the Plebs directly, bypassing the Senate, and to present the wars as just and pious, fought in self-defence.

The classicist Ruth Breindal thinks Caesar probably dictated much of the work to a scribe, while keeping an overwhelming hand in it, and regards its main purpose as propaganda to protect his reputation. The last chapters of Book 8 were written after Caesar's death in 44 BCE by the consul Aulus Hirtius, who died in 43 BCE.

The work opens with the often quoted Gallia est omnis divisa in partes tres, "Gaul is a whole divided into three parts". It is divided into eight books of roughly 5,000 to 15,000 words. Gaul here means the Celtic regions outside the province of Gallia Narbonensis, which Rome already held. The narrative begins in 58 BCE with the migration of the Helvetii, whom neighbouring allies asked Caesar to resist, and draws in further tribes and the Germanic Suebi.

Among the Gallic leaders, Diviciacus of the Haedui (Aedui) is shown as the one man in whom Caesar had absolute confidence, and his appeals led Caesar to act against the German leader Ariovistus. Book 6 describes the Germans, the Druids and their sacrifices. Book 5 tells of the centurions Lucius Vorenus and Titus Pullo, rivals who saved each other's lives when the garrison of Quintus Tullius Cicero was besieged in a revolt of the Belgae led by Ambiorix.

Most contemporaries and later historians took the account as truthful until the 20th century. After the Second World War historians began to question it, above all its claim that the Romans faced Gallic forces of up to 430,000, a size thought impossible for an army of the time, and suffered no deaths against them. From the 1970s some critics read the work less as history than as literature.

Its clear, direct Latin has made it a mainstay of Latin teaching. About 240 medieval manuscripts preserve it, the oldest written at Fleury Abbey in the later ninth century, and the first printed edition was published by Giovanni Andrea Bussi at Rome in 1469. Caesar appears in the Astérix albums, whose jokes include his speaking of himself in the third person.
commission-for-historical-clarification: The commission grew out of an agreement signed in June 1994 by the Guatemalan government and the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unity (URNG), under the advice of the UN Secretary-General and the United Nations Verification Mission in Guatemala. The Catholic Church, through the Human Rights Office of the Archdiocese of Guatemala, also pressed for it, while the army opposed it as a tool for the insurgents. Its mandate was not to judge but to clarify the past with "objectivity, equity and impartiality": it could name no individual, its findings had no judicial effect and it had no subpoena powers.

The commission worked from February 1997 to February 1999 under the German law professor Christian Tomuschat, with the Mayan scholar Otilia Lux de Coti and the lawyer Edgar Alfredo Balsells Tojo. At its height it had a staff of 269 and 14 field offices; it visited 2,000 communities and received testimony from about 20,000 people. Austria, Canada, Germany and the United Kingdom gave support, and the United States provided declassified documents. The 12-volume report was presented to the parties and to Kofi Annan in February 1999.

It registered 42,275 victims of human rights violations and acts of violence, among them 23,671 arbitrary executions and 6,159 forced disappearances. Of the fully identified victims, 83% were Mayan and 17% Ladino, and 3% of the violations were attributed to insurgent groups. The commission named structural injustice, the closing of public spaces, an anti-democratic trajectory and the Cold War as the main causes, and stated that the guerrillas never had the military potential to pose an immediate threat to the state.

Its seven recommendations included preserving the victims' memory, exhuming remains, investigating disappearances and paying reparations; a National Reparations Program was set up in 2003. The former military dictator José Efraín Ríos Montt was tried and convicted of genocide and crimes against humanity, but the proceedings were later suspended and he died while the trial was still under way. Scholars such as Rachel Sieder, Jeff Corntassel and Cindy Holder have questioned how far the commission brought justice to Indigenous victims and lasting peace.
commission-of-government: Newfoundland's finances had been strained by debt from the First World War and then by the collapse of fish prices in the Depression. In 1933, after years of crisis, a severe budget deficit and a riot that brought down the previous government, Prime Minister Frederick C. Alderdice asked the British and Canadian governments to set up a royal commission. Chaired by Lord Amulree, appointed by the British government, with Charles Alexander Magrath for Canada and Sir William Ewen Stavert for Newfoundland, it recommended suspending responsible government for a time. Alderdice put this to the House of Assembly, which approved it and so voted itself out of existence.

The Commission was sworn in on 16 February 1934, with Alderdice as vice-chairman. Its members were civil servants answerable to the British Government, and it set out to reform the administration and balance the budget. With grants in aid from the United Kingdom it tried to encourage agriculture and reorganise the fishing industry, and it did much to extend government health services to rural areas, but it could not solve the basic problems of a small export economy in a time of worldwide stagnation.

American and Canadian military spending in the 1940s brought a boom and allowed the Commission to consider restoring democratic government. The British government, believing wartime prosperity would not last, set up the Newfoundland National Convention in 1946 to debate the constitutional options, which went to the people in two referendums in 1948. By a slender majority they chose confederation with Canada over a return to dominion status, and the Commission governed until Newfoundland joined Canada on 31 March 1949.
commission-on-the-truth-for-el-salvador: The civil war between the Salvadoran government and the Farabundo Martí National Liberation Front (FMLN), a union of five leftist guerrilla groups formed in October 1980, followed the coup of October 1979 and the assassination of Archbishop Óscar Romero on 24 March 1980. By its end in 1992 an estimated 75,000 Salvadorans had been killed, about 1.4 percent of the population. The United States gave the government approximately $4.5 billion in military and other aid during the 1980s.

Talks mediated by the United Nations began in July 1990. The Mexico Agreement of 1991 called for a truth commission, and the Act of New York of December 1991 brought the agreements together before the Chapultepec Peace Accords of 16 January 1992. With the consent of both sides, Secretary-General Javier Pérez de Cuéllar appointed three foreigners: Belisario Betancur, former president of Colombia, Thomas Buergenthal, former president of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, and Reinaldo Figueredo Planchart, former foreign minister of Venezuela.

The commission worked from July 1992 to March 1993 with offices in Chalatenango, Santa Ana and San Miguel and a staff with no Salvadorans. Its mandate covered serious acts of violence between January 1980 and July 1991 whose impact demanded that the public know the truth. It heard about 2,000 witnesses and gathered statements from more than 20,000 others through human rights groups. In November 1992 the Argentine Forensic Anthropology Team exhumed remains of at least 143 victims at El Mozote, supporting testimony that they were summarily executed.

The report attributed approximately 85 percent of the abuses to government forces and named more than 40 senior members of the military, the judiciary and the armed opposition. It recommended removing those responsible from public office, reforming the judicial system, paying reparations to victims and creating a forum to oversee all this.

The army's high command called the report unfair, biased and insolent, and President Alfredo Cristiani said Salvadorans wanted to forget the past; others criticised it for passing over the role of the United States. About 200 senior officers were removed, retiring with full honours, and a new Criminal Procedure Code followed in 1996. In 2016 the Supreme Court ruled the amnesty law of 20 March 1993 unconstitutional, opening the way to prosecutions.
committee-for-the-preparation-of-korean-: The committee, known for short as the Preparatory Committee, was set up to take over executive authority from the Governor-General of Chōsen. Lyuh Woon-hyung founded it on the evening of 15 August 1945 on the basis of the National Establishment Alliance, which he had formed a year earlier, in August 1944. Its headquarters were in Gye-dong, Seoul, and its name was first proposed by Ahn Chai-hong.

Lyuh Woon-hyung was chairman and Ahn Chai-hong vice-chairman; Jeong Baek headed organisation, Choi Geun-u general affairs, Lee Gyu-gap finance, Jo Dong-ho publicity and Kwon Tae-seok enforcement. Its statement of aims pledged a completely independent nation, a democratic administration able to meet the basic political and social demands of all groups, and the keeping of domestic order and the people's livelihood during the period of transition.

Lyuh's younger brother, Lyuh Woon-hong, described its members as ranging from Communist Party members on the extreme left, through non-communist leftists and moderate socialists, to right-wingers such as Ahn Chai-hong and Lee Gyu-gap, and men such as Jang Gwon and Song Gyu-hwan who supported Lyuh unconditionally as an elder brother figure.

A plenary session on 4 September 1945 reorganised the executive committee and made the lawyer Ho Hon vice-chairman. On the evening of 6 September more than 1,000 people met in a lecture hall of Kyunggi Girls' High School. After Ahn Chai-hong and the nationalist faction withdrew, the communist and socialist wings took control and declared the People's Republic of Korea. The committee then became the government organisation of that republic, the People's Committees, and was later dissolved into the People's Republic Executive Committee.
committee-for-the-relief-of-the-black-po: The Black Poor, as the destitute Black residents of London were called, lived mostly in East End parishes such as Mile End, in Seven Dials and in Marylebone. Many had come through the Atlantic slave trade or had escaped their owners, and from 1731 the Corporation of London barred Black people from apprenticeships with freemen of the livery companies. Their numbers grew after the American War of Independence, when Black Loyalists who had fought for Britain reached London. On 5 January 1786 a notice in the Public Advertiser announced that Mr. Brown, a baker of Wigmore Street, would give a loaf to every Black person in distress, and a first meeting followed on 10 January.

The group found about 250 Black people in distress, of whom 35 came from the East Indies; one hundred men said they had served in the Royal Navy. Meeting at Batson's Coffee House, it drew George Peters, Governor of the Bank of England, John Julius Angerstein and the abolitionists Samuel Hoare and Henry and Samuel Thornton, with Jonas Hanway in the chair after Montagu Burgoyne and Benjamin Johnson. By 18 April it had raised £890 1s, the largest sum collected among the Quakers. It gave out alms at the White Raven tavern in Mile End and the Yorkshire Stingo in Lisson Grove, and kept a sick house in Warren Street.

Unable to find enough work for the men, it turned to settlement abroad. The scheme proposed by the entomologist Henry Smeathman drew Granville Sharp and the government of William Pitt the Younger. About 700 signed up but only 441 boarded at first, and the authorities, with the Committee's support, tried to force beggars to join. Olaudah Equiano and Ottobah Cugoano criticised the scheme, and Lord George Gordon advised against going.

In April 1787, 411 passengers sailed from Plymouth, and 96 died on the voyage. The survivors landed on 15 May 1787 and founded Granville Town, but fighting with a local chief and enslavement by traders left only 64 settlers. The colony was later repopulated by Black Loyalists recruited in Nova Scotia, and the descendants of the Black Poor form part of the Sierra Leone Creole people.
committee-of-public-safety: A widespread belief held that revolutionary France was in immediate peril, threatened by foreign armies, the revolts in the Vendée and foreign agents plotting from within. The Girondin leader Maximin Isnard proposed a nine-member committee, supported by Georges Danton, who called it "a hand to grasp the weapon of the Revolutionary Tribunal". The National Convention created it on 6 April 1793, after a proposal by Bertrand Barère. It supplemented the Committee of General Defence of early January 1793, and at first it was called the Danton Committee. Danton was not included when it was recomposed on 10 July 1793.

Maximilien Robespierre was elected to the committee on 27 July 1793. It governed the war, named the judges and juries of the Revolutionary Tribunal, provisioned the armies and the public and oversaw the state bureaucracy. It applied the Convention's decrees and so carried out some of the harshest policies of the Terror, among them the levée en masse of 23 August 1793 and the Law of Suspects of 17 September. The Law of 14 Frimaire on 4 December 1793 codified its powers.

The Hébertists were arrested and executed in March 1794, and Danton and Camille Desmoulins, who had turned the newspaper Le Vieux Cordelier against the committees, went to the guillotine on 5 April 1794. The Law of 22 Prairial, enacted on 10 June 1794, limited the legal recourse of the accused and made death the punishment for all the crimes it covered. Discord grew within the government, and Robespierre quarrelled with Collot d'Herbois and Billaud-Varenne and almost stopped attending in June 1794 because of illness.

On 26 July 1794 Robespierre told the Convention that the committees needed purifying. The next day, 9 Thermidor, Saint-Just was interrupted by Jean-Lambert Tallien and Billaud-Varenne, and the Convention ordered the arrest of Robespierre, his brother Augustin, Saint-Just and their supporters. Philippe Le Bas killed himself, and the others were guillotined on 28 July 1794. The Thermidorian Reaction that followed repealed many of the year's most unpopular laws and restricted the committees. The committee's influence diminished over 15 months, and it disappeared on 25 October 1795, the day the National Convention ended, under the Constitution of the Year III, which began the Directory.
committee-of-safety-hawaii: The committee grew out of the leadership of the Missionary Party, whose members ran as Independent Party candidates. A Committee of Nine, formed on 14 January 1883, led the Independent ticket at the elections of 1884, at which the party won 13 seats; reconvened as the Committee of Thirteen for 1886, it fell to ten. In January 1887 the Committee of Thirteen founded the Hawaiian League, a secret society illegal under the kingdom's law, whose 405 members, all of European or American descent, swore to protect the white community against arbitrary action by the government. Lorrin A. Thurston drafted its constitution.

Many members wanted annexation by the United States rather than reform of the monarchy, and the League was also called the Annexation Club. By early 1887 its members controlled the Honolulu Rifles, about 200 armed non-Hawaiian men under Volney V. Ashford, and in June 1887 they used them to force King Kalākaua to accept the Bayonet Constitution, which limited his power.

When the Marshal of the Kingdom, Charles B. Wilson, learned of the planned coup on 16 January 1893, his requests for warrants to arrest the committee were refused, and he and Samuel Nowlein gathered 496 men to protect the queen. On 17 January a policeman was shot while trying to stop a wagon of weapons, and the Rifles occupied Ali'iolani Hale. At the committee's request the American minister John L. Stevens had landed 162 sailors and marines from the USS Boston; they fired no shot but intimidated the royalists, and the queen ordered her forces to surrender to avoid loss of life.

The committee's proclamation, read to a crowd before ʻIolani Palace on 17 January, abolished the monarchy and established a Provisional Government until terms of union with the United States were agreed. Every government with a diplomatic presence in Hawaii recognised it within 48 hours, though Heihachiro Togo, commanding the Japanese gunboat Naniwa, at first refused to strike the kingdom's colours. President Grover Cleveland's administration blocked annexation, which Congress approved only in 1898, under William McKinley.
commius: Caesar recounts in his Commentarii de Bello Gallico that he made Commius king of the Atrebates after conquering the tribe in 57 BCE. Sent ahead to persuade the Britons not to resist the first expedition, Commius was arrested as soon as he landed and was handed back only when the Britons failed to stop the Roman landing. He then supplied a small troop of cavalry, and on the second expedition he negotiated the surrender of the British leader Cassivellaunus.

He stayed loyal through the Gaulish revolts of 54 BCE, and Caesar in return left the Atrebates independent and free of tax and gave Commius rule over the Morini. According to Aulus Hirtius, who wrote the last book of the De Bello Gallico, the legate Titus Labienus suspected him of conspiring with other tribes and sent the tribune Gaius Volusenus Quadratus to kill him at a sham meeting. Commius escaped with a severe head wound and vowed never again to associate with Romans.

After Alesia he joined a revolt of the Bellovaci, bringing some 500 Germans to their side. In 51 BCE he waged guerrilla war with a small mounted band until Volusenus, sent after him by Mark Antony, beat his horsemen. Commius sued for peace, offering hostages on condition that he never had to meet a Roman again, and Antony agreed.

Sextus Julius Frontinus, writing in the 1st century CE, tells how Commius escaped to Britain with Caesar in pursuit, raising his sails on ships stranded by the tide so that Caesar thought them afloat. John Creighton argues instead that Commius was sent to Britain under his truce with Antony and set up there as a friendly king. Coins in Gaul pairing his name with Garmanos or Carsicios suggest he kept some power there, perhaps through regents or sons.

By about 30 BCE he was king of the Atrebates in Britain, issuing coins from Calleva Atrebatum (Silchester). Coins with his name continued until about 20 BCE, and some have suggested two kings of the name, father and son, pointing to coins stamped COM COMMIOS. From about 25 BCE he seems to have ruled with Tincomarus, whose coins, like those of Eppillus and Verica, name him as a son of Commius.
commodus: Commodus was born on 31 August 161 at Lanuvium, the son of Marcus Aurelius and Faustina the Younger. His twin brother died in 165 and a younger brother in 169, leaving him his father's only surviving son. He was the first emperor born in the purple, during his father's reign. He was with the army at Carnuntum in 172 and received the title Germanicus, and in 175, when Avidius Cassius declared himself emperor in Syria, he assumed the toga virilis on the Danube front. On 27 November 176 his father gave him the title Imperator, and on 1 January 177 he became consul at fifteen, the youngest up to that time.

Marcus Aurelius died on 17 March 180, leaving Commodus sole emperor at eighteen. He soon made peace with the Danubian tribes. He had little interest in administration and left it to favourites: the chamberlain Saoterus, the praetorian prefect Perennis and the freedman Cleander. He devalued the denarius and paid for handouts and shows partly by taxing the senators. Cassius Dio, a contemporary, saw his accession as a descent from a kingdom of gold to one of iron and rust; the Historia Augusta is unreliable.

Conspiracies followed. In 182 his sister Lucilla plotted against him; her accomplices were executed and she was exiled to Capri and later killed. Cleander sold senate seats and commands, and in 190 appointed a record 25 suffect consuls; a food shortage and a riot brought his fall. Commodus presented himself as Hercules. After a fire damaged Rome in 191 he declared himself a new Romulus in early 192, renamed the city Colonia Lucia Annia Commodiana and renamed the months after his twelve names. He also fought as a gladiator in the arena.

In late 192 Commodus announced that he would take office on 1 January as both consul and gladiator. His mistress Marcia found a list of people he meant to execute, with her own name, the prefect Laetus and the chamberlain Eclectus on it. On 31 December she poisoned his food; he vomited it, and the conspirators sent his wrestling partner Narcissus to strangle him in his bath. The Senate declared him a public enemy and demolished his statues. His death ended the Nerva–Antonine dynasty, and Pertinax succeeded him. In 195 Septimius Severus had the Senate deify him. His sole reign is commonly thought to mark the end of the Pax Romana.
common-law: The common law was so named because it was common to all the king's courts across England. It originated in the practices of the courts of the English kings in the centuries following the Norman Conquest of 1066. Before the Conquest much legal business took place in local folk courts of the shires and hundreds, boroughs, fairs and large landholders held courts of their own, and the Catholic Church ran a separate system for canon law. How far the common law drew on Anglo-Saxon traditions such as the jury, ordeals and writs is still much discussed.

King Henry II is regarded as its establisher. He wanted to preserve public order, though providing law was also profitable, since fines and forfeitures brought the government large sums. He developed the practice of sending judges from the Curia Regis, the king's court, to hear disputes round the country, and as these circuits spread, a law emerged that was common to all England.

Common law is the body of law developed mainly through judicial decisions rather than statutes. It rests on the principle of stare decisis, to stand by things decided: courts follow the precedents set in earlier similar cases, and in a case of first impression the judge resolves the issue and sets a new one. Supporters value the predictability this gives commercial parties. Common law courts usually use an adversarial system, in which two sides present their cases to a neutral judge.

Equity developed beside it. From the 15th century litigants who felt cheated by the common law petitioned the king, and the resulting system was administered by the Lord Chancellor in the courts of chancery. The two often conflicted, and in England the courts were merged by the Judicature Acts of 1873 and 1875, with equity prevailing in a conflict.

In the 12th and 13th centuries continental European countries began receiving Roman law, including the Corpus Juris Civilis, but England already had the common law in place, so common law and civil law jurisdictions differ in judicial reasoning and sources of law. England spread its system to Wales, Ireland and overseas colonies, and the British Empire continued this; the laws of India, Pakistan and Bangladesh are largely based on it from the period of the British Raj. Many former colonies kept it after independence. Today about one third of the world's population lives in common law jurisdictions or in mixed systems that combine common and civil law.
common-program: The Common Program was the primary general policy document of the first plenary session of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, which adopted it unanimously as the basic political program of the country after the success of the Chinese Communist Revolution. It replaced the constitution of the Republic of China and so served as the provisional constitution of the new People's Republic.

The document had a preamble and seven chapters. It defined China as a New Democracy that would practise a people's democratic dictatorship led by the proletariat and based on an alliance of workers and peasants, uniting all the democratic classes, defined as those who opposed imperialism, feudalism and bureaucratic capitalism and favoured an independent China. People's congresses were to be the primary organs of state power, with the National People's Congress as the highest, and all state organs were to practise democratic centralism. The first task of the new government was to eliminate feudal, compradorial and fascist ideologies.

In the economy the program gave priority to the state-owned sector but did not seek to eliminate capitalism, encouraging private enterprises seen as beneficial to the national economy within a mixed economy. Article 26 made the development of production the basic aim, Article 34 tied every step of land reform to the revival and development of farming, and Article 35 called for heavy industry, from mining, iron and steel to power, machinery and chemicals, as the foundation of industrialisation. Articles 54 and 56 based foreign relations on respect for mutual sovereignty.

The Common Program remained the provisional constitution until September 1954, when the 1st National People's Congress passed and ratified the first formal constitution of the People's Republic. The researcher Zheng Qian has compared its support for an economy with mixed forms of ownership to Vladimir Lenin's New Economic Policy in the transitional period after 1921 in the Soviet Union.
commonwealth-of-independent-states: In March 1991, amid perestroika, Mikhail Gorbachev, president of the Soviet Union, proposed a referendum to preserve the Union as a federation of sovereign republics. The new treaty was never signed, because Communist Party hardliners staged a coup attempt in Moscow in August. After it collapsed, many republics declared independence. A week after the Ukrainian independence referendum, the leaders of Belarus, the Russian SFSR and Ukraine met at the Belovezhskaya Pushcha Natural Reserve and on 8 December 1991 signed the Belovezha Accords, declaring that the Union had effectively ceased to exist and proclaiming the CIS in its place. On 21 December these three republics and eight others signed the Alma-Ata Protocol.

The Charter of the CIS, signed on 22 January 1993, set up its institutions and rules. All who had ratified the creation agreement were founding states, but only those ratifying the Charter became member states. Ukraine, which never ratified the Charter, therefore remained a founding state and not a member. The CIS Interparliamentary Assembly was established on 27 March 1992 in Kazakhstan, and in 1995 the CIS adopted a Convention on Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms.

In May 1992 six post-Soviet states signed the Collective Security Treaty, also called the Tashkent Pact; it took effect in 1994. An Agreement on the Economic Union was signed on 24 September 1993. Three organisations later originated from the CIS: the Collective Security Treaty Organization, the Eurasian Economic Union and the Union State of Russia and Belarus.

A joint CIS team, the Unified Team, competed in the 1992 Winter and Summer Olympics. Between 2003 and 2005 three member states experienced changes of government in the colour revolutions: Eduard Shevardnadze was overthrown in Georgia, Viktor Yushchenko was elected in Ukraine and Askar Akayev was toppled in Kyrgyzstan. Georgia left the CIS after the Russo-Georgian War.
commonwealth-of-nations: On 18 January 1884 Lord Rosebery, visiting Adelaide, described the changing British Empire as a Commonwealth of Nations, as some of its colonies became more independent. Conferences of British and colonial prime ministers began in 1887 and led to the Imperial Conferences created in 1911. In the Balfour Declaration at the 1926 Imperial Conference, the United Kingdom and its dominions agreed that they were autonomous communities within the British Empire, equal in status and in no way subordinate one to another, though united by a common allegiance to the Crown and freely associated as members of the British Commonwealth of Nations. The term Commonwealth was officially adopted for the community, and the United Kingdom formalised it by the Statute of Westminster in 1931.

The Commonwealth and Empire took part in every major theatre of the Second World War, and the governments of Australia, Canada, New Zealand and the United Kingdom set up the British Commonwealth Air Training Plan for pilots from across the Empire. After the war the Empire was gradually dismantled, and most of its components became independent countries and members of the Commonwealth.

Membership at first required dominionhood. On 18 April 1949 Ireland formally became a republic and so left the Commonwealth, although it had not taken an active part since the early 1930s. Other members wished to become republics without losing their ties, and at a meeting of prime ministers in London in April 1949 the London Declaration, drafted by V. K. Krishna Menon, allowed India to remain a member when it became a republic in January 1950, accepting the British sovereign as a symbol of the free association and as Head of the Commonwealth. The word British was dropped from the title.

In 1961 respect for racial equality became a requirement, which led to the withdrawal of South Africa's re-application, and the Singapore Declaration of 1971 committed members to world peace, liberty, human rights, equality and free trade. Mozambique in 1995 and Rwanda in 2009 were admitted without any constitutional link to Britain.

The main decision-making forum is the biennial Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, successor to the Imperial Conferences, and the Commonwealth Secretariat, established in 1965, is the main intergovernmental agency. The Commonwealth Foundation works with civil society. Members have no legal obligations to one another, and their countries are represented to one another by high commissions rather than embassies. The headship is symbolic. The Commonwealth Games, begun in 1930 as the Empire Games and first held at Hamilton, Canada, were designed to be the Friendly Games. The Commonwealth War Graves Commission, founded in 1917 as the Imperial War Graves Commission, maintains the graves of 1.7 million service personnel who died in the two world wars.
communal-award: Separate electorates had first been introduced for Muslims by the Indian Councils Act 1909 and were extended to Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians and Europeans by the Government of India Act 1919. Ramsay MacDonald, who considered himself a friend of the Indians and wished to resolve the country's problems, announced the award after the failure of the second of the Round Table Conferences, and it drew severe criticism from Mahatma Gandhi.

The award kept separate electorates for these communities, added the Depressed Classes to them and applied the principle of weightage. Its ninth and last paragraph applied directly to the Depressed Classes, and Sir Samuel Hoare asked for it to be clarified. In the Punjab it reserved 19% of seats for the Sikhs, against 51% for the Muslims and 30% for the Hindus, and the Akali Dal, the representative body of the Sikhs, was highly critical of it.

Many Hindus saw the award as aimed at dividing Indian society, while many of the minorities supported it. According to B. R. Ambedkar, Gandhi was ready to grant separate electorates to Muslims and Sikhs but not to the Scheduled Castes, fearing division within both the Congress and Hindu society. The Poona Pact that ended the dispute satisfied the other communities, whose electorates remained separate, but rejected any further advance for the Untouchables.

Gandhi also agreed to the revival of Swaraj, which became policy when the All-India Congress Committee ratified it in May 1934. The government reluctantly lifted its ban on the Congress and received in return the anxious support of the All-India Muslim League. In the parliamentary debates on the Government of India Act, the Conservative MP Albert Goodman argued that the poverty of the Untouchables should be eased by greater representation in the provincial assemblies, while the Muslim League remained ambivalent about the award.
communards: The Prussian siege of Paris from September 1870 left the poor eating cat or rat meat or going hungry, and radical and socialist clubs and newspapers grew out of their resentment. On 18 March 1871 the government at Versailles sent troops to collect a reserve of cannons, but units of the Paris National Guard surrounded them and killed two generals, and by the end of the day the insurgents held the city and declared the Commune. Adolphe Thiers refused to bargain with them, and the Communards built barricades.

After the army retook Paris, 43,000 Communards were taken prisoner and 6,500 to 7,500 fled abroad. The number killed in combat or executed has long been disputed: Prosper-Olivier Lissagaray gave 20,000, while more recent historians put it between 10,000 and 15,000. A government inquest blamed the rising chiefly on a lack of belief in God, and some 4,500 were deported to New Caledonia, where the Isle of Pines was set aside for them. About two-thirds received simple deportation, while about 300 sentenced to forced labour were held with criminal convicts and suffered whippings and thumbscrews.

Food, clothing and shelter were short, and many built their own huts and traded clothes with the Kanak for food. In 1874 six déportés, among them François Jourde and Henri Rochefort, escaped by ship to Sydney, after which the rules grew stricter. Some Communards, such as Achille Ballière, formed friendships with the Kanak, and Louise Michel ran a school for them and supported those who joined the Kanak insurrection of 1878.

In January 1879 the prime minister Jules Armand Dufaure granted mass pardons, though more than one thousand were left off the list. Louis Blanc and Victor Hugo introduced bills for a total amnesty, which parliament voted in July 1880, and nine ships brought the déportés home between August 1879 and July 1880 to celebrating crowds. Some stayed in New Caledonia or settled in countries such as Australia. An inquiry into torture in New Caledonia from December 1879 put the Communards' accounts of abuse on the public record.
communist-international: The Communist International descended from the First International (1864 to 1876) and the Second International (1889 to 1914), which collapsed in the First World War. On 24 January 1919 Moscow sent a wireless invitation to thirty-nine communist parties and groups, timed to pre-empt a conference of reformist socialists in Berne. The founding congress met in the Kremlin from 2 to 6 March 1919. Of fifty-one delegates only nine came from abroad, because of the Allied blockade of Russia. Its aim was a world party for the armed overthrow of capitalist private property, and its founding split the labour movement between communists and social democrats.

The Comintern first expected revolutions in post-war Europe, especially Germany. When these failed in 1920 and 1921, Lenin concluded that revolution was not on the immediate agenda, and a united workers front was adopted in December 1921. After Lenin's death in January 1924 the Comintern was increasingly marked by Russian dominance. In China it directed the Communist Party to enter the Kuomintang in August 1922, forming the First United Front. From 1928 to 1933 it denounced social democrats as social fascists; after the Nazi seizure of power it turned to the Popular Front, ratified in 1935, and helped organise support for the Spanish Republic.

During the Great Purge many Comintern officials and foreign communists in Moscow were arrested and shot, and the Communist Party of Poland was dissolved in 1938. After the Nazi–Soviet Pact of August 1939 the Comintern called the war an imperialist war until Germany invaded the Soviet Union in June 1941.

Stalin unilaterally dissolved the Comintern on 15 May 1943 as a gesture to the Allies. Its formal structures were dismantled, but Soviet control over the international communist movement persisted and was partly revived through the Cominform, which existed from 1947 to 1956.
communist-party-of-burma: The party was set up at a secret meeting of seven men in a small room in Barr Street, Rangoon, on 15 August 1939. Among them were Thakin Aung San, Thakin Ba Hein, Thakin Soe and Yèbaw Ba Tin (H. N. Goshal). An armed wing soon followed. In July 1941, in Insein Prison, Thakin Soe and Thakin Than Tun wrote the Insein Manifesto, which named fascism the main enemy and called for temporary cooperation with the British, following the popular front line of the Bulgarian communist Georgi Dimitrov.

After the war the party fell out with the more moderate socialists of the Anti-Fascist People's Freedom League over how an independent Burma should be governed. Once the moderates led the government after independence in 1948, they cracked down on the communists, whose leaders left Rangoon for the countryside. The party fired the first shots of its insurgency at Paukkongyi, Pegu Region, on 2 April 1948.

In 1949 the party had between 4,000 and 15,000 armed troops and 25,000 members. Peace talks with Ne Win's Union Revolutionary Council government broke down in 1963. Frustrated, and inspired by the Cultural Revolution in China, the chairman Thakin Than Tun ordered a Cultural Revolution of the party's own: a campaign of purges and summary executions killed much of the old guard and several student leaders who had joined after the failed talks.

In the early 1970s the party moved its activities to the Chinese border, and its dwindling ranks were refilled by Kachin, Shan and Wa cadres. By 1973 its membership was mostly Wa, and analysts of the time regarded the parties before and after the purges as two different organisations. Further talks in Beijing and Lashio in 1980 and 1981 failed when the government demanded the abolition of the party, its People's Army and its liberated areas.

After the military crushed the 8888 Uprising, the party won a victory at Kongsa, near Kutkai, but many of its ethnic troops had come to see it as a Bamar organisation using non-Bamars as cannon fodder. The defections began among the Kokang on 12 March 1989, and the leadership fled to China. After the coup of 1 February 2021, cadres re-entered Myanmar on 15 March 2021 and in August announced a new armed wing, the People's Liberation Army, to fight the military junta.
communist-party-of-indonesia: The Communist Party of Indonesia, known as the PKI, was a Marxist-Leninist and Maoist party in the Dutch East Indies and later Indonesia. Its forerunner, the Indies Social Democratic Association, was founded in 1914 by the Dutch socialist Henk Sneevliet with about 85 members. Its Dutch members introduced communist ideas to educated Indonesians looking for ways to oppose colonial rule. After Sneevliet moved its headquarters from Surabaya to Semarang, it attracted many Indonesians. At its congress of 23 May 1920 in Semarang the association changed its name to one that called it communist, with Semaun as chairman, and the PKI name was adopted in 1924.

The party planned a revolution against the Dutch in 1926, but a clampdown that year drove it underground, and its leaders disagreed about timing. A limited revolt began in Batavia on 12 November, with similar ones at Padang, Bantam and Surabaya. The Batavia revolt was crushed within a day or two and the others within a few weeks, and the colonial government banned the party. It re-emerged after the Japanese surrender of 1945 and took part in the Indonesian National Revolution.

Under D. N. Aidit, who became General Secretary in January 1951, the party grew from 3,000–5,000 members in 1950 to 1.5 million in 1959. It finished fourth in the 1955 election with 16.35 percent of the vote and 39 of 257 seats. It supported President Sukarno's Guided Democracy and in 1960 accepted his Nasakom formula of nationalism, religion and communism. By 1965 it had about three million members and was supported by large labour, peasant, youth, women's and cultural organisations.

On the night of 30 September 1965 six of Indonesia's top generals were killed by a group calling itself the 30 September Movement. General Suharto put down the coup by 2 October, and the army blamed the PKI. The extent of the party's responsibility remains disputed: some leaders, Aidit among them, were involved, but evidence linking the party is inconclusive.

In the anti-communist purge that followed, an estimated 500,000 people or more were killed, with estimates running from 100,000 to two million, among them members, alleged sympathisers and people killed by mistake. A tribunal at The Hague concluded in 2016 that the killings were crimes against humanity, and declassified United States cables released in 2017 show that the United States supplied aid and lists of names. The party's leadership was destroyed and the PKI was banned in 1966.
communist-party-of-nepal-maoist-centre: The party was formed in 1994 after the Communist Party of Nepal (Unity Centre) split into two factions, one led by Pushpa Kamal Dahal and the other by Nirmal Lama. The electoral front, the United People's Front of Nepal, split too, and its faction under Baburam Bhattarai allied with Dahal's group. The Election Commission recognised only the party backed by Nirmal Lama, and Bhattarai called for a boycott of the 1994 mid-term elections.

Dahal's Unity Centre then went underground to prepare for a new phase of struggle. At its Third Plenum in March 1995 it renamed itself the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist) and decided to give up parliamentary elections and concentrate on a people's war, which it held would bring a new people's democratic form of government.

The People's War was formally launched on 13 February 1996, when a Gorkha district agricultural bank office was overrun and its loan papers destroyed, followed that evening by attacks on police posts in Rukum, Rolpa and Sindhuli. Talks with the government began in August 2001, and the Maoists demanded a constituent assembly, an interim government and a republic. A ceasefire was announced in January 2003, but Dahal, who is known as Prachanda, broke it on 27 August 2003 when the sides could not agree on a constituent assembly.

The Twelve-Point Agreement between the seven-party alliance and the Maoists, reached in Delhi, opened a path to peaceful agitation against the king's direct rule. In the 2008 Constituent Assembly elections it became the largest party. Dahal was elected prime minister with 464 of 577 votes, and the first meeting of the Assembly declared that the monarchy, in power for 240 years, had ended and that Nepal was a federal democratic republic.

In 2013 the party won only 80 seats and fell to third place, rejecting the result as the work of an international and national conspiracy. Dahal became prime minister again on 3 August 2016 and resigned on 25 May 2017. The party took its present name after ten Maoist groups merged with it in May 2016.

Maoists in Nepal take their philosophy from Mao Zedong and draw inspiration from Peru's Shining Path and the Revolutionary Internationalist Movement. Women were prominent in recruitment: reports suggest that one fifth to one third of the cadre and combatants in the civil war may have been women. The party's use of children as soldiers was criticised; UNMIN verified nine thousand child soldiers in its cantonment camps.
communist-party-of-nepal-unified-marxist: The party's predecessors were the Communist Party of Nepal (Marxist), led by Man Mohan Adhikari, and the Communist Party of Nepal (Marxist-Leninist), led by Madan Bhandari. The second had its origins in the 1969 Jhapa rebellion, inspired by the Naxalite movement in India and begun after land reform programmes introduced by King Mahendra in 1964. Both belonged to the United Left Front, formed in 1990 against the Panchayat system, which with the Nepali Congress helped restore multi-party democracy. On 6 January 1991 they merged, with Adhikari as first chairman. Its guiding principle is Marxism-Leninism, and in 1993 it adopted People's Multiparty Democracy, proposed by Bhandari, accepting periodic elections and the rule of law.

In the 1991 election the party won 69 of 205 seats. After Bhandari died in a vehicle accident in 1993, Madhav Kumar Nepal became general secretary. In 1994 the party won 88 seats, and Adhikari formed a minority government that lasted nine months. A split in March 1998 over the Mahakali treaty took 46 MPs into a reconstituted Marxist-Leninist party, which reunified with it in 2002. During the royal rule of King Gyanendra the party joined the Seven Party Alliance, and the 2006 revolution restored the House of Representatives. In the 2008 Constituent Assembly election it won 108 of 575 seats, and Madhav Kumar Nepal and Jhala Nath Khanal each led a government.

K. P. Sharma Oli became party chair in July 2014 and prime minister on 12 October 2015. After an alliance with the CPN (Maoist Centre), the party won 121 seats in 2017 and Oli became prime minister again in February 2018. On 17 May 2018 the two parties merged as the Nepal Communist Party, but on 8 March 2021 the Supreme Court ruled that the name belonged to another party and voided the merger, and the party was revived. In August 2021 Nepal and Khanal split away with 25 members of the House of Representatives to form the CPN (Unified Socialist). In the 2022 election the party won 79 seats. Oli became prime minister for a fourth time on 15 July 2024.

On 4 September 2025 Oli's government ordered most social media shut down for failing to register. The government said the aim was to raise tax revenue; critics linked the ban to anger at the display of wealth by politicians' children. Protesters were killed when forces used live ammunition, and by the end of 8 September 51 had died and more than 347 were injured. Oli resigned on 9 September, and former chief justice Sushila Karki was named interim prime minister until elections set for 5 March 2026.
communist-party-of-the-soviet-union: The party began in 1898 as part of the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party. In August 1903 a split opened between the followers of Julius Martov, called Mensheviks, meaning the minority, and those of Vladimir Lenin, called Bolsheviks, meaning the majority, although the two factions were of fairly equal size. Before the February Revolution of 1917 the party worked underground, and many of its leaders, Lenin among them, were in exile. The Bolsheviks seized power in the October Revolution of 1917, and the party took the name Russian Communist Party (Bolsheviks) on 8 March 1918 and All-Union Communist Party (Bolsheviks) on 31 December 1925.

After Lenin's death Joseph Stalin, the general secretary, and Leon Trotsky struggled for power. Trotsky argued for permanent revolution abroad, Stalin for building socialism in one country. By 1929 Stalin was leader, and he formalised Marxism-Leninism as the guiding ideology. The party pursued state socialism, with nationalised industries and a command economy, and Stalin's rule was marked by an extensive cult of personality.

After Stalin's death Nikita Khrushchev won the struggle for the top post and began the Thaw, which ended the mass terror of the earlier decades. At the 20th Congress in 1956 he denounced Stalin's crimes. Mikhail Gorbachev became general secretary on 11 March 1985, and his policies of perestroika and glasnost, with multi-candidate elections, weakened the party. In 1990 the Congress of People's Deputies changed Article 6 of the 1977 constitution, which had given the party a monopoly of the political system. Its activities were suspended on 29 August 1991, after a failed coup by conservative party leaders, and Boris Yeltsin banned it by decree on 6 November 1991.

The party was based on democratic centralism, conceived by Lenin: policy was discussed openly, but once the party line was agreed discussion had to cease, and dissent could mean expulsion. The 10th Congress approved a ban on factions. The Congress met every five years and was nominally the highest body, though under Stalin it became largely symbolic. Between congresses the Central Committee was the highest body, and daily business fell to the Politburo and the Secretariat. The party leader was General Secretary, a title renamed First Secretary from 1953 to 1966. Below them stood a nested system of regional, city and district committees and workplace organisations. The Komsomol was the party's youth wing.
communist-party-of-vietnam: The party traces its history to 1925, when Nguyen Ai Quoc, later Ho Chi Minh, established the Vietnamese Revolutionary Youth League. Its aims were to end French colonial rule, win national independence and redistribute land to working peasants, and the Comintern supported the groundwork financially. In 1928 the Kuomintang destroyed the League's headquarters in Guangdong, China, and the group was driven underground and split. On 17 June 1929 more than twenty delegates from cells in the Tonkin region met in Hanoi and declared the League dissolved and a Communist Party of Indochina established. The League's other faction, based in Cochinchina, declared itself the Communist Party of Annam in late 1929.

In 1941 the party set up the Viet Minh as a coalition front. In March 1945 Japan overthrew the French colonial regime in Indochina, and by August Japan had surrendered. The Viet Minh used the power vacuum to launch a nationwide uprising, and Emperor Bao Dai abdicated on 25 August. Ho Chi Minh proclaimed the independence of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam on 2 September 1945, but no country recognised it at first. The party led the First Indochina War, after which it became the ruling party in the north in 1954.

The third party congress, held in Hanoi in 1960, set the task of building socialism in North Vietnam and committed the party to the liberation of the south. After the party took power in the whole country in 1975, it unified Vietnam as the Socialist Republic in 1976. It had run a command economy in the north since 1954 and introduced the market reforms known as Đổi Mới in 1986. In 1988 it became the only political party when it absorbed its two sister parties, the Socialist Party and the Democratic Party.

The party is organised on the principle of democratic centralism. Its National Congress, held every five years, elects a Central Committee, which in turn elects the Politburo and the Secretariat and appoints the general secretary, the highest party office. The supremacy of the party is guaranteed by Article 4 of the constitution. The party holds to Marxism-Leninism and to Ho Chi Minh Thought, which became its official ideologies in 1991. At its 10th National Congress in 2006 it amended its statutes to let members engage in private business. It describes its economic system as a socialist-oriented market economy.
community-of-true-inspiration: The movement grew from the Inspirés, Huguenots of southern France who were radicalised after King Louis XIV's Edict of Fontainebleau of 1685 suppressed their religion. Claiming prophetic inspiration, they wandered as refugees through the Netherlands and England, and many settled in Halle. They influenced three brothers named Pott, exiled from Halle in 1714 to Hanau and Wetteravia, east of Frankfurt, under the tolerant counts of Isenburg-Eisenberg, where they gave ecstatic speeches in a trance-like state, their bodies seized by jolting motions. Eberhard Ludwig Gruber, Johann Friedrich Rock and Ursula Meyer of Thun were among the early leaders who preached in this way.

Their refusal of military service and of oaths kept the Inspirationists in conflict with German authorities, and their leaders were often banished. Their main centres were in turn Himbach near Hanau until 1740, the castle of Gelnhausen until 1753, Lieblos and then Herrnhaag. Gruber stayed for a time with the Brethren of Schwarzenau, whom the Inspirationists found legalistic, and poor relations probably helped drive the Brethren to the Netherlands in 1720. The movement declined after the deaths of Gruber and Rock until a revival led by Michael Krausert.

Renewed restrictions in the 1840s led the community to emigrate as a group. On land bought from the Seneca's Buffalo Creek Reservation, at West Seneca and Elma near Buffalo, they founded the Ebenezer Colonies and held their goods in common, working in textiles and agriculture. Finding the area crowded and in conflict with the Seneca, many moved in 1854 to the Iowa River Valley. Official membership was 1,534 in 1925 and still more than a thousand in the 1980s.

Worship begins with a period of silence, followed by a hymn, the Apostles Creed recited by a member, prayers, a Bible reading with the presiding elder's commentary, a psalm and a closing hymn. The year includes a Repentance Service (Buss Versammlung) at the start of Lent, a Faith Review Service (Glaubenslehre) before the annual Communion in the autumn, and a Covenant Service (Bundversammlung) on Thanksgiving Day.
comoro-islands: The Comoro Islands are a group of volcanic islands in the Mozambique Channel, to the north-west of Madagascar and facing Mozambique, covering a total area of 2,034 square kilometres. They are Ngazidja (Grande Comore), the largest and the seat of the capital Moroni, Ndzuwani (Anjouan), Mwali (Mohéli) and Mayotte (Maore). Mayotte is the oldest island still above sea level, while Grande Comore is the youngest and still volcanically active; its shield volcano Karthala rises to 2,361 metres. The climate is tropical maritime, with a hot and humid season from November to April and a dry season from May to October.

The islands may have been settled as early as the 6th century. Among the peoples who crossed the sea to populate them were Bantu-speaking peoples, Austronesian peoples including Malagasy, Arabs, Somalis, Portuguese, French and Indians. Islam probably arrived during the 10th century. With Zanzibar, Pemba, Lamu and the coastal towns of Kenya and Tanzania, the Comoros formed a prosperous region of Swahili culture, trading in local goods that were exported to the African coast, Madagascar, the Middle East and India, and political power lay with local rulers. The Portuguese made landfall in 1505; the Arabic word qamar means moon, hence the name Islands of the Moon.

French settlers later established plantations, first for sugar, which depended on the labour of numerous Africans, and in the 20th century for perfume plants and spices such as ylang-ylang, vanilla and cloves. In 1946 France redefined the islands as an overseas territory. In a referendum of 1974 the population voted overwhelmingly for independence, except in Mayotte, and after a unilateral declaration of independence in 1975 France kept sovereignty over Mayotte. The three other islands formed the Etat Comorian, later the Federal Islamic Republic of the Comoros Islands, and in 2001 became the Union of the Comoros under a new constitution. Mayotte became a French department on 31 March 2011.

The archipelago is divided between the Union of the Comoros, formed by Grande Comore, Anjouan and Mohéli, and the French department of Mayotte, which the Union's constitution also claims. The islands hold eight native land mammal species, among them two lemurs and the endemic Livingstone's fruit bat, and the coelacanth, a deepwater fish known from fossils over 300 million years old, lives in their waters.
compagnie-des-iles-de-lamerique: In 1635 Cardinal Richelieu, a shareholder in the struggling Compagnie de Saint-Christophe, charged François Fouquet, head of a small group of his councillors, with reviving it, and Fouquet renamed it. The company took over the administration of the French part of Saint-Christophe, then the only French settlement in the Caribbean, with a mandate to develop the other islands of the Antilles and convert their inhabitants to Catholicism.

On 15 September 1635 Pierre Belain d'Esnambuc, French governor of St. Kitts, landed at St. Pierre in Martinique with 150 settlers after being driven off St. Kitts by the English, claimed the island for Louis XIII and the company, and founded Fort Saint-Pierre under governor Jean Dupont. After d'Esnambuc's death in 1636 his nephew Jacques Dyel du Parquet became governor in 1637; he colonised Martinique, founded the first settlement in Saint Lucia in 1643 and led the expedition that settled Grenada in 1649.

Saint Martin and Saint Barthélemy followed in 1648 and St. Croix in 1650. In 1642 the company's charter was extended for twenty years: the king would name its governor general and the company the governors of the islands. On Saint Christopher, Phillippe de Longvilliers de Poincy, Bailiff Grand Cross of the Knights of Malta, governed from 1639 until his death in 1660, first for the company and then for the order itself.

By the late 1640s Mazarin took little interest in colonial affairs and the company languished. It dissolved itself in 1651, having sold its rights: the du Parquet family bought Martinique, Grenada and Saint Lucia for 60,000 livres, the sieur d'Houël Guadeloupe, Marie-Galante, La Desirade and the Saintes, and the Knights of Malta Saint-Christophe, Saint Croix, Saint Barthélemy and Saint Martin. In 1665 the Knights sold their islands to the Compagnie des Indes occidentales, formed in 1664.
companion-cavalry: The Companions, in Greek hetairoi, served as the elite heavy cavalry of the Macedonian army from the time of Philip II, and gained their highest prestige under Alexander the Great. They are regarded as the first or among the first shock cavalry used in Europe. The name means those near the king.

Companions could be members of the Macedonian aristocracy or commoners of any origin who enjoyed the trust and friendship of the king, and a festival called the Hetairideia marked the bond between king and companions. Even the Athenian playwright Euripides was honoured as a hetairos of King Archelaus. The king's Friends, or basilikoi hetairoi, were named for life by the king from among the aristocracy.

The Companions came from the most powerful nobles, who could acquire and maintain the best horses and armour. In Alexander's day they mostly carried a xyston, a long thrusting spear, and wore a bronze muscle cuirass or linothorax, shoulder guards and a Boeotian helmet, but no shield. A kopis or xiphos served for close combat if the xyston broke. In the age of Philip II and Alexander they were organised in eight territorial squadrons, called ilai, each of 200 to 300 horsemen.

The Royal Ile, which Alexander himself commanded, was about twice as large, at c. 400. Squadrons could be combined in twos, threes or fours into a hipparchy under a hipparch. Philotas first commanded the whole force, and after his execution command was split between Cleitus the Black and Hephaestion. Arrian says Alexander did not want anyone, even his intimate friend, to be the centre of attention. As the army campaigned towards India, non-Macedonians played a growing part, and the Macedonian mutiny at Opis may have been partly caused by this.

In battle the Companions formed the hammer to the Macedonian phalanx's anvil: the phalanx pinned the enemy while the cavalry attacked a flank or the rear. Alexander personally led the charge at the head of the royal squadron, usually in a wedge, and in a pitched battle the Companions usually fought on the right wing, next to the hypaspists. Their role was decisive in most of his battles in Asia.

The Companions of the successor states were more heavily equipped. At the Battle of Magnesia in 190 BCE the Seleucid Companions wore lighter equipment than the cataphracts but otherwise similar. Ptolemaic and Antigonid Companions carried a large round cavalry shield. The Seleucids replaced the title with grades of King's Friends but kept Companions as the name of a regiment, and the Byzantine Hetaireia, a bodyguard of the 9th to 12th centuries composed chiefly of foreigners, echoed the name.
companions-of-the-prophet: The Arabic word sahaba, the companions, comes from a verb meaning to accompany or keep company with. The term covers the disciples of Muhammad who saw or met him in his lifetime and embraced Islam while he lived. The last of them, Abu al-Tufayl, died in 110 AH (728 CE). Their followers are named by generation: the Tābi'ūn knew at least one companion, and the next generation knew at least one of them.

Companions are also classed in groups: the Muhajirun, the migrants who left Mecca with Muhammad when he was persecuted, the Ansar, the people of Medina who protected them, and the Badriyyun who fought at the Battle of Badr. Lists of prominent companions usually give 50 or 60 names, but al-Qurtubi's work holds 2,770 biographies of men and 381 of women.

The companions played a major part in the Muslim battles, in hadith narration and in governance after Muhammad's death. According to the History of the Prophets and Kings, Abu Bakr, Umar, Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah and the Ansar of Medina held consultations and chose Abu Bakr as the first caliph, and Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf and Uthman then selected Umar as the second. Later scholars accepted the companions' testimony about Muhammad's words and deeds and about the occasions of the Quran's revelation. Passed down through chains of trusted narrators, it became the basis of the developing Islamic tradition, from which the way of life (sunnah), the code of conduct (sharia) and jurisprudence (fiqh) are drawn.

The most widespread Sunni definition, given by Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, holds that a companion is one who met Muhammad while believing in him and died a Muslim, however long or short the time. Anyone who later left Islam is not counted. Sunni scholars assume all companions to be just unless proven otherwise. The Shia, and some modern Sunni scholars, follow a stricter definition requiring substantial contact, such as living with Muhammad, joining his campaigns or preaching. The Shia therefore judge each companion individually, assess righteousness by loyalty to Muhammad's family after his death, and hold that some companions bear responsibility for the loss of the caliphate by Ali's family.
company-of-merchants-trading-to-africa: The company was set up by the African Company Act 1750 to replace the Royal African Company, founded in 1660. Unlike its predecessor it was a regulated company, not a joint-stock company: the act forbade it to trade to or from Africa in its corporate capacity, to hold any joint or transferable stock, or to borrow money on its common seal. It received the Royal African Company's assets, chiefly nine trading posts: Fort William, Fort James, Fort Sekondi, Fort Winneba, Fort Apollonia, Fort Tantumquery, Fort Metal Cross, Fort Komenda and Cape Coast Castle, the administrative centre, on a coast dominated by the Fante people.

The company was run by the African Committee of nine members, three each from London, Liverpool and Bristol, elected every year from the traders of those cities, who paid 40 shillings to join; a member could serve no more than three years. In 1772 a series of pamphlets claimed that the committee was not acting properly. The annual parliamentary grant paid for the London office and the forts, and the committee reported to the Exchequer, the Admiralty and, from 1782, the Secretary at War. John Shoolbred (1740–1802) served for several years as its secretary.

Britain prohibited the slave trade after 1807, but the company went on trading in enslaved people illegally for some years. In 1817 it signed a treaty of friendship recognising Asante claims to sovereignty over large parts of the coast, including areas the Fante claimed. Controversy in Britain once it became known that the company had continued the slave trade within its territory contributed to its abolition by the government in 1821. Authority over its territory passed to Governor Charles MacCarthy of Sierra Leone, a colony founded as a refuge for freed formerly enslaved people, and the Gold Coast became a formal British colony; MacCarthy was later killed in the First Anglo-Asante War.
company-of-one-hundred-associates: French and Basque fishermen had used the Atlantic coast of North America as summer trading stations since the 16th century, and attempts at settlement on the Saint Lawrence followed the expeditions of Jacques Cartier in the 1540s, all of them failing. Under a monopoly granted by King Henry IV in 1603 to Pierre Dugua, Sieur de Mons, Port-Royal was founded in Acadia, and in 1608 an expedition led by Samuel de Champlain founded the colony that grew into Quebec City.

The Compagnie des Marchands held the trade from 1613 to 1620 but lost its rights in 1621 to the Compagnie de Montmorency. In 1627 Cardinal Richelieu withdrew that monopoly and founded the Compagnie de la Nouvelle France as part of a plan to develop trade.

Each of the hundred investors put in 3,000 livres, which gave the company its common name. They included officials of the French court, merchants and financiers; Champlain appears as investor number 52 in a list published on 14 January 1628. Twelve directors managed it under Richelieu's close control, with authority over Acadia, Canada, Newfoundland and French Louisiana. The charter required it to bring an average of 160 settlers to New France over the next twenty-five years and to support them for three years. Colonists not maintained by the company could barter with the Indians if they sold their furs to it.

The first fleet sailed in April 1628, after war had broken out with England in 1627. Holding a letter of marque from King Charles I, David Kirke and his brothers sailed up the Saint Lawrence and seized the fleet, and the company lost 90% of its initial investment. By 1631 it needed new investors and passed parts of its monopoly to subsidiary companies, such as the founders of the Compagnie des Habitants, to which control of the colony later shifted for a time. War with the Iroquois in the 1650s hampered the fur trade.

The situation changed when King Louis XIV came of age, ending the long regency of his minority. In 1663, as one of his first major acts as a reigning monarch, he dissolved both companies and gave the fur trading rights of North America to the French West India Company. In 1665 he sent the Carignan-Salières Regiment to Canada, the first European regular unit deployed to the Western Hemisphere, to deal with the Iroquois.
complutensian-polyglot-bible: The edition grew out of Spain's long tradition of translation and a debate, more than a century before the Reformation, about how religious texts could be rendered faithfully. Cardinal Francisco Jiménez de Cisneros, who initiated and financed the project, hoped a polyglot would settle the question. Its chief editor was Diego López de Zúñiga; his second, Alfonso de Zamora, was a converted Jewish scholar whose first language was Hebrew. Other conversos on the team were Alfonso de Alcalá and Pablo de Coronel, while Demetrius Ducas of Crete, Hernán Núñez de Toledo and Juan de Vergara worked on the Greek and Antonio de Nebrija on the Latin Vulgate.

The New Testament was printed in 1514 and the Old Testament completed in 1517. Cisneros died in July 1517 without seeing the work published, and Emperor Charles V confiscated the text. Erasmus's four-year privilege of 1516 may also have caused delay; Pope Leo X sanctioned the work in 1520, just as the Revolt of the Comuneros broke out.

The first four volumes hold the Old Testament in three columns, Hebrew outside, the Latin Vulgate in the middle and the Greek Septuagint inside, with the Aramaic Targum Onkelos and its Latin translation at the foot of each page of the Pentateuch. The editors compared the Vulgate's place to Christ crucified between two thieves, the Roman Church rising between the Synagogue and the Eastern Church. The fifth volume gives the New Testament in Greek and Latin, and the sixth holds dictionaries and study aids. Nebrija resigned after Cisneros refused to let him correct the Latin. The editors appear to have relied on the methods of Lorenzo Valla's Adnotationes in Novum Testamentum.

It contains the first printed editions of the Greek New Testament, the complete Septuagint and the Targum Onkelos. Of 600 six-volume sets printed, 123 are known to survive, and according to a much later letter of King Philip II many copies were lost in a shipwreck on the way to Italy around 1521. Erasmus's Greek New Testament reached readers first, though he acknowledged using the Complutensian in his 1527 edition. Its Septuagint underlay the 1518 Aldine Bible, and the work was re-edited as the Antwerp Polyglot of 1572, reprinted with additions as the Paris Polyglot of 1645 and developed further into the London Polyglot of 1654-1657.
complutum: The town grew up near the junction of several routes, beside the Henares river and the arable meadows around it. Before the Romans the Carpetani had a hill fort on the Viso Hill across the river. The Roman city followed an orthogonal grid of 15 decumani and 16 cardines over about 48 hectares, with an eastern quarter of rectangular blocks from the 20s and 30s CE and a western one of square blocks from the 60s, and at its height it housed 10,000 to 15,000 people. Its decumanus maximus carried the road from Emerita Augusta and Toletum to Caesaraugusta.

After the Roman conquest in the 1st century BCE a first city project on the hill failed, and the citizens then built a new city in the valley in two stages, under Augustus and under Claudius around 50 CE. Vespasian gave it the status of municipium in 74 CE, and it became the capital of a territory covering most of the present regions of Madrid and Guadalajara. The city was enlarged in the 3rd century, when a monumental forum with a basilica, baths, shops and a curia made from the old north baths was built, its façade bearing a verse inscription based on Virgil's Aeneid.

Among its houses, the House of the Griffins, built in the middle of the 1st century and destroyed by an accidental fire in the 4th, kept fine wall paintings, and the so-called House of Hippolytus, seat of the Youth College, has a fishing mosaic signed by the mosaicist Hippolytus. Tradition placed the martyrdom of Justus and Pastor, aged 13 and under 9, at the Paredón del Milagro in the curia, though they were probably executed at the Campo Laudable just outside the town.

The remains lie in the Complutum archaeological site, about a kilometre south-west of the medieval centre of Alcalá de Henares. About half of the city was destroyed between 1970 and 1974 by the building of the Reyes Católicos suburb, and regulated excavations followed the Spanish Historical Heritage Law of 1985.
