A Roman villa 5 km to the east, at El Val, bred horses for chariot races and has a mosaic of a victorious charioteer.
composite-bow: Composite bows are made from several materials, such as horn, antler, bamboo, wood or sinew, laminated together with glue. It is not known exactly when and where they originated, nor whether they had a single origin. The composite bow probably dates from the Bronze Age. Reliable evidence suggests that the first bows containing horn appeared in the Near East, probably in Syria, Anatolia or Mesopotamia, and then spread to Egypt, which led to the angular bow; several composite bows were found in the tomb of Tutankhamun, who died in 1324 BCE.

The Indo-Iranian Andronovo culture and the Srubnaya culture carried the composite bow to East Asia. The Scythian bow, probably evolved from the angular bow, was the first form suited to mounted archery, and it was the dominant shape in Europe and Asia until the 1st century CE.

The wooden core gives the bow its shape. A thin layer of horn is glued to the belly, the side facing the archer, because horn stores more energy than wood in compression. Sinew, soaked in animal glue and laid along the length of the back, has greater elastic tension than wood. Hide glue or gelatin from fish bladders holds the layers together, and after months of drying the bow is ready, often covered with leather or bark against moisture.

Their main advantage is high power in a small size, which suits an archer on horseback or in a chariot. Making one takes much longer than making a self bow, and the glue weakens in humid conditions: the 6th-century Byzantine Strategikon advised cavalry to keep their bows in leather cases.

The mounted archer became the archetypal warrior of the steppes, and the composite bow was his main weapon. Classic tactics were skirmishing, approaching, shooting and retreating, and the Parthian shot, fired backwards over the horse's rear. Infantry also used composite bows: the archers of classical Greece and the Roman Empire did, and Roman composite bows were made as far north as Britannia.

Skill with the composite bow remained part of the qualification for officers in the Chinese imperial army until reforms early in the 20th century, and Persian bows were used into the 1820s before muskets replaced them. Composite bows are still made and used in Korea and China, and archery with them is part of the Naadam festival in Mongolia.
composition-of-connacht: Connacht was made a Presidency in 1569 and later divided into counties, but the county administration did not work efficiently until the Composition. Clare, under the name Thomond, belonged to the Presidency from 1569 until about 1600. In 1577 the lord deputy Henry Sidney began a first Composition, which collapsed when the president, Nicholas Malby, died. The agreement of 1585 was made by Sir John Perrot as Lord Deputy of Ireland and Sir Richard Bingham as Governor of the Presidency of Connacht, with the Gaelic and Gaelicised chiefs of Connacht and Thomond. It was a form of surrender and regrant, part of the Tudor reconquest of Ireland.

Before the Composition a landholder owed several charges: to the English a cess to pay for the garrisons, and to the Gaelic chief coyne and livery for his private army and cuttings and coshery for his household. These were replaced by a single tax on land: a fixed annual rent of 10 shillings for each quarter of inhabited land, payable to the Presidency, together with a variable Composition rent payable to the local chief. Some lands, known as freedoms, were exempt from the Composition rent.

The territorial divisions of the chiefs, the countries known as cantreds or trícha céts, became baronies of the counties. The Composition book recorded the names of the holders of many quarters together with the rent each would owe.

The Composition put the county administration of Connacht on a working footing for the first time since the Presidency was created, and fixed in writing what each landholder owed to the Presidency and to his chief. The arrangement did not survive the next century's upheavals: after the civil wars of the 1640s, land in Connacht was assigned anew as part of the Cromwellian conquest of Ireland.
comprehensive-anti-apartheid-act: The legislation was initiated by Congressman Ron Dellums and sponsored in the Senate by William Roth. Democrats first tried to pass it in September 1985 but could not overcome a Republican filibuster. President Ronald Reagan saw the bill as an intrusion on his authority to conduct foreign policy, pursued as a policy of constructive engagement, and he issued sanctions of his own by executive order; Democrats called them watered down and ineffective.

Reintroduced in 1986, the bill passed the House unexpectedly in June on a voice vote, which Republicans allowed in the hope that it would die later. In August the Senate passed a weaker version by 84 to 14, and House Democrats accepted it to keep a margin large enough to override a veto. Reagan vetoed it on 26 September, calling it economic warfare that would chiefly hurt the poor black majority; Desmond Tutu said he would be judged harshly by history. Senator Richard Lugar, chair of the Foreign Relations Committee, led the override against a president he usually supported.

The House voted to override on 29 September by 313 to 83, and the Senate on 2 October by 78 to 21, all 47 Democrats joined by 31 Republicans. It was the first time in the twentieth century that a president's veto on foreign policy had been overridden, and it was seen as a major defeat for Reagan at the hands of his own party.

In 1989 the General Accounting Office reported that the Reagan administration had enforced the sanctions only in part, and President George Bush ordered full enforcement. After F. W. de Klerk repealed apartheid laws and released Nelson Mandela and other political prisoners, Bush lifted almost all the bans by executive order in 1991, though many state and city sanctions remained. Mandela called for those to be lifted in September 1993, and the last sanctions under the act were repealed in November 1993. How far the sanctions helped end apartheid has been debated: their opponents argued that the economy was already struggling and that the political process brought the change.
compromise-of-caspe: Aragonese succession rested more on custom than on legislation. The will of James I of Aragon had usually been followed, and since the union of Catalonia with Aragon in 1137 the crown had passed to the eldest son, the next younger brother or the only daughter. Earlier cases suggested that males in the male line came before daughters: Martin himself had succeeded over the daughters of his elder brother, King John I. By that rule the throne should have gone to James II, Count of Urgell, Martin's closest agnate and his lieutenant of the kingdom.

Other claimants were Louis of Anjou, a grandson of John I through his mother; Alfonso I, Duke of Gandia, who died in March 1412; Frederic, Count of Luna, an illegitimate grandson of Martin; and Ferdinand, a grandson of Peter IV of Aragon through his mother and regent of Castile.

The cortes of Aragon, Valencia and Catalonia had diverging interests, and the interregnum turned violent when Antón de Luna, a partisan of James of Urgell, assassinated the Archbishop of Zaragoza, García Fernández de Heredía. Rival cortes met in Aragon and in Valencia, and Ferdinand's troops entered both kingdoms; their victory at the Battle of Morvedre on 27 February 1412 left Valencia in Trastamarist hands. Pope Benedict XIII of Avignon proposed a body of nine compromisarios, accepted in the Alcañiz Concord of 15 February 1412.

According to the chronicler Jerónimo Zurita, whom most historians follow, the votes were cast on 24 June 1412. Vincent Ferrer spoke first for Ferdinand and five others joined him; Pere de Sagarriga, archbishop of Tarragona, and Guillem de Vallseca favoured James, and Pere Bertran abstained. Ferdinand was proclaimed on 28 June. Some Aragonese historians have argued since 2011 that the choice was unanimous, a view Ernest Belenguer rejected.

James of Urgell first swore allegiance to the new king but revolted in May 1413. His supporters were defeated outside Lleida on 25 June 1413, and the Gascon and English troops Antón de Luna had enlisted were beaten on 10 July. Ferdinand besieged Balaguer from August, and James surrendered there in October 1413. The County of Urgell was dissolved and its lands shared among Ferdinand's supporters. The Crown of Aragon was drawn into Castile's sphere, and about 50 years later the marriage of Ferdinand II to Isabella I of Castile joined the two crowns in a dynastic union.
conaie: CONAIE was founded at a convention of some 500 indigenous representatives on 13-16 November 1986, from the union of two confederations: the Confederation of Indigenous Nationalities of the Ecuadorian Amazon (CONFENIAE) in the east and the Confederation of Peoples of Quichua Nationality (ECUARUNARI) in the central highlands. It represents the Shuar, Achuar, Siona, Secoya, Cofán, Huaorani, Záparo, Chachi, Tsáchila, Awá, Epera, Manta, Wancavilca and Quichua peoples. At first it forbade its leaders to hold political office and kept away from parties and presidential candidates, promoting local campaigns instead.

Its aims include a positive indigenous identity, the recovery of land rights, environmental sustainability, opposition to neoliberalism and the rejection of U.S. military involvement in South America. During the 1990 uprising its leaders issued 16 demands, the first being the declaration of Ecuador as a plurinational state; others concerned bilingual education, control of archaeological sites, development programmes and local autonomy. In December 1995 it played a major part in forming the Pachakutik Plurinational Unity Movement, an electoral coalition that won 10% of the congressional seats in 1996.

The 1990 uprising, in which protesters blocked roads with trees and boulders and shut the country down for a week, is generally regarded as the emergence of indigenous peoples as national political actors. In April 1992 two thousand Kichwa, Shuar and Achuar people marched 385 kilometres from the Amazon to Quito to demand title to their lands, and in June 1994 an uprising forced President Sixto Durán to amend an Agrarian Reform Law. The constitution of 1998 defined Ecuador as a multiethnic and multicultural state, and the 2008 constitution took up CONAIE's position on the plurinational state.

On 21 January 2000 some 20,000 protesters reached Quito, and demonstrators led by Colonel Lucio Gutiérrez and CONAIE's president Antonio Vargas stormed the Congress; for less than 24 hours a junta of Vargas, Gutiérrez and the retired judge Carlos Solórzano ruled. CONAIE backed Gutiérrez for president in 2002, broke with him six months after his election and took part in the uprising that ousted him in 2005. Later it led protests against water laws in 2010 and 2014 and against rising fuel and food prices in 2022.
conakry: Conakry was originally settled on the small Tombo Island, one of the Îles de Los, and later spread to the neighbouring Kaloum Peninsula, a stretch of land 36 km long and between 0.2 and 6 km wide. The expanding urban area has since spread north-eastwards to occupy the whole of the peninsula. The climate is tropical monsoon, with a wet season of very heavy rainfall, more than 1,100 mm in both July and August, and a dry season dominated between December and April by the harmattan wind.

The city was essentially founded after Britain ceded the island to France in 1887. In 1885 the two island villages of Conakry and Boubinet had fewer than 500 inhabitants between them. Conakry became the capital of French Guinea and prospered as an export port, particularly after a railway to Kankan, now closed, opened the interior of the country to the large-scale export of groundnuts.

After Guinea gained independence in 1958 the population boomed, from 50,000 in 1958 to 600,000 in 1980. The city's small land area and relative isolation from the mainland, an advantage to its colonial founders, created an infrastructural burden after independence. In 1970 the conflict between Portuguese forces and the PAIGC independence fighters in neighbouring Portuguese Guinea spilled into the Republic of Guinea, when 350 Portuguese troops and Guinean loyalists landed near the capital, attacked the city and freed 26 Portuguese prisoners of war held by the PAIGC before withdrawing. Camp Boiro, a feared concentration camp, stood in Conakry during the rule of Sekou Touré.

Conakry is the capital and largest city of Guinea and its administrative, communications and economic centre. It forms a region and a prefecture of its own, the Conakry Special Zone, divided into communes. Its port ships alumina and bananas, and its manufactures include food products, cement and metal goods. Among its buildings are the Grand Mosque and the Roman Catholic Cathedral of Sainte-Marie, and the Sandervalia National Museum and the National Library of Guinea are in the city. Its population is roughly one fifth of that of Guinea, more than eight times that of the next city, Kankan.
conall-gulban: Conall Gulban is counted among the sons of Niall Noígiallach, and Irish tradition makes him the founder of the kingdom of Tír Chonaill in the 5th century. His by-name comes from Benn Ghulbain in the north of what is now County Sligo, the centre from which, in the tradition, the sons of Niall set out on their conquest of the North. He is said to have been very close to his brother Eógan mac Néill, ancestor of the Cenél nEógain.

In the history of Irish Christianity he is remembered as the first nobleman baptised by Saint Patrick, a step that tradition holds opened the way for the conversion of the ruling classes of Ireland. He also appears in the tale Acallam na Senórach (Colloquy of the Ancients) as host and companion of Caílte mac Rónáin, one of the Fianna, who tells him the meaning of place names in Tír Conaill and uncovers treasures of the Fianna from megalithic tombs.

Conall was murdered by the Masraige at Magh Slécht in Tullyhaw, in what later became Bréifne and is now the west of County Cavan, in 464, on a Friday. Saint Caillín buried him at Fenagh, in the south of present-day County Leitrim. His brother Eógan is said to have died of grief the following year.

His sons included Fergus Cendfota, Dauí, founder of the Cenél nDuach, and Énna Bogaine, founder of the Cenél mBogaine. The territory of his descendants was organised as the Diocese of Raphoe at the Synod of Ráth Breasail in 1111, at first without the Inishowen peninsula, which the Ó Dochartaigh, a Cenél Conaill family, later took from the McLoughlins. With the Cenél nEógain of Tír Eógain, the Cenél Conaill were the leading Uí Néill septs of the North until the Flight of the Earls.
conan-i-of-brittany: Conan, nicknamed Le Tort (The Crooked), was the son of Judicael Berengar and succeeded his father as Count of Rennes in 970. In 973 he married Ermengarde-Gerberga of Anjou, daughter of Geoffrey I, Count of Anjou, and Adele of Vermandois, which made Fulk Nerra, Count of Anjou, his brother-in-law. Brittany at the time was divided: after the regency during the life of Drogo, the duchy had been ruled in pieces by Drogo's illegitimate brothers Hoël and Guerech and by Guerech's son Alan, and the ducal title fell briefly vacant.

Conan took the title of Duke of Brittany in the spring of 990, after his attack on Nantes and the death of Count Alan. To reach that point he had allied himself with Odo I, Count of Blois. In a charter dated 28 July 990 he gave the lands of Villamée, Lillele and Passille to Mont Saint-Michel; all three later became part of the seigneury of Fougères.

The alliance with Blois became troublesome, and Conan freed himself from its influence through a pact with Richard I of Normandy, which established firm Breton-Norman links for the first time. Richard had married a daughter of Hugh I the Great and had revived his father's claim to be overlord of the Breton duchy. The pact strengthened that claim, but evidence for the overlordship is doubtful, since it rests largely on the writings of Dudo of Saint-Quentin, which historians do not regard as authoritative.

Conan died fighting Fulk Nerra at the Battle of Conquereuil and was buried at Mont Saint-Michel Abbey. With Ermengarde-Gerberga he had several children: Geoffrey, his heir, who lived from about 980 to 1008; Judith, who married Richard II, Duke of Normandy; Judicael, Count of Porhoët, who died in 1037; Hernod; and Catuallon, Abbot of Redon.
conan-ii-duke-of-brittany: Conan was the eldest child and heir of Alan III, Duke of Brittany, and his wife Bertha of Blois, of the House of Rennes. His father died while he was still a minor, and he inherited a difficult position: his grandfather Duke Geoffrey I's attempts at an alliance with Normandy had sunk into border skirmishes, Breton nobles such as Rivallon I of Dol were in revolt, and his uncle Odo, who governed as regent, refused to give up power once Conan came of age. By 1057 Conan had captured his uncle and had him chained and imprisoned.

Brittany, an independent Celtic duchy, had a long rivalry with Normandy, and Duke William of Normandy, later King of England, backed revolts among Conan's nobles. The war of 1064-1065 began when William supported Rivallon of Dol's rebellion. In 1065, before his invasion of England, William warned the neighbouring counties against attacking his lands, since his enterprise bore the papal banner; Conan replied that he would take the chance to invade Normandy. He is also said to have refused to help William's conquest, saying that the Normans had poisoned his father in 1040.

In his campaign of 1066 against Anjou Conan took Pouancé, long the border town of the Breton March, and Segré, and reached Château-Gontier, where he was found dead on 11 December after putting on poisoned riding gloves; he may have swallowed the poison when he wiped his mouth. William was widely suspected. Conan left no known children, and the marriage of his sister Hawise to Hoël II, who succeeded him together, may have been meant to bind the east and west of the duchy.
conan-iv-duke-of-brittany: Conan, called the Young, was the son of Bertha, Duchess of Brittany, and her first husband, Alan, 1st Earl of Richmond. From his father he inherited the earldom of Richmond, which made him a vassal of both the King of England and the King of France. When his mother died early in 1156 his stepfather, Odo II, Viscount of Porhoët, refused to give up power, perhaps in league with Conan's uncle Hoel, Count of Nantes. Within the year Conan captured and imprisoned Odo and took his inheritance.

Brittany had long been largely independent, with its own language and culture, and most of it was held by local lords. Henry II of England claimed to be its overlord and at first ruled through proxies, backing Conan, who had strong English ties. After Henry's brother Geoffrey, who had deposed Hoel at Nantes, died in 1158, Conan briefly held the city, but Henry opposed him, and at Michaelmas 1158 Conan surrendered Nantes and its lands to the king at Avranches. King Louis VII of France did not intervene.

In 1160 Conan married Henry's cousin Margaret, sister of the Scottish king William the Lion; their daughter was Constance. Facing revolts by his nobles, possibly encouraged by England, Conan asked Henry for help, and Henry demanded Constance's betrothal to his son Geoffrey. Henry seized lands on the Norman border in 1164 and invaded Brittany in 1166 to punish the barons, then forced Conan to abdicate in favour of Constance, an unusual arrangement since Conan might still have had sons. Henry held Brittany as her guardian, though he never claimed the ducal title himself.

Conan died on 18 or 20 February 1171. He and Constance were the only members of the House of Penthièvre to rule Brittany. A son named William appears to have been alive towards 1200. Breton historians have usually remembered Conan as a weak ruler unable to defend his duchy against the Angevin king, a view the historian Eric Borgnis-Desbordes has recently qualified. He appears in Jean-François Ducis's tragedy of 1791 and in novels by Sharon Kay Penman.
concentration-camp: The English term concentration camp comes from the reconcentration camps (Spanish: reconcentrados) set up by the Spanish military in Cuba during the Ten Years' War of 1868–1878. Spain used such camps again in the Cuban War of Independence of 1895–98, when Valeriano Weyler's Reconcentration policy moved rural Cubans into them. The label was later applied to camps run by the United States during the Philippine–American War, by the British during the Second Boer War, and by the German Empire during the Herero and Nama genocide of 1904–1907, in which the death rate in the camps was 45 per cent, twice that of the British camps. Civilian internment may be older still, since a first example may date to the 1830s.

A concentration camp is a prison or other facility used to intern political prisoners or politically targeted groups, such as national or ethnic minorities, on grounds of national security, exploitation or punishment. The term covers systems that differ greatly in severity, mortality and architecture. What they share is that the inmates are held outside the rule of law. Extermination camps, whose main purpose is killing, are also loosely called concentration camps, and historians debate whether other cases of civilian internment should be called concentration camps or internment camps.

In the Russian Empire, katorga was a punishment for the most serious crimes; about 6,000 convicts were serving it in 1906 and 28,600 in 1916. During the Russian Civil War the Bolsheviks created separate prison camps under the Cheka. In 1929 the camps were put under the Joint State Political Directorate and expanded into the Gulag, which held some 18 million people from 1929 until 1953.

During the Armenian genocide, deported Armenians reaching Aleppo from mid-1915 were sent into camps across Syria and Upper Mesopotamia, including Ras al-Ayn and Deir ez-Zor, where hunger, disease and killings followed. It is estimated that up to 700,000 Armenians were killed in these camps between 1915 and 1918.

Nazi Germany opened camps in 1933 for tens of thousands of political prisoners, mainly members of the Communist Party and the Social Democratic Party, then arrested so-called anti-socials from 1937 and Jews increasingly from 1938. About 1.65 million people were registered as prisoners, and about a million of them died.
concepcion-chile: Concepción was founded by Pedro de Valdivia in 1550 north of the Bío Bío River, at the site now known as Penco. It was named Concepción de María Purísima del Nuevo Extremo. The settlement lay a few kilometres north of La Frontera, the boundary between Spanish territory and the land of the Mapuche, who remained independent until the 1870s. Spanish authorities formally recognised it as a town two years later by royal decree and gave it a coat of arms still in use today. When the Spanish arrived, the chronicler Jerónimo de Vivar noted that local Mapuche wore gold and silver bracelets and crown-like ornaments, interpreted either as Incan gifts, war spoils or the adoption of Incan metallurgy.

The city was the capital of the Kingdom of Chile between 1565 and 1573 and kept the unofficial position of military capital for the rest of the colonial period. After a serious earthquake in 1751 it moved to the Valle de la Mocha, where the city centre and historic district now stand. Its inhabitants are still called penquistas, after Penco. The city was an important site in the struggle for Chile's independence, and the declaration of independence was held at the Plaza de la Independencia. Until the election of Manuel Montt as president in 1851, executive power in independent Chile was dominated by Concepción elites.

Concepción is the capital of the Biobío Region and of Concepción Province, about 500 km south of Santiago. It is the core of the Greater Concepción metropolitan area, the second largest city in Chile by urban area, and sits in the most heavily industrialised region of the country. It is known as the university city, with the Universidad de Concepción, the Universidad del Biobío and the Catholic University of the Most Holy Conception. Like most of Chile it is seismically active: an earthquake in 1939 destroyed much of the city, one in 1953 damaged 15 per cent of its buildings, and a major earthquake in 1960 had a nearby epicentre.
concepcion-del-uruguay: The city lies on the western shore of the Uruguay River in Entre Ríos province, some 320 km north of Buenos Aires. A settlement known as Arroyo de China, with no formal foundation, was recorded about 1778, and its first chapel was raised that year. Tomás de Rocamora, commissioned by the viceroy Vértiz and Juan José Salcedo, founded the town of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception of Uruguay on 25 June 1783, north of the older settlement. Its citizens are called uruguayenses, to tell them from Uruguayans, who are uruguayos.

In 1810 the town was the first in the region to join the revolution begun at Buenos Aires. In 1814 the Supreme Director Gervasio Antonio Posadas named it capital of the newly created province of Entre Ríos. After his victory at Cepeda on 1 February 1820, Francisco Ramírez proclaimed the Republic of Entre Ríos on 29 September, which also took in Corrientes and Misiones, with Concepción as its capital. It ended with Ramírez's death on 10 July 1821. In 1826 Justo José de Urquiza, as governor, promoted the law that made the town a city.

Urquiza founded the Colegio del Uruguay in 1848, the first secular school in the country. In 1851 the pronouncement of Urquiza against Juan Manuel de Rosas was made in the central plaza, and it led to the Battle of Caseros on 3 February 1852 and to the National Constitution of the following year. The city remained the provincial capital until 1883, when the seat moved to Paraná. Its railway opened on 30 June 1887, and its port was among the busiest in the country by 1910.

The city is sometimes called La Histórica for its part in the formation of the nation. The Palacio San José, Urquiza's former residence, stands 23 km away, and in 1994 the oath of the constitutional reform was taken there. The economy rests on the port, an industrial park making poultry products, wood and auto parts, and public administration. The city has four universities, and the Colegio del Uruguay educated many presidents of Argentina and Paraguay.
concertacion: In 1987 General Augusto Pinochet legalised political parties and called a plebiscite on whether he would stay in power after 1990. The Christian Democracy, the Socialist Party and the Radical Party had already gathered in the Democratic Alliance, and in 1988 the Humanist Party, the Ecologist Party, the Social Democrats and several Socialist splinter groups joined them as the Concertación de Partidos por el NO, though some Socialist factions held back for fear of fraud. Campaigning under the slogan La alegría ya viene, Joy is coming, the NO won with 54% on 5 October 1988.

Renamed the Concertación de Partidos por la Democracia in 1989, the coalition ran the Christian Democrat Patricio Aylwin, who won, but for over 15 years it lacked a majority in the Senate and had to negotiate its laws with the right-wing UDI and RN. In 1993 Eduardo Frei Ruiz-Tagle, son of the former president Eduardo Frei Montalva, won with 57%, and the Humanist Party, the Christian Left and the Greens left the coalition, accusing it of betraying its purpose. In the 1999 election Ricardo Lagos won the first runoff in Chilean history with 51%.

In 2005 Michelle Bachelet became the candidate after Soledad Alvear withdrew, and in the December parliamentary elections the coalition won a majority in both houses for the first time. Bachelet won the runoff of 15 January 2006 to become Chile's first female president. In the 2009 elections the coalition kept its Senate majority but lost the lower house, and Frei, its candidate again, lost the runoff of 17 January 2010 to Sebastián Piñera, ending twenty years in government.

Its years in office saw a large expansion of spending on social programmes and a steady fall in poverty. In opposition, the Concertación drew closer to the left-wing Juntos Podemos, led by the Communist Party, and together they won the municipal elections of 2012. On 30 April 2013 its parties and other opposition groups formed the Nueva Mayoría pact. Some of its members saw this as the end of the Concertación and the birth of a broader centre-left, while critics such as Marcel Claude and Carlos Larraín called it a change of name.
concession-of-evoramonte: The agreement, also called the Convention of Evoramonte, closed six years of civil war between the Constitutionalists and the Miguelites, fought from 1828. To end the bloodshed, Dom Miguel I of Portugal surrendered and gave up his claim to the throne. The Constitutionalists were represented by two marshals of the army, the Duke of Terceira and the Count of Saldanha, and the Miguelites by Lieutenant General José António Azevedo e Lemos.

The concession first had nine articles. It granted a general amnesty for all political crimes committed since 21 July 1826 and let anyone covered by it leave the kingdom freely with their property. Officers kept the ranks lawfully given them, and public and church employees could keep their allowances if their services made them worthy. Miguel received an annual pension of 60 contos de réis and could dispose of his own property, returning any jewels and other articles belonging to the Crown or to private people.

He could sail from any port he chose in a warship of the Allied Powers, with safety assured for him and his followers, and was banished for ever from the kingdom and its colonies within a fortnight. His troops were to hand in their weapons and his regiments to disband peacefully.

Four more articles were added the next day. Orders went at once to every garrison commander and every authority still recognising Miguel's government, in Portugal and in the colonies, to submit to the government of Queen Maria II. Miguel was to leave Évora on 30 May for Sines, where he would embark, and on 31 May his troops were to lay down their weapons at the college in Évora.

Soon after reaching Genoa, his place of exile, Miguel addressed the courts of Europe on 20 June 1834, declaring the concession illegal because it had been imposed on him by force by the governments of the Quadruple Alliance. He wrote that his acceptance had been a provisional act, made to spare his subjects further misfortune after a surprise attack by a friendly and allied power, and that the capitulation of 26 May, which he had been obliged to sign, must be considered null and void.
concordat-of-bologna: The agreement replaced the Pragmatic Sanction of Bourges of 1438, which had failed to guarantee the privileges of the Church in France. Under it bishoprics and abbacies were fought over, even before the Parlement of Paris, and the historian R. Aubenas observes that hardly anywhere were elections held in due form, since the king pressed his own candidates on the electors by every means. After his victory at Marignano in September 1515, Francis I met Pope Leo X in person at Bologna from 11 to 15 December 1515, and these meetings prepared the concordat, which was signed in Rome on 18 August 1516.

The king's right to nominate archbishops, bishops, abbots and priors was confirmed, and with it the crown's power to choose who led the Gallican Church. He also kept the right to tax the clergy and to restrict their appeals to Rome. Canonical installation of those chosen was reserved to the pope, who could thus veto a candidate held to be truly unqualified. The fiction of elections, of bishops by cathedral canons and of abbots by their monks, was given up.

The Apostolic Camera's right to collect annates was confirmed, a right that, when abused, led to the shuffling of prelates from one diocese to another. On his side Francis conceded that the pope's powers were not subject to any church council, a point that affirmed the papal position against the long-defeated Conciliar Movement. The concordat marked a stage in the development of the Gallican Church, but it was not a simple triumph for the French monarchy: it met bitter opposition from the Parlement and from the University of Paris.
concordat-of-worms: The Investiture Controversy began in the middle of the 11th century, when a reforming movement in the Church sought to reassert the rights of the Holy See. Pope Gregory VII forbade secular rulers to make clerical appointments, and Emperor Henry IV, who habitually invested the bishops and abbots of the Empire, rejected the claim. The dispute outlasted both men. In 1111 Henry V made an agreement with Pope Paschal II at Sutri, but when it was not carried out he imprisoned the pope, who then yielded under duress and later went back on his promises.

Callixtus II resumed talks, and in autumn 1119 the emperor agreed in principle at Strasbourg to give up investing bishops and abbots with ring and crosier. A planned summit at Mouzon broke down, and Henry was excommunicated at the council at Reims. Afterwards most of the clergy became willing to compromise. In 1121 a faction of nobles led by Archbishop Adalbert I of Mainz pressed Henry to make peace, and in February 1122 Callixtus wrote to him in a conciliatory tone.

The talks seem to have taken place at nearby Mainz while Henry waited at Worms. The papal delegation was led by Cardinal Bishop Lamberto Scannabecchi of Ostia, the future Pope Honorius II. On 23 September 1122 delegates signed the documents outside the walls of Worms, which had no room for the crowd. The agreement was issued as two charters, the Calixtinum, addressed to the emperor, and the Henricianum, addressed to God. Neither was signed.

Henry renounced investiture with ring and staff, opened ecclesiastical appointments in his realm to canonical election, recognised the papal patrimony and promised to return church lands he or his father had seized. Callixtus allowed the emperor or his officials to be present at elections and to judge disputed ones, and let him invest bishops and abbots with a sceptre representing their temporal lands. In Germany this came before consecration, elsewhere in the Empire within six months. The charters were deliberately brief, and the word regalia meant different things to each side.

The First Lateran Council confirmed the concordat in March 1123 with nearly 300 bishops and 600 abbots present. Some followers of Paschal II cried non placet, and Callixtus told them that they had not to approve but to tolerate it. Henry V died in 1125. Historians disagree about how decisive the settlement was. Some stress that it ended the Ottonian and Salian imperial church system and showed that the emperor held no religious authority; others note that the king was left in possession of the field and that the controversy over investiture continued for at least another decade. Successive emperors found its terms favourable enough that it remained almost unaltered until the Empire was dissolved in 1806.
conde-sur-lescaut: Condé-sur-l'Escaut is a commune of the Nord department on the border with Belgium, 12 km north-east of Valenciennes. It lies at the confluence of the Haine and the Scheldt. The name comes from the Celtic word Condate, meaning confluence. A Romanised form, Condatum, was in use in the Roman period, and Condé was in use by the 14th century. The present name dates from 1886. The region is noted for its coal mines, which made it a strategic objective in both world wars.

The meeting of two rivers gave the site military importance from before Roman times. It was first occupied by the Nervians, then was the site of a Roman military camp and later a settlement of Franks. Saint Wasnulf preached at Condé and died there around 650, and Vikings held the town from 855 to 889. During the Middle Ages and the Renaissance it changed hands many times, falling to the Flemish forces of Jacques van Artevelde, to Louis XI of France, to Les Gueux in the Eighty Years' War and to Turenne.

Louis XIV seized the town in 1676, and it became part of France in 1678 with the Treaty of Nimègue. Vauban improved its fortifications. Prince Josias of Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld captured it after a 92-day siege in 1793, and forces of the Seventh Coalition took it from Napoleon in 1815 and returned it to French control three years later. Germans occupied the town in the Second World War and used its people to run the adjacent coal mines. The U.S. 5th Armored Division liberated it on 2 September 1944.

Coal mining ended in 1989. The population peaked at 13,994 in 1975 and has since declined. The town is the eastern member of the Valenciennes metropolitan area, which administers 35 communes. It is known in music history as the home, retirement place and burial place of the Renaissance composer Josquin des Prez, who was provost of the church of Notre-Dame, which had one of the most sumptuous musical establishments in Hainaut. His house stood on the market square, and the church, with his tombstone, was destroyed in 1793.
condor-legion: After the military coup of 17 July 1936 began the Spanish Civil War, the Nationalists asked Germany and Italy for support. The first request for German aircraft, on 22 July, was for ten transport planes. Adolf Hitler decided to help on 25 or 26 July, though he was wary of provoking a wider European war. The first mission, Operation Magic Fire, used Junkers Ju 52 aircraft to carry the Spanish Army of Africa from Spanish Morocco to Spain, and German involvement was hidden through a dummy company and funded with three million Reichsmarks. The first contingent of 86 men left Germany on 1 August 1936, many of them believing they would only train the Nationalists.

The Legion was commanded by Hugo Sperrle, with Wilhelm Ritter von Thoma leading its ground element, which included small armoured units of Panzer I tanks. It had bomber, fighter, reconnaissance, anti-aircraft and signals groups. In 1937 it supported the Nationalist offensive in Biscay, a Basque region of northern Spain. Its aircraft attacked Otxandio and Durango, where the Basques said 250 civilians died on 31 March, and on 26 April it bombed Guernica in Operation Rügen. Casualties there are disputed: perhaps 200 or 300 people were killed, while the Basques reported 1,654 dead. The Times reporter George Steer wrote the first full account, noting German involvement.

The Legion also fought at the Battle of Brunete and in the campaign that ended with the fall of Santander and of Gijón on 21 October 1937. After the Nationalist conquest of Asturias, much of its industrial and mineral output was shipped to Germany as repayment for the Legion's service. Its maritime unit attacked Republican shipping and ports. The Legion left Spain in May 1939, sailing from Vigo to Hamburg, where crowds and ceremonies awaited it.

Many have regarded the intervention as a proving ground for the Second World War. Hermann Göring said at Nuremberg that he urged Hitler to help Franco partly to test the young Luftwaffe. The Messerschmitt Bf 109 entered service in Spain from about January 1937, and Wolfram von Richthofen, who commanded the Legion, later led ground-attack units in Poland, France and Operation Barbarossa. Adolf Galland, however, held that the value of the lessons was exaggerated and the wrong conclusions drawn. In 1997 German President Roman Herzog apologised to survivors of the Guernica raid, and in 1998 the German parliament had the names of former Legion members removed from military bases.
condroz: The Condroz is a natural region of Wallonia, the French-speaking part of Belgium, lying between the Ardennes and the Meuse. Compared with other parts of Belgium it is sparsely populated and agricultural, a country of low hills averaging about 200 to 300 metres. It lies mainly in the provinces of Liège and Namur, with smaller parts in Hainaut and Luxembourg, and is bordered by the Meuse to the north, the Ardennes to the east and the Famenne to the south. Today a western section also stretches beyond the Meuse, south of Namur and the Sambre, towards the Thiérache.

Very little is known of the Condrusi. Julius Caesar placed them, with the Segni, between the Eburones to the north and the Treviri to the south. Fragmentary evidence shows that their pagus lay within the Civitas Tungrorum, with its capital at Tongeren, and that its people served in the Roman military and could earn Roman citizenship.

The Pagus Condrustis reappears in medieval records from 747, in an area matching the old country of the Condrusi. It did not then extend west of the Meuse, where the Lommegau lay, but it included the Famenne to the south and reached east over the Ourthe. In 839 the Carolingian emperor Louis the Pious granted the county of Condroz and the county of the Ardennes to his son Louis the German, making the Meuse the boundary between the eastern and western Frankish kingdoms. The Treaty of Meerssen in 870 allotted the Condroz for some decades to the kingdom of the western Franks.

In the church the Condroz belonged to the Bishopric of Liège, which covered the old Civitas Tungrorum, its seat moved from Tongeren to Liège. About 800 the Pagus Condrustinsus was one of only four divisions of the bishopric, with Lomme, the Ardennes and the Hesbaye. The later archdeaconry of Condroz did not match the region: it held the deanery of Hanret in the Hesbaye and the deanery of Saint Remacle, which stretched along the Vesdre to the present German border.
confederacion-nacional-del-trabajo: The Confederación Nacional del Trabajo was founded in 1910 in Barcelona at a congress of the Catalan trade union Solidaridad Obrera. It was meant to be an opposing force to the then majority union, the socialist UGT, and to speed up the economic emancipation of the working class through the revolutionary expropriation of the bourgeoisie. It started small, with 26,571 members, and its first congress in 1911 coincided with a general strike that led a Barcelona judge to declare the union illegal. From 1918 it grew stronger, while employers hired thugs to intimidate unionists. The CNT was among the main leaders of the 1919 La Canadiense strike, which paralysed 70% of industry in Catalonia, and that year its membership reached 700,000.

The CNT joined the International Workers' Association at its founding in Berlin in 1922, and was outlawed under the dictatorship of Miguel Primo de Rivera. After the fall of the monarchy in 1931 it gave the Second Republic only minimal support and clashed with it in successive general strikes. In the Civil War it declined Largo Caballero's first invitation to join the national government, but in September 1936 it joined the Generalitat in Catalonia, and in November it accepted four ministries. Federica Montseny became Minister of Health, the first female minister in Spain. In February 1937 a congress at Caspe formed the Regional Federation of Collectives of Aragon.

In 1939 the Law of Political Responsibilities outlawed the CNT and seized its assets. One estimate says that roughly 160,000 to 180,000 of its members were killed by the Franco government. After Franco's death in November 1975 it was the only social movement to refuse to sign the 1977 Moncloa Pact. A dispute over taking part in works council elections split it in the 1980s, and in 1989 the Supreme Court of Spain barred the dissident faction from using its name, so that it became the General Confederation of Labour, while the CNT stayed small.

The CNT rests on workers' self-management, federalism and mutual aid. It prefers workers' assemblies, union sections and direct action to union elections and works councils. Its administrative posts rotate and are unpaid. Industrial unions form its base, deciding by direct democracy and consensus in the union assembly, and delegates bring agreements from their assemblies to the Congress, which decides the confederation's line of action.
confederate-ireland: The Irish Catholic Confederation was formed after the rebellion of 1641, both to control the popular uprising and to organise a Catholic war effort against the English and Scottish armies in Ireland. The initiative came from the bishop Nicholas French and the lawyer Nicholas Plunkett. On 17 March 1642 the nobles signed the Catholic Remonstrance to Charles I at Trim, and on 10 May the clergy met in synod at Kilkenny and drafted the Confederate Oath of Association, swearing allegiance to the king and obedience to the Supreme Council. Its members were Catholics of both Gaelic and Anglo-Norman descent, who wanted an end to anti-Catholic discrimination, greater self-government, and in many cases the reversal of the plantations.

The first General Assembly met at Kilkenny on 24 October 1642 and sat until 9 January 1643. It was a parliament in all but name, with 14 lords temporal, 11 lords spiritual and 226 commoners, and it elected a Supreme Council of 24 members.

The Confederates claimed to be loyal to Charles I, in part to protect their estates from confiscation under the Adventurers' Act of 1642, and never claimed independence. In September 1643 they agreed a cessation with the Royalist governor, the Duke of Ormonde, and in 1644 sent about 1,500 men under Alasdair MacColla to Scotland. They defeated the Covenanter army at the Battle of Benburb in June 1646. Pope Innocent X backed them, and sent the nuncio Giovanni Battista Rinuccini, whose supplies gave him much influence over the militants.

A peace with Ormonde in 1646 divided the Confederation, because the clergy, Owen Roe O'Neill and most of the General Assembly rejected it, and the Supreme Council was arrested. In 1647 the Confederates lost at Dungan's Hill and Knocknanuss. A new agreement with the Royalists then split them again, and Owen Roe O'Neill fought a brief civil war inside the Confederation in the summer of 1648. Historians dispute how far the split ran between Old English and Gaelic Irish.

Oliver Cromwell invaded in August 1649, and Kilkenny fell after a short siege in 1650. The Cromwellian conquest was the bloodiest warfare Ireland had known and came with plague and famine. The pre-war Catholic landowning class was nearly destroyed, and almost all Catholic-owned land was confiscated in the 1650s, though some was regranted in the 1660s. Most Confederate leaders spent the period in exile in France.
confederation-of-cologne: King Valdemar IV of Denmark had spent much of his reign reducing the autonomy of his nobles, enlarging the crown lands and putting his finances in order. He then reconquered Scania from Sweden in 1360 and took Gotland in 1361 after a decisive victory at the Battle of Visby. Because Visby and Gotland lay within the Hanseatic sphere, the League declared war, but after it nearly lost at the Battle of Helsingborg it agreed a truce with Denmark at Vordingborg in 1365.

In 1367 the Hansetag met at Cologne, chosen for its nearness to the Dutch towns, which were vital to the war. Lübeck, Rostock, Stralsund, Wismar, Kulm and Thorn were present, with Kampen, Harderwyk, Elburg, Amsterdam and Briel.

The members agreed to levy taxes on all goods in their ports and, to simplify collection, chose the currencies of Lübeck, Flanders, Pomerania, Prussia and Livonia for the main regions of the League. Each member was to provide a fixed number of ships and men, and departure dates were set for towns across the Baltic and North Sea so that the combined fleet could assemble in the Oresund for the attack on Denmark. Unusually for a medieval treaty, the text was written not in Latin but in Middle Low German, the language of the Hanseatic towns.

Support was uneven. Bremen and Hamburg, exhausted by earlier wars, gave money but no military help, and inland towns, untouched by the war at sea, refused to aid it; the Westphalian towns gave nothing. The Confederation nonetheless won allies in Mecklenburg, Holstein and among Danish nobles opposed to Valdemar, broke the truce of Vordingborg and invaded Denmark. The years after the peace marked the golden age of the Hanseatic League.

The Confederation outlived the war by fifteen years. When the League gave up the Danish forts in Scania in 1385, the Teutonic Order wished to keep it, but the other towns chose to dissolve it. In the 15th century several groups tried to form similar alliances, known as Tohopesaten, without success.
confederation-of-the-equator: The dissolution of the Brazilian Constituent Assembly in 1823 was badly received in Pernambuco. Its liberal leaders, Manuel de Carvalho Pais de Andrade and the friar Joaquim do Amor Divino Rabelo e Caneca, known as Frei Caneca, were republicans pardoned after the revolt of 1817, who had accepted the monarchy hoping for provincial autonomy. On 13 December 1823 the liberals forced the emperor's appointed president, Francisco Paes Barreto, to resign and illegally elected Pais de Andrade in his place, and they refused both Paes Barreto's return and a compromise president, José Carlos Mayrink da Silva Ferrão.

A naval division under John Taylor blockaded Recife from April 1824, but rumours of a Portuguese naval attack drew it away, and on 2 July, a day after it left, Pais de Andrade declared Pernambuco independent and invited the northern and northeastern provinces to join a Confederation of the Equator. None did, apart from a few villages in southern Ceará and Paraíba. In Ceará the president was deposed in favour of the confederate Tristão Gonçalves de Alencar Araripe, but Fortaleza soon reaffirmed its loyalty, and in Pernambuco the rebels held little beyond Recife and Olinda, recruiting even children and old men by force.

In August the emperor sent Admiral Thomas Cochrane's squadron and 1,200 soldiers under Brigadier General Francisco de Lima e Silva, who landed at Maceió and marched overland, gathering about 3,500 men. They attacked Recife on 12 September; Pais de Andrade fled secretly on a British ship, and the leaderless rebels were defeated at Olinda five days later. Frei Caneca and a few others escaped towards Ceará but were defeated weeks later.

Prosecutions ran from October 1824 to April 1825. Of the hundreds who had taken part in the three provinces, sixteen were condemned to death, among them Frei Caneca. Sentenced to be hanged, he was shot instead because no executioner would hang him, on 13 January 1825, outside the walls of the Forte de São Tiago das Cinco Pontas. Pedro I pardoned the others on 7 March 1825.
confederation-of-the-rhine: The Final Imperial Recess of 1803 transformed the Holy Roman Empire. About 112 immediate territories east of the Rhine were absorbed by larger states, all ecclesiastical territories but one were secularised, and most free imperial cities were mediatised. The Emperor lost important political support, and in 1804 Francis II took the title of Emperor of Austria to offset the loss of prestige. When the War of the Third Coalition began in 1805, Bavaria, Baden and Württemberg allied with Napoleon, and after Austerlitz Francis II had to assent to raising Bavaria and Württemberg to kingdoms.

The formation was not altogether voluntary. On 12 July 1806 Talleyrand summoned the princes' envoys in Paris and compelled them to sign a treaty whose terms were far harsher than expected. King Maximilian I Joseph of Bavaria was aghast that foreign policy would pass to Napoleon, the Protector of the Confederation, but his envoy was detained at the border until all the others had signed. Sixteen German states joined. On 1 August 1806 they seceded from the Holy Roman Empire, and on 6 August, after an ultimatum from Napoleon, Francis II declared the empire dissolved.

The treaty provided for common constitutional bodies, but the larger states wanted unlimited sovereignty. The highest office was held by Karl Theodor von Dalberg as Prince-primate, who presided over a Diet that never assembled. After Prussia's defeat in 1806, 23 more states joined, and in 1808 the confederation reached 36 states, ruling over some 14.5 to 15 million people. It served as a buffer between France and the two largest German states, Prussia and Austria.

It was above all a military alliance. Members had to keep substantial armies and supply France with troops, and found themselves more subordinated to Napoleon than they had been to the Habsburgs. Its states were of three kinds: model states ruled by Napoleon's relatives, such as the Kingdom of Westphalia under Jérôme Bonaparte; reform states, among them Bavaria, Württemberg, Baden and Hesse-Darmstadt; and smaller states that joined after 1806, in which change was minimal. After Napoleon's failed invasion of Russia many members changed sides at the Battle of Leipzig, and the allies dissolved the confederation on 4 November 1813.

On 30 May 1814 the Treaty of Paris declared the German states independent. The Congress of Vienna abolished Napoleonic creations such as the Kingdom of Westphalia and the Grand Duchy of Berg, and most members in central and southern Germany survived with minor border changes. With Prussia and Austria they formed the German Confederation, created on 8 June 1815.
conference-of-ambassadors: The Conference of Ambassadors of the Principal Allied and Associated Powers was an inter-allied organisation of the Entente, formed in Paris in January 1920 as a successor to the Supreme War Council. Its task was to enforce the peace treaties that ended the First World War and to mediate territorial disputes between European states. It was later incorporated de facto into the League of Nations as one of its governing bodies.

The Conference was made up of the ambassadors of the United Kingdom, Italy and Japan accredited in Paris, together with the French minister of foreign affairs, who chaired it. Among its chairmen were Georges Clemenceau, Raymond Poincaré and Aristide Briand. The ambassador of the United States attended only as an observer, since the United States was not an official party to the Treaty of Versailles. The French diplomats Jules Laroche and René Massigli served as its secretaries-general, and a series of committees and commissions, some permanent and some ad hoc, advised them.

The disputes brought before the Conference included Cieszyn Silesia, contested between Poland and Czechoslovakia, the Vilnius Region between Poland and Lithuania, the Klaipėda Region between Germany and Lithuania, and the Corfu Incident between Italy and Greece. On 15 March 1923 it recognised the eastern borders of Poland that had emerged from the Polish–Soviet War of 1920, together with Polish sovereignty over the Vilnius region and Eastern Galicia.

At a meeting in March 1925 Marshal Foch briefed the Conference on German disarmament. He reported that the old Imperial German Staff still existed, that the German army stood at 500,000 men rather than the 100,000 allowed by the Treaty of Versailles, that surplus war materials had been found, that no law limited the size of the armed forces, and that the police force of 150,000 men was kept on a military footing. Foch asked for a treaty of security between France and the United Kingdom, but the British ambassador, Lord Crewe, blocked further discussion. The Conference became less active after the Locarno Treaties of 1925.
conference-of-rulers: The Conference traces its origins to the Durbar, the Council of Rulers of the Federated Malay States, which first convened in 1897. Only the four federated states of Perak, Selangor, Negeri Sembilan and Pahang were represented, and Resident-General Frank Swettenham described its purpose as being to "bring home to the Malays, in the most striking manner possible, the reality of federation".

After World War II a Council of Rulers was set up under the short-lived Malayan Union, presided over by the Governor of the Union, with the nine rulers and three British officials as ex officio members; it considered legislation on Islam and advised the Governor. The first Conference of Rulers met on 31 August 1948, in the year the Federation of Malaya was established, and the body was formally established by Article 38 of the Constitution after independence.

Membership follows the succession of the Malay rulers, each state having its own rule of succession (Negeri Sembilan is itself an elective monarchy), and the appointment of the governors of Penang, Malacca, Sabah and Sarawak by the king. The governors take no part when the Conference elects or removes the king or his deputy, or deals with the rulers' privileges and the observance of Islam. Each ruler attends with his Menteri Besar, and the king, when he attends, with the Prime Minister.

The Conference generally meets three times a year, usually at the Istana Negara, and the Malay rulers chair its meetings in turn, none taking precedence over another. Its secretary is the Keeper of the Rulers' Seal. Although the National Library has called it the supreme institution in the country, its role is largely symbolic in practice, and the election of the king generally follows a fixed order based on the rulers' seniority at independence in 1957.

Its part in amending the Constitution was set by the Constitution (Amendment) Act 1971, passed after the May 13 Incident of racial rioting in Kuala Lumpur. The Act protected Articles 152, 153 and 181 and Part III, on the Malay language, the special position of the Bumiputra, the rulers and citizenship, which could now be altered only with the Conference's consent. The Democratic Action Party and the People's Progressive Party opposed the changes, and The Times of London attacked them, but the Alliance government passed them with its two-thirds majority.
confucianism: Chinese has no term that corresponds directly to Confucianism. The nearest catch-all is rú, which in modern Chinese means scholar or learned man and in Old Chinese carried meanings such as to tame, to mould and to educate. Confucius regarded himself as a transmitter of cultural values from the earlier Xia, Shang and Western Zhou dynasties. The Zhou made their claim to rule rest on moral power, the Mandate of Heaven, which Tian, Heaven, gave to virtuous rulers. By the 6th century BCE the Zhou system of rites had become diffuse and was claimed by different rulers in the Zhou states.

Tradition held that Confucius wrote or edited the Five Classics, whose received versions were edited about 500 years later by the Imperial Librarian Liu Xin. The scholar Yao Xinzhong adds that nothing can be taken for granted about their early versions. Philosophers of the Warring States period built on his legacy, which is compiled in the Analects.

Confucianism seeks the unity of the individual self and Tian, and extends self-cultivation to family and society. Its ethics are summed up in the Five Constants worked out by Han scholars: ren, benevolence; yi, righteousness; li, propriety or rites; zhi, wisdom; and xin, sincerity. The junzi, literally son of a lord, became in the Analects a person of noble character, a model any individual may reach through discipline of mind and action. Confucius also taught the rectification of names, holding that disorder stems from failing to call things by their proper names.

Social harmony requires everyone to play their part, as when Confucius tells Duke Jing of Qi that there is government when the prince is prince, the minister minister, the father father and the son son. A ruler governs by his own virtue rather than coercion. Confucius admitted students of different classes, and the Analects has him say that in teaching there should be no distinction of classes.

Confucianism was suppressed under the Legalist Qin dynasty and flourished under the Han, becoming the dominant ideological framework. Neo-Confucianism arose in response to the rising influence of Buddhism and Taoism and became central to the imperial examination system and the scholar-official class of the Song. The examination system was abolished in Korea in 1894, in China in 1905 and in Vietnam in 1919. Critics were present from the start, among them Mozi and the Legalist Han Fei. Jesuit missionaries translated Confucian texts in the 17th century, and the translations influenced Enlightenment thinkers, including Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz.
confucius: The name Confucius is a Latinized form of the Mandarin Kǒngfūzǐ, meaning roughly Great Master Kong, coined in the late 16th century by early Jesuit missionaries to China. His family name was Kong and his given name Qiu, meaning hill or mound. His courtesy name was Zhongni, the Zhong indicating that he was the second son in his family.

It is thought that he was born on 28 September 551 BCE in Zou, in modern Qufu, Shandong. The area was formally controlled by the kings of Zhou but effectively independent under the local lords of Lu. His father Kong He, an elderly commandant of the local Lu garrison, died when Confucius was three years old, and his mother Yan Zhengzai raised him in poverty.

Traditional accounts trace the family back through the dukes of Song to the Shang dynasty, though not all modern scholars accept this descent. He was born into the class of shi, between the aristocracy and the common people, and was educated at schools for commoners. At 19 he married Qi Guanshi, and a year later their son Kong Li was born. He is said to have held various government jobs in his early 20s and to have mourned his mother for three years.

In the Analects, Confucius presents himself as a transmitter who invented nothing. He put the most emphasis on study and wanted his disciples to master older classics rather than build a systematic theory. Tradition credits him with authoring or editing the Five Classics, but modern scholars are cautious about attributing particular assertions to him, since some of the texts and philosophy associated with him are more ancient, and the Analects were compiled many years after his death. His ethics stress self-cultivation and emulation of moral exemplars over rules, and he taught a negative form of the Golden Rule, sometimes called the Silver Rule.

His disciples and his grandson Zisi continued his school, and Mencius in the 4th century BCE and Xunzi in the 3rd century BCE elaborated his ideas in different ways. The Qin state, which conquered all of China in 221 BCE, adopted Legalism as its official doctrine. Under Emperor Wu of Han, works attributed to Confucius were made the official imperial philosophy and required reading for civil service examinations in 140 BCE, a practice continued nearly unbroken until the end of imperial China in 1912.
congal-caech: No early source preserves Congal's ancestry. Later materials make him the son of Scandal Sciathlethan and grandson of Fiachnae mac Báetáin, of the Uí Chóelbad, the main ruling line of the Dál nAraidi, based in Mag Line east of Antrim. He may instead have belonged to a rival branch of the Cruithne. The saga Fled Dúin na nGéd makes him a grandson of Eochaid Buide of Dál Riata, and so a nephew of his later ally Domnall Brecc, a link no other source confirms.

His epithets cáech and cláen mean squinting or half blind. The Bechbretha, a law tract on bees written within a generation of his death, says he was blinded in one eye by bees belonging to Domnall mac Áedo, and that this put him out of the kingship of Tara.

Congal is presumed to have become king of the Dál nAraidi in 626 and king of Ulaid some time after the death of Fiachnae mac Demmáin in 627. He first appears in the record in 628, when he killed Suibne Menn of the Cenél nEógain at Traig Bréni on Lough Swilly. That killing brought Domnall mac Áedo of the Cenél Conaill, said by the saga to be Congal's foster-father, to the headship of the Northern Uí Néill. In 629 Domnall defeated Congal at the Battle of Dún Ceithirn, near Coleraine.

His bid for the kingship of Tara came after 629, and victories of his allies the Clann Cholmáin in Leinster and Meath in 633 and 634 may belong to it. From 635 Domnall's allies gained the upper hand, and the tracts about his blinding may have been part of a propaganda war against him.

Congal and Domnall Brecc of Dál Riata challenged Domnall mac Áedo at the Battle of Mag Rath, at Moira in County Down, where Congal was killed. The battle and its hero passed into literature: Congal is the protagonist of the Fled Dúin na nGéd, appears in the Cath Maige Rath and the Buile Shuibhne, and was the subject of a long heroic poem by Sir Samuel Ferguson, Congal: A Poem in Five Books.
congo-arab-war: At first the Free State worked with the Arab-Swahili traders. In 1887, at the proposal of Henry Morton Stanley, Tippu Tip became governor of the Stanley Falls District under Free State authority, but he behaved more as a vassal than an official, and rival traders such as Rumaliza of Lake Tanganyika called the deal treason. The two sides competed for ivory, and King Leopold II had pledged at the Berlin Conference to end slavery; the war came to be presented as a Christian anti-slavery crusade. When Tippu Tip left for Zanzibar in 1890, his son Sefu bin Hamid ruled from Kasongo and his nephew Rashid bin Mohammad held Stanley Falls.

In March and April 1892 Sefu's men attacked Free State personnel, among them the ivory trader Arthur Hodister, who was killed. Ngongo Lutete, leader of the Batetela and Bakusu, went over to the Force Publique on 19 September 1892, and other local leaders followed. Open war began in late November. Rumaliza's troops besieged the anti-slavery post of Albertville on Lake Tanganyika for nine months until a relief column arrived.

After Nyangwe fell in March 1893, a rising there ended with most of the town set ablaze; an officer, Sidney Langford Hinde, wrote that a town of about thirty thousand inhabitants had been reduced to one fortified house. Kasongo fell in two hours on 22 April. Commandant Pierre Ponthier was killed attacking Rumaliza's forts. Sefu died in the battle on the Luama River on 20 October 1893, and on 9 January 1894 a shell blew up Rumaliza's ammunition store; more than two thousand prisoners were taken, but Rumaliza escaped to German East Africa. The last Zanzibari force was captured in December 1894 and all its members were executed.

The war caused tens of thousands of deaths among combatants and civilians. The market around Nyangwe ceased to exist and Kasongo was all but destroyed, so much of the Congo's trade was turned from East Africa towards the Stanley Pool and the Atlantic. The colonial authorities kept much of the Arab administrative structure in the east until the 1920s, while the Batetela and Bakusu, mistrusted for their part in the slave trade, were neglected under colonial rule. The historian Bruce Vandervort called it one of the most obscure wars of imperial conquest in Africa.
congo-basin: The Congo Basin is the sedimentary basin of the Congo River, a massive depression within the Congo Craton, in a region of Central Africa known as west equatorial Africa. It begins in the highlands of the East African Rift system, with the Chambeshi, the Uele and Ubangi rivers in the upper reaches and the Lualaba River draining wetlands in the middle reaches, and it ends where the Congo River empties into the Gulf of Guinea. The basin covers a total of 3.7 million square kilometres. Rainfall is between 1,500 and 2,000 millimetres a year and temperatures usually lie between 20 and 30 degrees.

The first inhabitants of the basin are believed to have been hunter-gatherers, whose small numbers reflect the dense forests and wet climate; remnants of their culture survive. Bantu peoples later migrated into the region and founded the Kingdom of Kongo. By the late 19th century Belgium, France and Portugal had established colonial control over the whole region. The General Act of the Berlin Conference of 1885 gave a precise definition to the conventional basin of the Congo, which included the entire actual basin plus some other areas, and bound its signatories to neutrality there, though this was not respected during the First World War.

Countries wholly or partly in the Congo region include Angola, Gabon, Burundi, Cameroon, the Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the Republic of the Congo, Rwanda, Tanzania and Zambia. The basin holds some of the largest undisturbed stands of tropical rainforest on Earth, with humid forests covering 1.6 million square kilometres, and large wetlands. Its animals include the okapi, African forest elephant, bonobo, chimpanzee and western lowland gorilla. Eight sites in the basin are on the World Heritage List, among them national parks such as Virunga, Salonga and Garamba.
congo-crisis: Colonial rule in the Congo began in the late 19th century with the Congo Free State, the personal colony of King Leopold II of Belgium, recognised internationally in 1885. Violence by its officials against Congolese and its system of economic extraction brought diplomatic pressure on Belgium, which took control in 1908 and created the Belgian Congo. A nationalist movement grew among the évolués in the 1950s, divided into parties along ethnic and regional lines. The largest was the Mouvement National Congolais, in which Patrice Lumumba became a leading figure.

At a Round Table Conference in Brussels in January 1960 Belgium, which had hoped for at least thirty years before independence, was pressed into fixing 30 June 1960. Delegates did not agree on federalism, ethnicity or Belgium's future role. Few preparations had been made, and white technical experts stayed in post, which many Congolese resented.

In the first week of July 1960 the army mutinied and violence broke out between black and white civilians. Belgium sent troops to protect fleeing whites. On 11 July Moïse Tshombe declared Katanga independent, saying 'We are seceding from chaos', and South Kasai also seceded. On 14 July the United Nations Security Council called for Belgian withdrawal and a UN force, but Secretary-General Dag Hammarskjöld would not use it against the secessionists. Lumumba then asked the Soviet Union for help, which split the government. On 5 September President Joseph Kasa-Vubu dismissed him, and Colonel Joseph-Désiré Mobutu took control in a coup.

Lumumba was captured on 1 December 1960 and handed to Tshombe's forces, who executed him on 17 January 1961 with the help of Belgian officers. Hammarskjöld was killed in a plane crash in late 1961, and the UN then took a firmer line. With UN troops the central government ended the secessions of Katanga and South Kasai by the start of 1963. In 1964 Maoist-inspired Simba rebels took territory in the east. Belgium and the United States intervened at Stanleyville in November 1964, and mercenaries helped the army retake the ground. About 100,000 people are believed to have died.

After elections in March 1965 a new stalemate between Tshombe and Kasa-Vubu paralysed the government, and on 25 November 1965 Mobutu seized power in a bloodless coup. He centralised the state, created a single party in 1967 and renamed the country Zaire in 1971. He remained in power until 1997. A Belgian inquiry led to an official apology in 2001 for moral responsibility, though not direct involvement, in Lumumba's killing. Historians usually portray the crisis as a time of intense disorder, and it was also a proxy conflict of the Cold War. Its turmoil helped to ignite the Portuguese Colonial War in neighbouring Angola.
congo-free-state: Until the middle of the 19th century the Congo lay in the middle of independent Africa, since fierce local resistance, rainforest and diseases such as malaria and sleeping sickness kept Europeans from settling the interior. In 1876 Leopold II of Belgium hosted the Brussels Geographic Conference and founded the International African Association, which he presented as a humanitarian enterprise but used to promote his plans to seize central Africa. At the Berlin Conference, convened by Otto von Bismarck in November 1884, he persuaded the powers that he would do philanthropic work and not tax trade. On 29 May 1885 he announced the name Congo Free State. Leopold ruled it from Brussels and never visited.

Leopold held the title Sovereign of the Congo Free State. He could not meet the costs of the state and set up a system to maximise revenue. Land without a habitation or cultivated plot was declared vacant and belonged to the state, and communities had to deliver set quotas of rubber and ivory. By the late 1890s wild rubber far surpassed ivory as the main revenue, and it peaked in 1903. Failure to meet rubber quotas was punishable by death, and soldiers of the Force Publique had to bring in the hand of each person they shot, so that quotas were in part paid in severed hands.

A reduction of the population between the start of Leopold's control and 1908 is noted by all who compared the two dates, but estimates of the death toll vary considerably. Some contemporary observers suggest a decrease by half. Roger Casement named war, starvation, reduced births and disease as the main causes. Joseph Conrad's Heart of Darkness, published in 1899, and the Congo Reform Association, founded by Casement and E. D. Morel, drew international opposition.

Under international pressure the Belgian Parliament reluctantly annexed the state on 15 November 1908 as the colony of the Belgian Congo, and Leopold died in Brussels on 17 December 1909. The state included the entire area of the present Democratic Republic of the Congo. Whether the killing amounts to genocide is debated: Adam Hochschild wrote that it was of genocidal proportions but not strictly speaking a genocide, while Robert G. Weisbord argued that the conditions would qualify under the UN convention.
congo-ocean-railway: The line runs 502 kilometres from the Atlantic port of Pointe-Noire to Brazzaville and bypasses the rapids of the lower Congo River, so that from Brazzaville river boats can go up the Congo and its tributaries, including the Oubangui River to Bangui. It is built to a gauge of 1,067 mm and includes the 1,690-metre Bamba tunnel and 14 large reinforced concrete viaducts, with gradients of up to 1 in 50. The first locomotives were 2-8-2 tender engines and articulated tank engines with six driving axles.

In 1921 the French colonial administration contracted the Société de Construction des Batignolles to build the railway with forced labour recruited from what is now southern Chad and the Central African Republic. Workers suffered rampant physical abuse, poor housing and hygiene and extreme deprivation, and deaths from industrial accidents and diseases such as malaria are estimated at more than 17,000 by the time construction ended in 1934. Resentment of conscripted labour and other oppression led to the Kongo-Wara rebellion of 1928 to 1931. France did not ratify the International Labour Organization's Forced Labour Convention of 1930 until 1946.

In 1962 a branch was built to Mbinda near the border with Gabon to meet the COMILOG Cableway and carry manganese ore to Pointe-Noire; the cableway closed in 1986, when Gabon built its own railway, but the branch stayed in use. The line closed for six years from the start of the civil war in 1997 and reopened in 2004. On 21 June 2010 a derailment between Bilinga and Tchitondi threw four carriages into a ravine and killed at least 60 people. A passenger train, La Gazelle, with Korean-manufactured passenger cars, was introduced in 2012, and ten diesel locomotives from Electro-Motive Diesel entered service in 2015. The railway is a state-owned enterprise.
congo-reform-association: In the mid-1890s Edmund Dene Morel, a shipping clerk for Elder Dempster in Antwerp, noticed that steady exports of firearms and cartridges to the Congo were matched by vast imports of rubber and ivory, and concluded that no real trade was taking place and that the goods were extracted by force. He resigned in 1901 and founded the West African Mail in 1903, drawing on missionaries, travellers and former agents of the Congo Free State and its concession companies. The Aborigine Protection Society under Henry Fox Bourne and Sir Charles Dilke MP had already denounced the regime.

A parliamentary debate in 1903 led the Foreign Office to send Roger Casement, its consul at Boma, into the interior. From June 1903 he recorded the testimony of victims and saw the mutilations himself. His report of 1904 confirmed the scale of the atrocities, though officials softened it and removed the names of witnesses and perpetrators. Disillusioned, Casement turned to Morel, and the two founded the association.

Morel led the campaign as a non-partisan and Christian cause and won the support of church leaders, businessmen, peers and MPs; Casement, as an official, stayed out of direct involvement. Regional branches spread across Britain, and lectures used the magic lantern to show photographs of the atrocities. The missionaries John and Alice Harris gave some six hundred public talks in two years. The historian Felix Lösing has argued that racist dynamics, rather than evangelical philanthropy or humanitarian feeling, were the main reason for its success, since activists warned that the atrocities threatened imperial rule across Africa.

An American Congo Reform Association, led by Baptist missionaries and the academic Robert E. Park and backed by Booker T. Washington and Mark Twain, ran a parallel campaign. Leopold answered with a covert Press Bureau, which the Kowalsky Scandal of December 1906 exposed. On 23 January 1908 Britain and the United States jointly demanded that Belgium annex the territory, which it did later that year.

Reform after annexation was slow and gradual. When Britain recognised the Belgian Congo in 1913, the association publicly disbanded on 16 June 1913, Morel declaring that the native of the Congo was once more a free man, although he and the movement knew this was not so.
congo-river: The Congo River, formerly also called the Zaire, is the only major river to cross the equator twice. Its basin covers about 4 million square kilometres and ten countries, around 13 percent of Africa; the Chambeshi River in Zambia is generally taken as its source, and the Lualaba is the river upstream of the Boyoma Falls. From Kisangani it flows north-west, then south-west to Pool Malebo, where Kinshasa and Brazzaville face each other. Below the Pool it falls through the Livingstone Falls, a series of 32 falls and rapids, to the sea at Muanda. Its flow is stable because its basin lies on both sides of the Equator, and it is one of the deepest rivers in the world.

The whole basin is populated by Bantu peoples, whose expansion is estimated to have reached the middle Congo by about 500 BCE. The name Congo comes from the Kingdom of Kongo, once on the southern bank, formed in the late 14th century. The name Zaire is a Portuguese adaptation of the Kikongo nzere, river. European exploration began in 1482, when the Portuguese explorer Diogo Cão found the estuary and made contact with the Kingdom of Kongo. The full course remained unknown throughout the early modern period.

Henry Morton Stanley's expedition of 1876-77 proved that the Lualaba fed the Congo and not the Nile. It reached Boma on 9 August 1877, having most probably lost 132 people to disease, hunger, drowning, killing and desertion. Stanley founded Kinshasa as a trading post in 1881, named Léopoldville for Leopold II of Belgium, who claimed the basin privately as the Congo Free State in 1885.

The Democratic Republic of the Congo and the Republic of the Congo are both named after the river.
