Although the Livingstone Falls block access from the sea, nearly the whole river above them is navigable in sections, especially between Kinshasa and Kisangani, and it remains a lifeline in a land with few roads or railways. Its basin holds the Congo rainforest, the second-largest rainforest area in the world, and almost 800 fish species have been recorded there, many found nowhere else.
congress-of-angostura: The assembly, also called the Second National Congress of Venezuela after the congress of 1811, met during the Venezuelan wars of independence as the congress of the re-established Republic of Venezuela. Much of the country was still under Spanish rule, so elections were held only in the parts of southern Venezuela and Margarita Island held by the patriot forces. Twenty-six delegates represented six Venezuelan provinces; representatives of Casanare, the only liberated province of New Granada, chosen from exiles fighting beside the Venezuelan patriots, joined later.

Not all of the proposals in Bolívar's Address at Angostura were accepted. The congress rejected his plan for an exalted ceremonial president for life governing through ministers answerable to parliament, a hereditary senate on the British model, and a fourth, moral branch of government loosely modelled on the Classical Areopagus. Its chief work was the Venezuelan Constitution of 1819, adopted on 15 August, which was soon made obsolete. Francisco Antonio Zea was chosen vice president, Juan Germán Roscio vice president for Venezuela and Francisco de Paula Santander for Cundinamarca.

The Fundamental Law of the Republic of Colombia, enacted on 17 December 1819, had fourteen articles. It declared Venezuela and New Granada united in one republic out of necessity and mutual interest, joined their debts, and divided the state into three departments, Venezuela, Cundinamarca and Quito, with capitals at Caracas, Bogotá and Quito. A new capital was to bear Bolívar's name, the flag would take the Venezuelan colours, and a congress would meet at Rosario de Cúcuta in January 1821 to write a constitution. The republic was to be proclaimed with public celebrations on 25 December 1819.

Zea, as president of the congress, and the secretary Diego de Vallenilla signed the law, with deputies including Manuel Cedeño and Diego Bautista Urbaneja, and Bolívar approved its publication. Historians call the new state Gran Colombia to tell it apart from the present Republic of Colombia; its constitution was drawn up at the Congress of Cúcuta in August 1821.
congress-of-berlin: The Treaty of San Stefano of March 1878, which ended the Russo-Turkish War of 1877-1878, created a large Principality of Bulgaria as an autonomous vassal of the sultan. This extended Russian influence over the Balkans and alarmed the other powers. Britain saw the entire Mediterranean as its sphere of influence, and Austria-Hungary wanted Habsburg control over the Balkans. Otto von Bismarck therefore called the Congress and presided over it as an impartial mediator, since Germany stood to gain nothing from the crisis. Before it opened, Britain concluded the Cyprus Convention on 4 June 1878, a secret alliance with the Ottomans that let Britain occupy Cyprus.

The Congress met from 13 June to 13 July 1878 at Bismarck's Reich Chancellery in Berlin. Britain, Austria-Hungary, France, Germany, Italy, Russia and the Ottoman Empire were members. Delegates from Greece, Romania, Serbia and Montenegro attended only the sessions that concerned their states. The Congress revised or eliminated 18 of the 29 articles of the Treaty of San Stefano.

Romania, Serbia and Montenegro were recognised as independent. Romania received Northern Dobruja but had to give Southern Bessarabia to Russia. Bulgaria was divided into the Principality of Bulgaria, with nominal autonomy under the Ottomans, and Eastern Rumelia, an autonomous province under a Christian ruler. Macedonia stayed under the Ottoman Empire. Austria-Hungary was given the administration of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the right to garrison the Sanjak of Novi Pazar, and Britain took over the administration of Cyprus.

The result was at first hailed as a success for peace, but most participants were dissatisfied. Russia, which had won the war, felt humiliated, and Gorchakov called the Treaty of Berlin the darkest page of his life. Bulgaria was left with less than half the territory planned at San Stefano. The Serbs resented Russia's consent to the Austrian administration of Bosnia, and Bismarck was hated by Russian nationalists. The League of the Three Emperors was destroyed. Historians see the settlement as having sown the seeds of the Balkan Wars of 1912 and 1913 and the First World War.
congress-of-chilpancingo: Miguel Hidalgo had called for a National Congress in a manifesto of 15 December 1810, but his government at Guadalajara ended after the defeat at Calderón Bridge on 17 January 1811. On 19 August 1811 insurgent generals at Zitácuaro set up the Suprema Junta Nacional Americana under Ignacio López Rayón, which still claimed to defend the authority of Ferdinand VII. Driven out by Félix María Calleja in January 1812 and divided between Rayón and those, like José María Morelos, who wanted a clear break with the monarchy, the Junta was nearly dissolved by August 1813, when Morelos called a congress of provincial representatives.

Morelos raised Chilpancingo to the rank of a city, and the Congress was installed in its parish church of Santa María de la Asunción. Since full elections could not be held, it combined elected deputies such as José Manuel de Herrera with members of the old Junta and substitutes named by Morelos, among them Carlos María de Bustamante, José María Cos and Andrés Quintana Roo. In his opening address Morelos linked 14 September 1813 to the fall of Mexico-Tenochtitlan in 1521 and presented the Sentimientos de la Nación, a 23-point programme of independence, popular sovereignty, division of powers, the end of slavery and castes, and the Catholic religion alone. Offered the title of His Serene Highness, he chose to be called Servant of the Nation.

The Act of 6 November 1813, drafted mainly by Bustamante, declared the permanent end of dependence on the Spanish throne. Royalist pressure then made the Congress itinerant, and at Apatzingán it sanctioned the Constitution of 22 October 1814, which set up a republic with a strong legislature and a three-member executive, first held by Morelos, José María Liceaga and Cos.

At Puruarán in July 1815 the Congress decreed the first national symbols: a seal with an eagle on a nopal holding a snake, and flags for war, parley and commerce. A letter asked President James Madison to recognise América Mexicana, but no recognition followed. On 6 September 1815, at Uruapan, the Congress created the Junta Subalterna, which outlived it as the insurgents' last organised government, moving between places such as Taretan, Ario and the fort of Jaujilla, until around 1820 it handed its authority to Vicente Guerrero before the Plan of Iguala.
congress-of-cucuta: The congress grew out of the rebuilding of republican government in the last phase of the Spanish American wars of independence. In the Spanish reconquest of 1815–1816 the United Provinces of New Granada collapsed and the viceroyalty was restored under Pablo Morillo, who by the end of 1816 had eliminated most of the republican leaders in Santafé. Resistance survived in peripheral regions such as Casanare, whose army later crossed the Andes in Bolívar's campaign to liberate New Granada in 1819. A separate republic continued in Venezuela, where the Congress of Angostura met in 1819 with only Casanare represented from New Granada.

The union of New Granada and Venezuela was first proclaimed at Angostura in 1819 and reaffirmed, with reservations and changes, by an assembly in Bogotá in 1820. Bolívar drew the new state's borders on the principle of uti possidetis, so Panama and Ecuador were included as parts of the old Viceroyalty of New Granada, although neither sent deputies; Bogotá, Caracas and Quito were to be regional capitals.

Formally the General Congress of Colombia, it was installed by Antonio Nariño and brought together deputies of New Granada and Venezuela to ratify the union. When its sessions began, most of the territory was already independent of Spain, except southern Colombia and Ecuador. The constitution it wrote set out the law of the republic and fixed its capital and boundaries.

At 11 o'clock on the morning of 3 October 1821 Bolívar entered the chamber, then in the sacristy of the parish church of Villa del Rosario de Cúcuta, accompanied by a commission of deputies and his chiefs of staff. Seated beside the speaker while the assembly stood, he was sworn in as president of the Republic of Colombia, made up of Venezuela and Cundinamarca, the republican name of New Granada. After his speech and the naming of Santander as vice-president, the text of the constitution was read out.

The congress gave the new republic its constitutional organisation and set principles on which republican institutions would replace those inherited from three centuries of Spanish rule. The places connected with it, together with the House of Santander, are now protected as part of the Park of the Great Colombia.
congress-of-erfurt: The meeting was meant to reaffirm the alliance concluded the previous year at Tilsit after the War of the Fourth Coalition. Napoleon had made an admirer of Alexander there, but by 1808 anti-French feeling at the Russian court was beginning to threaten the alliance. Napoleon and his foreign minister, Jean-Baptiste Nompère de Champagny, sought to strengthen it in order to settle affairs in Spain and prepare for the expected war with Austria. Charles Maurice de Talleyrand-Périgord, convinced that Napoleon was leading France to destruction, worked against them.

Erfurt was then under Napoleon's direct control as the Principality of Erfurt, and he set out to impress Alexander with the glories of his empire. The meeting grew into a gathering of kings, princes, dukes, barons and notables from all over Europe. The actor Talma and the whole Comédie-Française presented sixteen French tragedies, and the twenty-year-old Arthur Schopenhauer arrived in Goethe's train and watched the proceedings with a cynical eye.

The outcome was the Erfurt Convention of fourteen articles. It called on Britain to end its war against France, recognised the Russian conquest of Finland from Sweden, and stated that in case of war with Austria Russia should aid France "to the best of its ability". The two emperors left for home on 14 October.

The war with Austria began six months later, and Alexander gave France as little help as he could. Erfurt was the last meeting of the two emperors, and by 1810 each was considering war with the other. By 1812 Russia no longer complied with the Continental System, had raised its defence spending and had moved troops to the border to prepare an invasion of Poland; Napoleon struck first and with greater force.

From Tilsit onwards few observers believed the two powers could live side by side with the Grand Duchy of Warsaw, a French satellite, on Russia's border. Erfurt may have delayed the war, but conflict between them was likely in the end. Leo Tolstoy refers to the congress in War and Peace.
congress-of-gniezno: Bishop Adalbert of Prague died in 997 on a mission to the pagan Prussians and was quickly canonised through the joint efforts of Duke Bolesław I and Emperor Otto III, becoming the first Slavic bishop to be made a saint. Bolesław bought his body back from the Prussians for its weight in gold and placed it in a tomb at Gniezno Cathedral. According to Thietmar of Merseburg, Otto, Adalbert's friend and pupil, made a pilgrimage there as part of his plan to renew the empire on a federal basis, the renovatio imperii Romanorum, with Poland and Hungary as its eastern partners.

Bolesław received the emperor at the Polish border on the Bóbr river near Małomice, and Bishop Unger of Poznań escorted him to Gniezno. There, according to the Gesta principum Polonorum of Gallus Anonymus, written in 1115, Otto named Bolesław frater et cooperator Imperii, brother and partner of the empire, and populi Romani amicus et socius. Whether this raised Bolesław to the rank of king has not been established; he had himself crowned at Gniezno Cathedral in 1025.

Adalbert's brother Radzim Gaudenty became the first archbishop, and the new sees went to Bishop Poppo at Kraków, Bishop Jan at Wrocław and Bishop Reinbern at Kołobrzeg. Otto gave Bolesław a replica of the Holy Lance and received an arm of Saint Adalbert. Bolesław then accompanied the emperor to Charlemagne's grave at Aachen, where he received Charlemagne's throne, and the two arranged the betrothal of Bolesław's son Mieszko II Lambert to Otto's niece Richeza of Lotharingia.

Otto's death in 1002 left his policy unfinished. His successor, King Henry II, changed course, and Bolesław's expansion into Lusatia and Bohemia led to a German–Polish War that ended with the Peace of Bautzen in 1018. The see of Kołobrzeg was overthrown by a pagan resurgence around 1007. Scholars debate whether Poznań stayed under the pope or went to Magdeburg, but the congress is generally seen as freeing the Polish church from Magdeburg, and the archdiocese of Gniezno, subject directly to the Holy See, kept Poland independent of the empire throughout the Middle Ages.
congress-of-lushnje: After the First World War the Congress of Durrës, on 25 December 1918, set up a provisional government under Turhan Pashë Përmeti. It could not extend its authority over the borders set by the Treaty of London of 1913 while General Piacentini's Italian forces remained, and it was willing to accept Italian protection to keep Albania whole. In July 1919 the secret Venizelos–Tittoni agreement traded concessions over Albanian territory, and on 20 August 1919 an Italian-Albanian agreement accepted an Italian high commissioner, Captain Fortunato Castoldi, to oversee the administration in the most sensitive matters.

Many Albanians saw this as a curtailment of independence, and revolts broke out across much of the country. On 14 January 1920 David Lloyd George, Georges Clémenceau and Francesco Nitti signed an agreement at the Paris Peace Conference to partition Albania among Greece, Montenegro and Serbia. Nationalists of a secret group, the Krahu Kombëtar, had meanwhile been planning a second congress to replace the government.

The Durrës government tried to stop the meeting. On 15 January 1920 the prefect of Durrës, Abdyl Ypi, one of its organisers, was shot dead, and the finance minister, Fejzi Alizoti, ordered that delegates from the north be kept from travelling; many delegates went straight from Ypi's funeral to Lushnjë. A militia of about 1200 men sent on Italian orders to disperse the gathering instead agreed with Meleq Frashëri not to interfere. The 56 delegates, from Albania, neighbouring Albanian-inhabited lands and emigrant communities, met at the house of Kaso Fuga, with Aqif Elbasani as president and Ferid Vokopola as secretary.

The congress declared the Durrës government invalid, resolved on armed resistance to the Italian forces and formed a new cabinet under Sulejman Delvina. Leadership of the state passed to a High Council of Luigj Bumçi, Aqif Pashë Elbasani, Abdi Toptani and Mihal Turtulli, while a National Council elected by the delegates acted as parliament, sitting from 27 March to 20 December 1920.

The decisions led a few months later to the Vlora War, the total withdrawal of the Italian army and the final affirmation of Albania's territorial integrity in 1921. The congress is regarded as the most important meeting of Albanian political leaders since the Declaration of Independence of 28 November 1912, and the building where it met became a museum in 1970.
congress-of-panama: Simón Bolívar called the congress from Lima on 7 December 1824, and José Faustino Sánchez Carrión, Peru's Minister of Government and Foreign Relations, who shared his ideal of Hispanic American unity, sent the invitations. Its other name, the Amphictyonic Congress, honoured the Amphictyonic League of Ancient Greece. Its aim was a common policy of the new republics towards the Spanish Empire: it proposed a league with a shared military and diplomatic policy, a mutual defence pact and a plan to liberate Cuba and Puerto Rico, but never the formation of a unitary state.

Chile and the United Provinces of South America declined to attend, out of mistrust of Bolívar's influence; the Empire of Brazil stayed away, expecting a hostile reception during its war with Argentina over present-day Uruguay; and isolationist Paraguay was not invited. Bolívar also invited the United Kingdom and the Netherlands as observers, for their commercial interests in Hispanic America.

The British observer, Edward James Dawkins, had orders from George Canning to seek trade agreements and to dissuade Gran Colombia and Mexico from backing expeditions to free Cuba or Puerto Rico from Spain. The Dutch envoy, Jan van Veer, came to offer mediation between the republics and Spain, but lacked accreditation, and since the Dutch monarchy recognised none of the republics he was received only as an individual.

Bolívar's project soon foundered amid civil war in Gran Colombia, the disintegration of Central America and the rise of nationalism, while the United Kingdom secured many favourable trade deals at the congress. In the United States, President John Quincy Adams and Secretary of State Henry Clay wanted to take part, but politicians from the Southern United States, wary of republics that had mostly outlawed slavery, held up the funds and the confirmation of the delegates. Richard C. Anderson Jr. died on the way to Panama, and John Sergeant arrived only after the discussions had ended.
congress-of-peoples-deputies-of-russia: The Congress was created by an amendment to the constitution of the RSFSR on 27 October 1989 and first met on 16 May 1990. It officially had 1,068 deputies, 900 elected from territorial districts in proportion to population and 168 from national-territorial districts, and two thirds had to be present for a quorum. It alone could adopt and amend the constitution, approve the prime minister, call referendums and impeach the president. Between its sessions, held in the Grand Kremlin Palace, a Supreme Soviet of 252 deputies that it elected passed laws, 333 in all.

At the first session 86% of the deputies were members of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union. Some 24 factions formed, grouped into a Communist bloc and a Democratic Russia bloc, which at first held the majority.

Yeltsin twice fell short of the 531 votes needed before he was elected chairman on 29 May 1990 with 535, after Mikhail Gorbachev had spoken against him. After a referendum of 17 March 1991 created a presidency, Yeltsin won the election of 12 June 1991 and was sworn in before the Congress on 10 July; Ruslan Khasbulatov became chairman on 29 October. On 1 November 1991 the Congress gave the president extraordinary powers for 13 months, and its revisions of the 1978 constitution recorded the renaming of the republic as the Russian Federation on 25 December 1991.

In December 1992 it refused to approve Yegor Gaidar as head of government, and in March 1993 it cancelled the president's extraordinary powers. On 28 March 1993, 617 of 1,033 deputies voted to impeach Yeltsin, short of the two thirds required, and in the referendum of 23 April voters expressed support for him and his policies. Against the Reform Coalition and Democratic Centre stood the Russian Unity and Creative Forces blocs, which together opposed many of his policies.

Decree No. 1400 of 21 September 1993, which dissolved the Congress without constitutional authority, led the deputies to dismiss Yeltsin and approve Vice-President Alexander Rutskoy as head of state, and the standoff brought street fighting to Moscow. Pro-presidential forces stormed the White House on 4 October 1993. A new constitution was approved by referendum on 12 December 1993, when the Federal Assembly was elected, and in February 1994 that assembly declared an amnesty for the conflict.
congress-of-peoples-deputies-of-the-sovi: The Congress was created as part of Mikhail Gorbachev's reform agenda. On 1 July 1988, the last day of the 19th Party Conference, Gorbachev won the delegates' backing for a last-minute proposal for a new supreme legislative body. Frustrated by the old guard's resistance to liberalisation, he turned to amending the 1977 Constitution in order to separate party and state and so isolate his conservative opponents.

Detailed proposals were published for public consultation on 2 October 1988, and in a session from 29 November to 1 December 1988 the Supreme Soviet enacted the amendments and a law on electoral reform and set the election for 26 March 1989. The new body was to be the de facto successor of the Congress of Soviets of the Soviet Union, which had existed from 1922 until 1936.

The Congress had 2,250 deputies, elected in three ways: 750 by the system used for the Soviet of the Union, 750 by that used for the Soviet of Nationalities, and 750 representing public organisations such as the Communist Party, the Komsomol and the trade unions.

It was to meet twice a year and elect a smaller Supreme Soviet of 542 deputies, replacing the old one of 1,500, to serve as a permanent legislature. The Congress kept the most important matters: amending the constitution, electing the Supreme Soviet and its chairman, ratifying the head of the Council of Ministers, holding referendums, and settling questions of borders and the structure of the union.

On 7 March 1989 a final list of 5,074 candidates was published, about 85 per cent of them members of the Communist Party. 8 per cent, and run-offs and fresh elections followed in April and May. The difference from earlier Soviet elections was that they were competitive, with several candidates allowed for a seat, and the Congress included many political positions, from Communist to pro-Western.

At its first session, from 25 May to 9 June 1989, deputies criticised the state of the Soviet Union in speeches that were televised live and watched by millions; industrial output is said to have declined as people stayed at their screens. Further sessions were held in December 1989 and March 1990. After the attempted coup of August 1991 the Congress dissolved itself on 5 September 1991, passing its powers to the Supreme Soviet and a new State Council, both of which ended with the Soviet Union on 26 December 1991.
congress-of-soviets-of-the-soviet-union: Before 1922 the Soviet republics had signed a number of treaties with one another. By the early 1920s the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic and the Ukrainian, Byelorussian and Azerbaijan Soviet Socialist Republics had taken steps to combine their economic and military strength, which drew them closer politically. The first congress met in Moscow on 30 December 1922 with delegates from the Russian, Ukrainian and Byelorussian republics and the Transcaucasian Socialist Federative Soviet Republic, which joined Azerbaijan, Georgia and Armenia; these four became the founding Union Republics.

Delegates were sent from the soviets of all the republics: one for every 25 thousand voters from the city soviets and one for every 125 thousand inhabitants from the provincial and republic congresses. They were elected at the provincial and autonomous republican congresses of soviets, or directly at the congress of a union republic that had no provincial congresses. The congress set the general direction of all public bodies and elected the Central Executive Committee of the Soviet Union, which answered to it.

Its exclusive powers included concluding treaties, conducting diplomacy and declaring war, establishing a union citizenship, settling disputes between republics, coining money and running the postal service, drawing up a general plan for the national economy, directing transport, the telegraph and foreign trade, admitting new republics and amending the constitution. The only chairman of its presidium was Mikhail Kalinin.

The Second Congress met in January 1924, a few days after Lenin's death, to ratify the first Constitution of the Soviet Union; it heard Stalin swear to Lenin that his commandment would be fulfilled with honour. The Uzbek and Turkmen Soviet Socialist Republics were admitted in 1924, and the Tadzhik republic became a Union Republic in 1929. Further congresses met in 1925 and 1927. At the Seventh Congress, in February 1935, Stalin proposed constitutional reform, and the congress voted for secret and direct voting, equal representation of town and country and a constitutional commission. The Extraordinary Eighth Congress of November and December 1936 ratified the new constitution and dissolved itself.
congress-of-troppau: The congress met on 20 October 1820 to discuss how to suppress the revolution in Naples of July 1820. Tsar Alexander I of Russia and Emperor Francis I of Austria attended in person, and King Frederick William III of Prussia was represented by the crown prince, the future Frederick William IV. The three eastern powers were also represented by their foreign ministers, among them Prince Metternich for Austria and Prince Hardenberg for Prussia.

Britain objected on principle to joint action against the Neapolitan liberals and sent no plenipotentiary, only Lord Stewart, its ambassador in Vienna and half-brother of the Foreign Secretary, Viscount Castlereagh. France also gave its representatives no full powers, though its policy was less clearly defined, so a division between the eastern and western powers was plain from the start. The meeting was intimate and informal. In a three-hour conversation over tea at a small inn, Alexander told Metternich that he deplored all he had said and done between 1814 and 1818 and asked what Metternich wanted of him.

With the three eastern courts in agreement, the views of Britain and France, whose governments were bound by constitutional forms, could be set aside. Their representatives were kept out of a series of conferences on the ground that they could only report, not decide, and the preliminary protocol was signed by Austria, Russia and Prussia on 8 November; the Troppau Protocol itself was signed on 19 November 1820. It declared that states changed by revolution in a way that threatened others ceased to be members of the European Alliance, and that the powers would bring them back, by peaceful means or if need be by arms.

The powers made no immediate effort to apply the protocol, and the conferences were adjourned after its announcement, to resume at the Congress of Laibach the following January. In Britain the protocol was received with dismay. The government was reluctant to attack it openly but found it hard to answer the opposition's claim that, read literally, it entitled Russia or Austria to invade England over its rule of Ireland; one opposition member asked whether a horde of Cossacks would be seen encamped in Hyde Park.
congress-of-tucuman: After the May Revolution of 1810 replaced the viceroy with the Primera Junta, the provinces moved towards full independence, but royalist forces from the Viceroyalty of Peru held the upper hand in Upper Peru and threatened the revolution. On 15 April 1815 a revolt ended the rule of Carlos María de Alvear and called a general congress. Each deputy represented 15,000 inhabitants, and the provinces of Upper Peru, now Bolivia, sent delegates. The Banda Oriental, today Uruguay, and the other provinces of the Liga Federal loyal to José Gervasio Artigas had their deputies rejected on formalities, and Paraguay, already independent, stayed apart.

The congress opened on 24 March 1816 in the house of Francisca Bazán de Laguna, with 33 deputies and a presidency that rotated each month; free to set its own agenda, it debated at length. On 9 July, under the presidency of Francisco Narciso de Laprida of San Juan Province, it declared the independence of the United Provinces of South America, a name meant to draw in other independence movements of Spanish America that had no deputies there. Among the signatories were Juan José Paso and Tomás Godoy Cruz. Later debates turned on the form of government and where the congress and the executive should sit.

From 1817 the congress sat in Buenos Aires, and its constitution of 1819 was rejected. It was dissolved in 1820, after the Federal League provinces of Santa Fe and Entre Ríos defeated a weakened army of the Directorship at the Battle of Cepeda, which carried the conflict between centralists and federalists onto the battlefield. The house where independence was declared was rebuilt and is now a museum and monument, the House of Tucumán.
congress-of-vienna: The Congress of Vienna was a series of diplomatic meetings held from September 1814 to June 1815 to agree a new layout for the European order after the fall of Napoleon Bonaparte. It was chaired by the Austrian statesman Klemens von Metternich. Its aim was a long-term peace: the main powers were to be resized so that they could balance each other. Conservative leaders such as Metternich also wished to restrain Bonapartist, republican and liberal movements. More than 200 states and princely houses were represented, and much business was done informally at salons, banquets and balls.

The four victorious powers, Austria, the United Kingdom, Prussia and Russia, hoped to exclude France, but Talleyrand made himself part of the inner councils. The hardest question was the Polish-Saxon crisis, since Russia wanted most of Poland and Prussia all of Saxony. Austria and Britain opposed this, and on 3 January 1815 they and France signed a treaty promising war on Russia and Prussia if necessary. The Final Act was signed on 9 June 1815, nine days before the Battle of Waterloo.

Russia received most of the Duchy of Warsaw, Prussia three-fifths of Saxony and land on the Rhine, and Austria Lombardy-Venetia. A German Confederation of 39 states replaced the nearly 300 states of the former Holy Roman Empire. The Netherlands and the Southern Netherlands were united as a kingdom under the House of Orange-Nassau. The Congress gave rise to the Concert of Europe. Critics have judged the settlement a reaction that ignored national and liberal movements. Others, among them Henry Kissinger and Paul Schroeder, credit it with preventing a widespread European war from 1815 to 1914.
congreve-rocket: Tipu Sultan of Mysore employed up to 5,000 artillerymen who specialised in rockets with cases of hammered iron, which could travel almost 1,000 yards, while rockets in Europe had no iron case and a shorter reach. Several of these rockets were sent to Great Britain after 1799. William Congreve began work in 1804 by buying the best rockets on the London market, which reached only 600 yards. After experiments at his own expense, and then at the Woolwich Arsenal's laboratory with the permission of Lord Chatham, he was producing 32-pounder rockets with a range of 3,000 yards by the spring of 1806.

The cases, first of cardboard, were made of sheet iron by 1806. The propellant used the ingredients of gunpowder, and a wooden stick fixed to the side steadied the flight. Warheads were incendiary, explosive or filled with shot, and the rockets could be fired from a frame, a tripod or even a sloping bank.

The Royal Navy was the main user in the Napoleonic Wars, and the Royal Marine Artillery became expert in the weapon; the army formed two Rocket Troops of the Royal Horse Artillery on 1 January 1814. The first attack on Boulogne in 1804 failed in strong winds, and the second Boulogne expedition is usually counted the first success. In the War of 1812 rockets were used against Lewes, Delaware, in April 1813 and helped rout the American forces at the Battle of Bladensburg, which led to the burning of Washington, D.C. They served at the bombardment of Algiers in 1816, against fighting elephants in the First Anglo-Burmese War in 1825, and in the Opium Wars, the Crimean War and the Indian Rebellion of 1857.

Other states took them up. Captain Józef Bem experimented with them in the Kingdom of Poland, and Polish rocketeers broke Russian cavalry charges at the Battle of Olszynka Grochowska on 25 February 1831. Paraguay fired them in several battles of the war of 1865–1870.

Rockets were quick to set up and fire, and their shrill whistle and smoke trails could make horses bolt, but wind and instability scattered them by hundreds of yards and duds were frequent. They remained in regular use until the 1850s, when William Hale's spinning design replaced them, and from the 1870s they carried rescue lines to ships in distress.
conimbriga: Conímbriga lies on a triangular spur above two deep valleys, 2 kilometres from Condeixa-a-Nova and 16 kilometres from Coimbra, the Roman Aeminium. Its name joins conim, the local word for a place of rocky eminence, with the Celtic suffix briga, citadel. It stood where the road from Olisipo to Bracara Augusta passed by way of Aeminium. Occupation began in the 9th century BCE with the Castro culture, and before the Romans the Conii people lived there.

Romans arrived around 139 BCE with the campaigns of Decimus Junius Brutus, and Romanisation was quick. Under Vespasian, between 69 and 79 CE, the town became a municipium, a new forum, baths and street plan were laid out, and settler families from the Italian peninsula intermarried with local ones. Its houses included the Casa dos Repuxos and the House of Cantaber, the largest known private residence on the site, with 40 rooms and a hypocaust. A paleo-Christian basilica was built later, in a converted house.

Between 465 and 468 the Sueves destroyed the city and its people dispersed, some taken into slavery. Cantaber, its leading aristocrat in the 5th century, is said to have been murdered in his own house, and his wife and children sold as slaves. A bishopric was founded between 561 and 572 under its first bishop Lucêncio, but by 589 the see had moved to Aeminium.

Conímbriga, a National Monument since 1910, is not the largest Roman city in Portugal but the best preserved, and archaeologists estimated in 2005 that only 10 percent of it had been excavated. Its rough walls, about 1,500 metres long, were built from large reused blocks. Systematic excavation began after the state acquired land in 1930, a Monographic Museum opened in 1962, and from 1964 a mission with the University of Bordeaux under J. Bairrão Oleiro, Robert Étienne and Jorge de Alarcão uncovered the centre of the town. The amphitheatre was identified in 1993.
conn-of-the-hundred-battles: In medieval tradition Conn was the son of Fedlimid Rechtmar. The Annals of the Four Masters relate that on the night of his birth five roads to Tara, never seen before, were discovered. The Lebor Gabála Érenn says he took power by killing his predecessor Cathair Mór, while other sources name Dáire Doimthech as the king before him. The Lia Fáil, the coronation stone at Tara said to roar under the rightful king, roared under Conn for the first time since Cúchulainn had split it. In the saga Baile in Scáil, Lugh and a woman who is the sovereignty of Ireland foretell to Conn the length of his reign and the kings who will follow him.

The versions of the Lebor Gabála give his reign as twenty, twenty-five, thirty-five or even fifty years, much of it spent at war with Mug Nuadat, king of Munster. In the medieval text Cath Maige Leana, Conn defeated and killed Mug Nuadat's father, Mug Neit, and Mug Nuadat escaped by sea to Beare Island and then to Spain. Nine years later he landed with an army near Bantry Bay and forced Conn into a treaty dividing Ireland: Leth Cuinn, Conn's half in the north, and Leth Moga, Mug's half in the south, with the border running from Galway to Dublin.

After fifteen years of peace Mug Nuadat broke the treaty, and Conn destroyed his army in a surprise night attack at Mag Leana, near Tullamore in County Offaly, where Mug Nuadat was killed. Geoffrey Keating tells the war differently, with Conn killing his rival in his bed in an early morning attack. A medieval source sets the birth of the hero Fionn mac Cumhaill in Conn's time, and Conn later made Fionn head of the fianna. Of Conn's two sons, Connla went with a fairy woman to Mag Mell, and Art was known afterwards as Óenfer, the lone.

The Lebor Gabála, Baile in Scáil and the Annals say Conn was defeated in battle in Túath Amrois by Tipraite Tírech, king of the Ulaid, while Keating and the Great Book of Lecan have Tipraite send fifty warriors dressed as women from Emain Macha to kill him at Tara. His son-in-law Conaire Cóem succeeded him as High King, and his son Art later reigned after him. The Lebor Gabála places his reign in the time of the Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius (161–180), Keating's Foras Feasa ar Éirinn dates it to 116–136 and the Annals of the Four Masters to 122–157.
connachta: The Irish word for a province, cúige, earlier cóiced, literally fifth, points to a prehistoric pentarchy of the Connachta, the Ulaid, the Laigin, the region of Mumu and the central kingdom of Mide. By the early 5th century this order seems to have broken up, as the Ulaid were reduced and new Connachta dynasties expanded north and east. Medieval tradition traced them to the sons of Eochaid Mugmedon: Brion, Ailill, Fiachrae, Fergus Caech, perhaps a literary addition, and Niall of the Nine Hostages.

David Sproule argued that the name may first have meant headship or supremacy, from cond or conn, head, and that Conn Cétchathach himself was derived from the name Connacht rather than the reverse. Historians such as Paul Byrne have accepted this view.

The descendants of Brión, Fiachrae and Ailill were known as the Three Connachta of the province itself, the line of Ailill later being replaced by the Uí Maine. Niall's descendants, the Uí Néill, at first surpassed their parent dynasty, holding the so-called High Kingship of Ireland at Tara, and remained the most powerful dynasty in Ireland down to early modern times. The lands of the Connachta also took in at times parts of southern and western Ulster and northern Leinster, and their traditional capital was Cruachan, now Rathcroghan in County Roscommon.

In the sagas of the Ulster Cycle the Connachta, ruled from Cruachan by King Ailill mac Máta and Queen Medb, are the enemies of the Ulaid of Conchobar mac Nessa at Emain Macha, and their wars, above all the Táin Bó Cúailnge, frame most of the stories. As the sagas are set around the time of Christ while Conn was placed in the 2nd century, later texts gave the province older names. The saga tradition is older than that chronology, however, and may rest on real wars between the two peoples; Kenneth H. Jackson dated the origin of the Ulster saga to the 4th century.
connecticut: Connecticut is bordered by Long Island Sound to the south, New York to the west, Massachusetts to the north and Rhode Island to the east. It is named after the Connecticut River, the longest in New England, which roughly bisects the state. The river's name derives from anglicised spellings of Quinnetuket, a Mohegan-Pequot word for long tidal river. Many coastal towns lie less than 20 feet above sea level, and because the coast is on Long Island Sound, an estuary, it is relatively protected from high storm waves.

Evidence of human presence dates back 10,000 years. The peoples were semi-nomadic and shared Algonquian languages. In the early 17th century about 8,000 Pequots lived in the south-east, a number roughly halved by the smallpox epidemic of 1633–34, and 1,500 to 2,500 Mohegans lived west of the Thames. Their economies combined hunting, shellfishing, gathering and maize agriculture, and wampum from quahog and whelk shells served as currency and as a record of agreements.

In 1633 the Dutch West India Company established a short-lived settlement, House of Hope, in Hartford. The Dutch colony of New Netherland initially claimed half of Connecticut, but the English founded the first major settlements at about the same time. Thomas Hooker led followers from the Massachusetts Bay Colony to form the Connecticut Colony, and the Saybrook and New Haven Colonies, founded by other settlers from Massachusetts, had both merged into it by the mid-1660s. The Fundamental Orders of 1638–39 framed its first government, and King Charles II granted a charter in 1662.

Connecticut was one of the Thirteen Colonies that rejected British rule. At the Constitutional Convention of 1787 its delegates Roger Sherman and Oliver Ellsworth proposed the Connecticut Compromise, a bicameral Congress with proportional representation in the House and equal representation of the states in the Senate. In January 1788 Connecticut became the fifth state to ratify the Constitution. Hartford became the sole capital in 1875; before then New Haven and Hartford alternated.

Hartford is the capital and Bridgeport the most populous city. Connecticut is the third-smallest state by area. Its nickname, the Constitution State, was adopted in 1959. Yale University stands in New Haven, and the United States Coast Guard Academy in New London.
connecticut-river: The Connecticut River flows roughly south for 406 miles (653 km) through four states. It rises from Fourth Connecticut Lake, a small pond 300 yards south of the Canadian border in Pittsburg, New Hampshire, and for 255 miles forms the border between New Hampshire and Vermont. After the last ice age the middle valley lay at the bottom of Lake Hitchcock, and its rich, almost rockless soil comes from that lake's sediments. The name is a corruption of the Mohegan word quinetucket and the Nipmuc kwinitekw, meaning beside the long, tidal river. Because of large shifting sandbars at its mouth, it is the only major river in the northeastern United States without a port there.

Archaeology shows human habitation of the valley for 6,000 years before the present. The Pequots dominated the southern part, from the river's mouth to just below Middletown, and kept an uneasy stand-off with their rivals the Mohegans. In 1614 the Dutch explorer Adriaen Block became the first European to chart the river, which he called the Fresh River and claimed for the Netherlands as the northeastern border of New Netherland. Dutch traders built a fortified post at the site of Hartford in 1623. Puritan groups followed: settlers from Plymouth Colony founded Windsor after 1632, a group from Watertown in the Massachusetts Bay Colony founded Wethersfield in 1633, and Hartford and Springfield were established in 1635 and 1636.

The valley's fertile soil and central position made it the object of centuries of border disputes. Springfield broke away from the Connecticut Colony in 1641, which brought the Massachusetts Bay Colony to the river. The Treaty of Paris of 1783 set the border between New Hampshire and the Province of Canada at the northwesternmost headwaters of the Connecticut. Several streams fit that description, and the dispute produced the short-lived Indian Stream Republic, from 1832 to 1835.

The river's numerous falls powered mills and waterwheels, and industry grew up on its banks, especially at Springfield and Hartford. From about 1865 the river carried massive logging drives to sawmills, and these spring drives stopped after 1915, with a final drive in 1918. In March 1936 a flood destroyed numerous bridges. Its watershed of 11,260 square miles covers parts of five states and one Canadian province, and its valley holds some of the most productive farmland in the northeastern United States.
connemara: Connemara lies on the Atlantic coast of western County Galway. One common definition takes it as most of the county west of Lough Corrib and Galway city, bounded by Killary Harbour, Galway Bay and the Atlantic; narrower ones limit it to the old territory of Conmhaicne Mara in the far north-west, and there is argument about where it ends near Galway city. Its name comes from that tribal name, a branch of the Conmacne who lived by the sea (muir, genitive mara). The Twelve Bens and the Owenglin River, which reaches the sea at Clifden, traditionally divided North from South Connemara. The landscape holds mountains, peninsulas, coves, islands and small lakes.

Clifden, the main town, is surrounded by an area rich in megalithic tombs, and Connemara green marble, found between Streamstown and Lissoughter, was a trade treasure in prehistoric times. The wider area was a sovereign kingdom called Iar Connacht under the Ó Flaithbertaigh until it became part of the English-administered Kingdom of Ireland in the 16th century. In the east, the territory called Delbhna Tír Dhá Locha was ruled by kings who claimed descent from the Delbhna and Dál gCais and kinship with Brian Boru; they took the surname Mac Con Raoi, anglicised as Conroy or King.

The Dominican Order had a monastery north of Roundstone before the Suppression of the Monasteries reached the region. Under the Anglo-Irish Blake family, who remained until the 1920s, local memory recalls bad landlords and support for the Irish Church Missions. By contrast, the landlord John D'Arcy (1785-1839), who bankrupted himself and his heirs to found Clifden, is recalled fondly. In the War of Independence the IRA had active companies at places such as Maam, Carraroe and Rosmuc, while the Royal Irish Constabulary held fortified barracks at Clifden, Letterfrack and Leenane. Éamon de Valera addressed a large anti-Treaty rally at Oughterard on 23 April 1922.

Connemara contains most of the Connacht Gaeltacht, the largest Irish-speaking area in Ireland, with between 20,000 and 24,000 native Irish speakers among about 32,000 people. Its largest settlement is Clifden, and Connemara National Park lies in the north-west. In the Victorian era the district was often called the Irish Highlands, for its likeness to the Scottish Gàidhealtachd. A railway branch from Galway to Clifden ran from 1895 to 1935.
conon: Shortly after the Battle of Notium, Conon took over the Athenian fleet from Alcibiades. The Spartan navarch Callicratidas caught his seventy ships and chased them towards Mytilene on Lesbos, where Conon lost thirty. He drew the other forty onto the beach, but Callicratidas blockaded him by sea and land. Conon slipped a messenger ship out to Athens, and the relief force defeated the Spartans at Arginusae, where Callicratidas was killed. In 405 BCE Conon pursued the fleet of Lysander to the Hellespont, where Lysander held a strong position at Lampsacus; the Athenians fell back to Aegospotami, an open beach without harbours. Alcibiades warned them and advised a move to Sestos, but was apparently ignored.

On the fifth day of the standoff Lysander caught almost the whole Athenian fleet unprepared while the crews had disembarked for their meals. It was generally believed that treachery was involved, but Conon was never implicated. His ship was one of nine that escaped, and he and eight others fled to Evagoras of Cyprus, fearing the judgement of the Athenian people. By 397 BCE the satrap Pharnabazus had persuaded the Persian king Artaxerxes to wage war by sea with a fleet of 300 Phoenician and Cypriot ships, and they found Conon on Cyprus to command it. At Cnidus in 394 BCE the Spartans, under the inexperienced Peisander, were overwhelmingly defeated, and the Aegean cities expelled their Spartan garrisons.

Conon then returned to Athens. Pharnabazus let him keep part of the fleet and supplied money to fortify Piraeus and rebuild the long walls. Athens regained its position as a major power in Greece, though without its empire. The next year the Athenian delegates, Conon among them, protested at Sparta's offer to hand over the cities of Anatolia to Persia, and Tiribazus threw them into prison. Ancient writers give conflicting accounts of his end: some say he was sent inland and put to death, others, probably more likely, that he retired to Cyprus and died there. His son Timotheus later became another prominent general.
conques: Conques lies at the confluence of the rivers Dourdou de Conques and Ouche, in a valley, and takes its name from the Occitan word conca, meaning basin, which comes from the Latin concha, a shell. The village is built on a hillside with narrow medieval streets, so that large vehicles cannot enter the historic centre and most day visitors arrive on foot. It was largely passed by in the nineteenth century and was saved from oblivion by the efforts of a small number of dedicated people. The historic core therefore has very little construction dating from between 1800 and 1950.

The first monastery building at Conques was an eighth-century oratory built by monks fleeing the Saracens in Spain. In the eleventh century the original chapel was destroyed to make way for a much larger church, since the arrival of the relics of Saint Faith, a young woman martyred in the fourth century, had shifted the pilgrimage route from Agen to Conques. A second phase, finished by the end of the eleventh century, added five radiating chapels. A third phase, completed early in the twelfth century, was inspired by the churches of Toulouse and Santiago de Compostela, with galleries over the aisles and a western aisle for the increased pilgrim traffic.

The Abbey Church of Sainte-Foy was added to the UNESCO World Heritage Sites in 1998, as part of the Routes of Santiago de Compostela in France. Conques is counted among Les Plus Beaux Villages de France. On 1 January 2016 it was merged into the new commune of Conques-en-Rouergue. The American author Hannah Green wrote Little Saint, a book about the town and its church, after visiting in 1975.
conquest-of-ceuta: Ceuta, on the Strait of Gibraltar, traded with the Levant, Egypt and Libya, exported coral, and was a haven for Berber pirates who raided Iberian coasts. It controlled one of the outlets of the trans-African gold trade, though by the 15th century it had declined since the 13th. Morocco was in disorder: the Marinids of Fez were at odds with the Nasrids of Granada, and in 1414 the Kingdom of Tlemcen briefly installed a governor of Ceuta before Salah ben Salah ousted him.

King John I prepared the expedition for years in secret, raising loans rather than taxes, which would have required the Cortes. A false embassy to Blanche of Navarre in Sicily stopped at Ceuta to study its defences, and a staged quarrel with William VI, Count of Holland, spread the rumour that Portugal meant to attack Holland.

The fleet numbered about 200 ships and carried as many as 50,000 men, of whom about 19,295 were soldiers, with English, French and German mercenaries among them. At Lagos the royal chaplain João de Xira read the crusade bull and revealed the objective. Winds scattered the ships off Ceuta, and the governor, Salah ben Salah, believing the attack abandoned, dismissed the volunteers who had come to defend the city, leaving only its usual garrison. Ceuta received no help from Sultan Abu Said Uthman III of Fez.

On 21 August 1415 the king was wounded in the leg as he went ashore, and Prince Henry led the landing. With his brother Duarte and about 300 men he drove the defenders back to the Almedina gate, which was breached before it could be shut, and the Portuguese forced their way into the city.

The main mosque was consecrated as a cathedral the same day, and the princes were knighted there. The looting was great but less profitable than the king had hoped; the Count of Barcelos took more than 600 marble and alabaster columns for his residence. Against the wishes of many of his men, John kept the city, set up the Casa de Ceuta to supply it, and left on 2 September 1415.

In 1419 Abu Said Uthman III and Muhammad VIII of Granada besieged Ceuta without success against its captain, Pedro de Meneses. The city became a base for Christian privateering in the western Mediterranean and remained Portuguese until it passed to Spain in 1668.
conquest-of-mecca: In 628 the Quraysh of Mecca and the Muslims of Medina made a ten-year pact, the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah. The Banu Bakr aligned with the Quraysh and the Banu Khuza'ah with the Muslims. Old grievances from the pre-Islamic era, sharpened by a desire for revenge, led to renewed fighting, and the treaty was breached when the Banu Bakr attacked the Banu Khuza'ah.

According to Al-Tabari, three days before the news of the breach arrived, Muhammad told his wife 'Aisha to prepare for a campaign. 'Amr ibn Salim Al-Khuza'i then reached Medina with forty horsemen to seek help for his people. Muhammad summoned all Muslims able to fight and set out, joined on the way by his uncle Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib. Accounts differ on the dates: he is variously said to have left on 2, 6 or 10 Ramadan and to have entered Mecca on 10, 17 or 18, 19 or 20 Ramadan 8 AH.

Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, with Hakim ibn Hizam and Budayl ibn Warqa', went out to learn the Muslims' position and met Abbas, who brought them to Muhammad. Abu Sufyan accepted Islam, and Muhammad declared that whoever took refuge in Abu Sufyan's house, stayed in his own house or entered the Sacred Mosque would be safe. Muhammad then divided his army: Khalid ibn al-Walid led the right flank into the lower part of the city, Zubayr ibn al-Awwam the left from above, and Abu 'Ubaidah the infantry through a side valley, with orders to kill only in self-defence. Khalid met resistance led by Ikrima ibn Amr, Safwan ibn Umayya and Suhayl ibn Amr; twelve of the Quraysh and two of his own men were killed.

Muhammad went to the Kaaba, took the key from 'Uthman ibn Talha and ordered the idols and images inside destroyed. He then addressed the Meccans from the doorway, and Bilal ibn Rabah called the adhan from the Kaaba. Muhammad had decreed that nine people might be killed even under the curtains of the Kaaba; four were put to death, including 'Abdullah ibn Khatal and Miqyas ibn Sababa, who had killed Muslims and left Islam. Others, among them Ikrima, Wahshi and Hind bint Utba, were forgiven.

On the second day in the city Muhammad declared Mecca a sanctuary. Muhammad stayed nineteen days, teaching, sending envoys to invite people to Islam and sending men to destroy remaining idols near Mecca, among them al-Uzza at Nakhlah and Suwa' of the Hudhayl.
conquest-of-the-desert: Since the founding of Buenos Aires in the 16th century the frontier between colonial ranches and Indigenous lands had moved slowly outwards, reaching the Salado River by the end of the 18th century, while cattle drove off the game the native peoples hunted. After independence the government wanted to occupy the lands the republic claimed, in part to forestall Chile, whose occupation of Araucanía began in 1861, and to open them to immigrants. Raids on frontier towns, in which cattle were driven to Chile for trade, gave the campaign its spur: in 1872 Calfucurá and 6,000 warriors killed 300 settlers and took 200,000 head of cattle.

In 1875 the war minister Adolfo Alsina began a slower advance, linking forts by telegraph and digging the trench of Alsina, 374 km long, to hinder cattle drives. After his death in 1877 Roca, who held that the Indigenous peoples had to be extinguished, subdued or expelled, took his place. His first sweep in late 1878 swept the land between the trench and the Rio Negro, and in 1879, with 6,000 soldiers armed with Remington rifles, he reached Choele Choel in two months, killing 1,313 people and capturing more than 15,000.

As president he sent Colonel Conrado Villegas south in 1881; the last battle was fought on 18 October 1884, and the chiefs Inacayal and Foyel surrendered with more than 3,000 warriors two months later in present Chubut Province. Chilean soldiers fought beside Mapuche allies in clashes in the Pulmarí Valley in 1883.

Settlers of European descent turned the land to farming, which made Argentina a great agricultural exporter in the early 20th century, and Chilean trade east of the Andes was cut. Argentine troops displaced more than 15,000 Mapuche and enslaved some of the survivors, and peoples such as the Teushen were destroyed within a generation. The campaign remains disputed: the literary scholar Jens Andermann notes that contemporary sources point to an aim of extermination, with prisoners killed and captives kept from having children, while apologists describe a response to raids on settlements. Roca's statue in Bariloche is a frequent site of protest.
conquest-of-wales-by-edward-i: After 1066 the Normans seized much of Wales and set up Marcher lordships, but Welsh principalities such as Gwynedd, Powys and Deheubarth survived, and by the 13th century Gwynedd was dominant, its princes styling themselves Prince of Wales. By the Treaty of Montgomery of 1267, Henry III recognised Llywelyn ap Gruffudd in that title in return for homage. Under Edward I tension grew: in 1274 Gruffydd ap Gwenwynwyn of Powys and Llywelyn's brother Dafydd ap Gruffydd defected to the English, Llywelyn refused to do homage at Chester in 1275 and planned to marry Eleanor, daughter of Simon de Montfort, and in November 1276 Edward declared war.

In July 1277 Edward marched from Chester into Gwynedd with 15,500 men, 9,000 of them Welshmen from the south, supported by a fleet from the Cinque Ports. Llywelyn surrendered without a major battle, and by the Treaty of Aberconwy in November 1277 he kept only western Gwynedd and his title.

In 1282 Dafydd, discontented with his reward, rebelled, and the war became a national struggle provoked largely by Edward's attempts to impose English law. The Welsh won at Llandeilo Fawr in June 1282 and at Moel-y-don on 6 November, but Llywelyn was lured into a trap and killed at the Battle of Orewin Bridge on 11 December. Edward marched into Snowdonia in January 1283 and took Dolwyddelan Castle; Dafydd was captured in June and executed as a traitor at Shrewsbury.

Lands not kept by the crown became new Marcher lordships, such as Denbigh for the Earl of Lincoln. In 1301 the royal lands were granted to Edward of Caernarfon with the title Prince of Wales, thereafter the customary endowment of the heir to the throne. English settlers took Welsh land and new towns such as Flint, Aberystwyth and Rhuddlan were founded, while James of Saint George oversaw the building of castles such as Beaumaris.

Revolts followed, under Madog ap Llywelyn in 1294, Llywelyn Bren in 1316 to 1318 and Owain Glyndŵr from 1400, but none succeeded, and the Laws in Wales Acts 1535 to 1542 incorporated Wales into England. The conquest cost Edward around £173,000, against an annual revenue of about £40,000, and his need for taxes helped widen the role of Parliament.
conrad-count-palatine-of-the-rhine: Conrad was the son of Frederick II, Duke of Swabia (1090–1147), and his second wife, Agnes of Saarbrücken, a daughter of Frederick, Count of Saarbrücken. As the only half-brother of Frederick Barbarossa, he received the family's possessions in Franconia and the Rhineland, above all those that came from his mother's ancestry.

At the Reichstag held at Worms in 1156, Barbarossa conferred on him the dignity of Pfalzgraf, Count Palatine of the Rhine, and Conrad became the first to hold it by inheritance. With the title came the Vogtei, or advocacy, of Schönau Abbey and of the chapter of Worms Cathedral, as well as the Staufen family estates around Speyer and Worms. His efforts to widen his sphere of influence brought him into conflict with the Bishops of Trier and Cologne.

Conrad married twice. His first wife, a daughter of Count Gottfried I of Sponheim whose name is not known, probably died in 1159 or 1160. From about 1160 he was married to Irmengard of Henneberg, a daughter of Count Bertold I of Henneberg, burgrave of Würzburg, and the marriage brought him the Vogtei of Lorsch Abbey.

Conrad died on 8 November 1195 and was buried in Schönau Abbey near Heidelberg, where both his wives were also laid to rest. None of his sons survived to continue the family: Gottfried, the son of his first marriage, died probably in 1187 or 1188, and Frederick and Conrad, sons of the second, died before 1189 and probably in 1186.

His inheritance passed to his daughter Agnes, who had married Henry V of the House of Brunswick at Burg Stahleck late in 1193. Henry held the palatinate from 1195 to 1212, and Agnes died on 9 May 1204. Their heiress in turn passed the inheritance to the Wittelsbach dynasty, who thereby became lords of the Palatinate and Electors Palatine.
conrad-i-duke-of-zahringen: Conrad was a son of Duke Berthold II of Zähringen and his wife, Agnes of Rheinfelden. His elder brother Berthold III held the duchy before him, and in 1120 the two brothers granted city rights to Freiburg. In 1122 Conrad succeeded Berthold III as Duke of Zähringen, and from 1127 he was also Rector of Burgundy, holding both titles until his death.

Much of his life was spent resisting the growing power of the House of Hohenstaufen, to which end he allied himself with the House of Guelph. In 1127 he and Count Reginald III of Burgundy both claimed the inheritance of Conrad's murdered nephew, William III. Emperor Lothar III, who urgently needed support against his Hohenstaufen rivals, backed Conrad and rejected Reginald's claim on the dubious ground that Reginald had failed in his duty to attend the emperor's court. The title of rector of Burgundy made Conrad, at least in theory, a kind of representative of the emperor in the Kingdom of Burgundy.

In 1138 King Conrad III of Germany grabbed power, and the conflict between the Guelphs and the Hohenstaufen relaxed. His family changed sides with it: from then until the late 1150s the dukes of Zähringen were among the most loyal supporters of the Hohenstaufen.

Conrad died at Constance on 8 January 1152 and was buried in the family vault at the Abbey of Saint Peter in the Black Forest. With his wife, Clementia of Namur, a daughter of Godfrey I, Count of Namur, he had at least five children: Berthold IV, later Duke of Zähringen; Adalbert I, founder of the line of the Dukes of Teck; Clementia, who married Henry the Lion; Rudolf, Archbishop of Mainz; and Hugh, Duke of Ullenburg.
conrad-i-of-burgundy: Conrad belonged to the Elder House of Welf. He was the son of King Rudolph II, the first ruler of the united kingdom of Upper and Lower Burgundy since 933, and of Rudolph's consort Bertha, a daughter of Duke Burchard II of Swabia. Some sources call him Conrad III, since he was the third Conrad in his family: his great-grandfather was Duke Conrad II, whose father was Count Conrad I.

Conrad succeeded his father in 937 while still a minor. His future brother-in-law, the German king Otto I, later Holy Roman Emperor, exercised the regency, and under it Conrad began a close collaboration with the Germanic kings. Burgundy became central to Otto's Italian policy because it held the Great Saint Bernard Pass. Conrad extended the kingdom's control over important monasteries, among them Lure Abbey, Payerne Priory, Romainmôtier Priory and Moutier-Grandval Abbey.

The chronicler Ekkehard IV told a story, probably apocryphal, of how Conrad dealt with a double invasion by the Magyars and the Arabs of Fraxinetum. He sent envoys to each army warning it of the other and offering Burgundian aid against it, then reported to each where the other was. When the two armies met, the Burgundians held back until the invaders were spent, then attacked, destroyed both and sold the captives into slavery.

Conrad died on 19 October 993 and was buried at the Abbey of Saint-André-le-Bas at Vienne. His first wife, Adelaide of Bellay, bore him at least one daughter, Gisela, who married Henry II, Duke of Bavaria. By 966 he had married Matilda, a daughter of Louis IV of France and Gerberga of Saxony. Their children included Rudolph III, who was king of Burgundy from 993 until his death on 6 September 1032, and daughters who married the Count of Blois, later Robert II of France, and Herman II, Duke of Swabia. A son by his concubine Aldiud, Burchard, became Archbishop of Lyons.
conrad-i-of-germany: Conrad, called the Younger, was the son of Duke Conrad of Thuringia, called the Elder, and his wife Glismoda, who was probably related to Ota, wife of the Carolingian emperor Arnulf of Carinthia. The Conradines, counts in the Franconian Lahngau region, had been loyal supporters of the Carolingians, and they competed with the sons of the Babenberg duke Henry of Franconia for predominance in Franconia. In 906 the two parties fought near Fritzlar. Conrad the Elder was killed, as were two of the three Babenberg brothers, and King Louis the Child took the Conradines' side. Conrad then became the undisputed duke of all Franconia. He failed, however, to extend Conradine rule over western Lotharingia.

After the death of Louis the Child, Conrad was elected king of East Francia on 10 November 911 at Forchheim by the rulers of Saxony, Swabia and Bavaria. He was the first king not of the Carolingian dynasty, the first elected by the nobility and the first to be anointed. The dukes kept Charles the Simple, king of West Francia, from the throne. Only Reginar, duke of Lotharingia, refused allegiance and joined West Francia.

Because he was himself one of the dukes, Conrad found it hard to establish his authority over them. Henry of Saxony rebelled against him until 915, and Burchard II of Swabia demanded and received more autonomy. Erchanger of Swabia revolted in 913, defeated the royal army near Lake Constance and was executed on 21 January 917 with his brother Berthold. Arnulf of Bavaria called on the Magyars for help. His campaigns against Charles the Simple to regain Lotharingia and Aachen failed. The Magyar raids, continuing since the Bavarian defeat at the Battle of Pressburg in 907, further weakened his authority.

Severely injured in one of his battles with Arnulf, Conrad died on 23 December 918 at Weilburg Castle and was buried in Fulda Cathedral. According to the chronicler Widukind of Corvey, he persuaded his brother Eberhard of Franconia on his deathbed to offer the crown to Henry the Fowler, duke of Saxony and one of his main opponents, whom he thought the only duke able to hold the kingdom together against the rivalries of the dukes and the Magyar raids.

Eberhard and the Frankish nobles accepted this advice in May 919, and Henry was elected king at the Diet of Fritzlar. Kingship passed from the Franks to the Saxons. Eberhard succeeded Conrad as duke of Franconia and was killed in 939 at the Battle of Andernach during a rebellion against Otto I; the duchy then became a direct possession of the Ottonian dynasty until 1024.
conrad-ii-holy-roman-emperor: Conrad was the son of the Franconian count Henry of Speyer and Adelaide of Metz, and as a child he inherited the titles of count of Speyer and Worms. He was a great-great-grandson of Otto the Great. In 1016 he married Gisela of Swabia, a twice-widowed duchess whose son Ernest II was a minor duke. Conrad hoped to act as regent in Swabia, but Emperor Henry II gave the guardianship to Archbishop Poppo of Trier, which strained relations between the Salian family and the Ottonian house.

Henry II died childless in 1024, and on 4 September an assembly of princes at Kamba chose Conrad as king. He toured the kingdom to win recognition, gaining the Saxon nobles at Minden by promising to respect their customs and laws, while the princes of Lorraine rejected his claim. In Italy many nobles considered the throne vacant, and the Lombard cities offered the crown to Robert II of France and then to Duke William V of Aquitaine, who both refused. On 26 March 1027 Pope John XIX crowned Conrad and Gisela in Rome, in the presence of Cnut the Great and Rudolph III of Burgundy.

His stepson Ernest II rebelled in Swabia and rose again during the Italian expedition. Conrad continued the Ottonian system of using bishops and abbots as imperial servants but ended the favouritism once shown to churchmen. From his second Italian expedition in 1036 he won the lesser nobles, the valvassores, against the bishops. When Rudolph III died childless in 1032, Conrad claimed Burgundy and incorporated it into the empire, so that Germany, Italy and Burgundy formed the royal triad.

In 1038 Conrad went to southern Italy to settle a dispute over Capua, took the city and gave it to Guaimar IV of Salerno. An epidemic then killed many of his troops on the return. He died of gout at Utrecht on 4 June 1039 and was buried at Speyer Cathedral, which he founded and which holds the Salian emperors. His son Henry, elected and anointed king in 1028, succeeded as Henry III. His chaplain Wipo of Burgundy wrote a biography in chronicle form.
conrad-ii-of-znojmo: Conrad was the son of Prince Luitpold of Znojmo and his wife Ida, a daughter of the Babenberg margrave Leopold II of Austria. When his father died in 1112, Znojmo passed to his uncle Ulrich I of Brno, who died the following year. From 1115 both the Brno and Znojmo principalities were held by Soběslav I, the youngest son of the late King Vratislaus II of Bohemia.

Conrad first ruled Znojmo from 1123, when Soběslav fell out with his elder brother, Duke Vladislaus I of Bohemia. Vladislaus died two years later, and as the dynastic struggle came to a head at the Battle of Chlumec in 1126, Soběslav had Conrad deposed in 1128 and imprisoned at Dohna Castle. Seeking to reconcile with his Moravian cousin and to steady his rule, Soběslav later restored him as prince of Znojmo, which he held again from 1134 until his death, and arranged his marriage to the Vukanović princess Maria, a daughter of Grand Prince Uroš I of Serbia.

The quarrels revived when Vladislaus II, son of Vladislaus I, came to the Bohemian throne in 1140. Two years later Conrad and his cousins of Brno and Olomouc marched on Prague, but the castle was held by the duke's younger brother, Prince Děpold I of Jamnitz, while Vladislaus went to the court of King Conrad III of Germany at Würzburg and returned with a large royal army. The Moravian forces had to retire, and Conrad, excommunicated by Jindřich Zdík, Bishop of Olomouc, had to accept Bohemian overlordship.

Some time after 1134 Conrad commissioned the wall paintings of the Znojmo Rotunda. He died in 1161. He and Maria of Serbia had five children. Their son Conrad III Ota married Hellicha of Wittelsbach, became the first Margrave of Moravia in 1182 and Duke of Bohemia in 1189, and their daughter Helena of Znojmo became High Duchess of Poland by her marriage to Casimir II the Just.
conrad-iii-of-germany: Conrad was the son of Duke Frederick I of Swabia and Agnes, a daughter of Emperor Henry IV. After his father's death in 1105 his elder brother Frederick II inherited Swabia. In 1116 their uncle, Emperor Henry V, made Conrad Duke of Franconia. When Henry V died in 1125, Conrad unsuccessfully backed Frederick for the kingship.

Frederick was banned and Conrad lost Franconia. With the support of the imperial cities, Swabia and Austria he was elected anti-king at Nuremberg in December 1127, was crowned King of Italy at Monza but achieved little there, and in 1135 acknowledged Lothair III as emperor. After Lothair died in December 1137, Conrad was elected king at Coblenz on 7 March 1138 and crowned at Aachen six days later. Henry the Proud, the most powerful prince in Germany, refused to accept this, and Conrad stripped him of his lands. The civil war that followed is considered the first act of the struggle between Guelphs and Ghibellines. A peace was made at Frankfurt in May 1142.

In 1146 Conrad heard Bernard of Clairvaux preach the Second Crusade at Speyer and joined Louis VII. He had his son Henry Berengar elected king before leaving. His army of about 20,000 men crossed Anatolia rather than taking the coast, and on 25 October 1147 the Seljuk Turks defeated it at Dorylaeum, killing or capturing most of the foot soldiers. Conrad fell ill at Ephesus, recovered at Constantinople, and later took part in the failed Siege of Damascus.

In 1150 Conrad and Henry Berengar defeated Welf VI and his son at Flochberg. Henry Berengar died that year, and the Welfs and Hohenstaufen made peace in 1152. Conrad was never crowned emperor and styled himself King of the Romans until his death on 15 February 1152. According to the account of his last hours, he named his nephew Frederick Barbarossa as successor rather than his six-year-old son Frederick. Barbarossa was elected king at Cologne a few weeks later, and the son received Swabia.
conrad-of-montferrat: Conrad was born around 1146 in Montferrat, then a margraviate of the Kingdom of Italy in the Holy Roman Empire, the second son of Marquess William V of Montferrat and Judith of Babenberg. Little is known of his early years, but from his twenties he was active in diplomacy and became an effective commander. After the family's alliance with the Byzantine emperor Manuel I Comnenus, he defeated Barbarossa's forces under Archbishop Christian of Mainz at Camerino in September 1179 and took the chancellor hostage. In 1187 he married Theodora, sister of Emperor Isaac II Angelos, and received the rank of Caesar, but soon left for the Kingdom of Jerusalem.

Conrad arrived off Acre, which had fallen to Saladin, and sailed north to Tyre, where he found the remnants of the crusader army after the Battle of Hattin. With the support of the Italian merchant communities he reorganised the city's defences. Tyre withstood Saladin's siege. When Saladin returned in November 1187 he produced Conrad's captive father, William V, before the walls and offered to release him if Tyre surrendered; the old man told his son to stand firm, and William was later released unharmed. On 30 December Conrad's forces captured many Egyptian galleys.

When Guy of Lusignan came to Tyre in 1189, Conrad refused him entry, saying that Guy had forfeited his rights at Hattin. After Queen Sibylla died of disease in 1190, her half-sister Isabella, the heiress, had her marriage to Humphrey IV of Toron annulled, and Conrad married her on 24 November 1190. Richard I of England supported Guy, while Conrad had the backing of Philip II of France. Conrad inherited Montferrat in 1191.

In April 1192 the barons of the Kingdom of Jerusalem unanimously elected Conrad king. He was never crowned. On 28 April, riding home from a meal at the house of Philip, Bishop of Beauvais, he was stabbed by two men who turned out to be members of the Order of Assassins, a Nizari Isma'ili sect. His guards killed one and captured the other. He was buried at Tyre, and Isabella, pregnant, was married to Henry II of Champagne only seven days later.

The murder remains unsolved. The surviving assassin claimed under torture that Richard was behind it, which cannot be proved, and a letter attributed to the leader of the Assassins blamed a dispute over a captured ship but is believed to be forged. English-language fiction and film have mostly depicted Conrad as a villain, notably Walter Scott's The Talisman.
conradin: Conradin was born on 25 March 1252 at Wolfstein, Bavaria, the son of Conrad IV of Germany and Elisabeth of Bavaria. His father died in 1254, and he grew up at the court of his uncle and guardian, Duke Louis II of Bavaria. Supporters of the Hohenstaufens recognised him that year as king of Sicily and Jerusalem. Pope Alexander IV forbade his election as king of Germany and offered the Hohenstaufen lands in Germany to King Alfonso X of Castile and Richard of Cornwall. His half-uncle Manfred acted as regent in Sicily and was crowned king there in 1258 on a false rumour of Conradin's death.

Conradin took possession of the Duchy of Swabia in 1262. After Charles I of Anjou, called by Pope Clement IV, defeated and killed Manfred at Benevento in 1266, envoys from the Ghibelline cities urged Conradin to come and free Italy. He pledged his lands, crossed the Alps and issued a manifesto at Verona setting out his claim to Sicily. His uncle Louis and other companions turned back, and he lacked funds, yet his cause prospered. He was welcomed at Pavia, Pisa and Siena. In September 1267 a Spanish fleet under Frederick of Castile landed at Sciacca, and most of Sicily rose against Charles. The pope excommunicated him in November, and in July 1268 he entered Rome to a popular reception.

On 23 August 1268 his army of Italian, Spanish, Roman, Sicilian and German troops met Charles at Tagliacozzo. A charge by Spanish knights led by Henry of Castile captured the banner of Charles and seemed to promise victory, but Charles had hidden veteran French knights behind a hill, and their entry turned the battle. Conradin escaped to Rome and then to Astura, hoping to sail for Sicily, but was arrested and handed to Charles. He was imprisoned in the Castel dell'Ovo in Naples with Frederick of Baden, and both were beheaded on 29 October 1268.

With his death at sixteen the male line of the Hohenstaufen dynasty became extinct. His remains and those of Frederick of Baden lie in the church of the monastery of Our Lady of Mt. Carmel at Naples, founded by his mother. In 1847 Maximilian, crown prince of Bavaria, erected there a marble statue by Bertel Thorvaldsen. Two songs attributed to Conradin appear in the 14th-century Codex Manesse.

The Kingdom of Jerusalem passed to the heirs of Isabella I of Jerusalem, and Hugh III of Cyprus kept it as Hugh I of Jerusalem. Sicily passed to Charles of Anjou, and after the Sicilian Vespers of 1282 the Aragonese heirs of Manfred kept the island while the southern mainland, popularly called the Kingdom of Naples, stayed with Charles's party.
consell-de-cent: In 1249 James I laid down the basic structure of Barcelona's municipal government: a board of four advisers, helped by eight counsellors and an assembly of probi homines, or leading men, all drawn from the mà major, the senior hand, the upper class of wealthy merchants. After several changes the organisation took its lasting form by 1265, when the city's authority rested on three counsellors elected by a council of one hundred men, from which the body took its name, cent being Catalan for one hundred.

In 1335 Peter III the Ceremonious allowed the council to use the royal insignia of the four red bars. The council played an important part in the government of the Principality of Catalonia beyond the city. In 1401 it rejected Martin the Humane's foundation of a General Medical School in Barcelona with the same privileges as the University of Montpellier, holding that it encroached on the city's jurisdiction, a dispute that led in the end to the creation of the University of Barcelona in 1450. In 1464 the council proclaimed Peter the Constable of Portugal count of Barcelona as Peter V of Aragon.

In the last decades of the 17th century the council was represented in the Conferència dels Tres Comuns, the Conference of the Three Commons. After the Siege of Barcelona ended in 1714, Philip V of Spain occupied the city and abolished the council through the Nueva Planta decrees, and from then on the city's government was controlled directly by the monarchy. A main street of the city, the Carrer del Consell de Cent, is named after the council.
consensus-tigurinus: The agreement was meant to unite the Protestant churches in their teaching on the sacraments, above all the Lord's Supper, on which Calvin's view stood between the Lutheran doctrine of the Real Presence and the Zwinglian view of the elements as symbols. Calvin wrote a first draft in November 1548, with notes by Bullinger, and sent it to the Swiss churches, but the Synod at Bern opposed his view strongly and went on doing so until after his death. In May 1549 Calvin met Bullinger and William Farel in Zürich, and the three revised the text into its final form.
