The Consensus sets out 26 articles of Reformed teaching on the sacraments. It holds that the sacraments do not of themselves confer grace, but that God acts through them as means by the Holy Spirit; that their inner effect appears only in the elect; that in baptism the remission of sins comes primarily from the blood of Christ; and that in the Supper believers eat and drink the body and blood of Christ not by a carnal presence of his human nature, which is in heaven, but by the power of the Holy Spirit and the elevation of the soul to heaven. It rejected both transubstantiation and the Lutheran sacramental union.

The text was published in Zürich and Geneva in 1551, with a German translation by Bullinger and a French one by Calvin. It was accepted by the churches of Zürich, Geneva, St. Gallen, Schaffhausen, the Grisons, Neuchâtel and in time Basel, and was received favourably in France, parts of Germany and England, where Martin Bucer praised it and Peter Martyr Vermigli endorsed it. Melanchthon said that he now understood the Swiss for the first time and would no longer write against them, but the Gnesio-Lutheran Joachim Westphal attacked it, calling Zwingli and Calvin heretics, and it became the occasion of the second sacramental war.
conservatism: The Anglo-Irish statesman Edmund Burke, who opposed the French Revolution, is credited as one of the forefathers of Western conservative thought in the 1790s, along with the Savoyard statesman Joseph de Maistre. Burke served as private secretary to the Marquess of Rockingham and as official pamphleteer to the Rockingham branch of the Whig party, which together with the Tories made up the conservatives of the late 18th century United Kingdom. The first established use of the term in a political context came in 1818 from François-René de Chateaubriand, during the Bourbon Restoration.

Conservatism seeks to promote and preserve traditional institutions, customs and values, and its central tenets vary with the culture in which it appears. In Western countries conservatives have sought to preserve institutions such as the family, organised religion, the nation-state, property rights, aristocracy and monarchy. Political scientist Andrew Heywood names five central beliefs: tradition, human imperfection, organic society, authority and hierarchy, and property. The philosopher Michael Oakeshott wrote that to be conservative is to prefer the familiar to the unknown and the tried to the untried.

The ideology has many variants. Paternalistic conservatism first arose in the United Kingdom under Benjamin Disraeli's One Nation Toryism and stresses the obligation of the privileged towards the poor. Liberal conservatism joins a minimal role for the state in the economy to a strong state for law and order. Reactionary conservatism seeks to return to an earlier state of affairs.

Early European forms of conservatism were often reactionary and romantic, idealising the Middle Ages with their feudal order, aristocratic rule and established church. In the late 19th century conservatism became more progressive, adopting capitalism and nationalism, which until then had been anti-traditionalist forces. In the first half of the 20th century, as socialist movements grew stronger and the Tsarist regime fell in the Russian Revolution, conservatism in Austria, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Italy, Portugal, Spain and Romania moved to the far right and became more authoritarian. After the war it took a more moderate form, with Christian-democratic parties dominating Western Europe. In Latin America conservative elites held power through the Catholic Church and the military.
conservative-judaism: By the early 19th century the rise of centralised European states ended Jewish judicial autonomy and social seclusion, and emancipation and acculturation quickly changed the values of the public. The new academic study of Judaism, Wissenschaft des Judentums, became a source of controversy over how far its findings could decide present conduct. Modernised Orthodox rabbis in Germany such as Isaac Bernays and Azriel Hildesheimer studied it cautiously but refused it any say in religious matters, while Abraham Geiger, who became the founding father of Reform Judaism, opposed any limit on critical research.

Rabbi Zecharias Frankel's positive-historical school lay between these. In the United States the movement took shape in a free-spirited environment of loose communities. The term Conservative Judaism was used, still generically, in Alexander Kohut's dedication speech for the Jewish Theological Seminary of America in 1887. Its alumni formed the Rabbinical Assembly by 1901, and the boundary with Orthodoxy was institutionalised only in the aftermath of World War II.

The movement employs historical-critical research alongside traditional methods and gives great weight to its constituency in deciding practice. It views Halakha as normative and binding, requiring observance of the Sabbath, dietary rules and daily prayer with phylacteries, while holding that the law has always evolved. Its Statement of Principles of 1988, Emet ve-Emunah, called Halakha indispensable. The movement sees the Orthodox as having petrified the process and Reform as having abandoned it. Louis Ginzberg wrote that one may conceive of the origin of the Sabbath as a professor would, yet observe the smallest detail known to strict Orthodoxy.

Its theology is deliberately plural. Frankel thought the very idea of theology alien to traditional Judaism, and a course on Conservative theology opened at the seminary only in 1985. Emet ve-Emunah affirmed God as Creator but said his nature was elusive and acknowledged many positions. On revelation, JTS faculty who embraced Biblical criticism in the 1920s held that a verbal revelation occurred at Sinai but that the text was composed by later authors.

The Rabbinical Assembly and its legal committee made rulings that shaped practice. In the 1940s mixed seating in synagogues became common after public demand. In 1950 it was ruled that closing an electrical circuit is not kindling a fire and so is permitted on the Sabbath, and the committee also permitted driving to the synagogue on that day for that purpose alone, a ruling heavily disputed within the movement. The United Synagogue of America was founded in 1913 as the congregational arm, and the World Council of Conservative Synagogues in 1957.
conservative-party-uk: The Conservative Party was founded in 1834 from the Tory Party and was, with the Liberal Party, one of the two dominant parties of the 19th century. Writers differ about its deeper roots. Some trace it to the Tory Party; others point to a faction rooted in the 18th-century Whig Party that gathered around William Pitt the Younger in the 1780s, known as Pittites, who never used the terms Tory or Conservative. From about 1812 the name Tory was commonly used for a new party that, in the historian Robert Blake's words, are the ancestors of Conservatism.

Under the Earl of Derby and Benjamin Disraeli the party carried the Reform Act 1867. In 1886 it allied with the Liberal Unionist Party and, under Lord Salisbury and Arthur Balfour, held power for all but three of the next twenty years, until a heavy defeat in 1906 when it split over free trade. The Liberal Unionists merged with it in 1912.

After the landslide of 1918 the Conservatives dominated the government of David Lloyd George. In May 1940 a National Government was formed under Winston Churchill, but the party lost the 1945 general election in a landslide to Labour. It returned in 1951. Margaret Thatcher deposed Edward Heath in 1975 and won the 1979 general election. John Major won the 1992 election, the party's fourth successive victory.

The party comprises the voluntary party, the parliamentary party and the professional party. Membership peaked in the mid-1950s at about 3 million. Its factions have included one-nation conservatives, dominant in the 20th century until the rise of Thatcherism in the 1970s, free-market Thatcherites, who sought lower taxes and privatisation, and traditionalists, who support the Church of England, the unitary British state and the family. Historically the party favoured protectionism and the British Empire, and since the 1980s it has generally favoured free markets. It opposes independence for any part of the United Kingdom.
consistori-del-gai-saber: The seven founders, literary men of the bourgeoisie, set out their aims in a manifesto in Old Occitan verse, pledging prizes for poetry in the manner and language of the classical troubadours of roughly 1160 to 1220. The academy was first called the Consistori dels Sept Trobadors, the Consistory of the Seven Troubadours. It was governed by a chancellor and seven judges known as mantenedors, or maintainers. In 1390 John I of Aragon founded the Consistori de Barcelona in imitation of it.

At the yearly contest the most excellent poet received the violeta d'aur, the golden violet, for the best poem or cançó. Other forms had other flowers: a silver marigold for the best dança and a silver dog rose for the best sirventés, pastorèla or vergièra. The first prize went on 3 May 1324 to Arnaut Vidal de Castelnou d'Ari for a sirventes in praise of the Virgin Mary, and the last of this early period in 1484 to Arnaut Bernart de Tarascon. Records of around a hundred prizes survive, won by men and women from both sides of the Pyrenees.

To judge these contests the Consistori commissioned an Occitan grammar with the laws of poetry. Its first compiler, Guilhem Molinier, completed the Leys d'amor between 1328 and 1337, and it went through two later redactions. By 1471 the academy was losing its Occitan character, and in 1513 it became the Collège de rhétorique et de poésie françaises. In 1554 it gave a silver eglantine to Pierre de Ronsard for his Amours, and in 1694 Louis XIV refounded it as the Académie des Jeux Floraux.

The Consistori is often credited with encouraging a monotonous poetry, and its poets are judged to have lacked the force of the last troubadours, such as Cerverí de Girona. Martí de Riquer criticised the Toulouse school for its narrow themes and strict rules and for exporting occitanisms into Catalan poetry, comparing it to French neoclassicism. Its idea of a gay science later inspired Friedrich Nietzsche's The Gay Science of 1882.
conspiracy-of-cinadon: Xenophon describes Cinadon as a young man, fine in body and brave in spirit, but not one of the equals. His own lower status is not named. He was a valued and respected man, sent at times on missions for the city, and he resented that he did not belong to the highest class of citizen, the Spartiates. The only other conspirator named is Teisamenos, a seer, whose status is not given. Besides Xenophon's Hellenica, the plot is mentioned by Polyaenus and Aristotle.

The first warning came at a sacrifice presided over by King Agesilaus II, when the omens were very bad and the seer foresaw, in Xenophon's words, a most terrible conspiracy. Several days later an informer came to the ephors. Besides the count in the agora, he reported that Cinadon called the Spartiates the enemy of most of the crowd, and that among the disaffected classes no one could hide that he would be glad to eat the Spartiates raw. Only some of the conspirators were armed, but the rest had axes, sickles and other tools that could serve as weapons.

The ephors feared that an open arrest would set off the revolt. By an elaborate ruse they sent Cinadon to Aulon on the Elean frontier, with an escort of men from the king's guard chosen by their commander and a detachment of cavalry, the hippeis, as reinforcement. Questioned at Aulon, he named the principal conspirators, who were arrested in Sparta when word arrived.

Brought back to Sparta, Cinadon was questioned further until all his accomplices were named. He and the others were bound, collared and led around the city, struck with whips and goads. Asked why he had plotted, Cinadon answered that he wished to be inferior to no one in Lacedaemonia. Polyaenus, in a shorter version of the event, adds that the ephors ordered the other conspirators executed while Cinadon was still away, and so put down the plot without resistance; where he found this is not known.
constaffel: In legal texts the word Konstaffel meant the residents of a castle, city or city quarter, and in Strasbourg it also named an institution of the upper class. In Zürich, Rudolf Brun gathered the urban upper class into the Constaffel during his guild revolution of 1336. At first it was a personal association with no internal constitution, made up, as in Strasbourg, of members of the upper-class drinking rooms; Brun chose from it thirteen members of the council, who sat facing an equal number of guild masters. It is comparable to the Achtburger of Basel.

In 1348 the Society of Nobles, part of the Constaffel, built the Haus zum Rüden, which served as the city hall until 1401 and as the Constaffel's assembly house. In 1417 came the Gemeine Konstaffel, a fraternity with military, charitable and religious purposes. From the end of the 14th century the body declined through emigration, social decline and the dying out of leading families, reaching its lowest point in the Old Zurich War.

After the Waldmann affair, the Fourth Oath Letter of 1489 made it a political guild, and in 1490 the council required it to take into the Gemeine Konstaffel all men and women of the city without guild rights, among them the residents of the Kratzquartier. After the Reformation the drinking society became the closed Noble Society zum Rüden, dissolved in 1878; from 1600 it gave guild families only conditional membership as Stubenhitzer, who reached the council seats through a new Bürgerliche Konstaffel.

The Constaffel was dissolved in 1798, restored in 1803 and 1815 as one of thirteen cantonal and municipal electoral guilds, and dissolved again in 1838 and 1866. In 1841 it formed itself into the Gesellschaft zur Konstaffel, a society whose purpose is to take part in the Sechseläuten.
constans-i: Constans was the third and youngest son of Constantine the Great and Fausta. He was educated at Constantinople under the poet Aemilius Magnus Arborius, who taught him Latin. On 25 December 333 his father raised him to caesar. He was engaged to Olympias, daughter of the praetorian prefect Ablabius, but never married.

After Constantine's death, Constans and his brothers Constantine II and Constantius II were proclaimed augusti and divided the empire on 9 September 337. Constans received Italy, Africa and Illyricum, and in 338 he campaigned against the Sarmatians.

Constantine II tried to issue legislation for Africa in 339 and invaded Italy a year later, but was ambushed and killed by Constans' troops, and Constans took over his territories. From 341 to 342 he campaigned against the Franks, after an initial setback ending in victory and a favourable peace. In early 343 he visited Britain, for reasons that remain unclear.

He issued an edict in 341 banning pagan sacrifices but soon legislated against the destruction of temples. His support for Nicene orthodoxy and Bishop Athanasius of Alexandria brought him into conflict with Constantius II. The Council of Serdica of 343 failed to settle it, and by 345 Constans was threatening civil war, until Constantius let Athanasius return. He also used the army against Donatism in Africa.

On 18 January 350 the general Magnentius was proclaimed emperor at Augustodunum (Autun) with the support of court officials such as Marcellinus. Constans, on a hunting trip, tried to reach Hispania but was cornered at Helena (Elne) in the eastern Pyrenees and killed after seeking sanctuary in a temple.

Ancient sources, which may reflect Magnentius' propaganda, blame his fall on corruption, neglect of parts of the empire and contempt for soldiers. Jill Harries and others doubt this and see the revolt as the work of an apprehensive official, noting that Constans often travelled with only a small escort.
constans-ii: Constans was born on 7 November 630 in Constantinople, the son of Constantine III and Gregoria. Constantine III was a son of Emperor Heraclius. When Heraclius died in February 641, Constantine III and his younger half-brother Heraclonas succeeded him, and Constantine III died suddenly after three months. In September 641 the ten-year-old Constans was crowned co-emperor, amid rumours that Heraclonas and his mother Martina had poisoned his father. Around 5 November the general Valentinus deposed Heraclonas, leaving Constans sole emperor. He reigned at first under a regency of senators led by Patriarch Paul II of Constantinople.

His reign coincided with the Arab conquests. The Byzantines withdrew completely from Egypt in 642. A fleet under the admiral Manuel retook Alexandria in 645, but its commander plundered the countryside and was forced to leave. In 647 Arab forces entered Armenia and Cappadocia, and a major offensive in 650 and 651 led Constans to negotiate with Mu'awiya I, the governor of Syria. In 655 Constans led a fleet against the Muslims at the Battle of the Masts, off Lycia. About 500 Byzantine ships were destroyed and the emperor was almost killed. Peace with the Arabs followed in 659, and in 658 he defeated the Slavs in the Balkans.

In religion he tried to steer a middle line between Orthodoxy and Monothelitism, forbidding discussion of the natures of Christ by the Typos of 648, which satisfied few. Pope Martin I condemned both the doctrine and the decree at the Lateran Council of 649. He was arrested in 653, brought to Constantinople, condemned and exiled to Cherson, where he died in 655. Constans also forced his younger brother Theodosius to take holy orders and had him killed in 660.

Having earned the hatred of the people of Constantinople, he left the city for Syracuse in Sicily. From 663 he campaigned in Italy against the Lombard Duchy of Benevento, besieging Benevento without success before withdrawing to Naples. That year he spent twelve days in Rome, the first emperor to visit it since 476, where Pope Vitalian received him with honour. He stripped buildings, the Pantheon among them, of their bronze, and his later demands in Calabria and Sardinia enraged his Italian subjects.

On 15 July 668 Constans was assassinated in his bath by his chamberlain, either with a bucket or with a knife. His son Constantine succeeded him as Constantine IV and quickly suppressed a brief usurpation in Sicily by Mezezius. Chinese histories record an embassy from the Byzantine ruler in 643, which they name Boduoli, to the Tang emperor Taizong.
constantin-caratheodory: Constantin Carathéodory was born in Berlin on 13 September 1873 to Greek parents and grew up in Brussels. His father Stephanos, a lawyer, was the Ottoman ambassador to Belgium, St Petersburg and Berlin, and his mother Despina came from the island of Chios; she died in 1879. He twice won a prize as the best mathematics student in Belgium at the Athénée Royal d'Ixelles, and from 1891 trained as a military engineer at the Belgian Royal Military Academy.

When war broke out between the Ottoman Empire and Greece in 1897 he sided with the Greeks, while his father served the Ottoman government. He took a post in the British colonial service in Egypt, working on the Assiut dam until April 1900 and teaching himself mathematics during the flood stoppages.

He studied at Berlin and at Göttingen, where he took his doctorate in 1904 and his habilitation in 1905. He became professor at Hannover in 1909 and at Breslau in 1910, succeeded Felix Klein at Göttingen in 1913 and moved to Berlin in 1919. At the invitation of Prime Minister Eleftherios Venizelos he submitted a plan on 20 October 1919 for a university at Smyrna, and in 1920 he became its dean, touring Europe to buy books and equipment.

It never admitted students because the war in Asia Minor ended in the Great Fire of Smyrna. A journalist rowed him to the battleship Naxos, and he brought part of the library to Athens, where he taught until 1924. He then held the chair at the Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität in Munich until his retirement in 1938 and worked at the Bavarian Academy of Sciences until his death on 2 February 1950. In 1936 he handed out the first Fields Medals in Oslo.

His dissertation extended solutions in the calculus of variations to discontinuous cases, and his method of equivalent variational problems became known as the royal road to the subject. The Carathéodory extension theorem is fundamental to modern measure theory. In complex analysis he proved that conformal mappings extend to the boundary of Jordan domains and originated the theory of prime ends.

In 1909 he formulated the second law of thermodynamics axiomatically, without Carnot engines, and coined the term adiabatic accessibility; Max Born praised the work, while Max Planck doubted it was a fundamental formulation. In 1926 he proved that no system of lenses and mirrors can avoid aberration, except plane mirrors.
constantine-algeria: Constantine, also spelled Qacentina, lies about 80 kilometres from the Mediterranean coast on the banks of the Rhumel River. It stands on a plateau 640 metres above sea level, framed by a deep ravine, and is often called the City of Bridges because of the many bridges that connect the hills and ravines it is built on. It is the railhead of an agricultural area and a centre of the grain trade, and is regarded as the capital of eastern Algeria.

In antiquity the city was Cirta, capital of the Berber kingdom of Numidia. In 112 BCE it was the capital of King Jugurtha, and the Roman generals Metellus and Gaius Marius used it as a base against him. In 311 CE it was destroyed in a war between the emperor Maxentius and the usurper Domitius Alexander, and in 313 it was rebuilt and renamed Constantina for Constantine the Great. Under Roman rule it exported wheat. The Vandals captured it in 432 and it returned to the Byzantine Exarchate of Africa in 534. After the Arab conquest of the 8th century it became known as Qacentina.

The city recovered in the 12th century and under the Almohad and Hafsid rulers was a prosperous market with links to Pisa, Genoa and Venice. The Ottoman Empire took it in 1529, and it was ruled by a bey subordinate to the dey of Algiers. Salah Bey, who ruled from 1770 to 1792, built much of the Muslim architecture still visible. The last bey, Ahmed Bey, led a fierce resistance to the French, who captured the city by 13 October 1837. In 1880 Charles Louis Alphonse Laveran, working in its military hospital, discovered that the cause of malaria is a protozoan.

Constantine is the capital of Constantine Province and the third largest city in Algeria, with about 450,000 inhabitants. Its monuments include the Great Mosque of 1136, the El Bey Mosque of 1703, the Ahmed Bey Palace and the ruins of a Roman aqueduct. The Roman city of Tiddis and the mausoleum of the Numidian king Massinissa lie nearby.
constantine-bodin: Constantine Bodin was the son of Mihailo Vojislavljević, the King of the Slavs, who held the Byzantine title of protospatharios and ruled Duklja, the most powerful Serbian principality of the time. His mother was a niece of the Byzantine emperor Constantine IX Monomachos.

In the fall of 1072 Bulgarian nobles led by Georgi Voiteh, the exarch of Skopje, asked Mihailo for a son whom they could crown as their emperor in a revolt against the Byzantines. Mihailo sent Bodin with 300 troops to Prizren, where he was proclaimed emperor of the Bulgarians and renamed Petar, and is therefore sometimes counted as Peter III. His forces took Niš, but he was defeated and captured at Pauni in southern Kosovo and taken to Constantinople and then Antioch. Venetian merchants whom Mihailo paid freed him in 1078, and he returned to become co-ruler of his father.

Bodin succeeded Mihailo in 1081. By 1085 he and his brothers had put down a revolt by cousins in the župa of Zeta, and he then ruled unchallenged. In 1081 he answered the Byzantine emperor Alexios I Komnenos's call for aid against the Normans but stood aside at the Battle of Dyrrhachion and withdrew when the Byzantines were beaten. His support for Pope Urban II in 1089 won his bishop of Bar the rank of archbishop, though the Catholic Church gained ground only on the coast, while the inland parts remained under Constantinople.

According to the Chronicle of the Priest of Duklja, written in the 14th century, he campaigned in Bosnia and Serbia, installing his relative Stephen as knez in Bosnia and his nephews Vukan and Marko as župans in Serbia. The Byzantines, once they had dealt with the Normans, attacked him, defeated him and imprisoned him again. He got himself freed, but his reputation declined.

What happened in Duklja is not fully known, and there may have been a civil war during his captivity. Queen Jaquinta persecuted possible claimants to the throne, including his cousin Branislav and his family. In the 1090s the centre of Serbian state life moved to the mountains of Kopaonik, where his subject Vukan led the fight against the Byzantines. Dynastic conflicts and a struggle with Dubrovnik pushed Bodin into the background, and he ended his reign without power or reputation. After his death Duklja was engulfed in dynastic strife.
constantine-i: Constantine was born on 27 February at Naissus, in Moesia Superior; the day is recorded but not the year, and scholars have proposed dates between 271 and 280, most favouring 272 or 273. His father was Flavius Constantius, an army officer who became one of the four emperors of the Tetrarchy, and his mother Helena was a woman of low birth, probably from Bithynia. He was educated at the court of Diocletian, where he was held as something of a hostage, and served Diocletian and Galerius against the Danube tribes and the Persians. In 305 he left Galerius's court and joined his father in Gaul.

After his father's death in 306 the army at Eboracum proclaimed Constantine augustus. His share was Britain, Gaul and Spain, and he drove back the Picts and the Franks. In 307 he married Fausta, daughter of Maximian, who rebelled against him in 310 and hanged himself that July. Galerius's edict of 30 April 311 ended the persecutions. Constantine then defeated the emperors Maxentius and Licinius in the civil wars of the Tetrarchy, and in 324 became sole ruler of the empire.

Constantine separated civil and military authority, disbanded the Praetorian Guard and introduced the solidus, a gold coin struck in similar weight and purity for seven centuries. He won victories over the Franks, Alamanni, Goths and Sarmatians. He favoured Christianity from 312, had a part in the Edict of Milan of 313, and convoked the First Council of Nicaea in 325, which produced the Nicene Creed. He was baptised by Eusebius of Nicomedia, and some modern scholars debate his beliefs.

He chose the Greek city of Byzantium as capital, founding it in 324 and dedicating it on 11 May 330 as Constantinopolis. He left the empire to his sons, replacing the Tetrarchy with dynastic succession. Eastern Churches venerate him as a saint equal to the Apostles. The Donation of Constantine, a document of the 8th century, was shown by Lorenzo Valla in 1440 to be a forgery.
constantine-i-of-greece: Constantine was born in Athens on 2 August 1868, the eldest son of King George I and Queen Olga. As the first Greek-born member of the royal family, he was greeted with great enthusiasm, and crowds shouted for him to be named Constantine, after the king who in popular legend would reconquer Constantinople. He was educated in the Hellenic Military Academy and in Germany, where he served in the Imperial Guard. In 1889 he married Princess Sophia of Prussia, the sister of Wilhelm II. As crown prince he commanded the Army of Thessaly in the Greco-Turkish War of 1897, which ended in a humiliating defeat.

In the First Balkan War of 1912 Constantine commanded the Army of Thessaly. He defeated the Ottomans at Sarantaporos and Giannitsa, and accepted the surrender of Thessaloniki on 27 October 1912 (Old Style), less than a day before Bulgarian forces arrived. His father, George I, was assassinated at Thessaloniki on 18 March 1913 and Constantine became king. The Balkan Wars doubled Greece's territory and population.

When the First World War began he rejected Wilhelm II's request to join the Central Powers but also refused to bring Greece in on the Allied side, as Prime Minister Eleftherios Venizelos wished. He held that neutrality best protected Greece, while his opponents accused him of German sympathies. He dismissed Venizelos twice, and in August 1916 Venizelist officers set up a rival government in Thessaloniki. The division of Greek society between Venizelists and royalists is known as the National Schism. Under Allied pressure and a blockade, Constantine left for Switzerland on 11 June 1917, and his son Alexander became king.

Alexander died on 25 October 1920. Venizelos lost a general election the following month, and a plebiscite in which nearly 99 per cent voted for his return brought Constantine back on 19 December 1920. The war against the Turkish nationalists in Asia Minor continued. In August 1922 the Greek army, overextended after an advance towards Ankara, was driven back to the coast. After a revolt of Venizelist officers he abdicated on 27 September 1922 in favour of his eldest son, George II. He died at Palermo, Sicily, on 11 January 1923. The royalist slogan 'bread, olives and King Constantine' dates from the Allied blockade of 1916 and 1917.
constantine-ii-of-georgia: Constantine was the son of Prince Demetrius. In 1465 he and his uncle, King George VIII, were taken prisoner by the rebel Qvarqvare II Jaqeli, atabeg of Samtskhe. He escaped and, while King Bagrat VI of Imereti was away campaigning in Kartli, tried in vain to seize the Imeretian capital, Kutaisi. He nonetheless called himself king and gained some power in Kartli, but only after Bagrat's death in 1478 could he drive out Bagrat's son Alexander II and take the crown of a kingdom already torn by civil war.

In 1483 Qvarqvare II defeated him at the Battle of Aradeti, and Alexander established himself in Imereti, though Constantine retook Kutaisi in 1484. In the winter of 1488 the Ak Koyunlu Turkomans under Sufi Khalil Beg Mawsilu besieged Tbilisi, taking it in February 1489. The occupation was short, but Alexander used it to seize Kutaisi and the rest of Imereti. From 1490 to 1493 Constantine recognised Alexander I of Kakheti and Alexander II of Imereti as independent sovereigns and granted Qvarqvare wide autonomy, leaving Georgia divided into three kingdoms and five autonomous principalities.

Between 1492 and 1496 he sought foreign help to reunite the country and defend it against the Ottomans and Safavid Iran, sending envoys to the Burji sultan of Egypt, Qaitbay, Pope Alexander VI and Isabella I of Castile, without result. In 1500 Shah Ismail I drew him and Alexander II of Imereti into a campaign against Ottoman possessions near Tabriz, promising to cancel the tribute Constantine still paid to the Ak Koyunlu. Each Georgian ruler sent 3,000 men, and by 1503 they had helped Ismail recapture Nakhchivan, but Ismail broke his promise and made Kartli and Kakheti his vassals.

Constantine died in 1505 and was succeeded by his son David X; church records suggest he may have abdicated in 1503 or 1504 and become a monk under the name Cyril. His wife Tamar died in 1492. Their sons included two later kings of Kartli, David X and George IX, and Bagrat, Prince of Mukhrani, who founded the House of Mukhrani. Another son, Demetrius, is recorded as co-king with his father, as were his brothers.
constantine-ii-of-greece: Constantine was born on 2 June 1940 in Psychiko, a suburb of Athens, the only son of Crown Prince Paul and Crown Princess Frederica. His father was the younger brother and heir of King George II. Italy invaded Greece in October 1940 and Germany in April 1941, and the infant Constantine was evacuated with his mother and sister to Crete and then, on 30 April 1941, to Egypt. The family later found refuge in South Africa. They returned to Greece in 1946, during the Greek Civil War, and when George II died on 1 April 1947, Paul became king and Constantine crown prince at the age of six.

He was a keen sailor. At the 1960 Rome Olympics he was helmsman of the yacht Nireus, which won the gold medal in the Dragon class with Odysseus Eskitzoglou and Georgios Zaimis, the first Greek gold medal since 1912.

Paul died of cancer on 6 March 1964, and Constantine, aged 23, succeeded him. Later that year he married Princess Anne-Marie of Denmark. His reign was marked by political instability. In the Apostasia of 1965, the king refused the prime minister Georgios Papandreou's wish to take over the defence ministry after the ASPIDA affair, and Papandreou resigned on 15 July; at least 39 members of parliament then left his Centre Union. Historians suspect the king and his mother were interested in a coup from mid-1965, though the royalist C. M. Woodhouse rejected such evidence as certainly untrue.

The Colonels' Coup of 21 April 1967 left Constantine with no loyal forces to rely on, and he reluctantly agreed to swear in the junta on condition that it include mostly civilian ministers. He disliked the regime from the outset and planned a countercoup, which failed. On 13 December 1967 he fled the country.

He remained head of state in exile until the junta abolished the monarchy on 1 June 1973, a decision confirmed by a referendum in July that he contested. After the junta fell, a second referendum in December 1974, which he was not allowed to return to campaign for, confirmed the abolition by a majority of almost 70 per cent. He publicly accepted the verdict. Archives published later show that between 1975 and 1978 he was involved in a conspiracy against the government of Konstantinos Karamanlis, which never materialised.

He lived for decades in London, returning to Greece only briefly, as for his mother's funeral in 1981, which he was allowed to attend for six hours. A dispute over royal property ended in 2002, when the European Court of Human Rights awarded his family €13.7 million. In 2013 he moved back to Athens, where he died on 10 January 2023 after a stroke, aged 82.
constantine-ii-of-scotland: Constantine was a grandson of Kenneth I, the first of the family recorded as a king, though as king of the Picts. His father Áed succeeded Constantine I in 876 and was killed in 878, so Constantine cannot have been born later than 879. He may have spent a period in exile in Ireland, where his aunt Máel Muire was married to two successive High Kings. He became king on the death of his cousin Donald II, who was probably killed fighting Vikings at Dunnottar in 900. The change of title from king of the Picts to king of Alba belongs to a wider transformation of Pictland, and the origins of the Kingdom of Alba are traced to his lifetime.

In 906 Constantine and Bishop Cellach met at the Hill of Belief near Scone and pledged that the laws and disciplines of the faith should be kept. Historians debate the meaning of the phrase pariter cum Scottis. Around 918 he and Ealdred son of Eadulf fought Ragnall at Corbridge, a battle that appears to have been indecisive. In 920 or 921 he was among the kings who chose Edward the Elder as father and lord, and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle then first uses the word scottas for his subjects.

At Eamont Bridge on 12 July 927 Constantine, Owain, Hywel Dda and Ealdred agreed to renounce all idolatry, that is, not to ally with the Viking kings. In 934 Æthelstan invaded by land and sea and ravaged southern Alba, with no record of battles. Constantine witnessed a charter with him as subregulus, but there is no record that he submitted to Æthelstan's overlordship. In 937 he joined Olaf Guthfrithson and Owain ap Dyfnwal against Æthelstan and was defeated at Brunanburh, where a son named Cellach was killed.

Constantine abdicated in 943 and entered a monastery, leaving the kingdom to his nephew Malcolm I. The Prophecy of Berchán states that this was not voluntary. The monastery was probably St Andrews, refounded in his reign and given to the Céli Dé reformers, and he is said to have been abbot there. He died in 952. His reign of 43 years is believed to have played a defining part in the Gaelicisation of Pictland, and the words Scots and Scotland were first used in his time. The form of kingship that appeared then lasted until the Davidian Revolution of the 12th century.
constantine-iii-of-abkhazia: Constantine was the son and successor of Bagrat I, of the Anchabadze dynasty, and his reign was a constant struggle for supremacy among the Georgian lands. The kingdom's growing expansionism carried its realm to the east, and in 904 he annexed a large part of Kartli, bringing his frontier close to Arab-controlled Tiflis. King Smbat I of Armenia and Adarnase IV of Iberia, both his relatives and his rivals in Gugark and Inner Iberia, then joined against him. Adarnase captured him and handed him to Smbat, who held him prisoner at Ani before freeing him to make an alliance against the resurgent Muslims, sealed by a marriage.

The alliance turned Adarnase against Smbat. When Emir Yusuf ibn Abi'l-Saj invaded Armenia in 912, Adarnase barred Smbat's way to refuge in Abkhazia, and Smbat was captured and hanged at Dvin in 914. Yusuf's campaign, one of the last major attempts of the Abbasid Caliphate to hold the Georgian lands, then a patchwork of rival native states and Muslim holdings, devastated and weakened Tao-Klarjeti. Constantine used Adarnase's weakness to restore his authority over Kartli, and Adarnase, confined to his family's lands in Tao, had to recognise himself as Constantine's vassal.

This began almost sixty years of Abkhazian dominance over Tao-Klarjeti. Constantine also invaded Hereti, a principality in the Georgian-Albanian marchlands, and divided its major strongholds with an ally, and he sought influence over Alania by supporting its Christianization. His son George II became king of Abkhazia and reigned until 960; another son, Bagrat II, was co-king, and a daughter married Ashot of Klarjeti.
constantine-iii-western-roman-emperor: Little is known of Constantine before he was declared emperor; his date and place of birth are unknown. He was a common soldier, not an officer. In 406 the roughly 6,000 troops of the field army of Roman Britain, unpaid for years, revolted and chose their own leader. They first appointed Marcus and killed him, then Gratian, who was killed after four months. On 31 December 406 the Vandals, Sueves and Alans crossed the Rhine, and in this insecurity the army chose a man named after Constantine the Great. Early in 407 his fellows acclaimed him emperor. A contemporary called Britain a province rich in usurpers.

Constantine crossed the Channel at Bononia with all the mobile troops left in Britain and their commander Gerontius, and set up his headquarters at Lyon. The army in Gaul declared for him, followed by the civil administration in Hispania, and he negotiated agreements with the Franks, Alamanni and Burgundians that secured the Rhine. Honorius sent Sarus the Goth against him, but after Sarus killed Justinianus, one of Constantine's generals, he was forced to retreat to Italy.

By May 408 Constantine had captured Arles and made it his capital, and he raised his oldest son, a monk, to caesar under the name Constans. Late in 408 Honorius, needing to placate him while the Visigoths under Alaric were in Italy, acknowledged him as co-emperor and sent a purple robe. They were joint consuls in 409.

In 409 Gerontius rebelled, proclaiming his client Maximus emperor at Tarraco and inciting the barbarians in Gaul against Constantine. Saxon raids on Britain began in 408, and in 409 the Roman inhabitants expelled his officials. In spring 410 Constantine led an army into northern Italy but withdrew to Arles at the River Po after a false report that the general Allobich was dead. Gerontius defeated and killed Constans at Vienne, probably early in 411, and then besieged Constantine at Arles.

In 411 Honorius's new general Constantius III arrived at Arles. Much of Gerontius's army deserted to him, and Gerontius retreated to Hispania, where he committed suicide. Constantius defeated a relief force in an ambush, and Constantine, whose troops on the Rhine had abandoned him to support the Gallo-Roman Jovinus, surrendered with his son Julian. Despite a promise of safe passage, Constantius had both beheaded in August or September 411, and Constantine's head was presented to Honorius on 18 September.

The historian Peter Heather describes the Roman Army of Gaul as emerging from these wars in tatters. Roman rule never returned to Britain after Constantine stripped its defences. He has been associated with the Constantine of Geoffrey of Monmouth's fictitious Historia Regum Britanniae, who through his son Uther Pendragon becomes the grandfather of King Arthur.
constantine-iv: Constantine IV was the eldest son of the emperor Constans II and Fausta, daughter of the patrician Valentinus. His year of birth is unknown, though often given as around 650. He was made co-emperor with his father in 654 and became emperor in September 668, when news arrived that Constans II had been assassinated in Sicily.

His first task was to suppress the revolt in Sicily, where conspirators had proclaimed an officer named Mizizios emperor. Pope Vitalian withheld recognition and the navy stayed loyal. Constantine landed at Syracuse, captured Mizizios and had him executed.

Constantine faced severe pressure from the Caliphate of Muʿāwiya I. The Arabs captured Cyzicus and used it as a base, and their fleet took Smyrna and other coastal cities. Possession of the fleet allowed Constantine to defend the capital, and the Byzantines gradually regained the initiative, with counteroffensives into Egypt and Syria that helped end fifteen years of continuous raids. Muʿāwiya's death in 680 closed this period. At home Constantine reintroduced the heavy copper follis of Justinian I to restore the currency.

In November 680 he convened the Sixth Ecumenical Council, also called the Third Council of Constantinople, which reaffirmed the doctrines of Chalcedon and ended the Monothelite controversy; it closed in September 681. In 680 the Bulgars under Khan Asparukh crossed the Danube. Constantine besieged their camp in Dobruja but, in poor health, left the army, which panicked and was defeated. In 681 he acknowledged the Bulgar state in Moesia and agreed to pay tribute.

His brothers Heraclius and Tiberius had been crowned with him, and the populace demanded that this stand, but in late 681 Constantine had their noses slit so that they would be ineligible to rule. He died of dysentery on 10 July 685, succeeded by his son Justinian II. The Eastern Orthodox Church venerates him as a saint for calling the council.
constantine-mavrocordatos: Constantine Mavrocordatos was born in Constantinople on 27 February 1711, a member of the Phanariote Mavrocordatos family. With the support of the boyars he succeeded his father, Nicholas Mavrocordatos, as Prince of Wallachia in 1730, but was removed the same year.

He returned to the Wallachian throne five more times and ruled Moldavia four times. Through the Treaty of Belgrade of 1739, after the Austro-Turkish War of 1737 to 1739, he regained control of Oltenia, the Banat of Craiova. He was a personal rival of Grigore II Ghica: the chronicler Ioan Neculce wrote that once both were on their thrones they quarrelled and denounced each other to the Porte openly.

His fiscal and administrative reforms were partly modelled on those of the Habsburg monarchy during its rule in Oltenia. He abolished several indirect taxes, such as the văcărit on cattle, in favour of a single tax of 10 löwenthaler payable in four quarters. Faced with the flight of serfs to Transylvania, he let them move between estates for a fee, while imposing a quitrent and a corvée of 12 days and allowing boyars a tax-exempt retinue of serfs, the scutelnici. He also forbade slave owners to separate married Roma belonging to different masters.

Against boyar protests he built a salaried administration of ispravnici whom he appointed himself and who could act as judges, merged the prince's personal treasury with that of the state, and denied boyar title to families no longer holding office. In 1761 the Ban of Oltenia moved his seat from Craiova to Bucharest, leaving the region to a kaymakam.

During the Russo-Turkish War, on 5 November 1769, he was wounded and taken prisoner by the troops of Catherine II after resisting at Galați. He was taken to Iași, where he died in captivity on 23 November 1769. The boyars tried to have his reforms overturned, but successive rulers confirmed them.
constantine-of-preslav: Evidence about Constantine's life is scarce, but he is believed to have been a disciple of Saint Methodius. After Methodius died in 885, the Germanic clergy in Great Moravia jailed Constantine and sold him as a slave in Venice. He escaped to Constantinople and around 886 moved to Bulgaria, where he worked at the Preslav Literary School at the end of the 9th century and the beginning of the 10th.

His Didactic Gospel is usually dated to the first years of the reign of Tsar Simeon I, 893–894. A compilation of lectures on a number of church holidays, it is the first systematic work of sermons in Slavic literature, and it opens with the poetic preface known as the Alphabet Prayer. In 894 Constantine wrote the Histories, the first historical chronicle in Slavic literature. In 906, commissioned by Simeon I, he translated the Four Epistles against the Arians of Saint Athanasius of Alexandria, in response to the heresies then beginning to spread in Bulgaria.

He is also said to be the author of the Service for Methodius, which tells of Methodius's struggle for the recognition of Old Church Slavonic, and of the Proclamation of the Holy Gospels, which rejects admiration for the foreign Greek language and champions Old Bulgarian as the means of developing and raising Bulgarian culture.

Constantine was one of the most prolific writers in Old Bulgarian and one of the leading scholars, writers and translators of the Preslav school. None of his original manuscripts survived the burning of Preslav by the Byzantine emperor John I Tzimisces in 972 and the period of Ottoman rule from 1396 to 1878. All of his works are known from later copies, the earliest of which date from the 12th and 13th centuries.
constantine-p-cavafy: Cavafy was born in Alexandria, then in Ottoman Egypt, where his parents had settled in 1855. His father Petros Ioannis, a prosperous merchant who had lived in England and held Greek and British citizenship, died suddenly in 1870. Two years later the family moved to England, and in 1877, after the Long Depression ruined their business, returned to Alexandria. Disturbances in 1882, when Alexandria was bombarded and the family apartment at Ramleh burned, took them to Constantinople, where the nineteen-year-old Cavafy began researching his ancestry and first wrote poetry systematically. In 1885 he returned to Alexandria and lived there for the rest of his life.

He worked as a news correspondent, then at the stock exchange, and was finally hired as a temporary clerk in the British-run Egyptian Ministry of Public Works, a post renewed annually for thirty years. He published from 1891 to 1904 in broadsheets for close friends, and a favourable review by Gregorios Xenopoulos in 1903 introduced him to literary circles on the Greek mainland. Kostis Palamas and his followers criticised his mixture of Katharevousa and Demotic. He quit his post in 1922, calling it a liberation. E. M. Forster, who knew him, introduced his poems to English readers in 1923.

Cavafy classed his poems as historical, philosophical and hedonistic or sensual. Waiting for the Barbarians, of 1904, shows a city whose people wait for barbarians who never come, and ends, "Those people were a solution of a sort". Ithaca, of 1911, draws on the Odyssey and says that the journey matters more than the destination.

Cavafy died of cancer of the larynx on 29 April 1933, his seventieth birthday. His canon of 154 poems appeared in book form only in 1935, in an anthology by Heracles Apostolidis. After the Greco-Turkish War, younger poets such as Karyotakis found inspiration in him, and Forster, Arnold J. Toynbee and T. S. Eliot promoted him before the Second World War. The Cavafy Museum, set up in his Alexandria apartment in 1992, holds his manuscripts and translations in 20 languages.
constantine-phaulkon: Phaulkon was born to Greek parents within Assos Castle in northern Cephalonia, then under Venetian rule; his father was named Zuane, and the family name was Gerakis or Gerachi. At 13 he left the island on an English ship and spent ten years in London, where the name became Falcon before it was given a Greek form again as Phaulkon. He may have fought under Prince Rupert of the Rhine in the Second Anglo-Dutch War. In 1669 he sailed to Bantam as an assistant gunner and joined the English East India Company as a clerk.

He reached Siam as a merchant in 1675 and learned Siamese within a few years, besides English, French, Portuguese and Malay. In 1681 the Phra Khlang Kosa Lek introduced him to the court of King Narai, where he worked as an interpreter and in the royal treasury. In 1682 he became a Catholic and married Maria Guyomar de Pinha, a woman of mixed Japanese, Portuguese and Bengali descent. In 1686 he led royal troops against the Makassar Revolt and was nearly killed in the fighting.

Phaulkon engineered a rapprochement with France that brought an exchange of embassies, among them that of the Chevalier de Chaumont in 1685 and Kosa Pan's to Versailles, and a French expeditionary force by 1687. Louis XIV made him a knight of the Order of Saint Michael. Meanwhile his English protégés Richard Burnaby and Samuel White used the port of Mergui for piracy against Golconda, and the Company's reprisal in 1687 ended in a massacre of English residents there and a Siamese declaration of war on the Company.

As Narai lay terminally ill, a rumour spread that Phaulkon meant to rule through the designated heir, Phra Pi. Phetracha, Narai's foster brother, staged the 1688 Siamese revolution: on 18 May Narai and Phra Pi were arrested and Phaulkon was seized, imprisoned and tortured, and the French commander Desfarges made no move to save him. On 5 June 1688 he was beheaded near Wat Sak by Luang Sorasak. Narai died on 11 July, and Phetracha, proclaimed king, expelled almost all the French troops.

His place in Thai history is disputed. Supporters of Phetracha present him as a foreign opportunist serving Western interests, while more sceptical historians see a convenient scapegoat for Phetracha's seizure of the throne.
constantine-tikh: Konstantin Tih was a wealthy Bulgarian boyar whose estates lay in the region of Sofia or Skopje. In a charter to the Saint George Monastery near Skopje he stated that Stefan Nemanja of Serbia was his grandfather, and the Byzantine historian George Pachymeres called him half-Serbian. He may have been related to the Serbian royal house through either parent. Some scholars hold that he was a son or nephew of the boyar John Tihomir, who controlled Skopje in the late 12th century.

Michael II Asen was murdered by his cousin Kaliman in late 1256 or early 1257, and Kaliman was soon killed too, ending the male line of the Asen dynasty. Rostislav Mikhailovich of Macsó and the boyar Mitso claimed Bulgaria, but neither won the support of the boyars of Tarnovo, who offered the throne to Konstantin. He divorced his first wife and in 1258 married Irene Doukaina Laskarina, daughter of Theodore II of Nicaea and Elena, a daughter of Ivan Asen II. The marriage strengthened his claim, and he was thereafter called Konstantin Asen.

War with Hungary and with the Byzantine Empire followed. In 1260 he retook Vidin from Rostislav, and in 1261 Hungarian troops under Stephen, son of Béla IV, stormed into Bulgaria and restored the north-west to Rostislav. After Michael VIII Palaiologos blinded John IV Laskaris, Irene persuaded Konstantin to fight Michael.

He took Stanimaka and Philippopolis in 1262, but a Byzantine army recovered them, and by the end of 1263 Bulgaria had lost significant territory to the Byzantines and the Hungarians. In late 1264 he joined Tatar forces against Michael and took the fortress of Ainos. In 1266 Stephen captured Vidin and plundered the region of Tarnovo.

In 1268, to keep him out of an anti-Byzantine coalition, Michael VIII gave him his niece Maria Palaiologina Kantakouzene as a third wife and promised Mesembria and Anchialos as her dowry, but did not hand them over. A riding accident left Konstantin paralysed from the waist down, and Maria took control of the government. Nogai's Tatars raided Bulgaria regularly.

Costly and unsuccessful wars, repeated Mongol raids and economic instability, including Konstantin's minting of coins on a vast scale, led to a revolt in 1277. A swineherd or swine-owner named Ivaylo led the discontented and took control of a significant area. Konstantin marched against him with his guard but was decisively defeated and killed in his chariot. His son Michael Tih by Maria succeeded as co-emperor of Bulgaria from 1277 to 1279.
constantine-vi: Constantine was born on 14 January 771, the only child of Emperor Leo IV and Irene. His father crowned him co-emperor in 776, and he succeeded as sole emperor in 780 at the age of nine, with his mother and her minister Staurakios as regents. In 788 Irene broke off his engagement to Rotrude, a daughter of Charlemagne.

After the Armeniac troops rebelled against Irene, Constantine came to actual power in 790. After an unsuccessful campaign in the Balkans he restored his mother as co-ruler in 792, the year he was defeated by Kardam of Bulgaria at the Battle of Marcellae. A plot then formed in favour of his uncle, the Caesar Nikephoros. Constantine had his uncle blinded and the tongues of his father's four other half-brothers cut out. He also blinded the Armeniac general Alexios Mosele, and the Armeniacs revolted, a rising he crushed with extreme cruelty in 793.

He then divorced his wife Maria of Amnia, who had borne no male heir, and married his mistress Theodote. The marriage was unpopular and canonically illegal and began the Moechian controversy. Patriarch Tarasios refused to officiate, and Theodote's uncle Plato of Sakkoudion was imprisoned after breaking communion with him. The controversy cost Constantine most of his support in the church, which Irene took care to back in public.

On 19 August 797 supporters of Irene captured Constantine, blinded and imprisoned him, and she was crowned as the first empress regnant. When he died is unknown, but it was before 805, and he may have died of his wounds soon after. He was buried in the Monastery of St Euphrosyne, which Irene had founded. In 800 Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne as Emperor of the Romans, on the assertion that a woman could not rule in her own right, so Constantine was the last ruler recognised by the eastern empire, the papacy and the Western powers alike.
constantine-vii: Constantine was born in Constantinople on 17 or 18 May 905, the son of Emperor Leo VI by his fourth wife, Zoe Karbonopsina, a marriage the church regarded as uncanonical. To help legitimise him, his mother gave birth to him in the Purple Room of the imperial palace, where legitimate children of reigning emperors were normally born, hence the epithet Porphyrogennetos, born in the purple. His father and uncle raised him to the throne as a two-year-old child on 15 May 908. In early 913 his dying uncle Alexander appointed a seven-man regency council headed by Patriarch Nicholas Mystikos.

Most of Constantine's reign was dominated by others. The patriarch made an unpopular peace with Tsar Simeon of Bulgaria, and Zoe drove him out of the regency, but the Bulgarians defeated her general Leo Phokas in 917. In March 919 the admiral Romanos Lekapenos replaced her as regent and married his daughter Helena to Constantine; he became co-emperor on 17 December 920, and Constantine was eclipsed by a senior emperor. Constantine spent those years studying the ceremonies of the court.

Romanos was deposed by his sons in December 944, and Constantine became sole emperor on 27 January 945, aged 39. He left government largely to bureaucrats, generals and his wife Helena. In 947 he ordered the return of peasant lands without compensation. A fleet sent against the Arab corsairs of Crete in 949 failed, but in the east Nikephoros Phokas took Adata in 958 and John Tzimiskes captured Samosata a year later. Olga of Kiev, regent of the Rus', visited him in 957 and was baptised. Constantine died on 9 November 959 and his son Romanos II succeeded him; it was rumoured that he had been poisoned.

Constantine was a writer and scholar who gathered educated men round him. He wrote or commissioned the Geoponika, a compilation of earlier agronomic works; De Ceremoniis, on court ceremonies; De Administrando Imperio, advice for his son on running the empire and dealing with its enemies; and the Excerpta Historica, selections from ancient historians, of which only six of fifty-three titles survive. A history praising his grandfather Basil I is also attributed to him, though his authorship is uncertain. John Julius Norwich calls him the Scholar Emperor.
constantine-xi-palaiologos: Constantine was born on 8 February 1404, the fourth son of Emperor Manuel II Palaiologos and the Serbian noblewoman Helena Dragaš. Little is known of his youth, but from the 1420s he showed skill as a military commander, and his older brother John VIII Palaiologos twice named him regent in Constantinople. In 1428 he was proclaimed Despot of the Morea, the Peloponnese, which he ruled with his brothers Theodore and Thomas; together they extended Roman rule over almost the whole peninsula for the first time since the Fourth Crusade and rebuilt the Hexamilion wall. A campaign into Central Greece and Thessaly in 1444–1446 failed.

John VIII died childless in October 1448 and Constantine, his preferred heir, was supported by their mother Helena against his brother Demetrios, who had the backing of those opposed to church union. The Ottoman sultan Murad II accepted the succession. Constantine remained unmarried and childless. Like John, he supported the union of the Greek Orthodox and Catholic Churches proclaimed at the Council of Florence, and appealed for help to Pope Nicholas V and to Venice, but the pope required full acceptance of the union and Venice promised aid only if others joined it. In October 1452 the legate Isidore of Kiev arrived with 200 Neapolitan archers to confirm the union, which inflamed its opponents in the city.

In April 1453 Mehmed II led an army of perhaps 80,000 men against Constantinople, defended by probably fewer than 10,000. Constantine had laid a great chain across the Golden Horn to keep out the Ottoman fleet. The city fell on 29 May 1453. No eyewitness to the emperor's death survived, and the sources differ: most, among them Michael Critobulus and Cardinal Isidore, say he died fighting at the gate of Saint Romanus; others report that he was trampled, that he hanged himself, or that he escaped.

His death ended the line of Roman emperors begun by Augustus. In Greek folklore he became the Marble Emperor: an angel was said to have turned him to marble and hidden him beneath the Golden Gate, to be raised when God wills the city restored.
constantinople: The city stood on a peninsula at the south-eastern tip of Thrace, with the Bosporus to the east, the Golden Horn to the north and the Sea of Marmara to the south. Its position between the Aegean and the Black Sea, and between Europe and Asia, gave it command of the trade routes between the two seas. Before Constantine it was Byzantion, settled around 657 BCE by colonists from Megara, and briefly renamed Augusta Antonina by Septimius Severus. Constantine at first called his city New Rome; it soon became known as Constantinople, the city of Constantine.

The land side was protected by the Theodosian walls, a double wall with a moat and palisades in front, and from the fifth century by the Anastasian Wall, a chain of walls about 60 kilometres long across the Thracian peninsula. The city was built to rival Rome, and it was claimed that several of its elevations matched Rome's seven hills.

Constantine chose the site because Rome lay too far from the frontiers and the armies, and because Byzantion could be readily defended, with easy access to the Danube and Euphrates frontiers and supplies from the workshops of Roman Asia. It became the eastern capital in 330 and the sole capital once the western provinces were lost in the fifth century. Its standing grew gradually: it received its first known urban prefect, Honoratus, in 359. Under Justinian I the expedition to reconquer Africa sailed from the city in 533. In 618 Heraclius ended the free grain supply, since Egypt could no longer feed the city during the Persian wars, and the population fell substantially.

From the mid-fifth century to the early thirteenth, Constantinople was the largest and wealthiest city in Europe. In 1204 the Fourth Crusade, diverted against it, sacked the city and set up the Latin Empire, which lasted until Michael VIII Palaiologos retook the city in 1261. It then had about 35,000 people, a number he raised to about 70,000 by the end of his reign. The Black Death reached it in 1347. Mehmed II took the city in 1453; his soldiers had three days to pillage, and he ordered an imam to call the adhan in Hagia Sophia, turning the cathedral into a mosque.

The city remained the Ottoman capital until the empire's dissolution and the founding of the Republic of Turkey in 1923, when the capital moved to Ankara. It is now known internationally as Istanbul and lies in both Europe and Asia. Byzantine architecture, from St Mark's Basilica in Venice to churches across the Slavic East, was widely copied, and Byzantine gold coinage, the bezant, was prized throughout the Middle Ages.
constantius-i: Marcus Flavius Valerius Constantius was born on 31 March in a year that is unknown, probably no later than about 250, in Moesia Superior, a Roman province on the middle Danube. He was of humble origin. The Historia Augusta, an unreliable source, makes him the son of a nobleman named Eutropius and of Claudia, a niece of the emperor Claudius Gothicus; modern historians suspect this link was invented under his son Constantine. The nickname Chlorus, the Pale, was popularised by Byzantine-era historians and was not used in his lifetime.

He served in the guard under Aurelian, fought against the Palmyrene Empire in the east, and later became governor of Dalmatia. By 288 he was praetorian prefect in the west under Maximian, and he took part in campaigns against the Alamanni. Around 289 he divorced Helena, the mother of Constantine, and married Maximian's daughter Theodora.

In 293, under the power-sharing arrangement known as the Tetrarchy, Constantius was appointed caesar to Maximian at Milan on 1 March. His command included Gaul and Britain, and his capital was Trier. He first defeated the forces of the usurper Carausius in Gaul, capturing Boulogne. Carausius was then murdered by his finance officer Allectus, who held Britain until 296. Constantius spent two years against the Franks and Alamanni before launching two fleets across the Channel. The one under his prefect Julius Asclepiodotus landed near the Isle of Wight and defeated and killed Allectus; Constantius occupied London and killed the Frankish mercenaries roaming the province.

He reorganised the British provinces and restored Hadrian's Wall and its forts. In 298 he defeated the Alamanni at Langres and again at Vindonissa, and in 300 he fought the Franks, settling some of them in deserted parts of Gaul. When the Diocletianic Persecution began in 303 he ordered the demolition of churches but made the least effort of the four rulers to enforce the edicts; Eusebius denied that he destroyed any, while Lactantius says he did.

Diocletian and Maximian abdicated on 1 May 305, and Constantius became augustus in the west. His son Constantine, who had been passed over for the rank of caesar, joined him in Gaul as he prepared to campaign in Britain. Constantius advanced into the far north of the island against the Picts and, by 7 January 306, claimed a victory and the title Britannicus Maximus. He wintered at York and died there on 25 July 306, recommending his son to the army, which acclaimed Constantine emperor. This helped bring down the Tetrarchy and began civil wars that ended in 324.

Christian writers made Constantius secretly Christian, and medieval Welsh and Geoffrey of Monmouth's tales gave him a British wife; these have no historical validity, as he had divorced Helena before going to Britain.
constantius-ii: Constantius was born on 7 August 317 at Sirmium in Pannonia, the third son of Constantine the Great and the second by his wife Fausta. His father made him caesar on 8 November 324, when he was seven. In 336 war broke out with Sasanian Persia under Shapur II, and Constantine sent him east to command the frontier. He defeated and killed the Persian general Narses at Narasara, recaptured Amida and strengthened its walls.

When Constantine died in 337, Constantius buried him in the Church of the Holy Apostles. Soon afterwards the army massacred two of his uncles and seven cousins, among them Hannibalianus and Dalmatius. The official account blamed a mutinous army, but Ammianus Marcellinus, Zosimus, Libanius, Athanasius and Julian blamed Constantius himself. He and his brothers Constantine II and Constans then divided the empire at Sirmium, and he received the eastern provinces.

For years Constantius defended the eastern frontier against Shapur II, whose attacks were mostly sieges of Nisibis, Singara and Amida; Shapur won most of these encounters but gained little. In the west, Constantine II died in an ambush in 340, leaving Constans in control until he was killed in 350 by forces loyal to the usurper Magnentius. Constantius made his cousin Gallus caesar in the east and married his sister Constantina to him. He defeated Magnentius at Mursa Major in 351, one of the bloodiest battles between Roman armies, and at Mons Seleucus in 353, after which Magnentius killed himself.

Sole ruler from 353, he had Gallus arrested and executed after reports of his conduct, and on 6 November 355 made his last male relative, Julian, caesar and sent him to Gaul. He campaigned against the Alamanni, and in 357 against the Sarmatians and Quadi across the Danube; that year he visited Rome for the only time. Laws of the 350s forbade pagan sacrifice under penalty of death, though he never disbanded the priestly colleges. He pressed a compromise position between Arianism and the Nicene Creed on the church, and he restricted Jewish ownership of slaves.

When Shapur destroyed Singara and took Amida in 360, Constantius travelled east. Julian's Gallic legions, ordered to send reinforcements, proclaimed him augustus. Constantius could not answer at once and in 361 set out west, but he fell ill with fever and died at Mopsuestia on 3 November 361. Sources say he was baptised by the bishop Euzoius and named Julian his successor. He was buried in the Church of the Holy Apostles.

His reputation is divided. Ammianus portrays a conscientious but vain emperor open to flatterers, while orthodox churchmen and Julian saw a heretic and a murderer. Some modern historians think he suffered at the hands of unsympathetic authors, and note that many contemporaries held him in high esteem.
constitutio-antoniniana: Before 212 CE full Roman citizenship was mostly held by the inhabitants of Roman Italy. Colonies of Romans in the provinces, Romans and their descendants living there, the inhabitants of various cities and small numbers of local nobles, such as kings of client states, also held it. Provincials were usually non-citizens, although some held Latin rights, and veterans of the auxiliary troops received citizenship on discharge. Citizenship remained a sought-after status until 212.

The edict, issued by Caracalla, declared that all free men in the Roman Empire were to receive full Roman citizenship, and by extension free women were to have the rights of Roman women, such as the jus trium liberorum. One exclusion occurs in a disputed passage referring to the dediticii, technically free people without citizenship or Latin rights. These were foreigners who had surrendered under treaty and former slaves counted among them because of a penal status. The exclusion is most often taken to refer to the freedmen.

The jurist Ulpian states in the Digest that all persons throughout the Roman world were made Roman citizens by an edict of Antoninus Caracalla. Many new citizens took the name Aurelius, after the emperor's full name, Marcus Aurelius Antoninus. Seven of the eleven emperors between Gallienus and Diocletian, among them Claudius Gothicus, Probus and Carus, bore the name Marcus Aurelius.

The reasons for the decree are still discussed. Cassius Dio held that Caracalla's real purpose was to increase his revenues, since aliens did not pay most of the taxes, though he generally regarded the emperor as contemptible. Few of those who gained citizenship were wealthy, and the measure is thought to have had other purposes, perhaps to enlarge the number of men able to serve in the legions, since only citizens could be legionaries.

Recent scholars see the edict as a milestone in the provincialisation of Roman law: private law in the provinces had to be rewritten to conform with that applying to citizens, and imperial constitutions became the main source of Roman law. Provincial law at variance with it still held in places, as papyri from Egypt show. Mary Beard describes the era after 212 as effectively a new state masquerading under an old name.
constitutio-romana: The agreement was drawn up between Lothair I, King of Italy and since 817 co-emperor with his father Louis the Pious, and Pope Eugene II, and it was confirmed on 11 November 824. Eugene's election was then being challenged by Zinzinnus, the candidate of the Roman populace, and the pope agreed to several concessions to imperial power in central Italy in return for Lothair's military and juridical support.

The constitution was divided into nine articles. It declared inviolable those under the special protection of pope or emperor, required obedience to the pope and his officials, forbade the plundering of church property after a pope's death and ordered the Church's property restored. It restored the custom set by Pope Stephen III in 769 under which both clergy and laity of Rome took part in papal elections, and it set out to check the power of the nobles and to put down robbery with violence.

Two commissioners, one named by the pope and one by the emperor, were to report how justice was administered, so that failures could be corrected by the pope or, if he did not act, by the emperor. Each person was to be judged under the law, Roman, Salic or Lombard, under which he had chosen to live. The people swore to obey the emperors Louis and Lothair, saving their fidelity to the pope, and to allow no uncanonical election. The constitution also introduced the earliest known papal oath.

Sixty years later Pope Marinus I set it aside for a time with a decree that the emperors should not interfere in the election of a pope, either directly or through their ambassadors. In 962, however, many of its clauses were reintroduced in the Diploma Ottonianum. Modern scholars debate whether it was a dead letter with little practical impact or marked a stage on the road to imperial domination of the papacy.
constitution-act-1867: The preamble records that New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and the Province of Canada had asked to form one Dominion with a constitution similar in principle to that of the United Kingdom. The act made Canada the name of the new federation and Ottawa its seat of government, left executive authority vested in the Queen, exercised by the Governor General with a Privy Council, and created a Parliament of the monarch, a Senate and a House of Commons. Senators were appointed rather than elected, 72 at the union, in equal regional divisions, and money bills had to begin in the Commons.

Sections 91 and 92 list the subjects of federal and provincial law: Parliament may legislate for the peace, order and good government of Canada and on criminal law, marriage and divorce, and Indians and lands reserved for the Indians, while the provinces hold property and civil rights and the administration of justice. Education went to the provinces with protections for denominational schools, reflecting the Protestant and Catholic quarrels of the time. Section 133 allows English and French in the federal Parliament, the Quebec legislature and their courts, and section 146 provided for admitting further colonies.

The courts have read much into the act's brief text. The Privy Council held that the peace, order and good government power is a limited federal competence rather than a general residue, and the Supreme Court of Canada relied on the preamble in 1993 on parliamentary privilege and in the Provincial Judges Reference of 1997 to hold that judicial independence is guaranteed. Until the decision in Edwards v Canada (AG) of 1929 the provision on appointing senators was read as excluding women. Section 91(24) allowed the government to act as if the treaties between Indigenous peoples and the Crown before Confederation, such as the Treaty of Niagara of 1764, did not exist.

The act has no written bill of rights. When the constitution was patriated in 1982, the British North America Acts were renamed the Constitution Acts and section 92A added, giving the provinces greater control over non-renewable natural resources. The day the act took effect, 1 July 1867, is kept as Canada Day, called Dominion Day before 1982.
constitution-act-1982: Under the Statute of Westminster, 1931, the British Parliament kept the power to amend the British North America Act, 1867, until Canadian governments could agree on an amending formula of their own. After substantial agreement on such a formula in 1981, both houses of the Parliament of Canada asked the British Parliament to give up that power, which it did by the Canada Act 1982 in March 1982. On 17 April 1982 Queen Elizabeth II, Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau, the Minister of Justice Jean Chrétien and the Registrar General André Ouellet signed the proclamation that brought the act into force.

Part I is the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, which replaced the Canadian Bill of Rights of 1960, a federal statute that did not apply to provincial laws. The Charter greatly widened judicial review, and its section 24 let courts grant new remedies and exclude improperly obtained evidence. Section 35 recognises and affirms the existing aboriginal and treaty rights of the Indian, Inuit and Métis peoples; amendments of 1983 guaranteed them equally to men and women and extended them to land claims agreements. Section 36 sets out a commitment to equal opportunity and the principle of equalisation payments.

Part V lays down five amending procedures, among them the general 7/50 formula of section 38 and the unanimity procedure of section 41. A new section 92A of the 1867 act gave the provinces exclusive jurisdiction over non-renewable natural resources and electrical generation. Subsection 52(1) declares the Constitution the supreme law of Canada, and subsection 52(2) defines it as including the Canada Act 1982 and 30 acts and orders listed in a schedule, the 1867 act renamed the Constitution Act, 1867 among them.

The Supreme Court concluded that Quebec's formal consent was never necessary, and the Meech Lake and Charlottetown Accords both failed to obtain it. In New Brunswick Broadcasting Co v Nova Scotia the Supreme Court held that the list in section 52(2) is not exhaustive and added parliamentary privilege to the Constitution as an unwritten principle. Section 55 required French versions of the parts enacted only in English; a committee set up in 1984 presented them in 1990, but they have not been put forward for enactment. Canada's patriation set an example for the Australia Act 1986 and New Zealand's Constitution Act 1986.
constitution-of-3-may-1791: The Government Act, as the Constitution was titled, was adopted by the Great Sejm that met from 1788 to 1792, in response to the perilous situation of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, which had been a major European power only a century earlier. Since 1652 the liberum veto had allowed any Sejm deputy to nullify all the legislation of that Sejm, and deputies bribed by magnates or foreign powers had paralysed government for over a century; only a confederated sejm was immune to it. The Great Sejm opened on 6 October 1788 and became a confederated sejm on its second day. Russia and Austria were at war with the Ottoman Empire, and a new alliance with Prussia seemed to offer security.

On 18 April 1791 the Sejm adopted the Free Royal Cities Act, expanding the rights of townspeople after their Black Procession in Warsaw demanded enfranchisement. The Constitution was drafted by King Stanisław August Poniatowski, with contributions from Ignacy Potocki, Hugo Kołłątaj and others. The King is credited with the general provisions and Kołłątaj with the document's final shape.

The Constitution reflected Enlightenment influences, among them Rousseau's social contract and Montesquieu's balance among legislative, executive and judicial branches and a bicameral legislature. It sought a more effective constitutional monarchy, introduced political equality between townspeople and nobility and placed the peasants under the government's protection, mitigating the worst abuses of serfdom. Article I acknowledged the Roman Catholic faith as the dominant religion but guaranteed tolerance and freedom to all religions. Article II confirmed many old privileges of the nobility, and Article III made the Free Royal Cities Act integral to the Constitution: personal security was extended to townspeople, including Jews, who also gained the right to acquire landed property and became eligible for officers' commissions and public offices.

The Commonwealth's neighbours reacted with hostility. Magnates opposed to the reform formed the Targowica Confederation and asked Catherine the Great to intervene, and Russian armies allied with them in the Polish–Russian War of 1792, while Frederick William II of Prussia broke the Prussian alliance. The Constitution was in force for less than 19 months. The Grodno Sejm of 1793 declared it null and void, and the Second and Third Partitions of 1793 and 1795 ended the sovereign existence of Poland and Lithuania until 1918.

Over the following 123 years its memory helped sustain Polish and Lithuanian aspirations for independence. Two of its authors, Potocki and Kołłątaj, called it the last will and testament of the expiring Homeland. The holiday of 3 May was banned during the partitions, reinstated in 1919 and restored in April 1990.
constitution-of-india: In 1928 the All Parties Conference convened a committee at Lucknow to prepare a constitution for India, whose report became known as the Nehru Report. The constitution that was eventually adopted drew mainly on the Government of India Act 1935, which was largely drafted by Samuel Hoare.
