Its framers also borrowed features of earlier legislation: the Government of India Act 1858, the Indian Councils Acts of 1861, 1892 and 1909, the Government of India Act 1919 and the Indian Independence Act 1947. The last of these, which led to the creation of Pakistan, divided the former Constituent Assembly in two, and each new assembly had sovereign power to draft a constitution for its own state.

The Constituent Assembly was elected by the members of the provincial assemblies. It first met on 9 December 1946, and on 11 December appointed Rajendra Prasad as its president and B. N. Rau as constitutional legal adviser. Its 389 members were reduced to 299 after partition. On 13 December 1946 Jawaharlal Nehru presented an Objective Resolution laying down the underlying principles, which later became the Preamble. The assembly took almost three years to draft the constitution, holding eleven sessions over 165 days. Rau's initial draft had 243 articles and 13 schedules; after discussion, debate and amendment the text came to 395 articles and 8 schedules, in 22 parts. A seven-member drafting committee chaired by B. R. Ambedkar considered and amended Rau's draft.

The constitution declares India a sovereign, socialist, secular and democratic republic, though the words socialist and secular were added to the Preamble by the 42nd amendment in 1976. It sets up a parliamentary system in which the Council of Ministers, headed by the prime minister, is collectively responsible to the lower house, the Lok Sabha. Its first article describes India as a Union of States. The states retain important powers and are represented in the Rajya Sabha, but the Union List gives the national government exclusive authority over matters such as defence and international relations. Article 368 sets the procedure for amendment, which needs a two-thirds majority in each house of Parliament.

The framers repealed earlier British acts in Article 395, to ensure constitutional autochthony. The text is deliberately worded in generalities, to ensure flexibility. The American historian Granville Austin called it first and foremost a social document, with its Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles as its chief instruments and conscience. It does not limit Parliament's power of amendment, but in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala the Supreme Court held that certain features are so integral to the constitution that they can never be removed, a principle known as the Basic Structure doctrine. The Hindi translation was the first into an Indian language, made by the linguist Raghu Vira.
constitution-of-ireland: The Constitution replaced the Constitution of the Irish Free State, in force since 6 December 1922. There were two main reasons. The Statute of Westminster 1931 made the dominions sovereign in their own right, and the 1922 text was associated in many eyes with the controversial Anglo-Irish Treaty. Éamon de Valera, leader of the anti-treaty faction, founded Fianna Fáil in 1926, and the party entered government after the 1932 general election.

De Valera supervised the writing personally. John Hearne, legal adviser to the Department of External Affairs, drafted it, a group under Micheál Ó Gríobhtha translated it into Irish, and John Charles McQuaid, president of Blackrock College, advised on religious, educational and family questions. Dáil Éireann approved the draft on 14 June 1937.

It was put to a plebiscite on 1 July 1937, the day of the general election, and passed with 56 percent in favour, 38.6 percent of the whole electorate. Fine Gael and Labour supporters, Unionists and some independents and feminists opposed it. It came into force on 29 December 1937. The text of about 16,000 words opens in the name of the Most Holy Trinity and asserts the sovereignty of the people. It provides for a directly elected, largely ceremonial president, a head of government called the taoiseach, a parliament, the Oireachtas, with Dáil Éireann and Seanad Éireann, and a judiciary headed by the Supreme Court, which can strike down unconstitutional laws.

Article 8 makes Irish the first official language and English the second, and the Irish text prevails in a conflict. Article 45 sets out directive principles of social policy that no court may enforce. Amendment requires a referendum.

As adopted, Article 2 claimed the whole island as the national territory. The Good Friday Agreement of 1998 led to amended Articles 2 and 3, in force from December 1999, which say a united Ireland may come about only with the consent of majorities in both jurisdictions.

On publication the Irish Independent called the draft one of de Valera's finest tributes to his predecessors, while the Irish Times criticised the territorial claim on Northern Ireland and the omission of the British Commonwealth, and the Daily Telegraph objected to the special position of the Roman Catholic Church. The British government protested in a communiqué on 30 December 1937.

The Fifth Amendment removed the recognition of named denominations and the special position of the Catholic Church. The constitution contained a prohibition of abortion from 1983 to 2018, and the 34th amendment in 2015 provided for same-sex marriage. Referendums in March 2024 rejected proposed changes to the articles on the family and on women's life within the home.
constitution-of-japan: The Meiji Constitution of 1889, the fundamental law of the Empire of Japan, was modelled on Prussian and British examples and made the prime minister and cabinet accountable to the emperor rather than to the elected Imperial Diet. On 26 July 1945 the United States, the United Kingdom and the Republic of China issued the Potsdam Declaration, which demanded surrender, demilitarisation and democratisation. Japan accepted its conditions, which implied changes to the constitution after the surrender.

General Douglas MacArthur, the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, at first directed Prime Minister Kijūrō Shidehara to prepare a new constitution, but Emperor Hirohito and most of the cabinet were reluctant to replace the 1889 document. In February 1946 MacArthur presented a draft prepared under his own supervision, which Japanese scholars reviewed and modified. To preserve legal continuity, the new text was adopted as an amendment to the Meiji Constitution under Article 73 of that document.

The constitution has a preamble and 103 articles in 11 chapters, and is short at about 5,000 words. The preamble declares that sovereign power resides with the people. The emperor is 'the symbol of the State and of the unity of the people', and his role is entirely ceremonial. Article 9 states that the Japanese people forever renounce war as a sovereign right of the nation and the threat or use of force to settle international disputes.

Thirty-one articles describe the rights and duties of the people, which the Meiji Constitution had granted only within the limits of law. The constitution sets up a parliamentary system. A bicameral National Diet is made up of a House of Representatives and a House of Councillors, and the old House of Peers, composed of nobles, was abolished. The Cabinet is headed by a Prime Minister and answerable to the Diet. Amendments need a two-thirds vote of each house and a majority in a referendum.

The Diet's two houses made amendments of their own without interference from MacArthur, adding provisions for suits against the State for officials' torts and for wrongful detention. The text took effect on 3 May 1947, after a six-month transitional period. A government body, the Kenpō Fukyū Kai, was established to promote acceptance of the new constitution among the people.

The necessity and extent of Article 9 have been debated in Japan since its enactment, particularly after the Self-Defense Forces were set up in 1954. Some lower courts have found them unconstitutional, but the Supreme Court has never ruled on the question.
constitution-of-latvia: The Satversme was drafted by the Constitutional Assembly of Latvia, which had 150 members, later 152, elected in April 1920. A Constitutional committee presented its draft on 20 September 1921, in two parts: the first regulated the state's institutions and the second the rights and obligations of citizens. The text was influenced by Germany's Weimar Constitution and the Swiss Federal Constitution, and German was one of the working languages of the Assembly. The first part was passed on 15 February 1922.

The second received 62 votes in favour and 6 against on 5 April 1922, with 62 abstentions counted as noes, mostly because the parties of Latgale opposed it, and so it was not adopted. A law of 20 June 1922 set the constitution to come into force at midnight on 7 November 1922.

The constitution consists of 116 articles in eight chapters, covering general provisions, the Saeima, the President, the Cabinet, legislation, the courts, the State Audit Office and, since 1998, fundamental human rights. It declares Latvia an independent democratic republic whose sovereign power is vested in the people. The Saeima has 100 members, elected for four years in general, equal and direct elections by secret ballot on proportional representation.

Executive power lies with the President and the Cabinet; the President's orders must be countersigned by the Prime Minister or the relevant minister, with two exceptions, dissolving the Saeima and choosing a new Prime Minister. Articles 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 77 can be amended only by national referendum. Eight amendments were made after independence was restored; among them the voting age fell from 21 to 18 in 1994, the Constitutional Court was established in 1996, and the Latvian language was given official status in 1998.

After Kārlis Ulmanis's coup of 15 May 1934 his cabinet gave the functions of parliament to the Cabinet of Ministers, until a new constitution could be drafted, which never happened. After the Soviet occupation of June 1940 the Latvian SSR adopted constitutions modelled on the Soviet ones, in August 1940 and April 1978.

Latvian lawyers and historians hold that the 1922 constitution remained in effect, since Ulmanis's declaration cancelled none of its parts and the People's Saeima of 1940 was elected under the Russian SFSR's constitution. On 4 May 1990 the Supreme Soviet of the Latvian SSR declared the restoration of independence and reintroduced articles 1, 2, 3 and 6; the whole constitution was reintroduced by the 5th Saeima on 6 July 1993.
constitution-of-medina: According to traditional Islamic belief, in Muhammad's last years in Mecca a delegation from twelve important clans of Medina invited him, as a neutral outsider, to be chief arbitrator for the whole community. Fighting among Medina's pagan and Jewish inhabitants had gone on for around a hundred years before 620, and after the Battle of Bu'ath it was clear that tribal blood feud was no longer workable without one man with the authority to adjudicate.

After the emigration Muhammad is said to have drafted the constitution, a kind of alliance or federation of the Medinan tribes and the Muslim emigrants from Mecca. It made him chief magistrate, the final authority in disputes, the interpretation of law and the maintenance of public order.

The document has about 47 clauses. It declares that the believers form a separate community, the ummah, and sets out the duty of each clan, among them the emigrants from the Quraysh, Banu Awf and Banu an-Najjar, to pay its own blood money and ransom its own prisoners. Believers are allies of one another, are to relieve anyone burdened with debt, and are to raise their hands together against a rebel, even a son. Disputes are to be referred to God and to Muhammad.

The Jews of several named clans are 'one community along with the believers', each with their own religion, and are to share the costs of war when they fight alongside the Muslims. The Quraysh are to be given no protection, and the valley of Yathrib, Medina, is declared sacred for the people of the document. Jonathan Berkey finds the inclusion of the Jewish tribes in the ummah one of its most interesting features, and it sets faith ties above blood ties.

The text is known only from excerpts in early Muslim sources, chiefly the biography of Ibn Hisham, a recension of Ibn Ishaq, and the Kitab al-Amwal of Abu Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Sallam. It lacks the chain of narrators that hadith scholars require, yet most historians accept it as authentic, because it includes non-Muslims, portrays the Quraysh as enemies of God, and has an archaic style full of allusions only contemporaries would have understood.
Some remain sceptical. Robert Bertram Serjeant held that it consists of eight distinct documents issued over the first seven years or so of the Medinan period, while others take it as a single text.

The dating is disputed. W. Montgomery Watt placed it in the early Medinan period, in 622 or shortly after, Hubert Grimme after the Battle of Badr in 624, and Leone Caetani before it. It is also unclear with which Jews the agreement was made, since it does not name the three major clans, Banu Qaynuqa, Banu Nadir and Banu Qurayza.
constitution-of-the-lacedaemonians: The work survives in the collection of Xenophon's writings, and Plutarch also names him as its author; most scholars of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries agreed, attributing its imperfections to copying and later editing. Its fourteenth chapter is dated to around 378 BCE, about the time of the Second Athenian League of 375 BCE, and the chapters before it to the years 387 to 378 BCE. It is the only contemporary account of the Spartan political system to survive.

In his introduction Xenophon says he wondered how Sparta, one of the most sparsely populated cities, became the most powerful and best known in Greece, and ceased to wonder once he saw the Spartans' practices. Scholars suggest that a Spartan victory, most likely the defeat of Athens in the Peloponnesian War during Xenophon's youth, drew his attention.

Of its fifteen chapters, the first thirteen describe what made Sparta great. Chapter I deals with parenting, and Chapters II to IV with an education that begins in early childhood and lasts into adulthood, producing citizens who are humble and law-abiding yet daring and ingenious, and who hunt for most of their lives. Later chapters treat moderation and exercise, equality and indifference to wealth, contempt for money, obedience to the laws and magistrates, the preference for an honourable death over surrender, public rewards for good citizenship, and the army's strategy and leadership.

Chapter XIV changes course, describing a Sparta that had grown corrupt and no longer obeyed the laws of Lycurgus, so that other Greek states now joined against it instead of looking to it for leadership. Chapter XV ends with the city's continued loyalty to its kings. Xenophon traces every law to Lycurgus, whose reforms were believed to have been sanctioned by Apollo at Delphi.

Most modern scholars classify the treatise as an encomium of Sparta. Together with Plutarch's Life of Lycurgus it gives the most detailed surviving description of the Spartan state, and it is considered the best source on Spartan women in classical antiquity.
constitution-of-the-united-states: The Constitutional Convention assembled at Independence Hall in Philadelphia and sat between 25 May and 17 September 1787. Twelve states were represented, Rhode Island refusing to take part, and 55 of the 74 appointed delegates attended. The convention's mandate was limited to amending the Articles of Confederation, which had proved ineffective, but the delegates soon began considering a replacement. The framers drew on English common law, on Magna Carta for the principle of due process, and on Enlightenment writers such as John Locke and Montesquieu, whose ideas lie behind the separation of powers. Some scholars argue that Haudenosaunee political ideas also influenced the document, a claim other historians dispute.

The text has a Preamble, seven articles and a closing endorsement signed by 39 framers. Articles I to III set up Congress, the presidency and the courts. Articles IV to VI deal with federalism: relations among the states and with the federal government, the amendment process, and the supremacy of the Constitution and federal law over state law, with a ban on religious tests for office. Article VII set the way of ratification. Instead of the unanimous approval that the Articles of Confederation required, it called for conventions in the states and for the approval of nine of the thirteen.

The first ten amendments, the Bill of Rights, took effect in 1791. They protect freedoms of religion, speech, press and assembly and the right to keep and bear arms. The Eleventh Amendment of 1795 overturned the Supreme Court's decision in Chisholm v. Georgia (1793). Amendments are appended to the document, not written into the original text.

The convention's secretary, William Jackson, signed a note verifying four changes made by hand to the final text. Within three days of the signing the document went to the Congress of the Confederation, which voted unanimously on 28 September 1787 to send it to the states. It replaced the Articles on 4 March 1789. Early justices of the Supreme Court included men who had framed or ratified it, among them John Jay and John Marshall. Marshall's Court held in Barron v. Baltimore (1833) that the Bill of Rights restricted only the federal government, not the states. Abroad, the Constitution has been taken as a model, and its amendments and judicial review informed Benito Juárez, José Rizal and Sun Yat-sen, among others.
constitutional-act-1791: The act was passed by the Parliament of Great Britain in the reign of George III and repealed the Quebec Act of 1774. It reformed the government of the Province of Quebec to accommodate, among others, the 10,000 United Empire Loyalists who had arrived from the United States after the American Revolution, in a province whose population included 145,000 French-speaking Canadiens. Before it, the province had no legislative assembly.

The division took effect on 26 December 1791. The largely unpopulated western half became Upper Canada, now southern Ontario, and the eastern half Lower Canada, now southern Quebec, the names following their relative elevation along the St. Lawrence River. Upper Canada received English law and institutions, while Lower Canada kept French civil law, seigneurial land tenure and the privileges of the Roman Catholic Church. Assemblies elected by freeholders gave both colonies a form of representative government.

The act also tried to create an established church through the clergy reserves, grants making up one-seventh of the territory of the two provinces. Income from leasing or selling them went from 1791 to the Church of England alone and from 1824, in a complex ratio, also to the Presbyterian Church of Scotland.

The reserves hindered economic development and bred resentment against the Anglican church, the Family Compact and the Château Clique. French Canadians and the Catholic Church feared being overshadowed by Loyalist settlement and Protestant rights, while English-speaking settlers felt the French kept too much power, though both preferred the new arrangement to the Quebec Act. The act is often seen as a watershed in French Canadian nationalism, since it created a province the French considered their own; continued Anglo-Canadian political and economic dominance there fuelled discontent and, in time, the Lower Canada Rebellion of 1837-38.

After the Act of Union 1840, provisions on the clergy reserves remained in force, and the rest was repealed in stages by the Statute Law Revision Act 1871 and later acts of 1872 and 1950, with final repeal in British law, though not in Canadian law, in 1966. In 1896 Parliament gave it the short title Clergy Endowments (Canada) Act 1791, but in Canada it is still called the Constitutional Act, 1791.
constitutional-convention-united-states: During the American Revolution the Thirteen Colonies replaced their colonial governments with republican constitutions based on the separation of powers. These endorsed legislative supremacy: most power lay with the legislature, state governors lacked significant authority, and courts were under legislative control. Massachusetts elected delegates to its own constitutional convention in 1779, setting a precedent. The convention in Philadelphia was originally planned to begin on 14 May 1787, but few delegates had arrived, and a quorum of seven states was secured only on 25 May. It met in the Pennsylvania State House, later renamed Independence Hall, and was known at the time as the Federal Convention. Most delegates came expecting to improve the Articles of Confederation.

George Washington was elected president of the convention. James Madison arrived eleven days early and had studied republics and confederacies throughout history. His Virginia Plan, presented by Edmund Randolph on 29 May, proposed a supreme national government with a bicameral Congress. Small-state delegates, alarmed at proportional representation in both houses, offered William Paterson's New Jersey Plan on 15 June. The Virginia Plan became the basis, and the delegates quickly agreed on three branches. Disputes over the legislature, the executive and slavery slowed progress for weeks, and the presidency was settled only after debate on whether to divide the executive among three people or vest it in one.

The Connecticut delegation, including Roger Sherman, proposed a House with proportional representation and a Senate with equal representation, and a Grand Committee examined the question. The Three-Fifths Compromise, counting three fifths of other persons, was adopted as part of it. Progress was slow until mid-July. The Committee of Detail, chaired by John Rutledge, produced a first draft in August, and Northern and Southern delegates agreed to let Congress end the slave trade from 1808 and to strengthen the Fugitive Slave Clause. A Committee of Style, including Gouverneur Morris and Madison, produced the final text.

The Constitution was inscribed on parchment by Jacob Shallus and signed by 39 of the 55 delegates on 17 September 1787. Seventy representatives had been appointed, but some did not accept or could not attend. At least a third of the 55 delegates owned slaves, and slavery was among the hardest questions: Georgia and the two Carolinas refused to join the Union if slavery were not allowed. The proposed Constitution was printed in several copies and then in newspapers, which began the debates and ratification process. It remains the only federal constitutional convention, although the fifty states have held 233 of their own.
constitutional-monarchy: A constitutional monarchy is also called a limited, parliamentary or democratic monarchy. The monarch exercises authority in accordance with a constitution and does not decide alone. It differs from an absolute monarchy, in which the monarch is the only decision-maker, because the ruler works within a legal framework. The powers of constitutional monarchs vary widely. Some are hereditary symbolic heads of state with almost no executive power, in what are sometimes called ceremonial monarchies or crowned republics. In executive or semi-constitutional monarchies the monarch keeps significant powers, such as appointing and dismissing ministers or dissolving the assembly. Many constitutional monarchies are democratic, but some are not.

The oldest example from ancient times was, according to this account, that of the Hittites, whose king shared authority with an assembly called the Panku. Herodotus says that Demonax created a constitutional monarchy for King Battus III the Lame of Cyrene in about 548 BCE. In England the first form of constitution came with Magna Carta in 1215, and the Glorious Revolution of 1688 furthered limits on the crown through laws such as the Bill of Rights 1689 and the Act of Settlement 1701. In Scotland the Claim of Right Act 1689 placed similar limits.

Queen Anne was the last British monarch to veto an Act of Parliament, on 11 March 1708. George III still blocked Catholic Emancipation, which led to the resignation of William Pitt the Younger in 1801. William IV was the last to dismiss a prime minister, Lord Melbourne, in 1834, and Queen Victoria was the last to exercise real personal power, which declined over her reign. Poland produced the first constitution for a monarchy in continental Europe, the Constitution of 3 May 1791. Hegel gave the concept a philosophical justification in 1820.

The modern form developed mainly in the United Kingdom, where an elected parliament and a government led by a prime minister hold real power while the monarch is bound by convention to act on ministers' advice. In France's July Monarchy Louis-Philippe I was styled King of the French rather than King of France. In the German Empire, shaped by Otto von Bismarck, the Kaiser kept considerable executive power and the Imperial Chancellor needed no parliamentary confidence vote. That model was discredited and abolished after Germany's defeat in the First World War. Italy's monarchy was discredited under Benito Mussolini and abolished in 1946. After the Second World War surviving European monarchies almost always adopted the British model.

The Commonwealth realms keep reserve powers for emergencies, as in November 1975, when the Governor-General of Australia dismissed the prime minister Gough Whitlam. Walter Bagehot named three rights of a constitutional monarch: to be consulted, to encourage and to warn.
constitutionalist-army: Also called the Constitutional Army, it was formed in March 1913 by Venustiano Carranza, its self-styled First Chief, in answer to the murder of President Francisco I. Madero and Vice President José María Pino Suárez during La Decena Trágica (the Ten Tragic Days) and Victoriano Huerta's seizure of the presidency. Carranza had few forces whose loyalty he could count on. Pancho Villa and Emiliano Zapata gave him their support in theory, but they turned against the Constitutionalists after Huerta's defeat in 1914.

In July 1913 Carranza divided the country into seven areas of military operations, each in theory under a general commanding an army corps: Northeast, Northwest, Central, East, West, South and Southeast. The last four existed only on paper. In practice the army was made up of the Northwest Corps, renamed the Army of Operations, under Álvaro Obregón, the Northeast Corps under Pablo González, and the Central Corps under Pánfilo Natera.

When fighting broke out in 1914 between the Constitutionalists and the Conventionalists of Villa and Zapata after the Convention of Aguascalientes, the Constitutional Army numbered 57,000 men against their 72,000. The Constitutionalists grew stronger as their opponents weakened, and by 1917 only minor revolts remained, among them those of the Felicistas, supporters of Félix Díaz, nephew of the ousted president Porfirio Díaz.

The army Carranza had created became the threat to his own rule. When Obregón stood for the presidency against Carranza's chosen successor, Ignacio Bonillas, Carranza tried to have him arrested on false charges. Under the Plan of Agua Prieta Obregón marched on Mexico City with his army, and Carranza fled the capital and was killed in the Sierra Norte of Puebla on 21 May 1920. Obregón was elected president in 1920, and other former Constitutionalist generals later became presidents and leading politicians.
constitutionalist-revolution: The Revolution of 1930 brought Getúlio Vargas to the presidency with the backing of the military and the political elites of Minas Gerais, Rio Grande do Sul and Paraíba. It overthrew President Washington Luís, kept the São Paulo governor Júlio Prestes, elected president in 1930, from taking office, and ended the First Brazilian Republic. Paulistas resented the loss of the autonomy the states had held under the 1891 constitution. The federal government accused the movement of seeking secession, but there is no evidence that its commanders were separatists.

On 23 May 1932 government troops killed four protesting students, Martins, Miragaia, Dráusio and Camargo, whose initials gave the movement its name, MMDC; a fifth, Alvarenga, died months later. The uprising began on 9 July 1932.

São Paulo's politicians expected a quick war with the support of Minas Gerais and Rio Grande do Sul, which never came. According to Javier García de Gabiola, the rebels won over only one of the army's eight divisions, the 2nd Division in São Paulo, reinforced by the Força Pública Paulista and MMDC militias. With 15,000 to 29,000 rifles, depending on the source, they could never arm more than 35,000 men, while Brazil equipped about 100,000.

The 2nd Division's advance on Rio de Janeiro was stopped in the Paraíba Valley by the loyalist 1st Division under General Góis Monteiro, and three months of trench warfare followed. In the south federal forces broke the rebel line at Itararé on 17 July, and the Minas Gerais front, active from 2 August, proved decisive: federal troops broke through at Eleutério on 26 August and came within 70 kilometres of São Paulo. The Paulistas surrendered on 2 October to General Valdomiro Lima. There were 934 official deaths, though unofficial estimates reach 2,200.

Despite the defeat, Vargas granted several of the movement's main demands: a non-military state governor, the election of a Constituent Assembly and a new constitution in 1934. That constitution was short-lived. In 1937 Vargas dissolved the National Congress and, after a coup d'état, enacted another that established the Estado Novo. The uprising was the first major revolt against the Vargas government, and 9 July, the day it began, is a holiday and the most important civic date of the state of São Paulo.
constitutions-of-melfi: The Liber Augustalis was promulgated on 1 September 1231 at Melfi, the town from which Frederick's Norman ancestors had first set out to conquer the Mezzogiorno two centuries earlier. It began as a reform of the Assizes of Capua of 1220, which were themselves Frederick's reform of the Assizes of Ariano of 1140. Frederick is presented as its author, with Giacomo Amalfitano, Archbishop of Capua, as an influence; the pope reproved the archbishop for advising clauses against the church's wishes. Tradition attributed the work to Pier delle Vigne, but it was almost certainly the product of months of work by a committee.

Written in Latin and translated into Greek before its promulgation, the code applied to all the peoples of the realm: Lombards, Greeks, Saracens, Germans and Jews. Its 253 clauses fall into three books, on public law (107 clauses, one missing in all manuscripts), judicial procedure (52) and feudal, private and penal law (94). Continuing the centralising legislation of Roger II, it strengthened the king and weakened his feudatories. Bearing arms without permission was forbidden, a standing Saracen army was created, the sale of fiefs was banned and all vassals became subject to the king's taxes. Clergymen were made subject to the common courts, and cities could not become communes or elect consuls or podestàs.

Penal justice passed to the king and his magistrates, who were elected for a year and paid a salary by the state; the master justiciar headed the Magna Curia, the final court of appeal. State monopolies were imposed on silk, iron and grain, tariffs on trade within the kingdom were abolished and weights and measures made uniform. The code affirmed the equality of freemen before the law and banned trial by ordeal, rejecting the ordeals of hot iron and cold water with reasoned argument, as well as trial by battle, with exceptions for knights and for cases without witnesses. It also required practical experience of anyone who would practise medicine.

The Constitutions formed the basis of Sicilian law for the next six centuries, remaining in force in the Kingdom of Naples until 1809 and in Sicily until 1819. The historian Ernst Kantorowicz wrote that the Liber "is the birth certificate of the modern administrative state." James M. Powell published the code as The Liber Augustalis in 1971, and Wolfgang Stürner edited the text for the Monumenta Germaniae Historica in 1996.
constructivism-art: Constructivism was a development of Russian Futurism after the First World War, and particularly of the counter-reliefs that Vladimir Tatlin exhibited in 1915. The term was coined by the sculptors Antoine Pevsner and Naum Gabo, whose Realistic Manifesto of 1920 is its first appearance. Its geometric abstraction owed something to the Suprematism of Kazimir Malevich. As theory and practice it grew out of debates at the Institute of Artistic Culture in Moscow from 1920 to 1922, which defined the style as a combination of faktura, the material properties of an object, and tektonika, its spatial presence.

The key work was Tatlin's proposal for the Monument to the Third International (1919-20), known as Tatlin's Tower, which joined a machine aesthetic to searchlights and projection screens. It was never built, for lack of money after the revolution. Gabo and Pevsner held that the movement had a spiritual core, while Tatlin and Alexander Rodchenko held a utilitarian view. The debates led to Productivism, which demanded direct participation in industry and an end to easel painting.

Constructivists designed street festivals and propaganda for the Bolshevik government during the Civil War, and later advertising during the New Economic Policy. Rodchenko and the poet Vladimir Mayakovsky called themselves advertising constructors. Others worked in theatre, where Vsevolod Meyerhold developed his biomechanical acting, and in cinema, photomontage, book design and poster design, as with the Stenberg brothers.

Tatlin's designs were hailed in Germany, and exchanges between Moscow and Berlin led to a short-lived Constructivist International that met Dadaists and De Stijl artists in 1922. Teachers at the Bauhaus drew on Constructivist ideas and the teaching methods of VKhUTEMAS. Its main early political patron was Leon Trotsky, and after his expulsion in 1927-28 the movement came under suspicion. The Communist Party gradually favoured realist art, and about 1934 Socialist Realism was instituted in its place, although some Constructivists kept working for the state. Naum Gabo carried a version of Constructivism to England, and Joaquín Torres García helped spread it to Latin America.
consulate-of-the-sea: The name belonged first to a court. The institution can be traced to the Carta Consular granted to Barcelona by Jaume I of Aragon in 1258, which let the city's merchants settle their commercial disputes without interference from the royal courts, in return for money the king needed for his wars of expansion. Similar bodies already existed at Messina and Genoa. As the Crown of Aragon expanded, new consulates were set up in its major ports; at Valencia, in 1283, the charter of Peter III ordered disputes to be settled according to maritime customs as accepted in Barcelona.

The full Catalan title is Les costums marítimes de Barcelona universalment conegudes per Llibre del Consolat de mar, the maritime customs of Barcelona universally known as the Book of the Consulate of the Sea. The printed book holds a code of procedure issued by the kings of Aragon for the consuls' courts, a collection of ancient customs of the sea, and rules for the government of cruisers of war. A document called The Acceptations follows, claiming that the chapters had been approved by the Roman people in 1075 and by princes and peoples in the 12th and 13th centuries; it is generally regarded as having no historical value. An appendix adds ordinances of the kings of Aragon and the councillors of Barcelona.

Of two Catalan manuscripts in the Bibliothèque nationale de France, the older, MS. Espagnol 124, gives the two first treatises, the most ancient part, in a 14th-century hand on paper of that century; its later parts are on 15th-century paper and hold no document more recent than 1436. The other, MS. Espagnol 56, was written in the 15th century under the superintendence of Peter Thomas, a notary and the scribe of the Consulate of the Sea at Barcelona. The epistle dedicatory of the early printed book calls the work an amended version compiled by Francis Celelles with the help of many shipmasters and merchants.

With its appendix the book circulated in Europe as The Consulate of the Sea and was translated in the 16th century into Castilian, Italian and French. The Italian version, printed at Venice by Jean Baptista Pedrezano, circulated most widely in northern Europe and led many jurists to think the work Italian. Dutch and German translations by Westerven and Engelbrecht followed in the next century. Pardessus published a French translation of The Customs of the Sea in his Collection des lois maritimes (Paris, 1834), and Sir Travers Twiss gave an English one with the Catalan text in the Black Book of the Admiralty.
continental-congress: The idea of a joint colonial body first arose in 1754, at the start of the French and Indian War, when representatives of seven of the thirteen colonies met at the Albany Congress and Benjamin Franklin proposed a confederation. The proposal was rejected. A further step came with the Stamp Act Congress, which met in New York City in October 1765 and sent a Declaration of Rights and Grievances to Parliament. The Stamp Act was repealed in March 1766. The Continental Congress drew its organisation less on Parliament than on that congress, and nine of its delegates sat in the First Continental Congress.

The First Continental Congress met in Carpenter's Hall, Philadelphia, from 5 September to 26 October 1774. Fifty-six delegates from twelve colonies attended, among them George Washington, Patrick Henry and John Adams, with Peyton Randolph of Virginia as president. Georgia did not take part. The delegates organised an economic boycott of Britain, adopted the Continental Association and petitioned the King for redress. Most were not yet ready to break away from Britain.

The Second Continental Congress convened on 10 May 1775 at the State House in Philadelphia, shortly after fighting began. It raised armies, directed strategy, appointed diplomats and made treaties. On 14 June it established the Continental Army and on 15 June appointed Washington its commander. It sent the Olive Branch Petition to King George III, but after the Proclamation of Rebellion of August 1775 some members concluded that peace would not come. It adopted Richard Henry Lee's resolution for independence on 2 July 1776 and, two days later, the Declaration of Independence, drafted by Thomas Jefferson. It created standing committees, including a board of war and a navy board, and approved the Articles of Confederation on 15 November 1777.

The Articles came into force on 1 March 1781, and the body became the Congress of the Confederation, a single chamber in which each state had one vote. It could declare war, sign treaties and borrow or print money, but it could not tax. It met in Philadelphia and later in other cities, including Annapolis and New York City, and its authority declined after the war. Its Northwest Ordinance of 1787 placed the land north of the Ohio River under federal control. The Philadelphia Convention of 1787 was authorised to amend the Articles, and the first Congress under the new Constitution replaced the Confederation Congress in 1789.
continental-system: Britain declared war on France in May 1803. Napoleon could not invade because of the Royal Navy's control of the sea, and after the British victory over a Franco-Spanish fleet at Trafalgar on 21 October 1805 he abandoned his plans and turned to economic warfare. On 16 May 1806 the Royal Navy imposed a blockade of French and French-allied coasts. Britain was then Europe's manufacturing and business centre as a result of the Industrial Revolution, and Napoleon believed that, as an island nation, it could be forced to sue for peace if its trade with the continent were cut off.

Napoleon issued the Berlin Decree on 21 November 1806, forbidding the import of British goods into any European country allied with or dependent on France and cutting all connections with Britain, even mail. Britain replied with orders in council in January and November 1807, and Napoleon answered with the Milan Decree of 1807, under which neutral ships using British ports or paying British tariffs were to be treated as British and seized. The embargo was applied intermittently and ended on 11 April 1814, after Napoleon's first abdication.

Enforcement drew Napoleon into further wars. Portugal, allied with Britain, refused to comply. After the Treaty of Tilsit in July 1807 Napoleon failed to capture the Portuguese fleet, which sailed with the court to Brazil, and the Peninsular War began in 1808. Britain bombarded Copenhagen and seized the Danish fleet in 1807, and used bases at Heligoland, Gothenburg and Hanö to smuggle goods into the Baltic. Russia reopened trade with Britain in 1810, which was a motive for Napoleon's invasion of Russia in 1812.

The blockade did not cause lasting damage to Britain. Smuggling was extensive, and British exports to the continent fell by between 25 and 55 per cent compared with the period before 1806, but trade with the rest of the world rose sharply and covered much of the loss. Britain did suffer high unemployment and inflation from 1810 to 1812, and unrest, including the Luddite movement, was put down by the yeomanry and militia.

The system hurt France and its allies. Shipbuilding and other industries that depended on overseas markets declined, ports such as Marseille and Bordeaux suffered, and food prices rose across the continent. The Dutch economy, built on trade, suffered greatly. The industrial north and east of France and Wallonia gained from the lack of British competition. Napoleon's St Cloud Decree of July 1810 admitted limited British trade, and the resentment of allied governments weakened his coalition. The embargo also contributed to the War of 1812 between Britain and the United States.
continuation-war: The Winter War of 1939 to 1940 ended with the Moscow Peace Treaty. Finland distrusted Germany afterwards, but the fall of France ended any Western orientation in its foreign policy. On 31 July 1940 Hitler ordered planning for an attack on the Soviet Union, and Germany reversed its refusal to sell arms to Finland and allowed its troops to transit through Finland and Sweden. Its leaders said they would fight only to redress the balance of the 1940 treaty and described themselves as co-belligerents rather than allies of Germany, though President Risto Ryti envisioned a Greater Finland and Mannerheim often called the war an anti-Communist crusade. Historians still disagree on whether Finland was an ally of Nazi Germany.

German forces invaded the Soviet Union on 22 June 1941, and Finnish troops occupied the demilitarised Åland Islands. After a Soviet air raid on Finnish cities on 25 June, Finland declared war. By September 1941 it had regained the territory conceded in 1940, and it went on into East Karelia, halting some 30–32 km from the centre of Leningrad. Historians debate how far Finland took part in the siege of the city. In Lapland the joint German–Finnish Operation Silver Fox, begun on 29 June, failed to take Murmansk or cut the Kirov Railway.

From 19 July 1941 the Finns ran a military administration in occupied East Karelia, intending to prepare its incorporation into Finland; almost 30% of the remaining Russian civilians were interned in concentration camps. On 9 June 1944 the Soviet Leningrad Front began the Vyborg–Petrozavodsk Offensive. The Red Army retook Viipuri on 20 June and Petrozavodsk by 28 June, though the Finnish army halted the offensive in August.

A ceasefire took effect on 4 September 1944, and the Moscow Armistice was accepted by the Finnish Parliament on 19 September. Finland restored the borders of 1940, ceded Petsamo, leased the Porkkala Peninsula to the Soviets, paid war reparations, held war-responsibility trials and banned fascist groups. A Soviet-led Allied Control Commission oversaw the terms. The demand that German troops leave led to the Lapland War between Finland and Germany. According to Finnish historians, Finnish forces lost 63,204 dead or missing and around 158,000 wounded.

The 1947 Paris Peace Treaty described Finland as an ally of Hitlerite Germany during the war. The Finnish Jewish community of about 2,000 had full civil rights, but in November 1942 officials secretly deported eight Jewish refugees to the Gestapo, of whom only one survived; the government then refused to hand over any more.
contras: The Contras, from the Spanish contrarrevolucionarios, were anti-communist rebels who fought the Sandinista National Liberation Front (FSLN) and the Junta of National Reconstruction, which took power after the Nicaraguan Revolution of 1979. In July 1979 the FSLN took Managua after weeks of heavy fighting, and President Anastasio Somoza Debayle fled the country. Dissidents of the new government and members of the former National Guard formed groups that met and established the Contras in 1980.

They were not a single body but three elements of Nicaraguan society: former National Guardsmen and other right-wing figures; anti-Somoza activists who had supported the revolution but felt betrayed by the Sandinistas, such as Édgar Chamorro and José Francisco Cardenal; and Nicaraguans who had stayed out of the revolution but opposed the Sandinistas.

In September 1981 the CIA and Argentina's intelligence agency persuaded the 15 September Legion, the Nicaraguan Democratic Union and several smaller groups to merge as the Nicaraguan Democratic Force (FDN). It was led by the former National Guard colonel Enrique Bermúdez as military commander and the businessman Adolfo Calero as head of its political directorate, and was based in Honduras. In April 1982 Edén Pastora, a former Sandinista, organised the Sandinista Revolutionary Front in the south and declared war on the government. In June 1985 most groups reorganised as the United Nicaraguan Opposition, and in May 1987 the Nicaraguan Resistance was organised on similar lines.

The United States provided military assistance and funds. On 4 January 1982 President Ronald Reagan signed a secret directive giving the CIA authority to support the Contras with 19 million dollars in military aid. After Congress blocked further aid, the Reagan administration raised funds from third countries and private sources through a National Security Council operation run by Lieutenant Colonel Oliver North, which culminated in the Iran–Contra affair of 1986–1987. In 1986 the International Court of Justice found that the United States had violated international law by supporting the Contras and mining Nicaragua's harbours.

Americas Watch and Human Rights Watch accused the Contras of attacks on civilians, kidnapping, torture and executions, and Human Rights Watch called them major and systematic violators of the laws of armed conflict. Calero denied that his forces deliberately targeted civilians, and the Reagan administration contended that the Contras did not deliberately attack them. After a cutoff in United States military support, five Central American presidents, including Daniel Ortega, agreed with the Contras that voluntary demobilisation should begin in early December 1989, ahead of the elections of February 1990.
control-of-fire-by-early-humans: The use and control of fire was a gradual process of more than one stage. One stage was a change of habitat from dense forest, where wildfires were rare but hard to escape, to savanna, where they were common but easier to survive; this may have happened about 3 million years ago. Hominins then foraged in the wake of wildfires, as savanna chimpanzees and vervet monkeys do, used the hot spots left behind, carried fire from burned to unburned areas and kept it burning over a season, which may have led to base campsites. Building a hearth came later, and making fire with a bow drill later still.

Most evidence from the Lower Paleolithic is uncertain, because natural processes can explain many findings. The reddened clay at Chesowanja in Kenya, dated to 1.4 million years ago, could have come from burning tree stumps. Stronger evidence comes from Kalambo Falls in Zambia, where charred logs, charcoal and fire-hardened wooden implements date to about 180,000 years ago, and from Qesem Cave in Israel, where cut-marked bones lie near fireplaces from before 382,000 years ago.

The Barnham site in Suffolk gives the earliest evidence of making fire: baked earth with flint and pyrite, which can be used to strike a spark. Pyrite is rare there, so people must have travelled tens of kilometres to obtain it, and several short-lived fires burned in the same spot. The excavators attribute the fires to early Neanderthals; Wil Roebroeks, of Leiden University, regards most of the evidence as circumstantial.

Fire kept people warm at night, warded off predators and allowed expansion from tropical to temperate climates. About 164,000 years ago, at Pinnacle Point in South Africa, people heated silcrete to make it easier to knap. Cooking made starchy and fibrous plants edible, reduced toxins and released more nutrients, and the molar teeth of Homo erectus gradually shrank.

The cooking hypothesis, set out in Richard Wrangham's Catching Fire and first presented by Friedrich Engels, proposes that cooking allowed brain size to increase. Critics argue that species such as Homo ergaster had large brains when evidence for cooking fires is slight, and that cooking fires began in earnest only about 250,000 years ago.
convention-of-kanagawa: From the beginning of the 17th century the Tokugawa shogunate pursued a policy of isolation. Foreign trade was kept to the Dutch and the Chinese and was conducted only at Nagasaki under a strict government monopoly. The policy aimed to suppress the spread of Christianity and to prevent foreign trade from raising up a daimyo powerful enough to overthrow the Tokugawa. By the early 19th century the policy was increasingly challenged. In 1844 King William II of the Netherlands urged Japan to end its isolation, and in 1846 an American expedition under Commodore James Biddle asked for ports to be opened but was sent away.

In 1853 President Millard Fillmore sent Commodore Matthew C. Perry with a fleet to open Japanese ports to American trade, by gunboat diplomacy if necessary. Perry reached Uraga with four warships on 8 July 1853, refused to go to Nagasaki, and threatened to proceed to Edo. He landed at Kurihama on 14 July and delivered the President's letter. Abe Masahiro of the Council of Elders then polled all the daimyo, which showed the shogunate weak and indecisive; of 61 known answers, 19 favoured accepting and 19 opposed.

Perry returned on 11 February 1854 with eight warships and made clear he would not leave without a treaty. Negotiations began on 8 March and lasted about a month, and the Japanese side gave way on almost every demand, except for a commercial agreement, which was deferred. The main dispute was the choice of ports, Perry rejecting Nagasaki. The treaty, was signed on 31 March 1854 at what is now Kaikō Hiroba in Yokohama, and Perry concluded it with representatives of the shogun led by Hayashi Akira. It opened the ports of Shimoda and Hakodate to American vessels, ensured the safety of American castaways and established an American consul in Japan. It was ratified on 21 February 1855.

The treaty effectively ended the 220-year policy of seclusion and was followed by similar agreements with the United Kingdom in October 1854, Russia in February 1855 and France in 1858. The Harris Treaty of 1858 with the United States allowed foreign concessions and extraterritoriality, and the Japanese chafed under what was called the unequal treaty system.

Within Japan, the suspension of earlier military restrictions led many domains to re-arm and weakened the shogun. Popular outrage over perceived appeasement fuelled the sonnō jōi movement and shifted political power from Edo towards the Imperial Court in Kyoto. Emperor Kōmei's opposition to the treaties lent support to the movement to overthrow the shogunate and, eventually, to the Meiji Restoration.
convention-of-london-1786: The Treaty of Versailles of 1783 between Britain and Spain, which ended the Anglo-Spanish War, required British settlements on what it called the Spanish Continent to be evacuated. Its wording was close to that of the Treaty of Paris of 1763, which had ended the Seven Years' War. British settlers on the Mosquito Coast resisted the new agreement, as they had resisted the earlier one, arguing that Spain had never actually controlled the area, so that it belonged to the American Continent rather than to the Spanish one.

Both sides then increased their military activity around the Black River Settlement, where most of the British settlers lived. The Kingdom of Great Britain and the Kingdom of Spain then decided to open further negotiations over the status of the British settlements in Mosquitia and the Bay of Honduras.

In the convention signed on 14 July 1786, Britain agreed to evacuate all British settlements from the Country of the Mosquitos. In exchange, Spain agreed to enlarge the territory open to British loggers on the Yucatan Peninsula and allowed them to cut mahogany and other hardwoods, timbers that were then rising in value.

The agreement was carried out over the opposition of the Mosquito Coast settlers, and the British evacuated more than 2,000 people. Most of them went to Belize, while others were moved to Jamaica, Grand Cayman or Roatán. Control of Black River was formally handed over to the Spanish on 29 August 1787 by William Pitt Lawrie, the grandson of the settlement's founder, William Pitt, who had lived from 1699 to 1771.
convention-of-moss: Denmark–Norway ended the Napoleonic Wars on the losing side, and under the Treaty of Kiel of 14 January 1814 Norway was ceded to the king of Sweden. The Norwegians instead convened a constitutional assembly at Eidsvoll, signed the Constitution of Norway on 17 May 1814 and elected as king Prince Christian Frederik, viceroy and heir to the thrones of Denmark and Norway. Crown Prince Charles John, de facto ruler for King Charles XIII and, as Jean Baptiste Bernadotte, one of Napoleon's foremost generals, rejected an independent Norway.

The Swedish army was larger, better equipped and better trained. After a naval attack on the Norwegian gunboats at Hvaler, from which they escaped, the main Swedish force crossed the border at Halden, bypassing the fortress of Fredriksten, while 6,000 soldiers landed at Kråkerøy outside Fredrikstad, which surrendered the next day. The Norwegian army around Rakkestad struck back several times, pressing Sweden to negotiate. Talks began on 7 August, Charles John accepted the Norwegian constitution, and the armistice was concluded by Norway at Moss on 14 August and by Sweden at Fredrikstad on 15 August.

The convention comprised four documents. Because Sweden did not recognise Christian Frederik as king, it was signed for the Norwegian government by two of his ministers, Niels Aall and Jonas Collett. The Storting was to meet and ratify it; the King of Sweden accepted the constitution with only the changes the union required, which the Storting had to approve; and Christian Frederik was to renounce the crown and leave the country. At Norway's insistence the wording avoided treating the Swedish king as king of Norway before the Storting elected him, so the union would rest on Moss rather than Kiel.

Many Norwegians were at first shocked by the concessions, and the Swedish negotiator, General Magnus Björnstjerna, met an unfriendly welcome in Christiania. Opinion shifted over time, since Norway entered the union as an equal state with its own parliament and institutions, sharing only the king and the foreign service. The union lasted until Norway declared it dissolved in 1905. The war was the last between Sweden and Norway and Sweden's last war.
convention-of-ocana: By 1826 Gran Colombia was economically exhausted by the long campaigns that freed Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia from royalist control, and divided by tensions between its civil administration and the military and between local leaders and the central government. In 1826 General José Antonio Páez, a leading caudillo of the department of Venezuela, rebelled in the separatist movement known as La Cosiata. Simón Bolívar settled it peacefully in 1827 by intervening in person and promising a constituent congress, although the Constitution of Cúcuta forbade any reform before ten years had passed, that is, before 1831.

The convention met from 9 April to 10 June 1828, with José María del Castillo y Rada as its president and Andrés Narvarte as vice-president. Two currents divided it: Bolívar's followers wanted a strong presidency, while the supporters of Vice-President Francisco de Paula Santander wanted a more decentralised government. Early on, Bolívar proposed a highly centralised constitution based on the one he had written for Bolivia in 1826, but it proved unpopular. The debate over centralism and federalism grew bitter, and Santander's side, pointing to the ban on revision before 1831, came to argue for keeping the existing constitution in the name of national unity.

Santander left for Cúcuta and then Bogotá. On 13 June 1828 a popular movement in Bogotá led by General Pedro Alcántara Herrán, intendant of Cundinamarca, called for the military command to take power. On 27 August Bolívar issued an organic decree he called the Fundamental Law, which set aside the Constitution of Cúcuta and abolished Congress and the vice-presidency, and he annulled the powers of the Bogotá deputies to the convention. Santander was named minister plenipotentiary to the United States in September. Weeks later Bolívar survived an attempt on his life, but the country stayed unstable until 1831, when separatist movements prevailed and Gran Colombia was dissolved.
convention-parliament-1660: The Convention Parliament followed the Long Parliament, which had voted for its own dissolution on 16 March 1660. It was elected as a "free parliament", with no oath of allegiance either to the Commonwealth or to the monarchy, and first assembled on 25 April 1660. Former Parliamentarians held a technical plurality over Royalists, 180 to 110 by one count, but the Royalists outmanoeuvred them, relying on the many new and inexperienced members and on the disunity and lack of leadership of the former Parliamentarians on most contested questions.

After receiving the Declaration of Breda, Parliament proclaimed on 8 May that Charles II had been the lawful monarch since the death of Charles I in January 1649. It then prepared the Restoration Settlement, providing for land and revenue so that the new regime could govern. The Indemnity and Oblivion Act, law from 29 August 1660, limited reprisals against those who had served under Oliver Cromwell, but those accused of regicide, the trial and execution of Charles I, were prosecuted, and an act attainted several of them.

Its statutes are cited as 12 Cha. 2. Because the acts of the Commonwealth parliaments were struck from the legal record, it re-enacted some it wished to keep, such as the Navigation Act of 1651. Its other acts included the Tunnage and Poundage Act, whose high customs duties remained largely unchanged until the 18th century, a poll tax to pay for disbanding the New Model Army, the Tenures Abolition Act, the establishment of the General Post Office, bans on wool exports and on tobacco plantations in the British Isles, the confirmation of marriages, and a perpetual thanksgiving on 29 May.

Charles II dissolved the Convention Parliament on 29 December 1660. Its successor, elected in May 1661 and called the Cavalier Parliament, set about systematically dismantling or recasting the legislation and institutions of the Interregnum, and confirmed the acts of the Convention Parliament.
convention-peoples-party: The United Gold Coast Convention, formed in August 1947 and led mainly by professional and business men, invited Kwame Nkrumah home from London as its general secretary on the proposal of the lawyer Ebenezer Ako Adjei. Nkrumah had helped George Padmore organise the Fifth Pan-African Congress in Manchester in 1945. He arrived late in 1947 amid discontent over shortages and rising prices, the uncompensated cutting-out of cocoa trees with swollen-shoot disease and the meagre gratuities of ex-servicemen, which led to a boycott of mostly foreign-owned firms from 26 January 1948.

In June 1949, after a three-day meeting at Tarkwa, the CYO agreed to form a new party that kept the name Convention. On 11 June the UGCC's Working Committee declared membership of the two bodies incompatible and announced charges against Nkrumah, and on 12 June, before a crowd of some 60,000 on the Old Polo Ground, he resigned and launched the CPP.

While Nkrumah was in James Fort prison, K. A. Gbedemah kept the party running, and its manifesto was smuggled out on toilet paper. The CPP swept the municipal elections of 1950 in Accra, Cape Coast and Kumasi. Its government moved the Motion of Destiny on 10 July 1953 asking Britain to name a date for independence, and in the first direct elections, on 19 June 1954, it won 72 of 104 seats. Against the National Liberation Movement, which called for a federal constitution, it won again in 1956, and at midnight on the night of 5 to 6 March 1957 Nkrumah proclaimed Ghana's independence on the Polo Ground in Accra.

On 24 February 1966, while Nkrumah was travelling on a Commonwealth mission seeking a resolution of the Vietnam crisis, a military and police junta overthrew the CPP government. The party stayed banned, and its followers regrouped in the People's National Party, whose candidate Hilla Limann won the 1979 elections before Jerry John Rawlings overthrew him on 31 December 1981. After party politics returned in 1992 the Nkrumaist movement split into several parties. The CPP won three of 230 seats in 2004 and one in 2008, for Nkrumah's daughter Samia Nkrumah, and it joined the Socialist International as a consultative member in June 2018.
conversion-of-paul-the-apostle: According to the New Testament, Saul of Tarsus, later Paul, was "a Pharisee of Pharisees" who "intensely persecuted" the followers of Jesus, and Acts places him at the stoning of Stephen. In Galatians he writes that he was advancing in Judaism beyond many of his own age and was extremely zealous for the traditions of his fathers. Both Acts and his letters hold that he was not a follower of Jesus and did not know him before the crucifixion.

Paul's own letters describe the experience briefly. In 1 Corinthians he lists himself last among those to whom the risen Christ appeared, and in Galatians he says he received the gospel "by revelation from Jesus Christ" and did not consult any human being. Acts tells the story three times, at far greater length. In Acts 9 Saul is travelling from Jerusalem to Damascus with a mandate from the High Priest to arrest followers of Jesus when a light from heaven flashes around him and a voice asks why he persecutes it. He is blind for three days until Ananias of Damascus lays hands on him, something like scales fall from his eyes, and he is baptised.

The second account is in a speech to the crowd after his arrest in Jerusalem, tailored to a Jewish audience; the third, before King Agrippa, is briefer and stresses obedience to a heavenly vision. The accounts differ in detail. Acts 9:7 says his companions heard the voice but saw no one, while Acts 22:9 says they saw the light but did not hear it. Some commentators read the Greek words differently in each place to harmonise them; Craig Keener notes that ancient historians did not trifle over minor differences.

Protestants saw the conversion as a demonstration of faith alone, while Counter-Reformation Catholics saw it as showing the power of preaching. Many readers take it as evidence of divine grace, and as a commissioning of Paul as apostle to the Gentiles. Natural explanations have been proposed, among them temporal lobe epilepsy (D. Landsborough, 1987), which James R. Brorson and Kathleen Brewer challenged in the same journal.

The Feast of the Conversion of Saint Paul falls on 25 January and has been kept since the 8th century; it closes the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity. Painters from the Renaissance onward, among them Michelangelo and Caravaggio, depicted the scene, often showing Paul on a horse that the biblical accounts never mention. "Road to Damascus" has become a phrase for a sudden change of mind.
cooch-behar-palace: The palace, also known as the Rajbari, was built during the reign of Maharaja Nripendra Narayan of the Koch dynasty, and it shows how far the Koch kings had accepted European ideals. The original palace was in part a three-storey structure, and it was afterwards destroyed by the Assam earthquake of 1897. It is listed among the Monuments of National Importance in West Bengal.

Built of brick in the Classical Italian manner, the palace covers about 51,000 square feet and is 296 feet wide, set on a base 4 feet 9 inches above the ground. Arcaded verandahs run along the front on the ground and first floors, their piers arranged alternately in single and double rows. The building projects slightly at its southern and northern ends, and in the centre a projecting porch leads into the Durbar Hall.

The Durbar Hall, the hall of audience, is crowned by a metal dome rising 124 feet from the ground and topped by a cylindrical louvred ventilator. The inside of the dome is carved in stepped patterns, and it rests on four arches supported by large Corinthian columns, with small balconies around it.

The palace has more than 50 rooms, among them drawing rooms, a dining hall, a dancing hall, a billiard room, a library, bedrooms and dressing rooms, a kitchen, the Toshakhana and a ladies' gallery. The objects and precious things these rooms once held are now lost.
coolgardie: Coolgardie lies about 558 kilometres east of Perth and 38 kilometres south-west of Kalgoorlie. Gold was first found at a place called Fly Flat, at a time when the great rushes of the previous three decades, mostly in eastern Australia, were largely exhausted. In the 1890s four goldfields were gazetted with the town as their reference point: Coolgardie and East Coolgardie in 1894, North Coolgardie in 1895 and North-east Coolgardie in 1896.

Thousands flocked to the new field, and the Municipality of Coolgardie was established in 1894. By 1898 the town had an estimated 15,000 people, and at its peak 700 mining companies based there were registered on the London Stock Exchange. It had a railway connection between Perth and Kalgoorlie, the first public baths in the state, many hotels and several newspapers. Most miners, working in harsh conditions, left poorer than they came.

Afghan cameleers, not all of them from Afghanistan, carried supplies to the field. In 1894 a caravan of six men, forty-seven camels and eleven calves crossed the desert from Marree, arriving in July. By 1898 the Muslim community of Coolgardie numbered about 300, the main one in the colony, with simple mud and tin mosques; they later moved, mostly to Perth.

The goldfields gave the town political weight: Britain and the eastern colonies threatened to create a new state, Auralia, around them unless Perth held a referendum on federation, and Western Australia joined as a founding state in 1901. Coolgardie became the centre of a federal electorate, and Alf Morgans of Coolgardie was briefly Premier in November 1901. As the gold dwindled the electorate was abolished in 1913, and the population fell to about 200; the main street, lit by electric light in March 1896, had four hurricane lamps by April 1924.

Coolgardie has about 850 people and is known as a tourist town and mining ghost town, its surviving buildings from the boom years having helped a small revival. The Great Eastern Highway runs through it as Bayley Street, and the town still has a Mining Registrar.
cooperative-cyber-defence-centre-of-exce: In 2003, before it formally joined NATO, Estonia proposed the creation of a Centre of Excellence. NATO's 2006 Riga summit listed possible cyber attacks among the asymmetric threats to common security, and the cyber attacks on Estonia in 2007 showed for the first time how vulnerable NATO countries, their institutions and NATO itself could be to disruption of their information and communications systems. Estonia's proposal won strong support from NATO Secretary-General Jaap de Hoop Scheffer. NATO completed an assessment in April 2007, approved a policy on cyber defence in January 2008, and announced at its Bucharest summit that April its readiness to help allies counter a cyber attack on request.

The centre was established on 14 May 2008; General James Mattis, speaking in Brussels that day, called the need for it compelling. On 28 October 2008 it received full accreditation from NATO and the status of an International Military Organisation. Its founding states were Estonia, Germany, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Slovakia and Spain. Hungary joined in 2010, Poland and the United States in 2011 and the Netherlands in 2012. In 2013 France, the United Kingdom and the Czech Republic joined, together with Austria, the first non-NATO country.

Finland, Greece and Turkey followed in November 2015, Bulgaria, Denmark, Norway and Romania in June 2019 and Ireland in October 2019. Colonel Jaak Tarien succeeded Merle Maigre as director on 30 August 2018. Ukraine applied in August 2021 and was accepted as a contributing participant in March 2022. South Korea joined in May 2022 as the first Asian country, and Japan in November 2022. In March 2024 the centre had 32 sponsoring nations, a status open only to NATO members, and seven non-NATO contributing participants.

The centre is one of 21 accredited NATO Centres of Excellence, funded nationally and multinationally and closely linked with Allied Command Transformation. Its mission is to improve the capability, cooperation and information sharing of NATO, its member nations and partners in cyber defence through education, research and development, lessons learned and consultation. Its work covers the doctrine and concepts of cyber defence, education and training, support for experimentation, exercises and the legal aspects of cyber defence. It may also establish cooperative relations with non-NATO states, universities, research institutions and businesses.
coosa-river: The Coosa River begins in Rome, Georgia, at the confluence of the Oostanaula and Etowah rivers, and around 90% of its length lies in Alabama. The Oostanaula is itself formed by the Conasauga and Coosawattee Rivers. The Coosa ends just north-east of Montgomery, the state capital, where it meets the Tallapoosa River south of Wetumpka. Shoals and waterfalls along its lowest 65 miles, among them the Devil's Staircase, long kept boats on the upper river from reaching the Alabama River and the Gulf of Mexico.

Native Americans had lived in the Coosa Valley for millennia before Hernando de Soto and his men arrived, and the Coosa chiefdom was then one of the most powerful in the south-east. More than a century after the Spanish left, the British built strong trading ties with the Muscogee Creek bands of the valley around the late 17th century. France, whose settlements on the coast included Mobile, saw the river as a gateway to the whole South and contested the valley until it gave up its lands east of the Mississippi River in the Treaty of Paris of 1763.

By the end of the American Revolutionary War the Creek held the lower valley and the Cherokee the upper. After the Creek defeat at the Battle of Horseshoe Bend, the Treaty of Fort Jackson of 1814 forced the Creek to cede a large amount of land, leaving them a reserve between the Coosa and Tallapoosa rivers. In the 1820s and 1830s the Creek and Cherokee were removed to Indian Territory; the Cherokee capital, New Echota, had stood on the river's headwater tributaries in Georgia. Settlers then filled the valley with cotton plantations worked by enslaved African Americans.

The first river town of the basin grew at the foot of the Devil's Staircase and took the native name Wetumpka, meaning rumbling waters or falling stream. Riverboats used some 200 miles of the upper river as a commercial waterway into the early 20th century.

Most of the river is impounded, and Alabama Power, a unit of the Southern Company, owns seven dams and powerhouses on it. While building the first of them, Lay, Mitchell and Jordan, the company pioneered methods of controlling malaria that the Medical Division of the League of Nations came to study. The dams have harmed several species found only in the Coosa, a system that has already lost a significant portion of its aquatic fauna to extinction. Cities on its banks include Rome, Gadsden and Wetumpka.
coosawattee-river: The Coosawattee is 49.3 miles (79.3 km) long. It begins at the confluence of the Ellijay and Cartecay rivers in the city of Ellijay, in central Gilmer County, and flows west through the foothills of the North Georgia mountains. Its tributaries include Mountaintown Creek, Talking Rock Creek and Salacoa Creek. Below Carters Dam it forms the boundary between Murray and Gordon counties before entering Gordon County, and near New Echota it meets the Conasauga River to form the Oostanaula, itself a tributary of the Coosa River.

The country around the confluence was the centre of the Cherokee Nation's territory in north Georgia and south-eastern Tennessee. In the early 1820s, after the United States had forced them to cede their lands in eastern Tennessee and they had moved south, the Cherokee made New Echota, near the meeting of the rivers, their capital. It remained so until their removal in 1838. The American writer James Dickey based the fictional Cahulawassee River of his first novel, Deliverance (1970), on the Coosawattee, and the book was made into a feature film directed by John Boorman in 1972.

In Murray County the river is impounded by Carters Dam, completed in 1977, the tallest earthen dam east of the Mississippi River; the lake behind it, Carters Lake, lies mostly in Gilmer County, and below the dam the river flows into a reregulation reservoir. The Coosawattee Foundation, based in Calhoun and established in 1987, works to protect Native American resources in the American Southeast through excavation, education and advocacy.
cop28: The United Nations Climate Change Conference is held each year for the countries that signed the 1994 United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, with the host rotating among members. In early 2021 the United Arab Emirates offered to host the 2023 event, and Dubai was chosen as the host city in November of that year. It was the third conference hosted by a member of OPEC. The UAE committed to net zero emissions by 2050, the first Middle Eastern government to make such a pledge.

Before the summit the climate envoys of the United States, China and the European Union met regularly, and on 15 November the United States and China announced an agreement to triple global renewable energy use by 2030.

COP28 was the largest climate summit to that date, with over 80,000 accredited participants, up from 49,000 the year before, among them more than 150 heads of state and government. King Charles III gave the opening speech, saying the world was dreadfully far off track in meeting its climate targets. Numerous sessions treated the effect of climate change on public health, a first for a conference of the parties, and it was the first to discuss food systems.

The UAE Declaration on Sustainable Agriculture, Resilient Food Systems, and Climate Action was adopted by 159 countries. The conference was criticised for the choice of Sultan Al Jaber, chief executive of the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company, as its president, and for the size of the meeting's carbon footprint.

A first draft of the final agreement, released on 11 December, was widely rejected by most Western countries because it avoided calling for a fossil fuel phase-out. The Alliance of Small Island States called it a death certificate for small island nations, while OPEC urged participants to reject any mention of phasing out fossil fuels. The conference, scheduled to end on 12 December, was extended after Saudi objections.

On 13 December Al Jaber announced a compromise, the UAE Consensus, the first in the history of the summits to mention the need to move away from every type of fossil fuel. It called for a tripling of global renewable energy capacity by 2030, further efforts towards the phase-down of unabated coal power and a cut in methane emissions. China and India did not sign the pledge on renewable energy. The head of the International Monetary Fund welcomed the creation of the loss and damage fund.
copan: Copán lies in a fertile mountain valley in the alluvial basin of the Copán River, on the south-eastern edge of Mesoamerica. The valley made it a trade hub between the Maya lowlands and the non-Maya peoples of southern Central America, and its polity controlled access to the upper Motagua River valley, a main source of jadeite and obsidian. Its ancient name was probably Oxwitik, meaning the Three Witiks.

Little is known of the rulers before a new dynasty with origins at Tikal was installed in the early 5th century. Texts record that a warrior named K'uk' Mo' Ajaw took the throne in 426 as K'inich Yax K'uk' Mo', probably sponsored from Tikal; he may have strengthened his claim by marrying into the old Copán royal family. K'ak' Chan Yopaat, the eleventh ruler, was crowned in 578 and reigned until 5 February 628.

Uaxaclajuun Ub'aah K'awiil became the thirteenth king in July 695. Under him Copán's sculpture developed into the full in-the-round style characteristic of the city, and he ranked his city among the four most powerful Maya states with Tikal, Calakmul and Palenque. In 724 he installed K'ak' Tiliw Chan Yopaat as a vassal on the throne of Quiriguá, but in 738 that ruler captured and beheaded him. Copán lost its domain and the Motagua trade route, though its rulers began building monuments again within a few decades.

At its peak the kingdom had at least 20,000 people. The population fell in the 8th and 9th centuries to fewer than 5,000, and the valley held only a few farming hamlets when the Spanish arrived in the 16th century.

Copán is in western Honduras, near the border with Guatemala. It is known for its portrait stelae, the Acropolis, a ballcourt and the Hieroglyphic Stairway. Altar Q, dedicated by Yax Pasaj Chan Yopaat in 776, shows the first sixteen kings of the dynasty. John Lloyd Stephens and Frederick Catherwood described the site in 1841. UNESCO made it a World Heritage Site in 1980.
copenhagen: Copenhagen lies on the eastern shore of the island of Zealand, partly on the island of Amager and on a number of natural and artificial islets between the two. It faces the Øresund, the strait that separates Denmark from Sweden and connects the North Sea with the Baltic Sea. The Swedish city of Malmö lies directly across the sound, 42 kilometres away by road.

The Danish name København reflects the city's origin as a harbour and a place of commerce.
