The Old Norse form was Kaupmannahǫfn, meaning 'merchants' harbour', and the present form developed through sound changes that took place around 1400. The Latin name Hafnia is the source of the name of the element hafnium.

Flint tools show settlement in the Stone Age, and many historians believe the town dates to the late Viking Age, possibly founded by Sweyn I Forkbeard. The first habitations were probably centred on Gammel Strand, 'old shore'. The natural harbour and good herring stocks attracted seasonal fishermen and merchants from the 11th century and more permanent residents in the 13th. Excavations have uncovered the remains of a large merchant mansion from about 1020 near Kongens Nytorv, and a well from the late 12th century in Pilestræde.

Copenhagen became the capital of Denmark in the early 15th century, and the University of Copenhagen was founded in 1479. In the 16th century it served as the de facto capital of the Kalmar Union and its monarchy, and by the 17th century it was the centre of the Danish government and military. The 18th century brought a devastating plague outbreak and urban fires, followed by the building of the district of Frederiksstaden and of institutions such as the Royal Theatre and the Royal Academy of Fine Arts. In this period the city was the centre of the Danish slave trade.

A British fleet bombarded the city in 1807 during the Napoleonic Wars. The Danish Golden Age that followed gave Copenhagen a neoclassical look. After the Second World War the Finger Plan guided the growth of housing and businesses along five urban railway routes running out from the centre.

Copenhagen is the capital and largest city of Denmark and its cultural, economic and governmental centre. Since the completion of the Øresund Bridge it has been increasingly integrated with Malmö and the Swedish province of Scania in the Øresund Region. Its landmarks include Tivoli Gardens, the Amalienborg and Christiansborg palaces, Rosenborg Castle and Frederik's Church, and the University of Copenhagen is the oldest university in Denmark.
copper: Copper is a chemical element with the symbol Cu, from the Latin cuprum, and atomic number 29. It is a soft, malleable and ductile metal with very high thermal and electrical conductivity, second only to silver among pure metals at room temperature. Pure copper is orange-red, one of the few metals with a natural colour other than grey or silver. In air it slowly forms a protective layer of copper oxide, and on old roofs and the Statue of Liberty a green layer of verdigris appears. Copper is also one of the few native metals, found in nature in a directly usable, unalloyed form.

The use of native copper dates to about 9000 BCE in the Middle East, and a native copper pendant found in northern Iraq dates to 8700 BCE. The history of copper metallurgy is thought to run from cold working of native copper to annealing, then smelting, and finally casting. The earliest archaeological evidence of hot metallurgy in Eurasia, in the Balkans and Carpathian Mountains, dates to between 6200 and 5000 BCE. An amulet from Mehrgarh in Pakistan, dated to 4000 BCE, is the earliest example of lost-wax casting in copper. Ötzi the Iceman, who lived between 3300 and 3200 BCE, was found with a copper axehead of 99.7 per cent purity.

Smelting was probably discovered in China before 2800 BCE, in Central America around 600 CE and in West Africa about the 9th or 10th century. Experience with copper helped the development of other metals, and copper smelting likely led to the discovery of iron smelting.

Copper was alloyed with zinc to make brass and with tin to make bronze, and copper-tin bronzes have been used to make bells for centuries, the composition of the alloy affecting the tone. Alloys of copper and nickel, called cupronickel, are used in low-denomination coins. In Japan, shakudō is a decorative alloy of copper with 4 to 10 per cent gold, which can be patinated to dark blue or black. For more than two centuries copper paint has been used on boat hulls to control the growth of plants and shellfish.
copperbelt: The region lies on the border between central-western Zambia and the south-eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, though in some contexts the term excludes the Congo entirely. It takes in the mining towns of Zambia's Copperbelt Province, among them Ndola, Kitwe, Chingola, Luanshya and Mufulira, and those of the Congo's Haut-Katanga and Lualaba provinces, such as Lubumbashi, Kolwezi and Likasi. The ores lie in the Katanga Supergroup, a Neoproterozoic sequence of formations with rich stratiform copper-cobalt deposits; chalcopyrite, bornite and chalcocite occur in the Lower Roan Formation.

Since the Bantu expansion both Katanga and Zambia's Copperbelt have been called Ilamba, or Lambaland, after the Lamba people, who came from the Luba and Lunda kingdoms, settled at Lake Kashiba and spread outward from there. In 1895 the American scout Frederick Russell Burnham led the expedition of the Northern Territories (BSA) Exploration Co. that established the presence of major copper deposits. Along the Kafue River he met people wearing copper bracelets, and he reported that the natives had worked the ore for ages, as their old dumps showed, and traded their handiwork as far as the Portuguese of the west coast and the Arabs of the east.

Years later the British South Africa Company built towns along the river and a railway to carry the copper through Mozambique. During the 1950s the Copperbelt was the largest copper-producing area in the world, with the Roan Antelope, Nkana, Nchanga, Mufulira and Rokana mines.

Zambia's part became a province soon after independence in 1964 under the name Western Province, and President Kenneth Kaunda renamed it Copperbelt Province in 1969. Its mines include Chambishi, Kansanshi, Lumwana and Konkola, and those in the Congo include Kamoto, Kipushi, Kolwezi and Ruashi.
coptic-orthodox-church: According to Coptic tradition the church was founded by Saint Mark the Evangelist, a companion of the Apostles, around 42, and it regards itself as the subject of many Old Testament prophecies. The Catechetical School of Alexandria, which Jerome records as founded by Mark himself, is the oldest catechetical school in the world. It became a leading centre of the allegorical method of biblical interpretation and sought a rapprochement between Greek culture and the Christian faith.

In the 4th century an Alexandrian presbyter named Arius began a dispute about the nature of Christ. Emperor Constantine I convened the Council of Nicaea in 325 after Pope Alexander I of Alexandria proposed a council, and it led to the Nicene Creed. After the Council of Chalcedon in 451, disputes over the nature of Christ left the Oriental Orthodox churches in schism.

The Muslim invasion of Egypt took place in 639. Bishop John of Nikiu, whose Chronicle survives in Ge'ez, gives a hostile account of the conquest, though he says that Amr ibn al-As took none of the property of the churches. The population remained mainly Christian at first, but gradual conversion to Islam made Egypt a largely Muslim country by the end of the 12th century. Scholars point to the repression of Coptic revolts, Arab-Muslim immigration and conversion, and to higher Umayyad taxes on Christians, which weakened the church's economic base. The church moved its seat from Alexandria to Cairo in the 12th century.

The position of Copts began to improve early in the 19th century under the Muhammad Ali dynasty, and Sa'id Pasha abolished the jizya tax in 1855. Pope Cyril IV founded the first modern Coptic schools in 1853, including the first Egyptian school for girls, and a printing press. The Theological College of the School of Alexandria was re-established in 1893.

The pope of Alexandria heads the church, which follows the Coptic Rite. The language of its liturgy descends from Ancient Egyptian and uses the Coptic alphabet, derived from the Greek with added letters from the Demotic. Since Coptic was supplanted by Arabic after the Arab conquest, service books carry Arabic in parallel columns. Believers use a breviary called the Agpeya to pray seven times a day, facing east.

The church has long consecrated the archbishops of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, whose first native head, Abuna Basilios, was crowned patriarch by Pope Cyril VI in 1959. The Eritrean church gained autocephaly in 1998.
coptos: Qift, ancient Gebtu and in Greek Coptos, lies in the Qena Governorate about 43 kilometres north of Luxor, on the east bank of the Nile. Its closeness to the Red Sea made it an important trading centre between India, Punt, Arabia Felix and the north. It was the chief city of the fifth Upper Egyptian nome, Harawî, the Two Hawks. Mining expeditions into the Eastern Desert, and expeditions to Punt, left the Nile valley from Qift and Qus. Gebtu stood at the start of two caravan routes to the Red Sea, one to the port of Tjau and one further south to Berenice.

Under the native pharaohs the whole trade of southern Egypt with the Red Sea passed over these roads, and merchants followed them under the Ptolemies and in Roman and Byzantine times. Gebtu was politically important especially under the Eleventh Dynasty, but was later overshadowed by Thebes. Its chief god, Min, became a male fertility deity and the god of the eastern desert, and in the Middle Kingdom he was linked with Horus as Min-Horus.

Augustus built the city up. It fell to the Blemmyes in the third century CE and was almost destroyed by Diocletian in 292 after a long siege. In the sixth century it was renamed Justinianopolis after the emperor Justinian I. In 1176 the Copts rose against al-Adil I, brother of Saladin, who put the revolt down by crucifying 3,000 Copts around the city. The Ottomans levelled much of the medieval town in the sixteenth century, and it never regained its former importance.

The village of Qift stands on the ancient site. W. M. Flinders Petrie found remains of three temple groups inside an enclosure wall in 1893 to 1894, and American excavations took place from 1987 to 1992. The northern temple of Min and Isis dates to the Ptolemaic period, on earlier foundations of the Middle Kingdom and of Thutmose III. The southern temple yielded the Coptos Decrees, stelae of the Sixth and Seventh Dynasties that copy royal decrees concerning the temple and its personnel.
copts: The word Copt entered English in the 17th century through Neo-Latin from the Arabic Qubṭ, an Arabization of the Coptic word for Egyptian, itself adapted from the Greek Aigýptios. It originally referred to all Egyptians and became synonymous with native Christians after Egypt's Islamization and Arabization following the Muslim conquest. Copts are descended from the ancient Egyptians and historically spoke the Coptic language, the latest stage of the Egyptian language.

According to sacred tradition Mark the Evangelist introduced Christianity to Alexandria around 42, during the reign of Claudius. A fragment of the Gospel of John in Coptic from the first half of the 2nd century shows it had spread across Egypt. By the beginning of the 3rd century Christians were the majority of the population, and the Church of Alexandria was one of Christendom's four apostolic sees.

The Catechetical School of Alexandria, founded around 190 by Pantanaeus, taught Athenagoras, Clement, Didymus and Origen. The first three ecumenical councils were presided over by patriarchs of Alexandria: Alexander I at Nicaea in 325, Timothy I at Constantinople in 381 and Cyril at Ephesus in 431. The Council of Chalcedon in 451 condemned and deposed the Alexandrian patriarch Dioscorus I. The Egyptian delegation rejected it, and so did most native Egyptians, whose church became the predecessor of the Coptic Orthodox Church, while the church that accepted the council became the Greek Orthodox Patriarchate of Alexandria. Byzantine emperors repeatedly deposed and exiled non-Chalcedonian patriarchs.

After the Arab conquest in the 7th century the Copts were subjected, in the historian Roger S. Bagnall's account, to a system that prioritised fiscal exploitation, particularly through taxation. Their treatment ranged from relative tolerance to open persecution, in cycles that varied with the ruler. Under Islamic rule Copts held important administrative and commercial positions. When Napoleon conquered Egypt in 1798, a Coptic Legion under General Yaqub was raised, and it left for France with the French army in 1801.

Most Copts follow the Coptic Orthodox Church, an Oriental Orthodox church, while a minority belong to the Coptic Catholic Church, which is in communion with Rome. Coptic remained a literary language until the 13th century and was supplanted by Arabic toward the 16th. In the early 19th century it helped Champollion decipher the Egyptian hieroglyphs.

Copts keep the Coptic calendar, based on the ancient Egyptian calendar and reformed under Augustus in 25 BCE to match the Julian calendar. It has twelve months of thirty days and a short thirteenth month, and farmers still use it to follow the agricultural seasons. Coptic music is thought to preserve elements of ancient Egyptian music, with Byzantine and Hebrew influences.
cora-people: The Cora live in the rugged mountain and canyon country of Nayarit and across its borders in Jalisco, Durango and Sinaloa; the Mexican state of Nayarit takes its name from their own name for themselves. Historically their southern subgroups included the Coanes around Magdalena in Jalisco, the Huaynamota and the Zayahuecos, and the Totorames of the coastal plain between the Piaxtla River and the Río Grande de Santiago were related to them.

In the early 18th century the Cora had never allowed Catholic missionaries to live in their country, an island of the old religion among Christian Indians and Hispanic culture. A Spanish expedition of 1716 failed to bring them under control, but in 1722 the Spanish returned in force and the Cora yielded. According to Spanish accounts many then became Christian, and they keep Catholic-derived customs to the present.

The Cora live within comunidades indígenas, colonial land grants, and ejidos, agricultural communes, in the municipalities of El Nayar, Rosamorada, Ruiz and Tepic in Nayarit, in Mezquital in Durango and in a few settlements in Jalisco. They cultivate maize, beans and amaranth and raise some cattle. Their language belongs to the Corachol branch of the Uto-Aztecan family and, according to INALI, has eight dialects, among them Meseño of Mesa del Nayar and Tereseño of Santa Teresa del Nayar.

Cora religion joins the pre-Conquest religion with Catholicism. The supreme god is the sun, Tayau, our father, who crosses the sky by day and sits on his golden throne at noon; clouds are smoke from his pipe. In earlier times his priests, the tonatí, were the highest authority in Cora communities. His wife Tetewan is the underworld goddess, associated with the moon, rain and the west, and their son Sautari, the flower picker, is associated with maize, the afternoon and Jesus Christ.

Some Cora myths, such as the creation of the fifth sun, have Mesoamerican origins. Others are shared with the neighbouring Huichol, among them the myth that humanity descends from a man and a dog-woman who were the only survivors of a cataclysmic deluge.
corazon-aquino: María Corazón Sumulong Cojuangco was born on 25 January 1933 in Paniqui, Tarlac, the sixth of eight children of the businessman and former congressman José Cojuangco and Demetria Sumulong, a pharmacist. Both parents came from prominent political families. While studying law in 1953 she met Benigno Aquino Jr., known as Ninoy, and she gave up her studies to marry him on 11 October 1954. They had five children, among them Benigno Aquino III. Her husband became a leading critic of Ferdinand Marcos.

After her husband was assassinated on 21 August 1983 she became a figurehead of the opposition. Marcos announced a snap election on 3 November 1985, held on 7 February 1986. A petition with 1.2 million signatures urged her to run, and she declared her candidacy on 3 December, with Salvador Laurel as her running mate. The Batasang Pambansa proclaimed Marcos the winner, which prompted allegations of fraud and her call for civil disobedience.

On 22 February 1986 Juan Ponce Enrile and General Fidel V. Ramos announced their defection from the Marcos government. Cardinal Sin appealed over the Church's Radyo Veritas, and millions gathered on Epifanio de los Santos Avenue. The People Power Revolution ousted Marcos, and Aquino, who had held no earlier political office, was sworn in on 25 February 1986.

She issued a provisional Freedom Constitution, and the 1987 Constitution limited the presidency to a single six-year term. Her government produced the Family Code of 1987 and the 1991 Local Government Code, and in 1989 created the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao after talks with the Moro National Liberation Front. It faced coup attempts, the deadliest in August 1987 leaving 53 dead and the most serious in December 1989. Marines killed 12 farmers at the Mendiola Massacre in January 1987. Aquino declined to seek re-election and left office in 1992.

She chaired the Benigno S. Aquino Jr. Foundation and spoke abroad on democracy and human rights. She died of colorectal cancer on 1 August 2009, and her family declined a state funeral. Time named her Woman of the Year in 1986, and she received the Ramon Magsaysay Award in 1998.
corbie-abbey: The abbey, dedicated to Saint Peter, was founded under the patronage of Balthild, widow of Clovis II, and her son Clotaire III. Its first monks came from Luxeuil Abbey, founded by Saint Columbanus in 590, and carried on the Irish respect for classical learning encouraged there; their rule was the Benedictine rule as Columbanus had modified it. Theodefrid was the first abbot. Gifts of estates supported the community, and exemptions freed the abbots from interference by local bishops, as Pope Benedict III confirmed in 855. The abbots ranked as counts and had the privilege of a mint.

Corbie kept close links with the Carolingians. Desiderius, last King of the Lombards, was exiled there in 774 after his defeat by Charlemagne, and Charlemagne's cousin Saint Adalard served as abbot, under whom the monastic school became widely known. In the 9th century Corbie was larger than St. Martin's Abbey at Tours or Saint Denis at Paris and housed up to 300 monks; its scholars included Ratramnus, Paschasius Radbertus and Hadoard.

After a fire in 1137 the buildings were rebuilt on a larger scale. Saint Colette, whose father was a carpenter at the abbey, became a hermit under the direction of the abbot in 1402 and lived near the abbey church. Commendatory abbots, Cardinal Mazarin among them, were introduced in 1550, and in 1618 Corbie was one of the first houses incorporated into the new Congregation of Saint Maur.

The library, gathered from as far as Italy, was an important channel for the works of Antiquity into the Middle Ages and held unique copies of works of Tertullian, the corpus Corbiense. In 1638 Cardinal Richelieu had 400 manuscripts moved to Saint-Germain-des-Prés in Paris, and many of these were later obtained by the Russian diplomat Peter P. Dubrovsky and sent to St. Petersburg. At the suppression in 1790 the 300 manuscripts still at Corbie went to Amiens. The buildings were partly demolished, but the church survives with its portal and western towers.
corbinian: Corbinian was born and baptised as Waldegiso at Châtres, near Melun, in Frankish territory, and was named after his father, who may have died when he was an infant. His mother, Corbiniana, then renamed him after herself. Nothing else is known of his childhood. The early source for his life is the Vita Corbiniani written by Bishop Arbeo of Freising. For fourteen years he lived as a hermit at Châtres, on the road to Orléans, near a church dedicated to Saint Germain, until his reputation drew students who distracted him from his solitude.

Devotion to Saint Peter the Apostle led him to travel to Rome with some of his disciples. There Pope Gregory II urged him to evangelise Bavaria. Corbinian, who may already have been a bishop or was consecrated by Gregory, was sent to Grimoald, the Frankish Duke of Bavaria. On a mountain near Freising, where a sanctuary already stood, he built a Benedictine monastery and a school, dedicated to Saint Vitus and later to Saint Stephen, which became Weihenstephan Abbey in the 11th century.

Corbinian denounced Grimoald's marriage to Biltrudis, the widow of the duke's brother. She called him a foreign interloper and arranged to have him murdered, and he fled Freising until Grimoald was killed and Biltrudis carried off by invaders in 725. He returned at the invitation of Grimoald's successor, Huebert, and worked at Freising until his death.

Corbinian was buried at Merano. In 769 Bishop Arbeo translated his body to Freising, and it now lies in Freising Cathedral. His feast day is 8 September, and the translation of his relics is commemorated on 20 November. His brother Erembert governed the monastery after him and in 738, when Saint Boniface created four dioceses in the Duchy of Bavaria, became the first Bishop of Freising. The bear of his legend has been read as the bishop himself tamed by God's grace, the pack saddle as the burden of the episcopate. Joseph Ratzinger adopted it on becoming Archbishop of Freising-Munich in March 1977 and kept it as pope.
corcu-duibne: The name means "seed or tribe of Duibhne", the name of a goddess, and ogham inscriptions show that the Corcu Duibne claimed descent from a female ancestor, DOVINIA. They also claimed descent from Conaire Mór, a figure of legend, which would make them distant kin of Dál Riata, the Múscraige and the Corcu Baiscind, all of the Síl Conairi of legend and ultimately of the Clanna Dedad.

The 8th-century text The Expulsion of the Déisi gives them a founder, Corc Duibne. In its later version Corc and his twin Cormac are born of incest to Coirpre Músc and Duihind, the crops fail, and a druid and his wife Boí take Corc to the island of Inis Boí. There, after a year of morning purifications on the back of an otherworldly white cow with red ears, his curse passes into the cow, which leaps into the sea and becomes the rock of Bó Boí. As a hostage at the court of Cormac mac Airt, King of Tara, Corc is fostered by Óengus Gaíbúaibthech of the Déisi, follows him into exile, and finally stays on his old island to found his dynasty.

The Corcu Duibne are attested as early as the 5th century, and more than a third of all Irish ogham inscriptions come from their region. The Iron Age hill fortress of Caherconree on the Dingle Peninsula keeps the name of Cú Roí, a cousin of Conaire Mór in legend, and the peninsula's Modern Irish name is Corca Dhuibhne. Their relations with the Eóganacht Locha Léin are poorly understood, but they seem to have spent at least some time under its overlordship in the Kingdom of Iarmuman; rule from the Eóganacht Chaisil is not apparent. Their ruling clans were the O'Shea, O'Falvey and O'Connell.

The annals record their kings from the late 10th century: Congal son of Anrudán died in 989, Ua Ségda was slain in 1041, and Mathgamain Ua Ségda died in 1096. In 1064 Tairdelbach made a great raid into their country, taking cattle beyond counting, and in 1118 Tadc Ua Ségda was slain by the foreigners of Luimnech.
corded-ware-culture: The origin and spread of the Corded Ware culture is one of the unresolved issues of the Indo-European homeland problem, and archaeologists are divided over it. Some saw an influence from nomadic pastoral societies of the steppes, while others held that it developed independently in central Europe. A study by Haak and colleagues in 2015 traced much of its ancestry to a massive migration from the steppes about 4,500 years ago, but warned that the sampled Yamnaya individuals might not be directly ancestral, and that a more western or earlier steppe population may have been involved. Papac and colleagues argued in 2021 that differences in male lineages suggest the Yamnaya culture had no direct role in its origins.

Corded Ware occupied most of continental northern Europe, including much of Germany, Poland, the Baltic states and the European part of Russia, as well as coastal Norway and southern parts of Sweden and Finland. Archaeologists note that it was not a unified culture: groups had regionally specific economies and differed in settlement and society. They shared burial practices, cord-decorated pottery and distinctive stone axes. Few settlements are known, which led to a view of the people as nomadic pastoralists, but traces of emmer, common wheat and barley at Bronocice in south-east Poland show some sedentary farming. Wheeled vehicles, presumably drawn by oxen, are attested.

Burial was in flat graves or beneath small tumuli, in a flexed position. On the continent males lay on their right side and females on the left, both facing south, though in Sweden and parts of northern Poland the orientation differed. Men's graves typically held a stone battle axe, and beakers and other pottery were the most common gifts. Some graves held wagons and sacrificed animals. In Denmark the dead were buried below small mounds, with later burials placed above earlier ones.

The Corded Ware culture has long been regarded as Indo-European, and it may have done much to spread Indo-European languages in Europe. Mallory suggested in 1999 that it may have been the common ancestor of the later Celtic, Germanic, Baltic and Slavic languages and possibly some of those of Italy, while Anthony proposed that it introduced Germanic, Baltic and Slavic into northern Europe. The idea that it was the homeland of the Proto-Indo-Europeans has lost currency, as the steppe hypothesis is now the most widely accepted. Genetic studies link it with the later Sintashta and Andronovo cultures, which may reflect an eastward expansion.
corfinium: Corfinium stood in the valley of the Aternus, near the point where the river turns sharply from a south-easterly to a north-easterly course towards the Adriatic Sea. It lay 7 miles from Sulmo (modern Sulmona) and 30 from Alba Fucens by the Via Valeria. The bridge over the Aternus, 5 km from the city, is mentioned by both Caesar and Strabo and was always a military point of the highest importance; the town of Popoli grew up beside it, which led some authors wrongly to place Corfinium there.

During the Social War the confederates probably chose Corfinium for its military position, and seem to have meant it as the permanent capital of Italy and a rival to Rome, giving it a new and spacious forum, a senate house and other public buildings. Before the end of the second year of the war they had to abandon it and move their seat of government to Aesernia (modern Isernia).

In 49 BCE Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus held the fortress with 31 cohorts, the only place that offered Caesar effective resistance in his advance through Italy. Disaffection among his officers forced Domitius to surrender after a siege of only seven days, and Caesar released the leading Republicans captured with the garrison after they swore loyalty, oaths many soon broke.

Under the Empire Corfinium remained a flourishing municipium, never a colony, though it received settlers in the time of the Gracchi and again under Augustus. Its people built two aqueducts, largely cut in solid rock, one through a tunnel nearly 5 km long. In the 4th century it seems to have been the capital of the province of Valeria and the residence of its governor, and it was still in existence as late as the tenth century.

The town was later known as Pentima and then, in medieval times, as Valva, a name the neighbouring valley, La Pianata di Valva, still keeps. It took back its ancient name in 1928, and ruins of Corfinium have been found around the modern town of Corfinio.
corfu-declaration: During the First World War the South Slavs of Austria-Hungary increasingly supported trialist reform or a common South Slavic state. Serbia saw the war as a chance for expansion, and in its Niš Declaration of December 1914 its National Assembly announced the unification of its unliberated brothers as a war aim. After Austro-Hungarian, German and Bulgarian forces occupied Serbia in late 1915, its government took refuge on Corfu. The Yugoslav Committee, an ad hoc group of intellectuals and politicians from Austria-Hungary, was established in April 1915 under Ante Trumbić.

The May Declaration of 1917, issued by South Slavic members of the Vienna Imperial Council, demanded a state under Habsburg rule and took the initiative from both Serbia and the Committee. Russia had withdrawn diplomatic support from Serbia after the February Revolution. Nikola Pašić, the Serbian prime minister, therefore came to terms with the Committee, whose members, most of them from Dalmatia, feared the Treaty of London's promises of territory to Italy.

Talks ran from 15 June to 20 July 1917. Pašić wanted a centralised government in Belgrade, while Trumbić wanted a federation. Pašić said that if the Croats insisted on federation, Serbia would abandon unification in favour of a Greater Serbia, and Frano Supilo resigned from the Committee in protest. Most other members sided with Pašić, being preoccupied with Italy.

The declaration passed over the system of government. It stated that Serbs, Croats and Slovenes were one tri-named people, and that the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes would be a parliamentary, constitutional monarchy under the Karađorđević dynasty. It promised equality of religions and alphabets, and left the constitution to a future Constituent Assembly, which would decide by an unspecified qualified majority, not a simple one.

It was hailed as a South Slavic Magna Carta, but it fixed the monarchy, the dynasty and the name of the state in advance and gave no institutional safeguards for national rights. The Serbian government disregarded the qualified majority but upheld the declaration when its terms matched Serbian interests, while Croatian autonomist politicians held the qualified majority to be binding. In Italy it was portrayed as anti-Italian.

In Geneva, from 6 to 9 November 1918, Pašić signed a declaration renouncing a unitarist union, which his government quickly repudiated. On 1 December 1918 Prince Regent Alexander accepted the National Council's offer to proclaim unification with no constraints.
coricancha: The Coricancha, from the Cusco Quechua Quri Kancha, meaning golden temple, was originally named Intikancha or Intiwasi and was dedicated to Inti, the Inca sun god. It stood in Cusco, then the capital of the Inca Empire, at the confluence of two rivers, one of them the Huatanay. According to Inca myth, Manco Cápac decided to build it there, as the foundation of Cusco and of the empire.

The Inca built it of ashlar masonry, using cuboid stones cut by hand and shaped to a similar size, and rejected any stone with a slight imperfection or break. This labour was costly, and the technique came to signify the Inca's imperial power to mobilise labour. Early Spanish accounts say the stones fitted so well that no joining or cement could be seen.

The high priest lived in the temple and offered the ordinary sacrifices with other priests. Pachakuti Inca Yupanqui rebuilt the House of the Sun, adding oracles, buildings and plates of fine gold, and supplied gold and silver vessels for the Mama-cunas, cloistered women who mostly wove, dyed wool and made chicha. The walls were once covered in sheets of gold, and the adjacent courtyard held golden statues.

During Inti Raymi the Sapa Inca and the curacas went from the Haucaypata, where they greeted the rising June solstice sun, to the inner court. The Sapa Inca sat with his ancestors' mummies in the sun room, and used a concave mirror to focus the sun's rays and light the fire for burnt sacrifices of llamas. Children were sacrificed in certain circumstances.

When the Spanish demanded a ransom in gold for the life of the emperor Atahualpa in 1533, most of the gold was collected from the Coricancha. Most of the temple was destroyed after the war with the Spanish conquistadors, and settlers took it apart to build churches and houses. Its stonework became the foundation of the Church and Convent of Santo Domingo, and construction took most of a century. Major earthquakes have damaged the church, but the Inca walls still stand. Four rooms of the ancient temple with sloping walls remain in the convent, and an underground archaeological museum nearby holds mummies, textiles and sacred idols from the site.
corinium-dobunnorum: The name is first recorded by Ptolemy around 150 CE, probably in the form Corinion; its meaning is unknown. The fort was built in the territory of the friendly tribe of the Dobunni, whose main settlement at the time was the hillfort at Bagendon. Three main Roman roads met there: the Fosse Way, Akeman Street and Ermin Way. The earliest known fort, Leaholme Fort, stood west of the River Churn, whose braided channels Roman engineers had to divert around the growing town.

By the mid-70s CE the army had left the fort. Over the next twenty years a street grid was laid out, with two market places, shops and houses, and a basilica decorated with Corinthian capitals, Italian marble veneers and Purbeck Marble mouldings. Built over the ditch of the old fort, its walls cracked and sank and had to be rebuilt in the mid-2nd century. A cattle market adjoined the forum, wooden water pipes point to an aqueduct, and the amphitheatre was set in an old quarry. No temples have been found, but many sculptures show religious activity.

The town was walled in the late 2nd century, with five gates and later polygonal towers. Wealthy people built stone houses from the 110s, most luxurious in the 4th century, and the town may have been the centre of a stone-carving industry under one Sulinus son of Brucetus and of mosaic workshops. Around 350 the amphitheatre became a storage and work space. The walls were repaired around 410 and the forum kept clean, but the town was abandoned around 430. A timber building with 5th- and 6th-century pottery in the amphitheatre may have been the stronghold of King Cyndyddan, who fought at the Battle of Dyrham in 577.

The grass-covered bowl of the amphitheatre, known as the Bull Ring, is in the care of English Heritage, and a short stretch of the Roman wall can be seen in the Abbey Park. Many finds, among them mosaic floors, inscribed stones, columns and capitals, are shown in the Corinium Museum in Cirencester.
corinna: Corinna came from Tanagra in Boeotia. The Suda, a tenth-century encyclopedia, records her as the daughter of Acheloodorus and Procratia and gives her the nickname Myia, "the fly". Ancient tradition placed her in the fifth century BCE as a contemporary of Pindar, either his teacher or a fellow pupil of Myrtis of Anthedon, and said she defeated him in at least one poetry competition, though some sources claim five victories.

Scholars have been divided over this chronology since Edgar Lobel argued in 1930 that there is no reason to think she predates the spelling used on the Berlin papyrus. Sceptics note that no ancient writer mentions her before the first century BCE; Martin Litchfield West and David A. Campbell favour a late date, and Campbell calls the third century "almost certain". Archibald Allen and Jiří Frel defend the traditional date.

According to the Suda she wrote five books of poetry, collected in a Boeotian edition in the late third or early second century BCE. About forty fragments survive, more than for any ancient woman poet except Sappho. The three substantial ones come from second-century CE papyri found in Egypt. One tells of a singing contest between Mount Cithaeron and Mount Helicon, ending with Helicon hurling down a boulder in anger. Another tells of the daughters of the river-god Asopus, abducted by gods, and a third invokes Terpsichore, the Muse of dance and chorus.

She wrote in a literary dialect that mixed her Boeotian speech with the language of epic, and her style is clear, simple and often humorous. Her subjects are local legends, including Orion, Oedipus and the Seven against Thebes, which she frequently reworks with details found nowhere else. In a story told by Plutarch, she rebuked Pindar for neglecting myth, and after he filled his next ode with allusions she advised him, "Sow with the hand, not with the sack."

Pausanias reports a monument to her in the streets of Tanagra and a painting of her in the gymnasium, and the theologian Tatian says the sculptor Silanion made her portrait statue. Her poetry was popular in the early Roman Empire: Antipater of Thessalonica counted her among nine mortal muses, Ovid may have borrowed her name for his lover in the Amores, and wall-paintings at Pompeii apparently show her victory over Pindar.

Modern critics have often judged her parochial and dull, while others now see her reworking Panhellenic traditions to give Boeotian figures a larger role. She has also drawn the interest of feminist literary historians as one of the few ancient Greek women poets whose work survives.
corinth-canal: The first to propose cutting through the isthmus was the tyrant Periander of Corinth in the 7th century BCE. He built instead the Diolkos, a stone trackway along which ships were towed from one side to the other, a change of mind attributed to the expense, a lack of labour or fear that a canal would rob Corinth of its role as a trading centre. Caligula commissioned a study in 40 CE, and Egyptian experts wrongly claimed that the Gulf of Corinth was higher than the Saronic Gulf.

Nero was the first to begin work. In 67 CE he broke the ground himself with a pickaxe, and about 6,000 Judean prisoners of war began digging trenches from both sides. According to Suetonius the cut reached about 700 metres, a tenth of the isthmus, before work stopped on his death. Herodes Atticus and the Venetians, after their conquest of the Peloponnese in 1687, considered the project but did not start it. The modern canal follows Nero's course.

The opening of the Suez Canal in 1869 gave new impetus, and in 1870 a law authorised construction. A concession of 1881 went to the Société Internationale du Canal Maritime de Corinthe, and work was inaugurated on 23 April 1882 in the presence of King George I of Greece. After eight years the company's money ran out and it went bankrupt. A Greek company resumed work in 1890, and the canal was completed on 25 July 1893.

It is a sea-level channel without locks, 6,343 metres long and 8 metres deep, 24.6 metres wide at the surface and 21.3 metres at the bottom, with near-vertical rock walls rising 90 metres above sea level. It saves ships a journey of 700 kilometres around the Peloponnese.

Traffic fell far below the hoped-for 4 million net tons a year. By 1906 it had reached only half a million net tons, and 1.5 million by 1913. The narrow channel, winds funnelled by its walls and strong tidal currents made navigation difficult, and the unstable limestone walls caused repeated landslides. Between 1893 and 1940 the canal was closed for a total of four years for repairs.

On 26 April 1941 German paratroopers captured the main bridge during the Battle of Greece, but British charges destroyed it. In October 1944 retreating German forces blocked the canal with landslides and wreckage. The United States Army Corps of Engineers began clearing it in November 1947, and it reopened to all traffic by September 1948. Because it is too narrow for most modern ships, it is now used mainly by smaller and tourist vessels.
corinthian-war: When the Peloponnesian War ended in 404 BCE, Sparta alone received the plunder and the tribute of the former Athenian Empire, which alienated its allies. In 402 BCE Sparta attacked Elis, and Corinth and Thebes refused to send troops. Thebes, Corinth and Athens also refused to join a Spartan expedition to Ionia in 398 BCE, in which King Agesilaus II campaigned as far inland as Sardis. In 395 BCE the Thebans encouraged their allies the Locrians to collect taxes from disputed territory, which led to fighting with Phocis, an ally of Sparta. Sparta mobilised, and Athens voted to support Thebes. In late 395 BCE Corinth and Argos joined, and the allies' council at Corinth gave the war its name. Sparta recalled Agesilaus from Asia.

At Nemea in 394 BCE the Spartans won a decisive victory, in which the coalition lost 2,800 men and the Spartans and their allies 1,100. In the same year, both right wings were victorious at Coronea, the Thebans breaking through before Agesilaus met them head on. At sea Agesilaus had raised 120 triremes under his brother-in-law Peisander, but the Persian fleet, commanded by the satrap Pharnabazus II and the Athenian admiral Conon, destroyed it at Cnidus, which effectively ended Sparta's attempts to become a naval power.

Pharnabazus and Conon then captured Spartan-allied cities in Ionia and in 393 BCE based their fleet on Melos, the first time in 90 years that a Persian fleet had gone so far west. In 391 BCE the Athenian general Iphicrates, with light troops and peltasts, defeated a Spartan regiment at Lechaeum, and Argos and Corinth were merged. Athens recaptured a number of islands, and Thrasybulus won over states in the Hellespont before he was killed on Lesbos.

Alarmed by Athenian successes, the Persians stopped backing the allies. Antalcidas arranged with the satrap Tiribazus that Persia would join Sparta if the allies refused peace, and his fleet threatened the grain route to Athens. The King's Peace of 387 BCE was dictated by Artaxerxes II: Persia was to control Ionia, all other Greek cities were to be autonomous, which in effect barred leagues and alliances, and Sparta was to enforce the terms. Thebes was the main loser, as the Boeotian League was disbanded and its cities garrisoned by Sparta.

Persia captured Egypt and Cyprus by 380 BCE, and Sparta used the autonomy clause to break up coalitions, splitting Mantinea into five villages. War between Sparta and Thebes resumed in 378 BCE and Spartan dominance ended at Leuctra in 371 BCE. Athens, with walls and fleet restored, began to recover power and formed the Second Athenian League.
corippus: Corippus's full name is known from a single document, and nothing is known of his life beyond what his own poems tell. A native of Africa, he is called africanus grammaticus in one medieval manuscript, and he has sometimes been identified, on insufficient grounds, with Cresconius Africanus, a Catholic bishop who compiled a collection of church law. He appears to have served as a tribune or notary under Anastasius, treasurer and chamberlain of Justinian I, and late in that emperor's reign he left Africa for Constantinople, apparently after losing his property in the Vandalic War and the Moorish revolts that followed.

The Iohannis, also called De Bellis Libycis, was dedicated to the nobles of Carthage. In eight books, the last unfinished, it follows John Troglita, magister militum of Africa, from his dispatch by Justinian to his decisive victory near Carthage in 548. Its picture of the land and peoples of late Roman Africa is that of an observer from the province, and many of its statements on customs are confirmed by Procopius and by what is known of the Berbers.

In laudem Iustini minoris, in four books and written when Corippus was old, tells of the death of Justinian, the coronation of Justin II on 13 November 565 and the reception of an Avar embassy, and throws much light on court ceremony, though critics have found it servile. He also wrote a panegyric for Anastasius, then quaestor and master of offices.

Corippus took Virgil, Lucan and Claudian as his models, and his Latin is counted unusually pure for his age; he is probably the last important Latin author of late antiquity. The absence of mythological machinery and his allusions to Scripture suggest he was a Christian. The Iohannis survived in a single full copy made in the late 14th century by Giovanni De Bonis and found in 1814 in the Trivulzio library near Milan.
cormac-mac-carthaigh: Cormac belonged to the Mac Cárthaigh clan of the Eóganacht Chaisil, the original royal dynasty of Munster, which had lost the kingship to the Dál gCais of Brian Boru in the 10th century and Cashel itself by the 1070s. His father, Muireadach mac Carthaig, died in 1092. The historian Henry Alan Jefferies argued in 1983 that Ceallachán O'Callaghan then usurped the kingship of the Eóganacht of Cashel, and that his death in 1115 at Mac Carthaigh hands opened the way for Cormac's brother Tadhg.

When the High King Muirchertach Ua Briain fell ill in 1114, his vassals saw a chance to assert themselves. In 1118 Tadhg defeated Brian Ua Briain at Glanmire, and Tairrdelbach Ua Conchobair, who wished to keep Munster divided, recognised him as the first King of Desmond, leaving Thomond to the sons of Diarmaid Ua Briain. Ua Conchobair ravaged Desmond in 1121, 1122 and 1123 after Tadhg rebelled. Late in 1123 Tadhg fell seriously ill and resigned the kingship to Cormac.

Early in 1124, while Ua Conchobair was distracted by an attack from Mide and Breifne, Cormac allied with the kings of Laghin, Mide and Breifne to invade Connacht. At the bridge of Átha Luain over the Shannon they found Ua Conchobair waiting with a great army. Seeing Cormac as the leader of the revolt, Ua Conchobair executed the hostages of Desmond, among them Cormac's son Mael Sechlainn, and Cormac, judging that victory would cost too many lives, went home.

In 1125 he seized Limerick from the Ua Briain, an act seen as a claim to the kingship of all Munster and an affront to Ua Conchobair, now fully recognised as high king. The next year Ua Conchobair defeated him decisively at his camp in Osraige, and in 1127 Cormac was deposed in favour of his brother Donnchadh, who submitted after the siege of Cork on Saint Brigid's Day 1127. Cormac was tonsured, took holy orders and withdrew to the monastery of Lismore.
corn-laws: Grain had long been regulated in Britain. Imports were controlled as early as 1670, and the Corn Act 1772 allowed imports only when the domestic price stood above 48 shillings a quarter, a compromise between producers and consumers. Amendments in 1791 and 1804 favoured agricultural producers. In 1813 a House of Commons committee recommended excluding foreign corn until the home price passed 80 shillings a quarter, a level the political economist Thomas Malthus thought fair.

Corn prices fell when the Napoleonic Wars ended in 1815. The Tory government of Lord Liverpool then passed the Importation Act 1815, which received royal assent on 23 March 1815 after the Commons and Lords had approved it on 10 and 20 March. It led to serious rioting in London. The ceiling of 80 shillings was so high that it was never reached between 1815 and 1848.

The laws blocked cheap corn, at first by forbidding imports below a set price and later by steep duties. The Importation Act 1822 allowed imports at 80 shillings and prohibited them again when the price fell to 70. In 1828 William Huskisson and the Duke of Wellington devised a sliding scale in which the duty fell as the domestic price rose.

Opposition came mainly from urban groups with little political power. The Merchants' Petition of 1820, written by Thomas Tooke, demanded free trade. Charles Pelham Villiers proposed repeal in the Commons every year from 1837 to 1845, and the Anti-Corn Law League was founded in 1838. Its leading advocate, Richard Cobden, promised that repeal would cheapen food and help manufacturers. Landlords answered that manufacturers wanted cheap food to cut wages, a view shared by socialist Chartists.

Poor harvests and the Great Famine in Ireland forced the issue in late 1845. Lord John Russell announced his support for repeal on 22 November, and Robert Peel resigned as prime minister on 11 December, then resumed office on 21 December when Russell could not form a government. The third reading of Peel's bill passed the Commons on 15 May 1846 by 327 votes to 229, and the Lords, persuaded by Wellington, passed it on 25 June as the Importation Act 1846. Peel resigned soon after and credited the success to Cobden.

The Conservative Party divided. Those loyal to Peel, among them the Earl of Aberdeen and William Ewart Gladstone, were known as Peelites, and in 1859 they joined the Whigs and Radicals to form the Liberal Party. Cheap grain from North America and the Russian Empire later reduced British wheat-growing, and Britain's dependence on imported grain rose from 2 per cent in the 1830s to 45 per cent in the 1880s. Benjamin Disraeli, once a leading opponent of repeal, did not restore the duties.
cornelis-de-houtman: Cornelis de Houtman was born on 2 April 1565 in Gouda, South Holland, the son of the brewer Pieter de Houtman. His younger brother Frederick was born in 1571. In 1592 his wealthy cousin Reynier Pauw and other Amsterdam merchants formed the Compagnie van Verre to finance a Dutch trading expedition to the East Indies, inspired by maps of the route supplied by the cartographer Petrus Plancius. That year Pauw sent Houtman and his brother to Lisbon. It is unclear whether he had real business there or went chiefly as a commercial spy on the Portuguese spice trade.

On 2 April 1595 four ships left Amsterdam under Houtman: the Mauritius, Amsterdam, Hollandia and Duifje. Scurvy broke out after a few weeks, and at Madagascar seventy-one of the 248 sailors had to be buried. Quarrels broke out among the captains and traders after a skipper died. The ships reached Banten, on Java, in June 1596, passing through the Sunda Strait rather than the Malacca Strait, which the Portuguese controlled, as Jan Huyghen van Linschoten had advised.

The Sultan of Banten entered a friendly treaty with the Dutch, but Houtman was insulting to him and was turned away for rude behaviour without buying any spices. Attacked by pirates on the way to Madura, he ordered his men to attack and rape the civilian population there in revenge. At Bali the ships obtained a few pots of peppercorns on 26 February 1597. The Amsterdam was deliberately burned at Bawean, the crew decided against continuing to the Moluccas, and another skipper died, with Houtman accused of poisoning him. Portuguese ships kept the fleet from taking on water at Saint Helena, and only 87 men returned, too weak to moor the ships themselves.

The voyage was a humanitarian disaster and probably only broke even, but it showed that the Portuguese monopoly on the spice trade was vulnerable. Within five years 65 more Dutch ships had sailed east, and the Dutch eventually displaced the Portuguese and took over the spice trade. The voyage may be regarded as the start of Dutch colonisation of Indonesia.

Houtman made a second journey east in 1599 for a different company and reached Aceh, where the sultan received him peacefully until Houtman insulted him. He was defeated by Admiral Keumalahayati and her Inong Balee army, and died on 11 September 1599.
cornelis-jol: Cornelis Corneliszoon Jol came from the fishing village of Scheveningen, now a borough of The Hague. He lost a leg when young, for reasons unknown, and became one of the earliest documented pirates to use a wooden peg leg, known as Perna de Pau to the Portuguese and Pie de Palo to the Spanish, who also called him El Pirata. He joined the Dutch West India Company in 1626 during the Eighty Years' War and rose quickly to admiral. Contemporary chroniclers praised his courage and prudence, his integrity, resoluteness and tenacity of purpose.

Jol crossed the Atlantic nine times to attack the Spanish and Portuguese on the coast of Brazil and in the Caribbean. On one of his early voyages he took the island of Fernando de Noronha, which remained part of Dutch Brazil under the name Pavonia until 1654. In 1633 he and Diego el Mulato raided Campeche in Yucatán with ten ships, one of several early buccaneer raids on the town. In 1635 the Dunkirk privateer Jacob Collaert captured him near Dunkirk, but he was released some six months later.

In 1638 he fought the Spanish admiral Don Carlos Ibarra off Cuba while trying to take the treasure fleet, but none of the ships were captured, as his captains, jealous of his promotion over them, refused to fight; in Spain he was wrongly reported killed. In 1639 he commanded a squadron of seven ships under Admiral Maarten Tromp at the Battle of the Downs, a decisive Spanish defeat. In 1640, waiting again for the treasure fleet off Havana, he lost four ships wrecked ashore in a hurricane.

In 1641 he sailed from Brazil to Africa and took Luanda and the island of São Tomé from the Portuguese. On São Tomé he caught malaria and died on 31 October 1641. His son, also named Cornelis Corneliszoon Jol, or Hola, served as an officer in the Dutch navy and commanded the Leiden under Tromp in the First Anglo-Dutch War of 1652 to 1654. A street in Scheveningen bears Jol's name.
cornelis-matelief-de-jonge: Born in Rotterdam, Matelief was given command of a fleet of eleven ships of the Dutch East India Company bound for Malacca, which stood in the way of non-Portuguese ships heading for the Indonesian Archipelago, China or Japan. The fleet left Zeeland on 12 May 1605 with 1400 men on board, 600 of them soldiers. Officially it was on a trading mission, but its real aim was to break Portuguese power in the region. At Mauritius in January 1606 Matelief met Steven van der Hagen, and he was among the first to describe the island's dodo, black rat and macaque.

He reached Malacca in April 1606 and in May made a formal pact with Sultan Alauddin Riayat Shah III of Johor: the Dutch would receive Malacca and trade with Johor, and each side would tolerate the other's religion. The siege was repulsed on land by Portuguese troops under André Furtado de Mendonça, helped by Japanese samurai from red seal ships.

On 14 August the Viceroy of Goa, Dom Martim Afonso de Castro, arrived with twenty ships. In the fighting from 17 August the Dutch lost the Middelburg and the Nassau, and Matelief withdrew with about 150 dead against some 500 Portuguese. Returning a month later, he sank or burned all ten Portuguese ships Castro had left behind, on 21 September 1606.

From Ternate Matelief sailed to Canton, capturing a Chinese junk laden with Banda spices on 4 June 1607, but turned back when six Portuguese ships under André Pessoa appeared, without an agreement with China. By the end of his voyage he had lost six ships. In 1608 he brought home an embassy from King Ekathotsarot of Siam, which met Maurice of Nassau, Prince of Orange, in The Hague on 10 September 1608; a treaty between the Dutch Republic and Siam followed in 1617.

Back in Rotterdam he sat in the city's vroedschap from 1618 and later served as burgemeester, though in 1625 he lost his seat as a deputy in the States-General after staying too long in Warsaw. He died in Rotterdam on 17 October 1632. The Dutch took Malacca in 1641, again allied with Johor and now also with Aceh.
cornelis-speelman: Speelman was born on 2 March 1628, the son of a Rotterdam merchant, and in his 16th year sailed for the Indies aboard the Hillegersberg as an assistant of the Dutch East India Company (VOC). He reached Batavia in 1645, became bookkeeper in 1648 and second merchant in 1649, and went as secretary with the ambassador Joan Cunaeus to Persia, where Shah Abbas II received them with great festivity; he wrote an account of the voyage. He married Petronella Maria Wonderaer, the fifteen-year-old daughter of the receiver-general.

Back in Batavia he became bookkeeper-general in 1657, head of the company's clerical staff in 1659 and a schepen, a kind of alderman, of Batavia in 1661. Appointed governor and director of Dutch Coromandel on 12 June 1663, he was suspended for illegal private trading, having bought a diamond for his wife and resold it when she disliked it, and was sentenced to a 15 months suspension and a fine of 3,000 guilders. In 1666 he was named admiral of an expedition to Makassar, and on 18 November 1667 he concluded the Treaty of Bongaya.

A second expedition in 1669 completed the subjugation of Makassar, for which he received a gold chain and medallion. He became a full Counsellor of the Indies in 1671 and commanded a fleet against the French the next year. From December 1676 he led an expedition to Central Java in support of the ruler of Mataram and fought the rebel Trunajaya on the east coast until his recall at the end of 1677. Made Director-General of the Indies in 1678 and governor-general on 29 October 1680, he took up office on 25 November 1681, succeeding Rijckloff van Goens.

During his term the sultan of Ternate was defeated and ceded all the lands of his kingdom to the company, and Speelman also subdued the city of Bantam. He died in the Castle at Batavia on 11 January 1684 and was buried in the Kruiskerk with great splendour, to a salute of 229 cannon shots. Johannes Camphuys succeeded him as governor-general.
cornelis-van-vollenhoven: Cornelis van Vollenhoven was born in Dordrecht on 8 May 1874 and entered Leiden University at the age of 17. There he took a master's degree in law in 1895, a bachelor's degree in Semitic languages in 1896, a master's in political science in 1897 and a doctorate in law and political science in 1898. His thesis, Omtrek en inhoud van het internationale recht (Scope and content of international law), earned him a cum laude and already pointed towards his later interest in the law of Southeast Asia.

After his studies he became private secretary to J.Th. Cremer, a colonial businessman and minister of Colonial Affairs. In 1901 Leiden made him professor of the adat law of the Dutch East Indies. He had a strong influence on his students and colleagues, and several became leading scholars of adat law, among them Frederik David Holleman, whose doctorate he supervised.

He campaigned for the preservation of adat and argued against the view that it was quackery or inefficient, writing many pamphlets on it. His work Het adatrecht van Nederlandsch-Indië (The adat law of the Netherlands Indies) also covered the law of the so-called Foreign Orientals, the Arabs, Chinese, Indians and others living in the colony. Nearly all of this was done from Leiden: he visited the East Indies only twice, in 1907 and in 1923. The University of Amsterdam gave him an honorary doctorate in 1932.

Van Vollenhoven died in Leiden on 29 April 1933. Known as the Man for Adat Law, he was remembered as the great champion of the customary law of the archipelago and is still held in high regard by many of the older generations in Indonesia. The Van Vollenhoven Institute for Law, Governance, and Society, part of Leiden Law School, bears his name.
cornelius-fuscus: Little is known of Fuscus before the civil war of 69. According to Tacitus he was born into an aristocratic family but gave up a senatorial career for a life of quiet repose as an equestrian. He enters history with the accession of Galba in 68, after the revolt of Gaius Julius Vindex and the suicide of Nero. Fuscus was among the first to declare for the new emperor and, according to Tacitus, won him the support of an unnamed Roman colony, for which he was rewarded with the procuratorship of Illyricum.

In the Year of the Four Emperors, after Galba's murder and the defeat of Otho by Vitellius, Fuscus and Marcus Antonius Primus brought Illyricum, Pannonia and Dalmatia over to Vespasian. Tacitus wrote that he found his pleasure less in the rewards of peril than in peril itself. Fuscus commanded the Legio V Alaudae and the fleet of Ravenna when it turned to Vespasian, fought at the Second Battle of Bedriacum and led the legion in the conquest of Rome. Nothing is recorded of him under Vespasian and Titus, but under Domitian he was prefect of the Praetorian Guard from at least 81.

Around 84 or 85 the Dacians under King Decebalus crossed the Danube into Moesia and killed its governor, Gaius Oppius Sabinus. Domitian travelled to the region with a large force commanded by Fuscus, who drove the Dacians back across the border in mid-85, and the emperor returned to Rome to celebrate a triumph.

Fuscus then led an expedition into Dacia, where the forces of Decebalus attacked his men from all sides. His attempt to rally them failed. Fuscus was killed, the Legio V Alaudae was destroyed and the battle standard of the Praetorian Guard was lost. The Praetorian cohorts were restored, but the Fifth Alaudae was never re-formed.
cornelius-vanderbilt: Vanderbilt was born on Staten Island on 27 May 1794 and left school at eleven to work on his father's ferry in New York Harbor. At sixteen he began his own ferry to Manhattan, and other captains called him the Commodore in jest, a nickname that stuck. In 1817 he began working for Thomas Gibbons, who was fighting a steamboat monopoly granted by the New York legislature. In Gibbons v. Ogden the Supreme Court ruled for Gibbons on 2 March 1824, holding that states could not interfere with interstate commerce.

From 1829 Vanderbilt worked for himself and built steamboat lines around New York, on Long Island Sound and on the Hudson, where in 1834 he competed as The People's Line until the monopoly paid him to stop. By the end of the 1830s he dominated steamboats on the Sound and began to take over connecting railroads. With the gold rush he turned to ocean steamships and founded the Accessory Transit Company to carry passengers across Nicaragua. During the Civil War he gave his largest steamship, the Vanderbilt, to the Union Navy and received a Congressional Gold Medal.

In 1863 he took control of the New York and Harlem Railroad through a stock corner, and in 1864 he sold his last ships to concentrate on railroads. He bought the Hudson River Railroad in 1864 and the New York Central in 1867, and in 1870 merged two lines into the New York Central and Hudson River Railroad, one of the first giant corporations in the United States. His attempt to corner Erie Railway stock led to the Erie War with Jay Gould and James Fisk Jr.

In 1869 he married Frank Armstrong Crawford, and at her urging gave one million dollars, then the largest charitable gift in American history, to found Vanderbilt University in Nashville. He died on 4 January 1877, aged 82, with an estimated fortune of 105 million dollars, 95 per cent of it left to his son William and four grandsons. Two daughters and a son challenged the will in court, and William settled. His biographer T. J. Stiles credits him with expanding the nation's transport infrastructure, while critics call him a robber baron for monopolies helped in part by political manipulation.
cornplanter: Cornplanter was born at Canawaugus on the Genesee River, in present-day New York State, the son of a Seneca woman, Gah-hon-no-neh, and a Dutch-American fur trader from Albany, Johannes Abeel II, after whose family he was also known as John Abeel III. Raised by his mother among the Seneca, he belonged by matrilineal descent to her Wolf Clan; his maternal uncle Guyasuta was an important Seneca leader. His Seneca name, Gayë́twageh, means the planter.

When the American Revolutionary War began in 1775 he urged neutrality, but after the Seneca met the British officer John Butler at Irondequoit in July 1777 and chose to support the British, he honoured the decision. With Sayenqueraghta he was named war chief of the Mohawk, Seneca, Onondaga and Cayuga. He fought in the ambush at the Battle of Oriskany in 1777, joined Butler's Rangers at the Battle of Wyoming in 1778 and led the Seneca at the Cherry Valley Massacre that November, in which many non-combatants were killed or taken captive.

In 1779 he fought a delaying action against the Sullivan Expedition, whose burning of villages and stores left many Seneca to freeze or starve that winter. In a raid of May 1780 his warriors captured his own father, whom he had escorted home in safety.

After the war he negotiated with the United States, signing the Treaty of Fort Stanwix in 1784, the Treaty of Canandaigua in 1794 and the Treaty of Big Tree three years later. He kept the Seneca neutral in the Northwest Indian War, met President George Washington in Philadelphia in 1790, and invited Quakers to teach skills such as carpentry and smithing on his land.

Later he turned to the teaching of his half-brother Handsome Lake, burned his uniform, broke his sword and closed the schools, and his influence gave way to that of Chainbreaker and Red Jacket. He died in 1836 at home on the Cornplanter Tract, 1,500 acres along the Allegheny River granted to him in 1796. In 1866 Pennsylvania placed a monument over his grave, believed to be the first in the United States to honour a Native American. When the Kinzua Dam was completed in 1965, the tract was flooded and his grave and monument were moved to the Riverview-Corydon Cemetery.
cornwall: Cornwall forms the tip of the south-west peninsula of Great Britain and is exposed to the full force of the Atlantic winds. Its only land border is with Devon, formed almost entirely by the River Tamar. The coast is mostly resistant rock and tall cliffs, and the interior is a spine of infertile upland made of granite intrusions, among them Bodmin Moor, Hensbarrow, Carnmenellis and the Penwith peninsula. These are the exposed parts of the Cornubian batholith, which also includes Dartmoor and the Isles of Scilly. The Lizard peninsula is mainland Britain's only ophiolite, a section of oceanic crust now found on land.

The area was inhabited from the Palaeolithic and Mesolithic periods, and in the Late Bronze Age it belonged to a maritime trading culture, the Atlantic Bronze Age system, that reached from Ireland to Portugal. Cornwall had a minor Roman presence and later formed part of the Brittonic kingdom of Dumnonia. The Battle of Deorham in 577 separated Dumnonia from Wales, after which its people often fought the expanding kingdom of Wessex. Centwine of Wessex drove the Britons as far as the sea in 682, and the Annales Cambriae report a British victory at Hehil in 722. King Æthelstan set the boundary at the Tamar in 936.

By the Norman Conquest Cornwall was administered as part of England but kept its own culture. Breton allies of the Normans took many lands, and a new Cornish-Norman ruling class later emerged, some of its members involved in the Stannary Parliament system. Cornwall became a duchy in 1337. In 1548 the college at Glasney was closed and looted, and objections to the English language Book of Common Prayer led to the Prayer Book Rebellion; reprisals have been estimated to account for 10 to 11 per cent of the civilian population and began the slow decline of the Cornish language. During the Industrial Revolution the tin and copper mines expanded and then declined, and china clay became a major industry around St Austell.

Cornwall is a ceremonial county with an area of 1,375 square miles; its only city is Truro. It is recognised by Cornish and Celtic political groups as one of six Celtic nations, and its flag is Saint Piran's, a white cross on a black field. Efforts to revive the Cornish language began in the nineteenth century, and the language is recognised under the European Charter for Regional or Minority Languages. The Newlyn School and later the artists of St Ives made the county a centre of painting, and the derelict mine workings survive as a World Heritage Site.
coro-venezuela: Coro stands on a coastal plain at the south of the Paraguaná Peninsula, a few kilometres from its port, La Vela de Coro, on the Caribbean Sea. The Médanos de Coro National Park, a field of dunes, lies to the north. The climate is hot and semi-arid, with strong winds. According to tradition the name comes from the Caquetio word curiana, meaning place of winds.

The city was founded on 26 July 1527 by Juan de Ampíes as Santa Ana de Coro. Ampíes agreed to respect Manaure, the leading chief of the Caquetio people, but in 1529 Ambrosius Ehinger arrived as first governor for the Welser, a banking family of Augsburg to whom the emperor Charles V had granted the Province of Venezuela. As Neu-Augsburg it was the first German colony in the Americas, and expeditions set out from it in search of El Dorado. The Welser government ended in 1545. The diocese of Coro, created in 1531, was the first bishopric in South America.

Coro was the first capital of the captaincy general of Venezuela until 1578, when Caracas replaced it because of repeated pirate attacks and its harsh climate. Francis Drake sacked the cathedral in 1567, and in the 17th century a hurricane and more raids struck the city. In 1795 José Leonardo Chirino led a rising of enslaved and other dominated people in the Sierra de Coro that aimed to end slavery and was defeated. In 1806 Francisco de Miranda landed at La Vela de Coro, bringing the tricolour later adopted by Gran Colombia. Coro stayed loyal to Spain in 1810 and joined the independence movement in 1821.

Coro is the capital of Falcón State. Its centre joins the Spanish chequerboard plan with irregular streets of German origin, and its houses are built of adobe and bahareque, an earth and plant-fibre technique unique in the Caribbean. The cathedral is the oldest Catholic church on the South American mainland. Coro and its port were inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 1993 and have been on the List of World Heritage in Danger since 2005 because rain damages the earthen buildings.
coromandel-coast: The delimitations of the coast vary, but it is generally taken to be bounded by the mouth of the Krishna river to the north, the Bay of Bengal to the east, the cape of Point Calimere to the south and the Eastern Ghats to the west, although some extend its northern boundary to Ganjam. It covers about 22,800 square kilometres, with an average elevation of 80 metres, backed by the low, flat-topped hills of the Eastern Ghats. It is home to the East Deccan dry evergreen forests, whose leathery leaves stay on the trees all year, and to mangrove forests along the low coast and river deltas. Kaliveli Lake and Pulicat Lake are important wetlands for migrating and resident birds.

The name comes from Cōḻamaṇḍalam, Tamil for the realm of the Cholas, from which the Portuguese derived Coromandel. Another derivation is Karaimaṇḍalam, the realm of the shores. In Muslim sources from the 12th century on the coast was called the Maʿbar Coast. An Italian explorer, Ludovico di Varthema, perhaps first gave the name Coromandel in 1510, and the Portuguese then used it on maps.

By late 1530 the coast had three Portuguese settlements, at Negapatão, São Tomé de Meliapore and Paliacate. In the 17th and 18th centuries it was the scene of rivalry among European powers for control of the India trade. The British established themselves at Fort St George, Madras, and at Masulipatnam, the Dutch at Pulicat and Sadras, the French at Pondicherry, Karaikal and Nizampatnam, and the Danish at Dansborg, or Tranquebar. Eventually the British won out, though France kept the small enclaves of Pondicherry and Karaikal until 1954. The Dutch took up serious trading there.

The coast supplied Indian Muslim eunuchs to the court of Siam. In the 18th century Chinese lacquer goods such as boxes, screens and chests became known as Coromandel goods, because many Chinese exports were consolidated at its ports. Two works on its economic history are Merchants, Companies and Commerce on the Coromandel Coast, 1650 to 1740, by Arasaratnam, and The World of the Weaver in Northern Coromandel, by P. Swarnalatha. The name was later given to places elsewhere: the Coromandel Peninsula in New Zealand took it from a Royal Navy ship called HMS Coromandel, and Coromandel Valley in South Australia from a ship that reached Holdfast Bay in 1837 with 156 English settlers.
corpus-christi-feast: The feast resulted from some forty years of work by Juliana of Liège, a Norbertine canoness born in 1191 or 1192, who had been raised by the Augustinian nuns of Mont-Cornillon. She reported a first vision of Christ in 1208, in which she was told to plead for a feast of Corpus Christi, and kept it secret for about twenty years. She then petitioned the Dominican Hugh of St-Cher and Robert of Thourotte, Bishop of Liège, who in 1246 ordered the feast kept each year in his diocese on the Thursday after Trinity Sunday. The first celebration was at St Martin's Church in Liège.

In 1251 Hugh of St-Cher, as Cardinal-Legate, found the feast unobserved at Liège and reinstated it, and the next year he established it across his jurisdiction. Jacques Pantaléon, who had served as archdeacon at Liège, became Pope Urban IV and in 1264 made the feast universal for the Latin Church by the bull Transiturus de hoc mundo. The bull gave as the chief reason that so many other themes crowded Maundy Thursday that the Eucharist was almost lost sight of.

Tradition says that Urban IV was moved by a procession to Orvieto in 1263 after a bleeding host was witnessed at Bolsena. Scholars have questioned this, noting problems in dating the miracle, whose tradition begins in the 14th century. Thomas Aquinas, at Orvieto from 1259 to 1265, is credited with the office and Mass of the feast, including the hymn Pange Lingua.

The feast was not widely kept for half a century. It became truly universal only after the bull was included in the Clementines, promulgated in 1317 by Pope John XXII. The central observance is a procession of the Blessed Sacrament in a monstrance, followed by Benediction, with flower wreaths on doors and windows. In medieval Europe it was also a time for mystery plays: those at York were performed on Corpus Christi Day for some 200 years until the 16th century.

During the Reformation the feast was suppressed in many Protestant churches, especially Calvinist ones, because it affirmed the real presence. Martin Luther condemned processions with the consecrated elements as vain idolatry, yet Lutheran calendars kept the feast until about 1600, and it continues in some Lutheran churches. England abolished it in 1548, and the Church of England has since allowed a Day of Thanksgiving for the Institution of Holy Communion on the same Thursday.
corpus-juris-civilis: Justinian came to the throne in Constantinople in 527. Six months later, to reduce the great number of imperial constitutions and so of lawsuits, he arranged a new collection of them, the Codex Iustinianus. The commission could leave out or change text and delete what was obsolete or contradictory. The first edition was completed on 7 April 529 and replaced all earlier constitutions; it is lost, and a second edition of 534 survives.

A little over a year later Justinian appointed a commission headed by Tribonian to compile the writings of the jurists in a shorter, more contemporary form. It finished the Digest in 533. How far the editors amended their material is not recorded and mostly cannot be known. The text was almost entirely in Latin, though Greek was the language of most citizens.

The work has four parts. The Code collects imperial pronouncements having force of law back to the time of Hadrian; its first law requires all peoples under imperial rule to hold the Christian faith. The Digest is an encyclopedia of brief extracts, mostly from the second and third centuries, from 38 jurists, and was given full force of law.

The Institutes, a student textbook in four books made by Tribonian and the professors Theophilus and Dorotheus, is largely based on the Institutes of Gaius, of which two thirds is literal quotation. It became law on 30 December 533, with the Digest. All three were meant to be the sole source of law, but Justinian had to pass further laws after 534, counted as the fourth part, the Novels.

In the Eastern Empire the Corpus was revised into Greek and remained the basis of law, in the Basilika of the late 9th century, until the 15th century. In the West it took effect in areas regained under Justinian, such as Ravenna, but was otherwise recovered only in the Middle Ages. Historians disagree on how it was recovered in northern Italy about 1070. It was taught at Bologna by Pepo and then Irnerius, whose pupils, the Four Doctors of Bologna, were among the first glossators.

The recovered law became the foundation of law in all civil law jurisdictions and influenced the canon law of the Catholic Church. Its influence on common law is markedly less. The name Corpus Juris Civilis was adopted only in the 16th century, when Dionysius Gothofredus printed it under that title in 1583.
corrective-move: When South Yemen became independent of Britain on 30 November 1967, the ruling National Front was divided between an Aden-based right wing that favoured a capitalist system and a Hadhramaut-based left inspired by Lenin's The State and Revolution. The economy was in crisis: the British withdrawal left more than 20,000 Yemenis unemployed, the closure of the Suez Canal cost Aden 75 per cent of its shipping and trade income, and unpaid British aid cost the state 60 per cent of its revenue. Qahtan al-Shaabi, president from 1 December 1967, also made himself prime minister and supreme commander.

At the Fourth General Congress at Zinjibar on 2–8 March 1968 the left, led by Abdul Fattah Ismail, won a majority of the 41-member General Command and resolutions for purges, land reform and popular councils, accepting a compromise leadership under al-Shaabi. An army coup on 20 March, a right-wing purge on 30 March and a left-wing counter-coup on 14 May all failed, and in October 1968 the left was reintegrated into the leadership.

By early 1969 Qahtan was losing support in every faction for his autocratic style, and on 6 April he was forced to give up the premiership to his cousin Faysal al-Shaabi. On 15 or 16 June he dismissed the interior minister, Muhammad Ali Haitham, who had been drawing closer to the left. The General Command called the decision unilateral and accused him of seeking to become a dictator. On 22 June Qahtan and Faysal offered to resign, believing their opponents too weak to accept; the offer was accepted and troops secured the radio station for the announcement. Qahtan was held in prison and under house arrest until his death in 1981; Faysal was arrested on 31 March 1970 and shot after an escape attempt.

Salim Rubaya Ali became president and chairman of a five-member Presidential Council, with Haitham as prime minister, Ismail as general secretary of the National Front and Ali Nasser as commander-in-chief. The main sectors of the economy were nationalised on 27 November 1969, and a constitution drafted with East German and Egyptian help was adopted on 30 November 1970. The National Front became the only authorised party, merging into the Yemeni Socialist Party in 1978. A Family Code of 1974 set minimum marriage ages and restricted polygamy, and adult literacy rose from about 15 per cent to an estimated 53 per cent by 1985. The historian Noel Brehony called the Corrective Move "the most decisive event in the early history of independent south Yemen".
corrientes: Corrientes lies in the Argentine Littoral, on the eastern shore of the Paraná River, near the border with Paraguay. It is about 1,000 km from Buenos Aires and 300 km from Posadas, on National Route 12. Across the river, which marks the natural border with Chaco Province, lies its twin city Resistencia, joined to it by the General Belgrano Bridge. The Guarani name of the city is Taragui, meaning 'Currents'. The climate is humid subtropical, with an annual average temperature of 21.3 °C and annual rainfall of around 1,500 millimetres.

Europeans reached the region early.
