Sebastian Cabot established the fort of Sancti Spiritu upstream on the Paraná in 1527, and in 1536 Pedro de Mendoza went further north into the river's basin, searching for the Sierras of Silver. Juan Torres de Vera y Aragón founded the city on 3 April 1588 and named it San Juan de Vera de las Siete Corrientes, later shortened to Corrientes.

The seven currents refer to seven peninsulas on the shore at this place, which produced wild currents that made navigation difficult. Its position between Asunción and Buenos Aires made it an important middle point, helped by its land, 55 metres high, which prevents flooding when the river rises. In 1615 Jesuits settled near the Uruguay River. In 1807 the city resisted the British invasions. During the Argentine War of Independence it was in permanent conflict with the centralist government of Buenos Aires, but the Paraguayan War united them after Paraguayan forces attacked the city in 1865.

Corrientes is the capital of the province of Corrientes and had a population of 346,334 at the 2010 census. It combines colonial and modern architecture with several churches, and it is home to one of Argentina's biggest carnival and chamamé celebrations.
corsica: Corsica is the fourth-largest island in the Mediterranean, lying south-east of the French mainland, west of the Italian Peninsula and immediately north of Sardinia. It is 183 km long at its longest and 83 km wide at its widest. It is the most mountainous island in the Mediterranean, a mountain in the sea: a single chain makes up two-thirds of the island, with Monte Cinto the highest peak at 2,706 metres. Its granite backbone on the western side formed about 250 million years ago.

People have lived on Corsica since the Mesolithic, and a permanent presence is documented from the Neolithic. After the western Roman Empire collapsed in the fifth century CE the island was invaded by the Vandals and the Ostrogoths, briefly recovered by the Byzantine Empire, then became part of the Kingdom of the Lombards. Pepin the Short, king of the Franks, expelled the Lombards and nominally granted Corsica to Pope Stephen II.

In the first quarter of the 11th century Pisa and Genoa together freed the island from the threat of Arab invasion, and it then came under the influence of the Republic of Pisa. Immigration from Tuscany gave the island its place names and made the language of the northern two-thirds close to Tuscan. The Republic of Genoa ruled Corsica from 1284 to 1755.

The Corsican Revolution against Genoa began in 1729 under Luiggi Giafferi and Giacinto Paoli, later led by Giacinto's son Pasquale Paoli. An independent Corsican Republic was proclaimed in 1755 and remained sovereign until France conquered the island in 1769. Napoleon Bonaparte was born in Ajaccio in 1769. In 1814 British troops briefly occupied the island and the Treaty of Bastia gave the British crown sovereignty, but Lord Castlereagh later repudiated it. Corsica was freed in 1943, the first French department to be liberated.

Corsica is one of the 18 regions of France and a single territorial collectivity, with a Corsican Assembly that has more extensive powers than other French regional bodies. Ajaccio is the capital and Bastia the second largest town. The population is 365,636. French is the official and most widely spoken language, while Corsican, an Italo-Dalmatian language close to medieval Tuscan, is recognised as a regional language. The Scandola Nature Reserve, within the regional natural park, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
cortes-of-aragon: The King of Aragon was bound to summon the Cortes at least once every five years, and every year after the union with Catalonia. Their main business was judicial: settling disputes between individuals or towns and hearing complaints about the king's officers or the estates. They also approved legislation and voted on taxes. The four estates were the clergy, the great nobles or ricos hombres, the knights and the towns.

The more important laws required unanimity among the four estates. Any member could veto a law, and the decision was then recorded as agreed with the exception of that member, which allowed further debate and discussion, though these often ended in stalemate. Such cases were referred to a permanent committee of two representatives of each estate, which judged whether the existing will of the majority was sound.

The Cortes of Aragon served as the model for the parliaments of Sardinia and Sicily. They survived until 1707, when Philip V issued the Nueva Planta decrees, which centralised political power and abolished the former regional assemblies of the Crown of Aragon, including the Cortes themselves.

The Cortes were revived in 1983 as the regional parliament of the Spanish autonomous community of Aragon, under Article 12 of the Statute of Autonomy for Aragon. Article 16 of the statute sets out their functions: electing the President of Aragon and approving the president's actions and legislation, making laws, supervising planning and economic projects, monitoring borrowing and spending, appointing an Auditor General for Aragon and electing senators to the Spanish Senate.
cortes-of-cadiz: After the Tumult of Aranjuez of March 1808 forced Charles IV to abdicate, Napoleon drew him and his son Ferdinand VII to Bayonne, made both give up the throne and handed it to his brother Joseph Napoleon. Local juntas rose against the French, and a Supreme Central Junta met in Aranjuez on 25 September 1808 in place of the absent royal government. It called for an Extraordinary and General Cortes, but after defeats at Ocaña and Alba de Tormes it retreated to Cádiz and dissolved itself on 29 January 1810, leaving a five-person Regency to convene the assembly.

Unlike traditional cortes, the assembly met as a single body rather than by estates. When it opened on 24 September 1810, 104 deputies were present, 30 of them interim delegates for overseas territories who were living in Spain; Ramón Power y Giralt was the only American deputy to arrive in time. Eventually about 300 deputies took part, including 63 from Spanish America. About one-third were clergy, one-sixth nobles and the rest from the middle class. Cádiz's powerful merchant guild, the consulado, pressed to keep its trade advantages, while the Americans wanted freer trade.

In its first session the Cortes declared that it, not the king, held national sovereignty, and it divided government into legislative, executive and judicial branches. The deputies split into liberals and conservatives; conservatives saw the assembly as an interim body until Ferdinand, whom his supporters called the Desired One, returned. The liberal majority turned it into a constitutional convention. The Constitution of 1812 created a unitary state with equal laws across the empire, a limited monarchy governing through ministers under parliamentary control and new provinces and municipalities, but it denied people of African ancestry political rights and representation.

On his return in 1814 Ferdinand dismissed the Cortes on 4 May and ruled as an absolute monarch, foreshadowing a long conflict between liberals and traditionalists. In Spanish America most of the Criollo people rejected the Cortes' claim to sovereignty, and conservatives there found the constitution too liberal, which hastened the move to independence. By the second half of 1826 only Cuba and Puerto Rico remained Spanish in the Americas.
cosenza: Cosenza is the capital of the province of Cosenza in Calabria. It stands 238 m above sea level at the confluence of the Busento and the Crati, in a valley between the Sila and the coastal range of mountains. The old town, overshadowed by its Swabian castle, descends to the Crati, and the modern city lies to the north, beyond the Busento. Almost surrounded by mountains, it has cold winters and hot summers.

The ancient Consentia was the capital of the Italic Brettii, a bulwark against Hellenic influence. In their territory the Battle of Pandosia was fought, in which Brettii and Lucanians defeated Alexander of Epirus. According to the historian Jordanes, Alaric advanced south after sacking Rome and died near Cosenza. Tradition says slaves diverted the Busento to dig his tomb and were killed to keep it secret.

Later the town was disputed between Saracens and Lombards, destroyed and rebuilt around 988, and became the capital of the Norman dukedom of Calabria. Frederick II promoted building and an annual fair. The Spanish army occupied it in 1500, and in the sixteenth century it was the seat of the Viceroy of Calabria and home of the Accademia Cosentina, whose members included Bernardino Telesio. During the French period of 1806 to 1815 it was a birthplace of the Carbonari. The Bandiera Brothers were executed there after the uprising of 15 March 1844, and in 1860 a plebiscite annexed Calabria to the new Kingdom of Italy.

Cosenza has a population of 63,240, and its urban area more than 250,000. The cathedral of Santa Maria Assunta was destroyed by an earthquake on 9 June 1184 and consecrated by Frederick II in 1222. The Castello Svevo was restored by Frederick II, who added its octagonal tower in 1239. The University of Calabria lies in neighbouring Rende.
cosimo-de-medici: Cosimo di Giovanni de' Medici was born in Florence on 27 September 1389, to Giovanni di Bicci de' Medici and Piccarda Bueri. Cosimo inherited his wealth and banking skill from his father, who had founded the Medici Bank in Florence in 1397. Under Giovanni the bank opened branches in Rome, Geneva and Venice, and most of its profit came from Rome, where its manager handled Church finances. Cosimo later extended it with offices in London, Pisa, Avignon, Bruges, Milan and Lübeck. About 1415 he married Contessina de' Bardi, and they had two sons, Piero the Gouty and Giovanni.

Cosimo's power rested on his wealth, which he used to influence the votes of office holders in the city councils, above all the Signoria. Because Florence was proud of its republic, he pretended to little ambition and seldom held office. Enea Silvio Piccolomini, later Pope Pius II, said of him that political questions were settled in his house and that he was king in all but name. Yet his fellow politicians saw him as first among equals, and the councils resisted his proposals throughout his career.

In September 1433 the anti-Medici party, led by figures such as Rinaldo degli Albizzi, had him imprisoned in the Palazzo Vecchio. Some demanded his execution, but the sentence became exile. Cosimo went to Venice, taking his bank with him. Within a year so much capital had left Florence that the decree was lifted, and he returned in 1434. In foreign policy he worked for a balance of power between Florence, Naples, Venice and Milan, and he sent Francesco I Sforza to establish himself in Milan after 1447. The settlement brought nearly half a century of peace.

Cosimo died at Careggi on 1 August 1464 and was succeeded by his son Piero, the father of Lorenzo de' Medici. The Signoria awarded him the title Pater Patriae, Father of the Fatherland, and had it carved on his tomb in the Church of San Lorenzo. He had commissioned Michelozzo to build the Palazzo Medici, and he was a patron of Fra Angelico, Fra Filippo Lippi and Donatello. His support enabled Brunelleschi to complete the dome of Santa Maria del Fiore in 1436. In 1444 he founded the first public library in Florence, at San Marco, and he supported Marsilio Ficino's translation of Plato.
cosimo-i-de-medici: Cosimo was born in Florence on 12 June 1519, the son of the condottiere Ludovico de' Medici, known as Giovanni delle Bande Nere, and Maria Salviati. He came from a different branch of the family, descended from Giovanni il Popolano, and a successor was sought outside the senior branch because the only male child of Alessandro was illegitimate and four years old.

Until his accession Cosimo had lived only in Mugello and was almost unknown in Florence. Many influential men favoured him in the hope of ruling through him, but the Florentine writer Benedetto Varchi observed that the innkeeper's reckoning was different from the glutton's: Cosimo proved strong-willed, astute and ambitious, and soon rejected the clause that entrusted much power to a Council of Forty-Eight.

Toward the end of July 1537 exiles under Bernardo Salviati and Piero Strozzi marched into Tuscany. Alessandro Vitelli defeated them at Montemurlo and stormed the fortress, and the prominent prisoners were later beheaded. Cosimo won recognition from Charles V in exchange for help against France in the Italian Wars. This restored the power of the Medici, who ruled Florence until Gian Gastone de' Medici died in 1737, and helped free Tuscany from Imperial garrisons.

With Charles V's support Cosimo defeated the Sienese at the Battle of Marciano in 1554 and besieged their city, which fell on 17 April 1555 after 15 months, its population diminished from 40,000 to 8,000. Montalcino, the last redoubt of Sienese independence, was annexed in 1559, and in 1569 Pope Pius V elevated him to Grand Duke of Tuscany. He was an authoritarian ruler who kept a guard of Swiss mercenaries and had Lorenzino de' Medici assassinated in Venice in 1548. He built fortresses, laid heavy taxes on his subjects and developed a navy, entrusted to the Knights of St Stephen, which took part in the Battle of Lepanto.

Cosimo created the Uffizi, or offices, to consolidate his administrative control of the committees, agencies and guilds of Florence's republican past; it now houses a major collection of art. He finished the Pitti Palace, laid out the Boboli Gardens and supported Giorgio Vasari, Benvenuto Cellini, Pontormo and Bronzino. In 1539 he married Eleanor of Toledo, who died of malaria in 1562 with their sons Giovanni and Garzia. In his last ten years, struck by the deaths of two sons, he gave up active rule to his son and successor Francesco I and retired to the Villa di Castello. He died on 21 April 1574.
cosimo-ii-de-medici: Cosimo was born on 12 May 1590, the elder son of Ferdinando I de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany, and Christina of Lorraine. His father took care to give him a modern education, and Galileo Galilei was his tutor between 1605 and 1608. In 1608 Ferdinando arranged his marriage to Archduchess Maria Maddalena of Austria, daughter of Archduke Charles II. The wedding was marked by an elaborate display on the Arno that included a performance of the Argonautica, in which Jason sailed around an artificial island and gave Maria Maddalena six red apples, alluding to the Medici balls, or palle. The couple had eight children in eight years.

Ferdinando I died in 1609 and Cosimo succeeded him. Because of his precarious health he did not take an active part in governing and delegated administration to his ministers for most of his twelve-year reign, but he was a great patron of science and letters. He extended the Palazzo Pitti, rebuilt the Villa del Poggio Imperiale and enlarged the navy. The artist Jacques Callot worked at his court until 1621, recording feasts and carnivals in Florence.

In 1610 Galileo was named court mathematician, a post that freed him from teaching mathematics at universities and let him work as philosopher, mathematician and astronomer in Florence. He had dedicated his Sidereus Nuncius to the grand duke, and the four moons of Jupiter he found were named the Medicean Stars in reference to Cosimo and his three brothers. Tuscan ambassadors in Prague, Paris, London and Madrid received copies of the book and telescopes made by Galileo, paid for by the court treasury.

Cosimo died of tuberculosis on 28 February 1621. His elder son Ferdinando II was still a minor, and, as Cosimo wished, the regency went to Cosimo's wife and his mother. Of his children, Ferdinando II became grand duke, Margherita married Odoardo Farnese, Duke of Parma, and Anna married Ferdinand Charles, Archduke of Austria; two of his sons became cardinals.
cosimo-iii-de-medici: Cosimo was born on 14 August 1642, the eldest surviving son of Ferdinando II and Vittoria della Rovere of Urbino. Ferdinando wanted him to have the finest scientific education, but the pious Vittoria opposed it and prevailed, and the Sienese theologian Volunnio Bandinelli became his tutor. On 17 April 1661 he married Marguerite Louise d'Orléans, a granddaughter of Henry IV of France, by proxy at the Louvre. The marriage was unhappy from the start: she demanded the crown jewels and eventually left Tuscany for the Convent of Montmartre. They had three children: Ferdinando in 1663, Anna Maria Luisa in 1667 and Gian Gastone in 1671. Accompanied by Lorenzo Magalotti, Cosimo toured Europe in 1667 and 1668 and met Rembrandt in Amsterdam.

When Ferdinando II died on 23 May 1670, the grand duchy had 720,594 people, its exchequer was nearly bankrupt and Siena was virtually abandoned. Cosimo began with fervour but soon left day-to-day administration to his mother. He turned to persecuting Tuscany's Jews: a law of 1 July 1677 forbade Christians to work in Jewish establishments on pain of a fine of 50 crowns, and later decrees of 1679 and 1680 banned Jews from visiting Christian prostitutes and from cohabitation. His reign was also marked by laws regulating prostitution and May celebrations, and by economic decline.

In 1689 the Duke of Savoy obtained the style Royal Highness, which angered Cosimo, who later obtained it for his own family through the Elector Palatine. Anna Maria Luisa married the Elector Palatine, Johann Wilhelm; Cosimo's elder son Ferdinando married Violante Beatrice of Bavaria and Gian Gastone married Anna Maria Franziska of Saxe-Lauenburg on 2 July 1697, but no marriage produced children. On 9 October 1691 France, England, Spain and the United Provinces guaranteed the neutrality of Livorno, and Tuscany stayed neutral in the War of the Spanish Succession. Cosimo visited the Convent of Saint Mark daily.

Cosimo fell ill on 22 September 1723 and died on 31 October. Six days earlier he had proclaimed that Tuscany should remain independent and that Anna Maria Luisa should succeed after Gian Gastone; the proclamation was ignored, since Charles VI held that the Tuscan succession was his to alter as an imperial fief. Gian Gastone repealed the laws against Jews and eased tariffs. On his death in 1737 Tuscany passed to the House of Lorraine. Among Cosimo's lasting edicts was the establishment of the Chianti wine region.
cosmas-indicopleustes: Cosmas came from Alexandria in Egypt and lived in the 6th century. He made several voyages to the Kingdom of Aksum and elsewhere in the Red Sea and Indian Ocean during the reign of the emperor Justinian. He was a pupil of the East Syriac Patriarch Aba I and a follower of the Church of the East. His surname Indicopleustes means Indian voyager, although he cannot be shown to have reached India or Ceylon himself.

He seems to have visited Aksum, in what is now northern Ethiopia, as well as Eritrea, and he sailed along the coast of Socotra. Around 525 he was at Adulis, on the Red Sea coast of modern Eritrea, when the king of Aksum was preparing an expedition against the Jewish king Dhu Nuwas in Yemen.

Around 550 Cosmas wrote the Christian Topography, once copiously illustrated and partly based on his experience as a merchant. It is thought to have been written in Alexandria, though it is said to have been composed in a Sinai cloister. He described the ports of the Malabar Coast and was the first traveller to mention Soriyani Christians in present-day Kerala. He reported churches in Taprobane, in Malê where pepper grows, and at Calliana, with clergy appointed from Persia. He also learned at second hand that there was a sea east of China, which Ptolemy had not known.

At Adulis he recorded inscriptions, including the Monumentum Adulitanum, that have since vanished. His cosmology held that the earth and ocean are flat and that the heavens form a box with a curved lid, modelled on the tabernacle described to Moses. The inhabited earth lies at the centre, surrounded by ocean, beyond which lies the paradise of Adam. The sun circles a conical mountain in the north, which accounts for the length of the day. He was scornful of Ptolemy and others who held the earth to be spherical.

Cosmas's view was never influential, even in religious circles, and the Christian John Philoponus sought to refute it. The ninth-century patriarch Photius judged his style very poor and thought him more a fable writer than a truthful historian. David C. Lindberg observes that Cosmas is the only medieval European known to have defended a flat earth, so that his use to support a claim that most medieval people believed in a flat earth is false. Apart from his cosmology, his account of Aksum, India and the Indian Ocean is valued by historians. The work survives in a 10th-century manuscript in Florence and in 8th and 9th century manuscripts at the Vatican that contain some of his sketches.
cosmas-the-priest: Almost all that is known of Cosmas comes from the few words he writes about himself in his treatise. He calls himself unworthy, as medieval priests customarily did, but his wide criticism of the high clergy of the Bulgarian Patriarchate shows he was of some rank. The historian Plamen Pavlov suggests that he was a senior churchman who wrote on the direct orders of the Bulgarian emperor. Where he worked is unknown: suggestions range from the capital Preslav and eastern Bulgaria to Ohrid and Macedonia, and even Veliko Tarnovo.

His dates are a difficult question. Most scholars place him in the middle or second half of the 10th century, though some have argued for the first half of the 11th or even the early 13th century. He calls the heresy newly appeared, mentions John, the new presbyter and exarch, whom most identify with the writer John Exarch, and says the heresy spread under Tsar Peter I, whose reign, according to Dimitri Obolensky, he treats as already over.

The Sermon Against the Heretics falls into two parts. The first describes the Bogomil heresy, names a priest called Bogomil as its founder while blaming the devil himself, and accuses its followers of degrading Bulgarian society; its roughly 70 quotations from the Apostle Paul suggest Cosmas knew of the sect's ties to Paulicianism. It is the earliest and fullest account of Bogomil dualism, and so of the Balkan forerunner of Catharism. The second part attacks abbots and bishops for greed, gluttony and neglect of their flocks, questions the influence of hermits, and hints that the state of the Church was partly to blame for the heresy.

The work survives in 25 full copies, all from East Slavic sources, the earliest of the 15th century, and in 116 excerpts or compilations, some of South Slavic origin. It was popular in medieval Russia and Serbia, where it was taken as a model for writings against other heresies. Cosmas is not known to have been canonised, but the copies often call him blessed or a saint. The village of Kozma Prezviter in Omurtag Municipality has borne his name since 1934, and Kozma Cove in Antarctica is named after him.
cossack-hetmanate: The official name of the state was the Zaporizhian Host. The term Hetmanate was coined in the late 19th century from hetman, the title of the host's general. The state emerged from the Cossack uprising of 1648 under Bohdan Khmelnytsky, whose causes included corruption in the royal administrations of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, social disenfranchisement, the growing activity of the Orthodox Church and the growth of the Cossack population despite government limits. The Treaty of Zboriv, signed on 18 August 1649 by Khmelnytsky and Adam Kysil, gave it legal recognition in the Commonwealth's eastern territories.

Khmelnytsky weighed several courses, among them an alliance with Orthodox and Protestant states, equal partnership within the Commonwealth, or a place in the Ottoman orbit. The unreliability of his alliance with the Crimean Khanate led him to seek a protector, and after long negotiations the Cossacks chose Tsar Alexis. A second Pereiaslav Council in 1659 restricted the Hetmanate's independence. The period from 1657 to 1687, known as the Ruin, was marked by constant civil wars. It ended with the election of Ivan Mazepa, who served as hetman from 1687 to 1708 and reunited the left bank under one ruler.

After Mazepa's failed attempt in 1708 to break the union with Russia, Cossack autonomy was severely restricted. His successor Pylyp Orlyk, elected in April 1710, ruled in exile and approved the Pacts and Constitutions of the Zaporozhian Host. In 1722 the Little Russian Collegium, six Russian officers, was set up as a parallel government, and Pavlo Polubotok, elected hetman in opposition, was arrested and died in prison. The collegium ruled until 1727, when Danylo Apostol was elected. The hetman Rozumovsky was called to the capital in January 1764 and forced to resign, and a decree of 21 October 1764 abolished the post.

Supreme power belonged to the General Cossack Council, with a Council of Officers (the starshyna) as an advisory body. By the end of the 17th century the hetman came to be chosen by the officers, and after the Battle of Poltava in 1709 the tsar had to confirm him.

The state was divided into regiments, which served as military and administrative districts. Society had five groups: nobles, Cossacks, clergy, townspeople and peasants. Peasants were never fully enserfed and kept the right to move, though their duties to landlords grew. Visitors remarked on high literacy: in the 1740s 866 of 1,099 settlements in seven regimental districts had primary schools. Under Mazepa the Kyiv collegium became an academy.
cossacks: The Cossacks are a predominantly East Slavic, Eastern Orthodox people who originated on the Pontic-Caspian steppe of eastern Ukraine and southern Russia. Their origins are disputed. The Tatars used a word meaning free men, qazaq, for independent horse-riding communities of the steppe. By the end of the 15th century the term was also applied to Slavic peasants who had fled to the devastated lands along the lower Dnieper and Don, where they founded self-governing, cavalry-based communities. In the 16th century there were major hosts on the Dnieper, Don, Volga and Ural rivers, and the Zaporozhian Cossacks west of the Dnieper.

The Zaporozhian Cossacks became known for raids on the Ottoman Empire and its vassals. Several uprisings against the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth in the early 17th century culminated in the Khmelnytsky Uprising of 1648, after the King refused to enlarge the Cossack Registry. It was one of the catastrophes known as the Deluge, which weakened the Commonwealth. The Treaty of Pereyaslav of 1654 brought most of the Cossack state under Russian rule. Cossacks took part in the rebellions of Stepan Razin and Yemelyan Pugachev, and after a late 18th-century uprising Russian forces destroyed the Zaporozhian Host. Their service in the Napoleonic wars made them folk heroes.

In return for military service under the nominal suzerainty of various states, Cossacks were allowed a great degree of self-government. They were organised into hosts, each responsible for a territory of affiliated villages called stanitsas. An ataman, later called hetman, commanded a band and was elected at a rada, as were other officials; his symbol of power was a ceremonial mace, the bulava. Zaporozhian Cossacks were mostly infantry using war wagons, and Don Cossacks mainly cavalry. Women ran families while men were away at war, and relations between the sexes were relatively egalitarian. Cossacks appeal to some as symbols of freedom and to others as symbols of repression.
costa-rica: Costa Rica lies between the Caribbean Sea and the Pacific Ocean, with Nicaragua to the north and Panama to the south, and shares a maritime border with Ecuador to the south of Cocos Island. Its land area is nearly 51,180 square kilometres. The highest point is Cerro Chirripó at 3,819 metres, the highest volcano is Irazú at 3,431 metres, and Lake Arenal is the largest lake. Of the 14 known volcanoes, six have been active in the last 75 years. The climate is tropical, with a dry season from December to April and a rainy season from May to November.

Historians place the Indigenous peoples of Costa Rica in the Intermediate Area, where the peripheries of the Mesoamerican and Andean cultures overlapped. The oldest evidence of human occupation is stone tools, linked to hunter-gatherers who arrived about 10,000 to 7,000 years BCE in the Turrialba Valley. In some accounts the name la costa rica, the rich coast, was first applied by Christopher Columbus, who sailed along the eastern shore in 1502 and reported much gold jewellery worn by the natives. It may instead come from Gil González Dávila, who landed on the west coast in 1522 and obtained gold, sometimes by violent theft.

Like the rest of Central America, Costa Rica never fought for independence from Spain. On 15 September 1821 the authorities in Guatemala declared the independence of all Central America, and the date remains Independence Day. Coffee was first planted in 1808 and by the 1820s had passed tobacco, sugar and cacao as the main export, creating a wealthy class of growers, the Coffee Barons. General Federico Tinoco Granados ruled as a military dictator from 1917 to 1919. In 1948 José Figueres Ferrer led an armed uprising after a disputed presidential election between Rafael Ángel Calderón Guardia and Otilio Ulate Blanco. The 44-day civil war left more than 2,000 dead and was the bloodiest event in Costa Rica in the 20th century.

San José is the capital and largest city, with around 350,000 residents and two million in its metropolitan area, and the country has about five million inhabitants. It is a presidential republic under the constitution of 1949, divided into seven provinces and 82 cantons. The army was abolished on 1 December 1948, and the constitution of 1949 made the abolition permanent. Education has been free and compulsory since 1886. Spanish is the main language, and at least five Indigenous languages are still spoken, among them Bribri, Maléku and Cabécar. Catholicism is the state religion, and the constitution guarantees freedom of religion.
cotabato-city: Cotabato City lies at the mouth of the Rio Grande de Mindanao and the Pulangi River, facing Illana Bay, part of the Moro Gulf, on the island of Mindanao. It covers about 176 square kilometres and is basically a delta formed by the Tamontaka River and the Rio Grande de Mindanao. About 70 per cent of its land area is below sea level, and the only elevated areas are PC Hill and Timako Hill. The climate is tropical rainforest, hot, humid and wet through the year. Before Hindu and Muslim traders arrived, the area was swamp and rainforest, home to numerous ethno-linguistic groups.

Later, Hindu traders arrived and the people of the area embraced Hinduism. By 1515, after a Muslim establishment in Sulu, Muslim merchants came to Maguindanao and converted many people to Islam. The Sultanate of Maguindanao was formally established that year, with Tubok as its first capital, and the sultan's seat moved around Tamontaka in 1711. After Spain defeated the Sulu Sultanate and forced it to sign a peace treaty in 1851, it turned to Maguindanao. Datu Amirul, father of Sultan Muhammad Makakua, consented to a Spanish military base at the stone fortress of Kota Wato in what is now Barangay Tamontaka.

The Spanish raised their flag there on 30 April 1861 and renamed the place Cotabato. They agreed that the local Maguindanaons became subjects of the Spanish Crown while their Islamic beliefs would be respected.

Cotabato was the capital of the original Province of Cotabato from 1920 until 1967. In 1942 Japanese forces entered the area, and Maguindanao was liberated in 1945. The city was chartered on 20 June 1959 under Republic Act No. 2364, and now has 37 barangays. It long resisted inclusion in the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao, though it was the region's government centre. Its voters ratified the Bangsamoro Organic Law on 21 January 2019, and it was formally turned over to the Bangsamoro regional government on 15 December 2020.

Cotabato City is an independent component city, not subject to the provincial government of Maguindanao del Norte, where it lies geographically, and serves as the regional centre of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region. About half of its people are Maguindanaon, with sizeable Cebuano, Tagalog and Iranun populations, and Tagalog is the main lingua franca. Most residents are Sunni Muslims. The city is the seat of the Archdiocese of Cotabato and has the Sultan Haji Hassanal Bolkiah Masjid, the largest mosque in the Philippines, and the Church of the Immaculate Conception at Tamontaka, built by the Jesuits in 1872.
cotentin-peninsula: The peninsula lies wholly within the department of Manche. To its west lie the Gulf of Saint-Malo and the Channel Islands, and to the southwest the peninsula of Brittany. It is part of the Armorican Massif, apart from the Plain, which lies in the Paris Basin, and it falls into three areas: the headland of Cap de la Hague, the Cotentin Pass and the valley of the Saire River.

The oldest stone in France is found in outcrops on the coast of Cap de la Hague. Some historical documents call the northern part an island, because a broad marshy area that flooded separated it from the mainland, and only a small strip of land in the heath of Lessay joined them. Gates at river outlets on the west coast and in the Baie des Veys later made it a true peninsula.

In Roman times the peninsula belonged to Armorica. The town now called Coutances, capital of the Gaulish Unelli, took the name Constantia in 298 under Constantius Chlorus. The base of the peninsula, the pagus Constantinus, joined the pagus Coriovallensis around Cherbourg and became known as the Cotentin. Under the Carolingians it was administered by viscounts of the Saint-Sauveur family.

After Frankish power collapsed, Norse settlers from the Irish Sea region, of Norwegian origin, settled the peninsula heavily. Place names such as La Hague, La Hougue and those ending in -tot and -bec derive from Old Norse, and the pagi of Haga, Sarnes and Helganes bore Norse names as late as 1027.

In 933 the peninsula passed from Brittany to the Duchy of Normandy, and there was at first much hostility between the new Danish overlords and the Norwegian settlers, including a pagan rebellion against Longsword's rule. In 1088 Robert Curthose, Duke of Normandy, gave the Cotentin to his brother Henry, who later became king of England and made it his first power base.

During the Hundred Years War Edward III of England landed in the bay of La Hougue and knighted his son Edward, the Black Prince, at Quettehou. The naval Battle of La Hogue was fought in 1692. In the World War II the westernmost of the D-Day landings came at Utah Beach, followed by a campaign to take Cherbourg.

The peninsula has about 250,000 inhabitants. Its largest town, Cherbourg-en-Cotentin, is a cross-channel port and shipbuilding centre. Agriculture is the main economic resource, and the La Hague plant reprocesses nuclear fuel. The local Norman dialect, Cotentinais, survives, and the painter Jean-François Millet was born on the peninsula.
coto-war: The border between Panama and Costa Rica had never been well defined since colonial times, when the limits of the province of Veragua were left vague. Treaties of 1856, 1865 and 1873 were never ratified by both governments. Under an 1886 convention the President of France, Émile Loubet, arbitrated, but Costa Rica rejected his award of 11 September 1900 as favouring Colombia.

After Panama separated from Colombia, a new arbitration conducted in the United States produced the White award of 12 September 1914, which favoured Costa Rica and which Panama would not accept. The status quo held until February 1921, when a Costa Rican force under Colonel Héctor Zúñiga Mora occupied Pueblo Nuevo de Coto, then in the Alanje district of the Panamanian province of Chiriquí.

Panama had dissolved its army in 1904 and had to hand over its long-range weapons in 1915, but President Belisario Porras had kept 50 rifles secretly and ordered a mobilisation. Police from Panama City under General Manuel Quintero Villarreal sailed to Rabo de Puerco, and with police from David and volunteers from Bugaba they reached Coto on 27 February under Second Lieutenant Justiniano Mejías, capturing Zúñiga Mora without a fight.

The same afternoon they ambushed the motorboat La Sultana bringing Costa Rican reinforcements, killing five and taking 54 prisoners; on 1 March the ship La Estrella met a similar fate. On the Atlantic side, in Bocas del Toro, Costa Rican forces advanced without meeting resistance.

The United States demanded that both countries stop fighting and withdraw their forces, and both governments ordered their troops off the positions they held. The Panamanian soldiers were welcomed as heroes in David and Panama City, but under pressure from the United States, which acted in defence of its banana companies' interests, Panama had to accept the White award and give up the Coto region to Costa Rica. The Arias-Calderón treaty of 1941 settled the border.
cotonou: The name Cotonou means by the river of death in the Fon language. At the beginning of the 19th century, when it was spelled Kutonou, it was a small fishing village, and it is thought to have been formally founded by King Ghezo of Dahomey in 1830. It grew as a centre of the slave trade and later of palm oil and cotton. In 1851 the French Second Republic made a treaty with Ghezo that allowed it to establish a trading post there.

During the reign of King Glele (1858–89) the territory was ceded to the Second French Empire by a treaty signed in 1878, and in 1883 the French Navy occupied the town to prevent a British conquest. After Glele's death in 1889 King Béhanzin tried unsuccessfully to challenge the treaty. The town grew rapidly after the harbour was built in 1908, and its population was still only 70,000 in 1960.

Cotonou lies on the coastal strip between Lake Nokoué and the Atlantic Ocean. A canal, the lagoon of Cotonou, dug by the French in 1855, cuts the city in two, and the Ouémé River flows into the Atlantic at Cotonou. Coastal erosion worsened from 1961 after the building of the Nangbeto Dam and the deep-water port; a United Nations Environment Program pilot project found that in 40 years the coast east of Cotonou had retreated by 400 metres.

Cotonou is the seat of government and the largest city of Benin, though the official capital, where the national legislature sits, is the smaller city of Porto-Novo. The city proper had 679,012 inhabitants in 2012. French is the official language of Benin, and Fon, Aja and Yoruba are also spoken in the city. The Autonomous Port of Cotonou is one of the largest in West Africa, and a railway links the city with Parakou in the north.
cotswolds: The Cotswolds rise from the meadows of the upper River Thames to an escarpment above the Severn Valley and the Vale of Evesham. Jurassic limestone forms the bedrock, creating a grassland habitat and a golden stone that is quarried for building. The region lies across several English counties, mainly Gloucestershire and Oxfordshire, with parts of Wiltshire, Somerset, Worcestershire and Warwickshire. The highest point is Cleeve Hill at 330 m, just east of Cheltenham; the northern and western edge, known as the Cotswold Edge, is a steep escarpment, while the dip slope falls to the southeast. The stone is rich in fossils, particularly of sea urchins, and varies from honey-coloured in the north to golden in the centre and south.

There is evidence of Neolithic settlement from burial chambers on the Cotswold Edge, and there are remains of Bronze and Iron Age forts. The Romans built villas such as the one at Chedworth, founded settlements including Gloucester, and paved the Celtic path later known as the Fosse Way. In the Middle Ages the breed of sheep known as the Cotswold Lion made the region prosperous through the wool trade with the continent. The most successful era was 1250 to 1350, when much of the wool was sold to Italian merchants, and much of the money went into building churches. Numerous large stone wool churches survive.

The place name is popularly believed to mean a sheep enclosure in rolling hillsides, but the English Place-Name Society derives it from the 12th-century form Codesuualt, meaning Cod's high open land, with Cod taken as an Old English personal name. Chipping Campden is noted as the home of the Arts and Crafts movement, founded by William Morris at the end of the 19th and beginning of the 20th century, and for the annual Cotswold Olimpick Games, a celebration of sports dating to the early 17th century.

A large part of the Cotswolds has been designated a National Landscape, legally still an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, since 1966. It covers 787 square miles and stretches south-west from just south of Stratford-upon-Avon to just south of Bath. Roughly 80 per cent of the region's nearly 800 square miles is farmland, and it has 4,000 miles of historic stone walls. Its stone-built towns and villages include Chipping Campden, Stow-on-the-Wold, Bourton-on-the-Water and Broadway, and the 93-mile Cotswold Way runs from Bath to Chipping Campden.
cottbus: Cottbus, in Lower Sorbian Chóśebuz, lies on the River Spree in Lower Lusatia, about 125 km upstream of Berlin. The name comes from the Lower Sorbian personal name Chóśebuz, said to mean cheerful watchman or vigilant hero, so that the place is the settlement of Chóśebud. It was first documented in 1156 as Chotibus, and the spelling Kottbus first appears in 1391.

The settlement was established in the tenth century, when Sorbs built a castle on a sandy island in the Spree. The March of Lusatia captured it in 965, and in 1002 it passed to Poland under Bolesław I the Brave. In the German-Polish war of 1015 to 1018 it was an important Polish stronghold, and in 1032 it passed again to the March of Lusatia. In 1514 Jan Rak founded the Universitas Serborum, a Sorbian gymnasium, in the city. In 1635 Bohemia ceded Lower Lusatia to Saxony, which made Cottbus an enclave of Saxony, and from the 1690s French, Walloons and Palatines settled there.

After the Second World War Cottbus lay in the Soviet Occupation Zone and then in the German Democratic Republic, and in 1952 it became capital of the new district of Cottbus. On 17 June 1953 its people joined the uprising against living-standard restrictions and made political demands, and Soviet tanks and workers' militias suppressed it. The city grew with lignite mining and reached its historic peak of 128,943 inhabitants in 1989. After German reunification in October 1990 privatisation brought a deep structural change.

Cottbus is the second-largest city of Brandenburg, after Potsdam, and the political and cultural centre of the Lower Sorbian-speaking Sorbs, or Wends. Signs are mostly in German and Lower Sorbian, and the Wendish Museum is there. The Brandenburg University of Technology has its seat in the city, and the State Theatre, built in Art Nouveau style by Bernhard Sehring and opened in 1908, is the only state theatre in Brandenburg. Branitz Park, laid out from 1845 by Hermann von Pückler-Muskau, is a landscape park of international significance with two grass pyramids.
cottian-alps: The Cottian Alps (French: Alpes Cottiennes; Italian: Alpi Cozie) lie in the south-western part of the Alps and form the border between France (Hautes-Alpes and Savoie) and Italy (Piedmont). The range is drained by the Durance and Arc and their tributaries on the French side, and by the Dora Riparia and other tributaries of the Po on the Italian side. Its limits include the Maddalena Pass to the south, the Col du Galibier to the west and the Mont Cenis Pass to the north. The Fréjus Road Tunnel and Fréjus Rail Tunnel between Modane and Susa are important links between France and Italy.

The name comes from Marcus Julius Cottius, a king of the tribes of this region in the 1st century BCE. His father Donnus had opposed Julius Caesar and later made peace with him. Cottius was succeeded by his son Gaius Julius Donnus II (reigned 3 BCE to 4 CE) and his grandson Marcus Julius Cottius II (reigned 5 to 63 CE), whom the emperor Claudius granted the title of king. On his death Nero annexed the kingdom as the province of Alpes Cottiae.

For much of the Middle Ages the range was divided between the Duchy of Savoy, which held the north and the easternmost slopes, and the Dauphiné, then independent of France, which held the south-western slopes and the upper parts of some Po valleys. The Dauphiné's Alpine territory, the Escartons, had limited autonomy and elected its own parliament. That status lasted after the Dauphiné was annexed to France in 1349 and was abolished in 1713, when the Treaty of Utrecht gave the House of Savoy the mountainous area on the eastern side.

After the Treaty of Turin of March 1860 the north-western slopes became French. Two eastern valleys, the Pellice and the Germanasca, were for centuries a sanctuary for the Waldensians, a Christian movement persecuted as heretical by the Catholic Church from the 12th century.

The range is divided between the Italian province of Cuneo and the Metropolitan City of Turin on the eastern slopes, and the French departments of Savoie, Hautes-Alpes and Alpes-de-Haute-Provence on the western slopes.
cotton: Cotton was domesticated independently in the Old and New Worlds. In the Americas the indigenous species Gossypium barbadense has been identified at a site in the Nanchoc District of Peru and dated to the 7th to 6th millennia BCE, and cultivation at Ancon in Peru has been dated to about 4200 BCE. It was the backbone of the coastal cultures of Norte Chico, Moche and Nazca, whose people grew it upriver, made it into nets and traded them to fishing villages for fish. In South Asia a cotton thread dated to the sixth millennium BCE was found at Mehrgarh in Pakistan. The Spanish who reached Mexico and Peru found people growing cotton and wearing clothes made of it.

Cotton is a soft staple fibre that grows in a protective boll around the seeds of plants of the genus Gossypium, in the mallow family. The fibre is almost pure cellulose. Four species are grown commercially, all domesticated in antiquity: upland cotton, native to Central America, Mexico and the Caribbean, which supplies about 90 per cent of production; extra-long staple cotton from tropical South America; tree cotton, native to India and Pakistan; and Levant cotton, native to southern Africa and the Arabian Peninsula. The English word derives ultimately from a Hebrew word for a garment of linen, which was the usual word for cotton in medieval Arabic.

Hand-held roller gins had been used in India since the 6th century, and dual-roller gins appeared in India and China between the 12th and 14th centuries. The earliest clear pictures of the spinning wheel come from the Islamic world in the 11th century. Under the Mughal Empire cotton production increased, helped by agrarian reforms that favoured cash crops.

The English East India Company introduced cheap calico and chintz in the 1660s, and the cloth overtook its spice trade by value in the late 17th century. Weavers objected, and Parliament passed the Calico Act of 1700 and a stricter act in 1721. The exemption of raw cotton led to a native industry and to mechanised spinning and weaving, with imports rising to seven thousand bales a year by the early 1770s. In the United States, before 1865 cotton was largely produced by enslaved African Americans and enriched both southern landowners and the textile industries of the north and of Britain.
cotton-gin: Cotton fibres grow in the seed pods, or bolls, of the cotton plant, tightly interwoven with the seeds, and before the gin the two had to be separated by hand, which took hours of labour. The earliest evidence of a gin is a single-roller gin shown in Buddhist paintings of the 5th century in the Ajanta Caves in western India. These early gins had a roller of iron or wood and a flat piece of stone or wood, resembling a mealing stone, and needed a great deal of skill.

Their early history is ambiguous because archaeologists probably mistook gin parts for other tools. The two-roller gin appeared in India and China between the 12th and 14th centuries, and by the 16th century the Indian version was common in the Mediterranean cotton trade. The worm-gear roller gin and the crank handle, both developed in India under the Delhi Sultanate or the early Mughal Empire, greatly expanded textile production, and the worm-gear gin is still used in the Indian subcontinent.

The Indian roller gin reached the southern United States in the mid-18th century but suited only long-staple cotton, not the short-staple cotton common in Georgia. Eli Whitney applied for a patent on his gin on 28 October 1793, and it was granted on 14 March 1794. It used a wooden cylinder covered with rows of slender wires that caught the fibres and pulled them through a comb-like grid too narrow for the seeds, while a second cylinder with brushes wiped the cleaned fibres off to keep it from jamming.

His model cleaned 50 pounds of lint a day. Other inventors, among them Hodgen Holmes, also patented improvements, and after years of litigation the courts declared Whitney the inventor. Fones McCarthy's roller gin of 1840 later suited extra-long staple cotton, and the Munger system of 1879 joined the ginning machinery into one flow.

The gin made cotton farming far more profitable. Production in the United States grew from 750,000 bales in 1830 to 2.85 million in 1850, and ports such as New Orleans, Mobile, Charleston and Galveston prospered on the trade. Whitney had hoped to reduce the labour needed, but picking by hand was now the bottleneck, and cotton harvesting machines did not appear until the 1930s. Planters bought more enslaved workers, whose number rose from about 700,000 in 1790 to about 3.2 million in 1850. For this reason the gin is frequently cited as one of the indirect causes of the American Civil War.
cotubanama-national-park: The park lies on the lower south-eastern coast of the Dominican Republic, in the provinces of La Altagracia and La Romana, joining the coast around La Romana-Bayahibe and Boca de Yuma. It includes Saona Island, across the Catuano Strait, and the small Isla Catalinita. Much of the ground is limestone and coral, through which underground currents connect with the sea, and the coast is lined with mangroves, beaches and cliffs.

A study made before the park was declared found over 539 plant species, more than 50 of them endemic, among them mahogany, sea grape and guayiga. Its animals include the rhinoceros iguana, the hutia and the solenodon, more than 300 species of birds such as the Hispaniolan parrot, and on the coast coral reefs, manatees and dolphins.

Before 1492 the island was divided into five Taíno chiefdoms, and the park lies in that of Higüey, ruled at the time of the Spanish conquest by the cacique Cotubanamá. After the Spanish conquistador Juan de Esquivel had the caciques of Saona Island killed, Cotubanamá led a rebellion. A truce failed after Spanish soldiers under Martin de Villaman committed atrocities against the Taíno, and a war of eight to nine months followed. Cotubanamá fled to Saona, was captured by a soldier, Juan López, and was hanged in Santo Domingo on the orders of Governor Nicolás de Ovando in 1504.
The park was declared by Decree No. 1311 in 1975, and in 2014 the National Congress gave it the name of the cacique in place of Parque Nacional del Este.

The park protects more than 20 ceremonial plazas, over eight indigenous cemeteries and hundreds of caves and sinkholes. Caves such as Jose Maria, Ramoncito and Berna hold thousands of Taíno pictographs and petroglyphs, while the freshwater pools of the Padre Nuestro complex and the spring of Manantial de la Aleta, where many intact ceramics have been found, supplied drinking water. The park also includes a buffer zone of 12,000 hectares around its boundaries, and by 2021 it had been admitted to the Specially Protected Areas and Wildlife protocol of the Cartagena Convention.
cotys-i-odrysian: Cotys was born during the reign of Seuthes I. An Athenian inscription of 330 BCE honours Reboulas, brother of Cotys and son of a King Seuthes, and scholars who once took his father to be Seuthes II now hold it was Seuthes I, since Seuthes II was only seven when Seuthes I abdicated in 411 BCE. His standing before he became king is obscure, but he is tentatively identified as a brother of Hebryzelmis, the Odrysian king honoured by Athens in 386/385 BCE. Around 390 BCE the Athenian general Iphicrates, in Thrace to make peace between Amadocus I and Seuthes II, married a daughter of Cotys in opulent circumstances.

Cotys may have ruled at first in the interior. With the help of Iphicrates he established himself as the heir of Hebryzelmis and removed rivals, possibly including Amadocus II and Saratocus. Inscribed objects found to the north and west, among them pieces of the Rogozen Treasure that bear his name, suggest an expansion the written sources do not record. His push towards the Aegean and the Chersonese alarmed Athens, and in the early 370s BCE cities joined the Second Athenian Confederacy partly as a safeguard against him.

In 365 BCE he welcomed back Iphicrates, now dismissed by Athens, and the mercenary commander Charidemus, who married another daughter. His general Miltokythes starved Sestos into surrender in 363 or 362 BCE, then rebelled, seizing the royal treasury at Hieron Oros. Athens backed Miltokythes, but Cotys, aided by Iphicrates and Charidemus, defeated its fleet and forced him out in spring 361 BCE; according to Demosthenes, they bribed the Athenian commanders. By 360 BCE Cotys held almost all of the Chersonese.

In September 360 BCE Python and Heraclides of Aenus, two students of Plato thought close to the king, killed Cotys at a feast in his palace, claiming he had wronged their father. Athens made them honorary citizens and gave them gold wreaths. Some authors put his death in 359 BCE, but the arrival of the Athenian commander Cephisodotus in 360 BCE makes the earlier date certain.

Cotys was the last ruler of a relatively unified Thrace for centuries. His son Cersobleptes had to share the kingdom with Amadocus II and Berisades. Because Cotys turned from ally of Athens to dangerous foe, the sources, above all Demosthenes, depict him as drunken, cruel and perfidious, while Plutarch tells of him breaking a gift of fine pottery so that his temper would not lead him to punish servants who broke it.
coudenberg-palace: The first castle on the Coudenberg, Dutch for Cold Hill, is generally dated to the middle of the 11th century, when the counts of Leuven and Brussels left the valley of the Senne for the heights, where floods were less likely, near the road to Leuven and the Sonian Forest. Its existence is well attested in the 12th century. After the Holy Roman Emperor Frederick Barbarossa created the Duchy of Brabant in 1183, the castle was enclosed by the city's first great wall, and early in the 13th century the court settled there.

Once a second city wall was built after the occupation of 1356 by Louis II, Count of Flanders, the castle was gradually turned into a residential palace. Philip the Good added new wings and the Aula Magna, a great hall where the States General of the Burgundian Netherlands held their first regular meetings in 1465 and where Duchess Margaret of Austria gave up her regency to Charles of Habsburg in 1515. Charles V added Renaissance galleries and rooms, a late Gothic chapel in memory of his parents and a market square in front of the palace.

In the 17th century the Archdukes Albert VII and Isabella, sovereigns of the Spanish Netherlands, held their court there, restored the façade, refitted the apartments and gardens and brought artists such as Jan Brueghel the Elder and Peter Paul Rubens to decorate it. To protect the Archduchess on her way to her devotions, the street beside the Aula Magna and the chapel was extended almost to the Church of St. Michael and St. Gudula and renamed the Rue Isabelle.

The fire of 3 February 1731 broke out in the kitchens; frost made water hard to bring, and by morning the palace, many works of art and the government archives were lost. The court moved to the Palace of Orange-Nassau, and the ruins, the Cour brûlée, stood for more than forty years until Prince Charles Alexander of Lorraine proposed a royal square in 1774, approved by Empress Maria Theresa. The Place Royale was built over them between 1775 and 1782.

The main buildings stood roughly where the BELvue Museum and the Rue Royale are now, and the whole area was levelled in the 18th century. Excavations have uncovered the cellars of the main palace, the rooms beneath the banqueting hall of the Aula Magna and the warehouse under the chapel, which can be visited through the museum.
council-of-aragon: The council arose from the composite nature of the Spanish monarchy, in which kingdoms shared a king but kept their own laws, customs and government. Ferdinand II, with his wife Isabella the first ruler of both Castile and Aragon, became king of Castile in 1474 and of Aragon in 1479, and spent most of his time at the Castilian court in Valladolid. To govern lands their king seldom saw, the system of viceroys and councils grew up, and in 1494 the council was formed out of the former royal council of the kings of Aragon.

Its official name was the Royal and Supreme Council of Aragon. It consisted of a Treasurer-General, a Vice-Chancellor and five Regentes; all but the Treasurer-General were native-born Aragonese, many of them drawn from the letrados, the class of lawyers on whom Ferdinand and Isabella relied. It administered the Kingdom of Aragon, the Principality of Catalonia, with Roussillon until 1659, and the kingdoms of Valencia, Majorca and Sardinia.

While the viceroy remained the supreme authority in each territory, the council supervised the viceroys and linked them with the king. It received their reports, advised the king on policy and sent out his orders. The Aragonese possessions in southern Italy, Naples and Sicily, passed in 1556 to the Council of Italy, together with the Duchy of Milan.

The council served as the model for those created as the Spanish monarchy grew in the 16th century: councils for Italy, Portugal and Flanders, and others for general affairs such as the Council of the Inquisition, the Council of War and the Council of State. Gaspar de Guzmán, Count-Duke of Olivares, explained to Philip IV that a council for each kingdom made the king present in each. The system bound the territories only through their common king, however, and did nothing to create a common government or economic ties between them.
council-of-brabant: Presided over by the chancellor of Brabant, the council had among its duties the task of judging whether new legislation conflicted with the rights and liberties set down in the Joyous Entry. This duty brought it into conflict with Emperor Joseph II, whose reforming measures it resisted as contrary to the duchy's established liberties.

On 1 January 1787 Joseph II decreed the abolition of the council and ordered that it be replaced by a number of newly created tribunals. On 20 April the council declared the decree void as contrary to the liberties of the duchy and told its members to ignore it. At the end of May 1787 the government in Brussels postponed its judicial innovations, and in September it withdrew the decree.

The conflict returned two years later. On 18 June 1789 the emperor's representative in Brussels, Ferdinand von Trauttmansdorff, declared that the powers of the Council of Brabant would from then on be exercised by the Great Council of Mechelen. This coup by the government was one of the direct causes of the Brabant Revolution. The council was finally abolished during the French occupation, which lasted from 1794 to 1814.

In the late 18th century the architect Gilles-Barnabé Guimard designed a palace in Brussels for the Council of Brabant, and the Belgian Federal Parliament now sits in that building. Among the council's members over the centuries were Willem Van der Tanerijen, who died in 1499, Cornelius Wytfliet, Petrus Peckius the Younger, Ferdinand van Boisschot and Guillaume Wittouck.
council-of-castile: John I of Castile created the first Royal Council in 1385, after the disaster at the Battle of Aljubarrota. It had 12 members, four each from the clergy, the cities and the nobility. In 1442 the nobility increased its influence by adding many nobles as titular members, and the number rose to sixty. The council proved ineffective, and in 1480 the Catholic Monarchs, Ferdinand II of Aragon and Isabella I, passed the Act of Resumption at the Cortes of Toledo, which let them appoint its officials directly instead of leaving power with the nobles.

The reformed council had a president, a treasurer, a prelate, three caballeros, often of the minor nobility, and between eight and ten letrados, lawyers or jurists. Nobles who had not been appointed could attend but had no vote, so the council and its bureaucracy were made up chiefly of new men: minor nobles, townsmen and civilian magistrates. It advised the Crown on military and civil appointments and on pensions and favours, supervised expeditions and colonisations until the Council of the Indies was created, and served as the supreme court of the Crown of Castile. When there was no fit monarch, it ruled as a regency council.

After Isabella's death in 1504 the council again grew corrupt and fell under noble influence, ignoring nobles who seized royal and peasant land by force. When the Revolt of the Comuneros broke out in 1520, much of the rebels' anger was aimed at the council and its president, Antonio de Rojas Manrique. Once the revolt was defeated, Charles I replaced Rojas with Juan Pardo de Tavera, Archbishop of Santiago, brought in gentry and educated lawyers, and passed most civil cases to the audiencias so that the council could concentrate on administration.

In this period it became known as the Council of Castile. A Council of Finance and the Council of the Indies were split from it, and in 1555 the Council of Italy. It came to prominence again during the minority of Charles II, when Mariana of Austria was regent, and under Charles III and Charles IV. The Cortes of Cádiz abolished it in 1812; Ferdinand VII restored it in 1814, and Isabella II dissolved it in 1834.
council-of-chalcedon: The First Council of Nicaea in 325 determined that Jesus Christ was God, consubstantial with the Father, and rejected the Arian view that he was a created being; later councils at Constantinople in 381 and Ephesus in 431 reaffirmed this. About two years after the death of Cyril of Alexandria in 444, an aged monk of Constantinople named Eutyches began teaching a variation on the traditional Christology, to stop what he saw as a new outbreak of Nestorianism. Many believed he was denying that Jesus was fully human, though Pope Leo I thought his error came from a lack of skill rather than malice.

In 449 Emperor Theodosius II called a council at Ephesus, with Dioscorus of Alexandria presiding. Leo sent legates with a letter, known as Leo's Tome, which confessed that Christ had two natures, and later called that council the Latrocinium, the Robber Council. After Theodosius died and Marcian became emperor, Marcian announced a new council to set aside the council of 449.

Leo had pressed for the council to meet in Italy, but Marcian called it at Chalcedon, closer to Constantinople, so that he could respond quickly to events on the Danube, which was being raided by the Huns under Attila. It sat from 8 October to 1 November 451 and was attended by over 520 bishops or their representatives, the largest and best-documented of the first seven ecumenical councils. It also approved the Creed of Nicaea, the Creed of Constantinople, two letters of Cyril against Nestorius and the Tome of Leo, and dealt with church discipline and jurisdiction.

The Chalcedonian Definition repudiated the notion of a single nature in Christ and declared two natures in one person, 'without confusion, without change, without division, without separation'. A canon later numbered 28 declared that the See of Constantinople, as New Rome, had equal privileges with Rome, because of the importance of the city in the empire. The seventh session gave the bishop of Jerusalem authority over the three Palestines.

The near-immediate result was a major schism. Bishops uneasy with the language of Leo's Tome held that accepting two natures amounted to Nestorianism, and the sees of Alexandria and Antioch were the most significant to reject the council. The Oriental Orthodox churches still reject it and hold that their teaching, which they call Miaphysite, has been misunderstood as monophysitism. The Eastern Orthodox and Catholic Churches treat its definitions as normative.
council-of-charroux: The council met on 1 June 989 at Charroux Abbey, south-east of Poitiers, which kept relics of the True Cross. It sat under the patronage of William IV, Duke of Aquitaine and Count of Poitiers, and the authority of Archbishop Gunbald of Bordeaux, with the bishops Gislebert of Poitiers, Frotaire of Périgueux, Abbon of Saintes, Hugues I of Angoulême and Hildegaire of Limoges present. Its aim was to end the private wars between lords, or at least to limit them, since the weakened duke, despite his nickname Fier-à-Bras, could not prevent them alone. The bishops, who held their sees from the duke, are said to have feared a destabilisation of their own position and of the social order.

The council reaffirmed the immunity of churches: anyone who violated a church or took something from it by force was anathema unless he made reparation. Anyone who attacked, captured or struck a priest, deacon or other cleric who bore no arms committed sacrilege, unless the cleric had been judged by his own bishop for an offence. What was new was that protection reached beyond the clergy to civilians and their property. Anyone who seized the sheep, oxen, donkeys, cows, goats or pigs of farmers and other poor people was anathema, unless the poor person was at fault and had not made amends.

The council did not bring peace, but it told the feudal lords that they no longer had the sole right to begin and wage war, and it set out for the first time rules and limits for war. It showed that the authority of the Church could make up for royal or princely authority where that was lacking. A second council met at Charroux in 1028, called by William VI, Duke of Aquitaine, to consider how to fight Manichaeism, but its acts do not survive.
council-of-clermont: The Byzantine emperor Alexius I Comnenus had sent envoys to the Council of Piacenza asking for military assistance against the Seljuk Turks, and Pope Urban II reacted to that request. The council that followed was a mixed synod of clergy and laymen held from 17 to 27 November 1095 at Clermont in Auvergne, then part of the Duchy of Aquitaine. About 300 French clerics attended. No official list of the participants or of the signatories to its decrees survives.

The council was above all a synod for implementing the Cluniac reforms, enacting decrees and settling local and regional issues. It extended the excommunication of Philip I of France for his adulterous remarriage to Bertrade of Montfort and renewed the Truce of God, an attempt by the church to reduce feuding among Frankish nobles.

Urban's speech on 27 November is known from several accounts that vary widely. Fulcher of Chartres, who was present and wrote from memory around 1100 to 1105, is generally considered the most reliable. In his version Urban first urges the clergy to vigilance and calls for the restoration of order in the Frankish provinces. He then asks the Franks, once peace is re-established, to aid the Christians of the East, whom the Turks had attacked and from whom they had taken Byzantine Anatolia as far west as the Mediterranean. He ends with the words 'Christ commands it' and promises immediate absolution to all who die on the way or in battle against Muslims.

Robert the Monk, writing in 1107, gives a more vivid sermon and has the audience burst out with the cry Deus vult. His Urban stresses the reconquest of the Holy Land more than aid to the Greeks, a theme many historians consider an insertion shaped by the success of the First Crusade.

In a letter of December 1095 to the faithful in Flanders, Urban called on the princes to free the churches of the East, named Adhemar of Le Puy as leader of the expedition and set the departure for the feast of the Assumption, 15 August 1096. The anonymous Gesta Francorum records that news of the call spread quickly through Gaul and that the Franks had crosses sewn on their right shoulders. The call led to the First Crusade, the capture of Jerusalem and the founding of the Kingdom of Jerusalem.
council-of-constance: The council's main purpose was to end the schism that followed the Avignon Papacy. After Pope Gregory XI returned to Rome in 1377 and died in 1378, the controversial election of Urban VI led a number of cardinals to defect and elect a rival pope at Avignon. The Council of Pisa then deposed both claimants and elected a third, so that there were three claimants: Gregory XII at Rome, Benedict XIII at Avignon and John XXIII. Many voices, including that of Sigismund, King of the Romans and of Hungary, pressed for another council. John XXIII called it, and it sat in Constance from 16 November 1414 to 22 April 1418.

Sigismund arrived on Christmas Eve 1414 and influenced the council continuously as protector of the church. Instead of voting as individuals, the members voted in national blocs, a practice carried in February 1415. On 2 March 1415 John XXIII promised to resign, but on 20 March he fled secretly to Schaffhausen. On 6 April 1415 the fifth session issued the decree Haec sancta, which declared that a general council has its power directly from Christ and that everyone, even a pope, must obey it in matters of faith.

On 4 July 1415 Gregory XII's proxies convoked the council in his name and then announced his resignation. The council delayed choosing a new pope, fearing that he would restrict discussion of reform. Two years passed before the antipopes were deposed and Martin V was elected in November 1417. Constance was the last papal election held outside the Italian peninsula.

The council also dealt with reform. It condemned John Wycliffe on 4 May 1415. Jan Hus, summoned under a letter of safe conduct, was found guilty of heresy and handed to the secular court, which sentenced him to be burned. His supporter Jerome of Prague suffered the same fate. The council also heard the dispute between the Kingdom of Poland, the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and the Teutonic Knights.

The status of Haec sancta and of Frequens, which ordered councils every ten years, remained disputed. Frequens was never put into practice. Parts of the church, notably in France, upheld Haec sancta, and the Gallican Articles of 1682 reaffirmed it. The Catholic Church today generally regards it as invalid.
council-of-elvira: The bishops, presbyters, deacons and laymen who met at Eliberri, mostly from Hispania Baetica and Carthago Nova, gathered probably at the urging of Hosius of Córdoba, under the presidency of Felix of Accitum, now Guadix, perhaps as the oldest bishop present, to restore order and discipline in the church. Apart from Hosius almost nothing is known of them, and the scholar Victor De Clercq notes that neither the date nor the reason for the meeting is known with certainty. With the Synod of Arles of 314 and the Synod of Ancyra, it is one of three councils that first approached the character of general councils and prepared the way for the first ecumenical council.

The canons concern conduct and discipline, not doctrine, and their penalties ranged from long delays to baptism to exclusion from the Eucharist for years or for life. Christians were barred from marrying pagans or Jews, from sharing meals with Jews, from serving as flamen or duumvir and from pagan festivals. Canon 1 refused communion to lapsed Christians even at death, and canon 33, held to be the oldest canon of clerical celibacy, bound the clergy to continence. Canon 36 declared that images should not be in churches, the church's first official statement on art. Maurice Meigne holds that only the first 21 canons were issued at Elvira and the rest added later.

After the Reformation canon 36 became a point of dispute: according to Philip Schaff, Protestants cited it against image worship, while Catholic writers read it as banning images of the deity alone or as a guard against pagan desecration. The date also remains debated. Louis Duchesne and De Clercq place the synod before the persecution under Diocletian, others between 303 and 314, while Karl Josef von Hefele and Robert William Dale follow the early compilers Mansi and Hardouin in dating it to 305 or 306. Ferdinand de Mendoza first gathered its scanty documentation in 1593.
council-of-europe: The French Foreign Minister Aristide Briand floated the idea of a federal union of European nations in 1929. Winston Churchill first publicly suggested a Council of Europe in a BBC radio broadcast on 21 March 1943, while the war was still being fought, and returned to the idea in a speech at the University of Zurich on 19 September 1946.

The Council was founded on 5 May 1949 by Belgium, Denmark, France, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden and the United Kingdom. Greece and Turkey joined three months later. Its first meetings were held in Strasbourg's University Palace, and it soon moved into its own buildings in the city.

In its early years the founders drafted the European Convention on Human Rights, drawing in part on the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, signed only months earlier. Where the Universal Declaration was aspirational, the Convention provided an enforcement mechanism, an international court, to judge alleged violations and hold governments to account.

West Germany became a full member in 1951 and Austria joined in 1956. Greece, suspended in 1967 after a military coup, withdrew and was readmitted in 1974. Portugal and Spain joined in 1976 and 1977 after their transitions to democracy. After the revolutions of 1989 and the collapse of the Soviet Union, Hungary joined in 1990 and Poland in 1991, followed by most states of Eastern and South-Eastern Europe.

The Council cannot make binding laws, unlike the European Union. It works through treaties, called conventions, which set common legal standards; some are open to states outside Europe, such as the Budapest Convention on Cybercrime. In 1955 it adopted the flag of twelve golden stars on a blue ground, and in 1972 an anthem based on the Ode to Joy theme from Beethoven's ninth symphony. The European Union later adopted both.

Its two statutory bodies are the Committee of Ministers, made up of the foreign ministers of the member states, and the Parliamentary Assembly, composed of members of national parliaments. A Secretary General, elected by the Assembly for five years, heads the secretariat. English and French are the official languages.

Membership is open to any European state that accepts the rule of law and the human rights and fundamental freedoms of all persons within its jurisdiction. Judgments of the European Court of Human Rights are legally binding on the state concerned, which may have to pay compensation or change its laws or practices.
council-of-flanders: The council grew out of the less formal justice that the counts of Flanders and their advisers had long exercised. Philip the Bold sought to turn this into a permanent court with written rules and a fixed jurisdiction at Lille, at the same time as he set up the Lille Chamber of Accounts to audit government spending. The cities of Ghent, Bruges and Ypres and the Franc of Bruges, however, refused to accept that the council could hear appeals against their own magistrates.

The court moved to Ghent in 1407, where it sat mainly in the Gravensteen castle, and on 17 August 1409 Duke John the Fearless gave it statutes in 44 articles. Article 26 required French in closed hearings and left the choice of language to the parties in open ones.

When Ghent was at odds with the dukes of Burgundy in the 15th century, the council often sat elsewhere, at Kortrijk, Dendermonde, Ypres or Bruges, until it was settled again in Ghent in 1498. The counts had accepted appeals to the Parlement of Paris from the parts of Flanders anciently attached to the kingdom of France, essentially those west of the river Scheldt, but in 1521 Charles V gave the Great Council of Mechelen sole appellate jurisdiction over the whole county, and by the Treaty of Cambrai of 1529 Francis I of France gave up all claim to sovereignty or jurisdiction there.

During the Dutch Revolt Calvinists seized power in Ghent in 1578, and from 1580 to 1585 the council sat at Douai under the presidency of Willem van Pamele, loyal to Spain, while a rival president, Adolf van Meetkercke, served the side in revolt. In 1694 Charles II of Spain disbanded the Admiralty Council and gave its maritime jurisdiction to the Council of Flanders. The council pronounced its last sentence of death on 24 July 1772. Among its first presidents were Pieter van der Zijpe, from 1386, and Simon van Formelis, who held the office from 1409 to 1440.
council-of-florence: The council grew out of the Council of Basel, convoked by Pope Martin V shortly before his death in February 1431 and seated on 14 December 1431, when the conciliar movement was strong and the papacy weak. It took place amid the Hussite Wars and the rise of the Ottoman Empire, and at stake was the conflict between the conciliar movement and papal supremacy. The fathers at Basel proclaimed the superiority of a council over the pope. In December 1431 Pope Eugene IV tried to dissolve it and open a new council at Bologna but was overruled, and in December 1433 he conceded the point in a bull.

After the death of Emperor Sigismund in 1437, Eugene IV translated the council to Ferrara on 8 January 1438, where it drew some of the Byzantine delegates who had been at Basel. Some members rejected the papal decree and stayed at Basel, where this rump council suspended Eugene and in November 1439 elected Amadeus VIII, Duke of Savoy, as the antipope Felix V. The council moved to Florence in 1439, because of plague at Ferrara and because Florence agreed to finance it.

At Florence the delegates reached agreements on the Western insertion of the Filioque into the creed, the number of the sacraments and Purgatory. Papal supremacy and the promise of military aid against the Ottoman Empire were also at issue. On 6 July 1439 the union was proclaimed in Latin and Greek in the document Laetentur Caeli, signed by Eugene IV and the emperor John VIII Palaiologos. Some Greek bishops accepted it reluctantly, and others, such as Isidore of Kiev, out of conviction. Mark of Ephesus refused and led the opposition in Byzantium.

Delegates of the patriarchates of Jerusalem and Antioch signed, but their patriarchs later rejected the union. The Serbian Patriarch Teofan I did not attend, and the Russian Orthodox Church rejected the union on learning of it, although Avraamy of Suzdal had signed.
