In Constantinople the great majority of clergy and laity rejected it, accusing the emperor and the patriarch of betrayal. Western military help proved insufficient, and Constantinople fell in May 1453.

The council declared the Basel group heretics, and in the bull Etsi non dubitemus of 20 April 1441 it affirmed the superiority of the pope over councils. The rump council was driven out of Basel in 1448, moved to Lausanne and closed in 1449, when Felix V resigned.
council-of-italy: Before the council existed, the Spanish possessions in Italy were administered by the Council of Aragon, since the Crown of Aragon had long ruled most of them. Local councils and viceroys in Naples and Palermo, and a governor in Milan, controlled their internal affairs. To coordinate Spanish rule in Italy better, Philip II separated the Italian states from the Council of Aragon, and Naples, Sicily and Milan passed to the new council. The Kingdom of Sardinia stayed under the Council of Aragon, as its own Stamenti demanded.

Officially the Royal and Supreme Council of Italy, the council was second only to the monarch in governing these lands, which also included the State of the Presidi and, until 1713, the Marquisate of Finale. It had a president drawn from the Spanish high nobility and six regents, two each for Sicily, Naples and Milan, one Spanish and one a native of the territory, all experts in canon and civil law. Three secretaries, a fiscal advocate who looked after the interests of the state and a conservator general of the crown's patrimony completed its staff.

Its role was solely consultative. It nominated the viceroys of Naples and Sicily and the governors of Milan to the Spanish Council of State, over which the king presided, and approved the more important civil and military appointments. Its opinion went to the king in a document, the consulta, edited by the secretary, which he annotated with his own decision; when the council was not unanimous, every member's opinion was reported.

After the War of the Spanish Succession the former Spanish states in Italy passed to the Austrian Habsburgs, and in 1713 Emperor Charles VI set up a Supreme Council of Spain in Vienna to assert his sovereignty over them. Left without any territories to govern, the Council of Italy was abolished by Philip V of Spain on 1 May 1717.
council-of-jerusalem: According to Acts, Jerusalem was the first centre of the Christian Church, and James the Just, the brother of Jesus, led the early community there. Barnabas and Paul went to Jerusalem to meet the Pillars of the Church: James, Peter and John. At the time most followers of Jesus were Jewish by birth, and even converts would have regarded the early Christians as part of Judaism. Scholars hold that these Jewish Christians affirmed every aspect of Second Temple Judaism, with the addition of the belief that Jesus was the Messiah. Circumcision, the sign of the covenant with Abraham, was disdained in the Greco-Roman world.

The purpose, according to Acts, was to resolve a disagreement at Antioch. Men who had come down from Judaea were preaching that those not circumcised according to the custom of Moses could not be saved, and some Pharisees who had become believers said it was needful to make Gentiles keep the law of Moses. The dispute lay between those who followed the Pillars, led by James, who thought the church must observe the Torah, and Paul, who called himself the Apostle to the Gentiles and held that faith in Christ was sufficient.

After advice from Peter, Barnabas and Paul gave an account of their ministry among the Gentiles, and James quoted the prophet Amos. He then proposed that Gentile converts not be burdened but be told to abstain from food polluted by idols, from sexual immorality, from the meat of strangled animals and from blood. The assembly accepted this, and a letter in those terms was written. The Western textual tradition of Acts adds the negative form of the Golden Rule.

The Apostolic Decree was binding on Christian congregations in other regions. Its purpose, scope and origin are debated. Bruce Metzger's summary of research around 1994 judged the fourfold decree original, covering food offered to idols, strangled meat, blood and unchastity, with the shorter threefold forms explained as variants; Jacques Dupont wrote that scholarship was practically unanimous in reading its prescriptions as ritual rather than ethical. According to the 19th-century German Catholic bishop Karl Josef von Hefele, the decree had been obsolete in the West for centuries.

Most scholars identify the council of Acts 15 with the meeting Paul describes in Galatians 2:1–10, and recent scholarship inclines towards treating the council and its rulings as historical, though some scholars of the mid to late 20th century were sceptical.
council-of-lithuania: After the last Partition of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth in 1795, Lithuania belonged to the Russian Empire, and the uprisings of 1830 and 1863 failed to free it. Germany occupied the country in 1915. After the Russian Revolution of 1917 the Germans, preparing for peace talks with Russia, allowed the Vilnius Conference to meet from 18 to 23 September 1917, hoping it would ask for closer ties with Germany. Instead it called for an independent Lithuania, with any closer relationship to depend on German recognition, and on 21 September it elected a council of twenty to carry this out. The Germans banned publication of the resolution and censored the council's newspaper, Lietuvos aidas.

The first twenty members were aged from 25 to 66 and included eight lawyers, four priests and three agronomists; eight were Christian democrats. Antanas Smetona was elected chairman at the first meeting on 24 September, and the chairman, two vice-chairmen and two secretaries formed the presidium. On 13 July 1918 six members were added, among them Augustinas Voldemaras, while four socialists, among them Steponas Kairys, resigned over the invitation to a king. Six members of the Vilnius Belarusian Council joined in November 1918 and three Jewish activists in December, and by the spring of 1919 the council had almost doubled. There were no women, despite a petition with 20,000 signatures.

On 11 December 1917 the council agreed to a firm and permanent alliance with Germany, but Germany did not recognise the state or invite it to the talks at Brest-Litovsk, and Lithuanians, including those abroad, disapproved of the declaration. On 16 February 1918, temporarily chaired by Jonas Basanavičius, the council declared independence again without naming any tie to Germany. Germany recognised Lithuania on 23 March, on the basis of the December declaration. Germany proposed a personal union with the Prussian Hohenzollern dynasty; as an alternative the council invited Wilhelm Karl, Duke of Urach, who was elected king as Mindaugas II on 13 July 1918.

With Germany's defeat the council adopted a provisional constitution on 2 November 1918 and annulled the invitation to the king. Voldemaras formed the first government on 11 November, the day of the armistice at Compiègne, and the council began building an army, police and local government. Smetona left the chair in 1919 on becoming the first President of Lithuania and was succeeded by Stasys Šilingas.
council-of-liubech: The council met at Liubech on 19 October 1097 and is one of the best documented princely meetings of Kievan Rus'. Vladimir Monomakh initiated it to end the Chernigov war of succession of 1093–1097, in which he and Sviatopolk II had fought Oleg I of Chernigov, a son of Sviatoslav II, over his father's inheritance. Besides Sviatopolk and Oleg, the princes present included Vasilko Rostislavich and Davyd Sviatoslavich. The meeting aimed to stop the war, to pacify the people and to present a united front against the Cumans, also known as the Polovtsians.

The council gave each prince his principality as a patrimonial domain, to be inherited by his immediate family. This broke with the rota system, lestvichnoe pravo, followed in Kievan Rus' for two centuries, under which the throne passed by seniority to the eldest of the dynasty and princes moved gradually upwards from one region to another.

Sviatopolk II received Kiev, Turov and Pinsk with the title of grand prince. Vladimir Monomakh received Pereyaslavl, the Rostov-Suzdal lands, Smolensk and Beloozero, and his son Mstislav held Great Novgorod. The sons of Sviatoslav II, Oleg, Davyd and Yaroslav, received Chernigov, Tmutarakan, Ryazan and Murom. David Igorevich of Volhynia received Vladimir-in-Volhynia, and Volodar and Vasilko Rostislavich received Peremyshl, Terebovl and Cherven.

Some scholars hold that the settlement established a feudal system in Kievan Rus', while others argue that it created a federative structure. It ended the struggle for Chernigov, but the feuding between the princes continued, and Vladimir Monomakh called the Council of Uvetichi on 10 August 1100. After Sviatopolk's death in 1113 the citizens of Kiev revolted and summoned Vladimir Monomakh to the throne.

The new arrangement allowed regional centres to grow in power, most notably Galicia–Volhynia and Vladimir-Suzdal. The period also saw continued work on the legal code known as the Russkaya Pravda and the first chronicle compilation, the Initial Compilation or Nachalnyy svod, on which the Primary Chronicle was later based. A monument to the congress of princes by Gennady Ershov was raised in 1997.
council-of-peoples-commissars: The Council of People's Commissars, known as the Sovnarkom, was the highest executive authority of the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic, the Soviet Union and the Soviet republics from 1917 to 1946. The Sovnarkom of the RSFSR was founded soon after the October Revolution of 1917, and its role was formalised in the 1918 Constitution of the RSFSR, which made it responsible to the Congress of Soviets of the RSFSR for the general administration of the affairs of the state.

Unlike the Russian Provisional Government, which had included representatives of various parties, it was a government of a single party, the Bolsheviks, apart from a brief two-party cabinet with the Left Socialist-Revolutionaries from December 1917 to March 1918.

When the Soviet Union was created, its Sovnarkom and its Congress of Soviets were modelled on the RSFSR system, and identical Sovnarkom bodies were founded in the Soviet republics and autonomous republics, which kept their own governments for domestic matters. The all-Union Sovnarkom grew into the main executive of the Soviet government, and its head, the Premier of the USSR, served as head of government. It issued decrees with the force of law when the Congress was not in session, and decrees not approved at the Congress's next session were considered revoked.

The first council, elected by the Second All-Russian Congress of Soviets in late 1917, included Left-Communists, Trotskyists and other ex-oppositionists, although the party had banned factional groups at its Eleventh Party Congress in 1921. Many of the early commissars later opposed the majority organised by Stalin and were allegedly accused of conspiring with the Trotskyist or another opposition; they were expelled from the party or arrested, and most of those accused were executed for treason during the Great Purge, while some had their sentences reduced to imprisonment. In 1946 the Sovnarkoms were transformed into the Council of Ministers, at the all-Union and Union Republic levels.
council-of-preslav: Boris I abdicated in 889 and retired to a monastery, leaving the throne to his eldest son Vladimir-Rasate, who tried to restore Tengrism, the country's traditional religion since 681. In 893 Boris deposed him and called a People's Council at Preslav to give the change legitimacy, with the higher and lower nobility, the clergy and representatives of every province.

No medieval source mentions the council directly. The fullest account of Vladimir's fall comes from the Benedictine abbot Regino of Prüm, whose Chronicon tells how Boris left the monastery, captured his son, had his eyes put out and imprisoned him, then gathered his whole realm, set up his younger son as prince and threatened him with the same punishment should he betray Christianity.

Historians hold that the council, presided over by Boris, took four main decisions. Simeon I, who had been meant for a high church career, was released from his monastic vows and replaced his brother, and the rule of succession was changed so that a ruler's brother could follow him. The capital moved from Pliska, where memories of the pagan past were strong, to Preslav, home of the Panteleimon Monastery where Boris had retired.

Byzantine clergy were to be sent away and replaced by Bulgarian clerics, among them Clement of Ohrid, sent as bishop to Devol. Old Bulgarian was to replace Greek in the liturgy, becoming the official language of the state.

The official status of Old Bulgarian gave impetus to the Preslav and Ohrid Literary Schools, and under Simeon Bulgarian culture and literature entered a golden age, making the country a cultural centre of Slavic Europe. Removing the Byzantine clergy and Greek liturgy kept Bulgarian religious life and policy free of direct Byzantine influence. Byzantium answered in 894, when Emperor Leo VI moved the Bulgarian merchants' market from Constantinople to Salonica, a move that led to war, won by Simeon at the Battle of Boulgarophygon in 896.
council-of-ten: Until 1582 an additional zonta of around 15 to 20 members also sat with the council. No more than one member of a family could serve at a time, and members could not be re-elected to successive terms. Elections were held in August and September, and the council met at least weekly. Its deliberations were secret and its members swore an oath of secrecy. According to the historian Thomas Madden, the three capi of the Ten served for a month at a time and, to avoid any chance of bribery, were forbidden to leave the Ducal Palace while in office.

Besides Doge Marino Faliero in 1355, the council ordered the execution of the Count of Carmagnola in 1432. Formally charged with the security of the republic, it was also handed more ordinary business because it was small and could decide quickly, and by 1457 it held almost unlimited authority over government. It oversaw diplomacy and intelligence, managed military affairs and handled legal matters; during the War of the League of Cambrai it found ways to pay for the state's military costs.

From the 1490s through the 1530s the Ten and other authorities enacted sumptuary laws. An anti-banqueting law of 1506 sought to stop ambitious noblemen from buying votes with lavish dinners at the compaginie della calza, exclusive social societies. In 1539 the council created the State Inquisitors, a tribunal of three of its members with authority equal to the whole council, who could try treason cases on their own, held secret trials on a low standard of proof and built a large network of spies at home and abroad. From 1624 the council prosecuted all crimes involving the private lives of patricians.

The council received denunciations through the bocche dei leoni, lion's mouths placed around the city into which Venetians could drop written reports of suspected crimes. Later observers such as Mark Twain saw them as the sign of an oppressive government spying on its citizens, but the reports were examined and only credible ones were investigated. The council lasted until the end of the republic in 1797.
council-of-the-european-union: The Council first appeared in the European Coal and Steel Community (ECSC) as the Special Council of Ministers, set up to counterbalance the High Authority, the supranational executive that later became the Commission. Its powers were limited: coal and steel matters lay in the Authority's domain, and the Council's consent was needed only for decisions outside them. The Treaties of Rome of 1957 established two new communities, the European Atomic Energy Community and the European Economic Community, each with a Council of its own.

In 1965 France, under President Charles de Gaulle, boycotted all Council meetings over disagreements about the Commission's agriculture proposals, among other things. This empty chair crisis halted the Council's work until the Luxembourg compromise resolved it the following year. The Merger Treaty of 1967 merged the two Councils into a single Council of the European Communities, which took the name Council of the European Union in 1993, after the Maastricht Treaty created the Union.

Maastricht added intergovernmental elements, but Parliament and Commission gained strength at the same time. The Treaty of Lisbon abolished the pillars, gave Parliament further powers and merged the Council's High Representative with the Commission's foreign policy head, who chairs the Foreign Affairs Council in place of the rotating presidency. It also made the European Council a separate institution with a permanent president. The development of the Council has been marked by the rise of Parliament, with which it has had to share legislative power.

The Council is one of two legislative bodies of the Union, with the European Parliament. Together they amend, approve or veto proposals of the European Commission, which holds the right of initiative, and they share the budgetary power. Most laws now pass under the ordinary legislative procedure, which needs the consent of both bodies. Ministers of the member states meet in different configurations according to subject.

Most decisions are taken by qualified majority: at least 55 per cent of member states, at least 15 of them, representing at least 65 per cent of the population. Foreign and security policy generally requires unanimity. The presidency rotates every six months among the member states, whose government sets the agenda and chairs meetings, and from 2007 three successive presidencies have shared a common programme.
council-of-the-indies: In 1493 Isabella I withdrew the wide powers she had granted Christopher Columbus and placed the affairs of the Indies in the hands of her chaplain, Juan Rodríguez de Fonseca. He became in effect minister for the Indies, laid the foundations of a colonial bureaucracy and presided over a Junta de Indias of about eight counsellors drawn partly from the Council of Castile. Charles V was already using the name Council of the Indies in 1519, and after the conquest of the Aztec Empire in 1521 showed the importance of the Americas, the council was formally created on 1 August 1524 on the model of the Council of Castile.

At first it followed the itinerant court of Charles V; Philip II placed it in Madrid in 1561. It oversaw the Casa de Contratación, the House of Trade founded at Seville in 1503, and had two secretaries, one for the Viceroyalty of New Spain and the other for Peru, Chile, Tierra Firme and the New Kingdom of Granada. Unrest in Peru and the efforts of Bartolomé de las Casas on behalf of the native peoples led Charles to reshape it in 1542 with the New Laws, which limited the rights of encomienda holders.

The council was usually headed by a churchman, but its members were mostly laymen trained in law. Its power peaked in the 16th century. Finance passed to the Council of Finance in 1556–57, and the Inquisition established in Mexico and Lima in the 1570s lay outside its control. Juan de Ovando y Godoy, president in 1571–75, was appalled by the councillors' ignorance of the Indies, and his project for a general description of the territories produced the Relaciones geográficas. Under Charles II the council's decisions were codified in the Laws of the Indies of 1680. In the last Habsburg years some places were sold or given to the plainly unqualified, among them a nine-year-old boy.

In 1714 Philip V created a Secretariat of the Navy and the Indies whose minister took over the council's administrative work, though it continued in a secondary role and regained prestige late in the 18th century. The Cortes of Cádiz abolished it in 1812, Ferdinand VII restored it in 1814, and it was finally abolished in 1834 by the regency for the four-year-old Isabella II. Its records form the General Archive of the Indies in Seville, a major centre of documentation for Spanish and Spanish American history.
council-of-trent: Martin Luther issued his 95 Theses in Wittenberg on 31 October 1517. In 1520 he appealed to the German princes for a council in Germany, free of the papacy, and German opinion came to see a council as the best way to reconcile the differences. It took a generation to meet. Popes feared reviving the schism over conciliarism, the Lutherans demanded the exclusion of the papacy, France and the Holy Roman Empire were rivals, and the Turkish danger weighed on the Mediterranean. Paul III summoned a council to Mantua for 23 May 1537, but war between France and Charles V prevented it, and it was postponed indefinitely in 1539.

The council met for twenty-five sessions between 13 December 1545 and 4 December 1563, in three periods: 1545–1549, 1551–1552 and 1562–1563. It opened at Trent with only about 30 bishops. Julius III reopened it on 1 May 1551, but Maurice, Elector of Saxony, defeated Charles V and marched into Tirol in April 1552. Protestants had been invited and given safe conduct, and Melanchthon and Johannes Brenz set out for Trent, but they were refused a vote and the victory of Maurice ended their cooperation.

Pius IV reconvened it from 18 January 1562. The French monarchy boycotted the council until a delegation led by Charles de Guise, Cardinal of Lorraine, arrived in November 1562. The decrees were signed in 1563 by 255 members, two-thirds of the bishops being Italians. No pope attended in person; legates represented them.

The council affirmed that scripture and tradition are both authoritative, confirmed the traditional canon including the deuterocanonical books, endorsed the Latin Vulgate and reaffirmed the seven sacraments. On justification it declared that grace is offered through human cooperation, rejecting the Protestant doctrine, and it reaffirmed purgatory, indulgences and the veneration of saints, while forbidding the sale of indulgences. Pius IV ratified the decrees on 26 January 1564. The Tridentine Creed followed in 1565, and Pius V issued the Roman Catechism and revised the Breviary and Missal in 1566, 1568 and 1570, which led to the Tridentine Mass. Italy, Portugal and Poland accepted the decrees, and France only recognised their doctrinal parts. More than three hundred years passed before the next ecumenical council, in 1869.
council-of-troubles: In the last years of Margaret of Parma's regency, the discontent of the high nobility, anger at the persecution of heretics and the new dioceses, and the famine of 1565 shook the regime. A League of Nobles petitioned against the persecution, and in the summer of 1566 Calvinists attacked Catholic churches. Philip II sent the Duke of Alba with Spanish troops, and his first measures so offended the regent that she resigned in early September 1567. The council he created on 9 September was presented as advisory, but it set aside the older councils and ignored privileges such as Brabant's Joyous Entry.

Alba presided, with Charles de Berlaymont and Philippe de Noircarmes as vice-presidents and jurists from the provinces such as Jacob Hessels as members, but the most influential were the Spaniards Juan de Vargas and Luis del Río, apparently the only ones allowed to vote. As the cases grew into thousands, Alba set up two criminal and two civil chambers in 1569. Commissioners hunted heretics in the provinces, trials were conducted wholly in writing, and the usual charge was high treason, whose content the councillors shaped to the needs of the moment; many contemporaries saw the proceedings as arbitrary.

Lamoral, Count of Egmont, and Philip de Montmorency, Count of Horn, were denied trial by their peers of the Order of the Golden Fleece and executed on 5 June 1568, four days after eighteen lesser nobles were put to death in Brussels. According to Jonathan Israel, almost nine thousand people were convicted of heresy or treason, most of them in absentia, and lived in exile with their property confiscated; the exodus has been estimated at 60,000 people. The confiscations brought in half a million ducats a year, according to a letter of 1572.

Luis de Zúñiga y Requesens abolished the council on 7 June 1574 in return for a subsidy from the States-General, but as it went unpaid the council sat on without pronouncing further death sentences. On 4 September 1576 revolutionary bands under Jacques de Glymes arrested the Council of State in Brussels, which ended the tribunal. Hessels was hanged by the rebel government of Ghent, while Vargas and Jeronimo de Roda escaped.
councils-of-braga: Braga was the metropolitan see of an ecclesiastical province and the chief bishopric of the Kingdom of Galicia in the Suevic period, and again in the High Middle Ages, when it lay in the Kingdom of Portugal. A council said to have met there in 411 is probably an invention of the historian Frei Bernardo de Brito. The first council was presided over by Lucretius and the second by Saint Martin of Dume, as Martin of Braga is also known.

Eight bishops took part in the first council, which issued twenty-two decrees. All were to follow the same rite and readings, and to greet the people with Dominus vobiscum without the alterations of the Priscillianists. Mass was to follow the order sent from Rome to Profuturus, and nothing was to be sung in church but the Psalms and texts of the Old and New Testament. Priests who abstained from meat had to eat vegetables cooked with it, to avoid any suspicion of Priscillianism, and no one was to be buried inside a church.

The second council, held to increase the number of bishops in Gallaecia, was attended by twelve bishops, from the suffragan sees of Braga and from the Diocese of Lugo, and issued ten decrees. Bishops were to inspect how priests administered the sacraments, catechumens were to receive twenty days of instruction before baptism, and no fee was to be taken for ordination, the chrism or the consecration of a church. The metropolitan was to announce the date of Easter, and anyone saying Mass without fasting was to lose his office.

A third council met in 675 under Leodegisius in the reign of King Wamba and issued eight decrees, among them a ban on offering milk and grapes in place of bread and wine. Councils were held at Braga again in 1137, 1148, 1262, 1286, 1292, 1426 and 1470, and in 1566, when the council was meant to apply the reforms of the Council of Trent. Forty synods are also recorded there from the 13th century onwards.
counter-reformation: The term Counter-Reformation translates the German Gegenreformation, coined in the late eighteenth century by German historians as a negative concept for Catholic repression and popularised by writers such as Leopold von Ranke. Protestant historians have tended to treat Catholic reform as part of it. The period is frequently dated from the Council of Trent (1545 to 1563) to the end of the European wars of religion in 1648, though this dating is controversial. Catholic reform had earlier roots in the Gregorian reforms of the late 11th century, the Benedictine Bull of 1336 and the Capuchins, who arose from Matteo de Bascio's proposal of 1526 to return to the original Franciscan rule.

Pope Paul III, considered the first pope of the Counter-Reformation, initiated the Council of Trent, which dealt with corrupt clergy and the sale of indulgences. The council upheld the medieval church's sacramental system and doctrine and rejected compromise with Protestants. Pius V made the Tridentine Mass obligatory in 1570. Other measures included the Roman Catechism of 1566, the Index Librorum Prohibitorum of 1559 and seminaries to train priests, and new orders such as the Jesuits, Discalced Carmelites and Ursulines arose. The effort also used regional Inquisitions and state power, and had a missionary side in lands colonised by Catholic nations.

Rudolf II began suppressing Protestant activity in Habsburg lands in 1576. In France, Catholics and Huguenots fought wars from 1562, and the Edict of Nantes of 1598 brought peace; in 1685 Louis XIV abolished the right of Huguenots to worship.

The Counter-Reformation drastically diminished Protestantism in Lithuania, Poland, France, Italy and the Habsburg lands, including Austria, southern Germany and Bohemia, but did less in Hungary. War and discriminatory laws caused large migrations of religious refugees, and towns such as Freudenstadt and Glückstadt were founded as homes for them. By the Union of Brest in 1596, Ruthenian Orthodox bishops entered full communion with Rome while keeping their Byzantine liturgy and married clergy. The Church was also a leading patron of the arts, and the Baroque style of Bernini's Rome and Rubens's Flanders served to restore Catholic centrality.
counts-feud: After the death of Frederick I in 1533, the Jutland nobility proclaimed his son, then Duke Christian of Gottorp, king as Christian III. He had already made Lutheranism the state religion in Schleswig and Holstein by 1528. Count Christopher of Oldenburg rejected the election and demanded that Christian II, forced from power in 1523, be set free. Troops from Oldenburg and Mecklenburg, parts of the Zealand and Skåne nobility and the cities of Copenhagen and Malmø joined him, and Lübeck agreed to finance him if he kept Dutch shipping out of the Danish straits.

In 1534 the privateer Skipper Clement, once in Christian II's service, raised the peasants of Vendsyssel and North Jutland against the nobles at the count's request, and many manors were burned. The rebels defeated a noble army at the Battle of Svenstrup on 16 October 1534. Christian III then forced a peace on Lübeck, and Johan Rantzau pursued the peasants to Aalborg, which his troops stormed on 18 December; at least 2,000 people are thought to have died in the storming and the plundering after it. Skipper Clement was captured and executed in 1536.

Gustav Vasa of Sweden sent an army to help Christian III, which plundered its way through Skåne and Halland. At Helsingborg in January 1535 Tyge Krabbe turned the castle's cannons on its own defenders and opened it to the Swedes, and Denmark east of the Sound was lost to the count. Rantzau crushed the rest of his army at the Battle of Øksnebjerg on 11 June 1535, and Copenhagen and Malmø capitulated in 1536 after months of siege.

The peasants paid dearly: many bought their lives with great gifts to the king and nobles, and Christian III's reign saw the rise of royal absolutism and greater repression of the peasant classes. Jürgen Wullenwever was ejected from Lübeck, which the war plunged into lasting decline, and was executed at Wolfenbüttel in 1537. That year Christian III invaded Norway and made it a puppet kingdom under Denmark. Bringing a Swedish army into Skåne also whetted Swedish ambitions for the province, which passed to Sweden in 1658.
county-antrim: County Antrim is one of the six counties of Northern Ireland, in the historic province of Ulster, and one of the thirty-two traditional counties of Ireland. It is named after the town of Antrim, from the Irish Aontroim, 'lone ridge', and covers 3,086 square kilometres next to the north-east shore of Lough Neagh. A large part of the county is hilly, especially in the east. On the northern shore the hills end in abrupt cliffs, notably the basalt columns at Fair Head and the Giant's Causeway. The fertile lowlands lie in the valleys of the Bann and the Lagan.

The earliest known inhabitants were Mesolithic hunter-gatherers, and the Mount Sandel site at Coleraine, beside the Bann, shows human habitation around 7000 BCE. In the early Middle Ages southern County Antrim belonged to the Kingdom of Ulidia, and the north was part of Dál Riada, which stretched across the sea into what is now western Scotland. The Dál nAraide held lower County Antrim. Between the 8th and 11th centuries the Vikings raided the coast.

In the late 12th century Antrim became part of the Earldom of Ulster, conquered by Anglo-Norman invaders. Edward Bruce's campaign of 1315 brought a revival of Gaelic power and left Carrickfergus as the only significant English stronghold. In the 15th century the MacDonnells, a gallowglass family from Scotland, became the most powerful in the Glens, and in the 16th century many Scots settled in the county. In 1588 the Spanish ship La Girona was wrecked off the Giant's Causeway with the loss of nearly 1,300 lives. In 1689, in the Williamite War, Antrim was a centre of Protestant resistance to the Catholic James II.

Belfast, the capital of Northern Ireland, lies mostly in County Antrim, with the rest in County Down. Antrim was administered by Antrim County Council from 1899 until 1973, and its traditional county town is Antrim. Carrickfergus Castle, dating from the Norman invasion of Ireland, is one of the best preserved medieval structures in Ireland, and Dunluce Castle stands on a dramatic rocky outcrop. The Giant's Causeway is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Slemish, near Ballymena, is traditionally the place where Saint Patrick spent his years as a slave.
county-carlow: County Carlow lies in the province of Leinster. It is the second smallest of Ireland's 32 traditional counties by area and the third smallest by population. It is landlocked, and its southern, western and eastern boundaries follow the River Barrow, the River Slaney and the Blackstairs Mountains. The county is named after the town of Carlow, on the Barrow, which is the county town and largest settlement. The name is an anglicisation of the Irish Ceatharlach; the 19th-century scholar John O'Donovan proposed that it came from Ceatharloch, four lakes, though P. W. Joyce noted that there was no evidence such lakes ever existed. Granite underlies about 70 per cent of the county.

The area may have the highest concentration of megalithic monuments per square kilometre in Ireland. The Brownshill Dolmen, a portal tomb about 6,000 years old, has a capstone weighing an estimated 100 tonnes and is reputed to be the heaviest in Europe, which gives the county its nickname, the Dolmen County. Carlow contained both the navigable Barrow and the Slighe Cualann, one of the roads leading to Tara, so control of it was vital to anyone claiming the kingship of Leinster. By the 11th century the Mac Murchada branch of the Uí Ceinnselaig had established themselves as Kings of Leinster.

After the Norman conquest the Borough of Carlow was founded, and in 1247 the independent Liberty of Carlow was established. It was then over three times its present size. In the 14th century it was the capital of the Lordship of Ireland from 1361 to 1374. After the Irish Confederate Wars of the 1650s most Gaelic Irish and Anglo-Norman landowners were dispossessed, but after the Restoration many Irish nobles petitioned the king and recovered their lands, so the Cromwellian conquest had a limited impact on Carlow. During the War of Independence the Carlow Brigade of the Irish Republican Army used the estate at Duckett's Grove as headquarters from 1919 to 1922.

Carlow town holds about 44 per cent of the county's population, which was 61,968 at the 2022 census. Agriculture is strong, notably dairy, cereals and vegetables, and Carlow was historically Ireland's main producer of sugar beet, with the Irish Sugar Manufacturing Company founded there in 1926. Together with Kilkenny and Tipperary the county keeps the historic Butler coat of arms, first recorded in 1665.
county-clare: County Clare lies in the province of Munster, bordered on the west by the Atlantic Ocean. The River Shannon and the Shannon Estuary lie to the southeast and south, Lough Derg to the northeast and Galway Bay to the north. It covers 3,450 square kilometres. The county contains the Burren, a karst region with rare flowers and fauna, and at its western edge the Cliffs of Moher. Its nickname is the Banner County, for which two origins are suggested: the banners captured by Clare's Dragoons at the Battle of Ramillies, and the banner of Catholic emancipation raised by Daniel O'Connell's victory in the 1828 by-election.

Clare holds the oldest known evidence of human activity in Ireland: a bear's patella with butchery marks, found in the Alice and Gwendoline Cave near Clarecastle and dated to about 10,500 BCE. It is also one of the richest places in Ireland for dolmens, the best known being Poulnabrone in the Burren, where remains have been dated to 3800 BCE. In the Early Middle Ages the area was part of the Kingdom of Connacht. It was then annexed to Munster, settled by the Dalcassians and renamed Thomond, meaning North Munster, and Brian Boru rose to leadership from there. From 1118 the Kingdom of Thomond was a petty kingdom ruled by the O'Brien clan.

After the Norman invasion Thomas de Clare established a short-lived Norman lordship of Thomond, and his son Richard de Clare was killed at the Battle of Dysert O'Dea in 1318. In 1543 Murrough O'Brien became Earl of Thomond by surrender and regrant to Henry VIII. The Lord Deputy Henry Sidney transferred Thomond from Munster to Connaught and shired it, so that Thomond became County Clare. The name is explained either from Thomas de Clare's Castle of Clare, after which the county was named in 1590, or from the settlement of Clare, now Clarecastle, whose Irish name Clár means a plank bridge.

The county seat and largest settlement is Ennis, and Clare County Council is the local authority. The population was 127,938 at the 2022 census. Clare is known for traditional music, among it the Willie Clancy Summer School at Milltown Malbay. Shannon Airport, which opened in 1945, was the first in Ireland to receive transatlantic flights. Bunratty Castle and the Cliffs of Moher are among its places of interest.
county-cork: County Cork is the largest county of Ireland by land area and the southernmost. It borders Kerry to the west, Limerick to the north, Tipperary to the north-east and Waterford to the east. The Bandon, Blackwater and Lee and their valleys dominate the centre, and the south-western coast has many peninsulas, among them the Beara Peninsula, Sheep's Head, Mizen Head and Brow Head, the most southerly point of mainland Ireland. The county contains the southern part of the Golden Vale pastureland. It has twenty-four historic baronies, the most of any county.

Much of the county was once part of the Kingdom of Deas Mumhan, anglicised as Desmond, ruled by the MacCarthy Mór dynasty. After the Norman invasion in the 12th century the McCarthy clan were pushed west into what is now West Cork and County Kerry, and the north and east were taken by the Hiberno-Norman FitzGerald dynasty, who became the Earls of Desmond. Cork City received an English royal charter in 1318. The Desmond Rebellions of 1569–1573 and 1579–1583 destroyed the FitzGerald dynasty, and afterwards much of the county was colonised by English settlers in the Plantation of Munster.

In 1491 Perkin Warbeck, who claimed to be Richard of Shrewsbury, landed at Cork and sought support against Henry VII. The mayor and several citizens went with him to England and were executed when the rebellion collapsed, and the nickname rebel county is traced to these events. The Battle of Kinsale in 1601 all but ended the rebels' hopes in the Nine Years' War. County Cork was officially created in 1606 by dividing the older County Desmond.

In the Irish War of Independence of 1919–1921 Cork saw considerable fighting, including the Kilmichael Ambush in November 1920 and the Crossbarry Ambush in March 1921. On 11 December 1920 fires started by the Black and Tans gutted Cork City centre. Most IRA units in Cork opposed the Anglo-Irish Treaty, and the Irish Free State took the city and county in August 1922. Michael Collins, born near Clonakilty, was killed at Béal na Bláth during the civil war.

The county lies in the province of Munster, and its city, Cork, is the second-largest city in the Republic of Ireland. It has two Gaeltacht areas where Irish is the main everyday language, Múscraí in the north and Cape Clear Island. The port of Cobh, then called Queenstown, was the point of embarkation for many Irish emigrants and the last stop of the RMS Titanic. Blarney Castle holds the Blarney Stone.
county-donegal: Donegal lies in the north-west corner of Ireland and is the island's northernmost county, the largest in Ulster and the fourth largest in Ireland. It shares a short border with only one other county of the Republic, Leitrim, while 93 per cent of its land border is shared with three counties of Northern Ireland. The county is named after the town of Donegal, from the Irish Dún na nGall, fort of the foreigners, though Lifford is the county town and Letterkenny the largest town. It is the most mountainous county in Ulster. Errigal, at 751 metres, is the highest peak, the Slieve League cliffs are among the highest sea cliffs in Europe, and Malin Head is the most northerly point on the island.

Donegal was the home of the Clann Dálaigh, whose best-known branch was the O'Donnell dynasty. From the early 13th century to the start of the 17th the O'Donnells were the second most powerful ruling family in Ulster, after the O'Neills of Tír Eoghain. They ruled Tír Chonaill, a Gaelic kingdom covering almost all of the modern county. The head of the family was called An Ó Domhnaill and Rí Thír Chonaill, King of Tír Chonaill, and was based at Donegal Castle.

Their power ended in the newly created County Donegal in September 1607, after the Flight of the Earls from Portnamurray, near Rathmullan. The city of Derry was officially part of the county until 1610. The partition of Ireland in the early 1920s cut the county off from Derry, which had been its main port and financial centre for centuries, and left it joined to the rest of the Irish Free State only by a border of a few kilometres. Its narrow-gauge railways lost their goods traffic to the roads after the First World War.

The county had 167,084 inhabitants at the 2022 census. It contains Gaeltacht districts, Irish-speaking areas, in Gweedore, the Rosses and Cloughaneely; the Donegal Gaeltacht is the second largest in Ireland, and its Ulster Irish shares many traits with Scottish Gaelic. Glenveagh National Park, a nature reserve of 170 square kilometres around the late Victorian Glenveagh Castle, is among its best-known places.
county-dublin: County Dublin lies on the east coast of Ireland in the province of Leinster, bordered by Meath to the west and north, Kildare to the west, Wicklow to the south and the Irish Sea to the east. Its coastline is 155 kilometres long and is marked by bays and estuaries, most prominently Dublin Bay. The southern part of the county is dominated by the Dublin Mountains, which rise to around 760 metres, while the northern section, now known as Fingal, ranges from commuter towns to flat, fertile plains used for horticulture and agriculture. The offshore islands include Lambay Island, the largest off Ireland's east coast, and Ireland's Eye, a name that results from a mistranslation of the island's Irish name by Vikings.

The earliest recorded inhabitants settled along the mouth of the River Liffey. Five wooden fish traps found near Spencer Dock in 2007 were dated by radiocarbon to the Late Mesolithic, c. 6,100–5,700 BCE. The county takes its name from the city, an anglicisation of the Old Norse Dyflin. Viking settlers founded the city in the 9th century and established the Kingdom of Dublin, on the site of a Christian ecclesiastical site called Duiblinn, from the Middle Irish for a dark tidal pool where the River Poddle entered the Liffey. Dublin is the longest-established county in Ireland, the first part of the island to be shired after the Norman invasion in the late 1100s.

Until 1994 the historic county was governed in two parts, the city council area and the local government area called County Dublin. That year the county council area was divided into three administrative counties, Dún Laoghaire–Rathdown, Fingal and South Dublin. The Dublin and Kingstown Railway, opened in December 1834 between Westland Row and Dún Laoghaire, was Ireland's first railway and the world's first commuter railway line. The First Dáil of the Irish Republic met in the Round Room of the Mansion House in January 1919.

Dublin city is the capital and largest city of the Republic of Ireland, and Leinster House on Kildare Street is the meeting place of both houses of the Oireachtas. The county had 1,458,154 inhabitants at the 2022 census, about 28 per cent of the Republic's population. Its places of interest include Dublin Castle, Christ Church Cathedral, Kilmainham Gaol, Glasnevin Cemetery and the Custom House.
county-fermanagh: Fermanagh is the least populous of the six counties of Northern Ireland, with a little over a third of the population of Tyrone, the next smallest. Nearly a third of the county is covered by lakes and waterways, including Upper and Lower Lough Erne and the River Erne, and Enniskillen, the county town, stands in the middle of it. It is the only county of Northern Ireland that does not border Lough Neagh. Its uplands include the Cuilcagh range on the southern border, whose summit of 665 metres is the county's highest point, and its limestone has produced cave systems such as the Marble Arch Caves.

The name comes from the Irish Fir Manach, men of Manach. According to the account given, the Menapii, a Celtic people named on Ptolemy's map of Ireland, later settled around Lough Erne and became known as the Fir Manach. The Annals of Ulster, covering medieval Ireland from 431 to 1540, were written at Belle Isle on Lough Erne. In the early 9th century the Fir Manach proper belonged to the Airgíalla group-kingdom of Uí Creamthainn, seated at Clogher.

Fermanagh was a stronghold of the Maguire clan, whose first chief, Donn Carrach Maguire, died in 1302. When the lands of Hugh Maguire were confiscated, the county was divided among Scottish and English undertakers and native Irish: Scottish undertakers received Knockninny and Magheraboy, English undertakers Clankelly, Magherastephana and Lurg, and servitors and natives the rest. A statute of Elizabeth I made Fermanagh a county, but it was brought under civil government only with the Plantation of Ulster. The county's railway lines were closed in 1957, leaving it the first non-island county in the United Kingdom without a railway service.

Fermanagh was run by a county council from 1899 until 1973. Agriculture and tourism are among its most important industries, with beef, dairy and sheep farming and heavy use of the waterways by pleasure craft and anglers. Enniskillen Castle houses the museum of the Royal Inniskilling Fusiliers, and the National Trust looks after the Crom Estate, Florence Court and Castle Coole.
county-kilkenny: Kilkenny is the 16th-largest of Ireland's 32 counties by area and borders five others: Tipperary to the west, Waterford to the south, Carlow and Wexford to the east and Laois to the north. The River Nore flows through the county, and the River Suir forms the border with Waterford. Most of the county is hilly, with uplands in the north-east, north-west and south, and its highest point is Brandon Hill at 515 metres.

Most of the rock is limestone. A large area in the north and east, around Castlecomer, holds coal beds, generally with culm, which was used extensively for burning lime. Near Ballyhale the Kiltorcan Formation, at the top of the Old Red Sandstone, contains a fossil assemblage that includes Archaeopteris.

The county takes its name from the city of Kilkenny, the anglicised form of Cill Chainnigh, the church of Cainneach or Canice. This probably refers to the church and round tower that became St Canice's Cathedral. The county was based on the Gaelic Kingdom of Osraige, or Ossory, which existed from at least the 2nd century until the 13th century. Its kings, the Mac Giolla Phádraig family, ruled from a stronghold at Cill Chainnigh. The medieval Diocese of Ossory was established in 549 and its territory matched the kingdom's. In historic times Kilkenny replaced Aghaboe as the chief church of Osraige.

Kilkenny was the last county in Leinster, apart from Louth, to have native speakers of Irish. Its dialect, part of the Ossory dialect region shared with Laois, had most of its features in common with the surviving dialect of Ring in County Waterford.

The county had 103,685 people at the 2022 census, and the city of Kilkenny on the Nore is its largest settlement and seat of local government. Its buildings include Kilkenny Castle, Rothe House, St Canice's Cathedral and St Mary's Cathedral in the city, Jerpoint Abbey near Thomastown and Kells Priory. Dunmore Cave at Ballyfoyle is one of the most documented archaeological sites in Ireland. In 1966 the county's village creameries amalgamated to form Avonmore Creameries. Hurling is by far the dominant sport, and the county's colours are black and amber, first worn by Tullaroan in 1886.
county-laois: Laois is the 23rd of Ireland's 32 counties in both area and population. It is landlocked and, uniquely, doubly landlocked, since none of the counties that border it touches the coast. The county was formerly divided into nine baronies, among them Ballyadams, Cullenagh, Portnehinch, Slievemargy, Stradbally and Upper Ossory.

The first people in Laois were hunter-gatherers who passed through about 8,500 years ago. Neolithic farmers left burial mounds at Clonaslee and Cuffsborough, and Bronze Age people left a stone circle at Monamonry and hill forts at Clopook and Monelly. The body of Cashel Man indicates that ritual killing took place around 2000 BCE. The county takes its name from Loígis, a medieval kingdom of which it is only a part. By the first century CE the western third of Laois belonged to the Kingdom of Ossory, while the east was divided among the Seven Septs of Loígis, including the O'More, O'Lalor, O'Doran, O'Dowling and O'Devoy.

Holy men and women founded religious communities in Loígis. St Ciarán of Saighir founded a monastery in the western Slieve Bloom Mountains as first bishop of Ossory. Between 550 and 600 St Canice founded Aghaboe Abbey, and St Mochua a community at Timahoe. The Synod of Rathbreasail, which established the Irish dioceses, met near Mountrath in 1111. The Rock of Dunamase was part of the dowry of the Irish princess Aoife, who married the Norman Strongbow in 1170. From 1175 until about 1325 the Normans held the best land while Gaelic society withdrew to the bogs, forests and mountains, and in the early 14th century a Gaelic revival drove them out.

In 1548 the English confiscated the lands of the O'Mores and built the Fort of Leix, today's Portlaoise. In 1556 Queen Mary made the area a county, Queen's County. Two plantations followed, in 1556 and 1607. The first, led by Thomas Radclyffe, 3rd Earl of Sussex, who sought to dispossess the O'Moore clan, provoked a long guerrilla war and is widely regarded by historians as a failure; the second, after the Nine Years' War, was more successful. Quakers settled at Mountmellick in 1659 and Huguenots at Portarlington in 1696. The Great Famine of 1845 to 1849 devastated the county, and Irish was still spoken there in the 1870s.

The county was known as Queen's County from 1556 to 1922 and received its present Irish name after the Irish War of Independence. Portlaoise, formerly Maryborough, is its main town and the seat of Laois County Council. The county had 91,657 people at the 2022 census. Houses built by Anglo-Irish landowners include Durrow Castle, Heywood House and Emo Court.
county-limerick: County Limerick borders Kerry to the west, Clare to the north, Tipperary to the east and Cork to the south. The River Shannon flows through the city of Limerick and continues as the Shannon Estuary to the Atlantic. Because the estuary is shallow, the county's most important port is Foynes, several kilometres west of the city. The land is mostly a fertile limestone plain, ringed by mountains: the Slieve Felims, the Galtees, the Ballyhoura Mountains and the Mullaghareirk Mountains. The highest point is Galtymore, at 919 m, on the border with Tipperary.

People were established in the Lough Gur area as early as 3000 BCE. From the 4th to the 11th century the kingdom of the Uí Fidgenti was approximately co-extensive with the county, with its capital at Dún Eochair near Bruree. Christianity came in the 5th century, and monasteries were founded at Ardpatrick, Mungret and Kileedy. Vikings established the city on an island in the Shannon in 922, and the O'Briens of Dál gCais raided the area and kept their power until late in the 1100s. After the death of Domnall Mór Ua Briain in 1194 the Normans took control, and in 1210 the County of Limerick was formally established as Uí Fidgenti lands were granted to what became the Fitzgerald dynasty.

The Desmond Rebellions, a war in Munster that began in 1569, ended with the confiscation of the estates of the Geraldines and others. The county was ravaged again in the Cromwellian conquest of 1649–53, when Henry Ireton's army besieged the city for twelve months until its surrender in October 1651. In the Williamite War the city endured sieges in 1690 and 1691. In 1690 Patrick Sarsfield destroyed the Williamite guns at Ballyneety, and the second siege ended with the Treaty of Limerick, which was later dishonoured, so that the city became known as the City of the Broken Treaty. The Great Famine of the 1840s began mass emigration and a steep decline in Irish as a spoken language.

The county's population was 209,536 at the 2022 census, of whom 102,287 lived in Limerick City, the county town. Limerick City and County Council has governed both since 2014. In the late 1930s and early 1940s Foynes was the last port of call for seaplanes on the eastern side of the Atlantic, until Shannon Airport opened in 1942. Places of interest include King John's Castle, Adare, Lough Gur and the Treaty Stone.
county-louth: Louth is the smallest of Ireland's 32 counties by area, at 826 square kilometres, and is known colloquially as the Wee County. It is bounded by Meath to the south, Monaghan to the west, Armagh to the north and Down to the north-east across Carlingford Lough, and by the Irish Sea to the east. It is the northernmost county in Leinster and the only one in the province to share a border with Northern Ireland. The county is named after the village of Louth, which takes its name from Lugh, a god of the ancient Irish.

The county is the setting of part of the epic Táin Bó Cúailnge. The Vikings left their mark in the name of Carlingford Lough and founded a longphort at Annagassan in the ninth century. At that time Louth consisted of three sub-kingdoms: Conaille, Fir Rois and Fir Arda Ciannachta. Early in the 12th century the whole area became part of the O'Carroll kingdom of Airgíalla under Donnchad Ua Cerbaill. The Normans occupied it in the 1180s and formed the County of Oriel, in time distinguishing 'English' Oriel, the later Louth, from 'Irish' Oriel, which passed to the McMahon lordship of Airgíalla.

In 1316 Edward Bruce was crowned on the hill of Maledon near Dundalk, and his Scottish army laid waste much of the Anglo-Norman colony, including Ardee and Dundalk, before it was defeated and Bruce killed at the Battle of Faughart. In 1412 a royal charter united the two towns of Drogheda as a county in its own right. Louth was considered part of Ulster until 1596, when a conference at Faughart led to its becoming part of Leinster.

Because Louth lay on the main route to the Gap of the North, the 16th and 17th centuries brought many skirmishes. Oliver Cromwell attacked Drogheda in 1649 and slaughtered the Royalist garrison and hundreds of citizens. Late in the same century the armies of James II and William of Orange faced each other in south Louth before the Battle of the Boyne, fought 3 kilometres west of Drogheda. In 1798 several leaders of the United Irishmen came from the county, and were betrayed by informers; several were hanged.

Dundalk is the county town and Drogheda is the larger of the two main towns; the county had 139,703 people at the 2022 census. Its historic sites include Mellifont Abbey, Monasterboice, the St Mary Magdalene Dominican Friary and King John's Castle at Carlingford. The Cooley Peninsula was the last Gaeltacht outpost in Leinster, and its dialect, Gaeilge Oriel, died out with its last native speaker in 1960.
county-mayo: County Mayo lies on the Atlantic coast of Ireland, bounded by the ocean on the north and west, by County Galway on the south, County Roscommon on the east and County Sligo on the northeast. It has 1,168 km of coastline, about 21 per cent of the State's total. The west of the county is largely poor subsoil under extensive Atlantic blanket bog, while the east is limestone country, where farmland is more productive. Clew Bay opens on the west coast. The county is named after the village of Mayo, now generally called Mayo Abbey, and its name comes from the Irish Maigh Eo, meaning 'Plain of the yew trees'.

Human occupation reaches far back. At Belderrig on the north coast there is evidence of Mesolithic communities around 4500 BCE, and the county holds many Neolithic remains, particularly megalithic tombs and stone circles. Examples of all four Irish tomb types, court, portal, passage and wedge tombs, can be found, notably near the Céide Fields. Ringforts, crannógs and Ogham stones survive from the Iron Age and after. From the middle of the 6th century hundreds of small monastic settlements were founded, among them Mayo Abbey, Aughagower, Ballintubber, Killala and the island sites of the Inishkea Islands and Inishglora. Tradition holds that Saint Patrick spent forty days praying on Croagh Patrick.

The county came under Norman control in 1235. Richard Mór de Burgh invaded and settled it in the 1230s with Anglo-Normans and Welsh, introducing families such as Burke, Gibbons, Staunton, Joyce and Walsh. After the collapse of the lordship in the 1330s these families became estranged from the administration in Dublin and adopted Gaelic language, law and customs. The county's boundaries, formed in 1585, reflect the Mac William Íochtar lordship of that time. Grace O'Malley is probably the best-known person from Mayo in the late 16th century. In the 1640s, Cromwell's regime sent displaced Irish families to lands west of the Shannon, under the phrase 'to hell or to Connaught'.

The Great Famine of 1845–47 fell with particular force on Mayo, where nearly ninety per cent of the population depended on the potato. The population fell from 388,887 to 274,830 between 1841 and 1851, and emigration reduced it to 199,166 by 1901 and a low of 109,525 in 1971.

Castlebar is the county town and the largest town, followed by Ballina and Westport. The population was 137,231 at the 2022 census. Mayo County Council is the local authority, and about 9 per cent of the county's people live in the Gaeltacht. Among its notable places are Croagh Patrick, Achill Island, Ashford Castle, Ballintubber Abbey, Cong Abbey, Knock Shrine and the Céide Fields.
county-monaghan: County Monaghan is the fifth-smallest of the Republic's 26 counties by area and the smallest of Ulster's nine counties by population. It is divided into five baronies: Cremorne, Dartree, Farney, Monaghan and Truagh. Slieve Beagh on the Tyrone and Fermanagh borders is its notable mountain, and the county has many small lakes, among them Lough Muckno and Lough Egish. Lead was once mined at Annaglogh and Lisdrumgormley. Only small pockets of native woodland remain after a long history of intensive farming and forestry.

The county has many ancient burial sites, including court cairns, dolmens and wedge tombs. The English Lord Deputy of Ireland, Sir John Perrot, visited the area and met the Irish chieftains, who asked that Ulster be divided into counties and that the land of the kingdom of Airgíalla be apportioned among the local chiefs. A commission was set up, and County Monaghan came into being, divided into five baronies, four of them controlled by the MacMahon chiefs and Truagh by McKenna.

After the defeat of the Earl of Tyrone and the Ulster chieftains in 1603, Monaghan was not planted as other Ulster counties were, and the land stayed in the hands of the native chieftains. In the Irish Rebellion of 1641 the McMahons and their allies joined the general rising of Irish Catholics, and after their defeat some Scottish and English families settled in the county. Following the Irish War of Independence and the Anglo-Irish Treaty, Monaghan was one of three Ulster counties to join the Irish Free State rather than Northern Ireland.

The Ulster Railway linked Monaghan with Armagh and Belfast in 1858 and with Clones in 1863. After the partition of Ireland in 1922 the boundary with County Armagh became an international frontier, and trains were delayed by customs inspections. The lines from Armagh were closed in 1957, and the last goods service between Clones and Monaghan ended in 1960, leaving the county with no railway.

Monaghan is the county town, and the county's population was 65,288 at the 2022 census. Agriculture employs a larger share of people than in the country as a whole, and the county is the main source of egg supplies in the Republic. The poet Patrick Kavanagh was born there and wrote of its stony grey soil. Monaghan County Museum received a Council of Europe Award in 1980, and the best of the county's architecture, in the Georgian and Victorian styles, includes The Diamond in Monaghan town and St Macartan's Cathedral.
county-of-geneva: The county arose within the Burgundian Kingdom of Arles, or Arelat, which passed to the Holy Roman Empire in 1032, and it corresponded largely to the later province of Genevois. The early counts are hard to trace. Medieval historians linked the figures Reynier and Olivier of the late 12th-century poem Girart de Vienne to the Genevois, but this is pure fiction. The House of Geneva itself is traced from Gerold of Geneva, count from about 1045.

The county never played a major part as a feudal power. Its counts kept the city of Geneva and its surroundings, but soon lost the approaches to the western end of Lake Geneva, which had made the position strategic. In 1124 the Bishops of Geneva had their rule over the city acknowledged and went on to make themselves an independent force, while the Counts of Savoy encircled the territory and controlled its trade routes. From 1219 the counts' stronghold and capital was Annecy.

As the male line neared its end, Robert of Geneva was raised to a rival papacy by the French cardinals who broke with Urban VI: elected on 20 September 1378, he took the name Clement VII. On the death of his brother Peter he unexpectedly succeeded as count in 1392, though he depended on the goodwill of the count of Savoy. With his death in 1394 the House of Geneva died out. The title passed to Humbert VII of Thoire and Villars, who held it until his death in 1400.

In 1401 Humbert's heir, Odo of Thoire and Villars, sold the county to Amadeus VIII of Savoy. Other members of the Genevan house protested, and the legal processes were completed only in 1424, after which the county was joined to the lands of the House of Savoy. It was at times granted as an appanage to cadet branches, among them Philippe, Duke of Nemours, and his heirs, and the title Count of Geneva survives in the House of Savoy as a courtesy title.
county-of-pallars-jussa: Pallars Jussà, or Lower Pallars, was a county of the Hispanic March in the 11th and 12th centuries, long after the march had ceased to be effectively administered by the kings of France. It was a division of the County of Pallars, which had been de facto, and possibly de jure, independent since the late 9th century. Under the testament of Sunyer of Pallars the eldest son, Raymond III, received Pallars Jussà and the younger, William II, Pallars Sobirà. The lower county comprised the valley of Flamicell, the left bank of the Noguera Ribagorzana and Pobla de Segur, and roughly matched the modern Catalan comarca of Pallars Jussà.

Pallars Jussà was wealthier and more populous than mountainous Pallars Sobirà and was able to expand against the Muslim lands to its south, but Raymond III left the frontier war largely to Arnau Mir de Tost, a baron from the County of Urgell. Under his son Raymond IV comital power was violently reduced by rebellious nobles, backed by Artau I of Pallars Sobirà and Ermengol III of Urgell. The peasants bore arbitrary exactions, forced labour and military service, and the barons claimed customary levies.

In the war that followed Raymond IV lost most of his fortresses, including Segur, and many nobles renounced their obligations and held their castles as private property. Only with help from the Moors, received some time before Artau's death in 1081, did he recover his position, and Artau II (1081–1124) is recorded as never having fought his relatives in the lower county. In 1055 Raymond IV had married his daughter Valença to Arnau Mir. The counts ruled until 1124, when the last of the line, Bernard Raymond, who had fought beside Raymond Berengar III of Barcelona against Lleida, died at the Battle of Corbins.

His nephew Arnau Mir followed Alfonso the Battler and later Raymond Berengar IV of Barcelona and Alfonso II of Aragon, who granted him the city of Fraga. Around 1161 he founded Vilanova de Pallars (Palau Noguera), giving it a charter of tax exemption in 1168. His will placed the county under the suzerainty of the Knights Hospitaller, but his son Raymond V repudiated it. When the heiress Valença died without heirs, Dolça de Só, daughter of Bernard Raymond, succeeded, and on 27 May 1192 she donated the county to Alfonso and the Crown of Aragon. It was the last major county annexed to the Crown.
county-of-pallars-sobira: Pallars Sobirà, meaning Upper Pallars, came into being when Count Sunyer of Pallars died in 1011 and his testament divided the county between his sons: the elder, Raymond III, received Pallars Jussà and the younger, William II, Pallars Sobirà. The upper share held the original heartland of Pallars, the upper valley of the Noguera Pallaresa, which roughly matches the modern Catalan comarca of Pallars Sobirà. By then, however, the wealth and population of Pallars lay in Pallars Jussà, which could also expand southwards against Muslim territory.

In the 11th century Count Artau I of Pallars Sobirà, allied with Ermengol III of Urgell, made repeated attacks on the richer lowland county. Artau acted less as a count than as the war leader of powerful feudatories who sought plunder and the repeal of the lower communities' tax exemptions; at home the peasants bore arbitrary exactions, forced labour and military service. Raymond IV of Pallars Jussà lost most of his fortresses, his capital Segur among them, but regained his position after Artau's death. Artau II (1081–1124) is recorded as never having fought his kinsmen.

Isolated high in the Pyrenees, the county played little part in wider Catalan affairs. By 1199 it was inherited by Guillelma, who sold it to her husband, Roger of Comminges, and retired to a convent. In 1295 Sibil·la succeeded her uncle Raymond Roger I and married Baron Hug de Mataplana, whose family became the third dynasty of Pallars. Between 1298 and 1332 the counts repelled three attacks by the Viscounts of Couserans, backed by the Counts of Foix and the Kings of France.

The last count, Hugh Roger III, led the army of the Council of the Principality of Catalonia in the Catalan Civil War. After his defeat in that war and in the rebellions that followed, his county passed to the Crown in 1487.
county-offaly: Offaly lies in the province of Leinster and the Eastern and Midland Region. Tullamore is the county town and its largest town. The county borders seven others: Galway, Roscommon, Tipperary, Laois, Westmeath, Kildare and Meath. The Slieve Bloom Mountains rise in the south on the border with Laois, and their highest summit, Arderin, reaches 527 metres.

Most of the county is flat and known for its bogs. The Bog of Allen, Clara Bog and Boora Bog are among the largest, and peatland covers about 420 square kilometres, 21 per cent of the land. The floodplain of the River Shannon lies in the north-west, and the Grand Canal runs across the county from Edenderry to Shannon Harbour, where it joins the Shannon.

One of the earliest known settlements is at Boora Bog, where stone axes, arrowheads and blades date to between 6,800 and 6,000 BCE. No structures were found, which suggests a temporary camp. The Dowris Hoard, found in a bog near Birr, is the largest collection of Late Bronze Age objects found in Ireland. After Christianisation the monastic complex of Clonmacnoise was built on the Shannon.

Before the Tudor period the area belonged to several small Gaelic kingdoms, all outside the Pale around Dublin. Uí Failghe, ruled by the Ó Conchobhair Failghe (O'Conor Faly), stretched from the east of the present county into north Kildare and was part of the Kingdom of Leinster. Firceall, ruled by the O'Molloy clan, held much of the centre and belonged to the Kingdom of Meath. The south, with northern Tipperary, was held by the Ó Cearbhaill of Éile (O'Carroll Ely) within the Kingdom of Munster.

The Tudor plantations of Laois and Offaly under Queen Mary I swept these kingdoms aside. The Settlement of Laois and Offaly of 1556, an Act of the Parliament of Ireland, created King's County, named after Philip, king of Ireland by marriage to Mary. It replaced the old kingdoms with baronies and the county system. The older kingdoms were not coterminous with the counties formed from them.

Offaly County Council is the local authority, and the county's population was 82,668 at the 2022 census. Bord na Móna, founded in 1946, employed many people cutting peat, and the Grand Canal of the 18th century brought prosperity to Banagher and Tullamore. Sites to visit include Clonmacnoise, with its high crosses and round tower, and Birr Castle, home of the 19th-century telescope known as the Leviathan of Parsonstown.
county-tipperary: Tipperary is the largest landlocked county in Ireland and the sixth largest of the 32 counties by area. It shares a border with eight other counties, more than any other: Offaly, Laois, Kilkenny, Waterford, Cork, Limerick, Clare and Galway. The county lies on the central plain of Ireland, but its terrain includes the Knockmealdown, Galtee and Silvermine Mountains and the Arra Hills, and Galtymore is its highest point. Most of the county is drained by the River Suir, which rises at the Devil's Bit. The centre is the Golden Vale, a rich pastoral stretch in the Suir basin. No part of the county touches the coast.

After the Norman invasion of Ireland the Kingdom of Ormond, ruled by the O'Kennedy, was claimed as a lordship. By 1210 the sheriffdom of Munster had been divided into the shires of Tipperary and Limerick, and the county was established in the early 13th century. In 1328 Tipperary was granted to the Earls of Ormond as a county palatine, or liberty. The grant excluded church lands such as the archiepiscopal see of Cashel, which formed the separate county of Cross Tipperary. The Earls gained jurisdiction over the church lands in 1662, but the two were not definitively united until a statute passed when the 2nd Duke of Ormond was attainted for supporting the Jacobite rising of 1715.

The county was divided again in 1838. Clonmel, the county town, where the grand jury held its assizes, lay at the southern limit of the county, and the roads leading north were poor, which made the journey inconvenient for jurors from the north. A petition to move the county town was opposed by the MP for Clonmel, so the county was instead split into two ridings, South and North, whose juries met at Clonmel and Nenagh. Each riding became a separate administrative county in 1899, and the Local Government Reform Act 2014 amalgamated them into a single county again.

The county had 167,895 people at the 2022 census, and its largest towns are Clonmel, Nenagh and Thurles. It is called the Premier County, a description attributed to Thomas Davis, editor of The Nation in the 1840s, who is said to have written that where Tipperary leads, Ireland follows. The Gaelic Athletic Association was founded at Thurles in 1884. Landmarks include the Rock of Cashel, Cahir Castle, Ormonde Castle at Carrick-on-Suir and the Ahenny High Crosses. The song It's a Long Way to Tipperary was written by Jack Judge, whose grandparents came from the county.
county-waterford: County Waterford lies in the province of Munster and is named after the city of Waterford. It has two mountain ranges, the Knockmealdown Mountains and the Comeragh Mountains, and Knockmealdown, at 794 m, is its highest point. It is crossed by many rivers, among them the Suir, 184 km long, and the Munster Blackwater, 168 km long. Its volcanic coastline has over thirty beaches, and a large stretch of it, known as the Copper Coast, is designated a UNESCO Geopark for its geological importance. The county has eight historic baronies, the westernmost being Decies-within-Drum and Decies-without-Drum, which are separated by the Drum-Fineen hills.

The county is based on the historic Gaelic territory of the Déise, and is still colloquially called the Déise, anglicised as Decies. The name comes from the Déisi, an Irish tribe who, some time between the 4th and 8th centuries, were driven from southern County Meath and north Kildare, and moved into the Waterford region, conquering and settling there. Their ancient territory was roughly coextensive with the present Roman Catholic Diocese of Waterford and Lismore, and so included part of south County Tipperary.

Megalithic tombs and ogham stones are found throughout the county. Viking influence survives in Reginald's Tower, one of the first buildings in Ireland to use brick and mortar construction. At Woodstown, 5.5 kilometres west of Waterford city, a settlement of the 9th century has been discovered. It was the largest Viking settlement found outside Scandinavia and the only large-scale 9th-century Viking settlement discovered to date in Western Europe. Other architectural features of the county are products of the Anglo-Norman invasion of Ireland and its effects.

The population of the county, including the city, was 127,363 at the 2022 census. Since 2014 Waterford City and County Council has governed both the city and the county. To the west of Dungarvan lies Gaeltacht na nDéise, an Irish-speaking region that includes An Rinn and An Sean Phobal, where the language is still spoken daily.
county-westmeath: Westmeath is the 20th largest of Ireland's 32 counties by area. It formed part of the historic Kingdom of Meath, called Mide, meaning middle, because the kingdom lay at the geographical centre of Ireland. The Hill of Uisneach, in the barony of Moycashel, is sometimes regarded as the notional centre of Ireland, though the actual centre lies in neighbouring County Roscommon. The summit of Mullaghmeen, at 258 metres, is the highest point in the county and the lowest county top in Ireland. The county's many lakes include Lough Derravaragh, Lough Ennell, Lough Owel, Lough Sheelin and Lough Ree.

After the Norman invasion the territory of the Gaelic Kingdom of Meath became the basis of the Anglo-Norman Lordship of Meath, granted by Henry II of England to Hugh de Lacy in 1172. When de Lacy's male heirs failed in 1241 the lordship was split between two great-granddaughters. Maud (de Geneville) received a central eastern portion as the liberty of Trim, while her sister Margery (de Verdun) received the north-eastern and western portions, which became the royal county of Meath in 1297. The liberty and the royal county were merged in 1461.

While the east of the county lay within the English Pale, the west was Gaelicised in the 14th century and passed outside the control of the sheriff of Meath. As part of the better administration of the new Kingdom of Ireland, the Parliament of Ireland passed the Counties of Meath and Westmeath Act 1543, by which the eastern portion kept the name Meath and the western portion was called Westmeath. The first meeting of Westmeath County Council was held on 22 April 1899. After the Great Famine the population declined for a century as many people emigrated, and it has grown since the middle of the 20th century.

Mullingar is the county town and Athlone is the largest town. Athlone developed because of its military significance and its position on the main Dublin to Galway route across the River Shannon, and Mullingar gained from the Royal Canal, which carried produce cheaply to Dublin, while both grew further with the Midland Great Western Railway in the 19th century. The county had 95,840 people at the 2022 census. Whiskey is distilled at Kilbeggan, and the county has an extensive beef and dairy trade and many stud farms.
county-wicklow: County Wicklow lies in Leinster, bordered by the Irish Sea to the east and by Wexford to the south, Carlow to the southwest, Kildare to the west and Dublin to the north. The county is named after the town of Wicklow, about 50 kilometres south of Dublin, whose name derives from the Old Norse Víkingaló, meaning Vikings' Meadow. The Wicklow Mountains are centred on the Leinster batholith, a mass of granite covering 1,500 square kilometres, the most expansive mass of intrusive igneous rock in Ireland or Britain. The River Liffey, 132 kilometres long, rises near Tonduff mountain. The coastline is relatively short, at 64 kilometres, and Wicklow Head is the most easterly mainland point of the Republic of Ireland.

In 431 Saint Palladius, a bishop from Britain or Gaul sent to the Irish believing in Christ, landed with companions at Wicklow harbour. The local tribe, the Cualann, had a chief named Naithi who opposed the missionaries, but Palladius still founded three churches, at Donard, Tigroney and Colbinstown. After a rather unsuccessful stay he left for Scotland.

Wicklow was the last of the traditional counties of Ireland to be shired, in 1606, from land previously part of Dublin and Carlow. It was established as a distinct county to control local groups such as the O'Byrnes. After the failed Irish Rebellion of 1798, government forces built the Military Road across the mountains, from Rathfarnham to Aghavannagh, to help defeat rebels still active in an area that had been a hotbed of rebellion for centuries. Wicklow was the first county in Ireland to lose the Irish language: only about 2 per cent of people spoke it in the 1770s. Andrew and Hannah Byrne of Glenealy, who both died in 1830, were among the last native speakers in the county.

The county town is Wicklow, though Bray is by far the largest town, and Wicklow County Council is the local authority. The population was 155,258 at the 2022 census. The county is colloquially called the Garden of Ireland for its scenery and woodlands, and the Wicklow Way is the oldest waymarked long-distance walking trail in Ireland. Places of interest include the ruins of the monastic city of Glendalough, Powerscourt Estate and Waterfall, Wicklow Gaol and the Wicklow Mountains National Park.
coup-of-18-brumaire: The French Republic under the Directory had been at war with the major European powers since 1792. Emmanuel Joseph Sieyès, elected to the Directory in May 1799, opposed the Constitution of 1795, which gave the Directory limited powers and no parliamentary control, and saw a coup as the only way to change it.
