He looked for a strong man who would restore the Republic on his terms and first had General Joubert in mind; when Joubert fell at the Battle of Novi in August 1799, he turned to Napoleon on the advice of General Moreau.

Napoleon reached Paris on 16 October but was under the minimum age of 40 for the Directory. When Paul Barras refused to support a coup on 4 November, Napoleon allied with Sieyès. The coup was planned for 7 November and postponed by 24 hours to Saturday, 9 November.

On 9 November the Council of Elders was summoned to the Tuileries, where Sieyès persuaded it, on the pretext that a Jacobin plot was imminent, to move the legislature to the Château de Saint-Cloud, outside Paris, and gave Napoleon command of the troops in the Paris area. The directors Gohier and Jean Moulin were placed under house arrest, and Talleyrand persuaded Barras to resign. On 10 November Napoleon had the palace at Saint-Cloud surrounded by 6,000 soldiers.

In the Orangery, where the Council of Five Hundred sat, deputies shouted 'Kill him!' and tried to seize him, and Murat and Lefebvre saved him, dazed and bleeding. Lucien Bonaparte told the guards that Napoleon had been attacked, and the chamber was cleared by force. By 2 am Lucien had gathered a quorum of stragglers from the Five Hundred and fifty members of the Elders, who dissolved the Directory and swore allegiance to three provisional consuls: Napoleon, Sieyès and Ducos.

Napoleon moved to isolate Sieyès, who resigned after Napoleon publicly criticised his ideas. Napoleon kept the main features of his draft, with four assemblies able to block one another and ministers answering only to the Consul. The constitution was adopted on 12 December, with Jean-Jacques Cambacérès and Charles Lebrun as co-consuls.

It was put to a referendum, which gave 3,011,007 votes for and 1,562 against. Half a million of these votes were cast by the army without valid ballots, and some 900,000 were forged by Lucien Bonaparte. With a turnout of 25 per cent, Napoleon secured only about 17 per cent of the genuine votes, on this reckoning. Most historians regard the coup as the end of the French Revolution.
courland: Courland, in Latvian Kurzeme, is one of the Historical Latvian Lands. It lies in western Latvia, bordered on the north by the Gulf of Riga, on the west by the Baltic Sea and on the south by Lithuania, and its name means Land of Curonians. The landscape is low and undulating, with marshy coastlands and, inland, wooded dunes of pine, spruce, birch and oak, swamps and lakes. Its largest city is Liepāja. Of nearly a hundred rivers, only the Daugava, the Lielupe and the Venta are navigable.

The Curonians were a Baltic tribe with a strong warrior culture and a reputation for seafaring, living on the Baltic shore from before the 5th century. During the Livonian Crusades they resisted German crusading orders for a long time. After the Samogitians defeated the Livonian Order at the Battle of Durbe in 1260, uprisings followed, but in 1266 the whole of Courland was partitioned between the Livonian Order and the Archbishop of Riga. Curonian nobles in Kuldīga kept their personal freedom and some privileges.

From 1561 until 1795 the Duchy of Courland and Semigallia was a semi-independent state, nominally a vassal of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth. The future Empress Anna served as regent from 1711, and after the ducal line died out in 1737 she arranged for the duchy to pass to Ernst Johann von Biron. The duchy was one of the smallest European states to found overseas colonies, on Tobago and Trinidad and on James Island in the Gambia. In 1795 the last duke, Peter von Biron, ceded it to the Russian Empire, and it became the Courland Governorate, where most land was held by nobles descended from German invaders and most Latvians were landless labourers.

German forces took Courland in 1915. After Latvia declared independence on 18 November 1918, Courland became one of its provinces. In 1944–1945 some 200,000 German troops were trapped in the Courland Pocket until their surrender on 8 May 1945.

Courland is part of Latvia but is no longer an administrative unit; the Kurzeme Planning Region covers much of it. Its population has long been predominantly Lutheran, with Orthodox, Catholic and Jewish communities.
courland-pocket: In June 1941 Army Group North swept through the Baltic states, which the Soviet Union had occupied since June 1940, on its way to Leningrad, which it besieged for more than two years without taking it. After the siege was lifted in January 1944 the army group fell back to the Panther Line. Operation Bagration, launched on 22 June 1944, almost destroyed Army Group Centre by late August and forced Army Group North to retreat through the Baltic states. On 9 October 1944 the 1st Baltic Front reached the Baltic Sea near Memel (Klaipėda), cutting the army group off from East Prussia in a pocket between Tukums and Liepāja.

Heinz Guderian, Chief of the German General Staff, urged an evacuation to strengthen the front in Central Europe, but Adolf Hitler ordered the troops to hold out, believing them necessary to protect submarine bases on the Baltic coast. Thirty-three divisions under Feldmarschall Ferdinand Schörner withdrew onto the peninsula, abandoning Riga, which the 3rd Baltic Front took on 13 October. Between 15 October 1944 and 4 April 1945 Soviet forces launched six major offensives. In the battle that began on 21 December, the Latvian 130th Rifle Corps of the Red Army faced the Latvian 19th SS Division.

On 25 January 1945 the force was renamed Army Group Courland under Colonel-General Lothar Rendulic, and some divisions were evacuated by sea. In seven months the Soviets advanced no more than a few kilometres in difficult terrain and bad weather. Western historians hold that after December 1944 the Soviet command aimed mainly to keep the Germans from escaping; the Russian historian Aleksei Isaev calls Courland a peripheral front for both sides. German losses are estimated at over 150,000, and Grigoriy Krivosheev counts 160,948 Soviet casualties between 16 February and 8 May 1945.

After the German Instrument of Surrender of 8 May 1945, Karl Dönitz ordered the last commander, Colonel-General Carl Hilpert, to surrender, but the cut-off troops received the order only on 10 May, making Army Group Courland one of the last major German formations to lay down its arms. The prisoners, Germans and Latvians, were taken to camps in the Soviet interior. Hilpert was executed for war crimes after a trial in Soviet captivity in 1947. The Soviets detained all men aged 16 to 60 and burned tracts of forest to flush out resisters.
court-of-justice-of-the-european-union: The Court began as a single court, the Court of Justice of the European Coal and Steel Communities. When the Euratom and the European Economic Community were founded in 1957, its name changed to the Court of Justice of the European Communities. In 1988 the Court asked the Commission to create a Court of First Instance, and in 2004 a Civil Service Tribunal was added to deal with cases brought by EU staff. That Tribunal was later ended, its competence passing to the Court of First Instance, which was renamed the General Court. The Treaty of Lisbon in 2009 gave the system its present name and renamed the older court simply the Court of Justice.

The institution is seated in the Kirchberg district of Luxembourg City and consists of two courts. The Court of Justice hears applications from national courts for preliminary rulings on the interpretation of EU law, direct actions against member states for failure to fulfil an obligation, direct actions against EU institutions, and appeals from the General Court. It has one judge from each member state, assisted by Advocates General, each of whom prepares an independent, non-binding opinion in the cases assigned to them.

The General Court hears actions brought by individuals or companies against acts of EU institutions and agencies, claims for damages, intellectual property cases and employment disputes between institutions and their staff. It has two judges from each member state. Judges and Advocates General are appointed by national governments jointly, for a renewable term of six years. The working language of the Court is French.

The Court's mission is to ensure that the law is observed in the interpretation and application of the Treaties. It reviews the legality of the actions of EU institutions, enforces compliance by member states with their obligations and interprets EU law, working with national courts so that the law is applied uniformly. It is described as a sui generis court system, of its own kind, and as a supranational institution.
court-of-policy: The Court of Policy was established in 1732 by the Dutch authorities, at a time when the colonies of Berbice, Demerara and Essequibo were under the control of the Netherlands. It held both legislative and administrative functions. At first it consisted of the governor, five appointed officials, among them the Fiscal Officer and the Vendor Master, and five colonists chosen by the governor from a list of nominees put forward by the College of Kiezers. When the British took over the colony in 1803, they kept the Dutch administrative bodies, the Court of Policy among them.

Sitting together with the College of Kiezers, the Court of Policy at first formed the Combined Court. In 1812 Hugh Lyle Carmichael, Lieutenant Governor of Demerara, abolished the College of Kiezers and gave its duties to the Financial Representatives, who were elected by the public on a severely limited franchise. The College of Kiezers was re-established in 1831, but only as an electoral college for the Court of Policy. For most of its existence the Court and the six Financial Representatives together made up the Combined Court.

The constitutional reforms of 1891 took away the Court's executive powers, which passed to the Executive Council. The reformed Court had 16 members. Eight were unelected: the governor and seven officials, among them the Attorney General, the Government Secretary, the Immigration Agent General and the Receiver General. The other eight were elected from seven constituencies, Georgetown returning two. Elections were held in 1892, 1897, 1901, 1906, 1911, 1916, 1921 and 1926, but only 1.08% of the population could vote in 1921 and 4.2% in 1926.

The Court of Policy was abolished in 1928, when a new constitution created the Legislative Council, and it met for the last time on 17 July 1928. Its name is kept by the Court of Policy building of 1752, a one-storey clay brick building with walls 61 cm thick. Its middle room was the church and its northern room the court; the southern room, first meant as a prison, was later used for slave auctions. It is the oldest non-military structure in Guyana, and the Dutch Heritage Museum opened there on 19 February 2007. With Fort Zeelandia it was placed on UNESCO's World Heritage Tentative List on 15 November 1995.
court-of-the-myrtles: The court is the centre of the Comares Palace, the core of the palace complex known as the Qaṣr al-Sultan or Dār al-Mulk, which Isma'il I, who came to the throne in 1314, planned as the official palace of the sultan and the state. Yusuf I (r. 1333–1354) built the Comares Tower and the Hall of the Ambassadors on its north side. Muhammad V refurbished the court and the hall between 1362 and 1367, and the decoration seen today is his; his name appears in many of the surviving inscriptions.

The courtyard measures 23 to 23.5 metres wide and 36.6 metres long, its long axis running roughly north to south. A reflective pool 34 metres long lies on that axis, with the myrtle hedges that name the court along both sides; it is also called the Patio de la Alberca, Courtyard of the Pool. Circular floor fountains at either end feed the pool through short channels designed to slow the water, so that its still surface reflects the sunlight and the architecture around it.

At each end stands a portico of a wide central arch flanked by three smaller arches, its stucco carved with arabesque, sebka and epigraphic motifs. The northern portico leads through the Sala de la Barca, whose name most scholars derive from the Arabic baraka, blessing, to the Hall of Ambassadors inside the Comares Tower, the throne hall and audience chamber, 11.3 metres square and 18.2 metres high under a wooden dome of 8017 pieces.

After the conquest of Granada in 1492 the Catholic Monarchs linked the Comares Palace to the Palace of the Lions for the first time and flew the royal flag from the Comares Tower when they visited. In the 16th century the southern halls were largely demolished for the Palace of Charles V, only their façade being kept to preserve the look of the courtyard. A fire in 1890 destroyed the wooden ceiling of the Sala de la Barca, which was reconstructed from surviving fragments by 1965.
couserans: Couserans lies in the Pyrenees and makes up the western half of the Ariège département, around the towns of Saint-Girons and Saint-Lizier, with a small part in the far south of Haute-Garonne. It covers 1,162 km². At the 1999 census it had 21,260 inhabitants, a density of only 18 per km², one of the lowest in western Europe; the only urban area, Saint-Girons with Saint-Lizier, held 9,484 of them.

The Consoranni were probably essentially Aquitanian, speaking a language related to old Basque, and held an oppidum on the hill of present-day Saint-Lizier. The Romans came into contact with them around 80 BCE and placed the area in the Provincia. After the conquest of Aquitania around 50 BCE it belonged to Aquitania and later to Novempopulana, as the Civitas Consorannorum, whose capital at the old oppidum the Romans named Austria. The people slowly adopted Latin, which later evolved into Gascon.

Charlemagne created Couserans as a border county during his campaigns in the area. In 1180 a viscounty of Couserans was created for Roger of Comminges, brother of Count Bernard IV of Comminges, separating it from Comminges; at first it covered only the upper areas, without Saint-Lizier or Saint-Girons. The viscounty was united to the French crown in the 1450s. Couserans was not touched by the Cathar heresy, and in the 16th century the bishops of Saint-Lizier fought Protestantism with success.

In 1789 Couserans sent three representatives to the Estates-General. In 1790 Saint-Girons and Saint-Gaudens could not agree which should be the préfecture of a joint département with Comminges, so Couserans was joined with the County of Foix to form Ariège. A promise that the préfecture would alternate between towns was broken and Foix kept it, while Pamiers replaced Saint-Lizier as the seat of the diocese.

Couserans has no official status; the arrondissement of Saint-Girons matches the old province most closely. Saint-Girons, once a small suburb of Saint-Lizier, is its largest town and is regarded as its capital, while Saint-Lizier preserves some of the best medieval and Romanesque architecture in southern France. The region lost much of its population to rural exodus in the 20th century.
covenant-chain: The Covenant Chain grew out of agreements made early in the 17th century between Dutch settlers in New Netherland and the Five Nations of the Haudenosaunee, which centred on trade. When the English took New Netherland in 1664 and established the Province of New York, they renewed them. King Philip's War in New England, in which more than 600 colonists and 3,000 Indians died, and Bacon's Rebellion in Virginia led New York's governor Sir Edmund Andros to ask the Haudenosaunee in August 1675 for help in ending the conflicts; he worked with the Onondaga leader Daniel Garacontié.

The name came from the image of a silver chain tying the English sailing ship to the Haudenosaunee Tree of Peace in the Onondaga Nation. A three-link silver chain was made for the first agreement, its links standing for peace, friendship and respect between the Haudenosaunee and the Crown. Virginia's governor Lord Effingham used the phrase covenant chain at a council in 1684, and a Seneca speaker answered that the chain should be kept clean and bright as silver.

A treaty of 1676 between the Mohawk and the colonies of Massachusetts Bay and Connecticut ended King Philip's War in New England, the Mohawk having denied Metacom gunpowder and attacked his winter camp. A treaty of 1677 brought the Five Nations and the Lenape to peace with Virginia and Maryland and their Susquehannock allies, many of whom then settled among the Seneca and Onondaga. The Chesapeake had nearly eighty years of peace. In the historian Daniel Richter's words, "Iroquois and New Yorkers played dominant but seldom dictatorial roles" in keeping the treaties.

Colonial officials later assumed that the treaties had placed the Haudenosaunee under the English sovereign, which the Haudenosaunee rejected; at a council in 1692 their leaders said they would be not like father and son but like brothers. In 1753 the Mohawk, saying they had been cheated of their lands in New York, declared the chain broken. The Albany Congress failed to repair it, and the British government set up the British Indian Department in 1755. In a council that year Sir William Johnson renewed the chain, promising yearly meetings to strengthen and brighten it.

In June 2010 Queen Elizabeth II of Canada renewed the Covenant Chain Treaties, presenting eight silver hand bells each to the chiefs of Tyendinaga Mohawk Territory and Six Nations of the Grand River to mark 300 years of the chain. The bells were inscribed The Silver Chain of Friendship 1710–2010, a name often used when the chain was renewed.
covenanters: The movement grew out of disputes with James VI and Charles I over the organisation and doctrine of the Church of Scotland, the Kirk, which the Scottish Reformation had made Presbyterian in structure and Calvinist in doctrine. James held that as king he was head of the church, governing through bishops he appointed. In 1636 Charles replaced the Book of Discipline with a new Book of Canons, and when William Laud introduced the Scottish Prayer Book in 1637 it caused rioting across Scotland, among it the stool Jenny Geddes is said to have thrown in St Giles Cathedral.

Supervised by Archibald Johnston and Alexander Henderson, representatives of all sections of Scottish society agreed the National Covenant in February 1638. Support was widespread except in Aberdeenshire and Banff, and the General Assembly that met in Glasgow in December 1638 expelled the bishops from the Kirk.

The Bishops' Wars of 1639 and 1640 left the Covenanters in control of Scotland. Charles I's refusal to take the Covenant himself in 1647 split them into Engagers and the Kirk Party, and after defeat in the Second English Civil War the Kirk Party took control of the General Assembly. Defeats at Dunbar and Worcester led to Scotland's incorporation into the Commonwealth in 1652, and the movement divided again into Resolutioners and Protestors.

After the Restoration the Rescissory Act 1661 undid the reforms of 1638 and 1639, and bishops were restored. About 270 ministers who refused to renounce the Covenant lost their positions, and many held open-air conventicles instead. Risings were defeated at the Battle of Rullion Green in 1666 and the Battle of Bothwell Bridge in 1679, after the murder of Archbishop James Sharp. The Cameronians, led by Richard Cameron and Donald Cargill, renounced allegiance to the king in the Sanquhar Declaration of 1680, and in the period called the Killing Time the Privy Council authorised the execution without trial of Covenanters caught in arms.

After the Glorious Revolution the General Assembly met in November 1690 for the first time since 1654 and abolished episcopacy again. A minority of the United Societies stayed outside the Kirk and in 1743 formed the Reformed Presbyterian Church of Scotland. The graves of the Killing Time were marked by the United Societies from 1701, a work Sir Walter Scott portrayed in his novel Old Mortality of 1816, and many Covenanters from Ulster carried their faith to North America.
coventry-carol: The author is unknown, and the exact date of the text cannot be fixed, though the Coventry guild pageants are recorded from 1392 onwards. The only surviving text was edited by Robert Croo, or Crowe, who for some years acted as manager of the city pageants: he was paid for playing God in the Drapers' Pageant, for making costumes and props, for new dialogue and for copying out the Shearmen and Tailors' Pageant newly corrected. He seems to have adapted older material and added verse of his own.

The music was added to Croo's manuscript by Thomas Mawdyke, probably a tailor of St Michael's parish, as part of an unsuccessful attempt to revive the plays in the summer of 1591. Whether he composed it is debated, and its style may point to an earlier date.

The carol is sung by three women of Bethlehem, who come on stage with their children just after an angel warns Joseph to take his family to Egypt. It refers to the Massacre of the Innocents, in which Herod ordered all boys under two in Bethlehem to be killed, and takes the form of a lullaby sung by the mothers of the doomed children. Mawdyke set it in three parts, alto, tenor and baritone, since the mothers were played by men, and the setting contains a startling false relation at the words by, by, and an example of a Picardy third.

The plays were suppressed in the later 16th century, but Croo's prompt book survived. The Coventry antiquarian Thomas Sharp published a transcription in 1817 and, with the music, in 1825. This proved fortunate, since the manuscript was destroyed by fire at the Birmingham Free Library in 1879, and Sharp's careful copies are the only source. The carol reached a wide audience in the BBC's Empire Broadcast at Christmas 1940, sung in the ruins of Coventry's bombed cathedral. A variant that John Jacob Niles claimed to have collected in Gatlinburg, Tennessee, in 1934 may be his own composition, though Joel Cohen has argued for it.
covid-19-pandemic: The disease is caused by severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), a virus closely related to bat coronaviruses, pangolin coronaviruses and SARS. The first known outbreak began in Wuhan, Hubei, China, in December 2019. Many early cases were linked to people who had visited the Huanan Seafood Wholesale Market, but human-to-human transmission may have begun earlier, and molecular clock analysis suggests that the first cases occurred between October and November 2019. The scientific consensus is that the virus is most likely of zoonotic origin.

Cases in Hubei reached at least 266 by 31 December. A genetic sequencing company reported a novel coronavirus to the China CDC on 28 December, and eight doctors, including the ophthalmologist Li Wenliang, were detained by police on 3 January 2020 for spreading false rumours. On 31 December the World Health Organization (WHO) office in China was notified and launched an investigation.

The disease spread to other parts of Asia and then worldwide in early 2020. The WHO declared a public health emergency of international concern on 30 January 2020 and assessed the outbreak as a pandemic on 11 March. Governments responded with measures that ranged from public advisories to stringent lockdowns, travel restrictions, quarantines, mask mandates, testing and contact tracing. By the first week of April 2020, 3.9 billion people were under some form of lockdown, more than half the world's population.

Vaccines were developed rapidly and deployed to the general public beginning in December 2020, through government and international programmes such as COVAX. Several variants arose, and the WHO named some as variants of concern.

The pandemic caused severe social and economic disruption, including the largest global recession since the Great Depression. Travel collapsed, schools and public areas closed in many places, events were cancelled or postponed in 2020 and 2021, and telework became much more common. Supply chain disruptions and panic buying caused widespread shortages. The WHO declared an infodemic of incorrect information in March 2020.

On 5 May 2023 the WHO declared that the pandemic was no longer a public health emergency of international concern. The WHO noted that this did not mean the pandemic was over, and the end of a pandemic has been defined in many ways, as a social phenomenon as well as a biological one.
cowal: The peninsula is joined to the mainland in the north by the Arrochar Alps and bounded by Loch Fyne to the west, Loch Long to the north-east and the Kyles of Bute, a narrow channel separating it from the Isle of Bute, to the south. Loch Goil, the Holy Loch, Loch Striven and Loch Riddon cut into it, dividing the south into forks. It runs some 51 km from the Rest and be Thankful pass to Ardlamont Point and is some 27 km wide from Dunoon to Otter Ferry. Most of it is mountainous, of resistant metamorphic rock, with moorland, peat and forest, and settlement lies mainly on the coast.

Bronze Age cairns, such as one near the summit of Creag Evanachan above Loch Fyne, mark early occupation. When the Irish invaded the region it became part of Dal Riata, and the Cenél Comgaill controlled the peninsula. After an 11th-century Norse campaign transferred Lorn, Kintyre, Knapdale and the islands to Suðreyjar, Cowal and the land between Loch Awe and Loch Fyne were all that Alba kept of Argyll. Clan traditions trace Clan MacLachlan, Clan Ewen of Otter and Clan Lamont, which ruled from Toward Castle, to descendants of Anrothan, a grandson of a king of the Cenél nEógain.

In the wars between John Balliol and Robert de Bruys, the English held Carrick Castle and Dunoon Castle until de Bruys expelled them with the help of the Campbells, who later received both castles. During the civil war the Lamonts pushed back Campbell control, and in 1646 the Campbells overran Toward Castle and hanged many Lamonts in what became known as the Dunoon massacre. After 1740 William Caulfeild built the military road from Dumbarton to Inveraray across the north of Cowal, known as the Rest and Be Thankful.

Dunoon, the only burgh, became a resort for Glaswegians brought by paddle steamer in the late 19th century. No railway has reached the peninsula, which is served by roads and by ferries from Dunoon and Hunters Quay to Gourock, from Colintraive to Bute and from Portavadie to Tarbert in Kintyre. The Cowal Highland Gathering is held in Dunoon each August.
cowkeeper: Ahaya was born around 1710 to the Hitchiti-speaking Oconee, who lived at a site now called Oconee Old Town on the Oconee River, in what is now central Georgia. In the late 1720s the Oconee moved to the Chattahoochee River, among the Lower Towns of the Muscogee Confederacy, perhaps to distance themselves from whites encroaching on their lands. Peoples of Georgia used Florida as a hunting ground after the collapse of the Spanish missions, and in 1740 Ahaya, by then chief of his town, led 45 men to join James Oglethorpe's siege of St. Augustine.

About 1750 he led his people south, meaning to settle near the Atlantic coast, but stopped at the Alachua Savanna, now Paynes Prairie, where game, fish and feral cattle and horses from abandoned Spanish ranches were plentiful; the herds they gathered gave him the name Cowkeeper. Hitchiti-speakers from Sawokli, Tomathli, Apalachicola, Hitchiti and Chiaha joined them. His band fought the Yamasee and remnants of the Timucua, allies of Spain, and in 1757 he told Henry Ellis, lieutenant governor of Georgia, of a vision that he would find no peace in the afterlife unless he killed 100 Spaniards.

When Spain ceded Florida to Britain in 1763, Ahaya met John Stuart, the Indian Superintendent, at St. Augustine in 1764. He stayed away from the conference at Picolata in 1765, where Weoffke signed for Cuscowilla, but late that December he came to St. Augustine with 60 of his people and received a great medal from Governor James Grant. Jonathan Bryan of Georgia's scheme to acquire the Alachua lands in the early 1770s came to nothing. In the American Revolution the Alachua Seminoles stayed loyal to Britain, and Ahaya answered Governor Patrick Tonyn's calls to repel invasions from Georgia.

When Britain ceded Florida back to Spain in 1783, Ahaya asked the British to take him with them and said he would kill any Spaniard who entered his territory. He died soon afterwards, and relations between the Seminoles and the Spanish then improved. Much of what is known of him comes from the naturalist William Bartram, whom Ahaya called Puc Puggee, the flower hunter. Bartram described Cuscowilla as about thirty houses around a square with a council house, with Yamasee slaves waiting on the chief. His successors included King Payne, Bolek (Bowlegs) and Micanopy.
coxen-hole: Coxen Hole lies on the island of Roatán in the Bay Islands off the Caribbean coast of Honduras, and is the largest town of the department. The island's Juan Manuel Gálvez International Airport is located there. English settlement on Roatán is older than the town: records show Port Royal on the island occupied again in 1742, when the British tried to gain possession of most of the Caribbean coast of Central America and rebuilt the old fort there.

The archives at Belize record a Major Caulfield in command of Roatán as early as 1745. On 2 August that year he wrote to Edward Trelawny, Governor of Jamaica, describing Spanish harassment of the English settlements, which appear to have been well established on the island by 1775. The town itself was founded in 1835, when several British families moved to Roatán from the Cayman Islands. It takes its name from the pirate Captain John Coxen; in the 17th century Roatán was home to over 5,000 pirates.

The Caymanian slave-owners brought their slaves and their seafaring culture to Roatán, and these settlers came to form most of the island's permanent population. After the Bay Islands passed from the British Empire to Honduras through the Wyke-Cruz Treaty, the British settlers took Honduran nationality. The fruit trade of the late 1800s, the era of the so-called banana republics, increased the American and European presence in the region.

Coxen Hole had a population of 8,307 at the 2021 census. Various dialects of English remain the main language of the Bay Islands. Buses connect the town with other places on the island, and it has a stadium and a small hospital, the Woods Medical Facility.
coxs-bazar: Cox's Bazar lies on a coastal plain in the south-eastern corner of Bangladesh, about 150 km south of Chittagong, bounded by the Bakkhali River on the north and east and by the Bay of Bengal on the west. Along the shore is an extensive area of beach and dunes, one of the longest natural sea beaches of South-East Asia. Most of the town stands on a floodplain, so it is exposed to flooding from cyclones and storm surges.

In the early 9th century the greater Chittagong area, including Cox's Bazar, was under the Arakan kings until the Mughals conquered it in 1666. When the Mughal prince Shah Shuja passed through the hills on his way to Arakan he is said to have camped there; a place named Dulahazara, meaning one thousand palanquins, recalls his retinue. After the Mughals the area came under the Tipras and the Arakanese, then the Portuguese and then the British.

The name comes from Captain Hiram Cox, an officer of the British East India Company who was superintendent of the outpost of Palonki. He took on the settlement of Arakanese refugees and died in 1799 before finishing the work, and a market named after him commemorated this. The town was first established in 1854 and became a municipality in 1869. During the Bangladesh Liberation War of 1971 Pakistani soldiers killed many people in the town. The subdivision became a district in 1984, and in 2017 hundreds of thousands of Rohingya refugees from Myanmar arrived in the district.

Cox's Bazar is a fishing port and tourism centre and the headquarters of its district; its population was 196,385 in the 2022 census. Nearby are Himchari National Park, established in 1980, and the Buddhist monastery of Aggmeda Khyang. The town is linked by road and rail to Chittagong.
cradle-of-civilization: The earliest signs of a move to settled life appear in the Levant as early as 12,000 BCE, when the Natufian culture became sedentary and went on to become an agricultural society by 10,000 BCE. Fully developed Neolithic cultures emerged in the Fertile Crescent by 10,200 BCE, and Jericho in the Jordan Valley is believed to be the earliest established city, first settled around 9600 BCE. Proto-urban settlements with several thousand inhabitants followed, and by the 31st century BCE Susa in Elam and Memphis in Egypt joined the cities of Mesopotamia as places of tens of thousands.

Scholars once held that civilisation began in the Fertile Crescent and spread outward by influence. They now think that it arose independently at several places in both hemispheres, and that sedentary and nomadic communities kept interacting rather than standing as separate groups.

The concept focuses on peoples who built cities, created writing systems, worked pottery and metals, domesticated animals and developed class systems. If civilisation is taken to coincide with writing growing out of proto-writing, the earliest cases are the Near Eastern Chalcolithic of the 4th millennium BCE and proto-writing at Harappa around 3300 BCE, followed by Chinese writing that developed into the oracle bone script, and Mesoamerican systems from about 900 BCE.

In Mesopotamia, where the Tigris and Euphrates supplied soil and water for irrigation, the Ubaid period, c. 6500 to 3800 BCE, is the earliest known on the alluvial plain and saw the start of urbanisation. In South Asia the Indus Valley Civilisation begins around 3300 BCE with the Early Harappan Phase, which includes the earliest examples of the Indus script. In China the earliest evidence of cultivated rice, at Chengtoushan, dates to 6500 BCE, and the Yangshao culture lasted from 5000 to 3000 BCE.

In the Americas the Caral–Supe civilisation on the coast of Peru emerged around 3200 BCE, and Ruth Shady established it as the oldest known civilisation of the Americas in the early 21st century. During the third millennium BCE it may have been the most densely populated area of the world, northern China possibly excepted. The roots of the Olmec civilisation lie in early farming cultures of Tabasco that began around 5100 to 4600 BCE.

Ancient Greece and Ancient Rome are called the cradles of Western civilisation because of their part in shaping politics, law, philosophy, art and science. The phrase has also been used to describe the origin of a cultural group or as a basis for national mysticism, as in Indian and Taiwanese nationalism, and it appears in esoteric pseudohistory.
crati: The Crati is the largest river of Calabria and the third largest river of southern Italy after the Volturno and the Sele. In classical antiquity it was called the Crathis or Crater. It rises in the central Sila Mountains, in the comune of Aprigliano, as the Craticello at an elevation of 1,742 metres, and descends steeply northward towards Cosenza, where the Busento river joins it and doubles its size. It then crosses a large plain, the Vallo del Crati, where it receives tributaries from the right, including the Arente, the Mucone, its main tributary on that side, and the Duglia. Its drainage basin covers 2,448 square kilometres.

At Tarsia a dam forms an artificial lake of the same name. The river then turns northeast and meets the Coscile, its main tributary on the left, about five kilometres from the Gulf of Taranto, which again doubles its size. It passes immediately south of the archaeological site of Sybaris and Thurii, and its mouth is near the marina of Corigliano-Rossano. In the time of Sybaris the Coscile was not a tributary of the Crati but ran directly to the gulf, probably a short distance north of the city. The Crati's flow is very seasonal, averaging about 36 cubic metres per second, and it can bring disastrous winter floods.

Because it lay close to the ancient city of Sybaris, many ancient writers noticed the Crati. Lycophron and Theocritus mention it in their poetry, Euripides praised it and claimed it turned hair auburn, and Pliny the Elder wrote that it made sheep white. Strabo said the river was named for being a mixture, like the Krathis in Achaea, whereas Pausanias and Herodotus say it was named after that river.

Strabo also claimed that the people of Croton diverted the Crathis to submerge Sybaris, and research has not confirmed this. The Crati carries coarse sand and pebbles in its channel, which would have been deposited as sediment above the city if the river had flooded it. An analysis of core samples taken at the site of Sybaris by Stanley and Bernasconi found no such river deposits directly above the former city, and further cores and facies analysis may eventually confirm or discredit Strabo's account.
crazy-horse: Reports differ on Crazy Horse's birth year. Oral accounts from relatives and the biographer Kingsley Bray give 1840, while He Dog, who said they were born in the same year, is placed by census records and interviews in 1842. His father, also named Tȟašúŋke Witkó, was Oglala, and his mother, Rattling Blanket Woman, was Miniconjou. In the most widely repeated account of his vision, which comes from the interpreter William Garnett, a man rode out of a lake with an unpainted face and a single eagle feather and told him never to wear a war bonnet, to rub dust over himself before battle and never to take anything for himself.

On 21 December 1866, during Red Cloud's War, he led a decoy party that drew Captain William J. Fetterman and eighty-one soldiers out of Fort Phil Kearny into an ambush by nearly 1,000 Lakota, Cheyenne and Arapaho warriors. On 2 August 1867 he led the Oglala contingent in the Wagon Box Fight near the same fort.

In the Great Sioux War of 1876-1877 he was among the leaders who struck General George Crook's column on Rosebud Creek on 17 June 1876. Crook retreated the next day, and his delay in joining George Armstrong Custer's 7th Cavalry contributed to Custer's defeat at the Little Bighorn about a week later, where Crazy Horse helped lead the combined Native forces. Contemporaries described him as reserved and shy, generous to the poor, the old and children, and he avoided being photographed.

After months of pursuit, famine and military pressure, Crazy Horse arrived at the Red Cloud Agency near Fort Robinson, Nebraska, on 6 May 1877 with about 900 Oglala warriors and laid down his arms. In September 1877 he was fatally wounded by a bayonet while being confined in the guardhouse, during what the army described as a struggle with a guard. Seventeen eyewitness accounts survive and they disagree. He left no written statements and signed no treaties, so nearly all that is known comes from interviews made decades later. He is remembered as a symbol of Lakota resistance. The Crazy Horse Memorial in the Black Hills of South Dakota was begun in 1948 and remains incomplete.
credit-suisse: Alfred Escher, called the spiritual father of the railway law of 1852 for his work against a state-run railway system in Switzerland, founded the bank with the Allgemeine Deutsche Credit-Anstalt on 5 July 1856. Its first name was the Swiss Credit Institution (Schweizerische Kreditanstalt). Its main purpose was to provide domestic funding for railway projects and so avoid French banks that wanted to exert influence over the railways.

Escher aimed to start with three million shares and instead sold 218 million in three days. The bank opened on 16 July 1856 and was modelled on the Crédit Mobilier, a French railway-financing bank founded two years earlier, though with a more conservative policy of short-to-medium-term loans. In its first year 25% of its revenues came from the Swiss Northeastern Railway, which was being built by Bruno Hildebrand and Escher's company, Nordostbahn.

The bank issued loans that helped create Switzerland's electrical grid and the European rail system. In the 1900s it began to shift towards retail banking, responding to the rise of the middle class and to competition from the Swiss banks UBS and Julius Bär. In 1978 it partnered with First Boston to form Credit Suisse First Boston in Europe and bought a 44% stake in First Boston's American operations, and in 1988 it acquired a controlling share of First Boston itself. Between 1990 and 2000 it bought institutions such as the Winterthur Group, Swiss Volksbank and Bank Leu.

Credit Suisse came through the credit crisis better than many competitors and did not have to borrow from the government. In 2007 two of its traders pleaded guilty to mismarking securities positions to overvalue them by $3 billion and so raise their year-end bonuses. 6 billion in fines and restitution.

On 15 March 2023 its share price fell nearly 25% after its largest investor, Saudi National Bank, said it could not provide more financial assistance. UBS took the bank over, and in July 2024 Credit Suisse (Schweiz) ceased to exist as a separate legal entity.

Credit Suisse Group AG was a joint-stock company registered in Zurich that operated as a holding company, with offices in the major financial centres. It offered investment banking, private banking and asset management, and it was known for strict bank-client confidentiality and banking secrecy.
cree: The word Cree comes into English from the French Cris, short for Christinaux, which came from the Ojibwe word Kinistino. The Ojibwe used it for the many communities they met north and west of Lake Superior, mostly in Manitoba. The Cree are generally divided into groups by dialect and region, among them the Plains Cree, Woodland Cree, Rocky Cree, Swampy Cree, Moose Cree and East Cree, and the Atikamekw, Innu and Naskapi are closely related.

Cree homelands cover much of eastern and central Canada, from Eeyou Istchee in what is now Quebec to northern Ontario, much of the Canadian Prairies, and into British Columbia and the Northwest Territories. The Cree number more than 350,000 in Canada, where they are one of the largest First Nations groupings. Small communities live in the United States, mostly in Montana.

In Manitoba the Cree were first contacted by Europeans in 1682, at the mouth of the Nelson and Hayes rivers, by a Hudson's Bay Company party travelling about 160 kilometres inland. In 1732 Pierre Gaultier de Varennes, sieur de La Vérendrye, met 200 Cree warriors in what is now north-western Ontario, near present-day Fort Frances, in war paint for an attack on the Dakota and another group of Ojibwe.

A westward movement over time is strongly associated with the Cree role as traders and hunters in the fur trade. After acquiring firearms from the Hudson's Bay Company they moved onto the plains as traders and acted as middlemen with the company. The Cree and the Ojibwa were displaced from a large area north of Winnipeg by the Canadian government between 1905 and the 1930s. The Numbered Treaties cover most Cree homelands.

Historically the Cree were hunter-gatherers. The basic units were the lodge, perhaps eight to a dozen people, usually the families of two related married couples sharing a wigwam or tipi, and the band, a group of lodges that moved and hunted together. Lodges could leave bands, and bands formed and dissolved with ease. Beyond regional gatherings there was no higher formal structure, and decisions of war and peace were made by consensus. Clans each had a representative and a vote in important councils. Cree is a group of closely related Algonquian languages, a chain of dialects in which neighbours understand each other easily, and the most widely spoken Indigenous language in Canada.
creek-war: The Upper Creeks held the Coosa, Tallapoosa and Alabama rivers, while the Lower Creeks, trading partners of the United States, had adopted more American practices. A sharp fall in the price of deerskin from 1783 to 1793 deepened debt, and treaties from 1790 to 1805 ceded Creek land in Georgia and opened the Federal Road through Creek territory. The Red Sticks especially resisted the civilisation programme of the Indian agent Benjamin Hawkins. In 1811 the Shawnee leader Tecumseh spoke for an hour to 5,000 Creeks at Tukabatchee, and the Great Comet of 1811 and the New Madrid earthquakes were taken as signs of his power. Prophets such as Josiah Francis and Peter McQueen led the war party, named for the red clubs that symbolised war.

Creeks who opposed the war were killed, and on 22 July 1813 the Red Sticks attacked the council town of Tuckabatchee. On 27 July militia intercepted a party returning with gunpowder from Pensacola and were defeated at the Battle of Burnt Corn. On 30 August Peter McQueen and William Weatherford attacked Fort Mims, north of Mobile, and killed 400 to 500 people, among them women and children. Spanish officials and British traders supplied the Red Sticks, who had at most 4,000 warriors and perhaps 1,000 muskets.

Georgia, Mississippi Territory and Tennessee all sent forces. Brigadier General John Coffee destroyed a Red Stick band at the Battle of Tallushatchee on 3 November, where women and children were among the dead, and Jackson won at Talladega on 9 November. Major General John Alexander Cocke's attack on a friendly village on 17 November became the Hillabee Massacre. Short enlistments and lack of supplies nearly dissolved Jackson's army, until the 39th United States Infantry arrived on 6 February 1814 and his force grew to about 5,000. Some 600 Cherokee and Lower Creek allies fought with him at Horseshoe Bend on 27 March.

About 50 Creek settlements were destroyed and a dozen more abandoned. Jackson made no distinction between his Lower Creek allies and the Red Sticks, and the Treaty of Fort Jackson, forced on headmen of both on 9 August 1814 over the protests of the chiefs who had fought for him, took land from both, including hunting grounds claimed by the Cherokee. Jackson went on to drive the British from Pensacola and defeat them at New Orleans on 8 January 1815. In 1818 he invaded Spanish Florida, where some Red Stick leaders had fled, in the First Seminole War. As president he championed the Indian Removal Act of 1830, which led to the forced removal of the south-eastern peoples known as the Trail of Tears.
cremieux-decree: France conquered Algeria in 1830-1834, and a sénatus-consulte of 1865 allowed indigenous Algerians to apply for French citizenship, though few did. French officials believed the Jews of Algeria, many of whom had Sephardic and Ashkenazi relatives in France, would assimilate more readily than their neighbours. France had already given citizenship to the Sephardic Jews of France in 1790 and to the Ashkenazi Jews in September 1791. The aim in Algeria was the rapid acculturation of Algerian Jews into French Jews loyal to France.

Decree 136 of 1870 declared the indigenous Jews of the departments of Algeria French citizens, so that their civil and personal status would be settled by French law. It was signed by Adolphe Crémieux, Léon Gambetta as Minister of the Interior and Léon Martin Fourichon as Minister of the Navy and the Colonies, members of the provisional government then sitting at Tours while Paris was besieged. It made about 35,000 people citizens. Decree 137 confirmed that Algerian Muslims were not French citizens, a rule fixed in 1875 in the Native code. The Berber Mozabite Jews were also left out and gained citizenship only in 1961.

Within a generation most Algerian Jews spoke French and had embraced French culture. Many French colonists refused to accept Jews as citizens, and a wave of antisemitism followed that continued to worsen well into the mid-1900s. Muslim Algerians could in principle apply individually for citizenship, but only by renouncing Islam and its laws, and few requests were accepted.

Under Vichy, the Interior Minister Marcel Peyrouton abolished the decree on 7 October 1940. After the Anglo-American landings of November 1942 and the assassination of Admiral François Darlan, General Henri Giraud reinstated it on 14 March 1943. It remained in force until Algerian independence in 1962, when more than 80 per cent of Algerian Jews, about 110,000 of some 130,000, left for France.
crete: Crete lies about 100 kilometres south of the Peloponnese, closing the southern edge of the Aegean Sea, with the Sea of Crete to the north and the Libyan Sea to the south. It is the fifth largest island in the Mediterranean. The island is elongated, 260 kilometres from east to west, and a range of six mountain groups crosses it, among them the Idi Range, rising to 2,456 metres, and the White Mountains, cut by the Samariá Gorge. The earliest references call it Kaptara, in texts from Mari of the 18th century BCE.

Permanent settlement dates from the Neolithic, around 7,000 BCE, at sites such as Knossos. In the Bronze Age Crete was the centre of the Minoan civilisation, notable for its art, its writing systems such as Linear A and its palace complexes, with trade reaching Cyprus, Canaan and Egypt. Mycenaean Greeks took over in 1420 BCE, and the Linear B archive from Knossos holds the oldest identified writing in Greek. Rome conquered the island in 69 BCE after a three-year campaign under Quintus Caecilius Metellus, and Gortyn became capital of the province.

In the 820s Andalusian Muwallads led by Abu Hafs founded the Emirate of Crete, and Nikephoros Phokas restored Byzantine rule in 960 to 961. Venice ruled from 1212 for more than four centuries, a time of the Cretan School of painting, to which El Greco belonged. The Ottomans took the island in 1669 after the siege of Candia. After uprisings, the Great Powers decreed autonomy under Ottoman suzerainty in 1898, and Crete became part of Greece in December 1913. The Battle of Crete in May 1941 left more than 11,000 soldiers and civilians killed or wounded.

Crete is the largest and most populous island of Greece, with 624,408 people in the region in 2021, and Heraklion is its capital and largest city. Its Minoan sites include Knossos, Malia, Zakros, Petras and Phaistos. It has its own Mantinades poetry, music played on the Cretan lyra and laouto, and dances such as the Pentozali. In Greek mythology Crete is the birthplace of Zeus.
criccieth: Criccieth faces south on the boundary between the Llŷn Peninsula and Eifionydd, 5 miles west of Porthmadog and 9 miles east of Pwllheli. The town is built round the rocky rhyolite outcrop that carries the castle and divides the shore, with a sandy beach to the east and the quieter Marine Beach to the west. The cliffs on either side are softer glacial drift, protected by sea walls since before 1891. The earliest recorded form of the name, Kastell Krukeith, appears in Brut y Tywysogion; the most popular explanation, crug caeth or prisoner's rock, may instead refer to a bond community, since caeth chiefly meant serfs in Middle Welsh.

The area was settled in the Bronze Age, and the chambered tomb of Cae Dyni, with seven upright stones and 13 cup marks, survives on the coast east of the town. Llywelyn ab Iorwerth, who had controlled the area since 1202, is thought to have built the castle, first recorded in 1239, when the administrative centre of Eifionydd moved there from Dolbenmaen. After Llywelyn's death in 1240 his legitimate son, Dafydd ap Llywelyn, held his elder, illegitimate half-brother Gruffydd prisoner there until handing him to Henry III of England in 1241.

In 1284 Eifionydd became part of the new county of Caernarfonshire under the Statute of Rhuddlan, and Edward I granted Criccieth a borough charter. The constable of the castle customarily served as mayor, and by 1835 the office had become hereditary and the corporation had very few powers. The Criccieth Improvement Act 1873 replaced it with an elected local board. St Catherine's Church was built around 1300, and in 1749 a circulating school of Griffith Jones taught 543 illiterate people of a population of 600 to read. In the 19th century the herring catch, a coal yard and a lime kiln worked from the quay, and after Porthmadog's new harbour opened in 1811 sea captains built houses for summer visitors.

Criccieth is a seaside town and community in Gwynedd, with 1,753 people at the 2011 census, 64.2% of those aged three and over able to speak Welsh. It holds fairs every year on 23 May and 29 June. David Lloyd George, who grew up in nearby Llanystumdwy, is among the people associated with the town.
crimea: Crimea covers 27,000 square kilometres on the northern coast of the Black Sea and the western coast of the Sea of Azov. It is almost an island, joined to the mainland only by the Isthmus of Perekop, a strip about 5 to 7 kilometres wide. It was called the Tauric Peninsula, after the Tauri, until the early modern period; the name Crimea comes from the Italian la Crimea. Most of the peninsula is semiarid steppe, scattered with the burial mounds of the ancient Scythians, while the Crimean Mountains shelter a narrow southern coast with a Mediterranean climate.

The recorded history of Crimea begins around the 5th century BCE, when Greek colonies were founded on the south coast, the most important being Chersonesos near modern Sevastopol, with Scythians and Tauri in the hinterland. The south later became the Bosporan Kingdom, a client kingdom of Rome from 63 BCE to 341 CE, and stayed Greek in culture under the Byzantine Empire, the Empire of Trebizond and the Principality of Theodoro, which ended in 1475. In the 13th century the Venetians and the Genoese held some ports, while the interior fell to the Golden Horde.

In the 1440s the Crimean Khanate formed from the collapse of the Horde and soon became subject to the Ottoman Empire, which also conquered the independent coastal areas. Raids on Eastern Europe for slaves were a major source of prosperity. The Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca in 1774 made the Tatars of Crimea politically independent, and in 1783 Catherine the Great incorporated the peninsula into the Russian Empire. From 1853 to 1856 it was the site of the principal engagements of the Crimean War, in which Russia lost to a French-led alliance.

Crimea changed hands many times in the Russian Civil War, and Wrangel's White Army made its last stand there. In 1921 it became an autonomous republic within the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic. Germany occupied it from 1942 to 1944, and after the Soviets regained control in 1944 they deported the Crimean Tatars and several other nationalities. It became an oblast in 1945 and was transferred to the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic in 1954, on the 300th anniversary of the Treaty of Pereyaslav.

After Ukrainian independence in 1991 most of the peninsula became the Autonomous Republic of Crimea, and a 1997 treaty let Russia keep basing its fleet in Sevastopol, the largest city. In 2014 Russia occupied and annexed the peninsula, a step most countries do not recognise. Its population is about 2.4 million.
crimean-karaites: The Crimean Karaites are a traditionally Turkic-speaking Judaic ethnoreligious group native to Crimea. Most modern scholars regard them as descendants of Karaite Jews who settled in Crimea and adopted a Kipchak language, while others see them as descendants of Khazar or Cuman converts. Many Crimean Karaites identify as descendants of the Khazars, a theory specialists question: the Karaim language is Kipchak, Khazar Judaism was probably Rabbinic, and the Khazars disappeared in the 11th century while the first written mention of Crimean Karaites dates from the 13th. They lived alongside the Krymchaks, who practise Rabbinic Judaism, and under the Crimean Khanate had major communities at Çufut Qale, Sudak, Kefe and Bakhchysarai.

According to Karaite tradition, Grand Duke Vytautas of Lithuania moved a branch of the community to Trakai, although modern historians doubt the Crimean origin of the Lithuanian Karaites. Rabbinic leaders, who taxed all Jews from 1580 to 1646, regarded the Karaites as apostates, and in 1646 the Karaites obtained the expulsion of Rabbinites from Trakai. They suffered severely in the Khmelnytsky Uprising of 1648 and the wars of 1654 to 1667.

In the 19th century leaders such as Avraham Firkovich and Sima Babovich worked to change the community's status in Russian law, and Firkovich has been accused of forging documents to link the Karaites to the Khazars. The tsarist government exempted them from many restrictions on Jews, and in 1863 they gained the same rights as their Christian and Tatar neighbours, while the Krymchaks stayed under the anti-Jewish laws. Yevpatoria became their main centre.

In 1934 the Reich Agency for the Investigation of Families ruled that Karaites were not Jews under German law. Even so, German soldiers in the Soviet Union killed some of them, including 200 at Babi Yar. Ashkenazi rabbis in Crimea told the Germans that Karaites were not Jews, and many Karaites risked their lives to hide Jews. After the Soviet recapture of Crimea in 1944, 6,357 Karaites were counted. They were spared the mass deportation of Crimean Tatars, Greeks and Armenians. Assimilation and emigration have greatly reduced the community.
crimean-tatars: The Crimean Tatars are a Turkic people native to Crimea. They formed as a people there over hundreds of years and descend from various peoples who lived in Crimea, among them the Tauri, Scythians, Sarmatians, Alans, ancient Greeks, Huns, Khazars, Cumans and Italians. The connecting elements were a shared territory, the Turkic language and the Islamic religion. At the beginning of the 13th century the Cumans, the majority of the population, became part of the Golden Horde. The Crimean Tatars mostly adopted Islam in the 14th century.

In 1441 an embassy from several Crimean clans invited Hacı Giray from Lithuania to rule in Crimea. He founded the Giray dynasty, which ruled until Russia annexed the Crimean Khanate in 1783. The Khanate was among the strongest powers in Eastern Europe until the early 18th century. It officially was a vassal of the Ottoman Empire, with great autonomy after 1580. Until the 18th century it also kept up slave raids into present-day Ukraine and Russia, and Kefe was a major slave market. The Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca of 1774 made Crimea independent, but Russia annexed it in 1783, and many Tatars were forced to leave for the Ottoman Empire. At least 800,000 left Crimea between 1783 and the beginning of the 20th century.

More than 100,000 Crimean Tatars starved in the famine of 1921. In May 1944 the Soviet State Defense Committee ordered the deportation of all Crimean Tatars, mainly to Uzbekistan, and between 18% and 46% of the population was lost. A few were allowed to return from 1967, and in 1989 the Supreme Soviet adopted a full right of return.

The Crimean Tatar language belongs to the Kipchak group of Turkic languages and has three dialects. It was written in the Arabic script, in Latin from 1928 and in Cyrillic from 1938. The people are divided into three core groups: the Mountain Tats, the Yaliboylus of the coast and the Steppe Tatars. Large diaspora communities live in Turkey, Romania and Bulgaria.
crimean-war: The causes of the war lay in the Eastern question, the decline of the Ottoman Empire, Russia's expansion in earlier Russo-Turkish wars, and the British and French wish to preserve the Ottoman Empire to keep the balance of power. The proximate cause was Tsar Nicholas I's demand that the Ottoman Empire's Orthodox subjects be placed under his protection. After the Ottoman refusal, Russian troops occupied the Danubian Principalities in July 1853, and the Ottomans declared war in October.

Britain and France joined the Ottoman side in March 1854, after public outrage at the destruction of the Ottoman squadron at Sinop. In September 1854 the allies landed in Crimea to take the naval base of Sevastopol, won the Battle of the Alma, repulsed a Russian attack at Balaclava on 25 October, where the Charge of the Light Brigade took place, and defeated a second at Inkerman. The Siege of Sevastopol then lasted until 8 September 1855 and brought brutal conditions to both armies. Sardinia-Piedmont joined in 1855. Sevastopol fell after a French assault on the Malakoff redoubt. The British government of Lord Aberdeen fell in January 1855 after Parliament voted to investigate the war's mismanagement.

The Treaty of Paris, signed on 30 March 1856, forbade Russia to base warships in the Black Sea, made Wallachia and Moldavia largely independent, and gave Christians in the Ottoman Empire a degree of official equality. Estimates of the dead vary widely: 95,615 French, 22,182 British and between 450,000 and 630,000 Russian, most from disease. The war was one of the first to use explosive naval shells, railways and telegraphs, and was reported by William Howard Russell and photographed by Roger Fenton. Its failures led in Britain to a demand for professional nursing, associated with Florence Nightingale. For Russia, defeat drained the treasury and became a catalyst for reform, including the emancipation of the serfs in 1861.
criminal-tribes-act: Historians trace the idea of hereditary robber communities back before colonial rule. The anthropologist Anastasia Piliavsky argues that the stereotype has a deep history in Indian texts, and the historian Divya Cherian shows the 18th-century Rathor state of Marwar treating the Thori and Bavris as inherently given to crime. Colonial law built on this: under Warren Hastings in 1772, regulations allowed an offender's family and village to be punished, and Regulation XII of 1793 let wandering communities be put to work on roads or forcibly settled. The Thuggee Act of 1836, which allowed conviction for belonging to a criminal group without evidence of a crime, set the precedent for the law of 1871.

The act was first applied in the North-Western Provinces, Oudh and Punjab. An inquiry of 1883 approved extending it to the rest of India; an amendment of 1897 let local governments set up reformatory settlements for boys of four to eighteen, away from their parents; and from 1908 special settlements were built where notified tribes did hard labour. Applied in the Madras Presidency in 1911, it affected 1,400,000 people of nomadic communities, especially Yerukalas, Koravars and Korachas. Adult men had to report weekly to the police, and later amendments made fingerprinting compulsory.

The law of 1871 also created the category of eunuch, which covered hijras and other gender non-conforming communities and banned public dancing or wearing women's clothes. By 1931 the colonial government listed 237 criminal castes and tribes in the Madras Presidency alone.

Not all British officials supported the practice, and much of the nationalist press backed the act as a social reform. In 1936 Jawaharlal Nehru wrote that its "monstrous provisions" constituted "a negation of civil liberty". After independence the Government of Bombay set up a committee in January 1947, and campaigns led by P. Ramamurthi, P. Jeevanandham and U. Muthuramalingam Thevar cut the number of listed tribes before repeal. A central committee reported in 1950 that the system violated the spirit of the Indian constitution. In February 2000 the National Human Rights Commission recommended repealing the Habitual Offenders Act, and in March 2007 the UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination asked India to repeal it.
crinan-of-dunkeld: Crínán, also called Crinan the Thane, was born around 975. His ancestry is uncertain: Iain Moncreiffe argued that he belonged to a Scottish sept of the Irish Cenél Conaill royal dynasty, while Christopher Cairney proposed a Cenél nEógain descent for the House of Dunkeld. He may have spent some time in exile in England under the patronage of King Æthelred the Unready or Cnut, and Neil McGuigan has suggested that he was the moneyer named Crínán who appears on some coins of Cnut's reign between 1017 and 1023.

Crínán was the erenagh, or hereditary lay abbot, of Dunkeld Abbey, a daughter house of Iona founded on the north bank of the River Tay after the missions of St Columba among the Picts. Although the title was often held in name only, Crínán seems to have acted as abbot in charge of the monastery, which made him a man of high standing in both church and secular society. Like the Irish warrior-abbots of his time he led armies, and he was very likely also the Mormaer of Atholl. The later chroniclers Walter Bower and John of Fordun instead make him abbot of Dull and seneschal of the Isles.

In the year 1000 he married Bethóc, daughter of Malcolm II. As Malcolm had no surviving sons, the claim to the throne passed through Bethóc to their son Duncan I, who reigned from 1034 to 1040. A daughter, mother of Moddan, Earl of Caithness, and a son, Maldred, have also been attributed to him, though Maldred's parentage is disputed by scholars such as G. W. S. Barrow.

In 1045, by then an elderly man, Crínán rose against Macbeth in support of the claim of his 14-year-old grandson Malcolm III and was killed in a battle at Dunkeld. Through Malcolm he became the ancestor of every later king of the House of Dunkeld, which ruled Scotland until the death of Alexander III in 1286. Dunkeld Cathedral, built between 1260 and 1501, now stands on the site of his monastery.
cripps-mission: When Britain declared war on Germany in September 1939, Viceroy Linlithgow declared India a belligerent on Britain's side without consulting Indian leaders or the elected provincial representatives. The Congress provincial governments resigned en masse, while the All India Muslim League, the Hindu Mahasabha and regional parties supported the war effort in exchange for concessions. Japan's entry into the war in December 1941, the fall of Singapore on 15 February 1942 and the retreat from Rangoon made an invasion of India a real threat.

The War Cabinet was divided. Labour ministers and moderate Conservatives wanted progress towards self-government, while Winston Churchill, supported by the Secretary of State for India, Leo Amery, opposed any dismantling of the empire. The United States, which needed India as a base for aid to Chiang Kai Shek's Nationalist China, pressed for a settlement, and by 9 March 1942 the cabinet had agreed to send the mission. Cripps landed in Delhi on 22 March.

Cripps, a member of the Labour Party and a friend of Jawaharlal Nehru, held talks with Congress leaders and with Muhammad Ali Jinnah. Chakravarti Rajagopalachari, backed by Vallabhbhai Patel, Maulana Azad and Nehru, offered full support in return for immediate self-government, but in public Cripps could offer little in the short term beyond more Indian members of the Viceroy's Executive Council. Gandhi called the offer of dominion status after the war a post-dated cheque drawn on a failing bank. Jinnah objected that the proposals made no clear concession for Pakistan.

In August 1942 the Congress working committee threatened civil disobedience unless its Quit India call was conceded, and the British imprisoned the Congress leadership for the rest of the war. Jinnah's Muslim League condemned the movement, and encouraged Muslims to join the war effort. Historians give two main reasons for the mission's failure: its promises were to be kept only after the war, and Linlithgow and Amery worked against it behind the scenes, as correspondence released in 1970 shows. After the war even Churchill accepted that the offer of independence could not be withdrawn, and the Labour government of Clement Attlee granted India independence.
crisis-of-the-third-century: After the death of Marcus Aurelius in 180 the long period of stability ended. Septimius Severus emerged as sole emperor in 197 after the Year of the Five Emperors, and to keep the armies loyal he raised legionaries' pay and gave large donatives, a policy his successors continued. There were also no clear rules for the imperial succession, since the empire kept the facade of a republic, and any general with a large army had an incentive to seize power whenever the succession looked uncertain.

The crisis began in 235, when troops assassinated Severus Alexander, whom they judged too lenient with Germanic chieftains, and proclaimed Maximinus Thrax, the first of the barracks emperors. In 238 the Year of the Six Emperors killed all the original claimants. Generals fought each other and neglected the frontiers, where the Goths, Vandals and Alamanni raided across the Rhine and Danube while the Sasanian Empire attacked in the east. The Plague of Cyprian broke out in 251, and in 260 the Sasanians captured Emperor Valerian.

The empire then broke apart. The Gallic Empire, including Gaul, Britain and briefly Hispania, split off in 260, and the Palmyrene Empire, covering Syria, Palestine and Egypt, in 267. Claudius II Gothicus defeated a Gothic invasion at Naissus in 268 or 269, which historians see as the turning point. Aurelian, who reigned from 270 to 275, defeated the Palmyrene Empire and the Gallic Empire, so that by late 274 the empire was one again.

Many cities, especially in the west, were ruined, and towns including Rome itself, which had not needed fortifications for centuries, now built thick walls. The economy was crippled by the breakdown of trade and the debasement of the currency. Diocletian broke the cycle of usurpation by sharing rule with a colleague and then, in 293, establishing the Tetrarchy of four co-emperors. Most historians now see the crisis as marking the transition from classical antiquity to late antiquity. The empire survived until 476 in the West and until 1453 in the East.
crispo-family: The Crispo were a family of Lombard stock from Verona who settled on Venetian Negroponte, where their head, Francesco, was Baron of Astrogidis. He married Fiorenza Sanudo, daughter of Marco Sanudo, Baron of Milos, and a cousin of Nicholas III dalle Carceri, Duke of the Archipelago, who had angered Venice and his own subjects. When Nicholas died in unclear circumstances while hunting with Francesco, Francesco seized the castle of Naxos and the islanders proclaimed him duke. Venice, wanting a strong ruler against Ottoman raids, recognised him as Francesco I in 1383.

Francesco's son Giacomo I, who ruled until 1418, introduced salic law in his will, and later disputes turned on it: Venice enforced it to exclude claims through women, crowning William II over Adriana, aunt of the child duke Gian Giacomo Crispo, and later defeating Domenico Pisani's bid. Several dukes succeeded as minors under regencies. William II agreed to pay the Ottoman Empire an annual tribute, yet Naxos was occupied in the Ottoman-Venetian War of 1463-1479 and most of its people were carried off as slaves.

Heavy taxes under John III provoked a revolt of the Greek Orthodox peasants against the Catholic Italian nobility, put down with galleys of the Knights Hospitaller; John was poisoned in 1494, and Venice governed directly until his son Francesco III came of age in 1500. Francesco III, called the Mad Duke, killed his wife Taddea Caterina Loredano and was overthrown in 1511. His son John IV, crowned in 1517, aided the Knights at Rhodes in 1522 but submitted to Ottoman suzerainty when Hayreddin Barbarossa landed on Naxos in 1537.

By 1563 a Venetian report called Naxos the shadow of a principality, kept alive by the bribes John IV paid Turkish captains not to raid for slaves. His elder son Francesco died before him, and Giacomo IV succeeded in 1564. The Ottomans, who had tolerated the family only for its tribute, deposed him after two years and installed the Jewish administrator Joseph Nasi.
cristero-war: The Mexican Revolution began in 1910 against the dictatorship of Porfirio Díaz. Under Díaz the Catholic Church and the state had an informal modus vivendi in which the anticlerical articles of the liberal Constitution of 1857 were kept on paper but not enforced. The Constitution of 1917, drawn up under Venustiano Carranza, strengthened them: Article 3 made education secular, Article 27 limited the property religious associations could hold, and Article 130 separated the state from the churches. Carranza and his successor Álvaro Obregón were lenient in enforcing these articles, especially where the Church was powerful.

The rebellion was a response to President Plutarco Elías Calles's decree to enforce Article 130 strictly, an act known as the Calles Law. In July 1926 Catholic bishops endorsed an economic boycott, particularly effective in Jalisco, Michoacán, Guanajuato, Aguascalientes and Zacatecas. In September the Mexican Congress rejected the bishops' proposal to amend the offending articles, and Pope Pius XI denounced the persecution in the encyclical Iniquis afflictisque on 18 November 1926.

The government called the rebels Cristeros because they invoked Cristo Rey, Christ the King, and they soon took the name themselves. On 3 August 1926, in Guadalajara, some 400 armed Catholics shut themselves in a church and surrendered when their ammunition ran out; American consular sources reported 18 dead and 40 wounded. Further uprisings followed in Zacatecas, Guanajuato and Durango. Their leaders mostly used guerrilla tactics, since their forces were no match for federal troops, and Jalisco became the main focus. The Feminine Brigades of St. Joan of Arc helped smuggle guns and ammunition.

In October 1927 the American ambassador Dwight Morrow began a series of breakfast meetings with Calles, aided by Father John J. Burke of the National Catholic Welfare Conference. The assassination of the president-elect Obregón by the Catholic radical José de León Toral damaged the peace process. Emilio Portes Gil, interim president from September 1928, allowed the talks to resume, and in May 1929 the bishops said they would not demand repeal of the laws, only more lenient enforcement. The conflict ended on 21 June 1929.

The government often did not keep the terms of the truce; it executed some 500 Cristero leaders and 5,000 other Cristeros. Between 1926 and 1934 at least 40 priests were killed. Of 4,500 priests serving before the rebellion, only 334 were licensed to serve 15 million Catholics by 1934. A second wave of armed resistance in the late 1930s, partly against socialist education, is called the Second Cristero War. Historians interpret the rebellion as a stage in the church-state struggle that reaches back to the War of Reform, and as the last major peasant uprising after the Mexican Revolution.
cristobal-mendoza: José Cristóbal Hurtado de Mendoza y Montilla was born in Trujillo on 23 June 1772 and was first taught by his father in a Franciscan monastery. At 16 he went to Caracas, where he took a degree in philosophy in 1791, and in 1794 he became a doctor of canon and civil law in Santo Domingo. After working in law offices in Trujillo and Mérida, he moved to Barinas in late 1796, where he became known for defending local tribal groups, and in January 1807 the Council of Barinas elected him mayor.

Mendoza joined the movement of the Caracas elite against the Spanish crown on 19 April 1810 and was elected to represent Barinas in the Constituent Congress. Before he could take his seat he learned he had been named to the triumvirate, whose three members rotated the presidency every week; the other two chose him to go first, on 5 March 1811. He was the author of the Venezuelan Declaration of Independence, issued on 5 July 1811, and took part in drafting the first constitution in December 1811.

After the First Republic fell to the royalist invasion of Domingo de Monteverde, he became an aide to Simón Bolívar, who made him governor of Mérida, which he entered on 23 May 1813. As governor of Caracas he proposed the open meeting of 14 October 1813 at which Bolívar was given the title Liberator. When the forces of José Tomás Boves took Caracas in July 1814 he went into exile, and in Trinidad he wrote for the Correo del Orinoco under a pseudonym, arguing against monarchies in the Americas.

From late 1821 he served as Justice Minister of Gran Colombia. In April 1826 Francisco de Paula Santander made him intendant of the Department of Venezuela, but he failed to calm the conflict around José Antonio Páez's separatist movement, El Cosiata, and Páez exiled him to Saint Thomas. Bolívar restored him to the post in 1827.

In poor health, Mendoza resigned in the middle of 1828 and died in Caracas on 8 February 1829. With Francisco Javier Yanes he had published the first major collection of documents on Bolívar's public life. Since 1972 Venezuela has kept National Lawyer Day on his birthday, 23 June.
cristoforo-madruzzo: Madruzzo was born on 5 July 1512 at Calavino, into a noble family of Trento; his brother Eriprando was a mercenary captain who fought in the Italian Wars. He studied at Padua and Bologna, received from his older brother in 1529 a canonry at Trento and the parish of Tirol near Meran, and became a canon of Salzburg in 1536 and of Brixen in 1537. When he became Prince-Bishop of Trento in 1539 he was only a subdeacon, and he was ordained deacon, priest and bishop in 1542.

In December 1542 he was made administrator of the Bishopric of Brixen. Charles V and his brother King Ferdinand I, later emperor, esteemed him highly and sent him on many delicate missions. He took part in the imperial Diet of Ratisbon as the emperor's representative and upheld Catholic teaching against Martin Luther. In 1546, by the favour of Charles V, he received a yearly allowance of 2,000 ducats from the Archdiocese of Santiago de Compostela.

As bishop and temporal ruler of Trent he played a prominent part in the Council of Trent. He insisted that reform of the Church be taken up in earnest, as Charles V wished and in the hope of winning the Protestants back, and largely through his efforts reform enactments were passed in each session together with doctrinal decisions. He opposed Cardinal Pacheco and others who wanted to ban all vernacular translations of the Bible. Learned himself, he was a patron of the liberal arts.

In 1567 he resigned the see of Trento in favour of his nephew Ludovico and spent his last years in Italy, becoming in turn Cardinal Bishop of Sabina, Palestrina and Porto. He died at Tivoli on 5 July 1578, his 66th birthday. A few years later his remains were entombed in the family chapel in the church of Sant'Onofrio in Rome.
cristovao-da-gama: Cristóvão was a son of the navigator Vasco da Gama and a younger brother of Estêvão da Gama. He first went to India with Estêvão in 1532, returned to Portugal in 1535 and sailed to Diu with Garcia de Noronha on 6 April 1538. In 1541 Estêvão, then Viceroy of India, gave him command of a ship in the fleet he led into the Red Sea against the Ottoman naval base at Suez, where the brothers were defeated.

Back at Massawa, Estêvão sent him with 400 men-at-arms, 130 slaves, about 1,000 arquebuses and several bombards to aid Emperor Gelawdewos. The force marched inland to Debarwa, waited out the rains, and was joined by the emperor's mother, Queen Seble Wongel, from her mountain refuge. On 2 February 1542 it took a hill held by Imam Ahmad's troops at the Battle of Bacente, losing only eight men. Ahmad himself was defeated at Jarte on 4 April, when he was wounded, and again on 16 April. The eyewitness Miguel de Castanhoso wrote the main account of the campaign.

During the rains, camped at Wofla, Gama seized a weakly held mountain stronghold with about 100 men, gaining horses he badly needed. Ahmad meanwhile obtained 2,900 musketeers from the governor of Zabid in South Arabia, 900 of them handpicked Ottomans.
