On 28 August the Portuguese were heavily defeated at the Battle of Wofla, with only 170 surviving, and that night Gama, his arm broken by a bullet, was captured with 14 companions.

According to Castanhoso, and Jerónimo Lobo after him, whose accounts read like hagiography, Gama was tortured to force him to convert to Islam and then beheaded by Ahmad, who threw the head into a spring later said to heal the sick. Over 120 Portuguese joined Queen Seble Wongel, rearmed from the arms stockpiled at Debre Damo, and helped Gelawdewos raise a new army. Most sources agree that Gama's men killed Ahmad at Wayna Daga to avenge their commander. Richard Burton in 1856 called him "the most chivalrous soldier of a chivalrous age".
crnojevic-noble-family: The origins of the family are obscure. Its earliest known forebear is Đuraš Vrančić, a nobleman who served King Stefan Milutin of Serbia (r. 1282–1321). His grandson Đuraš Ilijić, a military leader under Tsar Stefan Dušan, was head of Upper Zeta from 1326 until 1362, when the family was still called Đurašević. In 1355 Dušan sent him to relieve Skradin, a Croatian city of his sister Jelena Nemanjić Šubić under Hungarian attack. The sons of Balša I killed him as a rival in 1362.

The Balšić family then greatly suppressed the Đuraševići, who kept to Budva and the Gulf of Kotor. The descendants of Crnoje Đurašević, a son of Đuraš, came to bear the name Crnojević. Crnoje's son Radič, master of Budva at the end of the 14th century, was an honorary citizen of the Republic of Dubrovnik, threatened Kotor and added Grbalj and Paštrovići to his domain, until he was killed in 1396 in a war against the House of Balšić.

From 1403 Radič's sons Đurađ and Aleksa ruled Upper Zeta as vassals of the Republic of Venice. Stefan I, called Stefanica (1451–1465), used the turmoil in Zeta to become its de facto ruler and married Mara, daughter of Gjon Kastrioti. After southern Serbia fell to the Turks in 1455, he acknowledged Venetian rule in return for autonomy in internal affairs and for the Orthodox Metropolitan.

His son Ivan (1465–1490), better known as Ivan-beg, began with a war on Venice but turned back to it in the face of the Turkish threat. The Ottomans took Upper Zeta in 1474 and his lands around Žabljak in 1478. He returned in 1481, after the death of Mehmet the Conqueror, as an Ottoman vassal, keeping the coast above Kotor to Lake Skadar, and moved the seat of the Zeta Metropolitan from Prevlaka to Cetinje, which became his capital.

Ivan's son Đurađ (1490–1496) founded the printing house of the Cetinje monastery, where the first book in the Cyrillic script of Church Slavonic among the South Slavs was printed in 1494. When his contacts with the King of France about an anti-Ottoman war became known to the Turks, he had to flee, and Montenegro fell under direct Turkish rule. His brother Stefan II then led its administration for the Ottoman Empire until 1499, and another brother, Staniša, islamised and renamed Skender-beg, ruled the ancestral lands from 1514 to 1528. Đurađ's descendants lived in Hungary and Venice and died out in 1660.
cro-magnon: The Aurignacian industry took hold, perhaps in south-central Europe, after 40,000 years ago, and replaced the Mousterian culture of the Neanderthals. The Gravettian replaced it by about 30,000 years ago; where it originated is debated, with Germany and the Buran-Kaya III rockshelter in Crimea as candidates. Cooling intensified from about 29,000 years ago and peaked about 21,000 years ago in the Last Glacial Maximum, when glaciers covered Scandinavia and the British Isles and most of Europe was polar desert. The Solutrean emerged in the south-west and the Epigravettian from Italy to the East European Plain. The Solutrean evolved into the Magdalenian by 20,000 years ago, whose peoples recolonised Europe.

Before the Last Glacial Maximum, Cro-Magnons lived at low population density, were tall, hunted big game and kept up trade routes as long as 900 km. Their weapons included spears, spear-throwers and harpoons, and the Gravettians built large huts of mammoth bone on the East European Plain. After the maximum, as big game grew scarce, they relied more on small and aquatic game. They made cave paintings, Venus figurines and bone flutes, wore beads and dyed plant-fibre clothes, and buried their dead, possibly only people of high status.

In March 1868 workers building a road to the new Les Eyzies railway station in the Dordogne broke into a rock shelter on the Vézère. Louis Lartet excavated it and reported on 21 May to the Society of Anthropology of Paris. The name comes from French abri, "shelter", Occitan cro, "hole", and Magnon, the landowner. Earlier finds, such as the Red Lady of Paviland, which William Buckland described in 1822 as a citizen of Roman Britain, had been read through a creationist model. After evolution gained acceptance, the Cro-Magnons were drawn into race theories that were overturned by the mid-twentieth century.
croatia: Croatia lies on the Adriatic coast, and the sea forms its entire southwest border. It covers 56,594 square kilometres and is divided into twenty counties within four historical and cultural regions. The Dinaric Alps rise to the highest point, the Dinara peak at 1,831 metres, near the border with Bosnia and Herzegovina. Insular Croatia consists of over a thousand islands and islets, 48 of them permanently inhabited; the largest are Cres and Krk.

In the north the hilly Hrvatsko Zagorje and the plains of Slavonia are crossed by the Danube, Drava, Kupa and Sava. Karst topography makes up about half of the country. The area around Dubrovnik is a practical exclave, separated by land from the rest by a short coastal strip belonging to Bosnia and Herzegovina, and linked to it by the Pelješac Bridge.

The area was inhabited throughout prehistory, and Neanderthal fossils from the middle Palaeolithic were found at Krapina. Illyrians and Liburnians lived there, and the first Greek colonies were established on the islands of Hvar, Korčula and Vis. In 9 CE the territory became part of the Roman Empire. Emperor Diocletian, a native of the region, built a large palace at Split and retired there after abdicating in 305 CE. In the 5th century Julius Nepos, the last de jure Western Roman Emperor, ruled a small realm from it after fleeing Italy in 475.

Avar and Croat invasions in the late 6th and first half of the 7th century destroyed almost all Roman towns. Survivors retreated to the coast, islands and mountains, and Dubrovnik was founded by survivors from Epidaurum. The origin of the Croats is debated: the predominant view is that the White Croats were a Slavic group who migrated during the Migration Period, while the Iranian theory proposes a Sarmatian-Alanic origin, drawing on names in the Tanais Tablets. The oldest stone inscription with the full ethnonym styles Duke Branimir as Dux Cruatorvm, probably between 879 and 892.

Croatia is a unitary constitutional republic with a parliamentary system. The president is directly elected for five years, and the Sabor, a unicameral parliament, holds legislative power. Its population was an estimated 3.87 million in 2024, down from a peak of 4.7 million in 1991. The 2021 census recorded 91.6% Croats and 3.2% Serbs, and about 4 million Croats live abroad. The country has ten sites on UNESCO's World Heritage List. The necktie derives from the cravat worn by 17th-century Croatian mercenaries in France.
croatian-academy-of-sciences-and-arts: The academy was founded in Zagreb under the patronage of the Croatian bishop Josip Juraj Strossmayer, a prominent advocate of higher education in the age of Croatian national romanticism. He set up a trust fund and in 1860 gave a large donation to the then viceroy, or ban, of Croatia, Josip Šokčević, so that the best minds could be brought together and books in the national languages produced in the Slavic South, with the academy taking all areas of human science under its aegis.

It was named the Yugoslav Academy of Sciences and Arts because Strossmayer wanted it to be the central scientific and artistic institution of all South Slavs. After some years of deliberation by the Croatian Parliament and the emperor Franz Joseph, it was sanctioned by law in 1866. Its first chairman was the historian Franjo Rački, and the Serbian linguist Đuro Daničić became its secretary general and played a key part in preparing its dictionary, the Croatian or Serbian Dictionary of JAZU.

The academy began with 16 full members, a number that has since grown to 160. He also initiated the Academy Palace in the Zrinjevac park, completed in 1880, and in 1884 the palace became home to the Strossmayer Gallery of Old Masters, with 256 works, mostly paintings.

The academy began publishing its journal Rad in 1867, each of its classes started its own journal in 1882, and in 1887 it issued the first Ljetopis, a yearbook, with other publications in history and ethnology. The name was briefly changed from Yugoslav to Croatian between 1941 and 1945, under the Independent State of Croatia, and the academy became the Croatian Academy of Sciences and Arts again in 1991, after Croatia became independent.

The academy operates under the Croatian Academy of Sciences and Arts Act and is divided into nine classes: social sciences; mathematical, physical and chemical sciences; natural sciences; medical sciences; philological sciences; literature; fine arts; music and musicology; and technical sciences. There are four kinds of member, full, associate, honorary and corresponding.

Full and corresponding members are each limited to 160, associate members to 100, and full members to 24 per class; only full members carry the title of academician. Its research units include the Institute for Historical Sciences, housed in a Renaissance villa in Dubrovnik with a manuscript and library collection, which publishes the journals Anali in Croatian and Dubrovnik Annals in English, and the Institute for Ornithology, which houses the Croatian bird ringing scheme.
croatian-hungarian-settlement: Before the Revolutions of 1848 the northern Croatian lands formed the Kingdom of Croatia and the Kingdom of Slavonia, separate Habsburg crown lands under the jurisdiction of the Kingdom of Hungary that functioned in practice as a single kingdom, subordinate to the government in Vienna; imperial officials called it the Kingdom of Croatia-Slavonia. The Kingdom of Dalmatia in the south, taken from the French Empire in 1815, stayed a separate division of the Austrian half of the monarchy.

After the Austro-Hungarian Compromise of 1867 placed Croatia and Slavonia under Hungarian jurisdiction, Levin Rauch replaced Josip Šokčević as acting ban. A new electoral law imposed by the king on 20 October 1867 cut the elected members to 66 and added unelected virilist members. In the election held from 19 November to 23 December 1867 the People's Party won only 14 seats, and Rauch's Unionist Party gained a majority in the Sabor, which accepted the Nagodba on 24 September 1868, though many Croats who wanted full autonomy for the South Slavs objected.

The settlement was a joint enactment of the Diet of Hungary and the Diet of Croatia, sanctioned by the Emperor of Austria as King of Hungary, and so became a fundamental law of both. The Croatian parliament elected 29 deputies to the House of Representatives of the Hungarian Diet and two members to its House of Magnates. The common Diet controlled the military, finance, commercial and mining law, customs, the post, telegraphs, railways, harbours and shipping. Article 66 listed the lands of the kingdom, including Dalmatia, although Dalmatia remained in the Austrian half.

The kingdom was now officially named the Kingdom of Croatia-Slavonia. Under Article 66 the city and port of Fiume, now Rijeka, became a corpus separatum attached to Hungary, a question the settlement left unresolved, for Croatia regarded the port as its own. In 1881 the Croatian Military Frontier and the Slavonian Military Frontier were incorporated into the kingdom, and its deputies in the Hungarian Diet rose to 40 and its magnates to three. The settlement lasted until 29 October 1918, when the Croatian Parliament ended all state ties with Austria-Hungary.
croatian-parliament: The oldest Sabor with surviving records met in Zagreb on 19 April 1273, as the general diet of the kingdom of Slavonia, and its decisions had legislative power. The earliest recorded Sabor of the Kingdom of Croatia and Dalmatia dates to 1350 at Podgrađe near Benkovac. In 1527 the session at Cetin freely chose Ferdinand I of the House of Habsburg as ruler, after centuries of personal union with Hungary. The Sabor then became a regular gathering of the nobility, and by 1558 its title had stabilised as the Parliament of the Kingdom of Croatia and Slavonia. Since 1681 it has been formally the Diet of the Kingdom of Croatia, Dalmatia and Slavonia.

In 1712 the Sabor again invoked its right to choose the ruler, supporting what became the Pragmatic Sanction of 1713 and electing Maria Theresa of Austria as monarch. During the Croatian-Ottoman Wars sessions became so impractical that in 1685 it had the ban appoint a six-member committee, which began work in 1689 and kept its mandate through the 18th and into the 19th century. Since the mid-1800s the Sabor has met regularly and its members have been regularly elected.

On 29 October 1918 the Sabor decided on independence from Austria-Hungary and the formation of the State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs, which later joined the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes. It did not meet between 1918 and 1945, apart from an unelected Sabor convened in 1942. It reconvened in 1943 as the assembly of the State Anti-fascist Council for the National Liberation of Croatia and evolved through several constitutions after the elections of November 1945. After the first multi-party elections and the constitution of 1990 it was bicameral, with a Chamber of Representatives and a Chamber of Counties, until constitutional amendments in 2001 made it unicameral.

Under the constitution the Sabor represents the people and holds legislative power. It has at least 100 and no more than 160 members, elected for four years by direct, universal and equal suffrage and secret ballot, with seats reserved for national minorities and for Croats abroad. It meets in two regular sessions a year and elects a Speaker. The Sabor has convened in Zagreb since the 13th century, but had no special building until the 18th, meeting before then in private houses, royal estates in Gradec and the bishop's residence. It first met in a new building on 6 May 1737. The present building, designed by Lav Kalda and Karlo Susan, was completed in 1911.
croatian-peasant-party: The party was founded on 22 December 1904 as the Croatian People's Peasant Party (HPSS), in the Kingdom of Croatia-Slavonia within the Hungarian half of Austria-Hungary. The Radić brothers distrusted the traditional parties and built a grassroots network around national unity and agrarianism, and they believed Croatian statehood could be achieved within a monarchy reformed into three equal parts, Austria, Hungary and Croatia. The party mattered little before 1918, but its antimilitarism and pacifism won wide support in the last year of the war, and universal manhood suffrage gave the vote to the peasants, then 80% of the population of Croatia-Slavonia.

In the new Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes it became the only significant party in Croatia. It took the name Croatian Republican Peasant Party in 1920 and called for a neutral peasant republic. After a campaign of arrests before the 1925 election, Stjepan Radić accepted the monarchy in return for his release and a place in a coalition led by the People's Radical Party, and the party became the Croatian Peasant Party (HSS).

The HSS left the government in January 1927 and in November formed the Peasant-Democratic Coalition with the Independent Democratic Party, the most popular party among the Serbs of Croatia. On 20 June 1928 the Radical deputy Puniša Račić shot several HSS members in parliament, killing two; Radić died of his wounds on 8 August. After King Alexander declared a dictatorship in 1929 the party was banned. Under Vladko Maček it set up a paramilitary force, the Croatian Peasant Defence, in 1936, and as part of the United Opposition won most votes in 1938 but only 67 of 373 seats. In 1938 and 1939 Maček also corresponded with the Italian foreign minister Galeazzo Ciano, but declined an Italian offer to finance an uprising.

The agreement of 26 August 1939 made Maček deputy prime minister, and the Ustaše denounced him as a traitor. In the Second World War some members joined the Ustaše and others the Partisans, though most supporters stayed passive. After the communist victory the party was outlawed; Maček led it in exile until his death in 1964 and Juraj Krnjević until 1988. It was restored in Croatia during the breakup of Yugoslavia and took part in coalition governments from 2000.
croesus: Croesus was a son of the Lydian king Alyattes and one of his queens, a Carian noblewoman whose name is unknown. He had at least one full sister, Aryenis, and a half-brother, Pantaleon. As governor of Adramyttium, a city Alyattes had rebuilt as a base against the Cimmerians, nomads who had attacked Lydia in several invasions, he supplied Ionian Greek mercenaries for a campaign in Caria. A rivalry grew with Pantaleon, who may have been meant as successor, and after Alyattes died it became an open succession struggle, which Croesus won.

Croesus first marched on the Ionian city of Ephesus, whose tyrant Pindar was his own nephew. Pindar went into exile, and Croesus annexed the city and patronised the rebuilding of the Temple of Artemis. He went on to subjugate mainland Ionia, Aeolis and Doris, but made treaties of friendship with the island Greeks rather than attack them. He kept the peace with the Medes, whose king Astyages was his brother-in-law, and good relations with Egypt and Babylonia.

He offered rich gifts to Delphi, among them a gold lion weighing ten talents, and the Lydians gained precedence in consulting the oracle. He is credited with the first true gold coins of standard purity, the Croeseid, which followed his father's coins of electrum. Herodotus tells how Solon, shown his wealth, said that no man's happiness can be judged before his death; the story is regarded as a moral tale rather than history.

In 550 BCE Cyrus the Great overthrew Astyages. Croesus attacked Pteria, a vassal state, and Cyrus defeated him there, then again at Thymbra, and besieged and captured Sardis, ending the Lydian kingdom. The traditional date is doubtful, since Herodotus is unreliable on the chronology.

His fate is uncertain. Herodotus, Bacchylides and Nicolaus of Damascus say he was placed on a pyre, from which rain saved him; in most versions Cyrus kept him as an adviser, while Ctesias says he became governor of Barene. Kevin Leloux argues that he was executed. After the conquest Cyrus adopted gold coinage, and the Croeseid remained in use until Darius the Great replaced it with the daric. His name became a byword for wealth.
cromarty-firth: The Cromarty Firth is an arm of the Moray Firth. Its entrance is guarded by two steep headlands, 151 metres high on the north and 141 metres on the south, called the Sutors from a fancied likeness to two shoemakers, souters in Scots, bent over their lasts. From there it runs inland westwards and then south-westwards for 19 miles (30.6 km), with an average width of 1 mile, widening to about 5 miles between Nigg Bay and Cromarty Bay. Its principal river, the River Conon, enters at its head.

Dingwall stands near the head, Cromarty near the mouth, from which the firth takes its name, and Invergordon on the north shore. One bridge crosses it, carrying the A9 road between Ardullie and Findon, and a four-car ferry runs between Cromarty and Nigg in summer. The firth is a Special Protection Area for wildlife, home to bottlenose dolphins, harbour porpoises, grey seals and harbour seals, and visited seasonally by minke whales.

The firth forms one of the safest and most commodious anchorages in the north of Scotland, and Invergordon was at one time a major base of the Royal Navy's Home Fleet. In 1931 the firth was the scene of the Invergordon Mutiny. An airfield near Evanton was built to take aircraft from the fleet carriers while they lay at anchor. During World War II a large training and operational base for Catalina amphibious aircraft and Sunderland seaplanes stretched from Invergordon to Alness point, and a memorial to the men killed on its missions was placed there in 2001.

The Evanton airfield and the wartime seaplane base are both industrial estates now. At Nigg a yard with a dry dock for fabricating and repairing oil platforms opened in 1972 as a joint venture of Brown & Root and George Wimpey; owned by Global Energy Group since 2011, it is a centre for North Sea oil and renewable energy known as Nigg Energy Park. Elsewhere along the firth are facilities for cruise ships, oil processing and bulk cargo, regulated by the Cromarty Firth Port Authority.
cross-of-lorraine: The Cross of Lorraine is a heraldic two-barred cross, a vertical line crossed by two shorter horizontal bars. In most renditions the upper bar is the shorter, though bars of equal length also occur. Its ultimate origin lies in the crozier of an archbishop. It reached the Duchy of Lorraine through the Kingdom of Hungary. Béla III was the first Hungarian monarch to use the two-barred cross as a symbol of royal power, in the late 12th century, and the historian Pál Engel thinks he probably took it from the Byzantine Empire. René the Good, a descendant of the Hungarian kings, used it as his personal sigil while laying claim to four kingdoms.

René II, Duke of Lorraine, inherited the symbol from his distant ancestors of the House of Anjou of Hungary and placed it on his flag before the Battle of Nancy in January 1477. He defeated the army of Charles the Bold, Duke of Burgundy, who had occupied the duchy, and regained his lands. All coins struck for him bore the cross afterwards, though it was still known as the Cross of Anjou in the 16th century.

The north-eastern part of Lorraine, the Moselle department, was annexed to Germany with Alsace from 1871 to 1918 and again from 1940 to 1944, and the cross served French patriots as a rallying point for recovering the lost provinces. Capitaine de corvette Thierry d'Argenlieu suggested it as the symbol of the Free French Forces led by Charles de Gaulle, as an answer to the Nazi swastika. It appeared on the flags of Free French warships, on aircraft and on the medal of the Order of Liberation.

Similar two-barred crosses appear in the heraldry of other countries. A golden double cross with equal bars, the Cross of Jagiellons, was used by Jogaila from his conversion to Christianity in 1386 and entered the arms of Lithuania. It is also a national symbol in Belarus, as the Cross of St. Euphrosyne of Polatsk. De Gaulle is commemorated by a Cross of Lorraine 43 m high at Colombey-les-Deux-Églises. In 1902 the Paris physician Gilbert Sersiron proposed it as the emblem of the crusade against tuberculosis, and it became the badge of the American Lung Association.
cross-of-the-angels: The cross, a pre-romanesque Asturian reliquary, is the first piece of jewellery made in the Kingdom of Asturias to have survived. It is a Greek cross measuring 46.5 by 45.7 centimetres and 2.5 centimetres thick, formed of two pieces of cedar wood with a round disc at the centre. From its side arms hang rings with chains of pearls and precious stones, the pendilia, comparable to the votive crosses and crowns of the Visigothic treasure of Guarrazar. Its present appearance is the result of careful reconstruction after it was damaged in the robbery of the Camara Santa in August 1977.

Alfonso II gave the cross to the Church of San Salvador in Oviedo, and the gift is usually read as the king's thanks for his restoration to the throne after the years of his incarceration in the monastery of Abelania. Its inscription, in which Alfonso offers the cross as a humble servant, declares that by this sign the pious are protected and the enemy defeated; and that whoever dares to take it, except where its own free will allows, shall be struck dead by divine lightning. It ends by dating the work to the era 846.

The cross became the symbol of Oviedo around the 15th century, though it is said to have been used as the city's seal as early as 1262. An engraving in the old city walls shows it with the Greek letters alpha and omega hanging from its arms as a sign of consecration. It appears today in the coat of arms of both the city of Oviedo and the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Oviedo.
cross-of-victory: According to legend, the plain wooden core was carried against the Muslims of al-Andalus by Pelagius at the Battle of Covadonga in 722, which is regarded as the founding event of the Kingdom of Asturias. It was then said to have been kept by his son Favila of Asturias in the Church of Santa Cruz at Cangas de Onís, the kingdom's first capital, which Favila and his wife Froiluba built in 737. A study of 2010, however, radiocarbon dated the wood to the late 9th century, roughly the age of its decorated casing.

The Latin cross measures 92 by 72 centimetres. Its core is two pieces of oak, 2.5 centimetres thick, with circular ends finished in three foils and joined at the centre by a circular disc. The whole is covered with gold leaf and filigree, and the front is decorated with coloured enamel, pearls, precious stones and gold thread; the casing holds 152 gems and imitation gems. An inscription in soldered gold letters on the back names the royal donors to the Church of San Salvador and records that the work was made at the Castle of Gauzón. Alfonso III gave it to mark a hundred years of the Asturian kingdom's victories and conquests.

Like the other treasures of the Cámara Santa, the cross was badly damaged during the Spanish Civil War of 1936-39. From 1942 it regained its gems through popular donations, but the goldsmiths Horacio Rivero Alvarez and Luis Aguilar altered the position of the medallions on both faces, and new enamels added in 1971 by the German goldsmith Werner Henneberger also departed from the original design. On 9 August 1977 it was stolen with the Agate box and the Cross of the Angels, and the thieves tore off its stones and gold plating; its present appearance is the result of a reconstruction of 1978. Since December 1990 the flag of the Principality of Asturias has shown the cross on a blue field, set towards the hoist.
cross-river-state: Cross River State lies in the South-South zone of Nigeria and takes its name from the Cross River, which bisects its interior before forming much of its western border and flowing into the Cross River Estuary. It covers 20,156 square kilometres. Benue State lies to the north, Ebonyi and Abia states to the west and Akwa Ibom State to the south-west, while the eastern border is part of the national border with Cameroon.

Most of the interior is covered by the Cross-Sanaga-Bioko coastal forests, with a forest and savanna mosaic in the far north and mangroves on the southern coast. Protected areas such as Cross River National Park, the Afi Mountain Wildlife Sanctuary and the Mbe Mountains Community Forest shelter some of Nigeria's last Cross River gorillas, drills and forest elephants. The climate is tropical, with heavy annual rainfall, and cooler on the high plateau of Obudu.

In the pre-colonial period the area was divided among its ethnic groups. Some joined the Aro Confederacy, while the Efik founded the city-state of Akwa Akpa, Old Calabar. Calabar became a British protectorate in 1884 as the capital of the Oil Rivers Protectorate, although the British did not gain formal control of the whole area until the early 1900s. The protectorate was renamed the Niger Coast Protectorate and then incorporated into the Southern Nigeria Protectorate. Much of the area became a centre of anti-colonial resistance during the Women's War.

After independence in 1960 the area was part of the Eastern Region. On 27 May 1967 General Yakubu Gowon's government created South-Eastern State from the region's eastern part. Within two months the Igbo-majority remainder of the old region attempted to secede as Biafra, and in the Nigerian Civil War Calabar and its port were hard fought over. The state was renamed Cross River State in 1976. In September 1987 its western part was separated to form Akwa Ibom State. The state had also included the Bakassi Peninsula, which was ceded to Cameroon under the Greentree Agreement.

Calabar is the capital and a major seaport on the navigable waters of the Cross River, and the state has eighteen Local Government Areas. Its peoples include the Efik, the Ekoi or Ejagham, the Yakurr, Bekwarra, Igede and many others. English is the common language, with Efik, Bekwarra and Ejagham among the principal local ones. The economy relies on farming and fishing, with crops such as cocoyam, oil palm, yam, cocoa and plantain. Visitors come to the Ikom Monoliths, a series of volcanic-stone monoliths of unknown age, to the Obudu mountain resort and to the annual Calabar Carnival held in December.
crossbow: A crossbow is a ranged weapon in which a bow-like assembly called a prod is mounted horizontally on a frame called a tiller or stock. It shoots arrow-like projectiles called bolts or quarrels. Unlike an archer, who must draw and shoot in one quick motion, the crossbow user spans the weapon and cocks it, and a trigger-released mechanism then holds the string under tension. The weapon can be carried ready to shoot, the user has unlimited time to aim, and it can be used effectively with much less training than the English longbow or the bows of steppe nomads.

The drawbacks were weight and slowness. High draw weights required gears, windlasses, pulleys or cranequins to span the weapon, which were awkward on a battlefield, and medieval crossbows had short draw lengths, so they needed very high draw weights.

The earliest known crossbows were invented in China in the first millennium BCE. Bronze crossbow locks dated to about 650 BCE have been found there, and bronze bolts from a Chu burial site date to the mid-5th century BCE. The Chinese trigger was made of three cast bronze pieces, which gave a mechanical advantage so that heavy draw weights could be released with a light pull. It shifted the role of projectiles in war, especially in the Qin unification wars. In Greece the gastraphetes, or belly-bow, appeared probably in the late 5th century BCE and was used at the Siege of Motya in 397 BCE. It was likely invented independently of the Chinese crossbow.

References to the crossbow in Europe are essentially absent from the 5th to the 10th century. It reappears in 947 as a French weapon at the siege of Senlis and in 984 at the siege of Verdun. Crossbows were used at the Battle of Hastings in 1066 and by the 12th century had become common battlefield weapons. European prods were wood until composite prods appeared in the 13th century and steel ones around the 14th, when winches and cranequins were also used. In the Islamic world the weapon was regarded as foreign, and Islamic texts do not mention it before the 14th century, though Mamluk cavalry used crossbows.
crossing-of-the-rubicon: In the late Roman Republic the Rubicon was a small river flowing east from the Apennine Mountains into the Adriatic Sea. With the much larger Arno on the western side of the mountains, it marked the boundary between the province of Cisalpine Gaul to the north and the lands ruled directly by Rome and its allies to the south. Caesar had been governor of a region stretching from southern Gaul to Illyricum, and as his term drew to a close the Senate ordered him to disband his army and return to Rome.

Provincial governors held imperium, the right to command, only in their provinces. Roman law allowed only elected magistrates, the consuls and praetors, to hold imperium within Italy, and a governor who entered Italy at the head of his troops lost it. Exercising imperium unlawfully was a capital offence, and so was obeying a general who lacked it: a general who led an army into Italy made himself and his soldiers outlaws condemned to death, so generals had to disband their armies first.

In January 49 BCE Caesar led the 13th Legion, Legio XIII, south over the river from Cisalpine Gaul into Italy, deliberately breaking the law on imperium and making armed conflict inevitable. The exact date is unknown, but scholars usually place it on the night of 10 to 11 January, judging from how fast messengers could travel. The Roman historian Suetonius shows Caesar hesitating at the river and attributes the crossing to a supernatural apparition, and reports that he said alea iacta est, the die is cast. The scene's importance is somewhat undermined by the fact that part of his forces had already entered Italy, with his legate Quintus Hortensius occupying the town of Ariminum.

Caesar's swift action forced Pompey, the consuls and much of the Senate to flee Rome. The civil war that followed ended with Caesar as dictator for life, dictator perpetuo. The phrase crossing the Rubicon survives as an idiom for committing oneself to a risky course with no way back, the point of no return.
crotone: Crotone is a city and comune in Calabria. The promontory of Kroton was inhabited in the Bronze Age by indigenous peoples. The Greek foundation was led by Myscellus of Rhypes in Achaea, after the Delphic Oracle told him to cross the vast sea and found Kroton next to the river Esaro. The Achaeans were driven by lack of cultivable land and population pressure. Excavation shows that most existing settlements in the area disappeared, and that Greek settlers married indigenous women from the first generation.

Croton became one of the most flourishing cities of Magna Graecia, reaching a population between 50,000 and 80,000 around 500 BCE. From 588 BCE it produced many Olympic winners, the best known being Milo, and its physicians were the foremost among the Greeks. Pythagoras founded his school there around 530 BCE. About 510 BCE Croton destroyed Sybaris with an army under Milo. A revolt led by the oligarch Cylon then massacred many Pythagoreans.

Croton declined, was captured by Dionysius of Syracuse in 379 BCE and by Agathocles in 295 BCE, and submitted to Rome in 277 BCE. Hannibal made it his winter quarters for three years in the Second Punic War. A Roman colony followed in 194 BCE. About 870 Saracens sacked it, and the Normans later conquered it. It became part of the Kingdom of Italy in 1861.

The city was known as Cotrone from the Middle Ages until 1928, and in 1992 it became the capital of the Province of Crotone. Archaeology has recovered the ancient wall circuit, enclosing at least 617 hectares, and the layout of the Greek town. The Castle of Charles V, of the 16th century, houses the town museum, and the cathedral holds the icon of the Black Madonna of Capo Colonna. The national archaeological museum, founded in 1968, holds finds from the Sanctuary of Hera Lacinia.
crowfoot: Crowfoot was born to Kainai parents, Istowun-ehʼpata (Packs a Knife) and Axkahp-say-pi (Attacked Towards Home). He was first called Shot-Close, later Bear Ghost and then Packs a Knife after his father was killed in a raid on the Crow when the boy was five. A year later his mother married Akay-nehka-simi (Many Names) of the Siksika, among whom Crowfoot grew up. He fought in as many as nineteen battles and was often wounded, and his people called him Manistokos, father of the people.

Crowfoot worked to keep good relations with the Hudson's Bay Company and the North-West Mounted Police. Late in 1866 he stopped warriors from looting a train of company carts and killing its Métis drivers and escorted the Métis back to Fort Edmonton. He refused Sitting Bull's call to fight the United States and the police together, though he later made peace with the Sioux when they fled into Canada.

At the Treaty 7 talks the government took him, wrongly, for the leader of the whole Blackfoot Confederacy. Red Crow of the Kainai said he would sign if Crowfoot did, and on 21 October Crowfoot told his people: The police have protected us as the feathers of the bird protect it from the frosts of winter.

When rations were cut in 1881 and 1882 and the chief Bull Elk was arrested unjustly, Crowfoot confronted the police but sent his men home; Bull Elk was acquitted, and Edgar Dewdney replaced the agent Norman Macleod with Cecil Denny. In the North-West Rebellion of 1885 Crowfoot's adopted son, the Cree chief Poundmaker, was deeply involved, and Crowfoot sheltered Cree refugees in his camp while keeping his warriors out of the fighting.

The farming programme that followed did not supply the tools and help it promised, and famine and disease killed most of Crowfoot's children. Poundmaker died while visiting him after his release from prison. Crowfoot died of tuberculosis at Blackfoot Crossing on 25 April 1890, and eight hundred of his people attended his funeral. His jacket, bow and pipe were returned from Exeter to the Blackfoot Crossing Historical Park in 2014, and Willie Dunn's film The Ballad of Crowfoot of 1968 was the first National Film Board of Canada film by an Indigenous director.
crown-colony: Early English colonies were often proprietary colonies, founded and run by companies under charters granted by the monarch. The first royal colony was Virginia, after 1624, when the Crown revoked the charter of the Virginia Company and took over the government. Bermuda followed in 1684, when the charter of the Somers Isles Company was revoked; until 1968 the government in London appointed its governor. Elected lower houses began earlier, with the House of Burgesses of Virginia in 1619 and the House of Assembly of Bermuda in 1620.

A Crown colony usually had a governor who represented the Crown, held executive power and was appointed by the British government through the monarch. He governed with or without a local council, which in larger colonies was split into an executive council and a legislative council. British citizens in Crown colonies had no representation in local government or limited representation in a lower house, and the House of Commons never included seats for any colony.

In 1918 there were three types. Some, such as Bermuda, Jamaica, Ceylon and Fiji, had an appointed upper house and an elected lower house. Others, such as British Honduras, Sierra Leone and Hong Kong, had bodies staffed by Crown appointees. The fewest, among them Gibraltar, Saint Helena and Singapore, were ruled directly by a governor.

Until the mid-19th century the term mainly meant colonies acquired through wars, such as Trinidad and Tobago. Later it covered every British territory other than British India, including self-governing colonies such as New South Wales and New Zealand. In the 1800s some gained self-government and delegated most internal legislation to elected assemblies, overseen by the Colonial Office. For some territories the Dominion Office replaced it in 1925.

The British Nationality Act 1981 renamed the remaining colonies British Dependent Territories from 1 January 1983, and since 2002 they have been British Overseas Territories. Hong Kong, a Crown colony without substantial autonomy, passed to the People's Republic of China in 1997.
crown-dependencies: The Crown Dependencies are three offshore island territories in the British Isles: the Bailiwick of Guernsey, the Bailiwick of Jersey, together known as the Channel Islands, and the Isle of Man. Their status is that of territories for which the United Kingdom is responsible, rather than sovereign states, and they are therefore not members of the Commonwealth of Nations, although all three take part in the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association and have their own teams in the Commonwealth Games. They are members of the British–Irish Council. The Kilbrandon Report of 1973 described them as like miniature states.

Each has its own legislative assembly. The Bailiwick of Guernsey has three jurisdictions, Guernsey, Alderney and Sark, with parliaments called the States of Deliberation, the States of Alderney and the Chief Pleas. The Isle of Man's Tynwald, consisting of the House of Keys and the Legislative Council, claims to be the world's oldest parliament in continuous existence, dating back to 979. Legislation ultimately requires the approval of the King in Council, though Acts of the UK Parliament do not normally extend to the islands without their consent on domestic matters.

The Crown Dependencies are distinguished from the British Overseas Territories, which are remnants of the British Empire. Their relationship with the Crown is much older and springs from their status as feudatory territories subject to the English Crown. Their political systems evolved in an ad hoc manner, so that each has particular and unique structures. Since 1290 the Channel Islands have been governed as two Bailiwicks, each headed by a Bailiff, with a Lieutenant Governor representing the Crown. In the Isle of Man the monarch is styled Lord of Mann, a title held at different times by Norse, Scottish and English kings and nobles until it was revested in the British monarchy in 1765.

The United Kingdom is solely responsible for defence and international representation, although framework agreements signed in 2007 and 2008 provide that it will not act internationally on the islands' behalf without consultation. Until a declaration agreed in 1950, the islands were considered part of British metropolitan territory for international agreements; afterwards the three were treated as distinct from the United Kingdom and from each other. The Crown Dependencies have never been member states of the European Union. They belong with the United Kingdom and Ireland to the Common Travel Area. Gavin St Pier, a former Chief Minister of Guernsey, has disputed the term itself, arguing that it was an administrative invention of Whitehall and that it wrongly implies dependence on the Crown.
crown-of-ireland-act-1542: Before the act, English monarchs had ruled Ireland as Lords of Ireland. Under the papal bull Laudabiliter the island had been made a feudal province of the Holy See under the temporal power of the English monarch, who handed to the papacy the annual tribute levied on the nobility and people of Ireland. The act made King Henry VIII of England the first monarch to hold the title King of Ireland.

Its long title was An Act that the King of England, his Heirs and Successors, be Kings of Ireland. The Parliament of Ireland, meeting in Dublin, heard it read in English and Irish, and in the upper house in Irish only. Section 2 ordered that a proclamation of the act be made in every shire of Ireland. Among the 18th-century Irish Patriot Party it was known as the Act of Annexation.

The papacy and Europe's Catholic monarchs at first refused to recognise the title, still regarding Ireland as a papal fief. Under the Catholic Mary I, Pope Paul IV's bull of 1555 recognised Philip and Mary as King and Queen of England and its dominions including Ireland, without naming Ireland a kingdom outright. When the Protestant Elizabeth I succeeded in 1558, Pope Pius V's bull Regnans in Excelsis of 1570 declared her a heretic and released her subjects from their allegiance.

Ireland remained a kingdom with its own parliament until 1801, when fear of revolution after the Irish Rebellion of 1798 led to its union with Great Britain. Words of section 2 were repealed by the Statute Law Revision Act 1950. The act stayed unamended after the Irish Free State was formed in December 1922, and although it ceased to have effect once the Republic of Ireland Act 1948 abolished the monarchy in Irish law, it was formally repealed there only in 1962.
crown-of-the-kingdom-of-poland: The Crown of the Kingdom of Poland, commonly the Polish Crown, was a political and legal concept that expressed the idea of the kingdom as a permanent entity, distinct from its reigning monarch and with its own rights, institutions and territories. It grew out of the Polish monarchy's consolidation under the last Piast kings and gained importance under the Angevin dynasty.

Poland had been regarded as a kingdom since Bolesław I the Brave was crowned in 1025, and even during the period of partition its Piast princes were seen as members of a royal dynasty. Kraków, where Wawel Cathedral held the royal jewels, and Gniezno, the place of coronation, were its two centres.

The idea of corona regni had earlier arisen in England, France, Aragon, Hungary and Bohemia. In Poland it gained force after Casimir the Great's death. The annulment of his testament in 1370 was in effect the first act taken in the name of the Crown: the court ruled that the ruler could not diminish the territory of the Crown, and Louis accepted. Jan Radlica began in 1381 to style himself supreme chancellor of the Kingdom of Poland.

On 13 and 14 August 1385 the Union of Krewo, a set of prenuptial agreements between the Lithuanian Grand Duke Jogaila and Polish lords, formed a personal union of Poland and Lithuania. Jogaila pledged to attach his Lithuanian and Ruthenian lands permanently to the Crown. He was baptised in Kraków on 15 February 1386 as Władysław and married Queen Jadwiga days later. The union lapsed and was renewed several times: Casimir IV Jagiellon accepted the Polish throne only on terms of equal states and was crowned on 25 June 1447, and in 1492 the Lithuanian Council of Lords chose a separate grand duke.

On 1 July 1569 the Union of Lublin created the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth as a real union. The Crown and the Grand Duchy kept separate territories, armies, treasuries and most institutions, under one monarch and a joint Sejm. The union also made the monarchy elective, and the Jagiellonian line ended once Henry de Valois was elected on 16 May 1573. The Constitution of 3 May 1791 was drafted over 32 months, mainly by Stanisław II Augustus, as a constitutional monarchy. Russia invaded in 1792, and the Grodno Sejm annulled it after less than 19 months.

After 1569 the Crown's lands formed two provinces, Greater Poland and Lesser Poland, divided into voivodeships. Royal Prussia was a semi-autonomous province from 1569 to 1772. Rzeczpospolita, Commonwealth, became an alternative name for the state.
crown-of-thorns: According to the New Testament, a woven crown of thorns was placed on the head of Jesus before his crucifixion, both to cause him pain and to mock his claim of authority. It is mentioned in the gospels of Matthew, Mark and John, and the gospels do not say what became of it. The oldest known mention of a crown venerated as a relic is by Paulinus of Nola, writing after 409. The Breviary of Jerusalem, dated to about 530, and Antoninus of Piacenza place it in the Basilica of Mount Zion, where it was still seen in 870. François de Mély supposed that the crown went to Constantinople not much before 1063.

The exact plant used to make the crown is not confirmed. The relic in Paris was examined in the nineteenth century and appeared to be a twisted circlet of rushes of Juncus balticus. The thorns kept in other reliquaries appeared to be Ziziphus spina-christi, the jujube tree, which grows around Jerusalem. According to de Mély, the sixty or seventy thorns that Louis IX and his successors distributed had already been separated from the band of rushes by the time it reached Paris. De Mély counted more than 700 holy thorn relics, many of them third-class relics, that is objects touched to a first-class relic.

Baldwin II, the Latin Emperor of Constantinople, anxious for support for his tottering empire, offered the crown to Louis IX of France. It was then in the hands of the Venetians as security for a loan of 13,134 gold pieces. It was redeemed and taken to Paris, where Louis IX built the Sainte-Chapelle, completed in 1248, to receive it. After the French Revolution, during which it was kept for a time in the Bibliothèque Nationale, the Concordat of 1801 restored it to the Church, and it was deposited in Notre-Dame de Paris.

Individual thorns were given by French kings to other European rulers: the Holy Thorn Reliquary in the British Museum was made in the 1390s for Jean, duc de Berry. In 1543 John Calvin, in his Treatise on Relics, listed the many places claiming parts of the crown and concluded that there must be falsehood and imposition, noting that the ancient Church never knew what had become of it. Members of the Paris Fire Brigade saved the relic from the fire at Notre-Dame on 15 April 2019, and it returned to the cathedral in December 2024.
crucible-steel: Pre-industrial fires of charcoal or coal could not melt iron or steel, but pig iron, with its lower melting point, could be melted. By heating wrought iron or steel together with pig iron for a long time, carbon spread from one into the other and gave a medium-carbon steel ingot, while slag and oxide floated to the surface. Such ingots were very hard but often uneven, with regions of high and low carbon. Slow cooling over several days could give the frost-like or woodgrain-like pattern seen on Damascus blades after polishing and etching.

Islamic writers such as al-Tarsusi and Abu Rayhan Biruni (c. 973–1050) describe three methods: carburisation of wrought iron packed with carbon, decarburisation of cast iron, and the fusion of wrought and cast iron together in a crucible.

The South Indian and Sri Lankan steel is commonly called wootz, generally taken as an English corruption of the Canarese ukko or the Telugu hookoo. Proven production sites in south India, such as Konasamudram and Gatihosahalli, date from at least the 16th century, and by the 17th century Hyderabad was the main centre. In Sri Lanka the earliest confirmed site, in the Knuckles range, dates to the 6th to 10th centuries CE. Excavations at Akhsiket and Pap in the Ferghana Valley and at Merv in Turkmenistan show large-scale production from the late 8th or early 9th to the late 12th century.

Benjamin Huntsman, a clockmaker of Handsworth near Sheffield seeking better steel for clock springs, used a coke-fired furnace reaching 1,600 °C that held up to twelve clay crucibles of about 15 kg each. Charged with blister steel and a glass flux, the pots stayed in the furnace about three hours before the slag was skimmed off and the steel poured into moulds. Full melting gave an even structure, and the steel was later used for scissors, axes, swords, tools and cutlery. Robert Hadfield and Robert Forester Mushet used the process to make the first alloy steels.

European scientists turned to wootz from the 1790s; George Pearson's report to the Royal Society in 1795 was the first to use the word in print, and Michael Faraday was also fascinated by it. Huntsman's process was used to make tool steel until methods using an electric arc were developed in the early 20th century, and the crucible process is now obsolete.
crucifixion: Crucifixion was common in the ancient world, and Greece, Persia, Carthage and Rome are among the civilisations known to have used it widely. The earliest clear reference may be a post-mortem one in Herodotus, who says that Polycrates, the tyrant of Samos, was executed in 522 BCE by Oroetus, satrap of Lydia, and that his dead body was then crucified. In earlier pre-Roman Greek texts the verb anastauroo usually meant impale.

In Rome the Greek and Latin words covered many painful forms of execution. Crucifixion was generally meant to deter others, and victims were sometimes left on display after death. It was intended to be slow, painful, gruesome, humiliating and public, and the word excruciating comes from it. In Japan it was introduced during the Sengoku period (1467–1573) and was called haritsuke.

Crucifixion is a method of execution and torture in which the condemned is tied or nailed to a large wooden cross, beam or stake and usually left to hang until death. The gibbet took many shapes. It could be a simple upright stake, called crux simplex, or have a crossbeam at the top, in a T shape (crux commissa), or just below it (crux immissa), the form familiar in Christian symbolism. The oldest image of a Roman crucifixion, a graffito at Puteoli of the time of Trajan or Hadrian, shows a T-shaped cross.

Death could take minutes, hours or days according to the method, the victim's health and the environment. If a nail severed an artery death could follow within minutes. Josephus records that three of his acquaintances, crucified captives, were taken down at Titus's order, and that one of them recovered.

Josephus and Appian refer to thousands crucified in the Roman–Jewish wars, but archaeological remains are few. The best-known was found in a Jewish tomb of the 1st century at Givat HaMivtar in Jerusalem in 1968, in an ossuary inscribed Jehohanan, the son of Hagakol. Nicu Haas found a heel bone with a nail driven through its side, suggesting that the feet were nailed from the side.

Jesus was crucified, and the event became central to Christianity and is represented by the cross and the crucifix. Tradition holds that Saint Peter was crucified upside down and Saint Andrew on an X-shaped cross. Between 73 and 71 BCE, about 6,000 followers of Spartacus were crucified along the Appian Way between Capua and Rome.
crucifixion-of-jesus: The crucifixion is described in the four canonical Gospels, referred to in the epistles of the New Testament and attested by later ancient sources. Paul is the earliest surviving source to document it, and the earliest detailed accounts are in the Gospels. In the Synoptic Gospels Jesus predicts his death in three places. All four Gospels end with an extended narrative of his arrest, a trial before the Sanhedrin and a final trial at the court of Pontius Pilate, who governed Judaea from 26 to 36 CE.

According to the Gospels, Pilate had Jesus flogged and condemned him to death, not for being found guilty but to satisfy either a crowd or the religious leaders before him. The Synoptic Gospels say the Roman soldiers made Simon of Cyrene carry his cross, while John says only that Jesus bore it himself. At Calvary, or Golgotha, he was stripped of his clothing and hung between two convicted men. Mark places the crucifixion at the third hour, about 9 a.m., and his death by the ninth hour, around 3 p.m.

John says a sign above the cross read "Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews" in Hebrew, Latin and Greek. The Synoptic Gospels report darkness from noon to mid-afternoon and the tearing of the Temple veil; John mentions neither. The exact location is a matter of conjecture, though the accounts place it outside the walls of Jerusalem.

Scholars hold the fact of the crucifixion to be accepted by a near universal consensus, though not its details. There is no consensus on the date. It is generally agreed to have been on a Friday on or near Passover, with estimates between 30 and 33 CE; Rainer Riesner holds that 7 April 30 is the most likely, and 3 April 33 is another preferred date. Josephus wrote that Pilate condemned Jesus to the cross, though the passage includes later interpolations, and Tacitus, writing about 116, said that Christus suffered the extreme penalty under Tiberius at the hands of Pontius Pilatus.

Christians call his suffering and death the Passion and treat it as central to doctrines of salvation and atonement. Muslims maintain that Jesus was not crucified, on the basis of Quran 4:157–158, and some early Gnostic sects also denied it. The cross became a central element of Christian symbolism and the crucifixion a key subject of Christian art.
crusade-of-varna: After 1430 the Ottomans returned to their aim of controlling all lands south of the Danube. Sultan Murad II began raiding Transylvania in 1432, and the attacks intensified after King Sigismund died in 1437. In 1439 Smederevo capitulated and Serbia became an Ottoman province, and Despot Đurađ Branković fled to Hungary. In 1440 Murad besieged Belgrade but failed to take it. Hungary meanwhile fell into civil war over the succession, and Władysław of Poland was crowned king on 17 July 1440. John Hunyadi won him the position of nádor of Transylvania, with responsibility for the southern border, and defeated Ottoman raids in 1441 and 1442. The Church had long urged a crusade, and Pope Eugene IV published a crusading bull on 1 January 1443.

War was proclaimed on Palm Sunday 1443 at the diet of Buda. With an army of 40,000, mostly Hungarians, Władysław and Hunyadi crossed the Danube and took Niš and Sofia. The crusaders expected that Murad's fief-holding cavalry, who had to gather the harvest to pay taxes, could not mobilise quickly, and Hunyadi's winter experience and better armour added to their advantage. They won at Niš and Aleksinac but were defeated at Zlatitsa Pass on 12 December 1443. On the march home they ambushed a pursuing force at Kunovica and took Mahmud Bey prisoner, so that they returned to Buda in February 1444 as heroes, and the king and Church spread word of victories and contradicted anyone who mentioned the loss.

Murad, pressed by his wife Mara, daughter of Branković, and by the sister of his vizier, sought peace. Talks at Edirne and Szeged ended in the Peace of Szeged, sworn on 15 August 1444, though Cardinal Julian Cesarini pressed for the crusade to continue. Soon after the treaty's requirements were met, Władysław gathered an army of 16,000 men, mostly Hungarian regular troops with forces from Poland, Transylvania, Croatia and Bosnia and mercenaries, joined by 4,000 Wallachians at Nicopolis. Murad, who had retired, came back to lead his army.

On 10 November 1444 the armies met at Varna. The Ottomans won a decisive victory despite heavy losses, and the crusaders lost King Władysław and over 15,000 men. Hungary fell back into civil war until Hunyadi was elected regent for the infant Ladislaus in June 1446. Together with the Ottoman victory at the Second Battle of Kosovo in 1448, Varna deterred European states from sending substantial help to the Byzantines before the fall of Constantinople in 1453. Hunyadi's victory at the siege of Belgrade in 1456 halted Ottoman expansion beyond the Balkans for seventy years, until the Hungarian army was crushed at Mohács in 1526.
crusader-states: The Crusader states, also called Outremer, from the French for overseas, were four Catholic polities in the Levant and south-eastern Anatolia, existing from 1098 to 1291. From north to south they were the County of Edessa (1098 to 1150), the Principality of Antioch (1098 to 1268), the County of Tripoli (1102 to 1289) and the Kingdom of Jerusalem (1099 to 1291). Their foundation followed the First Crusade, proclaimed by the Latin Church in 1095. At the Council of Piacenza that year the Byzantine emperor Alexios I Komnenos asked Pope Urban II for help against the Seljuks, and Urban went far beyond what the emperor probably had in mind by calling for the First Crusade at the Council of Clermont.

The settlers were called Franks or Latins, and were mainly French-speaking Roman Catholics, while the natives were mostly Arabic- or Greek-speaking Muslims, Christians of other denominations, and Jews. The name Crusader states can mislead, because from 1130 onward very few of the Franks were Crusaders.

In 1098 Baldwin of Boulogne took over Edessa in a coup and Bohemond of Taranto remained ruling prince in captured Antioch. The siege of Jerusalem in 1099 ended in a decisive victory over the Fatimid Caliphate. Edessa fell to the Zengid Turks in 1144. In 1244 Khwarazmian troops sacked Jerusalem, and at La Forbie on 18 October the Franks were defeated, with 16,000 Frankish warriors killed.

The Bahri Mamluks took power in Egypt in 1250. They captured Antioch in 1268 and Tripoli in 1289, and the fall of Acre in 1291 ended the Kingdom of Jerusalem nearly 200 years after its founding. The survivors fled to the Kingdom of Cyprus.

The states were feudal. Jerusalem's royal administration sat in the city until its loss and then in Acre, with the usual household officers of European rulers, and the courts of Antioch produced the Assizes of Antioch. Historians now regard the Franks as a minority society, largely urban and living apart from the native peoples under separate legal and religious systems. Estimates of their number range from 120,000 to 300,000, perhaps at least 15 per cent of the population. Castles blended European, Byzantine and Muslim traditions, and historians regard them as the most impressive artistic achievement of the crusaders.

The military orders emerged here. The Knights Templar, whose rule was confirmed at the Council of Troyes in 1129, grew from a brotherhood attached to the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, and the Hospitallers took up military functions in the 1130s. The states were economic centres tied by sea to Europe and by land to Mesopotamia, Syria and the Nile.
crusades: Sites linked to Jesus's ministry, including the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem, were popular pilgrimage destinations in Roman Palestine. Jerusalem fell to Caliph Umar in 638, and by the mid-10th century three rival caliphates had emerged: the Umayyads in al-Andalus, the Shi'ite Fatimids in Egypt and the Abbasids in the Middle East. By the late 11th century, Christian just war theory, increasing aristocratic piety and the popularity of penitential journeys to the Holy Land had created a context for armed pilgrimages. In March 1095 Pope Urban II received envoys from Emperor Alexios I Komnenos, who asked for military aid at the Council of Piacenza.

On 27 November 1095, at the Council of Clermont, Urban announced a military campaign against the Turkomans. According to most accounts he promised spiritual rewards, though accounts differ on whether he offered reduced penance or full remission of sin. Popular enthusiasm outran his wish to enlist only trained warriors, and Peter the Hermit attracted thousands of peasants and townsfolk. No crowned ruler joined; the leaders included Godfrey of Bouillon, Bohemond of Taranto and Raymond of Saint-Gilles, Count of Toulouse, who led the largest force.

The campaign's successes led to four Crusader states: the Kingdom of Jerusalem, the Principality of Antioch and the counties of Tripoli and Edessa. When Edessa fell on 26 December 1144, most of its Frankish population was killed or enslaved, and the Second Crusade failed in 1148. Saladin destroyed the Jerusalemite field army at the Battle of Hattin on 4 July 1187, and Jerusalem surrendered on 2 October. The Fourth Crusade, first aimed at Egypt, was diverted to the Byzantine Empire and ended in the Sack of Constantinople and the Latin Empire in 1204. Jerusalem was regained by negotiation in 1229, but the Mamluks, who had reunited Egypt and Muslim Syria by 1260, captured the Crusaders' last mainland strongholds in 1291.

The fall of the Frankish East caused dismay rather than shock in the West, and Western Christians mostly blamed the Franks' alleged immorality. Schemes to recover the Holy Land inspired treatises, and only the Alexandrian Crusade briefly revived crusading activity in the region in 1365. Over time the crusading movement expanded to campaigns against pagans, Christian dissidents and other enemies of the papacy, promoted with similar spiritual rewards and continuing into the 18th century. The Crusades created national mythologies, tales of heroism and a few place names, and modern Muslim thinkers have drawn parallels between them and later political developments.
crypteia: The name comes from the Greek kruptos, meaning hidden or secret, and its members were called kryptai. Its structure is debated, partly because few classical texts mention it and Xenophon's Constitution of the Lacedaemonians does not. According to Aristotle it was established by the Spartan lawgiver Lycurgus, and there is no known date for its founding. Plutarch, writing centuries later, doubted that Lycurgus would have put such harsh customs into the Spartan constitution and thought the Crypteia had been introduced, if at all, only after the helot revolt that followed an earthquake in Sparta in the mid-460s BCE.

Its ranks were young upper-class Spartans, probably aged between 21 and 30, known as hêbôntes, who had finished the agoge so well that officials marked them as future leaders. They may have been chosen as those judged most intelligent. According to Plato, they went barefoot in winter, slept without cover, had no attendants, and roamed the countryside by night and by day. The length of service is unknown, and a scholion on Plato's Laws suggests it may have been a single year.

Plutarch and Heraclides Lembus, who may both draw on a lost work of Aristotle, describe kryptai sent into the countryside armed only with daggers, hiding by day and killing helots on the roads by night, sometimes working in the fields by day. Aristotle added that the ephors declared war on the helots each autumn so that they could be killed without breach of religion. Some scholars see a form of secret police, others military training like the Athenian ephebia, and the French historian Henri Jeanmaire saw a rite of passage. Plutarch also names Damoteles as commander of the Crypteia at the Battle of Sellasia, where Cleomenes III sent him to observe the army's rear and flanks, which shows it as a unit with a commander.

Some have linked the Crypteia to Thucydides' account of how the Spartans, in the eighth year of the Peloponnesian War, invited helots to claim freedom for bravery and then did away with about two thousand of them, though Thucydides does not name it. Whether the Crypteia was disbanded after Sellasia, when Cleomenes III began emancipating helots, is only speculation. The historian Stephen Hodkinson notes that Plato and Plutarch portray it in almost contradictory ways, and that modern scholars have adopted a composite understanding of it.
ctesias: Ctesias came from Cnidus in Caria, a town then part of the Achaemenid Empire, and served as physician to King Artaxerxes II. He accompanied the king in 401 BCE on his expedition against his brother Cyrus the Younger and was in the king's entourage at the Battle of Cunaxa, where Cyrus fought with his Greek mercenaries, the Ten Thousand. There Ctesias treated a flesh wound of the king. He reportedly took part in negotiations with the Greeks after the battle, and he helped the Spartan general Clearchus before his execution at the royal court at Babylon.

Ctesias wrote treatises on rivers and on the Persian revenues, an account of India called the Indica, and a history of Assyria and Persia in 23 books, the Persica. The Persica was drawn from documents in the Persian Royal Archives and written in the Ionic dialect in opposition to Herodotus. Its first six books cover the history of Assyria and Babylon to the founding of the Persian empire by Cyrus the Great in 550 BCE, and the remaining seventeen cover the years to 398 BCE.

It survives in an abridgment by Photius and in fragments preserved by Athenaeus, Plutarch, Nicolaus of Damascus and especially Diodorus Siculus, whose second book derives mainly from it. According to the Encyclopædia Britannica, Ctesias mentioned that the grave of Darius I at Persepolis lay in a cliff face reached by an apparatus of ropes.

Opinion of the Persica has long been divided. Many ancient authorities valued it highly and used it to discredit Herodotus, while one modern author writes that its unreliability makes Herodotus seem a model of accuracy. His account of the Assyrian kings does not agree with the cuneiform evidence, and the satirist Lucian placed Ctesias, with Herodotus, on an island of torment for writers of false histories.

The Indica records the Persian view of India, with descriptions of artisans, philosophers and people with the qualities of deities, and of gold beyond counting. It rests on the testimony of travellers to Persia rather than on his own observation, and modern readers place it between fact and fiction. It states that the Indus varies from 40 to 200 stades in width and that India makes up half of Asia. It survives only in fragments and in the reports of later authors.
ctesiphon: Ctesiphon stood on the eastern bank of the Tigris, about 35 kilometres south-east of Baghdad, at the place now called al-Mada'in. It merged with the surrounding cities on both shores, including the Hellenistic city of Seleucia, and the whole group was known as The Cities, Mahuza in Aramaic and al-Mada'in in Arabic. The city measured about 30 square kilometres, more than twice the area of imperial Rome in the 4th century.

Ctesiphon was founded in the late 120s BCE on the site of a military camp set up opposite Seleucia by Mithridates I of Parthia. Strabo says the Parthian kings used it as a winter residence. It became the capital of the empire around 58 BCE under Orodes II. Because of its importance it was a major target for Rome: Trajan captured it in 116 and Hadrian returned it in 117, Avidius Cassius took it in 164 and abandoned it at peace, and in 197 Septimius Severus sacked it and sold thousands of its inhabitants into slavery.

By 226 the Sasanians held the city, ended the Parthian dynasty and made it their capital, enlarging it greatly. The western quarter, Veh-Ardashir, had many wealthy Jews and the seat of the church of the Nestorian patriarch. After taking Antioch in 541, Khosrow I built a new city near Ctesiphon for its captured people. The Byzantine emperor Heraclius surrounded Ctesiphon in 627 and left after the Persians accepted his terms.

After the Battle of al-Qādisiyyah in the mid-630s the Arabs occupied Ctesiphon in early 637, finding it deserted by the royal family, nobles and troops. The city then declined rapidly, especially after the Abbasid capital Baghdad was founded in the 760s, and Caliph al-Mansur took building material from its ruins.

The most conspicuous remaining structure is the Taq Kasra, sometimes called the Arch of Ctesiphon, once part of the royal palace and estimated to date between the 3rd and 6th centuries. It stands in the Iraqi town of Salman Pak. German expeditions excavated the site in 1928–29 and 1931–1932, and an Italian team from the University of Turin worked on the western side, which it identified as Veh Ardashir, in the late 1960s and early 1970s.
cu-chulainn: In the Ulster Cycle Cú Chulainn is born Sétanta, the son of the mortal Deichtine, sister of King Conchobar mac Nessa, and of the god Lug. He gets his better-known name as a child, after killing the fierce guard dog of Culann in self-defence and offering to take its place until a replacement is reared, so that he becomes the Hound of Culann. The word cú, hound, was also a figurative term for a warrior in early Irish literature.

As a small child he sets out alone for the boy-troop at Emain Macha, and when the boys attack him he has a ríastrad, a battle frenzy in which he beats them single-handed. He wants no wife but Emer, daughter of Forgall Monach, whose father opposes the match and sends him to train in arms with the warrior-woman Scáthach on the Isle of Skye. She gives him the spear Gáe Bulg.

At the age of seventeen he defends Ulster single-handedly against the army of Queen Medb of Connacht in the Táin Bó Cúailnge, the Cattle Raid of Cooley. Medb has invaded to steal the stud bull Donn Cúailnge, and the men of Ulster are disabled by a curse. Cú Chulainn invokes the right of single combat at fords and defeats champion after champion in a standoff lasting months.

In Bricriu's Feast he competes with two other heroes for the champion's portion, and only he submits to the beheading challenge set by Cú Roí mac Dáire, a challenge that reappears in the Middle English poem Sir Gawain and the Green Knight. In another tale he kills his own son Connla, whom Aífe had bound never to give his name or refuse a challenge. Cú Chulainn takes him for an intruder and wounds him fatally with the Gáe Bulg.

Medb conspires with Lugaid, son of Cú Roí, and others whose kin Cú Chulainn had killed. His fate is sealed when he breaks his geasa, or taboos: an old crone offers him dog meat, which he is forbidden to eat, but he cannot refuse hospitality. Lugaid kills his charioteer Láeg with the first of three magical spears, his horse Liath Macha with the second, and wounds Cú Chulainn with the third. He ties himself to a standing stone, traditionally identified as Clochafarmore near Dundalk, to die on his feet. His enemies believe him dead only when a raven lands on his shoulder.

Irish nationalists have often invoked his image. Oliver Sheppard's bronze of the dying Cú Chulainn stands in the Dublin General Post Office in memory of the Easter Rising of 1916, and Éamon de Valera unveiled it in 1935. Lady Gregory retold the legends in Cuchulain of Muirthemne in 1902, and W. B. Yeats wrote several plays and poems on them.
cuauhtemoc: The name Cuauhtémoc means one who has descended like an eagle. His date of birth is unknown, since he does not enter the historical record until he became emperor. He was the eldest legitimate son of Emperor Ahuitzotl, and according to several sources his mother, Tiyacapantzin, was a Tlatelolcan princess, though this is inferred from his rank. After education in the calmecac, the school for elite boys, and military service, he was named ruler of Tlatelolco in 1515 with the title cuauhtlatoani, eagle ruler. He married the princess later known as Isabel Moctezuma, a daughter of Moctezuma II.

In 1520 Cuauhtémoc was elected tlatoani, the most able candidate among the high nobles being chosen by their vote, to succeed his cousin Cuitláhuac, who died of smallpox shortly after succeeding Moctezuma II. He was around 25, and Tenochtitlan was besieged by the Spanish and devastated by smallpox. It was increasingly isolated, as many polities once under its control deserted and swelled the numbers of Spanish allies. He oversaw Moctezuma's funeral without the usual pomp, since he believed in armed resistance while Moctezuma had believed in negotiation.

After eighty days of warfare he called for reinforcements. Of all the Nahuas only the Tlatelolcas remained loyal, and the surviving Tenochcas took refuge in Tlatelolco. Cuauhtémoc was captured on 13 August 1521 while fleeing across Lake Texcoco with his wife, family and friends. According to Spanish sources, he asked Hernán Cortés to strike him dead with his knife, and Cortés refused. Later, when the booty fell short of the Spaniards' expectations, he was tortured by fire. Baptized as Fernando Cuauhtémotzín, he kept the title of tlatoani but was no longer sovereign and was mostly held in guarded custody.

In 1525 Cortés took Cuauhtémoc and other indigenous nobles on his expedition to Honduras, fearing an insurrection in his absence. At Itzamkanac he had Cuauhtémoc hanged for allegedly conspiring to kill him. The accounts differ. Cortés wrote that he learned of the plot on 27 February 1525 and hanged Cuauhtémoc, Tetlepanquetzal and Tlacatlec. Bernal Díaz del Castillo portrays the executions as unjust and based on no evidence, and Fernando de Alva Cortés Ixtlilxóchitl, drawing partly on Texcocan oral tradition, wrote that Cortés invented the plot. Tlacotzin was appointed his successor and died the next year.

Cuauhtémoc is the embodiment of indigenist nationalism in Mexico, being the only Aztec emperor who survived the conquest. He is honoured by a monument on the Paseo de la Reforma in Mexico City. An ossuary at Ixcateopan said to hold his remains was excavated in 1949, but the Instituto Nacional de Antropología e Historia rejected its authenticity.
cuba: Cuba is an archipelago of 4,195 islands, cays and islets in the northern Caribbean Sea, where the Gulf of Mexico meets the Atlantic Ocean. Key West, Florida, lies about 150 kilometres across the Straits of Florida to the north and northwest, Mexico 210 kilometres west across the Yucatán Channel, Haiti 78 kilometres to the east and Jamaica 148 kilometres to the south. The main island is 1,250 kilometres long and makes up most of the land area of 104,338 square kilometres. It consists mostly of flat to rolling plains apart from the Sierra Maestra in the southeast, whose highest point is Pico Turquino at 1,974 metres. The second-largest island is Isla de la Juventud.

Humans first settled Cuba around 6,000 years ago. The Arawakan-speaking ancestors of the Taíno arrived from South America about 1,700 years ago and, unlike the earlier settlers, produced pottery and practised intensive agriculture. The earliest evidence of the Taíno on Cuba dates to the 9th century. Descendants of the first settlers persisted in the west of the island until European contact as the hunter-gathering Guanahatabey. Christopher Columbus first arrived on 27 October 1492, claimed the island for Spain and named it Isla Juana after John, Prince of Asturias.

The first Spanish settlement was founded by Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar at Baracoa in 1511, and San Cristóbal de la Habana was founded in 1514 and moved to its present place in 1519, becoming the capital in 1607. The Taíno were forced to work under the encomienda system.

Within a century they suffered high mortality, primarily from Eurasian infectious diseases against which they had no immunity, aggravated by harsh colonial subjugation. In 1529 a measles outbreak killed two-thirds of the few who had survived smallpox. Cuba remained part of the Spanish Empire until the Spanish–American War of 1898, was then occupied by the United States, and became independent in 1902. The Cuban Revolution of January 1959 overthrew the government of Fulgencio Batista and established a communist government under Fidel Castro.

Havana is the capital and largest city. Cuba is a socialist republic whose constitution names the Communist Party as the leading force of society and the state. Spanish culture, West African culture and the Guanahatabey and Taíno inheritance together shape Cuban culture. Cuba's population descends primarily from Spanish settlers, sub-Saharan Africans brought through the transatlantic slave trade, and pre-Columbian peoples, chiefly the Taíno and Ciboney. Havana, Camagüey, Cienfuegos and Trinidad, with colonial centres in Baroque and Neoclassical styles, are inscribed as UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
cuban-missile-crisis: The crisis was a 13-day confrontation, from 16 to 28 October 1962, in which Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba matched American missiles deployed in the United Kingdom, Italy and Turkey, all within range of Moscow. In April 1961 a CIA-led force of Cuban expatriates had tried to invade Cuba. Khrushchev decided in May 1962 to counter the American lead in strategic missiles by placing intermediate-range missiles in Cuba. At a meeting in July 1962 he and Fidel Castro agreed to deploy them to deter a future American invasion.

On 15 October analysts identified what appeared to be medium-range ballistic missiles in U-2 photographs. President John F. Kennedy formed the Executive Committee of the National Security Council, EXCOMM, which considered doing nothing, diplomacy, a secret approach to Castro, an air strike and an invasion. On 22 October Kennedy announced a naval blockade, which he called a quarantine because a blockade is an act of war. The Strategic Air Command was raised to DEFCON 2 on 26 October, the only confirmed time in American history. On 27 October, called Black Saturday, the United States Navy dropped practice depth charges on the Soviet submarine B-59, whose captain proposed to launch a nuclear torpedo; Vasily Arkhipov, aboard, did not consent.
