Khrushchev agreed to dismantle the offensive weapons in Cuba, under United Nations verification, for a public American declaration not to invade Cuba. The United States secretly agreed to dismantle its missiles in Turkey. The quarantine ended on 20 November 1962. The need for quick contact led to the Moscow-Washington hotline. Khrushchev was embarrassed because the withdrawal was secret and the Soviets appeared to retreat, and his fall two years later was in part due to this. Castro saw the outcome as a Soviet betrayal. The crisis is widely considered the closest the Cold War came to full-scale nuclear war.
cuban-revolution: Batista overthrew the emerging Cuban democracy in the coup of 1952. In the 1950s Cuba ranked among the more advanced Latin American countries by averages such as life expectancy, but the averages hid sharp disparities. The economy depended on sugar and on the United States, nearly one-third of the labour force lacked full-time work, and only 15 per cent of the rural population had running water. Batista's regime kept close ties with organised crime, and was marked by police corruption, censorship and anti-communist campaigns that suppressed opposition with violence, torture and public executions.

Fidel Castro, a young lawyer, first challenged the coup in the courts. When that failed, he and his brother Raúl led the assault on the Moncada Barracks on 26 July 1953. At his trial he spoke for hours in his own defence, ending 'History will absolve me', and was sentenced to fifteen years. Under political pressure Batista freed all political prisoners on 15 May 1955, and the brothers went to Mexico.

The yacht Granma left Tuxpan on 25 November 1956 with the Castros and eighty others and landed on 2 December. Batista's army attacked three days later; no more than twenty of the eighty-two survived to reach the Sierra Maestra. In 1958 about 12,000 soldiers, around 7,000 of them untrained recruits, entered the mountains in Operation Verano, and the guerrillas defeated them. The Battle of El Jigüe in July 1958 is widely considered a turning point.

Batista left the country at the turn of the year, and on 2 January 1959 the army commander in Santiago de Cuba ordered his soldiers not to fight. Castro reached Havana on 8 January. Manuel Urrutia Lleó took office as president on 3 January with José Miró as prime minister. After the government nationalised American property in August 1960, the United States froze Cuban assets, severed relations and tightened the embargo in January 1961. The Bay of Pigs invasion of 1961, by 1,500 mostly Cuban exiles, was repulsed. The Soviet Union became Cuba's main ally, and the 26th of July Movement became the Communist Party in October 1965. Historians debate whether Castro was a communist from the start.
cucurrucucu-paloma: Tomás Méndez wrote the song in the huapango style, and its lyrics allude to love sickness. It reached audiences first through Mexican cinema. It appeared in the comedy Escuela de vagabundos, screened in 1955, where it was sung by the film's star, Pedro Infante. Ten years later it gave its name to the Mexican film Cucurrucucú Paloma of 1965, directed by Miguel Delgado, in which it was performed by Lola Beltrán, who played the part of Paloma Méndez.

The song was first released on record in 1956, in a version sung by Harry Belafonte. It has since been recorded by many other popular singers, among them Luis Miguel, Rocío Dúrcal, Perry Como, Miguel Aceves Mejía, Nancy Ames, Hibari Misora, Dario Moreno, Gaby Moreno, Nana Mouskouri, Julio Iglesias, Shirley Kwan, Rosemary Clooney, Natalia Lafourcade, Lila Downs and The Del Rubio Triplets. Joan Baez included it on her album Gracias a la Vida, and Franco Battiato took up its refrain in his own song Cuccurucucù, on La voce del padrone.

Its use in film continued well beyond its Mexican beginnings. It was heard in The Last Sunset (1961), Le Magnifique (1973), Happy Together (1997), The Five-Year Engagement (2012) and Moonlight (2016). In Pedro Almodovar's film Talk to Her of 2002 it was sung by the Brazilian singer Caetano Veloso in an art-song style quite unlike the mariachi presentation of its first appearances on screen. In 2019 the operatic tenor Juan Diego Florez sang it at La Scala in Milan, accompanying himself on the guitar, in a performance that was circulated as a video and widely watched.
cudjoe: The name Cudjoe corresponds to the Akan day name Kojo or Kwadwo, given to a boy born on a Monday. The Leeward Maroons most likely emerged in 1690, when a Coromantee rebellion broke out on Sutton's estate in western Jamaica and most of the enslaved Africans there ran away into the mountainous interior. Cudjoe was probably the son of one of the leaders of that revolt. The oral history of the Accompong Town Maroons, as told by Milton McFarlane, holds that he was the freeborn son of Naquan, who led those who fled from the estate.

According to contemporary white enslavers, Cudjoe challenged a Madagascan for the leadership of the Leeward Maroons in 1720, and by defeating and killing him became their undisputed leader. His community was known as Cudjoe's Town, or Trelawny Town. For about half a century, until the treaties of 1739 and 1740, the Maroons operated outside direct British control.

During the First Maroon War of the 1730s the English colonial forces failed to win any significant victory over Cudjoe's Leeward Maroons. The agreement of 1739 recognised them as a semi-autonomous entity and freed their land from taxes. In the 1740s some Leeward Maroons who opposed the treaty rose in revolt, and Cudjoe crushed these risings.

Two descriptions of him survive from colonial writers. The physician R. C. Dallas, writing half a century after Cudjoe lived, claimed that he was short and stout, with a large lump of flesh on his back. The slaver Thomas Thistlewood, who met him in 1750, noted in his diary that he wore a feathered hat, with a sword at his side and a gun on his shoulder, barefoot and with "somewhat a Majestic look".

One source claims that Cudjoe died in 1744, but Edward Long and Thistlewood wrote of meeting him in the 1750s and 1760s. Long described him leading his Maroons in a martial performance at Montego Bay for Governor Sir William Lyttleton in 1764, and in the same year Thistlewood heard that he had been dead for some time. The treaty had named Accompong as his successor, but Governor Roger Hope Elletson had the Trelawny Town badge of authority given instead to a Maroon officer named Lewis, leaving Accompong authority over Accompong Town only. Cudjoe Day is celebrated in Jamaica on the first Monday in January.
cudjoe-lewis: His father was Oluwale, or Oluale, and his mother Fondlolu; he had five full siblings and twelve half-siblings through his father's two other wives. He crossed with 115 other captives on the Clotilda, a ship recently built in Mobile and owned by Timothy Meaher, and was sold at Ouidah to its captain, William Foster. The import of slaves had been illegal since 1808. Meaher, his brother Burns and their associate John Dabney were charged, but the captives were hidden and the case was dismissed in January 1861. The scuttled ship was found in May 2019.

Bought by James Meaher, Kossola worked as a deckhand on a steamer and took the name Cudjo, a day-name for boys born on a Monday, when Meaher could not pronounce his own. After emancipation the Clotilda Africans tried to raise money to return home; when that failed and Timothy Meaher refused them land, they bought it, and on 30 September 1872 Lewis paid $100.00 for about 2 acres.

He became a naturalised citizen on 24 October 1868 and joined a Baptist church in 1869. He married Abile, called Celia, formally on 15 March 1880; she died in 1905, and he outlived all six of their children. After a train hit his buggy in 1902 he sued the railroad and won $650.00, overturned on appeal, and became sexton of the church.

Emma Langdon Roche interviewed him for her 1914 book Historic Sketches of the South, and Arthur Huff Fauset published his tales in 1927. Zora Neale Hurston interviewed him in 1927 and 1928, filmed him and wrote Barracoon, published only in 2018.

Lewis died on 17 July 1935 and was buried at the Plateau Cemetery in Africatown. In 1959 a bust of him was set up before the Union Missionary Baptist Church on a pyramid of bricks made by the Clotilda captives. Long thought the last survivor of the Clotilda, he was outlived by two who had crossed as children, Redoshi, who died in 1937, and Matilda McCrear, who died in 1940, as the historian Hannah Durkin found.
cuenca-ecuador: Cuenca lies in the south-central inter-Andean region of Ecuador, in the Paute river basin, at about 2,538 metres above sea level, roughly 470 kilometres south of Quito and 200 kilometres south-east of Guayaquil. Four rivers cross it, the Tomebamba, Yanuncay, Tarqui and Machángara, and their confluence gives the city its Spanish name, which means a basin. The first three rise in the páramo of El Cajas National Park to the west. Its full name, Santa Ana de los Ríos de Cuenca, honours Saint Anne and the Spanish city of Cuenca, home of the viceroy who ordered its founding.

Archaeological finds trace the first inhabitants in the area to about 8060 BCE, in the Cave of Chopsi, where nomadic hunters followed the animals. Later peoples grew potatoes, quinoa and squash and kept guinea pigs, llamas and alpacas. From around 2000 BCE society became more organised, with specialised administrative and religious authorities, and later came the Cañari, who were absorbed by the Incas in the 15th century. Archaeologists believe a Cañari settlement called Guapdondelic, said to mean land as big as heaven, was founded around 500 CE.

After a bitter struggle the Incas conquered the Cañari, likely in the 1470s. They replaced the Cañari architecture with their own but did not suppress the Cañari or their achievements in astronomy and agriculture, and they renamed the city Tomebamba. The emperor Tupac Yupanqui ordered the building of a grand city called Pumapungo, said to rival Cusco, and Tomebamba became known as the second Cusco. When the Spaniards found it, they saw only ruins, and it was sparsely populated until the 1550s.

Gil Ramírez Dávalos founded the Spanish city on 12 April 1557 on the orders of the viceroy of Peru, Andrés Hurtado de Mendoza, decades after Quito (1534), Guayaquil (1538) and Loja (1548). The city achieved independence on 3 November 1820 and reached the peak of its importance in the first years of independent Ecuador, as the capital of one of the republic's three provinces, with Guayaquil and Quito.

Cuenca is the capital of Azuay province and one of the largest cities of Ecuador. Its historic centre was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1999. The Old Cathedral, built in 1557, is now a museum, and the New Cathedral, completed in 1975, has blue and white domes that symbolise the city. The Universidad de Cuenca, founded in 1867, is among the oldest universities in the country. Cuenca is known for its textiles and for the straw hats called Panama hats, which are made there by local artisans.
cuenca-spain: Cuenca stands on a steep spur whose slopes fall into the deep gorges of the Júcar and Huécar rivers, on the western fringes of the Iberian System mountains, at about 1,000 metres in the old town. It is also known as the Eagle's Nest. Its name may come from the Latin conca, 'river basin', or from the Arab castle Kunka. The Roman settlements of the province lay elsewhere, at Segobriga, Ercavica and Gran Valeria, and the site of Cuenca itself was uninhabited in Roman times.

Under Muslim rule Cuenca was a fortress with a wall about a kilometre long, and an economy of agriculture and textiles. In the early 11th century it fell to the taifa of Toledo. Sancho Ramírez of Aragon besieged it in 1076 without success; the first Christian troops entered in 1093, and the Almoravids took it in 1108. From 1147 Muhammad ibn Mardanis was king of Cuenca, Murcia and Valencia until 1172. In 1177 Alfonso VIII of Castile, leading a coalition, conquered the city. Cuenca received a Latin law code, the Fuero, and the diocese was established in 1183; its second bishop, St Julian, became the patron saint. Alfonso X made it a city in 1257.

Textiles and livestock brought prosperity. A Jewish community, first recorded in 1177, lasted until the expulsion of 1492, and the Inquisition prosecuted the descendants of conversos until a last trial from 1718 to 1725. In the 18th century the textile trade declined and the city lost population. It suffered great destruction in the war against Napoleon's troops.

Cuenca is the capital of the province of Cuenca in Castilla–La Mancha. The cathedral was built from 1182 to 1270 under the influence of Queen Eleanor, wife of Alfonso VIII, and is regarded as one of the first Gothic cathedrals in Spain, with Ávila's; its façade was rebuilt after the collapse of the Giraldo tower in 1902. The Bridge of Saint Paul, begun in 1533, was replaced in 1902 by an iron and wood bridge up to 40 metres high, and the old Dominican convent of Saint Paul is now a hotel. The old town was declared a World Heritage Site in 1996.
cuffy: Cuffy was an Akan man, born in the 18th century on the Dutch Gold Coast, in what is now southern Ghana. Captured into slavery and carried across the ocean in the Atlantic slave trade, he was taken to Berbice, where he lived on Lilienburg, a plantation on the Berbice River, as a house slave for a cooper, owned by the widow Berkey.

The rising began on 23 February 1763 on plantation Magdalenenberg on the Canje River, where enslaved people protesting harsh treatment burned the plantation house. On 27 February a revolt broke out on Hollandia, next to Lilienburg, and Cuffy is said to have organised the rebels into a military unit. The revolt spread from plantation to plantation towards the capital, Fort Nassau, and the rebels seized guns and gunpowder. By 3 March they numbered 600; at the brick house of Peerenboom they let the Dutch leave, then killed many and took prisoners, among them Sara George, whom Cuffy kept as his wife.

Accepted as leader, Cuffy declared himself Governor of Berbice, named Captain Accara his deputy for military affairs and had farms organised to supply food. On 2 April 1763 he wrote to Governor Wolfert Simon van Hoogenheim that he did not want war and proposed a partition, the Dutch holding the coast and the rebels the interior. Van Hoogenheim delayed, saying the Society of Berbice in Amsterdam must decide, while reinforcements arrived from Suriname, Barbados and Sint Eustatius.

An attack Cuffy ordered in May 1763 cost many losses and divided the rebels, and Accara led a faction against him. On 19 October 1763 the governor was told that Captain Atta had revolted against Cuffy and that Cuffy had taken his own life. The last rebel captain, Accabre, was captured on 15 April 1764. Since 1970 the anniversary of the rising has been Republic Day in Guyana, and Philip Moore's 1763 Monument, also called the Cuffy Monument, stands in the Square of the Revolution in Georgetown.
cuiaba: Cuiabá lies near the geographical centre of South America, in a transition zone between the Amazon, the Cerrado and the Pantanal, and is called the Southern gate to the Amazon. Its name is a Bororo word meaning 'arrow-fishing'. It is known across Brazil as one of the hottest cities, with temperatures often above 40 °C. An obelisk in the centre marks the middle of the continent as calculated in 1909; more accurate measurements in the 1990s placed it about 45 kilometres to the north-east, near Chapada dos Guimarães.

The first Portuguese in the region were bandeirantes, explorers, slavers and fortune hunters from São Paulo. In 1718 Pascoal Moreira Cabral of Sorocaba arrived and, after losing a battle with the Coxiponé people, found gold up the Coxipó River. The bandeirantes enslaved indigenous people to work the site. Cabral reported the discovery in a letter of 8 April 1719, and a gold rush followed. An earthquake in 1746 destroyed much of the town. In 1751 Dom Antônio Rolim de Moura Tavares became first governor of the Captaincy of Mato Grosso and founded Vila Bela as its capital.

Cuiabá replaced Vila Bela as capital of the province in 1835. The town stayed small until the Paraguayan War (1864 to 1870), which brought a brief boom as it supplied the troops, and afterwards governments used it as a place of exile for troublesome politicians.

Roads and then aviation ended the isolation from 1930, and the city grew rapidly after 1960, from 50,000 inhabitants to more than a quarter of a million by 1980, as commercial agriculture carried soybeans and rice abroad. Cuiabá is the capital and largest city of Mato Grosso and, with Várzea Grande, forms its metropolitan area. It is a trading centre for a cattle-raising and farming region and the seat of the Federal University of Mato Grosso.
cuicuilco: Cuicuilco lay on the southern shore of Lake Texcoco in the south-eastern Valley of Mexico, in what is now the borough of Tlalpan in Mexico City. It stood about 4 km from Lake Xochimilco and near the Sierra de las Cruces and Ajusco, with springs and streams close by, and some experts link its growth to its position near the pass of Toluca. Teotihuacan lay about 60 km to the north-east. The meaning of the name is unknown, though the archaeologist Zelia Nuttall believed it meant place where songs and dances are made.

Cuicuilco began as a farming village, with early religious practices shown by stone offerings and pottery placed in graves. It grew around a ceremonial centre of pyramids, with plazas and avenues beside shallow pools fed by runoff from the hills of Zacayuca and Zacaltepetl, as well as terraces, fortifications and irrigation canals. Its people were in contact with distant places such as Chupicuaro and Monte Albán. At its height the population is estimated at 20,000, and the city may have covered nearly 400 hectares. A four-tier settlement hierarchy makes it one of the early Mesoamerican sites to show state formation.

Relations with Teotihuacan were mostly hostile, each city taking defensive positions against the other. Cuicuilco weakened as Teotihuacan rose, and lava from Xitle finally buried it. Pottery and other evidence suggest that refugees moved north and joined the population of Teotihuacan, which became the ruler of the Central Highlands. People kept making offerings on the lava, and smaller settlements went on at the site in later periods, down to the Spanish conquest.

The site lies under the Pedregal de San Ángel, a lava field of about 80 km² that is over 10 m deep in places. The lava preserved the city but makes excavation difficult, and the area is also built over, partly by buildings of the National University of Mexico. Finds made in 1990, among them a circular pyramid in a plaza, were destroyed to build an office complex. The ceremonial centre forms Cuicuilco A, and Cuicuilco B lies to the west; the site museum was designed by the architect Luis Macgregor Krieger.
culavamsa: The name means Lesser Chronicle. The work is generally considered a sequel to the Mahavamsa, the Great Chronicle written in the 6th century by the monk Mahanama, and the two are sometimes treated as a single work spanning over two millennia of Sri Lankan history. Unlike the Mahavamsa, the Cūḷavaṃsa was written by different authors at different periods. Tradition ascribes its first part to the Buddhist monk Thera Dhammakitti, though many historians now believe it to be the collaborative work of several monks.

The chronicle falls into two parts. The first, chapters thirty-seven to seventy-nine, written in the 13th century, begins with the arrival in Sri Lanka of a tooth relic of Siddhartha Gautama and runs to the reign of Parakramabahu the Great (1153–1186). The second, by an unknown author, continues from Vijayabahu II to Parakramabahu IV (chapters 80–90). Within it the section from Parakramabahu IV to the death of Kirti Sri Rajasinha was compiled by Tibbotuvāve Sumangala Thera, and the last chapter was carried to 1815 by Hikkaduve Siri Sumangala. These later portions are generally considered inferior to Dhammakitti's in style and in factual reliability.

Wilhelm Geiger, who translated it from Pali into German, saw the history of Parakramabahu as the real kernel of the work, as the life of Dutugemunu is of the Mahavamsa. In his view the compiler drew from his reading an ideal picture of an Indian king and fitted the king to it, without asking whether the details were probable. Geiger held that the chronicle does not consciously relate false information but exaggerates and embellishes, and that its truth can be recovered with caution. Carvings, edicts and monuments confirm parts of it, such as Parakramabahu's wars with Gajabahu II and Manabharana, and it is the primary source for his reign.

In 1871 the British colonial government commissioned a 101st chapter covering 1815 to 1871. In 1935 the monk Yagirala Pannananda wrote Mahavamsa Part III, a further extension in Sinhala, and in 1977 the government of Prime Minister JR Jayawardene set up a commission to extend the chronicle to cover 1935 to 1977.
cultivation-system: By the late 18th century the monopolies of the Dutch East India Company had led to its ruin. A land tax raised revenue during the British occupation of Java but soon failed, because tenants could not pay what was asked. From the late 1820s the colonial government came under heavy financial pressure from the Padri Wars (1821–1837) and the costly Java War (1825 to 1830), and the Belgian Revolution of 1830 and the cost of keeping the Dutch army on a war footing until 1839 brought the Netherlands close to state bankruptcy. In 1830 Johannes van den Bosch was appointed governor general to increase the exploitation of the colony's resources.

The system applied only to land the colonial government controlled directly, exempting the Vorstenlanden, or princely states, and the private domains. Instead of paying land tax, villages had to give 20% of their land to government export crops, or peasants had to work 66 days a year on government plantations; in practice far more land was taken, leaving little for food. Up to 1 million farmers were forced to work under it at its peak, and villagers were tied more formally to their villages. Local middlemen received cultivation percentages that grew with the revenue their territories yielded, and farmers were paid in new copper coinage worth less than half its face value.

The system brought the Netherlands back from the brink of bankruptcy and at its peak supplied 50% of Dutch state revenue; as early as 1831 the colonial budget was balanced and the surplus used to pay the debts of the defunct company. In the 1840s it caused widespread famines and epidemics, first in Cirebon and then in Central Java, as indigo and sugar had to be grown instead of rice. According to recent research the death rate rose by as much as 30%, and several tens of thousands died of starvation and disease. Resistance was widespread but was met with violence, harsh prison sentences and corporal punishment.

Political pressure in the Netherlands and merchants who wanted free trade led to its abolition through the Suikerwet and the Agrarische Wet of 1870, which opened the free-market Liberal Period. Forced labour persisted until the end of the colonial period, with prisoners and conscripted labourers building railways, bridges and irrigation systems in appalling conditions. Indonesian historians call the system tanam paksa, enforced planting.
cultural-revolution: Mao Zedong declared the People's Republic of China on 1 October 1949. His Great Leap Forward of 1958 to 1962 aimed to turn an agrarian society into an industrial one through people's communes, and the Great Chinese Famine of 1959 to 1961 that followed caused between 15 and 55 million deaths. After Nikita Khrushchev denounced Stalin in 1956 and began economic reforms, Mao and many other party members opposed the changes, fearing damage to the worldwide communist movement. In 1963 Mao launched the Socialist Education Movement, cleansing Beijing officials of questionable loyalty.

The movement has two periods: spring 1966 to summer 1968, when most key events took place, and a tailing period lasting until the autumn of 1976. On 25 May 1966 Nie Yuanzi, a philosophy lecturer at Peking University, posted a big-character poster attacking the university's leadership. Mao called on young people to Bombard the Headquarters and proclaimed that to rebel is justified. Mass upheaval began in Beijing with Red August in 1966, and young people formed Red Guard cadres across China. Quotations from Chairman Mao Tse-tung became the object of a cult of personality.

In 1967 radicals seized power from local governments and party branches and established revolutionary committees, smashing the public security, procuratorate and judicial systems. These committees often split into factions and fought each other. After the fall of Lin Biao in 1971, the Gang of Four became influential in 1972.

The Red Guards sought to destroy the Four Olds, old ideas, culture, customs and habits, which often meant destroying historical artefacts and cultural and religious sites. Tens of millions were persecuted, including Liu Shaoqi, Deng Xiaoping and Peng Dehuai, and millions as members of the Five Black Categories. Schools and universities were closed, the National College Entrance Examinations were cancelled and over 10 million urban youths were sent to the countryside. Estimates of the death toll range from 1 to 2 million, including the Guangxi Massacre, which involved cannibalism, and massacres in Beijing, Inner Mongolia, Guangdong, Yunnan and Hunan.

The revolution continued until Mao's death in 1976, followed by the arrest of the Gang of Four. In 1978 Deng Xiaoping became paramount leader, and his reform and opening up helped dismantle the ideology of the Cultural Revolution. In 1981 the Communist Party acknowledged it as responsible for the most severe setback and the heaviest losses suffered by the people, the country and the party since 1949. In China it is often called the ten years of chaos.
cumaean-sibyl: The word sibyl comes through Latin from the Greek sibylla, a prophetess, and there were many sibyls in the ancient world. The one at Cumae became the best known among the Romans because of her place in the legends of early Rome and her nearness to the city. Ancient writers give her several names: Herophile in Pausanias and Lactantius, Deiphobe, daughter of Glaucus, in the Aeneid, and Amaltheia, Demophile or Taraxandra elsewhere. A Cimmerian Sibyl, said to live underground near Lake Avernus, may have been a doublet of her, though some sources kept the two apart.

In the story of the Sibylline Books, an old woman offered nine books of prophecy to King Tarquin, burned three each time he refused her price, and sold him the last three for the original sum. The books were kept in the Temple of Jupiter on the Capitoline Hill and consulted only in emergencies. When the temple burned in the 80s BCE, prophecies were gathered again from across the empire, and Augustus later moved them to the Temple of Apollo on the Palatine.

In the Aeneid she prophesies by singing the fates and writing on oak leaves, and guides Aeneas to the underworld, whose entrance lay at the crater of Avernus. In Ovid's Metamorphoses she asks Apollo for as many years as grains of sand in her hand but not for youth, and withers until only her voice is left. Constantine the Great read Virgil's Eclogues as a coded prophecy of Christ, and Augustine quoted the Sibylline Oracles in The City of God. Michelangelo set her among the prophets on the Sistine Chapel ceiling, and T. S. Eliot took the epigraph of The Waste Land from the Satyricon of Petronius, where she says she wants to die.

In 1932 Amedeo Maiuri identified the Antro della Sibilla at Cumae, a trapezoidal passage over 131 metres long cut into the volcanic tuff, from Virgil's description and that of the writer known as pseudo-Justin. The identification is problematic, since the later writers may themselves have followed Virgil. A nearby tunnel, the Crypta Romana, was once taken for her grotto, and some archaeologists propose a tunnel complex near Baiae instead.
cumana: Cumaná lies at the mouth of the Manzanares River on the Caribbean coast, 402 kilometres east of Caracas. It is a busy maritime port with one of the largest tuna fleets in Venezuela and the seat of the first and most important of the five campuses of the Universidad de Oriente. The municipality of Sucre, which includes the city, had a population of 358,919 at the 2011 census. Its climate is hot and semi-arid.

Cumaná was founded in 1515 by Franciscan friars under the name Nueva Toledo, as the first Spanish settlement in Venezuela and in South America, a claim disputed by the town of Santa Fe. Successful attacks by the indigenous people, among them the Cumanagoto, forced it to be refounded several times, until Diego Hernández de Serpa's refoundation in 1569 gave it the name Cumaná. Bartolomé de las Casas, who attempted a peaceful colonisation, was preempted by Gonzalo de Ocampo's punitive raids in 1521, made in retaliation for the destruction of the Dominican convent at Chiribichi. In 1537 the Province of New Andalusia was established with Cumaná as its capital, so that it was also known as the Province of Cumaná.

The city gained independence on 15 July 1811. After the threat of Amerindian attacks faded, earthquakes destroyed it on various occasions, so that its oldest part dates from the late 17th and 18th centuries and almost none of the 16th-century architecture survived. The Castle of San Antonio de la Eminencia, begun around 1659, was built to defend the city against English, French and Dutch pirates, and José Antonio Páez was held there in 1849 until his expulsion on 24 May 1850. In the 18th century scientists including Pehr Löfling, Alexander von Humboldt and Aimé Bonpland worked in Cumaná.

Cumaná is the capital of Sucre State. It was the birthplace of Antonio José de Sucre, a leading general of the independence movement who also served as president of Bolivia and of Peru, and of the poets Andrés Eloy Blanco and José Antonio Ramos Sucre. The Basilica of Saint Agnes, restored around 1853, is the oldest church in the city, and Plaza Bolívar was built in 1930 on the site of the Sucre Museum, which collapsed in the 1929 earthquake. Mochima National Park lies near the city.
cumans: The Cumans, or Kumans, formed the western branch of the Cuman–Kipchak confederation and spoke the Cuman language. They are called Polovtsy in the chronicles of the Rus', Cumans in Western sources and Kipchaks in Eastern ones. Their original homeland is unknown. The writer al-Marwazi, about 1120, says that a Turkic people called the Qun came from the northern borders of China and drove out the Śari people, and that they were Nestorian Christians. Related to the Pechenegs, the Cumans held a shifting area north of the Black Sea and along the Volga known as Cumania.

The Cumans first met the Rus' in 1055. In 1061, under the chieftain Sokal, they devastated the Pereyaslavl principality, which began a war that lasted 175 years. At the Battle of the Alta River in 1068 they defeated the armies of the three sons of Yaroslav the Wise, and afterwards they repeatedly invaded the Rus' lands, taking captives who became slaves or were sold at markets in the south. Some Cumans were also allies: David IV of Georgia married the daughter of the Cuman king Atrak and invited her relatives to settle in Georgia.

The Mongols under Jebe and Subutai defeated the Cumans in 1220. After the Mongol invasion of Kievan Rus' in 1237 many Cumans sought asylum in the Kingdom of Hungary, where others had already settled. In 1239 and 1240 large groups crossed the Danube, and some were settled by John III Doukas Vatatzes of Nicaea in Thrace, Macedonia and Anatolia. Those who stayed on the steppe joined the Golden Horde and later adopted Islam.

Horses were central to Cuman life, and the main activity was animal husbandry. Robert de Clari described them as nomadic warriors who raised horses, sheep, goats, camels and cattle, moving north with their herds in summer and south in winter. They fought as light cavalry, later developing heavy cavalry, with composite bows, javelins, sabres and maces. Their religion was Tengrism, and the dead of high rank were buried under a mound with a horse and sometimes a servant or slave. The Codex Cumanicus, written between 1294 and 1356, was a manual to help Catholic missionaries communicate with them. Cuman names survive in places such as Kumanovo in North Macedonia.
cumberland: Cumberland is an area of North West England that was historically a county. It was bordered by Northumberland, County Durham, Westmorland and Lancashire, and by the Scottish counties of Dumfriesshire and Roxburghshire to the north. It included the city of Carlisle, part of the Lake District and the North Pennines, and the Solway Firth coastline, with the Irish Sea to the west. Its highest point, Scafell Pike at 978 metres, is the highest mountain in England, and Carlisle is the county town. The county's boundaries, formed in the twelfth century, were not changed substantially during its existence.

In the Early Middle Ages the region was part of the Kingdom of Strathclyde in the Hen Ogledd, the Old North, and its people spoke the Brittonic language now called Cumbric. The first record of the name Cumberland is in 945, when the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle says King Edmund I of England ceded the area to Malcolm I, king of Alba. The names Cumberland and Cumbria derive, like the Welsh name Cymru, from a Common Brittonic word meaning compatriots. When the Domesday Book was compiled in 1086, most of the future county belonged to Scotland.

In 1092 King William Rufus invaded the Carlisle district, settled it with colonists and granted it to Ranulf le Meschin as an earldom. Carlisle became the see of a new diocese in 1133. After Henry I of England died in 1135, King David I of Scotland regained the area and made Carlisle one of his chief seats of government while England fell into civil war. Henry II took it back in 1157 and formed two counties from the earldom, Westmorland and Carliol, which by 1177 was known as Cumberland. The border between England and Scotland was fixed permanently by the Treaty of York in 1237. Cumbric is believed to have died out in the twelfth century.

Cumberland had an administrative role from the twelfth century until 1974, when it was merged with Westmorland and parts of Lancashire and Yorkshire to form Cumbria. Local government had been reshaped in the nineteenth century, and a county council was created in 1889. Carlisle became a county borough in 1914.

The name survives in Cumberland sausages and in several newspapers and organisations, and in Macbeth it is the kingdom given to Prince Malcolm. A flag based on the arms of the former county council was registered as the flag of Cumberland in 2012, and in 2013 the government recognised the continued existence of the historic counties. A unitary authority named Cumberland, covering most of the historic county but not Penrith, was created in 2023.
cumbria: Cumbria is the most north-westerly ceremonial county of England and is mostly mountainous. It borders Scotland to the north, Northumberland and County Durham to the east, North Yorkshire and Lancashire to the south and the Irish Sea to the west. The uplands fringe the Vale of Eden, which broadens into the Solway Plain near Carlisle. The south-west holds the Lake District, with England's highest mountain, Scafell Pike, and its longest lake, Windermere. The North Pennines lie to the east.

In the Neolithic period the area held a centre of stone axe production, the Langdale axe factory, and stone circles and henges, such as Mayburgh Henge, were built across the county. The region lay on the border of Roman Britain, and Hadrian's Wall runs through the north. In the early Middle Ages parts of it belonged successively to Rheged, Northumbria and Strathclyde, and there was also a Viking presence. The names Cumbria and Cumberland both mean land of the Cumbrians, and Cumberland is first recorded in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 945. The first king unequivocally described as king of the Cumbrians is Owain ap Dyfnwal, who ruled from about 915 to about 937.

The region became the border between England and Scotland and was unsettled until the Union of the Crowns in 1603. In the Industrial Revolution mining took place on the Cumberland coalfield and Barrow-in-Furness became a shipbuilding centre. The Lake District came to be valued for its picturesque qualities, notably by the Lake Poets.

Cumbria was created in 1974 from Cumberland, Westmorland, the Furness area of Lancashire and a small part of Yorkshire. Its largest settlement and only city is Carlisle, and it is predominantly rural. The Lake District is a national park and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Cumberland sausage has protected geographical status, and Cumberland and Westmorland wrestling is practised at the Grasmere Sports and Show, held every year since 1852.
cumbric: Cumbric is an extinct Brythonic Celtic language or dialect spoken in the Early Middle Ages in the Hen Ogledd, the Old North, in what is now Northern England and the southern Scottish Lowlands. Place-name evidence suggests that it may also have been spoken as far south as Pendle and the Yorkshire Dales. Linguists are undecided whether to classify it as a dialect of Old Welsh or as a separate language. Koch calls it a dialect but says that some of its place names clearly reflect a developed medieval language, much like Welsh, Cornish or Breton.

The term is geographical rather than linguistic, referring to the variety of Brittonic spoken in a particular region of North Britain. Its speakers seem to have called themselves Cumbri, as the Welsh called themselves Cymry, probably from a reconstructed Brittonic word meaning fellow countrymen, and the two peoples probably felt they were one ethnic group.

No contemporary written records of the language survive, and the evidence comes almost entirely from secondary sources. Most of it is place names, found in Scotland south of the firths of Forth and Clyde and in Cumberland and neighbouring areas; Brittonic-looking names north of that line are Pictish. Examples are Bathgate, meaning boar wood, and Carlisle, recorded as Luguvalium in the Roman period, to which caer, fort, was added later. Other evidence comes from the personal names of Strathclyde Britons in Scottish, Irish and Anglo-Saxon sources and from a few words that survived as legal terms in south-west Scotland.

A distinctive naming practice joined Gos-, related to Welsh gwas, servant, to the name of a saint, as in Gospatric, Gosmungo and Goscuthbert. About 100 counting systems have been collected in northern England since the 18th century, and the scholarly consensus is that they derive from a Brittonic language closely related to Welsh. Whether they are survivals of Cumbric is disputed, though Markku Filppula, Juhani Klemola and Heli Paulasto consider it plausible.

It is impossible to give an exact date for the extinction of Cumbric. In the mid-11th century some landowners still bore what appear to be Cumbric names, among them Dunegal, lord of Nithsdale, and Eilifr, lord of Penrith. At the Battle of the Standard in 1138 the Cumbrians are noted as a separate ethnic group, perhaps still set apart by language. The prevailing view is that the language became extinct in the 12th century, around the incorporation of the Kingdom of Strathclyde into the Kingdom of Scotland. A number of words in Scots and northern English dialects have been proposed to be Brittonic in origin, such as croot, small boy, but their derivation is hard to establish.
cunedda: The name Cunedda, spelled Cunedag in the Historia Brittonum of 828, derives from the Brythonic *Cuno-dagos, meaning Good Hound or Warrior. His title Wledig literally means of a gwlad, a country; some scholars read it as a rendering of a Roman title, while the historian Rachel Bromwich doubted this, and as a cognate of the Irish flaith it may simply mean lord or ruler.

His family is traced to a grandfather in late Roman Britain, Padarn Beisrudd, Paternus of the red tunic. One traditional reading makes him a Romano-British official placed by the Roman Emperor Magnus Maximus in command of the Votadini troops in the Clackmannanshire region in the 380s or earlier; he may instead have been a frontier chieftain given Roman military rank. The command possibly passed to his son Edern and then to Cunedda.

According to section 62 of the Historia Brittonum, Cunedda came from Manaw Gododdin with his sons one hundred and forty-six years before Maelgwn reigned in Gwynedd, and drove out the Scotti with great slaughter. The Irish named are the Uí Liatháin. Cunedda is said to have settled in the territory of the Venedoti, and to have married Gwawl, daughter of Coel Hen, the ruler of Eboracum.

Two explanations have been offered: that he acted under Magnus Maximus or his successors, or under Vortigern. The Oxford genealogist Peter Bartrum's range of dates runs from the late 370s to the late 440s. David Dumville dismisses the idea of moving foederati from Scotland to Wales in this way, while Sheppard Frere argued that Vortigern moved the Votadini south no later than 442. Some historians suggest Cunedda never went to Wales at all and that the account is propaganda for Gwynedd, since Irish settlement continued there into the 6th century.

Maelgwn Gwynedd, his supposed great-grandson, died in 547 according to the Annales Cambriae, which points to the mid-5th century, though many claims about Cunedda's heirs surfaced only in the 10th century. A son, Ceredig, is named as grandfather of Saint David. The Marwnad Cunedda, or Lament for Cunedda, in the Book of Taliesin, has been called perhaps the earliest Welsh poem extant, but its age is disputed and its text dates from the sixteenth century.

A folk story recorded by Victorian antiquarians has Cunedda killed and buried at Allt Cunedda, a hill near Cydweli in Carmarthenshire, where poorly recorded digs found a hill fort and stone cists with skeletons, since lost. The House of Tudor, which flew the Red Dragon, claimed descent from him.
cuneglasus: The Welsh form of his name, Cynlas Goch, appears in several genealogies of the royal line of Rhos in Gwynedd: the Harleian genealogies, the genealogies of Jesus College MS 20 and the Achau Brenhinoedd a Thywysogion Cymru. They make him a son of Owain Danwyn and the father of Maig, though the Jesus College text gives the relationship differently, and only the Achau gives the epithet Goch or ties him to Rhos. The historian Peter Bartrum saw little doubt that Cynlas and Gildas's Cuneglasus were the same man.

Gildas counts Cuneglasus among the five tyrants of Britain in On the Ruin of Britain. He calls him a rider and ruler of many, a despiser of God and his order, and a tawny butcher, which Gildas says is what his name means in the Roman tongue. He accuses him of throwing his wife out of doors and of desiring her sister, who had vowed lifelong chastity as a widow; neither sister is named in any source.

Gildas's phrase about the guider of the chariot that is the receptacle of the bear is obscure. Some who identify Arthur with Owain Danwyn have read it as Cuneglasus driving the chariot that carried his father's coffin. In 1918 the historian Arthur Wade-Evans proposed that the bear's den was Dinerth, a name meaning bear's fortress, in Rhos-on-Sea. Excavations by David Longley for the Gwynedd Archaeological Trust in 1997 found there an early medieval fortress with a well-built limestone wall 3 metres high, fronted by a rubble rampart, so that the phrase may pun on Cuneglasus's chief court.

The Bonedd y Saint, a genealogy of British saints, names other children of Owain Danwyn as his siblings, among them the saints Einion Frenin, Seiriol and Meirion. Through Owain's brother Cadwallon Lawhir, the genealogies make Maelgwn his first cousin. Cynlas may have given his name to the old township of Cynlas in Llandderfel, Penllyn, and a source of 1745 places his grave in the church at Bangor in Caernarfonshire.
cuneiform: Cuneiform grew out of the token system used in the Near East for accounting. Clay tokens, some with pictographic shapes of animals and associated with numbers, were in use from the 9th millennium BCE, and they were pressed onto clay envelopes and then replaced by flat tablets on which signs were recorded with a stylus. Writing is first recorded at Uruk at the end of the 4th millennium BCE, and the first unequivocal documents date from around 3300 BCE. These early tablets were purely pictographic. Tablets with syllabic elements, clearly in Sumerian, date from about 2800 BCE, when pictographs began to be used for their sound, which allowed abstract ideas and personal names to be written.

Cuneiform is a logo-syllabic system named for the wedge-shaped impressions that form its signs. In the mid-3rd millennium BCE a wedge-tipped stylus pressed into soft clay replaced the pointed stylus and made writing quicker. Writing ran from top to bottom and right to left. Most surviving tablets were left moist, not fired, and were baked by accident when fires destroyed the buildings that held them.

The Akkadian Empire adopted the script from the 24th century BCE. Akkadian is a Semitic language, quite unlike Sumerian, and its scribes wrote it phonetically with Sumerian sound signs while keeping many Sumerian signs as logograms. The script was adapted for Elamite, Hurrian, Urartian and Hittite, and it recorded letters, business documents, laws such as the Code of Hammurabi, maps and medical manuals. Old Persian cuneiform, with 36 sound signs and 8 logograms, was designed independently under the early Achaemenid rulers. From the later half of the 1st millennium BCE cuneiform fell into disuse as Aramaic replaced Akkadian.

Cuneiform was rediscovered in the early 17th century, when the trilingual Achaemenid royal inscriptions at Persepolis were published. In 1621 Pietro Della Valle gave the direction of writing, and Carsten Niebuhr copied the inscriptions in 1778 and distinguished three kinds of writing. Georg Friedrich Grotefend began the decipherment of Old Persian in 1802, and bilingual and trilingual inscriptions then allowed the older scripts to be read, back to Sumerian. The British Museum holds the largest collection of tablets, about 130,000, and most tablets in museums have not been published.
cunigunde-of-luxembourg: Cunigunde was one of eleven children of Siegfried I of Luxembourg and a woman called Hedwig, whose identity genealogists dispute. Her paternal grandmother, also named Cunigunde, was a Carolingian, which made her a seventh-generation descendant of Charlemagne. She married King Henry in 999, when he was Duke of Bavaria. She is said to have long wanted to be a nun, and that the marriage was a white marriage, unconsummated by mutual agreement. The couple were childless. Some authors suppose that later hagiographers mistakenly read a virginal marriage into that fact, while others accept that it was purely platonic.

Cunigunde was crowned queen on 10 August 1002 at Paderborn by Archbishop Willigis of Mainz, the first known crowning of a German queen on her own, since earlier queens had married kings already crowned. She seems to have been politically active. Wives of Ottonian rulers were often styled consors regni, partner in the rule, in charters, and in a third of Henry's surviving charters she appears as an advocate or initiator. She sat in imperial councils and is reported to have influenced his gifts to the Church, including the cathedral and monastery at Bamberg. She and Henry were crowned in St Peter's Basilica in Rome on 14 February 1014.

During a grave illness she vowed to found a Benedictine monastery at Kassel if she recovered. Henry died in 1024 before it was finished. She then acted as regent with her brother, and handed over the imperial insignia when Conrad II was elected on 8 September 1024.

As a widow she was comparatively poor, because she and Henry had given away so much in charity. In 1025 she retired to Kaufungen Abbey in Hesse, the Benedictine house for nuns she had founded. At its dedication she offered a relic of the True Cross, took off her regalia and put on the nun's habit. She died there on 3 March 1040 and was buried at Bamberg Cathedral beside her husband.

Pope Innocent III canonised her on 29 March 1200. Her biography and the bull of canonisation relate miracles, among them one in which she walked unharmed over glowing ploughshares, which became her usual attribute. She is the patroness of Luxembourg, and her feast day is 3 March. Tilman Riemenschneider's limestone double tomb at Bamberg, made between 1499 and 1513, shows the imperial couple with two lions at their feet.
cunimund: The Gepids had held Sirmium, now Sremska Mitrovica in Serbia, since 536, when they took it from the Byzantine emperor Justinian I. By 549 they were at war with the Lombards, who received 15,000 troops from Justinian; the Gepids agreed to a truce, but only while the Byzantine soldiers stayed in the area. The peoples of Thurisind and of the Lombard king Audoin were locked in a long feud. Cunimund succeeded Thurisind, who according to several sources was his father, and his hatred of the Lombards was said to stem partly from the killing of his brother Turismod by Alboin.

Open war with the Lombards, now led by Alboin, broke out again in 565. Cunimund asked the new Byzantine emperor, Justin II, for help and promised him Sirmium. Justin agreed and the Gepids gained a temporary advantage, but Cunimund did not hand the city over.

When the Lombards allied with the Avars, Cunimund made the same offer again and this time gave Sirmium to the Byzantines. Their troops kept the city but did not join the Gepids in the fighting. The Avars did not appear either, and the Lombards defeated Cunimund's forces in the Lombard–Gepid War of 567. In 568 the Avars forced the Lombards to move on to Italy, and the former Gepid lands came under Avar rule.

In the account of Paul the Deacon, Alboin killed Cunimund and had his skull made into a drinking cup, called a scala or patera, and forced Cunimund's daughter Rosamund to marry him. At a feast in Verona, Paul reports, Alboin made her drink from her father's skull; humiliated, she later had him murdered in his sleep. J. R. R. Tolkien recalled the story of Thurisind, Cunimund and Rosamunda in his story The Lost Road.
cunipert: Cunipert, also written Cunibert or Cunincpert, was king of the Lombards from 688 to 700. He succeeded his father Perctarit, though he had been associated with the throne since 680. Alahis, duke of Brescia and formerly duke of Trento, had also rebelled during Perctarit's reign; according to Paul the Deacon in the Historia Langobardorum, it was Cunipert who persuaded his father to show mercy, and Perctarit is reported to have warned his son of the consequences.

Soon after Perctarit's death Alahis forced Cunipert to flee to Isola Comacina, an island in Lake Como. Paul the Deacon's Book V is the only surviving record of Alahis's rule, which he portrays as burdensome and tyrannical and particularly hostile to the Catholic Church.

Alahis lost the support of the Church and of the people, notably the brothers Aldo and Grauso of Brescia, and Cunipert returned to Pavia and resumed control. Alahis nevertheless gathered enough support to fight. Cunipert, with the men of Piedmont, defeated Alahis and the men of Venetia at the Battle of Coronate, on the Horn of the Adda near Lodi, in 689, and Alahis was killed.

Cunipert put down other insurrections, among them that of the usurper Duke Ansfrid of Friuli, and settled the schism of the Three Chapters between the patriarch of Aquileia and his rival, the patriarch of Grado. He is notable as the first Lombard monarch to strike coins in his own image. He died in 700 and was buried in the Basilica of Santissimo Salvatore in Pavia. His young son Liutpert succeeded him, with the regent Ansprand, and faced many rebels.
cunobelinus: His name, Common Brittonic Cunobelinos, means strong dog. The coins suggest that he took power on the death of his father Tasciovanus, a king of the Catuvellauni, and his earliest issues come from Camulodunum, capital of the Trinovantes, where he seems to have ruled first; some carry a palm or laurel wreath, a Roman sign of victory. He may have been emboldened by the Roman defeat in the Teutoburg Forest in 9 CE to move against the Trinovantes, allies of Rome since a treaty with Julius Caesar in 54 BCE. He minted also at Verlamion, the later Verulamium, and unlike his father named no co-rulers.

He kept good relations with Rome. He used the title Rex and classical motifs on his coins, and he may have been a client king. Imports of Italian wine, olive oil, fish sauces from Hispania, glassware and Gallo-Belgic tableware entered Britain through Camulodunum, and Strabo thought he was probably among the British kings who sent embassies to Augustus. His brother Epaticcus extended his power over the Atrebates and took their capital Calleva by about 25.

About 40 his son Adminius, who held Kent, was banished and fled to the emperor Caligula, whose planned invasion of Britain came to nothing. Cunobelinus died about 40, and was certainly dead by 43. The Lexden Tumulus near Colchester has been suggested as his tomb, though the earlier king Addedomarus is another candidate. When Caratacus completed the conquest of the Atrebates, their king Verica fled to Rome and gave the emperor Claudius a pretext for invasion.

His memory survived in legend. The Historia Brittonum of the early 9th century made him Bellinus, son of Minocannus, through scribal errors passed down from Suetonius by way of Orosius, and Welsh tradition turned this figure into Beli Mawr. Geoffrey of Monmouth's Kymbelinus, a warrior raised at the court of Augustus, passed through Raphael Holinshed's Chronicles of 1577 to William Shakespeare, though the king of Cymbeline has almost nothing in common with the historical ruler beyond his name.
cupbearer: A cupbearer was an officer of high rank in royal courts, whose duty was to pour and serve the drinks at the royal table. Because of the constant fear of plots and intrigues, such as poisoning, the holder had to be regarded as thoroughly trustworthy. He guarded against poison in the king's cup and was sometimes required to swallow some of the drink before serving it.

His confidential relations with the king often gave him a position of great influence. The role was also an honorific one: an Egyptian hieroglyph for cupbearer was used as late as 196 BCE on the Rosetta Stone, which names the canephora cupbearer Areia, daughter of Diogenes, and each Ptolemaic decree from the Decree of Canopus onward honoured a cupbearer.

Cupbearers are mentioned several times in the Bible, first in Genesis 40:1, and a chief of the cupbearers often presided over a number of such officials. In the post-exilic period Nehemiah rose to be cupbearer to King Artaxerxes, a position that put his life at risk every day but gave him authority and high pay. In Greek myth Hebe, the goddess of youth and daughter of Hera and Zeus, was the original cupbearer to the gods of Olympus, serving nectar and ambrosia, until Ganymede replaced her.

In Visigothic Spain the Comes Scanciorum, the Count of the Cupbearers, headed the royal cellars and poured the king's wine. In the Holy Roman Empire the king of Bohemia ranked as arch-cupbearer, though his duties were normally performed only at coronations. In Anglo-Saxon England the pincerna was drawn from the thegns, the third rank of nobles, after the king and ealdormen, and was in charge of drinks at royal feasts.

The office took many forms elsewhere. In Hungary the pohárnokmester, or Master of the Cupbearers, supervised the cupbearers at court, and the first mention of him dates from 1148. In Poland and Lithuania the cześnik was responsible for the king's wine cellar until the end of the 13th century, and from the 14th century the title was honorary.

In Russia the chashnik was chosen from among the boyars and served in the household of the monarch. Sargon of Akkad, in the 23rd century BCE, is the much older example of a cupbearer who rose to rule. In Shakespeare's The Winter's Tale, King Leontes of Sicily urges his cupbearer Camillo to use his place to poison King Polixenes of Bohemia.
cupisnique: The Cupisnique had a distinctive style of adobe clay architecture, and their artefacts share artistic styles and religious symbols with the Chavín culture that arose in the same area later. How the two are related is not well understood, and the names are sometimes used interchangeably. The scholar Izumi Shimada calls Cupisnique a possible ancestor of the Moche culture without mentioning Chavín, while Anna C. Roosevelt describes the coastal form of the Chavín Horizon as dominated by the Cupisnique style.

Little direct evidence survives of Cupisnique social organisation, demography or ways of making a living, and the buildings are decorated with painted and incised stucco reliefs of surreal creatures, so the Cupisnique are sometimes spoken of as a cult. Their society had a base of farmers and fishermen with a middle and an elite class. A recurring theme of their art is decapitation, in which the decapitators appear in five supernatural guises: human, monster, bird, fish and spider.

In 2008 a Cupisnique adobe temple was found at Collud, beside the temple of Ventarrón in the Lambayeque valley. It bears images of a spider deity, thought to be linked with rainfall, hunting and warfare, with a spider's head and neck, the mouth of a large feline and the beak of a bird. About three hundred years later the Chavín built a temple beside it at Zarpan. The team leader, Walter Alva, said that Cupisnique and Chavín shared the same gods and architectural and artistic forms. Other sites include Caballo Muerto in the Moche Valley and Limoncarro in the Pacasmayo area.

The religious motifs of the Cupisnique seem to have shaped the cultures that followed, among them the Salinar, Vicus, Gallinazo and Moche. Moche art keeps the five Cupisnique decapitators and adds the crab and the scorpion, and scholars see the Moche as heirs to the same belief rather than imitators by coincidence. The spider motif can be followed from the temple of Ventarrón to Moche artefacts of about 300 CE. In 2020 farmers clearing land in La Libertad found a shrine with a mural of a knife-wielding spider god some 3,200 years old.
cura-annonae: Rome's grain subsidies began as occasional emergency measures, importing cheap grain from allies in times of scarcity to feed citizen-farmers ruined by debt or dispossessed of their land. In the early Republic the consuls bought grain in emergencies on the Senate's behalf, and from the early 300s BCE the task passed to the aediles, who distributed the dole from their headquarters at or near the Temple of Ceres. Land, debt and grain became central to the popular politics of the late Republic, and Pompey was granted an emergency cura annonae that became an important source of his power.

By the end of the Republic the dole was a permanent programme, and Augustus and later emperors, reluctantly at first, made it a free monthly issue to about 200,000 adult male citizens, while the city as a whole, estimated at 1,000,000 people by the 2nd century CE, depended on imported grain. In 22 CE Tiberius declared the supply a personal imperial duty whose neglect would bring the utter ruin of the state. Most of the grain was traded privately as a profitable commodity, carried on privately owned ships that the government hired, subsidised and in effect insured; Claudius offered citizenship and freedom from harbour duties to owners who committed large vessels.

Kesler and Temin calculate that the early imperial supply required 2,000 to 3,000 voyages a year. The run to Alexandria might take 14 days with the wind behind, but the return took Lionel Casson's estimated average of nearly 70 days. At Ostia and Portus the grain was moved onto barges, hauled about 30 kilometres up the Tiber and stored in the horrea, most of them state-owned from the 1st century CE.

The dole and the public games earned the obedience of the urban poor, what the poet Juvenal mocked as bread and circuses. When the Vandals took the North African provinces around 439, the Western Empire lost most of its grain supply. As Rome's population fell, perhaps to about 100,000 by 500, local farms could feed it; some form of the system may have lasted into the 6th century, and at Constantinople it survived in reduced form into the 7th.
curicaueri: The name comes from the Purépecha Kurhikuaeri, the Great Fire or Great Bonfire; in the Zacapú region he was called Querenda-angápeti, the rock that is in the temple, and he was also known as Tatá Juríata, the one who makes the day. He was held to be the oldest Purépecha deity, from whom, with his wife Cuerauáperi, the other gods came. His five brothers, the Tiripe-mencha, governed the five divine houses of the earthly plane. Through a prophetic vision from Curicaueri, Tariácuri set out to create a unified Purépecha state.

In Purépecha belief everything in the universe was born of four unions of Curicaueri and Cuerauáperi, which eclipses recall: the stars and planets, then the four elements, then plants and animals, and finally men and women. With his son Cupantziere, the old sun who dies each evening playing ball with the Night, and his grandson Siratatáperi, the young sun, he formed the Trinity of Fire, seen in three stars of the Taurus constellation.

His image was painted black, with the lower face and nails yellow, a white fur headband and heron feathers; the Relación de Michoacán also describes him as a white eagle and, most often, as a stone that was the god himself. His priests, the curiti, and the Irecha painted themselves the same way, and warriors painted their bodies black in his honour. His main offerings were tobacco, blankets and blood thrown into the fire, and all rituals centred on bonfires whose smoke reached the gods; the Irecha themselves had to gather firewood for them.

War captives were sacrificed in great ceremonies in which the victim took the identity of Curita-Caheri, his celestial messenger. Made drunk and powdered with corn flour, the victims were held on the sacrificial slab while the Axame removed their hearts; their heads were placed on the eraquaréquaro, and the remains were cooked with corn and beans and eaten.
cursus-honorum: The cursus honorum mixed military and political posts, and the prize for winning each rung was eventually to become one of the two consuls of a given year. To have held each office at the youngest possible age, suo anno, was considered a great success: to miss a praetorship at 39 meant one could not become consul at 42. Cicero took extreme pride in being a novus homo, a new man whose ancestors had never been consuls, and in having become consul in his year.

The first official post was quaestor, which candidates could hold from the age of 30 after the reforms of Sulla. From the time of Augustus, twenty quaestors served in the financial administration at Rome or as second-in-command to a governor. At 36 a man could stand for aedile, an optional step; aediles looked after temples, public buildings, water and food supplies and markets, and organised games, which made the office valuable for gaining popularity.

A man of 39 could stand for praetor, a limit lowered to 30 under Augustus at the request of Gaius Maecenas. Six or eight praetors were generally elected a year, mainly as judges. Consul, with a minimum age of 42, was the highest office. The two consuls served for one year, each could veto the other, and each commanded two legions, with twelve lictors. After a consulship came a province as proconsul and possibly the censorship, which handled the census and the roll of the Senate.

The rules were altered and flagrantly ignored in the last century of the Republic. Offices officially presented as public service often became self-aggrandisement. Gaius Marius held the consulship five years in a row, and again in 86 BCE. Sulla's reforms between 82 and 79 BCE required a ten-year interval before holding the same office again. The dictatorship, which stood outside the cursus, was definitively abolished in 44 BCE after the assassination of Julius Caesar.
cursus-publicus: The Romans adapted their state post from the Persian network of royal mounted couriers described by Herodotus, in which letters passed from rider to rider along the Royal Road. A courier service may have existed under the Republic, but Suetonius states clearly that Augustus created the system, to carry messages, officials and tax revenues between the provinces and Italy. Augustus first stationed young men at short intervals along the military roads and then switched to vehicles, so that one man made the whole journey and could be questioned on arrival.

The service rested on obligations placed on private persons. Contractors called mancipes supplied the equipment, animals and wagons, and the stations were maintained from the resources of the areas the roads crossed; in Late Antiquity the cost was charged to provincial taxpayers. Along the main roads stood change stations with repair facilities, the mutationes, and full stations with lodging, the mansiones. Use required a diploma naming the holder, the period, the route and the lodgings, and governors and minor officials abused these to travel free.

Under Antoninus Pius a praefectus vehiculorum, Lucius Volusius Maecianus, supervised the service in Italy, while governors managed it in the provinces. After the reforms of Diocletian and Constantine I it had two sections, the fast cursus velox with horses and mules and the regular cursus clabularis with oxen for heavy goods. Julian, emperor from 361 to 363, tried to restrict the granting of passes.

From the Jerusalem Itinerary the night stations appear to have been about twenty-five Roman miles apart, and a typical day's journey was 38 to 62 miles, though a single rider could cover 160 km or more in an emergency. News of the accession of Pertinax on 1 January 193 was announced in Alexandria on 6 March.

The service was still fully working in the Eastern Empire in the first half of the 6th century, when Procopius accused Justinian of dismantling most of it except the route to the Persian border. The dromos continued through the Byzantine period, much reduced, under the logothetēs tou dromou, and by the 11th century its upkeep fell to local peasants. In the West it survived under Theodoric the Great's Ostrogoths in Italy.
curt-von-francois: Curt Karl Bruno von François was born in Luxembourg into a family of French Huguenot ancestry. His father, the Prussian general Bruno von François, was killed at the Battle of Spicheren on 6 August 1870; his younger brother Hermann von François later served as a general in the First World War, and the writer Louise von François was his aunt. Curt joined the Prussian Cadet Corps and fought in the Franco-Prussian War, for which he received the Iron Cross.

He then turned to exploration. In 1883 he worked as a geographer on an expedition along the Kasai River in the Congo Basin under Hermann Wissmann, and two years later he joined a second Congo expedition led by George Grenfell. After service on the German General Staff, where he rose to Hauptmann, he was sent to German West Africa in 1887 and explored Togoland and the trade route to Salaga as far north as the Mossi territory.

After Herero leaders expelled German officials from Okahandja in 1888, the German Colonial Society engaged François to secure German South West Africa. He landed at Walvis Bay in June 1889 with 21 troopers and based himself at Otjimbingwe, against the advice of the acting commissioner Heinrich Göring. In May 1890 he renewed a peace agreement with the Herero chief Maharero and occupied the ruined settlement of Windhoek, where he built the headquarters known as the Alte Feste. He served as Reichskommissar from March 1891 to November 1893, established Swakopmund as the colony's main harbour in 1892 and mapped much of the territory.

Fearing an alliance between the Herero and the Nama, he led 225 colonial troops against Hendrik Witbooi's village on 12 April 1893. Witbooi withdrew with most of his fighters, and the attack killed 88 Nama, 78 of them women and children. Newspapers reported and condemned the massacre, while German and Cape Colony officials tried to cover it up. Witbooi waged a guerrilla war from the Naukluft Mountains, and François failed to drive the Nama into the Omaheke Desert.

Theodor Leutwein replaced him in 1894, and François retired from the army in 1895. Living at Zernsdorf in Brandenburg, he wrote at length on Africa, including Deutsch-Südwest-Afrika (1899). He died in a hospital at Königs Wusterhausen on 28 December 1931 and was buried in the Invalids' Cemetery in Berlin; his grave, levelled in the Berlin Wall's border zone, was restored in 2018. A statue of him in Windhoek, unveiled in 1965, was taken down on 23 November 2022 after repeated calls for its removal.
cusco: Cusco lies in southeastern Peru, near the Sacred Valley of the Andes and the Huatanay and Urubamba rivers, at an elevation of about 3,400 metres. The Quechua name is Qusqu, which derives from the phrase qusqu wanka, rock of the owl, and relates to the foundation myth of the Ayar siblings: Ayar Awqa acquired wings and flew to the site of the future city, where he was transformed into a rock to mark his lineage's possession of the land.

The Killke people occupied the region from about 900 to 1200, before the Inca arrived in the thirteenth century. Carbon-14 dating established that the Killke built the fortress of Sacsayhuamán about 1100; the Inca later expanded it. The city was the capital of the Inca Empire, and many believe it was planned as an effigy in the shape of a puma. It had two sectors, hurin and hanan, which together took in the four provinces of the empire, and a road led from each quarter to the corresponding part of the empire.

The first three Spaniards arrived in May 1533, after the Battle of Cajamarca, and Francisco Pizarro officially entered the city on 15 November 1533. Early accounts record how the beauty of its buildings and the regularity of its streets astonished the Spaniards; the troops plundered the palaces and religious buildings, among them the Coricancha, the great temple of the Sun. The city was reestablished on 23 March 1534, with most of it built over Inca monuments.

Earthquakes interrupted urban development under Spanish rule. One in 1650 destroyed almost all the colonial buildings, and the effigy of the Lord of the Earthquakes is still carried in procession every year. Another on 21 May 1950 damaged more than a third of the city's structures, while Inca architecture withstood it, and restoration at the Santo Domingo complex exposed the Inca masonry of the Coricancha. UNESCO declared Cusco a World Heritage Site in 1983.
cusco-school: The tradition arose after the Spanish conquest of Peru in 1534 and is considered the first artistic centre in the Americas to teach European techniques systematically. Religious artists sent to Cusco taught drawing and oil painting to Quechua and Mestizo pupils, for the art's main purpose was didactic. The arrival of the Italian Jesuit painter Bernardo Bitti in 1583 brought Mannerism, with its elongated figures lit by focused light. Luis de Riaño, a disciple of Angelino Medoro, led local painting between 1618 and 1640, and Diego Cusihuamán painted murals in the churches of Chinchero and Urcos.

Baroque influence came through the tenebrism of Francisco de Zurbarán and engravings of Flemish art from Antwerp, above all in the work of Marcos Ribera, born in Cusco in 1630. Towards the end of the 17th century the growing number of Amerindian-Quechua and Mestizo painters gave the school its own character. In 1688, after continuous conflicts, the painters' corporation split and the Amerindian and Mestizo painters left it, citing exploitation by their Spanish colleagues, and from then on they followed their own sensibility.

Cusqueña painting kept to religious subjects, with little perspective, space broken into several compartmentalised scenes, a predominance of red, yellow and earth colours and lavish gold leaf, especially on images of the Virgin Mary. Its painters added Andean flora and fauna, warrior angels, portraits of Amerindian caciques and scenes such as the Corpus Christi procession. Most works are anonymous. Diego Quispe Tito, born in San Sebastián near Cusco in 1611, is regarded as its most original Amerindian painter, and the sixteen canvases of the Corpus Christi series, from the late 17th century, show the social strata of colonial Cusco in detail.

In the 18th century workshops made canvases in large quantities for merchants who sold them in Lima, Arequipa and other cities and as far as present-day Argentina, Chile and Bolivia; Mauricio García once contracted to deliver about five hundred in seven months. Marcos Zapata (c. 1710–1773), the leading artist of that century, painted more than 200 works between 1748 and 1764. The largest collection of the school's paintings is in the Cusco Cathedral, and the Lima Art Museum and the Inca Museum also hold important ones.
custom-of-paris: The Custom of Paris arose from a wider effort to centralise French law. France had no single law: its regions followed their own blends of jus commune and customary law, and the Custom of Paris was one of 360 uncodified custumals in force in 15th-century France. Because Paris was the capital, its customary law was held in high regard, and it was refined between the 13th and 15th centuries as part of the codification of all French custumals ordered by King Charles VII in the Ordinance of Montil-les-Tours in 1453. The revision of 1580 was ordered by King Henry III after a period of disuse.

Divided into 16 sections, the Custom held 362 articles on family and inheritance, property and debt recovery, and sought to join feudal land tenure to the growing town-based commerce of the Ancien Régime. Property was either movable or immovable, and to encourage trade movables could not be mortgaged. Land was held in allod or in fief, a fief either as a seigneurie or as a roture, whose holder owed the lord an annual cens and, on a sale, an entry fine (lods et ventes) of a twelfth of the price.

A married couple held its goods in community of property (communauté de biens). The husband was its head and master, but he needed his wife's consent to dispose of community property, and a widow was protected by dower (douaire). Children of either sex were entitled to a legitime, could not be disinherited and came into their inheritance at 25; a seigneurie passed half to the eldest son, while land held in roture was divided equally. Shaped by the canon-law ban on interest, the Custom forbade notaries to write interest into contracts, except for rentcharges.

The Custom had been part of the justice of Canada since the founding of the Company of One Hundred Associates in 1627, and Article 33 of the charter of the French West India Company introduced it officially in May 1664. At its widest it applied in Canada, Acadia, Newfoundland, Louisiana and Île Royale. By 1760, as applied in Montreal and Quebec City, it had become the law of Canada and on some points had diverged from its French origins.

After the British conquest the Royal Proclamation of 1763 introduced English common law, and French Canadians went on using notaries for their affairs until the Quebec Act of 1774 restored French private law on property and civil rights, while English law kept its hold over criminal matters.
cut-nyak-dhien: Cut Nyak Dhien was born in 1848 into a Muslim aristocratic family in the VI mukim district of Aceh Besar. Her father, Teuku Nanta Setia, belonged to the ruling Ulèë Balang class. She was educated in religion and household matters and at twelve was married, by arrangement, to Teuku Cek Ibrahim Lamnga. The Dutch declared war on Aceh on 26 March 1873, beginning the Aceh War, and captured VI mukim that year and the Sultan's palace in 1874. Her husband was killed in action at Gle Tarum on 29 June 1878, and she swore revenge on the Dutch.

The Acehnese hero Teuku Umar proposed to her. She refused at first but accepted when he allowed her to fight, and they married in 1880, to the great benefit of Acehnese morale. They had a daughter, Cut Gambang. On 30 September 1893 Teuku Umar surrendered with 250 men and was made a Dutch commander, but two years later he left with his troops and equipment and used them to help the Acehnese, which Dutch history calls his treason. He was killed in a surprise attack at Meulaboh. When Cut Gambang wept, her mother reportedly slapped and then embraced her, saying that Acehnese women might not shed tears for the martyred.

She went on resisting with a small force that shrank as the Dutch adapted their tactics, while nearsightedness and arthritis troubled her. One of her men, Pang Laot, revealed her headquarters at Beutong Le Sageu, and the Dutch captured her by surprise, though her daughter escaped and continued the resistance.

Taken to Banda Aceh, she was exiled to Sumedang in West Java, because the Dutch feared she would mobilise the Acehnese. She lived in the house of a cleric, Sanusi, taught the Quran to local women and was called Ibu Perbu, the Queen Mother. She refused colonial help, and the Regent of Sumedang provided for her. She died on 6 November 1908. President Sukarno proclaimed her a National Hero of Indonesia on 2 May 1964. The film Tjoet Nja' Dhien was shown at Cannes in 1989, and an airport and a navy corvette bear her name.
cuttack: Cuttack stands at the apex of the Mahanadi delta, on a strip of land between the Kathajodi and Mahanadi rivers. Four distributaries of the Mahanadi run through or beside the city. The name is an anglicised form of Kataka, from a Sanskrit word meaning capital, fort or military establishment, and refers to the ancient Barabati Fort around which the city first developed. While the fort stood the city was known as Bidanasi Kataka, Bidanasi Military Base.

According to the historian Andrew Stirling, who relied on the Madala Panji, the chronicle of the Jagannatha temple at Puri, the city was founded as a military cantonment by King Nrupa Keshari of the Keshari dynasty in 989 CE. A stone embankment to protect the new capital from flooding was built in the reign of Maharaja Markata Keshari, in 1002 CE. Barabati Fort, whose moat, gate and earthen mound of a nine-storied palace survive, is attributed to him. Chudangagarh, a fort about 8 km south-west of the city, was built by Chodagandadeva of the Ganga dynasty.

The Lal Bagh Palace on the Kathajodi shows the later rulers. It was built by a Mughal governor stationed at Cuttack, and the Naib Nazims lived there until 1751 and representatives of the Bhonslas of Nagpur from 1751 to 1803, when it passed to the British. The Maratha barracks at Chauliaganj, begun in 1775 and completed in 1795, housed artillery, cavalry and infantry. Under the British the Salt House was built in 1847–48. Cuttack was the birthplace of Subhas Chandra Bose, and Mahatma Gandhi stayed at the Swaraj Ashram on his visits during the Non Cooperation Movement of the 1920s.
